authors: Wang S, Wang Y, Wan Y, Oba BT.

title: Copper and zinc from slurry applications shape grassland soil microbial community structure in a long-term experiment.
abstract: Soil microbes are crucial in maintaining soil and plant health, underpinning agronomic productivity. This study investigates antimicrobial copper- and zinc-laden cow and pig slurry applications on soil microbial community structures in an approximately 50-year long-term slurry experiment on a permanent grassland located in County Down, Northern Ireland. Illumina and PacBio rRNA sequencing (analysing 16S and ITS genera) were used to investigate soil samples (to 15 cm depth) from the experiment's treatments. Slurry type and application rate were found to alter the soil microbial community structure. The highest slurry application rate resulted in the greatest log-2-fold changes in most relative abundances. Soil pH (ranging from ~6.5 to ~5.8) and carbon content (ranging from ~7% to ~5%) were also significantly elevated in the highest slurry treatments relative to the non-amended control. Soil pH, copper, and zinc concentrations were found to be significant key drivers of soil microbial community shifts (permutation test, p F ≈ 25) and zinc has the greatest influence on fungal (ITS; F ≈ 13) genera. A key finding was that these two community types responded differently to slurry management: Canonical analysis of principal components showed 16S community structure diverged by both slurry type and application rate, whereas ITS community structure was distinguished by application rate alone. Despite this, there is no sign that it has detrimental impacts on grass yield, and indeed, some promoted microbes (Nitrospira spp.) were associated with increased productivity. However, the potentially pathogenic organism (i.e., Fusarium spp.) observed in all treatments is of concern, given the contaminating mycotoxins they produce. The findings illustrate soil microbial responses to sustained and settled long-term organic-amended soils that could not be observed without the long-term nature of this experiment. These findings indicate that long-term Cu and Zn-loaded slurry application restructures the soil microbial community in significant ways with implications for antimicrobial resistance selection and a hypothesised link to mycotoxin-related food safety for further investigation, within a One Health framework linking soil, plant, animal, and human health.
authors: McCreanor C, Jia W, Carey M, Meharg C, Meharg AA, Holland J, Dhandapani S, Williams PN.

title: Integrated multi-omics reveals gut microbiota-metabolic mechanisms underlying the neuroprotective effects of Xijiao Dihuang Decoction against cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury.
abstract: BackgroundCerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) remains a major barrier to functional recovery after reperfusion therapy for ischemic stroke. Increasing evidence indicates that gut microbiota dysbiosis and metabolic disturbance are closely involved in post-stroke neuroinflammation and secondary brain injury. Xijiao Dihuang Decoction (XDD), a classical traditional Chinese medicine formula, has shown protective effects in cerebrovascular disorders; however, whether its effects against CIRI are associated with coordinated regulation of the gut microbiota and host metabolism remains unclear.MethodsCirculating XDD-derived components were characterized by ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS). Network pharmacology and molecular docking were used to predict potential targets and signaling pathways associated with CIRI. A middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion (MCAO/R) rat model was established, and rats were treated with low-, medium-, or high-dose XDD for 7 days, with edaravone as a positive control. Neurological deficits, cerebral infarct volume, hemorheological parameters, histopathological changes, and serum inflammatory cytokines were assessed. Cecal microbiota composition was analyzed by 16S rDNA sequencing, and cecal metabolic profiles were investigated using untargeted LC-MS metabolomics. Multi-omics integration and Spearman correlation analysis were performed to explore associations between differentially abundant bacterial genera and characteristic metabolites.ResultsA total of 54 XDD-derived circulating components were identified. Network pharmacology analysis indicated that the putative targets of XDD were mainly enriched in pathways related to inflammation, lipid and energy metabolism, and regulated cell death, with AKT1 and NLRP3 were predicted as potential hub targets. In MCAO/R rats, XDD improved neurological deficits, reduced cerebral infarct volume, alleviated hemorheological abnormalities, and attenuated neuronal injury. XDD also reduced serum IL-6 levels and lowered IL-1β levels mainly at medium and high doses. In addition, XDD partially restored gut microbial diversity and remodeled CIRI-associated microbial dysbiosis. Metabolomics analysis revealed marked metabolic disturbances after MCAO/R, and XDD reversed part of these alterations, particularly those related to lipid metabolism. Integrated analysis further linked specific bacterial genera with lipid mediators and fatty acid-related metabolites, indicating coordinated remodeling of the gut microbiota and host metabolism.ConclusionXDD exerts neuroprotective effects against CIRI through multi-target and multi-pathway actions. Its therapeutic effects may be associated with coordinated regulation of gut microbial homeostasis, metabolic reprogramming, and inflammatory/cell death signaling. These findings provide new evidence supporting the potential application of XDD in ischemic stroke and offer insight into microbiota-related mechanisms underlying its neuroprotective effects.
authors: Long YY, Feng YJ, Mao KN, Song ZG, Liu YC, Chen SY, Zheng CX, Zeng YD, Yin ST, Dai SS, Li H, Liu WH.

title: Biological and genomic characterization of Escherichia phage KBU_SV1 active against carbapenem-resistant Escherichia coli.
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Escherichia coli infections are increasingly difficult to treat, and bacteriophages have been highlighted as a promising tool to control such multidrug-resistant bacteria. Here, we isolated and characterized Escherichia phage KBU_SV1 using E. coli ATCC 25922 as the isolation and propagation host. Its morphology, host range, stability at various temperatures and pH, reduction growth of bacteria, effect on biofilm, in vivo efficacy, and genome were investigated. Transmission electron microscopy showed a polyhedral head and a long, non-contractile tail, corresponding to a siphovirus morphotype. The spot-test analysis of 106 bacterial strains showed spot clearance against 16 strains (host range index, 0.15), including carbapenem-resistant and carbapenem-susceptible E. coli isolates and, to a lesser extent, Klebsiella pneumoniae, while no such effect was observed in the other species tested. KBU_SV1 was stable between pH 4 and 12 and at 4-37 °C, but no infectivity was detected at pH 2 or 65 °C. Bacterial growth was suppressed at all multiplicities of infection (MOI) tested (100-0.01), followed by gradual regrowth. KBU_SV1 reduced established biofilms and inhibited biofilm formation in both E. coli ATCC 25922 and the carbapenem-resistant isolate Ec59. In the Galleria mellonella infection model, phage treatment significantly delayed larval mortality compared with the infection control, while no mortality occurred in larvae receiving phage alone. The genome of KBU_SV1 was found to be 45,190 bp with a G + C content of 53.56% and was complete with a 272-bp direct terminal repeat. The genome contains 71 putative open reading frames (ORFs) and no tRNA, while no virulence, antibiotic resistance (AMR) or lysogeny-associated genes were identified, and genome-based analyses predicted a virulent lifestyle. Comparative genomic analysis showed a high nucleotide identity (99.12%) with Escherichia phage EPIMAM03, and KBU_SV1 was assigned to the genus Dhillonvirus within the class Caudoviricetes. All these results showed that KBU_SV1 has favorable properties such as antibacterial potential against carbapenem-resistant E. coli, broad stability, antibiofilm and in vivo activity, and the absence of virulence and AMR genes. Based on all these features, this newly isolated phage is promising for the control of carbapenem-resistant E. coli infections, alone or in phage cocktails.
authors: Öztaş S, Karaynir A, Ozkan RG, Bozdogan B, Dündar D.

title: Mineralization mechanism and pollutant immobilization characteristics of vaterite induced by Bacillus velezensis and Pseudomonas putida.
abstract: Exploring strain-specific differences in bacterial vaterite biomineralization can supplement the basic theoretical research of biomineralization and reveal the biogeochemical linkages between microbially induced carbonate formation and in-situ pollutant sequestration in soil environments. In this study, Bacillus velezensis LB002 and Pseudomonas putida KT2440 were used as representative bacterial strains to compare strain-dependent vaterite formation and pollutant sequestration behavior. The biomineralization processes in the liquid medium were dynamically monitored, and the induced biominerals were characterized, with particular attention to their organic components. The differences in vaterite characteristics between both bacterial systems were evaluated, and their sequestration performance was assessed taking Cu2+ and tetracycline as target pollutants. Both strains induced vaterite formation under identical culture conditions, while B. velezensis exhibited a stronger biomineralization capacity than P. putida. In a 100 mL culture system, the Ca2+ mineralization percentage of B. velezensis reached 35.06%, and the dry weights of biomineral aggregates produced by B. velezensis and P. putida were 0.36 and 0.31 g, respectively. SEM observations revealed that the vaterite induced by B. velezensis had a loose and porous surface, whereas that induced by P. putida had a relatively smooth surface. For the high concentration of Cu2+ at 50 mg/L, the sequestration rate reached 84.93% for B. velezensis-induced vaterite, compared with 71.86% for P. putida-induced vaterite under the same conditions. Both biominerals demonstrated similar tetracycline sequestration efficiency, with values of approximately 60%. This study verifies that these two representative bacterial strains differ markedly in biogenic vaterite formation and mineral-mediated pollutant sequestration capacity, with interspecific variations in cell wall, EPS and CA activity accounting for these strain-dependent disparities. These findings help interpret why soil carbonate minerals show heterogeneous pollutant immobilization effects in natural edaphic environments, and offer experimental evidence for understanding microbe-carbonate-contaminant coupled biogeochemical cycling within soils and sediments.
authors: Li X, Nie W, Guo Z, Tang L, Liu F, Lian B.

title: From dietary exposure to organ injury: microbiome-mediated biotransformation of food-chain xenobiotics across the gut-liver-kidney axis.
abstract: Food-chain xenobiotics reach the intestine through food additives, processing-generated chemicals, environmental contaminants, and naturally occurring toxins. Their biological effects depend not only on intake but also on microbial metabolism and host handling. Gut microorganisms can detoxify parent compounds or generate metabolites with altered biological activity, while xenobiotic exposure can reshape microbial communities and host-microbial interactions. This review synthesizes evidence on these processes across the gut-liver-kidney axis, with particular attention to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and chronic kidney disease. We examine direct microbial biotransformation alongside exposure-related changes in intestinal barrier function, immune responses, and metabolic signaling. The resulting synthesis highlights compound-specific and host-specific responses, shaped by microbial enzyme capacity, dietary context, barrier integrity, and hepatic and renal clearance. Impaired organ function can, in turn, alter microbial ecology and promote metabolite accumulation, creating bidirectional interactions between exposure and disease. Although experimental studies provide mechanistic insights, human evidence establishing causal links between dietary xenobiotics, microbial transformation, and chronic liver or kidney injury remains limited. We also evaluate the potential of integrated biomarkers, dietary interventions, and microbial enzyme-targeting strategies, identifying the evidence needed for clinical translation. Future progress requires longitudinal cohorts and controlled dietary studies that combine measured exposure, microbial function, metabolite profiles, and organ-specific outcomes. This integrated perspective provides a framework for investigating individual susceptibility to dietary xenobiotics and evaluating microbiome-informed approaches to food safety and nutrition.
authors: Li G, Xiong Y, Yu X, Yu J, Xu R.

title: Manganese(II) oxidation by Bacillus wiedmannii DX3 isolated from electrolytic manganese residue: Mn(III) as an intermediate and characterisation of biogenic manganese oxides.
abstract: Manganese contamination in soil poses risks to plant growth and human health. In this study, we isolated the manganese-oxidising bacterium Bacillus wiedmannii DX3 from electrolytic manganese residue and investigated its Mn(II) oxidation characteristics. The strain exhibited efficient Mn(II) oxidation at different initial Mn(II) concentrations, with a maximum biogenic manganese oxide (BMO) production of 166.89 μM achieved at 5.0 mM Mn(II). Spectroscopic analysis revealed that Mn(III) serves as a key intermediate during microbial Mn(II) oxidation. The biogenic manganese oxides were further characterised using transmission electron microscopy (TEM), X-ray diffractometry (XRD), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), providing insights into their structural and functional properties. Overall, this study expands our understanding of manganese-oxidising bacteria and provides a mechanistic basis for the potential application of strain DX3 in the bioremediation of manganese-contaminated environments. The biogenic manganese oxides produced through the Mn(II) → Mn(III) → Mn(IV) pathway act as adsorbents for toxic metals and as oxidants for redox-sensitive contaminants. However, their efficacy in real soil and water matrices, as well as the biosafety of this B. wiedmannii strain, requires further evaluation.
authors: Zhong K, Zhang Q, Lu S, Yin J, Liao Y, Gu M, Zhang C.

title: Unleashing the industrial potential of microbial plant cell wall polysaccharide-degrading enzymes: recent advances in protein engineering.
abstract: Plant cell wall polysaccharide-degrading enzymes (PCWPEs) used in industry are predominantly of microbial origin. Key enzyme classes, including cellulases, lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases (LPMOs), β-xylanases, β-mannanases and pectinases, have attained technological maturity and are widely deployed across agro-waste biorefineries, food and feed processing, textile and pulp manufacturing. Low catalytic efficiency, insufficient thermostability, poor operational adaptability, restricted functionality, and product inhibition limit the industrial use of these enzymes. Structure- and sequence-guided design, supported by computational design tools, now allows more targeted improvement of PCWPE performance. Yet, the stringent and context-specific performance requirements imposed by diverse industrial applications continue to present substantial challenges. This review systematically summarizes current engineering strategies for PCWPEs in the past decade, aiming to provide a comprehensive understanding of the tailored strategies employed in different engineering directions and to offer insightful proposals for future research.
authors: Huang Z, Xu L, Zhou J, Gao R, Shi H.

title: Deletion of the Envelope gene attenuates SARS-CoV-2 infection by altered spike localization and increased cell-to-cell transmission.
abstract: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) causes COVID-19, a highly transmissible acute respiratory infection that can result in severe pneumonia and death. Many details of SARS-CoV-2 infection are not fully understood, including the cell biology and host-virus interactions involved in coronavirus assembly and release, in which the Envelope (E) structural protein is instrumental. Deletion of E in other coronaviruses has been shown previously to either attenuate or abrogate infection. To determine the role of E in SARS-CoV-2 virus production and infectivity, we produced a reporter SARS-CoV-2 with or without the E gene deleted using a bacterial artificial chromosome. Replication of ΔE SARS-CoV-2 was attenuated in Vero E6 cells expressing human ACE2 and TMPRSS2 and in human epithelial cell lines. Electron and immunofluorescence microscopy and virology assays showed that ΔE SARS-CoV-2 increased cell surface expression of Spike (S) glycoprotein, leading to reduced S incorporation into ΔE SARS-CoV-2 particles and promotion of increased cell-to-cell transmission that evades neutralizing antibody inhibition. Trans-complementation of E partially rescued ΔE SARS-CoV-2 S incorporation and restored cell-free transmission. In addition to validating the role of E in retention of S in the ER-Golgi intermediate complex (ERGIC), our results showed that a lack of E led to reorganization of the ERGIC and Golgi during SARS-CoV-2 infection. Improved understanding of E in SARS-CoV-2 replication and host pathogenesis may help the development of novel therapeutics.IMPORTANCENon-Spike coronavirus structural proteins, including Envelope, are conserved, making them potential pan-coronavirus therapeutic targets. Many details about these proteins and their roles in viral replication and host pathogenesis are unknown. In this study, we showed that severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) replicates without Envelope but is attenuated and impaired in virus particle formation, with less Spike incorporated into virions and more Spike expressed on the cell surface compared to wild-type virus. SARS-CoV-2 lacking Envelope transmitted primarily via cell fusion and evaded neutralizing antibodies. In addition, the absence of Envelope resulted in the reorganization of the cell secretory compartment during SARS-CoV-2 infection. A better understanding of how Envelope influences SARS-CoV-2 replication could guide directed design of novel therapeutics for treatment of COVID-19 patients, as well as the potential for pan-coronavirus protection against future coronavirus outbreaks.
authors: Fischer HL, Shanmugapriya S, Kline C, Duprex WP, McCarthy KR, Watkins SC, Conway JF, Ambrose Z.

title: Natural products regulate gut microbiota and SCFA metabolism in IBD: mechanisms and therapeutic potential.
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn's disease (CD), is a chronic relapsing inflammatory condition of the gastrointestinal tract. Over the past few decades, the global incidence of this disease has continued to rise, imposing a heavy socioeconomic burden. IBD is typically characterized by gut microbiota dysbiosis and reduced short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) levels, which in turn lead to impaired intestinal barrier function and decreased immune tolerance. Multiple studies have shown that natural products, including polysaccharides, polyphenols, alkaloids, and terpenoids, can modulate the gut microbiota in IBD, with changes in SCFA concentrations observed in some preclinical studies. These effects have been associated with alterations in bacterial taxa such as Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Bifidobacterium, and Christensenella minuta. These findings suggest that natural products may regulate the gut microbiota-SCFA metabolic axis; however, the direct causal relationships among changes in microbial composition, SCFA concentrations, and anti-inflammatory effects remain to be established. This review summarizes current mechanisms and translational opportunities for natural products targeting the microbiota-SCFA axis in IBD.
authors: He B, Xu Y, Wang Y, Pan Z.

title: Longitudinal integrated analysis of gut microbiota and metabolites in rectal cancer patients undergoing chemoradiotherapy.
abstract: BackgroundLongitudinal changes in the fecal microbiome and metabolome during concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) for rectal cancer remain incompletely characterized.MethodsIn this prospective single-center cohort, 19 patients with rectal cancer were enrolled and 17 were included in the longitudinal analysis after two prespecified sampling-window exclusions. Fecal specimens were scheduled at nine time points: R0, collected before the first dose of capecitabine and before radiotherapy, and R3 through R24 at three-fraction intervals during treatment. Twenty unmatched healthy volunteers provided one fecal specimen for a descriptive pretreatment comparison. Full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics were performed. Longitudinal microbial counts were analyzed using negative-binomial generalized linear mixed models, and metabolite features were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models; participant was included as a random intercept, and P values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR).ResultsNineteen genera and 27 of 176 analyzed species showed significant linear time trends during CCRT (FDR Parvimonas micra, Peptostreptococcus stomatis, and Gemella morbillorum decreased, whereas Lachnoclostridium pacaense, Blautia hydrogenotrophica, [Eubacterium] sulci, and Coprococcus eutactus increased. Of 2,873 analyzed metabolic features, 393 changed significantly over time. In a secondary same-cohort analysis, 17 of 50 correlation-selected taxon-metabolite pairs remained significant in time-adjusted mixed-effects models, including a positive association between C. eutactus and a feature annotated as stercobilin. Among 103 significant features with KEGG identifiers, three pathways met a nominal raw-P threshold, but none remained significant after FDR correction. Pretreatment patient samples had lower Shannon diversity and differed from healthy-control samples by ANOSIM; these comparisons were descriptive because the groups were not matched for age or sex. Five species shared the same case-control direction in this cohort and GMrepo reports, but only P. stomatis and G. morbillorum also showed significant longitudinal declines during CCRT.ConclusionThis small, intensively sampled cohort identifies exploratory fecal microbial and metabolic trajectories during capecitabine-based CCRT. The findings do not establish causal mechanisms, microbial functions, disease specificity, or biomarker performance and require independent confirmation in larger cohorts.
authors: Wang L, Zhang P, Zhang Y, Li Y, Qu B, Peng L.

title: Dietary whole sweet sorghum silage alters jejunal morphology, selected cecal bacterial taxa, and meat quality in heavy finishing pigs.
abstract: Whole sweet sorghum silage (WSS) is a locally available forage resource with potential application in sustainable swine production, yet its biological effects on the intestinal environment and production-related traits of heavy finishing pigs (defined here as pigs entering the trial at approximately 132 kg BW) remain unclear. This study evaluated the effects of replacing 20 percentage units of corn with WSS (on an as-fed basis) on growth performance, meat quality, jejunal morphology, and cecal bacterial composition. Seventy-two Duroc × Landrace × Yorkshire pigs were fed the corn-based control diet (CON) or the WSS diet for 30 d. Compared with CON, WSS reduced average daily gain and feed intake and increased the feed-to-gain ratio. It also decreased backfat thickness while increasing loin-eye area and marbling score. WSS reduced 48-h drip loss and increased inosine monophosphate concentrations in both the longissimus dorsi and psoas major muscles. Jejunal villus height and the villus-height-to-crypt-depth ratio were increased in WSS-fed pigs. No significant differences were detected in alpha-diversity indices or unweighted UniFrac community structure between diets, whereas an exploratory linear discriminant analysis effect size procedure identified Streptosporangium, Kribbella, Oxalobacter, and Planifilum as taxa associated with WSS and Bacteroides-related features as associated with CON. Because the diets were not nutrient-matched, these responses reflect the complete dietary contrast. Overall, WSS was associated with a pattern of reduced growth performance accompanied by selected changes in carcass and meat-quality traits, concurrent jejunal morphological adaptation, and exploratory cecal bacterial signals that warrant mechanistic validation.
authors: Shi S, Wei J, Zhang Y, Yuan X, Shang X, Li X, Zhou H, Jiang Y, Yang W, Zhou M, Jiang S.

title: Cereal-based solid-state production and storage stability of native Trichoderma harzianum isolates for biological control applications.
abstract: The effectiveness of Trichoderma-based biocontrol products depends on achieving high spore yields and maintaining viable propagules during storage. This study evaluated the effects of substrate type, isolate, and storage duration on spore production and viability of four Trichoderma harzianum isolates (BH10-2, KH5-1, MG7-2, and SH11-2) cultured on four cereal-based substrates: rice grain (RG), rice powder (RP), sorghum grain (SG), and sorghum powder (SP). The experiment was arranged in a factorial Completely Randomized Design (CRD) with three replications under laboratory conditions. Spore production was assessed 10 days after fermentation, while spore viability was determined after 30, 60, and 90 days of storage following a 7-day drying period. Colony-forming unit (CFU) data were log-transformed before analysis using two-way ANOVA for initial spore production and a linear mixed-effects model (LMM) for repeated measurements of spore viability during storage. Mean separation was performed using Tukey's HSD test at P ≤ 0.05. Initial spore production was significantly influenced by the interaction between isolate and substrate (P -1), whereas isolate MG7-2 grown on sorghum grain recorded the lowest initial spore production (5.81 log CFU g-1). Spore viability was significantly affected by isolate, substrate, storage duration, and their interactions (P Trichoderma. The combination of isolate MG7-2 and sorghum grain showed the greatest potential for developing stable Trichoderma-based bioformulations suitable for sustainable biological control.
authors: Londjiringa DD, Mabiki F, Madege R.

title: Targeting cariogenic virulence of Streptococcus mutans by pinosylvin: a promising anti-cariogenic natural agent.
abstract: Dental caries continues to be a serious worldwide public health issue, with Streptococcus mutans (S. mutans) identified as the primary etiological pathogen. This study aimed to evaluate the anti-cariogenic potential of pinosylvin (PIN) against S. mutans. A combination of in vitro and in vitro experiments was performed to characterize the anti-cariogenic effects of PIN. In vitro assays were conducted to determine the impacts of PIN on the growth, bacterial adhesion, biofilm formation, and lactic acid synthesis of S. mutans. Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) was applied to quantify the transcript abundance of key cariogenic virulence genes, including gtfB, gtfC, and gtfD. A rat dental caries model was adopted to assess the biosafety and in vitro anti-cariogenic efficacy of PIN. PIN inhibited the growth, bacterial adhesion, biofilm formation, and lactic acid synthesis of S. mutans. Consistent with these phenotypic alterations, qRT-PCR analysis demonstrated that PIN downregulated the expression of core cariogenic virulence genes gtfB, gtfC, and gtfD. In vivo, PIN exhibited favorable biocompatibility and anti-cariogenic effects in the rat caries model. Collectively, these findings suggest that PIN exerts anti-cariogenic activity against S. mutans by suppressing multiple virulence-associated phenotypes and downregulating key cariogenic genes. The in vivo findings further support its biocompatibility and potential anti-cariogenic effect. Nevertheless, the precise molecular mechanisms underlying these effects and suitable delivery strategies of PIN remain to be clarified in future studies.
authors: Shu J, Liu W, Qiu Y, Liao X, Xiong Y, Xie X, Xu Y, Liu Y, Liu Y, Peng J, Mei X.

title: Physiological and transcriptional responses of lactic acid bacteria to sub-inhibitory cadmium exposure.
abstract: IntroductionCadmium is a widespread environmental contaminant that can adversely impact microbial growth and metabolism. While the ability of Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) to bind and sequester cadmium has been extensively investigated, less is known about their physiological adaptation to sub-inhibitory cadmium exposure.MethodsFollowing the initial determination of the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), four selected LAB strains were exposed to sub-inhibitory cadmium concentrations (1/8, 1/4 and 1/2 × their respective MIC values) and investigated using a combined physiological and transcriptional approach. Growth performance, culturability, viability, and acidification activity were assessed alongside the expression of cadA, cadD, mntH, and czcA, genes involved in metal transport, homeostasis, and detoxification, respectively.ResultsThe results revealed marked strain-dependent differences in cadmium tolerance and adaptation. Even at sub-inhibitory concentrations, cadmium affected bacterial physiology by reducing growth and acidification activity. Limosilactobacillus reuteri showed the strongest reduction in relative growth, which decreased to 18.8% of the untreated control at 12 × MIC, while Nile Red fluorescence increased up to 5.61-fold, indicating pronounced alterations in the membrane lipid environment. LIVE/DEAD analyses demonstrated a concentration-dependent increase in the population of membrane-compromised cells, although proportional losses in cell viability did not always accompany reductions in culturability. Nile Red fluorescence analyses further revealed significant alterations in the cellular lipid environment, suggesting membrane remodeling as an important component of the adaptive response to cadmium exposure. Transcriptional analyses further showed heterogeneous expression patterns among strains, suggesting that adaptation to cadmium is regulated through strain-specific responses rather than a shared regulatory strategy.DiscussionOverall, these findings indicate that LAB responses to cadmium involve strain-dependent physiological and transcriptional changes. The study highlights the importance of considering strain-specific traits when evaluating bacterial responses to metal stress and provides a basis for future investigations into the molecular mechanisms underlying adaptation to sub-lethal cadmium exposure.
authors: Vardanyan D, Mancini L, Bernardi M, Filannino P, Calabrese FM, De Angelis M.

title: Gut microbiome taxonomic and functional capacity alterations in CHD and HFpEF.
abstract: The gut microbiome is known to modulate metabolic health, yet its role in coronary heart disease (CHD) and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) remains unclear. In the present study, we profiled the gut microbiome of 234 participants using shotgun metagenomic sequencing across controls (n = 43), individuals with low-risk atherosclerosis (LRAS, n = 23), and patients with CHD + HFpEF (n = 168). Species richness was significantly increased in CHD + HFpEF, with no disruption in taxonomic evenness. LRAS did not diverge significantly in alpha metrics. In contrast, beta diversity analysis demonstrated significant divergence of both LRAS and CHD + HFpEF taxonomic structure from controls, with the greatest divergence in CHD + HFpEF, particularly in older patients. Notably, all differences were attenuated when comparing obese controls and disease groups. However, significant heterogeneity in multivariate dispersion was observed, and a contribution of differences in variation cannot be excluded. Further differential analysis, adjusting for age, BMI, sex, and glucose and lipid profiles, revealed significant associations between specific taxa and CHD + HFpEF, including depletion of the saccharolytic fermenter Bifidobacterium and enrichment of taxa linked to proteolytic or inflammatory metabolism (notably Prevotella and Bilophila), regardless of age and BMI. Subsequent analysis of inferred functional features indicated increased potential for L-citrulline, L-glutamate, L-lysine, and pyrimidine metabolism in CHD + HFpEF. Collectively, the present analysis suggests that CHD + HFpEF is associated with distinct compositional and functional shifts in the gut microbiome. Further longitudinal and interventional research is required to determine which of these microbial features contribute to disease progression and to better characterize underlying mechanisms.
authors: Tauekelova A, Katkenov N, Kozhakhmetov S, Jarmukhanov Z, Vinogradova E, Abdrakhmanov A, Sailybayeva A, Bekbossynova M, Kushugulova A.

title: Microplastics as evolving particle-chemical-microbial interfaces: plastisphere ecology, ecotoxicity, and safety-informed remediation.
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) are not environmentally static particles; aging, fragmentation, contaminant acquisition, organic conditioning, and microbial colonization progressively convert them into dynamic particle-chemical-microbial interfaces. This transformation is central to their environmental fate and risk because plastisphere communities can alter particle transport, contaminant partitioning, nutrient cycling, antimicrobial-resistance dynamics, and polymer transformation. Experimental evidence shows that MP biofilms can increase conjugative transfer of antibiotic-resistance genes by approximately 7.2-19.6-fold relative to suspended bacteria, illustrating that microbial colonization can modify ecological function rather than merely change community composition. However, microbial presence, functional-gene enrichment, surface deterioration, and polymer mass loss should not be interpreted as equivalent evidence of biodegradation. Stable-isotope studies show that even biodegradable polymers may mineralize slowly and incompletely; approximately 65% mineralization of 1 3C-labeled PBS required 425 days, whereas direct mineralization of persistent polyolefins remains far more limited. Ecotoxicological effects are similarly conditional on particle size, morphology, aging, associated chemicals, exposure duration, and environmental context, and evidence for trophic transfer is stronger than that for generalized biomagnification. Interpretation is further constrained by substantial analytical heterogeneity in sampling, size cut-offs, recovery, contamination control, polymer identification, and number-vs.-mass reporting, making methodological harmonization and uncertainty assessment essential for cross-study comparison. Remediation should therefore distinguish particle capture from destruction and biodeterioration from depolymerization, microbial assimilation, mineralization, and true upcycling. Although enzymatic and microbial conversion technologies show considerable promise, most high-performance demonstrations involve defined polymers, post-consumer plastics, or prepared hydrolysates rather than heterogeneous environmental MPs. Safe application consequently requires carbon and contaminant mass balances, residue and product safety testing, microbial containment, and life-cycle verification. Climate-sensitive transport and toxicity further reinforce the dynamic nature of MP exposure, while circular-economy strategies should prioritize prevention, low-shedding design, reuse, and recovery before attempting energy-intensive reclamation of dispersed environmental particles. Overall, a microbiology-informed assessment of MPs requires progression from microbial identity to demonstrated function, from particle detection to exposure relevance, and from apparent removal or degradation to verified net risk reduction.
authors: Jiao H, Fodah AEM, Schagerl M, Yang B, Ali SS.

title: Reptiles in the One Health ecology of antimicrobial resistance, with insights into zoonotic pathogens: reservoirs, transmission pathways, and public health implications.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is a growing global health challenge at the interface of human, animal, and environmental health. Reptiles-including wild populations, pets, farmed species, and internationally traded animals-are increasingly recognized as participants in One Health AMR networks, occupying ecological interfaces that facilitate interactions among wildlife, domestic animals, humans, and the environment. Their diverse microbiota and exposure to both natural and anthropogenically influenced habitats create opportunities for the acquisition and dissemination of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria (AMR bacteria) and antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs), particularly in captive settings where close human contact and husbandry practices may favor bacterial exchange. Recent studies demonstrate that reptiles frequently harbor clinically relevant ARGs encoding extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBL), AmpC-β-lactamases, carbapenemases, and colistin resistance. Potential exposure pathways include direct contact, bites, environmental contamination of terraria and husbandry systems, and, in some regions, the handling and consumption of reptile-derived food products. Wild reptiles may additionally serve as valuable sentinels for anthropogenic AMR pollution within terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. Despite growing interest, the role of reptiles within the broader ecology of AMR remains incompletely understood. Available studies are geographically uneven, methodologically heterogeneous, and frequently lack high-resolution genomic characterization, limiting robust assessment of transmission pathways, transmission directionality, and the relative contribution of reptiles compared with other wildlife and environmental reservoirs. This review synthesizes current evidence on the occurrence, diversity, and transmission of AMR bacteria in reptiles and discusses their implications for public health, veterinary medicine, wildlife conservation, and One Health. It further highlights major methodological limitations, critical knowledge gaps, and priorities for harmonized, genomics-informed surveillance. Overall, current evidence suggests that reptiles should be viewed as ecologically relevant participants in the One Health ecology of antimicrobial resistance, although their relative contribution to AMR dissemination remains to be quantified.
authors: Ewers C, Unger F, Prenger-Berninghoff E, Eisenberg T.

title: Recognition-decision-execution: a new design principle for intelligent antimicrobial systems.
abstract: The continued rise of antimicrobial resistance highlights fundamental limitations of prevailing antibacterial strategies, which remain largely dominated by continuous, non-directed killing. Although combination therapies and multifunctional materials are frequently described as synergistic, many reported effects primarily reflect pharmacokinetic enhancement or local concentration increases, rather than genuine reprogramming of antibacterial behavior. As a result, most current approaches still impose sustained selective pressure and offer limited control over timing, location, and intensity of killing. Here, we propose the Recognition-Decision-Execution (RDE) framework as a function-driven organizational principle for antibacterial system design. In this framework, antibacterial activity is decomposed into three orthogonal yet logically coupled modules: pathogen recognition, decision-making, and killing execution. Recognition modules provide contextual information regarding pathogen identity, microenvironmental state, and infection dynamics; decision modules interpret these inputs to authorize action with defined spatiotemporal and intensity constraints; and execution modules eliminate pathogens only upon conditional approval. This architecture transforms antibacterial activity from a default, always-on process into a programmable, event-driven intervention that may reshape rather than universally reduce selective pressure. We discuss how functional decoupling enables a clear distinction between apparent (pseudo-) synergy and true mechanistic synergy, and how regulatory-execution interactions can qualitatively reshape killing mechanisms rather than merely amplifying them. Importantly, functional roles are not intrinsic to specific agents: antimicrobial peptides, nanomaterials, and nucleic acid aptamers can dynamically interchange between regulatory and execution functions depending on system architecture. The aptamer-nanomaterial-antimicrobial peptide triad serves as a minimal closed-loop example illustrating how sensing, decision-making, and execution can be independently optimized yet synergistically integrated. By emphasizing system logic, modular verifiability, and conditional authorization of killing, the RDE framework offers a unifying conceptual language for the design of programmable and adaptive antibacterial therapies. It should be emphasized that the RDE framework represents a unifying conceptual paradigm and set of testable design hypotheses. Most reported antibacterial examples only achieve partial pairwise functional slices rather than fully-validated ternary closed-loop RDE architectures.
authors: Ma J, Feng M, Li S.

title: Addition of Chinese medicinal herbal residues promotes the removal of antibiotic resistance genes during pig manure composting.
abstract: Aerobic composting is an effective methods for reducing antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and mobile genetic elements (MGEs) present in livestock and poultry manure. Chinese medicinal herbal residues (CMHRs) are rich in nutrients and antibacterial components, which may inhibit the spread of ARGs and MGEs. This study investigated the effects of adding different proportions of CMHRs added (0%, 10%, 30%, and 50% of the initial compost mixture mass) on ARGs and MGEs during pig manure composting. The results showed that CMHRs shortened the time required to reach the high-temperature stage and increased compost temperature. At the end of composting, the total nitrogen (TN) and available phosphorus (AP) levels in the M2 treatment group were significantly higher than those in the control group, reaching 8.11 g/kg and 333.73 mg/kg, respectively. High-throughput qPCR analysis showed that the total removal rates of ARGs after composting were 27.10%, 36.04%, 65.55%, and 40.55%, respectively; the corresponding removal rates of MGEs were 19.25%, 56.20%, 65.32%, and 14.03%, respectively; The 30% treatment was the most effective, with removal rates of aminoglycosides, β-lactam, multidrug resistance, sulfonamides, and tetracycline resistance genes of 78.09%, 81.11%, 74.09%, 54.27%, and 61.24%, respectively. Firmicutes, Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria, and Bacteroidetes were the dominant phyla in the compost. Clostridium-sensu-stricto1, Corynebacterium, Terrisporobacter, Anaerococcus, and Romboutsia were potential major hosts of ARGs and MGEs. During composting, changes in temperature and MGEs directly and significantly affected ARGs, while total organic carbon (TOM) and TN indirectly affected ARGs by regulating microbial communities. In conclusion, the addition of 30% CMHRs effectively reduces ARGs and MGEs in pig manure compost. These findings provide a basis for the use of CMHRs to reduce the spread of ARGs during pig manure composting.
authors: Wang B, Tian L, Wang Y, Tian Z, Yang Y.

title: Gut-liver axis dysregulation and restoration in decompensated hepatitis B cirrhosis: rationale and research progress of fecal microbiota transplantation.
abstract: Decompensated hepatitis B virus (HBV) related cirrhosis is associated with high mortality and a wide range of complications. Current antiviral and symptomatic treatments fail to reverse core pathological alterations, including disruption of the gut microbial ecosystem. Gut-liver axis imbalance represents a central hub in disease progression. Gut dysbiosis compromises the intestinal mucosal barrier, leading to endotoxin translocation into the bloodstream, which in turn exacerbates hepatic inflammation and fibrosis, thereby establishing a vicious cycle. This review synthesizes the key mechanisms, clinical efficacy, administration routes, and safety profile of fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) in this disease. It also identifies current technical bottlenecks and research gaps in FMT application and discusses future directions toward precision based and standardized clinical translation of this therapeutic approach.
authors: Gao S, Zhuang J, Cheng H, Hu K, Zhuang L, Pan Y.

title: Two myxobacterial strains against Rhizoctonia solani: comparative genomics of antagonistic potential and phenotypic evaluation of growth-promoting and disease-control effects.
abstract: IntroductionAlthough sugar beet (Beta vulgaris ssp. vulgaris) is a major sugar crop in China, continuous cropping obstacles frequently constrain its productivity and quality. The application of antagonistic microorganisms or plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) offers a promising biological method for alleviating these constraints. This study evaluated two previously isolated myxobacterial strains with documented antagonistic activity against Rhizoctonia solani: Cystobacter ferrugineus W14 and Cystobacter fuscus W11.MethodsTheir effects on sugar beet seedling growth under continuous cropping were assessed in a pot experiment, and whole-genome sequencing enabled the comparative profiling of disease resistance-related genes and functional pathways.ResultsInoculation with either strain significantly increased seedling growth parameters, including stem diameter, plant height, and leaf fresh weight, compared with the control (CK). Specifically, strains W14 and W11 significantly increased plant height by 38.40 and 33.62%, respectively, and stem diameter by 44.54 and 31.93%, respectively. Moreover, disease incidence was markedly reduced. W14 and W11 yielded disease index values of 16.11 and 19.46, respectively, corresponding to significant reductions of 70.49 and 64.35%, respectively, compared with the CK. Whole-genome sequencing revealed that strain W14 contained more GH19 family chitinase genes, GH5 family glucanase genes, and secondary metabolite biosynthetic gene clusters than strain W11. Functional annotation assigned more strain W14 genes to three major antagonism-related categories: cell wall degradation, antibiotic synthesis, and signal transduction. Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analyses consistently identified more genes involved in metabolic processes and secondary metabolite biosynthesis pathways in strain W14 than in strain W11.ConclusionBoth myxobacterial strains promoted sugar beet seedling growth and protected against diseases associated with continuous cropping, whereas strain W14 showed a greater genomic capacity for antagonistic traits. These findings provide a theoretical basis for the development of novel biocontrol agents. These genomic differences represent candidate correlates of antagonistic potential and require further functional validation.
authors: Gao Y, Fu Y, Jin C, Cheng J, Wang Y, Sun Y, Geng G, Sun Y.

title: Potato straw incorporation improves soybean agronomic traits and yield components and is associated with shifts in rhizosphere soil properties microbial communities and metabolites.
abstract: BackgroundThe soil-improving effects of cereal straw incorporation have been well documented; however, potato straw differs markedly from cereal straw in composition and degradation characteristics, and whether straw return is associated with the soil microbial ecosystem and with gains in yield components through pathways similar to those of cereal straw remains unclear.MethodsIn this study, a field-embedded pot experiment was conducted to characterize the interaction network among soil physicochemical properties, microbial communities, and metabolites under potato straw incorporation, and to elucidate its regulatory effects on soybean growth and yield components.ResultsCompared with no incorporation, straw incorporation significantly increased soil organic matter (by 21.60%), available potassium (35.39%), alkali-hydrolyzable nitrogen (16.94%), and available phosphorus (15.42%), and significantly enhanced the activities of acid phosphatase (28.63%) and polyphenol oxidase (16.04%). Amplicon sequencing identified treatment-associated enrichment of bacterial and fungal taxa previously linked to residue decomposition, nutrient cycling (e.g., Paenibacillus and Nitrosomonadaceae), or plant-beneficial interactions(e.g., arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi [Glomeromycota] and Bionectria). Correlation analysis between the soil metabolome and the microbial community showed that both bacterial and fungal communities exhibited a dichotomous pattern of contrasting metabolite preferences: among bacteria, Proteobacteria-dominated taxa were positively correlated with organic acid metabolites, whereas taxa dominated by Gemmatimonadota, Firmicutes, and Actinobacteria were positively correlated with aromatic amino acids and nitrogen-containing heterocyclic compounds, each group being negatively correlated with the metabolites preferred by the other; among fungi, root-symbiotic taxa were positively correlated with secondary metabolites such as flavonoids, whereas saprotrophic fungi were positively correlated with plant-residue decomposition markers such as 2-furoic acid and geranylgeraniol. Three relatively independent organic nitrogen transformation pathways-arginine metabolism, histidine degradation, and purine nucleoside catabolism-were also detected, and pH, organic matter, urease (S-UE), and soybean isoflavone metabolites (daidzein and genistin) showed strong co-occurrence patterns with other network members.ConclusionSoybean plant height, stem diameter, pods per plant, and 100-seed weight significantly increased by 14.93%, 17.77%, 19.10%, and 11.40%, respectively. In summary, potato straw incorporation broadened the soil organic nitrogen substrate spectrum by reshaping the soil physicochemical property-microbe-metabolite interaction network, thereby promoting soybean growth and yield components formation through multi-pathway synergy. These findings provide a theoretical basis for the resource utilization of potato straw.
authors: He A, Wang Y, Guo H, Li J, Zhang Y, Huang D, Yang F, Zhang R.

title: Inoculum-dependent activity of contemporary β-lactam agents against carbapenemase- producing Enterobacterales.
abstract: Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (CPE) pose a major therapeutic challenge because antimicrobial susceptibility measured at standard inoculum may not reflect activity at higher bacterial burdens. This Mini Review examines the biological basis, carbapenemase dependence, and agent-specific expression of inoculum effects among contemporary β-lactams. Increasing bacterial density can enhance β-lactamase burden and extracellular carbapenemase activity, alter the effective drug-to-enzyme relationship, and interact with permeability defects, bacterial physiology, and antimicrobial exposure. Available evidence shows substantial heterogeneity across carbapenemases and agents. Ceftazidime-avibactam appears comparatively stable in several CPE studies, whereas cefiderocol, aztreonam-avibactam, and other β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations can show marked density-dependent reductions in activity under specific conditions. However, in vitro MIC increases do not consistently translate into reduced in vivo efficacy. Standardized testing approaches, mechanism-informed susceptibility assessment, and clinically relevant pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies are needed to clarify the therapeutic significance of inoculum-dependent β-lactam activity.
authors: Sahu TK, Gadkari P, Rathored J.

title: An exploratory study of gut microbiota and serum metabolite profiles in type 2 diabetes patients with sleep disorders.
abstract: ObjectiveTo characterize gut microbiota composition and serum metabolites in T2DM patients with and without sleep disorders.MethodsThis single center cross sectional study enrolled 40 T2DM patients with sleep disorders (Group I), 40 T2DM patients without sleep disorders (Group N) and 30 age and sex matched healthy controls (Group ZC). Fecal and serum samples were collected for 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry metabolomics, respectively. Gut microbiota composition, serum metabolites and metabolic pathways, and microbe-metabolite correlations were analyzed.ResultsCompared with T2DM patients without sleep disorders, T2DM patients with sleep disorders showed reduced gut microbial diversity and evenness, as indicated by lower Shannon, Simpson, and Pielou's evenness indices. Beta diversity analysis showed a small but statistically significant difference in microbial structure between Groups I and N. At the genus level, nominal differences were observed between the two groups, including higher relative abundances of TM7x, Achromobacter, and Pseudomonas and lower relative abundances of Eubacterium_eligens_group, Lachnospiraceae_UCG-001, and Negativibacillus in Group I. Metabolomic results revealed 17 nominally differential metabolites between Groups I and N, involving caffeine metabolism and porphyrin and chlorophyll metabolism. Spearman analysis revealed that stercobilin abundance positively correlated with Lachnospiraceae_UCG-001 (R = 0.381, P Q = 0.095), Lachnospiraceae_ND3007 (R = 0.354, P = 0.002, Q = 0.121), and Odoribacter (R = 0.280, P = 0.01, Q = 0.301).ConclusionsT2DM patients with sleep disorders showed modest differences in gut microbial community structure and exploratory changes in serum metabolite profiles. Stercobilin and caffeine-related metabolic features may represent exploratory characteristics associated with sleep disorders in T2DM. These findings suggest potential microbiota-metabolite associations and provide a basis for future longitudinal and mechanistic studies.
authors: Ma J, Zhang X, Pan Y, Bao X, Yi H, Hua J, Mu Q, Liu L, Hu C, Zhao D, Gao S.

title: Autophagy in Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection: host defense, bacterial countermeasures, and therapeutic targeting.
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P. aeruginosa) is a major opportunistic pathogen whose diverse virulence strategies, increasing antibiotic resistance, and ability to establish persistent infections continue to compromise the efficacy of conventional antimicrobial therapies. Although traditionally regarded as an extracellular pathogen, P. aeruginosa can also enter and persist within host cells, triggering inflammatory responses and cellular injury while simultaneously modulating host autophagic responses. On the one hand, xenophagy and related autophagic processes recognize and deliver intracellular bacteria for lysosomal degradation. Mitophagy eliminates damaged mitochondria generated during infection and limits the accumulation of mitochondrial danger signals. Meanwhile, autophagy regulates inflammasome activation by controlling the removal of damaged organelles and inflammasome components, thereby shaping inflammatory responses during infection. Collectively, these processes contribute to the protective role of autophagy in host defense against P. aeruginosa infection. On the other hand, P. aeruginosa can interfere with or remodel host autophagy through secreted effector molecules, quorum sensing signals, and infection-induced host signaling pathways, resulting in a functional disconnect between autophagic activation and effective bacterial clearance or other antimicrobial responses. This review summarizes current advances in understanding the interplay between autophagy and P. aeruginosa, highlighting the protective functions of autophagy in host defense, the countermeasures employed by P. aeruginosa to evade autophagic clearance, and the therapeutic implications of these host-pathogen interactions. These insights may support the development of host-directed therapeutic approaches targeting autophagy to improve antibacterial defense against P. aeruginosa.
authors: Zhang B, Huang Y, Wen L, Hua Q, Zhao L, Shen J, Zhu M.

title: Biocontrol efficacy of Trichoderma asperellum TA-1 against Rhizoctonia solani AG-3 and its underlying mechanisms.
abstract: IntroductionRhizoctonia solani Kühn is a globally distributed soilborne pathogen responsible for severe diseases in various crops, including rice, wheat, tobacco, and maize, causing substantial economic losses. This study characterized a Trichoderma strain, TA-1, with significant biocontrol efficacy against tobacco target spot disease.MethodsTA-1 was isolated and identified through morphological characterization and molecular analysis as Trichoderma asperellum. Qualitative assays were conducted to assess ammonia production and laccase, amylase, and protease activities. Solid-state fermentation trials were performed to optimize spore production conditions, and greenhouse assays were conducted to evaluate biocontrol efficacy. Microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and transcriptomic analyses were used to characterize the interaction between TA-1 and R. solani AG-3.ResultsQualitative assays indicated ammonia production and laccase, amylase, and protease activities in TA-1. The optimal spore production conditions were wheat bran substrate, 0.5% glucose, 1.5% ammonium sulfate, a water-to-substrate ratio of 1:1, and a fermentation duration of 6 days, under which the spore yield reached 4.74 × 109 CFU/g dry substrate. Greenhouse assays showed that both TA-1 spore suspension and fermentation filtrate significantly suppressed disease symptoms caused by R. solani AG-3, with the spore suspension exhibiting stronger inhibition. Microscopy and scanning electron microscopy revealed clear mycoparasitic features during the TA-1-AG-3 interaction, including hyphal attachment and coiling, structural damage to pathogen hyphae, and colonization of the sclerotial surface. Transcriptomic analysis further identified strong upregulation of TrAFT101_005492, encoding a CFEM domain protein (log2FC = 4.99), and TrAFT101_000974, encoding a lipoxygenase (log2FC = 4.73), suggesting their potential association with the mycoparasitic interaction.DiscussionOverall, T. asperellum TA-1 possesses broad antagonistic activity and considerable biocontrol potential, supporting its further evaluation as a biological control agent for sustainable disease management.
authors: Liu S, Xia Y, Wang C, Hu B, Zhang C, Wang B, Li D, Liu T, Tang Q.

title: Efficacy of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome vaccines in animal models: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is an emerging tick-borne zoonosis that threatens both animal and human health across East Asia, yet no licensed vaccine is currently available. We therefore conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review and meta-analysis of preclinical murine and ferret studies to evaluate severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus vaccine efficacy. Seven electronic databases were searched for studies published between 2009 and 2025. Random-effects meta-analyses evaluated mortality, viremia, and post-challenge weight loss. Quantitative viral burden was further evaluated using standardized mean differences for mean and peak viremia, whereas body-weight trajectories were assessed using generalized linear mixed models. Twenty-three studies met the inclusion criteria. Vaccination markedly reduced mortality (RR = 0.10, 95% CI 0.05-0.21), post-challenge weight loss (RR = 0.21, 95% CI 0.12-0.37), and detectable viremia (RR = 0.45, 95% CI 0.27-0.73), although the effect estimate was attenuated in the trim-and-fill sensitivity analysis (RR = 0.74, 95% CI: 0.36-1.51). Furthermore, significantly suppressing both mean and peak viremia under homologous and heterologous challenge conditions. Longitudinal analyses further demonstrated improved preservation of body weight, particularly following mRNA and vector vaccination. These findings provide the strongest quantitative evidence supporting the development of broadly protective SFTSV vaccines for both human and veterinary use within a One Health framework.
authors: Sibomana E, Ntakiyisumba E, Hirwa F, Tanveer M, Inthavong N, Cabarles JC, Lee JH, Won G.

title: Vector-borne zoonotic bacteria in Tunisia: from fragmented data to an integrated One Health surveillance framework.
abstract: Vector-borne and vector-associated bacterial zoonoses represent an important component of infectious disease epidemiology in Tunisia. This review synthesizes available evidence on major bacterial groups, including Rickettsia, Bartonella, Anaplasma, Ehrlichia, Borrelia, Coxiella burnetii, and other arthropod-associated bacteria, using a One Health framework integrating human, animal, vector, wildlife, and environmental compartments. The available evidence reveals heterogeneous levels of knowledge across bacterial taxa. Rickettsia represents the most established tick-associated zoonotic system, with Rickettsia conorii as the main confirmed human pathogen, while additional species have been detected mainly in arthropods or animal-associated settings. Bartonella has a significant clinical association with blood culture-negative endocarditis, whereas other bacterial groups show predominantly animal- or vector-associated evidence. Coxiella burnetii remains a major zoonotic concern linked to livestock, camels, reproductive materials, and environmental exposure. For Borrelia, Anaplasma, and Ehrlichia, substantial evidence of circulation exists in vectors and animals, but human clinical relevance remains incompletely characterized. Across bacterial groups, a recurrent limitation is the imbalance between molecular detection in vectors or animal hosts and confirmed evidence of transmission or human disease. Detection of bacterial DNA should therefore be interpreted cautiously and not considered equivalent to infection, reservoir competence, or vectorial transmission. Additional arthropod-associated bacteria identified through microbiome studies require further investigation to clarify their ecological significance. The Tunisian evidence base demonstrates active circulation of diverse vector-associated bacteria but remains fragmented across clinical, veterinary, entomological, and ecological domains. Strengthening integrated One Health surveillance through coordinated human diagnosis, animal sentinel systems, vector monitoring, environmental investigations, and advanced molecular approaches is essential to better assess zoonotic risks in Tunisia and the wider North African-Mediterranean region.
authors: Ben Said M, Selmi R, Belkahia H.

title: Mendelian randomization of gut microbiota and exploratory testing of preventive effect of commercial Rothia mucilaginosa in constipated mice.
abstract: Constipation is linked to gut microbiota dysbiosis, but causal microbial contributors and tractable bacterial interventions remain incompletely defined. This study first performed two-sample Mendelian randomization using Dutch Microbiome Project gut-microbiome Genome-Wide Association Study (GWAS) data (N = 7,738) and a European constipation GWAS (N = 411,623) to identify gut taxa linked to constipation. Then, in vitro metabolomics and a loperamide-induced constipation mouse model were used in male C57BL/6 mice to exploratorily test whether the commercial Rothia mucilaginosa strain BNCC363031 prevents loperamide-induced constipation. In an exploratory two-sample MR screen across 207 gut taxa, genetically predicted Rothia was nominally associated with lower constipation risk [odds ratio (OR) = 0.916, p = 0.0041], and the species-level Rothia mucilaginosa showed a concordant nominal protective association (OR = 0.921, p = 0.0232). In mice (n = 8 per group), preventive gavage partially restored loperamide-suppressed defecation: the cross-day mean fecal pellet count in the last 3 h per day was higher in the Rothia mucilaginosa group (RG) than in model controls (MCs) (7.94 vs. 4.41; p = 0.0306) but lower than in normal controls (NCs) (13.16; p = 0.00162), whereas body weight; small-intestinal transit; and immunohistochemical zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1), Claudin-1, and mucin 2 (MUC2) H-scores were unchanged. A fecal 16S V4 signal corresponding to R. mucilaginosa was detected at a very low abundance in only 2/8 RG mice; in vitro metabolomics identified candidates of secreted metabolites, including acetic acid. This study provides a reference for research on Rothia mucilaginosa in the context of constipation.
authors: Jiang P, Yang X, Zhang C, Li Y, Xu C.

title: Comparative transcriptomics of outbreak-associated Salmonella Heidelberg, Typhimurium, and monophasic Typhimurium reveals differential expression of stress tolerance, virulence, and biofilm-associated genes.
abstract: Non-typhoidal Salmonella enterica remains a leading cause of foodborne illness worldwide, with certain serovars more commonly implicated in outbreaks linked to specific food matrices. However, gene expression differences between distinct serovars remain poorly understood, which may limit the ability to reduce the overall outbreak and illness burden. This study presents an RNA-Seq evaluation of six outbreak-associated, stationary-phase S. enterica transcriptomes representing serovars Salmonella Heidelberg, Salmonella Typhimurium, and monophasic Salmonella Typhimurium (I 4,[5],12:i-). Analysis of differential gene expression (padj   1) revealed upregulation of genes associated with enhanced pathogenicity among all strains; however, Salmonella Heidelberg exhibited a transcriptional profile consistent with enhanced invasion, iron metabolism, and biofilm formation, while Salmonella Typhimurium and monophasic Salmonella Typhimurium showed transcriptional profiles consistent with stress response and survival. Transcriptome patterns were concordant with previous research evaluating phenotypic stress responses, in which Salmonella Heidelberg demonstrated prolonged survival at lethal temperatures and enhanced biofilm-forming capabilities. Overall, these findings suggest that outbreak-associated strains may employ distinct transcriptional strategies that could contribute to serovar-specific outbreak characteristics. This work supports risk assessment modeling to ultimately improve food safety interventions and reduce the public health burden of S. enterica.
authors: Patch CA, Etter AJ.

title: Sub-lethal dose exposure of cyflufenamid, flutianil, quinoxyfen, trifloxystrobin and metrafenone effects on conidial germination and gene expression in the grape powdery mildew pathogen.
abstract: Erysiphe necator is a destructive obligate plant pathogen that infects grapevines worldwide. Recently, specialized fungicides have been widely employed to control grape powdery mildew. However, for some fungicides their modes of action and the transcriptome changes caused in E. necator upon application remain unclear. In this study, a conidial germination assay was conducted on E. necator conidia to determine if cyflufenamid (FRAC U06), flutianil (FRAC U13), quinoxyfen (FRAC 13), trifloxystrobin (FRAC 11) and metrafenone (FRAC 50) inhibit conidial germination. Further a transcriptomic analyses of E. necator conidia treated with sub-lethal doses of flutianil, quinoxyfen, and trifloxystrobin were conducted at 3 and 6 h. The results showed that cyflufenamid and metrafenone did not consistently inhibit conidial germination, even at chemical concentrations as high as 100 ppm. In contrast, flutianil, trifloxystrobin and quinoxyfen effectively suppressed conidial germination. The differential gene expression analysis revealed limited overlap in differentially expressed genes compared to the control group at their respective time frames, though all fungicide applications resulted in upregulated genes involved in cellular respiration. Quinoxyfen exposure led to reduced expression of protein kinase genes, suggesting a disruption in signal transduction, while flutianil treatment showed increased expression of sugar transporters and chitinases, possibly reflecting enhanced energy demand and cell wall remodeling. Additionally, in samples treated with quinoxyfen and flutianil, there was an overexpression of major facilitator superfamily (MFS) and adenosine triphosphate-binding cassette (ABC) multidrug transporters. Overall, these findings highlight that while flutianil, trifloxystrobin and quinoxyfen effectively inhibit conidial germination, their mode of action may also trigger altered gene expression of various gene families. This knowledge is valuable for developing improved fungicide resistance management strategies for managing E. necator.
authors: Sharma N, Mahey M, Naegele RP, Miles TD.

title: The multifaceted role of SsrB in S. Typhi H58 during THP-1 macrophage infection.
abstract: S. Typhi, the causative agent of typhoid fever, remains less well understood due to its human-restricted nature compared to S. Typhimurium, which enjoys a broad host range. Herein, we investigated the acid response of S. Typhi and the role of the SPI-2 master regulator SsrB during infection of human THP-1 macrophages. Using fluorescence lifetime imaging of the pH-sensitive probe mCherryTYG, we demonstrate that the S. Typhi cytosol acidifies during infection of THP-1 macrophages, similar to S. Typhimurium. This acidification triggers a marked up-regulation of SsrB, with S. Typhi expressing significantly more SsrB molecules than S. Typhimurium, as quantified by photoactivatable localization microscopy. Despite increased SsrB expression, activation of the SsrB-dependent reporter PsifA was reduced, indicating serovar-specific differences in SsrB activity. Unexpectedly, deletion of ssrB in S. Typhi increased net intracellular replication and host cell cytotoxicity, contrasting with its essential role in S. Typhimurium. Using phosphorylation incompetent (D56A) and acid-sensing deficient (H12Q) mutants, we demonstrate that the reduction in cytotoxicity is phosphorylation-independent, whereas restriction of net intracellular replication requires both phosphorylation and acid-dependent DNA binding. The SPI-2 effector SifB partially mediates this restriction. Our findings show that SsrB contributes to two infection phenotypes with distinct genetic requirements: it limits host cytotoxicity in a manner that requires neither phosphorylation nor acid-enhanced DNA binding, and it restricts intracellular replication in a manner that requires both activities. Whether these two phenotypes are executed by separate or by shared downstream targets was not established here. These results challenge the assumption that SsrB is dispensable for S. Typhi pathogenesis and highlight serovar-specific virulence strategies.
authors: Fernandez M, Deolankar S, Singh MK, Zangoui P, Kenney LJ.

title: Upper respiratory virome signatures reflect COVID-19 severity and post-recovery shifts.
abstract: IntroductionSevere acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection profoundly affects the upper respiratory tract, yet the dynamics of the resident virome across different stages of Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) and recovery remain poorly understood.MethodsThis study profiled alterations in the virome and microbiome in 143 SARS-CoV-2-positive adults, stratified by disease severity (Non-Severe, Severe, Critical), compared with 96 RT-PCR-negative controls. Nasal and oral swabs underwent targeted viral enrichment and next-generation sequencing, followed by virome profiling.ResultsThe respiratory virome of SARS-CoV-2-positive individuals was dominated by SARS-CoV-2, with co-detected viruses such as Human Mastadenovirus C, which increased with disease severity and persisting post-recovery. Alpha diversity was highest in Non-Severe cases and declined in Severe and Critical groups, suggesting increasing disruption of the virome with disease severity. Beta diversity showed clear separation between controls and cases, and across severity levels. LEfSe identified distinct viral signatures differentiating infection status, and logistic regression of key viral taxa accurately classified Critical versus post-recovery samples (AUC = 0.91). Although the study focused on viruses, bacterial taxa including Rothia mucilaginosa and Haemophilus parahaemolyticus were also detected with severity-linked variation, highlighting viral-bacterial interactions. Longitudinal paired analysis revealed consistent post-recovery enrichment of Streptococcus-specific bacteriophages across all severity groups, suggesting restoration of Streptococcus-associated phage dynamics during convalescence.DiscussionOverall, this study reveals SARS-CoV-2-associated alterations in the respiratory virome and microbiome and highlights specific microbial taxa with potential as biomarkers for disease severity and post-infection recovery.
authors: Gosain M, Kaur M, Talukdar D, Tanwar S, Jana P, Karmakar SP, Verma J, Bakshi S, Kamboj K, Verma P, Pareek M, Raghavan S, Kshetrapal P, Bhatnagar S, Bhattacharya J, Garg PK, Wadhwa N, Das B.

title: Identification and expression analysis of antibacterial peptides from venom of the scorpion Mesobuthus martensii.
abstract: IntroductionAs one kind of important component of animal innate immune system, many antibacterial peptides (ABPs) have been characterized from scorpion venoms. However, the genomic organization and structure of the genes encoding these venom-derived peptides have been rarely reported yet. It still remains unclear whether these ABPs are essential to the immune protection of scorpion venom glands and most of them could not be confirmed at the protein level. The scorpion Mesobuthus martensii (M. martensii) is an important raw material in Chinese Traditional Medicine for the treatment of some nervous system diseases.Methods and resultsHere, we tried to identify three ABPs (BmKb1, BmKn2 and BmKbpp) from the venom of M. martensii at the genomic, transcriptional and protein levels. We have cloned the genomic sequences encoding these three ABPs by analyzing the draft genome of M. martensii decoded previously by our group. Two of these ABP genes share the same genomic organization and structure of two exons and one intron with the GT-AG splice junction located in the DNA region encoding the N-terminal part of signal peptide. To further explore molecular mechanism of scorpion venom gland immunity, a modified method was applied to establish an infection model. Using this model, two genes (BmKb1 and BmKn2) were revealed to have a significant up-regulation at the transcriptional level after challenged by Staphylococcus aureus or Escherichia coli. This is even more strengthened by the presence of several immune response elements locating at their corresponding promoter regions. Finally, we also putatively identified the existence of these three ABPs in the natural venom of M. martensii.DiscussionThus, our work gained insight into the genomic organization and diversity of ABPs from scorpion and provides evidence supporting the key defense role of venom-derived ABPs in controlling scorpion venom gland infection.
authors: Liu G, Xu J, Tan Y, Wang W, Ling H, Cao Z, Li Z.

title: The effects of co-application of organic fertilizer and limestone powder on soil organic carbon and its fractions in rubber plantations: associations with microbial necromass carbon and Fe/Al oxides.
abstract: IntroductionRubber plantations serve as significant carbon reservoirs within China's terrestrial ecosystems. To provide a scientific foundation for improving soil fertility management, this study investigated the response of soil organic carbon and its components in rubber plantations to different soil amendments.MethodsSoil samples were collected from the 0-20 cm horizon of acidic soils in second-generation rubber plantations in Jinghong City, Yunnan Province. A laboratory incubation experiment was then conducted with four treatments: an unamended control (CK), organic fertilizer alone (T1), limestone powder alone (T2), and a combined organic fertilizer and limestone powder treatment (T3). The effects of these amendments on soil organic carbon and its fractions, iron and aluminum oxides, and microbial necromass carbon were systematically evaluated.ResultsThe results demonstrated that under T3, Organic carbon (SOC) increased significantly by 12.80%, relative to CK (p p o, Alo) and complexed (Fep, Alp) iron and aluminum oxides (p ConclusionIn summary, microbial necromass carbon, iron and aluminum oxides, and pH are closely related to soil organic carbon and its components. The combined application of organic fertilizer and limestone powder is highly effective in mitigating soil acidification and increasing SOC, microbial necromass carbon, and iron and aluminum oxides, and can serve as a reference for soil fertility management and carbon pool regulation in acidified soils of tropical rubber plantations.
authors: Yang J, Geng S, Shi X, Zhang Q, Yang C.

title: Endophytic Pseudomonas pergaminensis DR1 controls anthracnose and promotes growth of medicinal orchid Pleione bulbocodioides.
abstract: Pleione species are valued ornamental plants and the source of the traditional Chinese medicine "Bingqiuzi." In this study, pathogenic fungi were isolated from diseased leaves and pseudobulbs of Pleione bulbocodioides (Franch.) Rolfe in Yunnan Province, China. Through Koch's postulates, two pathogenic strains were obtained and identified as Colletotrichum orchidophilum based on morphological characterization and multilocus phylogenetic analyses (ITS, CHS, TUB2, GAPDH, and ACT). Notably, the two strains exhibited significant differences in sporulation capacity and conidial length. An antagonistic bacterial strain, DR1, was isolated from the roots of wild P. bulbocodioides and identified as Pseudomonas pergaminensis based on phylogenetic analysis of 16S rRNA and housekeeping genes (gyrB, rpoB, and rpoD). Strain DR1 exhibited strong antagonistic activity against C. orchidophilum in dual culture assays, with an inhibition rate of up to 71.28%, and demonstrated the ability to produce siderophores and proteases. The volatile organic compounds (VOCs) produced by DR1 achieved inhibition rates of 53.04% and 48.08% against the two pathogenic strains, respectively. In greenhouse trials, 4 months after application of the DR1 suspension, the disease index was significantly reduced, with a control efficacy of 62.5% (beta regression model), and the number of newly emerged leaves increased by 198% compared with the control (P P. pergaminensis type strain, the potential mechanisms by which DR1 may promote plant growth and suppress the pathogen were preliminarily discussed. This study conducted a preliminary identification of C. orchidophilum causing anthracnose on P. bulbocodioides and demonstrated that P. pergaminensis DR1 has promising biocontrol and growth-promoting potential, providing a valuable microbial resource for the sustainable cultivation of medicinal orchids.
authors: Xie YQ, Tao KF, Li NQ, Yue J, Su J, Gao JY.
