Among 101 specimens, 63 (62.4%) yielded polymicrobial results, of which mixed-species detection of M. avium-M. intracellulare accounted for 46 (73.0%). The Multiplex assay and mNGS showed no statistically significant difference in overall accuracy in this cohort (82.2% vs. 81.2%; raw agreement 83.2%, P = 1.000). The Multiplex assay achieved 100.0% sensitivity for all four species, with specificity of 87.8% and 87.5% for M. avium and M. intracellulare, respectively, and >98% for M. abscessus and M. fortuitum; mNGS showed the converse pattern, with lower MAC sensitivity (88.5%, 92.2%) but higher MAC specificity (93.9%, 95.8%). Requiring only a single PCR reaction without sequencing or bioinformatic analysis, the Multiplex assay showed no statistically significant difference in diagnostic accuracy from mNGS in this culture-positive cohort, without requiring library preparation or sequencing, representing a promising candidate for further evaluation as a routine NTM species-identification tool.
authors: Li Z, Wang Y, Lai L, Huang Y, Li L.

title: Fluoroquinolone resistance-associated determinants in ciprofloxacin-susceptible Shigella isolates from Senegal.
abstract: IntroductionFluoroquinolones remain important therapeutic options for shigellosis, but the accumulation of chromosomal and plasmid-mediated resistance determinants threatens their continued effectiveness. Genomic data on fluoroquinolone resistance-associated determinants in Shigella from West Africa remain limited. Here, we investigated the epidemiological, phenotypic, and genomic characteristics of clinical Shigella isolates recovered through Senegal's national sentinel surveillance system between 2020 and 2021, with particular emphasis on fluoroquinolone resistance-associated genomic determinants.MethodsStool specimens collected from patients with acute diarrhea were cultured for Shigella, followed by antimicrobial susceptibility testing and whole-genome sequencing. Genomes were analyzed for antimicrobial resistance determinants, quinolone resistance-determining region (QRDR) mutations, plasmid replicons, virulence-associated genes, sequence types, and core-genome phylogenetic relationships.ResultsAmong 900 diarrheal stool specimens, 22 Shigella isolates were recovered, including 12 S. flexneri, 7 S. sonnei, and 3 S. boydii. All isolates were phenotypically susceptible to ciprofloxacin, whereas qnrS1 was detected in 9/22 isolates (40.9%) and the QRDR substitution gyrA S83L in 4/22 (18.2%). These determinants occurred in non-overlapping isolates, and no gyrA S83V or parC QRDR mutation was detected. IncFII replicons were identified in all isolates, while additional replicons showed heterogeneous distributions across species and sequence types. The fluoroquinolone resistance-associated determinants were distributed across distinct genetic backgrounds rather than being restricted to a single lineage.ConclusionThese findings demonstrate that phenotypic susceptibility to ciprofloxacin may coexist with fluoroquinolone resistance-associated genomic determinants in clinical Shigella isolates. Integrating WGS with routine antimicrobial susceptibility testing may strengthen surveillance of emerging fluoroquinolone resistance in Shigella in Senegal and West Africa.
authors: Lo CI, Niang EA, Sadio O, Sankhe S, Guèye AB, Kane M, Ndiaye MO, Mbanne M, Yelkouni J, Ndongo S, Ly FP, Wane AA, Fall C, Diagne MM, Dieye Y.

title: Whole-genome sequence analysis of a clinical hypervirulent Klebsiella variicola strain recovered from a hospital in Ningxia, China.
abstract: Klebsiella variicola (KV) infections are being increasingly reported across diverse geographic regions and linked to high mortality. KV displays substantial geographical heterogeneity in antimicrobial resistance profiles, virulence phenotypes, and genetic backgrounds; genetic variants further promote its adaptability to varied environments. In this study, we isolated a strain designated KV7 from the sputum sample of an ICU patient at a tertiary hospital in Ningxia, China, with species confirmation achieved via whole-genome sequencing. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed using the VITEK 2 Compact automated microbial system. String test, immune cell phagocytosis assay, serum resistance assay, and mouse infection model were applied to evaluate virulence phenotypes. Genomic characterization revealed that KV7 belongs to ST8223 with an unassigned KL type and exhibits hypervirulence while remaining susceptible to tested antibiotics. Its hypervirulence is associated with the virulence plasmid pKV7-vir, which carries numerous virulence factor genes. Multiple mobile genetic elements were also detected on pKV7-vir. Moreover, comparative genomic analysis of KV isolates from China and other countries was performed, laying a theoretical foundation for regional surveillance of this pathogen.
authors: Kang Y, Zhang Z, Ma S, Tao W, Wang P.

title: Recurrent gene conversions and subcluster-specific variants are associated with Mycobacterium tuberculosis adaptation to intensive host pressure: a comparative genomic study.
abstract: BackgroundLong-read sequencing has revealed complex variations, such as gene conversions in immunologically critical PE/PPE gene families, yet their role in Mycobacterium tuberculosis host adaptation remains unclear.MethodsWe performed a comparative genomic analysis across a gradient of host-imposed selective pressure: chronic within-host infection, latent household transmission, and a 21-year clonal outbreak in Bern, Switzerland.ResultsWe observed a constrained accumulation of mutational events across distinct epidemiological settings, with rates ranging from 0.36 to 0.81 events per genome per year. Under minimal host-imposed selection, the pathogen accumulated only small-scale variants (i.e., SNPs and indels). During the outbreak, however, the genetic diversity landscape shifted toward larger-scale variants, including recurrent gene conversions and structural variations. Notably, an early PPE19-to-PPE18 conversion emerged in the ancestral strain and was maintained across the entire lineage. In contrast, 86% of variants were transient singletons, with only a small proportion persisting under selection.ConclusionThese findings suggest a framework in which M. tuberculosis maintains genomic stability through purifying selection, while retaining the capacity to generate adaptive diversity through large-scale genetic rearrangements in immunologically relevant genomic features under intensified host pressure.
authors: Lin T, Chen K, Chen Z, Jin Y, Chen W.

title: Editorial: Innovation fermentation empowers the new development of future functional foods.
authors: Cakmak H, García-Cayuela T, Li S, Wei J.

title: Clinical validation of a novel multiplex real-time PCR for diagnosing community-acquired pneumonia in the emergency department: a promising diagnostic tool for Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
abstract: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is a global public health burden with high morbidity, but timely diagnosis is hindered by limitations of conventional methods. We validated a novel multiplex real-time PCR (mRT-PCR) for CAP diagnosis in the emergency department, focusing on Mycoplasma pneumoniae (M. pneumoniae). A retrospective cohort of 371 CAP patients (2019-2021) from the Chinese PLA General Hospital was enrolled. The panel targeted 85 pathogens (40 bacteria, 18 viruses, 17 fungi, 10 other) plus 8 resistance genes, with a turnaround time (TAT) under 4 h and a cost of approximately US$100 per test. mRT-PCR showed performance comparable to mNGS for common pathogens (concordance >69% for bacteria/fungi) and high concordance with the final clinical diagnosis. Notably, it detected M. pneumoniae in 36.7% (136/371) of cases, outperforming conventional methods by identifying 204 exclusive positives (55.0% of cohort), with M. pneumoniae (40%) and viruses (30%) predominating. Polymicrobial infections occurred in 36.1% of cases; M. pneumoniae co-infections (38 cases) showed elevated neutrophils and reduced lymphocytes vs. single infections. An independent reference standard analysis excluding both index tests showed that 24.1% (210/873) of calls were independently corroborated - high for influenza, SARS-CoV-2 and M. pneumoniae, lower for S. pneumoniae, consistent with the limited sensitivity of sputum culture. Unlike conventional syndromic panels such as FilmArray, which profile fewer targets without concurrent resistance-gene detection, this mRT-PCR combines broad coverage with rapid TAT and low cost, making it promising for timely CAP diagnosis, particularly in resource-limited settings and for targeted therapy.
authors: Yang L, Guo C, Zhao Q, Yang J, Zhang H, Zhai Y, Ma Y.

title: SLA1 governs azole resistance in Candidozyma auris via mitochondrial ROS-driven efflux pump expression.
abstract: IntroductionCandidozyma auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant fungal pathogen, and widespread fluconazole (FLC) resistance severely limits clinical treatment options. Overexpression of the efflux transporter CDR1 represents a major driver of azole resistance; however, how oxidative stress modulates this process remains poorly understood. This study aimed to identify novel regulators that connect oxidative stress adaptation with azole resistance in C. auris.MethodsWe constructed SLA1 deletion mutants of C. auris. SLA1 encodes a conserved regulator of cytoskeletal organization and membrane trafficking. We evaluated mitochondrial homeostasis, mtROS accumulation, and CDR1 expression. Pharmacological mitochondrial perturbation was used to disentangle the individual effects of ROS accumulation and mitochondrial dysfunction on FLC resistance. We further assessed cell envelope integrity, in vivo virulence, and the transcriptional correlation between SLA1 and CDR1 using clinical isolates.ResultsSLA1 deletion triggered mitochondrial dysfunction, increased mtROS accumulation, upregulated CDR1, and enhanced azole resistance. Pharmacological disruption of mitochondria further raised ROS levels yet suppressed CDR1, depleted ATP, accumulated NADH, and abolished FLC resistance. This indicates that ROS elevation alone cannot sustain resistance under severe mitochondrial impairment. SLA1 knockout compromised cell envelope integrity and attenuated in vivo virulence, revealing a fitness trade-off during antifungal adaptation. Clinical isolates exhibited a significant inverse correlation between SLA1 and CDR1 transcript levels.DiscussionThis study identifies SLA1 as a previously uncharacterized modulator of oxidative stress adaptation and azole susceptibility in C. auris. Mitochondrial functional status governs the relationship between oxidative stress and azole resistance. The SLA1-dependent axis promotes antifungal resistance at the expense of reduced virulence. These findings reveal a new mechanism of drug adaptation in C. auris and point to a potential target for combating multidrug-resistant C. auris.
authors: Suo C, Zhang W, Li Y, Li C, Cui Y, Xiao Y, Lei J, Gao Y, Zhang H.

title: Sequence-activity mapping and model-guided engineering of the phenol-responsive DmpR-Po σ<sup>54</sup> promoter.
abstract: Promoters are core cis-regulatory elements that determine gene expression levels and dynamic responses, and their quantitative engineering directly dictates the performance of synthetic biological systems such as whole-cell biosensors. However, the transcriptional output of complex inducible systems, exemplified by σ54-dependent promoters, relies on long-range coordination among distal bacterial enhancer-binding proteins, DNA architectural proteins, and RNA polymerase. The combined effects of multiple regulatory regions on promoter output remain poorly understood, which limits the cross-background transfer of local sequence rules and hinders the accurate prediction and rational design of promoter activity. The phenol-responsive DmpR-Po promoter serves as both a classical model for investigating σ54-dependent regulation and a high-value sensing element for environmental pollutant detection and high-throughput enzyme activity screening. Resolving sequence-activity relationships across its complete regulatory region therefore holds both mechanistic and practical significance. To overcome the barriers to rational engineering of complex promoters, we established a modular design-measure-model-guide-validate framework targeting the full DmpR-Po regulatory region. A library of 17,500 designed promoter sequences was constructed to systematically perturb the upstream activating sequence (UAS), the IHF2 region, combined UAS-IHF2 mutational backgrounds, and downstream regulatory architecture. Fluorescence-activated cell sorting coupled with sequencing yielded a high-quality sequence-activity map covering 11,940 variants. At the regional level, identical UAS and IHF2 haplotypes generally preserved their relative activity rankings across single-region and joint-variant backgrounds, and the main effects estimated independently for UAS and IHF2 could approximately predict the activity of combined variants. At the nucleotide level, however, the effects of individual substitutions were strongly constrained by the overall DNA architecture and full-sequence context. A deep learning model trained on the complete regulatory sequence captured these context-dependent relationships, achieved robust predictive performance on held-out sequences and a separately transformed and processed Batch 2 derived from the same preconstructed plasmid-library pool, and enabled model-guided prioritization of targeted local variants. Single-clone validation further showed that model-guided edits produced variable experimental outcomes, supporting candidate prioritization while indicating that individual engineering predictions require experimental validation. Collectively, this study characterizes the transferability and context-dependent constraints of regional sequence effects and establishes a data-driven framework for quantitative prediction and model-guided engineering of complex σ54-dependent promoters.
authors: Xu Y, Song M, Xing W, Han J, Wu J, Cheng Y, Liu J, Wang L, Zeng J, Zhao Y, Guo J, Cai S.

title: Butyrate-associated antiproliferative and antitumor effects of Eubacterium limosum KGMB01548 in colorectal cancer.
abstract: IntroductionRecent work has shown that Eubacterium limosum suppresses colorectal cancer (CRC), but the contribution and cellular actions of its short-chain fatty acids remain incompletely defined.MethodsWe characterized E. limosum KGMB01548, a human gut isolate, and examined the antitumor activity of its cell-free culture supernatant (ElCFS).ResultsElCFS preferentially inhibited the proliferation of human HCT116 and murine CT26 CRC cells while having little effect on non-malignant CCD 841 CoN colonic cells. The activity persisted after heat and enzymatic treatments, and pH-dependent liquid-liquid extraction indicated that a small organic acid was a major bioactive component. High-performance liquid chromatography detected 13.77 mM butyrate and 23.33 mM acetate in ElCFS. At approximately the concentration delivered by 10% ElCFS, sodium butyrate (NaB; 1.3 mM) produced comparable antiproliferative activity, whereas sodium acetate did not, supporting butyrate as a major candidate contributor to ElCFS activity. ElCFS and approximately concentration-matched NaB increased histone H3 acetylation, consistent with histone deacetylase inhibition, and induced apoptosis, as evidenced by PARP and caspase-3 cleavage and p53 phosphorylation. Their antiproliferative effects were markedly attenuated under glucose-depleted conditions. In a CT26 syngeneic tumor model, peritumoral administration of ElCFS reduced tumor growth, indicating that secreted E. limosum metabolites retained local antitumor activity outside the intestinal route. Oral pre-administration of live E. limosum also reduced subsequent tumor burden. Furthermore, 16S rRNA gene profiling suggested modest changes in several putative short-chain-fatty-acid-producing taxa and in PICRUSt2-predicted butyrate-biosynthesis potential, without a major change in alpha diversity.DiscussionTogether, these findings link E. limosum KGMB01548 to butyrate-associated histone acetylation, apoptosis, glucose-sensitive antiproliferative activity, and tumor suppression, supporting further investigation of this gut commensal and its secreted metabolites as microbiome-derived approaches for CRC control.
authors: Yu SY, Bak JE, Oh BS, Ryu SW, Park H, Yu DJ, Lee J, Kim JS, Lee JH.

title: Metabolic adaptation of a methanogen to a ferruginous environment associated with intracellular Fe- and S-rich nanoparticles.
abstract: Across the great oxidation event (GOE) period, the oceans experienced a major transition from ferruginous (Fe2+-rich) to localized euxinic (HS--rich) conditions. In ferruginous oceans, sulfur is mostly sequestered into metastable aqueous Fe-S clusters (FeSaq) and sulfide minerals like mackinawite (FeSMack). Similarly, in euxinic oceans, iron is sequestered in such clusters and/or sulfide minerals. However, it is unclear how ancient methanogens, with high demands for sulfur and iron, adapted to this critical transition. We hypothesize that FeSaq and FeSMack could serve as sources of sulfur and iron to support cellular growth and methanogenesis. A model ancient methanogen Methanococcus maripaludis S2 (MmS2) was inoculated in a growth medium under either Fe2+-rich or HS--rich condition. Biological utilization of FeSMack was imaged using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and nanoscale secondary ion mass spectrometry (NanoSIMS). Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses were performed to characterize the cellular and biochemical responses of MmS2 under contrasting Fe-S conditions. The results revealed that MmS2 maintained a consistent methanogenic activity and growth irrespective of different Fe-S conditions. Under high-Fe2+ but limited HS- conditions, Fe- and S-rich particles accumulated inside cells, indicating utilization of FeSaq and/or FeSMack as sulfur sources. Intracellular Fe- and S-rich particles accumulation was accompanied by distinct transcriptomic and proteomic responses involving cellular metabolism and energy conservation. These findings provide new insights into the adaptive mechanisms of methanogens in response to evolving iron and sulfur environments during early earth, shedding light on the co-evolution of life and environment over geological history.
authors: Zhang Y, Zhang D, Sheng Y, Chen H, Li G, Dong H.

title: Targeted CPSF6 recoding reveals global fitness advantages of SPAD integration targeting and cell type-specific roles for capsid binding in HIV-1 DNA synthesis and nuclear import.
abstract: As part of the CFIm complex, CPSF6 regulates cellular gene expression via alternative polyadenylation. CPSF6 binds primate lentiviral capsids and has been implicated in HIV-1 reverse transcription, nuclear import, and integration targeting. However, interpretations of the role(s) of CPSF6 during HIV-1 replication are complicated by the transcriptional changes that occur when the protein is depleted from cells. To disentangle the role of CPSF6 in HIV-1 replication from alternative polyadenylation, we selectively recoded its capsid-binding phenylalanine-glycine motif to alanine-alanine in CD4-positive Jurkat T cells, CEM12D7 T cells, and THP-1 myeloid/macrophage cells using CRISPR/Cas9-based homology-directed repair. While large variations in single-round HIV-1 infection were observed among isolated T cell clones, en masse comparisons of recoded T cells to cloned control T cells failed to reveal any significant differences in infection levels. Consistent with an overall fitness advantage provided by DNA integration in speckle-associated domains, which was ablated by recoding across cell types, HIV-1 replicated more robustly in control T cell populations. Single-round infection, in addition to spreading replication, was reduced in recoded myeloid/macrophage cells, which correlated with reductions in reverse transcription, and more robust blocks to HIV-1 nuclear import. Recoded monocytes/macrophages, however, did not reveal any evidence for enhanced type I interferon production or sensing of HIV-1 nucleic acids. Altogether, we define endogenously recoded cell lines to uncouple capsid binding from CPSF6's role in RNA metabolism, which highlights a global fitness advantage of targeted DNA integration and cell type-specific roles for CPSF6 in HIV-1 reverse transcription, nuclear import, and virus replication proficiency.IMPORTANCEHIV-1 usurps cellular factors to effectively replicate and avoid innate immune sensing. HIV-1 capsid binds CPSF6, but the consequences of this virus-host interaction on HIV-1 biology are necessarily complicated by the cellular role of CPSF6 in pre-RNA processing. By endogenously recoding CPSF6 to selectively disrupt capsid binding while preserving its RNA-processing activity, we demonstrate in two different T cell lines that CPSF6-mediated targeting of HIV-1 DNA integration into nuclear speckle-associated domains correlates with optimal viral replication. Recoded THP-1 myeloid/macrophage cells revealed additional single-round and multi-round infection defects, which correlated with reductions in reverse transcription and HIV-1 nuclear import. These defects, however, did not correlate with enhanced type I interferon production or detection of HIV-1 nucleic acids by known innate immune sensors. Our work clarifies diverse roles for the capsid-CPSF6 interaction in HIV-1 infection of T lymphocytic versus myeloid cell lines and provides novel cell reagents for future research studies.
authors: Jang S, Radhakrishnan R, Greenwood J, Singh PK, Bedwell GJ, Robles-Sikisaka R, Routh AL, Engelman AN.

title: A validated sequence difference ratio framework distinguishes intrahost evolution from superinfection in Helicobacter pylori mixed infections.
abstract: BackgroundThe inability to quantitatively distinguish endogenous within-host evolution (mutation, homologous recombination, and heterologous recombination) from superinfection as the origin of intrahost Helicobacter pylori genetic diversity remains a critical bottleneck constraining precision therapeutics.MethodsWe developed a novel gene-based sequence difference ratio (SDR) framework utilizing single-nucleotide polymorphism counts and percentile-derived regional reference ranges to quantitatively classify the origins of mixed infections, including homologous and heterologous recombination (interspecies horizontal gene transfer). A dual-hospital cohort (34 patients, 114 flagellar isolates; 28 patients, 152 housekeeping isolates) was enrolled after excluding those with recent antibiotic or acid-suppressant exposure. Isolates were recovered using a patented single-colony culture system (US 18/278,425; EP 21927415.6) to eliminate conventional streaking bias. The model was validated using phylogenetic analysis, hierarchical clustering, and geographical divergence assessment.ResultsThe SDR framework achieved the first dedicated quantitative classification of five distinct H. pylori mixed infection mechanisms: mutation, homologous recombination, heterologous recombination, combined mutation-homologous recombination, and superinfection. Flagellar gene profiling identified a 51.5% mixed infection rate (17/33), with mutations as the dominant pattern (82.4%, 14/17); recombination involved the conserved flagellar genes flgE and flaA. Housekeeping gene analysis yielded a 14.8% superinfection rate (4/27), including the first documented triple-strain case; recombination involved the conserved housekeeping genes atpA and yphC. Strain H42 exhibited heterologous recombination in trpC (SDR 23.89-25.66%), providing the first nucleotide-resolution evidence of cross-species genetic exchange. Convergent mutations in fliD and mutY indicated niche-specific selective pressure. SDR thresholds were strongly correlated with evolutionary distance.ConclusionWe report the first validated quantitative framework for distinguishing intrahost microbial evolution (mutation, homologous recombination, and heterologous recombination) from superinfection in H. pylori. These findings challenge the long-standing single-strain therapeutic paradigm, and this scalable approach lays a universal foundation for the precise management of infectious diseases.
authors: Gu H, Shi Z, Chen W, Ye W, Zhang C, Li A.

title: Metabolic gene analysis of newly isolated Pseudochrobactrum sp. BJQ-1 and BJQ-2 reveals global dissemination of the chlorothalonil hydrolytic dehalogenase chd gene.
abstract: Chlorothalonil (TPN; 2,4,5,6-tetrachloroisophthalonitrile) is a globally used, persistent chlorinated fungicide. Its bacterial detoxification is driven mainly by the hydrolytic dehalogenase Chd. Although the chd gene and its association with mobile genetic elements have been reported, the extent to which identical chd modules have spread across distinct hosts on a global scale remains unclear. Here we isolated two chlorothalonil-degrading strains, BJQ-1 and BJQ-2, from geographically distinct sites. Both were identified as Pseudochrobactrum spp. by 16S rRNA phylogeny. Shotgun cloning and sequence comparison revealed that both strains harbor a chd ORF essentially identical (≥99.7% nucleotide identity) to those of Pseudomonas sp. CTN series, Paracoccus sp. XF-3 and Ochrobactrum lupini TP-D1. The same chd gene is embedded in three distinct mobile-element configurations, an IS21-like composite transposon in CTN series, an IS6-family transposase TnpA plus Pin recombinase in BJQ-1, and a λ Rac-like invertase in BJQ-2, a pattern incompatible with vertical inheritance. Upstream spacer analysis showed that a conserved IS21-like fusion promoter, composed of an IRR-borne -35 box fused to the native -10 element of chd gene, and the 179-bp istB-chd intergenic spacer (100% identical between the BJQ isolates and the CTN series) are preserved. Mining of the Prokaryotic Genome dataset retrieved chd-like sequences from diverse prokaryotic genomes spanning soil, aquatic and plant-associated habitats, confirming a broad phylogeography of the cassette. The recovery of an identical, transposon-associated chd module from two distantly sampled Pseudochrobactrum strains, together with its global genomic distribution, indicates that the chd detoxification cassette has disseminated worldwide, providing a general mechanism for the rapid recruitment of TPN biodegradation capacity in microbial communities.
authors: Ke Z, Wu Q, Gao M, Wang Q, Wang L, Yuan C.

title: Responses of cut-lily quality and rhizosphere soil microecology to different microbial inoculants.
abstract: Continuous cropping obstacles and soil-borne diseases have long constrained the development of the cut lily industry, and microbial inoculants have become an important tool for achieving green production. To screen for efficient inoculants suitable for cut lily and to reveal the mechanisms of action, this study used the dominant cultivar 'Siberia' (Lilium 'Siberia') as material and conducted a field experiment under solar greenhouse conditions in Lingyuan, Liaoning Province, using three commercial microbial inoculants: Treatment A (Shentai Trichoderma combination, containing Trichoderma harzianum and its metabolites), Treatment B (Moon composite inoculant, containing Trichoderma, Purpureocillium lilacinum, Bacillus subtilis, etc.), and Treatment C (Fengde composite inoculant, mainly Bacillus subtilis). The study systematically measured lily growth and commercial traits, soil physicochemical properties, and rhizosphere microbial community structure, and analyzed the linkage mechanism of "inoculant-soil physicochemical properties-rhizosphere microbial community-comprehensive lily quality." The results showed that Treatment A (Shentai Trichoderma combination) had the best comprehensive effect, significantly increasing plant height, stem diameter, and green leaf rate, and reducing leaf yellowing and abscission index. At the same time, it significantly increased soil total nitrogen, total phosphorus, available nitrogen, and organic matter content, and optimized the rhizosphere microecological environment. Further microbial community analysis indicated that Treatment A specifically enriched putatively beneficial taxa such as Pseudomonas and Streptomyces, and functional fungi such as Trichoderma and Mucor, while reducing the relative abundance of potentially pathogenic taxa such as Fusarium and Rhizoctonia. It also increased the modularity and proportion of positive correlations in the bacterial-fungal co-occurrence network, forming a stable growth-promoting and disease-resistant functional module. This study clarifies the core effects of the Trichoderma-based inoculant on lily growth, soil improvement, and rhizosphere microecological regulation, suggests a mechanism by which it synergistically improves cut lily quality and stress resistance through optimizing soil nutrients and reshaping microbial community structure, identifies a promising inoculant formulation with potential for green lily production, and provides a theoretical basis and technical support for the sustainable development of the cut lily industry.
authors: Yang Y, Zhou L, Zhang R, Hu X, Wang W, Li X, Bai Y, Irfan M, Chen Y, Chen L.

title: Volatile organic compounds from Streptomyces rochei TRM68247: fumigant biocontrol against postharvest diseases of Korla fragrant pear and identification of active antifungal components.
abstract: BackgroundLong-term application of synthetic fungicides leads to severe residue risks and pathogen drug resistance during postharvest storage of Korla fragrant pear (Pyrus sinkiangensis), making it urgent to develop low-residue gaseous biopreservation agents. This study investigated the fumigant biocontrol capacity of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) produced by desert-derived Streptomyces rochei TRM68247 against two dominant postharvest pathogens, Valsa pyri and Alternaria gaisen.MethodsWhole-genome sequencing was performed to identify biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) associated with volatile secondary metabolism. Volatile compounds were profiled by GC-MS, and core bioactive substances were screened and validated by in vitro dual-plate assays. Fumigation efficacy was further evaluated on pear twigs and on wounded, inoculated fruits under simulated storage conditions, with commercial eugenol included as a positive control.ResultsStrain TRM68247 harboured abundant BGCs supporting stable production of antifungal volatiles under storage conditions. GC-MS identified 44 volatile components, among which 2-ethyl-1-hexanol and 3,5-di-tert-butylphenol were screened as core bioactive substances. In vitro dual-plate tests showed that 2-ethyl-1-hexanol exerted broad and strong inhibitory activity against both fungi. Fumigation with VOCs from TRM68247 significantly retarded lesion expansion and blocked deep pulp infection, and the control efficacy against fruit black spot was comparable to that of commercial eugenol.ConclusionsVOCs from S. rochei TRM68247 are promising candidate fumigants for reducing postharvest rot loss of Korla fragrant pear, and the present work supplies two natural volatile antifungal compounds for the development of green fruit-preservation technology.
authors: Chen YH, Liu CW, Zhao JD, Wang TC, Zhang YX, Huang W, Luo X.

title: Effects of typical emerging pollutants on biological treatment systems: processes, mechanisms, and recovery strategies.
abstract: With the rapid advancement of industrialization and urbanization, human activities have released large quantities of persistent emerging contaminants into the environment. Among these, nanomaterials, microplastics, and perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances have emerged as research hotspots due to their widespread applications and increasingly significant environmental risks. These contaminants exhibit strong environmental persistence in aquatic environments and significantly affect the stability and treatment efficiency of conventional biological treatment systems, posing new challenges to the normal operation and pollutant removal. This article reviews the migration and transformation behavior of these emerging contaminants in biological treatment systems, the processes and mechanisms underlying their impacts on microbial communities and metabolic activities, as well as recovery strategies. By summarizing existing research results, this article aims to provide a scientific basis and technical support for the process optimization and the development of pollutant reduction technologies in wastewater treatment systems.
authors: Ren X, Song A, Shang D, Li H.

title: Marked variation in the bacterial microbiota of commercially produced Greek kefir products revealed by full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing.
abstract: Kefir is a fermented dairy beverage characterized by a complex microbial community that contributes to its technological and sensory properties and has been associated in previous studies with potential health-related effects. While the microbiota of kefir grains has been extensively studied, information regarding the bacterial communities of commercially produced Greek kefir remains limited. The aim of the present study was to characterize the bacterial community composition of commercially produced kefir products collected from different regions of Greece using full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing and to assess variation among the analyzed commercial product groups. A total of 32 kefir samples were collected from eight regions of Greece: Koufalia, Kilkis, Drama, Thrace, Katerini, Larissa, Volos, and Attica. Genomic DNA was extracted and subjected to Oxford Nanopore full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Taxonomic profiling was performed following quality filtering and bioinformatic analysis. The bacterial communities were predominantly composed of members of the phylum Bacillota, representing more than 92% of the total bacterial relative abundance in all samples. At the species level, Streptococcus thermophilus (45.89%) and Lactococcus cremoris (37.72%) were identified as the dominant shared taxa. Bray-Curtis dissimilarities and PERMANOVA supported differentiation among the commercial product groups (pseudo-F = 5.630, R 2 = 0.622, and permutation p = 0.001). Kefir samples from Koufalia were strongly dominated by L. cremoris (88.59%), whereas samples from Attica, Thrace, and Kilkis showed a predominance of S. thermophilus. In contrast, Katerini showed a compositionally heterogeneous bacterial profile with comparatively low dominance of the two core taxa. It also presented relatively higher abundances of Leuconostoc spp., Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus, Lactobacillus delbrueckii, and Bifidobacterium animalis. These findings demonstrate that commercially produced Greek kefir products share dominant bacterial taxa while exhibiting marked variation among commercial product groups. The observed variation among commercial product groups may be associated with product- and manufacturer-related factors, although the relative contribution of these factors cannot be determined from the present dataset.
authors: Vougiouklaki D, Lamprou P, Mouhtouris N, Fonazaki M, Batrinou A, Konteles SJ, Polanska M, Van Impe JFM, Tsakali E, Houhoula D.

title: Carbapenemase-producing rare Enterobacterales in hospital food: a Latin American one health blind spot.
abstract: IntroductionCarbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (CPE) are a global public health concern. These bacteria are very common in human infections, but reports of their presence in the food chain are increasing and could represent alternative routes for colonization and infection. Hence, we conducted a surveillance study to investigate CPE in food distributed to patients at a tertiary hospital in Brazil.MethodsThe samples were collected right before distribution and screened for β-lactam-resistant Enterobacterales. Isolates that exhibited carbapenem resistance were screened for NDM, IMP, VIM, OXA-48-like, and KPC carbapenemase genes by multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and those identified as CPE underwent whole-genome sequencing.ResultsAccordingly, we report the detection of a KPC-2-producing Superficieibacter electus, a KPC- 2-producing Pseudocitrobacter faecalis, and two NDM-1-producing Leclercia adecarboxylata isolated from four distinct food samples. The carbapenemase genes were harbored by plasmids, and the genomic traits indicate their potential to cause hard-to-treat human infections or serve as a reservoir of important antimicrobial resistance genes. Moreover, despite the 3-month time span between collections, the two L. adecarboxylata isolates exhibited high similarity, suggesting horizontal transmission of CPE associated with the hospital food service.DiscussionThus, the emergence of rare Enterobacterales raises concerns about the potential for silently spreading, hard-to-treat infections.
authors: de Godoy BLC, Rosa G, Nogueira MCL, Lincopan N, Casella T.

title: One Health genomic surveillance of Klebsiella pneumoniae in Belgium demonstrates large genomic diversity, presence of ESBLs and carbapenemases and circulation of clones across sectors.
abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae is an important reservoir and disseminator of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes. Multidrug-resistant lineages, particularly extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing and carbapenem-resistant strains, represent an important public health threat. This study characterized antimicrobial resistance and genomic diversity of K. pneumoniae across One Health compartments in Belgium and investigated genomic relatedness within and across sectors. Between 2019 and 2022, 888 presumptive K. pneumoniae isolates were collected from diseased animals (n = 311), wastewater (n = 299), the food chain (n = 178), and human clinical samples (n = 100). Following selection based on isolation source and AMR characteristics, 286 WGS-confirmed K. pneumoniae isolates were characterized for AMR and virulence determinants, plasmid replicons, population structure, and phylogenomic relatedness. Phenotypic and genotypic resistance showed high concordance for third-generation cephalosporins (93.4%) and carbapenems (89.2%). Carbapenemase genes encoding KPC, NDM, OXA-48-like, and VIM enzymes were detected in 67 isolates from humans (n = 56) and wastewater (n = 11), but not in food-chain or diseased-animal isolates. Population structure was highly diverse, with ST307, ST15, ST147, and ST11 representing the most frequently detected high-risk lineages. Thirteen novel STs were identified in 18 K. pneumoniae isolates. Seventeen genomic clusters were identified, including 13 within-sector and four cross-sector clusters. Notably, an ST147 cluster comprising two poultry-meat isolates and a human clinical isolate showed no SNP differences, indicating very close genomic relatedness across sectors. Overall, our findings demonstrate a genetically diverse K. pneumoniae population alongside the circulation of clinically relevant high-risk lineages across One Health compartments and support integrated genomic surveillance to better understand their dissemination.
authors: Debergh H, Bogaerts B, Van Damme I, Boland C, Vanneste K, van Hoorde K, Bogaerts P, Huang TD, Saulmont M, Botteldoorn N, Saegerman C, Garcia-Graells C.

title: Crosstalk between gut microbiota-associated metabolites and adaptive immunity in cholecystitis: a conceptual mechanistic framework and potential therapeutic implications.
abstract: The pathogenesis of cholecystitis involves the complex interplay of bile stasis, microbial dysbiosis, metabolic disturbances, and immune responses. Gut microbiota-associated metabolites can modulate adaptive immune components, including T helper 17 (Th17) cells, regulatory T (Treg) cells, CD8+ T cells, and B cells, through receptor-mediated signaling, immunometabolic reprogramming, and epigenetic regulation. Conversely, T cell-mediated immune selection and B cell-IgA responses can reshape microbial community structure and metabolic activity, thereby establishing a bidirectional microbiota-immune regulatory network. The immunological effects of metabolic signals, including secondary bile acids, short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan-related metabolites, polyamines, and lactate, are highly context dependent and may vary according to metabolite concentration, target cell type, receptor engagement, and the local tissue microenvironment. Importantly, direct mechanistic evidence specific to cholecystitis remains limited. Most of the mechanistic pathways discussed in this review are derived from studies of cholelithiasis, cholestasis, and other hepatobiliary or inflammatory disorders; therefore, several proposed links between microbial metabolism and adaptive immunity should currently be regarded as conceptual extrapolations rather than established mechanisms in cholecystitis. Focusing on this bidirectional crosstalk, we discuss its potential roles across distinct pathological settings, including gallstone-associated disease, acute inflammation, and chronic inflammation with tissue remodeling. We further summarize candidate therapeutic strategies targeting microbial ecology, bile acid metabolism, specific metabolic pathways, and adaptive immune responses. This conceptual framework may provide a basis for future mechanistic studies and facilitate the development of more precise therapeutic approaches for cholecystitis.
authors: Wang X, Zhang T, Ren Z, Ju B.

title: Characterization of a conjugative IncA plasmid co-harbouring bla NDM-5 and bla VIM-1 in a KPC-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae clinical isolate K27.
abstract: ObjectivesMultiple-carbapenemase-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae has emerged as a critical threat to global health due to limited treatment options and high mortality. This study aimed to characterize the genomic features of a triple-carbapenemase-producing K. pneumoniae clinical isolate.MethodsA carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae (CRKP) strain K27 was collected from a patient in a tertiary hospital in January 2025. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing, carbapenemase detection, S1 nuclease pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (S1-PFGE), conjugation experiments, and plasmid fitness cost assays were performed. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of strain K27 was carried out on Illumina and PacBio platforms, bioinformatic analyses were performed using tools such as PlasmidFinder, ResFinder and ISfinder to characterize plasmid architecture, including replicon typing, resistance gene profiling, and mobile genetic element identification.ResultsStrain K27 was an extensively drug-resistant ST11 K. pneumoniae producing three carbapenemases (NDM, KPC and VIM). Both S1-PFGE and WGS revealed that strain K27 carried four plasmids. The bla KPC-2 gene was located on an IncFIIpHN7A8:IncR hybrid plasmid (assigned as pK27-KPC2) and carried by a truncated transposon Tn6296, while the bla NDM-5 and bla VIM-1 genes were co-harboured on a single IncA plasmid (assigned as pK27-NDM5/VIM1), where they were carried by a truncated transposon Tn125 and integron In916, respectively. The two corresponding genetic elements were separated by ISCR1, and this arrangement was highly similar to that of plasmid p24A20009_B_NDM. Conjugation experiments demonstrated that the plasmid pK27-NDM5/VIM1 was transferable at a frequency of (4.5 ± 1.2) × 10-2, and the resulting transconjugant was designated as K27-C. Independent sample t-tests further revealed significant differences between the transconjugant K27-C and the Escherichia coli J53AziR groups, both in the area under the curve (t = 3.63, p = 0.002) and in the maximum optical density (t = 2.57, p = 0.02).ConclusionThe finding of two different class B metallo-carbapenemase genes co-harboured on a single conjugative IncA plasmid in a KPC-producing ST11 K. pneumoniae clinical isolate is alarming. This co-production of three distinct carbapenemases in a single strain could pose considerable challenges for the selection of clinical anti-infective therapies. Furthermore, the isolate may pose a high risk of subsequent clonal dissemination and/or horizontal gene transfer, necessitating ongoing epidemiological surveillance.
authors: Liu Z, Dong D, Jia N, Li Y, Gao Y, Zhu Y.

title: An acetophenone carboxylase homolog from Rhodococcus aetherivorans initiates acetone rather than acetophenone catabolism.
abstract: Ketones such as acetone and acetophenone are chemically inert and must be activated prior to microbial degradation. In aerobic bacteria such as Rhodococcus, ketone activation is accomplished either by oxygenation or carboxylation reactions. Acetone and acetophenone carboxylases are homologous enzymes, but have different subunit compositions. While acetone carboxylases form heterohexameric complexes out of three distinct subunits, the acetophenone carboxylase core complex contains an additional duplicate of one of these subunits, resulting in a heterooctamer of four different subunits. Moreover, acetophenone carboxylase comprises a detachable fifth subunit ε, which is not present in acetone carboxylases. Here, we show that an apparent acetophenone carboxylase from Rhodococcus aetherivorans initiates acetone rather than acetophenone catabolism. The same strain of R. aetherivorans also degrades acetophenone, but as revealed by proteomics and enzyme activity measurements, this substrate is activated by an oxygenation reaction. In contrast to the canonical enzyme variant, which is restricted to acetone and butanone, the acetone carboxylase from R. aetherivorans apparently also accepts more aliphatic ketones with longer chain length. Furthermore, gene deletion studies confirmed the indispensability of the unique subunit ε for enzyme activity. In conclusion, we identified a novel type of acetone carboxylase with acetophenone carboxylase-like subunit composition and extended substrate spectrum. Phylogenetic analyses suggest that heterodecameric acetone carboxylases are particularly widespread across Actinomycetota and Pseudomonadota.
authors: Müller K, Kahnt J, Paczia N, Heider J.

title: Elevated temperature exacerbates red sore disease caused by Vibrio vulnificus in American eels (Anguilla rostrata).
abstract: The marine pathogenic bacterium Vibrio vulnificus is linked to epizootics of a dermal ulcerative disease, causing high mortality in European and Japanese eels. American eels (Anguilla rostrata) experience a similar condition, commonly referred to as red sore disease (RSD). Field studies indicate that V. vulnificus infections highly correlate with RSD in American eels, but causation remains un-established. In this study, clinically healthy American eels were intraperitoneally injected with V. vulnificus and then held for 12 days at 18, 25, or 32°C. Presence of characteristic clinical signs, mortality, and consistent bacterial re-isolation fulfilled Koch's postulates for V. vulnificus as an etiological agent of RSD in American eels. Gross clinical signs included hyperemia, hemorrhage, epidermal erosion, and shallow to deep ulceration with sub-dermal tissue necrosis. Histopathology indicated widespread colonization by Gram negative bacteria; partial to complete loss of epidermis and dermis (including scales); as well as edema, hemorrhage, myonecrosis, and extensive leukocytic infiltration (inflammation) of affected tissues. Eels injected with V. vulnificus had 92 times higher odds of death than controls. Elevated temperature was an additional risk factor with the odds of V. vulnificus-injected eels dying being 13 times greater at 32°C compared to 18°C. This directly related to the increased growth of V. vulnificus at higher temperatures observed in vitro. These findings identify temperature as an important driver for RSD risk in wild American eel populations and a mitigation focus for eel aquaculture in the Chesapeake Bay region of the United States.
authors: Kohli AK, Brown HN, Cipriano CR, Gauthier DT, Vogelbein WK, Wargo AR.

title: Arbovirus diagnostics: from conventional methods to emerging technologies-a chikungunya virus-centric review.
abstract: Arboviruses remain an important global health concern because of their expanding distribution, diverse transmission patterns, and the challenges associated with accurate and timely diagnosis. This review is centered on Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) as a representative model, focusing on diagnostic strategies across different stages of infection and the key diagnostic pitfalls that affect CHIKV detection in co-circulation settings. In this review, we summarize current laboratory-based approaches for CHIKV detection and differential diagnosis, including virus isolation, antigen detection, nucleic acid amplification and serological assays, with discussion of their applications, strengths and limitations. We further review recent developments in emerging diagnostic technologies, including next-generation sequencing, CRISPR-based detection methods, aptamer-based recognition systems, biosensors, and point-of-care testing platforms, highlighting their potential advantages and current limitations. Comparative examples involving dengue virus (DENV) and Zika virus (ZIKV) are discussed specifically to illustrate cross-reactivity and misclassification risks relevant to CHIKV diagnosis. Particular attention is given to persistent issues affecting diagnostic accuracy and practical implementation, including serological cross-reactivity among co-circulating arboviruses and the challenges of translating advanced technologies into accessible tools for field and resource-limited settings. Overall, this review summarizes progress in CHIKV-relevant diagnostics and outlines future opportunities for developing more reliable, rapid, and widely applicable detection strategies.
authors: Zhu Y, Li J, Mao H, Chen K, Li J.

title: Evidence consistency analysis of the effect of a low-FODMAP diet on the abundance of Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii in patients with irritable bowel syndrome.
abstract: BackgroundThe low-FODMAP diet is recommended by clinical guidelines as an effective dietary strategy for alleviating symptoms in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). However, its effect on Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii (F. prausnitzii) remains unclear, largely due to methodological heterogeneity.MethodsWe systematically searched the literature up to September 2026 for randomized controlled trials comparing low-FODMAP diets with control diets in adults with IBS. Given the high methodological heterogeneity across studies, we performed a direction-of-effect and consistency analysis (vote counting and sign test) instead of a traditional meta-analysis.Results12 RCTs were included. For Bifidobacterium (11 studies), 9 (81.8%) reported a decrease and 2 reported no change; the sign test confirmed a consistent reduction (p = 0.033). A sensitivity analysis including only studies with direct between-group comparisons (9 studies) was consistent with the aforementioned analysis (8 reported a decrease, p = 0.020). For F. prausnitzii (7 studies), the evidence was inconsistent: 2 reported a decrease, 4 reported no change, and 1 reported an increase, with no statistically significant trend.ConclusionMost current evidence indicates that a low FODMAP diet reduces the abundance of Bifidobacterium in IBS patients, while its effect on F. prausnitzii remains unclear. This finding enables clinicians to conduct more evidence-based counseling with patients, clarifying the specific effects (and non-effects) of the low-FODMAP diet on microbiota and facilitating informed decision-making regarding dietary management. Furthermore, future research should investigate the dynamics of microbiota during the reintroduction phase and consider patient microbiota subtypes to clarify the overall impact of the diet on the microbiota.Systematic review registrationThis systematic review has been registered with PROSPERO (International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews) under the registration number CRD420261351146. The publicly accessible URL is: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/.
authors: Cao B, Zhou L, Hu S, Huang Y.

title: Two new sulfur-containing pyridine alkaloids from the co-culture of Diaporthe fungi.
abstract: The untapped metabolome of filamentous fungi represents a profound reservoir for therapeutic lead discovery. Although genomic mining confirms an abundance of cryptic biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs), axenic laboratory culture frequently lacks the ecological stimuli required to trigger their expression, inevitably leading to the redundant isolation of known metabolites. To circumvent this biosynthetic silencing and unlock hidden chemical diversity, strategies such as heterologous expression, the one-strain-many-compounds (OSMAC), epigenetic modulation, and microbial co-cultivation have been increasingly deployed. Herein, we harnessed an interspecies co-cultivation strategy to systematically investigate the biogenetic potential of mangrove-associated fungi belonging to the genus Diaporthe. Four fungal strains (Phomopsis phyllanthicola ZMU-32-2-1, Diaporthe kyushuensis ZMU-48-1, Diaporthe phaseolorum ZMU-49-3, and Diaporthe sp. ZMU-11) were initially isolated and purified. Subsequent co-cultivation screening revealed that strains ZMU-48-1, ZMU-32-2-1, and ZMU-11 showed altered metabolic profiles, with the appearance of novel chromatographic peaks that were not observed in their respective monocultures. Scaled-up co-fermentation and subsequent chromatographic purification led to the isolation of five structurally diverse compounds. Notably, this included two unprecedented sulfur-containing pyridine alkaloids, designated as diaridine A (1) and B (2), alongside three previously described secondary metabolites. The isolated compounds were evaluated for their antifungal properties; however, none displayed significant inhibitory activity at a concentration of 200 μg/mL. Despite the absence of potent antifungal efficacy, these findings highlight the power of microbial crosstalk in activating the cryptic chemical space of Diaporthe species, reaffirming their potential as a robust resource for novel drug discovery.
authors: Li JX, Gong YS, Lu MX, Shen HJ, Lu HX, Zhao XJ, Yin TP, Yuan S.

title: Correction: Can bio-H<sub>2</sub> compete with bio-CH<sub>4</sub>-unequal chances of anaerobic digestion metabolic pathways.
