Non-muscle myosin heavy chain IIA (NMHC IIA), as an actin-binding motor protein, has been recognized as a functional factor in herpesvirus entry. However, its precise mechanism in PRV invasion remains poorly defined. Our investigation demonstrated that targeted inhibition of NMHC IIA, using a specific chemical inhibitor, siRNA-mediated knockdown, C-terminus of NMHC IIA (sPRA, amino acids [aa] 1672-1981), or rabbit anti-sPRA serum, significantly decreases PRV infection in PK-15 cells in a dose-dependent manner. During the early stage of PRV infection, NMHC IIA underwent rapid and pronounced translocation from the cytoplasm to the cell surface, which is beneficial to the virus entry. The study identified that sPRA mediates PRV internalization by binding to viral glycoproteins gH and gL. Furthermore, we pinpointed the subdomain spanning aa 1831-1882 within sPRA as the critical domain for both mediating the interaction with gH/gL and facilitating viral internalization. These results advance our comprehension of the molecular pathways through which NMHC IIA supports PRV infection and highlight its potential as a therapeutic target for PRV intervention.ImportancePseudorabies virus (PRV), a member of the Alphaherpesvirinae subfamily, not only poses an ongoing threat to the global swine industry but also presents a potential zoonotic risk. Although the host protein NMHC IIA has been identified as a critical factor mediating virus entry, its precise molecular mechanism during PRV infection is still unclear. Herein, we demonstrated that NMHC IIA participates in PRV internalization through binding to viral glycoproteins gH and gL. Moreover, we precisely mapped the critical functional region, spanning amino acids 1831-1882 in the C-terminus of NMHC IIA, responsible for both the viral entry process and the interaction with viral proteins. These findings could deepen the understanding of the interaction mechanism between PRV and the host, and provide a promising broad-spectrum antiviral target.
authors: Wang L, Wang L, Ren B, Zhao J, Zhang L, Chen X, Tang T, Zhao Q, Sun Y.

title: Spacer peptide 2 inhibition of HIV-1.
abstract: HIV-1 virus assembly is organized by the precursor Gag (PrGag) protein, which, from its N-terminus to its C-terminus, is composed of the matrix (MA), capsid (CA), spacer peptide 1 (SP1), nucleocapsid (NC), spacer peptide 2 (SP2), and p6 domains. Evidence indicates that the full-length, wild-type (WT) HIV-1 envelope (Env) protein is incorporated into virus particles by virtue of interactions of plasma membrane-associated immature lattices assembled by the PrGag MA domains, but that Env proteins with cytoplasmic tail deletions (ΔCT) or truncations do not require such an interaction for virion incorporation. Remarkably, during PrGag proteolytic processing and viral maturation, the free SP2 peptide binds to MA proteins and drives the formation of a distinct mature MA lattice. This lattice maturation is necessary for efficient function of WT but not ΔCT Env proteins. Based on these observations, we tested whether ectopic expression of SP2 variants might inhibit HIV-1 by inappropriately driving the formation of mature MA lattices. We have found that the expression of a chimeric protein composed of the green fluorescent protein (GFP) and SP2 in virus-producing cells causes the assembly of defective viruses in a MA-dependent fashion. Viruses produced in the presence of GFP-SP2 had aberrant morphologies and incorporated significantly less Env, regardless of whether the Env protein was WT or CT-truncated. Our results suggest that it might be possible to develop SP2 derivatives into antivirals.IMPORTANCEThe matrix domain of the HIV-1 structural protein forms a hexagonal lattice at the plasma membranes of infected cells, and this lattice helps direct the assembly of immature virus particles. The immature matrix lattice is also instrumental in facilitating the incorporation of viral envelope proteins into virus particles. Surprisingly, when the HIV-1 protease processes the structural protein into its mature components, one of the peptides produced, spacer peptide 2, drives the reorganization of the immature matrix lattice into a mature form. This maturation step appears essential for envelope proteins to acquire their full activities. We have found that expressing a spacer peptide 2 variant in virus-producing cells results in the assembly of defective viruses. The viruses have aberrant morphologies and contain significantly less envelope protein than wild-type viruses. Our results suggest that it might be possible to develop spacer peptide 2 derivatives into antivirals.
authors: Barklis E, Alfadhli A.

title: Monitoring hCMV-specific T cell response in hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients via rapid whole blood cytokine release assay.
abstract: Human cytomegalovirus (hCMV) reactivations and disease frequently occur in hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) recipients as a consequence of the profound immunosuppression required to prevent graft rejection. Despite clear evidence of the role of hCMV-specific T cells in controlling hCMV replication, quantification of hCMV-specific T cells is not widely performed to inform the clinical management of hCMV reactivations after transplantation, largely due to the lack of a simple and reliable assay to assess hCMV-specific cellular immunity. Herein, we developed a simple and rapid whole blood IFN-γ/IL-2 release assay (CRA) that uses overlapping hCMV peptides to quantify the hCMV-specific T cell responses and validated it in the peripheral blood of 40 healthy donors and 20 HSCT patients post-transplant. We found that the CRA correlates well with classical IFN-γ ELISpot assays but demonstrates greater sensitivity in detecting hCMV-specific T cell responses in HSCT recipients. Notably, the CRA also captured dynamic changes in hCMV-specific T cell responses associated with hCMV reactivation. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the CRA is a simple and rapid method for longitudinal monitoring of hCMV-specific T cell immunity in HSCT recipients, with potential to inform clinical management of hCMV reactivations.ImportanceStem cell and organ transplant patients often experience human cytomegalovirus (hCMV) reactivations and disease due to the immunosuppression required to prevent graft rejection. While it is known that hCMV-specific T cells are effective in controlling hCMV replication, monitoring of these T cells after transplantations is not routinely done in clinics due to the lack of an easy and reliable assay to assess hCMV-specific T cells. Here, we developed a simple and rapid cytokine release assay to quantify hCMV-specific T cells directly in whole blood and validated it in the peripheral blood of healthy donors and hematopoietic stem cell transplant patients post-transplant. The assay correlated well with classical ELISPOT assays and captured the dynamic changes of hCMV-specific T cell responses associated with hCMV reactivation. Together with its simplicity, the assay is well suited for the longitudinal monitoring of hCMV-specific T cell immunity in transplant patients.
authors: Yuen N, Gan CLS, Chia A, Tan N, Young B, Ho AYL, Tan TT, Bertoletti A, Kalimuddin S, Tan AT.

title: Modeling the Epstein-Barr virus lifecycle in the rabbit.
abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a human gammaherpesvirus that establishes a lifelong, persistent infection in greater than 90% of people worldwide. EBV has lacked an animal model that depicts the viral lifecycle in B cells and epithelial cells, allows for the investigation of immune responses, and models persistence in a host. EBV establishes a robust infection in immunosuppressed rabbits, resulting in widespread infection of the spleen and the development of splenomegaly. Within the spleen, follicle formation was altered as a result of EBV infection. Similar magnitudes of infection were observed in immunosuppressed rabbits infected with the B95-8 and Akata viral strains. In immunocompetent rabbits, spleen morphology appeared similar to that of mock-infected rabbits. Rabbits infected with B95-8 and Akata viruses developed antibody responses to the EBNA family of proteins in a comparable manner to human infection. Akata infections were more consistent in both the immunosuppressed and immunocompetent studies, whereas B95-8 infections resulted in variable magnitudes of infection and immune responses. The persistence of EBV in rabbits and whether the full lifecycle of EBV in lymphocytes can be replicated remain to be further examined.ImportanceThe human gammaherpesvirus Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infects more than 90% of the global population and is associated with lymphomas and carcinomas. EBV develops a lifelong, persistent infection in its host, avoiding immune detection by limiting the expression of its productive and latency genes. Currently, the EBV field lacks an animal model that can have persistent infection and immune responses to the virus during the course of infection. We demonstrated that rabbits mount an immune response to EBV infection over 6 months and may be a good model of persistent infection, although the viral genome remained below our limit of detection similar to humans.
authors: Burgess CK, Young J, Christensen N, Sample CE.

title: Novel roles of the Epstein-Barr virus BRRF1 protein in post-transcriptional RNA regulation.
abstract: In lytic infection, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) proteins manipulate cellular processes in multiple ways to facilitate virion production and overcome host antiviral responses. Here, we screened a library of EBV lytic proteins for those that manipulate or localize to cellular processing bodies (PBs), known to play important roles in RNA surveillance and miRNA-mediated translational control. One EBV protein, BRRF1, was identified that partially localized to PBs, and affinity purification-mass spectrometry experiments showed that it interacted with the CCR4-NOT complex-a known component of PBs with multiple roles in post-transcriptional mRNA regulation. The CNOT9 subunit of CCR4-NOT was sufficient to bind BRRF1, and its downregulation diminished BRRF1 interaction with the CNOT1 scaffold protein, indicating its importance in mediating the CCR4-NOT interaction with BRRF1. A BRRF1 double-point mutant was generated that failed to bind CNOT9 or interact with CCR4-NOT and was used to assess the importance of the BRRF1-CCR4-NOT interaction. Luciferase reporter assays identified multiple roles for BRRF1 in post-transcriptional regulation, including polyadenylation-dependent destabilization effects and interference with miRNA function, the latter of which was dependent on BRRF1 binding to CCR4-NOT. In addition, mRNA sequencing experiments comparing cells with and without BRRF1 expression identified multiple transcripts affected by BRRF1, some of which were at least partly dependent on the BRRF1-CCR4-NOT interaction. These include Claudin 6, whose transcripts and protein were downregulated by BRRF1 expressed on its own, as well as in lytic infection. Thus, we have identified multiple roles for BRRF1 in post-transcriptional mRNA regulation, some of which involve interaction with CCR4-NOT.ImportanceTo efficiently generate virions, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) must manipulate cellular processes to optimize the environment and overcome host antiviral defenses. Through unbiased screening methods, we have identified an EBV protein (BRRF1) that localizes to cellular bodies, which play key roles in mRNA regulation, and that interacts with a cellular complex with multiple critical roles in post-transcriptional mRNA regulation. As expected from these interactions, we found that BRRF1 has multiple previously unknown roles in disrupting mRNA levels and translation. Interestingly, one of the transcripts targeted by BRRF1 is Claudin 6, which has multiple roles in cancers, leading to increased cell proliferation and invasion. Our study provides additional insight into how EBV proteins manipulate cells to promote infection and affect oncogenesis.
authors: Campbell AM, Shire K, Ho T, Sinay Z, Marcon E, Greenblatt JF, Frappier L.

title: Early innate immune signatures correlate with Ad26.COV2.S vaccine immunogenicity and protective efficacy.
abstract: The innate immune system is rapidly activated following antigen exposure and plays a critical role in shaping the ensuing adaptive immune responses. In this study, we performed bulk RNA sequencing and proteomic profiling in a cohort of 25 rhesus macaques following Ad26.COV2.S immunization to characterize early innate correlates of vaccine immunogenicity and protection. Our results show that innate immune activation occurred as early as day 1 post-vaccination and demonstrated a systemic enrichment of antiviral interferon pathways, cytokine signaling, and activation of innate immune cell signatures. These early transcriptomic signatures correlated positively with humoral and cellular immune responses at 6 weeks following vaccination and correlated inversely with viral loads following SARS-CoV-2 challenge. Similar correlates of immunogenicity were observed in a cohort of 25 adult healthy participants vaccinated with Ad26.COV2.S. Taken together, these findings highlight the importance of early activation of the innate immune responses following Ad26.COV2.S vaccination in shaping the protective adaptive immune response.IMPORTANCEEarly innate immune responses may shape vaccine immunogenicity and protection. We evaluated responses to Ad26.COV2.S vaccination in rhesus macaques and humans and found that day 1 innate immune signatures correlated with subsequent adaptive responses. These findings suggest that early post-vaccination immune programming influences immunogenicity and protective efficacy months later.
authors: Colarusso A, Stephenson KE, Collier A-RY, Wegmann F, Zahn R, Aid M, Barouch DH.

title: Peptidoglycan remodeling prevents antibiotic resistance during oxidative stress.
abstract: The bacterial small RNA (sRNA) OxyS is expressed in Escherichia coli during oxidative stress. The sRNA OxyS enhances cell survival by controlling genes involved in the regulation of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and iron-sulfur (Fe-S) cluster formation. Here, we used the MS2 affinity purification coupled with RNA sequencing (MAPS) technique to identify new target mRNAs of the sRNA OxyS. Our analysis revealed a significant enrichment of mepS mRNA, which encodes a peptidoglycan endopeptidase that promotes cell growth. Our results confirm a previous report on the sRNA OxyS repressing the translation of mepS. We also found that an ΔoxyS background facilitates the emergence of mutations, conferring increased resistance to the last-resort antibiotics polymyxin B and E (colistin), but only in the presence of the target mepS gene. This suggests that the translation repression of mepS by OxyS could prevent mutations in bacterial DNA during H2O2-induced oxidative stress. Moreover, we show that adding the antioxidant thiourea or sequestering iron in the ΔoxyS background effectively reduces the emergence of resistance against both polymyxin B and colistin. These results suggest that reactive oxygen species (ROS), in conjunction with intracellular iron, play a key role in driving the emergence of antibiotic resistance. Overall, our work underlines a mechanism of antimicrobial emergence implicating oxidative stress, intracellular Fe, and cell wall remodeling in E. coli.IMPORTANCEThis study uncovers an underexplored link between peptidoglycan remodeling and oxidative stress responses during exposure to antibiotics. By elucidating how MepS and the sRNA OxyS interact in the presence of polymyxins and oxidative stress, our study suggests that MepS may exert an anti-mutator function. The repression of mepS translation by OxyS seems to limit the emergence of antibiotic resistance driven by DNA mutations. Together, these findings suggest cell wall remodeling and oxidative stress response pathways as promising targets to enhance antibiotic efficacy and limit the emergence of resistance.
authors: Sukadi Miala J, Arcand-Carrier L, Lapointe R, Morin C, Sasseville C, Lalaouna D, Massé E.

title: Siderophore-mediated iron uptake in cyanobacteria: current insights and knowledge gaps compared with model heterotrophic bacteria.
abstract: Iron is indispensable for most organisms, but it is often not easily available in the natural environments. This constraint has considerable impact on cyanobacteria, which require large amounts of iron to support several physiological processes, prominent among them being photosynthesis and, in some species, nitrogen fixation. To overcome iron limitation, many cyanobacteria produce low-molecular-weight, strong iron-sequestering molecules called siderophores, and employ specialized transport systems for environmental iron acquisition. Although these systems share similarities with those of well-characterized heterotrophic bacteria, our understanding of siderophore-mediated iron uptake in cyanobacteria remains limited. To date, only a handful of cyanobacterial siderophores have been structurally identified, and few genes involved in their biosynthesis, transport, and regulation have been reported, but a complete understanding of these processes remains lacking. This review first briefly discusses the well-established siderophore biosynthesis, transport, and regulatory systems of the model heterotrophic bacteria Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, as a comparative framework. It further discusses the current understanding of siderophore systems in cyanobacteria, highlighting similarities and differences with heterotrophic bacteria, species-specific variations among cyanobacteria, and major knowledge gaps. The review also discusses the ecological significance of cyanobacterial siderophores and their emerging applications in heavy metal bioremediation. Overall, this review identifies important directions for future research, including expanded structural characterization of cyanobacterial siderophores, deeper investigation of their biosynthesis, transport, and regulatory pathways, and improved understanding of their ecological functions and environmental applications. Addressing these gaps will strengthen our mechanistic understanding of siderophore-mediated iron uptake in cyanobacteria and its environmental relevance.
authors: Srivastava A, Mishra AK, Mishra Y, Rajaram H.

title: Secretion of the Francisella pathogenicity island effector protein PdpE requires components of both the Sec and Type IV pilus secretion pathways.
abstract: Francisella pathogenicity determinant protein E (PdpE) is a protein of unknown function encoded within the Type VI secretion system (T6SS) gene cluster of the Francisella pathogenicity island, a region essential for bacterial intracellular replication and virulence. We previously showed that PdpE is secreted by the bacteria via a T6SS-independent pathway, but the specific pathway involved was unclear. In this study, we investigated PdpE secretion in Francisella novicida and demonstrated that it requires components of both the Sec general secretory pathway and the Type IV pilus (T4P) secretion system. F. novicida possesses two SecB paralogs, and either of the two paralogs is sufficient for bacterial viability and for T4P-mediated secretion of chitinase and PepO enzymatic activities. In contrast, we found that both paralogs are required for T4P-mediated secretion of PdpE. Bacterial two-hybrid and pulldown assays confirmed interactions between these two SecB chaperones. Genomic analyses indicate that the presence of two secB paralogs is a conserved feature across the family Francisellaceae, including species that lack pdpE, suggesting that-while they have overlapping and partially redundant functions-the two paralogs have evolved to fulfill additional specialized chaperone and/or regulatory functions.IMPORTANCEOur research shows that pathogenicity determinant protein E (PdpE) secretion in Francisella requires components of both the Sec general secretory pathway and the Type IV pilus (T4P) secretion system, making it the first gene product encoded within a Type VI secretion system gene cluster known to use an alternative pathway. Although genetically linked to PdpC, PdpE's reliance on an alternative secretion pathway may offer insight into its physiological role. Furthermore, we show that dual SecB chaperone paralogs are required for T4P-mediated PdpE secretion by Francisella, and bioassays indicate a direct interaction between the two distinct chaperones. Genomic analysis reveals that possession of two secB paralogs is a conserved trait within the Francisellaceae family.
authors: Lee B-Y, Clemens DL, Horwitz MA.

title: PBP1A and LdtJ transpeptidase activities are crucial for cell envelope homeostasis and counteract the selection of colistin resistance in Acinetobacter baumannii.
abstract: The multilayered cell envelope of Acinetobacter baumannii is an essential structure that maintains cellular integrity and protects the bacterial cell against external stresses and antibiotics. It consists of an inner membrane, a thin peptidoglycan (PG) layer, and an asymmetric outer membrane (OM) enriched in lipooligosaccharide (LOS), whose lipid A moiety is the target of colistin, a last-resort antibiotic. Although lipid A is essential in most Gram-negative bacteria, A. baumannii can survive without LOS through envelope remodeling, particularly in strains producing low levels of the bifunctional penicillin-binding protein PBP1A (encoded by mrcA) or in ΔmrcA mutants. Here, we identify a genetic and functional interplay between the LD-transpeptidase LdtJ, which generates 3-3 cross-links, and PBP1A, which catalyzes 4-3 transpeptidation during PG synthesis. We show that simultaneous inactivation of both enzymes severely affects growth, viable counts, morphology, and OM homeostasis. PG analyses revealed that the ΔldtJ ΔmrcA mutants display reduced overall cross-linking and shorter glycan chains, consistent with a weakened sacculus. Co-immunoprecipitation demonstrated that PBP1A associates with LdtJ, suggesting that the two proteins may act in close proximity during PG synthesis. Notably, ΔldtJ ΔmrcA mutants exhibited the highest recovery frequency of colistin-resistant, LOS-deficient variants compared with wild type or single mutants. Together, our findings indicate that 4-3 and 3-3 transpeptidase activities play complementary roles in PG synthesis and remodeling, contributing to envelope stability in A. baumannii, and that disruption of these activities favors the emergence of colistin resistance. This work further highlights the importance of PG remodeling in maintaining envelope homeostasis and suggests that proper PG cross-linking acts as a physiological constraint to limit the emergence of LOS-deficient colistin-resistant variants in A. baumannii, providing new insight into mechanisms that contribute to envelope destabilization.IMPORTANCEThe global rise of multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii represents an urgent clinical threat, driven by its capacity to withstand cell envelope damage and escape last-resort antibiotics such as colistin. Although peptidoglycan synthesis and remodeling are known to influence outer membrane stability, how these processes interact in A. baumannii remains unclear. Here, we identify genetic and functional interactions between two major peptidoglycan biosynthetic and remodeling activities, 4-3 and 3-3 transpeptidation, mediated by the bifunctional PBP1A and the LD-transpeptidase LdtJ, respectively. Disrupting these activities weakens the peptidoglycan, destabilizes the outer membrane, and increases the emergence of lipooligosaccharide-deficient, colistin-resistant variants. These findings highlight the importance of proper peptidoglycan cross-linking for envelope homeostasis in A. baumannii and provide insight into how disruptions in peptidoglycan architecture influence antibiotic resistance.
authors: Furlan B, Nandy S, Gong H, Whalen MB, Mattei N, Olea-Ozuna RJ, Vollmer D, Vollmer W, Boll JM, Massidda O.

title: Genetic basis of glycine and L-serine toxicity in Staphylococcus aureus and the case for glycine as an antibiotic adjuvant.
abstract: The toxicity of the amino acids glycine and L-serine at high concentrations in bacteria was discovered decades ago. In this work, we used transposon insertion sequencing (Tn-seq) experiments to determine the genes necessary to tolerate excess L-serine, diglycine, or glycine in the human pathogen Staphylococcus aureus. Our results indicate that intracellular accumulation of specific counterbalancing amino acids-such as alanine in the presence of excess glycine-is the primary mechanism of resistance to amino acid toxicity. Consistent with this model, specific amino acid and peptide uptake transporters were required for fitness in each treatment; the peptide transporter DtpT was crucial for fitness in excess L-serine or glycine, and the alanine transporter AapA was necessary for fitness in diglycine. Tn-seq results also identified the cystine/cysteine uptake transporter TcyABC as necessary in excess L-serine, suggesting that both peptide and cysteine uptake contribute to L-serine tolerance. In addition to uptake mechanisms, glycine and diglycine toxicity is neutralized by D-alanine aminotransferase (Dat), which is required for D-alanine synthesis. The requirement for Dat and DtpT function-but not AapA-in excess glycine is explained by excess glycine inhibiting alanine uptake. Building on this finding, we found that combined treatment with glycine and the alanine analog antibiotic D-cycloserine was strongly synergistic in inhibiting S. aureus growth. Overall, our findings identify targetable mechanisms underlying excess amino acid tolerance in S. aureus, with implications for developing novel combination treatments using the accessible and biocompatible amino acids glycine and L-serine.ImportanceGrowing evidence supports the beneficial effects of glycine and L-serine supplementation in combating bacterial infections. Previous researchers have found that combining antibiotic treatment with high glycine concentrations has additive effects with many antibiotics, even reversing resistance to antibiotics in some bacteria. In vivo, activating glycine and L-serine metabolism heightens the sensitivity of bacterial pathogens to the host complement system, and studies of glycine or L-serine treatments show low toxicity and reduced inflammation in mouse and human subjects. This study reveals that glycine may be an effective antibiotic adjuvant with D-cycloserine, and treatment with glycine or L-serine could potentiate other drugs that target alanine or cysteine metabolism, respectively.
authors: Brown TG, Barnum J, Killpack S, Griffitts JS, Wilson E.

title: Avian influenza A virus polymerase gene leads to temperature-resistant genome replication.
abstract: Influenza A viruses (IAV) pose a persistent pandemic threat. Successful cross-species transmission from waterfowl to mammals requires host adaptation for efficient replication and spread. Avian IAVs are adapted to the temperature of the avian gut, approximately 41°C, while human IAVs replicate at 33°C in the upper respiratory tract. PB1, the catalytic core of the viral heterotrimeric RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), is essential for viral RNA synthesis. Three pandemic IAV strains (1918, 1957, and 1968) carried an avian-origin PB1 gene, suggesting a selective advantage. Fever, a critical antiviral response, elevates body temperature to 38°C or higher and can restrict viral replication. We hypothesized that avian PB1 may allow IAV replication at febrile temperatures. Using a mini-replicon system, we demonstrate that a polymerase of a seasonal human H1N1 IAV fails to replicate viral RNA efficiently at 40°C, whereas substitution of the PB1 with that from the 1918, 1957, and 1968 pandemic viruses, or a low-pathogenic avian H2N1 virus, restores RNA synthesis. Chimeric seasonal human H1N1 viruses expressing avian or 1918 PB1 replicate at 40°C in MDCK cells, unlike wild-type H1N1. Activity assays with purified chimeric IAV polymerases further suggest that avian-origin PB1 may intrinsically enhance polymerase activity at elevated temperatures. Together, these data show that avian-origin PB1 enables IAV replication at febrile temperatures, highlighting its role in zoonotic emergence and host adaptation. Surveillance of avian-origin PB1 genes in IAVs circulating in mammals may help identify strains with pandemic potential and inform the development of countermeasures.IMPORTANCEInfluenza A viruses of avian origin remain a persistent threat to human health. The 1918, 1957, and 1968 pandemic influenza viruses each acquired an avian-origin PB1 gene, but the adaptive advantage conferred by these genes remains incompletely understood. Here, we show that avian-origin PB1 genes enhance viral RNA replication by a seasonal human influenza virus polymerase at elevated temperature and enable replication of a human influenza virus at 40°C, a temperature relevant to both avian hosts and human febrile illness. PB1-dependent effects were observed in cell-based polymerase assays, with purified polymerase, and during authentic virus infection. These findings identify temperature-resistant genome replication as a potential adaptive property of avian-origin PB1 and suggest that acquisition of an avian PB1 may help influenza viruses overcome temperature barriers encountered during adaptation to mammalian hosts.
authors: Williams SL, Gygli SM, Bjorgen JC, Fan H, Mudiwa M, Matthews L, Xiao Y, Freeman A, Legaspi SF, Qi L, Taubenberger JK, Fodor E.

title: Anabaena, a multicellular model for cyanobacterial cell biology and biotechnology.
abstract: Heterocyst-forming cyanobacteria (order Nostocales) are a monophyletic group of organisms that grow as filaments usually made of dozens to hundreds of cells (termed vegetative cells) that can perform oxygenic photosynthesis. Under combined nitrogen deficiency, some cells in the filament differentiate into N2-fixing heterocysts, which do not produce oxygen and, indeed, keep a microoxic environment appropriate for the expression and functioning of the N2-fixing enzyme, nitrogenase. Thus, in the diazotrophic filament, oxygenic photosynthesis and N2 fixation are segregated into two different cell types, vegetative cells and heterocysts, which require intercellular molecular exchange to feed each other with fixed nitrogen and reduced carbon, respectively. The current understanding of heterocyst biology, including regulation of heterocyst differentiation, which also involves intercellular signaling, is the result of studying mainly a few strains of the genus Anabaena. Here, we review the classical studies that established Anabaena as a model for the Nostocales and clarified the basics of N2 fixation in these organisms. Then, we show how molecular genetics came into the scene and how it was complemented by genomic analysis. This, together with the introduction of modern cell biology approaches, led to a renewed understanding of cellular differentiation and unraveled a system for intercellular communication that is unique in the biological world. In turn, the new accumulated knowledge on Anabaena physiology and genetics makes these organisms an excellent system for the development of new synthetic biology tools that will be crucial for their use in biotechnology.
authors: Flores E, Luque I, López-Igual R.

title: Real-time tracking of dual-labeled fluorescent SARS-CoV-2 reveals that the nucleocapsid mutations R203K/G204R accelerate viral uncoating.
abstract: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) remains a global health threat, and understanding the molecular events of its life cycle is critical for developing antiviral strategies. The nucleocapsid (N) protein is essential for RNA genome packaging and viral replication; however, the effects of N protein mutations on ribonucleocapsid disassembly or uncoating remain poorly understood. To address this, we developed dual-labeled fluorescent SARS-CoV-2 trans-complemented virus-like particles (DL-trVLPs) by inserting a tetracysteine (TC) tag at the C-terminus of the N protein. The DL-trVLPs enabled real-time visualization of viral RNA and N protein in living cells under BSL-2 conditions. Using single-virus tracking, we directly observed the uncoating events. By combining this approach with site-directed mutagenesis and molecular dynamics simulations, we found that the R203K/G204R double mutation present in multiple viral variants significantly accelerated uncoating and enhanced intracellular viral RNA accumulation and viral replication. These findings establish a mechanistic link between N protein mutations and uncoating efficiency and provide insights into variant-specific uncoating dynamics. This study not only presents a versatile visual platform for investigating SARS-CoV-2 infection but also identifies a key N protein mutational hotspot that could serve as a target for antiviral intervention.ImportanceSevere acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) variants pose persistent global public health challenges. Understanding variant-specific viral uncoating mechanisms, a rate-limiting infection step, is critical for antiviral development. The nucleocapsid (N) protein is essential for viral RNA packaging and replication, but how its mutations regulate ribonucleocapsid disassembly remains unclear, with technical barriers hindering real-time biosafe visualization. We developed a versatile dual-labeled fluorescent trans-complemented virus-like particle (DL-trVLP) system enabling single-virus tracking of viral RNA and N protein dynamics under BSL-2 conditions. Our findings show that the circulating R203K/G204R mutation accelerates uncoating and enhances viral RNA accumulation and replication, uncovering a mutation-pathogenicity link. This work advances SARS-CoV-2 lifecycle understanding, provides a valuable research tool, and identifies a key antiviral target for combating variants.
authors: Liu Z, Zhang J, Ding Q, Yang C, Wu H, Li S, Qin F, Zhang X-E, Wang D-B.

title: Natural variation in BtSARSr-CoV nsp12 harbors adaptive mutations that enhance viral replication and spillover risk in humans.
abstract: The non-structural protein 12 (nsp12) is essential for SARS-related coronavirus (SARSr-CoV) replication and a major antiviral target, yet the functional significance of its natural variation in bat reservoirs remains unclear. Here, by analyzing 183 bat SARS-related coronavirus nsp12 sequences, we identified mutation hotspots that overlapped with sites variable in human SARS-CoV-2 variants (14 of 33 sites analyzed, including P323L), suggesting shared functional constraints across species. Using a cell-based reporter assay for high-throughput profiling of nsp12 function, we found that 8 of 21 bat-derived mutations enhanced polymerase activity at 37°C, with several also conferring an advantage at 33°C or 40°C. Four of these mutations (I171V, A185S, R249K, and N611S) increased replication in a SARS-CoV-2 replicon system, and all have emerged independently in circulating lineages (A185S reached detectable global prevalence by 2025). These mutations did not affect remdesivir sensitivity. Structurally, the mutations localize to regions involved in RNA capping or the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) catalytic core. Notably, SARS-CoV-related strains naturally encode multiple such adaptive residues, whereas SARS-CoV-2-related viruses retain ancestral states. Our study demonstrates that bat SARSr-CoV nsp12 variation pre-encodes mutations capable of enhancing human-cell replication, providing a predictive framework for monitoring polymerase changes with zoonotic potential.ImportanceBat SARS-related coronaviruses (BtSARSr-CoVs) are closely linked to past human pandemics and represent an ongoing source of zoonotic risk. Proactive evaluation of their spillover potential is therefore critical for pandemic preparedness. Current risk assessments have focused largely on receptor compatibility, with limited experimental investigation of viral replication fitness in human cells. In this study, we demonstrate that specific mutations in the viral RNA polymerase non-structural protein 12 (nsp12), naturally circulating in BtSARSr-CoVs, can enhance viral replication in both bat and human cells. By functionally validating several such mutations that later emerged in SARS-CoV-2, we establish a direct link between reservoir virus diversity and pathways of human adaptation. The high-throughput reporter platform developed here provides a scalable tool for prospectively assessing the replication fitness of nsp12 variants identified through surveillance. Together, these findings enhance our ability to interpret genetic signatures from animal coronaviruses and contribute to a more predictive framework for monitoring variants with zoonotic potential.
authors: Li A, Si H, Wu K, Zhang Q, Luo Y, Chen J, Jia J, Zheng Y, Li C, Zhou P, Shen X.

title: A four-amino-acid deletion in gp41 enhances HIV-1 CRF01_AE Cluster 4 pathogenicity and fusion inhibitor resistance.
abstract: HIV-1 CRF01_AE Cluster 4 strains are spreading rapidly in China and Southeast Asia, yet the molecular characteristics and pathogenic mechanisms remain to be fully characterized. Here, we identified a characteristic RSSL tetrapeptide deletion in the gp41 region of CRF01_AE Cluster 4 strains. Compared with a Cluster 5 control strain (GX-C5), the RSSL-deficient mutant GX-C4 exhibited a higher replication peak in MT-4 cells, outcompeted the GX-C5 control in co-culture, and showed significantly enhanced infectivity in TZM-bl and MT-2 cells, accompanied by increased fusion activity but no difference in viral attachment. GX-C4 also showed reduced susceptibility to the fusion inhibitor Enfuvirtide (T20), with a 1.67-fold increase in IC50, and displayed even greater resistance to LP-98 (a novel and potent fusion inhibitor), with an approximately 12-fold increase in IC50. Further experiments revealed that RSSL mutation does not upregulate intracellular Env expression but significantly enhances Env incorporation into virions. Transcriptomic analysis identified 61 strain-specific differentially expressed genes between GX-C4- and GX-C5-infected groups, which were enriched in pathways related to muscle cytoskeleton regulation and motor protein function. The myosin gene MYH4 was significantly downregulated in GX-C4-infected cells, and the expression of the key immune molecule TICAM2 was also suppressed. The differential expression of these genes in host cells may further contribute to the differences in viral pathogenicity. Collectively, RSSL deletion significantly enhances viral pathogenic characteristics and reduces drug susceptibility, likely by promoting cytoskeletal rearrangement, and enhancing membrane fusion. These findings provide important theoretical insights into the differential pathogenicity of HIV-1 CRF01_AE Clusters 4 and 5.IMPORTANCEThis study identifies the RSSL tetrapeptide deletion in the gp41 region as a key molecular signature of CRF01_AE Cluster 4 strains and demonstrates its central role in enhancing viral replication capacity and resistance to fusion inhibitors through modulation of viral fusion efficiency. Notably, the RSSL-deleted strain exhibited up to 12-fold increased resistance to the clinical fusion inhibitor LP-98, suggesting that this deletion may impact therapeutic efficacy. Transcriptomic analysis further reveals enrichment in cytoskeletal pathways, the significant downregulation of MYH4 offering potential new targets for antiviral intervention. These findings provide a critical scientific basis for understanding the molecular evolution of CRF01_AE clusters, informing epidemic surveillance, and optimizing treatment strategies.
authors: Zhang D, Han J, Liu C, Lu J, Li N, Yang J, Wang F, Li Y, Sun Y, Lin D, Li H, Liu Y, Jia L, Wang X, Li J, Zhang B, Xue J, Li L.

title: Drift, selection and recombination bias drive the evolution of a non-ribosomal peptide.
abstract: Non-ribosomal peptides play important roles in microbial ecology and medicine, for example as toxins and antibiotics such as penicillin. Like ordinary proteins, non-ribosomal peptides are subject to evolutionary change, which is driven by rampant recombinations of their synthetases. The evolutionary dynamics and causes of non-ribosomal peptide diversification are not well understood, because recombinations complicate phylogenetic analysis and statistical tests for natural selection and drift. Here we study the non-ribosomal GameXPeptides, which entomopathogenic bacteria use to kill their insect prey. We use recombination-aware phylogenetics, ancestral sequence reconstruction and statistical analysis of historical recombination patterns to retrace the evolution of GameXPeptides. This uncovers dozens of new GameXPeptides, including striking patterns of structural convergence. We provide statistical and experimental evidence that this diversity is shaped by selection, but also that GameXPeptides experience substantial genetic drift and biased recombination rates that limit the space of accessible peptide variants. Our work illuminates the complex interplay of adaptive and non-adaptive evolutionary forces acting on some of the most versatile chemical weapons in nature.
authors: Kaiser S, Shahmohammadi N, Goel TSM, Buchanan CJ, Garg SG, Vidaurre-Barahona D, Qian Z, Lefèvre C, Schindler D, Kim Y, Bode HB, Hochberg GKA.

title: FibriLysins disrupt Staphylococcus aureus biofilms and abscess communities.
abstract: The rise of antibiotic resistance, particularly among pathogens such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, necessitates innovative antibacterial strategies. Here we introduce FibriLysins, a class of engineered enzymes combining staphylokinase and endolysin, which dismantle fibrin-encapsulated multicellular staphylococcal communities, including biofilms and staphylococcal abscess communities (SACs). We characterized diverse staphylokinases, developing a library of 27 FibriLysins, with a 78% positive hit rate. The lead variant, FL-028, has significant antibacterial activity against prevalent clinical S. aureus isolates. In vitro, FL-028 reduced bacterial counts in SACs by 3.4 log and in biofilms by 2.3 log. In vivo, FL-028 exhibits superior efficacy in a mouse model of bone fracture-related infection, outperforming vancomycin by 1 log and eliminating SAC presence in tissues. FL-028 shows no adverse effects on bone healing, as confirmed by histological examination, mechanical testing and micro-computed tomography analyses. These preclinical findings highlight the potential of FibriLysins as a robust and safe therapeutic approach against difficult-to-treat staphylococcal infections.
authors: De Maesschalck V, Chittò M, Siverino C, Gens L, Zeiter S, Hangartner A, Harzé S, Vanhoffelen E, Van Laere C, Kerremans A, Voet M, Boon M, Van Win T, Vande Velde G, Wagemans J, Metsemakers WJ, Richards RG, Moriarty TF, Lavigne R.

title: The Brief Case: Uncommon pathogen, unusual presentation-Ureaplasma urealyticum in a post-laminectomy infection.
authors: Collazos Blanco A, Fernández Gonzalez JA, Mata Forte T, Marín M, Santiño Gómez S, Molina Foncea AF, García Señán A, Nuñez Bello A, Simón Sacristán M.

title: Complete genome sequence of a carbapenem-resistant and hypermucoviscous Klebsiella pneumoniae strain KP110 isolated from a human urine sample in Dalian, China.
abstract: We report the complete genome sequence of a carbapenem-resistant and hypermucoviscous Klebsiella pneumoniae strain KP110 isolated from a urine specimen in Dalian, China. The isolate was identified as ST11-KL47 and comprised a 5.46-Mb chromosome with a 138.82-kb IncFII(pHN7A8) plasmid.
authors: Peng F, Guo Y, Hao Y, Wang G, Song M, Gao M, Liang Y, Wang T, Gao Y, Guo S, Hao C, Wu C, Yang Z.

title: Draft genome sequences of three Rhizopus strains relevant for solid-state food fermentation.
abstract: We report the whole-genome sequence of three Rhizopus strains relevant for the fermentation of plant-based foods: one Rhizopus microsporus var. oligosporus strain (CBS 112586) and two strains of the Rhizopus arrhizus/delemar complex (CBS 127.08 and CBS 329.47). Phylogenomics suggests reassignment of R. arrhizus CBS 329.47 to R. delemar.
authors: Vellozo-Echevarría T, Klusener JX, Braat M, Braat N, Beijen EPW, Meyer AS, Wösten HAB, Barrett K.

title: Near-complete genome sequence of a GII.P7-GII.7 norovirus from a 2026 California outbreak.
abstract: We report a 7,456-bp near-complete norovirus GII.P7-GII.7 genome recovered by metagenomic RNA sequencing from a pediatric stool swab collected during a 2026 gastroenteritis outbreak in Northern California. The genome expands the public genomic record of norovirus diversity and is available under GenBank accession PZ705759.
authors: Ivashin D, Glascock A, Lydon EC, Langelier CR.

title: Hybrid sequencing recovers highly contiguous genome assemblies from eight cultured Planktothrix rubescens isolates from Lake Zurich.
abstract: We report highly contiguous genome assemblies from eight cultured Planktothrix rubescens strains isolated from Lake Zurich, Switzerland. Hybrid Illumina and Nanopore sequencing produced high-quality, near-complete, near-contaminant-free assemblies, including seven single-contig genomes, four flagged as circular.
authors: Hofer C, Knapp D, Posch T, Andrei A-S, Pernthaler J.

title: AMRx Hub: a curated web platform for discovery of antimicrobial resistance resources.
abstract: AMRx Hub is an open-access web platform developed to address the fragmentation of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) resources by aggregating AMR-related resources into a centralized searchable repository, supporting researchers, educators, and policymakers through a One Health framework.
authors: Oladipo EK, Adeolu-Shittu AI, Fatuyi-Adene AD, Emmanuel JO.

title: Complete genome sequence of Mycobacterium avium subsp. hominissuis strain Jp1289, isolated from a lymph node of a pig in Germany.
abstract: Here, we provide the complete genome sequence of the Mycobacterium avium subsp. hominissuis strain Jp1289 isolated from an enlarged lymph node of a slaughtered pig in southern Germany. The strain has a 5,061,038 bp circular chromosome. Genome annotation predicted 4,081 coding genes and 59 RNA genes.
authors: Möbius P, Wibberg D.

title: Draft genome sequence of Bacillus cereus strain MHES1, a potential multiple stress-tolerant plant probiotic isolated from the rhizosphere of Rotala ramosior grown in the coastal belt of Barguna, Bangladesh.
abstract: This study reports the draft genome sequence of Bacillus cereus strain MHES1, isolated from the rhizosphere of Rotala ramosior in coastal Bangladesh. The 5.7-Mb genome contains 5,607 protein-coding sequences and genes associated with plant growth promotion, salinity tolerance, and resistance to arsenic, cadmium, and lead, supporting its potential for sustainable agriculture.
authors: Hossain MN, Islam R, Hannan MN, Nahar K, Rahman MM, Haque MM.

title: Complete circular genome sequence of an acne-associated Cutibacterium namnetense clinical isolate.
abstract: Herein, we report the first complete genome of Cutibacterium namnetense from a Malaysian human acne sample. The 2.40 Mb circular chromosome provides valuable resources to study this bacterial-related human disease. These genomic insights improve understanding of acne-related microbiomes, enhancing therapeutic approaches and human health outcomes globally.
authors: Sivasamugham LA, Goh M-S, Lee W-K, Hoh C-C, Kidd S, Gunawan S, Vythilingam R, Law D, Subramaniam G.

title: Isolation and genomic characterization of Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteriophage from Chennai, India.
abstract: In this study, we report the isolation and characterization of lytic bacteriophage TANUVAS_MVC-VPH-PA, which targets Pseudomonas aeruginosa. We investigated its genomic and structural features.
authors: Navya Sri B, Kannan P, Sundaram S, Anbazhagan S, Kumar TMAS, Rajalakshmi S, Savariraj WR, Mohanadasse NQ, Naveenkumar V, Cull CA, Amachawadi RG.

title: Draft genome sequence of Bacillus cereus MHES3, a potential plant probiotic isolated from the tomato rhizosphere in a saline-prone ecosystem of Bangladesh.
abstract: We report the draft genome of Bacillus cereus MHES3, a stress-tolerant plant probiotic candidate from saline tomato rhizosphere soil in Bangladesh. The 5.6-Mb genome (65 contigs; 35.0% GC; 5,507 CDS) harbors genes for growth promotion, nutrient acquisition, stress adaptation, and heavy-metal resistance, supporting future climate-resilient agriculture and bioremediation research.
authors: Islam R, Hossain MN, Hannan MN, Nahar K, Hoque MN, Rahman MM, Haque MM.

title: Genome sequence of Bradyrhizobium diazoefficiens WB74: a commercial nitrogen-fixing microsymbiont of soybean (Glycine max L.) in South Africa.
abstract: Bradyrhizobium spp. are a group of symbiotic bacteria within the rhizobia complex that fix atmospheric nitrogen in economically important legumes. Here, we present the Bradyrhizobium diazoefficiens WB74 genome, an exotic rhizobium strain locally developed as a commercial inoculant that has been used for sustainable soybean production in South Africa over the last three decades.
authors: Hassen AI, Swanevelder ZH, Muema EK, Bopape FL, Mtsweni P, Kubheka BP.

title: Complete genome sequence of Ancylobacter sp. strain SB2, a hydrogen-oxidizing bacterium isolated from an alkaline mineral water spring.
abstract: We report the complete genome sequence of Ancylobacter sp. strain SB2, a hydrogen-oxidizing bacterium isolated from an alkaline mineral water spring. The genome comprises 5,124,764 bp with 66.36% G + C content. Genome-based taxonomic analyses indicated strain SB2 is genomically distinct from the type strains of the Ancylobacter species examined.
authors: He S, Wei Q, Hayashi T, Kobayashi H.

title: Complete mitochondrial genome sequence of the green alga Mychonastes koreanus MKSC25 (Chlorophyta).
abstract: The complete mitochondrial genome of the green alga Mychonastes koreanus MKSC25 is 23,905 bp long, with a GC content of 44.88%. It contains 13 protein-coding genes, 22 tRNA genes, 2 rRNA genes fragmented into 7 segments, 1 putative open reading frame (orf158), and a 299-bp group I intron interrupting rrnL4.
authors: Kang NS, Jo CR, Kim SY, Tran BT, Lee T, Heo JS, Back J, Kim K-Y, An SM.

title: Metagenome sequences of unintended bacterial communities from a Pseudomonas fluorescens experimental evolution study.
abstract: We report 16 metagenome sequences from unintended contaminant communities that invaded an evolution experiment initiated with Pseudomonas fluorescens SBW25. Low-diversity bacterial assemblies from center and edge locations across eight populations in contrasting uniform or heterogeneous glucose agar plate environments feature four primary genera: Pseudomonas, Chryseobacterium, Delftia, and Moraxella.
authors: Moyo-Heath B, Chigome G, Mushamba R, Onyeaghala C, Bailey SF.

title: Whole-genome sequence of an ammonia-nitrogen-degrading Stutzerimonas kunmingensis strain JD1-4.
abstract: The genome of the ammonia-degrading bacterium Stutzerimonas kunmingensis JD1-4, isolated from mangrove sediment in Guangxi, was sequenced using PacBio Sequel II and Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platforms, yielding a single 4,852,889 bp chromosome without plasmids. Annotation identified 42 nitrogen metabolism genes, providing the genetic basis for its ammonia-degrading capability.
authors: Zhang J, Liao X, Yin Y, Chen H.

title: Draft genome sequence of the mammalian pathogenic Pythium insidiosum.
abstract: The reported genome represents a nearly complete reference assembly of the mammalian pathogenic oomycete Pythium insidiosum, generated from clinical isolates collected from animals in the southern United States. Genome assembly was performed from combined long- and short-read sequencing data obtained with the Oxford Nanopore Technologies and Illumina MiSeq platforms.
authors: Goncalves Ramos M, Yu F, Barber R, Nance-Richey R, Lawhon SD, Wu J, Davis CG, Green S, Goss EM, Santoro D, Hoffmann AR.

title: Complete genome sequence of the putative plant growth-promoting bacterium Pseudomonas gorinensis strain NG1 isolated from a high-lipid algae strain.
abstract: We report the genome sequence of Pseudomonas gorinensis NG1 isolated from alongside the alga Nannochloropsis gaditana. Bacteria capable of growing alongside algae cultured for biofuel production were isolated. The genome is 7,017,688 bp with 60.73% GC content and was sequenced with Oxford Nanopore technology and assembled with Flye.
authors: Wilbourn EK, Humphrey B, Lobitz M, Ricken JB, Smallwood C, Cahill J, Davis RW.

title: Draft genome sequence of the moderately halophilic bacterium Vreelandella alkaliphila strain WG10-512 isolated from a Himalayan salt mine in India.
abstract: Vreelandella alkaliphila strain WG10-512, isolated from Gumma salt mines, India, was sequenced via Illumina NovaSeq. The 183-contig draft genome contains 3,435 genes with 99.93% completeness and 0.41% contamination. Taxonomic analysis confirmed its classification with 98.94% ANI, providing a valuable resource for studying microbial adaptation in saline environments.
authors: Walia A, Rana P, Badiyal A, Verma SK.

title: Structural basis for N-glycopeptide preference in an infant-derived Bifidobacterium bifidum PNGaseA.
abstract: N-glycans are abundant nutrient sources for human gut bacteria, which deploy peptide: N-glycosidases to release them from glycoproteins. Breast milk is comprised of a high proportion of N-glycosylated bioactive proteins that can be accessed by infant colonic microbes. Here, we biochemically and structurally characterize a PNGaseA-family enzyme from infant-associated Bifidobacterium bifidum LMG13195. This enzyme acts on a broad range of N-glycan structures but shows a marked preference for N-glycans attached to glycopeptides rather than to denatured or native proteins, highlighting a specialized route for N-glycan acquisition in infant-associated Bifidobacterium species. Structures of the apo enzyme, an unliganded E236Q mutant, and a D107N-E236Q complex with a G2-peptide reveal a canonical two-β-sandwich PNGase core plus an additional ten-strand β-sheet cradle and are the first structures of this superfamily. Comparison of these states, combined with molecular dynamics simulations, indicates that glycopeptide binding is coupled to β-sheet cradle-loop movements that close against β-sandwich 1 over the peptide C terminus. The complex defines recognition of the two core GlcNAc residues and the central mannose, reveals that peptide contacts are concentrated around the +2 Thr residue of the NXT sequon, and positions the scissile amide at the active site. These findings, together with mutational and computational analyses, provide a structural basis for N-glycopeptide preference by linking glycopeptide binding to cradle closure and catalysis, thereby expanding the host-glycan nutrient landscape accessible to infant-gut Bifidobacterium species.
authors: Bakshani CR, Caulton SG, Taleb V, Ojuri TO, Coughlan K, Montesa A, Pérez-Latorre A, Merino P, Kozak RP, Çakaj S, Bottacini F, Lovering AL, van Sinderen D, Hurtado-Guerrero R, Crouch LI.

title: Algal symbiosis adaptively restructures the cnidarian microbiome to enhance holobiont metabolism.
abstract: Microbiomes are integral to the function and resilience of cnidarian holobionts, yet the spatial and functional integration of microbial communities within host tissues remains poorly understood. Here, we show that symbiosis with photosynthetic dinoflagellates induces adaptive, tissue-specific restructuring of the microbiome in the cnidarian model Aiptasia, fundamentally enhancing holobiont nitrogen assimilation and metabolic flexibility. Using laser microdissection, tissue-resolved metatranscriptomics, gnotobiotic hosts, and stable isotope tracing, we reveal that symbiosis profoundly restructures microbial communities across the epidermis and gastrodermis, enriching for taxa and pathways that support nitrogen assimilation in photosynthetically active tissues. Expression of microbial nitrite reductase is strongly upregulated in the symbiotic gastrodermis, and 15N-tracer experiments demonstrate that bacterial assimilation of nitrite synergizes with algal symbionts to fuel the biosynthesis of essential amino acids. These findings show that symbiosis drives spatially compartmentalized microbiome adaptation within animal tissues, aligning microbial metabolism with host-algal nutrient exchanges to enhance holobiont functioning.
authors: Cui G, Ngugi DK, Konciute M, Cheng S, Liew KX, Mi J, Al-Babili S, Aranda M.

title: Equipositioning of chromosomes in the polyploid archaeon Haloferax volcanii by HpaAB.
abstract: Proper genome segregation is essential for cellular survival, yet this process is poorly understood in archaea. Archaea show considerable variability in genome ploidy and organization. Haloferax volcanii DS2 is a polyploid archaeon with a fragmented genome consisting of a main chromosome, three secondary chromosomes and a plasmid. Due to high ploidy, genomic segregation in H. volcanii is typically considered random. However, we identified four two-gene operons encoding ParA-like proteins and uncharacterized partners. Here we characterized HpaA and HpaB, encoded on the secondary chromosome pHV3. HpaA contains conserved ATPase walker motifs and is a ParA protein with a bacterial origin. Mutation of key residues in HpaA alters its localization, while HpaA is necessary for proper HpaB spatial distribution. HpaB forms cytosolic foci and functions as a centromere-binding protein, analogous to bacterial ParB. Deletion of the genes hpaA and hpaB results in severe growth defects when xylose is the sole carbon source, consistent with the location of xylose degradation genes on pHV3. It also reduces the pHV3 to main chromosome ratio. Single-particle tracking suggests that HpaB influences HpaA dynamics. Together, these findings demonstrate an equipositioning of pHV3, likely supporting maintenance in the different cell morphologies observed in H. volcanii.
authors: Premrajka K, Johnsen U, Preidel H, Wienberg J, Corleis C, Ortjohann M, Giacomelli G, Bramkamp M.

title: Antimicrobial peptides derived from Nemuri induce ribosomal condensation to inhibit translation.
abstract: Antibiotic resistance is a global health threat requiring antimicrobials with alternative modes of action. Growing evidence indicates that bacteria organize key intracellular processes through biomolecular condensates and other forms of spatial organization, yet whether such spatial organization can be exploited as an antimicrobial target remains unclear. Here, we identify intrinsically disordered antimicrobial peptides, generated from the Drosophila sleep-inducing protein Nemuri, that inhibit bacterial growth by targeting ribosomal organization. Mechanistically, these peptides enter bacterial cells without overt membrane disruption and accumulate in ribosome-rich regions, where they bind broadly to RNA and ribosomal surfaces through multivalent interactions. This engagement remodels ribosome-rich regions into condensates with reduced ribosomal mobility, thereby suppressing global protein synthesis and distinguishing these peptides from canonical site-specific ribosome-targeting antibiotics. Furthermore, Nemuri-derived peptides exhibit broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, including activity against drug-resistant pathogens, with low cytotoxicity toward Drosophila and mammalian cells. Together, our findings identify the organization and material dynamics of bacterial ribosomes as a biophysical vulnerability that can be exploited by antimicrobial peptides, revealing how a naturally evolved metazoan host-defense system turns intracellular organization itself into an antibacterial target.
authors: Nishinami S, Hasan M, Niwa T, Inui T, Yokoyama T, Otsuki H, Ogasawara Y, Sugai H, Otobe Y, Machida M, Abdelaziz M, Ageta-Ishihara N, Sasaki R, Ishizaki Y, Iwasaki K, Fujioka Y, Ohishi T, Kajimoto S, Nakabayashi T, Tanaka Y, Yoshitane H, Kumeta H, Sehgal A, Igarashi M, Noda NN, Toda H.

title: A multimeric pore complex in the poxvirus core revealed by integrative structural analysis.
abstract: It has long been known that poxviruses transcribe more than a hundred early mRNAs within their viral core, yet how these transcripts exit the core remains unknown. Here, we combine cryo-electron tomography with deep-learning-based particle picking, subtomogram averaging, cross-linking mass spectrometry, and AlphaFold3 modeling to resolve the molecular architecture of a long-sought pore within the poxvirus core. The pore is formed by a heteromeric assembly of the viral proteins E8, E6, and L3, which together create a hollow hexameric tube spanning both the core wall and the surface-exposed palisade layer. Within the pore channel, we observe a rod-like density consistent with the viral RNA helicase I8, which may contribute to the release of the newly synthesized viral mRNAs from the core. We further observe a state of the pore lacking the outer and basal rings under transcription conditions. Together, our findings identify the structure and dynamics of a candidate mRNA-release pore within the surface layer of a double-stranded DNA virus and suggest that it may form part of the poxvirus transcription machinery.
authors: Liu J, Schäfer S, Lehnung S, Baumann LM, Mühlberg L, Steiner C, Schreiber M, Linder M, Welsch S, Liu F, Bogdanow B, Krijnse Locker J, Turoňová B.

title: Author Correction: Integrating central nervous system metagenomics and host response for diagnosis of tuberculosis meningitis and its mimics.
authors: Ramachandran PS, Ramesh A, Cresswell FV, Wapniarski A, Narendra R, Quinn CM, Tran EB, Rutakingirwa MK, Bangdiwala AS, Kagimu E, Kandole KT, Zorn KC, Tugume L, Kasibante J, Ssebambulidde K, Okirwoth M, Bahr NC, Musubire A, Skipper CP, Fouassier C, Lyden A, Serpa P, Castaneda G, Caldera S, Ahyong V, DeRisi JL, Langelier C, Crawford ED, Boulware DR, Meya DB, Wilson MR.

title: Widespread selection of antibiotic resistance within hospital sewers.
abstract: Environmental microbiomes are sources of diverse antibiotic resistance determinants that can be mobilized and transferred to human pathogens under a selection pressure from antibiotics. Hospital sewers contain more antibiotics than most environments and are thus increasingly recognised as potential arenas for resistance evolution. However, it is unknown if resistance selection occurs there and what the drivers are. Here we show selection of antibiotic-resistant bacteria within Swedish hospital sewers. Evidence include; consistent selection of multiple resistances in Escherichia coli exposed to filtered wastewater from ten hospitals, but not to corresponding municipal wastewaters; in-situ enrichment of resistant over sensitive E. coli from wastewater to sewer biofilms at hospitals, but not at municipal sites; and higher resistance in bacteria collected from hospital sewers than from municipal sites as assessed by culturing and metagenomics. Evidence for drivers includes complete rescue of sensitive E. coli by addition of resistance genes to fluoroquinolones and β-lactams, and cellular effects typical for β-lactams. Measured concentrations by liquid-chromatography-tandem-mass-spectrometry compared to selective thresholds identify ciprofloxacin and cefotaxime as principal selective agents. Antibiotic concentrations and use data allow extrapolation of risks beyond Sweden. Given the absence of detectable selection at municipal sites, mitigations of risks in hospital sewers should be prioritized.
authors: Gray DA, Nhung NT, Coertze RD, Ekwanzala MD, Waters N, Järhult JD, Wenzel M, Åhrén C, Fick J, Flach CF, Larsson DGJ.

title: Early-life bovine respiratory virome analysis reveals phage-driven adaptation and cross-host evolutionary signatures.
abstract: Past outbreaks of zoonotic viral infections highlight the importance of understanding respiratory virome ecology. As major food-producing animals with frequent human contact, cattle represent a critical host at the human-animal interface; however, the early-life establishment of their respiratory virome and its evolutionary connections to viruses from other hosts remain underexplored. Here, we longitudinally profile the upper respiratory tract (URT) virome of beef calves from birth to weaning using an optimized viral enrichment procedure and metagenomic workflow. Viral communities exhibited increased richness and turnover, reflecting ecological structuring during early life. Temperate phages dominate the URT phage community and share virulence- and mobility-associated genes with bacterial hosts, likely contributing to host adaptation and colonization persistence. Vertebrate-associated viruses emerge after the first week of life. Targeted reassembly from bovine URT viromes recovers near-complete betacoronavirus-like (CoV-D180) and adenovirus-like (AdV-D56) genomes positioned phylogenetically between bovine and human viral lineages. Competitive mapping of bovine-derived CoV-D180 and AdV-D56 to human respiratory metatranscriptomic datasets reveals genome-specific, regionally structured coverage patterns distinct from reference viruses, supporting shared sequence features in conserved genomic regions across host-associated viral lineages. Collectively, these findings reveal early-life assembly dynamics of the bovine respiratory virome and highlight cross-host signatures in a One Health framework.
authors: Wang Y, Kim H, Malmuthuge N, Zhou M, Chen Y, Alexander TW, Timsit E, Yao J, Liang G, Guan LL.

title: Statistical inference of keystone taxa reshaping the assembly rules of forest root microbiomes.
abstract: Root-associated fungi and bacteria play pivotal roles in terrestrial ecosystem processes. However, identifying keystone taxa driving below-ground microbial assembly remains a major challenge. Here, we present a statistical framework for identifying microbes that reorganize microbiome assembly. Using 1,270 root samples collected from a cool-temperate forest in Japan, we reconstruct assembly landscapes describing the probabilistic structure of community states. We then find that several endophytic fungi (e.g., Phialocephala and Oidiodendron) are strongly associated with the reorganization of assembly landscape topography along abundance gradients, coinciding with shifts in mycorrhizal symbiosis. Independent datasets from Europe confirm that the highlighted genera are significantly associated with changes in mycorrhizal colonization patterns. Prokaryotic communities exhibit transitions among states characterized by core taxa, Pseudomonadota, or Actinomycetota, strongly associated with abundance gradients of Candidatus Udaeobacter and several endophytic fungi. These findings provide a scalable framework for prioritizing candidate keystone taxa and linking microbiome assembly to ecosystem-scale processes.
authors: Noguchi M, Suzuki K, Fujita H, Toju H.

title: G-quadruplex structures affect the immune response to bacterial infection in mouse macrophages.
abstract: Macrophages orchestrate immunity via transcriptional reprogramming, largely controlled by the master regulator NF-κB. However, mechanisms of promoter selection remain enigmatic. Here, we reveal that DNA secondary structures called G-quadruplexes (G4s) modulate the macrophage transcriptome during inflammation. By investigating the G4 ligand pyridostatin (PDS) in lipopolysaccharide-stimulated macrophages, we establish that G4 stabilization significantly decreases the inflammatory response without affecting mitochondrial metabolism or pathogen clearance. Instead, NF-κB-dependent transcription of activation markers and proinflammatory cytokines is selectively repressed. Using chromatin accessibility profiling, NF-κB ChIP, and in silico predictions, we demonstrate that G4 stabilization sterically hinders NF-κB promoter occupancy. Furthermore, PDS stabilizes transient, transcription-induced G4s, prematurely shutting down transcription and reverting local chromatin to a dormant state. Thus, G4 formation represents a potential strategy to modulate dysregulated macrophage activation.
authors: Schult P, Kastl M, Szlapa J, Symeonidis K, Maasewerd S, Franklin B, Radcke A, Juranek SA, Abdullah Z, Paeschke K.

title: Discovery of direct-acting small-molecule RIG-I agonists through creation of a selective CARD activation platform.
abstract: Retinoic acid-inducible gene-I (RIG-I) plays a pivotal role in recognizing and combating RNA viruses in humans, and it has become a drug target of significant interest. RIG-I agonists composed of dsRNA represent antiviral and antitumor therapies, however the development of small-molecule RIG-I agonists, with their potential for improved pharmacokinetics, remains an unmet need. Here, we report small-molecule RIG-I agonists that directly activate the RIG-I receptor protein. These agonists stimulate the first step in RIG-I signaling by triggering release of the signaling domains (CARDs) from an autorepressed form of the protein. This was achieved by developing a sensitive high-throughput screening (HTS) assay that directly monitors CARD expulsion through optical methods. The resulting screen hits were refined and optimized, leading to a specific RIG-I agonist that induces a robust interferon response. This study establishes a pharmacophore and assay for development of small molecules that precisely modulate RIG-I signaling.
authors: Guo R, Norford K, Xu L, Wei M, Wang W, Halene S, Pyle AM.

title: FKS1/2-variant independent mechanisms underlying the emergence of resistance in echinocandin-refractory Candida auris infections.
abstract: The emerging fungus Candida auris is a drug resistant global public health threat and WHO critical priority pathogen. Recommended first-line invasive candidiasis treatment is echinocandin monotherapy, but C. auris can develop on-treatment resistance via FKS1/2 gene mutations and additional, previously unexplained mechanisms. To better understand echinocandin failure in C. auris, we sequenced the genomes of echinocandin refractory FKS1/2 wild-type C. auris serial isolates from two critically unwell patients in London, UK. Population analysis profiling revealed echinocandin heteroresistance, and in vitro culture of clinical isolates at supra-MIC concentrations of anidulafungin (8 μg/ml) exhibited morphotypic heterogeneity. Small colony variants (SCVs) and large colony variants (LCVs) showed elevated MICs with polyploidy (to 4n and above) alongside adaptive changes in cell wall β-1,3-glucan content. LCVs contained significantly more mutations in calcineurin-related stress tolerance pathway gene CRZ1 compared to clinical parents and SCVs, associated with further increases in MIC. These findings indicate progressive step-wise accrual of adaptation to echinocandins, including genomic instability, alterations in stress tolerance pathways, and cell wall remodelling, paving the way for resistance emergence.
authors: Gifford H, Pradhan A, Caswall B, Murphy SE, Leaves I, Edmondson MB, Chakraborty T, Wilson D, Taori SK, Gow NAR, Farrer RA, Brown AJP, Bicanic T.

title: Small viruses reveal bidirectional evolution between HK97-fold viruses and encapsulins via procapsids.
abstract: The HK97-fold is an ancient, conserved protein structure that assembles protein shells, forming the capsids of Duplodnaviria viruses and prokaryotic biochemical compartments called encapsulsins. It has been proposed that encapsulins evolved from HK97-fold viruses. But the higher complexity of viral capsids represents a biophysical paradox in the evolution of HK97-fold protein shells. To resolve this problem, we hypothesize the existence of simpler HK97-fold viral capsids associated with smaller genomes than those of known HK97-fold viruses. Such small viral genomes are searched in environmental metagenomes across public databases, including IMG/M and MGnify. Using hidden Markov models and protein language models, we identify and characterize small viral genomes encoding HK97-fold proteins that exhibit molecular similarities to encapsulins yet lack portal and tail genes. The phylogenetic analyses of HK97-fold proteins reveal independent mixed groups of viruses and encapsulins, and structural analyses identify similarities between encapsulins and procapsids, the immature state of viral capsids. The observations support a bidirectional evolution between encapsulins and HK97-fold viruses enabled by the viral procapsid state. Using biophysical and genomic arguments, we introduce an evolutionary model of HK97-fold protein shells, predicting that they emerged as lower-symmetry biochemical compartments and that HK97-fold viral capsids may retain biochemical functions.
authors: Aguilar A, Miranda Perez I, Nadel O, Nayfach S, Ruiz Pestana L, Segall AM, Rohwer FL, Roux S, White S, Luque A.

title: Characterization of silk-like materials from larval salivary glands of the dipteran, Keroplatus testaceus.
abstract: Silk-like secretions are well-studied in many insects but remain poorly characterized in Diptera. Larvae of the dipteran Keroplatus testaceus produce two distinct silk-like materials-a mucus web and a cocoon-from their labial salivary glands, differing in composition and function. Here we combined histology, transcriptomics, electron microscopy, proteomics, mechanical testing, and FTIR spectroscopy to characterize these secretions. Neither contains fibroin; instead, both comprise hydrophilic proteins including collagen-like, mucin, and novel proline-rich proteins. Structural predictions and FTIR analyses reveal β-sheets, α-helices, and polyproline II helices, contributing to mechanical robustness despite high hydration. The mucus web facilitates larval mobility and spore capture, while the cocoon provides mechanical protection during pupation. These findings reveal a fibroin-independent silk system adapted to humid, microbe-rich environments, expanding understanding of insect silk diversity and offering insights into novel biomaterials.
authors: Kmet P, Opelka J, Lopes TBF, Sehadova H, Sauman I, Hradilova M, Humenik M, Zurovec M.

title: Multivalent antiviral conjugates enhance activity against Influenza via cross-linking viruses.
abstract: Long-acting drug-Fc conjugate (CD388) has emerged as a new class of antivirals against influenza A and B, yet the mechanisms governing how Fc conjugation reshapes small-molecule function remain undefined. Here we establish a programmable multivalent antiviral conjugates (AVCs) platform by click chemistry that enables flexible combination of valencies and conjugated drugs, allowing systematic interrogation of valency-dependent antiviral mechanisms. Using zanamivir as a model, mono-, di-, and trivalent zanamivir are conjugated with Fc, with trivalent zanamivir-Fc conjugates (AVC-Z3) exhibiting higher activity than lower-valent AVCs. AVC-Z3 induces inter-virion aggregation, thereby coupling blockade of viral entry with restriction of viral release. This cross-linking-mediated dual-stage inhibition represents a mechanistic shift from neuraminidase suppression to physical viral immobilization. Furthermore, trivalent peramivir-Fc conjugate (AVC-P3) is synthesised and exhibits stronger antiviral activity than AVC-Z3 in vitro, with much longer half-life in vivo than AVC-Z3, and CD388 with YTE mutation. The in vivo antivirus efficacy of AVC-P3 surpasses other AVCs, baloxavir, and CD388 in H1N1-, H3N2-, H5N1-, and influenza B-infection mice models. Together, our findings define ligand valency as a determinant of antiviral mechanism.
authors: Feng X, Yuan L, Zhao L, Liu L, Xie F, Zhou M, Cheng G, Guan Y, Xia N, Cheng T, Zhong W, Xiao D, Zhou X, Li S.

title: A family of small proteins links c-di-GMP riboswitch signaling with sporulation in Clostridioides difficile.
abstract: Cyclic diguanosine monophosphate (c-di-GMP) is a second messenger that coordinates lifestyle transitions, virulence, and developmental processes in bacteria. In Clostridioides difficile, elevated c-di-GMP levels inhibit sporulation, but the underlying mechanism remained unclear. Here, we identified a conserved family of small, membrane-associated proteins encoded by c-di-GMP riboswitch-regulated genes. Transcriptomic analyses revealed that c-di-GMP represses these genes, and reporter assays demonstrated riboswitch-dependent transcriptional regulation via premature termination mechanism. Overexpression of a single gene, CD1980.2, was sufficient to trigger the transcriptional activation of sporulation genes, including sigma factors and their regulons, and to increase spore formation. Conversely, sporulation efficiency decreased proportionally with the number of deleted small-protein genes, and the strain lacking all seven genes displayed a severe sporulation defect, underscoring their cumulative and functionally redundant roles. Elevating c-di-GMP levels in the deletion mutant did not further reduce sporulation, supporting a model in which c-di-GMP inhibits spore formation by repressing the expression of this small-protein family. Thus, our work establishes these small proteins, encoded by c-di-GMP riboswitch-regulated genes, as important regulators of spore formation in C. difficile, a process essential for pathogen persistence and transmission.
authors: Badilla Lobo A, Waligora-Dupriet AJ, Penven L, Seifert R, Rodríguez C, Barbut F, Soutourina O, Peltier J.

title: Metabolization of human milk oligosaccharides by Streptococcus pneumoniae.
abstract: It is unclear whether human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) can be used as a nutrient source by Streptococcus pneumoniae. Here, we investigate whether and how S. pneumoniae metabolizes HMOs and whether these compounds inhibit pneumococcal adherence. We find that S. pneumoniae can metabolize several HMOs, except for 2'-fucosyllactose (2'FL). The process is regulated by the carbon catabolite repression system. Transcriptome analyses showed reduced expression of the lac operon I (lacABCD) in bacteria grown with two tested HMOs when compared to lactose (Lac). Genes for the Leloir pathway and exoglycosidases were upregulated. A genome-wide CRISPR interference screen showed that the lac operons I and II (lacEFG-2) are essential for metabolizing HMOs. Lac and non-metabolizable 2'FL were found to inhibit pneumococcal adherence to host cells in vitro. Importantly, 2'FL showed a stronger inhibitory effect compared to Lac in vivo. Further research is warranted to investigate whether the non-metabolizable 2'FL can be used to inhibit pneumococcal adherence.
authors: Bacher K, Martysiuk U, Bonifacio-Pereira GK, Mignolet J, de Bakker V, Ghazaghi M, Troxler L, Bommer TN, Gjuroski I, Furrer J, Müller L, Burgaya J, Mostacci N, Neill DR, Veening JW, Hilty M.

title: SARS-CoV-2-specific monoclonal antibody AER002 in Long COVID: an exploratory randomized phase 2a mechanistic trial.
abstract: Persistence of SARS-CoV-2 has been proposed as a biological driver of Long COVID, a disabling chronic illness with no proven treatments. We conducted an exploratory, placebo-controlled, double-blind, 2:1 randomized mechanistic trial (NCT05877508) of the SARS-CoV-2-specific monoclonal antibody AER002 in 36 participants who met the World Health Organization case definition of Long COVID. After baseline characterization, participants received a single infusion and were followed for 360 days.
