authors: Gu X, Gill A, Yang Q, Ross P, Hayward L, Stelmach M, Umina PA, Elahee Doomun SN, Berran M, Coakley L, Sharma S, Hoffmann A.

title: RiboTRAP-seq identifies spatially distinct functions for the anterior and posterior intestine in immune and metabolic regulation in Caenorhabditis elegans.
abstract: The intestine integrates food-derived cues to coordinate organismal physiology, yet the molecular specialization of discrete regions along the intestinal epithelium remains unclear. Here, we generate cell type-specific translatomes of the Caenorhabditis elegans intestine during fasting and refeeding using discrete promoters for the anterior quartet of intestinal cells (INT1) and the remaining eight pairs of intestinal cells (INT2-9). We found that the anterior-most INT1 cells are a translationally distinct intestinal subcompartment that is particularly enriched for immune- and stress response genes. Functional assays using novel INT1-specific genes emerging from this study reveal that these specialized cells play a previously unappreciated role in pathogen avoidance and organismal survival. A second critical function of INT1 cells is their role in sensing and responding to the contents of the gut lumen. We show that luminal pyruvate is the key signal linking bacterial nutrients in the gut to secretion of the gut insulin antagonist INS-7. These findings establish INT1 as sentinel enteroendocrine cells that integrate metabolic and immune cues to couple food status with immune and endocrine responses. Our studies also provide a rich resource for dissecting segment-specific intestinal biology, an overlooked and fertile area for future research.
authors: Liu CC, Seban N, Srinivasan S.

title: Separable downmodulation of meiotic axis protein deposition and DNA break induction at chromosome ends.
abstract: In many organisms, meiotic crossover recombination is suppressed near the extreme ends of chromosomes. Here, we show that multiple, often chromosome-specific, suppressive mechanisms with differing ranges contribute to the consistently low enrichment of recombination-promoting axis proteins and the downregulation of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) within 20 kb of telomeres in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Suppression of axis proteins is associated with cis-encoded signals and correlates with reduced coding density, although whether this sequence feature actively drives suppression remains to be determined. In addition, axis protein suppression requires the histone methyltransferase Dot1 and the Sir silencing complex. We show that Dot1 suppresses Sir complex activity at least in part independently of its canonical target, H3K79, to downmodulate axis protein deposition near chromosome ends. In parallel, the Sir complex, but not Dot1, suppresses the induction of DSBs at a small number of cryptic hotspots by limiting the openness of promoters, the preferred sites of meiotic DSB formation. Much of the reduced DSB induction near chromosome ends persists in dot1 and sir3 mutants, indicating that additional layers of regulation contribute to the robust reduction of meiotic recombination effectors near chromosome ends.
authors: Raghavan AR, May K, Subramanian VV, Blitzblau HG, Patel NJ, Houseley J, Hochwagen A.

title: In vivo virus-free lineage tracing and live imaging reveal that NeuroD1 does not reprogram microglia into neurons.
abstract: In situ glia-to-neuron conversion induced by a single transcription factor is a promising regenerative strategy for treating central nervous system injuries and neurodegenerative diseases. Previous studies reported that NeuroD1 can induce microglia-to-neuron cross-lineage conversion and improve recovery after brain injury. However, these findings remain controversial. To examine the ability of NeuroD1 in inducing microglia-to-neuron conversion, we employed virus-free genetic lineage-tracing systems in mice to specifically induce NeuroD1 expression in microglia and track the cell fate of NeuroD1-expressing cells at multiple timepoints. Meanwhile, we longitudinally monitored NeuroD1-expressing microglia via two-photon imaging and characterized their transcriptional profile by single-cell RNA sequencing. All observations across these methods revealed that NeuroD1-expressing cells retained their microglia identity and cannot convert into neurons, no matter under physiological and injury conditions. Instead, sustained expression of NeuroD1 facilitated microglia apoptosis in vivo. Collectively, our findings provide strong evidence that NeuroD1 alone is not sufficient to induce microglia-to-neuron conversion. This study further highlights the importance of rigorous lineage-tracing and cell fate-mapping strategies for validating in situ glia-to-neuron conversion.
authors: Li X, Li Y, Cao Y, Hu N, Yang B, Ouyang P, Jin Y, Gao S, Cao L, Peng B, Rao Y.

title: Scp160 deletion suppresses TDP-43 aggregation and toxicity in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
abstract: Protein misfolding and aberrant protein aggregation are central features of neurodegenerative disorders, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, where the RNA-binding protein TDP-43 accumulates in abnormal intracellular assemblies. Although yeast models have identified multiple modifiers of TDP-43 toxicity, the cellular factors that determine how aggregation-prone proteins are organized remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated whether the ribosome- and mRNP-associated proteins Scp160 and Bfr1 influence TDP-43 proteotoxicity and aggregate formation. We report that deletion of SCP160 or BFR1 improves growth during TDP43-GFP induction without reducing steady-state reporter abundance and decreases formation of prominent TDP43-GFP foci. Deletion of BFR1 produced an intermediate TDP-43 phenotype, with a weaker effect than SCP160 deletion on severe foci formation and toxicity. Importantly, the effect of SCP160 or BFR1 deletion on visible protein aggregation was not specific to TDP-43: severe Htt103Q-GFP aggregation was strongly reduced, and formation of VHL-GFP foci was suppressed, including under conditions of proteasome inhibition. Despite these shared effects, the two mutants were not phenotypically identical. Deletion of SCP160 produced a distinct spatial phenotype in which residual TDP43-GFP foci showed markedly increased association with Sec63-positive ER structures and reduced distance to these regions, whereas bfr1 Δ cells did not show the same Sec63-associated shift. Together, these findings uncouple TDP43-GFP abundance from toxicity and prominent foci formation and identify Scp160 and Bfr1 as factors that influence the intracellular partitioning of aggregation-prone and misfolded proteins, with an additional role for Scp160 in the spatial organization of TDP43 relative to the ER.

title: Recovering anaerobic bacterial genomes in saliva, tumour and blood whole genome sequencing data from patients with prostate cancer.
abstract: Microbial constituents in the gastrointestinal tract, the urine and prostate tissue are being linked with clinical differences in prostate cancer, and a recent meta-analysis has linked periodontal disease to this cancer. Several hypotheses exist regarding how specific bacteria can contribute towards the development of prostate cancer. Recovering microbial genomes, and their genomic features, from clinical samples and investigating fine-scale taxonomy is a critical first step in investigating causality. Here, we describe the microbial diversity of samples associated with prostate cancer. Metagenomic assembly of non-human reads from the PanProstate Cancer Group, derived from blood, saliva samples and prostate tissue whole-genome data (N = 247), successfully reconstructed 249 highly complete bacterial genomes, predominantly from oral samples. Our data, reveals eighteen bacterial species from the oral cavity without species level classification, while demonstrating a wide range of known species. This approach enables us to gain additional insights of the microbes in cancer patients at no additional sequencing cost and has the potential to reveal new links that could improve our understanding of cancer initiation and development.
authors: Gihawi A, Bampalis A, Subramanian S, Pan Prostate Cancer Group, Bova GS, Butler A, Corcoran NM, Favero F, Gnanapragasam V, Hamid A, Jung C, Kote Jarai Z, Leeman G, Loda M, Reimand J, Sahli A, Schlomm T, Yamaguchi TN, Weischenfelft J, Hovens C, Pope B, Bristow R, Brook MN, Cheng KCL, Girma EG, Gruber AJ, He HH, Imada EL, Jakobsdottir GM, Khani F, Lutsik P, Marchionni L, Molania R, Papenfuss AT, Pellegrina D, Queiroz LR, Rausch T, Robinson B, Zanettini C, Sørensen KD, Lamy P, Cancel-Tassin G, Cussenot O, Eeles RA, Annels N, Hayes VM, Hurst R, Cooper CS, Brewer DS.

title: Height From the Ground and Phytotelm pH Affect Prokaryotic Diversity in Epiphytic Bromeliads.
abstract: Tank bromeliads in the neotropics harbour complex communities of invertebrates and even provide food, water and shelter to various vertebrate species. However, few studies have sequenced the microbial communities within epiphytic bromeliad phytotelmata. We sequenced the 16S rRNA subunit extracted from swabs rubbed at the base within the central phytotelm of the epiphytic bromeliads Aechmea hoppii and A. nidularioides. We tested factors that we suspected could influence the alpha diversity and beta-diversity of prokaryotic communities in bromeliads. Height on the tree and size of the bromeliad influenced the alpha-diversity within plants. Height from the ground and pH of the phytotelm explained small proportions of the variation among communities, regardless of whether quantitative or qualitative distances were calculated. We used FAPROTAX to assign taxa to functional groups and found that a complex picture of correlations between function and variables emerged, with height on the tree, pH, plant size and species, forest type and sampling season correlating with different functional groups. This relatively large metabarcoding study of bromeliad phytotelmata prokaryotes contributes to the growing knowledge of these highly diverse and complex systems.
authors: O'Reilly-Berkeley X, Hughes TD, Mossman H, Rowntree JK, Preziosi RF.

title: Metagenomic Bioprospecting of Bioremediation-Related Genes in Amazonian Aquatic Ecosystems.
abstract: Environmental monitoring of contaminated freshwater systems still lacks curated genomic resources tailored to bioremediation-oriented screening. In this study, we developed a curated catalogue of 546 genes from 80 microbial species associated with heavy-metal resistance, hydrocarbon degradation, detoxification and related functions and applied it to river metagenomes from four municipalities in Pará, Brazilian Amazon: Altamira, Bragança, Marabá and Paragominas. Functional annotation was performed using eggNOG-mapper and metagenomic reads were aligned against the curated catalogue with Bowtie2. Mercury- and copper-related genes were the most frequently represented functional categories across all river systems, a pattern that may reflect both sequence representation in the metagenomes and the unequal composition of the curated reference catalogue. Bragança showed the largest detected gene repertoire, whereas diversity, Jaccard, UpSet and Dunn-based analyses revealed marked spatial heterogeneity and sites of localized functional enrichment. Recurrently associated bacterial taxa included Acinetobacter, Enterobacter, Pseudomonas, Stenotrophomonas, Cupriavidus and Sphingopyxis. These findings indicate that the catalogue provides a targeted genomic reference for environmental screening and bioprospecting, although metagenomic detection represents functional potential rather than experimentally confirmed remediation activity.
authors: Dos Anjos TMC, Macedo DB, Ferreira VBC, Dantas CWD, de Los Santos EFF, Cardenas-Alegria OV, Ramos RTJ.

title: Green Microbiology for Planetary Resilience: A Research Agenda for Microbial Sustainability Science.
abstract: The planet is facing a crisis occasioned by climate change, biodiversity loss, physical, chemical, and biological soil degradation, water insecurity and pollution, infectious disease crises, and unsustainable production systems and vulnerable food systems. These problems are deeply interconnected and share a common solution: microbial science. Microbes are central to maintaining or restoring water safety and quality, the carbon and nitrogen cycles responsible for maintaining and improving soil quality and fertility, plant productivity and immunity from pests and diseases, animal and human health and immunity, and other essential ecosystem services that maintain plant, animal, human, and environmental health. Despite the transformative potential of microbes and a growing body of recent scholarship recognizing their centrality to sustainability at a global scale, there is no coordinated, actionable research and policy agenda mobilizing microbial science toward planetary resilience. To this end, this perspective builds on established principles of Green Microbiology to advance a 10-year, forward-looking research agenda spanning climate science, food systems, water security, circular bioeconomy, One Health, biodiversity conservation, and artificial intelligence and their alignment to microbial research, technology, trends, and governance and policy structures with the fundamentals of planetary resilience.
authors: Akinsemolu AA, Onyeaka H.

title: Waste-Contaminated Sites Near Dhaka City Harbour Specific Biosurfactant-Producing Bacillus and Stutzerimonas Strains With Potential Biotechnological Applications.
abstract: Biosurfactants are eco-friendly surface-active compounds produced by microorganisms that lower surface and interfacial tensions, enhancing the bioavailability of hydrophobic compounds. The study reports the isolation and characterization of biosurfactant-producing bacteria from industrial waste effluent in a river near Dhaka, Bangladesh. Using diesel-enriched media, bacterial strains were isolated and screened for biosurfactant production using oil displacement, emulsification index (E24%), and drop-collapse assays. The microbial cultures were characterized based on biochemical activities and 16S rRNA sequencing. Biosurfactant characterization was carried out using chromatographic techniques. Six cultures passed the drop-collapse and oil-displacement tests with E24% ranging from 9% to 41%. The CTAB agar assay confirmed the anionic nature of the biosurfactants. The potential biosurfactant producers belong mostly to the Bacillus and Stutzerimonas groups, with one low-biosurfactant-producing isolate from the Enterobacteriaceae group. The presence of two consortia, Bacillus-Acinetobacter and Bacillus-Stutzerimonas, was also observed. The isolates and consortia exhibited varying levels of antibacterial, antifungal, adherence, and plant growth-promoting activity. Biosurfactant production capacity under extreme conditions has been characterized by pH stability (pH 2-pH 11), salinity tolerance (2%-10% NaCl), and temperature tolerance (40°C-100°C). Overall, they provide a green and economical alternative to synthetic surfactants, with low toxicity and potential applications in bioremediation, biocontrol, and plant growth promotion.
authors: Amina UFT, Mahzabin M, Rasul SSB, Elias SM.

title: Functional Redundancy Enables Stable Treatment Performance Across Taxonomically Diverse Dairy Wastewater Microbiomes.
abstract: Biological treatment of dairy wastewater depends on complex microbial communities that vary widely across reactors, influent sources and operating conditions. Whether stable treatment performance arises from conserved taxa or from redundancy in functional potential remains unclear. In this study, we conducted a meta-analysis and reprocessing of 239 samples from nine independent studies spanning six countries and multiple reactor configurations. Taxonomic profiles showed extreme heterogeneity, with no ASV detected in at least 50% of samples and most genera exhibiting strong study-specific patterns. In contrast, the predicted functional repertoire was highly conserved. PICRUSt2 analysis identified 196 MetaCyc pathways present in at least 90% of samples, and these pathways accounted for approximately 90% of total predicted functional abundance. Generalised linear latent variable models showed that temperature and pH created consistent but modest ecological gradients, while study- and reactor-level factors dominated community structure. Despite substantial taxonomic turnover, functional signatures associated with fermentation, biosynthesis, nitrogen cycling, and degradation of complex substrates remained stable across systems. Treatment-stage transitions also followed predictable metabolic trajectories. These results show that dairy wastewater treatment systems are taxonomically flexible but functionally robust, and that extensive redundancy supports consistent metabolic capacity across diverse operational and environmental contexts.
authors: Trentin AB, Dos Santos SLS, Bendix AF, Lopes LC, Mota TFM, de Souza SS, Ghisi NC, Leite DCA.

title: Regionally Divergent Relationships Between Microbial Communities and Environmental Gradients in Potato Production Systems.
abstract: Using soil microbiome data as indicators of soil health remains a challenging task in agriculture research. Microbiome data are complex and exhibit strong spatiotemporal variation and diverse responses to environmental factors. As a result, measurements of microbiota often are difficult to interpret and do not provide credible inferences about soil health status. In this study, we evaluated the distributions of soil microbial communities in three distinct potato growing regions of the Upper Midwest of the USA and compared their relationships with soil chemistry and management factors across regions. A total of 1270 soil samples were collected and analysed for microbial properties, including bacterial and fungal abundance, taxonomic and functional diversity and composition. We found substantial variation in the microbial community properties across spatial scales. Environmental factors were more strongly associated with community diversity at the class level than at finer taxonomic levels. Soil pH, soil organic matter (SOM), crop rotation schemes and fumigation correlated with different aspects of microbial properties, while most of the relationships were region-specific. Our results suggest that the microbiological component of soil health includes multiple aspects of the community properties, and region-specific recommendations are needed for developing soil health promoting practices.
authors: Shan S, George I, Kinkel LL, Lankau RA.

title: Validation of a Synthetic Wastewater Matrix as a Proxy for Municipal Wastewater for In Vitro Studies of E. coli.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major threat to global health and resistant bacterial populations have been observed to develop and spread in and around wastewater. However, in vitro studies on AMR development are typically conducted in ideal rich media conditions, which can differ in composition and nutrient density from wastewater. In this study, we compare the growth and AMR development of E. coli in a synthetic wastewater recipe to autoclaved wastewater samples from the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority (MWRA). We found that synthetic wastewater and real wastewater samples both supported less bacterial growth compared to LB broth and had similar susceptibility profiles to antibiotic pressure from Doxycycline, Ciprofloxacin and Streptomycin. More importantly, unlike in LB broth, AMR development over time during continuous passaging under subinhibitory antibiotic pressure in pH-adjusted synthetic wastewater was similar in fold change to real wastewater samples. Thus, we suggest that synthetic wastewater is a more accurate predictor of both E. coli growth and antibiotic resistance development in wastewater systems than standard nutrient broths such as LB. The validation of synthetic wastewater as a better proxy for real wastewater will allow for further recapitulation of the wastewater environment in future in vitro studies of AMR in these conditions.
authors: Sutradhar I, Gross N, Ching C, Nahum Y, Desai D, Bowes DA, Zaman MH.

title: Bacillaceae Within Galium aparine L.: A Plant-Associated Treasure of Biosynthetic Diversity and Growth-Promoting Potential.
abstract: Endophytic bacteria are key components of plant microbiomes, enhancing host growth, stress tolerance, and defence mechanisms. Ten cultivable strains affiliated with Bacillaceae, including putative novel Priestia and Bacillus species, were previously isolated from Galium aparine L.'s tissues. All tolerated diverse levels of abiotic stresses, produced ammonia and auxins, as well as all exhibited strong hydrolytic enzyme activities (amylase, protease, xylanase, and pectinase), indicating robust metabolic versatility. These bacteria stand out as prolific producers of industrially relevant compounds. Priestia megaterium GR4 demonstrated high production of hydrolytic enzymes and biosurfactants, and most strains synthesized and accumulated polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA), highlighting their potential as sustainable bioplastic producers. UPLC-MS/MS confirmed koranimine production by Peribacillus frigoritolerans GR2. Previous genome mining studies revealed diverse biosynthetic gene clusters, including those for surfactin and fengycin. Overall, G. aparine endophytes represent powerful biological factories capable of producing a wide range of valuable compounds, including enzymes, biosurfactants and biopolymers, with strong potential for applications in industrial biotechnology, sustainable agriculture, and biocontrol.
authors: Rutkowska N, Drożdżyński P, Boruta T, Sekuła B, Marchut-Mikołajczyk O.

title: Microbiome Continuum: Connecting Environmental, Host-Associated and Engineered Microbiomes Through One Health and Artificial Intelligence.
abstract: Microbiomes are increasingly understood as interconnected ecological systems spanning soil, water, plants, animals, humans and engineered environments rather than as isolated host-associated communities. This microbiome continuum provides a mechanistic perspective for One Health by linking microbial cells with the movement of metabolites, genes, signalling molecules and ecological functions across environmental boundaries. Here, we critically examined the biological processes that maintain this continuity, including dispersal, horizontal gene transfer (HGT), metabolic exchange, environmental exposure and host-microbe communication. We consider how climate change and anthropogenic disturbance reshape these interactions and influence antimicrobial resistance (AMR), non-communicable disease, ecosystem function and pathogen emergence. We further evaluate how artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, can integrate multi-omics and longitudinal data, while emphasizing that predictive performance does not establish causality and that AI remains dependent on data quality, biological knowledge and experimental validation. Engineered microbiomes offer opportunities for targeted intervention, but ecological stability, biosafety, HGT and translational uncertainty remain important constraints. We propose a One Health Microbiome Intelligence Framework (OH-MIF) as a conceptual architecture for cross-domain integration, with emphasis on standardized data, causal validation, equitable participation and human oversight.
authors: Bhuiyan MNI.

title: Isolation, Characterization and Molecular Identification of Putative Probiotic Bacteria From Red Tilapia Gut.
abstract: The use of probiotics is a promising strategy to enhance fish health and sustainability in aquaculture as alternatives to antibiotics. This study applied a systematic multi-criteria screening approach to identify autochthonous probiotic candidates from the intestinal microbiota of healthy red tilapia (Oreochromis sp.). A total of 26 culturable bacterial isolates were recovered and evaluated for antimicrobial activity against major fish pathogens (Aeromonas hydrophila, Streptococcus agalactiae and Streptococcus iniae), safety, tolerance to simulated gastrointestinal conditions, adhesion-related properties, enzymatic activities and environmental robustness. Only a small subset of isolates exhibited broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity and satisfied subsequent safety and functional criteria. Based on integrated performance, three isolates were shortlisted for advanced evaluation, of which two were retained for molecular identification. The selected isolates were identified by 16S rRNA gene sequencing as Pseudomonas aeruginosa PA4 (PA4) and Bacillus sp. BA4P (BA4P). Both strains demonstrated tolerance to gastrointestinal stress, measurable adhesion-related hydrophobicity, diverse enzymatic activities and stability under varying temperature and salinity conditions. These findings provide a robust framework for screening host-associated probiotics and support the further evaluation of PA4 and BA4P as potential candidates for sustainable tilapia aquaculture.
authors: Ntakirutimana R, Ashin MJ, Farhath AA, Bigirimana A, Hershey NR, Lovejan M, Mwangi P, Jijina MP, Fariq F, Varsha C, Rahiman KMM.

title: Volatile Emissions From Diverse Estuarine Bacteria Share Core Compounds With a Subset of Strain-Specific, Low Abundance Compounds.
abstract: Biogenic volatile organic compounds (BVOCs) are gases that influence atmospheric chemistry, nutrient cycling and species interactions, yet the contribution of heterotrophic marine bacteria to marine BVOC emissions remains poorly constrained. In addition, the extent to which the volatilome is linked to bacterial phylogeny is unknown. Here, we characterize the volatilome of 16 heterotrophic bacterial strains isolated from Baltic Sea surface water, spanning Alphaproteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria, Betaproteobacteria, Bacteroidota and Actinomycetes. Headspace BVOCs were quantified under standardized growth conditions using Proton Transfer Reaction Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometry (PTR-TOF-MS). A broadly overlapping bacterial volatilome was identified, with compound composition and proportional abundance similar across many strains, irrespective of phylogeny. Namely, most strains shared a set of core compounds with a subset of strain-specific, low abundance compounds. Acetone accounted for more than 50% of the emissions in most volatilomes. The remaining fraction of emissions was primarily comprised of other low-molecular-weight oxygenated compounds. Interestingly, two strains demonstrated strain-specific emission patterns, significantly diverging from the group in their emission rate and compound composition. Together, these findings suggest that marine heterotrophic bacteria may contribute a broadly conserved collection of BVOCs to the ocean-atmosphere interface, highlighting their role as a widespread source of trace gases in marine ecosystems.
authors: Galen E, Roslund K, Rinnan R, Riemann L.

title: Exploratory analysis of nasal and gut microbial community structure in preschool children with recurrent wheeze.
abstract: Early-life wheezing has been associated with microbial alterations along the gut-airway axis, yet few studies have examined bacterial communities in both compartments within the same children. This cross-sectional exploratory pilot study (n=25) characterized nasal and stool bacterial communities in children aged 1-4 years with recurrent wheeze and healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene metabarcoding. Across participants, nasal and stool bacteriomes were highly individualized and taxonomically diverse. Overall richness, evenness, and global community composition did not differ significantly between healthy controls and children with recurrent wheeze in either compartment. Nasal communities in the recurrent-wheeze group showed greater within-group dispersion, although the comparison did not reach the conventional significance threshold (p=0.054). Exploratory distance-based stratification identified a subgroup with nasal profiles farther from the healthy-control centroid; these profiles had lower richness and evenness, higher Moraxella abundance, and lower abundances of Prevotella spp., Alloprevotella, and Veillonella. No statistically supported genus-level differences were detected in stool samples. Community-assembly and co-occurrence analyses yielded group-specific descriptive patterns in both compartments. Different sets of cross-compartment correlations passed the multiple-testing threshold in healthy controls and children with recurrent wheeze, including correlations of stool Lactococcus with several nasal taxa in the recurrent-wheeze group. Because these analyses were performed in small groups, they are considered hypothesis-generating. These findings identify nasal microbial heterogeneity and exploratory differences in community organization in preschool children with recurrent wheeze, while providing no evidence for causal or Moraxella-driven effects. Larger longitudinal studies with functional measurements are required for validation.
authors: Gschwendtner S, Maison N, Illi S, von Mutius E, Rosenboom I, Tümmler B, Dittrich AM, Weckmann M, Abdo M, Waschki B, Kopp MV, Hansen G, Brinkmann F, Rabe K, Schaub B, Schloter M,  the ALLIANCE Study Group.

journal: International Journal of Systematic and Evolutionary Microbiology
authors: Oren A, Göker M.

title: Mining Impacts on a Threatened and Burnt Swamp Ecosystem: Responses of the Microbial Soil Community.
abstract: Peatlands are globally important carbon reservoirs that mitigate global warming while regulating biogeochemical cycles. However, these ecosystems are highly vulnerable to environmental disturbances, such as fire and mining. Despite the key ecological roles of soil microbes, descriptions of microbial assemblages in many peatland systems, and how they may shift under the dual disturbances of fire and mining, remain poorly addressed. Here, we assessed the composition and diversity of soil microbial communities in three mined and three unmined swamps in southeastern Australia, all affected by the unprecedented summer bushfires during 2019-2020. Bacterial and eukaryotic communities were analysed alongside soil chemical properties across a moisture gradient within each swamp. Our results revealed significant differences in communities due to mining activities, with the most pronounced differences observed within swamp communities rather than other sites along the moisture gradient. The eukaryotic community was significantly influenced by the combined effects of mining activity and fire history. The bacterial community was significantly correlated with pH. Our findings suggest that mining was associated with changes in eukaryotic diversity and bacterial community structure and functionality, with fire history potentially contributing to the observed patterns. This study underscores the critical, detrimental impacts that mining can have on peatland microbial composition.
authors: de Lima NM, Vázquez-Campos X, Thomsen A, Ooi M, Muñoz-Rojas M.

title: Bioremediation of Olein Industry Waste by Cytobacillus sp. OWB-43 Strain.
abstract: The disposal of industrial vegetable olein waste poses a significant environmental challenge. In the present study, we investigated the bioremediation potential of Cytobacillus sp. OWB-43 to treat a waste generated from vegetable olein production, a by-product of sunflower, soybean, corn, and peanut oil industries with a chemical oxygen demand (COD) of 160,000 mg L-1. Cytobacillus sp. OWB-43 decreased the COD in 18.75% (~30,000 mg L-1) and soluble solids in ether in 24.8% (7.2 g L-1). Moreover, maximum growth in population under stirring and static conditions was 3.7 × 108 CFU mL-1 and 1.5 × 109 CFU mL-1, respectively. Besides, bacterial treatment (both agitation and static), reduced phytotoxicity of the residues, as observed in both lettuce seedlings and onion bulbs, used as biosensors of toxicity. Furthermore, we demonstrated that treated residues can be safely disposed on soil without harmful effects. This statement was observed in soil irrigated with Cytobacillus sp. OWB-43-treated residue, which supported lettuce growth, with fresh and dry weight values comparable to those grown in water-irrigated soil. While genera such as Bacillus and Pseudomonas are known for oily wastewater treatment, this study identifies Cytobacillus sp. as a promising and previously unreported bioremediation agent on olein waste treatment.
authors: Escalante J, Lencina N, Piazza A, Burdisso P, Salazar MO, Furlan RLE, Gottig N, Ottado J, Garavaglia B.

title: Rainfall and Substrate Origin Driven Change of Ruminant Manure Microbiomes in Cyprus.
abstract: Microbial communities drive the stabilisation of organic matter during manure storage; however, the combined influence of substrate origin and sudden rainfall occurrences on these communities remains poorly understood. For the first time in Cyprus, we investigated the effects of manure type (dairy cow vs. goat) and a drying-rainfall simulation pulse on the community composition, diversity, and functional potential during manure storage, using 16S rRNA metabarcoding and shotgun sequencing. Under dry conditions, substrate composition set the baseline, with the more structurally heterogeneous goat manure supporting significantly higher diversity than dairy cow manure. Rainfall simulation then acted as a dominant environmental filter, sharply reducing diversity and driving compositional convergence across manure types. This shift coincided with a rapid rise of fast-responding, stress-tolerant taxa, primarily Bacillota, and an increase in functions linked to sporulation and rapid growth. Ordination and dispersion analyses further showed that substrate origin modulates stability: after rainfall simulation, cow-manure communities exhibited greater compositional displacement and greater variability than those from goat manure. Overall, the efficacy and stability of manure storage systems emerge from the interplay between initial physicochemical template and dynamic moisture stress. Optimising large-scale operations will require management approaches that consider substrate characteristics, microbial community structure, and moisture dynamics.
authors: Pissaridou P, Philippou K, Phokas A, Rodosthenous J, Hadjimichael C, Omirou M.

title: What is in the Dust? Species-Level Profiling Reveals Pathogenic and Protective Potential of Microbial Communities in Daycare and Home Environments.
abstract: Indoor environments are rich in microbial diversity, which is influenced by multiple factors, including human activities, occupancy levels and the presence of pets. Environment-associated taxa were found to be prevalent in daycare and human-associated taxa in home environments during the COVID-19 pandemic, a period marked by profoundly altered social mixing and hygiene practices. In this study, we investigated the structure of microbial communities and their ecological profiles in daycare and home dust in the post-COVID-19 era. Microbial communities in household dust remain more heterogeneous, with a higher prevalence of human-associated species, than daycare samples. Full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing enabled species-level taxonomic resolution, yet approximately 40% of amplicon sequence variants remained unclassified, underscoring the vast, novel microbial diversity within our indoor environments encountered in everyday life. AI-assisted ecological profiling revealed a higher burden of pathogens and opportunistic pathogens in home environments than in daycares. Interestingly, the presence of pets had limited influence on microbial diversity in household dust. Finally, several species with known probiotic properties and immunostimulatory potential were present in both environments, reinforcing the notion that microbial exposure during the critical window of early childhood may confer protection against various non-communicable diseases including asthma, childhood leukaemia and other cancers.
authors: McKay JA, Harding-Crooks R, Sangal V.

title: Shift Towards Syndiniales Prevalence in Protist Communities During a Marine Heatwave.
abstract: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are becoming more frequent and severe, yet their impact on natural marine protist communities remains poorly understood. Using 18S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, we examined the effects of the extreme 2017/2018 Austral summer MHW on protist communities in three water masses off the southeast coast of New Zealand. During the MHW, alpha diversity declined significantly in Subtropical Waters (Shannon: 1.78 ± 0.42, p = 0.03) and the Front (Shannon: 3.26 ± 0.19, p = 0.05), driven by reduced evenness in Subtropical Waters (Pielou: 0.36 ± 0.06, p = 0.03) and by both richness and evenness in the Front. Communities also became more homogeneous, with lower dispersion among samples, and the water mass driven structuring of communities seen in non-MHW summers disappeared during the MHW. The taxonomic composition shifted substantially: the parasitic dinoflagellate Syndiniales became the most dominant group in Subtropical Waters and the Southland Front (up 68 and 30 percentage points, respectively), while Dinophyceae decreased by 47% and 20%, respectively. Since host-parasitoid interactions play a significant role in carbon and nutrient cycling, the strong increase in relative abundance of Syndiniales underscores the need to consider biotic interactions, including host-parasitoid relationships, when studying MHW impacts on marine protists.
authors: Heynderickx H, Allen R, Summerfield TC, Currie K, Hoffmann LJ.

title: Helicobacter pylori In Free-Living Amoebae: A Potential Environmental Reservoir for Persistence and Transmission.
abstract: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) is a highly adapted gastric pathogen responsible for one of the most prevalent chronic bacterial infections worldwide and a major cause of gastritis, peptic-ulcer disease, and gastric cancer. Traditionally considered predominantly a human-associated microorganism transmitted via oral-faecal routes, growing evidence challenges this paradigm by demonstrating its persistence outside the human host through interactions with free-living amoebae (FLA). This review critically examines current knowledge of the biological and ecological interplay between H. pylori and FLA, focusing on amoeba-mediated internalisation, intracellular survival, morphological plasticity, and protection from environmental stressors. We highlight FLA's ability to support the persistence of spiral and viable but non-culturable (VBNC) coccoid forms of H. pylori, potentially enabling prolonged survival in aquatic and food-associated environments and raising concerns regarding potential waterborne and foodborne transmission. Given the limited direct experimental evidence, we integrate insights from amoeba-resistant bacteria to illustrate convergent intracellular persistence strategies. By considering FLA as a potential underrecognised environmental reservoir, this review expands current frameworks of H. pylori transmission and persistence, with potential relevance to settings with inadequate sanitation. We also outline key mechanistic and methodological gaps and call for standardised models to clarify the ecological significance of these interactions and inform surveillance and control strategies.
authors: Lamrabet O, Bekliz M, Qumar S, Sebastian M, Abdurahman U, Hamad M, Semerjian L, Khoder G.

title: Bacillus tropicus and Bacillus safensis: A Potential Siderophore Producing Rhizospheric Bacteria: Its Characterisation and Optimisation.
abstract: Siderophore-Producing Rhizobacteria (SPR) have emerged as a viable approach to plant protection and crop health management in agriculture. It brings iron molecules into bacterial cells for use in a variety of metabolic processes, with applications in agriculture, medicine, industry, and the environment. In this study, 22 bacteria were isolated and screened for siderophore production from maize field soil. Seven of the 22 bacterial isolates showed discrete zones of orange colour, indicating siderophore production. However, only two potent siderophore-producing strains, Bacillus safensis (BMS-01) and Bacillus tropicus (BMS-15), were optimised and identified using physiological characteristics and 16S rDNA sequencing. After optimising siderophore production with glucose and sucrose as carbon sources and NaNO3 and (NH4)2NO3 as nitrogen sources, Bacillus safensis (BMS-01) and Bacillus tropicus (BMS-15) were found to have a significant ability to yield siderophore (60%-70% units) under ideal conditions of pH 8, 28°C. The study concludes that the strains Bacillus safensis and Bacillus tropicus show potential for siderophore production, which may warrant further investigation as biocontrol agents and plant growth promoters in future field trials.
authors: Tilwari A, Kalam S.

title: Management-Driven Effects in Soil Physicochemical Properties and Microbial Communities in Eastern Amazonian Agroforests.
abstract: Agroforestry systems (AFS) are a promising bioeconomic strategy for sustainable land use and soil recovery in tropical regions. However, the potential effects of different management practices on soil microbial communities remain poorly understood. This study compared two neighbouring AFS in Tomé-Açu (PA, Brazil) with similar land-use, size, and productivity but contrasting management: organic inputs (AGF19) vs. chemical fertilization (AGF27), alongside a native forest reference area. Soil samples were evaluated through physicochemical properties, litter composition, and amplicon sequencing (16S rRNA and ITS) across three soil depths. Despite similar soil and litter characteristics, AGF19 showed a lower abundance of phytopathogenic fungi and associations with beneficial fungal taxa as biomarkers. In contrast, AGF27 exhibited signs of a microbiota shift towards a stress-related community. These findings could be partially associated with modest management changes like favouring organic inputs, influencing microbial diversity, functional guilds, and soil chemistry. Differences in management could be potentially linked with the identification of a phytopathogenic fungal taxon (e.g., Fusarium) as a biological marker of the community sampled in the AGF27 soil. Although different from the native forest, the results strengthen the role of AFS as a sustainable agroecological strategy. Regular soil monitoring and microbiome-informed practices are essential for sustainable management.
authors: Dextro RB, Rossmann M, Freitas AS, Domini JA, Martins GL, Shoichiro U, Coutinho LL, Cruz AF, Ono N, Tsai SM.

title: Airborne Bacteria Are Influenced by Surrounding Soil, Litter and Vegetation at a Forest Campsite.
abstract: Contact with natural environments is increasingly linked to human well-being, yet the environmental sources shaping forest airborne microbiota remain poorly resolved. Here, we examined the relationship between the forest aerobiome and nearby ground reservoirs, focusing on litter and surface soil in a recreational forest. Bacterial communities were compared among air, litter and soil at a campsite spanning two vegetation types: a secondary broadleaf forest with diverse understory and a conifer plantation with sparse understory. Air was continuously sampled for 1 week using membrane filtration, and litter and surface soil were collected adjacent to each air sampler. We identified 6146 amplicon sequence variants across 19 phyla. Habitat (air, litter, soil) was the primary driver of community composition. Airborne communities were significantly distinct from both litter and soil and showed lower diversity. Although dominant higher taxa were shared across habitats, airborne assemblages were compositionally distinct at the genus and amplicon sequence variant levels, whereas litter and soil were more similar to each other. Nonetheless, substantial genus-level overlap between air and ground habitats was detected in both vegetation types. These findings indicate that litter and soil act as important, but incomplete, environmental reservoirs of forest airborne bacteria in recreational settings.
authors: Kimura K, Kondo NI, Nakajima N, Ito HC, Kadoya T, Tsuchiya K.

title: Community context redirects evolutionary trajectories under stress.
abstract: Adaptation to abiotic stress is typically studied in single-species cultures, yet bacteria inhabit and evolve in multispecies communities where neighboring organisms reshape, for example, nutrient availability, redox state, and cellular physiology. We recently demonstrated that interspecies interactions can alter the fitness effects of antibiotic resistance mutations, and we suggest that this reflects a broader principle. Stress-response networks are extensively cross-regulated and draw upon a shared, finite pool of proteomic and energetic resources. Consequently, activation of one pathway constrains others, creating physiological trade-offs. Because microbial interactions routinely perturb the physiological inputs to these networks, they can systematically redirect evolutionary trajectories under abiotic stress. We discuss the evidence, limitations, and implications of this framework for predicting evolution and understanding microbiome stability.
authors: Warsi OM, Andersson DI.

title: Phylogenetic, genomic and morphological characterization of Rickettsia senegalensis sp. nov., a novel Rickettsia species detected worldwide.
abstract: Members of the genus Rickettsia are widespread obligate intracellular bacteria with high medical and veterinary relevance. While Rickettsia senegalensis was previously isolated from cat fleas, Ctenocephalides felis, in Senegal, a comprehensive polyphasic characterization is required to validly publish its name. This study aims to provide the first detailed phenotypic, ultrastructural and genomic characterization of the type strain PU01-02ᵀ. Cultivation assays demonstrated that strain PU01-02ᵀ grows aerobically in XTC-2, SF9 and LD652 cell lines at 28 °C in a CO2-free atmosphere. Ultrastructural examination via scanning electron microscopy using a backscattered electron detector confirmed its free cytoplasmic localization and a typical rickettsial morphology characterized by rod-shaped cells ~1.5 µm in length and 0.3 µm in width. Whole-genome sequencing yielded a 1.62 Mb genome with a G+C content of 33.2%, and three plasmids were detected. Genomic analyses confirmed its status as a distinct species, placing it within the transitional Rickettsia group, specifically inside the Rickettsia felis cluster. A review of epidemiological data revealed that rickettsial genes identical to those of R. senegalensis had already been identified in several haematophagous arthropods, including fleas and ticks parasitizing various hosts such as cats, dogs, opossums and rodents worldwide. It has also been detected in cat tissues, suggesting a potential host-pathogen association.Based on these comprehensive characterization data, we formally propose R. senegalensis sp. nov. as a new species, with PU01-02ᵀ (=CSUR R184ᵀ =DSM 28250ᵀ) as the type strain.
journal: International Journal of Systematic and Evolutionary Microbiology
authors: Labarrere C, Houmenou CT, Fournier PE, Fenollar F, Mediannikov O.

title: 'Candidatus Phytoplasma zeae': community-driven species delineation of the maize bushy stunt phytoplasma, a Dalbulus-transmitted corn pathogen confined to the Americas.
abstract: A novel phytoplasma species, 'Candidatus Phytoplasma zeae', is proposed based on ecological distinctiveness, vector specificity, whole-genome comparisons and community consensus. This phytoplasma is associated with maize bushy stunt (MBS) disease in corn (Zea mays) and is transmitted exclusively by Dalbulus maidis and Dalbulus elimatus, two leafhopper species endemic to the Americas that has been reported in Brazil, Colombia, Mexico, Peru and several U.S. states. Here, we sequenced and assembled the genome of MBS phytoplasma (MBSP) strains from Brazil and the USA to describe and propose this new species. Although the 16S rRNA gene sequence of the proposed reference strain, MBSP-BRRS, shares >99% identity with that of 'Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris', key nucleotide polymorphisms distinguish 'Ca. P. zeae' from other 16SrI-related phytoplasma species. Genome-wide average nucleotide identity between 'Ca. P. zeae' and all available 'Ca. P. asteris'-related strains genomes was between 92.6 and 98.4%. Comparative genomic analyses revealed unique gene clusters in 'Ca. P. zeae' associated with amino acid transport, defence mechanisms and protein turnover, which may contribute to its specialization in corn. The ecological profile of 'Ca. P. zeae', including its narrow host and vector range and restricted geographic distribution, supports its recognition as a novel species under Rule c of the IRPCM guidelines. The designation 'Ca. P. zeae' is, therefore, proposed by members of the research community who have studied this pathogen for over a decade, with the MBSP-BrazilRS strain serving as the reference.
journal: International Journal of Systematic and Evolutionary Microbiology
authors: Pellegrinetti TA, Molligan J, Santos AA, Canale MC, Duffeck MR, Olmedo-Velarde A, Jacques J, Valmorbida I, Faris A, de Andrade MVS, Manica MAP, Luna M, Reyes-Caldas P, Rodriguez-Chalarca J, Dumonceaux T, Pérez-López E.

title: Campylobacter aecornae sp. nov., isolated from surface water in Slovenia.
abstract: During a surveillance study conducted in Slovenia to investigate Campylobacter species from environmental waters, various Campylobacter coli isolates from clades 1 to 3 were isolated. Additionally, a Campylobacter isolate designated CCS1377, originating from the Classical Karst region near Illyrian Bistrica, was initially identified as a relative of C. coli through preliminary identification using multiplex PCR and MALDI-TOF MS. However, these methods did not allow a definite classification of the isolate. In-depth phenotypic analysis revealed characteristics of CCS1377 that were distinct from C. coli and Campylobacter jejuni type strains. This included a unique cell and colony morphology, non-motility, weak autoagglutination and an inability to assimilate succinate. MALDI-TOF MS analysis revealed distinct biomarker ions compared to C. coli RM2228, supporting the hypothesis that CCS1377 represents a novel species. Whole-genome sequencing and comparative genomics confirmed its distinct phylogenetic position. The chromosome of Campylobacter sp. CCS1377 was estimated to be 1,853,379 bp in size with a G+C content of 30.78 mol%, and the genome was predicted to contain 1,878 genes. Average nucleotide identity analysis against genomes available in the NCBI database yielded a maximum value of 81.2% when compared to C. coli type strain NCTC11366T, significantly below the established species threshold of 94.2%. The digital DNA-DNA hybridization (dDDH) value was also below the species threshold of 70%, with dDDH d4=22.0% [19.7-24.4%] in comparison to the C. coli type strain NCTC11366T. Based on these phenotypic and genomic characteristics, we propose the name Campylobacter aecornae sp. nov. for the newly recognized Campylobacter species. The proposed type strain is CCS1377T (=DSM 102056T=LMG 33651T).
journal: International Journal of Systematic and Evolutionary Microbiology
authors: Zautner AE, Dieckmann AL, Bohne W, Kahlfuß S, Lorenzen S, Bunk B, Spröer C, Overmann J, Hoppert M, Smole Možina S, Zelenik K.

title: dbcan-nf: a Nextflow pipeline for accurate CAZyme annotation in metagenomes.
abstract: MotivationCarbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) are crucial for carbohydrate degradation in any ecological environment. However, CAZyme annotation is not easy in whole-genome shotgun (WGS) metagenomes, due to the lack of accurate, scalable, robust, and reproducible workflows. We previously published dbCAN as a web server and associated standalone tool run_dbcan that performs CAZyme annotation with assembled genomes as the input but not with raw WGS reads.ResultsHere, we present dbcan-nf, an accurate and scalable Nextflow pipeline integrating run_dbcan as a component step, for automated CAZyme annotation in metagenomes. dbcan-nf supports multiple analytical routes, including individual sample assembly (IA), multisample coassembly (CA), assembly-free (AF), and subsampling (SS), and accepts both short and long reads. Using five benchmark datasets, we showed that dbcan-nf (IA and AF routes) had a much higher accuracy (recall and F1 score) and detected more CAZyme families than the competing tool Cayman. Among the different routes, dbcan-nf-IA produced the most accurate CAZyme annotation, especially when the sequencing depth is sufficient (e.g., >1.0 Gb). However, as a read assembly-based method, dbcan-nf-IA had a higher computational cost than Cayman. Finally, dbcan-nf leverages Nextflow-supported high-performance computing execution for workflow-level scalability through concurrent processing of multiple samples.Availability and implementationhttps://github.com/bcb-unl/dbcan-nf.
authors: Zhang X, Yi H, Zheng J, Yin Y.

title: CentroFinder: a multi-feature framework for de novo prediction of fungal regional centromeres.
abstract: MotivationCentromeres are essential chromosomal loci, yet their computational identification remains challenging due to rapid sequence evolution, high repeat content, and the absence of conserved defining motifs. This challenge is particularly pronounced in fungi, where centromere architectures vary widely in size, sequence composition, and chromatin organization, limiting the effectiveness of single-feature or motif-based prediction approaches.ResultsWe present CentroFinder, a fungal-specific computational framework for de novo centromere prediction from long-read sequencing-based genome assemblies. CentroFinder integrates multiple genomic and long-read-derived features into a weighted scoring model to identify loci where centromere-associated signals converge. Benchmarking against experimentally mapped centromeres in Cryptococcus deuterogattii, Magnaporthe oryzae, and Neurospora crassa showed that 27 of 28 predicted intervals overlapped the corresponding experimental domains, yielding 96.4% chromosome-level detection sensitivity. Application to 11 additional fungal genomes produced one contiguous predicted centromeric region per chromosome, supporting the transferability of the workflow for chromosome-level centromere prediction.Availability and implementationCentroFinder is freely available as open-source software at https://github.com/RahnamaLab/CentroFinder. The pipeline is designed for high-performance computing environments and leverages features derived from long-read sequencing data.
authors: Salimi S, Colson S, Renfro M, Ma LJ, Rahnama M.

title: Correction to 'A Rapid, Field-Deployable Diagnostic Platform for Getah Virus Based on RT-RAA and CRISPR EsCas13d'.
The Limits of Bayesian Estimates of Divergence Times in Measurably Evolving Populations.
abstract: Bayesian inference of divergence times for extant species using molecular data is an unconventional statistical problem: divergence times and molecular rates are confounded, and only their product, the molecular branch length, is statistically identifiable. Priors on times and rates are needed to break this identifiability problem, imposing a lower bound on the uncertainty attainable under infinite data. With infinite data, uncertainty in node ages increases proportionally with their mean age, such that older nodes have higher uncertainty than younger nodes. If extinct taxa with known sampling times are present (ie "heterochronous" data), times and rates become identifiable and uncertainties go to zero with infinite data. However, in real heterochronous datasets (such as viruses and bacteria), alignments tend to be small and how uncertainty scales with data size has not been explored. Here, we conducted extensive simulations and analyses of empirical data to develop the infinite-sites theory for heterochronous data. Contrary to expectations, we find that uncertainty in ages of internal nodes scales positively with the distance to their closest tip with known age (ie calibration age), not their absolute age. Estimation uncertainty decreases with calibration age more slowly in datasets with more site patterns, although overall uncertainty is lower in such datasets. Our framework establishes the minimum uncertainty attainable with perfect calibrations and effectively infinite sequence data. In a vast majority of cases, viral outbreak data are not sufficiently informative to display infinite-sites behavior, and estimates of evolutionary timescales will depend on dataset size, information content, and model complexity.
authors: Ivanov S, Fosse S, Dos Reis M, Duchene S.

title: TSLC: differential abundance analysis method for identifying biologically relevant known microbes.
abstract: MotivationIdentifying biologically relevant microbes is a crucial task in human microbiome studies. Numerous computational and statistical methods have been proposed for this task. However, most existing methods are based solely on taxonomic information, even when whole-metagenome sequencing data are available, and thus cannot account for the fact that different microbes can perform the same or similar functions (known as functional redundancy) and for the contribution of unknown microbes to functional abundance. Hence, the identified differentially abundant microbes might not be biologically relevant to manifested phenotypes.ResultsTo address the issues with existing methods, we propose a two-stage procedure: (i) determining differentially abundant functions between groups; and then (ii) determining microbes significantly associated with each identified differentially abundant function. This procedure involves ℓ1 -penalized log-contrast models and debiasing procedures to account for the compositional nature of microbiome data and the bias induced by the ℓ1 penalty. We performed extensive simulation studies to illustrate the consequences of ignoring functional redundancy and the contribution of unknown microbes, and to assess the performance of the proposed method. We applied the proposed method to two whole-metagenome sequencing datasets and showcased substantial differences between the typical taxonomic-based analysis and the proposed method.Availability and implementationAn R package for the proposed method is available at https://github.com/rgbeblavy/TSLC.
authors: Beblavy R, Monaco CL, Newkirk CE, Xiao J, Sohn MB.

title: Rhizosphere Fungal Community Responses to Nitrogen Addition Reflect Genotypic Versus Trait Variation in the Marsh Sedge Schoenoplectus americanus Over Time.
abstract: There is growing recognition that shifting environmental conditions can alter the nature and potential benefits of plant-microbe interactions. While it is well established that interactions with fungi can benefit plants under environmental stress, little is known about how plant exposure responses correspond to different factors that might shape fungal communities, particularly over time. Using a resurrection ecology approach, we examined the relative influence of contrasting environmental conditions and intraspecific variation in the foundational marsh sedge Schoenoplectus americanus on rhizosphere fungal communities. Cohorts of ancestral plants germinated from 100+ year old seeds and modern plants were grown under low and high nitrogen (N) concentration in a common-garden experiment. Fungal communities were characterized according to plant presence as well as genotypic and associated trait variation. The study revealed that the influence of S. americanus on fungal communities differed between the nitrogen regimes. Under low N, fungal taxonomic, but not guild, diversity was higher in rhizosphere soils than unplanted controls. Plant effects were, however, diminished under high N conditions. We also found that heritable traits had limited influence on fungal communities, whereas both taxonomic and guild diversity and composition reflected genotypic variation and G × E interactions. Cohorts of ancestral and modern plants also recruited distinct fungal communities depending on N conditions. These results indicate that shifts in plant-fungal associations over time are contingent on prevailing environmental conditions. Our findings also indicate that N-driven changes in plant-fungal interactions likely alter ecosystem processes that are central to saltmarsh resilience to shifting environmental conditions.
authors: Liu Y, Blum MJ, Lumibao CY.

title: Derivation of oligonucleotide barcodes that are absent from natural sequences.
abstract: DNA barcodes are short synthetic sequences used to uniquely identify target molecules, samples, or objects, and are essential for a wide range of biotechnology applications including high-throughput sequencing, lineage tracing, genetic screens, massively parallel reporter assays, and DNA-based data storage. However, randomly generated barcodes are prone to off-target hybridization and cross-reactivity with endogenous biological sequences, which can compromise experimental specificity and interpretation. Barcodes derived from sequences that are entirely absent from natural genomes, termed DNA primes, offer an ideal solution by eliminating the possibility of unintended interactions with biological material. Here, we present barcodesDB, a comprehensive database of synthetic DNA barcodes systematically identified by scanning 403 199 complete organismal genome assemblies across the tree of life, together with 215 Gbp of raw metagenomic sequencing reads spanning marine, soil, polar and host-associated environments. These barcodes are absent, on either strand, from every assembly and sequencing read examined in the release described, providing maximal specificity and minimizing cross-reactivity for downstream applications. We provide an open-access web application that enables researchers to search for barcodes satisfying user-defined constraints, including GC content and substring requirements, and to query whether candidate sequences occur in nature. This resource supports robust and scalable barcode design for diverse experimental and applied contexts. Our database is publicly available at: https://barcodesdb.com/.
authors: Patsakis M, Provatas K, Mouratidis I, Georgakopoulos-Soares I.

title: Modular Platform for Recombinant Production of Highly Toxic Bacterial Proteins.
abstract: Bacterial protein toxins constitute a vast, largely untapped reservoir of potent bioactive molecules for antimicrobial discovery and biotechnology. However, their intrinsic toxicity often prevents recombinant expression in microbial hosts, limiting biochemical and functional characterization. Here, we present a modular platform for the recombinant production of highly toxic bacterial proteins based on covalent fusion of polymorphic toxins (PTs) to their cognate immunity proteins (PIMs), enabling transient toxin neutralization during expression. This strategy enabled recombinant production and purification of three previously refractory toxin families, PT7, PT8 and PT9. We further streamlined the workflow by introducing intracellular protease-mediated cleavage of the toxin-immunity fusion, reducing purification from four steps to two and increasing the recovered yield of PT9 from approximately 1-2 mg/L to ~4 mg/L. Extending the approach to PT37 further showed that computational redesign of the immunity protein and fusion architecture can enable production when the native fusion is insufficient. Purified PT7 and PT8 retained nuclease activity following denaturation and refolding, while refolded PT9 was structurally validated by X-ray crystallography, demonstrating recovery of functionally and structurally competent proteins. Together, these findings establish a modular strategy for recombinant production of highly toxic bacterial proteins and facilitate their biochemical and functional characterization.
authors: Fraenkel R, Cahana I, Sivan T, Fisher T, Nadav H, Bruchim S, Weisz J, Deouell N, Cheskis S, Shalom M, Imbert L, Oppenheimer-Shaanan Y, Levy A, Tzarum N.

title: Position Effect Variegation of Penicillium rubens Genome and Application in Heterologous Production of the Plant-Derived Anthraquinone Physcion.
abstract: The filamentous fungus Penicillium rubens is well known as an industrial host for producing penicillin and also used as a promising chassis for secondary metabolite biosynthesis. Chromosomal position effect significantly influences the functional implementation of exogenous genetic modules, but it remains underexplored in filamentous fungi such as P. rubens. In this study, a PiggyBac (PB) transposon-mediated mutagenesis library was constructed in P. rubens. High-throughput sequencing confirmed a broadly distributed with moderate local hopping of PB insertions across this fungal genome. To characterize the genome position effect, two genomic loci libraries including low-expression (P4) and high-expression (P7) positions were obtained respectively by flow cytometry. Heterologous biosynthesis of the plant-derived anthraquinone physcion in P. rubens, via targeted integration of its biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) into the P7 genomic loci, substantially boosted the titre to a level significantly higher than that achieved via integration at the P4 loci, demonstrating a direct correlation between the integration locus and the secondary metabolite output. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic elucidation of chromosomal position effect on heterologous biosynthesis of secondary metabolites in P. rubens and it also provides an insight for rational selection of integration sites in filamentous fungi.
authors: Wu M, Fu Y, Tang L, Yao Y, Pan Y, Liu G.

title: Potential Roles of Escherichia coli in IgA Nephropathy: Evidence, Mechanistic Hypotheses and Microbiota-Targeted Strategies.
abstract: IgA nephropathy (IgAN), the most common primary glomerular disease, involves mucosa-kidney axis dysregulation, with gut dysbiosis increasingly implicated in its pathogenesis. Certain Escherichia coli (E. coli) strains harbour virulence-associated features that promote intestinal colonization, barrier disruption and immune activation. Recent microbiome and metagenomic studies have reported an enrichment of E. coli in patients with IgAN, suggesting a potential link to the mucosa-kidney axis. Nevertheless, E. coli may contribute to IgAN through two major pathways. First, sustained LPS exposure may induce aberrant production of galactose-deficient IgA1 (Gd-IgA1) by stimulating B cells and activate the NLR family pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome in macrophages, thereby amplifying systemic and renal inflammation. Second, metabolic reprogramming is associated with increased circulating sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) and altered production of indole and trimethylamine (TMA); S1P may promote mesangial proliferation and fibrosis, whereas indole- and TMA-related pathways may contribute to tubulointerstitial injury and chronic kidney disease (CKD) progression. Beyond conventional gut microbiota-targeted interventions, emerging precision therapeutic strategies offer promising new directions for the etiological treatment of IgAN. This review summarizes E. coli virulence factors, pathogenesis, and host, environmental, and ecological factors driving its gut expansion in IgAN patients and outlines corresponding therapeutic strategies.
authors: Liu Y, Ning X, Liu Y, Yu Z, Liu J, Xu X, Zhao J, Sun S.

title: Evolution and metabolite signaling of fumarases (class I and II): origin, function, and subcellular targeting.
abstract: This study explores the evolutionary origins of class I and II fumarases across the tree of life, focusing on the prevalence and phylogenetic patterns of their enzymes. Using a dataset of ∼21,000 complete proteomes and MMseqs2 easy-search against known fumarase sequences, we identified representative sequences for each class and constructed phylogenetic trees. Class I fumarases are found primarily in bacteria and in several eukaryotic groups, including Protozoa, SAR, and algae, with absence in fungi and archaea and low presence in plants and animals. Their patchy distribution and absence in archaea suggest horizontal gene transfer from bacteria to eukaryotes. Class II fumarases are ubiquitously distributed across bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes. Phylogenetic and genetic analyzes suggest a closer relationship between eukaryotic class II fumarases and bacterial homologs (particularly Alphaproteobacteria) compared to archaea. These results support the hypothesis that class II fumarase originated early on in bacteria and was then inherited by vertical gene transfer by eukaryotes. Analysis of protein sequences and structures for both classes demonstrates high evolutionary conservation, consistent with their essential catalytic function. Fumarases, TCA cycle enzymes, have been implicated in DNA damage response in numerous organisms, in all domains of life. These enzymes have also been shown to be dual targeted to mitochondria and the cytosol/nucleus in eukaryotes. We have examined how these two functions are linked to the evolution of fumarases and concluded that the extramitochondrial functions and subcellular localization of fumarases were determined much later in evolution. We conclude that metabolic signaling and its specific metabolites may provide the driving force for the fumarases' dual function, dual targeting, and interaction with different entities in the cell.
authors: Miller O, Jacobi D, Carmel L, Pines O.

title: Overcoming Detection Lag in a Cryptic Panzootic: Chytrid Invasion Linked to Historically Enigmatic Amphibian Declines in the Brazilian Atlantic Forest.
abstract: As human activity accelerates the spread of pathogens and other invasive species, reconstructing the cryptic early dynamics of undetected invasions has become a central challenge in disease ecology and invasion biology. Here, we leverage museum specimens to reconstruct the invasion of Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd), a fungal panzootic driving global amphibian biodiversity loss, across historically enigmatic declines in the Brazilian Atlantic Forest. Two hypotheses have been proposed to explain Bd's historical dynamics in this region: long-term enzootic persistence versus recent epizootic invasion coinciding with declines. Using molecular screening, histopathology, and genotyping of museum and modern specimens, we find no evidence of Bd infection prior to the decline, followed by widespread infection immediately thereafter. Only the global panzootic lineage (Bd-GPL) was detected during the first year of post-decline sampling, implicating its invasion in driving regional losses. Infection prevalence varied among species following the decline, likely reflecting species-specific interactions between baseline susceptibility and ecological exposure risk. Contemporary host populations exhibit more uniform prevalence regardless of decline history, consistent with the evolution of pathogen tolerance under enzootic conditions. Together, these results provide the first site-specific evidence linking Bd-GPL invasion to enigmatic amphibian declines in Brazil and demonstrate the power of museum collections for resolving detection lag dynamics in emerging infectious diseases.
authors: Boyette JL, Carvalho T, Rodriguez D, Neely WJ, Medina D, Martins RA, Ossiboff RJ, Gomez Z, Vuyk WC, Buttimer SM, Paniagua Torres KA, Assis AB, Navas CA, Muletz-Wolz CR, Campana MG, Richards-Zawacki CL, Becker CG.

title: Supervised and covariate-adjusted dimension reduction for prediction and visualization using microbiome data.
abstract: Given that the gut microbiome has been shown to play a critical role in human health, discerning the relationship between microbial taxa and disease outcomes or phenotypes is of interest. Often, this involves association testing, predictive modeling, and visualizing trends in the data. Principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) is a commonly used dimension reduction technique in microbiome studies. PCoA relies on pairwise distances between samples and serves as a nonlinear alternative to the classic principal component analysis when non-Euclidean distances are used. Its low-dimensional embeddings provide intuitive visualizations but do not incorporate outcome-related information. Therefore, the low-dimensional principal coordinates may have poor performance in visualizing outcome differences, as well as in downstream disease prediction tasks. Additionally, covariates, such as demographics, lifestyle factors, and technical artifacts, can obscure true biological signals, leading to masked or spurious associations and limited generalizability. To address these limitations, we propose a supervised and covariate adjusted PCoA algorithm. By utilizing outcome information, while simultaneously minimizing the influence of nuisance variables, our method produces low-dimensional embeddings that better separate disease outcomes in visualizations and result in improved accuracy in downstream regression and classification tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method and highlight its ability to extract important associations between the microbiome and disease outcomes while mitigating nuisance variation through simulations and application to real microbiome profiling studies.
authors: Zang C, Tang L, Deek RA.

title: DecBin: Bayesian-optimized deep clustering for long-read metagenomic binning.
abstract: Accurate metagenomic binning is essential for reconstructing microbial genomes, thereby facilitating the discovery of novel taxa, the identification of pathogens, and the characterization of antimicrobial resistance genes. Most existing methods are designed for assembled contigs and cannot be directly applied to raw long reads. Although a few dedicated long-read binning methods have emerged, challenges remain in bin-number estimation and representation learning. Here, we propose Deep Embedded Clustering for Long-read Binning (DecBin), an adaptive method for directly binning raw long reads through integrating a variational autoencoder (VAE), Bayesian optimization, and deep embedded clustering within a unified framework. Computational experiments on large-scale simulated and mock-community datasets demonstrate that DecBin outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both long-read binning and metagenome-assembled genome recovery, while also achieving strain-level resolution in a low-complexity natural microbiome. Further analysis shows that the advantage of DecBin is partly attributable to its Davies-Bouldin index-guided Bayesian optimization, which explicitly evaluates candidate cluster numbers using a global cluster-validity criterion, thereby improving bin-number estimation across communities of varying complexity. Meanwhile, joint fine-tuning of the VAE encoder and clustering layer enables clustering feedback to refine the latent space, yielding representations better aligned with genome partitions. These findings highlight the potential of adaptive deep clustering for metagenomic binning directly from raw long reads without prior assembly. The source code of DecBin is freely available at https://github.com/LorMeBioAI/DecBin.
authors: Zhu YH, Li X, Liu Z, Liu J, Ye R, Xue W, Jiang G.

title: Prediction of bacteria-specific drug metabolism using a cross-attention-based model.
abstract: Drug metabolism by gut microorganisms is bacteria-specific and can have clinically significant consequences, including prodrug activation, drug inactivation, and the generation of toxic metabolites. However, existing computational approaches have primarily focused on community-level predictions or drug-to-microbe effects, without resolving the metabolic contributions of individual bacterial strains or the bidirectional nature of drug-bacteria interactions, despite advances in computational frameworks. Here, we propose a bidirectional cross-attention architecture, multimodal Bi-MHA, that integrates atom-level molecular embeddings and protein-level bacterial embeddings from pretrained models to generate a combined representation for classification. The proposed model was developed using reliability stratification and a $\mathrm{\lambda}$-scaled loss function on the training dataset and achieved consistent performance across three unseen tasks: unseen drug (receiver operating characteristic area under the curve [ROC AUC]: 0.690), unseen bacteria (ROC AUC: 0.920), and unseen interaction (ROC AUC: 0.949), ranking first among all compared models in the rank-sum metric. Beyond prediction, attention-based analysis not only indicated enzymatic reaction sites that were experimentally validated in previous studies but also prioritized candidate bacterial proteins, demonstrating interpretability at both the atom and protein levels. The proposed model also achieved a 15 percentage point improvement in accuracy over the KNN baseline on an external validation dataset of 85 out-of-distribution drug-bacteria pairs. Furthermore, the model was extended to community-level prediction as a proof-of-concept application using a weighted-abundance pipeline on an independent microbiome dataset. These results demonstrate the model's potential as an interpretable screening tool for drug safety evaluation and personalized medicine. The source code is available at https://github.com/Jaehyeon-O-Ob/Bacteria-Specific_Drug_Metabolism.
authors: Park J, Kim SE, Yang H, Cho NC, Kim H, Shin HK.

title: BRIDGE-KO: auditable transfer learning with bridged knockoffs improves cross-cohort microbiome prediction of immunotherapy response
Thirteen quick tips for bacteriophage genome annotation.
authors: Zaki BM, Bouras G, Kropinski AM, Wattam AR, Edwards RA, Aziz RK.

title: In silico prediction of metabolic trait robustness in microbial cells.
abstract: Microbial strains undergo notable biomass expansion in industrial applications subjecting populations to Darwinian selection. The consequent adaptive evolution may threaten the often tediously developed desired metabolic traits of the strains, such as flavor or platform chemical production. Yet, it remains unresolved how to predict the evolutionary trait robustness. Here, we propose TRAEV (Trait Robustness Against EVolution), a computational framework for in silico prediction of evolutionary robustness of metabolic traits and trajectories of desired traits in application environments. TRAEV uses constraint-based metabolic models for predicting environment-dependent trait-fitness dependencies and accounts for the stochasticity of adaptive evolution by using Monte Carlo-based perturbation analysis. First, TRAEV predicts the immediate metabolic phenotype in the new environment, and then, the subsequent evolutionary trajectories of fitness and desired trait. Metabolic trait robustness is quantified from the evolutionary trajectories as two scores: Robustness Score (RS) and Trade-off Score (TS). RS represents trait robustness and the overall trait level during evolutionary adaptation, whereas TS captures trait-fitness trade-offs. We validated TRAEV by predicting relative evolutionary robustness of heterologous pigmentation of two engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains and two desired aroma generation traits by multiple wine strains of S. cerevisiae if they were developed via a laboratory selection process. Thus, we showed how TRAEV predictions could guide strain development.
