Within the 2021 DENV3 subset (96 accessions), 18 records dated August 2021 were identical across 10,707 nucleotides to the older Sri Lankan genome AY099336.1. There were 21 variable E positions within the original 96-accession DENV3 cohort. Whole-cohort deduplication (47 retained) and retaining one representative of the 18-record group (79 retained) preserved all 21 positions. Excluding the group (78 retained) resulted in eight variable positions: 13 of 21 (61.9%) were lost due to differences in state at those positions between the excluded group and retained cohort. Nextstrain reference-specific exclusions selected the same 18 records; applying its full saved list produced 77 accessions and the same eight variable positions. E270 and E383, which had pre-2021 antibody-related evidence, did not meet the sequence-variation criteria for follow-up; however, E223 and E224 remained variable. Antibody-position enrichment was not statistically significant. These results indicate that cohort eligibility decisions may impact dengue E-protein variant prioritization despite representative-retaining deduplication. Genome identity does not indicate specimen identity or an antigenic phenotype.
authors: Begum, K. T.; Rafea, K. A. G.

title: Language-guided domain adaptation improves protein sequence rep-resentations for antimicrobial resistance analysis
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR), particularly antibiotic resistance in bacterial pathogens, complicates infectious disease management. Because bacterial resistance is often mediated by protein functions, including antibiotic inactivation and efflux, protein sequence analysis provides a molecular basis for digital AMR surveillance and therapeutic intervention. We developed BacLLM, a language guided protein representation framework that integrates annotation-derived functional knowledge into protein language model representations for AMR analysis in WHO priority bacterial pathogens. Through sequence enhancement, semantic enrichment of UniProt annotations, and cross modal contrastive learning, BacLLM transfers LLM encoded annotation priors into the sequence encoder. Compared with baselines, BacLLM provided more informative representations for resistance-gene identification and mechanism prediction, captured resistance associated mutational signals at single-residue resolution, and preserved taxonomic relationships not reflected by phenotype based clinical groupings. Moreover, BacLLM recovered resistance associated functional organization within a TolC-centered protein association network, prioritizing proteins with low sequence identity to TolC but predicted structural similarity to TolC. Extending from AMR characterization to therapeutic prioritization, BacLLM also improved strain-level phage host matching for phage therapy candidate prioritization. Together, these findings establish BacLLM as a protein representation framework supporting AMR surveillance, functional characterization, and therapeutic candidate prioritization.
authors: Ye, R.; Li, L.; Geng, Z.; Song, S.

title: PREMISE: A Quality-Aware Probabilistic Framework for High-Resolution Source Assignment in Metagenomic Sequencing
abstract: Metagenomic applications, from influenza A virus (IAV) subtype tracking to bacterial strain resolution, frequently require sub-species resolution.However, traditional $k$-mer-based methods fragment reads into short $k$-mers and discard per-base quality scores.By omitting both intra-read linkage and error information, these methods confound closely related genomic variants, thereby impeding real-time pathogen surveillance and containment.We introduce \premise (Pathogen Resolution via Expectation-Maximization In Sequencing Experiments), a probabilistic, alignment-based framework implemented in Rust for high-resolution source assignment against near-complete reference databases.\premise aligns whole reads using a bidirectional run-length FM-index and quantifies reference abundances with a quality-aware Expectation-Maximization algorithm mapped over a taxonomy.This framework applies an optional sparsity penalty to resolve ambiguous assignments, which is particularly important when sparse samples are mapped against reference databases rich in highly homologous candidate references.On ten dense CAMI II strain-madness samples, \premise achieves the highest species-level read classification F1 score ($0.992$) among eight evaluated methods, with no false-positive or missed species.At the strain level, \premise maps reads to their source genome with top precision ($0.80$ vs. at most $0.64$ for competing methods), achieves 100\% recall, and estimates abundances as accurately as the best competing tool.These results demonstrate \premise's ability to provide rigorous, uncertainty-aware source resolution across both dense and sparse metagenomes, accurately resolving targets ranging from viral subtypes to bacterial strains.\\textbf{Availability:} \url{https://github.com/sriram98v/premise} under an MIT license.\\textbf{Contact:} \href{sriramv@iastate.edu}{sriramv@iastate.edu}\\
authors: Vijendran, S.; Dorman, K.; Anderson, T. K.; Eulenstein, O.

title: Secondary growth in the tomato stem is suppressed by the flowering regulators FUL2 and STM3
abstract: Herbaceous eudicot crops such as tomato accumulate substantial amounts of secondary xylem in their stems, particularly in the basal part. As plants progress from the vegetative phase to flowering and fruit development, secondary growth continues to provide mechanical support and facilitate transport. To uncover how secondary growth is regulated in the tomato stem, we used laser capture microdissection RNA-seq to establish tissue-specific transcriptomic profiles. This revealed that key regulators associated with wood formation in poplar are also acting in tomato. Furthermore, we found that the flowering regulators FUL2 and STM3 are substantially expressed in xylem tissue. Subsequent functional analysis identified FUL2 and STM3 as key repressors of secondary growth, with ful2 or stm3 knock-out mutants exhibiting strongly increased secondary growth in older tomato stems. Notably, a higher order mutant in which both ful2 and stm3 were knocked out displays a similar non-additive phenotype, indicating, together with yeast two-hybrid data showing physical interaction, that FUL2 and STM3 act together in a complex. The expression levels of both genes remain low until after the floral transition but strongly rise during subsequent stem development. Transcriptomic analyses in ful2, stm3, and wild-type stems at stages before and after detectable anatomical differences, showed that the FUL2-STM3 complex represses distinct sets of NAC and MYB candidate regulators associated with xylem development. Interestingly, FUL2 and STM3 control these regulators in a stage- and position-dependent way, with candidates showing upregulation only at later stages in mid-height stems being already upregulated at earlier stages in basal stem regions. Our findings provide a tissue-resolved transcriptomic resource for tomato stems and reveal a role for FUL2 and STM3 in limiting secondary xylem accumulation as stem development progresses.
authors: Pandey, K.; Appiah, A. P.; van Velzen, R.; Zahn, I. E.; Basu, E.; Angenent, G. C.; Deuss, P. J.; Bemer, M.

title: Dual regulation of chemical stress-induced DDI2/3 expression by a transcription factor Fzf1 and nucleosome in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
abstract: DDI2 and DDI3 (DDI2/3) are duplicated genes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that exhibit strong induction by a transcription factor Fzf1 in response to chemical treatments like cyanamide (CY) and methyl methanesulfonate (MMS). Although, like DDI2/3, SSU1, YHB1 and YNR064C also contain an Fzf1-binding consensus sequence CS2 and are coordinately regulated by Fzf1, these genes are only modestly induced by CY and MMS. To identify additional cis-acting elements in the DDI2/3 promoter, we made DDI2/3 promoter deletions in a reporter system and identified upstream repressing sequences (URS) spanning 480 nucleotides. To test a hypothesis that the chromatin structure constitutes the URS, we utilized a yeast strain capable of histone H3/H4 depletion by shifting carbon sources. Following histone depletion, DDI2/3 were strongly induced in an Fzf1 dependent manner, while YHB1 was repressed. Interestingly, under histone depletion conditions, CY or MMS treatment further increased expression of all Fzf1-regulated genes to comparable levels in an Fzf1 dependent manner. A genome-wide MNase-seq analysis showed that CY treatment reduced the nucleosome occupancy at the mapped DDI2/3 URS region in wild-type cells, but not in in fzf1{Delta} cells. These findings collectively indicate that Fzf1 plays dual roles in regulating the DDI2/3 response to CY. Firstly, it binds CS2 and serves as a transcription activator. Secondly, it is required for the chromatin remodeling at URS. This two-tier regulation at the DDI2/3 promoter helps to explain why DDI2/3 achieve much higher fold induction by CY and MMS than other Fzf1-regulated genes, suggesting Fzf1 to be a candidate pioneer transcription factor.
authors: Du, Y.; Lin, A.; Brown, J. A. R.; Howe, L.; Xao, W.

title: RNA-targeted aminopyridine compounds provide a new antifungal strategy
abstract: While RNA is an emerging therapeutic target class, progress is limited by a shortage of well-defined targets in which ligand binding is coupled to measurable function. The group I intron, a self-splicing ribozyme essential in fungal mitochondria but absent from humans, offers both a tractable platform for exploring first principles of small molecule-RNA targeting and a selective antifungal target. We recalibrated an intron-splicing assay to approximate cellular conditions and performed an extensive, cryo-EM-guided structure-activity relationship campaign against the Candida albicans mtLSU intron. Ligands containing a flexible diamine outperformed conformationally constrained analogues, suggesting a general principle for engaging dynamic RNA surfaces and yielding lead aminopyridine 56 (IC 21.6 nM). Compound 56 synergizes with amphotericin B against C. albicans, suggesting a path for combination therapies. RT-qPCR confirmed direct target engagement in cells. This work establishes the fungal group I intron as a viable, mechanistically distinct antifungal target and a model platform for RNA-targeted discovery.
authors: Hwang, J.; Sisto, L. J.; Shi, T.; Van Zandt, M. C.; Pyle, A. M.

title: Endothelial protein C receptor is an entry receptor for Langya virus
abstract: Langya virus (LayV) was recently discovered in infected individuals with febrile illness and classified as a Parahenipavirus, a group of poorly understood pathogens. LayV is distantly related to Nipah henipavirus which causes recurring outbreaks with case fatality rates reaching up to 90%. No vaccines or therapeutics are approved for use in humans for any parahenipavirus or henipavirus despite their broad geographic distribution and pandemic potential. Here, we discovered that human endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR) is an entry receptor for LayV and that the tetrameric LayV attachment glycoprotein (G) binds EPCR avidly. We reveal the molecular basis of LayV G recognition of the EPCR receptor and provide a blueprint of the determinants of receptor ortholog usage. We found that human and shrew EPCR orthologs promote cell entry of LayV and of the closely related Mojiang pseudoviruses. These results along with the detection of several Parahenipaviruses in shrews set these pathogens apart from Henipaviruses, which use Pteropid fruit bats as reservoir hosts. Our data support future surveillance efforts, by enabling prediction of EPCR utilization among newly discovered Parahenipaviruses, and the development and evaluation of countermeasures targeting this emerging group of human pathogens.
authors: Park, Y.-J.; Song, J.; Gen, R.; Stewart, C.; Lee, S.; Veesler, D.

title: A reporter mouse model to map RIG-I expression and function in vivo
abstract: The cytosolic RNA sensor RIG-I is a critical component of the innate immune response to RNA viruses, yet few tools exist to track RIG-I in vivo. Herein, we report the development of a RIG-I reporter mouse, termed RIG-ImScar, that enables fluorescence imaging and tractable immunoprecipitation of RIG-I in vivo. These mice revealed enrichment of RIG-I expression in circulatory, lymphoid, and mucosal tissues and broad expression across immune cell types. RIG-I itself is upregulated in response to IFN. To distinguish RIG-I sentinel cells, which are programmed to express RIG-I at steady state, from IFN-responder cells, we crossed RIG-ImScar mice with Mx1GFP mice. Blocking IFNAR with a monoclonal antibody showed that basal RIG-I expression in immune cells was largely independent of type I IFN signaling, although Ly6Chi monocytes required IFNAR for RIG-I expression. To probe functional responses in vivo, we intranasally administered a RIG-I-specific agonist, SLR14. Mapping RIG-I expression across the lung identified alveolar macrophages as a critical RIG-I sensor cell population, and depletion of alveolar macrophages, but not neutrophils, slightly impaired lung IFN responses. Together, these findings support the use of the RIG-ImScar model to probe RIG-I dynamics in vivo and predict functional sensor cell populations across tissues.
authors: Ehrenzeller, S. A.; Hinesley, A. C.; Borunda, S.; Liu, S.; Richards, D. O.; Kwon, D.-i.; Mehrmann, T. M.; Phillbrick, W. M.; Thoresen, D. T.; Flavell, R. A.; Pyle, A. M.; Iwasaki, A.

title: The mycotoxin zearalenone couples secondary metabolism to N-acetylglucosamine catabolism
abstract: Fungal secondary metabolites are often viewed as terminal products of specialized metabolism, yet how their production influences the physiology of the producing organism remains poorly understood. Here, we show that zearalenone (ZEA) production is functionally coupled to N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) catabolism in Fusarium graminearum. Transcriptome profiling of a ZEB2-overexpressing strain revealed enrichment of GlcNAc metabolic functions, and exogenous ZEA induced key catabolic genes independently of Zeb2. Among pathway components, NAG, encoding GlcNAc-6-phosphate deacetylase, was critical for GlcNAc utilization, and its loss caused severe GlcNAc-dependent growth inhibition. Genetic impairment of NAG was poorly tolerated under elevated ZEA pathway activity. Conversely, NAG overexpression increased tolerance to exogenous ZEA and alleviated the growth defect associated with ZEB2 overexpression. Together, these findings reveal a functional connection between secondary metabolite production and primary nutrient metabolism and suggest that ZEA-associated metabolic remodeling contributes to the fitness of the producing fungus.
authors: Lee, N.; Yang, J.; Park, J.; Han, J. W.; Kim, H.; Son, H.

title: Monounsaturated fatty acid depletion is a metabolic pattern of pathogenesis surveilled to activate p38 MAPK innate immunity
abstract: Pathogen infection profoundly remodels host metabolism. Whether hosts sense specific pathogen-induced metabolic changes to identify microbial infection is not known. Here, we find that depletion the monounsaturated fatty acid oleate is a metabolic pattern of pathogenesis, specifically surveilled by the nematode C. elegans to identify active infection with a bacterial pathogen. We previously demonstrated that the enzymatic TIR (Toll/interleukin-1 receptor/resistance)-domain containing protein, TIR-1/SARM1, the key upstream activator of p38 MAPK PMK-1 immunity, is a guard protein in an effector-triggered immune response, positioned specifically on the surface of lysosome-related organelles to sense the toxic effects of bacterial infection. Here, we show that acute loss of oleate in intestinal cells during bacterial infection causes lysosome-related organelles to collapse, which induces the aggregation and activation of TIR-1/SARM1. Further, we find that oleate deficiency is a host vulnerability that concomitantly activates the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) KGB-1 nutrient sensing pathway, an adaptive response that promotes expression of TIR-1/SARM1 on lysosome-related organelles and is required for survival during infection. These data establish a mechanistic connection between fatty acid nutrition and innate immune regulation, and reveal that specific changes in host metabolism are surveilled to identify pathogen attack.
authors: Wani, K. A.; Rahman, S. S.; Pukkila-Worley, R.

title: Stoichiometric Encoding of Amplification Kinetics Enables High-Level Multiplexing in Single-Channel TaqMan Real-Time PCR
abstract: Multiplexing in TaqMan real-time PCR (qPCR) is limited to four-six targets per reaction by fluorophore spectral overlap. Amplification curve analysis (ACA) can discriminate several targets within one fluorescence channel from amplification curves (AC) kinetic features, but has been confined mainly to digital qPCR (dqPCR) and is sensitive to domain shifts between instruments and specimen types. Here, we co-design biochemical encoding of target-specific information into ACs and their computational decoding to achieve single-channel 8-plex TaqMan qPCR on a standard thermocycler. Using asymmetric PCR, we show that forward primer, reverse primer and probe concentrations act as a programmable encoding mechanism, generating a 27-condition design space of reproducible non-canonical ACs, conserved from digital to bulk qPCR. Applying this stoichiometric encoding to an 8-plex central nervous system pathogens panel increased inter-target separability, raising the mean silhouette score from 0.329 to 0.711. To decode ACs without labelled target-domain bulk qPCR data, we pretrained a transformer encoder by self-supervised learning on more than 170,000 unlabelled dqPCR curves and aligned source and target domains using conditional domain adversarial training. On contrived clinical specimens, the framework classified a canonical 7-plex respiratory virus panel with 83.6% accuracy (versus 67.7% for a supervised baseline) and the encoded 8-plex panel with 89.8% accuracy. Furthermore, stoichiometric encoding enabled resolution of double- and triple-target co-amplification events with 98.7% accuracy in controlled dqPCR experiments. This approach expands the information capacity of existing qPCR instrumentation without new hardware, fluorophores or oligonucleotides, offering a low-cost route to syndromic molecular diagnostics.
authors: Kreitmann, L.; Malpartida-Cardenas, K.; Mao, Y.; Sobala, K.; Zhao, Z.; Hin, S. C.; Hazarika, A.; Xu, K.; Miglietta, L.; Breese, Z.; Holmes, A. H.; Brengel-Pesce, K.; Drazek, L.; Rodriguez-Manzano, J.

title: Commensal Engineered Living Materials for Sustained Secretome Delivery and Wound Healing
abstract: Using living cells as dynamic biological factories offers immense potential for the continuous, localized production of therapeutic proteins within compromised tissues. This strategy is particularly compelling for treating chronic non-healing wounds, which lack therapeutics that are able to function effectively in the inflammatory microenvironment. Commensal bacteria have been shown to promote healing in these hostile microenvironments, yet applying live microbes directly onto compromised tissue is clinically unfeasible due off-target safety risks and engraftment challenges. Herein, we establish a well-defined commensal Engineered Living Material (cELM) that allows encapsulation, retention, function, and delivery of native beneficial bacteria for localized production and release of a pro-healing secretome over weeks. We specifically encapsulated a pro-healing human wound bacterial isolate, Alcaligenes faecalis, using biocompatible, click-reactive hydrogel building blocks (thiol- or vinyl-sulfone-functionalized multi-arm poly(ethylene glycol)) and systematically varied the density of the polymer network and of the encapsulated bacteria to establish design rules for creating pro-healing cELMs. Physical confinement in the hydrogel network ensured bacterial biocontainment, while the hydrogel mesh size still permitted diffusion of the therapeutic secretome. Notably, controlling encapsulation density revealed an inverse relationship wherein lower cell densities yielded significantly enhanced per-cell metabolic activity and provided sustained production of pro-healing secreted factors. In a murine diabetic wound model, these A. faecalis cELMs shielded the encapsulated bacteria from host clearance, maintained biocontainment, accelerated re-epithelialization, and improved wound bed maturity. Together, these findings establish design principles for cELMs that couple bacterial biocontainment with sustained secretome delivery, providing a promising platform for localized treatment of chronic wounds.
authors: Lois, C. O.; Grice, E. A.; Kloxin, A. M.; Sullivan, M. O.

title: Hybrid RY-mers increase aDNA alignment sensitivity
abstract: One of the key steps in ancient DNA data analysis is the accurate identification of endogenous short reads that originate from the ancient genome. Currently, this step is performed using general-purpose sequence aligners, such as BWA-aln, with parameter settings optimized for sensitivity. This approach results in increased runtime, even relative to standard DNA alignment workflows, and is not sufficient for aligning samples that are highly divergent from a reference database. We introduce hybrid RY-mers, a seed construct designed to incorporate aDNA-specific sequence damage. We adapt hybrid RY-mers to the existing concept of multi-context seeds and implement them in the read aligner strobealign. On simulated genomic and metagenomic datasets, we show that hybrid RY-mers result in higher mapping accuracy, while also reducing runtime by 4-6 times compared to the state-of-the-art aDNA alignment method BWA-aln. Furthermore, substituting aDNA aligner MALT in the metagenomic tool-suite aMeta with our new alignment approach demonstrated that aMeta gave a faster and less memory consuming detection of ancient taxa present in the samples.
authors: Tolstoganov, I.; Sahlin, K.

title: Residual barcode-like sequences and barcode-associated artifacts after Dorado and Barbell preprocessing of metagenomic reads
abstract: Background Residual barcode-like sequences after preprocessing are a quality-control concern in multiplexed Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) sequencing data, particularly in low-biomass, host-dominated samples such as blood. Using blood datasets spiked with a microbial mock community and prepared with the Native Barcoding Kit 96 V14 (SQK-NBD114.96), we compared Dorado 1.1.1, Dorado 2.0.0, and Barbell 0.3.2. Results Dorado demultiplexing reduced barcode-positive reads to approximately 2% of reads, with internal barcode-like matches in 0.17-0.19% of reads. Barbell 0.3.2 applied to untrimmed Dorado basecalls yielded an approximately 50-fold lower detector-defined internal-match rate (0.0035-0.0037%) while retaining 91.2-91.8% of input reads. In the NCBI core_nt release of 12 September 2026, the focused screen identified complete, ungapped 24 nt identity for 64 of the 96 barcodes (66.7%), comprising 505 distinct barcode-accession pairs across 482 accessions and 195 exported TaxID groups of mixed taxonomic ranks. Records annotated as rRNA genes, chromosomes/genomes, and plasmids accounted for 35.6%, 23.2%, and 22.4% of the pairs, respectively. The barcode was located within its native ligation flanks in 224 pairs (44.4%), including 170 (33.7%) with the complete Dorado barcode search window and 3 (0.6%) with the full adapter construct. Conclusion Barbell combined 91-92% read retention with lower detected internal barcode signals. After demultiplexing, barcode-like sequences remained in sample data. Moreover, kit barcode sequences, often within their native ligation flanks, were detected in reference records. Both findings call for careful preprocessing, reference inspection, and downstream validation. Further research should determine whether barcode-associated artifacts in reads and reference records affect taxonomic classification in clinical metagenomic workflows.
authors: Dinse, T.; Englaender, V. R.; Metz, S.; Schrezenmeier, H.; Messerer, D. A. C.

title: Multimodal cellular context enables molecular phenotyping from single-molecule trajectories
abstract: Single-molecule tracking (SMT) provides direct measurements of molecular dynamics in living cells, but motion alone rarely specifies the underlying biological process, without accounting for the cellular environment in which that motion occurs. Here, we present MIST (Multimodal Interpretation of Single-molecule Trajectories), a framework that brings the paradigm of image-based profiling to single molecules by integrating trajectory dynamics, emitter properties and cellular context into a common, reusable phenotype space. Using a reference panel of nine proteins in live Escherichia coli, we show that multimodal context more than doubled protein-specific information relative to trajectory features alone, a gap that learned trajectory representations did not close. MIST allowed de novo identification of shared transcription-translation phenotype at the nucleoid periphery. A fixed reference space detected effects of previously uncharacterized MukB ATPase mutations without retraining. MIST provides an interpretable and extensible framework for comparing proteins, mutants and conditions within a common space of molecular phenotypes.
authors: Redchuk, T.; Rehm, L.; Sui, Y.; Mäkelä, J.

title: Multi-scale biophysical modeling of fungal colony growth
abstract: Fungal colony growth is shaped by the fundamental physical operating principles of hyphal elongation, branching, and anastomosis, which collectively organize into macroscopic foraging networks. While sophisticated 3D models utilizing adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) on high-performance computing architectures can explicitly capture these discrete cellular mechanics, their immense computational cost prevents their integration into predictive ecosystem simulators. Here, building upon the Biological Modeling and interface eXchange (BMX) framework, we combine high-fidelity discrete hyphal mechanics with an analytically tractable, stochastic traveling-wave surrogate (sBARE) to provide multiscale simulations of fungal colonies at a fraction of the computational cost. By leveraging demographic fluctuations at the advancing front, our framework uniquely resolves macroscopic parameter degeneracies, separating the directed forward drift of leading tips from their effective diffusion to capture the macroscopic signature of negative autotropism in 3D networks. Simulations reproduce experimentally observed traveling wave profiles and confirm that interior network density under replete conditions emerges as an invariant self-regulated by fusion. Furthermore, global sensitivity analysis reveals that expansion speed and network density are governed by largely disjoint microscopic parameters. We demonstrate that because the physics of hyphal growth permit networks that are both exceptionally fast and dense, the empirical trade-off between sparse 'explorer' and dense 'exploiter' strategies observed in nature is not a strict mechanical constraint, pointing instead to metabolic limits on local growth rules. Our mathematically tractable approach bridges exascale-level cellular mechanics with macroscopic wave dynamics, enabling the integration of trait-driven advective fluxes and carrying capacities into the spatial transport and reaction network schemes of large-scale biogeochemical models.
authors: Yan, L.; Marschmann, G. L.

title: Development of a Pan-Proteome Multi-Epitope Vaccine Candidate Against Nipah Virus Using Reverse Vaccinology and Immunoinformatics Approaches
abstract: Nipah virus (NiV) is a high-consequence zoonotic pathogen for which no licensed human vaccine is currently available. This study applied a consensus-guided pan-proteome immunoinformatics framework to design and prioritize a multi-epitope vaccine candidate using sequence information from all nine NiV proteins. A total of 901 NiV protein sequences were retrieved, of which 842 passed quality filtering and were processed through clustering, multiple-sequence alignment, and protein-specific consensus generation. Consensus-derived fragments were screened for cytotoxic T-lymphocyte, helper T-lymphocyte, and B-cell epitopes, followed by multi-criterion filtering based on antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, conservancy, class-specific immune-response properties, and human-proteome similarity. Ten epitope-selection strategies were combined with two adjuvant candidates and three construct architectures to generate 60 vaccine constructs. Shortlisted candidates were subsequently evaluated for physicochemical properties, HLA population coverage, structural characteristics, conformational B-cell epitopes, TLR3 docking, molecular dynamics, immune-response simulation, and expression-oriented optimization. VC033_V6_BD_L03 construct was prioritized as the lead candidate and showed combined predicted population coverage of 99.78% worldwide and 99.96% in South Asia. Docking against human TLR3 structure 1ZIW yielded a ClusPro score of -1624.8. During a 100-ns molecular-dynamics simulation, the complex underwent early conformational reorganization followed by lower late-phase structural variation and persistent interchain hydrogen bonding. MM/GBSA analysis yielded a mean interaction-energy estimate of -20.52, 15.42 kcal/mol. C-ImmSim predicted coordinated humoral and cellular responses, while codon optimization generated a 1,539-bp expression sequence compatible with virtual cloning into pET-28a(+). These analyses prioritize VC033_V6_BD_L03 as a consensus-derived, pan-proteome NiV multi-epitope vaccine candidate for experimental evaluation of expression, immunogenicity, safety, and protective efficacy.
authors: Nishan, R. K.; Nahian, M.; Akter, B.; Basher, T.; Nodee, T. A.; Asha, I. A.; Sany, M. R.; Sathy, S. A.; Shila, F. S.; Islam, M. A.; Azad, A. K.; Islam, M. S.

title: Coarse-graining genome-scale metabolic models for dynamic, multi-scale simulations of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in gel environments
abstract: Microbial communities are shaped by coupled interactions between microenvironment conditions and the intracellular adaptations that emerge in response external metabolic cues. For pathogenic microbes such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, these interactions can rapidly generate heterogeneous sub-populations that exhibit adaptations for sustaining host infection and resisting antibiotic treatment. Technological strides in -omics data collection, combined with robust computational tools like genome-scale metabolic models (GEM) for predicting cellular metabolism, have yielded promising multi-scale depictions of microbial population development in simulated spatial environments. These multi-scale model simulations help establish and evaluate mechanistic contexts for how infection-enhancing behaviors might emerge in the population or be influenced by variable perturbations in the biological system. However, the number and rigorous tuning of parameters influencing the connections between intracellular-extracellular events pose barriers when shaping simulations to different in vitro systems of interest. In this work, we present a genome-scale, metabolism-informed continuum model (GEM-CM), a computational framework for coupling a reaction-diffusion model to a surrogate GEM representation that generates metabolic rate predictions informed by flux balance analysis outputs. A key feature of GEM-CM is its application of random forest regression, or ensembles, to coarse-grain the interface connecting the GEM and reaction-diffusion models down to a small set of input metabolites methodically chosen through the random forests evaluation of feature importance. To demonstrate GEM-CMs utility, we evaluated simulation predictions against P. aeruginosa PA14 populations radially propagating in low weight percentage agar gels. In addition to biomass growth, we simulated PA14 populations producing the cytotoxic secondary metabolite pyocyanin (PCN). GEM-CM could capture PA14 growth dynamics in agar gels when ensembles were provided with three carbon source inputs describing the simulated growth media. Bacterial motility parameters and the random forest ensemble allowed GEM-CM simulations to accurately predict spatial biomass distributions for PA14 populations over time and probe their PCN production dynamics. Ensembles also demonstrated robust performance for single gene knockout conditions with GEM-CM simulation accurately capturing the partial or total biomass and PCN inhibition observed in transposon mutant screenings. When evaluating transposon mutant population development, the GEM-CM framework additionally suggested that metH may be a promising target to inhibit the spatial propagation of PA14. This works proof-of-concept applications illustrated GEM-CM utility as an early stage multi-scale modeling tool for interrogating in vitro metabolic behavior in microbial populations.
authors: Kim, M. S.; Papin, J. A.; Ford, R. M.

title: Deprivation of dietary fiber promotes low-grade neuroinflammation and anxiety-like behavior in mice
abstract: Background: Intestinal health is an important determinant of brain function in that an array of gut perturbants, especially those targeting microbiota, influence behavior. Fermentable dietary fiber nourishes gut microbiota and, consequently, promotes gut health. We hypothesized that depriving mice of fermentable dietary fiber would impact their brain and behavior. Methods: Male C57BL/6J mice were fed standard grain-based chow (GBC), a compositionally defined diet (CDD) which mimics macronutrient content of GBC but lacks fermentable fiber, or CDD supplemented with the fermentable fiber inulin (CDD+INU). Mice were subjected to behavioral testing 6-8 weeks later followed by analysis of the gut brain axis. Results: Relative to GBC-fed mice, CDD-fed mice exhibited low-grade gut inflammation and a reduction in open-field center exploration, signaling heightened anxiety-like behavior. CDD+INU fully reversed these abnormalities arguing they were a consequence of fiber deprivation. Analysis of the gut microbiome and serum metabolome showed that CDD+INU increased oxidative phosphorylation and immune suppressive metabolites. Flow cytometric and transcriptomic analyses of the brain revealed an array of pro-inflammatory alterations in myeloid cells, CD4+ T-cells, microglia and astrocytes in mice fed CDD but not CDD+INU. Most notably, microglia and astrocytes from mice fed CDD, but not CDD+INU, displayed reduced mitochondrial respiration and greater glycolytic activity. CDD, but not CDD+INU consumption also reduced the abundance of oligodendrocytes and neurons, and increased hippocampal pro-inflammatory gene expression. Conclusions: Deprivation of fermentable fiber results in coordinated changes in brain immune composition and glial metabolic state that is associated with increased anxiety-like behavior.
authors: Oyetunde, A.; Pyaram, D. N.; Ngo, V.; Li, C.; Abo, H.; Zou, J.; Mabb, A. M.; Gewirtz, A. T.

title: Massive inter-animal horizontal gene transfer contributes to stress tolerance in the fungus gnat Bradysia coprophila
abstract: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in animals is thought to be rare and largely restricted to transfers from non-animal sources. In contrast to this expectation, we discovered that 9.2% of the protein-coding genes in the genome of the dark-winged fungus gnat Bradysia coprophila (order: Diptera, family: Sciaridae) are of potential HGT origin. Most of these genes have phylogenetic affinity with sequences from other distantly related arthropods that inhabit a shared soil-dwelling niche with B. coprophila. We show that these findings are inconsistent with genomic contamination or widespread gene loss and instead suggest a level of inter-animal HGT that is, to our knowledge, unprecedented. Consistent with their potential functional importance, ~75% of putative B. coprophila horizontally transferred genes (HTGs) are transcribed, and nearly all are shared across multiple sciarid fungus gnat species that diverged tens of millions of years ago. Further, domain annotations suggest that HTGs participate in diverse processes potentially important to B. coprophila ecology. We tested the functions of eight putative B. coprophila HTGs through transgenic expression in the fly Drosophila melanogaster and the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and found evidence that HGT has likely endowed B. coprophila with the novel capability to biosynthesize NAD+, as well as enhanced capacity to withstand stressors imposed by arsenic, cyanide, alkylating agents, and reactive oxygen species. Our findings reveal a previously underappreciated contribution of inter-animal genetic exchange to the evolution of genomic, physiological, and ecological novelty.
authors: Kapoor, R. R.; Kumar, T.; Nanda, P.; Phuangphong, S.; Murray, A. W.; Extavour, C. G.

title: Starve, stress, and mate: Activation of the CCAAT-Binding complex overrides sterility of mating-type heterozygous Candida albicans
abstract: Sexual reproduction in the human fungal pathogen Candida albicans is typically restricted by a strict genetic lock: the a1-2 repressor present in standard mating-type heterozygous (MTLa/) diploid strains, which actively represses mating competency. While severe environmental pressures are known to influence fungal development, the molecular mechanisms that allow cells to override this genetic sterility block remain poorly understood. Here, we identify the highly conserved CCAAT-binding complex (CBC) as the critical developmental hub that integrates environmental stress to unlock mating in heterozygous diploids. By combining proteomic mapping (ChIP-SICAP) and transcriptomics (RNA-Seq) to define the regulatory network of the core CBC subunit Hap5, we demonstrate that CBC hyperactivation completely overrides the a1-2 repressor. This activation triggers a robust white-to-opaque phenotypic switch and initiates a mating-competence program in MTLa/ strains genetically locked in a sterile state. Crucially, this developmental transition is antagonized by the iron-regulatory partner Hap43, but is strictly dependent on physical interaction at the chromatin level with Cap1, the master regulator of the oxidative stress response. Our findings reveal that the CBC and Cap1 couple metabolic starvation (glucose and iron limitation) and oxidative stress to a core reproductive program, providing a mechanistic basis for how C. albicans bypasses genetic constraints on sexual reproduction to generate genetic diversity under hostile host conditions.
authors: van Wijlick, L.; Martinez de San Vicente, K.; Sertour, N.; Rai, L.; LeibundGut-Landmann, S.; Bachellier-Bassi, S.; d'Enfert, C.

title: Scaffold-level validation is needed for phage–host inference from metagenome-assembled genomes
abstract: AbstractAccurate phage–host prediction underpins ecological interpretation and experimental validation of uncultivated phages, yet most current approaches rely heavily on metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). This reliance implicitly assumes that MAG-level quality metrics, such as completeness and contamination, ensure scaffold-level correctness. Here, we demonstrate that this assumption can be violated under particular challenging conditions. Tetranucleotide frequency (TNF) analyses reveal that CRISPR-associated regions often diverge compositionally from their host genomes, increasing the risk of misbinning, while experimentally validated phage–host genome pairs show consistent TNF separation between phages and their hosts, challenging compositional binning assumptions. Through controlled simulations, we further show that the incorporation of substantial amounts of TNF-matched, non-host phage sequences into high-quality MAGs does not substantially alter standard completeness and contamination estimates, rendering such errors largely undetectable. Together, these results expose a systematic and underappreciated source of bias in MAG-based phage–host inference and highlight the need for explicit scaffold-level validation beyond conventional genome-quality metrics. We further propose a practical scaffold-level validation framework that integrates structural linkage and taxonomic consistency to improve the reliability of phage–host inference from MAGs.

title: Benchmarking genome recovery and ecological representation across aquatic communities of contrasting complexity
abstract: AbstractGenome-resolved metagenomics links microbial taxa to metabolic potential, but the ecological interpretation of reconstructed genomes depends on which taxa and genomic features are recovered. How sequencing inputs and reconstruction workflows influence this representation across communities of contrasting complexity remains insufficiently resolved. We generated 252 metagenomic assemblies spanning short- and long-read input volumes, assemblers, and polishing modes in coastal water and mangrove sediment communities, and paired each assembly with five binners. Three findings emerged. First, the relative contributions of tool choice and data volume differed among assembly strategies, with algorithmic factors often explaining comparable or greater variation in recovery scores than sequencing input. Second, conventional performance gains did not consistently translate into improved taxonomic representation or genomic feature retention: putative gene dropout was generally highest in short-read, intermediate in short-read-first hybrid, and lowest in long-read-first representatives of shared genome clusters, particularly for mobile genetic elements, and discrepancies between MAG-derived and read-based taxonomic profiles persisted, especially in sediments and at finer taxonomic ranks. Third, although recovery frequency was positively correlated with abundance, high-abundance taxa still frequently failed to yield MAGs, particularly in complex sediments. Genome recovery was thus jointly shaped by sequencing input and workflow choice, and technical gains did not reliably translate into ecological fidelity. Recovery bias is therefore likely to be underestimated by conventional performance metrics, and our results indicate that such bias is more pronounced in the complex sediment communities than in the water communities sampled here.

title: Rhizosphere microbiota co-occur with pea root rot disease complex pathogens
abstract: AbstractDisease results from interactions between the host, the environment, and the pathogen. However, in complex pathosystems such as the soil-borne pea root rot disease, multiple co-occurring pathogens interact differentially across the host–environment–pathogen triangle, adding additional layers of complexity. The soil microbiome, including beneficial microbes and opportunistic pathogens, adds a fourth dimension of complexity in which microbial communities may either ameliorate or exacerbate disease. Here, using a large-scale field trial of Pisum sativum and naturally occurring root rot disease complexes, we used amplicon-based and shotgun metagenomic sequencing approaches to investigate interactions within the host–environment–pathogen–microbiome disease tetrahedron. Metagenomic analysis identified taxa whose abundance correlated with members of a disease complex dominated by A. euteiches and Fusarium species, including Pseudomonas, Sphingomonas, Bacillus, and Pythium. We also found that pathogen abundance showed a weak correlation with disease severity, and similarly, pea lines exhibited low consistency in disease responses across years. However, we found that disease level affected total prokaryotic and fungal community diversity. We identified microbial taxa that are positively and negatively associated with plant health, suggesting their roles in either disease suppression or exacerbation. Collectively, this work sheds light on the complexity of interactions across plant genotype-environment-pathogen-microbiome interactions to provide insights into multivariate contributors to each disease axis.

title: Parasitic infection shapes host metabolism, thermal tolerance and microbial diversity
abstract: AbstractParasitic infections impose physiological costs on hosts. Infection can alter host thermal tolerance, metabolism and host-associated microbial communities. When combined with thermal stress, infection may interact neutrally, increase resistance to subsequent stress, or act synergistically to exacerbate physiological cost. However, the mechanism underlying how these stressors affect host physiology remains poorly understood. We integrated physiological measurements with bacterial community profiling and host and parasite transcriptomics to assess how infection with the trypanosomatid Crithidia mellificae alters heat tolerance in the insecthost, the solitary bee Osmia cornifrons. Infection significantly reduced the upper thermal limit for host locomotion by an average of 11 °C, while combined infection and heat exposure produced the highest metabolic rates. Infection and heat stress were also associated with differences in bacterial community composition and Shannon diversity. Host transcriptomes showed increased expression of genes associated with detoxification under heat stress and reduced expression of genes associated with ATP production and amino acid biosynthesis during infection. Heat-stressed parasites increased expression of genes associated with chaperone activity and metabolic regulation. These results suggest that infection and thermal stress converge on shared metabolic constraints that reduce physiological resilience and narrow thermal safety margins. Our findings suggest that rising temperatures may destabilize host-parasite interactions and increase host vulnerability.

title: Differential effects of moisture on surface versus mineral soil microbial communities in the High-Arctic
abstract: AbstractMicroorganisms play key roles in nutrient/carbon cycling and greenhouse gas fluxes in High-Arctic soils. However, the influence of soil conditions on tundra microbiomes remains poorly understood. Using high-throughput sequencing, we studied bacterial, fungal and micro-eukaryotic communities in surface soil-biocrust matrices and the underlying mineral soil along two environmental gradients in Svalbard. Both layers harboured highly different communities. Gravimetric water content and pH were the most important factors in explaining the variation in surface communities. Cyanobacteriota were the dominant phototrophs in wetter tundra soils, while Chlorophyta dominated drier ones. In mineral soils, soil texture explained community structure for all three groups, together with carbon-content and carbon: nitrogen-ratio for micro-eukaryotes and bacteria. Chloroflexota and Spirotrichea dominated mineral soils with high clay content, Actinobacteriota positively correlated with sand content. The effects of soil texture and water content were also reflected in co-occurrence networks. Surface communities split into two network clusters linked to either drier or wetter tundra. The mineral soil network was much less coherent, and clustering was related to soil texture. Our findings revealed the important interplay between soil layer, toposequence and soil microbiome in the High-Arctic. As precipitation patterns shift, the impact of topography on tundra microbial communities is likely to intensify.

title: Transcription of the uropathogenic Escherichia coli vat gene is driven by multiple promoters whose activity is modulated by the cyclic AMP receptor protein.
abstract: Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC), a cause of urinary tract infections, expresses various virulence factors to enable it to infect and persist, overcoming host defences. One of these is the vacuolating autotransporter toxin (Vat), which causes vacuole formation and cellular damage in bladder epithelial cells. Bacteria tightly regulate transcript initiation of most virulence factor genes using either bespoke transcription factors, or, sometimes, global transcription factors, such as the cyclic AMP receptor protein (CRP), which regulates hundreds of bacterial genes, typically responding to nutritional stress. We report that CRP binds to the regulatory region of the vat gene and describe the complex nature of regulation of vat gene transcription in UPEC CFT073. In vivo and in vitro analysis revealed that whilst the vat regulatory region contains a CRP-activated promoter, P1, two additional promoters, P2 and P3, ensure that net promoter activity is not dependent on CRP. Functional -10 and -35 elements were identified for the P2 promoter, which is suppressed by CRP binding, blocking the -35 element. Expression from the P3 promoter is also supressed by binding of CRP over the transcript start site.
authors: Hothersall J, Mao Y, Yang J, Bai G, Syeda N, Alhammadi MM, Haycocks JRJ, Grainger DC, Browning DF, Busby SJW.

title: Directed evolution and characterisation of light harvesting complexes with altered spectral properties in purple non-sulfur bacteria
abstract: AbstractPurple non-sulfur bacteria (PNSB) are metabolically versatile microorganisms that inhabit diverse environments taking advantage of a remarkably efficient photosynthetic machinery. In this work, we describe the creation of a workflow for experimental studies aiming to compare the light absorption properties of structural variants of the light-harvesting complex 2 (LH2) of PNSB. Through the creation of a library of LH2 variants using site-directed mutagenesis, we engineered proteins with different spectral properties to be expressed in a LH2-defficient mutant of the model PNSB Rhodobacter sphaeroides. We validated this approach by reproducing a previously described mutant with a blue-shift in the B850 absorption peak, in addition to identifying a novel mutant exhibiting a red-shift of this peak. We characterised the fluorescence lifetime of the purified LH2 spectral variants in vitro. Our results suggest that directed evolution approaches can be used to systematically explore the landscape of light absorption in LH2s variants.

title: Simulating Science Communication for Vulnerable Populations: A Project-Based Learning Exercise in Undergraduate Medical Microbiology
abstract: AbstractWhile undergraduate medical education relies heavily on traditional lectures to deliver foundational biomedical sciences, standard models frequently isolate pathogens and mechanisms from the socio-economic realities of healthcare and community communication. To address this gap, we implemented and evaluated a project-based active learning intervention conducted in a classroom setting in a Medical Microbiology course, challenging students to synthesize complex scientific literature and design educational brochures tailored for socially vulnerable populations. At the end of the academic semester, student perceptions were evaluated through an anonymous mixed-methods survey completed by 51 participants. The quantitative outcomes revealed high student satisfaction, with participants perceiving the instructions as highly transparent and the cognitive challenge as well-balanced. Notably, most of the students reported that the project successfully consolidated core microbiological content, while also stating that focusing on vulnerable communities significantly expanded their understanding of how social determinants impact infectious diseases. This strong positive feedback was also present in the thematic analysis of the open-ended responses, which showed that students highly valued practicing the translation of technical medical jargon into accessible, community-friendly language within this simulated exercise, which was conducted among peers and instructors. The primary challenges reported were operational, centered on group coordination and managing the heavy academic workload typical of the end of the semester. Overall, our findings suggest that integrating brochure design and public health context into the basic science curriculum effectively anchors microbiology to clinical and humanistic realities, fostering preliminary communication skills, teamwork, and social responsibility better than standard expository lessons.

title: Expanding arsenal of type III CRISPR-Cas antiviral defense
abstract: AbstractCRISPR-Cas systems are adaptive immune systems that protect prokaryotes from invading genetic elements through acquisition of foreign nucleic acid sequences and RNA-guided recognition of target molecules. Among the diverse CRISPR-Cas families, type III systems represent a highly complex and versatile branch that couples sequence-specific interference with nucleotide-based signaling and activation of diverse downstream immune responses. Recent discoveries have substantially expanded the functional diversity of type III CRISPR-Cas systems, revealing new subtypes, ancillary effectors, nucleotide second messengers, signal-degrading enzymes, and viral counter-defense strategies. Here, we summarize current mechanistic and structural insights into type III CRISPR-Cas biology, from adaptation and target recognition to immune signaling, ancillary effector-mediated responses, and defense regulation. We further discuss emerging biotechnological applications of type III systems and highlight key unanswered questions shaping future research in this rapidly evolving field.

title: Taxonomic validation of Saccharomycotina yeast genome assemblies through type-material-anchored BLAST-based average nucleotide identity analysis at the NCBI.
abstract: The extensive genomic resources available for Saccharomycotina yeasts, including assemblies derived from type material, make this group well suited for genome-based taxonomic verification. This study evaluates the effectiveness of type-material-informed Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI) analysis for verifying the taxonomic assignments of Saccharomycotina genome assemblies. Public yeast genome assemblies were compared against type material assemblies using an alignment-based ANI workflow. Operational thresholds were established, and results were compared with DNA-DNA hybridization and FastANI analyses. Assemblies were evaluated by best-match status and coverage, and problematic type assemblies were flagged for further review. A 95% ANI threshold yielded high concordance with declared species assignments among query-to-type comparisons. Cases of high similarity between different species and hybrid genomes were identified, highlighting the need for expert taxonomic review in certain instances. The alignment-based ANI showed a strong correlation with traditional DNA-DNA reassociation values and agreed closely with FastANI for highly alignable assemblies. Type-material-informed ANI is a reliable tool for automated taxonomic verification of yeast genome assemblies, but its effectiveness depends on the availability and quality of type assemblies and accurate metadata. The approach enables continuous quality control and supports broader application in fungal taxonomy, with recommendations for improving reference coverage and data submission practices.
authors: Robbertse B, Kannan S, DiCuccio M, Hoffman J, Schoch CL, Kimchi A.

title: The Fungal Response Regulator Skn7: Domain Architecture and Multifunctional Roles in Fungal Biology
abstract: AbstractThe two-component phosphorelay system (TCS) is an ancient signaling module that enables fungal adaptation to changing environments. It consists of a hybrid histidine kinase (HHK), a histidine phosphotransfer protein (HPt), and downstream response regulators (RRs). Among these, the nuclear response regulator Skn7 is unique to fungi and absent from mammalian and plant cells, making it an attractive antifungal target. This review integrates structural and functional evidence to describe the multi-layered regulatory architecture of Skn7 orthologs across fungal phyla. Structurally, Skn7 combines prokaryotic signaling with eukaryotic transcriptional features through a conserved receiver (REC) domain, a central coiled-coil oligomerization motif, and a winged helix-turn-helix heat shock factor (HSF) DNA-binding domain. Functionally, Skn7 coordinates oxidative stress responses through cross-talk with the osmotic and cell wall integrity (CWI) MAPK pathways while acting as both a transcriptional activator and co-repressor. Notably, Skn7 regulates fungal development, morphogenesis, secondary metabolism—including pigments, toxins, and volatile organic compounds involved in interspecific competition—and cell fate by controlling autolysis and programmed cell death cascades. Overall, this comprehensive review highlights the evolutionary plasticity and functional versatility of Skn7, supporting its potential as a therapeutic target against fungal infections.

title: gutDBase: a comprehensive database for uncovering heterogeneous molecular characteristics of 15 gut-related diseases.
abstract: The gut plays key roles in digestion, nutrient absorption, and immunity. A variety of gut-related diseases have shown great heterogeneity in many aspects, including molecular characteristics, cellular composition, and microbial communities, which may reveal disease-specific therapeutic targets. In recent years, large-scale datasets have emerged to decipher associations between gut-related diseases and characteristics. However, these valuable data are independently scattered in different studies, and no comprehensive resource is available for integrating these data, which limits systematic investigation and cross-disease comparisons. To address this, we developed gutDBase (https://bio-computing.hrbmu.edu.cn/gutDBase), a comprehensive database that systematically integrates transcriptomic and microbial data for 15 gut-related diseases, curated from 175 bulk and single-cell datasets derived from 161 publications. gutDBase provides a user-friendly, interactive interface, and rich visualization tools to display the expression patterns and microbial compositions of different diseases from multiple perspectives. This resource is intended to support studies of disease mechanisms, facilitate target discovery, and advance translational research in gut-related diseases.
authors: He G, Guan S, Qi C, Liu X, Zhang X, Lu M, Sun W, Liu C, Li Y, Cheng L.

title: BioLiP3: a protein-ligand affinity database integrating curated data with LLM-enabled literature mining.
abstract: Quantitative binding affinities and three-dimensional protein-ligand structures provide complementary information essential for structure-based drug discovery, yet these data remain largely disconnected across existing databases and the biomedical literature. We present BioLiP3, a major extension of BioLiP that expands quantitative affinity coverage 13-fold within its structure-centered framework for biologically relevant interactions. BioLiP3 contains 593 423 affinity records, of which 591 820 are linked to three-dimensional protein-ligand structures: 45 386 experimentally resolved PDB complexes, 528 732 BindingDB-derived records with computationally generated structures, and 17 702 structure-linked records derived from LLM-mined biomedical literature. For records lacking experimental complex structures, we generate structural models using available experimental or predicted receptor structures, binding-site identification, and molecular docking, with experimental and computational structures explicitly distinguished. To complement existing databases, we developed a hybrid literature-mining workflow combining large language models with rule-based validation and independent verification to extract Ki, Kd, IC50, and EC50 measurements from PubMed abstracts while preserving provenance. BioLiP3 further integrates ligand-binding sites and protein, functional, and structural annotations via cross-references to PDB, UniProt, NCBI Taxonomy, PubChem, and original literature. Taken together, these advances make BioLiP3 a unified resource for data-driven protein-ligand interaction studies and structure-based drug design. BioLiP3 is freely accessible at https://zhanggroup.org/BioLiP/.
authors: Lu H, Ma X, Zhang R, Zhang Y.

title: PmiREN3.0: a multi-omics integrated and AI-assisted encyclopedia for plant microRNA research.
abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are key post-transcriptional regulators in gene regulatory networks (GRNs). Comprehensive research on miRNAs increasingly requires the integration of large and heterogeneous datasets, together with more efficient approaches to knowledge exploration. Here, we present PmiREN3.0, a major update of the Plant MicroRNA Encyclopedia. Compared with PmiREN2.0, species/subspecies coverage increased from 179 to 340, adding 22 orders, 51 families, and 108 genera. Using the same standardized workflow and annotation criteria as previous releases, high-confidence miRNAs were identified from 5319 small RNA sequencing (sRNA-seq) datasets, with miRNA loci increasing from 39 751 to 87 667 and miRNA families from 7838 to 18 389. Resources and tools from previous releases were extensively updated, while six new modules were added for primary transcripts, DNA methylation, RNA modifications, stress-responsive expression, metabolic pathways, and core GRNs. PmiREN3.0 also introduces miRai+, a knowledge service powered by artificial intelligence (AI) that combines a language model fine-tuned on miRNA knowledge with retrieval augmented generation. Evaluation yielded scores of 0.910 for answer relevance, 0.965 for faithfulness, and 0.906 for factual correctness. Together, PmiREN3.0 provides an expanded plant miRNA dataset and an integrated platform combining multi-omics data and AI-assisted knowledge services for plant miRNA research. PmiREN3.0 is available at https://pmiren.com/.
authors: Zhang C, Zhao J, Yu X, Wang Q, Zhao A, Ren Y, Yang Y, Wei H, Ma Y, Xu KW, Li L, Guo Z, Yang X.

title: ECOD in 2027: a modernized interface and an updated classification of protein domains.
abstract: The Evolutionary Classification of Domains (ECOD) organizes protein domains into a hierarchy of evolutionary relationships, encompassing both experimentally determined and computationally predicted structures. ECOD now classifies 2.9M domains, of which ∼1.37M derived from the Protein Data Bank and 1.51M from predicted models in the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database. The principal development we report here is a complete rebuild of the ECOD web resource. Search has been reconstructed around three modalities: (i) sequence, (ii) structure, and (iii) keyword. Foldseek now is the primary search method for the ECOD web page, searching a ∼457k representative domain database that is also distributed for local use. Results are presented through a Mol* interactive viewer, and a new API has been developed for programmatic access to the database. Alongside the interface, the pipeline for classifying new PDB entries has been rebuilt and returned to a regular cadence, family groups have been synchronized with Pfam v38.2, the bulk distributables have been reorganized and now include the search databases, the ligands in contact with each domain are recorded for experimental structures and annotated with drug cross-references from DrugDomain, and a registry has been introduced through which ECOD assigns stable identifiers to gene-called proteins and records the structures it predicts. ECOD is freely available at http://prodata.swmed.edu/ecod.
authors: Schaeffer RD, Roy B, Guo R, Cong Q, Medvedev KE, Grishin NV.

title: DoriC 14.0: an updated database of prokaryotic replication origins with significantly expanded plasmid oriV annotations.
abstract: Replication origins are essential for both chromosome duplication and plasmid maintenance; however, their annotation remains challenging across different replicon types and across diverse phylogenetic lineages. DoriC 14.0, the latest update of the database of replication origins in prokaryotic genomes, restructures and greatly expands this resource, with particular emphasis on plasmid replication. The latest release contains 530 178 computationally derived origin records, associated with 432 232 distinct sequence accessions, including 434 060 chromosomal and 96 118 plasmid records from bacteria and archaea. For bacterial plasmids, OriV-Finder was applied with RNA II-based refinement, whereas a customized OriV-Finder pipeline was employed for archaeal plasmids, which relies on archaeal replication-associated proteins and origin recognition box motifs. DoriC 14.0 combines literature evidence with computational predictions, maintains traceable record identifiers, and offers versioned data with release history. New features include comparative sequence support, related-origin links, interactive candidate replication initiation protein (RIP) sequence-similarity networks, plasmid-level analyses of origin recurrence, RIP profiles, and RNA II variation. The updated website provides filter-based browsing, record-level views, BLAST searches, and standardized downloads, and is freely accessible at https://tubic.org/doric/ and https://tubic.tju.edu.cn/doric/ without registration.
authors: Li Y, Dong M, Geng Y, Luo H, Gao F.

title: The European Nucleotide Archive in 2026.
abstract: The European Nucleotide Archive (ENA, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena), hosted at EMBL's European Bioinformatics Institute, is an open resource that supports the global life sciences community by enabling submission, archiving, dissemination, and reuse of the world's nucleotide sequencing data. In 2026, the ENA continues to explore and address challenges related to a rapidly evolving landscape. This includes sustaining the growth of the data volume, increasing diversity in data types, the need for more standardized metadata, and the connection of sequence data with data from other disciplines. To address these challenges, the ENA has enhanced its services to adopt the INSDC minimum specification for data requirements, introduce new sample checklists and collaborate on an experiment checklist, and progress on the implementation of GFF3 for annotations. The ENA continues to support global science through its global engagement that includes understanding its Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) requirements to the wider community. Sustainability is a major aspect of the archive, which has seen updates to incremental indexing and SRA read removal. Additionally, the broker community continues to be supported and expanded. In this paper, we discuss these challenges and opportunities as we continue to keep pace with the evolving life science data resource ecosystem and requirements.
authors: Rahman N, Ahamed A, Devaraj R, Gupta D, Haseeb M, Ihsan M, Ivanov E, Kadhirvelu V, Teh WK, Kumar M, Lathi A, Liyanage I, Meszaros L, Paramasivam L, Pauperio J, Paz R, Pesant S, Rajan J, Tutis I, Ventouratou M, Woollard P, Yuan D, O'Cathail C, Finn RD, Sarkans U, Cochrane G, Gonzalez-Porta M.

title: BioImage Archive: bringing bioimaging data together.
abstract: The BioImage Archive (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/bioimage-archive) is EMBL-EBI's flagship resource for life sciences image data. It serves as a deposition database for biological images across scales from near-atomic through to whole organisms, and across imaging modalities. The Archive's mission is to support the reproducibility of quantitative results based on imaging, support methods development including modern deep-learning-based approaches, and allow large-scale reanalysis of image data. Across the Archive's ecosystem, we provide access to over 11 PB of image data. Recent developments in underpinning infrastructure now allow interactive exploration, visualization, and streaming access to a subset of the Archive's data using the new OME-Zarr file format, and will ultimately provide access to all of EMBL-EBI's archived image data, including data from the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive. Migration of all holdings and a unified submission system are in progress.
authors: Zulueta-Coarasa T, Yoldas A, Anita L, Babalola K, Bircan K, Cattavitello C, Clementel D, Ma M, Mandloi T, Marks D, Rookyard C, Sherwood F, Somasundharam S, Velasquez M, Weyand S, Hartley M.

title: Metabolomics Subcenter (Met-SC): an integrated metabolomics database and analysis platform.
abstract: The rapid growth of metabolomics data has increased the need for integrated storage, analysis, and reuse. Here, we present Metabolomics Subcenter (Met-SC) V1.0 (https://metabolomics.dicp.ac.cn/), an integrated database and platform for standardized data deposition, spectral-resource management, online analysis, and disease-focused knowledge mining. The deposition framework captures project, sample, pretreatment, and instrument metadata across chromatographic, capillary electrophoresis-mass spectrometry, and nuclear magnetic resonance workflows. Met-SC contains 7  756  867 reference spectra associated with 1 989 680 unique compounds and 73  014  049 unknown-feature spectra derived from diverse biological matrices and experimental conditions. Its web-based analysis module provides 27 functions for data preprocessing, quality-control visualization, and statistical analysis. Metabolism-centered knowledge graph for colorectal cancer (MetKG-CRC) comprises 108 679 biomolecular entities and 600 093 literature-supported evidence triples. By linking data deposition, spectral resources, analysis, and evidence-supported knowledge exploration in a single platform, Met-SC facilitates reproducible metabolomics data management and downstream discovery.
authors: Wen L, Wang M, Zeng Z, Song S, Zhao W, Xu G, Liu X.

title: GutBiomeDB: an integrated human gut microbiome database of 168 464 samples.
abstract: The gut microbiome plays an important role in maintaining human health. Despite the rapid growth of literature and publicly accessible data on the gut microbiome, a large-scale, well-curated database integrating a unified matrix with multiple analytical tools is still lacking. Here, we introduced GutBiomeDB, a comprehensive database and analysis platform for the human gut microbiome. GutBiomeDB contains 168 464 samples from 482 BioProjects, spanning 72 countries, 224 disease conditions, and seven life stages. To improve the reusability and accessibility of data, the uniformly processed taxonomic profiles generated by Abdill et al. were reused without reprocessing to construct a matrix of 4680 taxa and 3142 genera, and disease, life-stage, sex, and geographic metadata were manually curated by our team. Additionally, GutBiomeDB offers four tools for in-depth analysis: "Differential Analysis" for comparing diversity and abundance of user-selected cohorts and performing random-effects meta-analysis across projects; "Interaction Network" for comparing disease and healthy-control co-occurrence networks; "Lifecycle Atlas" for visualizing genus trajectories across seven life stages; and "Health Index" for searching similar samples and scoring uploaded genus profiles. GutBiomeDB serves as a versatile and valuable resource for advancing a broad spectrum of gut microbiome research and clinical relevance. GutBiomeDB is freely accessed at https://gutbiomedb.online.
authors: Zhai J, Liu BH, Guo LY, Li Y, Liu J, Su X, Cui R, Zheng D, Sun Y, Dai C.

title: SABIO-RK in 2027: enzyme kinetics data with modernized framework and enhanced data access.
abstract: SABIO-RK (https://sabiork.h-its.org) is a publicly available database providing expert-curated information on biochemical reactions, kinetic parameters, enzymes, and experimental conditions. For over 20 years, it has served as a central resource for experimentally measured enzyme kinetic data, as required for modeling in systems biology, in enzymology research, and lately to train machine learning predictors or AI-driven data extractors. Here, we report on SABIO-RK's comprehensive redesign of its infrastructure and interfaces for improved usability and scalability. The updated system integrates data input, curation, and public access into a unified JSON-based framework with full version control for transparency and reproducibility. The new web interface offers streamlined navigation and enhanced search with over 60 fields. Browse functionality provides structured database overviews, while the Results Explorer allows interactive refinement of search results, which can now be saved and reused. A secure RESTful API enables open programmatic access, returning results in JSON, CSV, SBML, or EnzymeML formats. As of September 2026, the database contains 76 973 entries from 8149 publications, covering 10 375 reactions, 2315 enzymes (EC (Enzyme Commission) numbers), and 14 224 chemical compounds. The new SABIO-RK also improves the curation workflow, simplifies user feedback, and facilitates future community curation. Upcoming features include AI-driven literature recommendations, entity recognition, and the integration of visual search.
authors: Rey M, Wittig U, Hu X, Müller W.

title: Ribocentre-FoldBridge: a comprehensive database bridging RNA chemical probing data and 3D structures.
abstract: RNA chemical probing generates nucleotide-resolved profiles in vitro and in cells, while X-ray crystallographic or cryo-electron microscopy models provide high-resolution structural models but remain comparatively low throughput. Aligning these experiments from different modalities may provide insights into RNA structure formation and molecular functions. Here, we present Ribocentre-FoldBridge (https://foldbridge.ribocentre.org/), an AI-assisted, curator-reviewed database linking curated chemical-probing profiles with experimentally determined 3D structures. This database catalogues 12 types of RNAs, linking 256 929 probing profiles across five experimental categories to 5321 structure-linked cases. It interactively visualizes the probing profiles that align with RNA secondary and tertiary structures at nucleotide resolution. We demonstrate probe-specific reactivity patterns across paired, unpaired, and solvent-accessible structural contexts. The database aims to provide a reproducible evidence layer for examining RNA structure-function relationships across heterogeneous experiments, and thus facilitate the development of new RNA structure or function prediction programs.
authors: Sun H, Hu L, Peng X, Zhang W, Lin J, Huang J, Zhang C, Huang L, Miao Z.

title: scSpAS: an integrated single-cell and spatial atlas of transcript isoform regulation.
abstract: Alternative transcript initiation, splicing, and 3'-end processing jointly shape transcript isoform diversity, but these regulatory layers remain fragmented across separate single-cell and spatial resources. Here, we present scSpAS, an integrated database of alternative transcription start site (ATS), alternative splicing, full-length transcript isoforms, and alternative polyadenylation (APA) in human and mouse. It contains 123 datasets, including over 418 000 cells and 82 000 spatial spots across healthy and disease contexts, covering 13 cancer types, 5 infectious conditions, 8 inflammatory diseases, and 90 healthy samples. Based on uniformly standardized pipelines, we utilized 5' capture and 3' capture single-cell RNA-sequencing data to identify ATS and APA sites, and the Smart-seq2 and long-read sequencing data to identify the alternative splicing events and isoforms. In total, scSpAS contains >648 000 alternative splicing events, 432 000 ATS, and 621 000 APA sites, as well as over 551 000 transcript isoforms. The database further integrates regulatory annotations derived from CLIP-seq, ATAC-seq, and CAGE-seq, together with predicted splicing regulatory motifs. scSpAS enables users to retrieve events, isoforms and genes, examine differential usage at cell-type and spatial levels, and in different biological and physiological conditions; furthermore, users can inspect the potential regulatory mechanisms of all events. It is freely available at https://scspas.chenlulab.com/.
authors: Chen L, Liu D, He Z, Xu Z, Li R, Yang Q, Gao Z, Xia R, Song J, He T, Wang Y, Lin JW, Chen L.

title: The UCSC Genome Browser database: 2027 update.
abstract: Since 2000, the UCSC Genome Browser (https://genome.ucsc.edu) has served as a standard tool for visualizing and comparing annotations across thousands of genome assemblies. Users can browse and visualize a wide range of data types from gene annotations to regulatory regions and comparative genome alignments. Once the data view is configured, the Genome Browser image can be exported for use in publications. Beyond visualization, users can use our tools to compare and export the annotations for further analysis. This year's feature updates include the full release of a tool to copy annotations between related assemblies, QuickLift; feature additions to our data-hosting service HubSpace to enable live editing of configuration files; two new display configurability options: "My Annotations" and custom item coloring; and several improvements to genome assembly discovery and track management. Beyond these new features, 28 new annotation tracks have been added across three broad categories: variant databases and interpretation, gene regulation, and transcriptome and gene expression. These include ENCODE4 cCREs and other ENCODE4 regulatory annotations, variant frequencies and phased variants from national sequencing projects, and two massively parallel reporter assay tracks.
authors: Speir ML, van Baren MJ, Barber GP, Benet-Pages A, Birgmeier J, Casper J, Clawson H, Diekhans M, Fischer C, Gonzalez JN, Hinrichs AS, Lee CM, Nassar LR, Perez G, Raney BJ, Robinson J, Smith AD, Alde E, Kitiyakara B, Haussler D, Kent WJ, Haeussler M.

title: GlyTouCan v4: a redesigned interface and expanded functionality for the international glycan structure repository.
abstract: GlyTouCan (https://glytoucan.org) is the international, species-neutral glycan structure repository that assigns stable, globally unique accession numbers to glycan structures independently of the experimental method used to determine them. Here, we describe GlyTouCan version 4, released on June 22, 2026, which introduces a completely redesigned user interface with substantially faster browsing and searching, including a new "archetype" view that groups registrations that differ only in the anomeric or ring form of the reducing-end residue together for clearer filtering of the >256,000 glycans now registered. Version 4 provides an improved graphical structure input, via the updated browser-embedded GlycanBuilder application, for both searching and registering structures. Users may now sign in with an ORCID ID in addition to a Google account, and all previously released v3 REST API endpoints remain fully backward compatible. Version 4 also introduces a framework for industry affiliates, providing a structured pathway for commercial organizations that work with or synthesize glycans, while all existing academic database-partner relationships are maintained. GlyTouCan remains freely available to all users without charge, login, or registration for browsing and searching. We also summarize the repository's data content, which spans >600 monosaccharide types and, judging from these, includes many glycans of probable bacterial or plant origin.
authors: Shiota M, Ono T, Matsubara M, Kimura N, Masding T, Tsukada N, Inoue K, Yamada I, Aoki-Kinoshita KF.

title: iGPSC-DB: a comprehensive database for an inferred single-cell genetic perturbation atlas.
abstract: Genetic perturbation-induced transcriptional reprogramming drastically remodels tumor cellular phenotypes and tumor microenvironment crosstalk.
