Unraveling the heterogeneous cellular responses to genetic perturbations is essential for the mechanistic dissection of tumors and the discovery of therapeutic targets. Here, we present iGPSC-DB (https://bio-bigdata.hrbmu.edu.cn/iGPSC-DB), a database designed to infer connections between tumor microenvironmental cells and diverse genetic perturbation events and to dissect the heterogeneous cellular responses to these perturbations. iGPSC-DB curates associations linking 178 114 perturbation events that target 7407 genes to 9 249 080 single cells from 1580 samples across 88 cancer types. iGPSC-DB also provides seven user-friendly tools for retrieving and analyzing: (i) inferred associations between genetic perturbation events and cells/cell types; (ii) the inferred perturbation-associated effects of perturbations on cellular functions, developmental trajectories, and cell-cell communication within the tissue microenvironment; (iii) the combined effects of different perturbations on cells, facilitating the design of combination therapeutic regimens; (iv) the impact of different perturbations on the differentiation trajectories and functional states of malignant cells; and (v) the association between perturbed target genes and clinical survival outcomes. iGPSC-DB will serve as a valuable resource to advance single-cell-resolution research on gene functions, regulatory mechanisms, and the discovery of tumor therapeutic targets.
authors: Wang P, Chen Z, Zhang Y, Kang A, Xing J, Wang X, Xu L, Lu S, Song X, Guo Q, Xu Y, Li F.

title: YEASTRACT+: the 2026 update with focus on global quantitative transcription regulation data and metabolic engineering applications.
abstract: YEASTRACT+ (http://yeastract-plus.org/) is a tool for the analysis, prediction, and modelling of transcription regulatory data at gene and genomic levels in yeasts. It incorporates three integrated databases: YEASTRACT, PathoYeastract, and NCYeastract, focused on Saccharomyces cerevisiae, pathogenic yeasts, and non-conventional yeasts of biotechnological relevance, respectively. In this release, YEASTRACT+ offers upgraded information on transcription regulation for 13 yeast species, extending the database to two additional yeasts of the basidiomycota phylum, the pathogenic yeast Cryptococcus neoformans, and the biotechnologically relevant Rhodotorula toruloides. A dramatic upgrade in the quality of the data provided occurred, as regulatory associations between transcription factors (TFs) and target genes are now associated with quantitative assessment. Quantitative impact of TFs on gene expression levels enabled the construction and release of two additional analytical tools: quantitative rank by TF, for the prediction of the most relevant TFs underlying a given transcriptomics dataset; and metabolic engineering based on integrating the quantitative impact of TF expression into genome-scale metabolic models. Altogether, this release of YEASTRACT+ provides unparalleled access to massive, curated, quantitative data associated with gene expression control in 13 yeast species, and a set of tools to enable its full exploitation towards fundamental, biotechnological, and health-related applications.
authors: Coutinho L, Paulo L, Couceiro D, Val T, Oliveira J, Costa IV, Zolotareva M, Matos M, Fernandes M, Mupueleque M, Sá-Correia I, Teixeira MC, Monteiro PT.

title: LncRNAfunc 2.0: an evidence-integrated knowledgebase for regulatory and functional interpretation of lncRNAs in cancer.
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) play diverse regulatory roles in cancer, yet their functional interpretation remains largely based on molecular associations and computational predictions, while experimentally derived evidence is fragmented across heterogeneous resources. Here, we present lncRNAfunc 2.0, an updated knowledgebase for systematic functional interpretation of cancer lncRNAs through multi-source evidence integration. Compared with the previous version, lncRNAfunc 2.0 reprocesses pan-cancer data from The Cancer Genome Atlas, incorporates normal-tissue and cancer-cell-line contexts from GTEx and CCLE, substantially expands binding and interaction evidence, and introduces perturbation evidence for lncRNAs and their regulators. These resources are integrated with association-based analyses and computational predictions as complementary evidence for interpreting lncRNA-associated regulatory relationships. lncRNAfunc 2.0 organizes functional knowledge into six biological dimensions: dysregulation, upstream regulation, lncRNA-mediated mRNA regulation, transcript remodeling, protein regulation, and tumor phenotypes. This framework connects regulatory determinants of lncRNAs with their downstream molecular relationships and phenotypic associations, including mRNA regulation, alternative splicing, protein regulation, survival, molecular and immune phenotypes, and drug response. Overall, lncRNAfunc 2.0 provides an evidence-integrated framework for exploring context-dependent lncRNA functions and regulatory mechanisms across cancers. lncRNAfunc 2.0 is freely available at https://lncrnafunc.xu-bioinfo.com/.
authors: Yang M, Li J, Lu X, Liu J, Zhou X, Zhao L, Wu X, Xu Y.

title: R-loopBase v2.0: species- and cell type-resolved quantitative R-loop maps and R-loop regulatory resources.
abstract: R-loops are non-canonical nucleic acid structures implicated in diverse cellular processes and diseases. We previously developed R-loopBase to address the pressing challenges of inaccurate R-loop maps and the limited understanding of the R-loop regulatory network. However, R-loopBase provided only human R-loop maps with categorical confidence and did not account for cell type specificity. These limitations, coupled with the emerging R-loop profiling technologies and advances in R-loop regulatory mechanisms, have motivated the development of R-loopBase v2.0 (https://rloopbase.nju.edu.cn). After uniformly re-analysing 358 R-loop mapping datasets generated by 16 technologies, we introduce a quantitative R-loop scoring framework that assesses genome-wide R-loop confidence in human, demonstrating strong concordance with known R-loop biology. We further extend the framework to specific cell types and mouse, fruit fly, and yeast. In parallel, we substantially expand the collection of R-loop regulators across species, enabling the inference of changes in R-loop homeostasis. Building on these expanded datasets, we implement several new interactive features and analytical tools, including an expanded multi-species genome browser, deep learning-based R-loop prediction, R-loop homeostasis analysis, and a streamlined data download portal. We anticipate that R-loopBase v2.0 will serve as an enhanced, up-to-date one-stop resource for the R-loop research community.
authors: Gu R, Hu J, Gao Y, Yang H, Lin R, Zhong X, Zhang KX, Li W, Hu Q, Wei L, Xing Z, Chen JY.

title: OrganiZymeDB: a comprehensive database of enzyme stability and function in the presence of organic solvents.
abstract: Low enzymatic tolerance to organic solvents is a major bottleneck for the development of industrial biocatalysis, since many substrates have limited water solubility, thus requiring the use of organic solvents for substrate solubilization and process economic viability. Yet, despite decades of experimental research in this field, no public resource currently exists that systematically collects and curates these data, limiting their accessibility and reuse for large-scale analyses and for the development and validation of computational methods. To address this gap, we present OrganiZymeDB (https://organizymedb.org/), a comprehensive, manually curated database of 28,121 experimental measurements of enzyme stability and function in the presence of organic solvents, compiled from 646 publications and covering 704 distinct proteins. Each entry is extensively annotated with the experimental conditions, including assay type, solvent identity and volume fraction, assay solution composition, pH, temperature, substrate(s), product(s), and enzyme production method, as well as the protein 3D structure and cross-links to other databases. OrganiZymeDB will assist both experimentalists, by providing straightforward access to solvent-compatibility data for enzymes of interest, and computational scientists, by providing a well-curated dataset to develop and evaluate methods for predicting enzyme solvent tolerance, ultimately enabling the design of robust industrial biocatalysts.
authors: Debruyne R, Pucci F.

title: GlycoPOST: expanding glycomics data sharing to glycoproteomics through the updated MIRAGE guidelines.
abstract: GlycoPOST (https://glycopost.glycosmos.org) is a public mass spectrometry (MS) data repository for submitting and sharing glycan-related raw MS data along with structured experimental metadata, in accordance with the Minimum Information Required for A Glycomics Experiment (MIRAGE) guidelines. As of 1 September 2026, GlycoPOST hosts 602 projects containing 7.6 TiB of data, of which 445 are publicly available. In this update, we implemented major updates to GlycoPOST, expanding its scope from glycomics to glycoproteomics by incorporating the recent revisions published on the MIRAGE MS guidelines, in addition to enabling users to filter "presets," which are units for metadata in GlycoPOST, by keywords and last update date. The newly introduced concept of "project type" enables each GlycoPOST submission, referred to as a "project," to be classified according to whether it contains glycomics or glycoproteomics data. This makes it easier to select reusable metadata profiles (presets) by displaying only categories relevant to the experimental field. Furthermore, with the introduction of a project type specifically designed for glycomics-assisted glycoproteomics experiments, it is now possible to register data and metadata from both glycomics and glycoproteomics within a single project. These updates will promote standardized data sharing and reanalysis across glycomics and glycoproteomics using GlycoPOST.
authors: Takahashi Y, Wang Z, Noguchi R, Seno A, Aoki-Kinoshita KF, Okuda S.

title: Early terminated transcripts and missing proteins reflect artifacts in bacterial proteomes.
abstract: The high redundancy of many bacterial proteomes can be used to evaluate proteome quality and identify sequence errors. We have used MMseqs2 clustering with subsequent filtering to identify clusters that contain sequences from at least 50% of the clustered proteomes to build sets of core proteins that include proteins from 95% of the clustered bacteria. These clusters typically capture >80% of proteins in the bacteria. Because these clusters have highly uniform length (the median cluster has >99% of its proteins at the mode length), short (133%) proteins are likely artifacts. Most "outlier" proteins are found in fewer than 10% of clusters, and "high-outlier" clusters are over-represented in a small fraction of proteomes, which often have poor proteome BUSCO fragment scores. Short-outlier proteins are artifacts; at least 80% of short-outlier genomes contain mode-length copies of the protein, which were missed because of frameshifts, termination codons, or initiation codon choice. MMseqs2 clustering with 50% participation provides robust sets of core bacterial proteins and can be used to identify lower-quality proteomes and proteins.
authors: Insana G, Martin MJ, Pearson WR.

title: DeSCENT: Deconvolutional Single-Cell RNA-seq Enhances Transcriptome-based Cancer Survival Analysis.
abstract: MotivationSingle-cell RNA-seq captures tumor heterogeneity, but it is rarely available together with patient survival outcomes. Bulk RNA-seq cohorts provide survival data but lack direct measurements of cellular expression.ResultsDeSCENT generates reference-informed cellular profiles from bulk RNA-seq and combines both representations for survival prediction. We evaluated DeSCENT with three survival models on eight TCGA cancer cohorts. Compared with Bulk, DeSCENT improved average C-index and generally improved time-dependent AUC, while integrated Brier score results were mixed. External validation showed higher average C-index than all three baselines, although performance was lower than in internal evaluation. These findings support the use of cellular representations in the evaluated transcriptome-only setting.Availability and implementationCode: https://github.com/YonghaoZhao722/DeSCENT. Archival snapshot: doi:10.5281/zenodo.22073099.Supplementary informationSupplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
authors: Zhao Y, You Z, Shen Y, Chu J, Gong X, Li T, Wang Z, Xu C, Luo Z, He Y.

title: scPhyloGRN: gene regulatory network inference guided by lineage topology in single-cell developmental data.
abstract: MotivationGene regulatory network (GRN) inference from single-cell transcriptomes is complicated by expression patterns associated with both cell state and shared ancestry. Cellular phylogenies provide developmental context, but incorporating relationships among individual cells into gene-level regulatory inference remains challenging.ResultsWe present scPhyloGRN, a supervised framework that integrates single-cell gene expression with cellular phylogeny to prioritize directed transcription factor (TF)-target candidates within the observed gene set. The framework maps cell ancestry to gene associations that guide graph construction, attention in a dual-stream encoder, and lineage-consistency regularization. We evaluated scPhyloGRN against ten methods across 17 dataset-reference settings spanning four mouse embryos and one Caenorhabditis elegans dataset. scPhyloGRN showed an overall advantage in regulatory edge prioritization, supported by additional evaluations using shared candidate spaces. Removing lineage information reduced AUPRC in the ablation analyses, while branch-level and regulator-level analyses showed improved ranking and recovery of reference-supported regulatory candidates.Availability and implementationSource code and analysis workflows are available at https://github.com/Maria0852/scPhyloGRN, with a versioned archive at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22793831.
authors: Meng R, Wang K, Hu J, Hu Z, Zhou D.

title: Inhibition of quorum sensing and biofilm in Pseudomonas aeruginosa by erythrinin B: Bioinformatic evidence for the LasR binding
abstract: Quorum sensing (QS)-regulated virulence factors and biofilm formation are major contributors to antimicrobial resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa. This highlights the urgent need for novel anti-virulence strategies that can disrupt these pathways and reduce such infections. The objective of this study was to evaluate the inhibitory potential of erythrinin B against QS-regulated virulence factors and biofilm formation in P. aeruginosa PAO1. Erythrinin B significantly suppressed pyocyanin (72.27%), pyoverdin (68.22%), protease (83.08%), and elastase (62.16%) production in a dose-dependent manner, while rhamnolipid inhibition was lesser (29.17%). Biofilm biomass was reduced by 73.02% at 300 μg/mL, corroborated by microscopy, which revealed diminished adherence and scattered planktonic cells. EPS (exopolysaccharides) and alginate levels were also markedly decreased, indicating disruption of biofilm matrix integrity. Molecular docking demonstrated that erythrinin B binds to LasR receptor (−11.7 kcal/mol), forming hydrogen bonds with Thr75, Tyr56, Tyr64, and Ser129, alongside hydrophobic and van der Waals contacts. MD simulations confirmed the stability of complex, with minor conformational changes compared to apo LasR. MM/GBSA analysis revealed favourable binding energy (−26.89 ± 2.04 kcal/mol), dominated by van der Waals interactions, with key contributions from Val76, Trp88, and Leu36. These findings indicate erythrinin B as potent QS inhibitor that attenuates virulence and biofilm formation in P. aeruginosa.
authors: Mohammed A. Alshuniaber

title: Two novel soil-derived Beauveria species from eastern China: integrative taxonomy and pathogenicity against Ostrinia furnacalis
abstract: Species delimitation in Beauveria is challenging because of conserved asexual morphologies and extensive cryptic diversity. Three soil-derived Beauveria isolates from Anhui, Jiangsu, and Shandong Provinces, China, were investigated using a concatenated four-locus dataset comprising ITS, Bloc, TEF, and RPB1. Detailed cultural and microscopic morphological characterization was performed on GDMCC 3.1077 (AH08D02) and GDMCC 3.1078 (JS02A02), the designated type strains of the two proposed novel species. Their separation was further supported by differences in conidial dimensions and pairwise nucleotide sequence identities of 520/539 bp (96.47%; 12 gap positions) for ITS, 925/997 bp (92.78%; 52 gap positions) for Bloc, 250/263 bp (95.06%; 23 gap positions) for TEF, and 919/926 bp (99.24%; no gaps) for RPB1 between two strains. The concordance of multilocus phylogenetic placement, nucleotide differentiation, and microscopic morphological characteristics supports their recognition as two novel species, described here as Beauveria anhuiensis sp. nov. and B. shunxiangii sp. nov. Laboratory immersion bioassays against third-instar larvae of Ostrinia furnacalis demonstrated concentration-dependent mortality for both type strains. At 1 × 108 conidia/mL, day-9 mortality was nearly 100% for GDMCC 3.1077 and 90.0% for GDMCC 3.1078. The day-9 LC50 were 0.763 × 106 and 2.018 × 106 conidia/mL for GDMCC 3.1077 and GDMCC 3.1078, respectively, while the corresponding LT50 at 1 × 108 conidia/mL were 5.06 and 6.01 days. Although GDMCC 3.1077 yielded numerically lower lethal concentration and lethal time estimates, the overall difference in day-9 mortality between the two strains was not statistically significant. These findings demonstrate the pathogenic activity of both type strains under laboratory conditions and support their further evaluation as potential biological-control resources.
authors: Qiongbo Hu

title: A mosaic of bacterial communities and their functional potential across Antarctic moss, lichen and soil
abstract: IntroductionBacterial community composition differed markedly among substrates, whereas broad community-level differences between sampling localities were not statistically detected. The recovered U. aurantiacoatra bacterial community was dominated by Pseudomonadota, while A. regularis and soil communities exhibited greater taxonomic diversity, with Pseudomonadota, Actinomycetota, and Cyanobacteriota as dominant phyla. Functional profiling revealed distinct metabolic patterns across microhabitats. Bulk soils exhibited the broadest metabolic potential and nearly complete nitrogen-cycling pathways. The A. regularis microbiome was enriched in autotrophic machinery, high-affinity transport systems, and environmental sensing pathways, whereas the lichen microbiome displayed a more streamlined functional profile, lacking diagnostic nitrogenase genes and dissimilatory pathways.DiscussionThese findings highlight the importance of substrate identity in structuring bacterial communities across adjacent Antarctic microhabitats. The observed differences in taxonomic composition and functional potential suggest that mosses, lichens, and soils provide distinct ecological niches, potentially influencing microbial contributions to nutrient cycling in Antarctic terrestrial ecosystems.
authors: Ekaterina Pushkareva

title: From gut education to central infiltration: microbiota-driven immune trafficking along the gut-brain axis
abstract: The classical paradigm of central nervous system (CNS) immune privilege has evolved toward recognizing a dynamic, multi-organ neuroimmune axis. In recent years, the gastrointestinal tract has been widely recognized as a major immune reservoir, where rather than functioning as a localized physical barrier, the gastrointestinal mucosa acts as a vital educational center that instructs systemic immune responses. Within the gut-associated lymphoid tissue, dietary inputs, microbial metabolites, and commensal colonization imprint intestinal adaptive and innate immune cells with distinct functional phenotypes and migratory signatures. Through coordinated molecular mechanisms, these gut-educated immune cells egress from the mucosa to reach distant sites, with the CNS representing a critical destination. In experimental models, under homeostatic conditions, gut-derived signals direct the physiological seeding of central border zones and parenchyma, where specialized populations maintain baseline tissue surveillance, reinforce barrier integrity, and calibrate neurodevelopmental behaviors. Conversely, pathobiont expansion, loss of short-chain fatty acid-producing commensals, and mucosal barrier disruption predominantly promote pathogenic gut priming, transforming gut-resident cells into autoreactive or pro-inflammatory effectors that breach central neurovascular borders. Once inside the CNS, these gut immune cells can contribute to neurodegeneration, ischemic injury, and neuroinflammatory pathology. However, this migration is not always destructive; specific gut-educated populations are simultaneously deployed to central boundaries to execute anti-inflammatory and counter-regulatory protection. By tracing this microbiota-driven intestinal priming to central infiltration, we highlight shared homing mechanisms identified mainly in preclinical models (mouse models, germ-free and photoconvertible animals), while outlining translational challenges in establishing their role in human neuroinflammatory pathology.
authors: Daniel Hevia-Magaña

title: Unique and novel methanotroph taxa from the tropics: taxonomic novelty and a gateway to methane mitigation and valorization applications
abstract: Methanotrophs, aerobic to microaerophilic bacteria that oxidize methane, play a critical role in mitigating greenhouse gas emissions. While most cultured methanotrophs have originated from temperate regions, tropical methanotrophs remained largely unexplored until recent efforts from India and Southeast Asia. The first methanotroph described from the tropical region was Methylomicrobium kenyense (renamed Methylotuvimicrobium kenyense, an alkalophilic methanotroph isolated from Kenyan soda lakes, in 2000). However, after that, there is a large gap till 2014–2015. In the last 10 years, six novel taxa have been described from tropical rice fields and wetlands. The present review focuses on the novel methanotrophs described from the tropics. India has contributed the most, with five novel methanotrophs, including two novel genera—Methylocucumis and Methylolobus —two novel species of Methylobacter, and one novel species of Methylomicrobium. Methyloterricola oryzae, a novel genus-species, was isolated from the rice fields of the Philippines. All novel tropical methanotrophs are Type I and belong to the Gammaproteobacteria, with unique morphologies ranging from the cucumber-shaped cells of Methylocucumis oryzae to the coccoid aggregates of Methylolobus aquaticus and the slightly polygonal cells of Ca. Methylobacter coli. The habitats are diverse: rice fields, wetlands, and mammalian guts, thereby extending the ecology of methanotrophs. Collectively, these discoveries expand global methanotroph diversity, establish tropical rice ecosystems and wetlands as hotspots for methane mitigation, and provide experimental models for linking genomic traits to ecological persistence. Future applications include biotechnological valorization of methane and enhanced methane mitigation strategies for climate change. By applying these microbes in industrial and environmental settings, methanotrophs can take center stage in ecological sustainability and climate resilience.
authors: Pratibha Srivastava

title: Engineering endolysins as antibacterial biologics: protein engineering design strategies and trade-offs
abstract: Endolysins, the phage murein hydrolases, are promising alternatives to conventional antibiotics. They are highly target specific, rarely induce resistance and spare commensal microbiota. Synergy between endolysins and certain antibiotics has also been well documented, which further supports their therapeutic potential. However, clinical translation is constrained by protein instability, immunogenicity, limited Gram-negative bactericidal activity and short in vivo half-life. This narrative review examines protein engineering strategies for endolysin development and reconciles conflicting mechanistic observations in the literature. It proposes a trade-off framework and context-dependent design principles for engineering next-generation endolysin-based therapeutics.
authors: Priyanka Bhowmik

title: Gut microbiome-derived metabolites in prostate cancer: microbial mechanisms of immune modulation, androgen metabolism, and therapeutic implications
abstract: The global burden of prostate cancer continues to rise, yet conventional biomarkers and therapies face substantial limitations due to tumor heterogeneity and treatment resistance. The gut microbiome has emerged as a critical regulator of host metabolism and immunity, with its bioactive metabolites influencing prostate cancer pathogenesis through multiple interconnected pathways. Short-chain fatty acids, secondary bile acids, microbiota-modulated tryptophan metabolites, and microbiota-derived androgens modulate immune surveillance, androgen metabolism, and therapeutic responses via hormonal and inflammatory signaling networks. These metabolites exert context-dependent effects that vary with concentration, disease stage, and the tumor microenvironment. This narrative review comprehensively synthesizes current mechanistic evidence on microbiome-derived metabolite signaling and evaluates the potential of circulating microbial metabolites as non-invasive biomarkers, while outlining future research priorities for clinical translation in prostate cancer management.
authors: Xi Xiao

title: A glycosylation-associated hemagglutinin substitution improves the breadth of an influenza B mRNA vaccine
abstract: IntroductionInfluenza B virus is an important cause of seasonal influenza, with its contribution varying across regions and seasons. Historically, influenza B viruses have been classified into two major lineages: B/Victoria (BV) and B/Yamagata. No naturally circulating B/Yamagata-lineage viruses have been confirmed after March 2020, making protection against BV the current priority of influenza B vaccination. In our previous study, we demonstrated that the T214A mutation significantly alters the cross-neutralization capacity of this antigen, potentially through altered glycosylation. Notably, the WHO-recommended vaccine strain for the season, B/Austria/1359417/2021 (BV21), lacked the relevant glycosylation position.MethodsWe used an mRNA platform to compare the cross-subclade protection provided by B/Wyoming/06/2014 (BW06) and BV21 within the B/Victoria lineage. We also introduced the D212N substitution into BV21 as a minimal antigenic modification.ResultsThe D212N substitution restored the glycosylation motif in BV21 and enhanced cross-neutralizing responses against the tested heterologous strains. Mice immunized with a high dose of the D212N-modified vaccine showed 100% survival following challenge with the tested viruses from different subclades.DiscussionOur findings provide valuable insights for the development of broadly protective influenza B vaccines.
authors: Chenyan Zhao

title: TLR2-dependent SOCS1 induction by Ureaplasma urealyticum attenuates IDO1 expression and amplifies chemokine production in human amniotic epithelial cells
abstract: Ureaplasma urealyticum is among the organisms most frequently recovered from the amniotic cavity during intra-amniotic infection. Using primary human amniotic epithelial cells, we found that IFN-γ–inducible IDO1 reduces the viable cell-associated burden of U. urealyticum, in part through tryptophan depletion, and that infection attenuates IFN-γ–induced IDO1 expression. This attenuation was mediated in part by TLR2-dependent induction of SOCS1, which reduced STAT1 activation and STAT1-dependent interferon-stimulated gene expression, and was reproduced to a lesser extent by heat-killed organisms. Reduced IDO1 activity lowered kynurenine, an endogenous ligand of the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), and the accompanying decrease in AhR activity was associated with increased CXCL8 and CXCL1 secretion; supplementing infected cells with kynurenine reduced chemokine release in an AhR-dependent manner. In a factorial analysis, TLR2 inhibition and kynurenine supplementation each lowered chemokine output, with TLR2 blockade producing the larger effect. Conditioned medium from infected cells increased neutrophil migration, adhesion and priming, with migration and respiratory-burst responses confirmed in primary human neutrophils. In fetal membranes from women with prelabour rupture of membranes, CXCL8 was higher in Ureaplasma-positive specimens and correlated with bacterial load. These findings indicate that TLR2-dependent SOCS1 induction attenuates IFN-γ–driven IDO1 expression in amniotic epithelium, and that the associated reduction in AhR activity acts alongside direct TLR2 signaling to amplify chemokine production. In human fetal membranes, both SOCS1 and CXCL8 expression were associated with bacterial load.
authors: Shuming Ouyang

title: Dietary polysaccharides as direct substrates for SCFA production: mechanisms and precision prebiotic intervention strategies
abstract: Conventional prebiotics lack the structural specificity to direct colonic fermentation toward defined outputs. Dietary polysaccharides (DPs) serve as direct fermentation substrates, and their architecture—monosaccharide composition, glycosidic linkages, molecular weight and branching—determines which short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing taxa can access them. This selectivity is governed by carbohydrate-active enzyme (CAZyme) repertoires and cross-feeding networks. We propose a dual-track precision framework: structure-guided matching of DPs to target SCFA producers, and individualized selection informed by baseline microbiota and disease-specific deficits. The proposed dual-track framework is a theoretical model that requires rigorous validation in human clinical trials. This work provides a mechanism-driven theoretical basis for advancing dietary polysaccharides from empirical prebiotics to precision nutrition tools.
authors: Yong Lai

title: Stochastic assembly outweighs deterministic filtering: crop phenological stages drive bacterial-fungal divergence between bulk and rhizosphere soils in saline-alkali fields
abstract: Soil salinization threatens crop productivity partly by disrupting rhizosphere microbiomes that support plant stress tolerance. However, most studies have focused on single growth stages or bulk soil, limiting a deeper insight into the temporal dynamics and assembly mechanisms of rhizosphere communities across the crop life cycle. We investigated bacterial and fungal communities in a long-term maize field with saline-alkali soil. Bulk and rhizosphere soils were sampled at seedling, heading, and maturity. Using 16S rRNA and ITS amplicon sequencing, iCAMP, functional prediction, and co-occurrence networks, we found that maize phenological stage significantly structured bacterial and fungal community composition, while the difference between the rhizosphere and bulk soil was not significant. Microbial diversity increased toward maturity in bulk soil, whereas rhizosphere bacterial diversity showed a seedling-stage bottleneck and fungal diversity remained higher than that in bulk soil. The rhizosphere enriched copiotrophic Proteobacteria and Actinobacteriota, whereas bulk soil favored oligotrophic Chloroflexi and Acidobacteriota. Drift (and others) represented the largest single assembly category across phenological stages in both compartments, with relative contributions exceeding 38%. Deterministic contributions to bacterial assembly remained stable across stages and compartments, whereas rhizosphere fungal assembly became more stochastic at maturity. Under the saline-alkali conditions examined here, stochastic processes remained dominant, and deterministic filtering did not become the predominant mode of community assembly. Predicted functional profiles shifted with plant development: organic phosphorus mineralization was enriched at seedling, phosphate transport and nitrogen fixation at maturity, and salt-tolerance functions shifted from compatible-solute synthesis to ion homeostasis and antioxidant defense. The rhizosphere showed reduced bacterial network connectivity but more positive fungal associations and a higher proportion of cross-kingdom associations. Together, these results characterize a “growth stage-rhizosphere effect-salinity stress” framework in saline-alkali maize field, in which environmental control shifts from salinity toward nutrient stoichiometry for bacteria and microbial biomass for fungi. These patterns may inform growth-stage-specific microbiome management in saline-alkali soil.
authors: Miao Gao

title: Association between systemic inflammatory markers and CD4 T-cell count in people living with HIV: a cross-sectional study
abstract: BackgroundPeople living with HIV (PLWH) experience persistent chronic inflammation even under effective antiretroviral therapy (ART) with viral suppression. The CD4 T-cell count remains the primary marker of immunodeficiency but does not capture the underlying inflammatory burden. Routine hematological inflammatory indices–including Absolute neutrophil count / Absolute lymphocyte count (NLR), Platelet count / Absolute lymphocyte count (PLR), (Absolute neutrophil count + Absolute monocyte count) / Absolute lymphocyte count (NMLR), (Neutrophil count × Monocyte count) / Lymphocyte count (SIRI), (Platelet count × Neutrophil count) / Lymphocyte count (SII)–have shown prognostic value in various diseases, yet their association with CD4 count in PLWH has not been systematically evaluated.MethodsThis single-center cross-sectional study enrolled 339 PLWH. Participants were categorized by CD4 count into binary ( 0.05), consistent with linear associations. SIRI showed only marginal association (OR = 1.46, P = 0.059), while SII was not significant. These associations remained robust in the virologically suppressed subgroup (87.9% with HIV RNA < 50 copies/mL) and survived Bonferroni and Benjamini–Hochberg corrections for multiple comparisons.ConclusionNLR, PLR, and NMLR are independently and linearly associated with lower CD4 T-cell counts in PLWH, with effect sizes increasing across worse immune strata. As these indices are derived from routine complete blood counts at no additional cost, they may serve as simple, accessible adjunctive biomarkers associated with lower CD4 T-cell counts, particularly in resource-limited settings. However, they should be regarded as indirect hematological indices rather than direct measures of systemic inflammatory burden; future studies incorporating established inflammatory biomarkers are needed to validate their clinical utility and prognostic value.
authors: Huichun Ji

title: Genome architecture, GC3 content, codon usage, and predicted translational adaptation of Salmonella temperate and virulent phages
abstract: IntroductionSalmonella enterica phages are important drivers of bacterial evolution and potential tools for phage-based applications. However, differences in genome architecture, codon usage, and predicted translational adaptation between Salmonella temperate and virulent phages remain uncertain and need to be determined.MethodsThis study elucidates genome-wide and functional-module-specific molecular signatures across Salmonella phage lifestyles. We analyzed 41 temperate and 41 virulent Salmonella phage genomes comprising 7,759 protein-coding genes. Because lifestyle is a genome-level attribute, statistical inference employed equal-genome-weight comparisons, whole-genome permutations, genome-cluster bootstrapping, and sensitivity analyses.ResultsThe virulent phages exhibited greater broad-scale genomic disconnectedness (81.7% versus 74.0% of within-group genome pairs lacking significant BLAST similarity) and larger mean genomes (80,784 versus 44,433 bp). The temperate phages showed higher genome-average overall GC and GC3 content, with “virulent”-minus-“temperate” differences of −4.484 and −7.706 percentage points, respectively (both q = 0.00013). Conversely, the virulent phages exhibited higher genome-average Codon Adaptation Index (CAI-2; difference = +0.0131) and Index of Translation Elongation (ITE; +0.0321), with associations persisting after adjustment for the nucleotide composition and coding-sequence length. The genome-equal effective number of codons (Nc) difference was not significant (q = 0.383). Genome-equal PERMANOVA detected significant differentiation across the complete molecular dataset (R2 = 0.1518; q = 0.0001) and all five gene functional categories, with the greatest effects in the DNA repair/recombination, lysis-associated, and structural genes. Only regulatory genes showed significantly different genome-level multivariate dispersion. Genome-average PCA scores differed significantly along GC-associated PC1 and a second axis associated with CAI-2, ITE, and sequence size. GC-adjusted CAI-2 -ITE correlations remained positive across both phage lifestyles (ρ = 0.771 and 0.776), with genome-cluster bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero. Genome-level relative synonymous codon usage analyses identified 23 of 59 codons with FDR-significant, large-effect differences. Principal findings persisted in functional-annotation and genome-relatedness sensitivity analyses.DiscussionCollectively, these results identify complementary compositional and predicted codon-adaptation signatures in the selected phage lifestyle groups, while taxonomic imbalance and the absence of direct translational measurements limit further interpretation.
authors: Mamuka Kotetishvili

title: Terbinafine-resistant Trichophyton indotineae and SQLE mutations in human and animal dermatophytosis: a One Health perspective
abstract: BackgroundDermatophytosis is an increasing public health and veterinary concern amid the emergence of terbinafine-resistant dermatophytes and recurrent treatment failures. This study characterized dermatophyte isolates from human and animal cases, assessed their antifungal susceptibility, and investigated terbinafine resistance-associated mutations in the squalene epoxidase (SQLE) gene.MethodsTwenty-two Trichophyton mentagrophytes complex isolates were recovered from skin scrapings of patients with recurrent tinea corporis and tinea cruris, and 39 isolates were obtained from animals with clinical signs of ringworm. Isolates were identified by sequencing the internal transcribed spacer (ITS) region, and antifungal susceptibility was determined by broth microdilution method. The SQLE gene was sequenced to detect resistance-associated substitutions.ResultsAll human isolates were identified as Trichophyton indotineae; animal isolates comprised T. mentagrophytes, T. verrucosum, Microsporum canis, and one feline-derived T. rubrum isolate. Fluconazole resistance occurred among both human and animal isolates, but terbinafine resistance was largely confined to human-derived T. indotineae, while most animal isolates, particularly T. verrucosum and M. canis, remained susceptible. SQLE sequencing identified several resistance-associated substitutions: Phe397Leu, the most frequent mutation in T. indotineae, was consistently linked to elevated terbinafine MICs (0.5–16 μg/mL), and Gln408Leu was associated with an MIC of 8 μg/mL and pronounced growth on terbinafine-containing medium. Resistance-associated substitutions were also detected in animal isolates, including Leu393Ser (T. rubrum) and Ile415Ser (T. mentagrophytes), both recovered from cats. Three isolates carried two concurrent substitutions, Phe397Leu and Ala448Thr. ITS-based phylogenetic analysis demonstrated that the studied human clinical isolates clustered with genetically related isolates from multiple countries, with no evident geographic segregation, suggesting widespread dissemination of closely related T. indotineae genotypes.ConclusionTerbinafine-resistant T. indotineae predominates among human dermatophyte isolates, driven largely by SQLE mutations, especially Phe397Leu. The presence of resistance-associated SQLE mutations in animal-derived dermatophytes indicates spillover of human-adapted resistant lineages into companion animals, underscoring the need for integrated antifungal susceptibility testing and One Health-based surveillance.
authors: Yasmine H. Tartor

title: Resting-cell biocatalysis as a platform for cadmium sulfide quantum dot biosynthesis
abstract: Biogenic quantum dots (QDs) have attracted interest as an alternative route for producing semiconductor nanomaterials. However, their potential advantages over chemical synthesis depend on the production system and require case-specific evaluation. However, current microbial platforms often suffer from limited control over chemical nanoparticle synthesis, low stability, and challenging downstream processing. In this study, we developed and characterized a resting-cell strategy for the biosynthesis of cadmium sulfide (CdS) QD using the environmental bacterium Pseudomonas putida KT2440 and explored, for the first time, the potential of Cupriavidus necator H16 as a microbial chassis for QD production. Optimization of production conditions in P. putida KT2440 were stablished. Structural and elemental characterization confirmed the formation of CdS nanomaterials, while spectroscopic and DLS analyses demonstrated a time-dependent increase in nanoparticle size from 2.6 ± 0.5 nm to 6.6 ± 0.7 nm. Purified QD retained fluorescence for up to 3 months when stored in Tris–HCl buffer, highlighting the importance of storage conditions for preserving nanoparticle integrity. Under resting-cell conditions C. necator H16 generated fluorescent nanoparticles with emission properties that differed from those observed in P. putida. Comparative analyses further demonstrated that resting cells outperformed actively growing cultures, enabling faster QD formation and prolonged fluorescence stability. Collectively, these findings establish resting-cell biocatalysis as an efficient platform for sustainable QD production and expand the repertoire of microorganisms available for the biological synthesis of semiconductor nanomaterials.
authors: Manuel Carmona

title: Delafloxacin activity against fluoroquinolone-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa: in vitro activity and mutant prevention concentration
abstract: IntroductionPseudomonas aeruginosa frequently develops resistance to fluoroquinolones limiting the usefulness of these agents for the treatment of healthcare-associated infections. This study evaluated the in vitro activity of delafloxacin in comparison with the older-generation fluoroquinolones against clinical P. aeruginosa isolates, and explored its potential to suppress the selection of resistant subpopulations.MethodsOne hundred clinical isolates were tested against ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and delafloxacin by broth microdilution method. Susceptibility was interpreted according to EUCAST criteria for ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin and FDA criteria for delafloxacin. Mutant prevention concentrations (MPCs) were determined for the three fluoroquinolones in 12 selected isolates using a high-inoculum agar-based method.ResultsResistance was observed in 29% of isolates for both ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin, compared with 25% for delafloxacin. Among isolates resistant to both ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin, 32.0% were susceptible or intermediate to delafloxacin. The median MPC/MIC ratio was 4 (IQR, 4–8) for delafloxacin, compared with 8 (IQR, 7–16) for ciprofloxacin and 16 (IQR, 7–64) for levofloxacin.DiscussionOverall, delafloxacin retained in vitro activity against a subset of fluoroquinolone-resistant P. aeruginosa isolates and showed a favorable mutant prevention profile in the isolates tested, with a lower median MPC/MIC ratio than ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin. These findings provide preliminary evidence supporting further investigation of delafloxacin against fluoroquinolone-resistant P. aeruginosa.
authors: Ángel Rodríguez-Villodres

title: Multi-omics integration for precision tuberculosis medicine: from molecular atlases to clinical translation
abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global health threat. Its management is constrained by incomplete prediction of antimicrobial resistance, limited ability to identify patients at risk of anti-tuberculosis drug-induced liver injury (AT-DILI), and heterogeneous treatment responses. This narrative review examines how multi-omics can address these challenges and adapts an established translational framework to TB-specific decisions. Clinically useful integration requires reproducible measurements, independent validation, and evidence that a result improves care. The relevant phenotypes emerge from interactions among Mycobacterium tuberculosis, host genetic and immune variation, lesion microenvironments, drug exposure, and microbial ecology. No single molecular layer adequately resolves this system. We examine pathogen and host genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, microbiome profiling, and single-cell and spatial technologies. We distinguish replicated resistance and NAT2-associated toxicity findings from emerging bacterial regulatory, immunometabolic, and microbiome associations. Selected diagnostic, prognostic, treatment-monitoring, and toxicity classifiers illustrate both the promise of integration and limitations in sample size, comparator selection, confounding, and validation. Their high training discrimination does not establish external performance or clinical utility. The framework links standardized biobanking and fit-for-purpose integration to analytical and clinical validation, functional testing, and evaluation of utility and equitable implementation. Explicit transition criteria distinguish these stages without treating proposed planning thresholds as universal standards. The clinical value of multi-omics will depend less on the number of measured features than on rigorous study design, affordability, and demonstrable benefit to patients.
authors: Wenping Gong

title: Data-driven investigation of bacterial growth dynamics in response to the medium-drug interplay
abstract: Bacterial responses to antimicrobial drugs are strongly influenced by environmental conditions, yet how drugs systematically reshape the contribution of individual nutrients across different growth phases remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated medium–drug interactions in Escherichia coli BW25113 using around 177 chemically defined media and six drug conditions, generating thousands of growth profiles. Lag time (t), growth rate (r), and carrying capacity (K) were analyzed to characterize responses across growth phases. By integrating large-scale growth profiling with machine learning, we quantitatively mapped how 41 medium components contributed to bacterial growth under different drug conditions. Drug exposure substantially reorganized these nutritional contributions and generally increased the number of components involved in determining growth, particularly for r and K. Glucose, isoleucine, K+, and PO₄3− emerged as common determinants, whereas their relative contributions changed with drug exposure. Importantly, drug-induced nutritional reorganization was both growth phase- and drug-specific: decreased contributions were enriched in amino acids, whereas increased contributions involved diverse nutritional categories, particularly metal ions. Thus, rather than viewing drug susceptibility as a fixed bacterial phenotype, our study provides a quantitative framework showing that antimicrobial responses emerge from dynamic interactions among drugs, nutrients, and growth phases.
authors: Bei-Wen Ying

title: Correction: The effect of cCMP and cUMP on growth of Pseudomonas aeruginosa
authors: Bastian Schirmer

title: Clinical and public genomic comparisons of carbapenem resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: BackgroundCross-setting comparisons of carbapenem resistance may reflect clinical contexts and selective genomic sampling. We examined reproducibility on two independent scales.MethodsWe analysed retrospective adult cohorts from a Chinese hospital (n = 1,362) and the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) v3.1 (n = 3,251), along with 26,417 publicly submitted clinical Pseudomonas aeruginosa BioSamples. Our clinical analyses compared susceptibility-defined carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa (CRPA), evaluated outcomes, adjusting for associations, and conducted exploratory reciprocal model transport. Our genomic analyses examined annotated determinants, submission-year patterns, single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) clusters, and co-resistance, including cluster-weighted sensitivity analyses.ResultsCRPA proportions were 36.9 and 9.3% in the two institutions. Unadjusted in-hospital mortality and post-index hospital stay were higher among patients with CRPA. Adjusted association directions agreed for 13 of 18 covariates. Transported models showed modest discrimination (area under the curves [AUCs], 0.641 and 0.619) and marked miscalibration (calibration slopes, 0.45 and 0.52). Among the included public Biosamples, 60.7% carried a defined carbapenem-associated determinant and 24.4% carried an acquired carbapenemase. Chinese submissions had higher serine-carbapenemase positivity, whereas US submissions had higher metallo-β-lactamase and chromosomal-determinant positivity. The country OR for blaKPC changed from 8.04 in the full sample to 1.59 in the cluster-assigned weighted analysis; the OR for acquired carbapenemase changed from 1.32 to 0.67.ConclusionClinical associations may recur without supporting a reliable transported prediction. Genomic contrasts are sensitive to sampling and analysis population. These exploratory, unlinked findings neither establish causal effects nor estimate national prevalence; genomic results do not confirm phenotypic CRPA.
authors: Zhao-Kun Fan

title: Biological legacy of large-scale coastal reclamation: Potential oxygen demand from pre-existing benthic biomass
abstract: Coastal-enclosure assessments commonly emphasize external organic loading, sediment processes, and hydrological exchange but rarely account for living benthic biomass that may become a transient internal organic load after habitat conversion. Omitting this pool may leave early post-closure oxygen budgets incomplete, particularly where water exchange and oxygen renewal are restricted. We evaluated this biological legacy in Saemangeum, Korea, using a three-step analysis: (1) estimating the pre-closure benthic carbon inventory and its complete-decomposition oxygen-demand upper bound; (2) using reanalyzed laboratory data to assess the temporal plausibility of rapid biomass loss and field-observed intertidal macrofaunal deficits to constrain potential demand; and (3) comparing the field-constrained estimates with standing dissolved-oxygen inventories across three effective receiving-water volumes. The compiled inventory contained 9,384 t C and yielded an all-component upper bound of 25,023 t O2; excluding the transferred bacterial estimate reduced this value to 14,461 t O2. At 120 days after closure, the net biomass-deficit and taxon-resolved minimum-loss estimators yielded potential demands of 3,547 and 4,663 t O2, respectively, equivalent to 54.0% and 70.9% of the intertidal macrofaunal upper bound. The corresponding point-estimate demand-to-inventory ratios exceeded one at an effective water volume of 0.35 km3 but remained below one at 0.83 and 1.27 km3. Among the tested assumptions, the inventory upper bound was most sensitive to the transferred bacterial stock, whereas the demand-to-inventory comparison was strongly influenced by receiving-water conditions. The tested alternative allocation and conversion-factor perturbations had smaller effects on the 120-day estimates. Conditional bootstrap intervals quantified sampling uncertainty in station-level means, while separate sensitivity analyses examined selected structural assumptions. These comparisons represent potential demand rather than realized oxygen consumption or predictions of hypoxia. The proposed tiered framework can identify coastal-enclosure projects requiring targeted monitoring and process-based oxygen-budget assessment.
authors: Bon Joo Koo

title: Distribution and export of dissolved organic carbon along a loop current eddy in the Gulf of Mexico
abstract: The ocean plays a major role in regulating the global climate by sequestering carbon, and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) represents one of the largest marine carbon reservoirs. Mesoscale eddies can enhance DOC export to the mesopelagic zone through eddy-wind interactions and eddy-induced strain, with this export often increasing during winter convective mixing. This study investigated how these processes affect DOC distribution and vertical fluxes within the anticyclonic Loop Current Eddy Yazoo in the oligotrophic Gulf of Mexico during the onset of Nortes winds in November 2022. Using high-spatial-resolution sampling along a transect, we mapped the spatial variability of DOC concentrations and hydrographic properties across LCE Yazoo and surrounding waters. We found pronounced horizontal and vertical variability in DOC concentrations and did not observe the hypothesized systematic enrichment within the eddy expected in a nutrient depleted environment. Total dissolved carbohydrates, which are important components of labile and semi-labile DOC fractions, accounted for 7.4% of total DOC in the epipelagic zone, decreasing to ~4% in the mesopelagic zone. Significant correlations were observed between DOC and Prochlorococcus, Synechococcus, picoeukaryotes, and heterotrophic bacterial biomass, indicating close spatial coupling between DOC and microbial community structure. Meanwhile, the relationship between DOC and apparent oxygen utilization in the oxycline indicated a greater apparent contribution of DOC remineralization to oxygen consumption within LCE Yazoo (~40%) than in adjacent waters (~29%). Upward and downward fluxes driven by eddy-Ekman pumping redistributed semi-labile DOC within the euphotic zone but did not result in net export. In contrast, upward and downward fluxes forced by eddy-induced strain led to the net subduction of semi-labile DOC, with particularly strong fluxes near the eddy edges. Overall, the findings support the idea that anticyclonic eddies may be important hotspots for semi-labile DOC export, potentially facilitating the microbial carbon pump in oligotrophic oceans.
authors: Julio Sheinbaum

title: Global surface-water microparticle carrier-load patterns across aquatic ecosystems: a spatial framework for prioritizing future plastisphere-associated antimicrobial resistance surveillance
abstract: Microplastic-associated biofilms can concentrate microorganisms, mobile genetic elements, and co-selective chemicals, but globally comparable measurements of plastisphere antimicrobial resistance (AMR) remain sparse. We therefore asked where surface-water particle carrier-load is sufficiently high to define candidate locations for paired, confirmatory plastisphere-AMR surveillance, without treating particle abundance as a proxy for AMR burden. We harmonized two worldwide surface-water datashares collected during 2013-2017. After removing three exact duplicate freshwater records and reserving 18 depth-profile samples for sensitivity analysis, 2,399 samples were classified as freshwater (n=1,006), estuarine (n=45), coastal (n=663), or open ocean (n=685). A two-part hurdle framework modeled particle detection and, among positive samples, log concentration, using 2-degree spatial-cell cluster-robust standard errors and adjustment for sampling year, platform, and container material. Operational surveillance-priority cells required at least three samples, at least 50% detection, and a median concentration at or above the ecosystem-specific 90th percentile among eligible cells. Detection increased from 49.5% in freshwater to 75.6% in estuaries, 79.3% at the coast, and 94.5% in the open ocean. Relative to freshwater, adjusted odds ratios for detection were 2.28 (95% CI 1.03-5.05), 2.20 (1.51-3.19), and 4.78 (2.62-8.75), respectively. The estuarine estimates should be interpreted cautiously because only 45 strict estuarine samples were available, and classification was based on text-derived source information. Among positive samples, adjusted geometric mean ratios were 1.45 (0.79-2.67), 1.40 (1.14-1.72), and 2.99 (2.33-3.84). Filaments constituted 82.7%-95.1% of classified particles. Twenty-eight operational hotspot cells were identified, although several open-ocean cells reflected concentrated campaign sampling. This analysis provides a transparent carrier-load layer for selecting candidate locations for future paired measurements of resistance genes, resistant organisms, antibiotics, metals, and mobile genetic elements. The identified cells are substrate-rich sampling priorities, not microbiologically verified AMR hotspots, and their value for AMR surveillance remains to be empirically validated.

abstract: Gut microbial single-nucleotide variants across 10,781 individuals reveal 940 associations that link strain-level genetic variation to 69 host traits, with structural analyses pinpointing host phenotype-associated variants, providing a base pair-resolution resource for mechanistic hypothesis generation.

title: Farnesol keeps fungal spores asleep.
abstract: Fungal spores must balance long-term survival in dormancy against the need to germinate and infect a host. A farnesol-sensing receptor controls this decision, and can be influenced by rhizosphere bacteria, shifting the balance between fungal persistence and plant disease based on cell density and nutrient availability.

title: Antagonistic second-messenger signalling coordinates Pseudomonas aeruginosa surface colonization and virulence
abstract: Second messengers cAMP and c-di-GMP regulate surface behaviours and virulence in Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Here, the authors show how the bacteria switch between attachment and surface movement by coordinating the two signalling systems, allowing distinct bacterial populations to work together to colonise and damage human airway tissue.

title: WASH orchestrates phagosomal maturation and bacterial killing in neutrophils through syntaxin 19-mediated lysosomal fusion
abstract: How actin regulates late phagosomal maturation and microbial killing in neutrophils remains unclear. The authors here show that WASH drives actin-dependent lysosomal dynamics and STX19 recruitment to phagosomes, enabling lysosome fusion and bacterial killing.

title: Erratum for the Report "Gut microbiome influences efficacy of PD-1-based immunotherapy against epithelial tumors".
Structure of the Chimalliviridae bacteriophage Goslar reveals host recognition and infection machinery.
abstract: Large-genome bacteriophages (phages) of the Chimalliviridae family have a distinctive life cycle, building compartments inside infected bacterial cells that broadly protect their genomes from host defenses. Here, we use cryo-electron microscopy to determine a structure of the Escherichia coli-infecting Chimalliviridae phage Goslar. We combine manual modeling of 25 structural proteins with AlphaFold structure predictions of an additional three proteins to generate a composite model with 2888 protein chains from 28 different structural proteins, totaling more than 1.4 million amino acid residues. Our structure reveals the architecture of the Goslar capsid, portal, tail, and baseplate, highlighting structural similarities and differences with other tailed phages. Combining our structural data with quantitative mass spectrometry of Goslar virions, we identify several high-copy virion-associated proteins that likely play key roles when injected into host cells upon infection. We also identify a Chimalliviridae-specific family of proteins that form long, flexible filaments anchored at the phage baseplate and which incorporate carbohydrate-binding domains, suggesting a key role in host recognition.

title: Effector-triggered stomatal immunity prevents leaf invasion by bacterial pathogens
authors: Tamar V. Av-Shalom, Yan Lai, Racquel A. Singh, Dora Yuping Wang, Reid Gohmann, David Mackey, Darrell Desveaux, David S. Guttman

title: A single-amino acid difference between rodent and human Andes virus affects viral glycoprotein trafficking.
abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), with rare outbreaks involving person-to-person transmission. A human ANDV isolate from one such outbreak and a rodent isolate from the same region differ in lethality in Syrian golden hamsters. Genomic analysis revealed 25 nonsynonymous substitutions, including one leading to a T641I change in the human ANDV glycoprotein precursor near its cleavage site. Although the isolates differed in growth kinetics, strand-specific RT-qPCR did not support major differences in viral RNA synthesis, whereas virion release was delayed in the case of the human isolate. In human cell expression systems, a single I641T substitution in the human ANDV glycoprotein resulted in decreased Golgi retention and faster release of virion-like particles relative to wild-type glycoprotein. Since ANDV egress takes place at the Golgi, the T641I change present in the human ANDV isolate may represent a human adaptive mutation influencing glycoprotein trafficking and virus particle release.
authors: Vidal-Freire S, Ferressini-Gerpe NM, Bellomo CM, Pastor AF, Tagliavia M, Somavarapu R, Shirsathe S, Zhang J, Giannetti E, Mena I, Krammer F, Tischler ND, Patiño-Galindo JA, Kaczmarek M, Sanchez-Lockhart M, Worwa G, Kuhn JH, Schmaljohn CS, García-Sastre A, Martínez VP, Palacios G.

title: The (amide-)N-methylnicotinamide is a microbe-derived NAD<sup>+</sup> precursor that drives gut stem cell renewal.
abstract: Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NAD) is a critical cellular coenzyme whose decline associates with various chronic and inflammatory diseases. Improved NAD restoration may reduce disease risks and extend healthy lifespan. We report here that certain commensal bacteria including specific probiotic species produce (amide-)N-methylnicotinamide (N-MNA), which is a structural isomer of methylnicotinamide, a nicotinamide degradative metabolite. Patients with gut dysbiosis and inflammation show reduced stool N-MNA. Stable isotope tracing revealed that N-MNA can be rapidly taken up and incorporated into NAD redox reactions by intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) and non-IECs of fruit fly, mouse, and human. Genetic and pharmacological analyses suggest that N-MNA is converted to NAD+ via the Preiss-Handler pathway, independent of the salvage pathway. Cell-type-specific ablation or overexpression of SIRT1, an NAD-consuming enzyme, in Drosophila, along with intestinal stem cell (ISC) lineage tracing in mice revealed that systemic N-MNA supplementation promotes ISC regeneration and gut epithelial repair. Compared to known NAD precursors, N-MNA brings a methyl group into host cells, representing a class of microbe-derived NAD precursor that stimulates the tissue regenerative power.
authors: Han J, Antonio JM, Bhupana JN, Choi G, Yang J, Chiles E, Tong Y, Rajmohamed MA, Wu HT, Wang D, Meadows V, Lapaque N, Etchegaray JP, Filip R, Liu TC, Kiela PR, Bessman N, Ferraris RP, Wong CO, Su X, Gao N.

title: Dual-acting compounds that deliver an acidifying domain via zanamivir to the virus surface are potent influenza inhibitors.
abstract: While contemporary antiviral development primarily strives to produce "lock and key" inhibitors, we present here a different approach to drug design that uses compounds devised to alter the microenvironment of the virion surface, making it incompatible with virus entry. We illustrate this strategy with inhibitors of influenza virus and show that compounds designed to produce a proton-rich mantle above the virion surface affect the ability of the viral hemagglutinin to interact with cellular receptors and gain entry to the cell. The compounds show exceptional antiviral activity both in vitro and in vivo and protect against influenza illness in ferrets and in mice after a single dose, either therapeutically or prophylactically.
authors: Mackenzie-Kludas C, Wu WY, Jin B, McKimm-Breschkin JL, Seah EL, Jones P, Fairmaid E, Tai CMK, Oh DY, Jenkins PJ, Hurt AC, Brown LE.

title: Viromic and metagenomic analyses reveal distribution and dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes in anaerobic digestion-composting systems: roles of quorum sensing and viruses
abstract:
Background
                     Under the “One Health” framework, untreated livestock waste serves as a critical vector for the cross-domain proliferation of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). While integrated anaerobic digestion-composting systems are increasingly adopted for agricultural waste treatment, the dynamic succession of ARGs and the regulatory roles of quorum sensing (QS) and viral communities during the drastic environmental transitions remain critically unexplored.
                  
                     Results
                     We applied comprehensive viromic and metagenomic analyses to track the dynamic fate of ARGs, ARB (antibiotic resistance bacteria), QS, and viral communities across a single campaign of full-scale anaerobic digestion-composting system treating cattle slurry. The relative abundance of total ARG (RPKG) was higher in cattle slurry digestate than in raw cattle slurry and lower in mature compost than in compost feedstock. The relative abundance of VFG-carrying contigs (RPKM) was also lower in mature compost than in compost feedstock. However, specific high-risk ARGs, notably aac(3)-VIIa and sul1, exhibited extreme recalcitrance. At the maturation stage, we revealed that thermotolerant taxa, predominantly Bacillota and Actinomycetota, dominated the ultimate high-risk ARB. Crucially, the carriage of specific QS regulatory genes (LuxR and DGC) within ultimate high-risk ARB exhibited a highly significant positive correlation (R2 > 0.82, P < 0.001) with ARG and virulence factor gene (VFG) abundances. Furthermore, while lytic phages dominated the viral community, the thermophilic stage coincided with a marked decoupling of phage and ARB-host abundance trajectories, consistent with reduced viral abundance under thermal stress.
                  
                     Conclusion
                     Within this campaign, mean ARG abundance (RPKG) was higher in cattle slurry digestate than in raw cattle slurry. Mean ARG and VFG abundances (RPKG) were lower in mature compost than in compost feedstock. Nevertheless, aac(3)-VIIa, sul1, and tet(M), together with ARG-carrying MAGs affiliated with Bacillota and Actinomycetota, remained detectable in mature compost. QS (luxR and DGC) is associated mainly with persistence and potential horizontal gene transfer, whereas phages act chiefly as ecological predators and rarely carry ARGs, so that resistant-bacteria persistence coincided with weaker virus–host coupling at high temperature, rather than providing evidence for transduction. These observations suggest biologically targeted interventions (e.g., QS inhibitors or sequential phage inoculation) as candidate strategies whose feasibility and efficacy remain to be tested across different feedstocks, seasons, and full-scale operating conditions before any general management recommendation can be made.

title: Antarctic intertidal sediments are overlooked hotspots of dimethyl sulfide production associated with Granulosicoccus-containing microbial communities
abstract:
Background
                     Dimethyl sulfide (DMS) is a volatile organosulfur compound that contributes to global climate regulation through its role in atmospheric aerosol formation. The Southern Ocean is an important source of DMS and represents a key region for marine sulfur cycling. However, previous studies have primarily focused on pelagic ecosystems, and the microbial drivers of DMS cycling in Antarctic coastal sediments remain poorly understood.
                  
                     Results
                     Here, we integrated 16S and 18S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, metagenomics, and DMSP-amendment incubation to characterize the DMS cycling in intertidal sediments of the climate-sensitive Fildes Peninsula. Our results revealed notable potential for DMS production via the DMSP cleavage pathway, in contrast to the demethylation-dominated pelagic ocean. Furthermore, the incubation experiments confirmed rapid DMS generation upon the addition of DMSP. Granulosicoccus, Ilumatobacter, and Cocleimonas were the potential drivers of DMS cycling, with genomic reconstruction demonstrating their roles in the biogeochemical cycles of sulfur and nitrogen.
                  
                     Conclusions
                     Our findings identify Antarctic intertidal sediments as potential hotspots of DMS production mediated by the DMSP cleavage pathway and Granulosicoccus-dominated microbial communities, necessitating their inclusion in polar biogeochemical models under climate change.

title: A novel digestive symbiont for both holobiont Rimicaris exoculata and Rimicaris chacei: the case of Lachnospirales
abstract:
Background
                     In deep-sea hydrothermal vent ecosystems, most animals harbor symbiotic communities that support their nutrition. This is the case for the shrimp Rimicaris exoculata and Rimicaris chacei, two endemic species of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge (MAR), housing three distinct bacterial symbiotic communities playing a major role in their nutrition and scaling up their immune systems. One is located in the cephalothoracic cavity, another in the foregut and the third in the midgut that is mostly represented by Candidatus Microvillispirillaceae. However, recent metabarcoding and metagenomics studies reported for the first time the presence of another abundant potential digestive symbiont representing a novel family of Lachnospirales. To date, their role and organization in the holobiont remain unknown. We combined Fluorescent in situ Hybridization, metabarcoding and genome-resolved metagenomics data to investigate their contribution to the holobiont functioning and their metabolic potential. For this purpose, we used the raw reads of a recent metabarcoding analysis and Metagenome-Assembled Genomes (MAGs) obtained in a previous study.
                  
                     Results
                     We studied two MAGs reconstructed from TAG and Snake Pit sites (MAR) revealing a novel midgut-associated Lachnospirales family. This novel symbiont shows the capacity to degrade host chitin, utilize oxygen and encode flagellar genes involved in host-symbiont recognition. In addition, this Lachnospirales family harbors CRISPR/cas genes that may contribute to the holobiont’s defense. This symbiotic lineage seems to colonize the ectoperitrophic space, undergo elongation without dividing and may be acquired after juvenile settlement at active vent sites. Consequently, they share many commonalities with Candidatus Microvillispirillaceae, with which they co-occur.
                  
                     Conclusion
                     Our data suggest that the Lachnospirales may engage in a syntrophic relationship with Candidatus Microvillispirillaceae. They may be able to degrade chitin, allowing Ca. Microvillispirillaceae to use degradation products for their metabolism. Like Ca. Microvillispirillaceae, Lachnospirales are acquired post-installation of juveniles between stage B and subadult metamorphosis. Consequently, both symbionts may strongly contribute to the holobiont fitness.

title: Divergent Responses of Bacterial and Microeukaryotic Diversity to Water-Level Fluctuations in a Lake-Floodplain System.
abstract: Water-level fluctuations (WLF) are widely accepted as key drivers of aquatic species diversity in lake-floodplain systems, with diversity increasing as water levels rise. However, microorganisms may challenge this pattern that their richness does not necessarily increase with water levels. To resolve this inconsistency, we applied 16S and 18S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing to bacterial and microeukaryotic assemblages in Dongting Lake, China, during the low-water (LWP; January 2024) and high-water periods (HWP; August 2024). Microeukaryotic richness was higher during HWP than LWP (p  0.3), consistent with their divergent fates in the water column: soil microeukaryotes are more likely to persist after flooding than soil bacteria. Co-occurrence networks evidenced substantially stronger bacteria-microeukaryote associations at high water and partial least squares path modelling resolved a DOC-to-bacteria-to-microeukaryotes pathway activated only during the HWP. These signals suggest that enhanced hydrological connectivity promoted community coalescence, possibly through intensified trophic coupling, although this interpretation requires experimental verification. This study highlights that natural WLFs reshape microbial richness by intermittently reconnecting terrestrial and aquatic microbial species pools.
authors: Tan C, Wantzen KM, Wu R, Li W, Lu L, Mbao E, Zhang L, Xie Z, Wang C, Lin W, Li Y, Zhou C, Zhu Z, Li X, Liang J.

title: Links Between Environmental Quality, Gut Microbiota, and Host Performance in Nutrient-Impacted Springs.
abstract: Microbial symbionts may enhance adaptation to environmental stress, yet their role in nutrient-enriched freshwater habitats remains unclear. We conducted a full-factorial laboratory experiment with least killifish, Heterandria formosa, manipulating water chemistry from four Florida springs and gut microbiota inoculations from conspecifics at those sites. Sequencing of 16S rRNA revealed that gut microbial richness was higher in fish reared in less nutrient-loaded waters, but inoculation treatments, if successful, did not produce significant shifts in composition. Gut communities consistently differed from ambient water, with enrichment of Pseudomonadota and Planctomycetota. Females grew more slowly in the most polluted water. In a parallel result, males displayed higher mass-specific metabolic rates in the most nutrient-loaded water. Reproductive output per female nearly doubled when experimental microbiota and water originated from the same site, despite stable microbial diversity, though parentage and inoculation success were not verified; therefore, these results should be interpreted cautiously. These results indicate that environmental quality shapes gut microbiota and host performance, and that matching microbial communities to habitat conditions can boost reproduction. Such interactions may contribute to freshwater fish resilience and merit integration into conservation strategies.
authors: Pluer B, Travis J.

title: Mycoviruses in the Genomic Era: Ecological, Evolutionary and One Health Perspectives.
abstract: Mycoviruses are widespread and ecologically significant components of the biosphere, acting as hidden modulators of fungal diversity, metabolism and symbiotic interactions. This review synthesizes historical and technological advances in mycovirus discovery within an integrative One Health framework linking human, animal, plant and environmental health. We trace the transition from early dsRNA-based detection and Sanger sequencing to modern metatranscriptomic, metagenomic and petabase-scale data-mining approaches that have dramatically expanded known mycovirome diversity, uncovering deeply divergent RNA virus lineages. We survey the major mycovirus families and their genomic architectures and compare the strengths and inherent biases of current discovery strategies. We critically assess evidence for horizontal viral transfer across kingdoms, distinguishing experimentally demonstrated cross-host replication from phylogenetic inference alone and review mycovirus roles in modulating fungal virulence in agricultural and clinical settings, explicitly separating robust findings from preliminary or speculative reports. Hypovirulence-based biocontrol of phytopathogenic fungi emerges as the only application currently supported by field-validated evidence, whereas mycovirus-based therapy for human fungal infection remains a long-term hypothesis rather than a near-term clinical strategy. We underscore the need to combine rigorous experimental and computational approaches to characterize mycovirome complexity and function and outline priority research directions for the coming decade.
authors: Jacquat AG, Bejerman N, Debat H.

title: Environmental Drivers of Nontuberculous Mycobacteria in Tropical Freshwater Systems
abstract:
In tropical freshwater ecosystems, nontuberculous mycobacterial diversity and distribution is mainly driven by habitat and sample type, and local environmental factors such as sediment texture and depth. These findings highlight the importance of microhabitat conditions over broad biogeographic patterns in shaping mycobacterial communities.

ABSTRACT
Whilst microbial diversity still remains largely unexplored across environments and scales, microbial biogeography is shaped by edaphic and ecological drivers, and shifts in microbial community composition are frequently associated with host community structure and health. Nontuberculous mycobacteria represent a striking example of environmental microorganisms with opportunistic pathogenic potential. Unfortunately, understanding of their diversity and distribution in tropical freshwater environments remains limited, while such knowledge is crucial for predicting disease emergence and transmission. Here we aimed at (i) identifying microhabitat abiotic and biotic drivers influencing their diversity and distribution in French Guiana, (ii) comparing their diversity and distribution between French Guiana and Côte d'Ivoire, and (iii) examining co‐occurrences between mycobacterial communities in different environmental contexts. By deploying an eDNA‐based metabarcoding approach from tropical freshwater ecosystems, we suggest that their diversity and distribution are mainly driven by habitat type (urban vs. rural), sample type (water vs. sediment), and local abiotic factors such as phosphorus levels in sediments (with species‐specific effects). Moreover, we found a stratified distribution of mycobacteria depending on sediment texture (fine silts vs. coarse sand) and depth. Overall, we suggest that their ecological interactions may occur at the microhabitat level rather than following clear biogeographic patterns.
