title: The Promise and Limitations of Metabolic Trait Prediction Across Diverse Bacteria
abstract:
Predicting metabolic capabilities of environmental bacteria holds great promise for microbial ecology, but the reliability of available tools is often unclear. This perspective suggests that phenotype predictions are often inaccurate in surprising ways, which makes experimental phenotyping essential for accurate ecological modelling.

ABSTRACT
Metabolic traits mediate microbial interactions and underpin mechanistic models of community assembly. With the rapid expansion of genomic data and bioinformatic tools, it is widely assumed that metabolic traits such as substrate utilization can be reliably inferred from genomes alone. Here, we systematically evaluate this assumption by comparing genome‐based predictions from four commonly used tools to high‐throughput growth phenotypes of 186 marine bacteria. For simple substrates, prediction accuracy was limited and highly variable across taxa and substrates, with many strains predicted at or near chance levels. For three of four tools, most errors were false positives, indicating that apparent pathway completeness frequently fails to translate into growth under laboratory conditions. In contrast, genomic prediction of polysaccharide utilization based on carbohydrate‐active enzyme content performed substantially better, suggesting that traits that depend on a few highly specific enzymes are easier to predict. While genome‐based approaches can recover broad statistical patterns in metabolic strategies, their limited strain‐level reliability constrains ecological inference and modelling. For the foreseeable future, large‐scale experimental phenotypic characterization will remain an indispensable component of microbial ecology, both to reveal trait distributions and to ground‐truth and improve genomic predictions.

title: Flagella‐Mediated Biofilm Formation and 3D Swarming Drive Virulence in the Honey Bee Pathogen Paenibacillus larvae
abstract:
The flagella of the bacterial pathogen Paenibacillus larvae, the etiological agent of American foulbrood in honey bees, were characterized and identified as virulence factors. These cellular appendages play key roles in biofilm formation and 3D swarming, two multicellular behaviours of P. larvae that contribute to pathogenesis.

ABSTRACT
American foulbrood, a devastating bacterial disease affecting honey bee larvae, represents a major threat to apiculture worldwide. Its etiological agent, the Gram‐positive, endospore‐forming bacterium Paenibacillus larvae, has therefore been extensively studied to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying its pathogenicity and to identify key virulence determinants. In the present study, we identified the peritrichous flagella of P. larvae as a novel and important virulence factor of the genotype ERIC II. A flagella‐deficient mutant was generated and shown to exhibit multiple defects in vitro associated with biofilm formation, including altered biofilm architecture, reduced adhesion, impaired floating capacity and loss of swarming motility. Survival assays using honey bee larvae, complemented by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analyses of infected larvae, further demonstrated the crucial contribution of flagella to virulence in vivo by mediating biofilm formation on the larval midgut epithelium as well as three‐dimensional swarming during epithelial invasion.

title: Bacterial protein function prediction via multimodal deep learning.
abstract: Bacterial proteins are specialized with extensive functional diversity for survival in diverse and stressful environments. A significant portion of these proteins remains functionally uncharacterized, limiting our understanding of bacterial survival mechanisms. Hence, we develop Deep Expression STructure (DeepEST), a multimodal deep learning framework that predicts protein function in bacteria by assigning Gene Ontology (GO) terms. DeepEST comprises two modules: a multi-layer perceptron that uses gene expression and gene location, and a protein structure-based module that uses predicted structures and amino acid sequences. Within DeepEST, we integrate these modules through a learnable weighted linear combination and introduce a novel masked loss function to fine-tune the structure-based predictor for bacterial species. These choices are well suited for bacteria, in which functionally related genes frequently colocalize and are cotranscribed within operons, allowing transcription dynamics to serve as informative, condition-dependent signals. We show that DeepEST outperforms existing protein function prediction methods on a 25-species benchmark, relying solely on amino acid sequence or protein structure. Averaged over the 25 species, DeepEST reaches a protein-centric F max of 0.689 and a term-centric micro-AUPRC of 0.756, a relative improvement of 4.4% and 11.6% over the second-best method, the structure-based predictor DeepFRI. Moreover, DeepEST predicts GO terms for unclassified hypothetical proteins across 25 human bacterial pathogens, supporting their experimental characterization. DeepEST bridges organism-specific data integration and structure-based transfer learning, providing a method tailored for bacterial protein function prediction in settings with structural and multi-condition expression data.
authors: Miklautz L, Fernandez L, Muzio G, Adamer M, Borgwardt K, Avican K.

title: Cryo-EM structures of an Acinetobacter baumannii podovirus reveal a canonical capsid maturation
abstract: Phages that hunting multidrug resistant bacteria represent a promising approach in precision medicine nowadays, including these infecting Acinetobacter baumannii. To data, a large number of A. baumannii phages has been isolated, however, complete structural information remains not adequately released. Previously, we reported a podovirus, AbP20, that infects A. baumannii with potent efficacy in mouse model. In the present work, we further report the high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of AbP20 and its procapsid. The near-atomic resolution reveals that AbP20 is composed of five distinct structural subunits, i.e., capsid, portal, nozzle, fiber, and adaptor. We then characterized the assembly mechanisms of molecular interactions within capsid and portal-tail complex. By co-expressing the scaffold protein and the capsid protein of AbP20, we constructed the self-assembled DNA-free procapsid of AbP20. A near-atomic resolution reconstruction reveals it a double-layered concentric spherical architecture with a nearly 1:1 ratio of these two proteins. Comparison between the mature and apo-form of the capsid of AbP20 uncovers a canonical model of conformational switch from procapsid to capsid. Altogether, the present work reports the first whole atom structure of a podovirus infecting A. baumannii, providing a reference for structure-based phage engineering and editing.
authors: Xue, H., Rao, G., Li, X., Zhong, M., Cao, S., Yang, H.

title: Identification and characterization of new P. aeruginosa phages using a surface receptor platform
abstract: Bacteriophages are of increasing interest for their potential use as alternatives to antibiotics for treating drug-resistant infections. Phage steering, specifically receptor-based steering, involves use of phages that bias the development of resistance in bacteria towards phenotypes such as reduced fitness. Phage therapy typically involves administering cocktails of phages with different targets to reduce the likelihood of resistance emerging. To ensure effective steering and cocktail design, there is a need to identify the receptors used by phages of interest, and to isolate phages that use diverse receptors. Here we describe a SURFAce Receptor (SURFAR) platform consisting of a set of defined Pseudomonas aeruginosa strains and mutants for rapid characterization of phage receptors. This platform can also be used to enrich for and isolate diverse phages from environmental samples, yielding novel phage genomes from wastewater. Using the SURFAR platform, two new phages were isolated and characterized: Dalewood, which targets both flagella and the conserved LPS outer core, and Bowman, a biofilm targeting phage capable of supressing growth of a subset of carbapenem-resistant clinical isolates. This tool helps to standardize the laborious but important task of phage receptor characterization, with the goal of expanding the known repertoire of P. aeruginosa phage receptors and phages.
authors: Tran, V. N., Lahane, T. S., Qaderi, I., Harvey, H., Burrows, L. L.

title: Magnetic organelle gene clusters enable bacterial growth and ATP homeostasis under oxidizing conditions
abstract: Biological organisms can produce magnetic nanoparticles made of magnetite to detect the Earth's magnetic field for orientation. The evolutionary mechanisms that led to the acquisition of this capacity remain unknown. The most ancient organisms known to perform magnetic orientation are magnetotactic bacteria. Under tight genetic control, they produce chains of magnetite nanoparticles in dedicated organelles to allow efficient navigation in aquatic environments containing molecular oxygen. Yet, these bacteria have been proposed to emerge before molecular oxygen became abundant on Earth, at a time when this navigation system could not have served its current function. Here, we show that gene clusters responsible of magnetite formation and organization enable resistance against hydrogen peroxide, a toxic oxygen-derived compound that was produced during the early stages of Earth's oxygenation when iron oxidation consumed molecular oxygen. Characterization of the nanoparticle's oxidation state supported the involvement of magnetite in resistance to hydrogen peroxide-induced oxidative stress. These findings are compatible with an early emergence of magnetotactic bacteria, before natural waters became oxygenated. We propose a conceptual framework to explain the origin of magnetic orientation in bacteria, and offer tools to identify the initiation of Earth's oxygenation in a time-resolved manner.
authors: Kojadinovic-Sirinelli, M., Garry, M., Wan, J., Dumont, A., Egli, R., Carlut, J., Modolo, L., Chevrier, D. M., Marcano, L., Choueikani, F., Gatel, C., Andersen, I. M., Scoppola, E., Li, C., Brutesco, C., Nonnon, M., Gachon, E., Yvert, G., Piazza, A., Faivre, D., Komeili, A., Amor, M.

title: Microbially conjugated bile acids differentially affect the lifecycle and pathogenesis of Clostridioides difficile
abstract: Clostridioides difficile is a Gram-positive bacterium that causes C. difficile infection (CDI). In healthy adults, it has been proposed that the gut microbiota provides colonization resistance against C. difficile by competition through nutrient limitation and antagonism through secondary bile acid metabolism, the latter of which is mediated by the deconjugation of host-derived bile acids with bacterial bile salt hydrolases (BSH). Recently, BSHs have also shown an ability to reconjugate non-canonical (i.e., not glycine or taurine) amino acids to sterol cores, resulting in novel microbially conjugated bile acids (MCBAs). MCBAs have been associated with the resolution of recurrent CDI, though the mechanism underlying these effects are not well understood. To address this gap, we synthesized 36 MCBAs with nine amino acids (cysteine, isoleucine, leucine, phenylalanine, proline, serine, tryptophan, tyrosine, and valine) conjugated to the primary and secondary bile acids found in the human gut (CA, DCA, CDCA, and LCA) and tested their impact on various stages of C. difficiles lifecycle including bacterial outgrowth, membrane integrity, sporulation, and toxin activity. We show that BSH-mediated amidation of bile acid sterol cores can either increase or decrease inhibitory effects on C. difficile in an amino acid-dependent manner. For example, serine MCBAs enhanced C. difficiles ability to grow in otherwise inhibitory bile acid concentrations, increased spore production, and elevated toxin activity. Tryptophan MCBAs increased inhibition. By demonstrating these variable effects, our work clarifies the molecular determinants of MCBA activity and highlights specific MCBAs as promising targets for the development of C. difficile microbial-based therapeutics.
authors: Theriot, C. M., Hamacher, S. W., Nandwana, N. K., Lyons, N. S., Gancz, A. S., Perkins, C. E., Cheng, B., Gentry, E.

title: Asymmetric division and polar growth define a non-canonical cell cycle in Bradyrhizobium.
abstract: Bradyrhizobia are widely used as plant growth promoters in agriculture, yet their cell biology remains poorly understood. Here, we described for the first time, nucleoid segregation dynamics and the cell cycle of Bradyrhizobium at the cellular level. We show that highly asymmetric polar growth generates a short daughter cell and a longer mother cell at each division. Nucleoid compaction and positioning change across growth phases, culminating in a highly compacted, asymmetrically positioned nucleoid in stationary phase. ParB presents a subpolar localization, at the nucleoid periphery. Despite this pronounced cellular asymmetry and the presence of a single large chromosome, chromosome conformation capture reveals a global chromosome organization similar to that of bacteria undergoing conventional binary fission Together, these findings uncover a distinctive cell cycle program in Bradyrhizobium. showing that such extreme asymmetry in growth and division, significantly different from closely related characterized -Proteobacteriota, is compatible with conserved principles of chromosome organization.
authors: Medici, I. F.; Bressano, J.; Comerci, D. J.; Mongiardini, E. J.; Lioy, V. S.; Soler-Bistue, A.

title: Decoding the molecular cues regulating the transition of Influenza virus polymerase from transcriptase to replicase.
abstract: Influenza virus polymerase (FluPol) dynamically transitions between distinct conformational states to coordinate viral gene transcription and genome replication. While vRNP-associated monomeric FluPol supports transcription, ANP32-dependent asymmetric and ANP32-independent symmetric polymerase dimers mediate genome and antigenome (vRNA/cRNA) replication. How FluPol coordinates these distinct functional states to maintain the transcription-replication balance remains poorly understood. Here, we identify and characterize interdomain interactions within PB2 that govern the stability of the replication-competent conformation of FluPol. Specifically, a highly conserved salt bridge between PB2 Mid-E282 and NLS-K752 stabilizes the replicase conformation, while the charge state of residue 627 (E or K) dictates ANP32 engagement, together coordinating polymerase dimerization and replication activity. Strikingly, bat influenza A viruses H17N10 and H18N11 harbor unconventional serine substitutions at both positions, compromising polymerase dimerization, ANP32 interaction, and vRNA/cRNA replication. Remarkably, introducing these bat-signature substitutions (E282S/K627S) into human H1N1 polymerase results in phosphorylation at both positions in human cells. These findings suggest that phosphorylation can partially compensate for the loss of negative charge at these residues, revealing a phosphomimetic adaptation mechanism that modulates polymerase conformational dynamics and function. Collectively, our study reveals how a conserved interdomain interaction within PB2 regulates conformational transitions and transcription-replication balance of FluPol, which might have been driven by phosphomimetic adaptations during the course of a diverse range of influenza virus evolution.
authors: De, A.; Roy, A.; Mondal, A.

title: Genomic analysis of the Streptococcus anginosus group; taxonomic implications, evolutionary insights and clinical considerations
abstract: Background: The Streptococcus anginosus group (SAG) (S. anginosus, S. intermedius, and S. constellatus) causes serious, potentially life-threatening, invasive infections, often in otherwise healthy individuals. However, the group's diversity is still poorly understood, and with it, the ability to identify prognostic markers of severe disease. Methods: Long-read sequencing produced closed genomes for 29 isolates from 25 patients hospitalised primarily for invasive SAG infections, and 21 isolates from 20 non-hospitalised controls. Genomes were classified with GTDB-Tk and combined with 211 reference genomes. After dereplication, 207 SAG genomes (38 isolate, 169 reference) representing 206 strains were analysed using: GTDB classification, average nucleotide identity, multi-marker and core-genome SNP phylogenies, recombination-aware analyses, mobilome, CAZyme and gapseq metabolic profiling, and lineage-aware genome-wide association testing for invasive phenotype. Results: Agreement between GTDB-Tk and MALDI-TOF taxonomic classifications was low (42.8%), including two S. massiliensis cases mis-identified by MALDI-TOF as SAG. S. anginosus resolved into four taxa (S. anginosus, S. hominis, S. whileyi and S. vaginalis). Phylogenies based on core genome single-nucleotide polymorphisms resolved these species into distinct clades, whereas 16S rRNA gene and multilocus sequence analysis phylogenies did not. The four ex-S. anginosus taxa showed a gradient of genomic cohesion, with S. vaginalis being near-clonal, in contrast to S. anginosus, which shared high levels of sequence ancestry with other neighbouring taxa. Carbohydrate utilisation was strongly lineage-associated, as was propensity for invasive disease. A ~15Kbp glycosaminoglycan utilisation locus was found in the three taxa of highest disease severity propensity (S. intermedius, S. constellatus, S. whileyi) which predicts a direct host glycosaminoglycan feeding mechanism that may contribute to invasive disease. No single functional feature, gene or core-genome SNP was associated with invasiveness however after lineage-adjustment. Combined feature analysis suggests S. vaginalis has undergone a niche restriction and has evolved for a primary existence in the female urogenital tract. Conclusions: Under-reported species may be mis-diagnosed as SAG invasive infections. SAG is more diverse than its current three-species definition, with the conventional S. anginosus species proposed to be classed into a complex of four distinct taxa. Invasive capacity appears to be an emergent system-level property rather than from individual features.
authors: Coleman, A.; Liaw, J.; Maresco-Pennisi, D.; Deehan, R.; Harris, P. N. A.; Cervin, A.; Edkins, O.; Zaugg, J.; Bialasiewicz, S.

title: Metabolites cross the membrane, the transcriptome does not follow: co-localization is required for the cyanobacterial response to a yeast partner
abstract: Interactions between phototrophs and heterotrophs are usually explained by cross-feeding, yet whether that exchange alone accounts for the phototroph's response has rarely been tested. We grew the sucrose-secreting cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus with the yeast Rhodotorula toruloides as a synthetic community, either in mixed co-culture or in membrane-separated co-culture (0.22 m pore size), each with a matched axenic control. Metabolite exchange occurred in both configurations: sucrose reached the yeast and was consumed, and yeast-derived metabolites reached the cyanobacterium. The yeast reached a higher final density behind the membrane, whereas the cyanobacterium gained about 9% over its axenic control only in mixed co-culture. Yet the cyanobacterial transcriptome responded only with co-localization: expression of 51 genes changed consistently across time points (day-averaged q < 0.05), against one gene behind the membrane, and the number of differentially expressed genes rose from 20 on day 4 to 91 and 127 on days 6 and 8. Nine regulatory programs (iModulons), mainly nitrogen and photosynthesis, responded in mixed co-culture and none behind the membrane. Reactor configuration alone changed 40 genes in axenic culture. These results suggest that co-localization, in addition to metabolite exchange, was required for the heterotrophic partner to trigger a response in the phototroph. Co-culture studies that infer interactions from shared metabolites may miss effects that depend on spatial structure. Importance Partnerships between light-powered microbes and the heterotrophs living alongside them move large amounts of carbon in oceans and soils, and are now built on purpose to turn carbon dioxide into fuels and chemicals. Such partnerships are usually described by the chemicals the partners trade, so we asked whether those chemicals are enough. The cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus and the yeast Rhodotorula toruloides were grown together in one vessel, or in two chambers divided by a membrane that molecules cross but cells cannot. The yeast fed on cyanobacterial sugar in both, yet the cyanobacterium changed its gene activity only when the two shared a space. Partners in nature are usually clustered rather than evenly mixed, so closeness may contribute as much as the chemicals themselves. Keeping partners apart in engineered cultures can still deliver carbon to the heterotroph, but may not deliver the benefits of partnership to the phototroph.
authors: Bohutskyi, P.; Johnson, Z.; Velickovic, M.; Kim, Y.-M.; Cheung, M.

title: The enemy of my enemy: A bacterial antagonist rescues Chlamydomonas by inactivating a toxin from a rival
abstract: Microbial interactions are shaped by multiple community members, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated a tripartite interaction between the microalga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and two Pseudomonas bacteria that coexist in the same soil habitat. In pairwise cultures, all three interactions are amensalistic (-like): Pseudomonas protegens Pf-5 antagonizes both C. reinhardtii and Pseudomonas fluorescens HKI0770 without benefit, while P. fluorescens inhibits C. reinhardtii without profiting from the alga. However, in a tripartite culture, P. fluorescens protects C. reinhardtii from P. protegens and promotes algal recovery. This protection is not stopped when the used carbon source, acetate, is supplemented. The P. fluorescens rescue effect is associated with reduced levels of the polyyne toxin protegencin produced by P. protegens. Protegencin levels, detected by Raman microspectroscopy, are decreased by application of spent medium or protein extracts from P. fluorescens, while heat- and protease-treatment abolish this activity. A heat-sensitive, proteinaceous factor, likely an enzyme(s), appears to contribute to protegencin inactivation. Our results show that P. fluorescens rescues C. reinhardtii by inactivating protegencin, despite being inhibited by P. protegens. These findings demonstrate the importance of investigating higher-order effects, since additional community members can transform pairwise antagonistic interactions into conditional protection through toxin inactivation.
authors: Vuong, T.; Schultz, C.; Suma, H. R.; Then, P.; Jana, S.; Schmitt, M.; Popp, J.; Stallforth, P.; Mittag, M.

title: CauloBrowser 2.0: an AI powered update
abstract: CauloBrowser is a systems-biology database for Caulobacter crescentus that organizes the largest repository of experimental data for this model bacterium. The original CauloBrowser provided a web interface for accessing these data, but the growing number of experimental datasets and advances in AI chatbots motivated an updated resource. We developed CauloBrowser 2.0 (CauloBrowser.org) as an open-source application that broadens access to RNA-seq, microarray, ribosome profiling, Tn-seq, ChIP-seq, and genome annotation data. The CauloChat AI interface allows users to query these datasets in natural language, generate visualizations, and achieve complex biological insights. While the database is hosted freely on the web, users may also download the database and run it locally, reducing dependence on the web-hosted service and allowing laboratories to use compatible unpublished datasets. Altogether, CauloBrowser 2.0 provides a significant update for exploring diverse systems biology data in C. crescentus.
authors: Aldikacti, B.; Lawal, V. A.; Chien, P.; Schrader, J. M.

title: Metatranscriptomic Profiling of Viral Diversity in Aquatic Environments with a Focus on Microalgal Viruses
abstract: Freshwater microeukaryotes contribute to aquatic productivity, yet the RNA viruses associated with these communities remain incompletely characterized compared with their marine counterparts. Here, we used metatranscriptomics to profile viral diversity across five Finnish freshwater sites (one river and four lakes) and one coastal marine sample from Hiroshima Bay in the Seto Inland Sea, Japan. We recovered 399 viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs), of which 285 (71.4%) represented RNA viruses distributed across five viral phyla and putatively associated with fungal, plant or algal, metazoan and bacterial hosts. DNA viruses formed a smaller component of the dataset, including bacteriophage-like vOTUs with transcripts encoding replication, structural, packaging, and lysis proteins. Two vOTUs, which were detected in the Vantaanjoki river sample, were putatively classified within the family Marnaviridae, which comprises RNA viruses that infect protists in marine and freshwater environments. Both vOTUs encoded conserved replication and picornavirus-like capsid domains, and one represented a near-complete dicistronic genome. RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) -based phylogeny placed these vOTUs in a strongly supported lineage outside the currently recognized genera within the family Marnaviridae, supporting their provisional assignment to the candidate genus Vandarnavirus proposed here within Marnaviridae. Whole-genome comparisons using the IMG/VR v4 database revealed genetic similarities between the vOTUs representing the candidate Vandarnavirus genus and picorna-like virus sequences from freshwater, wetland, saltmarsh, and estuarine metatranscriptomes. These findings expand the known ecological range of marnavirus-like RNA viruses and identify freshwater habitats as under-sampled reservoirs of microalgae-associated viral sequences.
authors: Ojha R, Demina T, Beltrani C, Abidizadegan M, Monttinen HAM, Oksanen HM, Peltomaa E, Tomaru Y, Ahola T, Sadeghi M.

title: The biochemical composition of coronavirus Nucleocapsid proteins drives the bicistronic properties of their sub-genomic mRNAs
abstract: The nucleocapsid (N) gene of coronaviruses (CoVs) encodes a structural RNA-binding protein required for viral assembly. In SARS- and MERS-CoV viruses, reading frame 2 of N contains an overlapping open reading frame (ORF) encoding an innate immune antagonist accessory protein. However, the extent of this dual coding capacity across the CoV family, and the genetic features driving overlapping ORF formation, remain unexamined. Here, we developed an in-silico tool (ORFan) to screen structural gene sub-genomic mRNA sequences from 152 species of coronavirus for the presence of overlapping accessory gene candidates. We found that frame 2 of the N gene in Alpha-, Beta- and Delta-CoVs frequently contains a potential accessory ORF (AcORF), conserved at the subgenus level, unlike the spike, envelope and membrane genes. We also show that CoV nucleotide biases in conjunction with codon biases integral to N protein function drive the relatively high abundances of start codons in frame two and stop codons in frame three, explaining the tendency towards frame 2 AcORFs. We further suggest that viral nucleotide biases and the codon composition required for RNA-binding function facilitate overlapping ORF formation in other virus families
authors: De Angelis, F.; Chook, H. W.; Apaa, T.; Seekings, A.; McElhinney, L.; Rademan, R.; Geldenhuys, M.; Markotter, W.; Pinto, R. M.; Gaunt, E. R.; Lu, L. R.; Lycett, S. J.; Digard, P.

title: High reproducibility demonstrated in a direct-to-consumer microbiome testing workflow under real-world conditions using fecal reference material
abstract: Recent studies have documented substantial variation in microbiome profiles recovered from identical biological samples across direct-to-consumer (DTC) gut microbiome testing providers and, in some cases, within individual providers. These reports underscore the need for transparent, published assessments of analytical performance from the companies offering these services. To assess analytical reproducibility in our own testing workflow, we processed 10 replicates of a homogenized National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) human fecal reference material (RM 8048) through our full sample processing pipeline, from sample collection to data generation. Replicates were shipped from five U.S. sites over a staggered 35-day window. They were processed amongst over 6,000 customer samples, batched for DNA extraction and sequencing based on their arrival in the lab in nine separate sequencing runs, and analyzed using our standard pipeline. The 10 reference material replicates yielded highly concordant community profiles regardless of shipping time or temperature. Technical variability was minimal (median Bray-Curtis dissimilarity = 0.04) compared with the variation observed in samples from the same Tiny Health customer collected the same day (median Bray-Curtis: 0.08), within one week (0.25), one to two weeks apart (0.28), and between unrelated individuals (0.88). When evaluated using NIST's Coefficient of Disagreement (COD) metric, our workflow yielded a maximum pairwise COD of 0.045, well below NIST's published upper bound of 0.073 for this reference material. All three spike-in control strains were successfully recovered from every sample. These results demonstrate the reproducibility of our DTC microbiome testing workflow under real-world conditions, with robust consistency across sample collection, shipping, laboratory processing, and bioinformatics analysis. They also highlight the value of RM 8048 and similar reference materials for evaluating and transparently reporting analytical performance in DTC microbiome testing.
authors: Trachsel, J. M.; Sturgeon, H.; Goad, D. M.; Straub, T. J.; Mars, R. A. T.; Sew Hoy, C.; Sukhum, K. V.

title: Dynamic allocation of MurJ coordinates bacterial growth and division
abstract: Rod-shaped bacteria grow by inserting peptidoglycan into the lateral cell wall during elongation and into the septal cell wall during division. These two modes of growth are driven by distinct peptidoglycan synthesis machineries that consume the shared precursor Lipid II and must be coordinated so that cell enlargement remains matched to division. However, how cells spatially allocate this shared precursor, and whether Lipid II translocation itself contributes to this coordi-nation, remain unclear. Here we show that the spatial distribution of the essential Lipid II flippase MurJ coordinates this balance in Escherichia coli. Increasing nonseptal MurJ abundance shifted cell-wall synthesis toward elongation and reduced septal synthesis. Single-molecule tracking revealed that MurJ diffuses throughout the membrane but is transiently captured at the division site, rather than stably incorporated into the septal synthesis machinery. This recruitment requires active septal cell-wall synthesis, but not ongoing Lipid II synthesis or flipping, indicating that MurJ recruitment is coupled to the active synthesis machinery rather than to substrate availability or transport. Thus, activation of septal synthesis creates transient MurJ capture at the division site, providing a mechanism to preferentially supply Lipid II for septal growth during cytokinesis. These findings reveal a capture-and-release mechanism that dynamically enriches MurJ at active division sites and thereby coordinates elongation and division in bacterial cells.
authors: Yan, D.; Duan, S.; He, H.; Sheng, J.; Zhang, Y.; Li, Y.; Du, S.; Tang, S.; Fu, Y.; Yang, X.

title: A Urinary Metabolomic Signature Associated with Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth in Children with Short Bowel Syndrome
abstract: Direct sampling of the small intestinal microbiome is challenging. Urinary metabolites may offer a noninvasive approach to studying microbial functional activity. We used clinically available gas chromatography/mass spectrometry to profile urinary organic acids in 94 children with short bowel syndrome, comparing those with clinically defined small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO; n=21) with those without SIBO (n=73). SIBO-associated metabolites included microbial fermentation products, dietary derivatives, and host metabolic intermediates. Metabolites enriched in SIBO mapped to aromatic amino acid metabolism, including tryptophan and tyrosine pathways, consistent with altered microbial fermentation. Many associations persisted after adjustment for intestinal anatomy, age, antibiotic exposure, and nutritional composition. These findings identified a urinary metabolic profile associated with clinically defined SIBO in children with short bowel syndrome and support further evaluation of urinary metabolomics as a noninvasive approach to studying small intestinal microbial function.
authors: Zong, W.; Gan, S.; Zarek, C.; He, M.; Alame, R.; Tovar, E.; Yang, S.; Huo, S.; Albenberg, L.; Zhan, X.; Wu, G. D.; Bales, C.; Koh, A.

title: Higher-order metabolic interactions among oral commensals gate pathobiont expansion through succinate-driven pH modulation
abstract: Despite advances in defining microbiome shifts associated with inflammatory mucosal diseases, the ecological interactions that constrain or facilitate pathobiont expansion remain poorly understood. Using a six-species synthetic oral microbial community and factorial interaction screening, we identified a higher-order interaction governing the growth of the periodontal pathobiont Porphyromonas gingivalis. The core community member Veillonella parvula was the strongest positive determinant of P. gingivalis growth, but this effect was substantially reduced by the health-associated commensal Actinomyces oris. A. oris-mediated antagonism resulted from extracellular acidification and was enhanced under anaerobic conditions. Genetic dissection of A. oris fermentation revealed that lactate dehydrogenase (ldh1) contributes to anaerobic lactate production, but ldh1 deletion only partially relieved P. gingivalis inhibition. Instead, succinate, produced through a succinate dehydrogenase/fumarate reductase pathway (sdh2), emerged as the principal driver of acidification and P. gingivalis suppression. At high cell densities, however, V. parvula consumed both lactate and succinate, reversing acidification and restoring conditions permissive for P. gingivalis growth. To assess the relevance of these interactions in vivo, we analyzed subgingival microbiome from 1,355 adults, including 555 with detectable P. gingivalis. Among these individuals, P. gingivalis abundance was negatively associated with Actinomyces abundance after adjustment for periodontitis severity, whereas this association was attenuated at high V. parvula abundance, consistent with the interaction observed in vitro. Together, these findings identify succinate as a previously unrecognized mediator of interbacterial antagonism and reveal how higher-order metabolic interactions among oral commensals regulate pathobiont expansion through pH modulation, with protective effects shaped by oxygen availability and metabolic cross-feeding.
authors: Soh, D.; Bhat, A.; Li, L.; Smardz, M.; Parker, C.; Tiede, E.; Nelson, B.; Frerichs, V.; Wood, T.; Ikonomou, L.; Ton-That, H.; Diaz, P. I.

title: Transcriptome reallocation during infection reshapes synonymous codon demand in Botrytis cinerea
abstract: While genomic codon usage is fixed within an individual isolate, the synonymous codons represented in its RNA pool can change when transcription shifts among genes. We tested whether this transcript-level phenotype accompanies infection by reanalyzing 39 libraries from three public Botrytis cinerea RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) time series in S. lycopersicum, Arabidopsis thaliana, and Physcomitrium patens. Gene counts were corrected for coding length, combined with fixed gene-specific codon inventories, and analyzed as centered log ratios within synonymous amino-acid families. Sampling time accounted for 95-98% of fungal codon-demand variation in each series. The association persisted after effective-length correction, unique-only competitive mapping, host-homology exclusion, depth equalization, protein-family weighting, and removal of translation-associated genes. Change vectors over the interpolated, time-aligned 16-24-h interval were positively aligned among studies, whereas later trajectories diverged. Matched reassignments of complete expression trajectories showed more full-series organization than expected in S. lycopersicum and Arabidopsis, but not in P. patens. Codon-preference-weighted abundance and expression breadth also changed through infection, although their directions were not universal. Across systems, large non-translation contributors repeatedly carried ATP-synthase/respiratory and extracellular annotations, although their timing and companion functions differed. Infection-associated transcriptional reallocation therefore repeatedly restructures the synonymous composition of the inferred fungal transcript pool. This establishes a dynamic allocation phenotype and a basis for testing consequences for RNA stability and translation during host-pathogen interactions.
authors: Dowell, J.; Pradhan, L.; Madrigal, M.

title: Sexing carnivores from faecal metagenomes: calibrating Rx for stone marten and red fox
abstract: Knowing the sex of the animal that deposited a scat adds value to non-invasive monitoring, but read-ratio sexing methods were developed for human ancient DNA. We examined their use in shotgun metagenomes of seven stone marten (Martes foina) and red fox (Vulpes vulpes) scats. Human DNA, present in every library, was removed by competitive mapping against the host assembly and the human reference. Applying the Skoglund Ry metric to the marten samples yielded 0 to 25 Y-mapping reads per sample and failed to identify either of the two animals that Rx places firmly in the male range, so we adopted the X-to-autosome ratio Rx of Mittnik et al. instead, reimplemented as an open-source, species-agnostic Python tool. To test whether its human-derived thresholds transfer, we simulated female and male genomes of both species and drew 200 replicate subsamples at each of fourteen depths from 1,000 to 100,000 mapped reads. Nine of 11,200 replicates were assigned to the wrong sex, all of them below 2,000 mapped reads; above that depth the only failure was non-assignment, in under 5% of replicates above 7,500 reads and under 1% above 15,000. Applied to the scats, Rx identified four females and two males; one sample with 596 host-assigned reads was left unassigned. With competitive removal of human reads, Rx and its original thresholds are usable in these carnivores.
authors: Vujic, V.; Mayer, C.; Helyes, G.; Maroti-Agots, A.; Maroti, G.; Csabai, I.; Solymosi, N.

title: NanoPAMDA enables rapid PAM characterization of metagenome-derived Cas9 effectors
abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 orthologs remain functionally underexplored despite the rapidly growing scale of publicly available metagenomic sequencing data. Here, we applied a multi-stage computational discovery pipeline to two independent sources of metagenomic sequence data, a multi-biome collection of 660,185 metagenome-assembled genomes spanning 17 public catalogs, and raw sequencing reads from human microbiome studies assembled de novo, to identify novel Cas9 orthologs. Candidates were filtered for guide RNA architectural plausibility, sequence novelty, conservation of catalytic residues, and structural integrity, yielding 14 candidates spanning both data sources for experimental characterization. To determine PAM preference at scale, we developed a cost-effective Nanopore long-read-based adaptation of the high-throughput PAM determination assay (NanoPAMDA), enabling rapid, time-resolved, kinetic PAM profiling across many candidates in parallel. One Cas9 effector, E10, showed PAM-specific activity in vitro and was catalytically active in E. coli. Together, these findings demonstrate a scalable, long-read sequencing-based framework for discovering and biochemically characterizing novel Cas9 orthologs from metagenomic data.
authors: Genel, I.; Suren, C.; Kurt, I. C.

title: Notch/NF-κB crosstalk signaling controls SASP gene expression during brain aging
abstract: AbstractBrain aging is associated with chronic, low-grade inflammation known as inflammaging, which is largely driven by senescent glial cells secreting pro-inflammatory factors termed as senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). In humans, the release of SASP factors in the brain is linked with an increased risk for the development of neurodegenerative disorders; thus, elucidating the underlying molecular mechanisms is essential for understanding the pathophysiology of brain aging. Both NF-κB and Notch signaling are known to regulate SASP expression; however, their mode of interaction in brain inflammaging is poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that brain aging is broadly associated with NF-κB activation but Notch suppression using different transgenic mouse models. Astrocytic NF-κB activation in young mice was able to mimic premature SASP formation but repressed Notch signaling in parallel. Bioinformatic analyses further identified conserved crosstalk sites within SASP genes co-occupied by Notch/RBPJ and NF-κB transcription factors in vivo, allowing specific combinatorial regulation. Importantly, selective physical interactions enable that activated Notch can act as a negative modulator of NF-κB signaling at different molecular levels. Consistently, pharmacological activation of Notch in primary astrocytes significantly reduced NF-κB-driven SASP gene expression. Together, these findings identify Notch–NF-κB crosstalk as a potential therapeutic target to mitigate brain inflammaging.

title: New pathogenic ZNHIT3 variants causing fetal hydrops and lethality disrupt snoRNP assembly
abstract: AbstractZNHIT3 is a conserved assembly factor required for biogenesis of box C/D small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein (snoRNP) complexes, which are key players in ribosome biogenesis. Pathogenic variants in ZNHIT3 cause Progressive Encephalopathy with Edema, Hypsarrhythmia, and Optic Atrophy (PEHO) syndrome, a severe neurodevelopmental disorder typically recognized postnatally. Here, we describe two fetuses from a single family who developed isolated hydrops in the early second trimester of pregnancy, resulting in intrauterine demise. Whole-genome quartet sequencing identified two new ZNHIT3 variants, c.40T > C; p.(Cys14Arg) and c.251_254del; p.(Glu84Alafs*8), inherited from healthy parents that present as compound heterozygous alleles in both fetuses. Functional studies using a ZNHIT3 knockdown-rescue system in HEK293T cells demonstrated impaired proliferation and increased apoptosis and revealed distinct molecular consequences for the two variants. One variant produced a stable ZNHIT3 protein lacking the region required for interaction with NUFIP1 and efficient box C/D snoRNP assembly, whereas the second variant reduced ZNHIT3 protein abundance. Both variants impaired snoRNP assembly, reduced the abundance of select box C/D snoRNAs, and caused site-specific losses of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) 2′-O-methylation. These defects were accompanied by changes in ribosome biogenesis and reduced translational output. Together, our findings expand the phenotypic spectrum associated with ZNHIT3 deficiency to include severe antenatal disease and demonstrate that impaired box C/D snoRNP assembly and rRNA modification represent convergent molecular consequences of pathogenic ZNHIT3 variants.

title: Transcription factor CCTF1 plays an important role in regulating proteasome activity during archaeal cell division
abstract: AbstractArchaea of the order Sulfolobales exhibit a highly ordered cell cycle progression similar to that of eukaryotes. It has been demonstrated that degradation of the cell division protein CdvB by the proteasome controls the progression of cell division. However, how the proteasome itself is regulated during the cell cycle is not fully understood. Recently, the cyclically expressed ArsR (arsenical resistance operon repressor) family transcription factor CCTF1 (cell cycle transcription factor 1) was shown to repress expression of PAN (proteasome-activating nucleotidase) in Sulfolobus acidocaldarius. Here, using biochemical approaches, comparative transcriptomics, and proteomics, we provide further insights into the CCTF1 function and show that it regulates PAN expression in Saccharolobus islandicus by binding to an AT-rich palindromic sequence within the pan promoter. We also reassessed the role of the cyclically expressed protein kinase aCcrK in the regulation of proteasome activity and conclude that CCTF1, rather than aCcrK, is the primary factor controlling the proteasome activity. These findings advance our understanding of the proteasome-mediated cell cycle regulation in archaea.

title: Systematic engineering of synthetic minimal promoters for tunable transgene expression in mammalian cells
abstract: AbstractFine-tuning transgene levels is crucial in fundamental and applied research. Native promoters are broadly utilized to regulate transgene expression. However, their large size and structural complexity hinder predictable tuning, constrain compatibility with viral vectors with limited capacity, and increase the risk of homologous recombination. Synthetic promoters are short de novo sequences, typically consisting of an enhancer region, which is positioned upstream of a minimal promoter that determines transcription initiation efficiency. Enhancer optimization typically yields coarse activation shifts, alters response curves, and requires case-by-case optimization. Synthetic minimal promoter architecture enables fine-tuning that is potentially compatible with any enhancer region. In this study, we systematically optimized minimal promoter sequences, core element composition, and regulatory motif sequences. Our findings support a modular model of minimal promoter function in which cis-regulatory elements from different minimal promoters can be mixed, altered, added, or deleted to yield predictable expression outcomes. We shortened and thereby enhanced the efficiency of known minimal promoters, engineered modular tunable minimal promoters, and generated candidate regulatory elements spanning 7–8 nucleotides that drive efficient transcription when combined with artificial ${5^{\prime}}$ untranslated regions (5'UTRs) that function as an additional regulatory layer. This framework broadens the utility of synthetic promoters for next-generation applications.

title: DNA mimic helical foldamers with up to 100 units: synthesis and recognition of a multiprotein complex
abstract: AbstractDNA mimic foldamers (DMFOs) are helically folded aromatic oligoamides that mimic the shape and charge distribution of double-stranded B-DNA. DMFOs consist of an alternation of two amino acid monomers, M and Q. Here, we introduce a new synthetic approach of (MQ)n oligomers on solid phase that enabled the production of sequences as long as a 100mer, formally equivalent to a 50-base pair DNA duplex. The approach takes advantage of dimeric Fmoc-MQ-OH as building blocks. Three such macromonomers were synthesized using Q and M units bearing different side chains. Solid phase synthesis protocols were validated in all series. Helix handedness was shown to be determined by a single chiral residue. The purified long oligomers were analyzed by reversed phase HPLC, mass spectrometry, circular dichroism, and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy for their purity, identity, and helix-handedness bias. Clusters of foldamers forming in the presence of Ca2+ could be visualized by cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM). Lastly, a 72mer DMFO was shown to bind to the A-module of the chromatin remodeling complex INO80 slightly tighter than a comparable DNA duplex. A cryo-EM structure of the complex at a resolution of 3.59 Å showed that the DMFO occupies the A-module DNA binding region.

title: Detection and quantification of DNA double-strand breaks by genomic and imaging methods: a critical appraisal of capabilities and limitations
abstract: AbstractDNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are the most genotoxic form of DNA damage. Unrepaired DSBs may cause loss of chromosome fragments at mitosis, while incorrectly repaired DSBs can cause chromosome aberrations and other adverse effects, leading to cell cycle arrest, senescence, cell death, or neoplastic transformation. Detecting and quantifying DSBs is important in studies of genome instability, aging, and cancer. Methods of detecting and quantifying DSBs fall into two broad categories: imaging-based methods, used to detect and localize DNA breaks in individual cells, and genomic methods, a new category utilizing massively parallel DNA sequencing to map DSBs genome-wide in a cell population. Imaging and genomic methods yield fundamentally different information. This review focuses on a critical evaluation of the capabilities and limitations of genomic and imaging methods for the detection and quantification of DSBs. It explains why the class of genomic methods, where quantification is based on counting the detected unique DSBs and the number of cells in the sample, results in inaccurate assessment of the average number of DSBs per cell and how this problem can be solved. We also discuss complementarity of genomic and imaging methods and potential directions of their future development.

title: Coupling metabolic enhancement to plasmid spread enables programmable antimicrobial control
abstract: AbstractThe rise of multidrug-resistant pathogens underscores the need for precise antimicrobial strategies beyond conventional antibiotics. Conjugation-based approaches offer a powerful yet underexploited means of delivering targeted genetic interventions within microbial communities. Here, we combine selective killing modules with optimized conjugative vectors to target antibiotic-resistant pathogens and clinically relevant resistance plasmids. First, we engineered toxin–intein modules, programmable cassettes that restrict toxic activity to specific regulatory contexts. We developed modules targeting Shigella spp., Salmonella enterica, and bacteria carrying the resistance plasmid pOXA-48, demonstrating tunable and selective activity at both species and strain levels. To identify the optimal delivery platform, we compared mobilizable and conjugative plasmids, finding that conjugative systems consistently outperform mobilizable ones by approximately one order of magnitude. We then streamlined the broad-host-range plasmid RP4 and enhanced its functionality by incorporating the metabolic fos locus, a type IV pilus operon or both features combined. Integration of the anti-pOXA-48 module into these vectors enabled effective suppression of resistance plasmid spread in complex microbial communities. Together, these results advance the use of conjugative plasmids as programmable antimicrobial platforms and identify delivery efficiency and ecological competitiveness as key determinants of the success of such interventions.

title: CFDP1 is required for histone variant H2A.Z deposition by the human SRCAP chromatin remodeling complex
abstract: AbstractCraniofacial Developmental Protein 1 (CFDP1) is a member of the evolutionarily conserved family of Bucentaur (BCNT) proteins and is required for cell survival and differentiation during tooth development. Its yeast homolog is involved in histone variant H2A.Z deposition by the yeast SWR1C remodeler. Direct connections between CFDP1, H2A.Z deposition, and the mammalian SWR1 homolog, Snf2-Related CREBBP Activator Protein (SRCAP), are poorly understood. Here, we perform detailed biochemical reconstitution and characterization of the human SRCAP complex (SRCAP-C). We find that CFDP1 weakly interacts with SRCAP-C in a salt concentration-dependent manner and is essential for H2A.Z dimer exchange by SRCAP-C. We show that CFDP1 stimulates the basal ATPase activity of reconstituted SRCAP-C, suggesting a requirement for CFDP1 in regulating intrinsic catalytic ATPase activity. Additionally, CFDP1 deficiency in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) leads to a genome-wide reduction of H2A.Z, H3K27me3, and H3K4me3 deposition, accompanied by the upregulation of developmental genes normally marked by these modifications. Taken together, our results provide mechanistic insights into how CFDP1 regulates histone variant H2A.Z deposition by SRCAP-C. Given mutations in the SRCAP gene cause Floating-Harbor syndrome, a rare, dominant developmental disorder, our study provides an additional link between craniofacial development and SRCAP-mediated H2A.Z deposition.

title: Correction to ‘Molecular basis for the regulation of retroviral nucleosomal integration by chromatin compaction’
abstract: This is a correction to: Delphine Lapaillerie, Yury Zgadzay, Fábio Gouveia Martins, Carole Bertinetti, Michel Autin, Julien Batisse, Camille Tumiotto, Paul Lesbats, Marc Ruff, Sergio Filipe Sousa, Vincent Parissi, Molecular basis for the regulation of retroviral nucleosomal integration by chromatin compaction, Nucleic Acids Research, Volume 54, Issue 13, 22 July 2026, gkag705, https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkag705

title: Drift-Driven Microbiome Simplification Generates Reconstructable and Ecologically Cohesive Microbial Communities
abstract: Engineering simplified microbial communities that retain function and ecological cohesiveness remains a major challenge because the taxa and interactions required for community establishment are rarely known a priori. Here, we experimentally evaluated drift-driven microbiome simplification as an alternative strategy for generating reduced and reconstructable microbial consortia. Using the tomato rhizosphere as a model system, three source microbial communities were subjected to different dilution bottlenecks and serial propagation. Increasing dilution was the main determinant of community composition and simplification, while repeated passage produced additional reductions in ASV richness, phylogenetic diversity, and evenness. Importantly, diversity loss was not accompanied by a uniform deterioration in bacterial colonization or plant performance, indicating that substantial simplification can occur without a parallel collapse in these system-level properties. Candidate Minimal Microbiome prototypes were selected from endpoint communities, reconstructed as synthetic communities, and their ecological cohesiveness was evaluated through invasion experiments. The reconstructed communities strongly restricted the establishment of the original complex microbial fractions, although invasion success depended markedly on invader identity. The drift-derived communities were at least as resistant to invasion as an independently designed bottom-up synthetic community. Together, these results provide experimental support for drift-driven simplification as a strategy to generate reduced microbial communities whose dominant members can be isolated, reconstructed, and experimentally evaluated. By allowing ecological assembly to generate candidate community configurations before cultivation and reconstruction, this approach provides a complementary route to rational bottom-up design and function-directed top-down microbiome engineering.

title: Diversity and Life-History Strategies of Rhizosphere Microbial Communities Associated with Deyeuxia Angustifolia Along a Wetland Degradation Gradient
abstract: Wetland degradation alters rhizosphere habitats and resource availability, yet its effects on bacterial and fungal diversity and life-history strategies remain unclear. We examined Deyeuxia angustifolia rhizosphere communities across four wetland types in the Sanjiang Plain, China: marsh (ZZ), typical meadow (DC), slightly degraded (DN), and severely degraded (DS). We measured plant biomass and soil properties and analyzed microbial communities using 16 S rRNA gene and ITS amplicon sequencing, life-history strategy indices, and partial least-squares path modeling (PLS-PM). Bacterial and fungal community composition differed significantly among wetland types (P ≤ 0.001 and P = 0.006, respectively). Bacterial alpha diversity did not differ significantly, whereas fungal Shannon and ACE indices were lower in DN than in DC (P < 0.05). The relative abundances of Acidobacteriota and Archaeorhizomyces increased with degradation, whereas Pseudomonadota and Actinomycetota peaked in DC; Ascomycota dominated fungal communities. The bacterial oligotrophic-to-copiotrophic ratio was highest in ZZ, followed by DN, with both exceeding DC and DS (P < 0.05). The fungal ectomycorrhizal-to-saprotrophic ratio showed no significant differences. PLS-PM indicated that degradation was negatively associated with soil environmental conditions (P < 0.001), which were positively associated with the bacterial oligotrophic-to-copiotrophic ratio (P < 0.05) and negatively associated with fungal alpha diversity (P < 0.05). Overall, fungal diversity in the rhizosphere soil of Deyeuxia angustifolia differed significantly across the wetland degradation gradient. Bacterial life-history strategies showed a significant, non-linear shift among degradation stages, reflected in changes in the relative dominance of oligotrophic and copiotrophic taxa. These findings provide insight into how wetland microbial communities respond to degradation and may inform wetland restoration.

title: The Ecology of Beech Bark Beetle Mycobiomes: Similar Fungal Composition Despite Host, Elevation and Site Gradients.
abstract: Bark beetles form varying associations with fungi, yet the mycobiomes of many deciduous phloem-feeding species are poorly studied and their ecological significance remains underexplored. Here, we used ITS2 metabarcoding to characterize the fungal communities of the beech bark beetles Ernoporicus fagi and Taphrorychus bicolor collected from 61 forest patches across six regions in Germany. Despite sampling two beetle species across an elevational gradient, experimental forest management treatments, and six regions, beetle species identity, treatment, and elevation explained little variation in beetle mycobiomes, and region showed only a weak effect that disappeared under closer inspection. However, we found mycobiome composition varied more consistently at the finer scale of individual forest sites, and geographic distance between patches had a weak but significant effect, suggesting that the fungal communities these bark beetles carry are shaped by local, patch-level factors rather than broader regional or host-related factors. The mycobiomes of both beetle species were largely similar and dominated by ubiquitous saprotrophs and yeasts.
authors: Carlson L, Kowallik V, Hübscher K, Rabenhofer L, Schernickau K, Biedermann PHW.

title: Towards a Superorganismal Perspective of Honey Bee Microbiota: Taxonomic Resolution by Niche and 16S rRNA Gene Variable Region
abstract: The honey bee (Apis mellifera) colony is a superorganism, but its microbiota is known mostly from the worker hindgut. Direct comparison across studies and niches is confounded by different regions of the 16S rRNA gene, bioinformatic processing choices, and reference database used for taxonomic assignment. We reprocessed 4,586 short-read Illumina libraries from 37 BioProjects, and added 345 full-length (V1-V9) PacBio libraries of dissected worker and queen gut tissues as a reference. Sequences were processed using one set of filtering and reporting thresholds and one species-level reference database. Each library was processed twice, with and without read denoising. The two methods agreed on genus-level composition but denoised reads produced far fewer amplicon sequence variants per library and significantly lower alpha diversity. Species resolution was highly dependent on 16​S rRNA gene region. Full-length reads named nearly every major genus to species, while some short regions named almost none. The superorganismal microbiota is comprised of both niche specialists, and generalists shared across multiple niches. We identified at least three abundant amplicon sequencing variants that lack species-level description. Contaminant reads were abundant throughout the dataset due to next generation sequencing of niches with low microbial biomass. Contaminants scaled inversely with bacterial load, dominating drone reproductive tissue, larvae, mouthparts, hive materials, control or lab reared worker guts and stored food. Thus, conclusions about honey bee microbiota and/or its integration with host information depend strongly on primer region, how sequencing error was handled, and the level of high-throughput sequencing contamination.

title: Phototrophic Fe(II)‐Oxidizers Can Use Multiple (In)Organic Substrates Simultaneously
abstract:
We demonstrated that photoferrotrophs generally utilized organics and Fe(II) simultaneously, and that two of the strains prefer Fe(II) over H2. For some photoferrotrophs, Fe(II) oxidation rates were significantly enhanced by the presence of acetate, lactate, and glucose. On the other hand, H2 typically slowed down Fe(II) oxidation.

ABSTRACT
Anoxygenic phototrophs are metabolically flexible bacteria. However, it is unclear how Fe(II) oxidation is affected by the simultaneous availability of organic or inorganic substrates. We therefore cultivated six green‐ and purple non‐sulfur photoferrotrophs from freshwater and marine environments with 2 mM Fe(II), amended with 0.6 mM organic co‐substrate or H2. We found that photoferrotrophs generally utilized organics and Fe(II) simultaneously, and that two marine strains preferred Fe(II) over H2. For some photoferrotrophs, Fe(II) oxidation rates were significantly enhanced by acetate, lactate, and glucose, whereas H2 typically slowed Fe(II) oxidation. All phototrophic Fe(II)‐oxidizers oxidized 80%–100% of the Fe(II) by the end of the experiment except for R. robiginosum, where Fe(II) oxidation reached only 52%–73%. We further observed for the first time that R. palustris TIE‐1 can grow with butyrate and glucose and that R. iodosum can utilize glucose. Comparison of genomic predictions with experimentally observed substrate consumption revealed discrepancies in four strains. Overall, our results demonstrate that Fe(II) remains an important electron donor despite the availability of alternative substrates, suggesting that maintaining photoferrotrophy is a common trait of photoferrotrophs and likely contributes to iron cycling in natural environments.

title: Spatial and Seasonal Structuring of Bacterial Communities and Putative Pathogen‐Associated Bacterial Taxa at Four Korean Coastal Locations
abstract:
Surface seawater bacterial communities across four Korean coastal locations exhibited differences in community composition among sampling locations and between the March and September sampling periods. Putative pathogen‐associated bacterial taxa (PPB), particularly Vibrio and co‐occurring taxa, showed location‐associated variation in relative abundance, providing preliminary baseline information for future coastal monitoring.

ABSTRACT
Coastal marine environments are dynamic transition zones where offshore water masses and terrestrial inputs shape microbial community structure. However, standardized comparisons of bacterial communities across geographically distinct Korean coastal waters remain limited, constraining the development of microbial baselines for long‐term monitoring. Surface seawater bacterial communities from four Korean coastal locations were analysed using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing. Total bacterial communities and putative pathogen‐associated bacterial taxa (PPB) assemblages differed among the four sampled locations and between the March and September sampling periods. PERMANOVA revealed significant effects of sampling location, sampling period and their interaction on community composition. Although Pseudomonadota dominated across all sampled locations, class‐ and genus‐level community compositions differed markedly among sites. Vibrio was a major component of PPB assemblages, while SIMPER analysis indicated that compositional differences among the sampled locations were associated with variation in combinations of co‐occurring taxa. Putative species‐level assignments further suggested location‐associated distribution patterns among dominant PPB taxa. Despite the absence of concurrent environmental metadata, these findings provide preliminary location‐specific baseline data for future coastal microbial monitoring and studies of environmental change.

title: The contextual pathogenicity of Porphyromonas gingivalis
abstract: In this Review, Lamont and Hajishengallis explore how the pathogenicity of Porphyromonas gingivalis is determined by microbial, metabolic and host context. They discuss how community interactions, nutrient-sensing and immune subversion regulate virulence and drive dysbiosis, inflammation and periodontitis progression.
authors: George Hajishengallis

title: Global change reshapes marine microbial communities, functions and One Health outcomes
abstract: Global change is transforming marine microbial communities. In this Review, Peixoto and colleagues explore the effects of climate and anthropogenic stressors on microbiome composition and function across marine environments, assess their consequences for ecosystem functioning, and propose management and mitigation strategies to improve ocean health through a One Health perspective.

title: High Hydrogen Yields During Continuous Photofermentative Valorization of Hydrothermal Carbonization Process Water by Engineered Rhodobacter capsulatus.
abstract: Photofermentative hydrogen (H2) production by purple non-sulphur bacteria (PNSB) is a promising route for sustainable energy generation, although large-scale application remains limited by substrate costs and process stability. Here, we demonstrate sustained H2 production using an H2-overproducing Rhodobacter capsulatus ΔhupAB mutant cultivated on process water (PW) derived from the hydrothermal carbonization of food waste. Batch assays showed that buffered PW supports phototrophic growth, soluble chemical oxygen demand (COD) removal, and H2 production without requiring defined carbon sources. Based on these results, continuous photofermentation was operated at a hydraulic retention time of 3.5 days using diluted PW supplemented only with phosphate buffer, operating for more than 600 h, with sustained COD removal and H2 production. Average H2 yields reached 178 mL H2 g-1 COD during the stable operational period (100-350 h), comparing favourably with literature values. Carbon partitioning analyses revealed lower inorganic carbon formation under PW feeding, consistent with a redistribution of reducing equivalents towards nitrogenase activity. This behaviour was associated with lower biomass yields and enhanced H2 production. Minimal CO2 formation resulted in an almost pure H2 stream. These results demonstrate the feasibility of continuous photofermentative valorization of PW for coupling waste valorization with high-purity biohydrogen production.
authors: Barahona E, Díez MP, Valverde Á, Cuesta D, Vilaró MG, Cicimov V, Prado A, Melero JA, de la Rubia MÁ, Mohedano ÁF, Diaz E, Puyol D.

title: Biofilm Engineering for Efficient Substrate-Enzyme Interactions to Enhance Enzymatic PET Degradation.
abstract: Despite extensive protein engineering efforts to significantly increase the catalytic efficiency of plastic-degrading enzymes, inefficient plastic-enzyme interactions during the interfacial biocatalytic process continue to impede their widespread applications. Here, we engineered the complete csgBACEFG curli operon through multicopy chromosomal integration to generate a csgBACEFG-optimized (CSGO) biofilm with enhanced curli assembly and plastic-surface adhesion. Unlike previou curli-based enzyme immobilization studies using individual CsgA curli components or pre-existing curli scaffolds, our strategy uses the complete curli assembly machinery to construct a dense, surface-associated catalytic biofilm. FAST-PETase was then embedded in a 2-day PET-surface CSGO biofilm through the SpyTag/SpyCatcher system, producing 2.5-fold more hydrolysis products from PET film depolymerization than soluble FAST-PETase with the same initial enzyme mass. The carrier-free biofilm-supported FAST-PETase also retained more than 50% of its first-cycle product formation after five 24-h PET nanoplastic (NanoPET) degradation cycles. These findings support biofilm-mediated enhancement of PET depolymerization and provide a proof-of-concept strategy that may inform future biofilm-assisted plastic treatment.
authors: Zhou X, Zhou X, Feng L, Wei R, Schwaneberg U, Blank LM, Xu A, Dong W, Jiang M.

Genetic Engineering Efforts to Generate Chlamydomonas Strains for Large‐Scale Biomolecule Production
abstract:
This represents the main aspects relevant to potential industrialization of Chlamydomonas.

ABSTRACT
Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is an established model microalga. Its easy manipulation, metabolic flexibility and tractable genomes allowed researchers to investigate fundamental processes such as photosynthesis using genetic studies for decades. Chlamydomonas is not naturally rich in lipids or pigments compared to industrially relevant microalgae. However, we highlight how its biotechnological potential relies on advanced genetic and metabolic engineering strategies, now possible due to the availability of extensive toolbox and synthetic biology platforms, which can improve industrial traits and allow to produce a variety of biomolecules of biotechnological interest. We provide examples of biomolecule production (terpenoids and recombinant proteins), and show that productivities (mg/L) are in the same range or could even be higher than those reached in other photosynthetic chassis (e.g., cyanobacteria or mosses). We point out that despite these achievements, the industrial implementation of C. reinhardtii is still lacking. Further technological advancements as well as clear international regulations and social acceptance are fundamental to reach the full potential of this microalga.

title: Reprogramming Native Cryptic Plasmids Enables Antibiotic‐Selection‐Free Urate Degradation by Escherichia coli Nissle 1917
abstract:
Reprogramming native cryptic plasmids of Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 enabled antibiotic‐selection‐free and oxygen‐adaptive urate degradation. The engineered strain reduced uric acid levels and alleviated hyperuricemia‐associated renal and inflammatory abnormalities in mice, supporting endogenous plasmid engineering as a strategy for live biotherapeutic development.

ABSTRACT
Hyperuricemia is associated with renal injury and disturbances in gut microbial ecology. Intestinal urate clearance by engineered probiotics is limited by antibiotic‐free functional maintenance and the oxygen requirement of urate oxidase (UOX). We reprogrammed the native cryptic plasmids of Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) to construct M12U, a marker‐free dual‐plasmid strain. pMUT2 carried an HucR‐regulated urate‐responsive UOX module, while pMUT1 encoded a low‐oxygen‐responsive UOX module and Tat‐targeted Vitreoscilla haemoglobin (tat‐VHB). M12U degraded urate in vitro and retained activity under low‐oxygen conditions. In hyperuricemic mice (n = 5 per group), oral M12U reduced serum urate, creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, inflammatory cytokines and renal histopathological injury. 16S rRNA profiling showed increased microbial richness and a partial shift in community composition toward healthy controls. Shotgun metagenomics revealed enrichment of Lactobacillus johnsonii and Bacteroides acidifaciens, together with increased metabolic potential related to the pentose phosphate pathway and glutathione metabolism. Faecal metabolomics showed reduced uric acid abundance and increased thiamine monophosphate and argininosuccinic acid. These results support further evaluation of dual‐native‐plasmid architectures for gut‐directed urate clearance.

title: Current Evidence Does Not Support Substantial DNA Cytosine Methylation in Myxosporean Genomes
abstract: AbstractSome invertebrate lineages are known to have lost their ability to methylate DNA cytosines. These lineages have often lost the enzymes responsible for cytosine methylation (DNMT1 and 3), as well as other enzymes that interact with methylated cytosines. Previous studies showed that myxosporeans, a group of parasitic cnidarians, lack recognisable DNMTs and other canonical methylation enzymes, and observed a lack of cytosine methylation in two myxosporeans using whole genome bisulfite sequencing. Recently, a study of five myxosporean samples using Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) sequencing reported high levels of methylation in two samples and low levels in the others and the presence of methylation-related genes in their assemblies. Here, we provide evidence that the two assemblies for which high levels of methylation were reported are heavily contaminated with fish-host sequences. In the other three samples, the lower apparent methylation signal resembles that observed in unmethylated negative controls and can be explained by ONT-background noise. Moreover, the CpG observed-to-expected ratios of the five assemblies differ from those of well-curated myxosporean assemblies. Additionally, the reported methylation profiles do not exhibit the typical distribution seen in invertebrates, possibly reflecting the presence of host contaminants. Finally, we found that most of the genes analysed are not canonical components of cytosine methylation pathways, and that the few candidate methylation-related genes reported in myxosporeans are more consistent with bacterial contamination than with genuine myxosporean genes. Together, these observations underscore important caveats in inferring the presence or absence of cytosine methylation in parasite genomes, particularly when using emerging technologies, and suggest that there is currently no robust evidence for substantial cytosine methylation in myxosporeans.

title: VENAS2: Bidirectional Mutation Modeling for Genomic Surveillance Reveals Reversions and Hidden Transmission Links in Pathogens
abstract: AbstractAccurately resolving pathogen evolution is essential for genomic surveillance, yet existing approaches often assume unidirectional mutation accumulation and fail to capture reversions that obscure lineage classification and transmission dynamics. Here we present VENAS2, a scalable framework that integrates genomic, temporal and geographic information to construct spatiotemporal evolutionary networks while explicitly modeling bidirectional mutational processes. Applied to 7.25 million SARS-CoV-2 genomes from GISAID between December 2019 and June 2024, VENAS2 reconstructed the evolutionary history of SARS-CoV-2 and precisely inferred the temporal dynamics of major variants of concern. Further application to the Viridian dataset revealed 4,654 distinct genomic sites with at least one potential reversion event, providing a systematic view of potential reversion signals during viral evolution. Extending to Mycobacterium tuberculosis, VENAS2 delineated major lineages and identified over threefold additional transmission clusters beyond conventional genomic distance-based methods, uncovering hidden links enriched for drug-resistant strains. These results demonstrate VENAS2’s capacity to uncover cryptic evolutionary processes across viruses and bacteria, providing a generalizable platform that bridges genomic surveillance with actionable public health response.

title: Symbiont-Derived Key Innovations Across the Diversity and Diets of Herbivorous Insects.
abstract: With prodigious biomass and diversity, herbivorous insects are among the world's most successful animals. It is widely believed, however, that some plant-based diets do not meet the needs of insect metabolism. Microbial symbionts may balance such deficits through diverse biochemistry. Here, we consider whether obligate nutritional symbioses between insects and microbes support large portions of insect herbivore diversity. In doing so, we assess the evidence that these highly integrated relationships are key innovations, circumventing nutritive shortfalls within particular plant tissues. Toward these ends, we compile nutrient data for 20 plant- and non-plant foods, plus data on diet and symbiosis across 874 families of insects-both herbivorous and non-herbivorous. Our results reinforce widely believed, but often uncited evidence that several insect taxa have long-consumed plant tissues with low concentrations of B-vitamins, nitrogen, or accessible carbon. Emerging as symbiont-enriched are seed-feeders, which face insufficient quantities of several B-vitamins in their food. Experimental and genome assessments show how symbionts surmount these B-vitamin shortcomings, showing also where this same challenge, and those of high fibre or low amino acid content are surmounted through symbiosis on other diets. We thus show where symbiont services are key innovations. Over half of the world's insect herbivores persist without nutritive assistance from obligate symbionts. This is largely because many consume leaves, which are reasonably good sources of amino acids and B-vitamins. Lateral transfer of microbial genes encoding plant cell-wall degrading enzymes has helped to overcome high fibre content, defusing the most challenging nutritive aspect of leaf-chewing diets.
authors: Russell JA, Smith HM, Bechade B, Cabuslay C, Carpenter M, Freeman D, Hansen A, Higashi C, Hu Y, Peng L, Williams A, Abbot P.

title: The Influence of the Antarctic Circumpolar Deep Water on Deep‐Sea Eukaryotic Biodiversity and Distribution in the Western Pacific Ocean
abstract:
ABSTRACT
The Antarctic region, a centre of biodiversity origin, influences deep‐sea ecosystems by supplying species to distant regions. Understanding the influence of Antarctic Upper Circumpolar Deep Water (UCDW) on deep‐sea eukaryotic diversity is therefore essential for outlining global biodiversity patterns. Our results showed the UCDW community exhibited ~1.5‐fold higher taxonomic and phylogenetic diversity than the Caroline Basin control community and contained a substantial proportion of unique taxa across multiple eukaryotic lineages. Source tracking using the available Southern Ocean surface‐water reference detected a 4.42% Antarctic‐associated contribution to the UCDW community. Indicators and generalists of the UCDW community shared > 97% sequence identity with Southern Ocean samples. The community analyses suggested that the Yap‐Mariana Junction choke point did not constitute a strong barrier to connectivity between adjacent basins, consistent with UCDW‐mediated dispersal into the Philippine Basin. The UCDW microbial dispersal into the Philippine Basin occurs through two potential routes: directly through the YMJ at 2000–3000 m and via upwelling across seamounts at 500–750 m. Governed mainly by neutral, dispersal‐driven processes, the UCDW community showed strong genetic exchange and connectivity. These findings suggest a role for deep‐water circulation in shaping the diversity and distribution of eukaryotes detected in western Pacific deep‐water samples.
