title: Biogeographic Barriers and Gut Microbiome Turnover Across the Peromyscus maniculatus Species Complex
abstract:
ABSTRACT
Biogeographic barriers are fundamental in shaping the distribution of animals and plants, yet the role of discrete landscape features in constraining microbial dispersal remains poorly understood. Identifying the barriers that partition gut microbial communities is essential for modelling the distribution of hosts and their symbionts across physical space and evolutionary time. The deer mouse (Peromyscus maniculatus species complex), which inhabits nearly all terrestrial environments in North America, provides an ideal model for testing these biogeographic drivers of the mammalian gut microbiome. Using NSF NEON biorepository samples, we characterized the gut microbiomes of 13 populations across the contiguous United States using full‐length 16S rRNA long‐read sequencing. The presence or absence of microbial taxa was best explained by eastern versus western regions compared to habitat or climate, suggesting a role of large fluvial systems as discrete barriers to microbial transmission, likely due to restricted host dispersal. Although we observed a consistent distance‐decay relationship across the continent, our results suggest that the Mississippi River is associated with increased microbial species turnover, with dissimilarity across the river exceeding levels predicted by geographic distance alone. Furthermore, we identified specific microbial lineages that exhibit varying patterns of isolation by distance across the continent, suggesting a gradient in microbial transmission patterns ranging from lineages that are freely shared across space to those that are dispersal limited. Together, these findings suggest that the gut microbiome may act as a bioindicator of landscape‐level ecological connectivity, revealing discontinuities in microbial transmission associated with large‐scale landscape barriers even among closely related host populations that lack reproductive barriers.

title: Genomic and functional characterization of quorum sensing and plant growth-promoting traits in Pseudomonas sp. P77
abstract:
Background
                     Eucommia ulmoides is a valuable medicinal and economic tree species whose seedling establishment is often constrained by slow early growth and vulnerability to stress. Plant growth-promoting bacteria (PGPB) represent sustainable alternatives to chemical inputs; however, PGPB associated with E. ulmoides and the genetic basis underlying their plant growth-promoting activities remain underexplored.
                  
                     Results
                     An N-acyl-homoserine lactone (AHL)-producing isolate, designated Pseudomonas sp. P77, was obtained from the root tissues of E. ulmoides. Functional assays showed that the strain displayed diverse plant growth-promoting characteristics, including phosphate and potassium solubilization, indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) production, and biofilm-forming capacity. UPLC–MS/MS analysis identified multiple AHLs in P77 culture samples, with C6-HSL, C8-HSL, and 3-oxo-C10-HSL among the major detected compounds. Inoculation with P77 significantly promoted the growth of E. ulmoides seedlings, as reflected by increased biomass, and was accompanied by enhanced antioxidant enzyme activities. Whole-genome sequencing generated a high-quality complete circular chromosome of 7.10 Mb with a GC content of 61.25% and an average sequencing coverage of 165.92×. Genome annotation identified genes encoding LuxI- and LuxR-family homologs potentially involved in AHL-mediated quorum sensing (QS), along with numerous genes potentially associated with plant growth-promoting traits. AntiSMASH analysis further predicted 25 biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs), including those potentially involved in the biosynthesis of pyoverdine, hydrogen cyanide, and other bioactive secondary metabolites.
                  
                     Conclusions
                     Phenotypic and genomic analyses indicate that Pseudomonas sp. P77 exhibits plant growth-promoting traits, nutrient-mobilizing activities, and biofilm-forming ability, as well as genetic potential for AHL-mediated QS. These findings provide a genomic basis for the development of P77 as a microbial inoculant for E. ulmoides nursery production and a valuable resource for future strain improvement.

title: Characterization of the organelle genomes of mycoheterotrophic Thismia angustimitra and evidence suggesting horizontal gene transfer.
abstract: BackgroundOur knowledge about mitochondrial genome evolution in plants is lacking far behind our knowledge of plastome evolution. In heterotrophic plants, it is well-known that plastome degradation and reduced or lost photosynthesis go hand in hand, and there is little if any difference between plastome evolution in mycoheterotrophic and haustorial parasites. The mitochondrial genome appears less affected by a heterotrophic lifestyle, although exceptions occur. In contrast to plastome evolution, mitochondrial evolution may differ between mycoheterotrophic and haustorial parasites, in particular with regards to the occurrence of horizontal gene transfer. However, data from mycoheterotrophs are scarce, and complete mitogenomes are only known from three of ten clades.ResultsHere we present data from the complete plastome and mitogenome from Thismia angustimitra, representing a fourth clade of mycoheterotrophs. The 18,215 bp plastome is much reduced and includes only few genes. The mitogenome has a multicircular structure consisting of 22 chromosomes with a total length of 422,400 bp. The gene content and the pattern of RNA editing are normal. The mitogenome includes only few repeats and recombinational activity is limited. A search for foreign DNA did not reveal any fungal sequences, the content of plastid DNA is low, but a large proportion of intergenic DNA shows similarity to distantly related angiosperms. Just a few plastid inserts appear to have originated through intracellular transfer, whereas others most likely stem from horizontal gene transfer. Synteny patterns of the intergenic sequences suggest that horizontal transfer may happen in either direction.ConclusionThe highly reduced plastome of T. angustimitra fits completely the general picture of plastome degradation in heterotrophic plants. Whereas the mitogenome in many aspects appears unaffected by the lifestyle, the recombinational activity is unusually low. Surprisingly, we find evidence suggesting horizontal gene transfer, indicating that this phenomenon may be more common among mycoheterotrophic plants than previously thought.
authors: Petersen G, Pedersen HÆ.

title: Rapid and sex-specific evolution of mouse saliva through regulatory rewiring and gene expansions
abstract:
Background
                     Mammalian saliva plays essential roles in digestion, immunity, and host-microbiome interactions, yet its protein composition varies widely across species and sexes. This diversity makes saliva a powerful model to study evolution of gene expression. Here, we compared mouse and human salivary glands as well as their secretions at the genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic levels to understand how saliva composition evolves.
                  
                     Results
                     We found that evolution of gene expression in mouse salivary glands is driven by rapid gene turnover and sexual dimorphism. In the submandibular and sublingual glands, 68% and 73% of expression from genes encoding secreted proteins derives from lineage-specific genes that lack one-to-one human orthologs. This contrasts the prevailing view that gene expression is largely conserved across tissues and highlights saliva as an unusually dynamic system of molecular evolution. Mouse submandibular gland shows striking sexual dimorphism, with 1537 tissue specific sex-biased genes, 3.8 times higher than in the liver (p < 0.001), a classic model of sex-biased expression. We also identified sex-specific expression of glycosylation genes associated with differential Muc19 sialylation. These results suggest that sexual dimorphism in mouse saliva arises from both transcriptional differences in secreted proteins and sex-specific post-translational modifications. Further, differentially expressed genes in submandibular gland cluster in genomic regions shaped by recent gene duplication, such as the kallikrein gene cluster, a mouse-specific expansion that accounts for ~ 16.4% of male-biased submandibular gland expression. Our analyses suggest that this bias arises through regulatory changes that are expanded by gene duplication, including the spread of a testosterone-associated regulatory motif and the expansion of a shared chromatin domain that promotes coordinated gene regulation.
                  
                     Conclusions
                     Together, our results reveal that lineage-specific genes disproportionately shape the mouse salivary transcriptome and that gene duplication and regulatory rewiring contribute to the rapid evolution of sex-biased expression in the submandibular gland. We describe a novel mechanism through which lineage-specific gene duplication and regulatory rewiring drive rapid, sex-specific evolution of the mammalian saliva. Our findings support saliva as an evolutionarily dynamic system and are consistent with developmental systems drift, whereby similar phenotypes across species may be maintained despite substantial divergence in their underlying gene-regulatory programs.

title: kinGEMs: A robust and scalable framework for resource-constraint models through stochastic tuning of deep learning-predicted kinetic parameters.
abstract: The construction of accurate enzyme-constrained genome-scale models (ecGEMs) remains a critical challenge in systems biology, limited by sparse kinetic data and the need for biologically meaningful representations. This work presents an integrated framework combining CPI-Pred, a deep learning model to predict kinetic parameters (kcat) from sequence and compound embeddings, with kinGEMs, a pipeline to incorporate these uncertainty-aware parameters into ecGEMs for metabolic optimization. By leveraging representations at multiple scales, the approach captures sequence, structure, and kinetic data to enhance model generalizability and accuracy. Rigorous benchmarking demonstrates the framework's capability to predict growth rates and fluxes that are consistent with experimental observations and measured proteome fractions, reduce median flux variability by several folds, and yield better-constrained metabolic models by explicitly accounting for the uncertainty inherent in ML-predicted kinetic parameters. kinGEMs successfully generated ecGEMs for 93 models spanning a phylogenetically diverse set of organisms including Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, mycobacteria, parasitic protists, fungi, and mammalian cell lines. These innovations breakdown the barrier to application of ecGEMs to non-model organisms and open new avenues for metabolic engineering and synthetic biology in more industrially relevant hosts.
authors: A Barghout R, Chiñas Serrano L, Sanchez-Lengeling B, Mahadevan R.

title: Autotroph–heterotroph relationships shape cyanobacterial bloom dynamics revealed by metatranscriptomics
abstract:
Abstract
Accelerated eutrophication and climate change are driving freshwater cyanobacterial blooms worldwide. Cyanobacteria–bacteria interactions shape phycosphere nutrient cycling and bloom dynamics, but their temporal shifts during bloom progression remain poorly understood. Using metatranscriptomics, we investigated the interactions between Microcystis and phycospheric bacteria throughout a bloom season in Lake Taihu, a heavily eutrophic lake in eastern China. During the early bloom, Microcystis and phycospheric bacteria co‐expressed genes associated with phosphate metabolism and oxidative stress response, whereas genes involved in nitrogen and iron acquisition were co‐expressed during the late bloom, suggesting potential nutrient competition. Carbohydrate metabolism‐related interactions persisted across bloom stages. As the bloom progressed, the dominant interacting taxa shifted from Hyphomicrobiales to Burkholderiales. We further assessed the generality of these patterns using metatranscriptomic datasets spanning multiple years and lakes. Phosphorus‐related interactions were consistently enriched during early blooms, whereas nitrogen competition‐related patterns predominated during late blooms; oxidative stress response‐related interactions, however, were more variable. Together, these findings reveal stage‐dependent shifts in phycospheric interactions that may contribute to bloom development and decline. The recurrence of these patterns across spatial and temporal scales suggests that shifts in phycospheric interactions are a general feature of bloom progression and may help predict bloom responses to environmental change.

title: Epidemiological surveillance of bacterial pathogens in cultured European sea bass (Dicentrarchus labrax) along the Aegean coast of Türkiye.
abstract: Intensive aquaculture of European sea bass (Dicentrarchus labrax) along the Aegean coast of Türkiye faces continuous production challenges from infectious diseases, yet comprehensive multi-year baseline data remain limited. This study presents a multi-year retrospective surveillance program (2020-2025) monitoring bacterial pathogens associated with 748 distinct cage-level disease outbreaks in fish across 19 discrete offshore commercial sea farms. To maintain industry confidentiality, diagnostic data from these separate facilities were fully aggregated and evaluated across three broad macro-regional surveillance zones. A total of 5,235 fish displaying clinical signs underwent diagnostic necropsy. Presumptive bacterial identification was conducted using phenotypic profiling through the API 20E system, and organ touch-imprint cytology. Six distinct bacterial species were isolated from positive clinical individuals, recovering a total of 2,490 isolates. Across the recorded outbreak events, etiological agents were ranked as primary drivers as follows: Photobacterium damselae subsp. piscicida (48.80%; N = 365), Tenacibaculum maritimum (35.83%; N = 268), Vibrio (Listonella) anguillarum (9.49%; N = 71), V. harveyi (3.74%; N = 28), V. ordalii (1.20%; N = 9), and V. alginolyticus (0.94%; N = 7). This hierarchy directly mirrored the overall bacterial isolation frequency, where P. damselae subsp. piscicida showed the highest relative distribution rate (46.18%; n = 1,150), followed by T. maritimum (34.10%; n = 849). Significantly lower isolation rates were recorded for V. (Listonella) anguillarum (11.41%; n = 284), V. harveyi (5.26%; n = 131), V. ordalii (1.77%; n = 44), and V. alginolyticus (1.29%; n = 32). Descriptive tracking of the purified laboratory isolates revealed localized variations in diagnostic recovery frequencies among the three sectors, while establishing a highly stable baseline dominated by P. damselae subsp. piscicida and T. maritimum across the Eastern Aegean Turkish mariculture network.
authors: Çelik P, Georgalas V, Çelik İ.

title: Antibiotic stewardship challenges in Madagascar's poultry sector: informality, knowledge gaps, and market constraints.
abstract: Antibiotic resistance (ABR) is a major global public health threat, largely driven by the overuse and misuse of antibiotics. Tackling its animal health component is particularly difficult in low- and middle-income countries, where data and resources are limited. This qualitative study aims to explore antibiotic use (ABU) and its underlying drivers in poultry farms in Analamanga, Madagascar's region with the highest poultry density. In April 2023, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 79 poultry farmers (13 backyard and 66 semi-intensive), 10 animal health professionals, and 10 agrovet shop sellers. Thematic analysis was used to examine farm characteristics, poultry health management, veterinary medicine supply and use, and interactions with poultry production stakeholders, in order to identify antibiotic stewardship challenges in Madagascar's poultry sector. Backyard and semi-intensive farmers shared several features: informality (absence of farm registration, rare cooperative membership, limited training), irregular profitability, easy access to antibiotics, recurrent antibiotic misuse (for example use in poultry viral infection treatment, first-line fluoroquinolone treatments), and limited veterinary inspection by competent authorities. However, the two farmer groups differed, as semi-intensive farmers had slightly greater knowledge of ABU and ABR than backyard farmers; they primarily consulted chick and feed suppliers for health advice and medicine purchase; and they widely perceived antibiotics as essential to maintaining poultry health and productivity. Practical roadblocks to invest in preventive measures or adopt effective antibiotic stewardship (ABS) were their narrow profit margins, limited access to credit, and weak bargaining power towards poultry product buyers. Tailored approaches such as supporting professionalization of poultry sector, building capacity of chick and feed suppliers to provide training in appropriate ABU and management of flocks, flock vaccination, deworming schedules, treatment record keeping and ABS principles may enhance antibiotic usage in the Madagascar poultry sector. Future research should build on this exploratory study, which used a convenience sample of stakeholders, by examining ABU trends and drivers in Analamanga with representative sampling and rigorous quantitative validation across Madagascar's poultry sector.
authors: Molia S, Tsimok'Haja Ramahatafandry I, Rakotoharinome M, Lienhardt C, Figuié M, Hobeika A, Kassié D.

title: Protocol for investigating the association between Helicobacter pylori exposure, antigen-specific serological responses, and resistant versus non-resistant hypertension in a South African cohort.
abstract: BackgroundHypertension is a leading contributor to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, with poor control in low- and middle-income countries. Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) has been associated with hypertension through inflammatory, endothelial, metabolic and immune pathways, but data from sub-Saharan Africa, particularly in resistant hypertension, are limited.MethodsThis cross-sectional observational study will enrol 200 adults aged ≥18 at a tertiary academic hospital in Cape Town, South Africa: 80 with resistant hypertension, 80 with non-resistant hypertension and 40 with normotension. Participants will undergo standardised clinical assessment, blood pressure measurement, and collection of blood, urine and saliva. H. pylori exposure will be assessed using the Pylori DuoTect® point-of-care assay, which detects antibodies to CagA and FliD. Laboratory analyses will include lipid profile, inflammatory and nitric oxide-related markers, homocysteine, insulin indices, complete blood count, ghrelin, multiplex cytokine profiling and flow cytometric immunophenotyping. PAXgene® blood RNA samples will be retained for future exploratory analyses. Saliva will undergo exploratory H. pylori antigen testing using CerTest® kits, which are validated for stool rather than saliva. Saliva analysis will be exploratory, and results will not define the primary H. pylori exposure variable. Remaining saliva will be kept for potential future oral microbiome analyses not defined in this protocol. Multivariable logistic regression will evaluate associations between H. pylori exposure and hypertension phenotype, adjusting for demographic, lifestyle, and clinical covariates.DiscussionTo our knowledge, this will be the first African study to integrate point-of-care H. pylori serology with detailed clinical, inflammatory, metabolic, and immunological profiling across resistant hypertension, non-resistant hypertension and normotension. Findings may clarify biological pathways linking H. pylori exposure to blood pressure dysregulation and inform future mechanistic and interventional studies.
authors: Mennen MC, Zulu MZ, Mabatha KC, Baguma R, Skelem S, Mbundwini NN, Aremu OO, Adriaanse M, van Dijk D, Pillay P, Africa S, Jones E, Setshedi M, Brink A, Burgers WA, Ntusi NAB.

title: Clinical and epidemiological characteristics of invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella disease in Ghana.
abstract: BackgroundInvasive non-typhoidal Salmonella (iNTS) disease remains a significant public health threat in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Although the disease is important, its clinical characteristics are not well described in literature. This study describes the clinico-epidemiological profile of iNTS disease in Ghana aiming to bridge important knowledge gaps and inform more effective management strategies.MethodsThe study spanned 8 years and utilized selected fever surveillance sites in Ghana. Patients with fever and/or history of fever for ≥ 3 consecutive days within the week prior to visit were approached and blood sample taken after consenting for investigations including blood culture. iNTS isolates were recovered using BACTEC blood culture, identified by Analytical Profile Index (API), sero-grouped using the Kauffmann-White scheme and confirmed by Illumina whole genome sequencing. Conditional logistic regression was used to assess associations between clinical and laboratory features and iNTS blood culture positivity in a 1:3 age-, sex-, and residence-matched case-control analysis.ResultsOf 271 blood-culture-derived bacterial pathogens, 15.5% (42/271) were identified as iNTS making it the second most common cause of bacteremia. iNTS disease exhibited seasonality with peak detections coinciding with the rainy seasons in Ghana. 23.7% (9/38) of iNTS isolates were multidrug-resistant (MDR), of which 5.3% (2/38) were extensively drug-resistant including resistance to ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin. Several factors showed crude associations with iNTS disease; however, only anaemia retained its association after adjustment of other factors (aOR=2.41 p = 0.030).ConclusioniNTS is a major cause of bloodstream infections with the highest burden in children under 5 years of age with susceptibility to the infection amplified by anaemia. The Salmonella serovars involved are increasingly becoming multidrug-resistant, including resistance to critical antibiotics.

title: Growth Conditions Shape the Fatty Acid Composition of Pedobacter lusitanus NL19.
abstract: Pedobacter lusitanus NL19 is a Gram-negative bacterium recognized for its potential to produce various antimicrobial metabolites, including lipids. However, how growth conditions regulate this production capability remains poorly understood. Like other bacteria, P. lusitanus NL19 adapts its membrane fatty acid (FA) composition in response to environmental conditions, a process that appears closely linked to its antimicrobial activity. In this study, we used GC-MS to identify and quantify FA, using alkaline transmethylation to produce FAME from esterified FA, and to track how different culture media (M9, R2A-B, PC25, and TSB) drive membrane FA remodeling in P. lusitanus NL19. The results revealed that cultivation in media associated previously with antimicrobial activity triggered an increase in monounsaturated and hydroxylated FA, in contrast to the saturated profiles observed under nutrient-rich conditions. This metabolic flexibility highlights an interplay between nutrient availability and membrane composition. Further research should evaluate whether FA provision triggers the release or excretion of bioactive secondary metabolites. Ultimately, this research advances our understanding of how environmental factors regulate lipid biosynthesis in P. lusitanus NL19.

title: Microbial plankton in southern Hudson Bay and James Bay in late summer
abstract: Hudson Bay and James Bay, on the southern margin of the Arctic, are warming and freshening as river discharge increases and surrounding permafrost thaws, yet their microbial plankton remain poorly described, and James Bay and the waters around the Belcher Islands have never been surveyed with environmental DNA. We conducted the first dedicated DNA-based survey of eukaryotic and prokaryotic plankton in southern Hudson Bay and James Bay, sequencing 18S rRNA (V9) and 16S rRNA (V4) gene amplicons from 72 samples collected at 51 stations in August 2022 and 2023. Hierarchical clustering resolved nine distinct communities; the primary division separated surface James Bay from Hudson Bay, with further structuring by year, distance to coast, depth, and riverine influence. Temperature, salinity, depth, and distance to coast together explained 31% of community variation (distance-based redundancy analysis), and threshold indicator taxa analysis placed an abrupt community-level change in offshore surface waters at 55.3°N and a salinity of ∼24.5. Across this boundary, primary producers shifted from large  Chaetoceros diatoms in Hudson Bay to the picoplanktonic green alga  Picochlorum and the cyanobacterium  Cyanobium in James Bay, while large  Gyrodinium dinoflagellates and  Calanus copepods gave way to  Gymnodinium ,  Pseudocalanus , and small cercozoans and ciliates. Heterotrophic bacteria in Hudson Bay were dominated by Proteobacteria, Bacteroidota, and Verrucomicrobiota, likely using diatom- and dinoflagellate-derived organic matter, whereas Actinomycetota and Planctomycetota dominated James Bay, likely using cyanobacterial and terrestrial dissolved organic matter. Prokaryotic diversity was highest in riverine, estuarine, and James Bay waters and declined northward and seaward. We also report the first strong presence of marine  Synechococcus CC9902 in Hudson Bay and identify cosmopolitan bacteria that provide a baseline for future monitoring. These results suggest that continued freshening of the Hudson Bay Complex will favour smaller primary producers and a stronger microbial loop, and that ecosystem shifts may occur abruptly once surface waters cross a salinity threshold.
authors: Kazmiruk ZV, Collins RE.

title: Draft genome of  Paraperlucidibaca  sp. CMO1 isolated from marine oil snow in the Churchill Marine Observatory, MB, Canada
abstract: An oil-degrading enrichment culture was inoculated from Marine Oil Snow (MOS) collected during an oil-spill experiment at the Churchill Marine Observatory in winter 2024. The complete metagenome-assembled genome for  Paraperlucidibaca sp. CMO1 was reconstructed, exhibiting the genetic potential to degrade hydrocarbons, including alkanes and aromatic compounds, as well as the ability to produce surfactants.
authors: Vidanage T, Collins RE.

title: Transpolar Drift and Atlantic inflow shape microbial biogeography and metabolic processes across the central Arctic Ocean
abstract: Abstract  The Arctic Ocean is changing rapidly. Sea-ice loss, advancing Atlantification and terrigenous inputs create contrasting ecoregions, yet their underlying microbial processes remain unresolved. Here, we combine high-resolution oceanographic observations and multi-omics data from the North Pole to the Svalbard shelf to determine how the shift from terrigenous influence to Atlantic-dominated waters shapes microbial biogeography, community assembly and metabolic processes. We demonstrate distinct, lifestyle-specific differences in microbial communities across four hydrographic regimes, with particle-attached communities showing a predominantly stochastic distribution while free-living communities were more regime-dependent. In the terrigenous-influenced Amundsen Basin, particle-attached microbial communities drive degradation of recalcitrant terrigenous organic matter with enrichment in denitrification, suggesting potential net nitrogen loss. Moving into Atlantic-dominated waters in the Nansen Basin during late summer, free-living communities increasingly rely on mixotrophic scavenging, trace gas oxidation and marine organic matter cycling as waters become progressively more nutrient-depleted. Surface-driven photoheterotrophy prevails in the warmest, ice-free waters. Comparative genomics across the Arctic Ocean further demonstrates highly connected yet regionally adapted microbial communities governed by these distinct hydrographic regimes. These results offer a mechanistic view of how microbial metabolic processes may restructure as the region becomes seasonally ice-free, Atlantification intensifies, and terrigenous inputs increase, thereby reshaping biogeochemical cycling across the Arctic Ocean.
authors: Venkatachalam S, Granskog M, Vipindas PV, Bratbak G, Assmy P, Vader A, Gonçalves‐Araujo R, Jabir T, Müller O, Chalari A, Shereef A, Murukesh N, Jain A.

title: A baseline for aquatic parasite diversity in West African mangroves: host-parasite records, DNA barcodes, and an experimental design for future use
abstract: Macroparasites represent a major fraction of biodiversity and biomass in marine ecosystems, yet remain substantially underrepresented in ecological surveys and food-web models, particularly in the Global South. This study addresses this geographic bias by providing the first comprehensive ecological survey of macroparasite communities of fishes in a West African Marine Protected Area (MPA) and adjacent Open-Access Area (OAA) characterised by mangrove forests. We collected 5,020 parasite specimens from 10 fish and one crab species in the Saloum Delta, Senegal, identifying 27 parasite species across all major taxa. Our findings include 15 new records for Senegal of which 11 are also new for West Africa. Additionally, 64% of host-parasite combinations constitute new host records. We provide 208 DNA barcodes, offering the first molecular data for 31% of these species globally and establishing a reference library for future DNA metabarcoding efforts in the region. Using sample size–corrected biodiversity indices and mixed-model analyses, we detected significant variations in parasite infracommunities and component communities between the MPA and OAA, demonstrating the feasibility of using comparative study designs to monitor fisheries impacts on parasite diversity in the Saloum Delta. Furthermore, the identification of trophically transmitted parasites provided evidence of unstudied food-web connections, e.g. predator-prey linkages between fishes and higher-trophic-level definitive hosts including birds and elasmobranchs. By integrating morphological identification, molecular data, and archiving of voucher specimens into publicly accessible, curated collections, this study establishes a new baseline for marine parasite biodiversity in West Africa and provides a methodological blueprint for surveying understudied regions.
authors: Cruz-Laufer AJ, Van Passel L, Sadio O, Dahdouh-Guebas F, Appy R, Bernot JP, Bouguerche C, Diamanka A, Hernández-Orts J, Kmentová N, Mendoza-Franco EF, Pantoja C, Shigoley MI, Vangelder N, Wood CL, Vanhove MPM.

title: Putative biosurfactants from polar microbial consortia
abstract: Biosurfactants (BS) are amphiphilic microbial metabolites that are biodegradable, low in toxicity, and environmentally compatible, making them attractive for applications in food, pharmaceutical, and bioremediation industries. This study investigated the phylogenetic composition and biosurfactant-producing potential of marine oil snow (MOS)-associated microbial consortia from the Churchill Marine Observatory, western Hudson Bay. MOS aggregates were cultivated in mineral Bushnell–Haas (BH) medium supplemented with 3% (w/v) NaCl, using motor oil as the sole hydrocarbon source. Enrichment cultures capable of growth in BH medium were subsequently evaluated for biosurfactant production using qualitative and quantitative assays at 4 °C and 20 °C. All cultures were maintained as enrichment consortia throughout the study. A total of eight enrichment cultures were identified as biosurfactant-producing consortia. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that  Pseudoalteromonas dominated all consortia, while  Paraglaciecola, Marinomonas , and other taxa were present at varying relative abundances. Although none of the consortia exhibited high emulsification activity (E  24 > 40%), biosurfactant yields were significantly higher at 4 °C. Additionally, three consortia tested positive for rhamnolipid-type biosurfactant production.
authors: Vidanage T, Desmond D, Collins RE.

title: NRT2.2 is essential for nitrate uptake and carbon-nitrogen balance in  Nannochloropsis oceanica
abstract: ABSTRACT  Nitrate is the dominant nitrogen source for marine microalgae, yet how it is taken up remains poorly understood in many ecologically and biotechnologically relevant species. Here we show that NITRATE TRANSPORTER 2.2 (NRT2.2) is the principal nitrate transporter of the oleaginous marine microalga  Nannochloropsis oceanica .  N. oceanica encodes only two NRT2 proteins and, unlike land plants and green algae, lacks a recognizable homolog of NITRATE ASSIMILATION-RELATED 2 (NAR2), the partner protein that green-lineage NRT2s require for activity and plasma membrane targeting. CRISPR knock-outs and confocal imaging showed that NRT2.2 is located at the plasma membrane and is required for nitrate uptake, whereas its paralog NRT2.1 cannot compensate for its loss. When nitrate was resupplied after nitrogen starvation,  nrt2.2 mutants did not take up nitrate and did not resume growth, while they recovered normally with ammonium. Their photosystem II efficiency fell below that of fully nitrogen-starved wild-type cells, and chlorophyll content was reduced, while total protein remained stable. Fixed carbon was redirected into storage, with lipids and carbohydrates accumulating above the levels of all strains after 3 days of nitrogen starvation. Loss of NRT2.2 therefore mimics a prolonged nitrogen starvation, even though nitrate is available. Because nitrate was present but could not be used, recovery from starvation depends on the capacity to take up nitrate, not only on its availability. In the ocean, where nitrate is depleted for long periods and resupplied episodically, NRT2.2 is thus likely to set how quickly  Nannochloropsis can use new nitrate inputs and resume growth.
authors: Santin A, Verdesca L, Bellan A, Minio M, Gerotto C, Morosinotto T, Perin G, Alboresi A.

title: Metabolic specialization in the gut microbiome of aquatic mammalian herbivores.
abstract: Sirenians, such as manatees, are the only extant mammals fully adapted to aquatic herbivory. Through specialized hindgut fermentation, they play a role in modulating nutrient fluxes and carbon cycling across tropical coastal and riverine ecosystems. However, our understanding of their gut microbiome and its metabolic potential remains elusive. Here we present an ultradeep genomic atlas of the gut microbiome from 47 freshwater and marine manatees spanning distinct developmental stages, comprising 1,215 non-redundant prokaryotic metagenome-assembled genomes and their associated virome. The manatee microbiome encodes a multilayered enzymatic repertoire for plant cell wall deconstruction, including free enzymes, cellulosomes and CAZyme-enriched outer membrane vesicles, alongside diverse pathways for aromatic catabolism. Combining biochemical and structural approaches, we characterize a previously unrecognized enzymatic pathway involving epilactase, which enables a specific Bacillota species to exploit a carbohydrate inaccessible to most microbial life, defining a specialized biochemical strategy for nutrient niche partitioning. Together, these findings uncover the microbial and metabolic basis of aquatic mammalian herbivory.
authors: Persinoti GF, Martins MP, Silva CBC, Streit RSA, Paixão DAA, Martins GH, Higasi PMR, Braatz GM, Silva MKP, Morão LG, Martins-Junior J, Stoffel F, Ciol H, Noske GD, Miyamoto RY, Oliveira GM, Martim DB, Oliveira CHM, Almeida OAC, Araújo EA, Andrade MO, Santos CA, Wolf LD, Souza AR, Gonçalves FAC, de Mello DMD, Morais MAB, Porto J, Lombard V, Giuseppe PO, Terrapon N, Lemos LN, Henrissat B, Carvalho VL, da Silva VMF, Murakami MT.

title: Cumulus cells mediate the protective effect of the marine carotenoid fucoxanthin against postovulatory oocyte aging via NRF2 signaling
abstract: Background  Oocytes awaiting insemination undergo postovulatory aging, an oxidative stress-driven loss of developmental competence. Fucoxanthin (FX), the major carotenoid of the brown alga Undaria pinnatifida, acts through NRF2, which requires a nucleus and transcription; the metaphase-II oocyte has neither, so its site of action is unresolved. Purpose  To determine whether FX delays postovulatory aging of mouse oocytes and identify the mediating compartment of the cumulus–oocyte complex. Study design  Ex vivo study of intact cumulus–oocyte complexes from superovulated ICR mice aged for 12 h, or 24 h for spindle analysis. Astaxanthin (AX) served as benchmark and the NRF2 inhibitor ML385 tested pathway dependence. Methods  Complexes were held in M16 medium with FX (1–10 µM) or AX (5 µM). Mitochondrial membrane potential, reactive oxygen species (ROS) and glutathione were measured with JC-1, DCFH-DA and monochlorobimane; spindle organization and cumulus-cell NRF2 localization by immunofluorescence. Results  At the optimal 5 µM, FX raised the JC-1 aggregate-to-monomer ratio eight-fold over untreated aged oocytes (1.24 ± 0.10 versus 0.15 ± 0.02; p Conclusion  FX preserves mitochondrial and redox status in postovulatory-aged oocytes through NRF2, which translocates in cumulus cells rather than the oocyte, identifying the cumulus cell as a target for extending oocyte usability in assisted reproduction.
authors: Oh C, Kwon S, Kwon HN, Woo J, Lee JE, Jung S.

title: Beyond PUE: A Boundary-Aware Primary-Energy Framework for Evaluating Self- Powered Computing Infrastructure, with Application to a Hybrid Offshore Floating Data Center
abstract: Abstract  Power usage effectiveness (PUE) is the dominant data-center sustainability metric, but it is defined only over the facility boundary: cooling and auxiliary overhead relative to the IT load. For self-powered infrastructure generating its own electricity on site, this boundary excludes exactly the losses—fuel-to-electricity conversion and any carbon-capture parasitic load—that determine whether total energy use is actually efficient. In this study, the hypothesis that facility-level PUE can systematically overestimate self-powered infrastructure sustainability is tested, and a boundary-aware primary-energy framework (η_primary = η_cycle × (1 − CCS penalty)/PUE) is developed to clarify that gap. The framework is applied to a proposal-stage architecture, the Hybrid Seabed-Energy Floating Data Center (HSE-FDC), offshore gas turbines, a wave-energy-converter array, carbon capture, and passive marine cooling, which had a PUE of approximately 1.04 with negligible grid dependency. Using literature-grounded parameters, the case study yields a plausible facility PUE of 1.08–1.09, which is comparable to that of real benchmarks, whereas the wave array contributes under 1.2% of the average power, which is far short of a genuine hybrid baseload. Critically, this favorable facility PUE corresponds to a primary energy efficiency of only 25.5–38.7%, below a conventional grid-tied facility (43.0%) and dramatically below a renewable-grid-tied facility (93.5%): a favorable facility PUE does not, by itself, indicate favorable total energy efficiency once onsite generation is included. The architecture's individual technologies are each already commercialized elsewhere; this study's contribution is the general framework and the demonstration that it changes the sustainability conclusion for a real architecture, generalizing to other off-grid contexts.
authors: Sandler L.

title: Particle-based representation of phytoplankton modulates emergent coexistence and biogeography in a model ocean
abstract: Phytoplankton communities sustain the marine food web through primary productivity. These communities sustain a high diversity of species, all of which must draw from the same finite nutrient supply. The mechanisms driving phytoplankton biogeography and succession, as well as those enabling high diversity, remain incompletely understood. Here, we compare emerging patterns of biogeography, richness, and diversity in a size‑structured phytoplankton community as it is advected and diffused within an idealized North Atlantic double‑gyre circulation, using both Eulerian and Lagrangian (particle‑based) modeling (PBM) frameworks. When a sufficient number of particles is modeled, the PBM, which resolves mortality at the particle level, produces stronger seasonal variability in biomass in the northern gyre and less stable and higher biomass in the southern gyre, while reproducing large-scale chlorophyll patterns observed by satellite. These contrasting dynamics are accompanied by distinct regional diversity patterns: local richness and diversity are generally higher in the PBM than in the Eulerian model in the northern gyre, with differences depending on the mortality threshold, whereas in the oligotrophic southern gyre, PBM local richness increases with particle number, while Eulerian richness is more sensitive to the mortality threshold. The PBM also produces a dynamic and emergent biogeographical structure that is more robust to the mortality threshold than the Eulerian model. Finally, Lagrangian variability in environmental conditions experienced by particles shows a stronger impact compared to the local Eulerian variability in the Northern gyre and stresses variable sensitivity to environmental histories. Together, these results suggest that the discrete representation of biomass fundamentally alters mortality, biogeography, and emergent coexistence patterns in model plankton ecosystems.
authors: Fremont P, Ribera d'Alcalà M, Hay Mele B, Jaillon O, Weitz JS, Iudicone D.

title: Natural Bioactive Compound Combinations in Alzheimer's Disease: Gut-brain Axis and Quantitative Interaction Assessment.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder for which singletarget therapies have repeatedly shown limited clinical efficacy. Natural bioactive compounds offer multi-target neuroprotective potential, yet contemporary research has predominantly focused on individual compounds rather than rationally defined combinations. This review examines natural bioactive compound combinations in AD through the gut-brain axis, with particular attention to distinguishing mechanistic complementarity from quantitatively demonstrated pharmacological synergy. The major pathways connecting gut microbiota dysbiosis to AD pathology were first summarized, and then discussed how compound combinations may produce enhanced effects through complementary microbiota modulation, metabolic regulation, and coordinated actions at intestinal and central nervous system targets. As an illustrative case, the combination of Icariin (ICA) and Panax Notoginseng Saponins (PNS), derived from the deconstruction of a traditional Chinese medicine formula, is critically evaluated. Available studies suggest combination-associated changes in gut microbiota, hippocampal protein expression, and AD-related outcomes, while evidence from the individual components supports biologically plausible complementary mechanisms. However, current evidence remains largely qualitative and does not establish that ICA-PNS produces supraadditive effects or that microbiota changes causally mediate its benefits. Improved combination efficacy should therefore not be equated with synergy. Future studies should use informative doseresponse matrices and pre-specified interaction models, including the Chou-Talalay combination index with complementary Loewe or Bliss analyses, together with multi-omics and microbiotacausality experiments, to enable more rigorous and reproducible evaluation and support mechanistic validation and future translational development of natural compound combinations.
authors: He W, Wang Z, Zheng S, Liu F, Zhang Y, Yang L.

title: Harnessing yeast biodiversity to identify superior chassis strains for metabolic engineering and precision fermentation.
abstract: Microbial cell factories are increasingly used for the sustainable production of fuels, chemicals and pharmaceuticals. Yeasts are particularly suitable as production hosts because of their metabolic flexibility, robustness, and expanding synthetic biology toolkits. Metabolic engineering of yeast historically relied on a narrow set of reference species and strains, especially Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Recent studies, however, show that applying identical pathway designs to different strain backgrounds or species can yield significant differences in titer, rate and yield (TRY). In this review, we examine how diversity within and between species in genomic features, metabolic regulation, substrate utilization and stress tolerance shapes chassis performance. We focus on eight species, including S. cerevisiae, Yarrowia lipolytica, Kluyveromyces marxianus, Komagataella phaffii, Ogataea polymorpha, Rhodotorula toruloides, Lipomyces starkeyi and Pichia kudriavzevii. We highlight that different species and strain backgrounds provide distinct advantages depending on the target product, pathway requirements, substrate, and process conditions. Finally, we discuss the transition from empirical strain screening toward diversity-informed and predictive chassis selection through multi-omics, phenotyping, metabolic modeling, and machine learning. We propose that chassis identity should be treated as a design variable, and that chassis selection should become an integral part of the Design-Build-Test-Learn cycle to develop optimal cell factories.
authors: Zhu Y, Voordeckers K, Steensels J, Verstrepen KJ.

title: Synthetic microbial communities enable sustainable restoration of coal gangue-impacted soils by reprogramming nutrient cycling.
abstract: Coal gangue disrupts microbial diversity and impairs nutrient cycling, constraining sustainable regional development. Traditional bioremediation relies on functional microbial traits, yet they often fail to colonize and perform in carbon-limited environments despite exogenous carbon inputs. We designed activity-oriented synthetic microbial communities (SynComs) to leverage exogenous carbon amendments and subsequently evaluated carbon use efficiency (CUE) as a community-level functional trait. High-activity SynComs were assembled from native and non-native strains based on their activity and metabolite interactions. The native-derived SynCom (SC3) enhances carbon and nitrogen cycling, whereas the non-native-derived SynCom (SC5) boosts diversity and phosphorus cycling (P < 0.05). These contrasts were associated with differences in strain functional contributions, community interactions, and carbon-source utilization. Metabolomics revealed greater functional microbial activation in SC5-conditioned biochar-derived metabolites than in glucose-derived metabolites. Multi-omics, single-cell Raman spectroscopy, and field studies confirmed the positive roles of SynComs in rhizosphere metabolism and nutrient cycling. Activity-driven SynComs approach was more efficient than single amendments, offering a potentially scalable strategy to restore carbon-limited tailing ecosystems and promote sustainability.
authors: Dong J, Zheng S, Chen Q, Zhang WR, Wu M, Huang Y, Wang P, Li HZ, Zhang Y, Corvini PF, Pan B, Xing B.

title: Host species identity drives temporally stable octocoral microbiomes in Florida.
abstract: Octocorals are foundational components of Caribbean reef ecosystems, yet their bacterial microbiomes remain poorly characterized compared to scleractinian corals. We present an extensive 16S rRNA gene survey of western Atlantic octocoral microbiomes, characterizing 180 samples from four co-occurring South Florida species over three years: the encrusting species Briareum asbestinum and Erythropodium caribaeorum, and the branching species Eunicea flexuosa and Muricea muricata. Host species identity was the strongest predictor of microbiome composition, explaining 14.4% of bacterial community variation, while temporal and spatial factors contributed less than 2% each. Core microbiome analysis at three prevalence thresholds (80, 90 and 100%) revealed host-specific bacterial associations. All four species harbored largely host-specific Endozoicomonas ASVs as dominant core members, with encrusting species maintaining larger and more taxonomically diverse cores than branching species. Phylogenetic reconstruction placed the dominant Endozoicomonas ASVs among described Endozoicomonas species, three lineages related to E. euniceicola, which was described from Florida octocorals, while the dominant Mycoplasma ASVs were highly divergent from described type strains, suggesting undescribed octocoral-associated lineages. Differential abundance analysis identified only a few significant temporally or spatially variable ASVs, reinforcing overall community stability. These findings demonstrate strong host control over microbial associations and provide a phylogenetic framework for understanding octocoral-bacteria symbioses in the western Atlantic.
authors: Liberman R, Gómez-Corrales M, Lopez JV.

title: CircoTax: a novel circular representation of differentially abundant microbial ranks.
abstract: One of the most relevant applications of NGS-based microbial abundance analysis is the discovery of taxa that appear as differentially represented between ecological niches. In the last years several methods have been proposed to accomplish this task, invariantly reporting the differentially represented taxa at the appropriate taxonomic rank as well as an adjusted p-value and a log2 fold change, representing the confidence on differential call and the amount of variation recorded. This work describes CircoTax, a specialized R ggplot2 plot representing a rank-aware collection of differentially abundant taxa in an intuitive, compact radial form. Specifically, the CircoTax is a circular plot with sectors encoding the taxonomy depth (from phylum to genus) and, departing from the center, a number of radial bars that reach rank-based sectors whose color and transparency are proportional to the log fold change intensity direction and p-value. The visualization of results is graphically appealing and allows to accommodate tens of differentially abundant ranks each with an associated amount of up or down variation so that results are easily intelligible for each differentially represented taxa at a glance. The software is freely available and can be run natively in R or through a dedicated ShinyApp for an interactive usage.
authors: Casbarra L, Di Gloria L, Ramazzotti M.

title: Structural characterization of a pseudaminic acid-modified lateral flagellar filament from Vibrio alginolyticus.
abstract: Bacterial flagellar filaments are often modified by glycans, but the structural basis and physiological significance of flagellin glycosylation remain poorly understood in many species. Vibrio alginolyticus produces lateral flagella for surface-associated motility in viscous environments, with LafA forming its filament as flagellin. A maf homolog encoding a putative flagellin glycosylation factor is located immediately downstream of lafA, suggesting that the lateral filament is glycosylated. To investigate this possibility, we purified the lateral flagellar filament from V. alginolyticus and determined the structure at 2.4 Å resolution by electron cryomicroscopy. Upon model building of LafA in the map, we identified additional densities connected to five serine residues, possibly corresponding to O-linked pseudaminic acid modifications. Mass spectrometric analyses identified these modifications as pseudaminic acid attached to Ser148, Ser173, Ser183, Ser189, and Ser197. Deletion of maf abolished lateral flagella formation and motility, and these defects were restored by complementation with maf. These results demonstrate that the Vibrio lateral flagellar filament is extensively modified by pseudaminic acid and that Maf is required for filament formation. Our findings provide the first structural insight into the glycosylation of the Vibrio lateral flagellar filament and establish a framework for understanding the role of flagellin glycosylation in surface-associated motility.IMPORTANCEA gene encoding a putative flagellin glycosylation factor (Maf) is located immediately downstream of lafA, the gene encoding lateral flagellin of Vibrio alginolyticus, suggesting that the lateral flagellar filament is glycosylated. Guided by this assumption, we determined the structure of the lateral flagellar filament by electron cryomicroscopy with mass spectrometry and identified five pseudaminic acid modifications on the filament surface. Genetic analyses further demonstrated that Maf is required for lateral flagellar formation and motility. These results provide the first structural characterization of a glycosylated Vibrio lateral flagellar filament and reveal a close link between flagellin glycosylation and motility organelle assembly.
authors: Kinoshita M, Minamino T, Nakatani H, Suzuki A, Takao T, Mishiro-Sato E, Kojima S, Namba K, Homma M.

title: Borrelia burgdorferi binds serum amyloid A and modulates subcutaneous adipose tissue immune signaling.
abstract: Following a tick bite, Borrelia burgdorferi spirochetes replicate in human skin and disseminate through tissues, including subcutaneous adipose tissue. Adipose is a complex organ containing both immune and non-immune cells that play a significant role in the immune response, yet little is known about adipose-specific immune signaling after B. burgdorferi infection. We investigated the landscape of immune signaling within adipose tissue-resident cells during B. burgdorferi infection in human tissue (skin and adipose tissue) ex vivo. Single-cell sequencing pathway analysis revealed upregulation of inflammatory pathways in skin, yet overall downregulation of immune pathways in adipose tissue cells during B. burgdorferi infection. Adipose-resident myeloid cells and adipose stem/progenitor cells (ASPCs) displayed an inflammatory profile characterized by the increased expression of IL-1β, TNF, and NFKB1. CellChat, a cellular communication comparative analysis, showed increased cell-to-cell communication across adipose-resident cell populations. ASPCs demonstrated the strongest outgoing signals, positioning them as key hubs of intercellular communication in adipose tissue. Interestingly, we observed adipose-specific downregulation of serum amyloid A (SAA), an inflammatory serum marker known to have antimicrobial properties and typically elevated in Lyme disease patients during acute infection. Therefore, we further evaluated the interaction between SAA and B. burgdorferi. Here, we show that human recombinant SAA protein directly binds B. burgdorferi spirochetes, reduces spirochete viability in a dose-dependent manner in vitro, and enhances phagocytosis. Taken together, these findings show that adipose tissue is a site of active immune signaling in the setting of infection and identify SAA as a host defense factor against B. burgdorferi.IMPORTANCEBorrelia burgdorferi is the bacterium that is transmitted by ticks and causes Lyme disease. These bacteria replicate in the skin to cause the localized skin rash erythema migrans, then disseminate to cause symptoms in other organs, including the joints and heart. Adipose tissue, or fat, is adjacent to skin, joints, and heart-all target organs of infection. In this study, we set out to understand how adipose tissue/fat plays a role in Lyme disease. We discovered that B. burgdorferi infection leads to an immune response in adipose tissue cells with specific downregulation of a gene called serum amyloid A (SAA). Our work shows that B. burgdorferi bacteria bind serum amyloid A (SAA), leading to decreased viability in vitro and enhanced uptake of B. burgdorferi by white blood cells. These findings highlight the dynamic role our fat can play during B. burgdorferi infection and can lead to the identification of new treatments for Lyme disease.
authors: Esterly AT, Du S, Lee B, Johnson E, Odell A, Sefik E, Yu Q, Cui Y, Ayyala H, Haykal S, Odell I, Flavell R, Fikrig E, Zapata HJ.

title: TRACER: Twin-contrastive learning for fine-grained and rare spatial domain identification in spatial transcriptomics.
abstract: MotivationFine-grained and rare spatial domains are difficult to identify in spatial transcriptomics because they contain few spots, show subtle transcriptional differences, and are strongly influenced by neighboring regions.ResultsWe present TRACER, a twin-contrastive learning framework that integrates a graph convolutional autoencoder with neighborhood-aware instance-level and cluster-level contrastive learning. By jointly preserving local spatial continuity and enhancing domain separability, TRACER achieved competitive and generally robust performance compared with representative spatial domain identification methods across multiple spatially resolved transcriptomic datasets, including human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex generated by 10x Visium, mouse brain datasets generated by STARmap, osmFISH, and BARISTAseq, and human breast cancer. TRACER recovered major cortical and anatomical structures, improved the identification of rare or transitional domains in the mouse somatosensory cortex, and revealed candidate functionally distinct small domains within a broadly annotated breast cancer region.AvailabilityThe source code of TRACER is available at https://github.com/luxin-heart/TRACER.Supplementary informationSupplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
authors: Liu Q, Lu X, Song B, Wei Q, Feng W, Guo K, Wang J, Zhou M, Zhao Y, Wang G.

title: Narrative-based explainable AI for precision oncology survival prediction.
abstract: MotivationExplainable and accurate Survival Prediction (SP) remain an open challenge in Precision Oncology. Early SP methods achieved interpretability through simple models, often at the expenses of prediction performance. More recent Machine Learning (ML) methods can learn complex patterns, but they often resemble inscrutable black boxes. Here we propose SurvXAI, a new framework that combines reliable SP with the latest eXplainable AI (XAI) approach.ResultsWe first train a Random Survival Forest model to predict the survival function of each patient. We then interpret these prediction by extracting patient-specific feature contributions with SurvSHAP, and we feed them into locally deployed Large Language Models (LLMs), to translate the numeric individual-level interpretation of the SP into natural language narrative explanations. Since conventional numerical breakdowns of the features contributions to the final predictions are often perceived as un-intuitive to non-ML experts, SurvXAI overcomes this limitation by automatically translating them into narrative explanations that can be readily used by clinicians, to facilitate the interpretation of model predictions.We validated our SP pipeline on six oncological datasets, including an in-house Multiple Myeloma cohort, comparing it with nine state of the art SP predictors. We then quantified the quality and usefulness of SurvXAI narrative explanations with a blind evaluation carried by seven human experts. This evaluation showed that larger LLMs produced more coherent explanations with accurate feature ranking and clinically plausible reasoning. SurvXAI demonstrates the potential of integrating explainable SP with LLMs to enable trustworthy, personalized interpretation in oncology and other clinical fields.Availability and implementationSurvXAI is available at https://github.com/AI-for-Genome-Inter  pretation-lab/SurvXAI_pipeline. The module for narrative generation is available at https://github.com/AI-for-Genome-Interpretation-lab/SurvX  AI_stories.
authors: Pan Z, Codicè F, Bret C, Garcia de Paco E, Thomas M, Mas A, Moreaux J, Raimondi D.

title: Domain-Aware Enzyme Classification via Multiple Instance Learning.
abstract: MotivationAccurate Enzyme Commission (EC) number prediction is fundamental to protein function annotation and metabolic pathway reconstruction. Recent methods based on protein language model embeddings or 3D structure have improved EC prediction, but important limitations remain. Whole-sequence embeddings can dilute local functional signals, such as catalytic residues and functional domains, whereas structure-based methods depend on accurate protein structures and are therefore difficult to apply broadly.ResultsWe present MIL-BC, a multiple instance learning framework for EC prediction that models each protein as a bag of domains rather than a single sequence-level object. This design is motivated by the observation that enzymatic function is often determined by constituent functional domains instead of the full-length sequence alone. Domain instances are generated automatically using our DCTdomain algorithm, avoiding dependence on curated domain annotations. MIL-BC aggregates domain-level evidence into protein-level EC predictions and assigns interpretable weights to domains that contribute most strongly to each prediction. We further combine the domain embedding with global embedding in MIL-BC+. MIL-BC+ achieved F1 improvements of 0.03 - 0.17 over the sequence-based baseline on all four test sets. The largest gains were observed for proteins with multiple enzymatic functions, where domain-level modeling better separates mixed functional signals. These results show that domain-centric multiple instance learning is an accurate and interpretable strategy for enzyme classification. By improving EC prediction without requiring structural data or curated domain labels, MIL-BC provides a scalable framework for large-scale protein function annotation.AvailabilityCode is available as a GitHub repository at https://github.com/omics-ai/enzyme-mil.git.
authors: Xiao Q, Ye Y, Tang H.

title: RNAactDrug 2.0: an updated resource for systematically exploring molecular features associated with drug sensitivity across multi-omics datasets.
abstract: RNAactDrug 2.0 (available at https://bio-bigdata.hrbmu.edu.cn/RNAactDrug or https://bio-datamining.hrbmu.edu.cn/RNAactDrug) is an updated resource for systematically exploring molecular features associated with drug sensitivity across multi-omics datasets. We have updated the RNAactDrug 2.0 database with significantly expanded data and improved features, including (i) ∼30 000 drugs, 38 908 RNA molecules, and 22 800 375 drug-RNA associations from large-scale pharmacogenomic databases, covering four molecular layers: expression, copy number variation (CNV), mutation, and methylation; (ii) 11 099 cases from The Cancer Genome Atlas across 33 cancer types are integrated to support clinical and pan-cancer analyses of drug sensitivity-associated RNA features; (iii) ∼3.8 million cells from >200 single-cell RNA sequencing datasets, spanning 34 cancer types and 38 tissues, enable analysis of cell type-specific patterns and intratumoral heterogeneity; (iv) 26 440 enhancers and 788 444 drug-enhancer associations, combined with potential target prediction, provide an exploratory epigenetic regulatory dimension; (v) enhanced search and browsing functionalities, together with seven tools for functional annotation, pan-cancer analysis, tumor microenvironment profiling, single-cell trajectory and CNV analysis, and enhancer-related analyses. In summary, RNAactDrug 2.0 is a crucial resource for the multi-omics dissection of drug sensitivity-associated molecules, providing important support for the discovery of drug resistance biomarkers and the advancement of personalized therapeutic strategies.
authors: Li F, Pei L, Xing J, Kang A, Chen Z, Liu W, Lu S, Xu L, Wang X, Zhang C, Xu Y.

title: PhenX Toolkit: a knowledgebase that enables consistent data collection and facilitates cross-study analysis and data reuse.
abstract: The PhenX (consensus measures for Phenotypes and eXposures) Toolkit (https://www.phenxtoolkit.org/) is a publicly available knowledgebase of well-established, broadly validated measurement protocols recommended for use in genomic, clinical, translational, and epidemiological research involving human participants. Consistent use of PhenX protocols, including questionnaires, bioassays, and physical assessments, improves the rigor, transparency, reproducibility, and comparability of research data. The Toolkit was recently highlighted in the National Institutes of Health (NIH) implementation plan, "Leading in Gold Standard Science," as an example of efforts to advance reproducible biomedical research. The Toolkit currently includes 1010 protocols spanning a wide range of diseases, exposures, and study designs. Content development is guided by the scientific community through a consensus-based process involving expert Working Groups, community input, and strategic oversight from the PhenX Steering Committee. Collaborations with NIH Institutes have expanded Toolkit content in priority areas, including substance use and cardiovascular disease. The PhenX Toolkit enhances study design and supports implementation of selected protocols. PhenX also collaborates with resources that facilitate data collection (REDCap), data standards (LOINC), and data repositories to promote interoperability and cross-study analyses. To date, the Toolkit has been recommended in 711 NIH funding opportunities and cited in >1300 publications. Future directions are discussed.
authors: Huggins W, Hendershot TP, Marazita ML, Bakalov VD, Ceger P, Cook B, Cox LA, Ives C, Nelms MD, Quattrone W, Reeve TC, Williams DN, Hamilton CM.

title: CircaVal: a gene-centric multi-omics platform for exploring circadian regulatory features.
abstract: The circadian clock orchestrates daily physiological processes through coordinated regulation of clock-controlled gene expression across multiple molecular layers. However, systematic characterization of this multilayered rhythmic regulation remains challenging because relevant information is distributed across independent datasets and rhythmicity is evaluated using diverse analytical approaches. Here, we developed CircaVal, a gene-centric multi-omics platform for the integrated exploration and interpretation of circadian regulatory features in humans, mice, and baboons. To support this framework, CircaVal processes public datasets using standardized, data-type-specific pipelines, and gene rhythmicity is integrated with tissue-specific expression, cross-species orthology, functional annotations, and multi-omics regulatory features. CircaVal further introduces an integrated rhythmicity score (IRS), which combines concordance across multiple rhythm-detection methods with reproducibility across independent datasets to provide a quantitative basis for prioritizing candidate rhythmic genes. The platform enables users to examine gene rhythmicity across datasets, identify tissue-enriched rhythmic genes, compare rhythmicity across species, and explore associated regulatory features. Additional functions include interactive gene-centric exploration, genome-browser visualization, rhythmicity analysis of user-uploaded time-series data, and programmatic data access. Together, these capabilities provide an integrated framework for rhythmic gene prioritization and gene-level interpretation of circadian regulatory features across tissues, species, datasets, and omics data types. CircaVal is freely available at https://CircaVal.com.
authors: Han G, Wu X, Li Q, Shi R, Xiao X, Liu J, Zhang H, Gao D, Li C, Wang A, Jin Y, Chuang TJ, Chao HW, Chen H.

title: tModBase v2.0: an expanded database of tRNA modifications with an AI-powered assistant.
abstract: Chemical modifications of transfer RNAs (tRNAs) are crucial for tRNA stability, codon decoding, translational fidelity, and tRNA-derived small RNA (tsRNA) biogenesis. Changes in these modifications are associated with stress responses, physiological regulation, and human disease, underscoring the need to integrate modification information with experimental evidence and biological context. We previously established tModBase, a web resource to organize and explore tRNA modification-related data. Its first release integrated modification sites, high-throughput sequencing-derived signals, and condition-dependent changes. Since then, tRNA profiling has expanded through modification-specific and direct RNA sequencing strategies, with rapidly growing datasets across species and conditions. Here, we present tModBase v2.0 (http://www.tmodbase2.com/), containing 528 datasets across 23 species, 40 sequencing and library-preparation methods, and 42 modification types. It includes 68 third-generation and 210 modification-specific sequencing datasets, extending coverage of direct-RNA and modification-specific approaches. tModBase v2.0 further integrates sequencing-derived signals, condition-dependent information, and biological annotations linking modifications with enzymes, genetic variants, tsRNAs, diseases, and expression profiles. The LLM- and retrieval-augmented generation-powered assistant tModBot enables natural-language exploration across database modules while grounding responses in retrieved tModBase evidence. tModBase v2.0 therefore provides an expanded resource for investigating the diversity, dynamics, and biological context of tRNA modifications.
authors: Tan Y, Xin NN, Wu T, Yu Tan Q, Zheng XN, Chen ZM, Feng X, Qu LH, Zheng LL.

title: InterPro: the protein sequence classification resource in 2027.
abstract: InterPro (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/interpro) is a freely accessible resource for the classification of protein sequences. It integrates predictive models, known as signatures, from multiple member databases to classify sequences into families and to predict the presence of domains and functionally important sites. The InterPro database provides annotations for hundreds of millions of sequences, ensuring extensive coverage of UniProtKB, the standard repository of protein sequences, and includes mapping to several other major resources, such as Gene Ontology, the Protein Data Bank in Europe (PDBe), and the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database. In this publication we report on the status of InterPro (version 110.0), detailing new developments in the database, its associated web interface, and software. Notable updates include InterPro-N, a deep-learning method that increases sequence coverage of UniProtKB to over 90%; the transition from InterProScan 5 to the completely re-engineered InterProScan 6; the integration of structure-based domain classifications and predicted structures from AlphaFold; a redesigned protein viewer offering a concise summary view; and a new Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that allows AI assistants to query InterPro programmatically. Over the past two years, 9484 new InterPro entries have been created, bringing the total to 54 922. InterPro data, software and tools are freely available.
authors: Blum M, Andreeva A, Chuguransky S, Florentino LC, Flores NM, Grego T, Hobbs EEM, Pinto BL, Polignano A, Meng-Papaxanthos L, Llinares-López F, Colwell L, Marchler-Bauer A, Bordin N, Bridge A, Haft DH, Klimke W, Letunic I, Mi H, Natale DA, Orengo CA, Piovesan D, Rivoire C, Sigrist CJA, Thomas PD, Tosatto SCE, Wu CH, Bateman A.

title: PlantVirDisConDB: an integrated resource linking plant virus sequence records with hosts, phenotypes, targets, antiviral evidence, and AI-assisted prioritization.
abstract: Research on plant viruses depends on taxonomy, nucleic acid sequences, host and disease records, molecular targets, and antiviral assays. These data are distributed across separate resources, making integrated retrieval and comparison difficult. PlantVirDisConDB (https://dpai.ccnu.edu.cn/PVDCDB) is freely accessible without login or registration and links these data through curated plant virus records. At the July 2026 reporting date, it comprised, in round numbers, 5000 virus and subviral agent records and 38 000 sequence accessions. It also included approximately1900 hosts, 9000 virus-host associations, 4800 disease names, 5000 structure records, and 25 000 small molecules. Direct assay records for plant viruses are distinguished from general antiviral background data; experimental and predicted structures, and measured activities and model outputs, are also labelled separately. Linked record pages support retrieval across these data types, access to individual sequence records, target searches, and molecular similarity searches. An activity prediction module ranks candidate molecule-virus pairs with applicability warnings and does not imply experimental or field efficacy. PlantVirDisConDB links viral nucleic acid entities to hosts, phenotypes, targets, and antiviral information and is updated through continuing curation and user feedback.
authors: Wang D, Zhu Z, Zhu Z, Yang R, Hu L, Ye Y, Wang F, Yang G.

title: THEOBROMA: an aggregated open database of 1.13 million natural products with per-compound license auditing, three-tier classification, and stereochemistry-aware deduplication.
abstract: Natural products remain one of the most productive sources of pharmacologically active compounds for drug discovery. Open aggregators attribute licenses at database granularity, and the consequences of that choice have become tangible as the field grows. A recent relicensing event in one constituent source (the September 2024 transition of the Natural Products Atlas to CC BY-NC 4.0) demonstrates how database-level licensing propagates across an aggregate and motivates the per-compound audit framework presented here. The same peer cohort separately leaves classification provenance and stereoisomer-family relations coarser than either layer warrants. THEOBROMA, accessible at https://theobroma.l3s.uni-hannover.de, integrates 1 132 805 natural products from 29 open sources under a per-compound license audit that resolves each compound's license tier across all attesting sources under a most-restrictive-wins rule. 896 242 compounds (79.12%) are identified under open-use licenses, and the per-source attestation chain, together with the resolved tier, is exposed through a dedicated audit endpoint and a query-time license filter. A three-tier classification labels all but 21 compounds by the provenance of the assignment (55.3% curated source labels, 18.2% NPClassifier tool assignments, 26.5% model-inferred). Deduplication at the full 27-character InChIKey retains 1 132 805 entries across 486 032 connectivity families, exposed via a dedicated /api/stereoisomers/ endpoint and a radial-family display. Any result set renders directly onto a taxonomic cladogram of its source organisms, so compositional queries are answered in the interface rather than downstream. Per-compound license provenance is the primary differentiator, while classification stratification and stereoisomer-family exposure add finer-grained access to two related axes. Together, they support license-compatible virtual screening and isomer-specific bioactivity analysis at corpus scale. As an evolving open resource, THEOBROMA pairs continuous pipeline maintenance with interactive geographic, taxonomic, and chemical-space exploration.
authors: Klamt T, Jaczkowski A, Franke J, Nejdl W.

title: mV2G: a multiomic atlas for tissue-specific variant-to-gene prioritization.
abstract: The multiomic Variant-to-Gene (mV2G; https://mv2g.hbliulab.org) is a comprehensive atlas that integrates diverse functional genomic evidence to prioritize tissue-specific variant-to-gene (V2G) associations. While genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified millions of associations between genetic variants and diseases, translating these findings into biological mechanisms remains challenging because >90% of variants reside in noncoding regions. Existing V2G resources provide complementary regulatory evidence but are fragmented and often lack tissue-specific interpretation. To address this challenge, we constructed the mV2G atlas by integrating 24 types of functional genomic evidence across 50 human tissues, including molecular quantitative trait loci, enhancer-gene predictions, 3D chromatin interactions, and experimental validation. The atlas contains 188 634 118 evidence-supported V2G pairs involving 13 618 039 variants and 69 521 genes. To prioritize high-confidence V2G pairs, we developed a CRISPR-informed, evidence-weighted model. Using this model, we prioritized 3 348 174 high-confidence V2G pairs, 88% of which were tissue-specific. The mV2G atlas provides searchable variant- and gene-centered interfaces, an interactive browser for visualizing variants, target genes, cis-regulatory elements, and chromatin states, as well as downloadable datasets. By integrating complementary regulatory evidence into a unified framework, mV2G provides an accessible resource for interpreting the functional and phenotypic impact of genomic variation in relevant tissues for human diseases.
authors: Zhang DY, Zhou H, Sheth MU, Gschwind AR, Engreitz JM, Lin X, Liu H.

title: The TCR Motif Atlas: a database of specificities for TCRs recognizing viral, cancer, and autoimmune epitopes.
abstract: T-cell recognition is elicited by the binding between T-cell receptors (TCRs) and epitopes. Many machine learning approaches have been proposed to model TCR-epitope recognition specificity, but most of them act as black boxes. To visualize TCR-epitope recognition specificity, we developed the TCR Motif Atlas (https://tcrmotifatlas.unil.ch). This database builds upon the probabilistic framework of TCR specificity profiles (TSPs) to visualize V and J genes as well as complementarity-determining Region 3 (CDR3) lengths and amino acids enriched in epitope-specific TCRs with respect to baseline TCR repertoires for hundreds of epitopes. An interactive interface enables users to build TSPs based on their own set of TCR sequences to investigate epitope recognition specificity or to explore potential biases in TCR repertoires of known or undetermined specificity. The TCR Motif Atlas further provides links to curated compilations of epitope-specific TCRs and crystal structures of TCR-epitope complexes.
authors: Tadros DM, Shah A, Roessner RA, Racle J, Gfeller D.

title: DectiSomes as broad-spectrum antifungal drugs.
abstract: SUMMARYFungal pathogens represent a significant threat to public health. Aspergillus fumigatus, Candida albicans, Cryptococcus neoformans, and Rhizopus delemar are the primary causative agents for aspergillosis, candidiasis, cryptococcosis, and mucormycosis. They and their closest relatives are responsible for more than 94% of fungal disease-related deaths. All four fungal diseases may lead to meningitis, with mortality rates approaching 99%. They are among the WHO-designated priority fungal pathogens needing new and more effective treatments. In response to this therapeutic gap, we developed DectiSomes-drug-loaded liposomes targeted to fungal cells by host-pathogen receptors. Host-pathogen receptors have many advantages over antibodies as liposome-targeting proteins, including a lack of immunogenicity. Of the pathogen receptors we tested, Dectin-1 and Dectin-2 are the most effective targeting proteins against the fungal pathogens tested. Liposomes loaded with amphotericin B and coated with one of these pathogen receptors bind specifically and strongly to the four pathogens and kill them, reducing the effective dose of amphotericin B by more than an order of magnitude over the untargeted control. DectiSomes are also more effective in murine models of fungal infection.
