In tumor-free mice, ROP-E7 induced greater helper and cytotoxic T cell responses than wild-type E7. In tumor-bearing mice, ROP-E7 reduced tumor burden and improved survival, while combination treatment induced complete tumor regression and tumor-free survival beyond 100 days. These effects were associated with increased intratumoral cytotoxic T cells and reduced regulatory and exhausted T cell populations. These findings provide preclinical support for combining therapeutic HPV16 E7 vaccination with T cell co-stimulation in HPV-associated cancers.
authors: Ou Y, Lu W, Zhao H, Demetrious C, Zhang Q, Zheng Q, Jiang Y, Kok-Ting Wan P, O'Neill E, Zhang L, Jiang S.

title: Toll-like receptor 4-driven translational reprogramming in macrophages is unaffected by Salmonella SPI-1 activity.
abstract: Changes in gene expression during bacterial infection are the combined result of altered transcription and translation, with the latter comparatively understudied. Gram-negative bacteria rapidly trigger cytokine gene transcription in macrophages through the activation of pathogen-associated molecular pattern receptors, for example the detection of Salmonella lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from the bacterial cell envelope by Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4). Here, through time-resolved parallel translatomic and transcriptomic profiling, we now show temporal TLR4-specific translational upregulation of cell signaling proteins in macrophages induced by Salmonella. While transcriptional upregulation of these genes is dampened through the activity of the Salmonella SPI-1 type 3 secretion system, a robust translational response remains. These data reveal an important host-pathogen translational regulatory network that modifies the innate immune response of macrophages to infection.
authors: Wood G, Johnson R, Brember MP, Lastovka F, Tourlomousis P, Bryant CE, Chung BY.

title: Non-triazole agricultural fungicides indirectly select for triazole resistance in the human pathogen Aspergillus fumigatus.
abstract: Agricultural intensification relies on chemical fungicides to manage crop disease,1,2 driving the evolution of resistance in plant pathogens.3 Fungicides persist in the environment, allowing activity beyond their intended targets, affecting downstream ecosystems and agricultural practices. The saprophytic and ubiquitous fungus Aspergillus fumigatus is an important human pathogen causing severe invasive fungal disease.4 Selection by agricultural triazoles, or demethylase inhibitors (DMIs), has led to cross-resistance to clinical triazoles, as both target the cyp51A gene.5,6 In the Netherlands,7,8 most triazole resistance arises from two cyp51A haplotypes, TR34 and TR46.9,10 Genomic surveys show that these resistance alleles often co-occur with resistance alleles to non-DMI fungicides, including quinone outside inhibitors (QoIs) and succinate dehydrogenase inhibitors (SDHIs).11 We hypothesize that agricultural environments with non-DMI fungicides can indirectly select for triazole resistance. Using grass mesocosms to compete A. fumigatus isolates, we found that low concentrations of DMI, SDHI, and QoI fungicides, comparable to agricultural residues, independently increased the proportions of triazole-resistant alleles. Resistance alleles for each class are not intrinsically cross-resistant, indicating that their co-occurrences result from linked resistance alleles. Consistent to these findings, environmental samples from heaps with only non-DMI fungicides contained high phenotypic triazole resistance (>20%). This work provides experimental and field evidence that triazole and non-DMI resistance can increase in parallel, consistent with genomic hitchhiking. We thus predict that novel resistance alleles are likely selected in isolates that have already accumulated resistance alleles to other fungicide classes. Therefore, managing selection and spread of environmental triazole resistance will require consideration of all fungicide classes.
authors: Kortenbosch HH, Kanellopoulos SG, Timmermanns L, Reyes Marquez F, Zwaan BJ, Auxier B, Snelders E.

title: Pole-to-pole LOV-domain receptor diversity points to an early stramenopile origin and global dominance of aureochromes.
abstract: Light regimes are a fundamental environmental cue for marine organisms. Yet molecular adaptations of photoreceptors to the extreme seasonality of polar regions remain poorly understood. We demonstrate that the diversity of candidate blue-light-sensing LOV-domain proteins increases at higher latitudes. We identify aureochromes, blue-light-sensitive transcription factors unique to stramenopiles, as the most frequent LOV-domain receptors across ocean latitudes. Phylogenetic reconstructions reveal early aureochrome diversification in the stramenopile lineage, originating in a heterotrophic ancestor before photosynthesis was acquired. This challenges the assumption that aureochromes are restricted to phototrophs, suggesting an ancestral role in spectral light signaling. We find that, despite changes in light quality and photoperiod by latitude, diatom aureochrome domain architecture remains conserved. This implies adaptation through regulatory tuning, such as altered expression dynamics or post-translational control. Our results emphasise the importance of spectral-light sensing in polar oceans and link the widespread dominance of aureochromes to their ancient origin and conservation.
authors: Misir M, Kroth PG, Wohlrab S.

title: Cardiovascular disease risk prediction models for people living with HIV in Sub-Saharan Africa: A scoping review protocol.
abstract: BackgroundThe landscape of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) care has dramatically shifted with the advent of effective antiretroviral therapy (ART), transforming HIV from a rapidly fatal illness into a chronic, manageable disease. This success, however, has unveiled new challenges, primarily the increased prevalence of non-AIDS-related comorbidities, with non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as cardiovascular disease (CVD) emerging as a critical concern for people living with HIV (PLWH). CVD has now become a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in this population, and its risk assessment is imperative. However, there is scanty data on CVD risk prediction models developed and/or applied among PLWH in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Therefore, this planned scoping review aims to systematically map existing literature on CVD risk prediction models developed and/or used among PLWH in SSA. The review will identify the models that have been developed, used, and validated in the region.MethodsThe scoping review protocol will follow an established framework for conducting scoping reviews. The study will employ the methodological approaches by Arksey and O'Malley and its recent advances, the Joanna Briggs Institute, and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis Protocols. The objective of the scoping review will be achieved through a comprehensive published literature search from 01 January 2000 to 03 June 2026 across five selected databases: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and CINAHL, based on a predefined strategy. Inclusion criteria will focus on studies written in English that develop, validate, or apply CVD risk prediction models among PLWH in SSA. The screening of search results and data extraction will be conducted by two independent reviewers.Expected outcomes and conclusionsThe review will synthesize and summarize the existing literature on CVD risk prediction developed and used among PLWH in SSA, identify knowledge gaps, and provide insights to inform the development of a novel CVD risk prediction model specific to PLWH in SSA. Registration: Open Science Framework https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/XVFUA.
authors: Ntiyani N, Letamo G, Keetile M, Disang M.

title: Validation of chemical inactivation methods for Select Agent compliance using HPAIV and low-pathogenicity influenza A virus in tissues and cultured cells.
abstract: The US Federal Select Agent program requires that inactivation procedures be validated before treated materials can be removed from biocontainment for downstream use. Although H5 avian influenza viruses are subject to temporary exemption from the Select Agent regulatory requirements, validated inactivation workflows remain critical for safe downstream handling of HPAIV-containing materials. Common treatments, including TRIzol, TRIzol LS, formalin, and ice-cold methanol, are frequently used to facilitate virus inactivation and downstream processing. However, facility-specific inactivation validation is required for Select Agent workflows and for safe handling of HPAIV-containing materials. In this study, HPAIV (H5N1)-infected samples were used to validate inactivation of material generated in cell culture, and low-pathogenicity (H1N1)-infected lung homogenates were used to validate inactivation of animal-derived tissues. Following inactivation, column-based buffer exchange was used to remove cytotoxic inactivants before viability testing. This step did not significantly reduce recovery of infectious virus, supporting the sensitivity of this approach. In inactivation tests, residual infectious virus was assessed by plaque assay and serial blind passages. No infectious virus was detected following any of the tested conditions. These data validate several procedures for inactivating influenza A virus-containing cell cultures, fluids, and tissue samples and provide a framework for facility-specific validation of similar workflows.
authors: Lang Y, Griffiths A.

title: Inactivation of microorganisms in the complex regions of transvaginal ultrasound probes by a UVC-LED light based disinfection system.
abstract: Endocavity ultrasound transducers, particularly transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) probes, contain intricate structures such as notches, grooves, lens surfaces, and handle edges that are highly susceptible to microbial contamination yet difficult to disinfect using conventional high-level disinfection (HLD) methods. This study evaluated the efficacy of a novel ultraviolet C light emitting diode (UVC-LED) HLD system in eliminating microbial contamination from these complex probe surfaces. Two TVUS probes were sampled from predefined high-risk regions before and after disinfection following clinical use. Probe A was sampled at the top and bottom notches and both sides of the handle, while Probe B was assessed at the lens, edges, and bent groove regions. Microbial contamination was quantified using swab sampling, culture on agar plates, and identification via Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization Time-of-Flight (MALDI-TOF). Environmental sampling of examination and disinfection rooms was also performed. To assess this system robustness, probe sites were repeatedly inoculated with Bacillus subtilis spores and evaluated following UVC treatment. Before UVC treatment, contamination rates ranged from 25% to 57% across sampled regions, with microbial loads reaching up to 3.9 log10 colony forming units (CFU). Identified organisms included Staphylococcus epidermidis, Pseudomonas koreensis, Bacillus cereus, and Propionibacterium spp. Probe sheaths were also predominantly contaminated with Staphylococcus epidermidis., with counts reaching up to 4.3 log10 CFU, Environmental sampling revealed diverse microbiota, with higher contamination levels in examination rooms compared to disinfection areas. Following 90 seconds of UV-C exposure, no microbial growth was detected on any sampled site, indicating 100% decontamination. Additionally, UVC treatment achieved > 6.5 log10 reduction of B. subtilis spores across all tested regions. These findings demonstrate that UVC-LED technology provides rapid, effective, and consistent high-level disinfection of complex TVUS probe surfaces, supporting its potential as a rapid and reliable disinfection modality in clinical setting.
authors: Yasir M, Willcox MDP.

title: Commonly expressed key driver genes in the pathogenesis of viral and non-viral liver cancer.
abstract: BackgroundHepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a common and lethal liver cancer primarily associated with viral infections like hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV), as well as non-viral causes. Understanding the molecular mechanisms of these subtypes is essential for identifying potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets.MethodsIn this study, an integrated bioinformatics approach was used to analyze publicly available datasets related to HBV-associated, HCV-associated, and non-viral HCC. Functional enrichment analyses and protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks were constructed to identify key hub genes.ResultsOur analysis identified dysregulated genes across all HCC subtypes. Among these, GPC3 and SPARCL1 were significantly upregulated, while ALB and HNF4α were downregulated, and are involved in critical cancer pathways such as Wnt, PI3K/Akt, and p53 signaling. Functional analysis linked these DEGs to essential processes in tumorigenesis, including cell cycle regulation and immune modulation. Notably, SPARCL1 has been identified as a potential inhibitor of SPP1, a key driver of HCC. Validation using databases such as GEPIA and TNMplot confirmed the dysregulation of these genes in numerous HCC tissue samples and their significant association with patient prognosis.ConclusionThis study provides a comprehensive overview of HCC pathogenesis by suggesting a shared gene profile between viral and non-viral forms, paving the way for universal diagnostic markers and targeted therapies while highlighting the need for further experimental validation to advance precision medicine in HCC.
authors: Zamanian M, Bajool N, Haghir-Sharif-Zamini Y, Araban SS, Nassiri F, Mirbahari SN, Ahangar-Parvin R, Shams R, Vosough M, Taleahmad S.

title: Antimicrobial-resistant Salmonella and Escherichia coli in fresh vegetables from Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso: Prevalence, β-lactamase genes, and food safety implications.
abstract: Fresh vegetables consumed raw are a recognized but underappreciated vehicle for foodborne pathogens and antimicrobial-resistant (AMR) bacteria, yet data on AMR determinants in fresh produce remain scarce for West Africa. This cross-sectional study characterized the prevalence of Escherichia coli and Salmonella spp. in 300 fresh vegetable samples from farms, markets, restaurants, and supermarkets in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, along with their antimicrobial resistance profiles, selected β-lactamase genes, and associated food-handling risk factors. E. coli was detected in 63.0% of samples (95% CI: 57.4-68.3%) and Salmonella spp. in 10.0% (95% CI: 6.9-13.9%). Prevalence did not differ significantly by season for either species (E. coli: 61.3% dry season vs 64.7% rainy season, χ²(1) = 0.36, p = 0.55; Salmonella: 8.0% vs 12.0%, χ²(1) = 1.33, p = 0.25). Per-agent resistance rates were likewise broadly similar between seasons for both species (e.g., Salmonella tetracycline resistance 23.3% dry vs 26.7% rainy). Salmonella isolates showed higher resistance for several individual agents than E. coli isolates, most notably tetracycline (25.0% vs 15.3%) and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (21.7% vs 12.8%; see Table 1). Multidrug resistance (non-susceptibility to ≥ 3 antimicrobial classes) was observed in 60% of resistant Salmonella isolates. Among eight resistant isolates screened by multiplex polymerase chain reaction (four E. coli and four Salmonella, selected to represent the range of resistance phenotypes observed), blaTEM was detected in 100% (8/8), blaOXA in 50.0% (4/8), and blaCTX-M in 50.0% (4/8), with co-occurrence of all three genes in 37.5% (3/8) of isolates. The detection of the extended-spectrum β-lactamase-associated blaCTX-M gene provides new surveillance data on vegetable-associated bacteria in Burkina Faso, an environmental compartment not previously included in national AMR monitoring. Risky food-handling practices were widespread: 98% of vendors stored vegetables at ambient temperature, 85% applied no disinfection, and 80% of settings presented cross-contamination risk with raw meat. A screening-level model yielded an indicative 2.0% exposure-risk estimate for antibiotic-resistant Salmonella per raw salad serving; this is a screening-level indicator rather than a confirmed infection probability (see Methods). A HACCP-based control framework with five critical control points is proposed as a preliminary, field-validation-pending tool. These findings support the integration of fresh produce into One Health antimicrobial resistance surveillance strategies in West Africa.
authors: Séré AP, Ouattara N, Sanou A, Dakuyo R, Kaboré K, Kaboré D, Konaté K, Dicko MH.

title: Formulation and biological evaluation of a bacterial nanocellulose-based nanoemulsion hydrogel loaded with Persea americana Mill. seed extract: An anti-aging assessment.
abstract: Avocado (Persea americana Mill.) seed is an underutilized by-product rich in catechins and fatty acids, with potential anti-aging properties. However, the utilization of avocado seed in topical formulations is limited by its poor solubility, physicochemical instability, and minimal skin penetration. Therefore, this study aimed to develop and evaluate a bacterial nanocellulose (BNC)-based nanoemulsion hydrogel incorporating avocado seed extract as a topical anti-aging delivery system. Nanoemulsions were prepared using avocado seed oil, Cremophor® RH40, and PEG 400, followed by incorporation into a BNC matrix to obtain a hydrogel-like formulation. Physicochemical characteristics were evaluated by globule size, polydispersity index (PDI), transmittance, pH, viscosity, morphology (TEM), FT-IR profile, and freeze-thaw stability. Skin permeation study was conducted using Franz diffusion cells, while anti-aging activities were assessed using the pinch test, skin hydration, and collagen density assessment in UVB-induced photoaging rat model.The optimized nanoemulsion exhibited a globule size of 20.3 ± 0.10 nm, PDI of 0.109 ± 0.029, transmittance of 99.62 ± 0.27%, and pH of 4.92 ± 0.01 with 1:6:3 ratio of oil, surfactant, and co-surfactant subsequently. The formulation was stable in globule size, PDI, or pH after three freeze-thaw cycles. Incorporation of avocado seed extract up to 5% did not adversely affect nanoemulsion characteristics. The cumulative permeation of BNC-based nanoemulsion was significantly higher than BNC-based conventional emulsion, reaching 198.28 ± 0.54 µg/cm2 after 120 min compared with 121.35 ± 0.54 µg/cm2. In vivo studies showed that the formulation significantly improved skin elasticity, hydration, and collagen density while reducing UVB-induced wrinkle formation (p < 0.05). In conclusion, the developed BNC-based nanoemulsion hydrogel successfully enhanced the delivery of avocado seed extract and provides a stable and effective platform for topical delivery of natural bioactive compound in anti-aging cosmetic applications.
authors: Ramadhani D, Suciati T, Elfahmi, Sujilah ARW, Rachmawati H.

title: Performance and carcass traits of nursery, growing, and finishing pigs fed fourth-generation phytase superdoses in diets severely restricted in calcium and phosphorus.
abstract: This study evaluated the effects of increasing inclusion levels of a bacterial phytase in diets with reduced calcium (Ca) and phosphorus (P) on growth performance and carcass traits of pigs across nursery, growing, and finishing phases. A total of 250 pigs (21 days of age; 6.079 ± 0.744 kg) were assigned to a randomized complete block design with five treatments: a positive control (PC), a negative control (NC; -0.18% available P and -0.16% Ca), and NC diets supplemented with 600, 1,200, or 1,800 FYT/kg. During the nursery phase, pigs fed the NC diet showed reduced average daily gain (ADG) and poorer feed conversion ratio (FCR) compared with PC (p  0.05). In the growing and finishing phases, performance variables were affected by treatment (p < 0.05), with NC pigs showing lower ADG and worst FCR, while phytase-supplemented pigs performed similarly to PC. Across periods, quadratic responses to phytase inclusion were observed for FCR (p < 0.001), with estimated optimal levels of 1,320 and 1,404 FYT/kg during nursery and growing-finishing phases, respectively. Carcass traits were also affected by dietary treatments (p < 0.05). Pigs fed the NC diet showed lower final body weight (FBW), hot carcass weight (HCW), carcass yield (CY), and lean meat percentage (LMP) compared with PC, whereas phytase supplementation restored these variables to values comparable to PC. Quadratic responses to phytase inclusion were observed for FBW (p = 0.004), HCW (p < 0.001), CY (p = 0.028), and LMP (p < 0.001), with estimated optimal inclusion levels of 1,377, 1,324, 1,416, and 1,246 FYT/kg, respectively. In conclusion, phytase supplementation effectively mitigated the negative effects of dietary Ca and P restriction, maintaining growth performance and carcass characteristics comparable to a nutritionally adequate diet across all production phases.
authors: Hideshima Marques CS, Callegari MA, Dias CP, da Silva Martins CC, Fascina VB, Oba A, de Carvalho RH, da Silva CA.

title: Simple and multiplexed tracking of bacterial growth in double emulsion droplets.
abstract: Droplet-based microfluidics enable researchers to observe phenotypic heterogeneity within complex biological mixtures through parallel encapsulation of individual samples followed by imaging. Observing or quantifying dynamic heterogeneity remains challenging due to complexities associated with trapping and tracking many individual droplets. Current approaches for time-lapse imaging require specialized devices with droplet traps that limit accessibility and throughput. Here, using readily available materials and software, we demonstrate a simple method for stabilizing and monitoring many, individual droplets for up to 12 hours. We leveraged our method to track bacterial growth within droplets in a high-throughput manner for over 6 hours. Our method allows tracking the changes and variation in growth rate within and across droplets, revealing heterogeneity in growth patterns hidden in batch assays. Improving the affordability and throughput of time-dependent phenotyping assays helps to advance biological discovery and biotechnology innovation.
authors: Somolinos Cedeño S, Thompson S, Fordyce P, Endy D.

title: Effectiveness of ultraviolet-C robots in isolation room disinfection: Impact of dose, distance, and direct exposure on environmental surface decontamination.
abstract: BackgroundTo minimize environmental services staff's exposure to pathogens, ultraviolet-C (UV-C) disinfection robots were applied before terminal manual environmental disinfection. This study aimed to evaluate the disinfection efficacy of the UV-C robot and to assess the effects of ultraviolet-C dose, distance, and direct exposure (line-of-sight irradiation) on disinfection outcomes.MethodsThis before-after study was conducted in a negative-pressure isolation ward comprising 17 single-patient rooms at a medical center in Taiwan between August 24, 2024, and January 3, 2025, yielding a total of 270 paired samples. An ultraviolet-C-emitting robot with a wavelength of 254 nm was sequentially positioned on both sides of the patient bed and operated for 5 minutes on each side before routine manual environmental disinfection. Total aerobic colony counts (ACC) and bacterial culture positivity rates were obtained from high-touch environmental surfaces (e.g., bed rails, call bells and bedside chairs) before and after UV-C disinfection. The effects of UV-C dose, distance between the robot and surfaces, and the presence of direct exposure (line-of-sight irradiation) versus indirect exposure on disinfection efficacy were analyzed using multivariate binary logistic regression, performed using SPSS version 27.0. The results of the regression analysis were expressed as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).ResultsThe median ACC and bacterial culture positivity rates on surfaces significantly decreased after UV-C disinfection (0.76 vs. 0.08 CFU/cm²; 83% vs. 57.4%, P ConclusionsUltraviolet-C robots serve as an effective disinfection intervention for hospital environments. Their efficacy is most pronounced when direct exposure (line-of-sight irradiation) is achieved in the isolation rooms. Therefore, aligning movable items toward the UV-C robot prior to disinfection, alongside subsequent manual environmental disinfection and physical debris removal, remains essential, particularly in shadowed areas.
authors: Chen YC, Liao WL, Wang SC, Tai CH.

title: Environmental enrichment is associated with changes in the gut microbiome and resistome of captive pythons.
abstract: Environmental enrichment is widely used to improve the welfare of captive animals, yet its effects on reptilian gut microbiota remain poorly understood. Here, we used shotgun metagenomic sequencing to investigate the gut microbiome and resistome of two captive python species: Burmese python (Python bivittatus) and reticulated python (Malayopython reticulatus), before and after environmental enrichment. We found that environmental enrichment was associated with increased α-diversity in Burmese pythons, as indicated by significantly higher ACE and observed species indices, while NMDS ordination revealed differences in the observed patterns of community composition between the two species. Pseudomonadota and Bacteroidota were dominant phyla in the gut microbiota of both python species, but their relative abundances responded differently to enrichment between hosts. Functional analyses suggested an enhanced metabolic potential in Burmese pythons, particularly in carbohydrate metabolism and environmental information processing, accompanied by increased abundance of carbohydrate-active enzymes. In addition, enrichment may influence the gut resistome, with Pseudomonadota contributing the majority of antibiotic resistance genes. Overall, our results demonstrate that environmental enrichment measures, such as dietary changes and improvements in water and air quality, are associated with changes in the gut microbiome and resistome of captive pythons in a host-dependent manner, highlighting the combined roles of diet and environmental conditions in the observed changes in the gut microbiota. These findings provide exploratory insights into the functional responses and host-microbiome evolution of reptile gut microbiota to captivity and have important implications for the management and welfare of captive animals.
authors: Chen J, Cheng YQ, Fan LP, Zhou X, Jiang JY, Wu F, Liang PW, Liu Y, Zuo ZL, Zhu GX.

title: Development of shelf-stable reagents and assay kits for bioluminescence applications using the capillary-assisted vitrification platform stabilization technology.
abstract: Luminescence is a powerful method for detecting trace analytes and monitoring biological processes. However, most bioluminescence reagents, including luciferase and its substrates, are sensitive to temperature, limiting their usable shelf lives, and resulting in inconsistent performance. Enhancing the stability of these reagents could reduce signal variability between experiments, simplify workflows, and address cold chain storage issues. In this study, we demonstrate the application of the platform stabilization technology, capillary-assisted vitrification (CAV), as a tool to stabilize different luciferases and their substrates, and the application of the stabilized reagents in both in vitro and in vivo bioluminescent assays. We demonstrate that CAV-stabilized reagents can be stored and shipped ambiently, maintain consistent performance over time, and are suitable for use in cell viability quantification, tumor monitoring, in vivo imaging, microbial detection, and immunoassays. Additionally, different reagents can be co-formulated to make ready-to-use assay kits that can also be shipped and stored ambiently. Our results demonstrate that CAV stabilization is a viable alternative to traditional storage methods, with broad potential to improve bioluminescence workflows.
authors: Radford S, Peris-Taverner Y, Dibble M, Corn K, Zhu T, Martello S, Mayeaux M, Ladd A, Renu S, Chunduri T, Jadhav A, Dart M, Rafat M, Shank-Retzlaff M, Bronsart LL.

title: Metagenomic analysis of tomato rhizosphere microbiomes detects Ralstonia phage sequences in Kenyan agricultural soils.
abstract: Bacterial wilt caused by Ralstonia solanacearum species complex is a major constraint in tomato production in Kenya, resulting in yield losses of up to 100% in heavily infested fields. This study used high-throughput shotgun metagenomic sequencing approach to characterize the rhizosphere microbiomes of tomato plants in three of the major production areas in Kenya (Kirinyaga, Kiambu, and Laikipia counties) focusing on detecting Ralstonia phage sequences. Soil samples were collected from the rhizosphere of bacterial wilt-infected tomato plants, and microbial DNA was extracted using a modified phenol-chloroform protocol and sequenced using Illumina NovaSeq platform. Taxonomic profiling revealed diverse microbial communities dominated by Actinobacteria and Proteobacteria. Four Ralstonia species were confirmed (R. insidiosa, R. pickettii, R. mannitolilytica and R. wenshanensis). Sequences similar to the R. solanacearum species complex were also detected but were too short for species-level confirmation. Metagenomic analysis detected sequences matching four previously described Ralstonia phages (RSL1, RSIBR3, Anchaing, and Cimandef). Functional annotation demonstrated abundant metabolic pathways, energy production systems, and stress response mechanisms, indicating highly adaptive microbial communities in the tomato rhizosphere. This study provides baseline data on rhizosphere microbiome composition in Kenyan tomato production systems and identifies Ralstonia phage sequences that could guide future isolation and host-range studies. If future work shows that these phages are active against Ralstonia, they could contribute to locally adapted biocontrol approaches that reduce reliance on chemical pesticides.
authors: Mogire DB, Neondo J, Muhonja C, Awuor C, Mureithi D, Ogada S, Wekesa TB.

title: Distribution characteristics of fungi on surfaces in the hospital environment: What have we overlooked?
abstract: Hospital environmental fungal contamination is a significant cause of healthcare-associated fungal infections, which are associated with high mortality rates in immunocompromised populations. However, current understanding of the distribution characteristics and high-risk colonization sites of fungi on hospital inanimate surfaces remains limited, hindering the development of targeted infection control strategies. A cross-sectional study was conducted in December 2024 in a large tertiary care hospital in central China. Using two-stage stratified sampling, 100 environmental surface samples were collected from 10 clinical departments. All samples underwent fungal culture and quantification, and culture-positive samples were further analyzed by 18S rRNA sequencing to characterize fungal community composition. A total of 20% of samples were culture-positive for fungi, and 7% exceeded the ECDC-recommended threshold of 5 colony-forming units per square centimeter (CFU/cm²). Water-related surfaces showed the highest culture-positive rate (32.1%), with the highest individual count observed in an endocrinology department handwashing pool (15 CFU/cm2), followed by air disinfection machine vents and faucets. Aspergillus was the dominant genus (43.8% of isolates), and 70% of identified genera included WHO-listed priority pathogenic fungi. Water-related surfaces and ventilation equipment outlets are high-risk sites for fungal colonization. Current cleaning protocols are insufficient for these areas, requiring enhanced targeted surveillance and disinfection to reduce healthcare-associated fungal infection risk.
authors: He W, Cheng F, Chen X, Chen N, Zhang Y, Li Y, Tan Y, Wu W, Feng B, Lin X, Huang X, Zhou W, Wang Y.

title: Genetic analysis of 7,000 year old preserved goat leather from Cueva de los Murciélagos (Albuñol, Spain).
abstract: Advances in ancient DNA research have expanded the range of materials from which genetic information can be recovered, enabling the analysis of atypical materials. These often preserve both host and exogenous DNA, for example due to handling or native microbes, offering a window into past diversity. Here we report one such exceptional material: a well-preserved goat leather specimen from Cueva de los Murciélagos (Albuñol, Spain), associated with an Early Neolithic context. Archaeozoological analyses show clear evidence of tanning and anthropogenic modification of the skin, while radiocarbon dating confirms it to be ~ 7,250-7,000 years old. We generated genome-wide data from the leather (Murciélagos1) and demonstrated that it derives from a domestic goat of European ancestry. Comparisons with modern goats show highest affinity to the Bermeya breed from northern Spain, demonstrating genetic connectivity in goat herds from the Neolithic to present day Iberia. We additionally recover fragmented DNA from the leather deriving from human and canid sources, the former likely reflecting handling/wearing of the leather and the latter indicating post-depositional disturbance. Murciélagos1 represents one of the oldest nuclear genome data from organic remains outside of high altitude, high latitude regions, and demonstrates the value of ancient DNA analysis in exceptional cases of organic preservation.
authors: Erven JAM, Guyet ZR, L'Hôte L, Mattiangeli V, Fernández-Domínguez E, Laidlaw G, Martínez Sánchez RM, Ramos Rodríguez B, Herrero-Otal M, Henríquez Valido P, Lozano Rodríguez JA, VarGoats consortium, Bradley DG, Daly KG, Martínez-Sevilla F.

title: Moisture and material shape microbial communities in the built environment through disturbance-productivity relationships.
abstract: BackgroundThe built environment houses diverse microbial communities whose diversity and composition differ among building materials and environmental conditions. Ecological theory makes predictions about how productivity and diversity shape communities, and experiments in the built environment provide an opportunity to test these predictions. We manipulated moisture (constant or repeated wet-dry cycling) on three common building materials to test hypotheses that environmental disturbance interacts with the potential productivity of building materials to influence alpha and beta diversity.MethodsCoupons of different building materials, medium density fiberboard, gypsum wallboard and oriented strand board, were sterilized before passive inoculation, then kept wet or periodically air-dried before rewetting. Microbial communities were sampled using swabs every 14 days for 7-week period. Productivity was measured using bacterial cell counts, fungal hyphal length, and fungal spore density, and microbial diversity was determined via community amplicon sequencing using universal bacterial (16S) and fungal (ITS) primers.ResultsThe most productive material (oriented strand board) supported the highest bacterial alpha and beta diversity, and these diversity levels were reduced by repeated drying disturbances. Diversity patterns for fungi were more variable, with the highest alpha diversity on low-moderate productivity material (gypsum wallboard). Fungal beta diversity was reduced by disturbance on high productivity material but increased on the other materials. These patterns were driven largely by members of Bacillaceae, Sphingomonadaceae, and Aspergillaceae that reached high abundances in some treatments.ConclusionsDisturbance regime interacted with building material, so disturbance effects depended on material type. There were also differences between bacteria and fungi, which may be due to the scale-dependence of productivity-diversity relationships, but this pattern was not uniform. Network analysis found evidence of multi-species complexes of bacteria and fungi known to form biofilms, as well as evidence of competitive exclusion on specific materials and conditions. Together, these results indicate that disturbances can interact with building materials, and that these disturbances may be strongly mediated by biotic interactions.
authors: Nannini K, Krutkin DD, Kelley ST, Ortiz-Velez A, Brown JD, Ogden S, Terrazas F, Barber NA.

title: Isolation and characterization of diverse Veillonella phages reveal novel lineages and distinct host interactions
abstract: The human oral microbiome is diverse and home to many species of bacteria, archaea, microeukaryotes, fungi and viruses. Homeostasis in the oral microbiome is important for health and dysbiosis in these communities leads to periodontal and systemic diseases. Veillonella are gram-negative, anaerobic, lactate-fermenting early colonizers of the mouth and are abundant in healthy oral microbiomes. Although considered commensals, Veillonella serve as bridging species in dental biofilms, promoting later colonization by pathogens, with mounting evidence supporting their roles as accessory pathogens in dental caries and periodontal disease. Bacteriophages are key regulators of bacterial community composition and are important drivers of microbial diversity, evolution, and ecology of the oral environment. Despite the ecological importance of Veillonella in the oral microbiome, phages infecting Veillonella remain largely uncharacterized. Here, we report the isolation of ten phages infecting natural isolates of three Veillonella species, representing seven distinct phage genomes. These phages exhibit diverse morphologies, genome organizations, and host ranges, with infection restricted to strains within the species of isolation. Several phages establish stable lysogeny, confer resistance to superinfection, and differ substantially in spontaneous production of infectious phage progeny. Genetic analysis of resistant mutants implicates lipopolysaccharide O-antigen as the receptor for one phage. Although none of the isolated phages had close matches in existing oral virome catalogs, related sequences were detected in oral metagenomes from geographically diverse populations. Together, these findings establish an experimentally characterized collection of Veillonella phages and connect previously uncharacterized oral viral diversity to bacterial hosts and infection phenotypes.
authors: Basu A, Lee H, Fenner J, Ruan J, Gaulke C, Vanderpool CK.

title: Metagenome-based analysis of metal resistance potential in microbial communities from Southern Mid-Atlantic Ridge surface sediments.
abstract: Deep-sea hydrothermal sediments are enriched in transition metals that exert selective pressure on resident microbial communities. Despite the recognized influence of metal toxicity on microbial diversity, the genomic basis of metal resistance and its phylogenetic distribution in hydrothermal deposits and the surrounding sediments of the Southern Mid-Atlantic Ridge (SMAR) remain poorly understood. Here, we performed metagenomic sequencing of surface sediments collected from five SMAR stations and reconstructed 157 high- and medium-quality non-redundant metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) to investigate the taxonomic diversity and genome-resolved distribution of metal resistance genes (MRGs). The recovered MAGs represented 15 bacterial and archaeal phyla, with Pseudomonadota dominating the community, followed by Nitrospirota and Bacteroidota. Annotation of the recovered MAGs revealed widespread resistance potential to multiple metals, indicating that diverse metal resistance mechanisms are broadly conserved across SMAR sediments. Genome-resolved taxonomic analysis further demonstrated pronounced lineage-specific patterns of MRG distribution. Gammaproteobacteria encoded the most diverse repertoire of resistance determinants, whereas Alphaproteobacteria preferentially harbored arsenic- and mercury-resistance genes. Other taxonomic groups exhibited specialized adaptive strategies, including zinc homeostasis in Bacteroidota. Our genome-resolved analyses demonstrate that metal resistance potential in SMAR sediments is taxonomically structured distribution, reflecting differences in genomic potential among microbial lineages to hydrothermal metal enrichment. These findings expand our understanding of microbial survival strategies in deep-sea hydrothermal ecosystems and provide a genomic framework for future studies of metal cycling in the deep ocean.
authors: Huang C, Deng A, Liu W, Cong B.

title: Proteomic signatures of cold adaptation and sponge host adaptation in marine Archaea
abstract: Temperature shapes the biochemistry of microbial proteins, and several amino acid compositional indices have been proposed to detect cold adaptation in microbial proteomes. Whether these indices capture cold adaptation in Archaea, which are abundant in cold marine environments such as the Arctic Ocean, has not been tested. We calculated six amino acid compositional indices (arginine to lysine ratio, acidic residue proportion, aliphatic index, aromaticity, grand average of hydropathicity, and proline residue proportion) across global protein families for 142 Marine Group I (MG-I; Thaumarchaeota) and 146 Euryarchaeota genomes from the Bacterial and Viral Bioinformatics Resource Center (BV-BRC), together with three MG-I metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) recovered from the Western Arctic Ocean. The Arctic MAGs fell within the range of index and phylogenetic distances of the wider MG-I population, and no signature of cold adaptation was detected. Instead, index values differed between the two main MG-I phylogenetic groups and between freshwater and marine genomes, and the Euryarchaeota formed five index-based clusters consistent with phylogeny. A group of 19 MG-I MAGs associated with sea sponges had significantly higher arginine to lysine ratios than other MG-I, differed in the usage of all amino acids except alanine and lysine, and had distinct codon usage and higher GC content; their anomalous placement in the MG-I phylogeny is consistent with long-branch attraction. These results indicate that amino acid compositional indices developed for Bacteria have limited power to detect cold adaptation in Archaea, but reveal strong proteomic signatures associated with host adaptation in sponge-associated Thaumarchaeota.
authors: Green K, Collins RE.

title: Metagenome-assembled genomes reveal water-mass-associated distribution ecotypes of marine Archaea in the Western Arctic Ocean
abstract: Archaea are important contributors to marine biogeochemical cycling, yet their ecology remains poorly characterized in the Arctic Ocean. The three dominant marine archaeal lineages, Marine Groups I, II, and III (MG-I, MG-II, and MG-III), are generally reported to have distinct, clade-consistent vertical distributions that are attributed to light penetration and temperature. Here, we used shotgun metagenomic sequencing of seawater collected during the 2015 U.S. Arctic GEOTRACES expedition (GN01) to recover archaeal metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from the Western Arctic Ocean and to relate their relative abundances to water mass structure. Temperature, salinity, silicate, and N  * distinguished four water mass layers: the summer surface layer, the Polar Mixed Layer, Atlantic Water, and Arctic Ocean basin water. Of 155 MAGs recovered from a metagenomic co-assembly, 17 were archaeal and represented all three marine groups (four MG-I, eleven MG-II, and two MG-III). Abundance-based clustering of samples from two deep central Arctic stations separated microbial communities according to water mass. Mapping MAG relative abundance across several hundred samples revealed surface, mid-depth, and deep distribution ecotypes; members of every marine group displayed more than one ecotype, and ecotype was not consistent with MAG phylogeny. These results indicate that archaeal distributions in the Western Arctic Ocean are more closely tied to water mass stratification than to clade identity, and that previously reported clade-specific depth distributions of marine Archaea may partly reflect the limited resolution of amplicon-based surveys and shallow sampling.
authors: Green K, Collins RE.

title: CAnDi: a global catalogue of anaerobic digestion microbiomes.
abstract: Methanogenic environments harbour complex prokaryotic consortia that drive the anaerobic conversion of organic matter into methane and carbon dioxide. Beyond being key to the global carbon cycle, such processes have been steered into powerful biotechnologies for energy production in bioreactors. Decoding the functional and taxonomic landscape of these communities requires comprehensive surveys, including bacteriophages and plasmids, which, however, remain vastly underrepresented in current databases. Here, we present the microbial Catalogue of Anaerobic Digestion (CAnDi), a database comprising 36 480 prokaryotic genomes spanning 11 149 species recovered from 1256 metagenomic samples collected across bioreactors worldwide. The reconstructed metagenomes also encode ∼1.9 million viral and over 130 000 plasmid sequences. Identity clustering revealed ∼536 000 candidate viral species, of which 85% are novel relative to existing databases, as well as over 15 000 unique plasmids. Clusters of viral and plasmid proteins were generated de novo, totalling 1 721 182 and 123 813 distinct protein families, respectively. Together, these resources substantially advance previous systematic approaches to characterize anaerobic digestion microbiomes, providing an expanded foundation for investigating the ecological and evolutionary roles of the virome and plasmidome in methane-producing ecosystems. CAnDi is accessible via https://www.candi-db.org/.
authors: Ghiotto G, Chasapi IN, De Bernardini N, Fraulini S, Ndela EO, Baltoumas FA, Treu L, Kyrpides NC, Pavlopoulos GA, Campanaro S.

title: Antibiotic resistance gene classes show no detectable shift despite extensive microcystin-associated river microbiome reorganization.
abstract: Antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) signals can reflect increasing environmental resistance or changes in the microorganisms carrying those genes. Cyanobacterial blooms make this distinction especially important because they can reorganize entire freshwater microbial communities. We combined repeated metagenomic sampling at ten sites over eleven rounds along an 85 km Nakdong River reach with taxonomic, functional, and genome-resolved analyses and site-aware machine learning. Sampling round explained 60.9% of microbial-community variation, compared with 5.0% for site, indicating that temporal turnover dominated persistent spatial structuring. After adjusting for site, season, and water temperature, high-microcystin conditions were associated with 3,241 microbial features. None of the 18 tested ARG drug classes showed a corresponding association. The resistance-candidate inventory sums candidate annotations in representative metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) assigned to origin samples; drug-class profiles partition the same annotations rather than measuring sample-wide ARG abundance. Across 301 representative MAGs, candidate counts were strongly positively associated with genome size, indicating that the inventory partly reflected the microbial genomic content represented. In exploratory models, predicted resistance-candidate inventories differed between community states. High-microcystin conditions therefore coincided with extensive microbial reorganization without a detectable parallel ARG-class response. Microcystin measurements should be paired with direct ARG measurements and community profiles to track toxin hazard, resistance determinants, and microbial turnover.
authors: Jeong M, Yeo S, Kang D, Park S, Hyun Y, Jeong SY, Shin JH, Lee S.

title: An AI-assisted genomic census of 193,342 assemblies finds a GFP-barrel family in unreported lineages, carrying pseudogenes in both fungi and cnidarians
abstract: Abstract  Green fluorescent protein and its homologues share an eleven-stranded beta-barrel enclosing a central helix, on which three consecutive residues cyclise to form the chromophore. A family of these barrels carrying a buried network of two arginines, two glutamates and a tyrosine, with a hydrophobic residue in place of the chromophore tyrosine, was recently assembled from protein records by Schneider and Zimmer. Here 193,342 genome assemblies were searched in all six reading frames, returning 396 loci, of which 140 read the complete buried network and collapse to 77 distinct carrying organisms. The charge network family reaches two sponge genera, a coronate jellyfish, three dinoflagellate transcriptome records and an archaeal genome, none of them represented in any proteome. In fungi and in cnidarians a substantial minority of loci carry an in-frame stop or a frameshift: 36 of 144 fungal loci, and 18 of 66 cnidarian loci across eleven genera. A Dollo reconstruction over a 28-genome Aspergillus clade requires two to six independent losses at the species level. The copies that survive are under purifying selection, at a median ratio of non-synonymous to synonymous substitution of 0.146 per species pair over 39 such pairs, and in one anthozoan lineage the gene is instead tandemly amplified to eleven copies. Two novel bacterial copies sit in mobile DNA, one inside a phiE-type prophage in Burkholderia pseudomallei and one beside an IS4 family transposase within a toxin-antitoxin array in a Myxococcota genome. A family that protein records show as intact is, in genomic sequence, intact in some lineages and breaking down in others.
authors: Sidaway A.

title: AnnelidaDB: a comprehensive platform of taxonomic and multi-omic resources across annelids.
abstract: Annelids inhabit marine, freshwater, and terrestrial ecosystems and are important models for studying animal evolution, regeneration, and host-microbe interactions, yet their rapidly growing omics resources remain dispersed across repositories and publications. We developed AnnelidaDB (www.annelidadb.com), a species-centred database built on an updated phylogenetic framework that integrates genomes, mitochondrial genomes, transcriptomes, proteomes, epigenomes, single-cell datasets, host-associated symbiont genomes, and comparative synteny for Annelida. The current release covers 1121 species, including 152 species with nuclear genomes, 177 with mitochondrial genomes, 591 with transcriptome data, 5 with single-cell datasets comprising 209 802 cells, and 30 bacterial symbiont genomes. AnnelidaDB organizes these resources through 10 navigation directories and connects species, genome, gene, functional annotation, and gene-family records. Users can browse genomic assemblies, explore interactive single-cell atlases and 12 200 precomputed Oxford plots, run BLAST queries and search genes against the annelid-specific database, and submit chromosome-level data for syntenic analysis against 20 Annelida linkage groups. Sequences, annotations, and private results are available for download. As a comprehensive multi-omics resource dedicated to annelids, AnnelidaDB provides an accessible platform for comparative investigations of annelid genome evolution, adaptation, regeneration, and symbiosis.
authors: Li Y, Liu H, Perez M, Li YX, Hui F, Shen Z, Sun Y, Martín-Durán JM, Rouse GW, Qian PY, Xu J, Xie X, Qiu JW.

title: Metagenome-assembled genomes reveal Labilithrix thermalis sp. nov., an uncultured microorganism in hot springs.
abstract: Geothermal environments harbor diverse microbial communities, including numerous phylogenetically novel lineages that remain largely unexplored. This study characterized two high quality metagenome assembled genomes (MAGs) from hot spring sediments in Yunnan Province, China. Phylogenetic analysis based on 16S rRNA gene sequences and genome sequences indicated that the two MAGs (JZ-3_bin_45TS and QQ_bin_234) should be assigned to the genus Labilithrix. Average nucleotide identity (ANI) and digital DNA-DNA hybridization (dDDH) values between the two MAGs and other genomes of the genus Labilithrix were below the recommended species thresholds (95% and 70%, respectively), indicating that the two MAGs represent a novel species within the genus Labilithrix. Genome annotation suggested an aerobic, chemoheterotrophic, and motile lifestyle, with the genetic potential for oxidative phosphorylation, tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, starch degradation, assimilatory sulfate reduction, arsenic detoxification, geothermal adaptation, and diverse biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs). Based on genomic and phylogenetic analysis, these MAGs should be classified as a novel species within this genus, for which the name Labilithrix thermalis sp. nov. is proposed following the rules of the published Code of Nomenclature of Prokaryotes Described from Sequence Data (SeqCode). This study expands the known diversity of the genus Labilithrix and highlights the value of metagenomics for uncovering previously uncultivated microbial taxa and function.
authors: Li MM, Liu MC, Lv AP, Ortúzar M, OuYang YT, Chen LB, Chen Y, Bian BR, Yuan Y, Gao L, Liu L, Jiao JY, Li WJ.

title: Evolutionary histories of microbial calcification-associated genes across the tree of life.
abstract: Biocalcification, a widespread process by which animals and algae form hard tissues and cellular structures, has played a major role in the global carbon cycle over the past 541 Ma. Extracellular or intracellular carbonates are formed by diverse bacteria, yet the genetic basis and evolutionary history of this process remain poorly resolved. Here, we present a large-scale survey of an intracellular calcification marker (calcyanin) and two calcification-associated genes with potential mineralization-promoting roles (carbonic anhydrase [CA] and urease) across the Bacteria and Archaea domains. High-sequence-coverage homologs of calcyanin are restricted to oxygenic cyanobacteria and consistent with vertical inheritance within seven families, suggesting a possible origin in a common ancestor of the Cyanobacteriia class, although some cases likely reflect horizontal gene transfer (HGT). In contrast, CA genes are widespread across all domains of life, with phylogenetic and structural analyses supporting independent origins of the α-, β-, and γ-classes, followed by extensive inter-phylum and possible inter-domain HGT events. Urease genes are distributed broadly and most likely originated in Pseudomonadota or Cyanobacteriota, and their phylogenetic placement is consistent with extensive bacterial and archaeal diversification and a possible bacterial contribution to plant and fungal ureases. Together, these findings not only reveal distinct evolutionary trajectories of microbial calcification-associated genes but also provide a genomic framework for generating hypotheses that microbial calcification may have interacted with ocean chemistry and the global carbon cycle since the Archaean.ImportanceMicrobes help regulate the global carbon cycle partly by influencing when and where carbonate minerals form on Earth's surface. However, the genes connected to microbial calcification have not been evaluated broadly across the bacterial and archaeal tree of life or in relation to early Earth history. Here, we analyze a previously experimentally validated intracellular calcification marker and two widespread enzymes that can influence carbonate chemistry under suitable conditions. Our results show that these gene systems have distinct and complex evolutionary histories, including inheritance within lineages, gene loss, duplication, transfer between distantly related microbes, and possible transfers between bacteria and eukaryotes. Compared with previous taxon- or gene-specific studies, this work provides a broader evolutionary view of how mineralization-promoting functions emerged, diversified, and spread across microbial lineages. It provides a genomic framework for studying how microbial physiology may have interacted with ocean chemistry and carbon cycling through Earth history.
authors: Liu P, Wang Y, Roberts AP, Meng F, Zhang R, Zhang C, Zhu K, Cao Z, Pan Y, Li J.

title: Shotgun metagenomic characterization of human adenovirus F40 and a non-cpe Clostridium perfringens strain in pediatric prolonged diarrhea: a genome-resolved case study.
abstract: BackgroundViral and bacterial pathogens may be concurrently detected in pediatric gastroenteritis, yet such findings are often missed by routine diagnostic methods. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing enables comprehensive detection and genomic characterization of microorganisms present in clinical specimens, including pathogens that may not be recovered by conventional testing.MethodsShotgun metagenomic sequencing was performed on a single pediatric diarrheic stool sample, followed by quality filtering, de novo assembly, taxonomic classification, phylogenetic reconstruction, and integrated virulome-resistome profiling, including plasmid-associated resistance elements.ResultsRoutine diagnostics identified adenovirus as the sole pathogen. Metagenomic analysis confirmed human adenovirus F40 (HAdV-F40), showing close phylogenetic relatedness to globally distributed HAdV-F40 reference strains and a clear distinction from HAdV-F41. In addition, metagenomics uniquely detected a Clostridium perfringens strain (SAM_A8, ST-5) that was not recovered by culture. The strain lacked the classical enterotoxin gene (cpe) but harbored a conserved histotoxic virulence profile, including cpa, pfoA, colA, hyaluronidases, and sialidases. Plasmid-associated tetracycline resistance genes (tetA(P) and tetB(P)) were also identified.ConclusionThis case study demonstrates the feasibility of shotgun metagenomic sequencing for comprehensive detection and genomic characterization of microorganisms present in pediatric diarrheal stool specimens, including organisms not identified by routine diagnostics. The findings are descriptive and highlight the value of metagenomics as a complementary diagnostic approach. However, no conclusions regarding pathogenic synergy, causality, or the clinical contribution of the co-detected organisms can be drawn from this single case.
authors: El-Shahidy SM, Zakaria AM, Ibrahim MA, Diab AM.

title: Assembly of minimally fragmented metagenomic pangenome graphs
abstract: Pangenome variation graphs are a powerful tool for representing genetic diversity within and across populations. For comparative and evolutionary genomic analyses leveraging these graph-based structures, it is important that graph topology reflects the underlying phylogenetic and genetic similarities of the genomes embedded within the graph. However, in metagenomic settings these approaches often produce highly fragmented multi-component graphs, hindering comparisons of genomes embedded across different components. This challenge is particularly pronounced for hypervariable viral families like Anelloviridae , whose short circular genomes frustrate existing variation graph construction methods. We present PANIMaSTA (Progressive Average Nucleotide Identity and Maximum Spanning Tree-Based Assembly), a workflow to construct minimally fragmented metagenomic pangenome sequence variation graphs through progressive assembly. The order in which the genomes are incorporated into the graph is informed by a maximum spanning tree (MST) inferred from an all-to-all genome similarity matrix comprised of pairwise Anelloviridae average nucleotide identities (ANI). Applied to over 5,200 diverse Anelloviridae genomes, we construct a sequence variation graph whose graph topology reflects the global genome similarities observed across the ANI matrix. PANIMaSTA constructs minimally fragmented metagenomic pangenome sequence variation graphs that are not achievable with existing methods suitable for similarity-aware sequence-to-graph mapping and downstream genetic analyses across highly diverse genomes.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
authors: Duchen D, Martino F, Panmei K, Kandathil AJ, Clipman SJ.

title: Senimuribacter muris sp. nov., a butyrate-producing bacterium isolated from mouse feces, and reclassification of members of the family Eubacteriaceae into the family Anaerovoracaceae.
abstract: Two strictly anaerobic, Gram-stain-positive, non-motile, and rod-shaped bacterial strains, designated rT4E-8T and mB4P-1, were isolated from the feces of specific-pathogen-free Mus musculus (C57BL/6J). Both strains were catalase- and oxidase-negative and produced butyrate as a major fermentation product, with optimal growth at 37 °C and pH 7. The two strains shared 100% pairwise 16S rRNA gene sequence similarity and showed high similarity to Senimuribacter intestinalis DSM 106208T (95.1-95.3%). Genome sizes of strains rT4E-8T and mB4P-1 were 2.9 Mbp and 2.8 Mbp, with genomic DNA G+C contents of 44.9% and 45.1%, respectively. Orthologous average nucleotide identity and digital DNA-DNA hybridization values between strain rT4E-8T and S. intestinalis were 75.9% and 25.4%, respectively, supporting their classification as a novel species. Based on the phenotypic, chemotaxonomic, and genomic evidence, strains rT4E-8T and mB4P-1 represent a novel species, for which the name Senimuribacter muris sp. nov. is proposed. The type strain is rT4E-8T (=KCTC 25664T =JCM 36407T). Phylogenomic analyses supported the reassignment of Senimuribacter and several related taxa from the family Eubacteriaceae to the family Anaerovoracaceae. In addition, Eubacterium sulci and Eubacterium infirmum are reclassified into Pareubacterium gen. nov., with Pareubacterium sulci comb. nov. and Pareubacterium infirmum comb. nov. Amplicon sequence variant analysis of mouse fecal microbiome datasets revealed that sequences corresponding to strain rT4E-8T exhibited a significant positive correlation with host age and were detected exclusively in C57BL/6J mice from a specific vendor. Large-scale metagenomic screening further supported the association of the novel strains with mouse gut environments.
authors: Kim B, Joe HI, Yang AI, Lee JY, Kim HS, Bae JW, Shin NR.

title: From saccharides to methane: substrate-driven microbial diversity and methanogenesis in anaerobic digestion revealed by 390 MAGs.
abstract: Anaerobic digestion (AD) is a key technology for organic waste treatment and renewable energy production, yet its microbial processes remain poorly understood. This study employed genome-centric metagenomics to investigate synthetic AD systems fed with five substrates: starch, glucose, butyrate, propionate-valerate, and acetate. A total of 390 high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) were reconstructed, 64.36% of which represent potentially novel species. Substrate-driven selection shaped distinct functional consortia, with Bifidobacterium enriched in starch hydrolysis and Syntrophomonas enriched in butyrate oxidation. A complete set of acetoclastic methanogenesis-associated genes was identified in a bacterial MAG (Armatimonadota UBA5829). A complete CO₂ reduction pathway was also identified in Methanothrix soehngenii. Glycine cleavage systems were prevalent in high-abundance MAGs, while key Wood-Ljungdahl pathway enzymes were absent. These findings provide genomic insights into substrate-driven assembly and methanogenic pathway distribution in synthetic AD systems.ImportanceAnaerobic digestion is a key technology for converting organic waste into renewable energy, yet the microbial processes underlying its efficiency remain largely hidden. By reconstructing 390 microbial genomes from digestion systems fed with different sugar-derived substrates, this study unveils how specific substrates shape microbial communities and reveals unexpected metabolic pathways for methane production. These findings challenge long-standing assumptions about which organisms perform key steps in the process, provide a valuable genomic resource for the field, and offer concrete targets for improving waste-to-energy systems through microbiome engineering.
authors: Pan X, Chen X, Xie H, Zhang Y, Dai Y, Yuan C, Kong F, Luo F.

title: BacMap 3.0: a comprehensive knowledgebase of annotated bacterial genomes.
abstract: BacMap 3.0 (https://bacmap.ca) is a comprehensive, freely accessible resource integrating 23 524 bacterial and archaeal species, 32 866 genomes, >100 million genes, 1756 primary metabolic pathways, and 45 284 metabolites within one interactive platform. Despite the extraordinary growth of bacterial and archaeal genome sequencing, relevant data remain distributed across numerous specialized databases, impeding comprehensive genome-to-function analysis. While existing microbial resources generally emphasize genome annotation, taxonomy, metabolic pathways, or phenotypes separately, BacMap 3.0 unifies these complementary information layers within an organism-centred framework. It resolves this fragmentation by consolidating genomic, functional, structural, metabolic, phenotypic, ecological, and phylogenetic information into richly detailed, organism-specific "BacCards". Each BacCard combines an interactive genome map with extensive annotations covering bacterium-specific taxonomy, physiology, morphology, metabolism, protein structures, pathways, and metabolites. To facilitate data exploration, BacMap 3.0 supports taxonomic and phenotype-based browsing, chemical structure searches, interactive genome visualization, as well as gene, genome, 16S RNA, and protein BLAST searches. Building on earlier releases devoted primarily to genome visualization, BacMap 3.0 increases organismal coverage by >13-fold and transforms BacMap into an integrated bacterial knowledgebase for genome-to-function investigation across multiple biological scales. By bringing diverse biological information together in a single searchable environment, BacMap 3.0 offers a powerful platform for comparative genomics, microbiome research, infectious disease investigation, and biotechnology with a goal of accelerating the interpretation of microbial diversity, biology, and function.
authors: Kruger R, Kyes M, Oler E, Saha S, Han S, Poelzer J, Wakoli J, López-Hernández Y, LeVatte M, Berjanskii M, MacKay S, Kovur P, Fitzsimmons CJ, Cahill JF, Wishart DS.

title: Genomic Characterization of Enterococcus gallinarum and Enterococcus avium Infecting Broiler Embryos; A Shared Integrative and Conjugative Element Associated with Avian Isolates
abstract: Enterococcus species are common opportunistic pathogens infecting a wide range of hosts, and often presenting multidrug resistance. Our research has identiﬁed several species of Enterococcus infecting broiler embryos or newly hatched chicks. Genome assemblies for Enterococcus avium and Enterococcus gallinarum isolated from broilers were compared with genomes from poultry and other hosts for phylogenomic relationships and pangenome associations. Three diﬀerent methods demonstrated that host preference in E. gallinarum is associated with genome evolution, with three prominent clusters. In E. avium there is no such evidence for clustering of isolates with respect to host range. The pange-nome analysis identiﬁed a 50- to 51-gene cluster spanning approximately 36 kbp enriched in avian and poultry isolates, relative to human isolates for both species. ChatGPT+ analysis of gene annota-tions from diﬀerent pipelines for this cluster predicted the cluster is likely a new Integrative and Conjugative Element (ICE). Representative ICE inserts were identiﬁed: ICE3 in E. gallinarum EGM181, with ICE1 and ICE2 from our hybrid assembly for E. avium 1788. Boundaries of these ICEs were identiﬁed by alignment to closely related genomes that lacked the ICE. ICE1 and ICE3 are 99% identical, while ICE2 is 94% identical to ICE1/ICE3. Two pipelines were constructed using ChatGPT+ to screen all available genomes from both species, for ICE1-like and ICE2-like, and subsequently extract intact ICEs, including identiﬁcation of ﬂanking genes. E. gallinarum genomes contained 13 ICE1-like and 1 ICE2-like, while E. avium genomes contained 15 ICE1-like and 4 ICE2-like. Only 1788 contained two ICEs. For 31 genomes the ICE insert is downstream of UDP-N-acetylmuramoyl-tripeptide--D-alanyl-D-alanine ligase (murF) and upstream of DEAD-box ATP-dependent RNA helicase (cshA), with all inserts in the same orientation relative to the ﬂanking genes. In 1788 the upstream gene for ICE2 is murF, and downstream gene is glucose uptake protein, while for ICE1 the upstream gene is sapS and downstream gene is cshA. The pipelines identiﬁed an additional 6 E. gallinarum and 5 E. avium genomes with an ICE1 or ICE2 split across two contigs. While 20 of the gene annotations are for hypothetical or poorly deﬁned polypeptides ChatGPT+ ascribes the remainder to Replication Control/Regulatory/Accessory, Conjugative Transfer, Stability/Maintenance, Recombination/Mobil-ity, or Adhesion/Bioﬁlm. Therefore, the role of the ICE in associating bacterial isolates with avian/poultry cannot be determined at this time but likely resides in the 20 hypothetical/poorly deﬁned genes in the adaptation region of these new ICE.
authors: Perry C, Lawal A, Pummill J, Alrubaye A, Rhoads D.

title: Coupled physicochemical and microbial recovery of aged premise plumbing following water-supply interruption.
abstract: Water-supply interruptions can cause pronounced deterioration of premise-plumbing water quality, yet the coordinated responses of bacterial communities, antibiotic resistance, bacteriophages, and microbial functional potential during water-supply resumption remain poorly resolved. Here, a full-scale 24-h water-supply interruption in an approximately 25-year-old cast-iron premise-plumbing system was investigated by integrating physicochemical measurements, quantitative PCR, metagenomics, virus-host prediction, and functional analyses. At 1 min after water supply resumption, residual chlorine was undetectable, whereas turbidity and total iron ranged from 149.9 to 155.3 NTU and 13.4 to 13.8 mg/L, respectively. By 40 min, residual chlorine reached 0.52 to 0.56 mg/L, while turbidity and total iron declined to levels of 0.56 to 0.61 NTU and 0.028 to 0.041 mg/L, respectively. Concurrently, Legionella pneumophila decreased from 4.12 to 0.83 log10 (gene copies/mL), and mexA from 5.55 to 1.77 log10 (gene copies/mL). Metagenomic analyses revealed pronounced succession of bacterial communities, putative human pathogen-associated taxa, and the resistome. Caudoviricetes dominated the viral community and showed coordinated temporal changes with predicted bacterial hosts. Biofilm-associated functional genes, extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), and putative phage-encoded auxiliary metabolic genes were more abundant in the initially discharged water and generally decreased following water supply resumption. The elevated EPS may have reflected both microbial production and detachment of pre-existing biofilm-associated material. Collectively, the results identify the initially discharged water as a distinct post-stagnation physicochemical and microbiological state. Water-supply resumption represents a rapid ecological transition in which restoration of disinfectant residual and displacement of stagnant/pipe-associated material jointly restructure the microbiome, resistome, and virome.
authors: Mi X, Wang Z, Ran M, Shi B, Wang H.

title: Genomic detection of domoic acid biosynthesis uncovers expanded toxigenic diversity across  Pseudo-nitzschia  diatoms
abstract: Domoic acid (DA) production by diatom genus  Pseudo-nitzschia causes recurrent harmful algal blooms with major consequences for marine ecosystems, fisheries, and human health. Predicting DA risk remains challenging because toxin production varies across morphologically similar and cryptic lineages. Consequently, morphology or single marker genes often fail to resolve toxigenic potential. Here, we expand genomic resources for  Pseudo-nitzschia by generating and compiling high-quality genomes spanning diverse species and biogeographic origins, establishing a genus-wide phylogenomic framework to investigate the distribution and evolution of the DA biosynthesis (  dab ) gene cluster. Among chemically characterized strains, the  dab pathway was detected in species only with confirmed DA production. While the cluster exhibits a conserved core structure, several lineages display signatures of ongoing evolution, including intronization, locus rearrangement, and pseudogenization. One striking example of  dab variation occurs in toxigenic  P. australis strains, in which its biochemically validated isodomoic acid A synthase-encoding gene  dabC is located outside the  dab locus. Metatranscriptomic surveys reveal widespread environmental  dab expression across size classes and species, implicating taxa not typically associated with environmental DA events, such as  P . cf.  obtusa and  P . cf.  plurisecta . To connect  dab expression with chemical output, nutrient limitation experiments in the historically inconsistent DA producer  P. pseudodelicatissima combined transcriptional profiling and nontargeted metabolomics demonstrating coordinated  dab expression across distinct co-expression modules and DA accumulation in response to silicon limitation. Together, these results refine the phylogenetic scope of DA production and provide a genome-resolved basis for improved molecular monitoring of toxigenic diversity.
authors: Wood-Rocca SM, Füssy Z, Thukral M, Caraballo-Rodriguez AM, Zheng H, Wanamaker SA, Polinski JM, DeSmidt A, Choisne N, Bill BD, McGrath H, Hammar F, Maumus F, Hubbard KA, Dorrestein PC, Delmont TO, Harke MJ, Moore BS, Allen AE.

title: Isolation and genomic characterization of a Teetrevirus phage infecting Klebsiella quasipneumoniae with a putative SAMase gene.
abstract: Phages regulate bacterial populations in engineered ecosystems. However, wastewater associated phage lineages remain uncultured and poorly characterized. Here, we describe vB_KquP_T1, a bacteriophage infecting Klebsiella quasipneumoniae and exhibiting a lytic growth phenotype, isolated from urban wastewater. Genome-based phylogenomic analyses revealed that vB_KquP_T1 represents a distinct species-level lineage within the Teetrevirus of the Autotranscriptaviridae, closely related to uncultured viral genomes. Metagenomic recruitment from 234 global wastewater datasets reveals that vB_KquP_T1-like phages are widespread, with pronounced regional variation. Notably, the vB_KquP_T1 genome encodes a putative S-adenosyl-L-methionine hydrolase (SAMase)-like protein. Structural modeling and comparative analysis revealed a conserved structural architecture, while molecular docking predicted potential interactions with SAM-related ligands. These findings link an uncultured viral lineage to a cultivated representative and support the conservation of SAM metabolism-related auxiliary genes across tailed phages.
authors: Chen K, Li J, Zhou L, Ge R, Zheng K, Xu C, Su Y, Sun S, Liang Y, Xing J, Wang M.

title: Characterization and Genome Analysis of a Novel Vibrio Alginolyticus Phage and Its Biocontrol Efficacy in Pearl Oyster Aquaculture.
abstract: A novel lytic bacteriophage, designated vB_ValS-L9, infecting the potentially pathogenic bacterium Vibrio alginolyticus L4, was isolated from a coastal aquaculture area in Beihai, China. Transmission electron microscopy revealed that vB_ValS-L9 possesses an icosahedral head (56.50 ± 4.19 nm in diameter) and a long tail (143.03 ± 5.32 nm in length), exhibiting a typical siphovirus-like morphology within the class Caudoviricetes. The phage demonstrated stability across various temperatures, pH levels, and salinities. Genomic sequencing showed that vB_ValS-L9 has a circular double-stranded DNA genome of 44,025 bp with a G + C content of 43.56% and 61 predicted ORFs. No tRNA, virulence, or antibiotic resistance genes were identified. Genomic and phylogenetic analyses, including ANI, VICTOR, VIRIDIC, and conserved protein phylogenies, identified vB_ValS-L9 as a novel species that, together with Vibrio phages Artemius and VapS30, forms a new genus in the class Caudoviricetes, for which the name Artemiovirus is proposed. Furthermore, in vivo trials using juvenile pearl oysters (Pinctada martensii) revealed that vB_ValS-L9 provides substantial prophylactic and therapeutic protection against V. alginolyticus L4 infection, especially when the phage was administered before bacterial challenge. Collectively, these findings suggest that vB_ValS-L9 shows potential as a safe, environmentally robust, and promising biocontrol candidate for managing vibriosis in aquaculture.
authors: Chen X, Li X, Zhu Y, Liang Y, Ren X, Zhang S, Tao J, Zou K, Lu L.

title: Jestvirus, a Novel Genus in the Family Autotranscriptaviridae Infecting Aeromonas.
abstract: Aeromonas species are ubiquitous, aquatic, opportunistic pathogens; however, their viral predators remain underexplored. Here, we isolated and characterized Aeromonas phage vB_AsaP_JS1, a dsDNA phage with a short non-contractile tail that infects Aeromonas salmonicida. Comparative analyses indicate that vB_AsaP_JS1 diverges from representative T7-like phages, with gene content similarity below 50% and a maximum amino acid identity of 70% or less. It forms a supported monophyletic clade in both phylogenomic and protein-based trees. Gene-sharing network analysis further shows that vB_AsaP_JS1 and its closest relatives form a distinct, isolated cluster, clearly separated from all currently recognized genera within the family Autotranscriptaviridae and related lineages of Caudoviricetes. Collectively, these features satisfy ICTV criteria for genus demarcation and support the establishment of a novel phage genus, tentatively designated Jestvirus. Functional annotation highlights a compact transcriptional module containing a single-subunit T7-like RNA polymerase and a streamlined replication packaging operon. Several putative host-interaction-related genes, including a deoxycytidine kinase homolog, a PelC-like protein, and a putative glycosidase, are encoded in the genome; their possible roles in nucleotide scavenging or host interaction during infection represent hypotheses that require experimental validation. Metagenomic read mapping reveals sequence-level signals related to vB_AsaP_JS1 in wastewater datasets from multiple geographic regions, suggesting a potentially wider environmental distribution for this phage lineage than previously recognized, though confirmation of phage identity and prevalence will require further investigation. Together, our results expand the known genomic diversity of T7-like phages and provide taxonomic, functional, and ecological evidence for a new phage lineage within Caudoviricetes.
authors: Chen K, Li J, Chen J, Zheng K, Zhou L, Su Y, Sun S, Chen X, Wang W, Liang Y, Shao H, Liu Y, Zou X.
