title: CnidoSite: A Multi-Omics Database for Cnidarians
abstract: The phylum Cnidaria, encompassing reef-building corals, sea anemones, hydroids, and jellyfish, includes both ecological keystones of the marine biosphere and indispensable models for reconstructing early animal evolution. However, escalating ocean warming, recurrent mass coral bleaching events, and intensifying jellyfish blooms have underscored the urgent need to dissect the molecular underpinnings of cnidarian thermal tolerance, symbiosis, and environmental adaptation. Progress in cnidarian research is hindered by the lack of centralized, high-quality multi-omics resources. To address this, we present CnidoSite (https://CnidoSite.org), a comprehensive, analysis-ready multi-omics platform dedicated to Cnidaria. Spanning 327 species across 120 families, 23 orders, and 7 classes, it integrates 147 full-annotated genomes, 15,642 bulk transcriptomes, 50 single-cell datasets, 46 proteomes, 723 epigenomes, 1,650 metagenomic samples, and 180,652 phenotype records. Complemented by advanced toolkits for multidimensional functional and comparative analyses, CnidoSite provides extensive functional genomic resources, including genome assemblies, phylogenies, fossil entries, functional annotations, BUSCO assessments, and mitochondrial annotations. Key features include 29 co-expression networks with cross-tissue visualization and single-cell atlases to map developmental trajectories and stress responses. In summary, CnidoSite serves as a centralized platform that bridges cnidarian biology, marine conservation, and evolutionary genomics to investigate coral bleaching, symbiosis breakdown, jellyfish blooms, and the mechanisms driving environmental adaptation.
authors: She J, Jiang C, Fan J, Qian P, Wu L.

title: Contrasting edaphic and land-use signatures of microbial phosphorus mobilisation and accumulation genes.
abstract: Phosphorus (P) is an essential nutrient that constrains productivity across many terrestrial ecosystems. Soil microorganisms regulate P transformation through distinct functional strategies, yet how these strategies vary with land use and environmental conditions across chronically P-impoverished landscapes remains poorly understood. Here, we combined 268 soil metagenomes from natural, pasture, and cropland systems across Australia with genome-resolved analyses of 1,077 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). Results revealed contrasting genomic distributions among P-cycling strategies. P accumulation genes were widely distributed across bacterial phylogeny, whereas mineralization gene and solubilisation gene were concentrated within specific lineages. Land-use-associated differences were most evident in the relative abundances of mineralisation and solubilisation genes, whereas accumulation genes showed comparatively little variation. Soil properties were stronger predictors of relative P-cycling gene abundance than climatic variables. Among these variables, soil pH was the strongest predictor of both the combined relative abundance of P-cycling genes and mineralisation genes, whereas accumulation genes were negatively associated with the mineral-associated organic carbon fraction. Continental predictions further suggested higher combined relative P-cycling gene abundance in wetter south-western and coastal eastern regions. These analyses reveal contrasting microbial P-cycling gene strategies across Australian soils and provide a genome-resolved framework for understanding their phylogenetic distributions and environmental associations at the continental scale.
authors: Du M, Xue P, Minasny B, Tang Y, Tran TKA, McBratney A.

title: Comparative multi-omics of host genome, metabolome and associated rhizosphere microbiota across karst-endemic and widespread Rhododendron species
abstract: Abstract    Background  To examine how classically calcifuge plants persist in phosphorus-poor, high-Ca  2+  karst bare-rock habitats, we compared genome, leaf-metabolome and associated rhizosphere-microbiome patterns in the karst-endemic  Rhododendron bailiense  Y.P.Ma, C.Q.Zhang & D.F.Chamb. with those in the widespread  R. delavayi  Franch. and allopatric  R. ambiguum  Hemsl. We integrated a multi-omics investigation across three natural microhabitats to decode these inter-kingdom interactions, combining whole-genome comparative analysis, UHPLC-MS/MS non-targeted leaf metabolomics, fungal internal transcribed spacer (ITS) amplicon profiling, and deep rhizosphere metagenomic sequencing. Results  Comparative genomics revealed significant expansion of secondary metabolism gene families in  R. bailiense  . Metabolomics showed a distinct chemical profile rich in specific flavonoids and polyacetylenes, such as luteolinidin and safynol. These species-specific metabolite profiles co-varied with microbial hubs, including  Piloderma  ,  Streptomyces  ,  Pseudorhodoplanes  and  Candidatus Sulfotelmatobacter  , whose reported or predicted functions are relevant to phosphorus mobilization, rhizosphere defence, recalcitrant-carbon turnover and mineral-associated sulfur cycling. In contrast, the  R. delavayi  and  R. ambiguum  rhizospheres were enriched in saprotrophic taxa, including  Mortierella  , consistent with broader nutrient-turnover potential. Conclusions  R. bailiense  showed a species-specific leaf-metabolite profile that co-varied with a distinctive rhizosphere microbiome. Together, these coordinated patterns suggest a potential functional link between species-specific host chemistry and rhizosphere-community organization, and highlight microbial and metabolic candidates relevant to karst persistence and conservation.
authors: Wen S, Leng Y, Yao H, Zhou K, Min Y, Peng L, Ou J, Qiao G, Wen X, Ding G.

title: Genomic and ecological specialization of Methanobrevibacter species shape human methane emission and overall gut ecosystem function
abstract: Abstract  Methane is a unique archaeal metabolite that links gut microbial ecology to host physiology. Although intestinal methane production varies by several orders of magnitude between individuals and has been associated with gastrointestinal transit and disease states, the ecological and functional determinants underlying this variation remain poorly understood. Here, we integrate breath methane phenotyping with shotgun metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, comparative genomics, cultivation and stable-isotope tracing in 80 deeply characterized individuals to determine the species-level and functional basis of human gut methanogenesis. Breath methane levels strongly reflected archaeal abundance but could not fully explain methane emission; species-resolved profiling revealed that methane emission represents distinct archaeome states rather than differences in methanogen quantity alone. High methane emitters were dominated by Methanobrevibacter smithii and M. intestini, whereas low emitters harbored a previously uncharacterized Methanobrevibacter lineage (M. sp900766745), for which we propose the name Candidatus Methanobrevibacter hominipaucus sp. nov. Comparative genomics revealed that M. sp900766745 represents a metabolically streamlined lineage lacking several methyl-compound utilization pathways and displaying reduced substrate acquisition capacity. Communities of low-emission individuals exhibited reduced microbial transcriptional activity and accumulated incompletely processed dietary metabolites, indicating lower fermentative turnover and altered hydrogen flux.
authors: Moissl-Eichinger C, Kumpitsch C, Mahnert A, Duller S, Blohs M, Mohammadzadeh R, Schmidberger L, Vrbancic S, Madl T, Habisch H, Leithner K, Haitzmann T, Lackner S, Holasek S, Högenauer C, Moser A, Zurabischvili T, Diener C.

title: Hologenomic Analysis of Anopheles plumbeus Reveals Genomic Complementarity with Its Endosymbiont Candidatus Tisiphia sp.
abstract: Anopheles plumbeus is a widespread forest mosquito species and an effective vector of human, animal, and avian malaria pathogens. In this study, we sequenced and assembled the genome of female An. plumbeus mosquitoes obtained from a laboratory culture. The mosquitoes were collected at the larval stage in the vicinity of Sochi (Black Sea coast of the Caucasus) and reared to adulthood on an artificial diet. The genome was generated using Oxford Nanopore Technologies long-read sequencing. The resulting hologenome comprises 1,449 contigs with a total length of 188,457,274 bp. It has been deposited in the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) and is publicly available as a metagenome-assembled genome. The high quality of the eukaryotic metagenome-assembled genome (eMAG) assembly was confirmed by BUSCO analysis, demonstrating 97.5% complete BUSCOs. A single intracellular bacterial symbiont, Candidatus Tisiphia sp., was identified within the hologenome. The symbiont genome was assembled via a Whole-Genome Shotgun (WGS) approach using the Flye assembler (v. 2.9-b1774), yielding a size of 1.7 Mb. The registered assembly of Candidatus Tisiphia sp. was designated as a 'reference sequence'. Genome annotation revealed 1,761 genes, including 1,525 protein-coding genes, 4 rRNA genes, and 38 tRNA genes. A distinctive feature of this novel Candidatus Tisiphia genome is the high abundance of IS DNA transposons belonging to several families. In total, 361 IS elements were identified in the Candidatus Tisiphia sp. genome. Eight identified IS transposon families—IS6, IS701, IS4, IS630, ISNCY, IS110, IS5, and IS1634—are multicopy. Crucially, we identified for the first time in this bacterial species the biosynthetic genes for folic acid (vitamin B9), biotin (vitamin B7), and thiamine (vitamin B1), as well as a gene cluster for heme biosynthesis, which is essential for the functioning of mitochondrial cytochromes in the mosquito's respiratory chain. These data provide a foundational framework for developing biocontrol strategies against this potentially dangerous malaria vector.
authors: Andrianov B, Bega A, Vasilenko O, Goryacheva I, Gorelova T, Moskaev A.

title: Microbial and antimicrobial resistance signatures differentiate healthy and inflamed ileal pouches in patients with ulcerative colitis.
abstract: Background and aimsFecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from healthy donors with a normally functioning colon has limited clinical effect in the treatment of chronic pouchitis. However, a normally functioning ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA) physiology differs from individuals with a healthy intact colon. We aimed to investigate the microbial characteristics of patients with a normally functioning IPAA (HealthyPouch) compared with chronic pouchitis (SickPouch), ulcerative colitis (UC), and a healthy intact colon microbiome (NormalGut). Furthermore, we investigated how repeated antibiotic use influences antimicrobial resistance on a bacterial genome level.MethodsFecal samples from 190 participants were collected; HealthyPouch (n = 38), SickPouch (n = 37), UC (n = 23), and NormalGut (n = 92) and sequenced with Illumina and taxonomically profiled. Samples from HealthyPouch, SickPouch, and NormalGut were also long-read sequenced using Oxford Nanopore Technologies for reconstruction of 12 282 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). DNA methylation motifs were used for plasmid-host association.ResultsThe HealthyPouch microbiome is distinct from both the UC, NormalGut, and SickPouch microbiome. Escherichia coli MAGs in the SickPouch (n = 21) microbiome had significantly higher co-occurring ciprofloxacin resistance mutations in the gyrA and parC genes, compared to both HealthyPouch (n = 26; BH adjusted P ConclusionsHealthyPouch microbiota differs from NormalGut microbiota, and could therefore be more appropriate for FMT treatment of chronic pouchitis. The association between E. coli and resistance gene-carrying plasmids underscores the importance of integrating plasmid analysis into metagenome-based approaches for personalized antibiotic treatment and resistance monitoring.

title: Public Goods Supply Structure Shapes Microbial Network Organization during Full-Scale Anammox Reactor Start-Up.
abstract: Key public goods (KPGs) are metabolites or functions produced at a metabolic cost by microbial populations but potentially benefiting the community. In engineered anammox systems, such functions may underpin interdependencies between anaerobic ammonium-oxidizing bacteria (AnAOB) and associated microorganisms, yet their supply-side organization and temporal dynamics remain poorly understood. We integrated genome-resolved metagenomics and metatranscriptomics to quantify relative transcriptional contributions to 33 KPG biosynthesis pathways during start-up of a full-scale anammox reactor. Across 42 high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), these transcriptional contributions were used to infer supply structure and temporal evolution. Inferred KPG supply structures were highly uneven across stages (Gini = 0.74-0.98), with the top 20% of populations accounting for up to 98.7% of total transcriptional contribution. Three resource-specific trajectories emerged: progressively concentrated, persistently concentrated, and dynamically fluctuating supply. AnAOB dominated contributions associated with low-cost amino acids, acetate, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, coenzyme A, oxidative-stress defense, and extracellular polymeric substance export potential, but showed apparent dependence on non-AnAOB populations for vitamins, cofactors, and high-cost amino acids. Restructuring was driven mainly by redistribution among retained populations rather than supplier turnover, with the strongest reorganization occurring during early start-up. These findings reveal a structured, resource-dependent, and dynamically reorganized KPG landscape during reactor establishment.
authors: Zhu D, Gong H, Zhou S, Yang J, Xie L, Azari M, Zheng M, Dai X.

title: A portable C-terminal rheostat calibrates RecE/Redα exonuclease activity for enhanced bacterial recombineering
abstract: Recombineering enables precise genome engineering across diverse bacteria, yet efficient tools for large DNA integration remain underdeveloped for Streptomyces and other biotechnologically relevant bacteria. Here we identify a panel of highly active RecET recombinase pairs from actinobacteriophages that mediate efficient homologous recombination in Streptomyces. The lead candidate, Che9cRecET, supports genomic integration of kilobase-scale DNA with only 50bp homology arms and enables accurate insertion of 79kb biosynthetic gene clusters, far outperforming conventional genome editing approaches. Structural and biochemical analyses reveal Che9cRecE as a distinct C3-symmetric toroidal homotrimeric 5′-3′ exonuclease, whose extended C-terminal loop acts as a tunable rheostat calibrating exonuclease activity to an optimal window for recombination. We further show this portable C-terminal loop enhances recombineering efficiency across phylogenetically diverse exonucleases including Escherichia coli Redα/RecE and Pseudomonas A. Our work uncovers a conserved regulatory mechanism of the RecE/Redα exonuclease family and delivers a generalizable strategy for advancing bacterial genome editing.
authors: Luan J, Jiang C, Guo R, Wang C, Wang S, Stewart AF, Fu J, Zhang Y, Wang H.

title: Exiguobacterium sargassi sp. nov., a novel seaweed-associated bacterium isolated from Sargassum henslowianum with a glycoside-hydrolase-enriched CAZyme repertoire
abstract: Abstract    Marine macroalgae are rich in complex polysaccharides, making them ideal habitats for finding undiscovered bacterial lineages with unique metabolic capabilities. A novel Gram-variable, facultatively anaerobic bacterium, designated strain RM11  T  , was isolated from the internal tissue of  Sargassum henslowianum  collected in Quang Ngai province, Vietnam. Growth occurred at 10–45°C, pH 7.0–10.0 and 1–12% (w/v) NaCl. Phylogenetic analysis of the 16S rRNA gene placed strain RM11  T  within the genus  Exiguobacterium  , with the highest sequence similarity to  E. qingdaonense  S82  T  (99.82%). Average nucleotide identity (ANI) values ranged from 86.46 to 90.92% and digital DNA–DNA hybridization (dDDH) values from 30.5 to 41.7%, both well below species-delineation thresholds (95–96% ANI; 70% dDDH). The genome (2,859,837 bp; G + C 47.79%) encodes genes for heavy-metal transport, ammonia assimilation, and oxidative and osmotic stress responses. Annotation of carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) revealed a glycoside-hydrolase-dominated repertoire enriched in GH13 family members predicted to participate in α-glucan metabolism, together with a candidate secreted GH16_3–CBM4 β-glucanase, whereas no polysaccharide lyase genes were detected. Based on the combined phenotypic, chemotaxonomic and genomic evidence, we propose  Exiguobacterium sargassi  sp. nov., with the type strain RM11  T  (= KCTC 43930  T   = InaCC B1791  T  ).
authors: Han HL, Vuong TQ, Nguyen TDP, Kim S, Dang MN.

title: Machine Learning based Classification of Ocular Pathogens using Host-transcriptomic Signatures: a proof-of-concept
abstract: Abstract  Background.  Diagnosis of infectious keratitis, uveitis, and endophthalmitis is constrained by the scarcity of pathogen-derived material in small-volume ocular specimens. The host transcriptome is an abundant alternative signal: infection elicits pathogen-class-specific transcriptional responses that may permit pathogen identification without direct detection. We tested this premise as a proof of concept using publicly available in-vitro infection RNA seq. We assembled 330 human RNA-seq samples (177 infected, 153 mock) spanning six pathogens (Herpes Simplex Virus-1, Human Cytomegalovirus Virus, Aspergillus Fumigatus, Candida Albicans, Pseudomonas Aeruginosa, Mycobacterium Tuberculosis) across 36 BioProjects and 24 host cell types. Results.  Per-study differential expression yielded a robust-gene feature matrix. Pathogen classification was evaluated with Random Forest under leave-one-study-out (grouped) cross-validation and contrasted against random cross-validation to quantify study-level information leakage. Under random (non-grouped) cross-validation, balanced accuracy reached 0.85–0.92 across gene panel sizes (8–700 + genes). Under honest, leakage-corrected leave-one-group-out validation, balanced accuracy was lower than random cross-validation and remained stable across panel sizes and gene-selection strategies, peaking at 0.70 (60–100 gene panel) and averaging 0.519–0.60 across the full range of gene sets tested (8 to 9,942 genes; chance level = 0.14 for 7 classes). Unsupervised UMAP visualization of the robust gene set showed distinct clustering by pathogen and by pathogen class (viral, fungal, bacterial), with cross-kingdom pathogen pairs showing more distinct separation than within-kingdom comparisons. Conclusions.  Beyond established diagnostics such as PCR and metagenomics, host transcriptomic signatures analyzed via machine learning offer a promising alternative approach to pathogen classification, achieving balanced accuracy substantially above chance under rigorous, study-independent validation. These findings support the feasibility of host-transcriptome-based diagnostic classification, with dataset provenance as the primary current limitation to clinical translation.
authors: Plumber¹ MT, Kumar R, Yadavalli T.

title: Transposable element content is associated with total genome size and host taxonomy in sulfur-oxidizing bacterial endosymbionts.
abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) are mobile genetic sequences that can disrupt, relocate, or create genes and regulatory elements, thereby contributing to genome evolution. Their potential role in shaping adaptation, including symbiotic relationships, has drawn increasing attention. Most research on TEs to date has focused on terrestrial environments, while less is known about TE function and prevalence in marine habitats. This study investigates the presence and distribution of TEs in marine chemosynthetic symbioses, specifically among the genomes of sulfur-oxidizing Gammaproteobacteria associated with animals living in a diversity of chemically reducing environments. Our data reveal that factors such as phylogenetic relationship and habitat type have no demonstrated association with TE abundance, while factors such as genome size, host family, and lifestyle are significantly correlated. Almost all vesicomyid clam symbionts lacked TEs likely because of reductive genome evolution, while mytilid symbionts had the highest TE abundance possibly due to increased rates of homologous recombination or TE proliferation related to adaptive genome streamlining. Transposase family diversity varied considerably among symbiont groups but was not associated with genome size, indicating that other factors influence transposase composition. Notably, a large fraction of transposase genes was flanked by genes involved in DNA replication and repair, membrane transport, and prokaryotic defense systems, implying a possible role in environmental or host adaptation. This study highlights the dynamic nature of TE content in symbiotic bacteria and allows for the formulation of hypotheses on TE function for the evolution of bacteria in diverse, chemically reducing environments.ImportanceTransposable elements are key drivers of bacterial genome evolution and environmental adaptation by creating new gene functions and altering existing ones, yet they remain comparatively understudied in marine microbes. In this study, we assessed TE content and the function of flanking genes in symbiotic and free-living sulfur-oxidizing bacteria from a variety of aquatic environments. Our analyses show that genome size, bacterial lifestyle, and host association have a significant impact on TE abundance, but not necessarily transposase diversity. Transposases were often flanked by DNA replication and repair genes, membrane transporters, and prokaryotic defense systems, which likely represent transposition cargo that might be relevant for habitat adaptation. The patterns observed within these data further our understanding of the distribution and function of transposases and lay a foundation for future studies investigating the role of transposases in bacterial genome evolution.
authors: Coste M, Breusing C, Travis BA, Girguis PR.

title: Transmission risk and mechanism of antibiotic resistance genes driven by glacier melt: Insight from Asian water tower to global significance.
abstract: Accelerated glacier melt due to climate change is increasingly releasing sequestered antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). However, ARG transmission risk and driven mechanisms that are associated with glacier retreat remain poorly understood. We employed genome-resolved metagenomics along a 246.5 km sampling transect spanning two distinct hydrological seasons and multiple habitats to track the dissemination of ARGs along the hydrological continuum of the Kuoqionggangri Glacier on Tibetan Plateau. Our results demonstrate that hydrological connectivity facilitates the physical transport of antibiotic resistant bacteria. Specific microbial lineages, particularly pathogenic Ralstonia pickettii were traced continuously from glacial sources to downstream rivers, disseminating both ARGs and virulence factors. Beyond host-mediated transport, glacier-derived ARGs can spread into downstream indigenous microbial communities via horizontal gene transfer. Genomic evidence confirmed that sulfonamide and β-lactam determinants transfer across taxonomic boundaries, disseminating from upstream environmental taxa (e.g., Novosphingobium) into downstream opportunistic pathogens. Finally, integrating 156 global glacier metagenomes revealed that the Tibetan Plateau yields an exceptionally high absolute ARG concentration (8.85 ± 0.07 log10 copies/L). Surpassing > 99% of the surveyed regions globally, the sheer magnitude of this genetic discharge identifies glacial melt as a critical emission hotspot, overwhelming downstream aquatic systems with severe ecological resistance risks.
authors: Zhang H, Zhang S, Zhuang W, Huang M, Mao D, Tong Y, Wang X, Luo Y.

title: Detection and whole-genome characterisation of Regana virus in the bicoloured shrew (Crocidura leucodon) from Graubünden, Switzerland.
abstract: BackgroundOrthonairoviruses are of medical and veterinary importance, but the genetic diversity and geographic distribution of shrew-associated orthonairoviruses remain unclear. Shrews are increasingly recognised as hosts for diverse orthonairoviruses, including Regana virus (REGV), which has been reported in the bicoloured white-toothed shrew (Crocidura leucodon) in Germany and the Czech Republic.MethodsWe examined archived shrew specimens collected in Graubünden Canton, Switzerland, between 2005 and 2006 using nested reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction, metagenomic next-generation sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, pairwise sequence comparison, and protein feature annotation.ResultsNairoviral RNA was detected in three C. leucodon from Luzein and Malans, whereas four Sorex araneus and one Neomys anomalus tested negative. Complete or near-complete REGV genome sequences were recovered from the three positive animals. Swiss REGV variants clustered with REGV from Germany and the Czech Republic across the S, M, and L segments. RdRp amino acid identities were 98.8-98.9% among Swiss variants and 92.1-95.6% between REGV Np12 and German or Czech variants. Comparative protein analyses identified conserved viral ovarian tumour protease catalytic residues, similar glycoprotein precursor organisations, and nairovirus-like nucleoprotein motifs.ConclusionsThese findings document REGV in C. leucodon in Switzerland and expand the known geographical and genetic ranges of REGV in European shrew populations.
authors: Park K, Lee J, Hyun D, Kim SG, Kim J, Hilbe M, Gu SH, Lim BK, Kadjo B, Ohdachi SD, Truong T, Truong N, Palacios G, Yanagihara R, Song JW.

title: Description of 10 novel species within genus Janthinobacterium isolated from alpine lakes.
abstract: Strains of genus Janthinobacterium are cosmopolitan and widely found in glaciers. As glaciers retreated, numerous lakes developed in alpine regions. It remains unknown whether Janthinobacterium strains inhabit these lakes. Numerous small freshwater lakes, formed following Quaternary glaciation, occur in the mountainous regions of Southwest China. Metagenomic approaches combined with isolation and cultivation methods are applied to investigate Janthinobacterium strains from seven alpine lakes in this region. The annotated reads using Kraken 2 reveal that the mean relative abundance of genus Janthinobacterium is 0.27%, but no metagenome-assembled genomes are recovered for this genus. Though 11 Janthinobacterium strains are isolated from these alpine lakes, none of the metagenomic reads could be mapped to these isolates. Nevertheless, the ANI, AAI, digital DDH and phylogenomic analyses support that these 11 isolated strains should represent 10 novel species of genus Janthinobacterium, for which the names Janthinobacterium altilacustre sp. nov., Janthinobacterium alpinum sp. nov., Janthinobacterium cryophilum sp. nov., Janthinobacterium lacus sp. nov., Janthinobacterium limneticum sp. nov., Janthinobacterium limnophilum sp. nov., Janthinobacterium montanilacus sp. nov., Janthinobacterium montanum sp. nov., Janthinobacterium oligotrophicum sp. nov. and Janthinobacterium yunnanense sp. nov. are proposed. Comparative genomic analyses further reveal that Janthinobacterium strains possess strong phosphorus metabolic potential but exhibit distinct capacities for nitrogen metabolism. Strains isolated from alpine lakes also harbor unique genetic traits, such as hydrogen metabolism. Taken together, this study expands our understanding of the ecological function potential of Janthinobacterium strains.
authors: Lu HB.

title: Phylogenomic and Comparative Genomic Analyses Support the Monophyly and Genomic Cohesion of the Pseudomonas Fluorescens Lineage but Not the Broader “Pseudomonas_E” Grouping
abstract: The genus Pseudomonas comprises a large and diverse group of bacteria of major clinical, ecological, and biotechnological importance. Genome-based studies have shown that species currently assigned to this genus are distributed among multiple distinct evolutionary lineages. In this study, we examined the evolutionary relationships and genomic cohesion of the Fluorescens lineage using genome sequences from more than 450 members of the family Pseudomonadaceae. Phylogenomic trees constructed from multiple datasets, including 987 core proteins, the Bac120 marker set, a six-protein housekeeping dataset, and 16S rRNA gene sequences, consistently recovered the Fluorescens lineage as a large and strongly supported monophyletic clade. Whole-genome similarity analyses based on average amino acid identity, percentage of conserved proteins, and Dice similarity further supported the genomic cohesion of this lineage. Pangenome analyses identified 18 protein families for which homologs sharing a minimum of 50% sequence identity and 50% sequence length were present in all examined members of the Fluorescens lineage but absent from other species in the analyzed dataset. In contrast, no protein family meeting these criteria was identified for the broader GTDB grouping formerly designated “Pseudomonas_E”. Additionally, our analyses identified a molecular signature consisting of a conserved one-amino-acid deletion in the SurA N-terminal domain-containing protein that was uniquely shared by all examined members of this lineage. In the GTDB classification, the Fluorescens lineage is included within the broader “Pseudomonas_E” grouping, more recently designated Aquipseudomonas. However, the composition and boundaries of this broader grouping vary among phylogenetic analyses, and it lacks the comparable genomic cohesion and defining molecular characteristics observed for the Fluorescens lineage. These results provide independent evidence that the Fluorescens lineage represents a stable, monophyletic, and genomically cohesive evolutionary group, whereas the broader GTDB grouping is not supported as a comparably coherent lineage.
authors: Gupta RS, Rudra B, Lalucat J.

title: Genomic insights into Agathobaculum and Butyricicoccus highlight taxonomic refinements and synonymization with proposal of a new genus within the family Oscillospiraceae, Parabutyricicoccus gen. nov.
abstract: Members of the family Oscillospiraceae are prominent anaerobic bacteria of the gut microbiota, with numerous taxa capable of butyrate production and other metabolically important activities. Despite their growing importance in microbiome research, the taxonomy of several Oscillospiraceae lineages remains unresolved. In particular, the genera Agathobaculum and Butyricicoccus were established largely on the basis of 16S rRNA gene phylogeny, yet accumulating genomic evidence indicates inconsistencies in their current classification. In this study, we performed a comprehensive genome-scale reassessment of all validly published species assigned to these genera using an integrated approach combining core-genome phylogenomic analysis and genome relatedness indices, including average nucleotide identity, average amino acid identity, digital DNA-DNA hybridization and percentage of conserved proteins, complemented by phenotypic and chemotaxonomic comparisons. Genomic similarity metrics revealed that Agathobaculum faecis Liu et al. 2022 and Agathobaculum ammoniilyticum Hitch et al. 2022 exceeded established species delineation thresholds, supporting their synonymization. In addition, Butyricicoccus faecihominis Takada et al. 2016 showed high genomic relatedness to members of Agathobaculum, justifying its transfer to this genus. Conversely, Butyricicoccus porcorum Trachsel et al. 2018 and Butyricicoccus intestinisimiae Li et al. 2022 formed a coherent and well-separated lineage distinct from both genera, warranting recognition of a novel genus within the family Oscillospiraceae, for which the name Parabutyricicoccus gen. nov. is proposed. These taxonomic revisions provide a robust phylogenomic framework for resolving relationships within Oscillospiraceae and improve the accuracy of bacterial classification in gut microbiome studies.
journal: International Journal of Systematic and Evolutionary Microbiology
authors: Menasria T, Zaatout N, Benhadj M.

title: Single-Cell Insights into Virus-Microbe Interactions in Emerging Contaminant Degradation.
abstract: Viruses are increasingly recognized as critical regulators of microbial ecology, yet their roles in pollutant degradation remain largely unexplored. Here, we integrate Raman-activated cell sorting-stable isotope probing (RACS-SIP) and single-cell genomics to elucidate virus-microbe interactions underlying methylnaphthalene biodegradation in petroleum-contaminated soils. Microcosm experiments demonstrated up to 80% removal of methylnaphthalene within 36 days, accompanied by pronounced shifts in microbial and viral communities. Correlation analyses suggested potential virus-host associations, with Ochrobactrum and an unclassified Caudoviricetes phage emerging as key contributors to degradation. RACS-SIP enabled in situ identification and isolation of active degraders, and single-cell genomic analysis indicated that viral auxiliary metabolic genes, including methyltransferases, aldehyde dehydrogenases, and decarboxylases, may complement host pathways for the multistep conversion of methylnaphthalene to naphthalene. Subsequent mineralization occurs through canonical catechol and gentisate pathways encoded by the host genome. This study provides preliminary evidence that viruses may act as metabolic collaborators rather than passive parasites in pollutant degradation, potentially enhancing host metabolic capacity and influencing biodegradation outcomes. Beyond revealing a virus-inclusive metabolic network, the RACS-SIP framework overcomes key limitations of traditional metagenomic methods by resolving virus-host linkages at the single-cell level. These findings broaden our understanding of viral ecological functions and highlight novel leverage points for bioremediation technologies targeting emerging contaminants.
authors: Li J, Liu J, Cai X, Mei W, Jiang L, Zhang D, Li B, Luo C.

title: Termite-Like Phylogenetic Conservation of Gut Microbiota in Passalid Beetles Suggests Evolutionary Convergence in Decaying Wood Degradation
abstract: Beetles of the family Passalidae are an important group of subsocial wood-decomposing (saproxylophagous) insects, spending their entire life cycle living inside and feeding on rotten logs. Decaying wood is an abundant resource, but nutritionally poor and challenging to digest. As in other saproxylophagous insects, digestion for passalids is only possible through symbiotic relationships with their gut microbiota, highlighting the critical roles of these symbionts in the evolution of wood-decomposing insects. Despite its importance, this critical symbiotic relationship remains poorly understood, hindering our ability to identify the factors shaping this association and assessing its role in the evolution of Passalidae. Using high-throughput sequencing of the microbial 16S rRNA we comparatively analyzed the composition and abundance of symbiont lineages in the anterior hindguts of passalid beetles from two independent mountain systems in the Colombian Caribbean region. We tested the influence of geographical co-occurrence and phylogenetic relatedness on gut microbial composition and structure. We posit that if shared locality was the primary driver of gut microbiome assembly, then sympatric species should harbor more similar microbiomes regardless of their phylogenetic relationships. Alternatively, if host evolutionary history is the dominant factor, congeneric species should exhibit more similar microbiomes regardless of geographic co-occurrence. Our results support that phylogenetic relatedness explained substantially more variation in both bacterial and archaeal communities than geographic locality, indicating that gut microbiome composition is primarily structured by host evolutionary history. Furthermore, bacterial and archaeal communities exhibited evidence of phylosymbiosis, although at different phylogenetic scales: bacterial communities more closely reflected relationships among genus level clades, whereas archaeal communities retained congruence mainly at deeper host lineages. We also uncovered extensive bacterial taxonomic novelty, with nearly half of bacterial reads remaining unclassified at the genus level, highlighting the large undescribed microbial diversity associated with Passalidae. These findings lead to establishing Passalidae as a promising comparative model for investigating the evolutionary processes governing gut microbiome assembly and the evolution of lignocellulose-feeding symbioses.
authors: Beza-Beza CF, Jiménez-Ferbans LA, Redondo-Soto A, Welsh MV, Mikaelyan A.

title: Functional genomic analysis of Vreelandella zhaodongensis BS253: a new isolate from hypersaline lakes from Brazilian Pantanal.
abstract: Natural ecosystems harbor an immense diversity of microorganisms whose metabolic capabilities remain unexplored. Therefore, the investigation of microbial life in diverse environments can reveal bacteria with unique physiological and biochemical traits, which may be useful for biotechnological applications. In this study, we report the complete genome sequencing and functional characterization of isolate BS253, isolated in a hypersaline alkaline lake from Brazil's Pantanal region. Using a hybrid sequencing strategy combining Oxford Nanopore long reads and Illumina short reads, we assembled a circular chromosome of 3.76 Mb and two plasmids. Phylogenetic and comparative genomic analyses identified the isolate as Vreelandella zhaodongensis. Digital DNA-DNA hybridization (76.4%) and ANI (96.83%) values supported the designation of BS253 as a strain of V. zhaodongensis. Genome mining revealed genes potentially associated with salt and alkali tolerance, hydrocarbon and plastic degradation, and the biosynthesis of secondary metabolites. Phenotypically, BS253 is a moderately halophilic, facultatively anaerobic, Gram-negative rod that also exhibits emulsifying activity (55.1%) under defined culture conditions. These findings highlight strain BS253 as a metabolically versatile extremophile and a promising candidate for future studies in environmental and industrial biotechnology.
authors: Lautert-Dutra W, Napp AP, Sivinski EAB, Staats CC, Dos Santos FM, Melo CL.

title: Polyphasic taxonomic characterization of Stenotrophomonas algeriensis sp. nov., a novel endophytic bacterium isolated from the halophyte Lygeum spartum L.
abstract: A halotolerant endophytic bacterial strain, IS26ᵀ, was isolated from the internal root tissues of the halophytic grass Lygeum spartum L. collected in the Algerian steppe. Its taxonomic position was determined using a polyphasic approach integrating genomic, phenotypic, chemotaxonomic, and functional analyses. Phylogenomic reconstruction placed strain IS26ᵀ within the genus Stenotrophomonas as a distinct lineage closely related to Stenotrophomonas rhizophila DSM 14405ᵀ and the non-validly published species "Stenotrophomonas nematodicola" W5ᵀ (= CPCC 101271ᵀ). Although the 16S rRNA gene sequence extracted from the draft genome assembly of strain IS26ᵀ (1,547 bp) was identical to that of S. rhizophila DSM 14405ᵀ and exhibited 99.73% sequence similarity to that of "S. nematodicola" W5ᵀ, genome-based analyses clearly supported its recognition as a novel species. Average nucleotide identity and digital DNA-DNA hybridization values with the closest relatives ranged from 85.86 to 86.06% and 29.9-30.8%, respectively, well below the accepted species delineation thresholds. Strain IS26ᵀ was distinguished from related taxa by several phenotypic and chemotaxonomic characteristics. It produced indole and grew optimally at 30 °C, pH 7.0, and in the presence of up to 5% (w/v) NaCl. The predominant polar lipids were diphosphatidylglycerol, phosphatidylglycerol, and phosphatidylethanolamine, the major respiratory quinone was ubiquinone Q-8, and the dominant fatty acids were anteiso-C₁₅:₀ and iso-C₁₅:₀. Functional genome annotation revealed genes associated with osmoadaptation, environmental stress response, ion homeostasis, and plant colonization, consistent with the ecological niche of the strain. Based on the combined evidence, strain IS26ᵀ represents a novel species, for which the name Stenotrophomonas algeriensis sp. nov. is proposed (IS26ᵀ = DSM 112992ᵀ = CECT 31263ᵀ).
authors: Dif G, Bouras N, Belaouni HA, Neumann-Schaal M, Nouioui I, Laassami A, Meklat A, Zitouni A.

title: Shimia rhodophyticola sp. nov., Neomarinovum algicola gen. nov., sp. nov., and Phycorhabdus gracilariae gen. nov., sp. nov., isolated from marine algae, and the taxonomic revision of nineteen taxa within the family Roseobacteraceae.
abstract: Three bacterial strains, W99T, S113T, and S268T, were isolated from marine algae and subjected to polyphasic taxonomic characterization. Phylogenetic and phylogenomic analyses placed W99T within the genus Shimia, whereas S113T and S268T formed two distinct genus-level lineages within the family Roseobacteraceae. The three isolates were Gram-stain-negative, non-motile, and obligately aerobic, with optimum growth at 25, 25, and 30°C, respectively, and at 2.0% (w/v) NaCl. Ubiquinone-10 was the sole respiratory quinone in all three strains. The major fatty acids were 11-methyl C18:1 ω7c and summed feature 8 (C18:1 ω7c and/or C18:1 ω6c) in strain W99T; C16:0 and summed feature 8 in strain S113T; and 11-methyl C18:1 ω7c, cyclo-C19:0 ω8c, and summed feature 8 in strain S268T. The major polar lipids were phosphatidylglycerol and phosphatidylcholine, with diphosphatidylglycerol additionally detected in strain S268T. Polyphasic taxonomic analyses demonstrated that strain W99T represents a novel species of the genus Shimia, for which the name Shimia rhodophyticola sp. nov. is proposed (W99T = KACC 24154T = JCM 38196T), whereas strains S113T and S268T represent two novel genera and species, Neomarinovum algicola gen. nov., sp. nov. (S113T = KACC 23417T = JCM 38210T) and Phycorhabdus gracilariae gen. nov., sp. nov. (S268T = KACC 24156T = JCM 38211T), respectively. In addition, comprehensive phylogenomic and genome-based relatedness analyses support the taxonomic revision of nineteen taxa within the family Roseobacteraceae, providing a revised genome-based taxonomic framework that better reflects the evolutionary relationships within the family.
authors: Won HS, Bayburt H, Choi BJ, Kim JM, Lee JK, Jia B, Jeon CO.

title: Molecular insights into the long terminal repeat regions of therapeutic staphylococcal Twortvirinae phages.
abstract: Staphylococcal bacteriophages with proven therapeutic efficacy in anti-staphylococcal therapy have large (~140 kb) genomes and belong to subfamily Twortvirinae. Representatives of four genera (Kayvirus, Silviavirus, Sepunavirus, and Twortvirus) are the most intensively studied and are advancing toward clinical applications. However, the functions of many of their genes remain unknown and cannot be predicted from sequence homology alone. The least explored and most diverse genomic regions are the long terminal repeats (LTRs), which comprise ~10% of the virion DNA. These regions were often omitted from early genome assemblies or misplaced in genomic maps. Only recent studies have shown that LTRs encode genes expressed immediately upon infection and involved in host takeover, genome establishment, and interactions with bacterial defense systems, highlighting their critical role in successful infection during phage therapy. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the genomic architecture, transcriptional organization, and molecular functions of LTR regions in Twortvirinae phages. By integrating comparative genomics with recent transcriptomic and phage-host interaction studies, we identify LTRs as key regulatory and evolutionary hubs in Twortvirinae biology and highlight major knowledge gaps concerning their roles in bacterial immunity and phage genome evolution. The enrichment of LTRs in targets of bacterial anti-phage defense systems, together with their dynamic evolution through gene gain, loss, and diversification, suggests a central role in phage adaptation to diverse hosts. Finally, our synthesis of available data allows us, for the first time, to infer which end of the phage genome enters the host cell first during infection.
authors: Amankwah S, Wicke L, Kałuski Ł, Stefańczyk E, Łobocka M.

title: Planetary-scale metagenomic analysis reveals CRISPR targeting dynamics across ecosystems.
abstract: Interactions between microorganisms and their mobile genetic elements (MGEs), including viruses and plasmids, impact microbiome dynamics. CRISPR-Cas systems are important regulators of these host-MGE interactions, but a global understanding of the diversity, activity and roles of CRISPR spacers across Earth's biomes is still lacking. Here we develop a computational approach to search short-read data and collect 794 million CRISPR spacers across 367,609 public metagenomes, from which we identified 1.18 billion hits between 41 million spacers and 2.5 million viruses and plasmids. While spacers were highly variable across samples, those matching known viruses were more prevalent and conserved, consistent with a positive selection pressure associated with phage targeting. Among these, however, we find evidence suggestive of recurrent entry of phage genomes into non-host microbial cells, further blurring the line between CRISPR targeting and virus-host interactions. These results highlight key drivers of CRISPR targeting patterns likely to influence strain-level diversification and selection processes in microbiomes.
authors: Roux S, Neri U, Bushnell B, Fremin BJ, George NA, Gophna U, Hug LA, Camargo AP, Wu D, Ivanova N, Kyrpides NC, Eloe-Fadrosh EA.

title: Decoding microbial diversity in roots of rice plants under flooded conditions: influence of the host genotype, root compartment, and mycorrhizal association.
abstract: Rice is a vital staple for more than half of the world's population, uniquely adapted to grow under flooded conditions. Our current understanding of root-associated microbiomes in rice plants under flooded conditions (anaerobic rice) is, however, limited. While rice plants are capable of establishing symbiotic associations with arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi, also under flooded conditions, little is known about the impact that mycorrhizal associations might have on the root microbiome. Here, we used metagenomic sequencing to characterize the root-associated microbiomes of cultivated rice grown under flooded conditions. The root endosphere and rhizosphere compartments were found to harbor distinct microbial communities, with bacterial taxa comprising approximately 95% of the total microbial community. At the phylum level, the root bacteriome was primarily composed of Pseudomonadota (Alphaproteobacteria, Betaproteobacteria, and Gammaproteobacteria), followed by Actinomycetota. The fungal microbiome was dominated by Ascomycota (Sordariomycetes, Eurotiomycetes, and Dothideomycetes) and Basidiomycota. Both root compartment and host genotype significantly influenced microbiome composition, with most genotype-specific recruitment occurring at the species level. These associations were further reshaped in plants pre-inoculated with the AM fungus Rhizophagus irregularis. Co-occurrence networks revealed a genotype-dependent effect in the complexity of microbial taxa in mycorrhizal rice plants. Key microbial species primarily involved in methane production and nutrient cycling (e.g., phosphate-solubilizing bacteria and nitrogen-cycling bacteria) residing in roots of flooded rice were identified. Functional analysis of gene abundance related to those microbial communities revealed compartmentalization, with nutrient-cycling bacteria being more prevalent at the endosphere. Overall, this study demonstrated that the rice genotype, root compartment, and mycorrhizal condition shape the root microbiome in rice plants, ultimately influencing holobiont dynamics in flooded rice fields.ImportancePlant roots harbor a large diversity of microorganisms that strongly influence plant health and improve stress tolerance. Among them, root colonization by arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi enhances mineral nutrition and mitigates environmental stress. Although most rice cultivated worldwide is grown under anaerobic conditions (flooded fields), investigation of microbial communities inhabiting root-associated compartments of flooded rice, including AM fungi, has received only little attention. Here, we demonstrated that the rice genotype, root compartment, and mycorrhizal condition markedly influence the microbiome in roots of rice plants in flooded conditions, thus illustrating the potential of the rice plant to shape its root-associated microbiome. Differential root-associated microbiomes of commercial rice varieties include microbes primarily associated with methane production and nutrient cycling. Elucidation of factors influencing root-associated microbiomes in flooded rice systems, including their association with AM fungi, offers practical guidance for exploiting root-associated microbial communities for sustainable rice cultivation while reducing reliance on agrochemicals.
authors: Busturia I, Martín-Cardoso H, Domingo C, Garcia-Molina A, San Segundo B.

title: Meta-omic insight into the community-level tolerance of the activated sludge to limited-dose ionizing radiation (LimDIR).
abstract: Ionizing radiation is a promising advanced oxidation process for wastewater treatment, yet the community-level tolerance mechanisms of conventional activated sludge (CAS) under limited-dose ionizing radiation (LimDIR, 2-50 Gy) remain poorly characterized. To address this knowledge gap, we investigated such tolerance mechanisms by integrating batch experiments, 16S rRNA profiling, metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, and metagenome-assembled genome (MAG)-resolved analyses of glucose-fed communities receiving a single acute X-ray dose. Under LimDIR, the CAS community maintained NH4+-N removal despite transient inhibition at 2-15 Gy and recovery at higher doses, and progressively enhanced carbon removal (from 64.5% to 71.6%, R2 = 0.85 with dose), while community diversity and the dominant phylogenetic framework were preserved even though genus-level composition shifted. In contrast, transcriptional profiles responded sensitively to irradiation, indicating that resilience was mainly driven by functional regulation rather than compositional turnover. Mechanistically, the dose-dependent increase in repair transcripts was carried by RecA-mediated homologous recombination together with the SOS/translesion damage-tolerance set, and enzymatic antioxidant systems constituted the major defense against oxidative stress. Community-level tolerance was further supported by quorum sensing, two-component systems, biofilm/extracellular polymeric substance (EPS)-related protection, and syntrophic carbon and nitrogen metabolism. MAG-resolved analysis suggested a core-partner cooperative tolerance model. In this model, self-protective core taxa encoded integrated DNA repair, antioxidant defense, and stress-responsive regulatory functions, whereas partner populations supplied essential structural components, including lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis, and metabolic complementarity required for community-level stability. Functional redundancy across taxa further buffered irradiation stress and sustained process performance. These findings indicate LimDIR tolerance in activated sludge as a cooperative, multilayer community property and provide a mechanistic basis for the resilience of biological wastewater treatment under irradiation stress.
authors: Liu W, Song B, Chen Q, Du M, Xu N, Huang R, Wei H, Bai H, Zhang S.

title: Light Perturbations Rapidly Reshape Community Structure and Functional Potential of Synechococcus and Its Co-occurring Bacterial Community in an Estuarine Ecosystem
abstract: Abstract    Estuarine ecosystems frequently experience rapid fluctuations in light availability, yet the short-term responses of microbial communities to such perturbations remain incompletely understood, particularly with respect to shifts in functional potential and organic matter cycling. Multi-omics and geochemical analyses were applied to examine microbial community responses during 24-h light/dark shipboard incubations using seawater from the Yellow River Estuary (YRE). The dominant  Synechococcus  OTU (OTU61), affiliated with S5.1 Clade IX, increased in relative abundance in both Light and Dark treatments relative to the  in situ  samples. Surface communities showed greater compositional turnover during incubation than bottom communities, as reflected by higher OTU loss rates (57.72% vs. 46.51%), though enclosure effects cannot be excluded as a contributing factor. Functional annotation of metagenomic data revealed differences in the relative representation of enzymes associated with carbon metabolism and redox processes between Light and Dark treatments. Metabolomic profiles and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations also varied between treatments, potentially reflecting differences in organic matter pools associated with light conditions. These results indicate concurrent changes in microbial community composition, functional gene representation, and metabolite profiles during short-term light perturbation in shipboard incubation. These observations provide an exploratory framework for understanding light-associated microbial processes in estuarine systems and highlight the need for further validation using direct process-based approaches.
authors: Zhou Y, Wang T, Li J, Gao H, Qin S.

title: Genomic and biological characterization of ΦAB114, a temperate siphovirus infecting colistin- and carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii.
abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii is a prominent opportunistic pathogen responsible for healthcare-associated infections. Its increasing association with multidrug resistance (MDR) severely constrains current therapeutic options, underlining the urgent need for alternative antimicrobial strategies. In this study, we aimed to isolate and comprehensively characterize a novel bacteriophage, ΦAB114, targeting MDR A. baumannii through morphological, biological, and genomic analyses. ΦAB114 was characterized using transmission electron microscopy (TEM), host range analysis, and Illumina-based whole-genome sequencing (WGS). Functional genome annotation, comparative genomics, and phylogenetic analyses were performed to determine its genetic features, evolutionary relationships, and the presence of antibiotic resistance or virulence-associated genes. TEM analysis revealed that ΦAB114 exhibits a siphovirus-like morphology and belongs to the class Caudoviricetes. ΦAB114 was able to infect 20 of 72 clinical A. baumannii isolates, including carbapenem- and colistin-resistant strains WGS identified a putatively linear double-stranded DNA genome of 37,423 bp with a GC content of 39.76%, encoding 55 putative ORFs. Functional annotation revealed genes involved in structural assembly, DNA packaging, replication, and regulation, while an integrase gene suggested a temperate lifestyle. Comparative genomic and phylogenetic analyses showed high sequence similarity to Acinetobacter phages Ab105-1phi and AbTJ. No antibiotic resistance or virulence-associated genes were detected. The genomic characteristics of ΦAB114, the absence of detectable antimicrobial resistance and virulence genes, and its observed activity against MDR A. baumannii clinical isolates contribute to the genomic and biological characterization of this temperate phage, underscoring the need for further experimental studies to fully evaluate its biological behavior and potential applications.
authors: Uluçam Atay G, Alpay Karaoğlu Ş, Bozdeveci A, Suyabatmaz Ş, Bayramoğlu G.

title: Data mining of global sequence datasets markedly expands known diversity within the Tobamovirus genus
abstract: High-throughput sequencing has transformed RNA virus discovery, producing vast datasets that often contain unexplored sequences of known and novel viruses across diverse sample types. Large-scale reconstruction of viral genomes within specific taxonomic groups remains a lengthy, labor-intensive process constrained by fragmented assemblies, heterogeneous workflows, and the limitations of percent identity cut-offs for taxonomic placement. Here, we focused on  Tobamovirus (family  Virgaviridae ), a genus that contains important emerging plant pathogens. Tobamoviruses are detectable in diverse environmental matrices and are thus expected to be present across a range of datasets. We mined global short-read datasets to uncover hidden tobamovirus diversity, combining expert curation with supervised machine learning to streamline the discovery of novel tobamoviruses. Using the Serratus PalmID tool, we first identified 253 candidate datasets that are most likely to contain novel tobamoviruses. We developed a reproducible Snakemake pipeline for quality control, de novo assembly, similarity searches, and preliminary taxonomic assignment, yielding 510 candidate tobamovirus contigs across 131 datasets. Following manual curation, we confirmed 228 tobamoviral contigs from 23 datasets based on BLAST similarity searches, coding sequence content, genome organization, and assessment of potential misassemblies. To expedite the curation process, we built a two-stage machine learning classifier of tobamoviral contigs. Based on alignment-derived features and sequence properties, each ORF is first scored to determine whether it is tobamoviral. ORF-level predictions are then merged into contig-level classification using stacked generalization. Through clustering and phylogenetic analyses, we identified at least 32 putative novel tobamoviruses in datasets derived from freshwater, wastewater, plants, animal gut, and soil. Most were placed within established  Tobamovirus subclades, whereas a few highly divergent sequences formed distinct basal branches related to recently identified soil-associated sequences classified as  Virgaviridae sp. These findings highlight the value of aquatic and wastewater systems for expanding our understanding of tobamoviral diversity and demonstrate how data mining and targeted curation can substantially expand recognized diversity within the genus. The workflow is readily adaptable to other viral taxa and supports continuous discovery as public datasets grow.
authors: Arambašič NP, Bačnik K, Kranjc L, Vogrinec L, Curk T, Kutnjak D.

title: Gut virome remodeling after fecal microbiota transplantation is associated with virus-bacteria co-variation and metabolic response in obesity and type 2 diabetes.
abstract: Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) modifies gut bacterial composition and improves metabolic outcomes in subjects with obesity and type 2 diabetes (ObT2), but bacterial changes alone do not fully explain the heterogeneity in clinical response. We performed virus-like particle (VLP)-enriched metagenomic sequencing coupled with bulk-DNA metagenomic sequencing on longitudinal fecal samples from a randomized controlled FMT trial in ObT2. Using random forest classification, post-FMT virome changes showed accuracy comparable to bacteriome changes (84.8% vs 81.4%) in distinguishing LDL responders from non-responders. Donor-derived viral contig engraftment was detected in 64.7% (11/17) of recipients receiving FMT alone and 58.8% (10/17) receiving FMT with lifestyle intervention (LSI), versus 5.6% (1/18) in the sham with LSI group. FMT was associated with increased virome diversity, compositional shifts toward the donor virome, and coordinated virus-bacteria associations, with most responsive viral contigs classified as Caudoviricetes. FMT-responsive viral contigs that were shared between the two FMT groups were predicted to infect Roseburia and Bifidobacterium, while contigs associated with clinical responses were predicted to infect Escherichia, Roseburia, Blautia, and Enterococcus. These findings suggest that the gut virome is a complementary ecological component associated with FMT responses and metabolic outcomes in ObT2.
authors: Jiang H, Peng Y, Lam B, Yang K, Lin Y, Mak JWY, Tse YK, Chan FKL, Xu Z, Ng SC.

title: WasteFams: a database of protein families from global wastewater microbiomes.
abstract: Wastewater surveillance has emerged as a critical tool for global epidemiology, yet the functional diversity of wastewater microbiomes remains poorly characterized at the protein level. Here, we present WasteFams, the first comprehensive database dedicated to the systematic exploration of protein families in wastewater metagenomic and metatranscriptomic studies worldwide. Integrating data from 580 metagenomes, 132 metatranscriptomes, and 1709 reference genomes (504 metagenomes, 129 metatranscriptomes, and 1151 reference genomes after filtering), WasteFams catalogs 3887 non-redundant protein families (containing ⪰100 members) derived from over 105 million predicted proteins. Each protein family is enriched with multi-layered annotations, including AlphaFold3 structural predictions, taxonomic classifications, and biome-specific metadata. To further expand their functional annotation, we integrated deep genomic context analysis to link protein families to mobile genetic elements, biosynthetic gene clusters, antibiotic resistance genes, and CRISPR elements. Accessible through the EnvoFams portal, WasteFams provides a user-friendly interface featuring advanced search capabilities, sequence and structural similarity tools, and interactive visualization modules. As global initiatives increasingly leverage wastewater for public health and environmental insights, WasteFams can serve as a critical resource for discovering novel microbial functions, monitoring resistance mechanisms, and exploring the biotechnological potential of secondary metabolites within wastewater-engineered ecosystems.
authors: Galaras A, Chasapi IN, Aplakidou E, Chasapi MN, Lamari E, Diplari S, Georgakopoulos-Soares I, Karatzas E, Baltoumas FA, Kyrpides NC, Pavlopoulos GA.

title: Isolation and genomic characterization of a novel Pseudomonas jumbo phage ΦBRkr.
abstract: Jumbo phages generally have large viral genomes packaged in large virions and exhibit a broad host spectrum. However, the detailed variation in host spectrum among jumbo phages, particularly in the context of bacterial phage defense systems, is not fully understood yet. In the present study, we isolated a novel Pseudomonas virus, ΦBRkr, from sewage water in Japan. Transmission electron microscopic analysis and whole-genome sequencing revealed that ΦBRkr is a jumbo phage with a total DNA length of 306,291 bp, and suggested a novel Pawinskivirus-like phage. Furthermore, ΦBRkr showed broader infectivity against 100 genetically diverse Pseudomonas aeruginosa clinical isolates (62.0% of host spectrum) compared with Phikzvirus ΦNK1 (40.0% of host spectrum). By examining the correlation between phage infectivity and the presence of predicted phage defense systems across these 100 strains in an exploratory screening, we found that among the 50 predicted defense systems evaluated, the Jumbo phage killer (Juk) AB system emerged as the potential candidate showing a distinct differential restriction between the two phages. While ΦNK1 completely failed to infect any strains harboring the predicted JukAB, ΦBRkr may evade this defense mechanism in some strains. Genomic comparisons revealed that, unlike ΦKZ and ΦNK1, ΦBRkr lacks a homolog of the KZ241 gene, which is known to trigger the JukAB system. It has been suggested that this absence likely confers a stealth advantage to ΦBRkr during P. aeruginosa infection. These results contribute to a deeper understanding of the diversity of Pseudomonas jumbo phages and provide insights into their advantageous properties for future applications.IMPORTANCEPseudomonas aeruginosa is an opportunistic pathogen causing severe multidrug-resistant infections, making phage therapy a promising alternative treatment. Jumbo phages are attractive candidates because they typically infect a wide range of bacterial strains. However, bacteria constantly deploy diverse defense systems to block viral infections, which can limit therapeutic efficacy. In this study, we isolated a novel jumbo phage, ΦBRkr, which exhibits a broad intra-species host range, infecting 62.0% of 100 diverse clinical P. aeruginosa isolates tested. Our results suggest that its ability to effectively evade the predicted Jumbo phage killer (Juk) defense system, a robust barrier restricting other well-known jumbo phages, contributed to its broader host range. Viral genomic evidence implies this phage employs a natural stealth strategy by lacking the specific protein targeted by the putative Juk system. Uncovering how certain phages naturally bypass robust bacterial immunities provides critical insights for selecting and developing highly effective phages for future applications.
authors: Sakata Y, Nakamura T, Fujiki J, Tamamura K, Ichikawa N, Nakamura K, Iwasaki T, Iwano H.

title: Unlocking the secrets of paired terminal genomic repeats utilised by the  Burkholderia  jumbo phage Matilda
abstract: Bacteriophages (phages) are viruses that infect bacteria. Jumbo phages have genomes exceeding 220 kb, which can support greater functional independence and complexity. This work identified vB_BceM_Matilda (φMatilda), a novel  Burkholderia -targeting jumbo phage. Before injecting its genome into the host bacterium, φMatilda binds to the bacterial flagellum, the rotation of which is required to drive a productive phage infection. Its linear 267 kb dsDNA genome has a previously undescribed tripartite architecture, with bidirectional terminal elements of 1.3 kb and 25 kb, each flanked by distinct inverted repeats of 1.5 kb and 18 kb, respectively. These architectural elements bookend the genome. Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses tracked the phage infection process and confirmed that genes within these terminal elements are transcribed and translated during infection. The presence of bidirectional terminal sequences in related jumbo phages suggests that the tripartite genome architecture may be conserved and functionally important. This work represents the first description of this genome architecture in any organism, expanding our understanding of genome organisation and raising new questions about the replication, packaging, and evolution of jumbo phage genomes.  Visual abstract
authors: Lewis JM, Burns O, Mogg H, Mistry T, Lee Y, Weigele P, Mahenthiralingam E, Chen Y, Scott NE, Baxter L, Mesquita CS, Stark R, Lithgow T, Barr JJ, Sagona AP.

title: Multilayered network analysis reveals the centrality of newly discovered Nucleocytoviricota in wastewater treatment plant communities.
abstract: Viruses of the phylum Nucleocytoviricota are remarkable entities due to their exceptionally large genomes and complex gene repertoires, which blur the lines between viral and cellular life. Previous research has leveraged computational approaches to map their extensive diversity. Experimental work has, in parallel, begun to elucidate their intricate interactions with hosts, bacterial symbionts, co-infecting virophages, and other mobile genetic elements.Although unlikely to replicate all simultaneously within the same host cell, the convergence of these entities within a single environment creates a dense hub of potential interactions that calls for a holistic, topology-based analysis. Here, we recovered high-quality genomes of 61 Nucleocytoviruses, 15 virophages and 14 polinton-like viruses from deeply sequenced metagenomes of 23 Danish wastewater treatment plants, and integrated them into a multilayered interaction network together with microbial contigs. This network recovered putative interactions across multiple levels, including Nucleocytoviruses co-occurring with hyperparasitic elements, associations with abundant activated sludge bacteria, and read-level signals of integration events. We show that the giants among viruses act as centrality-inducing entities, elevating others into highly central positions within the community and therefore are key players shaping the microbial community structure, ecology and evolution in wastewater treatment plants.
authors: Lücking D, Manzano-Marín A, Willemsen A.

title: Molecular Characterization of Previous Unclassified Dicistroviruses in Water Reservoir in São Paulo, Brazil.
abstract: In this study, viral metagenomics was applied to identify viruses related to the Dicistroviridae family in freshwater samples collected from urban reservoirs of the state of São Paulo, Brazil. Through next-generation sequencing, five complete RNA genomes similar to Dicistroviridae were detected. These genomes range from 8.032 to 9.425 nucleotides in length, and each contains two open reading frames (ORFs) with conserved protein domains and internal ribosome entry sites (IRES) characteristic of Dicistroviridae. Phylogenetic and genetic identity analyses based on the amino acid sequences of the nonstructural (ORF1) and structural (ORF2) polyproteins suggest that these five genomes represent four putative novel species provisionally named Hydro virus 1 to Hydro virus 4. These findings enhance our understanding of the diversity and distribution of Dicistroviridae in aquatic environments.
authors: Funada Barbosa MR, Foro Ramos EDS, Villanova F, Silva RLO, Zhang W, Ferreira NE, Tozetto-Mendoza TR, Mendes-Correa MC, Pandey RP, Sato MIZ, Leal E, da Costa AC.

title: Genome-resolved metagenomics reveals seasonally defined life strategies in hypersaline sediments
abstract: Background  Hypersaline sediments are long-standing models for microbial adaptation and are increasingly regarded as reservoirs of novel biosynthetic potential, including surface-active compounds. Inferences about biosurfactant production in such communities have rested largely on taxonomic affiliation, targeted single-gene surveys or metabolite detection, rather than on genome-resolved evidence that the pathways are encoded. The seasonal restructuring of these communities has also rarely been resolved at genome level. Results  We sequenced summer and winter sediments from the hyperarid Qaidam Basin on the northern Tibetan Plateau, recovering 44 metagenome-assembled genomes and 1,468 biosynthetic gene clusters from 2.98 Gbp of assembly. Evaporative and cryoconcentration processes raised winter porewater chloride by two to three orders of magnitude relative to summer. The community switched between osmoadaptation strategies. Summer sediments were dominated by salt-in haloarchaea with acidic proteomes and rhodopsin phototrophy, whereas winter sediments were dominated by salt-out bacteria with near-neutral proteomes and winter-enriched compatible-solute biosynthesis. The salt-in bacterium  Salinibacter occupied the expected intermediate position, providing an internal control. The winter surface-active response was envelope-associated rather than secreted, comprising phospholipase-derived lysophospholipids, desaturase-mediated membrane remodelling, substitution of phospholipids by phosphorus-free ornithine and sulfoquinovosyl lipids, and capsular exopolysaccharide export. Dedicated secreted biosurfactant pathways were not detected. Of 69 NRPS clusters, only one carried the starter condensation domain diagnostic of lipopeptide assembly, and it matched no characterised reference. Profile-based, read-level and orthology-based searches independently recovered no complete lipopeptide, rhamnolipid or trehalolipid pathway. Apparent biosurfactant genes in 40 of 44 genomes resolved to housekeeping homologues upon domain verification, and an independent catalogue of 1,773 regional genomes reproduced the same absence.  Conclusions  Surface activity in this hypersaline community is retained at the cell envelope rather than secreted, and dedicated biosurfactant biosynthesis is not a community-level trait. Because both taxonomic affiliation and gene-name annotation overestimate this capacity, genome-resolved verification is required before biosynthetic potential inferred from extreme environments is treated as real.
authors: Ullah H, Selvarjan R, Lau Vetter MCY.

title: Global population genomics and pangenome of the clubroot pathogen link clonal expansion and effector diversification to resistance breakdown in canola
abstract: Clubroot disease, caused by the obligate biotrophic protist Plasmodiophora brassicae, threatens Brassica crops worldwide. Novel pathogen virulence frequently breaks resistance in agricultural crops, and yet explanations for isolate evolution remain unknown. We combined whole genome sequencing of 192 isolates from 24 countries with a pangenome analysis of 55 high–quality complete or nearly complete genome assemblies and performed functional effector analyses to investigate potential mechanisms of virulence emergence. Three major phylogenetic clusters were identified, including two highly clonal lineages with contrasting virulence profiles, and a genetically diverse population retaining signatures of recombination. Our findings support a model in which genome–wide purifying selection maintained core genome integrity, while effector genes evolved under less constraint. Despite a compact closed pangenome, we identified chromosome 17 as a major hotspot of single nucleotide and structural variations, transposable elements and expansion of ankyrin repeat effectors. Within the variable chromosome 17, PbAnk2 alleles from virulent and avirulent isolates encoded proteins with distinct predicted structures. PbAnk2 interacted with the Arabidopsis co–chaperone DJC31 in yeast two–hybrid and BiFC assays, whereas co–immunoprecipitation did not detect an interaction for the allele found in isolates that break CRa–mediated resistance, suggesting that allelic variation may alter PbAnk2′s association with DJC31. These findings reveal the clonal expansion of virulent isolates and connect it to effector diversification that led to resistance breakdown and establish a genomic framework for pathogen surveillance and durable clubroot resistance.

title: Decoding horizontal transposon transfer across plants through a comprehensive HTT atlas.
abstract: IntroductionHorizontal transposon transfer (HTT) plays an important role in genome evolution; however, its prevalence, evolutionary patterns, and potential mechanisms in plants remain poorly understood due to limited taxonomic sampling and challenges in distinguishing HTT from vertical inheritance.ObjectivesThis study aimed to systematically identify HTT events across major plant lineages, investigate factors potentially associated with HTT, and assess the possible evolutionary significance of HTT in plant genomes.MethodsA total of 558 high-quality plant genomes representing 352 species spanning algae to angiosperms were analyzed. A conservative phylogeny-informed framework integrating transposable element (TE) annotation, orthology inference, sequence similarity analysis, and lineage distribution filtering was developed to identify putative HTT events. Co-transfer relationships, host gene enrichment, transport-related pathways, and exosome-associated sequences were further analyzed to investigate candidate factors associated with HTT.ResultsIn total, 1,548 putative HTT events involving 684 TE families were identified across diverse plant lineages, indicating that both RNA- and DNA-mediated transposons contribute extensively to HTT in plants. Co-transfer analyses revealed widespread associations among TE superfamilies, whereas functional enrichment analyses highlighted chromatin-related and transport-related host genes frequently associated with HTT regions. HTT-related TE sequences were also detected in publicly available plant exosomal sequencing datasets, and several hotspot TE families showed homology to viral-associated sequences, suggesting potential involvement of vesicle-mediated transport and viral interactions in HTT processes. In addition, genes associated with cold acclimation and stress responses were enriched near several HTT regions, suggesting that HTT may contribute to environmental adaptation in some plant lineages.ConclusionThis study provides a comprehensive atlas of HTT across plants and establishes a scalable framework for HTT detection in large-scale comparative genomics analyses. These findings generate candidate hypotheses regarding the mechanisms and evolutionary significance of HTT and provide a resource for future functional and experimental investigations.
authors: Huang Y, Sahu SK, Wang H, Lin Z, Hu J, Zhao Y, Varshney RK, Liu X.

title: Horizontal Gene Transfer from Fungi to Myxozoa: Genomic Evidence and Evolutionary Implications.
abstract: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is increasingly recognized as an important mechanism driving evolutionary innovation in eukaryotes, yet its functional significance in parasitic lineages remains poorly understood. Myxozoans are obligate cnidarian parasites characterized by extreme genome reduction and complex two-host life cycles, making them an intriguing system for investigating the evolutionary role of HGT. We conducted a comparative genomic and transcriptomic analysis to identify and characterize candidate genes putatively transferred from fungi to myxozoans. Phylogenetic reconstruction, sequence composition analyses, and functional annotation provided multiple lines of evidence supporting ancient HGT events retained across diverse myxozoan species. Candidate transferred genes encode proteins putatively involved in carbohydrate metabolism, defense, and regulatory processes. Exploratory codon-usage analysis revealed compositional differences between candidate genes and the sampled reference sets, a pattern that may be consistent with partial amelioration following ancient transfer, although broader quantitative comparisons will be required to evaluate codon adaptation more rigorously. Molecular clock analyses place the inferred fungi-to-myxozoan HGT events within a time interval that overlaps with the major diversification of myxozoans, around 300 Ma. Collectively, these findings suggest that candidate horizontally acquired genes may have contributed to functional innovation during myxozoan evolution, expanding our understanding of the evolutionary impact of HGT in these highly reduced parasites.
authors: Ibrahim AGA, Adriano EA.
