title: Novel Biomarkers for Bacterial Meningitis and Other Central Nervous System Infections.
abstract: Purpose of reviewTimely and accurate diagnosis of central nervous system (CNS) infections remains challenging because of nonspecific clinical characteristics and limited diagnostic accuracy of conventional tests. Novel cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers may improve early diagnosis and facilitate differentiation between infectious aetiologies. This review summarizes established and emerging CSF biomarkers for the diagnosis of CNS infections, with a focus on bacterial meningitis, and discusses their potential clinical application.Recent findingsSeveral novel CSF biomarkers have demonstrated excellent diagnostic performance for bacterial meningitis. Among these, CSF C-reactive protein (CRP) has recently been implemented in clinical practice, while heparin-binding protein and combinations of CSF CRP with inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-1β show similarly high diagnostic accuracy. Pathogen-specific biomarkers, including CXCL13 for neuroborreliosis and β-D-glucan and galactomannan for fungal CNS infections, further expand the diagnostic repertoire. In addition, multi-omics approaches, including metabolomics, lipidomics, and proteomics, have identified promising candidates such as pyruvate and phosphatidylcholines, although these require further validation. Untargeted techniques, including metagenomic next-generation sequencing and phage immunoprecipitation sequencing, further enhance pathogen detection and may complement microbiological testing. Novel biomarkers have the potential to substantially improve the diagnosis of CNS infections. Several biomarkers for bacterial meningitis are already available for clinical implementation, particularly in patients with intermediate CSF leukocyte counts, where diagnostic uncertainty is greatest. For viral and other CNS infections biomarkers remain scarce. Future studies should focus on validation of emerging biomarkers and on integrating biomarker panels with advanced molecular diagnostic techniques to enable rapid, accurate and clinically applicable diagnostic strategies.
authors: Nieuwenhuijsen BL, Olie SE, van de Beek D, Brouwer MC.

title: Characterization and Functional Analysis of the Oropharyngeal Microbiome in ICU staff via Metagenomic Sequencing
abstract: Abstract  Background  ICU staff face an elevated risk of colonization by drug-resistant bacteria, potentially associated with persistent occupational exposure to hospital environments. The oropharynx, as a key ecological niche at the interface of the respiratory and digestive tracts, serves as an important reservoir for opportunistic pathogens. This study employed shotgun metagenomic sequencing to systematically characterize the composition and functional profiles of the oropharyngeal microbiota in ICU staff. Methods  A cross-sectional study was conducted, enrolling 10 full-time ICU staff (with ≥ 5 years of clinical experience) and 10 healthy non-medical controls with no history of medical-related employment. Oropharyngeal swabs were collected for metagenomic sequencing. Multi-dimensional comparative analyses were conducted between the two groups, covering community structure, taxonomic composition, KEGG metabolic pathways, virulence factor profiles, and antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) profiles. Results  Compared with the control group, ICU staff exhibited significantly reduced genus-level richness (Chao1 index) but elevated community evenness, resulting in higher Shannon and Simpson indices, with a clearly distinct overall microbial community structure. The abundances of potential pathogenic genera including Pseudomonas, Streptococcus, Escherichia, Mycobacteroides, and Helicobacter were significantly enriched, whereas core oral commensal genera such as Prevotella were depleted. Functionally, ICU staff exhibited significant enrichment in bacterial biofilm formation, drug metabolism–cytochrome P450, and ABC transporter pathways; marked upregulation of virulence factors associated with adhesion, immune evasion, and endotoxin biosynthesis; and elevated abundances of five resistance genes primarily derived from Streptococcus and Haemophilus species (mel, patB, mdtG, hmrM, and rlmA(II)). Conclusion  ICU occupational exposure is associated with systematic remodeling of the oropharyngeal microbiota, characterized by depletion of core oral commensals and enrichment of opportunistic pathogens. Functionally, this remodeling supports the formation of a potential synergistic resistance system of "biofilm barrier–P450 metabolic inactivation–ABC active efflux," providing novel metagenomic evidence for microbiome-based surveillance and occupational health protection of healthcare workers.
authors: Zhou k, Li j, Ling B, Fan z, Xiu g.

title: Context-dependent and shared responses of the zebrafish gut microbiome to KH<sub>2</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> enrichment.
abstract: Anthropogenic phosphorus (P) enrichment is widespread in aquatic ecosystems, yet its effects on the functional potential of fish gut microbiomes remain poorly understood. We conducted a replicated 42-day experiment with zebrafish (Danio rerio), combining shotgun metagenomics with genome-resolved analyses to examine how sustained KH2PO4 exposure reshapes the gut microbiome in water-only and sediment-associated systems. Evidence for sediment-dependent modulation of microbial diversity and community composition was primarily observed during early exposure, indicating that these effects varied over time. Despite context-specific differences in functional profiles, both environmental backgrounds showed enrichment of genes or modules associated with P acquisition and turnover, selected carbon utilization pathways, energy transduction, and biosynthesis, accompanied by reduced potential for certain aromatic compound degradation and nitrate assimilation processes. Genome-resolved analyses further identified a Mycobacterium population that exhibited positive abundance responses to KH2PO4 addition in both environmental backgrounds. Its genomic traits related to P homeostasis, substrate utilization, and cellular biosynthesis provide candidate mechanistic explanations for this shared response. These findings reveal sediment-dependent responses of the zebrafish gut microbiome to extreme KH2PO4 input and identify microbial functional shifts that warrant further investigation as potential indicators of P-associated environmental disturbance.
authors: Zhu W, Yu X, Niu S, Ge K, Liu H, Zhang S, Li M, Ming Y, Li T, Zhao Z, An X, Niu M, Wu K, Xie W, He Z, Yan Q.

title: Extracellular polymeric substances drive Curvibacter host adaptation and cospeciation with Hydra.
abstract: The interactions between hosts and their microbial symbionts play a crucial role to host physiology. Bacteria can adapt to specific host environments over evolutionary timescales, leading to cospeciation and the formation of specialized host-microbe relationships. Understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying these adaptations provides key insights into the evolution of symbiosis and the stability of microbial communities. This study investigates the cospeciation and molecular adaptations of Curvibacter to its host Hydra, a well-established model for the study of host-microbe interactions. We provide strong evidence of cospeciation, as demonstrated by phylogenetic congruence between different Hydra species and their corresponding Curvibacter symbionts, along with preferential recolonization of germ-free Hydra by their native Curvibacter strains. Comparative genomic analyses reveal that host-associated Curvibacter strains exhibit distinct metabolic and biosynthetic adaptations compared to their free-living relatives. Specifically, the enrichment of proteins linked to host glycan interactions, extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), DNA metabolic processes, ABC transport, sugar metabolism, and bacterial chemotaxis highlights specialized adaptations of Curvibacter symbionts within the Hydra glycocalyx. Importantly, some of these signatures are only detectable within the Hydra vulgaris-associated Curvibacter subgroup, emphasizing the need to examine host-specific adaptations at a finer taxonomic resolution. Functional experiments identify a symbiont-specific EPS operon as a factor for host colonization, thereby establishing its role in facilitating symbiont specificity and stability. These findings provide insights into the molecular mechanisms driving host-microbe coevolution and highlight the evolutionary forces shaping microbial specialization within host-symbiont relationships.
authors: Becker L, Fürbach L, Minten T, Bathia J, Karbach M, Foret S, Winterfeldt NM, Usadel B, Pauly M, Axmann IM, Fraune S.

title: Expanding the range of habitats colonized by the Verrucomicrobiota: Description of three novel Oleiharenicola species thriving in a co-culture with methanotrophic bacteria.
abstract: In this study, we characterize five strains of ultra-small verrucomicrobia, which affiliate with the genus Oleiharenicola, the family Opitutaceae, and develop in trophic associations with methanotrophic bacteria due to the ability to utilize organic acids excreted by methanotrophs and their exopolysaccharides. First representative of these bacteria, strain Vm1ᵀ, was isolated from a laboratory bioreactor with a Methylococcus-dominated methane-oxidizing consortium. Four additional isolates, strains 1P4, E5ᵀ, A3, and T2ᵀ, were further retrieved from Methylocystis, Methylosinus, and Methylomonas-dominated methanotrophic enrichment cultures obtained from freshwater habitats. Cells of these strains were Gram-negative cocci, 0.35-1.6 μm in size, which reproduced by binary fission and formed micro-colonies on media prepared with semi-solid gellan gum. These aerobic bacteria utilized a variety of mono- and disaccharides, organic acids, yeast extract, peptone, and grew at 15-42 °C and pH 5.0-9.0. Their closest phylogenetic relative was Oleiharenicola alkalitolerans NVTT (97.4-98.3% 16S rRNA gene sequence similarity). The genomes determined for strains Vm1ᵀ, E5ᵀ and T2ᵀ were 4.5-5.0 Mb in size and contained gene clusters involved in the degradation of recalcitrant sugars, such as L-rhamnose and L-fucose, including an array of genes encoding planctomycetal-type bacterial microcompartments. The latter were expressed in L-fucose-grown cells. Phylogenomic analysis revealed that these isolates constitute three novel Oleiharenicola species, for which the names Oleiharenicola thermotolerans sp. nov. (type strain Vm1ᵀ = VKM B-3854ᵀ = BIM B-2222ᵀ), O. aggregatus sp. nov. (type strain E5ᵀ = VKM B-4035ᵀ = BIM B-2221ᵀ), and O. mucosus sp. nov. (type strain T2ᵀ = VKM B-4036ᵀ = BIM B-2220ᵀ) are proposed.
authors: Salova VD, Danilova OV, Gorbunov AM, Dedysh SN.

title: Environmental constraints reveal condition-dependent advantages of a defined benzene-degrading consortium.
abstract: Benzene-contaminated soils remain difficult to remediate because bioaugmentation strategies often rely on selecting individual strains with high degradation activity, while their long-term performance under environmental constraints is uncertain. Here, we show that a defined three-member consortium sustained benzene removal more effectively than the strongest degrader alone under environmental constraints. By integrating field microbiome analysis, 13C-benzene DNA stable isotope probing, genome-resolved metagenomics, cultivation, defined consortia, isotope labeling, and long-term soil incubation, we identified and reconstructed a functional benzene-degrading consortium. Field profiling identified a limited set of taxa associated with benzene contamination. DNA-SIP, genome-resolved metagenomics, and isolate assays further differentiated the roles of the focal lineages. Stutzerimonas showed the strongest benzene degradation, Rhodococcus encoded additional aromatic-catabolic potential, and Rhizobium exhibited nitrogenase activity. Although Stutzerimonas showed the highest degradation efficiency in monoculture (approximately 78%), the three-member consortium displayed a stronger advantage under environmental constraints. When the exogenous nitrogen source was omitted, corrected degradation reached approximately 73% in the three-member consortium, compared with approximately 38% in the Stutzerimonas-Rhodococcus consortium. At 700 mg L-1 benzene, the three-member consortium retained approximately 86% corrected degradation, whereas Stutzerimonas alone declined to approximately 44%. During 6 months of repeated benzene amendment in soil, the consortium maintained rapid benzene removal together with continued detection of all three focal bacterial lineages. These findings show that the benefit of the consortium depended on environmental context and provide a basis for evaluating candidate inocula for benzene remediation.
authors: Zhang B, Li Y, Du C, Xiong Y.

title: A novel nudivirus from the Jonah crab (Cancer borealis: Brachyura).
abstract: Nudiviruses are double stranded DNA viruses known to infect arthropod hosts. Around 20 different nudiviruses have been identified from crustacean hosts alone. In crustaceans, the hepatopancreas is the primary target of infection, where nuclei appear hypertrophic under histological preparation due to a growing intranuclear viroplasm. The Jonah crab, Cancer borealis, is the target species of an emerging fishery located in the New England (USA) region. Histological and metagenomic tools were used to characterize a new nudivirus, including pathological characterization and sequencing of the 97,677 bp genome, which encoded 93 open reading frames. The genome housed a genetic synteny that was similar to other gammanudiviruses. The virus also phylogenetically clusters with other members of the Gammanudivirus genus based on a 17-protein concatenated phylogenetic tree. Comparative genomics revealed up to 66 conserved genes across all Gammanudivirus species, including a putative deneddylase that appears not to be present in all other nudivirus lineages. Discovering and identifying this nudivirus provides greater detail on a new pathogen that poses a potential risk to the emerging fishery.
authors: Conover G, Behringer DC, Clark F, Montague AM, Jennings L, Scro A, Goldstein J, Bojko J.

title: Abundance-weighted analysis and deep functional metagenomic selection reveals unrecognized diversity of soil-derived streptothricin acetyltransferases
abstract: ABSTRACT  Streptothricins (STCs) are broad-spectrum antibiotics under investigation for their therapeutic potential against antibiotic-resistant Gram-negative pathogens. However, the extent and diversity of genes that confer resistance to STCs, or their environmental resistome, remains largely unknown and is essentially limited to a handful of STC acetyltransferases. Here, we used a deep functional metagenomic approach to uncover previously unrecognized STC resistance determinants. A functional metagenomic library containing  ca. 700 Gigabases of soil metagenomic DNA was selected for resistance to nourseothricin (NTC), a mixture of STC congeners, resulting in collection and sequencing of nearly 30,000 resistant clones. An abundance-weighted sequence analysis identified 265 acetyltransferase-like candidates spanning broad phylogenetic, taxonomic, and genomic diversity. Re-cloning and experimental testing of 18 candidates chosen to cover acetyltransferase sequence space confirmed that 10 conferred significant NTC resistance in  Escherichia coli . Phylogenetic analyses identified three previously uncharacterized STC acetyltransferase lineages, designated as SatC, SatD, and SatE. Despite substantial sequence divergence from characterized streptothricin acetyltransferases (maximum amino acid identities of approximately 31% for SatC and SatD and up to 47.5% for SatE), these enzymes largely retained key residues associated with streptothricin binding and catalysis. In addition to strongly increasing NTC resistance, expression of the SatC construct in  E. coli also significantly decreased susceptibility to the aminoglycoside antibiotics amikacin and kanamycin. Together, these findings reveal a substantially broader than previously known environmental repertoire of STC acetyltransferases and demonstrate how deep functional metagenomic selections, combined with abundance-weighted hit calling, phylogenetic analysis, and structural prediction, can uncover novel resistance functions.
authors: Yang L, Crofts TS.

title: Full-length genomes evolve in parallel in a long-term evolution experiment with phage φX174.
abstract: The study of evolution in organisms with high mutation rates requires detailed data on the genomic composition of the population. Here we report on an innovative use of high-throughput sequencing technology combined with rapid experimental evolution that allowed us to follow the genetic diversification of four independent bacteriophage populations for 412 generations in extraordinary detail. One of our goals was to assess phylodynamic methods that use genetic information to infer key parameters of the population history. Because phylodynamic methods assume neutral evolution, we did not actively impose any selection pressures in our evolution experiment (in addition to those inherent in the bacterial cell environment). Tracing over 80'000 bacteriophage genomes, representing 884 distinct genotypes, we find that the patterns of viral diversification result in largely non-congruent genotype distributions, but also document multiple instances of parallel evolution. Unlike previous observations of parallelism in viral evolution, we do not just see the parallel evolution of mutations at single sites, but on the level of full-length genomes. Computer simulations that recapitulate our experiments in great detail show that this degree of parallelism is inconsistent with neutral evolution. We further show that the observed extent of parallel evolution biases phylodynamic analysis of migration rates, and wrongly estimates significant migration between the independent evolution lines. Our approach is applicable to many other viruses and paves the way to advanced population genetic investigations that aim to shed light on phenomena that relate to genetic linkage across the genome.
authors: Bons E, Chabas H, MacDonald H, Escalera Ledermann A, Ösze S, Dunstan J, Ochsner N, Angst DC, Bonhoeffer S, Regoes RR.

title: BacPath: A Rapid Metagenomic Workflow with a Curated Reference Database for Species-Level Detection of Bacterial Plant Pathogens
abstract: The emergence of plant pathogens through geographic spread, host shifts, and climate change threatens disease management and global food security. Detection of emerging pathogens without prior genomic information is critical for preventing widespread outbreaks and enabling timely management to reduce economic impact. Accurate and reliable detection of infecting organisms using metagenome-based bioinformatic pipelines is therefore essential. To address this, we have developed and validated BacPath pipeline and a highly accurate complete genome database, BacPathDB. Raw read files obtained from Oxford Nanopore sequencers (MinIon and Flongle) were processed, quality-scored, and mapped against a curated database. The expandable BacPathDB contains high-quality genomes with accurate metadata and currently includes 317 genomes, representing species, within the genera Dickeya and Pectobacterium, including most type strains. The pipeline accurately detected all 32 species within these two genera in silico, with no false positives or false negatives. In vitro analyses with both Pectobacterium and Dickeya species further confirmed the accuracy of the developed pipeline for detecting pathogens from complex plant tissue samples infected with single or multiple pathogens. Detection can be achieved with as little as a single read, however, analyses based on five or more reads provide higher confidence in the results. The pipeline is rapid, enabling detection in approximately one minute, and can be performed on a 16 GB laptop without requiring high computational resources. This makes it well suited for field applications, while the curated reference database enhances its reliability for routine diagnostics, epidemiological investigations, disease surveillance, regulatory programs, biosecurity, and microbial forensics.
authors: Arif M, Montesinos S, Maurya N, Alvarez AM, Dobhal S.

title: Expanding the Repertoire of Associations Between Antibiotic Resistance Genes and Putative Mobile Genetic Element Carriers Using Metagenomic Long Reads
abstract: Antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and the mobile genetic elements (MGEs) that mediate their horizontal transfer are central to understanding the mechanisms, evolution, and dissemination of antimicrobial resistance. Although thousands of ARGs have been documented and numerous ARG–MGE associations have been reported, broader questions about the diversity and distribution of these associations remain underexplored. How comprehensive are the current catalogs of ARG–MGE associations? Are certain MGE families preferentially associated with particular ARGs, and vice versa? How are ARG–MGE associations distributed across microbial taxa? Is the environmental abundance of an ARG related to the diversity of its MGE associations? Do ARG–MGE association patterns vary across environments? Here we address these questions by analyzing multiple publicly available long-read metagenomic datasets from various environmental settings, leveraging the ability of long reads to capture ARGs along with their genomic contexts within individual reads. We identified numerous potential ARG–MGE associations not found in existing databases. A few MGE families were putatively associated with nearly all identified ARGs. ARG–MGE associations were unevenly distributed across taxa. ARG abundance was positively associated with both MGE association diversity and the taxonomic spread of those associations. Furthermore, ARG–MGE association patterns varied across environments. Overall, our findings reveal an extensive diversity of ARG–MGE associations that remains largely underrepresented in current knowledge bases. Importance  Antibiotic resistance is a growing global concern, in part because mobile genetic elements facilitate the spread of resistance genes across bacterial populations, taxa, and environments. Characterizing the associations between resistance genes and mobile genetic elements, and assessing their distribution across taxa and environments, can provide insights into the mobilization and dissemination of antibiotic resistance. Although these associations have primarily been investigated using assembled genomes, our findings demonstrate the potential of unassembled long-read metagenomic data to uncover previously uncharacterized gene–element associations. Our results reveal a substantial reservoir of such associations that remains underrepresented in existing knowledge bases.
authors: Go DJL, Shrestha AM.

title: Genomic Insights into the Pathogenicity and Host Adaptation of Pseudomonas amygdali pv. mori, the Causal Agent of Mulberry Bacterial Blight.
abstract: Mulberry bacterial blight (MBB), a devastating disease of mulberry (Morus spp.), causes substantial losses in yield and quality. This study isolated and characterized the highly virulent strain MYC18 from diseased tissues and identified it as Pseudomonas amygdali. The MYC18 genome comprises 6.39 Mb across a single chromosome and three plasmids, encoding 5,979 predicted coding sequences. Comparative genomic analysis indicates an open pan-genome and significant structural diversity among phylogenetically related strains. Genome annotation revealed 322 virulence-associated genes and 21 multidrug resistance determinants, along with a highly conserved type III secretion system (T3SS) encoding 29 predicted effectors. qRT-PCR analysis of eight representative T3SE genes revealed temporally partitioned expression patterns: early transient induction (hopF1, hopR1, hopD2), sustained high expression (hopI1, hopM1), and late-peaking (hopG1, hopX1, avrD). As the first high-quality reference genome for P. amygdali pv. mori, the MYC18 assembly provides a critical genomic resource for elucidating the pathogenic mechanisms of mulberry bacterial blight and developing targeted disease control strategies.
authors: Dai X, Tang Q, Wang S, Liu Y, Zhao W, Wang Z, Sheng S, Wu F, Li P.

title: Scaling laws link conserved gene-abundance distributions to adaptive expression in diatom communities worldwide.
abstract: Marine microbes sustain Earth's major biogeochemical cycles, yet how they maintain stable ecosystem functions across diverse environments remains unclear. We analyzed metagenomic and metatranscriptomic data from diatom communities sampled during the Tara Oceans global expedition. While gene abundance distributions remain statistically similar across sample, gene expression varies systematically across geographical locations, a global pattern we show reflects predictable scaling laws. Global distributions, scaling relationships, and variability among sampling stations are captured by a stochastic model linking gene abundance dynamics to gene expression. While colder waters are associated with higher transcriptional activity and warmer regions show more selective gene usage, we find that transcript abundance increases nonlinearly with transcript richness. This general scaling is captured by our model and suggests that diatom communities balance high expression of core genes with specific functional diversity. These scaling relationships hold consistently across ocean basins, with temperature, used as an effective large-scale environmental descriptor whose signature cannot be fully disentangled from spatial structure, sufficing to predict transcriptional patterns from genetic composition. Our findings reveal how the stability of gene-abundance structure in diatom ecosystems coexists with transcriptional variability, enabling flexible functional responses.
authors: Pigani E, Simoens K, Bernardi D, Campese L, Iudicone D, Azaele S, Suweis S.

title: Morphogenomic description of Cranifera cranifera (Chitwood, 1932) Kloss, 1960 from captive Blaptica dubia Serville, 1838 cockroach.
abstract: Nematodes of the superfamily Thelastomatoidea are found in the digestive system of various arthropods, feeding on their host microbiome. They are sometimes considered to be ecologically intermediate forms between free-living rhabditids and parasitic Spirurina, while phylogenetically they are nested within the latter. In addition to new morphological data on the male morphology, this manuscript presents the first nuclear genome assembly of a thelastomatid species, Cranifera cranifera, using a long-read sequencing approach, making a total of three nuclear genomes available for superfamily Thelastomatoidea. The C. cranifera nuclear genome assembly presented here is 243 Mb long, consists of 7563 contigs, has an N50 of 43 kb, and includes 94% of the BUSCO nematoda_odb12 genes. The mitochondrial genome is 24644 bases long, includes a complete set of protein-coding, rRNA, and tRNA genes, and a repetitive region 9731 bases long, which includes multiple copies of tRNA-Asn(gtt) and tRNA-Lys(ttt). The nuclear assembly also contained two sequence variants of the 28S rRNA and two of the 18S rRNA genes, highlighting the presence of intragenomic variation within the rRNA operon. The newly generated assemblies (nuclear and organelle) will add to a growing body of genomic resources for underrepresented and understudied animal parasitic nematodes from Clade 3, enabling comprehensive studies in their phylogeny and trait evolution in the future.
authors: Morffe J, Guiglielmoni N, Wassey N, Gueddach K, Schuster A, Becker K, Bast J, Schiffer P, Holovachov O.

title: ArthroVerse: mapping protein family diversity across arthropod-associated microbiomes.
abstract: Metagenomic studies of arthropod-associated microbiomes have generated vast amounts of sequence data, yet the functional and structural organization of these proteins remains largely unexplored. Here, we present ArthroVerse, the first comprehensive database of protein families derived from arthropod-associated metagenomes. Non-redundant protein families were generated after rigorous filtering, deduplication, and clustering. The protein families were further annotated with microbial taxonomy, host associations, protein structural information, and carbohydrate-active enzymes predictions. The resulting dataset integrates both metagenomic and reference genome-derived proteins, enabling systematic exploration of functional diversity, evolutionary relationships, and host-microbe interactions in insect microbiomes. ArthroVerse provides a valuable resource for the study of microbial ecology and arthropod physiology, offering unprecedented insight into the protein landscape of insect-associated microbial communities. ArthroVerse is publicly accessible at https://envofams.org/arthroverse/.

title: Ecological and metabolic signatures of biofilm viromes across a national river surveillance network
abstract: Benthic biofilms are biogeochemical hotspots in rivers, yet their endogenous viral communities remain poorly resolved at national scales. We analysed 447 biofilm metagenomes from 146 sites within England’s River Surveillance Network (RSN), sampled in spring and autumn from 2021 to 2023, integrating viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs), water-quality gradients, predicted host associations and auxiliary metabolic genes (AMGs). We recovered 38,534 vOTUs, revealing extensive viral novelty, where 93% of the vOTUs could not be assigned to a known family. Viromes were dominated by Caudoviricetes and unclassified lineages and were extremely heterogeneous: no vOTU occurred in more than 8.3% of samples. Season, but not sampling year, structured virome composition (family-level PERMANOVA R  2 = 0.050, p = 0.001; year p = 0.08), and within-site turnover between spring and autumn exceeded turnover between years. Bray–Curtis ordination linked virome structure weakly to pH, dissolved organic carbon, conductivity, nitrate-N and dissolved oxygen (envfit R  2 ≤ 0.066), while threshold indicator taxa analysis (TITAN) identified vOTUs with abrupt change points along alkalinity, dissolved oxygen, nitrate-N and temperature gradients. Predicted host associations were concentrated in Pseudomonodota, Cyanobacteriota and Bacteroidota, with  Microcoleus ,  Chamaesiphon and  Flavobacterium among the dominant host genera. Virus–host networks were modular, and module abundances correlated with water quality variables (dissolved oxygen, pH, nitrate etc.), suggesting that environmental filtering acts partly through host ecology. Predicted virus–host associations formed a sparse network organised around a few highly connected viral lineages. Functional profiling showed that the biofilm virome was dominated by nucleotide metabolism, DNA methylation, phosphate-stress, glycan-modification and photosynthesis-related AMGs, with  nrdA /  nrdB ribonucleotide reductase as the dominant AMG signal. Few vOTUs (1.2%) were detected as proviruses, although provirus fractions were higher in selected host-linked lineages. Collectively, these results show that river biofilm viromes are seasonally structured ecological communities whose composition, host associations and metabolic potential reflect the physicochemical and biological state of rivers. We propose that biofilm viromes provide a complementary layer of information for understanding river health, microbial ecology and the propagation of anthropogenic pressures in freshwater systems.
authors: Busi SB, Thorpe AC, Warren J, Walsh K, Read DS.

title: Structure, function, and evolution of topoisomerase modulatory proteins in bacteria.
abstract: SUMMARYDNA topoisomerases are essential for maintaining the integrity and functionality of the genome. By homeostatically controlling the genome topology in bacteria, these enzymes influence essential cellular processes such as gene expression, replication, recombination, and chromosome segregation. Although DNA topoisomerases were initially considered to act as stand-alone enzymes, they are now being recognized as integral components of dynamic protein complexes that perform diverse functions in vivo. The discovery of several proteinaceous modulators of DNA topoisomerases has expanded the understanding of their functional versatility. These are encoded either by the bacterial chromosome or extrachromosomal elements like plasmids and bacteriophages. Chromosomally encoded modulators are engaged in fine-tuning topoisomerase activity, enabling them to carry out specialized cellular functions beyond their canonical enzymatic roles. Crucially, they prevent genomic instability that may arise from dysregulated topoisomerase activity. By altering DNA topology, modulatory proteins can influence transcriptional bursting, leading to epigenetic heterogeneity within the bacterial populations, crucial for bacterial stress adaptation. In contrast, topoisomerase interacting proteins encoded by plasmids and phages have dedicated roles in facilitating plasmid maintenance and phage propagation by suppressing host defenses and promoting horizontal gene transfer. We present a comprehensive analysis of the topoisomerase modulatory proteins discovered so far, offering insights into the mechanisms by which DNA topology and homeostasis are maintained within the intracellular environment. We project the potential of topoisomerase modulator-based drug design as a promising strategy for combating multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens.
authors: Biswas P, Nagaraja V, Sengupta S.

title: Type III effector repertoires as a window into Pseudomonas syringae pv. actinidiae evolution and Actinidia defense responses.
abstract: Kiwifruit bacterial canker, caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. actinidiae (Psa), represents a complex disease system in which closely related bacterial populations differ in host association, pathogenicity, genomic composition, and geographic distribution as evidenced by pandemic spread of biovar 3 after 2008. Closely related Psa lineages differ in host association, virulence, and distribution, yet these differences arise largely outside the conserved core genome. Mobile genetic elements remodel accessory regions, and acquisition, loss, and redundancy of type III effectors shape whether a lineage colonizes or is restricted by a given Actinidia genotype. Virulence is therefore a host-dependent property, not a fixed lineage rank. On the host side, genome assemblies, QTL mapping, and infection transcriptomics indicate that resistance reflects the timing and persistence of immune signalling rather than receptor presence alone, although few candidate receptors have been validated in planta. Durable resistance is most likely to derive from recognition of non-redundant effector functions and from immune hubs, such as RIN4, that multiple effectors target. Integrating pathogen population genomics, effector biology, and host immune genetics is the route to predicting which lineages will emerge next.
authors: Asif M, Zhao Z.

title: Metagenomic insights into microplastic micro-interfaces: Transforming pollutants and spreading resistance.
abstract: Microplastic micro-interfaces (MPMI) in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) serve as critical hubs for microbial colonization, pollutant transformation, and antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) dissemination. In this study, a large-scale genome-resolved metagenomic approach was employed to reconstruct 463 quality-filtered metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from biofilms established on polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polyethylene (PE), and polypropylene (PP) within a municipal WWTP. Taxonomic profiling revealed that MPMI selectively enriched strict anaerobes and uncultured taxa, driving a profound ecological shift relative to the surrounding water and indicating the formation of localized hypoxic micro-niches. Functionally, the MPMI microbiome constructed a highly integrated metabolic network. Dominant lineages were found to synergistically couple aromatic hydrocarbon degradation (via the shikimate pathway and β-oxidation) with complex carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur cycling, while deploying energy-efficient nucleotide salvage strategies to ensure biofilm stabilization under nutrient stress. Crucially, horizontal gene transfer (HGT) emerged as a fundamental mechanism for functional diversification, facilitating the active cross-genomic exchange of key adaptive traits associated with pollutant metabolism and biofilm regulation. Furthermore, MPMI harbored a highly diverse resistome comprising 36 ARG categories and 289 subtypes, highlighted by the critical genomic co-localization of mobile elements and clinical resistance markers (e.g., mcr-5.1, mupA) in core colonizers. Ultimately, these genomic insights identify the MPMI as a major ecological hotspot driving the concurrent adaptation of metabolic networks and the resistome, thereby exacerbating the risk of ARG dissemination in aquatic environments.
authors: Tian H, Liu J, Zhang Y.

title: Reconstructing skin microbiome of G. Clemenceau (1929): paleoproteomic analysis of his bath sponge.
abstract: Paleoproteomic analysis of a bath sponge belonging to Georges Clemenceau explores the possibility of reconstructing the skin microbiome of a historical figure from a preserved personal item. Using high-resolution mass spectrometry and a cascade proteotyping strategy, several microorganisms were identified, dominated by environmental bacteria of the genus Pseudomonas and opportunistic fungi such as Aspergillus and Exophiala. Traces of Escherichia coli, human proteins, marine organisms, and plants were also detected. Overall, the results suggest that the sponge does not accurately reflect Clemenceau's stable skin microbiome, as microorganisms typically associated with human skin are absent, likely due to taphonomic biases and preservation phenomena. On the contrary, the object appears as a complex microenvironment that has accumulated contamination over time related to humidity, the domestic and coastal environment, as well as the conditions of use and storage. The presence of opportunistic microorganisms, notably Exophiala sideris, even suggests a potential risk of skin infections in an elderly diabetic individual. This study thus demonstrates that everyday objects can constitute unique biological archives for paleopathology, not for precisely reconstructing an individual microbiota, but for documenting dermatological hygiene practices, microbial environments, and the infectious risks associated with reusable, damp objects at the beginning of the 20th century.
authors: Charlier P, Armengaud J, Gebelin M, Lhortolary S.

title: Novel putative PETase candidates from metagenomic mining of Ebrié lagoon and Kassembié lake, Côte d'Ivoire
abstract: Plastic pollution threatens aquatic ecosystems in Côte d’Ivoire, yet their microbial potential for polyethylene terephthalate (PET) degradation remains poorly characterized. We applied shotgun metagenomics to five samples from Biétry bay, an urban site in the Ébrié lagoon, and Kassembié lake, a low-impact reference site. MetaPhlAn4 detected 131 site-specific, uncharacterized species-level genome bins, including 76 found only at Biétry. Functional annotation of the non-redundant gene catalogue identified 15,860 hydrolase genes and 195 genes assigned to the CE1 carbohydrate esterase family, used here as a proxy for general ester-cleaving potential. Structural prediction with ColabFold (AlphaFold2) and comparison with IsPETase using TM-align prioritized four novel PETase-like candidates, BietPETase1–4. These findings reveal under-explored microbial and enzymatic diversity in Ivorian aquatic ecosystems and provide candidates for experimental validation in PET-bioremediation research.

title: Comparative Genomics Analyses of Bacterial tRNA Modification Protein Families Using Clusters of Orthologous Genes (COG) and KEGG Orthology (KO) Classification Systems
abstract: Accurate identification of bacterial tRNA modification enzymes is essential for understanding translation, physiology, and genome evolution, yet annotation remains complicated by paralogy, multifunctionality, functional divergence, and non-orthologous replacement. We compiled an experimentally supported catalog of bacterial tRNA modification proteins and linked them to 71 Clusters of Orthologous Groups (COG) and 74 KEGG Orthology (KO) families. Their distributions, conservation, and copy-number patterns were examined across 1,322 bacterial genomes represented in both annotation systems. Comparison of COG and KO assignments revealed strong agreement for one-to-one family relationships but substantial discordance for broad COG families that encompass functionally distinct paralogs. Genome-scale profiling identified a conserved core repertoire of tRNA modification systems that was supported by both phylogenetic conservation and retention in bacteria with highly reduced genomes. Phylogenetic distribution patterns highlighted known and candidate cases of non-orthologous replacement, including alternative solutions for m5U54 and xm5(s2)U34 biosynthesis, and identified Actinomycetota as a promising source of currently uncharacterized tRNA modification enzymes. Gene-duplication analyses revealed that most core tRNA modification pathways were maintained as single-copy genes or highly conserved single-copy modules, whereas only a limited number of families, displayed substantial expansion. Predicted tRNA modification repertoires increased with genome size, but the relationship was weak, lineage dependent, and better described by log-linear than linear models, indicating diminishing gains in modification capacity with increasing genome complexity. Finally, phylogenetically informed analyses identified a small number of associations between specific tRNA modification pathways and physiological traits. Together, these results provide an updated COG-KO reference framework for bacterial tRNA modification systems, clarify the strengths and limitations of commonly used orthology resources, and highlight evolutionary processes shaping the diversification of bacterial tRNA modification pathways.
authors: Reed CJ, Yuan Y, Crécy-Lagard Vd.

title: Biological characterization of the lytic Pseudomonas aeruginosa phage BUCT980 and its therapeutic efficacy in a murine lung infection model.
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an important opportunistic pathogen whose increasing multidrug resistance limits conventional antimicrobial treatment options and underscores the need for alternative antibacterial strategies. In this study, we isolated and systematically characterized a novel lytic phage, BUCT980, and evaluated its antibacterial activity and therapeutic potential. Transmission electron microscopy showed that BUCT980 is a myovirus. One-step growth analysis indicated an apparent latent period of approximately 60 min and a burst size of approximately 173 PFU per infected cell. The BUCT980 genome is 60,697 bp in length, and comparative genomic and phylogenetic analyses support its placement within the class Caudoviricetes. No known lysogeny-associated genes, virulence factors, or antibiotic resistance genes were identified by genomic analysis. In vitro, BUCT980 markedly suppressed the growth of P. aeruginosa PAO1 across the tested multiplicities of infections (MOIs) and inhibited biofilm formation. In 10-fold serial-dilution spot assays, BUCT980 formed clear plaques on 4 of 29 clinical isolates and produced visible inhibition in 13 additional isolates representing multiple sequence types. In a murine model of acute P. aeruginosa pneumonia, intranasal administration of BUCT980 significantly improved survival, reduced pulmonary bacterial burden, and alleviated lung injury. No overt histopathological abnormalities were observed in the liver or kidney during short-term observation. These findings support further evaluation of BUCT980 as a candidate therapeutic phage for acute P. aeruginosa lung infection.IMPORTANCEPseudomonas aeruginosa is a major cause of difficult-to-treat respiratory infections because of its antibiotic resistance and biofilm-forming capacity. Here, we characterized BUCT980, a lytic phage that suppressed P. aeruginosa growth, inhibited early biofilm formation, and showed activity against clinical isolates from multiple sequence-type backgrounds. Genomic screening identified no known lysogeny-associated genes, virulence factors, or antibiotic resistance genes. In a murine acute pneumonia model, intranasal BUCT980 treatment improved survival, reduced pulmonary bacterial burden, and alleviated lung injury. Bacterial regrowth during prolonged exposure and limited activity against established biofilms indicate that combination strategies may be needed for sustained treatment. These findings support further preclinical evaluation of BUCT980 for acute P. aeruginosa lung infection.
authors: Yu X, Chen J, Zhang W, Tong Y, Xie L, Li M, Yao M.

title: Systematic mapping of the prokaryotic noncoding sequence space with a genomic language model
abstract: Prokaryotic genomes encode a vast repertoire of noncoding elements such as ribozymes, riboswitches, and CRISPR RNAs. The sequence-level diversity of these intergenic elements precludes alignment-based clustering that would enable annotation and discovery of novel noncoding RNA families. Here, we show that a genomic language model fine-tuned on prokaryotic intergenic sequences learns representations of noncoding elements from DNA sequence. We used these embeddings to organize 376 million intergenic regions from 1.3 terabase pairs of prokaryotic genomes and metagenomes into 5.14 million clusters. This approach nominated 20,149 clusters of putative structured RNAs with a candidate protein partner. Periodicity in token entropies revealed internal architecture, recovering CRISPR, TIGR and VIPR arrays together with their cognate effector proteins from sequence alone. Targeted clustering of bridge recombinase-adjacent sequences identified bridge RNA variants with longer guide recognition sequences than any characterized ortholog. Finally, we directed teams of AI agents to mine the database under researcher-defined criteria, uncovering divergent riboswitches, ribozymes, and other structured RNAs with biological hypotheses for their function. We release a publicly available database that transforms the dark matter of prokaryotic genomes into an explorable resource for human-agent molecular discovery.
authors: Sun G, Hudelmaier T, Gilligan JC, Gonzalez GA, Yin P, Wan F, Ma Z(, Durrant MG, Ricci-Tam C, Pawluk A, Puschnik AS, Konermann S, Hsu PD.

title: From assembly to yield: kingdom-specific rules, keystone networks and a Bayesian structural equation framework for the maize rhizosphere microbiome
abstract: Abstract    Background and aims.  The rhizosphere microbiome is an extension of the crop genome, yet the rules governing its assembly and its statistical links to yield remain unresolved. We asked whether bacteria and fungi follow kingdom-specific assembly rules across genotypes and stages (RQ1), which taxa form network backbones (RQ2), and through which statistical pathways microbial features connect to measured grain yield (RQ3).  Methods.  Bacterial and fungal communities of seven maize cultivars were profiled at seedling (V6) and tasseling (VT) stages, integrating diversity analyses, robustness-validated co-occurrence networks, FAPROTAX/FUNGuild annotation, BSEM, and machine-learning signature identification; grain yield was measured and no forecasting was attempted.  Results.  Bacterial assembly was dominated by developmental stage (ANOSIM R = 0.90), shifting from copiotrophic Proteobacteria toward oligotrophic lineages, whereas fungi retained stronger genotype structure at tasseling (R up to 0.74). Phenotypic and community distances were decoupled at the genotype level. Proteobacteria and Ascomycota formed network backbones whose removal eliminated 81.5% and 93.6% of edges. BSEM reproduced 68–69% of yield variance and resolved coherent phyla → functional guilds → agronomic traits → yield pathways (β = 0.55 for agronomic traits → yield), with cultivar effects ranging from + 0.50 (Nonghua 106) to − 0.49 (Dr. King 825). Machine learning confirmed complementary yield-associated signatures (Rhodanobacter ASV1138, ρ = 0.91).  Conclusion.  Bacteria and fungi obey kingdom-specific assembly rules; Proteobacteria and Ascomycota are structurally indispensable network backbones; and a Bayesian structural equation framework traces interpretable pathways from microbiome features to measured yield, offering testable hypotheses for microbiome-assisted maize breeding.
authors: Ban Y, Zhao G, Feng S, Han X, Lü Q, You Y, Huang T, Wang G.

title: Bioprospecting the Cultivable Bacteria Associated with Trididemnum maragogi from the Saint Peter and Saint Paul’s Archipelago (Brazil) for Bioactive Metabolites
abstract: Abstract    Ascidians and their associated microbiota represent one of the most prolific sources of novel bioactive compounds with application in marine biotechnology. This study investigates the pharmacological potential and metabolic diversity of the bacterial microbiota associated with the ascidian  Trididemnum maragogi  , collected at Saint Peter and Saint Paul’s Archipelago (SPSPA), Brazil. A total of 45 bacterial strains were taxonomically identified via 16S rRNA gene sequencing into 11 distinct genera, with a predominance of  Bacillus  and actinomycetes such as  Micromonospora  ,  Salinispora  , and  Streptomyces  . Crude organic extracts from bacterial cultures were evaluated for antiproliferative activity against human cancer cell lines (501-Mel and HCT-116). Extracts from  Micromonospora  spp. (BRB-810, BRB-814, BRB-832) and  Salinispora  spp. (BRB-803, BRB-808) exhibited potent cytotoxic activity. Metabolomic profiling via HPLC-MS/MS and Feature-Based Molecular Networking (GNPS) enabled the annotation of staurosporines, rifamycins, diketopiperazines, and other bioactive classes, while revealing that approximately 95% of detected features remain unannotated. Furthermore, whole-genome sequencing of  Micromonospora aurantiaca  BRB-832 unveiled 20 biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) related to macrolides, alkylresorcinols, anthracyclines, and novel uncharacterized pathways. These findings highlight  T. maragogi  and its microbial symbionts as a valuable, underexplored source of novel bioactive natural products with biotechnological potential.
authors: Fiasca JS, Martins BP, Oliveira RS, Feitosa LGP, Maldonado GP, Lopes NP, Lotufo TMC, Jimenez PC, Costa-Lotufo LV, Sahm BDB.

title: Pathogen profiling of inflammatory eye diseases with metagenomic deep sequencing in a tertiary referral center
abstract: Abstract    Background  Intraocular inflammation is a leading cause of blindness globally, but the precise etiology may be unknown in many cases due to challenges with traditional diagnostic modalities. Metagenomic deep sequencing (MDS) is an unbiased method for pathogen detection and may provide advantages over conventional diagnostic methods. Methods  Patients with possible infectious eye diseases were enrolled at the Emory Eye Center from January 2018 to March 2021 for MDS analysis of intraocular fluid samples in addition to standard-of-care conventional testing, including polymerase chain reaction and bacterial and fungal cultures. Samples were sent to the Proctor Foundation at the University of California, San Francisco for analysis. Pathogens were identified through a rapid computational pipeline that analyzed non-host sequences. Data were collected on patient demographics, medical history, ophthalmic exam, and conventional diagnostic results and summarized with respect to MDS findings. Results  Forty-one patients were included in this study with 25 females (61.0%) and a mean age of 55.3 years (SD:±16). The anatomic distribution of uveitis included anterior uveitis in 13 patients (31.7%), anterior/intermediate uveitis in 7 patients (17.1%), posterior uveitis in 4 patients (9.76%), panuveitis in 15 patients (36.6%), and scleritis in 2 patients (4.9%). Intraocular fluid was collected from 25 aqueous humor samples (61.0%) and 16 vitreous samples (39.0%). MDS identified pathogens in 11 of 41 samples (26.8%). The MDS positivity results by the site of sampling were 20.0% (5/25) from the anterior chamber and 37.5% (6/16) from the vitreous cavity. Pathogens identified included bacterial species such as  Klebsiella pneumoniae  ,  Serratia marcescens  , and  Streptococcus pneumoniae  ; viral pathogens including Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) and Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV); fungal organisms such as  Candida parapsilosis  and  Cladosporium  species; and parasites including  Toxocara canis.  Seven patients had an infectious etiology determined by MDS that was not detected by conventional diagnostics. Intraocular and systemic testing was concordant with MDS results in 4 patients. Conclusion  Infectious organisms associated with inflammatory eye diseases presenting to a tertiary referral center are diverse and include fungi, bacteria, parasites, and viruses. The unbiased nature of MDS may be advantageous in these tertiary settings, assisting in diagnostics and guiding appropriate therapies.
authors: Thomas J, Silva KD, Chen C, Zhong L, Liu Y, Abraham T, Yu D, Hinterwirth A, Arepalli S, Yeh S, Doan T, Shantha J.

title: Perspective: Evolutionary Genetics Is the Backbone of Genomic Epidemiology in Fungal Pathogens.
abstract: Genome sequencing is rapidly becoming a routine component of outbreak investigation and pathogen surveillance. In human fungal pathogens, however, the analytical framework has often remained centered on a single tree built from variants called against one reference genome. While that representation has been and will continue to be useful, epidemiological inference can also benefit from other approaches drawn from evolutionary genetics. Here, I review the transition from multilocus sequence typing to genome-scale epidemiology in human fungal pathogens, summarize representative successes in Coccidioides, Cryptococcus, Candida auris, Aspergillus fumigatus, Histoplasma, Sporothrix, Pneumocystis, and other fungi, and identify biological and technical sources of error that are still inconsistently addressed. More than a critique, this piece is a call to action. I argue that we need to start treating phylogenetic trees as one layer of evidence within a broader population-genetic framework and not as a stopping point. From a data collection point of view, we need a more robust epidemiological metadata collection scheme. From an analytical point of view, analyses of gene-tree discordance, demographic inference, ancestry, and structural variation can reveal features that a single tree derived from concatenated markers cannot. The amount of public sequence data is no longer the only limiting factor. The next pressing challenge is to translate the data generated by genomic and phylogenetic analyses into reproducible evolutionary inference while preserving and communicating the uncertainty that matters for public-health decisions.
authors: Matute DR.

title: On the Distribution of Synteny Block Lengths in Prokaryote Genomes under a Neutral Model of Genome Dynamics.
abstract: In bacterial and archaeal genomes, functionally linked genes often cluster in operons that enable coregulation of expression of these genes and production of their protein products in stoichiometric amounts. Many operons are shared by genomes of distantly related bacteria and archaea due in part to evolutionary conservation and in part to horizontal gene transfer (HGT). In contrast, similarity between species in their gene order along the chromosome can be merely a result of evolutionary closeness such that synteny has not yet been disrupted by genome dynamic events occurring during evolution. In general, however, accurate differentiation of operons from spurious gene clusters is a non-trivial task that depends on an underlying model of neutral genome evolution. Here, we employ a recently developed stochastic model of genome rearrangement ("jump model") that accounts for HGT across prokaryote species evolving along a phylogenetic tree to infer the size distribution of shared gene strings (synteny blocks) under neutral evolution. Analytic expressions are derived for the expected number of synteny blocks of a given size (or of maximal size) depending on the evolutionary distance between the genomes and the rates of different types of evolutionary events. This analysis is related to the well-studied family of stick-breaking problems, but the discrete structure and stochastic nature of the evolutionary process provide for the development of a simple, independent model. We demonstrate the predictive power of this model by computer simulations of synthetic data as well as by simulating genomes on real trees obtained from the Alignable Tight Genome Clusters database.
journal: Journal of computational biology : a journal of computational molecular cell biology
authors: Snir S, Wolf YI, Brezner S, Koonin EV, Steel M.

title: Phylogeography of clinical Burkholderia pseudomallei isolates in Cambodia demonstrates diversity, broad dispersal, and novel genes.
abstract: Burkholderia pseudomallei, the causative agent of melioidosis, is ubiquitous in Southeast Asia but remains understudied in many endemic countries. The species' high genetic diversity necessitates large-scale sampling to resolve fine-scale population structure. In countries bordering the Mekong River, the geographic range of B. pseudomallei strains may be increased by water-mediated dispersal. Between 2021 and 2023, we collected and sequenced 253 clinical B. pseudomallei isolates from patients admitted to six Cambodian hospitals and geotagged isolates by patient village. Isolates were genetically diverse and grouped into 11 clades, including one characterized by a chromosomal genomic island containing unique genes absent from other isolates, consistent with local evolution. Comparison with 3,234 publicly available global genomes revealed intermixing between Cambodian and other Southeast Asian isolates but clear distinction from Australian strains. Phylogeographic analyses further demonstrated spatial localization along major waterways, suggesting that river systems, including the Mekong, may contribute to bacterial dissemination in Cambodia. Taken together, these findings demonstrate the importance of localized data sets for contextualizing the population structure and evolution of this diverse pathogen in Southeast Asia.IMPORTANCEBurkholderia pseudomallei is a highly diverse bacterial species with genomic features that vary based on geographic sampling location. Existing data predominantly from Thailand show that isolates from Southeast Asia may be closely related to each other. Here, we sequenced isolates associated with human disease in Cambodia and compared these against genomes from public sequence repositories. We identified many distinct bacterial strains and found that some of these were localized either to the south or in the north of the country. We identified a unique group of genes in one cohort strain with putative roles in bacterial metabolism and genomic recombination. Finally, in a global phylogeny constructed from publicly available genomes, we found that Cambodian isolates intermixed with other Southeast Asian isolates. Our study is the largest genomic study of B. pseudomallei in Cambodia to date, with findings that contribute to the global understanding of the bacterium's diversity and evolution.

title: Exploring antimicrobial resistance in wild and domestic animal populations: combining publicly available data with BV-BRC resources to introduce bioinformatics in an undergraduate classroom.
abstract: Bioinformatics blends the fields of biology, statistics, computer science, and information technology for the processing and analysis of genomic data. Despite the growing demand for trained bioinformaticians and a positive job market outlook, most undergraduate institutions struggle to integrate bioinformatics into their life science curricula. Educators face numerous barriers to incorporating bioinformatics into their classes, including technical issues and expertise. To address this need, we are developing web-accessible, course-based materials for general microbiology, infectious disease, genomics, and other similar undergraduate and graduate classes that use bioinformatic workflows within the Bacterial and Viral Bioinformatics Resource Center (BV-BRC), one of three National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID)-funded Bioinformatics Resource Centers. Here, we present one such activity: a three-part exercise focused on antimicrobial resistance and metagenomics that uses six publicly available metagenomic samples collected from wild and domestic animal populations to explore the distinctions between their gut microbiomes and their respective antibiotic resistance genes. To analyze community composition and identify antibiotic resistance genes, students use two end-to-end services offered by the BV-BRC: Taxonomic Classification and Metagenomic Read Mapping. This assignment was developed to introduce students to core competencies in the field of bioinformatics and to highlight the BV-BRC as an educational resource for integrating bioinformatics without requiring students and instructors to possess the technical proficiencies and computing resources traditionally needed. We successfully implemented this exercise in an upper-level undergraduate microbiology course, demonstrating the feasibility of using the BV-BRC for bioinformatics education in the classroom.
authors: Sheriff J, Capria A, Bowers N, Wattam AR, Poretsky R.

title: Biosurfactant production under cold-saline stress is a strain specific trait independent from phylogeny and biosynthetic gene content
abstract: Microbial genomes code for far more biosynthetic potential than a single cell typically expresses, but the environmental and cellular controls that determine whether the latent capacity is realised remain poorly understood. Biosurfactants, surface-active metabolites proposed to aid survival in cold and saline habitats, exemplify this gap: capacity is often inferred from genomes or detected chemically, but is rarely linked to the specific conditions that stimulate its production in the same organisms. Here we combine whole-genome sequencing, untargeted LC-MS/MS metabolomics, and quantitative surface-tension assays across 25 bacterial isolates isolated from the cold, hypersaline Qaidam Basin (a terrestrial analogue for ancient Mars) and contrasting marine environments. We show that biosurfactant production is not a fixed lineage trait but a regulated, strain-specific response that emerges under combined cold and salt stress. This response is structured into three tiers: genomic capacity defines the accessible chemical space; the genomic complement of pathway-regulator genes tracks responsiveness; strain-level physiological state determines realised output. Regulatory-gene content, rather than biosynthetic-cluster count, predicted surfactant production across strains. Production was amplified by low temperature and high salinity and showed little phylogenetic signal, with near-clonal strains differing in their stress-response. These findings reshape biochemical adaptation in extreme environments as a problem of conditional activation, not only of genomic potential, but of cellular systems that permit its expression, which requires looking beyond biosynthetic-gene content to the cellular factors that determine whether that potential is expressed.

title: Detection of merbecoviruses in Danish bats using a novel broad-range RT-qPCR assay
abstract: Bat-associated merbecoviruses comprise a genetically diverse group of coronaviruses with variable receptor usage and host range, highlighting the need for efficient tools for their surveillance. Here, we developed and optimized a broad-range reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) assay for the detection of bat-associated merbecoviruses, including the lineage previously identified in brown long-eared bats (  Plecotus auritus ) in Denmark.  In silico analysis predicted detection of 898 of 941 (95.4%) merbecovirus sequences, and the assay detected all bat-associated merbecoviruses included in the experimental panel. The assay was applied to 33 bats sampled through the Danish national bat surveillance program in 2025. Merbecovirus RNA was detected in two samples, one from a  P. auritus and one from a Nathusius’ pipistrelle (  Pipistrellus nathusii ), representing the first detection of a merbecovirus in  P. nathusii in Denmark. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing recovered a complete merbecovirus genome from the  P. nathusii sample. Phylogenetic analysis assigned the virus to the MOW clade and showed that it was closely related to the Russian MOW15-22 virus, sharing 98.67% nucleotide identity across the complete genome and 99.85% amino acid identity in the spike protein. Limited sequence data obtained from the  P. auritus sample was consistent with the merbecovirus lineage previously identified in this species in Denmark. Together, these findings demonstrate the utility of broad-range RT-qPCR combined with metagenomic sequencing for surveillance and genomic characterization of bat-associated merbecoviruses.
authors: Johnston CM, Moreno A, Lelli D, Marving EL, Baagøe HJ, Elmeros M, Fjederholt ET, Lohse L, Rasmussen TB.

title: Metagenomic Characterisation of Antimicrobial Resistance Gene Profiles in Shrimp Farm, Pond Microbiomes From the Southern Coastal Areas of Kerala, India
abstract: Abstract  Aquaculture is the fastest growing animal protein production sector in worldwide and Asia contributing annually with about 90% of the global seafood production. Penaeus monodon commonly known as the giant tiger prawn is a marine crustacean that is widely reared for food. The global rise in antibiotic resistance vitalised by indiscriminate antibiotic usage presents a significant public health challenge. The detrimental impact of antibiotic resistance includes the persistence of antimicrobial residues in fish and the surroundings. It gradually leads to the accumulation of resistance genes with the consequent contamination of the environment and the human food chain. There is a scarcity of data regarding the antibiotic resistance of shrimp aquaculture farms and ponds in Kerala. In the present study the metagenomic analysis revealed the occurrence of AMR genes across the southern coastal areas of Kerala, India. The pooled shrimp gut, water and sediment samples were subjected to metagenomic analysis. The antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes were determined by various databases like RGI (Resistance Gene Identifier) and the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD).In addition to this, KEGG and COG databases revealed the important biochemical pathways, cellular functions and specific protein ortholog of bacterial and archaea genomes of the studied locations. The outcomes imply noticeable regional differences in presence of AMR genes in the shrimp gut, sediment and water samples of the different southern coastal areas of Kerala.
authors: S DCCSDCC, Sabu KKSDKK.

title: An Enzyme-Mediated Duplex Exponential Amplification Assay for Rapid Detection of Plasmodiophora brassicae.
abstract: Clubroot, caused by the soilborne obligate biotrophic protist Plasmodiophora brassicae, substantially reduces the yield and quality of cruciferous crops worldwide. In this study, an enzyme-mediated duplex exponential amplification (EmDEA) assay was developed for rapid detection of P. brassicae in extracted DNA. By comparing the P. brassicae strain 3A genome with representative bacterial, fungal, and oomycete genome assemblies, we identified 157 candidate regions that showed no detectable matches in the selected non-target genomes under the specified alignment criteria. Pbspec1, a fragment within the annotated locus PBTT_08698, was selected based on computational non-target screening, within-species conservation, and suitability for assay design. PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing were used to validate the target fragment. Six forward primers, six reverse primers, and six RNA probes were screened, and F2-R4-RNA2 was selected for subsequent EmDEA experiments. Using serial dilutions of purified recombinant plasmid DNA, the F2-R4-RNA2 combination consistently detected template concentrations of 1.0 × 103 copies/μL and above. No amplification was observed from the 12 non-target fungal or bacterial organisms. The assay detected P. brassicae in DNA extracted from four infected root samples and three naturally infested soil samples. All tested positive samples produced detectable fluorescence during a programmed 20-min run on a portable isothermal fluorescence instrument. These results support the potential use of EmDEA for rapid preliminary screening of P. brassicae following DNA extraction.
authors: Zhang Y, Qian K, Chang S, Chen Y, He M, Hu J, Zhao J, Mao Z, Ling J.

title: Dual-Track Genome Evolution in Curvularia muehlenbeckiae Suggests Host Jump to Pecan via Putative Mini-Chromosome Acquisition and Zn2Cys6-Centric Coadaptation.
abstract: Curvularia muehlenbeckiae (P-6) is an emerging fungal pathogen responsible for severe leaf spot disease in pecan (Carya illinoinensis); however, the genomic mechanisms underlying its host jump remain elusive. Here, we present the first near-complete genome assembly of P-6 (33.77 Mb), revealing a karyotype of 14 chromosomes, including two putative mini-chromosomes (Chr13/Chr14) that harbor 17 and 22% of the pathogen's candidate virulence factors, respectively. Notably, Chr14 contains a transposase-flanked secondary metabolite biosynthetic gene cluster, a configuration often associated with horizontal gene transfer in fungi. Pan-genome analysis exposed a conserved Curvularia virulome (99.55% of P-6 virulence orthogroups) alongside lineage-specific expansions of major facilitator superfamily (MFS) transporters (299 genes) and Zn2Cys6 transcription factors (126 genes) that facilitate adaptation to woody hosts-a signature distinct from graminaceous-infecting Curvularia species. Time-resolved transcriptomics revealed a Zn2Cys6-centric biphasic infection strategy: an early phase (0.5 h postinoculation [hpi]) governed by Zn2Cys6 hubs regulating MFS transporters and reactive oxygen species detoxification genes, and a late necrotrophic phase (72 hpi) mediated by distinct Zn2Cys6 factors inducing carbohydrate metabolism (AMY1 and INV2) and toxin production (PKS7 and NRPS3). Weighted Gene Coexpression Network Analysis confirmed stage-specific modules associated with these Zn2Cys6 transcription factors. Ecological profiling indicated optimal growth at 28°C and pH 5.0 to 6.0, consistent with subtropical disease epidemiology. Our findings support a dual-track evolutionary model where putative mini-chromosomes may facilitate virulence gene acquisition, while correlated expansions of Zn2Cys6 transcription factors and MFS transporters form a coregulated network associated with a biphasic infection strategy. The identification of these hubs will provide promising targets for eco-friendly management of pecan leaf spot.
authors: Deng 邓可 K, Guo 郭若奕 R, Lv 吕赛斌 S, Zhang 张莹 Y, Zhang 章初龙 C, Xiao 肖力宏 L.

title: Discovery of Molecular Factors in the Non-CYP51A Route for Tebuconazole Resistance: An Adaptive Laboratory Evolution Research.
abstract: Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a well-established model organism for studying antifungal responses and resistance mechanisms. Its well-characterized genetics and conserved cellular processes provide a useful framework for investigating responses to azole fungicides such as tebuconazole. The present work aimed to discover molecular factors underlying tebuconazole resistance in S. cerevisiae. For this purpose, genetically stable, tebuconazole-resistant S. cerevisiae mutants were obtained by adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) and were investigated at the physiological and genomic level to determine molecular factors responsible for the tebuconazole resistance. ALE analysis showed that tebuconazole-resistant mutants could be developed without using any physical and chemical mutagens prior to the selection, demonstrating a potential mutagenic effect of tebuconazole. The resistance analyses showed that the mutants could still survive at tebuconazole levels up to 40 μg/mL (130 μM). The cross-resistance and cell wall degradation analyses revealed that the selected three mutants exhibited resistance to cell membrane disruption (0.006% SDS), acid stress (30 mM acetic acid), lignocellulosic hydrolysate stress (8 mM vanillin), antifungal stress (100 μg/mL prochloraz), oxidative stress (1 mM H2O2), and cell wall disruption (lyticase), compared to the wild-type strain. Whole genome sequencing (WGS) analysis indicated that three mutants possessed 16 common nonsynonymous variations, and they were distributed into eight genes (Q0182, FLO9, FIT1, COS8, YHL008C, HSP150, YMR057C, and YMR306C-A) independent of the CYP51A pathway. Biological process annotation analysis by STRING revealed that the mutant proteins and their interacting partners were associated with cell wall-related functions (Hsp150p), iron metabolism (Fit1p), flocculation (Flo9p), and largely uncharacterized biological processes (Cos8p and Q0182). According to YEASTRACT analysis to determine the potential transcription factors responsible for tebuconazole resistance, Yap1p, Pdr3p, and Rpn4p were identified as common transcriptional regulators of the six mutated genes found in the three mutants, suggesting that these transcription factors may contribute to the development of tebuconazole resistance. The findings of this study suggested that FLO9, FIT1, COS8, HSP150, YHL008C, Q0182, YMR057C, and YMR306C-A were novel genes whose genetic variations were associated with tebuconazole resistance through a non-CYP51A (ERG11)-mediated mechanism.
authors: Kurt H, Altan H, Taş F, Yurdagül H, Velioğlu HM, Sürmeli Y.

title: Exploring the wild soybean derived cross-kingdom SynCom for mitigating continuous cropping obstacles: potential links to fungus-associated bacterial dispersal and root exudate reprogramming.
abstract: Continuous cropping obstacles severely constrain global soybean productivity, yet scalable biological solutions remain limited. While continuous monoculture typically causes yield decline in cultivated soybean, its wild relative persists in the same soils for decades without apparent decline, suggesting the presence of a protective native rhizosphere. By integrating long-term field surveys, metagenomic profiling, and stress-directed cultivation, we established a multi-tiered rational design framework to construct a functionally complementary, cross-kingdom synthetic community from wild soybean rhizospheres. Using a reductionist hydroponic model to isolate direct microbial effects from the complexities of the soil matrix, a simplified bacterial-fungal consortium successfully mitigated CCO-associated stresses. Specifically, SSC mitigated the growth inhibition caused by continuous cropping obstacles, enhanced disease resistance, and reduced the accumulation of phenolic autotoxins in the rhizosphere. Regarding the mechanism of action, compartmentalized experiments suggest that fungal hyphae can act as bacterial carriers, facilitating bacterial dispersal and increasing the accumulation of beneficial bacteria in the plant rhizosphere, thereby promoting rapid root colonization. SSC reprograms root exudates, significantly upregulating the biosynthesis of flavone and flavonol biosynthesis, which may act as chemotactic inducers to recruit beneficial microorganisms to soybean roots. Our research reveals that the wild soybean microbiome is an exploitable reservoir, providing a practical framework for translating the resilience of the native microbiome into sustainable agricultural solutions.
authors: Song W, Wei Y, Tang L, Wong FL, Lam HM, Prasad R, Zhang S.

title: Beyond the CaCl₂ Brine: Transient Microbial Communities at the Edge of Habitability in lifeless Don Juan Pond, McMurdo Dry Valleys, Antarctica
abstract: Abstract    Background  Don Juan Pond (DJP), located in the McMurdo Dry Valleys of Antarctica, is one of the most extreme aquatic environments on Earth due to its CaCl₂-rich brines, low water activity, exceptional chaotropicity, subzero temperatures, intense solar radiation, and recurrent desiccation. Although the central DJP brine has long been considered largely inhabitable, the surrounding basin seasonally harbors temporary streams, ponds, and sparse microbial mat. Here, we investigated the diversity, ecological organization, and environmental factor chaping the structure of microbial communities inhabiting these peripheral habitats by integrating hydrochemical analyses, in situ reflectance spectroscopy, DNA metabarcoding, and ecological network analysis.  Results  No DNA suitable for PCR amplification was recovered from the central CaCl₂ brine. In contrast, peripheral streams and ponds supported diverse prokaryotic, microeukaryotic, and fungal communities, with the highest alpha diversity consistently observed in the hydrologically heterogeneous S1 stream system. Prokaryotic assemblages were primarily associated with salinity-related variables, including chlorinity and Mg/Ca ratios, whereas eukaryotic and fungal communities were more strongly correlated with hyperspectral indices indicative of photosynthetic biomass. Transient habitats also hosted micro-metazoans, including rotifers, tardigrades, and nematodes, indicating ecological refugia capable of sustaining complex trophic interactions under polyextreme conditions. Hyperspectral indices successfully discriminated active microbial mats from inactive sedimentary crusts and were significantly associated with the distribution of multiple bacterial, fungal, and microeukaryotic taxa. Network analyses revealed highly interconnected multi-domain communities composed of bacteria, fungi, algae, protists, and microbial grazers.  Conclusions  The presence of life in the Don Juan Pond basin appears to be largely restricted to temporary habitats supported by seasonal meltwater inputs rather than the central CaCl₂ saturated brine itself, which is anathema to all life forms due to a number of strict physicochemical constraints imposed on life. The contrasting responses of prokaryotic and eukaryotic communities suggest that adaptation and persistence represent distinct ecological strategies in this polyextreme ecosystem. These findings indicate that environmental stability may be as important as salinity/chaotropicity in determining habitability limits and demonstrate the value of integrating molecular and hyperspectral approaches to investigate life in extreme terrestrial and exo-planetary analogous environments.
authors: Smedile F, Spada GL, Cono VL, Marturano L, Crisafi F, Azzaro M, Porcino N, Giani M, Laudicella VA, Pasti L, Chenet T, Traversa G, Mauro BD, Canini F, Zucconi L, Yakimov MM.
