title: Genomic convergence and geographical divergence: multi-scale salinity adaptation mechanisms of microbiomes in shale gas flowback and produced water.
abstract: Shale gas flowback and produced water (FPW) represents a spatially heterogeneous artificial hypersaline ecosystem, in which the salt‑tolerance‑related genetic repertoire of indigenous microorganisms and the mechanisms shaping in‑situ community salinity adaptation patterns remain poorly clarified. Here, we collected metagenomic data from major shale gas-producing regions worldwide, encompassing 68 FPW samples from five basins: the Sichuan Basin, Anadarko Basin, Denver-Julesburg Basin, Western Canadian Sedimentary Basin, and Permian Basin. Based on these data, we constructed a genomic dataset comprising 699 high-quality MAGs to unravel the multi-scale salt adaptation mechanisms of the FPW microbiomes. Genomic results revealed that over 80% of FPW microbes encoded salt-in and salt-out pathways, demonstrating widespread genetic functional redundancy across geographically isolated basins. Despite convergent genomic potential, FPW microbiomes exhibited basin-specific adaptive differentiation, with Sichuan and Permian Basins favoring the salt‑in pattern and Anadarko Basin favoring the salt‑out pattern. Given the high conservation of gene repertoires and the physicochemical differences across basins, such salinity adaptation patterns decoupling between genomic repertoire and community adaptation may be driven primarily by environmental filtering. Machine learning identified trehalose metabolism genes (e.g., K00697, K17311 and K17313) and K⁺ uptake genes (e.g., K03498) as the biomarkers governing salt‑out and salt‑in pattern biases, respectively. Metabolic cross-feeding mediated by trehalose public metabolites, supported by keystone taxa of Thermotogota and Bacillota, potentially further enhanced community-level salt tolerance via interspecific metabolic synergy. This study elucidates the hierarchical adaptation mechanism coupling intrinsic genomic potential and local environmental filtering, providing novel ecological insights into microbial salinity adaptation and theoretical support for hypersaline wastewater biological treatment.
authors: Shi X, Duan S, Zhang Y, Hou B, Zhang L.

title: Isolation, characterization, and therapeutic potential of a novel phage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 infecting Klebsiella pneumoniae.
abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae (K. pneumoniae) is an important opportunistic pathogenic bacterium that is often characterized by a multidrug-resistant phenotype, which can lead to the failure of antibiotic treatments. The emergence of multidrug-resistant K. pneumoniae, including carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae (CRKP), poses a significant threat to public health security. Bacteriophages, which are viruses capable of lysing bacteria, represent a promising alternative for treating infections caused by highly virulent K. pneumoniae and other antibiotic-resistant pathogens. In this study, we used K. pneumoniae 32b as the host bacterium and isolated the bacteriophage vB_KpiP_JZBo1. The optimal MOI of this bacteriophage is 0.01. And phage exhibited high activity across a wide range of temperatures (20°C - 50°C) and pH (4 - 11) following 1 h of incubation. Whole genome analysis revealed that the bacteriophage was a double-stranded DNA virus, encoding a total of 91 open reading frames (ORFs). Notably, genetic evolutionary analysis and BLASTN results indicated that phage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 shares the closest evolutionary relationship with K. pneumoniae phage KP8. However, genome-wide comparison revealed that they only exhibit 88% coverage and 93.03% nucleotide homology. This suggests that phage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 may be a novel species of phage. No genes associated with antibiotic resistance, virulence factors, and tRNA were found in the phage genome, and it belongs to Kaypoctavirus genus of the Schitoviridae family. Additionally, higher phage doses resulted in greater inhibitory and bactericidal effects against K. pneumoniae in LB medium. In model of G. mellonella, bacteriophage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 can effectively eliminate the infection of K. pneumoniae 32b and increase the survival rate of G. mellonella. These findings suggest that the bacteriophage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 has potential for the treatment and prevention of K. pneumoniae, and they also provide a theoretical basis for clinical applications.
authors: Peng D, Cao R, Sun X, Jia C, Huang L, Yao X, Han Y, Liu Y, Yang Y, Yang G, Wang Y, Li H.

title: Genomic Characterization and Environmental Adaptability of Burkholderia cenocepacia Isolated from Commercial Liquid Soap in Bangladesh
abstract: Abstract    Commercial liquid soaps may harbor opportunistic pathogens such as  Burkholderia cepacia  complex (BCC), yet genome-scale characterization of soap-associated BCC isolates remains limited in South Asia. In this study, a bacterial isolate, designated DG4, was recovered from a commercial liquid detergent and characterized using phenotypic, biochemical, whole-genome, and comparative genomic approaches. The isolate exhibited substantial growth under alkaline conditions, with optimum growth observed at pH 8 and detectable growth up to pH 10, while growth was severely restricted at pH 11–12. The isolate was catalase and lipase-positive and its crude supernatant demonstrated surface-active properties, producing a 1.08 ± 0.10 cm oil-displacement zone and an emulsification index (E24) of 53.07 ± 0.11%. The strain also exhibited strong biofilm-forming ability, with an OD570 of 0.508 ± 0.00. Whole-genome sequencing revealed a 7.89-Mb draft genome comprising 459 contigs, with 67.16% GC content and 40× sequencing coverage. Genome-based taxonomic analyses, including ANI and phylogenetic analysis, identified DG4 as  Burkholderia cenocepacia  , with an ANI of 98.28% against the reference strain  B. cenocepacia  J2315 genome. Multilocus sequence typing revealed a potential novel allelic profile not assigned to a previously recognized sequence type. Genome annotation identified 7,964 coding sequences, including genes associated with stress adaptation, membrane transport, biofilm formation, antimicrobial resistance, virulence, and diverse metabolic pathways. The genome contained multiple resistance determinants, including  adeF  ,  amrA  ,  qacG  ,  OXA-1142  ,  PEN-B1  , and a  vanF  -associated  vanH  gene. PathogenFinder predicted a human pathogenicity probability of 0.9819. In addition, numerous genes involved in hydrocarbon degradation, aromatic compound metabolism, desulfurization, and biosurfactant-associated functions were identified, supporting considerable bioremediation potential. AntiSMASH analysis detected 21 biosynthetic gene clusters, while prophage, mobile genetic element, and CRISPR-Cas analyses demonstrated substantial genomic plasticity and defense capacity. Comparative orthologous analysis revealed a conserved core genome of 5,243 gene clusters and only 14 DG4-specific clusters among six  B. cenocepacia  genomes. Commercial liquid detergent can harbor environmentally adapted  B. cenocepacia  with clinically relevant resistance and virulence determinants. These findings emphasize the importance of microbiological quality control and AMR surveillance of personal care products while highlighting the strain's potential for bioremediation research.
authors: Tasnim A, Uddin N, Islam S, Jashim A, Islam MI.

title: Comparative genomics reveals expanded cell-surface signaling and siderophore scavenging repertoires in Pectobacterium.
abstract: Iron acquisition in gram-negative bacteria relies on TonB-dependent receptors (TBDRs), some of which initiate cell-surface signaling (CSS) by activating extracytoplasmic function (ECF) sigma factors that induce cognate transport pathways. Although well characterized in Pseudomonas, CSS systems remain poorly explored in plant-associated bacteria. Surveying 6,847 plant-associated bacterial genomes revealed near-ubiquitous CSS systems in Pseudomonas and Pectobacterium, with markedly lower strain-to-strain variation in the latter. In 902 high-contiguity Pectobacteriaceae genomes, Pectobacterium averaged 5.03 CSS modules per genome, compared with 0.67 in Dickeya, despite their shared soft-rot lifestyle. De novo clustering identified 14 distinct CSS systems across the family, with nine found in Pectobacterium. The ferredoxin receptor gene fusA was conserved in 572 of 586 Pectobacterium genomes; however, only 126 carried fusA under CSS regulation. These strains were phylogenetically dispersed but formed a single fusA clade, a pattern consistent with co-acquisition of the receptor and regulator as a transferable module. Pectobacterium also encoded a more diverse repertoire of siderophore receptors than related taxa, suggesting broader potential for siderophore utilization across bacterial lineages. Notably, the predicted amonabactin-like biosynthetic gene cluster and its putative cognate TBDR were highly conserved within Pectobacterium but rare elsewhere in the family, supporting its potential role in the endogenous siderophore system in the genus. These findings reveal an expanded genomic repertoire of CSS systems and siderophore receptors in Pectobacterium, providing a framework for investigating their roles in environmental sensing and iron acquisition.IMPORTANCEBacteria often use cell-surface signaling systems to sense environmental cues and coordinate the uptake of substrates that cannot freely cross the outer membrane, including siderophores and host-derived proteins. Through comparative genomic analysis, we demonstrate that Pectobacterium harbors one of the richest and most diverse repertoires of these cell-surface signaling systems among plant-associated bacteria. Despite similar lifestyles, its repertoire far exceeds that of other Pectobacteriaceae and reveals extensive predicted siderophore producer-scavenger relationships within the genus and across the family. These expanded signaling and siderophore acquisition systems in Pectobacterium may contribute to its environmental adaptability and ecological versatility by broadening opportunities for nutrient acquisition and interactions with surrounding microbial communities.
authors: Seo J-Y, Park DH, Lee JH.

title: Targeting the Skin Microbiome in Dermatology: Translational Hype or Emerging Therapeutic Modality?
abstract: The human skin microbiome is a complex network of microorganisms, including bacteria, fungi, viruses, and archaea, that exist in a mutualistic relationship with the host. These microorganisms play important roles in maintaining skin homeostasis, defense against pathogens, regulation of immune response, and antimicrobial peptide synthesis. Dysbiosis, defined as an imbalance of microbial communities, has been linked to dermatological conditions including atopic dermatitis (AD), acne, psoriasis, and chronic wounds. Despite compelling mechanistic insights, the translation of microbiome science into clinically effective therapies remains inconsistent and prematurely optimistic. Emerging therapeutic strategies aim to restore and modulate the skin microbiome with precision, thereby moving beyond conventional broad-spectrum antimicrobial approaches. These encompass probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, live biotherapeutic products (LBPs), bacteriophage therapy, microbiome engineering, postbiotics, microbial consortia treatment, and antimicrobial peptides that selectively target microbial communities instead of eliminating them. While these strategies are biologically plausible and have initial-phase evidence, their clinical stability, reproducibility, and scalability are uncertain. Major limitations include inter-individual variability of microbiomes, transient colonization, methodological limitations in functional profiling, and regulatory uncertainties surrounding them. This review article critically evaluates microbiome-directed dermatologic therapies at the crossroads of real therapeutic potential and translational overextension. The field is not just hype; its clinical application has advanced more rapidly than the supporting evidence base justifies. Progress in this domain requires a shift from descriptive and associative research toward mechanism-driven, precision-based interventions. Such interventions must be validated against robust clinical endpoints. By critically assessing biological plausibility, clinical evidence, and translational barriers, this review provides a balanced perspective on the field and outlines realistic pathways for its evolution into a viable therapeutic paradigm.
journal: FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology
authors: Syed RA, Ahmed A, Hayat U, Qazi J.

title: Benchmarking nanopore-based strategies for antimicrobial resistance prediction.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) presents a pressing need to ensure that the right antimicrobials are used to target the right microbes at the right time. Ideally, the appropriate antimicrobial is selected after patient samples have been cultured and assessed with antimicrobial sensitivity testing (AST). However, the time needed for culture-based diagnosis leads to immediate empirical treatment, often with broad-spectrum and/or high-tier antimicrobials. Direct nanopore metagenomic whole-genome sequencing to identify pathogens and predict their AMR is a rapid and patient-side alternative. A limitation of this approach is potential inconsistencies in i predicted AMR phenotypes. Here, we benchmarked the current performance of in silico AMR prediction strategies for nanopore-generated long-read data. Using real-world nanopore data paired with AST phenotyping for 201 samples representing 27 bacterial species, we assessed the impact of basecalling mode, data volume and assembly strategy and compared the performance of eight in silico AMR prediction tools with seven AMR databases. We found that basecalling accuracy mode does not significantly affect the overall accuracy of in silico AMR predictions but assembly strategy and data volume both do. Prediction tools using the ResFinder database scored best for balanced accuracy (0.80±0.02 for both ResFinder and ABRicate), whilst DeepARG scored best for sensitivity (0.65±0.03); predictions were more accurate for some antibiotic classes and genera than others. However, even the best-performing in silico AMR prediction strategy missed some resistance identified by lab-based AST. We conclude, therefore, that currently in silico AMR prediction can supplement lab-based AST but cannot yet replace it.
authors: Ring N, Low AS, Evans R, Keith M, Paterson GK, Gally D, Nuttall T, Clements DN, Fitzgerald JR.

title: Biosynthetic Pathways and Regulation of Antibacterial Compounds From Endophytic Fungi: From Chemistry to Genomics and Biotechnology.
abstract: Endophytic fungi are non-pathogenic symbionts that represent a rich source of structurally diverse bioactive secondary metabolites. However, genome-mining studies reveal that most of their biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) remain transcriptionally silent under standard laboratory conditions, leaving much of their chemical diversity unexplored. This review examines antibacterial natural products from endophytic fungi by integrating three complementary aspects: metabolite chemistry, biosynthetic pathways, and strategies for activating cryptic BGCs. Endophytic fungi produce polyketides, non-ribosomal peptides, terpenoids, phenylpropanoid-derived compounds, and hybrid metabolites with antibacterial activities mediated through inhibition of ribosomes, cell wall and membrane biosynthesis, and bacterial resistance mechanisms. Their genomes encode diverse PKS, NRPS, TPS, and hybrid biosynthetic systems, many of which remain cryptic. Advances in chemical elicitation, co-cultivation, epigenetic modulation, CRISPR-based engineering, genome mining, and machine learning are accelerating the activation of silent clusters and the assignment of BGCs to their metabolites. Several fungal metabolites exhibit potent activity against multidrug-resistant pathogens, including MRSA, and some enhance the efficacy of existing antibiotics. This review highlights current progress, identifies remaining challenges in metabolite production and BGC annotation, and outlines future directions for translating endophytic fungi into a sustainable platform for next-generation antibacterial drug discovery.
authors: Eshboev F, Salihu AS, Khayrullaeva L, Khamdamov D, Gao AX, Mardieva K, Salleh WMNHW, Azimova S, Tsim KWK.

title: Haplotype-phased assemblies of the two poplar rust fungi species: Melampsora larici-populina and Melampsora allii-populina.
abstract: Dikaryotic rust fungi maintain 2 distinct haploid nuclei for most of their life cycle, making their large, repeat-rich genomes difficult to assemble and phase. Here we present haplotype-phased, near chromosome-scale genome assemblies for the poplar rust pathogens Melampsora larici-populina 98AG31 and Melampsora allii-populina 12AY07, generated using PacBio HiFi sequencing and Hi-C-guided scaffolding. For each species, we resolved 18 chromosomes per haplotype, providing the first near chromosome-level representations of poplar rust fungal species. M. larici-populina diploid assembly spans ∼203 Mb, while M. allii-populina reaches ∼416 Mb, with high completeness and strong collinearity between haplotypes. Compared with previous fragmented or collapsed references, these assemblies greatly improve contiguity, recover centromeric and telomeric features, and support the transposable element-driven genome size expansion in M. allii-populina. The haplotype-aware annotations of genes and predicted effectors derived from these resources will enable detailed analyses of genome architecture, repeat dynamics, and key loci such as avirulence genes. Together, these assemblies provide a robust genomic resource for investigating host adaptation, virulence evolution, and population diversity in poplar rust fungi.
authors: Corre E, Morin E, Sperschneider J, Abdalrahem A, Pernaci M, Grigoriev IV, Frey P, Duplessis S, Lorrain C.

title: Genomic characterization of the endangered medicinal polypore agarikon (Laricifomes officinalis syn. Fomitopsis officinalis).
abstract: Agarikon (Laricifomes officinalis syn. Fomitopsis officinalis) is an endangered fungus belonging to a unique lineage in the Polyporales (Basidiomycota) with a growing body of evidence supporting its medicinal value. In this study, we report the hybrid de novo assembly and annotation of the nuclear and mitochondrial genomes of L. officinalis, with a nuclear genome size of 28.76 Mb assembled across 66 contigs (51.96% GC content; BUSCO completeness of 99.4%) and a complete core mitochondrial genome size of 197.67 kb. Structural and functional annotation of the nuclear genome yielded 8,717 predicted genes including 8,604 protein-coding genes, with 287 genes in 27 candidate biosynthetic gene clusters. We characterized the mating type loci matA and matB, consistent with a tetrapolar mating system, and identified genes encoding key enzymes involved in triterpenoid and polyketide biosynthetic pathways that lead to the production of a diverse array of secondary metabolites. Additionally, we conducted maximum likelihood phylogenomic analysis to confirm the taxonomic position of L. officinalis among other species in the Polyporales using protein sequences for 730 shared BUSCO genes. This high-quality annotated genome of L. officinalis will serve as a foundation for further investigations into its evolutionary history, provide a reference for future population genomic analyses, and elucidate mechanisms underlying the synthesis of the bioactive compounds responsible for agarikon's wide-ranging medicinal benefits.
authors: Bennett PI, Bair ZJ, Bradshaw AJ, Stamets P.

title: Halophyte-derived rhizosphere microbiome transplantation improves physiological homeostasis and salt tolerance in alfalfa.
abstract: Halophyte-associated microbiomes are promising reservoirs of stress-adapted microorganisms, yet the consequences of transferring whole rhizosphere communities to phylogenetically distinct crops have remained unclear. Here, we evaluated rhizosphere microbiome transplantation (RMT) from Suaeda salsa to alfalfa (Medicago sativa) in a 2 × 2 factorial experiment comprising control and RMT treatments at 0 and 300 mM NaCl. Plant physiological responses were integrated with metagenomic profiling, community assembly analysis, microbial association networks, and functional gene analyses. Under salinity, RMT increased plant height, leaf area, and both shoot and root biomass, reduced shoot Na+ accumulation, and increased the shoot K+/Na+ ratio. RMT also reduced H2O2, malondialdehyde, and relative electrical conductivity while increasing antioxidant enzyme activities and osmolyte concentrations, whereas gas-exchange parameters showed no significant recovery. RMT altered rhizosphere community composition and assembly and was associated with greater network connectivity and simulated robustness. Metagenomic KO profiles showed higher relative representation of functions correlated to osmoprotection, ion transport, redox protection, and cell-envelope processes. These microbial functional shifts coincided with the physiological domains most strongly improved by RMT but did not establish direct causal microbial mechanisms. Overall, halophyte-derived RMT improved alfalfa performance under salinity, with coordinated physiological recovery accompanied by substantial reorganization of the recipient rhizosphere, supporting further evaluation of whole-community microbiome transplantation for crop production in saline soils.
authors: Hu J, He Y, Cui W, Wei L, Li L, Wang L, Alwathnani H, Rensing C, Zhang J.

title: A synthetic microbial community derived from the roots of Kalidium gracile enhances its salt tolerance by modulating gene transcription and reshaping the rhizosphere soil microbiota.
abstract: Soil salinization and alkalinization are severe environmental problems in the desert-oasis transition zone of the Hexi Corridor, China. Rhizosphere microbial communities are key regulators of plant adaptation to saline-alkali environments. However, the functional microbial resources and ecological mechanisms underlying the contribution of the rhizosphere microbiome associated with Kalidium gracile to its saline adaptation remain poorly understood. In this study, we characterized the rhizosphere microbiome of K. gracile inhabiting severely saline-alkali soil and isolated two Bacillus strains with strong plant growth-promoting potential, which were subsequently used to construct a synthetic microbial community (SynCom). Inoculation experiments under salt stress demonstrated that SynCom increased plant biomass and chlorophyll content and modulated host transcriptional responses associated with the "growth-defense trade-off." Shortly after inoculation, plant growth-related pathways were suppressed, while CAT and POD activities surged by 45% and 213%, respectively. At later stages after inoculation, the expression of growth-related pathways was significantly upregulated. Metagenomic sequencing revealed that SynCom reshaped the rhizosphere microbial community, with the relative abundances of the halophilic bacteria Halomonas and Marinobacter increasing by 317% and 1162%, respectively. The abundances of functional genes involved in soil carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur nutrient cycling were all significantly increased. Collectively, these findings indicate that SynCom enhances plant salt tolerance through a multi-layered regulatory mechanism by coordinating host physiological responses and rhizosphere microbial functions. Collectively, these findings reveal a multi-level regulatory mechanism through which SynCom enhances plant salt tolerance by coordinating host physiological responses and rhizosphere microbiome functions.
authors: Yue Y, Yuan M, Fan Z, Shan L, Zhao Y, He C, Ma Q, Zhang L.

title: Diversity-generating retroelements enable phages to expand their host range in the human gut
abstract: Diversity-generating retroelements (DGRs) are genetic elements that use error-prone reverse transcription to hypermutate specific target genes, most often the receptor-binding proteins of phages. They are enriched in human gut viruses, where they are hypothesised to enable phages expand their host range. Yet DGR-mediated host-range expansion across bacterial species has so far only been predicted  in silico and has not been examined directly within complex microbial communities. To test this hypothesis  in situ , we tracked phage-host interactions in the human gut, combining bulk metagenomic, virus-like particle (VLP), and Hi-C sequencing of longitudinal faecal samples collected over a five-week period. This culture-independent approach identified 380 interactions between 97 phages and 76 bacterial hosts. Nearly a third of these phages (31 of 97) encoded a DGR, and DGR-encoding phages were more likely to interact with multiple bacterial species. Moreover, nucleotide diversity in DGR-targeted genes increased with the number of hosts a phage interacted with and was concentrated in the surface-exposed, DGR-targeted variable region of its receptor-binding proteins. Together, these results provide  in situ evidence that DGRs enable phages to expand their host range in the human gut.
authors: van den Hurk AWM, Zuppi M, Kuida MD, Nieuwdorp M, Wortelboer K, Herrema H, de Jonge PA.

title: Proinflammatory strains of Mediterraneibacter gnavus are enriched during spondyloarthritis and bolster disease severity in animal model.
abstract: ObjectivesSpondyloarthritis (SpA) is a chronic inflammatory rheumatism with osteoarticular and extra‑articular manifestations. Intestinal dysbiosis has been implicated in SpA, notably the expansion of Mediterraneibacter gnavus (MG), a gram-positive coccus associated with several inflammatory disorders. We aimed to determine whether distinct MG strains were associated with SpA and contributed to disease pathogenesis.MethodsMG strains from patients with SpA and healthy controls (HCs) were identified based on metagenomic analysis, isolated and whole‑genome sequenced. Pathogenicity of selected strains was compared by mono-associating curdlan-treated germ‑free SpA-prone SKG mice. Putative strain selection under inflammatory pressure was examined by culturing MG in the presence of nitric oxide (NO). Functional effects were assessed by exposing monocytes from patients with SpA to MGstrains.ResultsPhylogenetic analysis separated MG strains into 3 main clades/subclades, using both metagenomic data and sequencing of 46 MG strains (39 from SpA and 7 from HCs). SpA-derived strains were significantly enriched in 2 clades/subclades, whereas the third clade was dominated by strains from HCs, suggesting clade-specific disease association. MG-mono-association of curdlan-treated SKG mice induced SpA, in which SpA-derived strains induced stronger colonic inflammation and arthritis. Consistently, MG DNA of these strains persisted in the inflamed colonic submucosa and SpA-derived strains showed enhanced resistance to NO. In vitro SpA-derived strains were enriched in toxic and proinflammatory properties.ConclusionsSpA is associated with a distinct repertoire of MG strains characterised by increased adaptability to inflammatory stress and heightened proinflammatory and toxic potential. These findings establish a link between strain‑level microbial diversity and disease susceptibility.

title: RDAR biofilm formation and in silico analysis of putative amyloid proteins in Azospirillum baldaniorum Sp245.
abstract: Azospirillum baldaniorum Sp245 is a plant growth-promoting rhizobacterium (PGPR) whose ability to benefit host crops depends on robust root colonization, a process driven by the transition from a planktonic state to a sessile, biofilm-associated lifestyle. This study investigated the capacity of A. baldaniorum Sp245 to form Red, Dry, and Rough (RDAR) morphotype biofilms. Through macroscopic evaluation and confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM), we visualized the presence of exopolysaccharides, putative amyloid proteins, and extracellular DNA (eDNA) within the RDAR biofilm matrix using Calcofluor White (CFW), Thioflavin S (TS), and Propidium Iodide (PI) fluorescent probes, respectively. Furthermore, formic acid treatment of extracellular matrix proteins extracts suggests the presence of resistant, putative amyloid proteins. Because genomic screening revealed the absence of homologs of a canonical curli-dependent amyloid system, we performed a genome-wide in silico analysis to identify genes encoding alternative biofilm-associated proteins. Using the Staphylococcus aureus Biofilm-Associated Protein (Bap protein) as a reference, we identified 20 candidate proteins characterized by extensive domain reiteration and diverse architectures, including bacterial immunoglobulin (Ig-like) domains, VCBS repeats, SWM motifs, DUF4347, PKD domains, and RTX β-roll structures. Three-dimensional modeling indicates that these candidates possess elongated, filament-like conformations with repetitive β-strand motifs typical of amyloid-like assembly and calcium-dependent adhesion. These findings suggest that in the absence of traditional curli machinery, A. baldaniorum Sp245 could be using a diverse, domain-rich repertoire of alternative matrix proteins to facilitate cell surface interactions, coordinate structural stability, and establish the RDAR biofilm morphotype. Ultimately, this study establishes a foundation for understanding the role of amyloid proteins in Azospirillum biofilm matrix formation and offers new insights into the potential mechanisms of bacterial persistence and ecological fitness in the rhizosphere.
authors: Cortés-Sotres DR, Xiqui-Vázquez ML, Reyes-Carmona SR, Barrera-Olvera NG, Baca BE, Mancilla-Simbro C, Ramírez-Mata A.

title: A bacterial chaperone–usher pathway links interkingdom association to antimicrobial protection of a fungal partner
abstract: ABSTRACT  Antimicrobial compounds (AMCs) influence species-level composition of microbial communities, governing beneficial and pathogenic interactions with plant and mammalian hosts. Phenazine-1- carboxylic acid (PCA) is a bacterially produced, redox-active AMC abundant in the rhizosphere. A recent study discovered the PCA-susceptible fungus  Aspergillus calidoustus can grow in PCA- abundant environments by associating with phenazine-tolerant bacteria, including the novel species  Paraburkholderia edwinii .  P. edwinii’s protection response is characterized by adherence to its fungal partner, bacterial aggregation, and sequestration and reduction of PCA, rendering PCA less toxic. Deletion of the bacterial transcriptional repressor HrcA generates a constitutively active protection response and enhanced protection of  A. calidoustus . Here, we use the Δ  hrcA strain to determine whether fungal protection uses bacterial self-protection machinery or dedicated interkingdom mechanisms. We identified a divergent archaic chaperone–usher pathway (CUP) operon encoding a predicted periplasmic chaperone, outer membrane usher, putative major pilin-like subunit, and putative adhesin-like tip protein. While many archaic CUP operons are annotated in diverse bacteria, their functions remain largely unexplored. We show these  f ungal  a ttachment  c omplex (  fac ) genes promote bacterial-fungal attachment, are required for  P. edwinii to sequester and detoxify PCA, and contribute to full fungal protection from PCA stress, despite not being required for  P. edwinii ’s own tolerance of PCA. We further identified the transcription regulator, FacR, that influences expression of the  fac system. Understanding the functions of divergent archaic CUP systems may illuminate protective interkingdom partnerships and inform how pathogenic and beneficial microbes gain entry to AMC-replete environments, shaping microbial communities in agricultural and clinical contexts.  IMPORTANCE  Some species of fungi can be opportunistic pathogens, while others promote rhizosphere stability. Antimicrobial compounds help govern the composition of microbial communities by excluding susceptible organisms and selecting for microbes with intrinsic resistance. However, susceptible fungi can gain entry into microbial communities containing antagonist compounds by partnering with protective bacteria, and it is unknown whether bacteria are extending the mechanisms of self-tolerance to fungal partners, or if there is dedicated machinery for interkingdom protection. Here, we show that  Paraburkholderia edwinii uses a divergent chaperone–usher system to associate with its fungal partner,  Aspergillus calidoustus , and protect it from phenazine stress. This system promotes fungal attachment, antimicrobial sequestration, and maintenance of a reducing environment, yet is dispensable for the bacterium’s own survival. These findings demonstrate that bacteria can deploy dedicated machinery to protect partners across kingdoms, revealing that antimicrobial tolerance can emerge from microbial interactions rather than intrinsic resistance alone.
authors: Gonzalez A, Dahlstrom K.

title: Genomic Dissection Explains Temporal Dynamics of Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans.
abstract: Bacterial spot of tomato caused by four taxonomically diverse Xanthomonas pathogens is one of the main seed-borne constraints of the tomato industry worldwide. Among the four bacterial spot xanthomonads, Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans has a particular importance in terms of competitive aggressiveness and global distribution. Bacterial spot of tomato was observed for the first time in Iran in 2015, where X. euvesicatoria pv. perforans was identified as the causal agent. While occurrence of this disease appeared to have subsided in the following years, a resurgence of the disease in the main tomato-growing areas of Iran has raised serious concerns since 2023. In this study, we assessed the range of new bacterial spot outbreaks in the country during 2023-2024. Our data showed that the disease is currently present in five Iranian provinces, including the two provinces where it had originally been reported in 2015. Whole genome sequence-based phylogenomic investigations suggested that the causal agent of tomato bacterial spot in Iran is still X. euvesicatoria pv. perforans, while genetic diversity was observed in the recently emerging population of the pathogen compared to the old population. The bacterial strains isolated in 2023-2024 surveys were phylogenetically distinct from those isolated in 2014-2016 surveys. Furthermore, type III effector repertoires varied significantly among the strains isolated in this study, regardless of their geographic origin. We provide novel insights into the ever-changing nature of tomato bacterial spot pathogens, highlighting the impact of seed-borne lineages of X. euvesicatoria pv. perforans in the population dynamics of the bacterium.
authors: Hajian-Maleki H, Briand M, Dittmer J, Koebnik R, Shams-Bakhsh M, Jacques MA, Chen NWG, Osdaghi E.

title: Diversity and Taxonomic Classification of Plasmids in Pantoea.
abstract: Plasmids play a key role in prokaryotic evolution by providing adaptive traits that may facilitate colonization of new ecological niches. Members of the genus Pantoea harbor diverse plasmids, several of which carry metabolic and phytopathogenicity functions relevant for the interactions with plants and other eukaryotic hosts. Pantoea species harbor mobile plasmids that are able to transfer between cells, as well as domesticated plasmids that are vertically inherited, similarly to chromosomes. Although knowledge of Pantoea plasmid function and evolution is expanding, a general framework for their classification is still lacking. Here, we propose a framework for classifying Pantoea plasmids into plasmid taxonomic units (PTUs). By analyzing 797 publicly available Pantoea genomes, we identified 5,320 plasmids, of which 1,925 were classified by plasmid gene content similarity into 82 prevalent clusters of homologous plasmids. Integrating the clusters with plasmid backbone gene phylogeny, we recovered three previously described PTUs-LPP1, LPP2, and pOnion-across a broader taxonomic range than previously recognized. Additionally, three novel PTUs-LPP3, pPLD, and pINT-with distinct functional traits and pangenomic characteristics are proposed. We show that phylogenetic placement can assign previously unclassified plasmids to the plasmid groups defined here. Our analysis supplies a unified framework for plasmid classification in Pantoea and provides a foundation for future comparative studies of plasmid diversity and evolution in this taxon. title: Thiamphenicol residues promote dark ammonia assimilation over oxidation in up-midstream of Jiulong River estuarine waters.
abstract: Estuaries receive large amounts of pollutants, including nitrogen nutrients and antibiotics, discharged by human activities. Ammonium (NH4+)/ammonia (NH3) is a preferred inorganic nitrogen nutrient utilized by microorganisms and an energy source for ammonia-oxidizing microorganisms. Nevertheless, the impact of residual antibiotics on NH3 transformation in estuary is not clear. So we investigated how thiamphenicol (TAP) - a ribosomal-targeting antibiotic widely used in aquaculture - alters dark NH3 transformations in the Jiulong River Estuary (JRE, 15NH4+ isotope tracing with metagenomic analysis. We found that tributaries are sources of antibiotics for JRE and single antibiotic concentration less than 0.1 μg/L, although the concentration varied with the seasons. In up-midstream dark zones, environmentally relevant TAP concentrations (0.01 μg/L) disproportionately stimulated NH3 assimilation over oxidation and the maximum stimulation was 118.6 ± 18.2% and 19.0 ± 1.1%, respectively. This made NH3 assimilation's contribution to total NH3 transformation maximally increased by 13 percentage points at upstream in winter and 15 percentage points at midstream in summer. Meanwhile, TAP had no directly significant effect on NH3 transformation in the downstream. Metagenomic analysis revealed that ammonia-oxidizing bacteria might be more sensitive to TAP exposure than ammonia-oxidizing archaea. Especially the ammonia-oxidizing bacteria community was composed of Betaproteobacteria. Our findings confirm that the hormetic effect of low-concentration antibiotics manifests in the NH3 transformation processes. The significant enhancement of NH3 assimilation by environmentally residual levels of TAP strengthens the flow of NH4+ to particulate nitrogen throughout the estuary, thereby potentially prolonging the residence time of NH4+ in aquatic systems. This provides a new perspective for understanding estuarine water eutrophication.
authors: Wan R, Ge L, Zheng ZZ, Zheng LW, Zou W, Xu M, Kao SJ.

title: Whole-genome Mining of a Lead-resistant Bacterial Strain (Bacillus cereus).
abstract: BackgroundHeavy metals cause neurotoxicity/neuroinflammation in animals, including humans, and heavy metal contamination of soil/water is one of the major factors in neurodegenerative diseases. Soil bacteria that persist in metal-impacted environments often carry genomic determinants for metal detoxification alongside biosynthetic pathways for the production of structurally diverse secondary metabolites. We combined phenotypic identification, whole-genome sequencing and annotation-based genome mining to characterise a soil Bacillus cereus isolate (designated as VLR6) recovered alongside five additional bacterial isolates (VLR1-VLR5) from the same sample set.PurposeAnnotation-based mining to identify heavy-metal resistance genes involved in metal transformation, which is essential for understanding metal detoxification mechanisms and their potential implications for neurodegenerative diseases.MethodsIsolates were identified by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionisation-time-of-flight mass spectrometry (Bruker Biotyper). The VLR6 genome (5,411,809 bp, single contig) was annotated with Bakta v1.12.0 (database v6.0) and screened for acquired antimicrobial resistance determinants with the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database Resistance Gene Identifier (CARD-RGI). Biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) were predicted using antiSMASH v8.0.4 (default rules; Minimum Information about a Biosynthetic Gene Cluster 3.0 KnownClusterBlast comparisons) and identified through systematic keyword screening of the Bakta functional annotation.ResultsVLR4-VLR6 were identified as B. cereus, VLR1 as Escherichia coli, VLR2 as Citrobacter braakii (within the C. freundii complex), while VLR3 yielded no interpretable spectrum. The sequenced isolate (VLR6) genome encoded 5,504 coding sequences, 108 tRNAs, 39 rRNAs and one clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats array (35.3% GC). CARD-RGI identified 14 antibiotic-resistance-associated loci, dominated by glycopeptide-resistance gene cluster components (vanT/vanW/vanY homologues) and B. cereus class A/B1 beta-lactamases. antiSMASH identified 12 complete BGC regions, including an NI-siderophore region matching petrobactin (BGC0000942) independently corroborated by annotation keyword screening of the asb/fpu/fat loci, non-ribosomal peptide synthetases-metallophore region matching bacillibactin and an azole-containing RiPP region matching the thiopeptides thiocillin I/micrococcin P1; six regions returned no significant known-cluster match. Annotation-based mining additionally identified a heavy-metal-resistance gene set including a zntA-annotated Pb(II)/Cd(II)/Zn(II)-class P-type ATPase homologue, a complete ars operon (arsRBC) and two czcR-family regulators.ConclusionThe VLR6 genome carries a genomically confirmed set of BGCs, most confidently a petrobactin siderophore cluster corroborated by two independent methods alongside an annotation-supported heavy-metal-resistance gene set. Phenotypic lead-MIC determination and metabolomic or transcriptomic validation are still required before any bioactivity, neuroactive or otherwise, can be attributed to this strain or its predicted metabolites.
authors: Raj V, Kumar B, Kumar A, Karn SK.

title: Whole-genome sequencing and phylogenetic analysis of Anolis adenovirus 2 reveals conserved genome organization and gene-specific evolutionary patterns.
abstract: Adenoviruses, which infect vertebrates, have a rich history of evolution that includes both host switching and coevolution, particularly within Barthadenovirus, a genus that infects squamate reptiles, birds, and mammals. Potential host-switching events can be identified by comparing the evolutionary histories between viruses and their hosts; however, many Barthadenovirus phylogenies have been inferred based on a limited number of easily-amplifiable gene segments. Whole-genome sequencing of novel strains of Barthadenovirus can provide greater phylogenetic confidence, and therefore more accurately identify host-switching when it occurs. Here, we present the coding-complete whole-genome sequence, annotation, reconciled species tree, and molecular evolution analyses of two isolates of Anolis adenovirus 2, a member of Barthadenovirus. Our two isolates of Anolis adenovirus 2 are sister lineages with very high sequence identity. Our results support existing hypotheses regarding the ancestral hosts of Barthadenovirus (squamate reptiles), and proposed host switching events within and between squamate reptiles and other vertebrate classes. We leverage our novel genome annotations to perform comparative synteny analyses, identifying a set of shared genes across Barthadenovirus whose gene order is largely conserved within the genus. Finally, our molecular evolution analyses highlight trends in evolutionary pressures on individual genes: Genes associated with viral replication and structure have experienced slower rates of evolution than those encoding proteins involved in host interaction. Our two sequenced isolates of Anolis adenovirus 2 add to an expanding number of adenovirus genomic resources and facilitate future investigations into the patterns and processes shaping adenovirus diversification.
journal: Infection, genetics and evolution : journal of molecular epidemiology and evolutionary genetics in infectious diseases
authors: Falvey CH, Geneva AJ.

title: Gut microbiome and metabolomics reveal the role of thioproline in attenuating colorectal cancer-associated inflammation.
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the top three cancers globally in terms of both incidence and mortality, and its development may be influenced by an inflammatory environment in the intestines, often associated with gut microbiota dysbiosis. Food bioactives could modulate gut microbiota through anti-inflammatory and epigenetic mechanisms. Given the significant role of thioproline as a food bioactive with antioxidant properties, its potential to modulate gut microbiota and mitigate CRC remains largely unexplored. This study aims to understand the effects of thioproline on gut microbiota community and investigate the mechanisms through which thioproline regulates gut microbiota and exerts its anticancer effects. Fecal and intestinal tissue samples were collected from health, CRC, and thioproline-treated CRC mice. The metagenome and metabolome data revealed that thioproline treatment significantly altered the gut microbiota community composition and metabolism in CRC mice. These CRC-associated gut microbiota and bacterial metabolites returned to normal levels. Moreover, under thioproline treatment, the microbial-metabolite interactions in CRC mice shifted toward patterns more closely resembling those observed in healthy mice. Thioproline treatment increased linoleic acid levels in mice, indicating its role in promoting linoleic acid metabolism to therapeutically restore homeostasis and alleviate inflammation in CRC. This was further supported by hematoxylin and eosin staining, which demonstrated that thioproline alleviated inflammation in CRC mice. Our study highlights thioproline's dual role in regulating the gut microbiota community and bacterial metabolism, modulating bacteria-host interactions, and ultimately reducing inflammation in CRC. These findings offer valuable insights for future research and therapeutic applications.IMPORTANCEColorectal cancer (CRC) is associated with gut microbiota dysbiosis and intestinal inflammation. While food bioactives can modulate the microbiome, whether thioproline exerts inhibitory effects against CRC through microbial regulation remains unknown. Using integrated metagenomics and metabolomics, we show that thioproline treatment restores the gut microbiota composition and bacterial metabolites disrupted by CRC to near-normal levels. Importantly, thioproline remodels microbial metabolite interaction networks, elevates linoleic acid levels, and alleviates intestinal inflammation. This study provides a systems-level perspective on how a single dietary bioactive compound reshapes the gut microbial ecosystem and its metabolic landscape to reduce inflammation in CRC. Our findings suggest a potential role for microbiome-targeted nutritional strategies in protecting against CRC progression through modulation of the gut microbiota and intestinal microenvironment.
authors: Liu J, Li W, Qi M, Zhao J, Wu J, Wang Y, Yang Y, Song X.

title: Genomic and functional characterization of compost-derived bacteria identifies a candidate bioinoculant that influences tomato physiology and leaf metabolism
abstract: Soil biodiversity is increasingly threatened by anthropogenic activities, with intensive agriculture having a particularly detrimental impact on soil microbial communities and potentially disrupting plant-microbe interactions that contribute to plant growth and resilience to environmental stresses. Biofertilizers based on Plant Growth-Promoting Rhizobacteria (PGPR) and organic amendments represent promising strategies to restore microbial diversity and promote crop health. Although compost is widely used as an organic fertilizer, its potential as a reservoir of culturable beneficial bacteria for the development of bioinoculants remains largely unexplored. In this work, we isolated and identified six bacterial strains from commercial compost derived from municipal organic waste and screened them for plant growth-promoting traits. Two representative isolates, Kocuria rhizophila and Glutamicibacter arilaitensis, were subjected to whole-genome sequencing and comparative analyses to investigate their taxonomy, functional potential, rhizosphere competence, secondary metabolism, plastic degradation associated features, and predicted human pathogenicity. K. rhizophila was subsequently tested as an inoculant on tomato plants grown in soil, compost-amended soil, or sterile compost-amended soil. Five of the six isolates exhibited many of the plant growth-promoting traits tested. Genomic analyses of the two strains supported several of the observed phenotypes and revealed functions potentially associated with nutrient metabolism, plant-root interactions, environmental adaptation, and degradation of plastic polymers. Neither strain was predicted to be pathogenic to humans, indicating a potentially low safety risk for their application as bioinoculants. Upon inoculation with K. rhizophila, plant responses were influenced primarily by substrate type, although the bacterium produced specific, substrate-dependent effects at 33 days post inoculation. Inoculation resulted in a trend towards increased dry biomass in plants grown in sterile compost and influenced leaf metabolic profiles at 33 days. These results support the potential of K. rhizophila as a compost-derived bioinoculant and indicate that enriching compost with beneficial strains isolated from the same matrix could be a useful approach to complement its effects on plant growth.
authors: Cipriani R, Strickler SR, De Biasio N, Angiolin CL, Ghirardello G, Zanardi W, Bonato T, Baldan B, Nigris S.

title: The pangenome of the human fungal pathogen  Cryptococcus neoformans  reveals that subtelomeres are hotspots for gene content variation
abstract: ABSTRACT  Cryptococcus neoformans is a human fungal pathogen that causes cryptococcal meningitis, primarily in individuals with advanced HIV disease. The  C. neoformans species is composed of four unique molecular types: VNI, VNII, VNBI, and VNBII, with thousands of global isolates within these groups. While previous descriptions of these molecular types have focused on nucleotide divergence between shared genes, there has been limited examination of variation in gene content between isolates. Here, we define the genome content diversity within a collection of 383  C. neoformans isolates spanning all four molecular types. To do so, we constructed a pangenome through  de novo assembly and annotation of short-read Illumina sequences. We defined 6,564 representative ortholog groups of the predicted proteins leveraging high-quality data from reference strain H99. We classified ortholog groups as either core (93.8%) or accessory (6.2%) based on their presence across the species. We next used long-read assemblies for a subset of our isolates to define the predicted accuracy of our classifications and account for errors in assembly or annotation of short-read sequences. We determined that while a subset of accessory genes are segregating across the entire species, many accessory genes are found only within specific molecular types, suggesting limited gene flow between groups. Additionally, we found many accessory genes are poorly conserved within the  C. neoformans species but share high sequence similarity to genes found in related Cryptococcaceae species, suggesting horizontal gene transfer. We also found that accessory genes were enriched within subtelomeric regions, implicating the subtelomeres in gene content variation between isolates. We show examples of accessory genes located within subtelomeres of  C. neoformans isolates that were conserved with subtelomeric proteins of other Cryptococcaceae species. Our pangenomic analysis of  C. neoformans gives species-level insights into its biology, potentially illuminating genetic contributions to pathogenesis.
authors: Reichardt CE, Billmyre RB.

title: Cross-kingdom metabolic regulation by a symbiotic virus: Transient viral microRNAs coordinate host metabolism and immune responses.
abstract: Symbiotic microorganisms and endogenous viruses play fundamental roles in shaping host physiology, yet the non-coding RNA-mediated mechanisms underlying viral-driven metabolic reprogramming remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate a novel mechanism of cross-kingdom metabolic manipulation mediated by symbiotic viral microRNAs. Using the tobacco cutworm Spodoptera litura, its endoparasitoid wasp Snellenius manilae, and the wasp-associated bracovirus SmBV as a model system, we identified two virus-derived microRNAs, SmBV-miR-2733 and SmBV-miR-3772, that target the host lipogenic genes encoding AGPAT and lipin, leading to the suppression of glycerolipid biosynthesis and reduced lipid accumulation. Functional analyses revealed that these symbiotic viral miRNAs concurrently attenuate host innate immune signaling pathways (Toll and JAK/STAT) and cellular encapsulation, establishing a mechanistic link between viral metabolic coercion and host immunomodulation. Crucially, this viral microRNA-mediated regulation is transient and highly dynamic; miRNA expression declines during later stages of infection, coinciding with an intermediate recovery of host lipogenic gene expression and lipid reserves, which may help sustain the developing parasitoids. Prolonged experimental maintenance of viral miRNAs disrupted host energetic homeostasis and compromised symbiotic success, underscoring the evolutionary necessity of temporally coordinated metabolic regulation. Comparative genomic analysis identified miR-2733- and miR-3772-like candidate loci with miRNA-precursor-like structures that are unevenly distributed across related bracovirus lineages. Together, our findings provide significant mechanistic insights into how symbiotic viral effectors post-transcriptionally rewire host metabolic and immune networks, offering a broader conceptual framework for understanding homeostasis in diverse host-microbe symbioses.
authors: Lin YC, Tseng YK, Chen P, Lin CY, Tang CK, Wu YL.

title: Divergent transcriptional responses of conserved cellular machinery to warming and phosphorus limitation in freshwater phytoplankton
abstract: Lakes are simultaneously warming and becoming phosphorus limited, but whether phytoplankton taxa of the same phylum respond through similar molecular mechanisms remains unclear, challenging a common assumption underlying predictions of ecological responses to environmental change. We cultured four freshwater phytoplankton species, including two diatoms (  Fragilaria crotonensis and  Nitzschia palea ) and two cyanobacteria (  Microcystis aeruginosa and  Synechococcus sp. ), across factorial gradients of temperature (20, 24 and 28 °C) and phosphorus (P) limitation, and characterized gene expression using RNA-seq, differential expression analysis and signed gene set enrichment. We generated predictions for expected responses for categories of gene functions derived from the growth rate (GRH) and temperature-dependent physiology hypotheses (TDPH). Warming and P limitation engaged largely the predicted functional categories in all species, however the direction of the response was not conserved, even within phyla—the two cyanobacteria regulated photosynthesis, ribosomal and chaperone genes in opposite directions. Ribosome- and translation-related genes gave the strongest warming response and, in  N. palea , reversed direction within the species, increasing between 20 and 24 °C and decreasing between 24 and 28 °C, below the strain’s thermal optimum estimated under moderate P limitation. Ribosomal allocation thus supported each hypothesis in different species and temperature ranges and was not predicted by thermal position alone. Where the interaction effects could be tested, P limitation rarely recruited novel pathways but modified existing warming responses, suppressing them in  F. crotonensis and amplifying and redirecting them in  M. aeruginosa . Molecular responses to combined drivers therefore diverge among related taxa, cautioning against aggregating species into functional groups when forecasting phytoplankton responses to global change.
authors: Santos JL, Weber de Melo V, Levasseur S, Weber AA, Narwani A.

title: Longitudinal Skin Bacterial Cluster Associated With Protection Against Allergic Co-Morbidity in Pediatric Atopic Dermatitis.
abstract: BackgroundAtopic dermatitis (AD) is an inflammatory skin condition that often portends the development of allergic comorbidities. Despite evidence supporting the role of the skin microbiome in AD, its temporal patterns and associations with risk or protection for allergic co-morbidity remain unclear. Our objective is to characterize core species of the pediatric AD bacterial microbiome, assess microbial networks and clusters, and identify global microbial changes relevant to AD and the atopic march.MethodsWe performed metagenomic shotgun sequencing on 353 non-lesional skin samples from children in the Mechanisms of Progression of Atopic Dermatitis to Asthma in Children (MPAACH) cohort across 5 annual visits. We assessed taxonomic composition and analyzed longitudinal skin microbial patterns with progression to allergic co-morbidities.ResultsWe identified 436 distinct species. Shannon diversity and richness declined with age, and socioeconomic factors explained the variance in species composition. Staphylococcus aureus (SA) was more abundant in severe AD. Cluster 5, comprised of typically gut-associated microbes, was more abundant in non-sensitized children who did not develop allergic co-morbidities over time.ConclusionsOur analyses revealed key patterns in core taxa, diversity and abundance of the skin microbiome over time in early life and highlighted previously unexplored factors such as socioeconomic status as key contributors to the variability in species composition. Abundance of SA confers risk, while gut-associated microbes may offer protection, influencing the clinical trajectory of AD and the atopic march. Thus, these results provide a novel and comprehensive understanding of the temporal dynamics of the skin microbiota in pediatric AD.
authors: Dahal A, Chang WC, Grashel B, Morgan D, Spagna D, Kim DH, Sachdeva S, Phelan KJ, Satish L, Biagini JM, Haslam DB, Ollberding NJ, Khurana Hershey GK.

title: Heptyl prodigiosin from estuarine Zooshikella sp. RANM57 induces caspase-dependent apoptosis and suppresses clonogenic survival in androgen-independent prostate cancer cells
abstract: Abstract    Estuarine microbiomes are rich ecological niches for discovering novel secondary metabolites with therapeutic applications. This study focuses on the isolation, purification, structural elucidation, and antineoplastic evaluation of a red pigment from a marine microbial isolate. The bacterium  Zooshikella  sp. RANM57 was isolated from the Netravathi River estuary. Biomass was recovered using an alum-induced flocculation technique and solvent extraction, after which the primary pigment was purified via flash chromatography and structurally characterized using HRLCMS-QTOF and NMR spectroscopy. Anticancer potential was evaluated against human PC-3 prostate cancer cells using MTT and clonogenic assays. The underlying apoptotic mechanism was delineated using Annexin V/PI staining, Caspase-3 quantification, and TUNEL assays. The purified pigment was identified as the tripyrrole alkaloid heptyl prodigiosin based on HRLCMS-QTOF, UV-Vis/FT-IR profiling, and 1D NMR spectral concordance with reported prodiginine features.  In vitro  evaluations revealed significant dose-dependent cytotoxicity against PC-3 cells (IC  50   = 9.00 µg/mL), demonstrating high anticancer efficacy relative to cisplatin. Mechanistic profiling confirmed that cell death occurred exclusively via an intrinsic apoptotic cascade, as evidenced by significant phosphatidylserine externalization (17.60%), executioner Caspase-3 activation (52.45%), and terminal DNA fragmentation (21.25%), without inducing primary necrosis. Furthermore, treatment also reduced clonogenic survival after 24 h exposure and 8-day outgrowth. The successful isolation and characterization of heptyl prodigiosin from  Zooshikella  sp. RANM57 underscores the value of estuarine bacteria in natural product discovery. Our biological evaluations demonstrate that the compound functions as a precise, potent inducer of caspase-associated apoptosis, positioning this tripyrrole scaffold as a highly promising candidate for further anticancer pharmacological development.
authors: Madtha RS, Balakrishna K, Deen KR, Rithick S, Ignacimuthu S, Pandikumar P, Chirakkara SP, Abraham A.

title: From partners to pathogens: Metabolic duality in algal-bacterial interactions.
abstract: Interactions between phytoplankton and bacteria are often classified as beneficial or harmful, yet interactions between the same partners can shift between these states. Here, we examine bacterial pathogenicity toward marine phytoplankton, focusing on how algal-bacterial interactions become harmful. In several Roseobacter-phytoplankton systems, bacteria repurpose metabolites produced or exchanged during the interaction by altering their concentration, signaling function, or metabolic fate, thereby contributing to host damage. We define this context-dependent repurposing as metabolic duality. We contrast this strategy with algicidal activity that does not require a demonstrated prior interaction with the algal partner or an algal-derived substrate. Examples include secreted proteases and small-molecule algicides that bacteria can produce independently of host-derived metabolites. Despite their different mechanisms, these routes often converge on oxidative stress and programmed cell death-like responses in the algal host. Bacterial identity alone does not determine the outcome. Host physiological state, microbial community composition, temperature, nutrients, and the chemical environment can all shift an interaction toward or away from pathogenicity. We therefore propose that phytoplankton pathogenicity is best viewed as an emergent property of the interactions among the bacterium, host, community, and environment. This perspective shifts the central question from which bacteria are pathogens to what makes an interaction pathogenic and provides a framework for understanding when and why algal-bacterial interactions become harmful in the ocean.
authors: Beiralas R, Segev E.

title: Insights Into The Early Diversification of  bla  NDM-1  Genetic Contexts Following its Emergence in  Acinetobacter  species and Spread to Enterobacterales
abstract: Since its emergence, the New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM) has become a major global antimicrobial resistance threat, enabling bacterial hosts to resist most β-lactam antibiotics, including carbapenems, and spreading widely across bacterial species and geographic regions. Believed to have originated in  Acinetobacter spp.,  bla NDM subsequently spread to Enterobacterales through mobile genetic elements, despite barriers to lateral gene transfer between these phylogenetically distant taxa. To investigate the genetic diversity and mechanisms underlying this interspecies transfer and subsequent global expansion, we sequenced and characterized 13  bla NDM-1 -positive Gram-negative bacterial isolates collected in India in 2007, among the earliest known isolates harboring  bla NDM-1 . Clonal diversity was observed among both  Escherichia coli and  Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates. Comprehensive genomic analysis revealed that  bla NDM-1 was consistently embedded within a conserved multidrug resistance region, often associated with mobile genetic elements involved in lateral gene transfer. Notably, the insertion sequence IS  Aba14 was identified in 6 of the 13 sequences, suggesting a potential role in the early dissemination of  bla NDM-1 among diverse bacterial hosts. These findings contribute to our understanding of the evolutionary origins and early genetic context of  bla NDM-1 , highlighting the importance of continued genomic surveillance and functional studies to better understand the persistence and dissemination of carbapenem resistance.  Impact Statement  This study characterizes 13 previously undescribed genetic contexts of the New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase-1 gene (  bla NDM-1 ) in Enterobacterales isolates collected in India in 2007. These isolates represent some of the earliest known  bla NDM-1 -positive Enterobacterales and are the earliest collected  bla NDM-1 -positive Enterobacterales for which whole-genome sequences are now available. Their genetic contexts include diverse combinations of antibiotic resistance genes and associated mobile genetic elements. Notably, the insertion sequence IS  Aba14 was identified in 6 of the 13 sequences, highlighting its frequent association with  bla NDM-1 during the early stages of its dissemination. Together, these findings reveal substantial genetic diversity surrounding  bla NDM-1 early in its emergence and suggest that diverse arrangements of mobile genetic elements may have contributed to its early dissemination across bacterial hosts and the subsequent spread of carbapenem resistance.
authors: Allard N, Touati D, Faille N, Grenier F, Beauchemin-Lauzon E, Lévesque S, Rodrigue S, Haraoui L.

title: First Report of Vibrio harveyi From Starry Flounder (Platichthys stellatus) With Phenotypic, Pathogenicity and Whole-Genome Characterization.
abstract: Vibrio harveyi is a prominent bacterial pathogen of marine aquaculture. Vibrio harveyi has not previously been reported in starry flounder. In this study, phenotypic and genotypic characterizations and pathogenicity assessments of V. harveyi isolated from starry flounder in South Korea were conducted. Phylogenetic analysis identified strains VH-SF-1, VH-SF-2, VH-SF-4 and VH-SF-5 as V. harveyi . Motility assays showed that VH-SF-2 displayed the highest activity at 27°C. In pathogenicity tests, VH-SF-2 caused 100% mortality within 16 and 48 h at doses of 3 × 108 and 3 × 107 CFU/fish, respectively, whereas a 10% mortality rate was observed at 3 × 106 CFU/fish. The lethal dose (LD50) was estimated to range from 3 × 106 to 3 × 107 CFU/fish, providing the first evidence of the pathogenicity of V. harveyi in starry flounder. These findings suggest that V. harveyi may emerge as a novel pathogen of this species. To investigate genomic characteristics and virulence factors, whole-genome sequencing (WGS) was conducted. Strain VH-SF-2 harboured multiple virulence-related mechanisms, including outer membrane proteins, motility, quorum sensing, bacterial secretion systems, iron uptake and regulation and virulence regulators. The study aimed to elucidate the biological and pathogenic characteristics of V. harveyi isolated from starry flounder.
authors: Park JH, Kim SW, Kim JO.

title: Chromosome-scale nuclear and mitochondrial genome assemblies reveal extreme genome compartmentalization in the hazelnut pathogen  Anisogramma anomala
abstract: Anisogramma anomala is an obligate biotrophic ascomycete and the causal agent of Eastern filbert blight, the most economically important disease of hazelnut in the United States. Here, we generated a chromosome-scale reference genome for  A. anomala isolate OR-Ennis-d and characterized its nuclear and mitochondrial genome architecture. The 344-Mb nuclear genome was resolved into 9 predicted chromosomes and is repeat-rich, with transposable elements comprising 88.8% of the assembly. Although transposable elements are abundant, their divergence landscape and low retention of conserved protein domains support a history of past extensive transposon proliferation followed by widespread degeneration. Repeat accumulation was highly uneven and generated pronounced genome compartmentalization. Approximately half of predicted genes occur in compact, TE-poor regions with short flanking intergenic regions that are enriched for conserved BUSCO orthologs. In contrast, genes in TE-rich, gene-sparse regions with long flanking intergenic regions are enriched for carbohydrate-active enzymes, secreted proteins, and candidate secreted effector proteins, consistent with a two-speed-like genome architecture. The 462-kb mitochondrial genome is among the largest reported for ascomycetes and contains 117 introns, including an intron adjacent to  cob codon 143 that may prevent acquisition of the p.G143A substitution associated with resistance to quinone outside inhibitor fungicides. Finally, we identified mitochondrial DNA insertions at 20 nuclear loci totaling at least 616.9 kb, an unusually extensive amount for a fungal genome. This chromosome-scale genome resource reveals the extreme nuclear and mitochondrial genome architecture in  A. anomala and provides a foundation for investigating genome evolution and adaptation to hazelnut resistance.
authors: Zaccaron AZ, Søndreli KL, LeBoldus JM, Weisberg AJ.

title: Comparative Genomics of Multidrug-Resistant and Extensively Drug-Resistant Acinetobacter Baumannii Clinical Isolates from an Intensive Care Unit in Northeastern Brazil
abstract: Abstract    Acinetobacter baumannii  is an opportunistic pathogen linked to healthcare-associated infections and the dissemination of multidrug-resistant phenotypes in critical hospital settings. In this study, we performed a comparative genomic analysis of clinical isolates identified as  A. baumannii  by routine hospital microbiology, obtained from an intensive care unit in Northeastern Brazil and classified as susceptible (SEN), multidrug-resistant (MDR), or extensively drug-resistant (XDR). Fifteen isolates were subjected to whole-genome sequencing; after quality control, 14 genomes were included in the main comparative analyses. Genome assembly metrics, functional composition, pangenome, resistome, virulome, Pasteur MLST, core-genome phylogeny, phenotype–genotype concordance, and FastANI-based taxonomic refinement were evaluated. MDR and XDR isolates carried a higher burden of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes than SEN isolates. Pangenome analysis revealed a conserved core genome combined with variable accessory content, whereas the virulome was relatively conserved across phenotypic groups. Quinolone resistance-determining region (QRDR) mutations in  gyrA  and/or  parC  were detected in ciprofloxacin-resistant isolates, supporting the role of chromosomal mechanisms in fluoroquinolone resistance that may not be captured by analyses restricted to acquired resistance genes. FastANI analysis further revealed taxonomic discrepancies in two susceptible isolates, highlighting the complementary value of WGS for hospital surveillance and taxonomic refinement within the  Acinetobacter calcoaceticus–baumannii  complex. Overall, our findings indicate that antimicrobial resistance in these clinical isolates is a multifactorial phenomenon shaped by clonal diversity, accessory genome variation, AMR gene burden, chromosomal resistance mechanisms, and taxonomic complexity within the ACB complex.
authors: Gondim R, Ribeiro S, Alves A, Lino L, Lima I, Nogueira L, Maia M, Magalhães L, Damasceno L, Filho JS, Silva D, Mendes C, Castro L, Damasceno C, França A, Miyajima F, Lima A, Havt A, Clementino MA.

title: Ultra-deep HiFi sequencing reveals rare structural-variant subpopulations in multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa from an LVAD-associated infection.
abstract: BackgroundPseudomonas aeruginosa is a Gram-negative opportunistic pathogen frequently associated with multidrug-resistant infections in clinical settings. The rise of antibiotic-resistant strains and their genomic complexity necessitate advanced tools for comprehensive genetic characterization, particularly in the context of resistance to antibiotic and phage therapies.MethodsHere, we use ultra-deep high-fidelity (HiFi) sequencing to analyze strain NRD619, a multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa isolate that had colonized the driveline of a left ventricular assist device of an 82-year-old male who was identified as a phage therapy candidate. Through HiFi long-read sequencing and bioinformatic analysis, we identified low-frequency heterogeneous structural variants (SVs) and investigated their potential phenotypic consequences through functional annotation and literature-based gene-function analysis.ResultsSmall variants in known resistance-associated genes, including an early frameshift in mexZ, were consistent with components of the multidrug-resistant phenotype, whereas several other genotype-phenotype associations remained uncertain. Ultra-deep long-read sequencing identified five low-frequency heterogeneous SV signals. A reciprocal 31.7-kb deletion and duplication of a phage-rich region were supported by 3 and 95 reads, respectively; three multi-kilobase insertion candidates were each supported by a single HiFi molecule. Observed variant allele frequencies ranged from 1.2119% to 0.0122%. The insertions intersected genes involved in type IV pili, transport, and stress response, providing plausible hypotheses for effects on biofilm-related behavior, device colonization, and other phenotypes.ConclusionsThis study demonstrates how ultra-deep sequencing can uncover cryptic genetic heterogeneity in bacterial pathogens, offering insights into P. aeruginosa population structure in a clinical isolate that are inaccessible to conventional-depth sequencing. Because sequencing followed single-colony recovery and laboratory expansion, the origin and in vivo frequencies of the rarest SVs cannot be established. The detected diversity may reflect structural states accessible in vivo or variation arising during ex vivo propagation; the latter remains relevant because culture-based genomic and phenotypic characterization interrogates the expanded population. Future applications could refine our understanding of multidrug resistance, phage susceptibility, and adaptations influencing host colonization.SignificanceChronic bacterial infections are usually represented by a single genome, even though clinicians and microbiologists know genetically diverse subpopulations can coexist within a patient. Using ultra-deep, high-fidelity long-read sequencing of a multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa clinical isolate from a left ventricular assist device-associated infection, we reveal structural heterogeneity distinguished by phage and mobile-element architectures and associated small variants. Coverage-based modeling shows that several of these rare structural states would be poorly sampled at standard sequencing depths, yet they occur in loci linked to virulence, surface interactions, transport, and stress response. Because the isolate underwent single-colony recovery before sequencing, the study cannot determine whether individual rare variants arose in vivo or during ex vivo propagation. Either possibility is informative: the former represents hidden within-host diversity, whereas the latter can alter the population used for culture-based genomic and phenotypic characterization. These findings establish ultra-deep long-read sequencing as a strategy for revealing hidden adaptive potential in chronic and device-associated infection isolates.
authors: Bosco A, Luong T, Jeshvaghane MA, Fallahpour M, Modlin SJ, Roach D, Valafar F.

title: Molecular and morphological characterization of nine new Gnomoniopsis species (Diaporthales, Gnomoniaceae): Genomic insights into evolution and phylogeny.
abstract: Gnomoniopsis comprises parasitic, endophytic, and saprophytic fungi. Since its establishment, this genus has presented considerable taxonomic challenges owing to extensive morphological overlap among species, rendering traditional classification systems that rely predominantly on phenotypic characteristics no longer applicable. To resolve the current taxonomic confusion and clarify the species diversity, phylogenetic relationships, and genomic adaptive characteristics of Gnomoniopsis, the present study was carried out. In this study, the internal transcriptional spacer (ITS), translation extension factor 1-α (tef1), and partial beta-tubulin (tub2) were analyzed and combined to observe morphological characteristics of Gnomoniopsis. The isolates were identified from chestnut (Castanea), Embelia vestita, tea (Camellia sinensis), and other hosts in Sichuan Province, as well as from Quercus species and partial leaf rot from Fujian Province. Nine new species, namely G. xiaoheijiangensis sp. nov., G. embeliae sp. nov., G. yunvfengensis sp. nov., G. quercus sp. nov., G. ledongensis sp. nov., G. yonganensis sp. nov., G. conghuaensis sp. nov., G. loropetali sp. nov., and G. qixiensis sp. nov., were obtained. Phylogenomic analysis based on 7,942 orthologous proteins' clusters revealed distinct species boundaries within Gnomoniopsis. Phylogenomics has thus effectively resolved the ambiguous phylogenetic relationships in this genus. This work identifies nine previously undescribed Gnomoniopsis species, clarifies the species diversity and conserved genomic characteristics within the genus, and lays a foundation for subsequent taxonomic analyses of Gnomoniopsis.
authors: Wang X, Jiang Y, Liu W, Yan X, Sheng J, Ai C, Liu X, Zhang X, Meng Z, Wang S.
