title: Archaea are more hospitable hosts for mobile inteins than bacteria.
abstract: Intervening proteins, or inteins, are mobile genetic elements characterized by their ability to rearrange peptide bonds through a post-translational, self-splicing reaction. Here, we expand the scope of a prior investigation to reexamine the distribution of inteins across archaea and bacteria. This update represents 20- and 50-fold increases in archaeal and bacterial genomes, respectively. In accordance with previous findings, inteins are enriched in DNA replication, recombination, and repair (RRR) proteins, but they are substantially more prevalent in archaea than bacteria, a difference twice that previously reported. Moreover, mini-inteins lacking homing endonucleases (HENs) are more common in bacterial inteins, suggesting bacterial inteins undergo HEN domain loss more frequently than archaeal inteins. This reduction in the prevalence of HENs, the drivers of intein mobility, offers a potential explanation for the lower density of inteins in bacteria than in archaea. Furthermore, certain classes of bacterial intein-containing proteins primarily contain mini-inteins rather than full-length inteins. The enrichment of mini-inteins within certain bacterial protein classes suggests that HEN domains may impose a greater functional cost in these proteins, creating selective pressure for HEN domain loss and resulting in reduced intein mobilityIMPORTANCEInteins are translated within host proteins and removed via a self-mediated splicing reaction. Prior comparative genomic analysis established that inteins are abundant in both bacteria and archaea, and that their distribution is strongly biased toward proteins involved in DNA transactions. Utilizing genomes made available over the last decade, this work increases the number of putative inteins by over twenty-fold. By investigating the distribution of inteins that can spread throughout/between genomes compared to those that have lost their ability to act as mobile elements, we provide a possible explanation for the higher abundance of inteins in archaea than bacteria. This work not only highlights that archaea are more hospitable intein hosts than bacteria but also serves to update the catalog of known prokaryotic inteins, which will function as a resource to the communities interested in inteins as mobile elements, tools in protein engineering, antimicrobial targets, and post-translational regulatory elements.
authors: Ariagno TM, Winkelman JD, Belfort M, Lennon CW.

title: Microdiversity drives resilience and niche partitioning in the bloom forming cyanobacteria  Limnospira platensis
abstract: The intraspecific evolutionary mechanisms of adaptation in blooming cyanobacteria, particularly those occurring on small spatial and temporal scales, remain poorly understood. Here, we used the unique properties of Lake Dziani Dzaha, which hosts a persistent population of  Limnospira platensis inhabiting distinct macro-habitats, to explore the spatial and temporal dynamics of microevolution. The Lake Dziani Dzaha (Mayotte), very stable at least since 2010, has experienced a seismo-volcanic crisis from May 2018 to November 2019, characterized by CO₂ outgassing that led to the mixing of the initially seasonally stratified water column, as well as changes in numerous physicochemical parameters. Phylogenomic analysis of 108 strains isolated during sampling campaigns in 2010, 2014, 2022, and 2024 revealed a population that remained highly phylogenetically cohesive over time. In 2022, genomic expansion was observed, characterized by an increase in genome size due to the proliferation of insertion sequences and a subsequent loss of adaptive genes. By 2024, a rapid recovery of the 2010-2014 genetic content took place through multiple independent events of horizontal gene transfer. At the spatial scale, although no significant differences in gene content were detected, distinct subpopulations were identified based on allele frequencies. Some alleles were specifically fixed and subject to different selection pressures among the subpopulations, suggesting the existence of distinct ecotypes. Overall, this study highlights the role of microdiversity in rapid resilience of blooming cyanobacteria populations within dynamic environments and in their adaptation through niche partitioning.
authors: Le Vern A, Duval C, Frère J, Bouly J, Troussellier M, Hugoni M, Agogué H, Jézéquel D, Marie B, Bernard C, Halary S.

title: Transgenerational immune priming (TGIP) and its potential association with EGR1 in Penaeusvannamei.
abstract: Acute hepatopancreatic necrosis disease (AHPND) caused by Vibrio parahaemolyticus remains one of the most serious bacterial diseases affecting Penaeus vannamei aquaculture. Immune priming has recently emerged as a promising strategy for enhancing disease resistance in aquatic animals. However, the molecular basis of immune priming and its potential effects on offspring remain poorly understood. In this study, UV-inactivated V. parahaemolyticus (V160807) was used to induce immune priming in P. vannamei. Primed F0 female shrimp were subsequently bred to obtain F1 offspring, and disease resistance, histopathology, cellular immunity, humoral immunity, transcriptome profiles, and DNA methylation patterns were evaluated. Both the F0 and F1 generations exhibited higher survival rates, lower bacterial loads, enhanced hemocyte-bacteria binding capacity, and stronger immune-related enzyme activities following bacterial challenge. Transcriptome analysis revealed significant enrichment of genes associated with pathogen recognition, melanization, and immune signaling pathways. In particular, pattern recognition receptor (PRR)-related genes, including CLEC4G and DSCAML1, were markedly upregulated. Whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) showed that histone H3 genes were hypomethylated, whereas ATP synthase-related genes displayed hypermethylation. These changes were accompanied by suppression of several energy metabolism pathways. Integrated transcriptomic and WGBS analyses identified EGR1 as a candidate regulatory gene. In F0 shrimp, EGR1 exhibited promoter and gene-body hypermethylation accompanied by reduced expression. Similar methylation changes were detected at the EGR1 locus in F1 offspring, including a conserved 61 bp hypermethylated region within the promoter. Pyrosequencing and RT-qPCR were further used to evaluate the methylation and expression patterns of EGR1. These findings demonstrate that prior exposure to UV-inactivated V. parahaemolyticus induces immune priming in F0 shrimp and is associated with enhanced disease resistance and immune response in F1 offspring. The EGR1 DNA methylation and gene expression changes may contribute to the establishment of maternal TGIP.
authors: Zhu Z, Liu Y, Zhang H, Luo K, Wang Y, Mu C, Yan M, Wang X.

title: Detection, characterization, and evolutionary inferences regarding a novel virus identified in Amblyomma dissimile Koch, 1844 (Acari: Ixodidae) from the Amazon, Pará, Brazil.
abstract: Ticks are among the primary vectors of infectious agents of medical and veterinary importance, second only to mosquitoes in the number of pathogens transmitted to humans. These arthropods are capable of transmitting a wide diversity of microorganisms, including protozoa, bacteria, and viruses. Notable among tick-borne viruses are those associated with viral encephalitis, which cause severe acute and chronic neurological infections in humans. This study aimed to characterize the RNA virome of an Amblyomma dissimile specimen collected from a Boa constrictor rescued in the municipality of Ananindeua, Pará state, in the Brazilian Amazon, using an RNA metagenomic sequencing approach. A total of eleven viral sequences were identified, distributed across five families: Chuviridae (n = 2), Rhabdoviridae (n = 2), Orthomyxoviridae (n = 5), Nodaviridae (n = 1), and Orthototiviridae (n = 1). A key finding was the identification of Dissimile tick rhabdovirus a potential new member of the Rhabdoviridae family described here for the first time, with no prior records in the scientific literature. Additionally, segments of Granville quaranjavirus were detected in Brazil for the first time, expanding the known geographic distribution of this virus. These results highlight the underrepresentation of viral diversity associated with Brazilian ticks in reference databases, underscoring the need to expand metagenomic surveillance and virological characterization efforts in the country, particularly given the potential impacts of climate change on tick distribution and virus circulation dynamics.
authors: da Silva E Silva LH, da Silva SP, de Castro PHG, Maurício KD, da Silva FS, Dias DD, Hernández LHA, da Silva SLS, Reis HCF, Dos Santos LEC, do Nascimento BLS, Brandão RCF, Vieira DBR, Nunes BTD, Cruz ACR, Nunes Neto JP.

title: Purification of filamentous phage ssDNA genomes using Chaotropic salt/silica methods
abstract: Filamentous phages play important roles in molecular biology and bacterial pathogenesis. There is therefore great interest in the genomes of the phages, including M13 and Pf, which infect  Escherichia coli and  Pseudomonas aeruginosa , respectively. However, efficient methods for purifying single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) from filamentous phages are scarce and rely mainly on repurposed commercial kits developed for dsDNA. These kits yield variable amounts of ssDNA, varying considerably from one phage to another, their solutions are proprietary and troubleshooting, and customizing the protocol to improve purification is not possible. Here, we developed and optimized two protocols based on ssDNA binding to silica columns in the presence of guanidine hydrochloride and potassium iodide chaotropic salts, for filamentous phages M13KO7 and Pf4. The protocols achieved 60 to 100% recovery, equal to or higher than the Monarch Spin gDNA Extraction and DNeasy Blood and Tissue kits, with similar A  260/280 and A  260/230 ratios, intact DNA in agarose gels, and no detectable host genomic DNA by PCR. Recovery depended critically on the chaotropic salts and on ethanol, and did not increase at lower pH, consistent with a water-exclusion model in which hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonding dominate over electrostatic repulsion. Phage-specific differences in recovery indicate that optimization may be needed for some phages, which the fully customizable nature of these protocols facilitates. Comparing the virion ssDNA with the double-stranded replicative form (RF) revealed genome variants in both phages, including a shorter M13KO7 form lacking the kanamycin resistance-p15A insert, and illustrates the value of analyzing both RF and ssDNA forms to study filamentous phage biology. Implementing these protocols in routine filamentous phage workflows should facilitate their characterization and engineering.
authors: Perez-Rodriguez S, Khosravi A, Milla C, Bollyky PL.

title: Early-life core microbiota are associated with postlarval survival of  Penaeus vannamei  : A meta-analysis
abstract: Larviculture is critical to the production of  Penaeus vannamei , the world’s leading farmed shrimp species, but remains constrained by erratic postlarval survival. Although early-life microbiome establishment is increasingly recognized as essential for larval health and survival, microbiome-based hatchery interventions are hindered by limited understanding of larval core microbiota. Here, we synthesized publicly available and self-generated 16S rRNA gene amplicon datasets of larval and rearing-water microbiota from 13 studies encompassing seven major producing regions worldwide to characterize shrimp larval core microbiota, their assembly processes, and their associations with larval survival. Although larval prokaryotic communities exhibited stronger geographic variation than developmental-stage succession, a conserved set of dominant bacterial families, including  Roseobacteraceae ,  Vibrionaceae ,  Flavobacteriaceae ,  Moraxellaceae , and  Pseudoalteromonadaceae , consistently prevailed across developmental stages and regions. By integrating occupancy, persistence, and ecological network centrality analyses, we demonstrated that common, temporal, and ecological core microbiota differ substantially in composition, diversity, stage specificity, and ecological roles in network stability. Compared with non-core taxa, core taxa were generally assembled more deterministically, irrespective of core category, suggesting stronger host selection and/or more rapid dispersal during microbiome establishment. Core microbiota also generally showed stronger associations with postlarval survival than total communities or non-core taxa, although contrasting survival associations among core members indicated that core microbiota are not ecologically homogeneous. Our work provides the first systematic categorization and characterization of larval core microbiota throughout the shrimp larviculture cycle, offering new insights into the ecological significance of core microbiota and identifying potential universal targets for microbiome-based intervention in shrimp larviculture.
authors: Chen R, Zhang W, Yu J, Song H, Zhou Y, Chen C, Huang X, Zhang D, Yan M, Wang K.

title: Estimating Gene Prevalence with Incomplete Genomes: Application to the Prochlorococcus Pangenome
abstract: Gene prevalence is an essential statistic in population genomics, defined as the proportion of a population carrying at least one ortholog of a given gene family. Common approaches to estimating gene prevalence either assume complete genomes or exclude genomes below a completeness threshold, resulting in biased and high variance estimates that fail to take advantage of all available data. Here we developed a maximum-likelihood framework that explicitly models genome completeness in order to estimate gene prevalence and associated confidence intervals from collections of complete and incomplete genomes. We applied the methodology to marine Prochlorococcus, a globally abundant photosynthetic bacterium for which the majority of available genomes are incomplete. Our methodology produced gene prevalence estimates with associated confidence intervals for a total of 52,500 gene families, more than 4 times the number quantifiable using complete genomes alone. We find a core of 714 genes are likely universal to the Prochlorococcus genus and a substantial majority of 49,828 gene families occur at low prevalence. Our results reveal a Prochlorococcus pangenome dominated by rare flexible genes and provide a general framework for incorporating incomplete genomes into quantitative analyses of microbial genomic diversity.
authors: Blaskowski S, Christie LG, Raut Y, Fuhrman JA, Bien J, Armbrust EV.

title: Dynamic changes of chicken gut microbiota and resistome during enrofloxacin treatment against multidrug-resistant Salmonella based on metagenomics.
abstract: Antibiotics are widely used to treat and prevent bacterial infections in human and animals. However, the impact of antibiotic dose on bacterial burden and diachronic changes and transfer of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in gut bacterial infections remains unclear. Here, we used enrofloxacin (ENR) at sub-inhibitory (1 mg/kg b.w.), prophylactic (3.03 mg/kg b.w.), and therapeutic (10 mg/kg b.w.) doses to treat infections with Salmonella harboring plasmid pJX-4, with infected but untreated groups as controls. We found that subtherapeutic ENR may pose potential risks to the gut ecosystem. Specifically, sub-inhibitory ENR led to persistently high Salmonella and its carried resistance gene qnrS1 levels; under this dose condition, preliminary evidence suggested that intestinal Escherichia coli was a potential host for in vivo transfer of plasmid pJX-4. The prophylactic dose group showed significantly higher relative abundances of human bacterial pathogens and ARGs, especially during treatment. Furthermore, this group was enriched in genes related to oxidative stress, cellular signaling, and secretion systems, and these functional genes were primarily associated with ARGs. Overall, different ENR doses shaped distinct evolutionary trajectories of the gut microbiome and resistome. This study provides a theoretical basis for the rational use of antibiotics in treating bacterial infections.
authors: Chen Y, Chu J, Guo Y, Farhan MHR, Lu X, Wei H, Xie C, Wang X, Huang L, Cheng G.

title: Microbial volatile humulene orchestrates plant-microbe alliance to establish disease-suppressive rhizosphere.
abstract: Microbial volatile organic compounds (mVOCs) suppress growth and virulence traits of soil-borne pathogens, yet their ecological roles in disease suppression remain unclear. Here, we show that the sesquiterpene humulene from Streptomyces acts as a multifunctional regulator that suppresses bacterial wilt through coordinated inhibition of Ralstonia solanacearum, plant metabolic reprogramming, and rhizosphere microbiome modulation. We combined in vitro pathogen assays, pot experiments, microbiota transplantation, rhizosphere 16S rRNA profiling, root-exudate metabolomics, and plant and pathogen transcriptomics to investigate the direct and microbiome-mediated effects of humulene. Humulene reduced disease severity and pathogen abundance via a microbiome-dependent mechanism. Microbiota transplantation confirmed that the humulene-conditioned microbiome retains transferable disease-suppressiveness. Humulene also selectively enriched antagonistic Streptomyces, not by direct growth promotion, but by reprogramming tomato root exudation to produce lipid-derived petroselinic acid, which promoted Streptomyces growth, humulene production, and pathogen suppression. Root transcriptomics further revealed activation of lipid metabolic pathways involving alternative fatty acid desaturation and oxylipin signaling. Together, humulene functions as an ecological signal that integrates pathogen suppression, host lipid metabolism, and microbiome assembly to establish a disease-suppressive rhizosphere, enabling microbiome-informed control of bacterial wilt.
authors: Huang Y, Zhang F, Zhang J, Zhang W, Wang N, Wang X, Wei Z, Jiang G, Raza W.

title: Core bacterial and host fruit-specific yeast microbiota in a polyphagous fly pest.
abstract: Holometabolous polyphagous insects undergo metamorphosis and exploit multiple host plants, exposing them to highly variable ecological conditions across both life stages and host plants. Whether these insects harbor a stable core microbiota, a life stage- or a host plant-specific microbiota remains open questions. Here, we characterized fungal and bacterial communities associated with Drosophila suzukii across life stages (larvae, pupae, and emerging flies) and host fruits (cherry, blackberry, and strawberry) using 16S and ITS metabarcoding. We tested the relative influence of life stage and host fruit on microbiota composition using community and network-based analyses. First, we identified that yeasts, but not bacteria, were strongly structured among host fruits. Bacteria and filamentous fungi were shared across fruits, constituting a fruit core microbiota dominated by Gluconobacter cerinus, Tatumella sp., and Cladosporium spp. In contrast, yeast were rather fruit-specific: the genera Hanseniaspora and Pichia were mostly associated with cherries and strawberries, contrary to Metschnikowia with blackberries. Second, we found that fungal, but not bacterial, communities of D. suzukii were structured among host fruits. D. suzukii harbored a core bacterial microbiota composed of G. cerinus and a niche-specific (host plant-specific) microbiota composed of yeasts: Hanseniaspora was typical in individuals related to cherry and strawberry, whereas Metschnikowia to blackberry. We also verified that individuals from artificial laboratory infestations and natural field infestations harbored similar microbial communities when they developed under the same laboratory conditions. Components of both core and niche-specific microbiota were most likely horizontally acquired by D. suzukii from host fruits. Taken together, our results underline the importance of metacommunity approaches to investigate tripartite interactions among insects, host plants, and microbiota.IMPORTANCEThe role of microbiota in mediating interactions between phytophagous insects and their host plants has been well illustrated in specialist species. However, it has been less comprehensively studied in polyphagous species, which infest multiple host plants, and across life stages in holometabolous species that experience separate ecological niches through development. We tested the existence of a core, a niche-specific, and a stage-specific microbiota in a polyphagous holometabolous species, D. suzukii. We examined both fungal and bacterial communities in larvae, pupae, and emerging flies infesting three host fruits. Our results showed, first, that the assembly of bacteria, filamentous fungi, and yeasts on fruits is driven by different ecological processes. Second, D. suzukii harbors a core bacterial microbiota, a niche-specific microbiota constituted by yeasts and no stage-specific microbiota. Our study emphasizes the importance of considering jointly the assembly of host plant and polyphagous insect microbial communities to better understand insect-microbe interactions.
authors: Dunis S, Lapègue M, Deschamps C, Cesari L, Loiseau A, Facon B, Rode NO.

title: Genome-wide conservation and locus-specific coding variation in  Teratoramularia rumicicola  , a candidate microbial herbicide for  Rumex  weeds
abstract: The  Rumex pathogen  Teratoramularia rumicicola is a candidate microbial herbicide, but its functional genomic repertoire and variation among isolates remain poorly characterised. We generated a PacBio HiFi reference and evidence-supported gene annotation for TR4 and a short-read assembly for GR1, then compared the isolates using assembly- and read-based analyses. The TR4 and GR1 nuclear assemblies comprised 22.34 Mb (13 contigs; N50, 2.90 Mb) and 21.23 Mb (486 contigs; N50, 0.350 Mb), respectively. The TR4 annotation predicted 8,898 protein -coding genes, and the representative protein set was 96.7% complete in the Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologues assessment. Functional annotation identified 593 putatively secreted proteins, 258 candidate effectors, 355 carbohydrate -active enzyme (CAZyme) candidates and 20 predicted secondary-metabolite biosynthetic regions. Seven secreted CAZymes were prioritised as potential host-barrier-associated factors based on predicted activities and homology to virulence -related entries in the Pathogen–Host Interactions database. Despite 99.81% average nucleotide identity across aligned regions, read-based comparison identified 28,040 high-confidence isolate-fixed differences. Of 158 reconstructed candidate GR1 alleles, 147 showed strong assembly support. Notable differences included predicted truncations of two Zn(II)₂Cys₆ transcription factors, one adjacent to an intact nonribosomal peptide synthetase-like core gene, and a separate gene showing a localised repeat-induced point mutation (RIP)-like substitution pattern and predicted premature termination. Together, these resources and candidate loci provide a foundation for investigating pathogenicity and strain variation relevant to microbial herbicide development.
authors: Izumi M, Oka T.

title: ARG-PASS v2.0 expands global resistome surveillance to reveal previously unrecognized antibiotic resistance genes reaching the human gut
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a significant global public health threat, and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) that bacteria depend on to withstand treatment are its molecular basis. How ARGs move from environmental reservoirs into the human microbiome, and eventually into human pathogens, remains one of the most important unresolved questions in AMR research. The environmental reservoir remains poorly described and the routes connecting it to human microbiomes are largely inferred rather than observed. Describing that reservoir requires computational methods able to recognise ARGs that share little similarity with known enzymes, yet retain accuracy after experimental validation to enable scalable applications. Dietary exposure through unprocessed ferments offers a tractable setting in which such a route can be observed directly. Here we introduce ARG-PASS v2.0 and first apply it to a lake metagenome from Kolkata, India, where 10 of 11 tested candidates across diverse ARG classes were functionally confirmed after expression in  Escherichia coli . Given their clinical relevance, we then predicted 918 class B1 metallo-β-lactamases (MBLs) from MGnify and the PLSDB, with most diverging from characterized enzymes, but as widely distributed. Often tracking their hosts’ distribution, we find that most class B1 MBL diversity lies outside human-associated microbiomes. Cross-referencing against the Unified Human Gastrointestinal Protein catalogue identified a carbapenemase, an ANT, and class A β-lactamases from  Bacillus sonorensis and  Bacillus licheniformis , detected in South Korean fermented soybean paste (  doenjang ) as well as gut isolates of populations consuming these foods. Together, these results point to a largely chromosomal reservoir of ARG diversity that reaches the human gut through both resident and generalist hosts. Once in the human microbiome, treatment may be compromised directly if the host is an opportunistic pathogen, or after transfer to a clinical pathogen.
authors: Bartrop L, Grenier F, Bielawski J, Rodrigue S, Haraoui L.

title: Glowing pathogenic bacteria discovered in the Aral Sea – a harmless evolutionary feature or a hidden threat?
abstract: Abstract  Bioluminescent bacteria are widespread in marine ecosystems, yet whether they can establish stable populations in long-isolated inland saline lakes has remained unknown. Here we report species-level identification and comprehensive characterization of the first isolated bioluminescent bacteria from the Aral Sea, a formerly extensive inland water body that has remained isolated from the world ocean since its Holocene formation while experiencing extreme fluctuations in salinity, temperature and water level. We show that the luminescent microbiota comprises two marine species, Vibrio cholerae and Vibrio vulnificus. V. cholerae isolates displayed enhanced tolerance to low salinity and possessed a thermolabile luciferase. In contrast, isolated V. vulnificus strains grew and emitted light over an exceptionally broad elevated salinity range (5–70‰) and retained luminescence at temperatures exceeding 40 °C, indicating remarkable adaptation to the highly variable physicochemical conditions of the Aral Sea. Phylogenetic analyses place isolates close to contemporary type strains, and the retention of virulence-associated genes indicates limited evolutionary divergence, suggesting a relatively recent colonization rather than long-term independent evolution. Together, these results demonstrate that bioluminescent bacteria from pathogenic species can successfully colonize ecological niches in isolated inland saltwater ecosystems typically occupied by other Vibrio species in the open sea.
authors: Bazhenov S, Matveeva V, Vlasov A, Viushinskij P, Scheglova E, Kudryavtseva A, Malysheva E, Sakharov D, Aianka R, Ten O, Rastorguev S, Alexyuk M, Bogoyavlenskiy A, Prokopiev V, Gordeliy V, Manukhov I.

title: Identification of Soybean Bush Dwarf Disease Associated with Coinfection of a Phytoplasma and Cowpea Mild Mottle Virus in Guangxi, China.
abstract: Phytoplasmas and viruses are important pathogens of soybean (Glycine max) and other legumes, posing a severe threat to global legume yields. In this study, three soybean plants exhibiting severe bush dwarfing, stem necrosis, leaf deformation, and wrinkling were collected from Nanning, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, China. High-throughput sequencing coupled with reverse transcription-PCR (RT-PCR) was employed for virome analysis, while nested-PCR and conventional PCR with 16S ribosomal RNA (16S rRNA) universal and tuf gene-specific primers were used for the specific detection of phytoplasmas. All three samples were confirmed to be coinfected with Cowpea mild mottle virus (CPMMV) and Candidatus Phytoplasma. The complete genome sequence of CPMMV was determined, which showed the highest nucleotide identity with the CPMMV isolate GX NiuDaLi, and the putative new isolate was named CPMMV GX-NN. Biological inoculation assays showed that CPMMV GX-NN could infect Glycine max, Vigna sinensis, and Nicotiana benthamiana, inducing typical viral symptoms. Phylogenetic analysis based on 16S rRNA sequences and virtual restriction fragment length polymorphism via iPhyClassifier was further conducted, and the phytoplasma was classified into the 16SrII Group. This is the first report of coinfection by CPMMV and a phytoplasma in soybean plants in Guangxi, China, providing critical insights for diagnosing and managing soybean diseases caused by these pathogens.
authors: Liu J, Chen Y, Tang Z, Xu X.

title: Earthworm-assisted enrichment of specific indigenous soil microbes for the preferential degradation of hexaconazole R-enantiomer.
abstract: This study examined the influence of earthworm addition on the enantiomer-specific degradation of the chiral triazole fungicide hexaconazole, focusing on the associated functional bacterial communities in soil and earthworm casts. S-hexaconazole was preferentially degraded in soil, whereas R-hexaconazole strongly inhibited soil microbial activities. Earthworm addition preferentially accelerated R-hexaconazole degradation and eliminated its inhibitory effects. Two soil bacterial families, Sphingomonadaceae and Xanthomonadaceae, and two biodegradation genes, p450 and ppo, were associated with the preferential degradation of S-hexaconazole. Two bacterial strains, HEX1 and HEX2, which belong to Sphingomonadaceae and Xanthomonadaceae, respectively, degraded R-hexaconazole but preferentially degraded S-hexaconazole in pure culture. In the R-hexaconazole treatment, earthworms selectively increased the abundances of Sphingomonadaceae, Xanthomonadaceae, and ppo, with Xanthomonadaceae and ppo levels being 23.1% and 25.1% higher, respectively, than those in the S-hexaconazole treatment, thereby shifting the community-level degradation preference toward R-hexaconazole. Notably, similar patterns were observed in earthworm casts. Network and metagenomic binning analyses revealed that Sphingomonadaceae and Xanthomonadaceae were potential hosts of the p450 and ppo. These findings suggest that earthworms facilitate the enrichment of specific indigenous soil bacterial families (Sphingomonadaceae and Xanthomonadaceae) to accelerate the preferential degradation of R-hexaconazole, highlighting the potential of earthworms to mitigate the risks in chiral fungicide-contaminated soil.
authors: Han L, Wang Y, Wang Y, Li Z, Liu M, Ju C, Nie J, Wang X.

title: Genomic Exploration of CRISPR-Cas Systems in Raoultella species: Diversity and Architecture.
abstract: Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats and CRISPR-associated protein (CRISPR-Cas) systems are adaptive immune mechanisms that protect bacteria against invading mobile genetic elements. They can influence horizontal gene transfer, phage resistance, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) dynamics. Although these systems have been investigated in several Klebsiella species, information on historically defined Raoultella species remains limited. In this study, 103 complete genomes representing Raoultella species, currently placed within the broader Klebsiella lineage, were analyzed to characterize the distribution, architecture, and diversity of CRISPR-Cas systems. CRISPR-Cas loci were identified using CRISPRCasFinder and CRISPRone, followed by subtype classification, direct repeat and leader sequence analyses, spacer matching, Cas1-based phylogenetic analysis, and AMR determinant screening. Complete CRISPR-Cas systems were detected in 23 genomes, predominantly in R. ornithinolytica strains. All complete systems were chromosomally located, whereas plasmid-associated orphan CRISPR arrays were observed in selected R. ornithinolytica strains. Two major architectures were identified, with Type I-E being dominant and Type I-F restricted to fewer strains. Direct repeat analysis revealed six consensus sequences, while leader regions displayed conserved AT-rich motifs and strain-specific divergence. Spacer analyses suggested historical interactions with phages and plasmids, particularly mobile genetic elements associated with Klebsiella and other Enterobacteriaceae. Cas1 phylogeny showed subtype-dependent clustering, indicating that CRISPR-Cas evolution does not strictly follow core genome phylogeny. The coexistence of predicted CRISPR-Cas loci and AMR determinants indicates that the presence of these loci does not necessarily preclude the carriage of resistance determinants. Overall, this study expands current knowledge of CRISPR-Cas diversity among the analyzed Raoultella genomes and provides a genomic framework for future functional studies.
authors: Abuden AV, Çolak ÇY.

title: Functional convergence despite taxonomic turnover across coral-associated microbiomes.
abstract: Coral-associated microbiomes are fundamental to holobiont health and resilience, yet their community structures often demonstrate high taxonomic variability across host species. Whether such variability results in functional instability or reflects pervasive metabolic redundancy remains unclear. Here, we investigated microbial taxonomic structure, functional potential, and community assembly mechanisms across 15 coral species using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics. These communities exhibited extreme taxonomic heterogeneity, high beta-diversity, and the absence of a universally shared core genus, indicating strong host-specific filtering that dictates microbial membership. In contrast, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathway-based functional profiles exhibited striking convergence across hosts, revealing a conserved metabolic landscape despite extensive taxonomic turnover. Mantel and Procrustes analyses identified a weak but significant correspondence between taxonomic composition and functional potential, a pattern consistent with functional redundancy across coral-associated microbiomes. Null model-based assembly analyses further revealed a decoupling between taxonomic and functional organization. Taxonomic structure was shaped by a host-dependent balance of stochastic and deterministic processes, whereas functional profiles were predominantly assembled through stochastic processes, maintaining consistently high functional redundancy across hosts. Metagenomic profiling uncovered a two-tier functional architecture underlying this stability: a conserved, high-abundance metabolic core enriched in carbon and phosphorus cycling and stress response functions that support microbial persistence in the coral microenvironment, together with lower-abundance host-specific metabolic modules involved in nitrogen and sulfur transformations that enable niche adaptation. Thus, functional requirements primarily govern the coral-associated microbiome rather than taxonomic identity. This synergy between conserved survival traits and flexible metabolic capacities maintains holobiont homeostasis despite extensive taxonomic turnover.IMPORTANCECoral reefs rely on complex partnerships between corals and their associated microorganisms to maintain health and withstand environmental stress. However, it remains unclear whether changes in microbial communities across different coral species lead to loss of important functions. In this study, we examined microorganisms associated with 15 coral species from the South China Sea and found that coral species hosted highly different microbial communities, while maintaining similar microbial functions. Our findings reveal that different microbial groups can perform similar ecological roles, allowing coral-associated communities to remain functionally stable despite changes in microbial membership. This functional flexibility may help corals maintain biological balance under changing environmental conditions and provides new insights into how coral holobionts preserve resilience in the face of ecological disturbances.
authors: Wen X, Han S, Wu M, Show PL, Liao B, Cai Z, Zhou J.

title: Correlation-based analysis of gene expression in Cardinium, Wolbachia, and Tyrophagus putrescentiae reveals distinct host-symbiont interactions and parallel evolutionary expansion of infection-associated genes.
abstract: Cardinium and Wolbachia are phylogenetically distinct intracellular symbionts that have convergently evolved mechanisms to infect a wide range of arthropod and nematode hosts. Here, we investigated the interaction dynamics of two basal strains, Cardinium (cTPut) and Wolbachia (wTPut), in the stored-product mite Tyrophagus putrescentiae (Acari: Astigmata). The KEGG-annotated gene expression profiles of mite samples were analyzed in single infections (Cardinium or Wolbachia) and mixed infections across three time points (2, 4, and 6 months). Temporal effects on gene expression were marginal; therefore, correlation-based network analyses were used to characterize host-symbiont interactions. The symbionts exhibited distinct host-targeting strategies: Wolbachia displayed a "broad" interaction pattern characterized by numerous weak correlations with host KEGG genes, whereas Cardinium showed a "focused" strategy involving fewer but stronger correlations. These patterns were consistent across global KEGG data sets, immune and regulatory pathways (including AMPK, autophagy, endocytosis, Hippo, lysosome, MAPK, mTOR, and Notch), receptor subsets, and metabolic pathways. Consistent with these interaction patterns, orthologous analyses across Cardinium and selected Wolbachia genomes revealed that infection-associated genes are not broadly conserved but are enriched in lineage-specific, duplicated gene families, particularly in T. putrescentiae-associated symbionts. These findings indicate that infection-related traits evolve primarily through lineage-specific gene family expansion rather than conservation and suggest that basal Cardinium and Wolbachia employ fundamentally distinct host interaction strategies.IMPORTANCEThe study provides novel insight into host-symbiont interactions: Cardinium, Wolbachia infecting mite Tyrophagus putrescentiae, an important producer of allergens (i) Cardinium gene expression responds to the presence of Wolbachia, whereas Wolbachia gene expression shows no reciprocal response; (ii) the two symbionts employ contrasting host interaction strategies with the host, with Cardinium exhibiting fewer but stronger associations and Wolbachia showing widespread but weaker correlations; (iii) distinct host pathways are differentially associated with each symbiont; and (iv) we identified 40 of the most correlated bacterial genes to the host that include candidates of viral origin, suggesting a potential role of horizontally acquired elements in the host. Furthermore, evolutionary analyses demonstrate that infection-associated genes are primarily lineage expanded rather than broadly conserved across symbiont genomes. Given the allergenic relevance of T. putrescentiae, these findings suggest that symbiont-specific interaction strategies can indirectly influence host physiology and allergen production.
authors: Hubert J, Glowska-Patyniak E, Stara J, Green S.

title: A novel clonal and axenic isolation pipeline for the human gut protist  Blastocystis  reveals within-subtype strain coexistence
abstract: Blastocystis is the most prevalent protist in the human gut microbiome, but its study is impeded by limitations in existing cultivation methods that hinder routine axenic and clonal isolation. These barriers have left open the question of whether multiple strains of a protist species can coexist within a single host, as observed within the bacterial gut microbiota. To address this, we introduce egg-based monophasic (EBM) medium, a novel optically clear liquid medium that supports exponential growth of  Blastocystis from low inoculum densities in standard tissue-culture plates and flasks, a capability not supported by existing media formulations tested here. Using EBM medium, we established a modular axenization and clonal isolation pipeline and recovered axenic and clonally isolated cultures representing  Blastocystis subtypes 1–4 from human and non-human primate hosts. To investigate within-host strain diversity, we sequenced a subtype 1 culture before and after clonal isolation. The non-clonal culture yielded a 21 Mb assembly with gene copy distribution and allelic polymorphism patterns consistent with multiple strains, whereas its clonal derivative yielded a 15 Mb assembly with patterns consistent with a single strain. These results indicate that the original culture contained multiple closely related strains co-colonizing one host. We identified the same genomic signature in published xenic cultures established from single human donors, supporting the presence of strain-level diversity within  Blastocystis subtypes. Our pipeline provides a scalable platform for  Blastocystis cultivation, imaging, and clonal isolation, enabling investigation of strain-level diversity that may be obscured in non-clonal cultures.  Importance  Blastocystis is the most prevalent protist in the human gut, yet experimental investigation remains limited by a difficulty in obtaining single-microbe and genetically defined cultures. Existing methods make it difficult to separate the protist from associated bacteria or recover individual lineages from mixed cultures. We developed a liquid growth medium compatible with standard tissue culture plates, live-cell imaging, and a modular workflow for producing axenic and clonal isolates. We use this pipeline to create axenic and clonal isolates across four common subtypes. Applying this workflow exposed a mixture of closely related strains in a single-subtype culture, a finding supported by analyses of independent published cultures. This culturing pipeline enables controlled investigation of strain-level diversity, and provides a new experimental framework for the study of  Blastocystis biology and its interactions with the gut microbiome.
authors: Leon F, Shih JB, Keller LE, Palaniappan S, Degaetano L, Nine GA, Lind AL.

title: Spatiotemporal genomic epidemiology of Eurasian avian-like H1N1 swine influenza viruses
abstract: Abstract    Background  Eurasian avian-like (EA) H1N1 swine influenza viruses pose a zoonotic threat, yet their genomic evolution and dissemination across Eurasia remain incompletely understood. This study investigated genotype diversity, temporal persistence, and geographic spread, and assessed the association between live-swine trade and viral migration to inform surveillance.  Methods  We analysed 1,703 publicly available EA H1N1 genomes sampled from 19 countries between 2009 and 2025. Lineage assignments across all eight gene segments were used to identify genotypes and describe their temporal and geographic distributions. Time-scaled Bayesian phylogenetics and discrete phylogeography were used to reconstruct evolutionary relationships and migration patterns. Generalized linear modelling assessed migration predictors, including directed live-swine trade and sampling intensity. The mixed effects model of evolution was used to detect episodic diversifying selection in hemagglutinin, followed by structural mapping of candidate residues.  Results  We identified 19 genotypes. The wholly EA-derived genotype G1 accounted for 57.0% of genomes and was detected across nearly the entire study period. Many reassortant genotypes carrying A(H1N1)pdm09- or triple-reassortant-derived segments were detected over short intervals, although several showed prolonged persistence. Genotype composition differed geographically, with reassortant genotypes enriched in Asia and predominantly EA-derived constellations more common in Europe. Phylogeographic reconstruction indicated asymmetric dissemination within and between Europe and Asia, with Western Europe occupying a central position in the inferred migration network. Directed live-swine trade received the strongest support among migration predictors after accounting for sampling intensity. Sixteen candidate hemagglutinin codons showed evidence of episodic diversifying selection. Most candidate HA1 residues mapped to exposed regions of the globular head near antigenic regions.  Conclusions  EA H1N1 evolution across Eurasia was characterized by a persistent EA genomic background, regional genotype diversification through reassortment, and spread associated with live-swine trade. These findings support integrating genomic surveillance with animal movement data to guide surveillance along trade networks and improve the detection and assessment of emerging variants of zoonotic concern.
authors: Liu H, Zhang Y, Yi J, Zhou Z, Li C, Xu F, Ren R, Liao M, Sun H.

title: Bioprospecting cultivable microorganisms from the Pantanal reveals taxonomic and functional enzymatic diversity
abstract: Abstract    The Pantanal is one of the world’s largest tropical wetlands, yet its cultivable microbial diversity remains underexplored for biotechnological applications. We bioprospected cultivable bacteria, filamentous fungi, and yeasts from environmental samples collected across 10 Pantanal sites and screened them for seven enzymatic activities. A total of 122 isolates were recovered, comprising 73 bacteria, 46 filamentous fungi, and 3 yeasts, representing 51 taxonomic groups and 37 enzymatic profiles. Protease activity was the most frequent among bacteria (71.2%), all filamentous fungi were cellulase-positive, and chitinase activity was detected in only five bacterial isolates. Taxonomic diversity among enzyme-positive isolates varied according to activity and sample origin, with Shannon–Wiener diversity index values ranging from 0 to 2.86. Significant positive associations were observed between protease–lipase, laccase–amylase, and protease–amylase, whereas no origin–activity association remained significant after multiple-testing correction. Phylogenetic analyses identified three particularly divergent or taxonomically unresolved bacterial lineages: P_1.1_002 within  Rothia  , P_13.1_002 within  Pseudomonas  , and P_10.3_001 within the order Enterobacterales. These findings reveal broad taxonomic and functional diversity among cultivable Pantanal microorganisms and identify lineages of interest for further taxonomic and biotechnological investigation.
authors: Motta MLL, Martins GM, Coelho BCS, Bastos KGF, Vasconcelos DC, Conceição L, Okamura LA, Silva DS, Medina-Gallardo JC, Gomes KS.

title: Efficient benzo[a]pyrene bioremediation by a novel halotolerant Rhodococcus ruber TN-1 in salinity environment: Mechanical insight from whole-genome, degradation efficiency and microbial properties.
abstract: Benzo[a]pyrene (BaP) contamination in highly saline environments has received increasing attention; however, efficient degradation of BaP by halotolerant BaP-degrading bacteria from contaminated water and soils remains poorly understood. In this study, a novel BaP-degrading bacterium, designated Rhodococcus ruber TN-1, was isolated, and its BaP degradation performance was evaluated. Whole-genome sequencing revealed genes and gene clusters associated with benzoate and xylene transport and degradation, naphthalene degradation, and the catabolism of other aromatic compounds. Strain TN-1 exhibited high BaP degradation efficiency in water, with a degradation efficiency exceeding 95% after 3 d of cultivation. Inoculation with strain TN-1 significantly improved the BaP degradation efficiency in three types of saline soil. After 14 d of reaction, the BaP degradation rate increased from 12.08% to 26.94% in the control to 44.03-59.12%. Correlation analysis revealed that the degradation rate of soil BaP was positively correlated with soil catalase (CAT) activity and negatively correlated with salinity. Metagenomic and quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) analyses demonstrated that the addition of strain TN-1 significantly increased microbial abundance in three saline soils, with strain TN-1 becoming the dominant microorganism and accelerating the microbial degradation of BaP. These findings highlight strain TN-1 as a promising bioaugmentation agent for the remediation of BaP-contaminated saline soils.
authors: Yan Y, Wang YN, Wang F, Gao Y, Wang H.

title: Why does a gene cassette keep the company of an orphan reverse transcriptase? Pollutibacter on five continents
abstract: Abstract  Several bacterial reverse transcriptases (RTs) protect cells from phage, yet some fit no known family. Screening 189,630 genomes, we found an RT that none of our comparisons (known RT types, trees, predicted structures) places in a known family (nearest published-library RT at most 34.6% identical), which we call ESOL RT. It sits beside a gene cassette in 16 genomes, chosen for carrying it, from lake, river, pond and other waters in nine countries on five continents, all in one Bacteroidota genus, Pollutibacter. The cassette has a conserved upstream element and four genes at fixed positions, including a MIDAS-motif protein and a predicted metalloprotease-like one lacking H[EDQ]xxH. At 27 further Pollutibacter loci, 97 of 99 observable positions beside the RT hold a cassette part, both exceptions at one locus. No observable copy of the four neighbouring genes is disrupted, codon models suggest purifying selection, and long reads from other freshwater samples span up to six modules. In a post hoc search of 794 genomes, the element lies upstream of an RT at 18 of 19 hits, the 19th cut by a contig end. Yet relatives of the -1 and +3 genes occur as an adjacent pair with no RT detected nearby in 54 of 149 genera carrying a +3-type gene, so why does the cassette keep the RT's company? The pairing is observed; two questions remain: did the RT join an existing module, and does it work with it, as DRT10 is reported to with an RNA and a protein partner?
authors: Pyo C.

title: Comparative Metagenomic Analysis of Fungal Communities and Genomic Analysis of Yeasts from the Chilean Altiplano and Central Mountains
abstract: Fungal communities inhabiting high-altitude environments are exposed to multiple environmental constraints, yet their diversity and genomic characteristics remain poorly characterized. Here, we investigated fungal diversity across 10 high-altitude localities in the Chilean Altiplano and Central Mountain region using ITS amplicon sequencing, complemented by comparative genomic analyses of 11 yeast isolates. Fungal commu-nities were evaluated based on taxonomic composition, alpha diversity, co-occurrence patterns, and relationships among sampling localities. Yeast isolates were analyzed using genomic similarity, synteny, functional profiles, stress-associated proteins, enzyme homologs, and mitochondrial genome characteristics. Ascomycota was the dominant phylum, but fungal community composition and alpha diversity varied among localities, with geographic structuring evident at the genus level. Co-occurrence networks revealed highly connected fungal communities, while many ASVs remained unclassified at lower taxonomic levels. Genome-scale analyses supported the classification of three isolates as Sporobolomyces salmonicolor and eight as Naganishia spp., highlighting the value of ge-nome-based approaches for resolving taxonomic relationships. Functional profiles were broadly conserved, but differences in GPI-anchor biosynthesis, galactose metabolism, steroid biosynthesis, and mitophagy were detected between isolates. In addition, stress-related and potentially biotechnologically relevant enzyme homologs were iden-tified. Mitochondrial genomes showed a conserved core of oxidative phosphorylation genes but substantial variation in introns, ORFs, and synteny, indicating marked mi-tochondrial genomic diversity. Together, these findings demonstrate substantial eco-logical and genomic diversity among fungi from high-altitude environments in Chile and reveal functional and genomic features that may be relevant to environmental adaptation and biotechnology.
authors: Baeza M, Gomez M, Veloso C, Alcaino J.

title: Functional divergence within mulberry-associated Pantoea ananatis: Insights from comparative genomics and host-contact metabolomics.
abstract: Pantoea ananatis is a widely distributed plant-associated bacterium that can exhibit contrasting ecological functions, ranging from plant-beneficial activities to pathogenicity. However, the genomic and metabolic features associated with such functional divergence among closely related strains remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized 18 mulberry-associated P. ananatis isolates using phenotypic assays and selected Pa-6 and YSFJ as representatives of two predominant functional types for comparative genomic and host-contact metabolomic analyses. Pa-6 exhibited a beneficial-associated phenotype characterized by several plant growth-promoting and antagonistic traits, comparatively limited tissue damage, and lower disease severity during the later stages of co-inoculation with Ralstonia pseudosolanacearum XZqk. In contrast, YSFJ caused progressive wilt accompanied by bacterial aggregation, xylem occlusion, vascular disorganization, and tissue damage. Despite these contrasting phenotypes, Pa-6 and YSFJ shared approximately 98.9% average nucleotide identity. Comparative genomic analyses revealed differences in accessory-gene content, plasmid composition, and strain-specific homologous clusters. Annotation comparisons highlighted a GH19-associated locus in Pa-6 and wbpZ- and feoB-associated loci in YSFJ as putative gene-content differences. Exploratory pathway mapping of host-contact extracellular metabolomic profiles highlighted central-carbon, organic-acid, and redox-related processes in the Pa-6 treatment and carbohydrate transport and utilization, aromatic-compound metabolism, and stress-related processes in the YSFJ treatment. These results document contrasting host-associated phenotypes and provide genomic and metabolic context for further investigation, while the contributions of individual loci and phylogenetic background remain unresolved.
authors: Yuan T, Yang P, Huang X, Li R, Liu Y, Huang M, Li J, Yi H, Liu J.

title: Microbiome-Informed Genomic Prediction of CH4:CO2 Ratio in Holstein Dairy Cattle Using 16S rRNA Profiles and SNP Markers.
abstract: Ruminant animals produce methane as a by-product of microbial fermentation in the rumen, with cattle being the largest contributors among ruminants. Methane emissions may be influenced directly by the host's genetics and indirectly through host-mediated effects on rumen microbiome composition. In this study, we investigated whether modelling both direct and indirect genetic effects could improve the genomic prediction of breeding values for methane emissions. We used genotype, methane CH4:CO2 ratio and 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data (16S), including 16S genus (16S-G), 16S species (16S-S) from Danish Holstein cows. A conventional genomic best linear unbiased prediction (GBLUP) model was used as a benchmark and compared with a microbiome-informed GBLUP approach based on three linked linear mixed models for the prediction of breeding values. In GMBLUP, the first model regresses methane emissions on three random animal effects (archaeal 16S, bacterial 16S and polygenic effects) using corresponding microbiome and genomic relationship matrices. The second and third models separately regress archaeal and bacterial 16S on random animal effects defined by the genomic relationship matrix. We evaluated prediction accuracy using five-fold cross-validation. The GBLUP model, which used only genomic marker information, achieved a mean accuracy of 0.20 across the five folds when evaluated in the animal subsets corresponding to the 16S-G and 16S-S datasets, while GMBLUP showed higher accuracy, particularly for the 16S-G dataset, with a mean accuracy of 0.48. These results highlight that incorporating microbiome information into genomic prediction models may improve predictive performance for the CH4:CO2 ratio, although further validation in larger and independent populations is required before practical implementation in breeding programmes.
journal: Journal of animal breeding and genetics = Zeitschrift fur Tierzuchtung und Zuchtungsbiologie
authors: Saedi N, Zhang S, Lund MS, Cai Z, Karaman E.

title: Pan-Genomic Insights into Bradyrhizobium ottawaense: Highlighting a Strain with Unusual Host-Specific Compatibility.
abstract: Biological nitrogen fixation occupies a paramount position in sustainable agriculture. The present study elucidates the genomic diversity and symbiotic capabilities of Bradyrhizobium ottawaense focusing on the commercial B. ottawaense strain RCAM0104 to decipher the genetic bases of plant-bacterial interactions and the evolutionary adaptability of these microorganisms. Experimental assessments of symbiotic compatibility revealed that RCAM0104 effectively nodulates Arachis hypogaea, Glycine soja, and Vigna unguiculata, but is ineffective on Glycine max. Histological examinations confirmed successful infection processes in most host plants, with the exception of white nodules observed on cultivated soybean. Prediction of type III effectors in the RCAM0104 genome identified effector proteins potentially involved in its promiscuous symbiotic phenotype. These findings highlight the genetic flexibility of B. ottawaense and its capacity to adapt to diverse host plants. The observed host-specific nodulation patterns correlate with specific variations in the accessory genome, suggesting their potential role in determining symbiotic compatibility, potentially through gene transfer from local strains. This research contributes significantly to our understanding of the evolutionary dynamics and ecological plasticity of rhizobia in symbiosis with legumes, providing insights into the mechanisms regulating plant-microbe interactions. Based on these results, we hypothesize an evolutionary trade-off, where a loss of compatibility with one host may have occurred concurrently with the putative acquisition in compatibility with another.
authors: Kirichek EA, Tsyganov VE.

title: Multi-omics analysis reveals microbial and metabolic signatures associated with neutral detergent fiber digestibility in dairy cattle.
abstract: BackgroundThe rumen microbiome is central to fiber degradation in dairy cows, yet the precise functional and metabolic networks driving variations in neutral detergent fiber (NDF) digestibility remain poorly understood. Elucidating these microbiome-host interactions is critical for improving forage utilization and advancing sustainable dairy production.ResultsEmploying an integrative metagenomics-metabolomics approach, we characterized the rumen microecology of lactating dairy cows exhibiting high and low NDF digestibility phenotypes (n = 10/group). Metagenomic profiling revealed a significant enrichment of fibrolytic taxa (Prevotella sp., Lachnospiraceae bacterium) and carbohydrate-active enzymes in the high-NDF group (HI). In addition, species-level differential abundance testing showed that Methanobrevibacter spp. was more abundant in the low-NDF group (LO) than in the HI group, whereas no archaeal differences were detected at the phylum or genus levels. Functional and metabolomic analyses indicated broader enrichment of amino acid degradation functions and higher concentrations of major volatile fatty acids (VFAs) in HI cows, consistent with stronger overall ruminal fermentation activity. Furthermore, VFAs and microbial composition explained 54.3% and 43.0% of the variation in NDF digestibility, respectively. An exploratory machine learning model based on selected annotated metabolite features showed moderate discriminatory performance, with an out-of-bag accuracy of 77.19%.ConclusionsOur findings suggest that coordinated shifts in rumen microbial composition, amino acid metabolism, and VFA production are associated with variation in NDF digestibility in dairy cattle. These results provide a basis for future studies aimed at improving fiber utilization through microbiome-informed nutritional or breeding strategies.
journal: Journal of animal science and biotechnology
authors: Ma B, Xiao J, Xu Y, Chen T, Liu S, Zou S, Gao D, Zhuang Y, Li M, Wang W, Li S, Cao Z.

title: BioDecryptors, a Bioinformatics Escape Game for Undergraduate and Postgraduate Learners in Clinical Microbiology: Prospective Before-and-After Study.
abstract: BackgroundBioinformatics is increasingly important in clinical microbiology with growing use of genomic sequencing, metagenomics, and phylogenetic analyses. However, introducing bioinformatics concepts and tools to medical learners can be challenging. Gamified educational approaches may allow introducing these concepts while supporting learner motivation.ObjectiveThis study prospectively evaluated BioDecryptors, an educational escape game to introduce bioinformatics principles and tools in clinical microbiology, by assessing short-term changes in knowledge and self-reported motivation and evaluating participant satisfaction.MethodsWe conducted a prospective before-and-after study between January and September 2025. Volunteers were recruited from undergraduate medical programs at Université Paris Cité and postgraduate programs or training activities for MDs and PharmDs at Université de Nantes, Université Paris-Saclay, and the French Society for Microbiology. Overall, 55 participants were included: 22 (40%) second-year medical students and 33 (60%) postgraduate MDs or PharmDs. Participants completed BioDecryptors in teams of 3 to 4 using versions adapted to their training level. Knowledge was assessed before and immediately after the activity using 2 distinct 10-item tests assessing the same predefined learning objectives. Motivation was assessed using a 12-item, 5-point Likert questionnaire covering 3 predefined domains, and satisfaction was assessed after the activity. Pre-post knowledge scores were compared using paired t tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, as appropriate. Motivation items were analyzed using paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Statistical significance was defined as a 2-sided PResultsPaired knowledge assessments were available for 50 participants. Mean knowledge scores increased from 7.0 (SD 2.0; 95% CI 6.4-7.5) before the activity to 7.9 (SD 2.0; 95% CI 7.4-8.5) afterward (PP=.79). Motivation increased for perceived usefulness (P=.04), willingness to learn (P=.01), understanding of bioinformatics in diseases (P=.002), and confidence in bioinformatics abilities (P=.002). Curiosity (P=.46) and interest in real-life applications (P=.33) did not significantly change. Among 50 satisfaction respondents, overall satisfaction was high (mean 4.7, SD 0.5; 95% CI 4.6-4.9); 98% (48/49) of the respondents to the corresponding item indicated an interest in other escape game modules.ConclusionsParticipation in BioDecryptors was associated with short-term increases in bioinformatics knowledge and self-reported motivation, together with high participant satisfaction. Unlike previously reported escape games focusing primarily on clinical or infection-control topics, BioDecryptors integrates hands-on bioinformatics analyses into a clinical microbiology scenario and offers versions adapted to undergraduate and postgraduate learners. Our findings provide preliminary evidence supporting the feasibility and acceptability of this approach as a complementary educational resource for introducing bioinformatics in health professions training. Controlled studies with longer-term assessments are needed to establish its comparative educational effectiveness and knowledge retention.
authors: Dellière S, Gschwind R, Salmona M.

title: msDNA: the story of a unique satellite DNA molecule in bacteria.
abstract: msDNA, or multi-copy single-stranded DNA, is a small satellite DNA observed in DNA extracts from a bacterial cell. A genetic element, usually found on the chromosome, called a retron, is responsible for producing msDNA. This small single-stranded DNA has a unique structure and is synthesized by reverse transcription from an RNA template. Retrons and msDNA are found in a large variety of different bacterial species. The msDNA molecule has also been developed into an important tool for genetic engineering and genome editing. But the biological function of this unique DNA molecule remained a mystery for decades. Recent discoveries show that a retron element can protect bacteria from infection with a virus (phage) using an abortive infection strategy. And the msDNA molecule is required for this anti-phage property. A historical perspective on this unusual DNA molecule, recent breakthroughs into its functions, and a discussion of the current and possible future directions of study are presented herein.
authors: Lampson BC.

title: The attachment rate of Vibrio anguillarum to microplastics strongly varies with strain identity, particle characteristics, and environmental conditions.
abstract: Microplastics (MPs), resulting from plastic objects and waste degradation, are increasingly abundant, particularly in marine environments. They exhibit a hydrophobic surface on which biofilms form easily. Metagenomic analyses of these biofilms have revealed that they often contain bacterial species potentially pathogenic to humans or animals. For this reason, MPs are suspected to present a risk to public health by acting as a vector for pathogenic bacterial species. To better understand this hazard, we studied different factors potentially affecting the bacterial attachment rate to MPs. Focusing on the fish pathogen Vibrio anguillarum, a collection of 16 GFP-labeled strains was assembled, including isolates from infected fish. Their attachment rates were measured using fluorescence microscopy on three types of MPs (milled polypropylene and polyethylene terephthalate particles, and commercially available polystyrene beads). A strong effect of the particle type was found, with higher attachment rates on milled particles, whose surface appeared qualitatively rougher based on visual examination of scanning electron microscopy images. Our results also revealed an intraspecific variation in attachment rate, highlighting the need for testing several strains of the same species to assess attachment rate and related hazards. Finally, it was observed that when a biofilm had formed by field incubation of the MPs, the differences in attachment rates between particle types were erased. The attachment of V. anguillarum depends on a combination of strain-related factors, particle characteristics, and environmental conditions, highlighting the need to combine microbiology, materials science, and environmental sciences to achieve a comprehensive risk assessment associated with MPs.IMPORTANCEMicroplastics (MPs) are increasingly abundant, particularly in marine environments. They are suspected to present a risk to public health by acting as a vector for pathogenic bacterial species. Focusing on the fish pathogen Vibrio anguillarum, we measured the attachment rates of 16 strains on three types of microplastics (milled polypropylene and polyethylene terephthalate particles, and commercially available polystyrene beads). This study highlights a strong effect of the particle type, with higher attachment rates on irregular particles, as well as a strong intraspecific variation. In a second experiment, it was observed that when a natural marine biofilm had already formed on the microplastic particles, differences in attachment rates between particle types were erased. Our findings emphasize the importance of accounting for multiple factors when assessing the risks of MPs as carriers of pathogenic bacteria, with our study addressing the first step of the conceptual pathway linking attachment, persistence, transport, exposure, and ultimately infection.
authors: Massot M, Wimmer L, Moussawi MA, Hamet J, Parac-Vogt T, Rajkovic A, Dailey L-A, Callens M, Bedhomme S.

title: Specialist-generalist trade-offs in microbial growth rates across soil habitats.
abstract: Microbial life strategies are shaped by a fundamental ecological trade-off: specialization enables peak performance in a narrow niche, while generalization allows persistence across diverse environments, but may constrain maximal growth rates. In soils, this trade-off is particularly relevant in the rhizosphere and detritusphere-and at their interface, where co-occurring living roots and decaying residues are hypothesized to generate emergent biogeochemical conditions. Using H₂¹⁸O quantitative stable isotope probing (qSIP), we measured bacterial and fungal growth rates in the rhizosphere, the detritusphere, and in the combined presence of rhizosphere + root detritus. We classified taxa operationally as specialists (defined as microbes actively growing only within a single habitat) or generalists (defined as microbes actively growing in two or more habitats), reflecting realized growth breadth under the conditions tested. Bacterial specialists exhibited faster growth than generalists within the habitats where they grew, a pattern consistent with a trade-off between niche breadth and growth rate. Net relatedness and nearest taxon indices showed that total bacterial communities were phylogenetically clustered, while specialist and generalist communities were phylogenetically random, consistent with functional traits-rather than lineage-predicting realized growth-breadth strategy. In annual grassland soils, fast-growing specialists may dominate ecosystem processes when resources abound, and slow-growing generalists may sustain element transformations when conditions shift; understanding this interplay may inform predictions of soil-carbon trajectories.ImportanceSoil microbes play a crucial role in cycling carbon and nutrients, but their strategies for surviving and growing in different environments remain poorly understood. This study asks whether soil microbes that grow rapidly in one habitat trade off that speed against the breadth of habitats they can occupy. Using quantitative stable isotope probing of H218O -an approach that measures active growth rather than mere presence-we tracked bacterial and fungal growth rates across three root-influenced habitats: the rhizosphere, the detritusphere, and the combined rhizosphere + detritusphere. We found that microbes detected growing in only one habitat ("specialists") tended to grow faster within their habitat than microbes detected growing across multiple habitats ("generalists"), a pattern consistent with a trade-off between niche breadth and growth rate. This pattern was clearer for bacteria than for fungi. Although these classifications describe realized growth breadth under the conditions tested rather than universal organismal traits, understanding where and when specialists or generalists dominate may help inform predictions about the fate of soil carbon under changing plant inputs.
authors: Foley MM, Sokol NW, Stone B, Blazewicz SJ, Estera-Molina K, Greenlon A, Hayer M, Kimbrel JA, Pett-Ridge J, Hungate BA.

title: Architecture and Evolution of Prokaryotic Multicellularity: Common Patterns and Diversity.
abstract: Prokaryotes form multicellular structures under both natural and experimental conditions, through developmental processes that sometimes echo those known from eukaryotes. Recent research has increasingly focused on the mechanisms underlying bacterial multicellular organization and its evolutionary origins. In this review, we first consider the modes of group formation, that is, clonal or aggregative, and show how mixed strategies in prokaryotic systems complicate this division. We then survey bacterial and, where known, archaeal multicellular structures, focusing on common patterns and differences in developmental dynamics across species, and highlighting the "soft" similarities with eukaryotic tissues and organismal organization. Next, we discuss the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying the canonical hallmarks of multicellularity in prokaryotes. Finally, we discuss recent research on the evolution of prokaryotic multicellularity, drawing on experimental, computational, and comparative approaches. Studying the specific forms of prokaryotic multicellularity, beyond simplified descriptions (aggregative vs. clonal), is necessary for understanding its complexity, and its consequences for microbial ecology, biogeochemical cycles and the evolution of bacteria per se. The prevalence of multicellularity in bacteria and emerging evidence from archaea raise the possibility that LUCA already possessed multicellular traits, suggesting that multicellularity may be an ancestral feature of life. The emerging picture is that bacterial multicellularity only partly matches eukaryotic models, instead reflecting multiple independent evolutionary origins and a striking capacity to regenerate and diversify developmental programs.
authors: Sohl G, Schubert A, Mascher T, Colizzi ES.

title: Genome-wide identification and integrative analysis of the cytochrome P450 superfamily in pea (Pisum sativum L.) reveals candidate genes associated with Aphanomyces root rot response.
abstract: Cytochrome P450 monooxygenases (P450) constitute one of the largest and most functionally diverse enzyme superfamilies in plants, underpinning the biosynthesis of a plethora of primary and specialized metabolites involved in growth and development as well as stress response. Here, we present the first integrated genome-wide analysis of the pea P450 superfamily (CYPome), combining phylogenetic, structural, evolutionary, transcriptional, and genetic approaches to identify defense-associated candidates. We identified 210 P450 genes encoding 241 proteins in pea genome, classified into 45 CYP families across 10 clans. Comparative analyses revealed both highly conserved legume P450 lineages and a substantial fraction of pea-specific expansions, reflecting dynamic CYPome evolution. Gene structure and motif analyses confirmed conservation of core catalytic features, alongside family-specific variation consistent with functional diversification. A conserved core of many PsP450 genes induced across multiple pea cultivars at a wide range of time points post Aphanomyces euteiches infection together with their expression in root tissue was discovered. Integration of aphanomyces root rot resistance-associated quantitative trait loci further refined candidate prioritization, identifying PsP450s that co-localized with resistance loci, exhibited strong co-expression with PsIFS genes, and were rapidly induced upon infection. Collectively, this integrative analysis defines the pea CYPome and identifies a focused set of high-confidence P450 candidates likely involved in defense-associated metabolic reprogramming during A. euteiches infection. These findings provide a foundational resource for functional genomics and offer promising targets for improving disease resistance in pea and related legume crops.
authors: Tahir MS, Dhaubhadel S.

title: Bacterial and fungal community dynamics in black pepper (Piper nigrum) across different processing plants using culture-based and amplicon sequencing approaches.
abstract: Black pepper (Piper nigrum) is among the most commercially relevant spices worldwide, yet its microbial ecology throughout processing remains insufficiently understood, particularly in relation to food safety. Despite being a low-water-activity product, black pepper may harbor diverse bacterial and fungal communities, including spoilage microorganisms, mycotoxigenic fungi, and foodborne pathogens. In this study, we investigated the dynamics of bacterial and fungal communities along the black pepper processing chain in three distinct processing plants. A total of 154 samples were collected from processing plants A, B, and C in São Mateus, Espírito Santo, Brazil. Culture-dependent analyses included enumeration of aerobic mesophilic bacteria, Enterobacteriaceae, lactic acid bacteria, total fungi, and xerophilic fungi; fungal isolation and identification; and Salmonella detection and confirmation. Culture-independent profiling was performed by amplicon sequencing targeting the V3-V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene and the V9 region of the 18S rRNA gene. Microbial counts increased throughout processing, indicating that post-drying operations represent critical contamination points. Fungal isolation revealed genera of hygienic and toxicological relevance, including Aspergillus, Fusarium, Penicillium, and Cladosporium. Salmonella was detected in 14.3% of the samples, comprising nine serotypes, with the highest occurrence after drying. Amplicon sequencing identified 5 phyla and 85 genera in the fungal community, whereas for the bacterial community, 24 phyla and 475 genera were identified, with Ascomycota, Proteobacteria and Firmicutes predominating across samples. Alpha and beta diversity analyses demonstrated significant differences among processing plants and confirmed processing as a major driver of microbial community assembly. Collectively, these findings reveal processing-associated microbial shifts and underscore the urgent need for improved hygienic practices, targeted monitoring, and effective decontamination strategies for black pepper.
authors: Furtado MM, Margalho LP, Amorim-Neto DP, Lemos Junior WJF, Duarte VS, Garcia MV, Santos AFM, Rodrigues DP, Copetti MV, Sant'Ana AS.

title: Mycobacteriophage Cluster A Immunity Repressors: A Conserved Protein Fold Adapted for Diverse Biological Functions
abstract: Abstract    Mycobacteriophage cluster A immunity repressors are unusual in that they silence lytic gene expression by binding numerous DNA binding sites located throughout the viral genome. They can also provide immunity to infection by genetically similar phages that contain the same or similar DNA binding sites. Despite containing similar DNA binding sites and repressor proteins, cluster A viruses often display heteroimmune phenotypes, the molecular details of which are currently unclear. Using a combination of small-angle X-ray scattering, protein crystallography, bioinformatics, and DNA binding and  in vivo  immunity assays, we show that cluster A repressors conserve a common protein fold yet appear to provide DNA specificity through a narrow region of the novel stoperator DNA binding domain. Additionally, both viral and bacterial genomes contain cluster A-like repressor proteins fused to diverse protein domains, which suggest that these repressors have evolved to do more than just silence viral lytic gene expression.
authors: Wallen J, McKinney R, Park S, Bonogafsky H, Tuhro A, Turner M, Hollis T, Gainey M.
