title: Rumen metagenomics of Tan sheep with divergent growth rate: functional gene and MAG profiles do not distinguish the groups
abstract: Abstract    Background  Feed conversion ratio (FCR) is a key economic trait in lamb production, and the rumen microbiome governs the energy the host obtains from feed. Because genus-level biomarkers are inconsistent across studies, we examined whether efficient and inefficient Tan sheep differ at the level of metabolic genes and metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). Sixteen Tan sheep, drawn from a finishing cohort of 100 animals, were ranked by average daily gain (ADG) and split into a high-growth/low-FCR group (n = 10) and a low-growth/high-FCR group (n = 6); individual feed intake was not recorded, so ADG, not measured FCR, defined the groups. Rumen contents were deep-shotgun sequenced, assembled and binned. Of 3,283 retained KEGG orthologues (KOs), a candidate required both a Wilcoxon between-group difference (P Results  Global community structure did not differ (ANOSIM taxonomy R = -0.139, P = 0.95; function R = -0.064, P = 0.682). The two-layer screen yielded 36 direction-concordant KOs (54 between-group and 94 ADG-correlated; union 112), enriched for sugar-transport (ABC/PTS) and energy genes, whereas canonical VFA genes showed no detectable difference (buk, pct, acs; all P > 0.7; absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence). However, 36 double-evidence KOs did not exceed the label-permutation null expectation (null mean 67, 95th percentile 195; P = 0.59), and the same was true for each single layer (between-group: 54 observed versus null mean 131, P = 0.83; ADG-correlated: 94 observed versus null mean 167, P = 0.67). A classifier built on the 36 KOs and evaluated with the feature set fixed in advance reached AUC = 1.000 and 87.5% accuracy, but under nested cross-validation the same pipeline gave AUC = 0.767 and 56.2% accuracy (9/16), which did not differ significantly from the permutation null (null mean AUC = 0.525, 95th percentile 0.883; P = 0.190). Initial body weight was confounded with group (Spearman rho with ADG = 0.67, P = 0.005). Only three MAGs were double-evidence, all inefficient-enriched and negatively correlated with ADG, representing unnamed novel genera (two Firmicutes-affiliated and one Bacteroidota-affiliated).  Conclusions  In this cohort of 16 Tan sheep, growth-efficiency divergence was not accompanied by any statistically detectable remodelling of rumen functional genes: the carbohydrate-uptake and energy-metabolism candidate panel did not exceed permutation-based null expectations, no KO approached FDR significance, and no classifier generalised under nested validation. The 591 MAGs recovered here provide a breed-specific genome resource for Tan sheep, and the contrast between the non-nested (AUC = 1.000) and nested (AUC = 0.767) estimates quantifies how much apparent signal feature selection performed outside cross-validation can manufacture at this sample size.
authors: Wang¹ J, Fan¹ Y, Zhang¹ H, Ma¹ J, Ma¹ Q, Li¹ X.

title: Codfishes survived essential gene loss by functionally co-opting freshwater ovulatory pathways to marine egg hydration.
abstract: Adaptive evolution associated with dispensable gene loss is widespread in the animal kingdom. However, loss of genes essential for embryonic survival and the mechanisms that evolved to bypass negative selection and extinction are less well known. Here, we show that all Gadiformes, an ecologically dominant order of codfishes, lost the aqp1ab-type genes that are essential for the formation of hydrated pelagic eggs and embryonic survival of marine teleosts in oceanic environments. Despite such gene loss, codfishes produce some of the most highly hydrated pelagic eggs of all marine teleosts. To resolve this apparent paradox, we initially confirmed that the mechanisms of osmotic drive are conserved with other pelagic-egg-producing marine teleosts, and then conducted comparative transcript analyses of aquaporin water channels in distantly-related freshwater and marine teleosts. This uncovered Aqp4-type channels that have been chromosomally linked to the Aqp1-type channels in jawed vertebrate genomes for >450 million years as the primary candidates. Using immunolocalization, functional assays, and inhibition experiments with zebrafish and Atlantic cod as model organisms, we show that short isoforms of Aqp4 are required for egg ovulation in more ancestral lineages of freshwater teleosts and were recruited to the oocyte hydration pathway of codfishes. By contrast, the oldest and most modern lineages of marine teleosts producing pelagic eggs still utilize the aqp1ab genes for egg hydration. Our data thus reveal that codfishes survived essential gene loss by functionally co-opting freshwater ovulatory pathways to marine egg hydration.
authors: Rey-Alfonso Á, Yilmaz O, Chauvigné F, Finn RN, Cerdà J.

title: Identification and Expression Analysis of MLO Genes in Poa pratensis in Response to Powdery Mildew Caused by Blumeria graminis f. sp. poae.
abstract: Poa pratensis L. is an important perennial grass that is widely used in seed and sod production for turfgrass establishment. However, its health and aesthetic value are frequently threatened by powdery mildew infection. In this study, the Mildew Locus O (MLO) genes of P. pratensis were identified through transcriptome analysis of Kentucky bluegrass in response to Blumeria graminis f. sp. poae. A comprehensive bioinformatics analysis, including physicochemical characterization, protein interaction prediction, EggNOG annotation, domain identification, and phylogenetic reconstruction, was conducted. Expression profiling revealed distinct patterns of PpMLO gene expression among varieties with different resistance levels. In this study, 33 PpMLO genes were identified from transcriptome data of plants under powdery mildew stress. Transmembrane domain analysis revealed that seven PpMLO proteins contain seven transmembrane domains, with leucine being the most abundant amino acid. The protein interaction network suggested a coordinated signaling system involving seven PpMLO proteins and functional proteins from Oryza sativa L. GO analysis revealed that the core members of the PpMLO gene family regulate immune and stress response biological processes by targeting the membrane and endomembrane systems and through molecular functions such as enzyme activities and ubiquitination. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the PpMLO gene family members of P. pratensis clustered in the same group as the homologous MLO genes of Arabidopsis thaliana and O. sativa, suggesting that they may have conserved biological functions in the response to powdery mildew stress. Expression profiling revealed that three key candidate genes, PpMLO2, PpMLO13, and PpMLO14, exhibited distinct expression patterns across cultivars with varying resistance levels. In the moderately resistant cultivar 'Taihang', PpMLO2 and PpMLO13 were significantly upregulated (Log2 fold change = 6.31 and 6.21, respectively). In the highly susceptible cultivar 'Explorer', PpMLO13 was moderately upregulated (Log2 fold change = 3.85). In contrast, PpMLO14 was strongly downregulated in the susceptible cultivar 'Black Jack' (Log2 fold change = -6.82). These differential expression patterns indicate that the MLO signaling pathway may adopt distinct regulatory strategies depending on the genetic background of the host. The identification of PpMLO2, PpMLO13, and PpMLO14 as key susceptibility candidates provides clear targets for precision molecular breeding. Targeting these genes through gene silencing or genome editing represents a promising strategy for reducing reliance on chemical fungicides and promoting sustainable green management of powdery mildew in P. pratensis.
authors: Liang Y, Zhang Y, Guo Z, Zhu H, Han L, Zhao X, Gao P.

title: Viral potential to modulate antibiotic resistance gene succession through host interactions during food waste composting.
abstract: Composting can mitigate antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) risks, yet viral contributions to their dynamics remain unclear. Using time-series metagenomics, we investigated viral roles in ARG succession during composting of two food waste types. In both composts, ARGs followed an enrichment-decline-rebound trajectory accompanied by substrate-specific ARG-host turnover. Particularly, the maturation rebound involved the re-enrichment of high-risk ARGs, including tet(L) and lnu(G). Procrustes analysis showed significant associations of viral communities with bacterial and ARG profiles. Meanwhile, virus-host networks were organized predominantly around Firmicutes, with both temperate and lytic viral abundances correlated with ARG-host dynamics during the heating-to-thermophilic transition. Viral auxiliary metabolic genes (AMGs), annotated for central carbon metabolism, nutrient acquisition, and stress responses, may aid environmental adaptation in key ARG hosts, including Bacillus spp. Although mobile genetic elements (MGEs) provided important genetic contexts for ARG mobility, only four putative virus-mediated ARG horizontal transfer records were detected. Structural equation modelling suggested potential viral involvement through host interactions, while highlighting the importance of ARG hosts and MGEs in resistome succession. Further viral perturbation experiments are needed to clarify causal contributions in future. Overall, this study provides new insights into viral roles in resistome succession, informing resistance risk management during composting.
authors: Zhang L, Luo D, Yang J, Yang M, Yang Y, Yao R, Zhan M, Zhang Y, Su Y, Wang B, Xie B.

title: Progress and disparities in fungal genomics in the long-read era.
abstract: Fungal genomics has expanded rapidly over the past three decades, yet this growth has been phylogenetically uneven and many taxonomic gaps persist. Here we review the field from early efforts such as the Fungal Genome Initiative to the current era of third-generation long-read sequencing and compile publicly available assemblies to quantify trends in contiguity, completeness, long-read adoption and taxonomic representation. We argue that fungal genomics has moved from a period of data scarcity to one in which the principal constraints are taxonomic bias, inconsistent annotation, sparse metadata and the interpretation of complex genome structure. Substantial phylogenetic gaps remain, particularly outside Dikarya and among unculturable taxa, and only a minority of assemblies are annotated. We therefore identify priorities for the fungal community, including coordinated efforts to close major taxonomic gaps, improved repository metrics to facilitate the identification of high-quality assemblies and standardized genome annotation, which is lacking for most assemblies.
authors: Kroll E, Zoclanclounon YAB, Urban M, Hill R, Hammond-Kosack KE.

title: The differential effects of dupilumab and Janus kinase 1-selective inhibitors on the skin microbiome in adult patients with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis using metagenomic sequencing: results from the BioDay registry
abstract: Abstract    Background  The skin microbiome in atopic dermatitis (AD) is characterized by decreased bacterial diversity and increased  Staphylococcus aureus  colonization. Although dupilumab has been shown to improve the skin microbiome in adult AD patients, little is known about the effects of Janus kinase 1-selective inhibitors (JAK1-i). Therefore, the aim of this study was to evaluate the differential effects of dupilumab and JAK1-i on the skin microbiome of adult AD patients. Skin swabs were collected from dupilumab-treated patients (N = 10) lesional/facial at baseline (T0) and week 16 (T16), from JAK1-i-treated patients (N = 15) lesional/facial at T0, week 4 (T4) and week 28 (T28), and from healthy controls (HCs; N = 17) at a single time point. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was used to assess microbial composition and diversity. Results  During both treatments, the Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI) scores significantly decreased over time (both p S. aureus  abundance significantly decreased after 16 weeks of dupilumab, whereas a nonsignificant decrease was observed after 28 weeks of JAK1-i. Microbial diversity increased in dupilumab-treated patients, approaching levels observed in HCs, while no such shift occurred during JAK1-i treatment. In both groups, commensal bacteria and fungi remained less abundant than in HCs. Conclusions  Despite comparable clinical improvements, dupilumab induced a more pronounced shift in the skin microbiome towards healthy skin compared with JAK1-i.
authors: Vroman F, Top J, Boesjes CM, Bayraktar D, Schürch A, de Graaf M, Bruin-Weller MS.

title: Pangenome and transcriptomics reveal the genomic basis associated with interspecific variation of sexually dimorphic nuptial spines in moustache toads.
abstract: Sexual dimorphism is a widespread phenotypic innovation that plays a crucial role in species diversification, yet its genetic origins and evolutionary trajectories remain poorly understood in vertebrates. Leptobrachium provides a tractable system in which male moustache toads develop maxillary nuptial spines used in male-male combat, whereas closely related pseudo-moustache toads lack this trait. To investigate the evolutionary genomics of these sexually dimorphic nuptial spines, we construct a pangenome from chromosome-level assemblies of six Leptobrachium species and integrate trans-species transcriptomic analyses. We find that keratin gene expansion predated the origin of nuptial spines, potentially providing genetic material for keratinized skin innovation. Recently duplicated hair keratin genes acquired putative Hoxc13 binding sites, and promoter reporter assays confirm that Hoxc13 can activate these genes in both moustache toads and pseudo-moustache toads. Differential hoxc13 expression may therefore be more important for affecting whether duplicated hair keratin genes are recruited to develop nuptial spines. Transcriptomic comparisons further reveal maxillary skin-specific expression of genes involved in keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation, as well as melanogenesis during the formation of nuptial spines. In Leptobrachium tengchongense, which has undergone secondary loss of nuptial spines, igfbp2, a conserved gene highly expressed in keratinized skin appendages across amphibians, shows positive selection and represents a candidate associated with this evolutionary transition. Our study provides amphibian pangenome resources and highlights how gene duplication coupled with regulatory recruitment may shape the evolution of novel sexually dimorphic traits in vertebrates.
authors: Li J, Feng Y, Huang S, Xie S, Ai Q, Huang C, Xiong R, Zhao M, Wu H.

title: Phage N4 uses a SAR endolysin-holin system for host cell lysis.
abstract: Bacteriophages (phages) cause active host cell lysis to terminate their infection and release progeny into the environment. However, some phages have systems to delay their lysis, and thereby increase progeny yield, in specific conditions: a phenomenon called lysis inhibition (LIN). Two dissimilar phages of Escherichia coli are known to exhibit LIN: T4 and N4. In T4, a multi-protein mechanism stalls lysis and maintains the LIN state in response to superinfection in a high phage population density. However, the lysis proteins responsible for T4 lysis and LIN are not conserved with phage N4. In this study, we characterize the phage N4 proteins involved in lysis by molecular and genetic means. We define the functions of the minimal gene set required for lysis through heterologous expression and complementation. Furthermore, by sequence comparison with a selected mutant library that does not induce LIN, we have identified genomic regions both within and outside the lysis cassette involved in N4 LIN. We propose a model where N4 lysis proteins that execute rapid N4 lysis can be regulated to induce LIN. Despite the lack of conservation with T4 components, our study suggests that direct modulation of lysis initiation may be common and provides a springboard for identifying similar mechanisms in other phages.IMPORTANCEPhages are viruses that kill only bacteria. To do so, they use lysis proteins to disrupt the structural components of the bacterial envelope. There are commonalities between the phages that infect bacteria with similar structures, but there are also interesting differences we can exploit to learn more about specific phages or their bacterial hosts. In this study, we characterize the lysis proteins of the E. coli phage N4. Our results suggest that lysis regulation controls phage yield in N4 differently than in the well-studied phage T4. Future studies on the relationship between lysis proteins and phage yield could provide handles to use this information for optimal large-scale phage production for clinical or industrial applications.
authors: Awuah MB, Martin C, Chamblee JS, Tomaszewski AJ, Sullivan TE, Emilia Q, Tran S, Snowden JH, Niemiec KA, Zhu J, Ramsey J.

title: Genome-resolved taxonomy, global distribution, and EPS potential of Zoogloea, the canonical floc-former in wastewater treatment systems.
abstract: The bacterial genus Zoogloea is the fourth most abundant genus in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) globally, where it plays key roles in floc formation and nutrient removal but can also contribute to viscous bulking when highly abundant. The taxonomic assignment of Zoogloea has historically been inconsistent, as several taxa were classified based on phenotypic characteristics and later reassigned to other families or orders. This has obscured both the identity and distribution of Zoogloea and hindered interpretation of its floc-forming mechanisms, which have been attributed to polysaccharides that may not originate from phylogenetically defined Zoogloea. Using our collection of more than 22,000 high-quality genomes from global activated sludge systems (MiDAS global genome catalog), we identified 47 genomes affiliated with the phylogenetically defined Zoogloea. In combination with abundance data, this enabled resolution of the genus' taxonomy, biogeographical distribution, and metabolic diversity. Building on this framework, we mapped the phylogenetic distribution of a recently identified Zoogloea-associated floc-forming polysaccharide biosynthesis gene cluster by screening the MiDAS global genome catalog and GTDB. The gene cluster was identified across multiple genera within the Burkholderiales order, including Zoogloea, Thauera, Azoarcus, and Ca. Accumulibacter, as well as several previously undescribed taxa. The gene cluster is broadly conserved, with minor variations in gene composition and synteny, suggesting corresponding differences in polysaccharide structure. Genomes encoding this cluster also consistently contained co-occurring floc-regulating genes, indicating a common and widespread mechanism underlying floc formation in activated sludge systems.IMPORTANCEOperation of activated sludge systems depends on stable microbial floc formation for the separation of biomass from treated effluent. Floc formation is mediated by extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) produced by microorganisms, yet the identity, distribution, and biosynthesis of these polymers remain poorly characterized. Zoogloea is widely regarded as a canonical and model floc-forming genus associated with EPS production in wastewater treatment systems. However, its taxonomic classification has historically been problematic, as organisms were often assigned to Zoogloea based on morphology, leading to widespread misclassifications. This has blurred the true origin of polysaccharides attributed to the genus as well as their wider phylogenetic distribution, which has not been systematically resolved. Here, we map the distribution of the Zoogloea-associated polysaccharide biosynthesis gene cluster across a global genome data set, providing a framework to link phylogenetically defined taxa with floc-forming potential. This improves our understanding of EPS production in activated sludge systems and may support strategies for enhanced resource recovery.
authors: Vestergaard SZ, Liu L, Dueholm MKD, Nielsen PH.

title: An integrated gut phage catalogue of nonhuman primates reveals functional adaptation to host ecology and evolutionary link to humans.
abstract: Nonhuman primates (NHPs), the closest evolutionary relatives of humans, are pivotal models for biomedical and ecological research. Gut phage are recognized as critical modulators of gut microbial communities; however, comprehensive insight into gut phage of NHPs is lacking. We used gut metagenomes spanning 25 NHP species and constructed an integrated gut phage catalogue (IGPC) comprising 11 389 nonredundant phage genomes. Our results revealed that the composition and function of NHP gut phage were significantly influenced by host clade, dietary niche and lifestyle. Host clade exerted a stronger influence than dietary niche on gut phage diversity. The lifestyle of NHPs influenced gut phage diversity and altered auxiliary metabolic gene profiles for different NHP species. Comparatively, 78.5% of IGPC phages were detected in human guts, with higher prevalence in nonindustrialized human guts. crAss-like phage-the most prevalent human-associated phage-were abundant in NHP guts, while exhibiting distinct evolutionary differences from crAss-like phage of humans. These findings comprehensively characterize the gut phageome of NHPs, revealing NHP host-driven and environment-driven functional adaptations, and provide an evolutionary understanding of the gut phageome between NHPs and humans.
authors: Yang S, Jin L, Deng W, Xiao H, Yao Y, Xie M, Xu H, Zou L.

title: Ecological Roles of Bacillus Lipopeptides in Mediating Plant-Microbe Interactions and Rhizosphere Community Dynamics.
abstract: The plant-beneficial bacterium Bacillus velezensis and related Bacillus species are increasingly recognized as important contributors to plant growth and health, yet the ecological functions of their secondary metabolites in situ remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated how lipopeptides produced by Bacillus species influence plant performance and root-associated microbial communities. Using Arabidopsis thaliana as a model host, we show that bacterial lipopeptides produced during root colonization promote plant growth by enhancing the uptake of essential mineral elements, including magnesium, calcium, iron, and zinc. Transcriptomic analyses revealed that lipopeptides upregulated host genes involved in metal transport and homeostasis in roots, while downregulating negative regulators of metal uptake. The lipopeptide production reshaped the composition of root-associated bacterial communities by increasing the relative abundance of putatively beneficial taxa and altering overall rhizosphere community structure. Functional genes indicated that lipopeptide enrichment was associated with microbial pathways related to metal transport, nutrient acquisition, and stress adaptation, suggesting that lipopeptides modulate both plant and microbial traits relevant to nutrient cycling. These results provide new insight into the ecological roles of B. velezensis-derived metabolites in plant-associated microbiomes and highlight lipopeptides as promising targets for harnessing beneficial plant-microbe interactions in sustainable agriculture.
authors: Li H, Zeng X, Xi Y, Li Q, Li Z, Huang Z, Peng Z, Liu S, Cui S, Li C, Wei H, Wang S, Jia Y.

title: Social Behaviour Drives Gut Microbiome Community Assembly Among Wild Long-Tailed Macaques (Macaca fascicularis) in Thailand.
abstract: The 'social microbiome' conceptualises gut microbial communities as 'islands' of host social organisation. Yet, in comparison to broader aspects of social organisation such as animals' group membership and composition, the impact of inter-individual differences in sociality on microbiome community ecology remains less well studied. Among a wild but human-provisioned group of long-tailed macaques (Macaca fascicularis), we assessed the relative effects of individuals' sociality, compared to their demographic characteristics, anthropogenic and abiotic environmental factors, and microbe-microbe associations, on the relative abundance and co-occurrence of bacterial taxa. Bipartite network analysis showed that bacterial communities among macaques were nested rather than segregated or modular structures. Several 'core' bacterial genera were found across all macaques, but other 'non-core' bacteria were found only in a few macaques suggesting that their occurrence/abundance may be influenced by transient environmental factors. Joint Species Distributions Models showed that macaques' sociality, particularly their dominance rank and their connectedness or centrality within their social grooming network, had the strongest impact on taxa abundance, followed by their demographic characteristics, and finally their exposure to both anthropogenic and abiotic environmental factors. Phylogenetically distant taxa were more likely to co-occur within the same macaque hosts than phylogenetically related taxa. These findings confirm that microbiome communities are strongly influenced by the social status and connectedness of individual hosts. Nevertheless, the finding that some taxa were more prevalent among high-ranking or well-connected macaques, while others were more prevalent among low-ranking or socially peripheral macaques, warrants further investigation into how individual differences in social microbiomes might affect their health and fitness. Future studies, through the collection of behavioural and microbial data on additional macaque groups, may provide further insights into the relative effects of animals' social organisation and social behaviours on microbiomes.
authors: Balasubramaniam K, Kesh J, Aiempichitkijkarn N, Atwill R, Malaivijitnond S, McCowan B, Nimnual J, Sawaswong V, Visedthorn S, Payungporn S.

title: Genome architecture shapes the appropriate unit of comparison in small plant DNA viruses.
abstract: Comparative viral genomics often assumes that a single unit of analysis can be applied across datasets. However, this assumption becomes difficult to justify when viral genomes may be monopartite or multicomponent, and when multicomponent genomes differ in whether their components are co-packaged or separately encapsidated. Here, we developed an architecture-aware, alignment-free framework to compare five plant DNA virus systems spanning monopartite and separately encapsidated multipartite architectures, including two-component and six-component systems: cacao swollen shoot virus complex (CSSV), banana streak viruses (BSV), Dioscorea bacilliform viruses, cassava mosaic begomoviruses (CMB) and banana bunchy top virus (BBTV). After curation of public GenBank records, 1,342 sequences were resolved into three analytical panels, including a 130-genome monopartite panel comprising CSSV and BSV and a 1,206-record componentized panel. In the monopartite panel, whole-genome compositional geometry robustly separated CSSV and BSV. A sliding-window mosaicity analysis further prioritized a subset of CSSV genomes with elevated internal discordance, consistent with mosaic-like compositional heterogeneity. The principal panel-level results were retained with canonical 5-mers, and mosaicity rankings were stable across 300-, 400- and 500-nt windows and concordant with an independent alignment-based similarity-profile benchmark. In the componentized systems, component identity formed a strong and reproducible axis of sequence organization in both CMB and BBTV. However, their isolate-level configurations differed: the complete CMB pairs examined here consistently selected different nearest external isolates, whereas complete BBTV sets showed more heterogeneous neighbour configurations and higher component-configuration tension. These results suggest that, within the systems examined here, the biologically informative unit of viral comparison may shift with genome architecture, from whole genomes in the monopartite panel to paired or distributed component configurations in CMB and BBTV. We therefore propose architecture-aware, alignment-free comparison as a cautious screening framework for identifying cases in which deeper phylogenetic or recombination-focused follow-up is most warranted.
authors: Ahn E, Baek I, Oh S, Kandpal L, Kim MS, Meinhardt LW.

title: Nuclear Functional Divergence and Genetic Basis of Cap Colour Variation Revealed by T2T Genomes of Two Compatible Monokaryons in Pholiota adiposa.
abstract: Basidiomycete fungi maintain a dikaryotic state throughout their life cycle, in which two genetically distinct haploid nuclei coexist within the same cytoplasm. However, the extent and functional significance of inter-nuclear genomic divergence remain poorly understood. Here, we present the first telomere-to-telomere assemblies of two compatible monokaryons (D1 and D11) from a wild isolate of Pholiota adiposa, achieving 13 complete chromosomes with zero gaps and Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs completeness of 98.6% and 98.3%, substantially outperforming the previous fragmented assembly. The two nuclei exhibit only 75% collinear genes, with 570 (D1) and 668 (D11) strain-specific genes. D1-specific genes are enriched in energy metabolism, consistent with faster mycelial growth, while D11-specific genes are enriched in genetic information processing and mitogen-activated protein kinase signalling, revealing functional complementarity between the two haploid nuclei. Resequencing of 18 wild accessions identified two candidate regions associated with red pileus colour on chromosomes 6 and 12, the former as a major-effect locus and the latter harbouring multiple pigment-associated genes. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment implicated phenylalanine metabolism, tyrosine metabolism, and terpenoid biosynthesis in colour formation, suggesting coordinated regulation across metabolic networks. This framework facilitates dissection of nuclear functional divergence and provides candidate targets for understanding fungal phenotypic variation.
authors: Liu T, Fan Y, Liu Y, Yan D, Liu Y, Song S, Lu C, Guo Y, Zhang D, Sun S, Wang S, Gao Q.

title: From expression profiling to functional validation: evidence hierarchy and biomarker readiness of circular RNAs in aquatic animals.
abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are covalently closed non-coding RNA molecules that are mainly generated from precursor mRNAs through back-splicing. Owing to the lack of free 5' and 3' ends, circRNAs exhibit high stability and pronounced spatiotemporal expression specificity. In aquatic animals, recent advances in high-throughput sequencing and bioinformatic analysis have greatly expanded the catalog of circRNAs and uncovered their regulatory roles in growth, gonadal development, tissue regeneration, immune defense, and environmental stress responses. This review provides a systematic overview of circRNA biogenesis, representative molecular functions, identification strategies, and bioinformatic resources in aquatic animals, with particular emphasis on circRNA-mediated regulation during bacterial and viral infection, antiparasitic defense, trained immunity, and responses to physicochemical stressors. We further summarize the current evidence supporting the potential of circRNAs as candidate biomarkers for economically important traits, infectious disease monitoring, and ecotoxicological assessment. Importantly, we highlight the major bottlenecks that currently limit progress in this field, including incomplete genome annotation, algorithm-dependent identification bias, and the lack of robust in vivo functional validation. Overall, aquatic animals provide valuable non-model systems for expanding our understanding of circRNA biology, although many proposed regulatory mechanisms and translational applications remain to be further validated.
authors: Song KS, Guo M, Li CH.

title: Comparative genomics of Sympodiorosea identifies genome evolution mediated through selective pressure on the metabolic gene repertoire.
abstract: Biological interactions involving host-associated fungi are driven by chemistry shaped over evolutionary time. For antagonistic fungi, specialization often involves acquiring genes for novel secretions-including proteins and specialized metabolites-that mediate nutrient acquisition and host defense interactions. Here, we conducted a phylogenomic investigation of Sympodiorosea, ascomycetes commonly found in basal fungus-growing ant gardens. While Sympodiorosea and related genera (Escovopsis, Luteomyces, Manidigitorum, Escovopsioides) are canonically viewed as virulent mycoparasites, non-virulent species may also emerge within these attine-associated fungi. We explored genomic variation in Sympodiorosea to assess potential alternative lifestyles, focusing on the diversity and evolution of metabolic genes. Our study revealed a constrained selective landscape across the Sympodiorosea genome. However, outcomes of in vitro host interactions were diverse and predictable based on the antagonist's ant-species-of-origin, suggesting functional diversification. Phylogenomics indicated that gene gain/loss events in carbohydrate-active enzymes and specialized metabolism drive this diversification. Although selection acts intensely on metabolism-related genes overall, specific metabolic genes experience diversifying selection, indicating their critical role in host associations. Furthermore, Sympodiorosea exhibits protease gene expansions and contractions discordant with a strictly mycoparasitic lifestyle, suggesting either an alternative lifestyle within ant gardens or recent evolution from other niches. These results provide novel insights into fungal genome evolution and the chemistry of the fungus-growing ant symbiosis.
authors: Robinson JC, Berasategui A, Vidaurre Montoya Q, Rodrigues A, Sosa-Calvo J, Zimmerman Z, Christoper Y, Fernández-Marín H, Read TD, Gerardo NM.

title: Structurally reorganized Wmk lineage with distinct genomic context and restricted distribution in Wolbachia.
abstract: Patterns of diversity in symbiont effector genes provide crucial insight into evolutionary processes shaping their diversification, particularly those arising from host-symbiont interactions. In the widespread symbiont genus Wolbachia, the male-killing candidate gene wmk encodes a putative transcriptional regulator with at least 5 known phylogenetic types based on sequence divergence. However, additional wmk homologs characterized by large in-frame deletions and protein reorganization suggest that diversity extends far beyond sequence variation alone. Yet, the full extent of structural diversification in wmk effectors remains poorly understood. In this study, I analyzed homologous proteins from 251 Wolbachia genomes using comparative sequence and structure-informed approaches to comprehensively characterize wmk effector diversity. These results demonstrate that sequence and structural diversification largely follow similar patterns, with one newly identified lineage standing out due to pronounced structural reorganization. The distinct genomic neighborhood of this divergent lineage, relative to other wmk lineages, suggests additional diversity at the regulatory level. Together, these findings reveal that variation in protein structure and genomic context complements sequence-level polymorphism in shaping wmk effector diversity in Wolbachia. Further analyses indicate that symbiont supergroup and host taxonomic order constrain the distribution of the divergent wmk lineage, providing new insights into the evolutionary forces governing effector gene diversification in this important symbiont system.
authors: Sahoo RK.

title: Research Note: Complete genomic characterization and biological phenotyping of a genotype VI.2.1.1.2.2 pigeon-derived Newcastle disease virus strain HN25.
abstract: Pigeon paramyxovirus type 1 (PPMV-1) is a major cause of mortality in domestic and wild pigeons worldwide and has the potential to infect chickens, thereby posing a threat to the poultry industry. In this study, a PPMV-1 strain, designated HN25, was isolated and characterized. Its complete genome was sequenced and analyzed, and its biological and physicochemical properties were evaluated. Phylogenetic analysis classified HN25 into sub-genotype VI.2.1.1.2.2 (formerly VIk), which is the predominant sub-genotype currently circulating in China. The fusion (F) protein of HN25 contains the cleavage site motif ¹¹²RRQKR↓F¹¹⁷. The virulence indices-an EID₅₀ of 10⁷·⁶⁷/0.2 mL, a mean death time (MDT) of 55.2 h, and an intracerebral pathogenicity index (ICPI) of 1.75-indicate that HN25 is a virulent strain. Physicochemical characterization showed that HN25 is sensitive to chloroform and unstable under acidic (pH 6.0, 37°C, 1 h) and thermal (56°C, 30 min) conditions. Sequence alignment identified four mutations in the F protein within functional domains (P5S, P12S, C25Y, and D170N), with P5S, Q445K, A522T, and A549V being strain-specific relative to the consensus sequence. In the hemagglutinin-neuraminidase (HN) protein, only one mutation (I514V) was found within a neutralizing epitope, along with a rare non-conserved substitution (N440H). These findings provide baseline data on the genetic evolution and potential antigenic variation of the predominant PPMV-1 sub-genotype in China. The identified mutations offer candidate targets for future antigenicity studies and vaccine design, though experimental validation is required.
authors: Xiao H, Wang H, Song L, Sang S, Wang C, Zhou B, Zhang Y, Wang X.

title: Aeration rate regulates organic acid metabolism during cereal vinegar solid-state fermentation: Insights from quantitative metagenomics and targeted metabolomics.
abstract: Aeration is a critical parameter regulating organic acid metabolism during cereal vinegar fermentation, but its regulatory mechanism remains unclear. We integrated absolute and relative quantitative metagenomics with targeted metabolomics to elucidate how aeration affects microbial metabolism and organic acid formation. Bacterial abundance in the L, M, and H groups declined from 2.80-2.98 × 1011 to 7.93 × 109-1.97 × 1010 copies/ng DNA, whereas fungal abundance declined from 6.02-6.67 × 109 to 7.90 × 106-4.56 × 109 copies/ng DNA. Relative quantification suggested increases in microbial relative abundance, whereas their absolute abundances decreased sharply during fermentation. Aeration was associated with changes in microbial community and functional gene abundance. Subsequent acid accumulation may further influence microbial succession. Phased aeration enabled targeted modulation of organic acid profiles. In the L-H-M group, succinic acid and GABA increased by 5.89-10.29% and 7.66-13.31%, respectively, compared with constant-aeration groups. These findings provide a basis for precise control of organic acid profiles through stage-specific aeration.
authors: Zhang A, Li N, Zhang W, Huo X, Zhang R, Zhou Y, Zhou J, Song J, Wang M, Zheng Y.

title: Silent travelers: the potential of migratory birds and their ticks to introduce emerging viruses into Switzerland
abstract: Switzerland hosts over 400 bird species, many of which are migratory. Through diverse movement patterns, ranging from short distances to almost global migrations, these birds can introduce zoonotic viruses, such as West Nile virus (WNV) or avian influenza virus (AIV), as well as unknown and potentially emerging viruses. Furthermore, they facilitate the global dispersal of infected ectoparasites, particularly ticks, risking the introduction of novel tick-borne diseases. To assess this risk, we sampled 42 bird species (39 migratory, 3 resident) over seven months in 2023 at the Bolle di Magadino nature reserve and the Piano di Magadino area in the canton Ticino (Switzerland). This region, because of its transitional climate, serves as an important resting and breeding ground for migratory birds. In total, 496 oropharyngeal-cloacal swabs, 164 sera, and 22 associated ticks were collected. While RT-qPCR of the swabs detected no active WNV or AIV infections, ELISA testing identified Orthoflavivirus antibodies in 15 of 164 sera, indicating prior exposure. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing revealed a viral landscape spanning 33 families (29 of which were identified in birds). Within this virome, DNA viruses, predominantly  Circoviridae, Genomoviridae, and  Parvoviridae , dominated in abundance but exhibited low diversity. In contrast, the highly diverse RNA virome primarily reflected the birds’ dietary habits and the local habitat at the nature reserve. Notably, we report the first detection of Bole tick virus 4 (BoTV4) in Switzerland, identified in several ticks (  Rhipicephalus turanicus ) associated with long-distance migrants. This member of the newly established  Pestiviridae family is already established in parts of Asia, Africa, and Europe. This study provides the first active surveillance of the wild bird virome in Switzerland. Our findings establish a framework for the early detection of emerging viruses and underscore the role of migratory birds as dispersal vectors for ticks and novel tick-borne viruses.
authors: Gerber CM, Zezza G, Guidi V, Wyler M, Bachofen C, Kubacki J.

title: tWhEEL: a transcript-aware workflow for quantifying CRISPR knockout feasibility using transcriptome assembly
abstract: ABSTRACT  Gene redundancy can complicate loss-of-function experiments (knockout), and its extent varies among organisms and biological functions. Relating variation in gene redundancy to the availability of genome-editing targets can help researchers select tractable biological functions and experimental organisms. Here, we present the transcript-aware Whole-genomic Evaluation for Editing Locus (tWhEEL), a pipeline that infers redundancy in silico from transcript information and cross-references it with specific guide RNA designs. tWhEEL integrates CRISPR-Cas9 guide design with Gene Ontology (GO) and pathway annotations to compute a knockout feasibility index (KFI) for individual genes and functional categories. Interactive HTML reports link GO-associated KFI and pathway-associated KFI summaries to the contributing groups, genes, and guide candidates with links to QuickGO or WikiPathways. By linking sequence-level guide candidates to functional-level targetability, tWhEEL can support the selection of biological functions and organisms for reverse-genetic experiments. Applications to model and nonmodel datasets revealed distinct targetability profiles, including high full targetability in yeast and query-protein-set dependence in zebrafish. A zebrafish Fanconi anemia case study recovered 14 of 19 published target-site designs. By connecting sequence-level guide candidates with function-level experimental planning, tWhEEL provides a framework for comparing reverse genetic tractability and prioritizing biological functions and organisms for further study.
authors: Nakamae K, Bono H.

title: Genome-wide association study integrated with transcriptomic validation reveals polygenic architecture of Vibrio parahaemolyticus resistance in hybrid abalone (Haliotis discus hannai ♀ × H. fulgens ♂).
abstract: Vibrio parahaemolyticus is a major bacterial pathogen threatening abalone aquaculture, yet the genetic basis of host resistance remains poorly understood. Here, we combined a controlled challenge test, super genotyping-by-sequencing (Super-GBS), genome-wide association study (GWAS), and RT-qPCR to investigate resistance to V. parahaemolyticus in DF(Green Pacific hybrid abalone, Haliotis discus hannai ♀ × H. fulgens ♂, DF)abalone. A challenge dose of 3 × 107 CFU/mL was selected to discriminate resistant and susceptible individuals, and after final quality control, 478,959 SNPs were included in the GWAS, which identified 862 FDR-significant SNPs, including 332 that also exceeded the Bonferroni-corrected threshold. Candidate gene and enrichment analyses highlighted multiple processes related to immune recognition, signal transduction, lysosome function, and metabolic regulation. Several genes, including tlr2, prkg1, slc7a9, man2b1, and htr6, were further supported by differential expression between resistant and susceptible groups. Functionally, these genes may represent different components of the host response to bacterial infection, including pathogen recognition, immune signal transduction, amino acid transport, lysosomal degradation, and metabolic regulation. Their coordinated involvement suggests that resistance to V. parahaemolyticus is mediated by an integrated immune-response network rather than by a single gene or pathway. Overall, this study demonstrates that resistance to V. parahaemolyticus in DF abalone is a complex polygenic trait and provides valuable genomic resources and candidate markers for the development of disease-resistant breeding strategies.
authors: Fan C, Gan H, Zhao Z, Wang L, Yao Y, Li L, Wang Y, Zhang Z.

title: Metagenomic features of oral microbiome in Tibetan dental caries patients: An exploratory study.
abstract: ObjectiveThis study aimed to preliminarily explore the composition and functional potential of oral bacteria in Tibetan patients with dental caries, and to explore potential associations between the observed functional features and the high-altitude living environment and dietary habits.MethodsSaliva samples were collected from nine Tibetan individuals with dental caries. Sequencing was performed on an Illumina high-throughput sequencing platform. The obtained genomes were annotated and analyzed using the non-redundant protein (nr) database, Clusters of Orthologous Genes (COG) database, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG), Carbohydrate-Active Enzymes (CAZy) database, Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD), and Virulence Factor Database (VFDB).ResultsAcross the nine samples, seven dominant phyla and ten dominant genera were identified. At the phylum level, Bacillota (44.06%) and Actinomycetota (26.2%) were predominant. At the genus level, Streptococcus (25.96%) predominated. Functional annotation showed that genes and pathways linked to cell wall/membrane biogenesis (32,623 genes) and carbohydrate metabolism (39,016 genes) accounted for a notable proportion of the total, thereby forming an efficient metabolic cascade encompassing carbohydrate uptake, metabolism, and acid production. Furthermore, multidrug resistance-related annotations represented the largest CARD category (53.05%), whereas immune modulation-related annotations predominated in VFDB annotation (52.48%).ConclusionsThis study provides a preliminary description of the community composition and functional annotation features of the oral microbiome in Tibetan patients with dental caries, showing prominent annotations related to carbohydrate metabolism and biofilm-associated functions, as well as resistance- and virulence-related annotations. These exploratory findings may serve as an initial reference for future studies on dental caries in Tibetan communities using larger cohorts and experimental validation.
journal: Journal of stomatology, oral and maxillofacial surgery
authors: Li Z, Shi B, Luo N, Zhao C, Weng Q, Chen J, Wang M, Zhu D.

title: Massilia danxiaensis sp. nov., a novel bacterium isolated from red sandy conglomerate of Danxia Mountain with an experimentally supported complete tryptophan biosynthesis pathway.
abstract: Strain SYSU DXS3249T was obtained from a sandy conglomerate sample originating from the red-bed geological formation of Danxia Mountain, PR China. The isolate is an aerobic, Gram-stain-negative bacterium that grows at pH 6.0-9.0 (optimum, pH 7.0), 15-37 °C (optimum, 28 °C), and in the presence of 0-1% NaCl (w/v; optimum 0%). Phylogenetic analyses based on 16S rRNA gene sequences and core genome datasets placed the strain within the genus Massilia, exhibiting highest 16S rRNA gene similarity to Massilia suwonensis CGMCC 1.12743 T (98.8%), followed by Massilia haematophila CCUG 38318 T (98.3%). The genomic DNA G + C content was 65.8%. The respiratory quinone of strain SYSU DXS3249T was Q-8. The polar lipid profile consisted mainly of phosphatidylglycerol, diphosphatidylglycerol and phosphatidylethanolamine, and the major cellular fatty acids (> 10%) were C16:0, C16:1 ω7c and C16:1 ω6c. Genomic analysis revealed a complete tryptophan biosynthesis module (M00023), and its functionality was experimentally supported by growth in M9 minimal medium without exogenous tryptophan. This trait may be ecologically relevant, as tryptophan is a precursor of auxin and other indole metabolites, and warrants future investigation of environmental adaptation and plant-microbe interactions. Based on the polyphasic characterization, strain SYSU DXS3249T represents a novel species of the genus Massilia, for which the name Massilia danxiaensis sp. nov. is proposed. The type strain of the proposed novel isolate is SYSU DXS3249T (= MCCC 1K09422T = KCTC 8716 T).
authors: Sun MM, He HH, Guo DY, Han JR, Hu CJ, Chen F, Zhou T, She TT, Lin HW, Fang SQ, Li WJ, Dong L.

title: Pangenomics as a framework for discovering structural variants underlying cold tolerance in chilli pepper.
abstract: Main conclusionPangenomics-based structural variant discovery offers a transformative framework to resolve missing cold-tolerance heritability in chilli pepper and accelerate climate-resilient cultivar development. Chilli pepper (Capsicum annuum L.) is a globally important crop severely restricted by cold sensitivity. SNP-based GWAS explain only 20-30% of the variance in cold tolerance, leaving a "missing heritability" gap. The GanZi/XianSheng paradox cultivars sharing >99% coding sequence identity yet exhibiting 5-10-fold differences in cold tolerance strongly implicates regulatory and dosage-based structural variants (SVs) as the primary drivers of phenotypic variation, a gap that pangenomics is positioned to address. This review synthesizes pangenomics, structural variant discovery, QTL mapping, and genome editing as an integrated framework for developing cold-tolerant chilli pepper cultivars. Based on cross-species evidence from rice, barley, and tomato pangenome studies, we propose four SV mechanisms predicted to underlie the GanZi cold-tolerance advantage: (1) regulatory SVs in promoters of CaMYB80, CBF/DREB (DREB, Dehydration-Responsive Element-Binding protein), and CaICE1; (2) copy number variations (CNVs) in antioxidant gene families (CaSOD (Superoxide Dismutase), CaCAT (Catalase), CaAPX (Ascorbate Peroxidase)) and the chlorophyll biosynthesis gene CaALAD (δ-Aminolevulinic Acid Dehydratase); (3) transposable element insertions creating novel regulatory elements in osmolyte biosynthesis genes (P5CS (Δ1-Pyrroline-5-Carboxylate Synthase), BADH (Betaine Aldehyde Dehydrogenase)); and (4) chromosomal inversions coordinating master cold-regulator gene clusters. A multi-SV haplotype in GanZi is predicted to explain 60-80% of phenotypic variance in cold tolerance, more than three times the explanatory power of SNP-based approaches. We outline a pangenome construction strategy (15-17 genomes, PacBio/Nanopore long-read sequencing, 18-24 months, $650K-$980K) followed by SV-GWAS on 200-500 accessions to identify 10-25 high-impact SVs. A four-phase breeding roadmap integrates QTL identification (1-2 years), candidate gene discovery via fine mapping and VIGS (1.5-2 years), CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing via TSWV/TRV viral vectors achieving 6.3-77.9% heritable editing efficiency (2-3 years), and multi-environment field validation across 4-6 locations (2-3 years).This integrated pangenomics-to-breeding strategy is projected to deliver climate-resilient chilli pepper cultivars with 2-5°C improvements in freezing tolerance within 7-10 years, substantially outpacing the 10-12-year timeline of traditional breeding. The proposed structural variant mechanisms remain to be experimentally confirmed in pepper and represent a testable research agenda for the chilli pepper genomics community.
authors: Ahmad SS, Nawaz MA, Can W, Zhao Y, Xin L, Chen R.

title: Influence of Gliricidia sepium living support on rhizosphere bacterial recruitment and fruit metabolomics in black pepper (Piper nigrum).
abstract: The ability of the rhizosphere to recruit beneficial microorganisms is central to the sustainable management of crops. Here, we investigated, through shotgun metagenomic sequencing and mass spectrometry techniques, the microbial composition, antimicrobial resistance (AMRs), and metabolomic profiles of Piper nigrum cultivated under two support systems: living Gliricidia sepium support (SL/RL) and dead wooden support (SD/RD). Bulk and rhizosphere soils were sequenced to assess taxonomic structure and ARGs, with emphasis on Actinobacteria due to their relevance in antibiotic production. Actinobacteria were highly represented across the samples (~ 35%). Dead-support rhizospheres exhibited a broader ARG repertoire and greater abundance of taxa known to include antibiotic-producing members, whereas living-support rhizospheres showed reduced ARG diversity. Metabolomic analysis further revealed support-dependent physiological responses in the host plant. PLS-DA distinguished the two cultivation systems, and three defense-related flavonoids, such as sakuranetin, isovitexin, and orientin, which were enriched in fruits of plants grown with dead support, indicating activation of stress - and defense - associated metabolic pathways. Their low abundance in living-support plants suggests reduced physiological stress, likely linked to improved nutrient cycling and rhizosphere stability provided by G. sepium. However, the volatile and total phenolic profile did not display significant chemical alterations in the samples. Together, these results suggest that support type influences both microbial functions and plant secondary metabolism. Dead support creates a more stressful ecological context that enriches antimicrobial resistance genes ARGs and defense metabolites, whereas living support promotes a more balanced soil-plant-microbe environment, supporting the use of G. sepium as a sustainable and biologically advantageous cultivation strategy for black pepper.
authors: Chaves VA, Alegria OVC, Dantas CWD, Ferreira VBC, Martins DT, Joseph RC, Almeida LS, de Souza SD, Gomes PWP, da Silva JKR, Ramos RTJ.

title: Description of two novel species, Flavobacterium suaedicola sp. nov. and Flavobacterium wonjuense sp. nov.
abstract: Two novel bacterial strains, designated HNIBRBA15423T and 25HG05S-40T, were isolated from the root of a halophyte and from a riverbank soil in the Republic of Korea, respectively. Cells of both strains were Gram-stain-negative, yellow-pigmented, non-motile, and rod-shaped. Phylogenetic analysis based on 16S rRNA gene sequences revealed that both strains belong to the genus Flavobacterium. Strains HNIBRBA15423T and 25HG05S-40T showed the highest sequence similarity to Flavobacterium jejuense EC11T (98.5%) and Flavobacterium dankookense ARSA-19T (98.3%), respectively. The major cellular fatty acids of both strains included iso-C15:0, iso-C15:1 G, and iso-C17:0 3-OH. Both strains contained menaquinone-6 as the respiratory quinone and phosphatidylethanolamine as the major polar lipid. The complete genome sizes and DNA G + C contents were 4.29 Mb and 29.7% for strain HNIBRBA15423T, and 3.45 Mb and 36.6% for strain 25HG05S-40T. The average nucleotide identity (ANI) and digital DNA-DNA hybridization (dDDH) values were calculated. For HNIBRBA15423T, ANI value compared to F. jejuense EC11T were 85.2% with dDDH value of 29.5%. For 25HG05S-40T, ANI values compared to F. dankookense DSM 25687T and F. wongokense WG47T were 76.0% and 78.6%, respectively, with dDDH value of 20.3% and 21.5%. Based on the polyphasic taxonomic data, strains HNIBRBA15423T and 25HG05S-40T represent two novel species within the genus Flavobacterium, for which the names Flavobacterium suaedicola sp. nov. and Flavobacterium wonjuense sp. nov. are proposed.
authors: Shin SY, Kang H, Jeon Y, Han SI, Choi A, Song J.

title: Validated small Col-like accessory elements in a near-clonal same-host stool-blood Salmonella pair.
abstract: BackgroundNontyphoidal Salmonella can cause bloodstream infection in vulnerable hosts, yet the bacterial differences that remain when paired stool and blood isolates are already near-clonal are not well defined. Core-genome SNP analysis is useful for assessing relatedness, but may overlook small circular accessory elements that are difficult to resolve using standard assembly workflows. This study investigated whether a clinically linked same-host stool-blood Salmonella pair contained validated small Col-like accessory elements not apparent from core SNP analysis alone.MethodsWe analyzed a temporally adjacent same-host stool-blood Salmonella index pair, FB1-XY1, together with two short-interval stool-stool comparator pairs. The analysis integrated strict reads-backed core SNP filtering, accessory-element analysis, Illumina and ONT read-level support, PCR/Sanger/qPCR validation and public-genome background screening.ResultsStrict reads-backed filtering retained only four core SNPs in the FB1-XY1 pair, whereas both stool-stool comparator pairs had no retained strict core SNPs. Despite this minimal core-genome divergence, the blood isolate XY1 carried two validated small Col-like accessory elements. The first was an assembly-resolved 13.8-kb ColRNAI-like plasmid containing ColRNAI-like replicon hits and duplicated cka/colicin K-like annotations, with a Proteinase K-sensitive inhibitory phenotype. The second was a 5,241-bp Col156-like circular element, contig_40, which was not represented as a near-full-length replicon in the final XY1 closed-assembly output but was supported by full-length XY1 Illumina and ONT read coverage, 116 ONT junction-spanning reads, PCR, Sanger sequencing, multi-colony screening and qPCR. FB1 Illumina reads showed no corresponding support for contig_40. In a screened public Salmonella background of 16,456 genomes, strict full-length hits were rare for both elements: 2 hits for the 13.8-kb plasmid and 15 hits for contig_40. Neither element had a strict full-length hit among 402 screened Muenster genomes.ConclusionsThese findings identify small Col-like circular accessory elements as a validated, assembly-sensitive layer of genomic variation in a near-clonal same-host stool-blood Salmonella pair. By showing that clinically linked stool-blood isolates can differ at the level of small circular accessory elements despite minimal core-genome divergence, this study extends paired-isolate interpretation beyond core SNP relatedness alone. Integrating read-level evidence, molecular validation and public-genome context may improve the interpretation of small circular elements in clinical microbial genomics.
authors: Tong K, Zhou J, Wang J, Huang Z, Ye M, Chen H.

title: Electroacupuncture alleviates chronic pain and comorbid depression through Gut-Metabolite-Brain axis remodeling to restore mPFC Glu/GABA balance.
abstract: The comorbidity of chronic pain and depression is increasingly recognized as a systemic disorder involving dysregulated microbiota-gut-brain communication. Although electroacupuncture (EA) has demonstrated therapeutic efficacy for both pain and depression, the mechanisms linking peripheral microbial-metabolic remodeling to central neurotransmitter regulation remain incompletely understood. Here, we employed an integrated multi-omics approach in a spared nerve injury (SNI) rat model to investigate the gut-metabolite-brain mechanisms underlying EA's efficacy. EA significantly alleviated mechanical hypersensitivity and depressive-like behaviors while restoring mPFC Glu/GABA balance, accompanied by normalization of the glutamate transporter EAAT2 and the GABA-synthesizing enzyme GAD67. Metagenomic analysis showed that EA remodeled the gut microbial ecosystem by increasing microbial diversity, suppressing opportunistic pathobionts, including Bacillus cereus, Alistipes onderdonkii, while enriching SCFA-associated genera, including Butyricimonas and Romboutsia. These alterations were accompanied by coordinated remodeling of amino acid and butanoate metabolism. Correlation network analysis identified Pipecolic acid as a central metabolic node linking gut microbial alterations with mPFC GABAergic neurotransmission and behavioral recovery. Although individual bacterial genera did not significantly mediate its restoration, causal mediation analysis demonstrated that the Pipecolic acid-GABA axis significantly mediated improvements in both mechanical allodynia and anhedonia, supporting Pipecolic acid as a functional metabolic hub linking peripheral metabolic remodeling to central GABAergic regulation. Collectively, these findings identify peripheral metabolic remodeling as a key mechanistic interface through which EA coordinates gut microbial ecology and central neurochemical homeostasis, providing a systems-level framework for understanding the therapeutic mechanisms of acupuncture in pain-depression comorbidity.
authors: Li S, Huang J, Lin D, Luo D, Fu W, Liu J.

title: Genome compartmentalization in a fungal insect pathogen reveals a second mating-type locus on an accessory chromosome.
abstract: The genomes of many fungal pathogens include rapidly evolving regions with high transposable element densities. Such regions often contain genes important for pathogenicity and may be non-core genomic elements carried on accessory chromosomes that are variably present among isolates considered to be members of the same species. Here we present a pangenomic analysis of a fungal insect pathogen, Metarhizium acridum, using six chromosomal assemblies that include isolates from four different continents. We show that the pangenome of M. acridum exhibits a continuum of compartmentalization, with a core genome that contains most of the carbohydrate-active enzymes, while accessory genes are primarily located in gene-sparse regions which encode many small secreted proteins, termed effectors, that are active during host interaction. Furthermore, we identified the first accessory chromosome in M. acridum. In contrast to the accessory chromosomes of many other fungal species, this chromosome does not encode any known effectors or secondary metabolite proteins related to pathogen-host interactions. Instead, the accessory chromosome is enriched in functions related to sexual reproduction and carries genes from both the MAT1-1 and MAT1-2 mating-type idiomorphs, in addition to the canonical MAT locus found on the core chromosomes. Notable as, within the genus Metarhizium, M. acridum is one of few species considered to regularly reproduce sexually. Our findings suggest that the presence of this accessory chromosome further facilitates sexual reproduction, possibly even primary homothallism, in the otherwise heterothallic M. acridum. Overall, our study suggests a novel mechanism in which an accessory chromosome may enhance the capacity for a fungal pathogen to undergo recombination.
authors: Parker DM, Wilson AM, Nogueira C, Nielsen KN, Posada SM, Hansen LH, Nielsen TK, Habig M, De Fine Licht HH.

title: Genomic epidemiology of human parvovirus B19 in Southern Brazil, 2015-2024.
abstract: BackgroundHuman parvovirus B19 (B19V) causes erythema infectiosum and, in severe cases, has been associated with hydrops fetalis and transient aplastic crises. Despite its clinical importance, particularly in vulnerable groups such as pregnant women and immunocompromised individuals, epidemiological and genomic data on B19V remain limited.Methods and resultsWe investigated 4,118 samples collected from patients with exanthematous illness in Rio Grande do Sul, Southern Brazil, between 2015 and 2024 using serological and molecular testing, and developed an amplicon-based whole-genome sequencing protocol for B19V, generating 47 near-complete genomes. B19V was detected across all age groups, with a higher frequency among females (62.4%), and among adults aged 21-40 years. Viral circulation was detected year-round, with a modest increase in July and a more pronounced peak in September, consistent with Southern Hemisphere winter seasonality. Forty-one genomes from the 46 included in the dated phylogeny clustered in a single well-supported clade containing sequences from other Brazilian states, with Rio Grande do Sul sequences interspersed rather than forming a single lineage derived from one introduction. The remaining five genomes clustered with sequences from other regions of Brazil and Argentina. This phylogenetic pattern reflects sustained endemic circulation through repeated local transmission and is not adequately captured by current genotype-level classification systems.ConclusionsThe findings of this study expand the genomic understanding of B19V in South America and provide important insights into its molecular epidemiology, seasonal patterns, and evolutionary history in Southern Brazil.
authors: Gregianini TS, Bermann TL, Möllman É, Martiny F, Munhós HC, Ruivo AP, Bauermann M, Crescente L, Patzer J, Baethgen LF, Nunes Z, Wallau GDL, Veiga ABG, Salvato RS.

title: Design and evaluation of probe-capture sequencing for clinical  Neisseria gonorrhoeae  specimens
abstract: ABSTRACT  Characterizing the molecular epidemiology of  Neisseria gonorrhoeae is essential for understanding disease burden, elucidating transmission dynamics, and informing clinical decision-making and public health interventions. Given that routine, culture-independent diagnostics rapidly and sensitively detect this difficult-to-cultivate pathogen, aligning genomic surveillance with these workflows is necessary to understand its epidemiology and evolutionary dynamics. To address this challenge, we investigated the utility of probe-capture sequencing to selectively enrich for pathogen-specific DNA during next-generation sequencing. Custom biotinylated oligonucleotide baits were designed using genetic information from publicly available genomes hosted on Pathogenwatch. Of the 32,574 assemblies, 2,877 representative genomes were selected to inform probe generation using core genome amino acid distance clustering and representation of unique resistance-associated genotypes and predicted resistance phenotypes. The resulting probe set provided generous coverage of the reference genome,  N. gonorrhoeae FA 1090, with 94.6% nucleotide coverage and 99.3% of annotated genes covered by at least one probe. Piloting this technology on 12 clinical urine specimens with variable relative pathogen abundances revealed that probe-capture sequencing substantially increased the relative abundance of  N. gonorrhoeae sequence reads from a complex sample (fold-change range, 226 - 2046), enabling considerable genome coverage, the construction of high-quality genome assemblies, and the detection of resistance-associated genotypes. These findings demonstrate that probe-capture sequencing is a viable method for enriching  N. gonorrhoeae genetic material from clinical samples, enabling culture-independent genomic investigations into the epidemiology of hard-to-culture pathogens and providing actionable insights to inform clinical and public health interventions.  IMPORTANCE  Understanding the molecular epidemiology of bacterial pathogens can illuminate population diversity, transmission dynamics, and genotypes associated with bacterial traits and clinical outcomes. Difficulties in cultivation hinder our ability to understand the epidemiology of  Neisseria gonorrhoeae . Aligning genomic surveillance methodologies with existing clinical diagnostic modalities is essential to guiding the implementation of innovative genomic surveillance. In this paper, we used representative public genome assemblies to design custom biotinylated oligonucleotide baits to successfully increase pathogen-specific DNA yield from complex clinical urine specimens during next-generation sequencing. Probe-capture sequencing markedly improved detection of pathogen-specific genetic material from clinical specimens, enabling construction of high-quality genome assemblies and detection of resistance-associated genotypes. Collectively, we demonstrate that probe-capture sequencing is a viable method for sequencing hard-to-culture pathogens from clinical specimens, highlighting how this technology could strengthen genomic investigations into the epidemiology of these pathogens and provide actionable insights to inform clinical decision-making and public health interventions.
authors: Singh A, Gontjes KJ, Badri Narayanan D, Won PM, Brunelle BW, Green SJ, Popovich KJ, Snitkin ES.

title: A Two-Stage ESM-Based Machine Learning Pipeline for Robust Hierarchically Evaluated Enzyme Function Prediction.
abstract: Accurate enzyme annotation remains a major bottleneck in translating rapidly growing protein sequence data into biological knowledge. Enzyme Commission (EC) prediction is particularly challenging because enzyme functions are organized hierarchically, annotations are often imbalanced across classes, and sequence similarity alone may be insufficient to resolve functional differences. To address these challenges, we developed ESM-ECForest, a 2-stage framework that combines protein embeddings generated by the pretrained language model ESM-2 (Evolutionary Scale Modeling 2) with random forest classifiers. The first stage distinguishes enzymes from nonenzymes, whereas the second assigns one or more EC numbers to proteins predicted to be enzymatic. On an external benchmark comprising 25,778 protein sequences, ESM-ECForest achieved competitive weighted F1 scores among the evaluated off-the-shelf methods, decreasing from 0.94 at Level 1 to 0.90 at Level 4. The largest relative improvements were observed for lyases (EC 4), ligases (EC 6), and translocases (EC 7), although EC 6 and EC 7 remained the most difficult classes internally. Uniform manifold approximation and projection of the ESM-2 embedding space showed clustering patterns that broadly reflected enzyme functional relationships, suggesting that the pretrained representations capture functionally relevant information. These results support the use of pretrained protein language model embeddings as an effective foundation for enzyme annotation. By combining pretrained protein representations with a lightweight supervised classifier, ESM-ECForest provides a scalable approach for EC prediction and may facilitate functional annotation of proteins from large microbial genomic and metagenomic datasets within the taxonomic and EC-label space represented during model development.
authors: Hua X, Grimaud GM.

title: Viral diversity and activity in Arctic tundra soils in wintertime
abstract: Arctic soils store vast amounts of carbon and are warming faster than the rest of the globe. Still, little is known about microbe-mediated feedback responses to the ongoing environmental changes in the warming Arctic. Specifically, viral diversity, functions, and virus-host interactions remain largely unknown in northern soils outside the growing season. Here, we analyzed the diversity and activity of viruses in oroarctic tundra soils during wintertime using metatranscriptomics. Through de novo virus prediction as well as targeted searches, we identified 995 viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs) in total. Most of these vOTUs, 93%, represented RNA viruses, part of which were presumably segments of multipartite genomes. RNA vOTUs were classified mainly within the phyla Lenarviricota (259), Kitrinoviricota (198), Pisuviricota (135), Ambiviricota (103), Negarnaviricota (79), and Duplornaviricota (42). Thirty-seven DNA vOTUs (mostly Caudoviricetes) were also detected, suggesting active viral infections. In total, 81% of all vOTUs were assigned with a putative host organism, mostly fungi (515 vOTUs). Viral communities were distinct across vegetation types, and pH and moisture contributed to the differences. Putative novel clades within Ambiviricota and Orpoviricetes were identified, expanding their known diversity. The study contributes to uncovering diverse RNA viruses and viroid-like elements in Arctic tundra soils and highlights that soil viruses remain active in wintertime.

title: Extensive and heterogeneous viral circular RNA production during Zika virus infection
abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are covalently closed RNA molecules with regulatory functions. Although virus-derived circRNAs (vcircRNAs) are well characterized in DNA viruses, their occurrence in RNA viruses remains poorly understood. Recent reports in coronaviruses and hepatitis C virus suggest that vcircRNA production extends beyond nuclear-replicating viruses. Here, we show that Zika virus (ZIKV), a vector-borne orthoflavivirus, produces vcircRNAs during infection of neural stem cells. Using a custom computational pipeline optimized for viral back-splice junction detection, we identified at 72 hours post infection a core set of 113 putative vcircRNAs shared across three biological replicates and distributed throughout the viral genome. Eight candidates spanning different genomic regions and abundance levels were experimentally validated by rolling-circle reverse transcription and Nanopore sequencing. These findings provide the first evidence of vcircRNA production in an orthoflavivirus, suggesting that circular RNA biogenesis may represent a previously underappreciated feature of RNA virus biology.
authors: Stradiotto M, Vezzi A, Vardeu M, Mercorelli B, Vogiatzis S, Loregian A, Barzon L, Toppo S, Lavezzo E, Trevisan M.

title: Artificial intelligence applications in microbiota-gut-brain axis research: Implications for Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Alterations in the gut microbiota (GM) are increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis through the microbiota-gut-brain axis (MGBA), influencing neuroinflammation, amyloid-β deposition, and tau aggregation. The inherent complexity of microbiota data necessitates artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) to identify novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets. In this narrative review, we examined AI applications in AD-related GM research, including metataxonomic and metagenomic approaches. AI methods facilitate microbial signature identification and enterotype characterization associated with AD progression, enable multi-omics integration clarifying molecular pathways linking GM dysbiosis to neurodegeneration, support predictive modeling for early AD detection, and inform personalized MGBA-targeted interventions. Employed techniques include classical ML (e.g., random forests) for taxonomic classification, deep learning (e.g., neural networks) for complex pattern recognition, and explainable AI for identifying key bacterial taxa and metabolic functions. Significant challenges persist regarding methodological standardization, larger longitudinal cohorts, and ethical considerations in clinical applications. Future priorities include developing interpretable models, integrating longitudinal multi-omics data to establish causality, and validating AI-derived insights for precision AD prevention and treatment. AI uniquely enables high-dimensional, non-linear analyses that advance understanding of microbiome-brain interactions, though clinical translation requires rigorous validation and interdisciplinary collaboration.
authors: Lista S, Emanuele E, Cuperlovic-Culf M, Mahdi A, Singh V, López-Ortiz S, Khoramipour K, Merino-País M, Minoretti P, Cisale GY, Heslegrave A, Imbimbo C, Sancesario GM, Bendlin BB, Imbimbo BP, Zetterberg H, Santos-Lozano A.

title: Exploring endophytic actinomycetes from Shiraia fruiting bodies to enhance fungal hypocrellin A biosynthesis.
abstract: The medicinal fruiting bodies of Shiraia harbor diverse microbial communities that are increasingly recognized as important regulators of fungal secondary metabolism. While endophytic bacteria and fungi associated with Shiraia have recently attracted considerable attention, the diversity and functional roles of endophytic actinomycetes remain largely unexplored. Here, we combined culture-dependent isolation with high-throughput 16 S rRNA amplicon sequencing to investigate the endophytic actinomycete community associated with Shiraia fruiting bodies. A total of 28 actinomycete isolates representing four genera were recovered, with Streptomyces being the predominant culturable genus. Functional screening identified the native endophyte S. pseudogriseolus A6 as the most effective elicitor of fungal hypocrellin A (HA) biosynthesis. Genome analysis revealed abundant carbohydrate-active enzymes and 27 secondary metabolite biosynthetic gene clusters, indicating a strong genetic potential for fungal colonization and metabolite-mediated communication. Co-cultivation with live strain A6 markedly enhanced both intracellular and extracellular HA accumulation without significantly affecting fungal biomass. Under the optimized co-cultivation conditions, total HA production reached 296.0 mg/L, representing a threefold increase over the monoculture control. Furthermore, A6 coordinately upregulated the expression of HA biosynthetic genes and metabolite transport genes. This study provides the first characterization of endophytic actinomycetes associated with Shiraia fruiting bodies and identifies actinomycete elicitors capable of stimulating fungal HA biosynthesis. These findings expand current knowledge of the Shiraia microbiome and highlight endophytic actinomycetes as promising microbial resources for enhancing fungal perylenequinone production.
authors: Shen WH, Zheng LP, Zhou JQ, Wang JW.
