title: Expanded comparative genomics supports labial gland disease viruses as a distinct and deeply divergent lineage within Naldaviricetes.
abstract: Labial gland disease viruses (LGDVs) are recently identified dsDNA viruses infecting ants, but their diversity, genomic coherence, and taxonomic boundaries have remained unresolved. Here, we expanded LGDV members by mining public arthropod genome assemblies and sequencing field-collected ants. Novel LGDV genomes were recovered from Pheidole selathorax, Proformica mongolica, Messor orientalis, and geographically distinct Anoplolepis gracilipes populations. Comparative genomic analyses demonstrate that LGDVs retain the conserved core genes in the order Lefavirales, class Naldaviricetes, share additional conservative genes with Apis mellifera filamentous virus and related viruses (AmFV/AmFLV), and encode an LGDV-restricted conservative gene set. Amino acid identity, conservative site, and gene neighborhood analyses support the internal coherence of LGDVs while distinguishing them from AmFV/AmFLV, which retained only partial local gene neighborhood similarities and lacked detectable genome-wide macrosynteny with LGDVs. Phylogenies inferred by protein sequences and structures were broadly congruent, showing that predicted protein structures retained complementary lineage-discriminating signal across deeply divergent naldaviricetes, and recovering LGDVs as a monophyletic sister group to AmFV/AmFLV. Molecular dating further supported a deep separation between these lineages, indicating that LGDVs and AmFV/AmFLV represent distinct, long-term divergent groups rather than recent derivatives of one another. Collectively, these findings support LGDVs as an internally coherent, deeply divergent, and ant-associated virus family in the order Lefavirales, class Naldaviricetes.ImportanceLarge dsDNA viruses within the class Naldaviricetes encompass deeply divergent lineages. The recent discovery of LGDVs suggests that these ant-associated viruses have a closer evolutionary relationship to the phylogenetically isolated honey bee-associated AmFV/AmFLV than other Naldaviricetes viruses. However, the classification status of LGDVs and AmFV/AmFLV remains to be determined. In this study, we identified five novel LGDV genomes from four different ant species. Comparative analyses of protein sequences and structures, as well as gene neighborhood and molecular dating analyses support that LGDVs belong to an internally coherent and divergent ant-associated lineage that is distinct from AmFV/AmFLV. This study expands the known diversity of ant-associated naldaviricetes. The broad congruence between sequence- and structure-informed phylogenies highlights the value of structure-informed approaches for resolving deep relationships among highly divergent large dsDNA viruses.
authors: Jiang S, Gong S, Gu Y, Hu J, Chen H.

title: Microbial profiling of Drosophila in French Guiana reveals candidate microbial taxa associated with native and invasive host.
abstract: Invasive alien species (IAS) threaten biodiversity, human health, and economies, yet host-associated microbiome differences between invasive and native species remain poorly understood in natural systems. We investigated bacterial and fungal microbiomes of IAS and native Drosophila species collected along an anthropisation gradient in French Guiana. IAS occurrence declined strongly from coastal anthropised habitats toward rainforest localities. Using bacterial 16S rRNA and fungal ITS metabarcoding of pooled flies, we assessed microbial diversity and community structure across host species, host category (invasive vs. native), and locality. IAS-associated bacterial communities showed reduced alpha diversity and differed in structure from those of native Drosophila. Bacteriome variation was also associated with host phylogeny and locality; because host category was partially confounded with these factors, differences cannot be attributed solely to invasion status. Fungal communities were primarily associated with locality and host species. We further identified core and exclusive taxa and compared bacteriome composition with global reference datasets and microbiome literature, identifying bacterial and fungal taxa preferentially or exclusively associated with invasive or native hosts. Overall, our study characterises microbiome variation between invasive and native Drosophila in French Guiana and identifies candidate taxa for future functional investigation.
authors: Laffargue TT, Pollet N, Brousseau L, Miller WJ, Hua-Van A, Chouteau M.

title: Breaking the ice: multiple origins of ice-binding/antifreeze proteins.
abstract: Ice-binding proteins (IBPs) enable organisms to survive freezing environments by binding to ice and inhibiting crystal growth. Their remarkable structural, taxonomic, and evolutionary diversity makes them an exceptional system for studying protein evolution. This review examines the origins, structures, and distribution of IBPs across fishes, arthropods, plants, microorganisms, and other taxa. Comparative genomic analyses have revealed the progenitor genes of all known fish antifreeze proteins (AFPs), with the alanine-rich α-helical AFPs demonstrating repeated convergent evolution from diverse progenitors. β-solenoid IBPs have arisen repeatedly in arthropods, plants, fungi, and microorganisms. Although these proteins share the ability to bind ice, they can have different functions and their structures differ substantially in fold, architecture, and ice-binding surface composition. Horizontal gene transfer has also played a major role in IBP evolution, including transfer of type II AFP genes among fishes, DUF3494 IBPs among bacteria and numerous eukaryotes, and likely transfer of a hyperactive β-solenoid AFP between distantly related beetle lineages. The identification of IBPs presents significant experimental challenges, requiring rigorous verification through thermal hysteresis or ice recrystallization inhibition measurements together with recombinant expression. Nevertheless, advances in genome sequencing, transcriptomics, protein purification, and structural prediction are rapidly accelerating IBP discovery. Collectively, IBPs demonstrate the extraordinary diversity of evolutionary solutions to a common environmental challenge and provide a powerful model for investigating the mechanisms by which novel protein functions arise.
authors: Graham LA, Davies PL.

title: A novel chromosomally encoded OXA-12-like β-lactamase variant (bla OXA-1433 ) in a new Aeromonas veronii sequence type (ST3591) from ready-to-eat oysters
abstract: Abstract    Antibiotic resistance, a natural feature of bacterial evolution, is not confined to clinical settings but actively circulates across aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems, food chains, and animal and human populations. Aquatic ecosystems serve both as reservoirs of resistance determinants and as sources of food production, making seafood a critical interface for human exposure to environmentally derived resistance genes. This study aimed to characterize a novel chromosomally encoded OXA-12-like β-lactamase variant (  bla  OXA−1433  ) identified in a new  Aeromonas veronii  sequence type (ST3591) isolated from ready-to-eat oysters, and to investigate its genetic, structural, and phenotypic features. The isolate was subjected to hybrid whole-genome sequencing using short- and long-read technologies, followed by genome assembly, multilocus sequence typing, genomic context characterization, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. The novel  bla  OXA−1433  variant was further characterized through sequence and phenotypic analyses. MLST analysis revealed a novel sequence type (ST3591), while genome mining identified a previously undescribed OXA-12-like β-lactamase variant. OXA-1433 shared 95.08% amino acid identity with OXA-12 and differed by 13 amino acid substitutions while retaining the conserved motifs characteristic of class D β-lactamases. Genomic context analysis demonstrated that  bla  OXA−1433  was chromosomally located within a conserved genomic region lacking detectable mobile genetic elements. Phenotypic assays demonstrated imipenem hydrolysis, consistent with carbapenemase activity. The identification of a novel  A. veronii  sequence type carrying a previously undescribed OXA-12-like β-lactamase variant expands current knowledge of the genetic diversity of this species in food-associated environments and highlights the value of genomic surveillance of seafood-associated bacteria for monitoring the evolution of antibiotic resistance determinants.
authors: Rocha G, Ribas MR, Palmeiro JK, Sincero TCM, Cunha MV.

title: Community structure and hidden phylogenetic diversity of marine fungi in the tropical Indian and western Pacific Oceans
abstract: Abstract    Background  Marine fungi remain a poorly understood component of ocean ecosystems despite their potential roles in marine biogeochemical cycling. Here, we investigated fungal diversity, community structure, vertical stratification, and environmental drivers across the tropical Indian and western Pacific Oceans using long-read 28S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing of 113 samples from surface waters, mesopelagic and bathypelagic zones, and sediments. Results  A total of 46,938 fungal OTUs were clustered, representing 35 phyla, 164 classes, 254 orders, 509 families, 940 genera, and 1,055 species. Ascomycota dominated fungal communities, followed by Basidiomycota, Chytridiomycota, Rozellomycota. Phylogenetic analyses revealed three deeply divergent fungal lineages distinct from currently recognized phyla. Pending further molecular and morphological validation, these lineages were provisionally designated as Candidate.Taichumycota, Candidate.Shizhenmycota, and Candidate.Xihemycota. Their distinct vertical stratification suggested potential ecological differentiation: Candidate.Taichumycota was restricted to surface waters, Candidate.Shizhenmycota was broadly distributed but enriched in surface communities, whereas Candidate.Xihemycota occurred across habitats and was particularly enriched in sediments. title: Elemental sulfur reinforces storage-driven denitrification through complementary electron supply and mitigates N₂O in carbon-limited wastewater.
abstract: Managing nitrogen removal while minimizing external organic-carbon addition remains a major challenge for carbon-limited wastewater treatment. Storage-driven endogenous denitrification improves carbon efficiency by storing influent organics as intracellular polymers, but the finite availability of these reserves constrains reducing-power supply during post-anoxic nitrogen removal. Here, we investigated whether elemental sulfur could complement intracellular-carbon-derived reducing power in a long-term anaerobic-aerobic-anoxic system treating real municipal wastewater with a low COD/TN ratio. S⁰ supplementation decreased effluent nitrate from 13.6 ± 2.7 to 3.4 ± 2.3 mg N L⁻¹, increased total nitrogen removal from 79.8 ± 2.5% to 94.1 ± 3.7%, and reduced total N₂O accumulation from 0.51 ± 0.04 to 0.09 ± 0.02 mg N L⁻¹. Direct cycle-resolved measurements showed that post-anoxic PHA/glycogen consumption decreased from 1.91 ± 0.17 to 1.28 ± 0.22 mM C L⁻¹ after S⁰ supplementation, demonstrating that sulfur-derived reducing equivalents partly substituted for intracellular-carbon oxidation while conserving the storage pool. Genome-resolved metagenomics and metatranscriptomics further identified putative carbon-storage sulfur-oxidizing denitrifying bacteria carrying linked functions for intracellular-carbon turnover, reduced-sulfur metabolism and stepwise denitrification. Dose-dependent respiratory inhibition, transcriptional responses and electrochemical characteristics were collectively consistent with reduced dependence on NADH/Complex I-mediated electron input and greater involvement of quinone- and cytochrome c-linked respiratory processes after sulfur amendment. These results demonstrate that coupling intracellular carbon storage with sulfur-derived reducing power can extend the electron-supply capacity of storage-driven denitrification and promote more complete nitrogen removal under carbon-limited conditions.
authors: Wang H, Peng Y, Weng H, Wu Y, Zhang L.

title: Evolutionary origin of the WHIRLY gene families across 330 plant species: from algae to land plants.
abstract: Main conclusionPhylogenomics of 921 WHIRLY genes across 330 plants reveals stepwise subfamily origins, purifying selection, and a novel AtWHY1/2/3 hetero-oligomeric stress complex. Whirly (WHY) transcription factors are a plant-specific, highly conserved family with central roles in organellar genome maintenance, retrograde signaling, and abiotic stress response, but their deep evolutionary trajectories across the full green plant lineage have remained largely unresolved. In the present study, 921 WHY genes were identified across 330 different species from algae to land plants, which were classified into three subfamilies (WHY I, WHY II, and WHY III) in this study. Structural characteristics of different subfamilies showed significant differences in the number of exons and protein motifs, which may have arisen due to functional differentiation. Collinearity was primarily observed among members of the same subfamily, and network clustering analysis further divided all WHY genes into three clusters, with genes within each cluster exhibiting significant collinearity. All three subfamilies are under intense long-term purifying selection, with average Ka/Ks ratios far below 1, indicating stringent evolutionary constraints on their core conserved single-stranded DNA binding domain. Using yeast two-hybrid assays, protein molecular docking and site-specific interaction validation, we further uncovered a previously unreported stable hetero-oligomeric complex formed by AtWHY1, AtWHY2, and AtWHY3, assembled via defined hydrogen bond networks and salt bridges at the conserved interface residues, which acts as a combinatorial regulatory switch to coordinate distinct subcellular stress responses. This work establishes a unified evolutionary framework for the WHY family and provides new mechanistic insights into how their hetero-oligomerization drives specialized stress adaptation during plant territorialization.
authors: Lan Y, Gong F, Dong R, Fang C, Cai P.

title: Systems biology and synthetic engineering of probiotic yeasts.
abstract: Yeast probiotics, particularly Saccharomyces boulardii, are used in clinical, nutritional and biotechnological settings, yet their strain-specific mechanisms remain incompletely understood. This review examines how systems biology and multi-omics approaches can improve understanding of probiotic yeast function. We discuss comparative genomics and pangenomics, transcriptomic responses to gastrointestinal stress, cell-surface proteins involved in pathogen interactions, and metabolomic outputs including organic acids and other potential postbiotic metabolites. We then consider genome-scale metabolic models, flux balance analysis, and 13C metabolic flux analysis as complementary tools for converting omics observations into testable hypotheses about pathway activity and strain-specific metabolic traits. Published comparisons of S. boulardii and S. cerevisiae illustrate this framework. Conserved and strain-specific genomic variation, differential stress responses, acetate production, pathogen binding and host-cell effects can be examined together, while causal links between most variants and probiotic effects remain unresolved. The review also compares the systems-data, metabolic-modeling, and genome-engineering readiness of Kluyveromyces marxianus and Debaryomyces hansenii, two non-conventional yeasts with thermotolerance or halotolerance, but less direct evidence for human probiotic function. Finally, we discuss CRISPR-based engineering, machine learning, data standards, regulatory considerations and future possibilities for strain-specific computational models. Progress will require standardized experimental conditions, well-annotated strain resources, integrated multi-omics datasets, and experimental validation of model predictions.
authors: Ali S, Che Hussian CHA, Goh HH.

title: Gapless Complete Genome and Multi-Omics Illuminate Immune Adaptation and Host-Virus Interactions in a Coronavirus Reservoir.
abstract: Bats are major reservoirs of emerging viruses, including severe acute respiratory syndrome-related coronaviruses, yet they exhibit remarkable tolerance to viral infections with limited clinical manifestations-a longstanding immunological paradox. Here, we generate a telomere-to-telomere (T2T) de novo genome assembly for Rhinolophus sinicus (R. sinicus), designated T2T-RSC1.0 (2.14 Gb), comprising 17 fully anchored autosomes and both sex chromosomes. This gapless assembly resolves 129.19 Mb of previously unresolved regions (PURs) and enables annotation of 848 previously unannotated genes, including 131 protein-coding genes and five pseudogenes on the 33.75 Mb Y chromosome. Using 2.12 × 105 newly identified single-nucleotide polymorphisms within PURs, population genomic analyses resolve three major genetic groups and provide improved resolution of genome-wide population structure. Comparative analyses further reveal population-level associations between major histocompatibility complex polymorphism and viral diversity. Multi-omics and functional analyses reveal a coordinated evolutionary remodeling of antiviral defense, antigen presentation, cytokine signaling, and inflammatory regulation in horseshoe bats. This study provides an unparalleled genomic resource for R. sinicus and establishes an integrated framework for investigating immune evolution, long-term host-virus coexistence, and mammalian adaptive evolution.
authors: Wang Y, Zhang S, Ouyang L, Du X, Huang X, Wang Z, Xie H, Tang J, Lou L, Ling W, Wang W, Zhou J, Liu Z, Hu Y, Wei F, Huang G.

title: Testing the Potential of Pseudomonas Bacteria for the Biocontrol of Ink Disease of Chestnut.
abstract: Ink disease, caused by the two oomycetes Phytophthora cinnamomi and Phytophthora × cambivora, is one of the most devastating diseases of sweet chestnut (Castanea sativa) in Europe. Its control is particularly difficult, with few fungicides showing a satisfactory effect, and those being progressively banned in forest ecosystems or in forest-like plantations because of ecological concerns. Therefore, alternative, nature-friendly control methods are urgently needed. The bacterial genus Pseudomonas includes many species with antifungal and antimicrobial properties. In this study, we isolated Pseudomonas bacteria from the rhizosphere of healthy and diseased chestnut trees in southern Switzerland. Out of 166 isolated Pseudomonas strains, 5 showed significant growth inhibition of P. cinnamomi and/or P. × cambivora in vitro. Three strains that significantly inhibited the growth of both pathogens were tested against a collection of 20 isolates of each species, showing that the in vitro inhibition is independent of the pathogen isolate. The mechanisms underlying this inhibition remain unclear because none of the three strains harbored biosynthesis genes coding for well-known antimicrobial secondary metabolites. Phylogenetic analysis of whole genome sequences showed that two of the strains belong to the P. fluorescens subgroup, whereas one strain probably belongs to a previously unrecognized species closely related to the P. putida subgroup. The results of this study indicate that Pseudomonas have the potential to be used as biocontrol agents against ink disease. Further experiments are needed to confirm their inhibitory effect against P. cinnamomi and P. × cambivora in vivo.
authors: Dennert F, Troxler V, Bossert OX, Schneider S, Maurhofer M, Prospero S.

title: Effects of environmental changes in the water column on microbial communities on microplastic surfaces during ocean entry.
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) act as mobile substrates for microbial colonization during their transport from land to sea, forming unique microbial reservoirs with potential ecological implications. Understanding the dynamics of these surface-associated communities is essential for assessing the environmental fate and risks of MPs. However, how shifts in aquatic environmental conditions influence the assembly and succession of MP biofilm communities remains unclear. In this study, water samples were collected from river, estuarine, and marine environments (the Jiuzhou River in Zhanjiang, China, and the Beibu Gulf region), and a laboratory based microcosm culture system was established to investigate changes in microplastic communities in response to shifts in the aquatic environment. It is worth noting that in marine environments, the number of taxonomic units exhibiting significant differences in abundance on MPs surfaces is higher than in river environments. Notably, the number of taxa exhibiting significant differential abundance on MPs surfaces was higher in marine than in riverine environments. Additionally, a rapid decrease in MPs-surface biomass was observed within 3 h following transitions from riverine to estuarine and from estuarine to marine conditions, suggesting that cross-environmental transport may temporarily inhibit biofilm biomass accumulation. This study indicates that changes in the aquatic environment and variations in salinity gradients may influence the colonization of microplastics by microorganisms, thereby deepening our understanding of the ecological role of microplastics in dynamic aquatic systems.
authors: Chen L, Tan Z, Zhang Y, Sun R, He L, Dai Z, Zhou JY, Li C.

title: From environmental gradients to putative intrinsic resistance: Deciphering the soil resistome across Mongolian Plateau grasslands.
abstract: Soils are important reservoirs of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), yet the ecological differentiation and host associations of grassland resistomes remain poorly understood. We investigated topsoil resistomes across desert steppe, typical steppe, and meadow steppe of the Mongolian Plateau using short- and long-read metagenomics. The resistome comprised 28 ARG types and 819 subtypes, dominated by rifamycin, vancomycin, and multidrug resistance genes. ARG abundance increased from desert steppe to meadow steppe. Soil pH, total organic carbon, total nitrogen, and climatic variables were strongly associated with resistome turnover, whereas grazing showed weaker associations. Mobile genetic element (MGE) abundance correlated positively with ARG abundance, but only 3.37% of ARG-carrying contigs contained detectable MGEs. An operational multi-indicator framework distinguished putative intrinsic and putative acquired ARGs with contrasting host and environmental associations. Both fractions were dominated by Actinomycetota, although Pseudomonadota contributed relatively more to putative acquired ARGs. Putative intrinsic ARGs were associated mainly with nutrient-related soil variables, whereas putative acquired ARGs showed stronger climatic and edaphic associations. Long-read assemblies markedly reduced the unclassified fraction. Among 195 ARG-carrying metagenome-assembled genomes, 65.6% represented reference-poor or previously uncultured lineages. These findings reveal spatially structured and heterogeneous grassland resistomes linked to ARG composition, host affiliation, and genomic context.
authors: Luo J, Dong S, Yuan M, Wen W, Li YA, Li Y, Zhao R.

title: Construction of a synthetic bacterial-fungal consortium for cephalexin biodegradation: transformation pathways and ecotoxicological assessment.
abstract: Cephalexin (CPX), a widely used β-lactam antibiotic, is frequently detected in aquatic environments and poses risks to ecological and human health, yet the biodegradation pathways underlying its microbial removal remain incompletely characterized. In this study, a synthetic bacterial-fungal consortium (CPXS), comprising Achromobacter aegrifaciens, Citrobacter amalonaticus, Elizabethkingia anophelis, Bacillus wiedmannii, and Geotrichum pandrosion, was constructed and evaluated for CPX biodegradation. Following systematic single-factor and multivariable optimization (pH 8, 30 °C, 85 mg/L CPX), the consortium achieved 98.5% CPX removal within 48 h, and degradation was further accelerated to 30 h with sodium acetate as a co-substrate. LC-MS-based accurate mass profiling was used to identify 19 transformation products, from which five plausible degradation pathways were predicted, proposed to be initiated by ring-opening hydrolysis of the β-lactam moiety and proceeding through key intermediates, including 2-amino-2-phenylacetamide, toward simple terminal metabolites such as N-methylacetamide and (Z)-but-2-enal, consistent with substantial progression toward mineralization. The consortium also degraded amoxicillin and ampicillin in synthetic and real municipal wastewater, indicating broad-spectrum activity and applicability under complex matrix conditions. Toxicity assays using Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, and HEK-293 cells showed that degraded samples retained negligible antibacterial activity and exhibited low cytotoxicity, confirming effective detoxification of CPX and its byproducts. Overall, this study proposes a detailed, multi-pathway degradation network for CPX mediated by a bacterial-fungal consortium, culminating in simple bioassimilable end products, and identifies CPXS as a promising candidate for the bioremediation of β-lactam antibiotic-contaminated wastewater.
authors: Moridshahi R, Etemadifar Z, Biria D.

title: Viral metagenomics reveals heterogeneity in mammalian virus hosting, sharing, and spillover.
abstract: Zoonotic viruses originating from mammals pose a persistent threat to global health. While rodents and bats are often considered "special reservoirs," it is debated if spillover risk is driven by specific taxa or merely reflects mammalian species richness. However, most tests have focused on published host-virus association datasets, which can reflect systematic biases in host and virus sampling effort. To address this limitation, we analyzed a comprehensive repository of 4,685 metagenomic datasets, minimizing bias toward any one viral taxon and spanning 296 species across 14 mammalian orders. We characterized the global mammalian virome and found substantial heterogeneity in the capacity of different mammalian orders to harbor and share human-associated viruses. Counter to conventional wisdom, carnivores exhibited significantly higher propensities to carry human-associated viruses, with bats ranked lower in this metric of zoonotic risk. Network analyses of viral sharing further revealed higher cross-order virus sharing among specific mammalian orders (e.g., carnivores and artiodactyls). Phylogenetic comparative analyses revealed that host life-history traits (e.g., longevity) and anthropogenic factors (e.g., urban land use) were key ecological drivers of both virus richness and transmission centrality. Our study provides a data-driven framework that challenges prevailing narratives of zoonotic risk and offers a refined strategy for prioritizing surveillance and mitigating emerging zoonotic threats.
authors: Wang Y, Qu G, Huang ZYX, Zhang X, Li H, Wei X, Hu L, Xu S, Becker DJ, Wei F, Xu Y.

title: Multi-Virus Surveillance Across Diverse Freshwater Systems in Tehran, Iran.
abstract: Environmental surveillance of viral contaminants in water systems is an essential tool for assessing exposure risk and supporting early-warning frameworks for emerging infectious diseases. In this study, a comprehensive one-year surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 and six enteric viruses was conducted across diverse freshwater systems in Tehran, Iran - including rivers, wells, and traditional qanat (underground aqueduct) infrastructures. Water quality parameters (turbidity, pH, Total Dissolved Solids, nitrate) and fecal bacterial indicators (total coliforms, fecal coliforms, and E. coli) were also measured to contextualize viral contamination within a broader environmental risk framework. Between September 2020 and August 2021, a total of 118 water samples were collected and analyzed using quantitative molecular detection methods. Overall, 61 of 118 samples (51.7%) tested positive for at least one virus. Surface water (rivers) showed substantially higher contamination rates (80.3%; 53/66 samples) compared to groundwater (15.4%; 8/52 samples). Among groundwater sources, qanat systems were markedly more vulnerable than conventional wells, with 25.0% (6/24) of qanat samples testing positive versus only 7.1% (2/28) of well samples. This elevated contamination in qanats was dominated by rotavirus (5/6 positive qanat samples, detection rate 20.8%) and was associated with higher fecal bacterial loads (total coliform geometric mean: 245 MPN/100 mL in qanats vs. 28 MPN/100 mL in wells), consistent with the susceptibility of shallow horizontal collection channels to fecal infiltration. SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detected in 34.8% of river samples and 3.9% of groundwater samples, with concentrations reaching 1.28 × 10⁴ genome copies per liter (GC/L) in surface waters, demonstrating sustained fecal contamination across all seasons. The most prevalent viruses in river water were norovirus GII (45.5%), adenovirus (43.9%), rotavirus (42.4%), and norovirus GI (40.9%), with mean concentrations ranging from 1.26 × 10² to 3.76 × 10³ GC/L. Hepatitis A and E viruses were not detected in any sample. Seasonal variation in viral detection was observed for enteric viruses, while SARS-CoV-2 and adenovirus showed year-round persistence. Strong correlations between fecal indicators and viral contamination (Spearman r = 0.61-0.63) support the use of bacterial monitoring as a cost-effective screening proxy. The results highlight the particular vulnerability of qanat systems and underscore the value of integrated environmental surveillance for water safety management in arid, water-stressed urban environments.
authors: Tanhaei M, Jiang G, Hosseini SM, Rafieepoor M, Nikpeyman Y, Saeedi Niasar M, Kazemian S, Nadalian B, Yadegar A, Mirjalali H, Ghaemi A, Moore MD, Zali MR, Mohebbi SR.

title: Genome-wide characterization of the PLATZ transcription factor family in chickpea reveals evolutionary diversification and genotype-dependent responses to drought and salinity
abstract: Abstract  Plant A/T-rich sequence- and zinc-binding (PLATZ) proteins are plant-specific, zinc-dependent DNA-binding transcription factors that regulate plant growth, development, and stress responses, yet this family remains poorly characterized in chickpea (Cicer arietinum L.). Here, ten non-redundant CaPLATZ genes were identified using three complementary approaches—keyword-based retrieval, BLASTP homology searching, and HMMER-based conserved-domain screening—and characterized through structural, evolutionary, regulatory, developmental, and stress-responsive expression analyses. Three segmentally duplicated gene pairs showed Ka/Ks ratios

title: Diversity and distribution of Bartonella spp. in domestic animals, wildlife, and ectoparasites in Brazil: a comprehensive review.
abstract: Bartonella are intracellular Gram-negative blood-borne bacteria capable of infecting a wide range of hosts, primarily mammals and birds. They are responsible for emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases characterized by persistent intraerythrocytic bacteremia in mammals. Out of 49 species described, 13 presents zoonotic potential. This review aimed to update the current knowledge on the occurrence, distribution, and genetic diversity of Bartonella in domestic animals, wild mammals and birds, and ectoparasites in Brazil. A total of 72 scientific articles published between 2007 and 2026 were included. The available information indicates that the Southeastern and Central-Western regions of Brazil account for most reports of Bartonella in animals and ectoparasites, whereas the Northern and Northeastern regions remain comparatively understudied. Overall, studies investigating Bartonella in Brazil have become increasingly frequent and geographically widespread over the years. Although some investigations rely on single-gene analyses, most employ multi-locus sequence analysis and phylogenetic reconstruction, providing stronger evidence for species identification and diversity. In contrast, relatively few studies have incorporated whole-genome sequencing or comprehensive phenotypic and biochemical characterization through bacterial isolation and blood culture. Future research should prioritize advanced genomic approaches and bacterial isolation to improve our understanding of the diversity, evolution, and epidemiology of Bartonella circulating in Brazil.
journal: Revista brasileira de parasitologia veterinaria = Brazilian journal of veterinary parasitology : Orgao Oficial do Colegio Brasileiro de Parasitologia Veterinaria
authors: André MR, Lee DAB, Neves LFD, Franco EO, Machado RZ.

title: CNTN4: A Possible Candidate Gene for Microbiota-Gut-Brain Axis in Autism Spectrum Disorders and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder.
abstract: The gut microbiota plays a significant role in autism spectrum disorders (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), though findings vary substantially across studies. Using gut microbiome data from a genome-wide association study of 5,959 participants and summary statistics from 46,351 ASD and 55,374 ADHD cases, we conducted bidirectional Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses with inverse variance weighting as the primary method. Reverse MR analysis assessed potential reverse causality. We annotated single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) with SNP-nexus to identify associated genes, followed by Gene Ontology (﻿GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses to characterize their functional roles. Seventeen gut microbial taxa showed causal associations with ASD risk, while 27 were linked to ADHD. Reverse MR analysis revealed associations between aSD and species Desulfovibrio piger as well as species Bacillus U, but no reverse causality was detected for ADHD. Biological annotation identified five novel conserved genes in host-microbiome interactions shared by ASD and ADHD, with CNTN4 emerging as a common candidate gene. These findings support a potential causal relationship between gut microbiota and ASD/ADHD risk while uncovering novel conserved genes implicated in host-microbiome interactions for both disorders.Lay AbstractDistinct gut microbiota profiles were observed in individuals with ADHD and ASD. Seventeen microbial species showed significant associations with ASD, while 27 were linked to ADHD. CNTN4 emerged as a potential candidate gene shared across both neurodevelopmental conditions and host-microbiome interactions.
journal: Autism : the international journal of research and practice
authors: Li Y, Wang W, Liu W.

title: Whole-genome analysis of avian orthoreovirus isolated in Japan reveals genetic divergence from vaccine strains.
abstract: Avian orthoreovirus (ARV) is an important pathogen associated with viral arthritis in chickens and causes substantial economic losses in the poultry industry. In recent years, ARVs belonging to clusters 2 and 6, which have rarely been reported in Japan, have been isolated from broiler chickens derived from breeder flocks vaccinated with the ARV vaccine strains 1733 and 2408. In this study, whole-genome sequencing and phylogenetic analyses were performed on ARV isolates circulating in Japan to clarify their genetic differences from the vaccine strains. Comparative analyses revealed considerable genomic diversity even among virus strains isolated from the same geographic region, suggesting frequent genetic reassortment among circulating ARVs. None of the genomic segments of our isolates showed high-sequence identity to the currently used vaccine strains. In particular, the σC protein showed low amino acid identities (49.39-56.48%) to strain 1733. These findings suggest substantial genetic divergence between recent Japanese ARVs and the vaccine strains. This study provide the first whole-genome characterization of recent Japanese ARVs. Continuous surveillance will contribute to a better understanding of ARV evolution and to the evaluation of the effectiveness of current vaccines against circulating field strains.
authors: Fujimoto Y, Tsunekuni R, Ikeda T, Nakagara K, Chuma T.

title: Core microbiota recruited by Salvia miltiorrhiza enhance resistance against Fusarium root rot disease
abstract: Abstract    Fusarium  root rot, caused by the soilborne pathogen  Fusarium oxysporum  , leads to substantial yield losses across multiple agriculturally crucial crops. While rhizosphere microbiota have been extensively studied in model species, a deeper understanding of the rhizosphere microbiome assembly associated with herb health is still needed. Given its economic importance in traditional medicine, we used  Salvia miltiorrhiza  and  Fusarium  root rot as a model to elucidate the rhizosphere microbiome assembly associated with plant health. Here, we employed 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing to profile the soil microbiome across three geographically distinct cultivation regions. Comparative analysis revealed marked divergence in bacterial community structures between healthy and diseased plants, identifying  Lysobacter  spp. as keystone bacterial taxa within the core microbiome enriched in healthy rhizospheres. Functional validation demonstrated potent antifungal activity of isolated  Lysobacter  strains against  F. oxysporum  , with  Lysobacter enzymogenes  strain Ly-1 exhibiting consistent biocontrol efficacy in both greenhouse and field experiments. Genomic and transcriptomic analyses further revealed that Ly-1 encodes specialized iron acquisition systems, including siderophore synthesis and transport machinery, with its antifungal activity being significantly amplified under iron-limited conditions, consistent with a model where iron competition cooperates with other biocontrol traits. Collectively, this study establishes a novel biocontrol paradigm and highlights the translational potential of core rhizobacterial enrichment for sustainable management of soilborne diseases in medicinal plants.
authors: You C, Gao Y, Ren P, Zhang W, Gong K, Zhang Q, Wang X, Zhou W, Kümmerli R, Xu Y, Shen Q, Wei Z, Wang X.

title: Genomic and experimental evidence from Antarctic geothermal sites indicates diverse thermophiles are globally cosmopolitan
abstract: Abstract  Mt. Erebus, the world’s southernmost active volcano, is highly isolated, yet a previous study found its heated soils contain prokaryotes found elsewhere globally. This was unexpected, as non-sporulating thermophilic microorganisms are thought to be dispersal limited. We searched for the presence of metagenome assembled genomes (MAGs) from Antarctic geothermal sites outside Antarctica, finding that 62% of MAGs had matching species globally. Three of these cosmopolitan thermophiles isolated from Mt. Erebus could survive atmospheric-like conditions, with UV being the strongest selective pressure. Moreover, hot soils from Hawaiʻi sampled four years after a lava flow hosted many thermophilic MAGs with identical strains elsewhere globally, indicating that dispersal/recolonisation by thermophiles can be rapid. Finally, ice core sections from Fang Glacier (Mt. Erebus) associated with volcanic events were enriched in thermophiles, implying that thermophiles could disperse via volcanic events. Our findings dispel the common conception of thermophilic microorganisms as being inherently dispersal limited.
authors: McDonald I, Noell S, Dragone N, Cano-Prasad M, Pyne R, Rea L, Bertler N, Kyle P, Saw J, Archer S, Herbold C, Galilee C, Stott M, Cary S.

title: Complete Chloroplast Genome of Nepeta griffithii and Comparative Genomics of 10 Nepeta Species.
abstract: Nepeta L. (Lamiaceae) is an ecologically and medicinally important genus, yet complete cp genome resources are available for fewer than 10 of the approximately 300 accepted species, with western Himalayan taxa almost entirely unrepresented. Here, we sequenced, assembled, and annotated the complete cp genome of Nepeta griffithii and compared it with nine previously published Nepeta cp genomes. The 10 cp genomes exhibited a highly conserved quadripartite structure, with genome sizes ranging from 151,254 to 152,348 bp, and contained 113 unique genes (79 protein-coding, 30 tRNA, 4 rRNA). Gene content, guanine-cytosine content, intron features, and inverted repeat contraction and expansion were highly conserved. SSR analysis identified 387 repeats across the 10 cp genomes, predominantly mononucleotide A/T motifs in intergenic spacers, yielding candidate cpSSR markers for population-level studies. Codon usage analysis revealed a strong bias toward A/T-ending codons, with leucine as the most frequent amino acid. Nucleotide diversity analysis showed intergenic spacers were more variable than both introns and genic regions. Highly polymorphic loci, including ccsA-ndhD, rpl32-trnL-UAG, and ndhG-ndhI, were identified as candidate markers for phylogenetic and population studies. Maximum likelihood phylogeny based on 79 concatenated protein-coding genes recovered a well-resolved topology within Nepeta and placed N. griffithii as sister to N. nuda with maximal bootstrap support of 100%. This study provides the first complete cp genome for N. griffithii, improves plastome sampling within the genus, and offers genomic markers for species identification, systematics, and evolutionary studies.
authors: Li X, Sammad A, Shah SA, Sun J, Karim A, Yir-Erong B, Tian X, Abdullah.

title: Genome-wide identification and expression profiling of IQM family genes in Chrysanthemum nankingense in response to abiotic stresses.
abstract: IQM proteins are plant-specific central modulators of calcium signaling, coordinating plant growth, development, and stress adaptation via calmodulin binding, yet no systematic characterization of the IQM family has been reported in Chrysanthemum nankingense. Here, we performed a genome-wide identification of the CnIQM gene family and conducted systematic bioinformatic analyses of their physicochemical traits, chromosomal distribution and phylogenetic relationships. RT-qPCR was used to detect transcriptional responses of CnIQM genes to exogenous phytohormones and major abiotic stresses, and yeast heterologous expression assays validated the stress tolerance of key CnIQM candidates. A total of nine CnIQM genes were identified. Most encode alkaline proteins predominantly localized to the nucleus or cytoplasm. Tandem duplication appears to be a major contributor to CnIQM family expansion, and all duplicated gene pairs are under strong purifying selection; high syntenic conservation of IQM loci is observed between C. nankingense and its congener Chrysanthemum lavandulifolium. All CnIQM proteins contain the canonical conserved IQ motif, whereas several paralogs exhibit structural variation with truncated UTR regions. Transcriptional profiling revealed differential induction under phytohormone, salt, drought, and cold treatments, with most genes rapidly upregulated by salinity and drought stress. Yeast heterologous expression assays showed that CnIQM5, CnIQM6, and CnIQM9 significantly improve salt and drought tolerance in yeast, while none enhances cold resistance in this heterologous system. This study clarifies the evolutionary and functional features of the CnIQM family and provides theoretical references and promising candidate genes for future functional research and stress-resistant molecular breeding of chrysanthemum.
authors: Wang T, Xie Z, Li S, Liu L, Lu N, Li C, Fan X, Han Q, Wang W, Pu S.

title: Large-genome phages encode diverse proteins associated with host cell envelope functions
abstract: Huge phages (or jumbo phages, >200 kilobases) encode extensive protein repertoires, yet their functional diversity and potential roles in host physiology remain poorly understood. Using protein structure-based analyses of dominant protein families across 7,187 non-redundant genomes of huge phages, we uncovered pronounced phylogenetic and habitat-associated diversification. Notably, we identified diverse proteins associated with bacterial cell envelope functions, particularly in human gut-associated huge phages. These included previously unreported phage-encoded sortase B, whose putative substrates contain signal peptides and cell-wall sorting signals, suggesting a potential route for displaying phage proteins on bacterial surfaces. Phage-encoded phage shock protein A (PspA) was distributed across diverse lineages and frequently neighbored genes associated with membrane organization and transport, implicating potential roles in membrane physiology. We also identified 1,603 β-barrel outer membrane proteins (OMPs) across 1,303 huge phages from diverse ecosystems. These OMPs exhibited structural diversity and associations with predicted host taxonomy, habitat, and neighboring envelope-related genes. Metatranscriptomic analysis supported expression of representative phage-encoded PspA and OMP genes in natural communities including the human gut. Together, these findings reveal bacterial cell envelope processes as a previously underappreciated potential interface for huge phage–host interactions.
authors: Yuan L, Chen L.

title: Newcastle disease virus research: pioneering scientists, landmark discoveries, and virological innovations.
abstract: Newcastle disease (ND) has been recognized for a century as one of the most consequential viral diseases of poultry, and its scientific history provides a distinctive example of how sustained investigation of a single pathogen can drive advances across veterinary medicine, virology, immunology, epidemiology, molecular biology, vaccinology, and biotechnology. The severe outbreaks reported in Java, Indonesia, and Newcastle-upon-Tyne, England, during 1926 marked the beginning of the recognized scientific history of ND and initiated an international research effort that progressed from disease recognition and experimental characterization to diagnostics, vaccination, molecular pathogenesis, and genomic epidemiology. During the 1940s and 1950s, investigations of viral propagation, antigenicity, pathogenicity, and attenuation established the foundations of live and inactivated vaccination. From the 1960s onward, molecular investigations progressively elucidated the determinants of ND virus (NDV) replication, protein processing, and virulence, particularly the role of the fusion-protein cleavage site. The emergence of nucleotide sequencing and phylogenetic analysis during the 1980s and 1990s subsequently transformed strain characterization and provided the foundations for molecular epidemiology and genotype classification. Complete-genome sequencing and the establishment of reverse-genetics systems in the late 1990s further transformed NDV from an organism studied primarily through observation and isolation into a genetically tractable experimental system. Subsequent international efforts standardized NDV genotype nomenclature and enabled increasingly detailed analyses of viral evolution and geographic dissemination. In parallel, NDV research expanded beyond conventional disease control into recombinant vaccine development, systems-level host-virus studies, molecular diagnostics, and oncolytic virotherapy. This historical perspective traces these major scientific transitions from 1926 to 2026, emphasizing the investigators, experimental systems, conceptual advances, and technological innovations that collectively transformed NDV research from disease recognition into a multidisciplinary molecular and translational fields.
authors: Ul-Rahman A, Munir M.

title: Modeling association networks from metagenome time series - a proof-of-concept from two contrasting estuaries.
abstract: Understanding microbial responses to environmental gradients is important for ecosystem assessment in estuarine environments. Here, we integrated time-series samples and shotgun metagenomics with association network inference, to examine patterns of taxonomic and functional co-variation. We collected and sequenced eDNA from two sediment time series from neighbouring but environmentally contrasting Basque estuaries, and compared the resulting taxonomic and functional association networks, based on Metagenome Assembled Genomes (MAGs) and KEGG Orthologous Groups (KOs), respectively. Networks inferred using 16S rRNA gene metabarcoding data were also included in this comparison. Several topology-based network properties differed strongly between the two sites, although differences were not always consistent when comparing the networks based on MAGs, KOs and metabarcoding. KO-based networks revealed distinct sets of associated Ortholog groups between sites, consistent with known environmental differences. Contrary to our expectations, metabolically related genes rarely formed complete pathway modules in gene networks, likely due to functional redundancy, gene copy number variation, synchronized pathway dynamics, or algorithmic constraints of correlation-based inference. Overall, the results illustrate both the potential and interpretative limitations of metagenome-based time association networks for functional ecosystem assessment, and support their use as hypothesis-generating tools that require further validation across a larger range of sites following environmental gradients.

title: Harnessing metatranscriptomics to unveil the metabolic landscape of microbiota in traditional fermented foods.
abstract: Traditional fermented foods are widely consumed and valued for their distinctive sensory properties and potential health benefits. These foods contain complex microbiota whose interactions and metabolic activities shape biochemical transformations relevant to product quality, safety, and functionality. Metatranscriptomics provides a culture-independent means of profiling community RNA and examining changes in microbial gene expression during fermentation. However, most fermented-food microbiome studies continue to infer function from community composition or genomic potential rather than from in situ gene expression. Existing metatranscriptomic applications also differ substantially in sampling, RNA processing, sequencing, and data analysis, limiting comparisons across food systems. This review examines the metatranscriptomic workflows applied to fermented foods, including sample preparation, sequencing strategies, and bioinformatic analysis. It identifies practical requirements for reproducible RNA-based studies in complex food matrices and compares transcriptionally represented taxa and pathways across fermentation systems. The review also distinguishes gene expression from realized metabolic activity, an important boundary when interpreting transcript annotations and reconstructed pathways. We further assess the strengths and limitations of metatranscriptomics, both alone and in combination with complementary omics, for resolving microbiota structure-function relationships. Key challenges include data integration, evidence interpretation, and the recovery of biologically meaningful information from complex transcriptomic datasets. When combined with complementary omics and experimental validation, metatranscriptomics can help relate expressed genes and pathways to fermentation phenotypes. These insights may guide the experimental evaluation of starter cultures and the development of more precise fermentation-control strategies.
authors: Li R, Fan X, Kang J, Huang X, Shi Y, Chen X.

title: Topoisomerase I participates in chromosome segregation of the polyploid bacterium Thermus thermophilus through its decatenation activity.
abstract: Thermus thermophilus, a polyploid thermophilic bacterium, lacks the canonical decatenases Topo III and Topo IV, posing a challenge for faithful chromosome segregation. This study aims to determine whether T. thermophilus topoisomerase I (TopoITth) has acquired decatenation activity and participates in chromosome segregation. Through gene deletion, we found that topA is essential; only a heterozygous ΔtopA::blm/WT-topA mutant could be obtained. Partial depletion of TopoITth caused severe Par- phenotypes, including cell filamentation, unsegregated nucleoids, anucleate cells, and DNA fragmentation, all of which were rescued by ectopic expression of wild-type topA, confirming the specificity of the defects. TopoITth localized to cell poles, mirroring the localization of classical segregation proteins SMC and XerD, and bacterial two-hybrid assays revealed physical interactions with both proteins. Truncation analysis mapped the interaction interfaces to the C-terminal domain of SMC and the N-terminal domain of XerD. In vitro, TopoITth exhibited decatenation and catenation activities, contrasting with Escherichia coli TopoI. SMC stimulated its decatenation in a dose-dependent manner, whereas XerD did not. Collectively, our results indicate that TopoITth acts as a decatenase integrated with the chromosome segregation machinery to compensate for the absence of Topo III and Topo IV. This study uncovers a functional expansion of type IA topoisomerases and offers a paradigm for how genome streamlining can drive the evolution of novel enzyme functions.ImportanceThis work refines the canonical view that bacterial topoisomerase I functions solely as a relaxase. By demonstrating that Thermus thermophilus Topo I has evolved robust decatenation activity and physically interacts with SMC to drive chromosome segregation, we uncover a functional expansion of type IA topoisomerases. This provides a paradigm for understanding how genome streamlining drives the acquisition of new functions by an existing enzyme. Beyond evolutionary significance, our findings may have translational relevance. Certain pathogens, such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium smegmatis, similarly lack canonical decatenases and depend on Topo I for survival. Although further studies are needed to validate whether this decatenase activity is widely conserved and essential in these pathogens, our work suggests that Topo I could be explored as a potential target for developing novel antibiotics against multidrug-resistant bacteria.
authors: Li H, He Y, Xu J, Zhang Y, Liu Y, Xiao W, Cao Z, Shen Y, Xu L, Liu X, Li X, Zhao Y.

title: Ocean depth modifies host-microbiome ecology and evolution
abstract: A major unsolved question in ecology and evolution is how similar free-living and symbiotic microbial communities are. In marine systems, depth homogenises free-living communities due to stronger dispersal and weaker environmental filtering compared to surface waters. We show that symbiotic communities of marine sponges follow a different pattern, with a subset of sponge species mirroring the increased similarity with depth seen in their free-living counterparts, while others remain highly host-specific both in shallow and deep waters. Moreover, in deep waters, more phylogenetically similar hosts harbor more similar microbiomes, yet host-symbiont cophylogeny nearly vanishes. This reveals two contrasting eco-evolutionary assembly rules: in more constant environments like the deep sea, community assembly is driven by host and environmental filtering with minimal signature of coevolution, whereas in variable environments, like shallow waters, host-symbiont coevolution is strong and key to maintain host-specific microbiomes.
authors: Díez-Vives C, Turon M, Lurgi M, Pita L, Nielsen S, Álvarez Fernández A, Thomas T, Riesgo A, Montoya JM.

title: GBactPro: cross-species bacterial promoter prediction using element-resolved promoter definitions
abstract: Accurate bacterial promoter prediction supports genome annotation, but many models use fixed-length promoter windows anchored to transcription start sites (TSSs) rather than promoter-element boundaries. We developed the  G eneral  Bact erial  Pro moter Predictor (GBactPro), a convolutional neural network–bidirectional long short-term memory (CNN–BiLSTM) framework using promoter sequences resolved by the Promoter Architecture Scanner. Using  Escherichia coli -trained models evaluated across 43 bacterial species, we compared eight input designs and identified the contiguous −35/spacer/−10 core as optimal (mean AUROC = 0.9859). Species-specific models showed broad transfer in a 43 × 43 evaluation. Joint training on all 43 species achieved a mean AUROC of 0.9943 across their held-out test sets and outperformed four established predictors under matched-length benchmarks. In genome-wide  E. coli scanning, GBactPro achieved AUROC and AUPRC values of 0.979 and 0.160 under stringent full-containment matching (0-bp tolerance), increasing to 0.997 and 0.323 under a 100-bp tolerance. False-positive predictions overlapped H-NS binding regions more frequently than true positives (24.4% versus 18.8%), and predictions also overlapped promoters derepressed in an H-NS-knockout dataset. Prediction precision varied across four TSS classes. These findings demonstrate that element-resolved promoter definitions improve cross-species prediction and support genome-wide identification of candidate bacterial promoters.
authors: Han HB, Kao YV, Kuo SA, Chou HD, Chang J.

title: Scalable phylodynamic inference of mutational and epistatic fitness effects with multi-feature birth-death models
abstract: Fitness is a complex phenotype determined by many different genomic features, their interactions with each other and the environment. For rapidly evolving microbes like viruses and bacteria, phylodynamic multi-feature birth-death (MFBD) models provide a way to infer the fitness of lineages with different genotypes from reconstructed phylogenies. However, existing phylodynamic methods assume very simple additive or multiplicative genotype-to-fitness (G-to-F) mappings that typically ignore epistatic interactions among features. We developed a gradient-based Bayesian MFBD framework for estimating the fitness effects of multiple features while allowing for both additive and epistatic G-to-F maps. The framework uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for posterior inference and incorporates shrinkage priors to regularize weakly supported fitness effects without cross-validation. In simulations, Bayesian inference performs well at recovering additive fitness effects, with accuracy and precision improving consistently with increasing tree size. While epistatic effects are more difficult to estimate because they depend on the co-occurrence of mutations, shrinkage improves estimation when interaction effects are weak or sparsely supported. Simulations with misspecified additive models show that ignoring moderate or strong epistasis can bias estimates of individual mutational effects. We applied the framework to a time-calibrated  Escherichia coli ST131 phylogeny with 1763 samples and estimated fitness effects for several mutations in the quinolone resistance-determining region (QRDR). These results show that Bayesian phylodynamic inference can be used to learn the genomic determinants of fitness while quantifying uncertainty in mutational and epistatic fitness effects.
authors: Cen S, Kepler LM, Lanzas C, Reich BJ, Rasmussen DA.

title: Isolation of polyethylene‑modifying soil bacteria from Egypt and Genome-based functional characterization of Sphingobacterium spiritivorum ASb3.
abstract: Polyethylene (PE) has been widely utilized, resulting in its accumulation in the environment due to its recalcitrant nature. In this study, seven bacterial isolates from garden soil and garbage dumps in Cairo and Giza, Egypt, grew on PE films as the sole carbon source, reduced PE weight, and formed biofilms. Scanning electron microscopy revealed surface perforations, while Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy detected new carbonyl and hydroxyl groups. Based on 16 S rRNA gene sequencing and phylogeny, the isolates exhibited high similarity to Sphingobacterium spiritivorum, Rhodococcus pyridinivorans, Pseudomonas putida, Ectopseudomonas mendocina, Zobellella taiwanensis, Achromobacter mucicolens, and Pseudomonas sp. To the best of our knowledge, S. spiritivorum, E. mendocina, Z. taiwanensis, and A. mucicolens have not previously been reported in PE biodeterioration studies. S. spiritivorum was selected for whole-genome sequencing. Comparative functional genomics revealed variation in enzyme families potentially associated with oxidation, hydrolysis, and β-oxidation. CAZy profiling identified carbohydrate-active enzymes, including proteins carrying predicted signal peptides. KEGG reconstruction supported alcohol- and aldehyde-to-fatty-acid conversion, fatty-acid activation, and β-oxidation-related metabolism. SignalP predicted secretion signals in selected proteins, while local synteny analysis showed conserved organization of these loci in Sphingobacterium strains. Overall, these findings suggest the potential of these isolates for PE biodeterioration.
authors: Elsayed AF, Amin DH, Gebreel HM, Mahasneh I, Youssef HI.

title: Prospecting for efflux pump and repressor genes in rivers of the Amazon region of Brazil.
abstract: BackgroundThe spread of multidrug-resistant bacteria in water bodies poses a significant public health concern. Efflux pumps represent critical mechanisms of antimicrobial resistance, regulated by genetic repressors that aid bacterial adaptation to environmental stress. This study profiles the diversity of efflux pump genes and genetic repressors in the surface waters of the Cereja (Bragança) and Uraim (Paragominas) rivers in the Amazon region of Brazil.Methods and resultsSurface water samples were collected along a gradient of anthropogenic impact, and environmental DNA was sequenced on the Illumina platform. The resulting sequencing data were subsequently subjected to metagenomic analysis, which identified a higher abundance of efflux pump genes in the Cereja River compared to the Uraim River, dominated by the RND and SMR families. Additionally, two-component system (TCS) repressor genes, particularly cbrB, were successfully recovered and modeled using Swiss-Model homology modeling.ConclusionsThe higher coverage of the cbrB repressor gene in anthropogenically impacted sites underscores its regulatory role in bacterial stress responses, suggesting its potential application as a novel biomarker of environmental pollution and antibiotic resistance spread in aquatic ecosystems.
authors: Chaves VA, Martins DT, Dantas CWD, da Silva SM, da Silva JAG, Queiroz Cavalcante AL, Macedo DB, Fernandes ALL, Tiwari S, Ramos RTJ, Cardenas-Alegria OV.

title: Elucidating changes in gene expression driving nuclear dynamics across a foraminiferal life cycle with Pheno2Seq
abstract: In many microeukaryotes, conserved morphology masks transitions between haploid and diploid phases of the life cycle, making it difficult to link gene expression to development. Hence, insights on such transitions come largely from ‘model’ lineages of animals, plants and fungi. To address this gap, we developed a method, Pheno2Seq, that enables visualization of fluorescently-stained individuals followed by identification of candidate genes through single-cell transcriptome analyses. We applied this method in  Allogromia laticollaris , a foraminifera with a complex life cycle that alternates between haploid and diploid phases and includes endoreplication to ∼11,000N. As this taxon lacks a reference genome, we used a conservative phylogenomic approach to identify gene families present across diverse foraminifera. We identified >800 differentially expressed genes underlying life cycle transitions along with a similar number of constitutively-expressed genes. During  Zerfall , a phase of extreme endoreplication, the transcriptome is largely silenced with the exception of gene families involved in genome processes and stability. Intriguingly, these gene families include chromatin modifiers, spliceosomal components and histone paralogs, some of which are known to contribute to cell type differentiation in multicellular eukaryotes. We also find numerous genes involved in DNA repair (e.g. DNA damage response and R-loop regulating genes). We speculate that these genes are part of an ancient eukaryotic toolkit, likely present in the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) and that regulates genomes during life cycle transitions. Our method, Pheno2Seq, can be adapted to diverse lineages to enable the study of life cycle regulation in microeukaryotes that lack morphologically distinguishable life cycle stages.  Significance  Unicellular eukaryotes represent most of the diversity across the eukaryotic tree of life, but life cycle transitions in many of these species can be cryptic (i.e. multiple stages share identical morphology despite changing nuclear phenotypes). We develop Pheno2Seq (Phenotype to Sequence), which characterizes nuclear phenotype by fluorescence microscopy, then elucidates gene expression underlying nuclear stage transitions. Changes in nuclear phenotype in the foraminifera sampled here demonstrates a central role of the reprogramming of histones and other genes involved in chromatin regulation, suggesting that the diverse life cycles observed across the eukaryotic tree of life emerged from a shared toolkit present in the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA).
authors: Sterner EG, Ribeiro GM, Leleu M, Katz LA.

title: Integrated multi-omics analysis reveals coordinated root and rhizosphere responses underlying AMF-mediated drought tolerance in kiwifruit.
abstract: Drought stress substantially restricts kiwifruit (Actinidia spp.) growth and productivity, yet the mechanisms through which arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) promote drought tolerance remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, root physiological and molecular analyses were integrated with multi-omics profiling of the rhizosphere microbiome to investigate AMF-mediated drought responses under well-watered and drought-stress conditions. Under drought stress, AMF inoculation improved plant growth, root development, cellular ultrastructure, and physiological performance. More importantly, root omics analysis revealed coordinated regulation of drought-responsive pathways involving glutathione metabolism, amino acid biosynthesis, phytohormone regulation, and energy metabolism. Beyond these plant responses, AMF inoculation altered bacterial and fungal community composition, enriched potentially beneficial taxa, and increased rhizosphere network connectivity under drought stress. Within the restructured microbiome, we identified an AMF-specific drought-responsive amplicon sequence variant (ASV) module composed primarily of bacterial taxa and associated with cross-kingdom microbial interactions. Integrated microbial-metabolite network analysis further identified a metabolite feature annotated as 1-piperideine as a candidate associated with selective microbial recruitment in AMF-colonized rhizospheres. Together, these findings suggest that AMF-associated drought tolerance in kiwifruit involves complementary changes in plant physiology, root molecular responses, and rhizosphere microbiome assembly. A mechanistic basis is thereby provided for developing AMF-based strategies to improve kiwifruit production under increasing water limitation.
authors: Shah OU, Shuchen F, Jia W, Hongfei S, Luyao C, Wenjie Z, Wenping X.

title: Molecular surveillance of adenovirus and coronavirus in Procellariiformes, Brazil: Detection of new divergent adenoviruses.
abstract: Adenoviruses are widespread DNA viruses that infect a broad range of vertebrate hosts and are recognized for their long-term host coevolution, remarkable genetic diversity, and broad pathogenic potential. Coronaviruses circulate among wild birds due to their evolutionary potential and are relevant to animal and public health. However, the diversity and ecological role of these viruses in pelagic seabirds remain poorly understood. This study provides the first molecular survey of adenoviruses and coronaviruses in Procellariiformes from the South Atlantic. Fifty stranded individuals representing 12 Procellariiformes species were collected along the southeastern Brazilian coast, between 2017 and 2023. Adenovirus and coronavirus survey were performed using nested PCR protocols, followed by sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, and histopathology of positive cases. Adenovirus was detected in seven individuals (14%; 95% CI: 5.8-26.7%) from three species: Southern Giant Petrels (Macronectes giganteus), Cory's Shearwaters (Calonectris borealis), and Black-browed Albatrosses (Thalassarche melanophris). Five sequence types were identified, including similar variants in Southern Giant Petrels and distinct adenoviruses in Cory's Shearwaters and Black-browed Albatrosses. All viruses clustered within a divergent lineage with adenoviruses previously detected in New Zealand seabirds and a Chimney Swift from the USA. No intranuclear inclusion bodies were found in histopathological analysis. All specimens were coronavirus-negative. This first molecular detection of adenoviruses in Procellariiformes expands the known diversity and host range of seabird adenoviruses and suggests circulation of genetically distinct viruses across oceanic regions, highlighting the need for genomic and epidemiological studies of their evolution, transmission, and health impacts.
journal: Comparative immunology, microbiology and infectious diseases
authors: Baes L, Reigada C, Duarte-Benvenuto A, Zamana RR, Sacristán C, Guerra JM, Schreiner TM, Murro RS, Catão-Dias JL, Ewbank AC.

title: Clonal integration drives divergent assembly of rhizosphere bacteria and fungi in Hydrocotyle vulgaris under cadmium heterogeneity.
abstract: Clonal plants enhance their fitness in heterogeneous environments through clonal integration, which enables resource sharing among interconnected ramets. However, how clonal integration shapes rhizosphere microbiome assembly and function remains poorly understood. In this study, we constructed patchy heterogeneous soils with cadmium-polluted and unpolluted substrates to simulate fragmented polluted habitats. Apical ramets were grown in cadmium-polluted soil and basal positions were cultivated in unpolluted soil, with stolons left either intact or severed. Rhizosphere and root-zone soils were sampled, and bacterial and fungal communities were characterized via 16 S rRNA and ITS amplicon sequencing. Our results demonstrated that stolon integration significantly altered rhizosphere microbial composition, with elevated relative abundances of Acidobacteriota, Actinobacteriota and Ascomycota and a reduction in Firmicutes. Beneficial genera Streptomyces and Savoryella were enriched under intact stolon treatments. Bacterial α-richness (Chao1) was significantly higher in the rhizosphere of stolon-intact plants, especially at the basal positions, whereas fungal α- richness showed no significant difference among treatments. Beta-diversity analysis revealed that bacterial communities were more sensitive to stolon integration than fungal communities, with fungal community structural shifts observed only in the basal rhizosphere. Amplicon sequence variant (ASV) analysis showed that intact stolons increased unique bacterial ASVs but reduced unique fungal ASVs in the basal rhizosphere. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that clonal integration differentially regulates the assembly of bacterial and fungal communities in the rhizosphere. This study highlights the distinct ecological roles of bacteria and fungi in plant-soil feedback and emphasizes multi-kingdom assessments of clonal integration under heterogeneous Cd condition.
authors: Wang XG, Liu B, Wang XX, Jing H, Zhao BN, Yan J, Li D, Zhang R, Si C.

title: A Gap-Free Telomere-to-Telomere Genome Assembly of Talaromyces marneffei Strain B33c Provides Insights into Chromosomal Architecture and Comparative Genomics.
abstract: Talaromyces marneffei is a thermally dimorphic fungal pathogen endemic to Southeast Asia and southern China, yet chromosome-scale genomic resources from early clinical isolates remain limited. Here, we combined PacBio HiFi sequencing with Oxford Nanopore and Hi-C validation to generate a gap-free, telomere-to-telomere genome assembly of strain B33c, a 1984 clinical isolate from China. The 28.1-Mb assembly comprises eight chromosomes and enabled detailed characterization of chromosomal architecture, including chromosome termini, the repeat landscape, and putative centromeric regions. Using 3314 single-copy orthologs, we reconstructed a time-calibrated phylogeny that recovered two major lineages among the sampled T. marneffei isolates, with B33c clustering closely with the Vietnamese isolates. Comparative synteny analyses showed a largely conserved chromosome-scale backbone within T. marneffei, alongside isolate-specific rearrangement-like patterns. Orthogroup profiling revealed a widely shared gene-family repertoire with isolate-specific variation, as illustrated by differences in the functional enrichment profiles of the ATCC 18224- and B33c-specific orthogroup sets. Overall, the B33c T2T assembly expands genomic resources for T. marneffei and provides additional strain-specific information for comparative studies of genome organization and evolution.
authors: Zhou X, Zheng Y, Jiang Z, Karki S, Pan K, Zheng D, Li X, Huang L, Liu G, Ling J, Tsui CKM, Cao C.

title: Chemical diversity analysis identifies inhibitory compounds in the secretomes of citrus-associated Bacillus spp. to the Huanglongbing pathogen, "Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus," and citrus root pathogens.
abstract: Huanglongbing (HLB) is a devastating and incurable citrus disease associated with the gram-negative, phloem-limited, and unculturable bacterium "Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus" (CLas), transmitted by the psyllid Diaphorina citri. Our goal was to identify high-performing microbial candidates from a previously established citrus-associated microbial collection for the management of HLB and associated root pathogens. Candidate selection was based on bioactivity, genomic, and metabolomic profiles. Eighteen Bacillus isolates were screened for antagonistic activity against Liberibacter crescens, CLas, and citrus-associated Phytophthora and Fusarium spp. Phylogenetic analysis grouped the isolates into four species groups: Bacillus velezensis, B. subtilis, B. pumilus, and B. cereus. Among these, B. velezensis exhibited the strongest and broadest inhibitory activity, followed by B. subtilis. This enhanced antagonistic potential is likely associated with the greater number and diversity of biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) identified. Notably, CLas-inhibitory isolates included B. velezensis (CB0021 and CB0909) and B. altitudinis (CB0086). Bacilysin and surfactin BGCs were conserved across all CLas-inhibitory isolates, suggesting a potential role in CLas suppression. Accordingly, surfactins were detected in bioactive fractions of B. velezensis (CB0027 and CB0909) and B. subtilis (CB0893), supporting their likely contribution to bioactivity and inhibiting L. crescens growth in vitro, highlighting their potential as candidate compounds for CLas management. Overall, this study underscores the importance of microbial discovery, screening, and characterization as an effective strategy for identifying sustainable solutions to manage HLB.IMPORTANCEHuanglongbing (HLB) is a severe disease of citrus that has altered the citrus landscape worldwide and currently has no cure. It is caused by the bacterium "Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus" (CLas) and transmitted by the psyllid Diaphorina citri. Currently, the most effective control strategy for this disease relies on trunk injection of antibiotics oxytetracycline and streptomycin, and there is a need to find alternative solutions to complement or replace chemical control. Here, we aimed to select high-performing candidates from our previously established citrus-associated microbial collection to manage HLB and root-associated pathogens. We screened 18 Bacillus isolates for antagonistic activity against Liberibacter crescens, CLas, and citrus-associated Phytophthora and Fusarium spp., and we generated their genomic and metabolomic profiles. Our research centers on selecting microbial candidates for their bioactivity and antimicrobial metabolite production, aiming to develop effective plant-protective bioinoculants for mitigation of HLB.
authors: Vieira FC, Ramasamy M, Mandadi K, Esteves MB, de Souza A, Allen M, Ruiz Rivera C, Yang C, Maloney KN, Roper MC.

title: The e14 cryptic prophage belongs to a temperate phage lineage distributed across Escherichia and retains genes with potential anti-phage defence functions
abstract: The e14 region of Escherichia coli str. K-12 is a cryptic prophage that retains functional excision and integration machinery despite extensive loss of phage reproductive functions. However, its evolutionary relationship to other bacteriophages remains poorly resolved. Here, we identify related prophages across four Escherichia species, alongside related, independently isolated bacteriophages. The putative prophages were 34.7–43.5 kb, more than twice the size of e14 (15.2 kb), and retained much of the genomic architecture required for phage reproduction. Comparative genomic and phylogenetic analyses support e14 as a highly reduced member of a broader lineage of temperate bacteriophages. The retention of genes with established or putative anti-phage functions further raises the possibility that e14 represents a form of ‘defence flotsam’, potentially protecting its host against subsequent phage infections. More broadly, cryptic prophages may provide reservoirs of anti-phage defence functions long after losing their capacity for phage reproduction.
authors: Gifford DR.
