title: Isolation and Probiotic Characterization of Bacillus stercoris VR19 from the polyherbal Ayurvedic fermented formulation Madhookasavam
abstract: Abstract    Probiotics are live microorganisms that provide health benefits to the host when administered in adequate amounts. In this study, bacterial isolates from Madhookasavam, a polyherbal Ayurvedic fermented formulation, were screened to identify potential probiotic candidates. Preliminary safety assessment included Gram staining, hemolysis testing, and antibiotic susceptibility profiling. Among the isolates, VR19 was the only strain to exhibit γ-hemolysis, indicating a non-hemolytic phenotype, and was susceptible to several clinically relevant antibiotics, including Chloramphenicol and azithromycin. The isolate VR19 demonstrated tolerance to acidic conditions and simulated gastrointestinal stresses, including pepsin (0.1–1%), bile salts (0.1–3%), and NaCl (1–10%). Functional characterization revealed cellulase activity of up to 1.95 U/mL, corresponding to the release of 0.959 mg/mL reducing sugars. The isolate also exhibited concentration-dependent antioxidant activity, reaching a maximum DPPH radical-scavenging activity of 72.9%. Probiotic performance was further evaluated using  Caenorhabditis elegans  as an in vivo model. VR19 showed effective intestinal colonization and persistence, as demonstrated by bacterial enumeration and Gram staining of colonies recovered from the nematode intestine. Molecular identification based on, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and phylogenetic analysis identified VR19 as  Bacillus stercoris  . Collectively, these findings show that  Bacillus stercoris  VR19 possesses promising probiotic properties, including a non-hemolytic phenotype, gastrointestinal stress tolerance, cellulolytic and antioxidant activities, and effective intestinal colonization. The strain therefore warrants further safety and efficacy evaluation for potential therapeutic and functional-food applications.
authors: Rathi V, Babu KR, Chauhan N.

title: Post-Transplant Gut Dysbiosis is a Targetable Axis
abstract: Abstract    Long-term graft attrition remains a critical challenge despite maintenance immunosuppression, which perturbs intestinal immune homeostasis and microbial communities, which may contribute to vascular inflammation and chronic graft injury. We previously identified  Muribaculaceae  expansion as a shared feature of long-term exposure to multiple distinct immunosuppressant classes in the murine gut microbiome. In this study, using a fully MHC-mismatched mouse heart transplant model under chronic tacrolimus treatment, we tested whether oral administration of the protolerogenic  Bifidobacterium pseudolongum subsp. globosum  (  Bifido  ) or pro-inflammatory  Desulfovibrio desulfuricans  (  Desulfo  ) could redirect this dysbiotic state and affect graft fate. Longitudinal metagenomic and metabolomic profiling showed an ordered tacrolimus-associated microbial succession that culminated in sustained  Muribaculaceae  enrichment with coordinated luminal and circulating metabolic remodeling.  Bifido  , but not  Desulfo  , redirected the community trajectory by reducing  Muribaculaceae  enrichment, increasing selected fermentative commensals, and establishing metabolites linked to epithelial and immune regulation, including kynurenic acid and N-acetylspermine. Spatial transcriptomics showed that  Bifido  partially attenuated early tacrolimus-induced colonic metabolic, stress, and epithelial-remodeling programs while later selectively reprogramming ileal antimicrobial defense, crypt-proximal metabolic adaptation, and mucosal humoral immunity. These changes were accompanied by minimal graft vasculitis and fibrosis, increased Foxp3⁺ regulatory T-cell localization in mesenteric and peripheral lymph nodes (LNs), and partial preservation of tolerogenic stromal laminin α4:α5 organization. In contrast,  Desulfo  -treated mice retained  Muribaculaceae  enrichment and developed progressive vascular injury. In an exploratory human-to-mouse fecal microbiota transfer (FMT) experiment, chronic allograft vasculopathy (CAV)-associated donor stool promoted expansion of endogenous murine  Muribaculaceae  and a distinct microbial functional state, together with increased graft fibrosis, T cell infiltration, LNs remodeling, and vasculitis. Whereas non-CAV donor stool favored  Bifido  enrichment and was associated with lessened graft pathology. Together, these findings provide proof of principle that the immunosuppressant-perturbed gut ecosystem is a targetable axis, supporting novel adjunct therapies that complement immunosuppression and mitigate chronic graft injury.
authors: Ma B, Kensiski A, Wu L, Gavzy S, Zhang T, Chaudry I, France M, Lwin HW, WillsonShirkey M, Lohmar B, Piao W, Mas V, Bromberg J.

title: Simplified Synergistic Rhizosphere Bacterial Consortia Enhance the Antagonistic Activities Against Ralstonia solanacearum and Improve Plant Health.
abstract: The rhizosphere microbiota plays a vital role in plant stress resistance and pathogen suppression. Bacterial wilt, caused by Ralstonia solanacearum, leads to significant economic losses in a wide variety of crops. The utilization of native microbial consortia has emerged as a promising strategy for combating this disease. In this study, we assembled a synthetic microbial consortium (Co-4) from rhizosphere bacteria with demonstrated antagonistic activity, comprising four strains of Bacillus sp., Heyndrickxia sp., Franconibacter sp., and Pseudomonas sp. Transcriptome analysis of tomato plants treated with Co-4 revealed significant alterations in gene expression, particularly in carbohydrate and energy metabolism, as well as translation processes. These changes correlated with enhancements in various plant growth traits, including height, stem thickness, biomass, leaf area, photosynthetic rate, and root development. Furthermore, two simplified consortia, SynCom1 (Bacillus, Heyndrickxia, and Franconibacter) and SynCom2 (Franconibacter and Pseudomonas), exhibited augmented antagonistic properties against R. solanacearum compared with their individual constituent strains. Using SynCom2 as a model, we demonstrated that its synergistic interactions resulted in increased biofilm formation, motility, biomass production, cross-feeding interactions, and volatile organic compound emissions, all of which likely contribute to disease suppression and enhanced plant defense. This study highlights the potential of simplified synthetic consortia for managing bacterial wilt through cooperative microbial functions, presenting an effective and environmentally sustainable biocontrol strategy.
authors: Liu X, Chen T, Qin X, Han M, Zhang X, Zhou J, Li P.

title: Characterization of Ralstonia pseudosolanacearum Phylotype I Isolates Causing Bacterial Wilt in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
abstract: Ralstonia pseudosolanacearum is a soilborne bacterial pathogen responsible for bacterial wilt disease in a wide range of host plants, including solanaceous crops. In this study, we collected 22 bacterial wilt isolates from solanaceous crops in seven sampling plots across the Kongo Central region of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). The genomic characterization of these isolates identified a single haplotype belonging to the R. pseudosolanacearum phylotype I sequevar 31 genetic lineage. We assembled the genome sequence of one representative strain, RUN6904, placed it in a phylogenetic context, and identified its type III effector repertoire. We demonstrated the virulence of the DRC isolates on tomato and showed the resistance of the AG91-25 eggplant accession likely triggered by the recognition of the RipAX2 type III effector from these isolates.[Formula: see text] Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). title: A new species in the Magnaporthiopsis genus from wild rice enhances rice yield and disease resistance by restructuring the microbiome.
abstract: Wild rice serves as a rich reservoir of beneficial endophytic fungi. However, the diversity and functional potential of these endophytes remain largely unexplored, limiting their utilization in sustainable rice production. In this work, we isolated and identified a novel endophytic fungus, Magnaporthiopsis oryzae (coded MB-9-27), from wild rice, Oryza granulata, and demonstrated that it directly promotes rice growth (yield increased by 12.66%) and enhances resistance to rice blast (disease rate decreased by 45.51%) in the field. Furthermore, MB-9-27 inoculation reshaped the rice microbiome, simplifying microbial interaction networks while significantly enriching beneficial bacteria (Methylobacterium sp., Sphingomonas sp.) and fungi (Mortierella sp., Rhizophagus sp., Mollisia sp., and Coniothyrium sp.). Among 75 fungi isolated from MB-9-27-treated rice plants, five representative strains (F14: Mortierella sp., F25: Trichoderma sp., F27: Clonostachys sp., F29: Podospora sp., and F30: Pseudeurotium sp.) corresponded to taxa ranked among the top 150 dominant fungal members identified through microbiome analysis. Functional screening revealed that Mortierella sp. (coded F14) markedly promoted rice growth, increasing shoot and root development by 55.8% and 51.6%, respectively, and reducing rice blast severity by 18.2%, indicating its dual role in promoting growth and suppressing disease. Metabolomic profiling of the rice-F14 holobiont identified significant accumulation of several metabolites, including Indole-3-glycerol phosphate (IGP), Adenine, and S-lactoylglutathione (SLG), suggesting alterations in pathways related to tryptophan metabolism, cellular metabolism, and redox homeostasis. Targeted LC-MS analysis further confirmed the production of IGP by F14. Bioassays demonstrated that IGP significantly promoted rice growth, supporting a potential role of tryptophan-derived metabolites in the plant growth-promoting activity of F14. Collectively, our findings demonstrated that MB-9-27 functions not only as a growth-promoting and disease-suppressive endophyte but also as a driver of beneficial microbiota assembly. Our results highlighted the potential of wild rice-derived endophytic fungi and their associated microbiota as valuable resources for microbial-assisted sustainable rice production.
authors: Li W, Zhu Q, Wu Y, Zhu J, Zhu X, Li L, Lin F, Su Z.

title: Biofilm-Controlled Molecular Crosstalk: Nitrogen Fixation, Arsenic Transformation and Antibiotic Resistance.
abstract: Biological nitrogen fixation, arsenic biotransformation and antibiotic resistance are conventionally studied separately, yet the environmental biofilm-bacteria's dominant organisational state in soils, sediments and rhizospheres-supplies a shared physicochemical and genetic context in which the three can intersect. The extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix imposes steep oxygen, redox and metabolite gradients across micrometre scales and demonstrably shelters oxygen-sensitive nitrogenase, retains arsenic-transforming enzymes (ArsC, ArsM and AioA) and elevates horizontal gene transfer (HGT) frequencies orders of magnitude above planktonic conditions. Individual circuits are genetically established in single organisms-RpoN coactivates pslA and nifA and the non-coding RNA NfiS stabilises nifK and katB transcripts, in Pseudomonas stutzeri A1501-but their assembly into one programme linking surface commitment, diazotrophic activation and oxidative stress defence, with additional c-di-GMP and ArsR stimulon input under arsenic stress, is proposed, not demonstrated. Arsenic-driven coselection of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) is the best-supported limb, operating through cross-resistance (RND efflux), co-resistance (ars-ARG colocation on Tn21, Class 1 integrons, IncP/IncQ plasmids) and coregulation (ArsR stimulon, SOS-derepressed intI1), whereas the proposal that diazotrophy-derived ammonium supports S-adenosyl-l-methionine supply for ArsM-mediated methylation rests on gene coenrichment and rate correlation rather than direct flux measurement. This review integrates these processes into a single biofilm framework, classifies each proposed linkage by the evidence behind it, identifies candidate trifunctional mobile elements carrying ars, nif and ARG cassettes in hyperaccumulator rhizospheres and paddy soils and specifies the minimum spatially resolved single-cell dataset (bacterial-MERFISH, par-seqFISH and SIP-NanoSIMS) needed to test the proposed couplings.
authors: Bagchi D, Majumdar A, Kotta-Loizou I, Buck M.

title: Identification of highly specific bacterial L-asparaginase through genome-wide computational screening and experimental validation.
abstract: BackgroundBacterial L-asparaginases are key therapeutics for acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), but their clinical efficacy is limited by off-target L-glutaminase co-activity, which contributes to severe side effects. This study aimed to identify highly specific bacterial L-asparaginases with minimal L-glutaminase co-activity.MethodsWe screened ~ 85,000 prokaryotic genomes using a workflow integrating AlphaFold2 structure prediction, molecular docking, binding-energy estimation, and molecular dynamics simulations. Six top-ranked enzymes were selected for experimental validation.ResultsRhAII protein from Acidobacteriota sp. showed high specificity toward L-asparagine (L-Asn), with a Michaelis constant (KM) of 12 ± 2 µM and turnover number (kcat) of 34 ± 2 s⁻¹, and negligible L-glutaminase activity. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations revealed a relationship between enzyme activity and the conformational dynamics of the flexible gating element (FGE), characterized by residue-level root mean square fluctuation (RMSF), and L-Asn positional fluctuations, evaluated by ligand root mean square deviation (RMSD) relative to the protein. High L-asparaginase activity was associated with optimal FGE dynamics and low L-Asn RMSD, consistent with stable substrate positioning within the active site. In contrast, enzymes with altered FGE dynamics relative to the reference EcAII enzyme from Escherichia coli, such as PoAII from Planctomycetota sp., showed poor L-asparaginase performance (KM 5797 ± 1143 µM; kcat 1.2 ± 0.1 s⁻¹).ConclusionsGenome- and structure-guided screening identified RhAII as a promising antileukemic candidate for further validation in biological models. A key limitation of the computational workflow was the lack of correlation between predicted substrate binding energies and catalytic efficiency, highlighting the importance of active-site dynamics in enzyme kinetics.
authors: Janicki M, Zielezinski A, Pieróg I, Śliwiak J, Ludwików A, Karlowski WM, Jaskolski M, Loch JI.

title: Endolysin potentiates depolymerase efficacy against Klebsiella pneumoniae under low-serum conditions.
abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a Gram-negative opportunistic pathogen responsible for severe healthcare-associated infections. The increasing prevalence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) strains, particularly those resistant to carbapenems, poses a significant clinical challenge. In this study, we isolated Jasmi2, a lytic bacteriophage targeting K2-type K. pneumoniae strains. Jasmi2 was classified within the genus Webervirus and contained a linear double-stranded DNA genome of 45,811 bp with 67 predicted open reading frames. ORF67 was identified as a K2-targeting tail depolymerase and designated DpoJ2. Recombinant DpoJ2 efficiently degraded the surface polysaccharide of K2-type K. pneumoniae and reduced biofilm biomass without significantly affecting viable cell counts. While DpoJ2 sensitized K. pneumoniae to serum-mediated killing, achieving an approximately 3.7-log reduction in bacterial counts in 25% human serum, its bactericidal activity diminished at lower serum concentrations. We successfully overcame this threshold by developing a novel combinatorial approach with the endolysin LysTS6. The DpoJ2-LysTS6 combination demonstrated superior efficacy compared to individual treatment, significantly enhancing bacterial eradication under low-serum conditions. DpoJ2 and LysTS6 exhibited no detectable cytotoxicity or hemolytic activity at the tested concentrations. The enhanced efficacy of the combination was further validated in vivo Galleria mellonella infection models, where the combination of DpoJ2 and LysTS6 increased larval survival to 20% at 72 h, whereas no larvae survived following either individual treatment. These findings establish a novel antibiotic-independent strategy combining a phage-derived depolymerase with an endolysin to enhance antibacterial activity against MDR K. pneumoniae, particularly under conditions where serum-mediated killing is limited.
authors: Suh E, Kim J, Lee J, Yong D, Yoo S, Ryu S, Kong M.

title: Phenotypic and genomic characterization of five novel Klebsiella bacteriophages: Exploring the relationship between spot-lysis patterns and host defense systems.
abstract: BackgroundIndividual Klebsiella phages typically exhibit narrow host ranges; novel phages must therefore continue to be isolated and characterized to assemble phage therapy cocktails. However, the determinants governing host range remain unclear.ObjectivesTo characterize five novel Klebsiella phages and examine relationships between their spot-lysis profiles and strain genotypes or host defense repertoires.MethodsFive sewage-derived phages were morphologically characterized, and their complete genomes were determined. Spot lysis was assessed against 249 clinical isolates of the Klebsiella pneumoniae species complex (KpSC). Genotypes, virulence and resistance determinants, and anti-phage defense systems were identified from draft genomes using Kleborate and DefenseFinder.ResultsTwo phages were Myovirus-like and three Siphovirus-like, representing novel species within Jiaodavirus and Sugarlandvirus, and the known species Slopekvirus matisse. Overall, 160 of 249 isolates (64.3%) showed spot lysis with at least one phage; ΦKpT256 produced spot lysis in 137 isolates (55.0%), comparatively broad for a single phage. Spot lysis extended across diverse K/O loci, sequence types, and virulence/resistance profiles. Although 2619 defense systems of 156 types were identified, descriptive comparison revealed no obvious one-to-one correspondence between spot-lysis patterns and individual defense systems.ConclusionsSpot-lysis patterns were not readily explained by the bacterial characteristics examined or by any single defense system, suggesting that additional host and phage factors may contribute. ΦKpT256 and the three Siphovirus-like phages showed differing species-level spot-lysis profiles and warrant evaluation as potential components of a KpSC-targeted phage cocktail.
journal: Journal of infection and chemotherapy : official journal of the Japan Society of Chemotherapy
authors: Nagashima S, Yamada K, Aoki K, Kajiwara C, Komori K, Wakui A, Aiba Y, Miyanaga K, Cui L, Tateda K, Harada S.

title: The origin of the MV Hondius Andes outbreak
abstract: In April-July 2026, Andes virus (ANDV) caused an outbreak aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship resulting in 12 confirmed cases and three deaths. Before symptom onset, the index case had travelled through hantavirus-endemic regions of Chile and Argentina, leaving the geographic origin of infection unresolved. We conducted phylogenetic and phylogeographic analyses using newly generated ANDV genomes from human cases and rodent reservoirs to investigate the likely origin of the outbreak. Through phylogenetic analyses, we show that the outbreak genome falls within a geographically structured lineage spanning southern Chile and Argentine Andean Patagonia. Using phylogeographic reconstructions across all three segments, integrated with the index case’s travel itinerary, we identified the Toltén-Lanco area of southern Chile as the most likely geographic origin of the outbreak genome, with two candidate locations accounting for >98% of the posterior support. However, the index case visited this area 62-66 days before symptom onset, exceeding the conventionally reported ANDV incubation period of 7-42 days. Thus, while genomic evidence supports a southern Chilean origin of the outbreak genome, the timing and circumstances of transmission to the index case remain unresolved.
authors: Ulloa-Zepeda L, Parker E, Gangavarapu K, Castillo A, Pavez C, Fernandez J, Vilches M, Vial P, Rambaut A, Andersen KG, Vial C.

title: Characterization of lactic and acetic acid bacteria and their phages from a California winery
abstract: Abstract    Spoilage of wine from volatile acidity or off flavors caused by uncontrolled growth of lactic acid bacteria (LAB) and acetic acid bacteria (AAB) results in significant economic losses. We aim to survey the persistence of LAB and AAB throughout the wine processing stages, and to evaluate the potential of phages as targeted microbial control. Cabernet Sauvignon samples were collected from a winery in Livermore, California during 2025 harvest season, covering grape rinse, juice/must, the end of primary fermentation and malolactic fermentation steps. Bacterial 16S amplicon sequencing of these samples identified key species that persist through the wine processing steps, including  Lactiplantibacillus plantarum  and  Levilactobacillus lactis  among LAB, and  Acetobacter oryzoeni  and  Acetobacter pasteurianus  among AAB. Phages targeting  L. brevis  ,  A. pasteurianus  and  A. fabarum  were isolated.  L. brevis  phages Indaco_L1 and Indaco_L2 (genome size of 135,623 bp and 141,184 bp, respectively) are related to phages in the  Tybeckvirus  genus of the  Herelleviridae  family, but distinct enough to form two novel species. The two novel  Acetobacter  phages, a first reported  Acetobacter  jumbo phage Vinphasol_A1 (genome size 397,952 bp) and Vinphasol_A2 (genome size 56,636 bp), share little DNA sequence similarity to phages in the current NCBI database. These isolated phages were able to inhibit the growth of  L. brevis, A. pasteurianus  and  A. fabarum  for up to 7 days in conditions simulating wine fermentation, suggests their potential application in controlling microbial spoilage during wine making processes.
authors: Boeckman J, Gill J, Jafri A.

title: Identification and Genomic Analysis of Lelliottia nimipressuralis JS203 and Its Production of 2-Phenylethanol with Broad-Spectrum Activity against Phytopathogens.
abstract: Colletotrichum dematium, a causal agent of anthracnose, poses an escalating threat to global agriculture, exacerbated by the emergence of resistance to conventional fungicides. In this study, we employed a "one strain-many compounds" (OSMAC) approach to screen 724 environmental bacterial isolates under varied media and temperature conditions to maximize secondary metabolite diversity. Isolate JS203, identified as Lelliottia nimipressuralis through whole-genome sequencing, demonstrated robust, broad-spectrum inhibition against C. dematium and several other major phytopathogens. Bioactivity-guided fractionation of JS203 extracts, followed by NMR and GC-MS analysis, identified the volatile aromatic alcohol 2-phenylethanol (2-PE) as the primary antifungal metabolite. Genomic analysis revealed that JS203 harbors Ehrlich pathway genes, including idpC and gpr_2, which share 100% amino acid identity with validated 2-PE biosynthetic enzymes from Enterobacter sp. CGMCC 5087. These results suggest a conserved metabolic route for 2-PE production in this understudied genus. Collectively, our findings highlight L. nimipressuralis JS203 and its production of 2-PE as a promising natural strategy for the sustainable management of anthracnose and other fungal diseases.
authors: Srok J, Wei SY, Yang CH.

title: Monitoring single-cell metabolic phenotyping changes of Daqu microbiota during fermentation by Raman spectroscopy.
abstract: Monitoring microbial community dynamics during natural food fermentation is essential for stabilizing fermentation processes and improving product flavor profiles. This study employed single-cell Raman spectroscopy to monitor the metabolic change of Daqu microbiota during fermentation. First, we developed an operational phenotypic unit (OPU)-based clustering method to process Raman spectral data of a nine-member microbial community. The clustering was validated by sorting out representative single cells from different OPUs and performing 16S/ITS region sequencing. Second, single-cell Raman spectroscopy was applied to the mixed Daqu sample throughout fermentation, identifying 10 OPUs and 54 sub-OPUs. Single cells from different OPUs were sorted and sequenced to obtain taxonomic annotation, which were correlated with the Raman spectral characteristics of each OPU. The OPU-based Raman spectroscopy method was successfully used to monitor the single-cell metabolic phenotypes of Daqu microbiota during fermentation, and taxonomic annotations revealed the succession of microbial community structure. This study presents a novel approach for monitoring the dynamics of metabolic phenotypes within Daqu microbial communities, offering a data-driven decision-making approach for subsequent production operations in multi-species fermentation processes.IMPORTANCEMicrobial communities play pivotal roles in diverse industrial processes, yet monitoring their metabolic dynamics remains challenging. Current omics approaches, including metagenomics, transcriptomics, and mass spectrometry-based metabolomics, fail to establish direct genotype-phenotype linkages at the single-cell level and often require destructive sampling. This study introduces operational phenotypic units (OPUs) as a novel framework to bridge this gap by integrating single-cell Raman spectroscopy with sequencing technologies. Our method enables non-destructive, rapid monitoring of metabolic phenotypes while preserving cells for downstream analysis. By applying this approach to solid-state Daqu fermentation, we demonstrate its capability to track microbial community succession and identify functionally distinct populations in real time. This data-driven strategy offers significant potential for optimizing multi-species fermentation processes across food, environmental, and biotechnological industries, providing a powerful tool for microbial community management and process control.
authors: Xu L, Liang P, Wang Y, Zhang X-J, Chai L-J, Xu H-Y, Wang S-T, Zhang S-Y, Shen C-H, Lu Z-M, Huang WE, Xu Z-H.

title: Metatranscriptomic profiling of active endophytic microbiome functions across diverse Musa cultivars.
abstract: Plant-endophyte symbioses play important roles in plant health and resilience, but the active functions of endophytic microbiomes remain less characterized than those of soil and rhizosphere microbiomes. We used metatranscriptomic profiling of culture-free enriched endophytic microbiomes from seven Musa cultivars grown under shared environmental conditions to characterize active microbial taxa and functional annotations across sampled tissues. Because each genotype and tissue combination had only one metatranscriptomic sample, this pilot study focuses on the microbial transcripts and functions detected in each sample rather than testing for cultivar or tissue differences. Culture-free enrichment produced metatranscriptomic profiles across samples, including 5,434 taxonomic annotations, and 32,694 gene annotations from expressed microbial transcripts. Functional annotations included pathways involved in secondary metabolism, energy production, environmental information processing, transport systems, oxidative phosphorylation, nitrogen metabolism, quorum sensing, biofilm formation, and xenobiotic biodegradation. Several taxa, including Bradyrhizobium sp., were detected across multiple samples and linked to diverse functional annotations. Approximately 30-35% of sequence reads were annotated as hypothetical proteins, showing that the functions of many detected transcripts are still unknown. Correlation analysis also showed sample-level associations among detected pathway profiles. Overall, this pilot metatranscriptomic data set provides a resource for banana endophyte research and identifies candidate microbial taxa and functional pathways for future studies of plant-microbiome interactions and microbe-microbe relationships.IMPORTANCEEndophytic microbiomes can influence plant health, but their active roles inside banana tissues remain poorly characterized. Here, we used metatranscriptomic profiling of culture-free enriched endophytic microbiomes from seven Musa cultivars to identify microbial taxa and functional pathways detected across sampled tissues. Metatranscriptomic data characterized pathways related to metabolism, transport, microbial signaling, biofilm formation, nutrient cycling, and secondary metabolism, suggesting potential variation in active microbiome profiles among sampled plants. This work provides a pilot resource for banana endophyte research and may help guide future studies on how plant-associated microbiomes interact with their hosts, how microbes function together inside plant tissues, and how these relationships could be used for microbiome-based crop improvement.
authors: Aghdam SA, De Souza R, Brown AMV.

title: Transposon mutagenesis identifies lon, csgF, and rfbF as critical genetic determinants of biofilm architecture and adhesion in multidrug-resistant Salmonella Typhimurium.
abstract: Salmonella Typhimurium relies on biofilm formation to withstand environmental stressors, resist antimicrobials, and establish persistent host infections. However, the genetic networks governing biofilm development remain poorly understood. Here, we assessed the biofilm-forming capacity of 708 S. Typhimurium isolates. Among them, 88.56% formed biofilms, with 3.81% classified as strong producers associated with extensive multidrug resistance. To elucidate underlying genetic determinants, we performed EZ-Tn5 transposon mutagenesis on a strong biofilm-producing clinical isolate (15E341), generating ~ 5000 mutants. Phenotypic screening and whole-genome sequencing identified three distinct loci-lon, csgF, and rfbF-whose disruption significantly impaired biofilm formation without affecting planktonic growth. Confocal and electron microscopy (LSCM and FESEM) revealed severely compromised 3D biofilm architecture and defective surface colonization. Furthermore, these mutants exhibited significantly reduced adhesion to Caco-2 epithelial cells, glass, and silicone. Transcriptomic analysis revealed a distinct regulatory shift, characterized by marked upregulation of flagellar assembly pathways and downregulation of fimbrial genes. In a murine model, the mutants exhibited attenuated virulence, evidenced by increased host survival and significantly reduced bacterial colonization in the cecum, liver, and spleen. Notably, whereas CsgF is an established curli-assembly factor and Lon is a well-characterized stress and virulence regulator, RfbF, an O-antigen biosynthesis enzyme, emerged as a previously undercharacterized determinant of biofilm capacity in S. Typhimurium. Collectively, these findings highlight multi-gene coordination in biofilm development and identify pathways that warrant further investigation for disrupting persistent Salmonella infections.
authors: Ge Q, Ye T, Ma S, Jiang L.

title: Metagenomic Next-Generation Sequencing of Mycoplasma hominis Infection in an Immunocompromised Patient: A Case Report.
abstract: Mycoplasma hominis is an underrecognized opportunistic pathogen that can cause extra-genitourinary infections, particularly in immunocompromised hosts. This case report describes a persistent soft tissue infection following a wooden splinter injury in a 52-year-old immunocompromised man, in whom M. hominis was identified by blood mNGS after conventional microbiological investigations were inconclusive. The patient developed recurrent fever, wound pain, swelling, and exudation. Empirical treatment with ertapenem and subsequent surgical intervention did not provide sustained clinical improvement, while conventional microbiological investigations remained inconclusive. Peripheral blood was therefore analyzed by mNGS, which detected M. hominis, human betaherpesvirus 5, and GB virus C. For M. hominis, nine species-specific reads were identified, with a relative abundance of 21.5% for the genus Mycoplasma and 99% confidence for species-level identification. The mNGS finding was interpreted together with the refractory clinical course and the absence of a convincing alternative bacterial pathogen. Following further surgical management and multidisciplinary evaluation, targeted antimicrobial therapy with intravenous moxifloxacin plus omadacycline was administered, followed by oral omadacycline after discharge. The patient subsequently became afebrile, pain improved, and inflammatory markers progressively declined. This case demonstrates the potential utility of blood mNGS for identifying an atypical pathogen in an immunocompromised patient with culture-negative, treatment-refractory infection. The findings also emphasize that low-read mNGS results should be interpreted in conjunction with clinical findings, conventional microbiological investigations, and treatment response.
authors: Li J, Zhou W, Cai L, Shen H, Lu H, Fan J.

title: A Baltic Sea microbiome-derived Type III polyketide synthase produces host-protective alkylresorcinols in E. coli.
abstract: Marine microorganisms are a prolific source of novel polyketide synthases (PKSs) that generate structurally diverse and functional polyketides. Here, we identify a novel type III PKS, ArsMB, from Pontimonas sp. via metagenomic mining of a Baltic Sea microbiome. Heterologous expression of arsMB synthetic gene in an Escherichia coli host that lacks a native type III PKS, combined with a two-step strategy to boost acyl-CoA precursor availability in a glucose-mineral medium, enabled the in vivo synthesis of two cell-associated alkylresorcinols, identified by GC-MS as 5-pentadecyl-1,3-benzenediol (ars1) and 5-tridecyl-1,3-benzenediol (ars2). The product profile is consistent with a tetraketide alkylresorcinol biosynthetic pathway utilizing C16 and C14 acyl starter units, drawn from the host acyl-CoA pool. In agreement, AlphaFold2-based structural modeling predicts a Cys139/His275/Asn308 catalytic triad and a long hydrophobic substrate tunnel compatible with long-chain acyl starter units. E. coli producing the amphipathic cell-associated alkylresorcinols ars1/ars2 exhibited increased resistance to muralytic digestion by endolysins and to hydrogen peroxide. These findings expand the known repertoire of marine-derived type III PKSs and highlight the biotechnological potential of ArsMB-derived alkylresorcinols.
authors: López-Gutiérrez S, Espinosa-Barrera LA, Soto-Hernández A, Zuleta-Prada H, Bustos-Brito C, Cardona-Félix CS, Utrilla J, Velazquez-Cruz B, Cárdenas-Conejo Y, Araujo-León JA, Aguilar-Hernández V, Osuna-Castro JA, Esquivel B, Serrano-Posada H, Centeno-Leija S.

title: Multi-Parameter In Vitro and Genomic Characterization of Bovine-Derived Bacteria with Probiotic Potential.
abstract: Raw milk and bovine feces represent important sources of microorganisms with probiotic potential. This study aimed to identify potential probiotic candidates from bovine-derived samples and to comprehensively characterize their functional and safety-related features by integrating multi-parameter in vitro evaluation with whole-genome analysis. Acid-producing bacteria were isolated from 12 raw milk and 15 bovine fecal samples using bromocresol green agar. Following PCR-based exclusion of Escherichia coli and RAPD-PCR dereplication, the isolates were evaluated for acid and bile tolerance, survival under simulated gastrointestinal conditions, and autoaggregation, leading to the selection of five candidate strains: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum MX13, Lacticaseibacillus paracasei MX165, Enterococcus faecalis MX179, Enterococcus faecium MX125, and Enterococcus durans FX198. Further in vitro characterization revealed marked strain-specific differences in gastrointestinal stress tolerance, autoaggregation, cell-surface hydrophobicity, and antibacterial activity, with the two lactobacilli displaying broader antibacterial spectra than the Enterococcus strains. Multivariate analysis further revealed distinct overall phenotypic profiles among the candidates, with MX13 exhibiting a relatively balanced functional profile across the traits evaluated. Whole-genome analysis revealed clear differences between MX13 and MX125 in antimicrobial resistance-associated, putative virulence-associated, and other functional genomic features, providing additional information for candidate prioritization. Overall, this study identified and characterized five bovine-derived potential probiotic candidates with distinct functional properties through integrated phenotypic and genomic evaluation, providing a basis for their further functional validation and application-oriented assessment.
authors: An M, Wang Y, Niu Y, Wang C, Zhang W, Wu Y.

title: Family-specific structure in infant gut viromes enables closed-set mother-child matching
abstract: Abstract  The early-life gut virome differs so strongly between individuals that the variation is usually treated as noise. We show it is structured by family, specifically enough that a child's virus set points to their own mother. Across 2,664 catalogue metagenomes, 142 twin libraries and 284 shotgun metagenomes re-quantified from raw reads, we ranked 32 candidate mothers by viral overlap with each of 125 child samples from 32 families. Using all detected vOTUs, the true mother ranked first for 67 of 125 samples (53.6%; median rank 1), against a median sample-level accuracy of 2.4% after permuting maternal labels across families. The mean within-family accuracy was 52.0% (family bootstrap 95% confidence interval 37.2% to 66.6%), and the true mother ranked first at least once in 22 of 32 families. Specificity comes from where the background is empty, not where the signal is large: the own-mother excess is largest for viruses of intermediate prevalence (+ 0.64) and small for the rarest (+ 0.09), yet rare viruses discriminate best because unrelated pairs share almost none. The same asymmetry appears independently in the twin cohort, where rare-virus sharing separates co-twins from unrelated pairs at AUC 0.997. Matching is not merely taxonomic: median agreement across cohort-variable consensus positions in shared vOTUs was 1.000 for mother-child pairs against 0.768 for unrelated pairs, positive in all 24 evaluable families. These findings support family structure in infant viromes, with additional within-vOTU consensus-sequence concordance in the evaluable subset of shared viruses. The comparisons are closed-set and do not resolve transmission direction or separate maternal acquisition from continued shared exposure.
authors: Wang A, Lai L, Johnson CP, Yang X, Ye C.

title: AI-driven structural informatics reveals diverse glycosylation machinery across double-stranded DNA viruses
abstract: Abstract  Glycosylation is widespread in biology and shapes molecular recognition, yet the diversity and biosynthetic organization of viral glycosyltransferases (GTs) remain poorly understood. Here we integrate structural-alphabet-guided searches and structure similarity networks with genomic-neighbourhood and biosynthetic gene cluster embedding analyses to examine viral GT-A proteins. This approach reveals extensive structural diversity overlooked by sequence-based annotation, including previously uncharacterized viral GT lineages. Most strikingly, we identified a jumbo-phage locus encoding five tandem glycosyltransferases alongside hydroxymethyl-pyrimidine biosynthetic and sulfation-associated enzymes, suggesting a previously unrecognized form of viral DNA modification involving a sulfated pentasaccharide. Beyond these examples, predicted saccharide-associated loci span divergent double-stranded DNA viruses, from giant viruses to tailed phages, and occupy multiple regions of the reference biosynthetic landscape. Together, our findings uncover an underappreciated repertoire of virus-encoded glycosylation machinery and suggest that viral glycan biosynthesis encompasses diverse molecular contexts and potential biological functions.
authors: Na L, Tajule R, Fang R.

title: Genome-wide analysis of the TAF gene family reveals a role for GhTAF8 in cottonseed oil accumulation.
abstract: TATA-box binding protein (TBP) associated factors (TAFs), together with TBP, com-pose transcription factor IID (TFIID), which is an essential complex for transcription initiation and regulation. TAFs are involved in regulating plant development. However, genome-wide identification and expression pattern analysis of TAFs in cotton remain unreported. In this study, a total of 124 TAF genes were identified in four Gossypium species. TAFs were divided into six subgroups based on the phylogenetic tree analysis. Analysis of collinearity and selection pressure indicated that TAF gene pairs have undergone strong purifying selection during evolution. Gene expression analysis of GhTAFs revealed that TAFs are expressed at all stages of cotton ovule development. Furthermore, a set of key GhTAF genes was identified, which are specifically or constitutively highly expressed across multiple stages of cotton ovule development. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis prioritized GhTAF8 (Ghir_D11G035840) from the blue module associated with 20 days post anthesis, a critical stage of rapid oil accumulation. GhTAF8 exhibited the highest module membership among the nine GhTAFs in this module. Overexpression of GhTAF8 in Arabidopsis thaliana increased seed oil content, whereas virus-induced gene silencing in cotton reduced seed oil content. A GhTAF8-centered co-expression network also identified genes potentially associated with seed development and lipid metabolism. These findings support a functional association between GhTAF8 and seed oil accumulation and provide a foundation for investigating its underlying regulatory mechanisms.
authors: Song J, Gao J, Feng P, Chen S, Jia B, Zhao W, Zhang B, Pei W, Wang L, Wu M, Zheng K, Yu J, Shu J, Liang Y, Ma J.

title: Host-microbiome asynchronous decoupling reveals systemic metabolic allostatic overload mediated by gut genomic potential degradation.
abstract: Background & aimsMetagenomic aging clocks predict chronological age but lose explanatory power during midlife (35-65 years). We hypothesized that cumulative allostatic load drives microenvironmental alterations, leading to asynchronous decoupling of metagenomic and metabolomic profiles.MethodsA metagenomic clock was trained on a lifespan cohort (N = 4551) and evaluated in a midlife sub-cohort (N = 1868). Independent metagenomic (N = 843) and fecal metabolomic (N = 106) cohorts assessed functional and phenotypic trajectories. Within a paired multi-omics cohort (N = 99), Procrustes and spatial dispersion analyses quantified topological decoupling. Metabolic biological age gap (metBAG) and metabolome-wide association studies (MWAS) characterized allostatic load signatures.ResultsThe lifespan model achieved R2 = 0.444 (MAE = 13.09 years). In midlife, model fit decreased (R2 = 0.187), whereas MAE narrowed to 6.73 years, indicating greater phenotypic stability. Concurrently, core taxa (e.g., Bifidobacterium breve) exhibited age-related declines. Paired analysis revealed significant spatial decoupling; microbial dispersion exceeded metabolic dispersion, suggesting host metabolic remodeling buffers microbial divergence. Elevated metBAG correlated with clinical parameters. Under high allostatic load, 1,3,7-trimethyluric acid enrichment and all-trans retinoic acid depletion were associated with the systemic aging transition.ConclusionsWe identified an asynchronous decoupling during midlife: basal microbial decline precedes systemic aging and is initially buffered by host metabolic remodeling. When allostatic load exceeds compensatory capacity, specific metabolite enrichment may accelerate systemic aging. This framework facilitates sub-health quantification and informs microbiome-targeted interventions.
authors: Wang Z, Xu X, Shang S, Fu Y, Wang J, Ren Y, Jin Z, Yue G, Guo Y, Yuan X, Zhang Q, Li S, He N.

title: Australian isolates of cell fusing agent virus and Culex flavivirus provide new tools to study insect-specific flaviviruses
abstract: Abstract    Cell fusing agent virus (CFAV) and  Culex  Flavivirus virus (CxFV) represent the prototype insect-specific flaviviruses (ISFs) found in  Aedes  and  Culex  species, respectively. While these viruses have been isolated from mosquitoes on several different continents, no isolates have been reported from Australian mosquitoes. In this study we successfully isolated CFAV from  Aedes aegypti  originating from Cairns in North Queensland, Australia and CxFV from  Culex quinquefasciatus  collected from Brisbane in South-East Queensland, representing the first field isolates for both viruses from Australia. Phylogenetic analysis of these isolates revealed that the new CFAV isolates were closely related to CFAV sequences previously detected by deep sequencing of pools of  Aedes aegypti  collected in North Queensland, while the genome sequences of the Brisbane CxFV isolates were most closely related to isolates of CxFV from  Culex quinquefasciatus  collected from Mexico in 2008. Using these Australian isolates, we report the first infectious clone created for CFAV, and the first infectious clone of the Australian strain of CxFV. Growth kinetics revealed that infectious clones of CFAV and CxFV replicated more efficiently than their wild-type counterparts, reaching titres more than 10  8  TCID  50  /ml. Deep-sequencing of these isolates indicated that differences in replication were due to co-infections of mosquito-derived native viruses with other viruses absent in infectious clone stocks. Using a panel of novel monoclonal antibodies raised against the CFAV virion proteins, we demonstrated antigenic relatedness between CFAV and CxFV and other lineage I ISFs, particularly those carrying the conserved FKW motif at positions 106–108 in the fusion loop region of the viral envelope protein. All generated mAbs bound CFAV with one mAb additionally recognising the ISFs CxFV, Palm Creek virus (PCV), Parramatta River virus (PaRV) and Niénokoué virus (NIEV). While these mAbs did not bind CxFV and CFAV proteins in mosquitoes injected with the infectious clones, the first immunofluorescence analysis of disseminated of CFAV in  Aedes  mosquitoes was visualised through anti-dsRNA staining, showing widespread infection across multiple mosquito tissues, including the midgut and ovaries. These advancements in the development of elementary tools provide opportunity to further our understanding of ISFs and pave the way for their potential application in laboratory research, as well as innovative mosquito-borne disease control strategies.
authors: Peterson AJ, McMahon IE, Hall LD, Johnston RA, Argent MS, Potter JR, Paramitha D, Parry RH, Newton ND, Ang CC, Rawle DJ, Darbro J, Hall RA, Hugo LE, Hobson-Peters J, Harrison JJ.

title: Replicon-resolved pangenomics reveals functional specialisation and genome evolution in Vibrio coralliilyticus
abstract: Abstract  Multipartite genomes define the genus Vibrio, yet replicon specialisation remains poorly understood, particularly in environmental species. We developed a machine-learning classifier to assign draft contigs to putative replicons with high accuracy, integrating complete and draft genomes in comparative analyses. Independent implementation in Vibrio cholerae yielded similar performance, supporting broader applicability. Analysis of 41 Vibrio coralliilyticus genomes revealed functional specialisation between chromosomes despite similar proportions of core and flexible gene families. Chromosome I was enriched in essential cellular processes, central metabolism, motility and regulation, whereas chromosome II was enriched in environmental sensing, signal transduction, transport and interaction-associated functions. Chromosome I also exhibited greater plasticity, with more extensive homologous recombination and higher densities of mobile genetic elements and defence systems. Two previously undescribed conjugative megaplasmid lineages (254–628 kb) displayed contrasting adaptive repertoires. One was broadly distributed across hosts and geographic regions, encoding a conserved accessory repertoire including a giant multidomain putative effector predicted to mediate host interactions. The other was restricted to Mediterranean coral isolates, with an expanded mobilome and a conserved Sofic-like anti-phage defence system. Together, these findings show that functional specialisation can coexist with similar gene conservation patterns, while chromosomes and megaplasmids make complementary contributions to adaptation and genome evolution.
authors: Rubio-Portillo E, Nadal-Molero F, Martin-Cuadrado A.

title: The Global Landscape of Publicly Available Norovirus Sequences: Genotype Annotations, Genome Completeness, and Geographic Representation
abstract: Background:  and Objectives: In the present work, we assessed genotype annotations, genome completeness, and geographic representation of norovirus in the National Center for Biotechnology Information Virus database. Methods: We analyzed metadata for 70,632 complete and partial norovirus sequence records retrieved on 17 August 2026. Major capsid protein (VP1) genotypes and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) types were extracted from deposited annotations. Genome completeness and geographic distribution were summarized descriptively, and 55 selected complete genomes underwent phylogenetic analysis. Results: GII.4 was the most frequently annotated specific VP1 genotype (18,503 records). Specific VP1 and RdRp assignments were unavailable in the analyzed annotations for 24,804 (35.12%) and 51,892 (73.47%) records, respectively. Only 1,859 records (2.63%) were annotated as complete genomes. Country metadata were available for 65,915 records (93.32%), of which Asia contributed 56.15%. The selected phylogeny showed broad genogroup clustering, with three animal-associated genomes belonging to GIV and GVI. Conclusion: This repository snapshot identified limited complete-genome representation, incomplete typing annotations, and uneven geographic representation. These findings describe deposited records rather than population prevalence. Improved genome coverage, annotation consistency, and metadata availability could support more informative comparative analyses.
authors: Vargas D, Godoy M, Gaggero A, Kibenge M, Kibenge F.

title: Proteomics-Guided Discovery of Candidate Enzymes for Degradation of a Rare Pyruvylated Glycosaminogalactan by a Newly Isolated Luteolibacter Strain.
abstract: Bacterial exopolysaccharides (EPS) display extensive structural diversity arising from variation in monosaccharide composition, glycosidic linkages, and non-carbohydrate modifications. However, the enzymes responsible for degrading many EPS structures remain unknown, reflecting the limited coverage of current carbohydrate-active enzyme (CAZyme) families. Here, we investigated the microbial degradation of EPSLp, a high-molecular-mass glycosaminogalactan from Lactiplantibacillus pentosus KW1 containing the uncommon GalNAcβ1 → 2(4,6-O-R-pyruvyl)Gal motif. Enrichment cultivation with EPSLp as the main carbon source led to the isolation of Luteolibacter sp. VK1, a novel strain capable of utilizing this biopolymer. Size-exclusion chromatography and MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry showed that VK1 depolymerizes EPSLp into defined oligosaccharides, consistent with endo-acting cleavage followed by further processing. By combining genomics, AlphaFold-based structural annotation and comparative proteomics, we identified candidate CAZymes potentially involved in EPSLp catabolism. Notably, a secreted GH123 protein and a distantly related GH123-like protein were strongly associated with EPSLp-dependent growth, suggesting that this enzyme family, or related structural homologues, may contribute to extracellular EPSLp depolymerization. Together, these findings support a candidate pathway for degradation of a structurally complex, pyruvylated bacterial glycan and highlight potentially novel EPS-active enzymes whose proposed roles, predicted through bioinformatic analyses, await experimental validation.
authors: Kietzmann VD, Mrozek PM, Boehlich GJ, Sandholm RM, La Rosa SL, Westereng B, Vaaje-Kolstad G.

title: FASTOP─Fast Editing Toolkit for Top Expression Sites in Yeast.
abstract: Budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a widely used chassis for producing food- and agriculture-related compounds, but construction of multienzyme pathways often requires repeated genomic integration. We developed FASTOP, a genome-editing toolkit for rapid engineering of eight transcriptionally active genomic hot-spot loci. FASTOP combines selectable markers, extended homology arms, and Cas9/gRNA-assisted integration, and enables PCR-free release of donor cassettes by restriction digestion to reduce sequence errors introduced during amplification. After characterizing the sites, we integrated a five-gene naringenin biosynthetic pathway into the hot spots as a proof of concept. Our results demonstrated that, upon expressing the five essential genes in simple shake-flask culture, naringenin production reached 505.7 mg/L, 6-fold higher than an episomal control expressing the same pathway genes and 4.5-fold higher than the previously reported strain using additional precursor engineering and controlled bioreactor cultivation. FASTOP therefore provides a practical platform for the rapid assembly of multienzyme pathways in yeast for stable heterologous gene expression.
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
authors: Borah M, Gautron N, Courdavault V, Naseri G.

title: The Hna Phage Defence Protein: A DNA-Stimulated Helicase With Cryptic Nuclease Activity.
abstract: The Hna phage defence system consists of a single protein containing helicase and nuclease motifs. Hna provides defence through abortive infection, meaning that it prevents production of new phages without saving the infected cell, but its specific mechanism of action is currently unknown. We previously observed that Hna causes cell death when phage 5A single-stranded DNA binding protein (SSB) is expressed in Sinorhizobium meliloti. Here, we recreated this response by expressing Hna and phage SSB in the heterologous host Escherichia coli, indicating that no other host-specific proteins are required for Hna-mediated cell death. We also find that increased expression of Hna is lethal in E. coli even in the absence of phage SSB. We tagged and purified the Hna protein from S. meliloti, as well as helicase and nuclease motif mutants, and show that wildtype Hna binds ssDNA, performs DNA-stimulated ATP hydrolysis and unwinds short DNA duplexes. The nuclease mutant exhibits increased DNA-dependent stimulation of ATPase activity. Hna demonstrates cryptic nuclease activity: we do not observe nuclease activity in vivo, but the purified protein showed inefficient degradation of phage and bacterial genomic DNA and a ssDNA oligonucleotide in vitro. Further research should elucidate how these activities contribute to cell death.
authors: Sather LM, Zamani M, Andres SN, Finan TM.

title: Genomic and phenotypic characterization of a honey-derived Enterococcus faecium isolate from the Brazilian semiarid region.
abstract: BackgroundEnterococcus faecium has attracted considerable scientific interest. While some strains are recognized as opportunistic nosocomial pathogens, several non-pathogenic isolates have demonstrated beneficial properties associated with food fermentation and probiotic potential. Therefore, this study aimed to perform a functional genomic characterization of the native E. faecium strain EFBI58, isolated from honey in the Brazilian semiarid region.Materials and methodsEnterococcus faecium strain EFBI58 was sequenced using Illumina MiSeq. Bioinformatic tools were employed for comparative genomics, phylogeny, and detection of resistance, virulence, prophage, CAZyme, and bacteriocin genes. Additionally, in vitro tests assessed antimicrobial susceptibility and survival under simulated gastrointestinal conditions.ResultsThe EFBI58 genome presented 2,457,210 base pairs, containing 2,330 coding sequences. Phylogenomic analyses demonstrated that honey-derived isolates formed a genetically distinct group. The ANI showing belonging to clade A2 of animal-associated species. Antimicrobial resistance assessment revealed the absence of acquired genes related to clinical resistance, which was confirmed by the phenotypic susceptibility profile to the evaluated antibiotics. In addition, genes associated with important virulence factors were not identified. A prophage was 21 kb also identified in the genome. The strain EFBI58 showed survival capacity under simulated gastrointestinal conditions and the presence of stress-response proteins, demonstrating mechanisms of adaptation to adverse environments. The profile of carbohydrate-active enzymes and growth in prebiotics sugars revealed a conserved metabolic repertoire associated with the utilization of different substrates.ConclusionsHoney- and bee-associated E. faecium isolates possess genomic characteristics that provide a basis for future investigations involving natural antimicrobial compounds, microbial interactions, and biotechnological applications.
authors: da Silva Santos D, Mendonça AA, de Lima E Silva MC, De Morais MMC, Xavier DE, da Rocha Neto JC, De Souza RB, De Morais Junior MA.

title: Productive or Transforming? How Epithelial Compartmentalization of HPV DNA and E6/E7 Transcripts Shapes Cervical Screening Assay Performance.
abstract: The human papillomavirus (HPV) life cycle is linked to epithelial cell differentiation, with viral genome amplification, E6/E7 transcription, and virion assembly spatially compartmentalized within the cervical epithelium. This organization is disrupted in transforming lesions. These fundamental observations determine what 'bulk' nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) of cervical exfoliates allow us to establish. DNA-based assays sensitively report high-risk HPV genome presence, which includes transient infections and virus particles. RNA-based assays target the E6/E7 transcripts in transcriptionally active disease, which accounts for their slightly higher clinical specificity for high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions. No single assay defines both viral presence and disease significance, however. Cytology, p16/Ki-67 dual stain, extended genotyping and host-cell methylation interrogate complementary axes of risk with strong biological rationale. The loss of spatial information that limits bulk NAAT approaches matters most in mixed-grade lesions and immunocompromised populations. Emerging spatial methods, AI-assisted cytology and cervical cell-lifts offer recovery of biological resolution.
authors: Schichl K, Doorbar J.

title: Duplication, Loss, and Feeding Ecology of Lysozyme Gene Copy Number in Insects.
abstract: Lysozymes are ubiquitous enzymes traditionally associated with immune defense via bacterial cell wall degradation. In some insect lineages, particularly Diptera with bacteria-rich diets, these enzymes have been secondarily recruited for digestion, but how widespread this shift is across other insect groups remains unclear. Here, we investigate the evolutionary dynamics and functional roles of C-type and I-type lysozymes across 275 insect genomes, inferring patterns of gene duplication and loss and testing associations between lysozyme copy number and dietary habits. Phylogenetic Generalized Least Squares method revealed few significant associations: a weak link between larval detritivory and C-type copy number, and a more consistent one between an omnivorous diet and I-type copy number across life stages. Duplication analysis revealed multiple independent expansions of C-type lysozymes within Brachycera. In Muscoidea, C-type lysozymes were highly expressed in the Musca domestica larval midgut, consistent with digestion, whereas in Blattodea, moderate C-type copy numbers and salivary gland-biased expression in Periplaneta americana adults instead suggest a primarily antiseptic role. I-type lysozymes lack the catalytic residues required for canonical muramidase activity, yet remain conserved throughout Insecta, including in lineages that lost C-type lysozymes, suggesting alternative, non-canonical functions. Together, these findings are more consistent with a predominantly lineage-specific pattern of gene family evolution, largely uncoupled from a single ecological driver, than with a broad, diet-driven adaptive signal. Digestive recruitment of C-type lysozymes may extend beyond the well-characterized cases of Musca domestica and Drosophila melanogaster to additional expanded lineages across Brachycera, although direct functional evidence remains lacking.
authors: Romão HAA, Canettieri CK, Moreira TR, Freire KZS, Pereira JM, Diniz-Filho JAF, Nunes R, Lopes AR, Terra WR, Borges CL, Dias RO.

title: Deciphering Polyomavirus-Mediated Carcinogenesis in the Genitourinary Tract.
abstract: Human polyomaviruses, particularly BK polyomavirus (BKPyV) and JC polyomavirus (JCPyV), establish persistent infections within the genitourinary tract and undergo reactivation under conditions of immunosuppression. Although their clinical relevance is well established in transplant-associated nephropathy and haemorrhagic cystitis, accumulating molecular, pathological, and epidemiological evidence suggests that these viruses may also contribute to genitourinary carcinogenesis. This review examines the emerging role of BKPyV and JCPyV in urothelial, upper urinary tract, renal, and prostate malignancies, with particular emphasis on the molecular mechanisms underlying viral oncogenicity. Polyomavirus large and small T antigens disrupt the p53 and pRb tumour-suppressor pathways, activate MAPK and PI3K/Akt signalling, interfere with DNA damage responses, and promote genomic instability. Viral genome integration and a potential hit-and-run mechanism involving APOBEC3-mediated mutagenesis provide complementary models for persistent or transient oncogenic effects. The review further explores viral microRNAs as regulators of viral persistence, immune evasion, and inter-polyomavirus competition, including JCPyV-mediated suppression of BKPyV replication. Clinically, polyomavirus-associated urothelial carcinomas demonstrate aggressive pathological features and are particularly relevant in kidney transplant recipients. Current diagnostic strategies integrating viral DNA quantification, urinary cytology, viral microRNA detection, immunohistochemistry, and RNA in situ hybridisation may facilitate risk stratification and tissue-level confirmation. Finally, therapeutic management remains challenging because effective oncological control must be balanced against preservation of graft function and restoration of antiviral immunity. Collectively, these findings position BKPyV and JCPyV as important, but mechanistically heterogeneous, candidates in genitourinary tumourigenesis and highlight critical priorities for establishing causal relationships and clinically actionable biomarkers.
authors: Sun G, Han H.

title: Reflections on the early days of the DNA damage response pathway in eukaryotes.
abstract: The DNA damage response (DDR) pathway has emerged as the central signaling network that preserves genome stability by using sensors to monitor the genome for aberrant structures and establishing signaling centers that promote organismal homeostasis. This review revisits the formative years of DDR research, focusing on the genetic dissection of the pathway in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and its evolution into a broadly conserved eukaryotic signaling system. Early studies of ribonucleotide reductase regulation, replication stress-induced transcription, and cell cycle control identified key regulators, including MEC1, DDC2, TEL1, MRC1, RAD53, DUN1, and RAD9, providing the first evidence that DNA damage signaling is propagated through a protein kinase cascade. This cascade is initiated when RPA binds to ssDNA generated by replication blocks and double-strand DNA breaks, thereby activating the apical MEC1/ATR kinase. These discoveries integrate the contemporaneous cell cycle checkpoint literature into a more comprehensive framework in which the DDR coordinates replication fork stability, replication origin firing, nucleotide metabolism, DNA repair, genome maintenance, and cell cycle control to maintain genomic stability. Parallel studies in Schizosaccharomyces pombe, Xenopus, and mammalian systems revealed the remarkable evolutionary conservation of the pathway and linked DDR dysfunction to a wide spectrum of human diseases, including cancer. In retrospect, the emergence of the DDR field highlights the extraordinary power of classical genetics combined with molecular biology to uncover a complex signaling network that now occupies a central position in chromosome biology, cancer research, aging, immunity, and therapeutic responses.
authors: Elledge SJ.

title: Morphological, Molecular Phylogenetic, and Mitochondrial Genome Characterization of a Deep-Branching Marine Flagellate, Katablepharis ulleungensis sp. nov. (Cryptista).
abstract: Katablepharids (or kathablepharids) are plastid-less, biflagellate protists widely distributed in marine and freshwater environments. Here, we report a new katablepharid species, Katablepharis ulleungensis sp. nov., isolated from a black sandy beach in Ulleung-do, South Korea. The stock strain was co-cultured with a small bicosoecid flagellate, serving as its prey. Cells were oblong, displayed two rows of Type I ejectisomes, and possessed two subapically inserted flagella with the posterior flagellum slightly longer than the anterior one. Rather than exhibiting linear or spiral locomotion, cells rotated in place using both flagella. Transmission and scanning electron microscopy revealed two types of ejectisomes, each consisting of two coiled ribbons. The feeding apparatus, situated at the cell apex, comprised a cytostome, 9-10 cytopharyngeal rings, numerous putative enzymatic vesicles, and inner microtubular arrays. Phylogenetic analyses using 18S rRNA gene placed the isolate within the genus Katablepharis; the phylogenetic placement together with distinct morphological characteristics supports its recognition as a new species. Using Illumina data, the complete mitochondrial genome (35,191 bp) was assembled and annotated to contain 60 genes, including 33 protein-coding genes, 25 tRNAs, and 2 rRNAs. This study expands our understanding of katablepharid diversity and contributes to mitochondrial genome resources for marine protists.
authors: Phanprasert Y, Lee HB, Kim JI, Kim SY, Lamothe OM, Kang NS, Jeong DH, Park JS, Kim E.

title: Identification of novel inhibitors of Mycobacterium smegmatis growth through genome-wide overexpression of Cluster P3 mycobacteriophage Xavia genes.
abstract: Bacteriophages encode numerous genes with no known function, many of which can affect essential cellular processes when expressed in the bacterial host. For mycobacteriophages, genome-wide overexpression in Mycobacterium smegmatis can be used to identify proteins that impair growth. To evaluate the cytotoxic potential of the Cluster P3 phage Xavia, we constructed a plasmid library containing 71 predicted Xavia genes under the anhydrotetracycline-inducible promoter pTet and screened this library in a plate-based cytotoxicity assay to measure impacts on M. smegmatis growth. Two genes prevented transformant recovery, consistent with toxicity under basal promoter leakiness, and inducible expression of 18 additional genes impaired growth. These inhibitory proteins include structural components; factors involved in DNA metabolism, lysogeny, and lysis; and several proteins with no known function. These results extend functional screening into a lineage of actinobacteriophages that has not previously been characterized, and identify new proteins that warrant further mechanistic analysis.

title: Gene expression is stable despite widespread cis and trans regulatory divergence in Saccharomyces yeasts.
abstract: Regulatory evolution can alter phenotypes, but cis- and trans-regulatory mechanisms may also diverge extensively while total transcript abundance remains stable. Comparisons of parental expression with allele-specific expression in F1 hybrids provide a framework for separating cis- and trans-regulatory effects because both parental alleles are measured in a shared trans-regulatory environment. Here, we analyzed RNA sequencing data from Saccharomyces cerevisiae, S. paradoxus, and their F1 hybrid. Among the 4,164 genes with sufficient allele-specific support for strict classification, 2,134 (51.2%) showed detectable cis- and/or trans-regulatory divergence. However, hybrid expression remained largely conserved, with 81.5% of genes not significantly different from either parent. Compensatory cis-trans divergence predominated over reinforcing divergence; cross-replicate estimation reduced the apparent magnitude of this excess, but opposite-sign effects remained predominant in all 20 nonoverlapping replicate comparisons. To connect gene expression to genome sequence, we analyzed the strongly cis-diverged locus LYS2 and found species differences in promoter architecture, including an S. cerevisiae-specific AT-rich insertion, altered spacing among candidate regulatory features, and a promoter-proximal TATA-like element unique to S. cerevisiae. Sequence-based nucleosome prediction suggests that these differences create a broader promoter-proximal nucleosome-depleted region in S. cerevisiae than in S. paradoxus. We also quantified allele-resolved intron retention and found that it was broadly conserved, with only rare locus-specific hybrid-associated shifts. Together, these results show that regulatory divergence is widespread but often buffered in the hybrid, whereas intron-retention divergence is comparatively limited.
authors: Rojas DS, Lang GI.

title: Antiviral agent modulates freshwater methanogenesis at the nanotrace level.
abstract: Antiviral drugs (ATVs), such as oseltamivir carboxylate (OTC), are widely used to treat viral infections. Although environmental levels are in the ng/L to µg/L range, knowledge on risks posed by this substance class is hindered by limited assessments. Evidence on effects on microbially-driven ecosystem processes is especially scarce, which is concerning because viruses are omnipresent in the microbiome and likely to influence microbial functioning. We assessed the influence of OTC on anaerobic methane production, a greenhouse gas largely emitted from natural systems and responsible for around one third of greenhouse gas-driven warming, as a proxy for microbial ecosystem function. Oseltamivir carboxylate inhibited initial methanogenesis between 15% and 40% even at nanotrace levels (i.e., 0.006-600 µg/L). Given that in most treatments methane levels returned to those of the control, the initial inhibition is potentially attributed to a temporally limited OTC-induced shift from a neutral/temperate viral infection of prokaryotes toward a lytic viral replication. Mostly unaffected 16S rRNA metabarcoding community data indicate that this effect might be uniform throughout the community. This study points to ecosystem-level effects at the ng/L range of ATVs, suggesting a significant knowledge gap, which warrants further attention to this group of chemicals.
authors: Bollinger E, Feckler A, Filker S, Bourassi H, Maccagnan A, McArdell CS, Bundschuh M.

title: Longitudinal associations of the gut microbiome with arterial stiffness in US adults: findings from the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging.
abstract: The gut microbiome affects arterial stiffness in experimental murine models; however, evidence in human longitudinal studies is lacking. In this study, we investigated longitudinal between-person (average) and within-person (change) associations of microbiome features with arterial stiffness. We assessed the fecal microbiome using whole genome metagenomic sequencing, and arterial stiffness using carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (cfPWV). Our analytic sample consisted of 349 adults from the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, who contributed 915 visits between 2013 and 2019. Using linear mixed models, we found higher microbiome evenness and butyrate-producing bacteria were associated with lower cfPWV on average (between-person), but changes in diversity were not associated with changes in cfPWV (within-person). Several potentially pathogenic bacteria were positively associated with cfPWV, both between- and within-person. Butyrate-production pathways were inversely associated with cfPWV between-person and borderline within-person. Trimethylamine-production genes were positively associated with cfPWV between-person and borderline within-person. In addition, changes in other functional pathways including peptidoglycan biosynthesis and L-arginine biosynthesis were associated with changes in cfPWV. In conclusion, cfPWV was associated with both between-person and within-person differences in gut microbiome features, with strength and consistency depending on the feature. These results can inform which microbiome features to target in interventions to improve arterial stiffness.
authors: Tilves C, Xiao S, Tanaka T, Differding MK, Spira AP, Ferrucci L, Mueller NT.

title: Effect of TiO<sub>2</sub>-coupled 405 nm LED light on hatching performance, production performance and environmental microbial in laying hens.
abstract: Intensive poultry production has led to biosecurity challenges, such as vertical pathogen transmission, disinfectant residues, and antimicrobial resistance. In this study, a two-strain incubation trial and a 62-week production trial were conducted, and the effects of TiO₂-coupled 405 nm LED treatment were evaluated throughout the entire layer production cycle. During incubation, eggs received either continuous darkness or a 12L:12D photoperiod (20 lx) of the 405 nm LED light from days 8 to 21. During production trial, hens were reared under conventional or TiO₂-coupled 405 nm LED light. Production performance, microbial loads, and community structures were measured. Light treatment significantly shortened the time to 90% hatch without impairing hatchability or chick quality. Under this treatment, hens reached 50% egg production significantly earlier than those in the control group. No significant differences were observed in the growth performance, egg quality, carcass, and eye health under the light treatment. Importantly, the treatment reduced the abundance of microbes on the eggshell surface by 26.47-27.78% and the concentration of incubator airborne bacteria by 58.37-66.68% (P < 0.05). During production, microbial counts on feed trough surface decreased by 36.11-40.00%, airborne bacterial counts by 35.58-54.75%, and Staphylococcus aureus counts by 29.39%, with evident biofilm disruption. Metagenomic sequencing revealed that the light treatment reduced the abundances of Chlamydia abortus, Chlamydia psittaci, and Klebsiella pneumoniae on eggshells by 94.64%, 95.15%, and 70.09%, respectively. Correspondingly, translocation of hepatic Klebsiella in chicks decreased and the liver microbial ecosystem stabilized. Furthermore, 16S/ITS sequencing of feed trough samples showed a 13.78% reduction in the abundance of the pathogenic phyla Firmicutes, with lower abundance of Basidiomycota allergens and enrichment of beneficial Ascomycota. In conclusion, light treatment did not adversely affect hatchability or production performance in this study. Instead, it significantly reduced environmental microbial loads, suppressed the growth of key pathogens, and optimized microbial ecology, thereby demonstrating its potential as a safe and environment-friendly auxiliary biosecurity strategy during the incubation and poultry production periods.
authors: Wu X, Su B, Su D, Ye R, Xu J, Li X, Zhang S, Fan Y, Wang S, Yao Y, Zhang R, Li H, Sun E, Zhao X, Chen Y, Hao E, Wang D, Chen H, Shi L.

title: Metagenomic insights into microbial adaptation and resilience of single-stage partial nitritation-anammox systems assisted by graphene oxide sponges under increasing salinity.
abstract: Salinity is an increasingly important challenge limiting the application of single-stage partial nitritation-Anammox (PN/A) processes for treating saline nitrogen-rich wastewaters due to osmotic stress and microbial activity inhibition. In this study, a graphene oxide sponge (GOS)-assisted PN/A system was operated for 164 days under progressively increasing salinity from 2,000 to 12,000 mg/L NaCl to investigate the long-term performance and the associated physiological, ecological, and functional responses to salinity stress. Despite transient performance deterioration following each salinity increment, the reactor rapidly acclimated and maintained stable nitrogen removal, achieving ammonia removal efficiencies above 98%. Salinity acclimation promoted extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) production, particularly tightly bound EPS, and enhanced the activities of ammonia-oxidizing bacteria and anammox bacteria. Scanning electron microscopy confirmed dense biofilm formation on the GOS, while elemental analysis indicated a lower surface-associated sodium signal in the attached biomass compared with suspended sludge. Microbial community analysis revealed the enrichment of salt-tolerant functional microorganisms, particularly Candidatus Kuenenia and Nitrosomonas. Metagenomic analysis further demonstrated that microbial adaptation was primarily associated with the enrichment of genes involved in two-component systems, ABC transporters, and quorum sensing pathways, suggesting increased functional potential for environmental sensing, transport regulation, and microbial communication, while the nitrogen transformation pathways remained relatively stable. These findings characterize the long-term performance and associated microbial responses of a GOS-assisted PN/A system under progressive salinity stress, providing new mechanistic insights into the salinity resilience of PN/A systems treating saline nitrogen-rich wastewaters.
authors: Wu S, Quan Y, Gao F, Shi L, Liu Z, Shen Z, Elsayed Ali EA, Veeramuthu A, Chen H.
