title: The stimulative effect of Cordyceps sinensis functionalized selenium nanoparticles on bone development in growing mice: involvement of the gut microbiota-bone axis.
abstract: IntroductionAchieving optimal peak bone mass (PBM) during adolescence through adequate intake of trace element such as selenium is crucial for reducing osteoporosis risk in later life. We previously developed novel functionalized selenium nanoparticles (Cs4-SeNPs) utilizing polysaccharide-protein complex isolated from Cordyceps sinensis for prevention of osteoporosis. The gut microbiota, functioning as the "second gene pool", plays a crucial role in maintaining bone homeostasis. However, how Cs4-SeNPs regulate bone metabolism via the gut microbiota-bone axis remains unclear.ObjectivesTo elucidate how the gut microbiota and microbial metabolites mediate the bone-promoting effect of Cs4-SeNPs.MethodsGrowing mice model was used to assess the effect of Cs4-SeNPs on bone development. Metagenomics, metabolomics, and proteomics analyses were conducted to uncover the mechanism of action of Cs4-SeNPs. In vitro osteoblast and osteoclast models were employed to validate the effects of key gut microbial metabolites regulated by Cs4-SeNPs on osteogenesis and osteoclastogenesis. Pseudo-germ-free mice model treated with antibiotics was employed to determine the role of gut microbiota in bone-promoting effects of Cs4-SeNPs.ResultsWe found that Cs4-SeNPs significantly enhanced bone mass in growing mice, as evidenced by improved bone microarchitecture and increased expression of bone extracellular matrix-related markers. Notably, antibiotic treatment-induced microbial depletion abolished the effects of Cs4-SeNPs on bone development in growing mice. Increased abundance of beneficial gut bacterial genera, notably Adlercreutzia and Parvibacter, were observed following Cs4-SeNPs administration. Proteomics analysis and subsequent verification experiments demonstrated that Cs4-SeNPs inhibited the TNF-R1/TAB2/NF-κB inflammatory pathway and upregulated the expression of antioxidant proteins including SERPINA3K, GPX1, and SOD in the bone tissue. Metabolomic analysis revealed that Cs4-SeNPs treatment significantly elevated fecal and serum levels of two key metabolites: kynurenic acid and trehalose. Further in vitro studies confirmed that kynurenic acid and trehalose could reproduce the effects of Cs4-SeNPs on osteoblastic and osteoclastic differentiation.ConclusionsOur findings suggest that Cs4-SeNPs optimize PBM and promote bone development in growing mice by improving the osteoblast/osteoclast balance via the modulation of the inflammatory TNF-R1/TAB2/NF-κB axis and the enhancement of antioxidant activity through the elevated levels of gut microbial metabolites kynurenic acid and trehalose in a gut microbiota-dependent manner.
authors: Liu ZW, Lai CH, Gan RY, Chen L, Zhang BB, Cheng WY, Dong XL, Wong KH.

title: Nucleic acid amplification testing for obligate intracellular and cell wall-deficient bacteria: from assay performance to clinical interpretation, a structured narrative review.
abstract: Obligate intracellular bacteria (Rickettsia, Orientia, Ehrlichia, Anaplasma, Coxiella, Chlamydia) and cell wall-deficient Mycoplasma species present profound diagnostic challenges due to their fastidious growth, low circulating burden, and genomic instability. Nucleic Acid Amplification Tests (NAATs) have revolutionized detection, yet critical gaps persist in distinguishing active infection from persistent DNA, standardizing cycle threshold interpretation, and integrating host-response biomarkers. This structured narrative review provides a comprehensive analysis of the complete diagnostic armamentarium for these pathogens. It is based on a reproducible, non-systematic literature survey and is not a PRISMA-compliant systematic review. We cover conventional methods (culture, serology), NAAT platforms (qPCR, digital PCR, isothermal amplification), and emerging technologies including CRISPR-Cas diagnostics, metagenomic sequencing, nanopore sequencing, biosensors, and host-response biomarker profiling. We introduce four conceptual frameworks: the "biological noise" paradigm reframing low-copy detection as a signal-to-noise challenge; a temporal-dynamic algorithm accounting for pathogen-specific detection windows; the "detection-disease disconnect" emphasizing clinical contextualization of NAAT positivity; and multi-analyte integration combining NAAT with viability markers and host inflammatory signatures. We also position these frameworks relative to prior diagnostic-interpretation theories, including STARD, QUADAS-2, MIQE, Bayesian pretest-posttest reasoning, Ct-value interpretation guidance, and host-response classifier frameworks. We compare ten clinically significant pathogens across technical and biological parameters, evaluate point-of-care deployment strategies, and address antimicrobial resistance testing. Performance metrics are presented as context-dependent estimates rather than fixed constants. The next frontier lies not in incremental assay improvements but in system-level integration of pathogen detection, viability assessment, host-response profiling, and clinical phenotyping, supported by artificial intelligence-enhanced interpretation and global standardization efforts.
authors: Naderi M, Sadidi R, Besharati R, Kebriae A, Azimian A.

title: Evaluation of the Safety and Efficacy of Fecal Microbiota Transplantations with Oral Capsules in Alzheimer’s Disease Patients Using Metagenomic Sequencing
abstract: Background:  Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease. Numerous studies have shown that the gut microbiota is closely related to the occurrence and development of Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that alterations in gut microbiota may represent a therapeutic strategy. However, the role and mechanisms of the gut microbiota in AD remain unclear, and standard research protocols for the gut microbiota are not uniform. The clinical safety and efficacy of oral capsule fecal microbiota transplantation, ( FMT) in patients with AD are not yet established, and related clinical studies are lacking. Objective: This study aimed to investigate the safety and effects of FMT capsule on cognitive im-pairment in patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease and to explore the re-lationship between cognition and gut microbiota by evaluating changes in gut microbial gene expression after FMT. Methods: In this study, 18 patients with clinically and radiologically confirmed mild to moderate AD aged 60-80years old were enrolled in this prospective single-arm clinical observation study. All subjects received allograft FMT (intestinal bacteria capsules with strict do-norscreening and in line with international FMT donor standards) three times at 0, 30 and 60 days. Serum and fecal samples were collected at 0, 30, 60 and 90 days, and MoCA, MMSE scores, HAMD, HAMA, ADL and fecal metagenomics sequencing were evalu-ated.During FMT and follow-up, safety was assessed by recording adverse events (AEs), vital signs, and laboratory parameters. Results After the intervention of FMT capsule, various cognitive and behavioral scores in FMT1 and FMT2 groups were not significantly changed, MMSE and MoCA scores in FMT3 group were significantly higher than those in FMT0 group (P Conclusion: In this study, FMT capsules can alter the intestinal microbiome structure and achieve intestinal microbiome remodeling, which may be a potential mechanism for microbiome capsules to improve AD related phenotypes.It is well tolerated and safe in the treatment of patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease.Despite the limited sample size and lack of control group, the results still provide clinical evidence for targeted inter-vention of the gut-brain axis in AD, but larger, randomized, double-blind place-bo-controlled trials are needed to further verify its efficacy and mechanism.
authors: Wu J, Cui D, Si Z.

title: PloidyPeaks: R package for automated flow cytometry cell cycle analysis and visualization in fungal microbes
abstract: ABSTRACT  Karyotypic variation in fungal populations from ecological, clinical, and industrial environments and is also a hallmark of many cancers. The evolutionary dynamics of karyotypic vriants (i.e., changes in the number of chromosomes, either as complete sets or single chromosomes) are the same as any  de novo mutation. To quantify karyotypic subpopulations within evolving populations, an unbiased computational method is required to identify subpopulations and quantify their abundance. Flow cytometry is the standard method to measure the genome size from large populations of individual cells. Cell populations typically include cells in all stages of the cell cycle (G0/G1 before DNA replication, S phase during replication, and G2/M after DNA replication but before cell division). Existing mathematical models can be fit to genome-size distributions to determine the base ploidy of a population, but existing algorithms assume a single base ploidy. Mixed-karyotype populations therefore require manual gating to subdivide the flow cytometry data before analysis, which introduces bias, as it is not always clear where or when gates should be drawn. To overcome this, we developed an new method that identifies and quantifies karyotypic subpopulations from flow cytometry data. The open-source R package  ploidyPeaks builds on existing Bioconductor tools to import and manipulate standard  .fcs flow cytometry files. Using reference populations of known ploidy, we established thresholds to distinguish single-genome size populations and identify candidate mixed-karyotype samples. We then developed a peak-detection algorithm to identify G0/G1 and G2/M peaks, resolve karyotypic subpopulations within mixed populations, and apply nonlinear least-squares fitting of the Dean-Jett-Fox cell-cycle model to each subpopulation, providing a confidence measure for model fit. Compared with existing methods, our approach quantifies genome size in mixed-karyotype populations without manual intervention while providing an objective measure of model fit. We demonstrate the utility of this method on 240 replicate populations initiated from 20  Candida albicans genetic backgrounds evolving for 100 generations to the antifungal drug fluconazole.
authors: Henry M, Kostna C, von Giese L, Gerstein A.

title: Genomic insights into environmental adaptation and metabolic versatility of Acinetobacter junii IK2 isolated from marine biofilm.
abstract: Biofilm formation is ubiquitous in the marine environment, driven by microbial colonization on submerged surfaces, and poses ongoing challenges to maritime industries. In this study, whole-genome sequencing (WGS) was carried out for Acinetobacter junii IK2, a strain isolated from the biofilm formed on stainless steel coupons immersed in a seawater microcosm setup to elucidate its genomic features and biofilm-forming potential. The genome consists of 3,215,808 bp with a GC content of 38.63%, assembled from Illumina-generated sequencing data. A total of 2990 protein-coding sequences (CDS), 10 rRNA genes, and 63 tRNA genes were predicted. Functional annotation through COG, GO, and KEGG databases resulted in the classification of 2909, 2389, and 2960 unigenes, respectively. Genome analysis identified the presence of thirteen genes associated with biofilm development, including the pgaABC operon, two-component systems (barA, ompR), and global regulators (crp, csrA, dksA), suggesting potential for biofilm formation. Genes such as oxyR, yfiB, yiaD, and pal further support oxidative stress resistance, adhesion, and envelope stability. The biofilm-forming ability of Acinetobacter junii IK2 was further validated using a crystal violet microtiter plate assay, confirming its ability to form biofilms. Additionally, 35 virulence genes, 6 multidrug resistance genes and 25 insertion sequences suggest enhanced survival, pathogenicity and genetic plasticity, reinforcing biofilm-mediated persistence. These genomic features provide insights into potential adaptive mechanisms that may contribute to the environmental adaptation of A. junii IK2 and offer insights into its role in the marine environment.

title: Advancing microbial pangenomics through human pangenomics.
abstract: Although the term pangenome originated in the study of microbial species, recent advances in eukaryotic pangenomics have been driven largely by the need to manage the substantial computational challenges posed by population-scale eukaryotic datasets. This review evaluates the extent to which existing eukaryotic pangenome tools and methods can be extended to microbial species. We first survey current eukaryotic and microbial pangenomic approaches and then examine opportunities and challenges in adapting eukaryotic methods to microbial genomes, with particular emphasis on scalability, data quality, evolutionary complexity, and benchmarking. Finally, we highlight areas where existing approaches generalize well and where substantive redesign and redevelopment are needed.
authors: Bravo JE, Sapoval N, Han Y, Kokroko N, Nakhleh L, Noyes NR, Treangen TJ, Boucher C.

title: Exploring sex- and captivity-associated gut microbial diversity in Bengal Tigers (Panthera tigris tigris).
abstract: BACKGRO​UND: The gut microbiome plays a critical role in host nutrition, immune regulation, metabolic stability, and overall physiological health in wildlife. However, gut microbiome data from large carnivores remain limited, particularly for endangered tiger populations. This study conducted a comparative analysis of fecal microbiomes from captive and wild Bengal tigers, integrated with publicly avai​lable datasets from Amur, Malayan, and South China tigers, to understand how captivity and host factors influence microbial assembly. ME​THOD​S AND RESULTS: Across all tiger subspecies, Firmicutes and Proteobacteria dominated as core bacterial phyla, with Actinobacteriota, Bacteroidota, and Fusob​acteriota forming a conserved microbial backbone. Wild Bengal tigers exhibited higher microbial richness and diversity than captive tigers​. Beta diversity analyses demonstrated clear clustering by habitat (captive versus wild), but substantial overlap between male and female captive Bengal tigers, indicating that captivity-associated conditions exert influences on gut microbiome structure than sex. Comparative analyses among tiger subspecies revealed broad overlap in microbial community composition, suggesting limited phylogenetic influence. South China and Amur tigers displayed the lowest richness compared to Bengal and Malayan tigers. Furthermore, analysis identified an enrichment of protein fermentation-associated taxa in captive tigers, whereas wild tigers showed a greater abundance of environmentally associated taxa. CONCLUSIONS: The study provides evidences that captivity promotes reduction in gut microbial diversity in Bengal tigers, and highlights the potential utility of microbiome-informed captive management. Integrating gut microbiome monitoring into conservation breeding, zoo exchange and reintroduction programmes may improve adaptive fitness in endangered tiger populations.
authors: Dolker S, Ghosh A, Singh VK, Joshi BD, Sharma LK, Thakur M.

title: Acute lethality and stress-responsive phenotypes differ among three Acinetobacter baumannii strains: phenotypic, genomic and transcriptomic analyses
abstract: Abstract    Background  Acinetobacter baumannii  exhibits substantial strain-level heterogeneity in antimicrobial resistance, virulence-associated phenotypes and responses to environmental stress. Whether acute lethality covaries with surface-associated and stress-responsive phenotypes across different strain backgrounds remains unclear. We compared three clinically distinct  A. baumannii  strains, LS01, AB5075 and XH386, using phenotypic assays, comparative genome annotation and transcriptomic profiling. Results  The three strains displayed distinct phenotypic profiles. Following inoculation with 5 × 10^4 CFU in  Galleria mellonella  , 96-h survival was 20% for LS01, 45% for AB5075 and 60% for XH386. In immunocompetent C57BL/6J mice challenged by oropharyngeal aspiration with a common inoculum of 5 × 10^6 CFU, 120-h survival was 25% after LS01 infection, whereas all AB5075- and XH386-infected mice survived. XH386 yielded the highest HBE-cell-associated bacterial recovery in both independent experiments. OD600 trajectories during exposure to non-heat-inactivated human serum varied with serum concentration and donor; at 10% serum, XH386 showed a higher late-phase OD600 than LS01 in both donor experiments. Transmission electron microscopy showed the most prominent capsule-associated extracellular layer in AB5075, whereas LS01 showed a thinner layer and XH386 markedly attenuated capsule-associated material. Attached biomass varied with strain and environmental condition, with XH386 showing the highest biomass under 10% heat-inactivated serum in repeated experiments. Comparative genome annotation showed extensive overlap in major pathogenicity-, biofilm-, iron-acquisition-, secretion- and stress-associated systems despite these phenotypic differences. title: Autonomous Hypothesis Testing Against Public Biomedical Data with Literature-Grounded Calibration
abstract: Public biomedical repositories contain petabytes of data, yet testing hypotheses against those resources still requires expert effort. I present a four-phase blinded workflow for autonomous computational hypothesis testing: an agent receives a natural-language hypothesis, discovers public datasets with academic publisher domains blocked, executes an analysis pipeline and validates findings against the literature. Published studies serve as calibration rulers, measuring how closely an autonomous workflow approaches known answers before it is trusted on unknown ones. Across five biomedical tasks spanning bacterial genomics, single-cell multiomics, metagenomics, cancer genomics and GWAS functional genomics, the agent scored 5–9 out of 10 on pre-specified rubrics in 20–188 minutes (the single-cell multiomics score was corrected from an initial 8 to 5 after blinded judge review identified over-credited criteria; see Methods). An exploratory comparison across three successive model generations found scores directionally higher for the first generation (claude-opus-4-6) on all five tasks (one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.031, rank-biserial r = 1.0; n = 5 studies), with newer models completing tasks faster; the benchmark also exposed generation-specific safety policy and schema differences that silently confound cross-generation comparisons if not corrected. Failures fell into three categories, tool-version sensitivity, data-scope limitation and analytical completeness, all self-diagnosed by the validation phase in all five cases examined here without human prompting. These results introduce a calibration framework and failure taxonomy for characterising when autonomous computational science workflows should and should not be trusted.
authors: O'Connell KA.

title: Population Genetic Evolution Analysis of Tsaoko Stripe Mosaic Virus and Development of RT-PCR and Real-Time RT-PCR Detection Methods for Strain Discrimination.
abstract: Tsaoko stripe mosaic virus (TkSMV) has been identified as the predominant viral pathogen of Amomum tsaoko in Yunnan Province of China. This virus induced various foliar symptoms, including chlorosis, stripe mosaic, and necrosis, while some infected A. tsaoko plants remain asymptomatic. Comprehensive investigation of the population genetic structure and molecular detection protocols for TkSMV is crucial for elucidating its evolutionary dynamics, epidemiology, and disease control strategies. Phylogenetic analysis based on 15 full-length genomic sequences and 29 coat protein (CP) gene fragments revealed three distinct evolutionary lineages (S1, S2, and S3) within the TkSMV population. Neutrality test analysis indicates that the genetic polymorphism of the TkSMV population is consistent with a neutral evolution model (Tajima's D > 0, not significant). The comparative evolutionary analysis demonstrated significant selective pressures across viral proteins: codon usage bias analysis revealed strong purifying selection (dN/dS A. tsaoko cultivation.

title: Molecular detection of Waddlia chondrophila in aborted bovine placental and vaginal mucus samples in Japan.
abstract: Chlamydia-related bacteria have recently raised medical and veterinary concerns as emerging causes of abortion and pneumonia in ruminants and humans in Europe and Africa. However, these bacteria have not yet been investigated in ruminants in Japan. In this study, two species, Waddlia chondrophila and Parachlamydia acanthamoebae, were examined as potential pathogens of ruminant abortion. Vaginal mucus and placental samples were collected from 29 cows that had experienced abortion or stillbirth in Japan between August 2023 and December 2023. In real-time PCR analysis, W. chondrophila DNA was detected in both the vaginal mucus and placenta from one cow, whereas P. acanthamoebae was not detected in any individual. An 856 bp 16S rRNA sequence was obtained and identified as W. chondrophila through phylogenetic analysis. The bacterial genomic copy numbers were 3.47 × 10⁴ copies/mL in vaginal mucus and 2.36 × 10⁶ copies/g in placenta, indicating that the placental load was 30- to 130-times higher. This study represents the first report of W. chondrophila detection in a bovine abortion case in Japan and highlights the need for further investigation of Chlamydia-related bacteria and other pathogens affecting animal and human health.

title: Assessing field-scale effects of treated wastewater on riverine biofilms: Community composition, functional genes, and micropollutant biotransformation.
abstract: Treated wastewater (WW) released from wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) leads to the influx of microorganisms and micropollutants (MPs) into receiving waters, and hence presents a continuous anthropogenic pressure on downstream riverine microbial communities; however, its impact on their composition and function remains insufficiently understood, particularly under environmentally realistic field conditions spanning multiple rivers, seasons, and wastewater treatment technologies. In this study, we investigated the effects of treated WW effluent on microbial community composition, functional profiles, the prevalence of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), and the fate of 189 MPs in riverine biofilms, including detailed biotransformation analyses for 122 reliably quantifiable MPs. Biofilms were grown under well-characterized field conditions across six Swiss rivers receiving effluent from WWTPs that varied in treatment technology, wastewater dilution, and season. At each river, pairs of biofilms were grown and collected at two sites upstream (up) and three sites downstream (dw) of the WWTP discharge point, resulting in a total of 60 biofilm communities. At the level of overall community composition and general functional profiles, differences between up- and downstream sites were inconsistent. However, clearer differences emerged when analyses focused on non-dominant taxa and specific functional traits, such as ARGs and MP biotransformation, indicating subtle but ecologically relevant impacts of treated WW that may be masked by broader trends. Approximately half of the analyzable MPs were measurably biotransformed, with the majority of these transformations likely occurring via co-metabolic processes, as suggested by MP structures and overall low variance in biotransformation rate constants. For a few MPs, which had previously been associated with catabolic biodegradation, enhanced biotransformation potential was detected in 8 out of 36 downstream biofilms. These observations of increased downstream biotransformation were predominantly associated with moving bed biofilm reactor (MBBR)-based WWTPs, suggesting that WW effects were highly technology-specific rather than ubiquitous. Fine-grained metagenomic analysis revealed an association between the abundance of relevant Enzyme Commission (EC) classes and enhanced saccharin biotransformation in downstream biofilms. While increased downstream biotransformation was heterogeneous and infrequent, multiple lines of evidence suggest that microbes transferred from the WWTP via treated WW effluent endowed these functions to downstream biofilms. Overall, our findings show that WWTP impacts on riverine biofilms are generally subtle at the level of overall community structure but become apparent when focusing on non-dominant taxa and specialized functional traits, which play a disproportionate role in shaping MP biotransformation potential.
authors: Kalt M, Poltorak V, Mastrorilli E, Ceppi E, Yu Y, Zimmermann M, Sunagawa S, Robinson SL, Fenner K.

title: Crossfeeding interactions in a minimal marine chitin-degrading community
abstract: Communities of heterotrophic particle-associated marine bacteria contribute to oceanic carbon cycling through interspecies interactions that can influence polysaccharide degradation. While these interactions have been extensively studied using single natural isolates or pairwise combinations thereof, their mechanistic relevance within multispecies communities remains unclear. To address this gap, we developed MCC4, a minimal chitin-degrading bacterial community consisting of two chitin degraders and two non-degrading isolates that represent globally prevalent marine bacterial taxa. We show that the community remains stable across ten growth-dilution cycles, establishing a reproducible model for controlled multi-isolate experiments. Using transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses combined with metabolite supplementation assays, we uncovered the underlying crossfeeding network. While one degrader drives chitin degradation, the other exploits chitin monomers and chitooligomers generated by the main degrader. The two non-degraders are sustained by consuming deacetylated chitin monomers, 2-carbon compounds, nucleotides, and branched-chain amino acids, likely released by degraders. Community assembly is driven by competitive scavenging abilities, potentially complemented by specific survival strategies such as increased motility and deployment of type VI secretion systems. Despite its simplicity, MCC4 captures dynamic microbial interactions characteristic of natural marine ecosystems. It offers a tractable, reproducible framework for investigating how environmental perturbations impact community function and testing ecological theories in particle-associated marine environments. authors: Haavisto V, Sauer U.

title: Unexplained Febrile Syndromes in Sub-Saharan Africa: Etiological Diversity, Diagnostic Challenges and Emerging Diagnostic Approaches—A Narrative Review
abstract: Unexplained febrile syndromes represent a major diagnostic and public health challenge in Sub-Saharan Africa. Although malaria remains an important cause of fever, an increasing proportion of febrile episodes is attributable to nonmalarial etiologies, encompassing a wide range of bacterial, viral, parasitic, and fungal infections, as well as noninfectious causes. Their etiological characterization remains limited by the low specificity of clinical manifestations, the heterogeneity of definitions and diagnostic algorithms, and insufficient laboratory capacity. Microscopy, rapid diagnostic tests, cultures, and serology remain essential in resource-limited settings, but their targeted nature and variable performance may lead to diagnostic dead ends. Emerging approaches, particularly multiplex PCR, next-generation sequencing, and clinical metagenomics, offer new opportunities to broaden the diagnostic spectrum, identify neglected or emerging pathogens, and strengthen surveillance. However, their integration requires strengthening laboratory networks, quality systems, and human resources, as well as evaluating their relevance and cost-effectiveness. An integrated approach based on the “One Health” concept appears essential to improve the diagnosis and surveillance of febrile illnesses in Sub-Saharan Africa.
authors: Keita AK, Gnimadi TAC, Kande A, Diallo H, Soumah AK, Kaba D, Toure A, Fenollar F, Mediannikov O, Keita AK.

title: Microbes as Key Players During Evolution Part II- From Unicellular to Multicellular Organisms
abstract: Microbes and thereof derived structures (plasmids, plastids, transposible elements, retrotransposons) are described as key drivers in the evolution of genes, genomes and new species in metazoa. This is a change of paradigm compared to the mechanisms of mutation and selection, and Mendelian genetics. The review first describes early metazoan developments and early symbiotic interactions. It presents examples of microbial influences on medusazoans, corals and sea anemones and then continues with microbial impacts on terrestrial ecosystems: Mutualistic associations of fungi, bacteroids and bacteria with lower plants (lichens, bryophytes) and higher plants (gymnosperms, angiosperms) and the exchange of reduced carbon for reduced nitrogen. The review goes on with animals, starting with the most recent common ancestor of vertebrates about 560 million years ago. Microbial impacts are described on insects, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals including homo sapiens. A further chapter deals with impacts of transposible elements. Special emphasis is directed towards the creation of new species. Chapter 6 describes bipartite and tripartite host-microbe cooperations which led to new holobiont species in metazoa. Defense systems and reticulate evolution are further topics of this review. The discussion points out that evolution is driven by net formation including multiple nods of primary, secondary or tertiary endosymbiogenesis events.
authors: Schirrmacher V.

title: Intracity-scale study reveals spatiotemporal variation of urban airborne microbiota and dynamics of antibiotic resistance/virulence genes.
abstract: Airborne microbiota are critical to urban air quality and public health, yet their spatiotemporal differentiation, community assembly, and profiles of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and virulence factor genes (VFGs) across urban functional zones remain poorly characterized. In this study, monthly 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing was combined with seasonal metagenomic profiling of 12 composite samples and environmental data to investigate airborne microbiota at three sites representing commercial, industrial, and recreational zones in Changsha, China. Airborne communities showed similar spatial patterns among the investigated functional zones but strong seasonal variation, with Shannon diversity below 2.0 in July and above 6.0 in January. Proteobacteria dominated most samples, while key seasonal taxa shifted among Delftia, Cupriavidus, and Achromobacter. Neutral community modeling supported stochastic dominance (R2 = 0.664, Nm = 1200), with 92.6% of operational taxonomic units within the 95% confidence interval. However, βNTI and RCbray analyses indicated increased deterministic selection in autumn-winter, coinciding with high pressure and pollutant accumulation. Metagenomics identified 25 ARG, 14 VFG, and 6 mobile genetic element (MGE) categories, with season explaining 53.9% of VFG compositional differences. Exploratory structural equation modeling identified associations between MGE abundance and ARG/VFG abundances (β = 0.75 and 1.09, respectively; both P < 0.001). Binning and contig co-localization showed that ARG-VFG-MGE co-harboring fragments were potentially affiliated with opportunistic pathogens such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Klebsiella pneumoniae, indicating potential biosafety concerns. These findings identify season as a key driver of urban airborne microbiota and genetic risk factors, providing a basis for atmospheric biosafety monitoring and assessment.
authors: Wang Y, Qing Y, Luo S, Tao M, Yang Y, Chen Z, Zhang X.

title: Hydrogen nanobubbles overcome metabolic bottlenecks and remodel transcriptional networks for high-rate methanogenesis in the anaerobic digestion of Paulownia leaf litter.
abstract: Volatile fatty acid (VFA) accumulation limits anaerobic digestion (AD) of lignocellulosic biomass by causing acidification and microbial metabolic imbalance. Paulownia leaf litter (PLL), an underutilized lignocellulosic residue with potential for renewable energy recovery, was selected as the substrate. This study evaluated hydrogen nanobubble water (H2-NBW) as a strategy to alleviate VFA inhibition and investigated associated microbial responses using integrated multi-omics analyses. H2-NBW increased cumulative methane yields by 26.4-34.5% compared with controls, accelerated VFA turnover, improved acid-base stability and buffering capacity, and enhanced extracellular hydrolytic enzyme activities by 12.7-42.4%. Coenzyme F420 fluorescence intensity increased by 11.5-30.7%, indicating enhanced methanogenic activity. Amplicon sequencing suggested that H2-NBW enriched microorganisms associated with carbohydrate degradation and fermentation, while overall community restructuring remained limited. Metagenomic analysis revealed increased functional potential for lignocellulose degradation, reflected in carbohydrate-active enzyme and H2 metabolism genes. Meta-transcriptomic analysis further showed increased transcription of genes associated with hydrolysis, acetate-forming metabolism, the Frh/Mvh-Hdr hydrogenase system, and hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis. These responses suggest that H2-NBW may support carbon conversion and hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis, accompanied by enhanced transcription of genes involved in substrate degradation, H2 metabolism, and methane formation. The observed improvements may be associated with exogenous H2 availability, microbial metabolic responses, and potential nanobubble-associated physicochemical effects. Overall, this study links improved AD performance with coordinated microbial functional and transcriptional responses, highlighting the potential of H2-NBW to improve lignocellulosic biomass conversion and methane recovery.
authors: Fan Y, Guo D, He Y, Zhai X, Zhao Z, Fan G.

title: Strain-dependent carbon partitioning and community-level functional responses during microalgae-based dairy wastewater treatment under CO<sub>2</sub> enrichment.
abstract: BackgroundMicroalgae-bacteria consortia offer a route for coupling dairy-wastewater treatment with carbon conversion, yet strain-dependent differences in carbon partitioning and microbial functional responses remain insufficiently resolved.MethodsChlorella vulgaris, Tetradesmus obliquus, and Synechocystis sp. were cultivated in dairy wastewater under air or a one-time 4% CO2 gas charge followed by closed-loop recirculation. Biomass production, nutrient removal, liquid-solid-gas carbon inventories, biochemical composition, bacterial succession, metagenomic profiles, and entropy-weighted TOPSIS were integrated.ResultsSynechocystis sp. treatment S1 showed the greatest liquid-phase total-carbon drawdown (72.1%), as carbon transferred to the suspended-solid pool, the proportion of liquid inorganic carbon within the instantaneous carbon inventory declined from 54.18% to 8.85%. T. obliquus treatment T1 achieved the highest biomass concentration (0.99 ± 0.01 g·L-1), NH4+-N removal (84.89%), and comparatively high carbohydrate and lipid accumulation, yielding the highest integrated TOPSIS score. Metagenomic analyses revealed treatment-associated shifts in CBB/TCA-related functions in C. vulgaris communities and late enrichment of glycogen-associated genes in Synechocystis sp. communities. RDA further linked central-carbon gene profiles with TC, TN, TP, EPS, and biochemical pools, while bacterial succession showed marked strain- and gas-condition dependence.ConclusionsThis divergence shows that maximizing biomass recovery and maximizing liquid-carbon drawdown represent different operational objectives rather than a single strain-independent response. The results identify distinct operational advantages among the tested phototrophs: T. obliquus favored biomass and resource recovery, whereas Synechocystis sp. promoted stronger short-term inorganic-carbon conversion. Together, carbon partitioning and community functional patterns indicate that tested-strains identity, carbon availability, nutrient demand, extracellular-carbon exchange, and phycosphere succession jointly shape system performance.
authors: Wang H, Xu J, Cao Y, Liu J, Liu K, Gong Y, Xu X, Zhi S, Zhang K, Wijffels RH.

title: Establishing Potosi Virus as a Human Pathogen: Fatal Neuroinvasive Disease in a B-Cell-Depleted Patient.
abstract: ObjectivesTo establish Potosi virus, a mosquito-borne member of the family Peribunyaviridae, as a neuroinvasive human pathogen.MethodsCase report.ResultsA 37-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis on long-term rituximab developed rapidly progressive dementia. Serial MRI demonstrated progressive generalized atrophy. CSF showed transient, minimal lymphocytic pleocytosis. Extensive infectious, autoimmune, and prion evaluations were unrevealing, but CSF metagenomic sequencing detected all 3 genome segments for Potosi virus. Postmortem examination revealed diffuse meningoencephalitis with T-cell-predominant leptomeningeal and perivascular inflammation. Molecular analyses confirmed multiple nucleotide sequences with >99+% concordance with a known Potosi strain, with widespread viral infection confirmed by immunohistochemistry demonstrating intracellular and extracellular viral antigen. Electron microscopy demonstrated particles of a size consistent with the Peribunyaviridae family. Metagenomic sequencing of RNA extracted from frozen brain tissue identified all 3 Potosi virus gene segments without other infectious entities. Findings were concordant across multiple laboratories and institutions.DiscussionPotosi virus can cause fatal neuroinvasive disease in humans, as evidenced by convergent postmortem neuropathologic, molecular, and ultrastructural evidence. Chronic B-cell depletion may increase susceptibility to severe disease with arboviral infections, which may present without conventional CNS inflammatory markers. CSF metagenomic sequencing should be considered in immunocompromised patients with unexplained progressive neurologic decline.
authors: Abbatemarco JR, Begum F, Villalba JA, Davis E, Bhatnagar J, Brault AC, Calvert AE, Chomyk A, Gould CV, Isada CM, Jung JU, Jones SE, Kang S, Ko Y, Li Y, Nakamura K, Najm L, Staples EJ, Trapp BD, Tipping P, Yeaney GA, Fox RJ.

title: Three new species in Lentistoma, Neolindgomyces, and Ophiocreas from freshwater habitats.
abstract: During a survey of saprobic fungi in Jiangxi and Zhejiang provinces, China, three fungal species were collected from decaying wood samples in freshwater habitats. We selected the internal transcribed spacers (ITS1-5.8S-ITS2), large subunit (28S ribosomal RNA), small subunit (18S ribosomal RNA), translation elongation factor 1-alpha (tef1), RNA polymerase II largest subunit (rpb1), and RNA polymerase II second-largest subunit (rpb2) genes for phylogenetic analyses. Maximum likelihood and Bayesian analyses were performed to clarify the phylogenetic affinities of the species. These species are separated from the other species in respective genera based on dimensions in ascomata, asci, and ascospores and DNA sequence data. Based on morphology and multilocus phylogenetic analysis, these species were confirmed as three new species and were named Lentistoma multiseptata, Neolindgomyces aquaticus, and Ophioceras jiangshanense. Newly added species are compared with other similar species, and comprehensive descriptions and micrographs are provided.
authors: Huang L, Jin ZH, Song HY, Zhang JB, Zhai ZJ, Zhou JP, Hu DM.

title: A candidate genetic trigger of female sex determination in Marsabit clawed frogs (Xenopus borealis).
abstract: A central question in biology asks why the genetic basis of sex determination evolves quickly in some groups even though disruption of this process carries severe risks such as sterility. A challenge to understanding mechanisms of this rapid evolution is a lack of functionally verified genetic triggers of sex determination. To begin to remedy this, we set out to identify, characterize, and functionally test the genetic trigger of female sex determination in Marsabit clawed frogs (Xenopus borealis), which has a species-specific and probably newly evolved W chromosome. Genomic and transcriptomic data identify a candidate that was expressed specifically in female gonads during sex determination. We knocked out this gene, which is a female-specific duplicate of wnt3.L - hereafter wnt3-W - and induced complete female-to-male sex reversal in 35 of 36 individuals. These sex-reversed individuals had male-typical external and internal morphology, mating behavior, mating calls, testis histology, and are fertile. This demonstrates that wnt3-W is generally necessary for feminization of X. borealis, and adds to only one other functionally verified candidate trigger of sex determination in amphibians. Phylogenetic and cytogenetic analysis indicates that wnt3-W originated recently on the tip of the X. borealis W chromosome, after this species diverged from all other extant Xenopus. Wnt3-W is the first known candidate genetic trigger of sex determination in the Wnt gene family, which is surprising because wnt3 is more generally involved with vital, but not sex-specific functions. Similarities in protein structure are consistent with the possibility that Wnt3-W is a genetic surrogate that utilizes the feminizing genetic network of Wnt4. The discovery of wnt3-W adds to a handful of other secreted peptides that trigger sex determination in animals; its proposed function as a positively acting female-determining gene - if confirmed - would further be distinguished from other known genetic triggers in vertebrates.
authors: Evans BJ, Murphy HA, Porter SR, Wasonga DV, Knytl M, Bergelová B, Horb M.

title: Microbial bioherbicides: Integrating bioprocessing, mechanisms of action and protein engineering for sustainable weed management.
abstract: The widespread use of synthetic herbicides in agriculture has intensified concerns regarding environmental sustainability and human health, while the evolution of herbicide resistance has outpaced the discovery of new modes of action. Bioherbicides have consequently emerged as a viable alternative, comprising biologically derived compounds capable of suppressing weed growth. This review adopts an integrated perspective on microbially derived bioherbicides, following the active biomolecules from the producing strain and its fermentation conditions to their physiological targets in the plant and to the molecular strategies available for their optimization. Unlike previous reviews, which address these dimensions separately and focus mainly on secondary metabolites, particular emphasis is placed here on enzymes with herbicidal activity and on protein engineering approaches. Based on a structured literature search, 39 original studies were analyzed. Phytopathogenic fungi, mainly Fusarium, Diaporthe, Phoma, Alternaria and Trichoderma, predominate as producing organisms, followed by bacteria of the genera Streptomyces, Pseudomonas and Bacillus, and submerged fermentation using low-cost agro-industrial substrates is the prevailing production strategy. Enzymatic classes such as cutinases, lipases, cellulases, pectinases and proteases act primarily by degrading the cuticle and the cell wall, whereas secondary metabolites frequently target the photosynthetic apparatus, particularly photosystem II; most of these compounds, however, still lack a defined mode of action within established herbicide classification systems. Molecular approaches, including heterologous expression, molecular docking and metabolic engineering, remain comparatively underexplored despite their potential to enhance activity, stability and specificity. Advances in formulation stability, bioprocess scalability, mechanistic characterization and regulatory harmonization are identified as the key requirements to translate these biomolecules into commercially viable products for sustainable weed management.
authors: Krein DDC, Conterato AAM, Plucinski R, Dotto GL, Dettmer A.

title: Pseudomonas spp.-based synthetic microbial community effects on nutrient dynamics in citrus plants under induced dysbiosis.
abstract: Main conclusionA targeted Pseudomonas-based synthetic microbial community reshaped rhizosphere bacterial communities and altered potassium partitioning under stress conditions, suggesting a potential role in mitigating antibiotic-induced dysbiosis. Sustainable agriculture primarily relies on biological practices to improve crop yield and resilience. Synthetic bacterial communities (SynComs) are a promising approach to promote plant growth; however, their effectiveness in situ is influenced by interactions with native microbial ecosystems and by environmental stressors, such as low pH and antibiotic use. In this context, beneficial microorganisms like Pseudomonas may enhance nutrient availability and mitigate antibiotic-induced dysbiosis by supporting microbial community reassembly and functional stability, thereby improving plant health. This study evaluated the effects of a Pseudomonas-based SynCom on nutrient accumulation and rhizosphere microbial dynamics in citrus plants subjected to streptomycin-induced dysbiosis and low-pH conditions. Selected Pseudomonas strains, chosen for their compatibility and adaptability to low-pH conditions, and through whole-genome sequencing, were applied at equal concentrations (OD600 = 0.1). SynCom treatment increased Chloroflexota abundance in the rhizosphere while reducing Actinomycetota and Pseudomonadota after 24 days. By Day 45, the abundance of Actinomycetota decreased, with slight increases in the other two phyla. At the genus level, SynCom application reduced the abundance of Pseudomonas and Agrobacterium, while enriching the Klebsiella community. Plants treated with SynCom under stress exhibited a 25% increase in leaf potassium levels, accompanied by a 29% decrease in root potassium (essential for stomatal regulation, osmotic adjustment, and photosynthetic efficiency, which are fundamental to tree growth and stress resilience) levels. Overall, our findings demonstrate that a targeted Pseudomonas-based SynCom can reshape rhizosphere communities and improve nutrient dynamics under abiotic stress, highlighting its potential as a sustainable strategy to mitigate antibiotic-induced dysbiosis and enhance citrus resilience.
authors: Ketehouli T, Trub MR, Goss EM, Martins SJ.

title: Human milk oligosaccharides are distinctly processed by early life gut microbial sialidases.
abstract: The infant gut microbiome in early life is shaped by numerous factors, including feeding method. Exclusively breastfed and formula-fed infants exhibit distinct microbiome compositions. While these effects are well-established, the underlying mechanisms that drive these differences are not fully understood. Here, we examine the removal of sialic acid from human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) influenced by human microbial sialidases in early life. We identify 351 and 214 unique sialidase sequences from adult and infant microbiome metagenomes, respectively, and characterize a diverse, representative set in vitro using sialylated HMOs normally present in human breastmilk. We find these proteins exhibit distinct abilities to metabolize 3'- and 6'-sialyllactose, which are the most abundant sialylated HMOs in breastmilk, and distinctly process other more complex substrates, as well. We provide structural insights into these functional differences by pinpointing active site features uniquely present in efficient enzymes and show that these results extend to activities on complex mixtures of sialylated HMOs purified from human breastmilk. Finally, we demonstrate in human clinical data that distinct profiles of sialidase-encoding bacterial taxa are observed in breastfed and formula-fed infants at 1 and 4 months of age, prior to the introduction of solid foods. Together, these findings show that specific bacterial sialidases are influential in shaping the early gut microbiome, data that may improve the supplementation of infant formulas for enhanced developmental outcomes.
authors: Plisko OL, Chapel VS, Sekela JJ, Talbert JA, Townsend SD, Zemel BS, Wu GD, R Redinbo M.

title: Identification of a novel equine rotavirus B from Missouri in 2025, which is distantly related to group B rotaviruses.
abstract: Despite the wide circulation of group B rotaviruses in animals and humans, rotavirus B was not found in horses until 2021 in Kentucky, USA. Little is known about the genetic diversity and evolution of rotavirus B in this new host. Here, we described a divergent equine rotavirus B (ERVB) from a foal with idiopathic diarrhea in Missouri (designated MO-ERVB-25). Full-genome sequencing and phylogenetic analysis revealed that MO-ERVB-25 is distantly related to all previously known group B rotaviruses, including ERVB strains identified in 2021 in Kentucky (KY-ERVB-21). The mean nucleotide substitution rate of the VP4 segment was estimated as 1.44 × 10-3 substitutions/site/year, which is a magnitude higher than the VP7 segment. We further demonstrated that MO-ERVB-25, like human RVB, binds chemically neutral LacNAc-containing complex N-linked glycans, while KY-ERVB-21 recognizes negatively charged polysialic acid (polySia) with α-2,8-linkage, which is a functional receptor for unrelated enteric human adenovirus 52. Using the AlphaFold-enabled structure prediction, we showed that both MO-ERVB-25 and human RVB VP8* lack a novel C-terminal α2 helix that is only observed in the KY-ERVB-21 VP8*, which may help explain the difference in glycan binding specificities. Finally, screening of foal samples by the reverse transcription quantitative PCR assay identified 4.2% of idiopathic foal diarrhea samples (6 out of 140) positive for MO-ERVB-25. These results suggest that MO-ERVB-25 represents a new rotavirus B subgroup that circulates in foals. Its circulation, together with KY-ERVB-25 subgroup, raises the possibility of reassortment and antigenic shift as mechanisms of rotavirus B evolution in equines.ImportanceEquine RVB (ERVB) has emerged as a significant cause of foal diarrhea since 2021. Our study describes a highly divergent RVB strain identified in a foal with severe diarrhea in 2025. This ERVB variant exhibited low amino acid identity compared with previously reported ERVB strains. The novel ERVB strain escaped routine diagnostic detection. Sequence analysis demonstrated that this new strain grouped with bovine, porcine, caprine, and equine RVB but formed a distinct, independent branch. In addition, glycan array studies revealed the substantial difference in glycan recognition between new and previously described ERVB strains, which is likely determined by the presence or absence of a novel C-terminal α2 helix in the VP8* receptor-binding domain. These results suggest that this novel ERVB variant may co-circulate with existing ERVB strains in horses, which may facilitate rapid viral evolution through antigenic diversity, a property previously reported in rotaviruses from other hosts.
authors: Soni S, Hause B, Uprety T, Yu J, Shuisong N, Eertink LG, Fang Z, Giri K, Erdal E, Morgan J, Lawson S, Nelson E, Graves AJ, Morrow JK, Adam EN, Sheng Z, Kennedy MA, Wang D, Li F.

title: Continent-wide Multi-Segment Phylogenomic Study of Host and Geographic Structuring of African Hantaviruses
abstract: Abstract    Background:  African hantaviruses remain among the least characterized members of the family  Hantaviridae  , with fragmented genomic data limiting our understanding of their evolutionary relationships, host associations, and geographic structuring. Here, we investigated the integrated continent-wide phylogenomic structure of African hantaviruses using all three coding genomic segments. Methods: We compiled and curated 281 full-length and partial coding sequences representing the L segment (  n   = 166), M segment (  n   = 48), and S segment (  n   = 67) from 13 African countries, alongside representative global reference strains. Temporal signal was evaluated using root-to-tip regression analysis. Segment-specific phylogenetic reconstructions were performed to characterize host-associated and geographic structuring. Additionally, pairwise tanglegram comparisons of the L, M, and S phylogenies were constructed to evaluate topological congruence and identify potential signals of genetic reassortment. Results  Root-to-tip regressions revealed weak temporal signal across the L (  R  ² = 0.069), M (  R  ² = 0.021), and S (  R  ² = 0.046) datasets, precluding reliable molecular-clock inference. Phylogenetic analyses demonstrated pronounced host-associated and geographic structuring across all three segments. Rodent, shrew, and bat-associated hantaviruses formed distinct evolutionary clades, with bat and shrew-borne lineages occupying basal, divergent positions relative to rodent-associated viruses. Endemic African hantaviruses exhibited marked regional clustering, forming distinct Malagasy, East African, and West African assemblages, whereas Senegalese, Beninese, and Malian sequences clustered within globally distributed,  Rattus  -associated Seoul orthohantavirus lineages. Comparative analyses highlighted complementary phylogenetic signals: the L segment provided a robust framework for resolving deep evolutionary relationships, the M segment offered clear discrimination among closely related host and geographic groups, and the S segment consistently recovered primary lineage boundaries. Pairwise tanglegrams demonstrated substantial topological concordance among segments highest between L and M with localized incongruences primarily in the L–S comparison restricted to closely related terminal taxa, consistent with but not definitive evidence of reassortment Conclusions  African hantaviruses display strong host-associated and geographic structuring, with major evolutionary relationships broadly conserved across all three genomic segments. These findings provide an integrated continent-wide phylogenomic framework, establishing a foundation for future genomic surveillance, evolutionary studies, and One Health strategies across Africa.
authors: Nicodemus M, Olumuyiwa O, Lanre I, Edet UO, Adeyinka AJ, Clement MA.

title: A genomic resource for a hidden endemic: the complete chloroplast genome of Allium aktauense from Uzbekistan.
abstract: Allium aktauense is a narrow endemic species from the Aktau Range in the Nurotau Mountains, Western Pamir-Alay, Uzbekistan, where it grows in rocky limestone crevices. Genomic resources for this species have previously been limited, restricting molecular assessment of its phylogenetic placement. In this study, we sequenced, assembled and characterized the complete chloroplast genome of A. aktauense and evaluated its phylogenetic position within Allium using comparative plastome data. The plastome is 152,443 bp long and has the typical quadripartite organization, comprising a large single-copy region of 81,522 bp, a small single-copy region of 17,907 bp and two inverted repeat regions of 26,507 bp each. Annotation identified 131 gene copies, including 85 protein-coding genes, 38 tRNA genes and 8 rRNA genes. Across the broad comparative dataset, the highest nucleotide diversity was observed in the ndhF-rpl32 region (Pi approximately 0.044), followed by ycf1 (Pi approaching 0.030); these regions are treated here as candidate variable loci requiring further validation within closely related taxa. Maximum-likelihood analysis of complete plastome sequences placed A. aktauense within subgenus Allium, with A. ophiophyllum as its closest sampled plastome lineage (bootstrap support 100%). The plastome provides a genomic resource for future phylogenetic, taxonomic and conservation-related research on endemic Central Asian Allium.

title: Calibrating public genome archives for AMR surveillance: Four decades of redundancy-aware phylogenomics of pandemic Escherichia coli ST131.
abstract: AimsEscherichia coli sequence type (ST)131 is a globally disseminated multidrug-resistant pathogen, yet public genome collections are skewed by uneven sampling and repeated sequencing of genetically near-identical isolates. Rather than another reconstruction of ST131 evolution, we quantified redundancy, reassessed population structure, and tested how sampling bias affects estimates of phylogenetic diversity, clade-specific dating, and fluoroquinolone-resistance-associated diversification.MethodsEnteroBase core-genome multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST) hierarchical clustering was used to reduce redundancy among 16,713 public ST131 complex genomes. Representative public genomes were combined with 390 unpublished New Zealand ST131 surveillance genomes from 1999 to 2019. Clade-specific phylogenetic and temporal analyses were performed for Clades A, B, and C, with sensitivity analyses using stricter cgMLST clustering and phylogenetic-diversity-guided subsampling.ResultsPublic genomes were highly redundant: just 2/409 cgMLST groups contained 85.2% of public genomes. After redundancy reduction, dated Clades A, B, and C phylogenies spanning 1999-2023 (n = 113), 1982-2025 (n = 240), and 1999-2025 (n = 614), respectively, were constructed. Clades A and B showed distinct temporal histories and evolutionary rates. Date-randomization supported temporal information in Clade C, although incomplete convergence of the observed-date relaxed-clock and Bayesian Skyline analyses means that exact Clade C molecular-date and demographic estimates should be interpreted cautiously. The broad Clade C reconstruction nevertheless indicated expansion of the dominant fluoroquinolone-resistant lineage in the late 1990s/early 2000s and again in the mid-2000s.ConclusionsPublic ST131 datasets reflect sampling distribution as well as number of available genomes. Redundancy in dominant cgMLST groups can obscure uncommon lineages and blur emergence with later expansion. In Clade C, redundancy-aware analysis was broadly consistent with previous estimates placing major fluoroquinolone-resistant diversification in the early 1990s, while indicating that early resistance diversification preceded later amplification of resistant sublineages.
journal: Drug resistance updates : reviews and commentaries in antimicrobial and anticancer chemotherapy
authors: White RT, Biggs PJ, Burgess SA, Collis RM, Cookson AL, Downing T, Elvy J, Featherstone LA, French NP, Pattis I, Price EP, Sarovich DS, Tiong A, Ussher JE, Winter DJ, Yang Z, Dyet K.

title: Does the mouth seed the small bowel? Mechanisms and hypothesis-generating framework via the oral-gut axis.
abstract: BackgroundAs the starting segment of the digestive tract, the oral cavity harbors a complex microbial community that closely interacts with the distal gut microbiota. Recent evidence suggests that oral hygiene status and oral dysbiosis may correlate with gut microbial homeostasis and play a potential role in the initiation or exacerbation of small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO).ObjectiveThis review aims to integrate existing evidence, outline a hypothesis-generating framework, identify critical knowledge gaps, and provide new perspectives for future interdisciplinary mechanistic research and clinical translation in SIBO and related gastrointestinal disorders.DesignThis narrative review synthesizes and evaluates preliminary clinical correlations, metagenomic surveys, and animal models that support the oral microbiota as a potentially modifiable factor associated with SIBO, and discusses the proposed underlying molecular pathways.ResultsExisting evidence supports the oral microbiota as a potentially modifiable factor associated with SIBO. However, direct high-level evidence testing oral hygiene interventions against definitive SIBO outcomes is currently lacking.ConclusionsThe oral-gut axis may play a critical role in SIBO pathogenesis. Future research requires high-quality clinical trials to validate the impact of oral hygiene interventions on SIBO outcomes, bridging the current critical knowledge gaps.
authors: He L, Wang J, Bai T, Hou X, Ran D, Yang J.

title: Genome-based identification of hydrocarbon-metabolism-associated genes with putative relevance to polyethylene modification in Rhodococcus pyridinivorans AAa3.
abstract: Polyethylene (PE) is a highly recalcitrant plastic that accumulates extensively in the environment. In this study, Rhodococcus pyridinivorans AAa3 was analysed using hybrid WGS to investigate its genomic features and identify candidate metabolic functions with putative relevance to PE modification. The assembled genome (5,078,411 bp) exhibited high completeness and continuity. Phylogenetic, phylogenomic, and ANI analyses confirmed the strain's classification, with 98.96 % ANI to R. pyridinivorans DSM 44555T. Genome mining identified diverse oxidative enzymes, including alkane monooxygenases, cytochrome P450s, Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenases, and multicopper oxidases. Analysis of AlkB proteins showed conserved motifs, transmembrane domains, and phylogenetic conservation. Orthology and synteny analyses showed conservation of AlkB proteins and their genomic neighbourhoods, with strain-specific variation. AAa3 contained five MCO genes, placing it toward the upper end of the copy-number distribution across 41 R. pyridinivorans genomes. Molecular docking showed accommodation of n-octane, n-decane, and n-dodecane within the targeted regions of AlkB1 and AlkB2. An AlkX-like TetR-family regulator was identified near alkB2, while targeted motif analysis detected an AlkX-like motif upstream of cytochrome P450 gene ACU6L1_03615. To the best of our knowledge, no previous genome-based study has specifically investigated R. pyridinivorans in the context of PE modification. These findings warrant further experimental investigation.
authors: Elsayed AF, Youssef HI, Gebreel HM, Mahasneh I, Amin DH.

title: Integrated assessment of mercury-tolerant plant-associated bacteria from a chlor-alkali site identifies candidates for bioaugmentation.
abstract: Mercury (Hg)-contaminated environments harbour microorganisms with traits that may be useful for plant-assisted remediation, but high Hg tolerance alone may not identify the most suitable strains for inoculation. In this study, plant-associated bacteria isolated from a chlor-alkali site were evaluated through phenotypic screening, whole-genome analysis, genome-scale metabolic modelling, and willow inoculation assays. Fifty-one Hg-tolerant isolates were recovered, of which 16 were selected for detailed characterization. All selected isolates displayed at least one plant growth-promoting trait, including indole-3-acetic acid production, siderophore production, or phosphate solubilization. Pseudomonas canadensis UFC_B020 and Pseudomonas umsongensis UFC_B021 grew at 200 µM Hg, the highest concentration tested. Genome-based analyses identified putative functions related to metal transport, membrane efflux, oxidative stress responses and plant-beneficial metabolism, while community-scale modelling predicted potential metabolite exchanges within three selected bacterial consortia. In willow inoculation assays, consortium 1 increased root projected area by 5.7% relative to the uninoculated control. The strongest root response was therefore associated with a different consortium from that containing the two isolates with the highest Hg tolerance, highlighting the value of considering both Hg tolerance and plant responses in candidate selection. Together, these results support an integrated strategy combining Hg tolerance, plant growth-promoting traits, genome-based functional information and consortium performance to prioritize site-derived bacteria for subsequent bioaugmentation studies.
authors: Meyer L, Zhou J, Pfendler S, Mishra A, Otero-Gonzalez L, Franco M, Gil-Guerrero S, Meunier A, Hocquet D, Guyot S, Capelli N, Chalot M.

title: Phylogenetic position and expanded host range of the photosymbiont Brandtodinium nutricula (Peridiniales, Dinophyceae)
abstract: Brandtodinium nutricula is a dinoflagellate species commonly reported in symbiosis with the marine protist host lineage, Collodaria (Rhizaria). Despite the widespread abundance of this symbiosis throughout the open ocean, and clear indications that the alga should be capable of existing outside of the symbiosis, there are no reports to date of the alga in free-living form in the environment. Even though B. nutricula molecular data are publicly available, the phylogenetic position of B. nutricula remains unclear. Our taxon-rich 18S rRNA gene phylogenetic analysis revealed a close association between B. nutricula and the copepod parasite lineage, Blastodinium. We next analyzed Tara Oceans metabarcode data to assess B. nutricula abundance outside of the Collodaria symbiosis and found that B. nutricula is common in free-living form throughout the sunlit ocean. Similarly, B. nutricula does not significantly correlate with Collodaria in terms of read depth in Tara Oceans samples, despite their tight association. We also determined that B. nutricula can live symbiotically within planktonic Foraminifera using fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy in combination with fluorescence in situ hybridization. These findings indicate that the radiolarian-B. nutricula symbiosis is less specific than previously suggested, highlighting the complexity of open ocean symbioses and the importance of weighing both host and symbiont perspectives when considering who benefits from the relationship.
authors: Coots NL, Blanco Bercial L, Gile GH, Keeling PJ.

title: An Integrated One-Click Python Pipeline for Bacterial Codon-Usage Analysis and Proteome-Wide Characterization
abstract: Abstract    Background:  Codon-usage analysis provides insights into synonymous codon preferences, nucleotide composition, and potential evolutionary constraints, while protein physicochemical indices offer complementary information about proteome characteristics. Together, these sequence- and protein-level measures can provide a broader computational view of genomic and proteomic variation across bacterial genomes providing insights into crucial functional mechanisms like pathogenicity and antibiotic resistance. However, integrating these analyses into a streamlined and reproducible workflow can be challenging.  Methods:  We developed an integrated one-click Python pipeline for bacterial codon-usage analysis and proteome-wide characterization. The workflow processes FASTA sequences, applies sequence-quality filters, calculates codon-usage and nucleotide-composition indices, performs parity analysis, and conducts principal component analysis (PCA) using relative synonymous codon usage (RSCU) and relative amino-acid usage (RAAU). It also estimates protein-level characteristics, including theoretical isoelectric point, molecular weight, grand average of hydropathicity, aromaticity, and sequence-length measures. Results are organized into two worksheets within a single Excel output.  Results:  The pipeline was applied to coding sequences from  Acinetobacter baumannii  ,  Pseudomonas aeruginosa  , and  Elizabethkingia anophelis  . Comparisons with previously reported values showed broadly similar estimates for selected indices, including GC content, GC3s, GRAVY, and aromaticity. However, differences were observed in third-position nucleotide composition, codon adaptation index (CAI), frequency of optimal codons (Fop), and sequence-length-related measures. These discrepancies highlight the influence of computational definitions, reference sets, and sequence-processing criteria on the resulting estimates.  Conclusion:  The pipeline integrates codon-level and protein-level analyses into an accessible workflow that generates structured outputs. Further benchmarking against established tools using matched sequences and standardized definitions is needed to establish its numerical agreement, robustness, and broader applicability. Future development could expand reference-set customization and validation across diverse bacterial genomes.
authors: Dahal U.

title: Construction and Evaluation of a Reference Strain System for Brucella melitensis Biovar 2 and Genomic Characteristic Analysis
abstract: Abstract    Objective  To establish a candidate national reference strain of  Brucella melitensis  biovar 2 according to relevant technical standards using a  Brucella  strain preserved in the local biological sample repository in Zhuhai City.  Methods  In accordance with the Technical Evaluation Standard for National Pathogenic Microorganism Strains (WS/T 812–2022), morphological identification of the candidate Brucella strain was performed via colony observation, Gram-staining and transmission electron microscopy. Species-level identification was carried out using matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF-MS), biochemical assays, serum agglutination tests and phage lysis assays. Whole-genome sequencing was applied for biovar typing, virulence- and resistance-associated gene profiling. Physiological characteristics were further characterized by antimicrobial susceptibility testing and strain stability assessment.  Results  Strain ZH25-Bru-002 (abbreviated as ZH25 throughout the text) was a Gram-negative bacillus. It grew well on modified Brucella agar and blood agar at 37°C, with cell dimensions of (0.3–0.4) µm × (0.6–0.8) µm. MALDI-TOF-MS identified it as  B. melitensis  with a score of 2.366. The strain was positive for oxidase, catalase and urease, and negative for hydrogen sulphide production. Plaque formation was observed in the Bk-phage lysis test. Agglutination titer for serum A was higher than that for serum M. Among the 12 tested antibiotics, the strain was resistant only to erythromycin (MIC > 32 µg/mL). Whole-genome sequencing together with 16S rRNA and  rpoB  gene typing confirmed its identity as  B. melitensis  biovar 2. Following serial in-vitro passaging to obtain the 1st-generation (G1), 5th-generation (G5), and 10th-generation (G10) derivatives of ZH25, colony morphology, biochemical profiles and biovar features remained stable. The strain has been deposited in the Pathogenic Microorganism Repository of Guangdong Provincial Center for Disease Control and Prevention and assigned a national preservation accession number.  Conclusion  The  B. melitensis  biovar 2 strain obtained in this study exhibits typical phenotypic and genotypic features of the pathogen. It qualifies as a reference strain for brucellosis surveillance, vaccine evaluation and diagnostic reagent development. The strain has passed review by the national repository and obtained the official preservation number NPRC(S) 01.0114.
authors: Yang W, Wu J, Fang Y, Liu X, Cui Y, Ke C, Yao S, Wu J, Huang H, Lin Y, Deng X, Huang W.

title: Biocontrol of postharvest Fusarium oxysporum on fruits and vegetables: mechanisms and efficacy of antagonistic microorganisms.
abstract: Fusarium oxysporum is a major postharvest pathogen causing significant losses in stored fruits, vegetables, tubers, and bulbs. Understanding its infection mechanisms is essential for developing effective biological control strategies. This review synthesizes current knowledge on postharvest infection by F. oxysporum, including wound-dependent penetration, production of toxins (beauvericin, fusaric acid) and cell wall-degrading enzymes (polygalacturonases, cellulases), and tissue colonization leading to rot and mycotoxin accumulation. It critically evaluates biological control agents (BCAs) from three major groups bacteria (Bacillus, Pseudomonas), yeasts (Metschnikowia, Wickerhamomyces), and filamentous fungi (Trichoderma) with emphasis on their modes of action: nutrient competition (iron chelation via siderophores or pulcherrimin), antimicrobial production (lipopeptides, volatile organic compounds, hydrolytic enzymes), and mycoparasitism (unique to Trichoderma). The interactions between the pathogen and BCAs are examined within the postharvest wound microenvironment, highlighting the competitive dynamics that determine infection outcomes. Based on published storage trials, the review identifies critical knowledge gaps limiting commercial translation: most BCA efficacy studies have been conducted at 25-28 °C, and in vivo data under cold storage (4-10 °C) remain scarce; direct quantification of pathogen virulence factors in infected fruit tissues is lacking; and transcriptomic analyses of F. oxysporum during biocontrol challenge are still unavailable. A research roadmap is proposed, including cold storage screening, in situ metabolomics, RNA-seq of the pathogen during BCA exposure, multi-strain efficacy testing, and LAMP diagnostics integration.
authors: Akpafi LM, He W, Zhu C, Fan Y, Wang Y.

title: Dynamic transcriptomic analysis of CCR4-NOT complex subunits identifies Cnot7 as an oogenesis-associated factor in Crassostrea gigas.
abstract: The CCR4-NOT complex is a conserved eukaryotic deadenylation machinery that plays essential roles in post-transcriptional regulation of mRNA metabolism, embryonic development, and reproduction. However, the composition and expression dynamics of the CCR4-NOT complex subunits in marine mollusks remain unexplored. Here, we systematically identified nine CCR4-NOT complex subunits in the Pacific oyster Crassostrea gigas. Phylogenetic and domain analyses revealed all CNOT proteins retained subtype-specific structural features in C. gigas. Notably, the oyster genome encodes CNOT7 but lacks CNOT8, consistent with the distribution observed in the analyzed invertebrates. Developmental expression profiling revealed typical maternal transcript expression patterns for six Cnot genes. Tissue-specificity analysis identified Cnot7 as the only Cnot gene meeting the predefined criterion for gonad-specific expression. Single-nucleus transcriptomic analysis further showed it was preferentially expressed in the oocyte lineage, with the highest expression in mature oocytes. These findings provide a molecular characterization of the CCR4-NOT subunits in a marine bivalve, and identify Cnot7 as a germline-associated candidate subunit potentially involved in reproductive development and early embryogenesis in C. gigas.
journal: Comparative biochemistry and physiology. Part D, Genomics & proteomics
authors: Zhou Y, Yu H, Li Q.

title: From substrate composition to microbial metabolism: performance, molecular, taxonomic and functional insights into sludge-derived hydrothermal carbon sources for denitrification.
abstract: Liquid recovered from hydrothermal sludge treatment is an attractive denitrification carbon source, but it carries nitrogen that raises effluent total nitrogen and recalcitrant organics that leave residual chemical oxygen demand (COD). Thermal hydrolysis (TH), wet air oxidation (WAO) and two-stage WAO with catalytic WAO (WAO-CWAO) liquids were compared with sodium acetate in sequencing batch reactors, and the mechanisms were resolved by Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metagenomics. TH and WAO liquids failed as carbon sources, with effluent COD and nitrogen above the Chinese discharge standard, whereas the WAO-CWAO liquid converted the recalcitrant organics into volatile fatty acids (VFAs), removed ammonia, and approached, but did not match, the sodium acetate control. An apparent nitrogen balance showed that residual nitrogen reflected the load introduced with the carbon source, and residual COD was traced to a CHON-rich pool unique to these effluents. Community composition followed carbon source quality, shifting from a diverse consortium sustained by slowly biodegradable organics to a streamlined assemblage of VFAs-utilizing denitrifiers. Genome-resolved analysis of the recovered metagenome-assembled genomes indicated a substrate-based division of labor: the dominant Saprospiraceae carried an expanded hydrolytic arsenal but no nitrate reductase, whereas Thauera carried complete denitrification and VFA-utilization gene sets but no polysaccharide hydrolases. A second, catalytic stage at higher temperature and oxygen pressure therefore alleviates the trade-off between nitrogen release and incomplete oxidation, yielding a sludge-derived carbon source that approaches sodium acetate.
authors: Fang K, Zhu Q, Zhu Y, Yao G, Zhao J, Xia S.

title: Genomic and In Vitro Characterization of the Candidate Probiotic Yeast Pichia kluyveri PK88™
abstract: Non-Saccharomyces yeasts are of growing interest as probiotic candidates, but strain-level charac-terization remains limited. We characterized Pichia kluyveri PK88™, isolated from coffee beans (NRRL deposit # 68561), using phenotypic assays, whole-genome sequencing, and in silico screen-ing. PK88™ was non-hemolytic and produced no detectable patulin, ochratoxin A, or aflatoxins. Genome analysis confirmed species identity (98.5–98.8% average nucleotide identity) and identi-fied no acquired antimicrobial-resistance genes, canonical virulence factors, or decarboxylases for harmful biogenic amines. By high-inoculum broth microdilution, MICs were low for echi-nocandins and amphotericin B and higher for fluconazole and posaconazole. Measured survival after acid, bile and anaerobic exposure was retained (93% at pH 2; 82–84% in bile), although sur-vival at pH 1 and under anaerobiosis was lower; hydrophobicity fell from 91% to 73–77% and auto-aggregation rose to 98–100%. PK88 supernatant inhibited Escherichia coli and Candida albi-cans in preliminary assays. In two independent experiments, Caco-2 cells exposed to PK88™ showed cytotoxicity ≤20% in every replicate up to 6 × 104 organisms/well and variable increases at higher doses. These preliminary data support further evaluation.
authors: Ahmed S, Fnu S, Valentin ES, Eltokhy A, Khater S, Goodwin E, Deaton J, McCormick TS, Ghannoum MA.
