title: Microbial-mediated degradation of aflatoxin B1 in agricultural soil.
abstract: Aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) is commonly present in agricultural soil and poses severe threats to soil ecosystems due to its high toxicity, yet its environmental fate and microbial-mediated degradation mechanisms remain insufficiently studied. In this study, the environmental behavior of AFB1 in an agricultural soil was investigated. Metagenomic analysis showed that exposure to a higher concentration of AFB1 (5.0 mg kg-1) altered soil bacterial community structure and reduced community diversity. After 30 days of incubation, AFB1 was slowly removed from natural soil microcosms but persisted in sterilized soil microcosms, indicating that indigenous soil microorganisms make a major contribution to AFB1 dissipation. Exposure to high-concentration AFB1 significantly enriched the genus Nocardioides, and a novel AFB1-degrading strain, Nocardioides sp. N13 (phylum Actinomycetota), was isolated from the agricultural soil. Strain N13 harbors three genes encoding putative F420H2-dependent reductase (FDR) homologs, which are hypothesized to be involved in the initial degradation of AFB1. Bioinformatics analysis revealed that putative FDR homolog-carrying bacteria are mostly assigned to the phylum Actinomycetota and are widely distributed across diverse soil environments worldwide. These findings provide a theoretical basis and potential microbial resources for mitigating AFB1 contamination in soil ecosystems.
authors: Lu P, Chen A, Feng Y, He S, Han G, Hu S.

title: Revitalizing simultaneous nitrification, endogenous denitrification and phosphorus removal under carbon starvation: Redox mediator-modulated electron transfer and metabolic coordination.
abstract: The simultaneous nitrification, endogenous denitrification and phosphorus removal (SNEDPR) process provides a resource-efficient paradigm for synergistic nutrient removal. However, its efficacy can be severely constrained by limited electron-donor availability and inefficient intracellular electron transfer under low carbon-to-nitrogen (C/N) ratios. Herein, we demonstrate that anthraquinone-2-sulfonate (AQS) serves as an effective redox mediator to alleviate these electron-transfer limitations. Under severe carbon-limited conditions, with an influent C/N ratio of 3.24±0.11, supplementation with 0.3 mmol/L AQS successfully restored the deteriorated system, recovering total inorganic nitrogen (TIN) removal efficiency to 96.57±0.87% while sustaining robust phosphorus removal (96.47±2.68%). Batch kinetic assays showed that AQS increased electron transfer system activity (ETSA) by over 100%, accompanied by enhanced nitrification-related activity, endogenous denitrification and phosphorus uptake. Integrated metagenomic and metatranscriptomic analyses further revealed transcriptional responses consistent with an electron-shuttling role of AQS, including enhanced ETC-associated electron-transfer potential and increased transcription of downstream denitrification enzymes. ATP synthase-related transcription was also enhanced, indicating an increased potential for PMF-coupled cellular energy conservation. Consequently, increased transcription was observed for key functional genes involved in nitrification (amoABC, nxrAB), denitrification (narGHI, napAB, nirKS, nosZ), and polyphosphate synthesis (ppk). Furthermore, AQS-amended operation was associated with microbial community succession toward a more specialized consortium, in which comammox, Thauera and Candidatus Accumulibacter clade ⅡC were associated with nitrification, endogenous denitrification, and denitrifying phosphorus removal, respectively. Although practical translation will require effective retention or recovery of soluble AQS, these findings demonstrate the potential of AQS-enhanced SNEDPR under carbon-limited conditions and provide multi-omics evidence linking improved nutrient removal with increased electron-transfer activity and coordinated microbial metabolic responses.
authors: Chen H, Chai Z, Song C, Zheng Y, Chen J, Zheng M.

title: GhHDZ-87, a cotton HD-Zip transcription factor, involved in regulating salt stress tolerance in G. hirsutum.
abstract: Salt stress severely constrains cotton seedling establishment, yield, and fiber quality. Although HD‑Zip transcription factors are known to play essential roles in abiotic stress adaptation in various plant species, their functions in cotton remain largely unexplored. In this study, we performed a comprehensive genome‑wide analysis of HD‑Zip genes in Gossypium hirsutum to uncover their evolutionary history and identify stress‑responsive regulatory components. Genome‑wide screening identified 90 HDZ members that were unevenly distributed across the 26 chromosomes of upland cotton. Phylogenetic analysis showed that the upland cotton HDZs were divided into six groups, with clade B absent from the seven clades identified across species. Analyses of gene structure and conserved domains provided strong evidence for the evolutionary conservation of HDZ members. The expansion of the GhHDZ family was primarily driven by duplication events, particularly whole‑genome duplication (WGD) and allotetraploidization, with purifying selection acting on these genes. The expression of GhHDZ-87 was upreglated under salt, drought, and ABA treatments. β-Glucuronidase (GUS) staining indicated that GhHDZ-87 was expressed in the roots, stems and leaves of ProGhHDZ-87::GUS transgenic Arabidopsis thaliana. VIGS(Virus-induced gene silencing) assays suggested that knockdown of GhHDZ‑87 reduced salt tolerance in cotton, potentially via ABA signaling and ion‑homeostasis pathways. Taken together, this study comprehensively characterized the GhHDZ gene family in cotton and identified GhHDZ-87 as a positive regulator of salt tolerance. This study not only provides genetic resources and theoretical support for improving salt tolerance in cotton, but also improves our understanding of the regulatory pathways underlying salt tolerance.
journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
authors: Zhang Q, Kang M, Zhang J, Guo X, Jian H, An L, Sun M, Wu H, Wei F, Lu J, Fu X.

title: Non-canonical nucleic acid structures in viruses: Regulatory modules and emerging antiviral targets.
abstract: Beyond their primary sequence, viral genomes contain structural information encoded in the ability of DNA and RNA to fold into alternative conformations. These dynamic non-canonical nucleic acid structures include G-quadruplexes (G4s), i-Motifs (iMs), R-loops, G4-associated R-loops and left-handed Z-conformations. Among them, G4s have been most extensively investigated in viruses and have been reported to modulate transcription, replication, translation, latency and immune evasion. However, the functional interpretation of these structures remains highly context-dependent: similar topologies can either promote or restrict infection depending on genomic location, folding dynamics, protein interactors and the stage of the viral life cycle. Here, we discuss recent advances in viral non-canonical nucleic acid structures, emphasizing the level of evidence supporting their formation and function. We also assess emerging antiviral strategies based on structure-targeting ligands, highlighting both their translational potential and the unresolved challenges of selectivity, target engagement and pharmacological validation in infected cells.
authors: Ruggiero E, Zanin I, Mattellone F, Richter SN.

title: Pervasive short hairpin folding in non-encapsidated RNA viruses
abstract: Genome-wide RNA secondary structure can influence viral replication, stability, translation, and interactions with host defenses, yet its distribution and significance across RNA viruses remain poorly understood. We developed the pervasive hairpin (peHaPi) metric to quantify densely distributed stem-loop structures and applied it to 817,234 GenBank virus sequences. This revealed a distinctive RNA architecture characterized by numerous short, highly uniform hairpins spanning most of the genome. The structure was strongly enriched in capsidless RNA viruses, encompassing nearly all ormycoviruses and a substantial fraction of narnaviruses, although it also occurred in several other RNA and DNA virus groups. Comparative analyses showed that increasing peHaPi scores appeared associated with more stable and constrained predicted RNA structures and altered codon base-pairing patterns, indicating selective constraints imposed by pervasive folding. Relationships between peHaPi and RdRp sequence similarity differed among virus groups, consistent with independent evolutionary origins of this structural phenotype. Analysis of virus-derived small RNAs provided no evidence that peHaPi(+) viruses elicit a reduced siRNA response, arguing against siRNA evasion as its primary function. Finally, combining peHaPi classification with DNA-read subtraction identified candidate RNA virus contigs lacking detectable protein homology or recognizable RdRp signatures across multiple independent datasets. These findings reveal pervasive short-hairpin organization as a novel feature of predominantly capsidless viruses and establish genome-wide RNA structure as a complementary signature for discovering highly divergent ormyco-and narnaviruses. Repositories  The raw sequence reads have been deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive under BioProject accession number  PRJNA1549704 .
authors: Dekker RJ, de Leeuw WC, van Olst MF, Ensink WA, van Leeuwen SM, Breit TM, Jonker MJ.

title: Plant Organellar Homologous Recombination Depends on Accessory Factors for Recombinase Activity
abstract: ABSTRACT  Plant mitochondrial and plastid genomes rely on homologous recombination (HR) for error-free DNA repair of double strand breaks. Here, we reconstructed the homologous recombination pathway of plant organelles from Arabidopsis, aiming to understand how proteins of diverse evolutionary origins assemble into a functional repair pathway. We found that the three bacterial-derived recombinases, AtRecAs assemble D-loop intermediates, but only chloroplast AtRecA1 independently execute end-joining recombination on large DNA substrates. AtRecA1-mediated end-joining recombination is enhanced by plant-unique single-stranded DNA-binding proteins of the Whirly and Organellar Single-Stranded Binding (OSB) families, in contrast these proteins are mandatory for the recombination activities of the dual-targeted AtRecA2 and mitochondrial AtRecA3. Recombinational intermediates generated by AtRecAs are resolved by a bacterial-like RadA helicase but not bacterial-like RecG. Finally, AtRecX inhibits the recombinase activities of AtRecA2, while the activities of AtRecA1 and AtRecA3 remains largely insensitive. Collectively, our results provide an integrative reconstitution of the plant organellar homologous recombination machinery, revealing that homologous recombination arises from a complex system of bacterial, phage-derived, plant-specific, and eukaryotic components. Plant-specific ssDNA-binding proteins emerge as key regulators of this process, promoting recombination efficiency and genome stability, that supports the essential functions of homologous recombination in DNA repair and DNA replication maintenance. GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT  DNA repair pathways mediated by homologous recombination in plant organelles
authors: Mora-Garduño J, Peralta-Castro A, Aguilar-Granados A, Raygoza CD, Díaz-Quezada C, Brieba LG.

title: Phagocytosis without mitochondria is a lineage trait of planctomycetal bacteria of prey
abstract: Phagocytosis is considered energetically out of reach for prokaryotes. Mitochondria-first models of eukaryogenesis therefore suggest a non-phagocytic archaeal host. Yet two recently described planctomycetes lack mitochondria and engulf entire bacteria. Whether this mode of predation is an oddity of two isolates or the hallmark of a bacterial lineage remained unresolved. Here, we report eight additional predatory  Planctomycetota from three aquatic habitats. The ten cultured strains now span two classes of the phylum  Planctomycetota , ‘  Candidatus Uabimicrobiia’ and one newly proposed class. Using engineered fluorescent prey, we show that nine strains internalize prey into fully sealed compartments whereas one digests its prey externally, a non-engulfing predator for comparison. The strains additionally divide by two distinct modes, however, not correlating with their feeding behavior. Sequence- and structure-based searches detect no eukaryotic phagocytosis protein conserved across the engulfing strains. The actin homologue previously proposed to mediate uptake occurs only in three engulfing strains. Routine engulfment by aerobic bacteria without mitochondria thus unsettles a premise of mitochondria-first models and reopens the question of which cell plans could have hosted the mitochondrial endosymbiont.

title: NMR metabolome and stool consistency in IBS: a layer-wise multi-omics comparison
abstract: Abstract    Background  Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is markedly heterogeneous [1], and existing biological subtyping based on taxonomy (16S/metagenomic species) has limited predictive ability under subject-level validation. Using real clinical labels (IBS subtype, IBS-SSS severity, and Bristol stool consistency), this study performs a unified, subject-grouped cross-validated comparison across multiple omics layers and completes held-out zero-shot validation and label-blind transductive cross-cohort stability selection in an external cohort (zero contact with target-domain labels). The core comparison task is Bristol stool consistency regression; the three-class task serves only as an auxiliary control.  Methods  We used the Cell 2020 longitudinal multi-omics cohort [2] (75 subjects, 464 clinically labeled stool samples: IBS-D 169, IBS-C 142, healthy 153; layer-specific availability differed: genus/species 457, KO/KEGG 459, NMR 445). The Bristol score constructed from stool diaries (441 samples, 67 subjects; IBS-D 4.92 > healthy 3.94 > IBS-C 2.93, direction validated) served as the core quantitative phenotype. Eight feature layers were compared: genus/species taxonomy, SHOGUN KEGG Orthology (KO) genes, KEGG pathways (375 aggregated), NMR metabolome (19), bile acids (12), tryptophan metabolites (12), and NMR+taxonomy combined (163 dimensions). All modeling used subject-grouped 5-fold cross-validation (StratifiedGroupKFold/GroupKFold) with nested tuning; Ridge/ElasticNet for regression (evaluated by OOF R² and Spearman  ρ  ) and L2 logistic regression for classification. Cross-layer consistency was assessed by Spearman correlation between functional potential and metabolite pools (n = 423). Cell 2020-trained models were frozen and blindly tested zero-shot on the Jacobs 2023 cohort [3] (368 samples × 601 metabolites). Finally, source-domain closed-loop stability selection was performed (  π  _uni_cell using only source-domain grouped bootstrap, B = 300; platform-shift KS using only target-domain unlabeled features; two sensitivity levels, pre-screening nested and fully nested, with gates recomputed within resampling). After freezing the selector, a fully held-out zero-shot evaluation was performed on Jacobs (2000× paired bootstrap) to define the cross-platform stable core (Iron-Core). Two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) was used to test potential causal effects of 27 candidate genera on IBS risk between the MiBioGen microbiome GWAS [4] and the IBS GWAS (GCST90016564) [5] (IVW/weighted median/MR-Egger plus Cochran Q and leave-one-out sensitivity, with global BH-FDR correction).  Results  ① The taxonomic layer showed limited signal for the IBS-D/C/healthy three-class task in the  full sample  (genus 0.506 ± 0.077, 95% CI [0.421, 0.595], permutation p = 0.005; species 0.520 ± 0.134, 95% CI [0.434, 0.611]; chance = 0.333), rising to 0.556/0.559 on the common complete subset and clustering with NMR (see ②); no reliable signal for IBS-SSS severity (genus balanced accuracy = 0.500, 95% CI [0.420, 0.578], permutation p = 0.458; only 2/70 features q ρ   = 0.468 (16/19 significant), and it remained highest on the common complete subset (0.193 vs 0.196). Its OOF R² point estimate exceeded those of taxonomy (genus 0.089/subset 0.037; species 0.043/subset − 0.023), bile acids (0.053/0.073), tryptophan (0.023/0.015), and functional gene layers (KO 0.005/−0.039; KEGG 0.036/−0.008); the unfiltered NMR+genus combined model was 0.171/0.165, lower than NMR; after filtering at the same prevalence = 0.10, the combined model was 0.204 (19 NMR + 68 genera, n = 424), not significantly different from NMR alone (  Δ  R²=+0.006, 95% CI − 0.081–+0.095, p = 0.454)—the earlier “combined dilution” was mainly caused by unfiltered low-prevalence genera. The ordering of mid-tier layers (genus, species, bile acids, tryptophan) was sensitive to sample composition (genus and bile acids swapped on the subset) and does not constitute a strong ranking claim. In the auxiliary three-class task, full-sample NMR balanced accuracy = 0.558 ± 0.085, but on the common subset NMR (0.556) clustered with genus (0.556), species (0.559), and combined (0.565), indistinguishable from one another—layer ordering in the classification task is sensitive to sample composition and does not provide evidence that “NMR is optimal for classification.” Within-NMR Shapley decomposition showed that  the SCFA group's marginal contribution was  φ     = 0.106, 2.4 times the amino-acid group's  φ     = 0.045  (remove SCFA  Δ  R²=0.076, p = 0.002; remove AA  Δ  R²=0.016, p = 0.085, not significant)—upgrading “SCFA dominance” from a qualitative ordering to a reproducible decomposition conclusion. ③ The markers most strongly positively correlated with Bristol were acetate (  ρ   = 0.414), butyrate (0.379), lysine (0.374), tyrosine (0.311), propionate (0.297), succinate (0.273), and branched-chain amino acids (0.19–0.23); the branched short-chain fatty acid 2-methylbutyrate was the only significant negative correlate (− 0.185). ④ Within subtypes (exploratory): NMR retained signal within IBS-C (  ρ   = 0.288, subject-cluster bootstrap 95% CI [+ 0.074, + 0.483]; R² CI crossed zero); no robust signal was detected within IBS-D (  ρ  =−0.263, 95% CI [− 0.573, + 0.128] crossing zero, P(  ρ   ≥ 0) = 0.083; R²=−0.048, 95% CI [− 0.226, − 0.001] on the negative side, indicating no predictive ability)—under the power constraint of n ≈ 150, this is only an exploratory hypothesis and is insufficient to support unsupervised subgrouping within subtypes. ⑤ Cross-layer validation: functional potential and metabolite pools were generally weakly coupled, but  the butyrate-producing community genomic abundance marker bcd (K00248, butyryl-CoA dehydrogenase gene, non-rate-limiting enzyme) was significantly positively correlated with the fecal butyrate pool (  ρ     = 0.265, q = 8×10⁻⁶)  ; BSH/bai showed no association with the bile acid pool—“potential ≠ activity.” ⑥ Zero-shot cross-cohort validation (Cell 2020 → Jacobs 2023): the 11 shared-metabolite model achieved Diarrhea vs Constipation+Mixed AUC = 0.647 (D vs C sensitivity 0.676),  ρ  =+0.278, with directional replication in 11/11 (one-sided sign test p = 4.9×10⁻⁴; features are not independent, so this p value is descriptive only); the random 11-feature baseline AUC = 0.506 (95% CI 0.434–0.589, p = 0.005), but a demographics-only (age/BMI/sex) baseline already reached AUC = 0.593 (95% CI 0.509–0.675), and R11's increment over demographics was + 0.053 (95% CI − 0.045–+0.153, p = 0.148), not significant; the full-feature model including unmeasurable SCFAs collapsed to AUC = 0.558—feature transferability is the first constraint on cross-cohort generalization. ⑦  Source-domain closed-loop stability selection (label-blind transductive  :  π  _uni_cell ≥ 0.8 + platform-shift KS   ; after freezing, zero-shot AUC on the fully held-out target cohort was 0.634 (95% CI 0.559–0.705),  ρ  =+0.243—not significantly different from the 11-shared-feature set (R11, 0.647; paired  Δ  AUC = − 0.013, p = 0.805), and significantly better than the full 16-feature set including imputed SCFAs (F16, 0.558;  Δ  AUC = + 0.075, p = 0.013). ⑧ Two-sample MR (genus→IBS causal test independent of the metabolite layer; 313 pruned SNPs → 259 harmonized SNPs): under the current instrumental-variable power and approximate distance-pruning framework,  no robust potential causal effect was detected  (minimum FDR = 0.835); the strongest nominal signals were Bifidobacterium (OR = 1.070 [1.004–1.141], p = 0.039) and Eubacterium hallii group (OR = 1.074, p = 0.062), both with low heterogeneity (Cochran Q p > 0.7), no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy (Egger intercept p > 0.85), and stable leave-one-out estimates, but observational and causal directions did not converge; Roseburia showed a nominal protective trend (OR = 0.930, p = 0.219), opposite to its positive observational correlation (  ρ  =+0.284).  Conclusions  Under subject-grouped cross-validation,  the layer with the highest point-estimate OOF R² for the Bristol continuous-trait regression task  was the metabolome (within NMR, dominated by the SCFA group: Shapley  φ   = 0.106, 2.4 times  φ  _AA = 0.045), not taxonomy or functional gene potential. The cross-cohort platform-robust core was data-driven and conditionally stable at 5 metabolites (lysine, tyrosine, uracil, glucose, leucine), achieving discrimination on the fully held-out target cohort that was not significantly different from the 11-shared-feature set with fewer features (0.634 vs 0.647), and significantly better than the 16-feature full model (0.558). The results support three mechanistic axes in terms of directional consistency, but with different levels of evidence:  SCFA→serotonin→intestinal motility  is supported mainly by within-NMR evidence (Shapley  φ   = 0.106, consistent marker direction spectrum); the  proteolytic fermentation fingerprint  is supported by the directional consistency of BCAAs/aromatic amino acids; and the  bile acid–TGR5 secretomotor  axis is supported only by the directional positive correlation of the bile-acid layer Top6 with loose stools, lacking functional/causal validation (“potential ≠ activity”). In the single-layer comparison, the feature-layer ranking was direct metabolic measurement > taxonomy > functional potential—this ranking applies only to the single-layer comparison for the Bristol regression task and should not be extrapolated to subtype classification (in the three-class task, NMR and taxonomic layers were indistinguishable on the common subset and the ordering was not robust), nor to combined models (after the same filtering, the combined model was not significantly different from NMR). It also shows that predictive magnitude and cross-domain transferability are not equivalent—the cross-cohort stable core is not the strongest within-domain feature. Two-sample MR further indicates that, under the current instrumental-variable power and approximate LD-pruning framework, no robust potential causal evidence was detected between mainstream candidate genera and IBS risk (none significant after FDR correction), and causal interpretation of observational microbiome–phenotype associations requires larger samples, bidirectional designs, and stronger instruments.
authors: Sui Y.

title: Detection and molecular characterization of Tomato yellow leaf curl virus in Ukraine
abstract: Abstract    Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (  Begomovirus flavisolanum  , TYLCV) is one of the most economically important viral pathogens of tomato worldwide, yet information regarding its molecular diversity in Ukraine has been limited. This study aimed to investigate the occurrence, molecular characteristics, and phylogenetic relationships of TYLCV isolates circulating in Ukrainian vegetable production systems. A total of 34 symptomatic tomato plants representing different cultivars were collected from several regions of Ukraine and analyzed by conventional PCR targeting the coat protein gene. Eighteen samples (52.9%) tested positive for TYLCV, while all healthy control plants were negative. In addition, TYLCV was detected in chili pepper (  Capsicum frutescens  ) and zucchini (  Cucurbita pepo  var.  giraumontia  ) growing adjacent to infected tomato plants, indicating a broader cultivated host range under field conditions. Partial genome sequencing of eight representative isolates generated GenBank accessions PX234052–PX234057, PX234062, and PX234063. Phylogenetic analyses based on Neighbor-Joining, Minimal Evolution, and Maximum Likelihood methods consistently demonstrated that Ukrainian isolates constitute a genetically homogeneous population with nucleotide identities exceeding 99%. Most isolates clustered tightly together, whereas isolate PX234052 represented the most divergent variant and the zucchini isolate (PX234057) formed a slightly differentiated branch while remaining within the TYLCV clade. Comparison with representative international sequences showed that all Ukrainian isolates grouped within the TYLCV-Israel (TYLCV-IL) lineage, exhibiting the closest relationship to isolates from Israel and Mediterranean countries, suggesting a common evolutionary origin. The limited genetic diversity observed among Ukrainian isolates indicates either a relatively recent introduction of TYLCV or the continued spread of a restricted number of closely related viral genotypes. These findings provide the first comprehensive molecular characterization of TYLCV populations in Ukraine and establish a baseline for future epidemiological surveillance, vector monitoring, and phytosanitary management. The detection of TYLCV in tomato, pepper, and zucchini further emphasizes the importance of integrated disease management and continuous monitoring of alternative cultivated hosts to reduce virus dissemination.
authors: Gerilovych A, Shevchenko N, Bashtan N, Miroshnichenko T, Chaiuk O, Ivchenko T.

title: Aquifer geochemistry shapes microbial diversity and carbon and nitrogen cycling potential
abstract: Abstract    Despite the importance of groundwater and its ecosystem functions, including nitrogen cycling, subsurface microbial biodiversity and ecology remain poorly understood globally. We investigated how aquifer geochemistry shapes microbial diversity and metabolic potential across Aotearoa New Zealand using shotgun metagenomics of 39 groundwater samples from 11 regions. We recovered 494 high- and medium-quality metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), which clustered into four groups (A, B, C1 and C2), based on hydrochemistry, and differed significantly in taxonomy and metabolic pathways. Cluster A had the highest microbial diversity and was dominated by uncultured taxa, particularly  Patescibacteria  . Carbon fixation pathways, predominantly the Calvin-Benson-Bassham and reductive tricarboxylic acid cycles, varied among clusters and were associated with different redox metabolisms. Aerobic respiration pathways also differed, particularly the microaerophilic  cbb  3  cytochrome  c  oxidase. Differences were also observed in nitrogen, sulfur, carbohydrate and organic acid metabolism, with several MAGs strongly correlated with nitrate, sulfate and potassium. Our findings demonstrate that aquifer geochemistry is a major determinant of microbial community structure and metabolic potential across Aotearoa New Zealand groundwater ecosystems.
authors: Houghton KM, Moreau M, Tschritter C.

title: KEGG for characterizing genomes and pathways in the biosphere.
abstract: The KEGG database (https://www.kegg.jp) has been developed as a model of the biological systems. By organizing knowledge of cellular and organism-level functions in the form of molecular wiring diagrams, the model enables generating new knowledge and finding practical applications. The KO (KEGG Orthology) dataset plays the basic role of organizing knowledge. KO is an ortholog with functional relevance, generalizing experimental evidence in specific organisms to other organisms. KEGG molecular networks, including pathway maps and modules, are generic networks with KOs as network nodes, and thus KEGG mapping from genomes to pathways can be applied to any organism. As the number of KOs increases and the KO annotation rate improves, KEGG mapping is further expanded. A set of KOs in the genome and a set of modules in the metabolic pathways are now used to characterize various data objects in the biosphere, including organisms, organism groups, microbiomes, viruses, and their combinations, such as endosymbiont-host, microbiome-host, and virus-host relationships. Furthermore, a simple measure of similarity either by KO compositions or module compositions is introduced to compare organism groups. The resulting similarity dendrograms possibly reflect similarity of cellular functions or, more specifically, metabolic functions, which can be compared with phylogenetic trees.
authors: Kanehisa M, Furumichi M, Sato Y, Matsuura Y, Ishiguro-Watanabe M.

title: The impact of OsASR5 on rice microbiome: Implications for nutrient cycling and stress response.
abstract: Plant-microorganism interactions contribute to plant health by enhancing nutrient acquisition. The transcription factor OsASR5 regulates detoxification gene expression under aluminum stress in rice and is implicated as a positive regulator of responses to iron and phosphorus deficiency. Given its role in nutrient regulation, we investigated whether OsASR5 influences the assembly of the rice microbiome. In this study, we characterized the bacteria communities associated with the leaves and roots of OsASR5-RNAi rice plants compared to wild-type Oryza sativa cv. Nipponbare. Notably, OsASR5-RNAi plants showed altered bacterial beta diversity compared with wild type. The bacterial composition of OsASR5-RNAi plants differed in both organs, with decreased Desulfobacteriota and increased in Acidobacteria abundance in leaves. At the genus level, Methylobacterium, a known plant growth promoter, was less prevalent in leaves, while Magnetospirillum, associated with iron cycling, was less abundant in roots. Conversely, several bacteria were more abundant in OsASR5-RNAi plants, including Aneurinibacillus, Anaeromyxobacter, and Methylobacter, which are associated with nitrogen cycling and phosphorus solubilization. Additionally, Geobacter and Geothrix, both known for their role in metal reduction, particularly iron, were more abundant in OsASR5-RNAi plants. These suggest that OsASR5 affects plant-microbe interactions, potentially influencing nutrient cycling and plant stress responses through microbiome modulation.
authors: Sánchez ICC, Margis-Pinheiro M, Dias-Oliveira M, Ponte LR, Ricachenevsky FK, Margis R.

title: Influenza A virus H5Nx genotypes assigned by genetic similarity are incongruent with global phylogenies
abstract: Influenza A virus H5N1 and related subtypes (H5Nx) have broad host ranges and pose a pandemic risk. Since early 2022, H5 clade 2.3.4.4b has predominated globally, causing unprecedented mortality in wild birds, poultry, and mammals, with spillovers to humans. Accurate viral classification is essential for tracking H5Nx variant emergence and spread, but reassortment among genome segments with distinct evolutionary histories complicates genotyping. H5Nx genotype assignment tools, GenoFlu in North America and Genin2 in Europe, assign segments to clusters by genetic similarity to reference sequences and define genotypes as constellations of segment clusters. However, genetic similarity does not necessarily imply recent shared ancestry due to independently re-occurring mutations and variability in the evolutionary rate. Furthermore, similarity is defined relative to references that may inadequately represent diversity. We evaluated the congruence of genetic similarity-based H5Nx clusters and genotypes with phylogenies of global sequences across eight segments. H5Nx genomes from 41,366 samples were assigned GenoFlu and Genin2 genotypes, and maximum likelihood phylogenies were inferred for each segment. CD-HIT and phylogenetic TreeCluster clusters were also generated for a range of distance thresholds. Clustering methods were evaluated based on phylogenetic purity, monophyly, and diversity. Reassortment within predominant GenoFlu and Genin2 genotypes was evaluated based on their phylogenetic cluster spans. Expectedly, GenoFlu was largely unable to assign genomes from outside of North America, South America, and Antarctica from 2022 to 2025, whereas Genin2 assignments struggled outside of Europe, Africa, and Western Asia. Only 14.2% of GenoFlu clusters were monophyletic, while Genin2 clusters were more variable across segments (overall 49.3% monophyletic). Despite CD-HIT yielding genetic distance clusters of similar size to TreeCluster, they were less monophyletic (44%) and encompassed greater phylogenetic diversity. We identified several genotypes, such as GenoFlu B3.13, D1.1, and D1.3, with segments that had diversified into separate subclusters. Similarly, GenoFlu genotypes B3.5 and A3, and Genin2 genotypes EA-2020-C, EA-2021-AB, and EA-2022-CH may erroneously combine multiple distinct reassortants. Genetic similarity-based H5Nx genotyping tools are rapid, stable, and sufficient for broad categorization, but may group viruses with distinct evolutionary histories and fail to assign divergent viruses, risking biased surveillance, modeling, and risk assessment.
authors: McLaughlin A, Tran H, Tait D, Nguyen H, Rudar J, Giacinti JA, Signore AV, Lung OA, Berhane Y, Poljak Z, Maguire F.

title: In Silico Validation of Contemporary East African Rift Valley Fever Virus Genomes Confirms the Enduring Robustness of the Bird et al. (2007) RT-qPCR Assay
abstract: Rift Valley fever virus (RVFV) is a zoonotic pathogen causing recurrent epizootics and epi-demics in East Africa. The quantitative reverse transcription PCR (RT-qPCR) assay devel-oped by Bird et al. (2007), targeting the large (L) genome segment, remains a global diag-nostic standard. However, continuous viral evolution raises concerns regarding diagnostic drift and potential assay failure. This study evaluated the contemporary robustness of this assay against East African RVFV genomes collected between 2005 and 2026. A total of 647 nucleotide records were retrieved from NCBI GenBank, from which a dataset of 193 L-segment sequences was curated based on geography, collection date, and segment an-notation. A custom sliding-window alignment algorithm quantified mismatches between the assay oligonucleotides and all valid sequences in both genomic orientations. Five se-quences initially exhibited high mismatch counts but were excluded after genomic coor-dinate mapping revealed they were partial fragments mapping outside the assay’s target region (nucleotides 4229–4723). Among the remaining 188 valid, target-spanning se-quences, 181 (96.3%) exhibited a perfect match to the forward primer, reverse primer, and TaqMan probe. Six sequences (3.2%) contained minor, biologically tolerable mismatches, and one (0.5%) showed probe-specific mismatches with intact primer binding sites. These findings confirm the enduring robustness of the Bird et al. (2007) assay against contempo-rary East African RVFV lineages, while simultaneously highlighting a critical genomic surveillance gap in Tanzania that warrants targeted infrastructural investment.
authors: Msoka KM.

title: Entamoeba invadens infection contributes to juvenile mortality in captive sea turtles.
abstract: Sea turtles are globally threatened marine reptiles, and infectious diseases are increasingly recognized as important causes of juvenile mortality. However, the etiology and pathogenesis of many diseases, including amoebiasis, remain poorly understood. Systemic amoebic lesions have been reported in sea turtles, yet the causative Entamoeba species has never been identified at the species level using molecular methods. We therefore investigated the etiology and pathogenesis of fatal amoebiasis using carcasses of 15 captive juvenile sea turtles (three loggerhead, Caretta caretta, and 12 green turtles, Chelonia mydas), integrating histopathological and molecular approaches. Histopathology revealed severe necrotizing enteritis, hepatitis, and pneumonia with abundant amoebic trophozoites and cysts. Polymerase chain reaction, Sanger sequencing, and in situ hybridization identified Entamoeba invadens in the intestine, liver, and lungs; 18S rRNA amplicon sequencing also detected E. invadens in fecal and intestinal samples. Phylogenetic analysis showed that the sea turtle-derived sequence clustered with E. invadens sequences from other reptile hosts. Bacterial and fungal aggregates were also observed within necrotic lesions, and 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing detected diverse bacterial communities without a consistently dominant taxon, consistent with secondary microbial translocation following intestinal barrier disruption rather than primary bacterial infection. These findings provide the first evidence that E. invadens causes fatal systemic amoebiasis in juvenile sea turtles and are consistent with polymicrobial invasion following parasite-induced intestinal damage. This study establishes a pathological and molecular basis for diagnosing systemic amoebiasis in sea turtles and has important implications for wildlife disease ecology and sea turtle conservation.
authors: Suenaga R, Ishizaki T, Katayama N, Nakashima E, Hamano H, Yamada M, Watanabe K, Mizuochi K, Kawazu I, Ueda K, Fukumoto S.

title: Hydroxyproline Enhances Branched-Chain Amino Acid Effects on Lifespan and Healthspan in Caenorhabditis elegans.
abstract: Food-derived protein hydrolysates frequently contain both collagen-associated hydroxyproline (Hyp) and branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs), but the biological consequences of their combination remain unclear. This study tested whether Hyp changes the effects of leucine (Leu), isoleucine, and valine on lifespan and healthspan-related phenotypes in Caenorhabditis elegans and whether these treatment effects are accompanied by coordinated microbial and metabolic remodeling. Amino acid concentrations that did not strongly disrupt bacterial food clearance were selected for lifespan, stress resistance, motility, muscle-integrity, biochemical, microbiome, metabolomic, and transcriptomic analyses. Hyp+BCAA combinations improved lifespan- and healthspan-related phenotypes in a BCAA- and dose-dependent manner. The strongest combined treatments enhanced resistance to thermal and oxidative stress, preserved age-associated motility and muscle structure, reduced oxidative and lipofuscin-associated markers, and increased adenosine 5'-triphosphate-related readouts. Multimomics profiling showed that these direct treatment effects were accompanied by distinct C. elegans-associated microbiota signatures, altered nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) precursor-related metabolites, including nicotinic acid ribonucleoside (NaR), and a Leu+Hyp transcriptional response enriched for energy metabolism, proteostasis, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Integrated microbiome-metabolome analysis identified a positive association between Rhodococcus abundance and NaR levels. These findings demonstrate that, under the tested culture conditions, Hyp+BCAA exposure improves longevity-related phenotypes and identifies microbial composition, NAD precursor metabolism, and host energy homeostasis as candidate, testable mediators.
authors: Liu L, Wu R, Gao Z, Fang F, Chang C, Hou Z, Wang H, Zhang D, Wang Z.

title: Distinct core minor pilin complexes prime specialized type IV filaments in cyanobacteria.
abstract: The model cyanobacterium, Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 encodes in addition to the major pilin of the Type IV pilus filament, an extensive, partially uncharacterized repertoire of minor pilins. For those cyanobacterial minor pilins that have been characterized, their roles span a surprisingly diverse range of functions. To elucidate the roles of uncharacterized minor pilins in a systematic way, we applied structural phylogenomics across 90 genomes, classifying cyanobacterial pilins into six conserved families that form two distinct putative core priming complexes. We demonstrate that these complexes initiate the assembly of two morphologically distinct Type IV pilus filaments: short, hyper-dynamic pili for natural competence, and long, adhesive pili for motility and phototaxis. Structural analysis revealed a conserved beta-solenoid domain in PilX subunits, which we propose fulfills the capping function of PilY1 homologs. Proteomic data indicate that the minor pilin PilX2 facilitates the assembly of motility pili, which is required to maintain DnaJ3 co-chaperone levels and trigger cAMP-dependent surface sensing. These findings challenge the concept of a single multipurpose pilus, establishing that cyanobacteria utilize a shared machinery to assemble two specialized filaments, each primed by distinct core minor pilin complexes to meet the conflicting biophysical requirements of DNA uptake and surface motility.
authors: Schuergers N, Wittig L, Enomoto G, Herz J, Sivabalasarma S, Ruoff K, Drepper F, Albers SV, Huesgen PF, Wilde A.

title: Genetic characterization of rabies virus circulating in crab-eating fox (Cerdocyon thous) in the State of Paraiba, Northeastern Brazil.
abstract: Rabies is a fatal viral zoonosis that remains endemic in more than two-thirds of all countries worldwide, causing approximately 70,000 human deaths annually-equivalent to one death every ten minutes. The rabies virus (RABV), a member of the genus Lyssavirus (family Rhabdoviridae), has bats and canids as its primary reservoirs, although infections have also been reported in other wild species, including Cerdocyon thous (crab-eating fox) and Pseudalopex vetulus (hoary fox). In this study, we performed a comprehensive genomic and biological characterization of a RABV variant circulating in wild foxes from the Northeastern region of Brazil. Using Next Generation Sequencing (NGS), phylogenetic analysis, and in vitro and in vivo assays, we identified genetic similarities between these isolates and previously described RABV strains from wild and domestic canids in Brazil. However, the presence of escape mutants indicates a heterogeneous viral population, suggesting ongoing adaptive evolution in wildlife reservoirs. These findings reinforce the importance of genomic surveillance to detect emerging variants that may compromise current vaccination or control strategies. Overall, our results provide new insights into the molecular diversity, pathogenicity, and ecological dynamics of RABV circulating among wild canids in Brazil, contributing to improved understanding and prevention of rabies in endemic regions.

title: Culture-free  Helicobacter pylori  genomics reveals within-host virulence heterogeneity and antibiotic resistance
abstract: Helicobacter pylori (Hp) infects over 40% of the world’s population and causes most cases of gastric cancer worldwide, yet fundamental questions about its within-host genetic diversity remain unresolved. Decades of work on Hp genomics depends on culturing clinical isolates, which can distort within-host genetic heterogeneity that informs Hp virulence and antimicrobial resistance. Culture-free alternatives have been limited by the extremely low Hp abundance in gastric tissue (usually 10  −3 to 10  −7 of total genomic DNA), making direct metagenomics prohibitively expensive and existing enrichment strategies insufficient for whole-genome recovery. Here we develop ultra-sensitive Hp sequencing (uHp-seq) for reconstructing Hp genomes directly from gastric biopsies. uHp-seq achieves a thousand-fold Hp DNA enrichment and recovers near-complete genomes across samples spanning orders of magnitude in Hp abundance. Notably, individual hosts may harbor multiple co-existing Hp strains or cagA EPIYA variants with different oncogenic potential. Resistance-associated variants for six commonly used antibiotics are resolved with greater accuracy than PCR-based and probe-based commercial panels. Applied to minimally invasive gastric string samples, uHp-seq delivers reliable resistance profiles without endoscopy, opening a path to genome-guided Hp eradication.

title: Genetic diversity, spatiotemporal dynamics and evolution of porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus 2 (PRRSV-2) lineage 1 in China
abstract: Abstract  Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus 2 (PRRSV-2) lineage 1 (L1) has become the dominant epidemic lineage worldwide, posing a serious threat to the swine industry. However, the fine-scale evolutionary history, spatiotemporal transmission dynamics, and molecular drivers of L1 in China remain poorly understood. In this study, 32,215 global PRRSV-2 ORF5 sequences including 1,213 ORF5 sequences from Chinese L1 strains were systemically analyzed. Phylogenetic analysis revealed a unipolar dominance of the L1C sublineage (NADC30-like strains), accounting for 86.12% of Chinese L1 strains and forming a well-supported monophyletic clade. Transmission network analysis identified Henan Province as the primary hub for cross-regional spread of L1C, with Shandong Province as the secondary hub and Fujian, Guangdong and Sichuan Provinces serving as tertiary transmission nodes. Positive selection analysis of ORF5 revealed that L1C accumulated a broader set of positively selected sites, highly enriched in B-cell epitopes and glycosylation sites, indicating a strong selective advantage in immune evasion. Furthermore, whole-genome recombination analysis of L1 identified major recombination hotspots concentrated in certain viral non-structural protein genes (nsp2, nsp9) and structural protein genes (ORF5, ORF6). Together, these findings demonstrate that the unipolar dominance of L1C in China is sustained by a synergistic cycle of transmission, antigenic evolution, and recombination, providing an important basis for precision molecular surveillance and region-specific control of PRRSV-2.
authors: Chi C, Yang N, Zhang P, Jiang S, Zheng W, Chen N, Zhu J.

title: Isolation and comparative genomic characterization of Ralstonia pickettii from bronchoalveolar lavage fluid of a cat with pneumonia
abstract: Abstract    The clinical significance of  Ralstonia pickettii  recovered from the feline lower respiratory tract remains poorly characterized. A 1.5-year-old neutered male cat presented with recurrent respiratory signs for approximately four months and pulmonary radiographic abnormalities. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid culture yielded a  Ralstonia  isolate, whereas concurrent lavage-fluid and instrument controls showed no bacterial growth. Identification as  R. pickettii  was supported by 16S rRNA sequencing and a digital DNA–DNA hybridization value of 77.2% with the type strain. Whole-genome sequencing yielded a 5.46-Mb draft assembly comprising 70 contigs. Broth microdilution testing identified susceptibility to levofloxacin, doxycycline and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and resistance to eight tested agents, including imipenem and meropenem. Marbofloxacin susceptibility was reported separately by the commercial laboratory. Clinical improvement occurred during ongoing marbofloxacin treatment and adjunctive nebulization. Comparison with 37 public reference genomes identified 3,389 core gene clusters. The feline isolate shared 99.9727% orthologous average nucleotide identity with the reference having the shortest estimated pairwise genetic distance, an International Space Station-associated isolate. Low support for the adjacent internal branch and unequal source representation limited interpretation of fine-scale relationships and acquisition source. This case documents a species-confirmed feline lower respiratory tract isolate and its genomic context. The single-case design, absence of concurrent lavage-fluid cytology and improvement during continuing combined treatment preclude firm conclusions about causation or treatment efficacy.
authors: Ma Y, Wang Y, Li B, Zhang S, Pan Z, Yao H.

title: Gut Clostridium aminophilum as a protective microbe in never-smoker lung cancer: insights from metagenomics and machine learning.
abstract: Lung cancer in never-smoking patients (LCINS) has gradually gained attention in recent years, and emerging evidence points to a potential role of the gut microbiota in LCINS by modulating host immunity and metabolism. In this study, metagenomics was performed on stool samples from 24 LCINS patients and 18 healthy individuals. LCINS patients exhibited reduced microbial richness in α-diversity compared with healthy controls, and differences in principal component distribution were observed. Pathway enrichment analyses revealed that LPS biosynthesis capacity was significantly increased, whereas the fatty acid biosynthesis pathway was significantly decreased in LCINS. A total of 317 differentially abundant species were identified, including 29 assigned to the module most strongly associated with LCINS based on weighted gene co-expression network (WGCNA). Then, 36 machine learning-based diagnostic models were constructed based on these 29 species, with the glmBoost + Ridge model showing the best performance for LCINS discrimination (AUC = 0.855). SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) identified Clostridium aminophilum as a protective factor and the top contributor to model performance (SHAP value = 0.068), with a single-species AUC of 0.743. In vitro, the culture supernatant of Clostridium aminophilum markedly suppressed A549 cell proliferation and migration. In vivo, oral administration of Clostridium aminophilum (5 × 106 CFU) for 21 days significantly suppressed tumor growth in subcutaneous A549-derived xenograft models. These findings suggest a significant association between LCINS and the gut microbiota, characterized by a marked depletion of Clostridium aminophilum. Notably, metabolites derived from Clostridium aminophilum were shown to inhibit lung cancer progression.IMPORTANCELung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer incidence and mortality worldwide, and the proportion of lung cancer in patients who have never smoked (LCINS) has been steadily increasing. However, the potential role of the gut microbiota in this disease has not been fully explored. In this study, we characterized the gut microbial spectrum of LCINS patients using metagenomic sequencing and developed a lung cancer predictive model with translational potential. Importantly, we identified a beneficial bacterium, Clostridium aminophilum, which may be developed as a probiotic to support conventional lung cancer treatments. These findings offer promising avenues for early diagnosis, adjunctive therapy, and personalized management of gut microbiota in LCINS patients.
authors: Zhang J, Fang L, Ma C, Hu Z, Chen C, Zhu T, Ying J, Zhu W, Huang G, Ni J, Zhang C, Yu G.

title: Isolation and characterization of humic acid-degrading microorganisms from natural environments.
abstract: Humic acid (HA) is an important component of natural organic matter and is widely present in soils, sediments, and wastewater. Due to its complex aromatic structure and high chemical stability, HA exhibits poor biodegradability and increases the difficulty of wastewater treatment. Microbial degradation has attracted increasing attention as an environmentally friendly approach for HA removal. However, functional HA-degrading microorganisms from natural organic matter-rich environments remain insufficiently explored. In this study, artificial lake sediment and humified soil beneath decayed ginkgo wood were selected as microbial sources for screening HA-degrading microorganisms. A total of 33 microbial isolates were obtained through enrichment culture, acclimation, and screening procedures. Among them, three representative strains, designated as HA-X1, HA-X4, and HA-Z3, exhibited relatively higher HA removal efficiencies. Based on morphological characteristics and molecular identification, HA-X1 and HA-X4 were assigned to Bacillus-related taxa, while HA-Z3 was affiliated with the genus Phoma. The growth characteristics and HA removal performances of the selected strains under different initial HA concentrations, pH conditions, and inoculum dosages were further investigated. The results showed that all selected strains could grow in HA-containing media and exhibited HA removal capability under the tested conditions. Among the three strains, HA-X4 showed the highest overall removal performance. The selected strains displayed different responses to environmental factors, indicating variations in their HA transformation characteristics. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis revealed the morphological characteristics of bacterial cells and fungal mycelial structures. This study provides functional microbial resources for further investigation of HA biodegradation and the development of biological treatment technologies for HA-containing wastewater.
authors: Cao Y, Lei Z, He Q, Wei S, Chen W, Pang T.

title: Rhizospheric Bacteria From Artocarpus heterophyllus Exhibit Antimicrobial Traits and Antagonistic Activity Against Pantoea stewartii subsp. stewartii, Causal Agent of Jackfruit Bronzing Disease.
abstract: The Jackfruit bronzing disease represents a significant phytosanitary constraint affecting Artocarpus heterophyllus production. In this context, the exploration of plant-associated microorganisms as a source of potential biological control agents aligns with sustainable agricultural strategies. This study is aimed at isolating, characterizing, and evaluating the in vitro antagonistic interactions, and antimicrobial potential of indigenous rhizospheric and endophytic bacteria with the potential to be developed as biocontrol agents for the control jackfruit bronzing causal agent Pantoea stewartii subsp. stewartii. A total of 138 bacterial isolates were obtained from rhizospheric soils and internal plant tissues, with a predominance of rhizospheric bacteria (78.3%). In vitro antagonism assays revealed that only rhizospheric isolates exhibited inhibitory activity against the phytopathogen, identifying 12 strains with consistent antagonistic capacity. These isolates were further characterized to elucidate the potential mechanisms involved in microbial antagonism. Functional analyses demonstrated that the antagonistic isolates possessed multiple extracellular enzymatic activities, predominantly lipase, followed by amylase and cellulase activities, whereas protease activity was absent. Additionally, selected isolates exhibited biosurfactant production, suggesting their role in pathogen inhibition. Antibiosis was confirmed through the production of diffusible antimicrobial compounds. Furthermore, molecular screening revealed the presence of nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) gene fragments in several strains, supporting their genetic potential to synthesize bioactive secondary metabolites. Phylogenetic identification based on 16S rDNA gene sequencing assigned the isolates to bacterial taxa known for their ecological versatility and functional attributes. Overall, this study provides evidence that rhizospheric bacteria associated with jackfruit harbor significant antagonistic and antimicrobial capabilities against jackfruit bronzing causal agent. These findings contribute to the understanding of microbial interactions and functional traits associated with plant microbiota. This study provides the first assessment of microorganisms associated with jackfruit.
authors: Arvizu-Gómez JL, Hernández-Morales A, González-Reyes C, Cervantes-Díaz CN, Campos-Guillén J, Pacheco-Aguilar JR.

title: Source apportionment and resistome signatures of community and hospital effluents in urban sewer networks.
abstract: Antibiotic resistance surveillance has traditionally focused on clinical settings, potentially overlooking broader microbial reservoirs in the community. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) provides a powerful tool for capturing these population-level signals. This study aimed to identify source-specific resistome characteristics and estimate the relative compositional contributions of hospital and residential wastewater to the downstream wastewater treatment plant (WWTP). By integrating droplet digital polymerase chain reaction (ddPCR) with metagenomic sequencing, spatiotemporal dynamics across an urban sewer network were characterized. Bacterial 16S rRNA gene concentrations did not differ significantly between hospital and residential wastewater. Under the specified flow scenarios, hospital wastewater represented a small fraction of the estimated total influent volume. Bayesian source tracking further indicated that residential sources collectively accounted for nearly 80% of the inferred source contribution to the influent antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) profile and 70.9% of the influent microbial community composition, whereas hospital wastewater accounted for only 5.5% of the inferred resistome contribution. These findings show that hospital wastewater contained clinically important resistance genes (e.g., blaKPC-2), whereas the sampled residential references accounted for the largest combined inferred contribution to the influent microbiome and resistome. Together, these results highlight the importance of incorporating community surveillance through wastewater-based approaches within the One Health framework.
authors: Li X, Liu H, Wu J, Xi C.

title: The Palatine Tonsil Bacterial Microbiota in Pigs: Diverse, Underexplored, Yet Functionally Relevant.
abstract: The palatine tonsils play a pivotal role in porcine upper respiratory tract immunity by acting as an interface between the host and the external environment. As such, the tonsillar microbiota represents a critical yet insufficiently characterized microbial ecosystem. This review provides an overview of current knowledge on the porcine tonsillar microbiota, beginning with a description of sampling strategies and laboratory approaches, including metabarcoding, shotgun metagenomics, and culturomics. The development of the tonsillar microbiota over time and the main environmental, host-related, and management factors shaping its composition are examined. Particular emphasis is placed on the core bacterial communities commonly identified in the palatine tonsils, which are largely dominated by members of the Pasteurellaceae, Streptococcaceae, and Moraxellaceae families. The review further discusses how infectious and non-infectious diseases can disrupt tonsillar microbial homeostasis, as well as the effects of antimicrobial treatments, vaccination, and other prophylactic interventions on microbial structure and function. Finally, methodological biases inherent to current studies are highlighted, key knowledge gaps are identified, and future research directions are proposed to advance metagenomic investigations and better elucidate the role of the tonsillar microbiota in swine health and disease.
authors: Hercouët K, Tardy F, Marois-Créhan C.

title: Agent_K: An Agent-Orchestrated Pipeline for Mapping Genes to Biosynthetic Pathway towards Metabolite Discovery
abstract: The identification of biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) and their associated metabolic pathways is central to genome-guided natural product discovery. However, existing computational tools depend on fragmented workflows for data processing, annotation, and analysis, which require substantial manual intervention and lack seamless integration across heterogeneous platforms and tools. Here, we present, Agent_K, an agent-orchestrated framework that automates the end-to-end process from bacterial whole genome sequence analysis to biosynthetic pathway mapping and metabolite discovery as candidate gene products for functional insights. The system employs a large-language-model (LLM) agent to coordinate multiple bioinformatics tools, enabling dynamic execution, data integration, result interpretation, and flexible and intuitive visualization. By integrating genomic sequences to functional annotations and pathway-level reconstructions, the framework facilitates the identification of candidate gene products, their biosynthetic pathways associated with individual BGCs, and the putative metabolites produced by those pathways. The developed novel agentic framework provides a user-friendly scalable and extensible solution for automated high-throughput analysis and mapping of bacterial secondary metabolism pathways for interactive exploration of candidate potential.
authors: Roy RS, Han JJ, Narayana JL, Zhou A, de Figueiredo P, Han A, Qian X.

title: Metagenomic Next-Generation Sequencing Enhances Pathogen Detection and Prognostic Stratification in Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation Recipients.
abstract: BackgroundAs an emerging detection technique, metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) provides superior genomic resolution and enhances detection precision relative to conventional pathogen detection methods. Patients with malignant hematological disorders are susceptible to infections following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). mNGS demonstrates a significantly higher positivity rate compared with conventional testing.MethodsA total of 100 patients who had undergone HSCT were retrospectively enrolled in this study. The detection rates and patient mortality rates associated with conventional diagnostic methods and mNGS were analyzed and compared. Additionally, the impact of mNGS results on the adjustment of antibacterial therapy was investigated, and the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve was utilized to assess the predictive value of mNGS for mortality.ResultsmNGS detected pathogens in 81% of patients (viruses 71.0%, with herpes simplex virus type 1 [HSV-1] at 26.7%; bacteria 25.0%, predominantly Enterobacteriaceae at 61.5%), outperforming conventional testing ( P P ConclusionCompared with conventional methods, mNGS has a broader pathogen detection spectrum, which may improve the overall detection rate of unknown, uncommon, and mixed infectious pathogens. The selection of diagnostic modalities may be guided by patient-specific factors including CRP levels, age, length of hospital stay, transplantation modality, and granulocyte reconstitution time. mNGS informs antibiotic adjustment, while combined biomarkers (AUC = 0.812) provide prognostic value.
authors: Liu Y, Bian X, Wang H, Tang D.

title: Chiral antibiotics amplify the phage-associated antibiotic resistome in salinized soil.
abstract: Anthropogenic global change is intensifying antibiotic pollution and soil salinization, yet how salinity shapes bacteria-phage interactions to drive the dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) under chiral antibiotic pressure remains poorly understood. Using viral metagenomic analyses and laboratory validation, we show that salinity amplifies the enrichment of total and high-risk ARGs along gradients of racemic ofloxacin and its S-enantiomer levofloxacin, concomitant with the parallel accumulation of mobile genetic elements and virulence factors. High-concentration antibiotic treatment in saline soils selected for stress-tolerant, fast-growing antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARBs) carrying abundant prophages and diverse defense systems, thereby promoting tight ARB-phage interactions. Under these dual extreme stresses, lysogenic phages were enriched, enhancing their carriage of ARGs, auxiliary metabolic genes (AMGs) that bolster host survival, and antidefense genes via a "piggyback-the-winner" strategy, thereby increasing ARG dissemination potential. Notably, high-concentration levofloxacin exerted stronger selective pressure than ofloxacin, increasing virus-to-host ratios and phage-associated ARG accumulation, as supported by incubation assays. Collectively, our findings support a mechanistic framework in which soil salinization interacts with chiral antibiotic exposure, particularly levofloxacin, to increase phage-associated ARG dissemination potential. This highlights a long-underappreciated, Anthropocene-driven pathway intensifying environmental resistance risks and posing new challenges for the One Health framework.
authors: Xie T, Lin D, Tong SQ, Wang Q, Ni N, Wang N, Yang Z, Liu XH, Zhu D.

title: Artificial intelligence in the diagnosis and identification of bacterial pathogens: Current advances and future perspectives.
abstract: Bacterial infections remain a major global health challenge, which are responsible for significant morbidity, mortality, and increasing antimicrobial resistance worldwide. Rapid and accurate identification of bacterial pathogens is therefore essential for guiding appropriate antimicrobial therapy, improving patient outcomes, and supporting effective infection control strategies. However, conventional microbiological diagnostic methods such as culture, microscopy, and biochemical testing are often time-consuming, labor-intensive, and dependent on expert interpretation. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly emerged as a powerful tool capable of transforming clinical microbiology by enabling rapid analysis of complex biomedical data. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the role of AI in the diagnosis and identification of bacterial pathogens and to discuss its current applications, advantages, limitations, and future perspectives. Key AI-assisted technologies, including machine learning and deep learning algorithms such as Random Forest, Support Vector Machines, Artificial Neural Networks, and Convolutional Neural Networks, are increasingly applied to diagnostic platforms, including automated microscopy, next-generation genomic sequencing, MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, and clinical data analysis systems. Current evidence indicates that AI-assisted diagnostic approaches can substantially improve the speed, accuracy, and automation of microbial pathogen detection while enabling large-scale analysis of microbiological and clinical datasets. In the future, AI-integrated microbiology laboratories, rapid diagnostic platforms, genomic surveillance systems, and AI-assisted clinical decision support tools are expected to further enhance infectious disease diagnostics and contribute to improved antimicrobial stewardship and global infection management.
authors: A Mohammed S.

title: Environmental microbial communities and host selection shape larval microbiomes.
abstract: Ocean warming is altering abiotic environments and biotic interactions experienced by marine organisms, where sensitive early developmental windows occur in biologically complex seawater communities. The impact of these interactions on developmental processes and fitness in hosts is not well understood, but likely contingent on the establishment of a host-associated microbiome. Here, we hypothesize that temperature and microbial exposure during embryogenesis influence larval microbiome assembly and host morphology. Strongylocentrotus purpuratus embryos were raised in low microbial richness (LMR) or high microbial richness (HMR) seawater at ambient (14 °C) or elevated (18 °C) temperature, then collected at 2, 4, and 6 days post-fertilization (dpf) following multiple feedings. Higher microbial diversity was observed in larvae that developed in HMR seawater when compared to LMR. Differences in relative abundances of dominant microbial families between seawater and larvae suggest some degree of host selectivity in microbiome assembly. Temperature did not strongly alter microbiome composition, but both temperature and microbial condition led to differences in larval morphology by 6 dpf, potentially due to enrichment of microbes with chemoheterotrophic functions. By linking how temperature and microbial communities interact with host development, we contribute novel insights into how early-life environmental conditions impact holobiont formation and morphology.
authors: Hendricks SF, Tan AL, Williams AG, Clark MM, Buckley KM, Strader ME.

title: Plasmid-mediated copper resistance in Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans: determination of plasmid copy number and stability.
abstract: The management of bacterial spot of tomato is challenged by the widespread occurrence of copper resistance among its causal pathogens. In Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans, a major causal agent, copper resistance is conferred by cop genes organized in an operon located on either the chromosome or plasmid. In the United States, copper resistance is predominantly chromosomally encoded. Plasmid-borne resistance is limited to a few phylogenetic groups but is prevalent in other bacterial spot pathogens. We hypothesized that plasmid-encoded copper resistance genes exhibit higher expression than chromosomally encoded genes but may be unstable in the absence of selective pressure for resistance. To test this hypothesis, we examined how the chromosomal versus plasmid-borne cop operon influences gene copy number and expression, as well as plasmid stability. Relative to strains with only chromosomal resistance, strains carrying plasmid-encoded resistance exhibited an increased copy number of copB, a key gene in the operon, while strains carrying both chromosomal and plasmid-encoded resistance showed an even greater increase in gene copy number. Correspondingly, copB expression was elevated in both groups. During in vitro growth without copper, partial or complete plasmid loss occurred in a subset of strains, and genome sequencing of colonies with reduced plasmid size revealed transposase-mediated plasmid rearrangements. These findings demonstrate that plasmid-borne copper resistance increases gene copy number and expression of copper resistance genes but can be unstable without copper selection in some strain backgrounds, highlighting the role of mobile genetic elements in shaping Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans adaptation to changing copper environments.IMPORTANCEPlasmids are key players in the dissemination of antimicrobial resistance. Although copper resistance is widespread among Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans strains, copper-based bactericides remain at the forefront of disease management. We previously demonstrated that distinct genetic elements, including plasmid- and chromosomally encoded genomic islands, contribute to the acquisition of copper resistance and the occurrence of multicopy resistance in X. euvesicatoria pv. perforans. Here, we show that the localization of copper resistance genes on a plasmid, chromosome, or both influences gene copy number and expression of copper resistance genes. Furthermore, rearrangements between co-resident plasmids affect plasmid stability, leading to the loss of copper resistance in X. euvesicatoria pv. perforans. These findings highlight how plasmid dynamics can shape bacterial evolvability and adaptation to selective environments.
authors: Kaur A, Bankole IA, Subedi A, Minsavage GV, Dillon MM, Goss EM, Jones JB.

title: Lineage II Escherichia coli O157:H7: genomes, prophages, colicins, and the absence of detectable Stx2.
abstract: The genomes of three lineage II strains of E. coli O157:H7 (FRIK2069, FRIK2455, and FRIK2533) with different pulsed-field gel electrophoresis patterns were sequenced, assembled, and compared. The genomes were closely related, with overall synteny, with the exception of a 302 kbp inversion in FRIK2069. FRIK2533 lacked pO157, which may account for its limited isolation. FRIK2455 was the dominant strain isolated over several years and was selected for comparison with lineage I (Sakai) and lineage I/II (EC4115) strains. Distinct polymorphisms were identified in prophages and MGEs among the three lineages. All lineages contained stx1 prophages and the locus of enterocyte effacement. The stx2a prophage was present in Sakai and EC4115, while the stx2c prophage was found in EC4115 and FRIK2455. Eleven geographically disparate LII strains from the United States were tested for functional phage and Stx2. Three of the 11 LII strains underwent delayed lysis after 24 h post-mitomycin C treatment. stx2 transcription was observed in two of the three lytic strains, but Stx2 was not detected in the lytic or non-lytic LII strains by Western blot. The supernatant of lysates from eight lineage II strains inhibited growth of the phage host (E. coli strain MG1655) due to the production of a colicin (D, B, or M). These findings add to the body of evidence that LII EHEC do not produce functional phage or a detectable level of Stx2. Additionally, colicin production and pO157 may be key characteristics to the persistence of EHEC strains in the bovine host and farm environment.IMPORTANCEEscherichia coli O157:H7 is a human pathogen that is phylogenetically separated into three lineages. Strains belonging to lineages I and I/II are isolated from both clinical and bovine samples, whereas lineage II strains are only isolated from bovine and environments they occupy. This study sequenced, assembled, and compared the genomes of three lineage II strains. The genomes were closely related and syntenic, with differences in plasmid content and a chromosomal inversion. Comparison of the genome from FRIK2455 (lineage II strain) with the genomes of lineage I and I/II strains found distinct polymorphisms in prophages and mobile genetic elements. None of the lineage II strains examined produced functional phage or Stx2, but eight strains produced a colicin. Results from this study support previous reports that lineage II strains do not produce a detectable level of Stx2. Additionally, colicin production and pO157 may contribute to the persistence of EHEC in bovine.
authors: Stanton E, Teng L, Lee C, Wahlig TA, Park D, Jeong KC, Kaspar CW.

title: Integrated epidemiological and genomic characterization of respiratory bovine coronavirus in U.S. cattle 2020-2025.
abstract: Bovine coronavirus (BCoV) is an important contributor to the respiratory disease complex in cattle; however, integrated genomic and epidemiological data describing currently circulating respiratory BCoV strains in the United States remain limited. The objective of this study was to monitor respiratory BCoV at the genomic level and analyze its epidemiological patterns over five years, in addition to assess the pathological findings of the currently circulating BCoV in cattle. A total of 4,505 respiratory samples submitted to a diagnostic laboratory between January 2020 and November 2025 were analyzed, of which 693 (15.38%) tested positive for BCoV. Positivity was highest in young calves (0-40 days; 20.0%) and declined significantly with increasing age based on logistic regression analysis. Temporal trend analysis using locally estimated scatterplot smoothing and the Mann-Kendall test showed no significant monotonic change in BCoV detection during the study period. Co-infections were commonly detected between BCoV and other viral respiratory pathogens, while bacterial pathogens predominated in many samples. Lung tissues submitted from bovine respiratory cases were screened by qRT-PCR, and selected samples with high viral loads were subjected to next-generation sequencing. Complete genome sequencing identified four respiratory BCoV isolates (~31 kb), all clustering within genotype GIIb with recent U.S. strains. Comparative genomic analysis revealed amino acid substitutions in structural and non-structural proteins that may influence viral attachment, replication, and tissue tropism. These findings provide updated epidemiological and genomic insights into respiratory BCoV circulating in U.S. cattle.IMPORTANCEThis study demonstrates continued detection and genetic evolution of respiratory bovine coronavirus (BCoV) among diagnostic respiratory samples submitted from U.S. cattle, with 15.38% positivity observed among 4,505 submitted samples and a higher proportion of positive submissions from young calves. Whole-genome sequencing of lung-derived isolates revealed consistent clustering within genotype GIIb alongside ongoing molecular diversification, including amino acid substitutions in spike, hemagglutinin-esterase, nucleocapsid, and membrane proteins, and the emergence of a previously unrecognized putative alternative ORF near 4.8-kDa NSP. These findings highlight that respiratory BCoV is continuously evolving at the site of disease. The observed genetic changes provide critical targets to refine diagnostic assays, support updating of vaccine strains, inform antiviral development, and enable more effective, evidence-based management strategies for controlling respiratory BCoV in cattle, requiring potential experimental validation.

title: Adaptive landscape and genetic divergence of Karnah sheep revealed by selection scans across multiple ovine breeds.
abstract: Indigenous sheep constitute vital reservoirs of adaptive genetic diversity, yet their genomic signatures of adaptation are poorly understood. The present study provides a comprehensive genomic characterization of the endangered Karnah sheep (Ovis aries) native to North Kashmir, India. A total of 41,812 high-confidence SNPs were used across 266 individuals representing nine geographically and functionally diverse breeds (i.e., Karnah, Garole, Deccani, Changthangi, Tibetan, Australian Merino, Rambouillet, Suffolk, and Texel). Population structure analyses revealed pronounced genetic stratification with PC1-PC3 explaining 13.81% variance, separating Asian indigenous clusters (high-altitude vs. lowland) from European-derived wool and mutton populations. This pattern was consistently supported by ADMIXTURE (optimal K value of 8) and neighbor-joining phylogenetic analysis, identifying two deeply rooted clades. Genome-wide nucleotide diversity (π) estimates indicated relatively uniform diversity across populations, with Australian Merino exhibiting the highest diversity (106% of the mean), followed by Karnah (102%), while Garole showed the lowest (93%). Pairwise FST values ranged from 0.03 to 0.188, reflecting moderate genetic differentiation, with the lowest differentiation observed between Changthangi and Tibetan breeds and the highest between Garole and European breeds. Selection signature analyses revealed strong adaptive signals in Karnah sheep. Intra-population iHS analysis (|iHS| > 3) identified key candidate genes such as RELN, ADIPOQ, and RAP1B associated with environmental resilience, metabolism, and reproduction. Cross-population XP-EHH and FST analysis further highlighted genes involved in lipid metabolism (ATP8B2, ELOVL1), calcium signaling (CACNA1C), and immune response (NFKB2, HS6ST3), indicating adaptive divergence driven by climatic and ecological pressures. Functional enrichment supported pathways related to immunity, metabolism, and reproduction. Collectively, these findings provide a robust genomic framework for understanding adaptive evolution in Karnah sheep and offer valuable insights for conservation and climate-resilient breeding strategies.
journal: Mammalian genome : official journal of the International Mammalian Genome Society
authors: Shanaz S, Ahmad SF, Gangwar M, Nabi N, Ganai NA.
