title: Host-like temperature unlocks glucose uptake and metabolism in pathogenic Leptospira.
abstract: Pathogenic Leptospira transitions between environmental reservoirs and mammalian hosts, exposing the bacterium to distinct temperature conditions. Although Leptospira is generally considered to rely primarily on long-chain fatty acids for growth and to have limited capacity to use glucose, whether host-like temperature alters glucose-associated metabolic capacity remains unclear. Here, we used transcriptome-integrated genome-scale metabolic modeling to examine temperature-dependent metabolic states in pathogenic Leptospira. Models contextualized with transcriptomic data from cultures at 37°C predicted increased flux through glucose transport, glucose phosphorylation, and downstream glucose-associated reactions than it did at 29-30°C. Similar temperature-dependent predictions were obtained for another pathogenic Leptospira species under in vitro conditions. Consistent with these findings, analysis of leptospires cultivated intraperitoneally in dialysis membrane chambers also predicted enhanced glucose uptake and metabolism under host-temperature conditions. In vitro validation experiments showed increased bacterial uptake or accumulation of a fluorescent glucose analog, elevated expression of candidate glucose transporter genes, and glucose-dependent enhancement of bacterial growth at 37°C. Treatment with a glucose degradation pathway inhibitor, 2-deoxy-d-glucose, further supported a contribution of glucose-associated processes to proliferation at 37°C. Together, these findings indicate that pathogenic Leptospira displays condition-dependent glucose uptake and glucose-associated metabolic activity that become apparent at host-like temperature, as opposed to being glucose-incompetent at environmental-like temperature. This prediction-driven framework refines the conventional view of Leptospira carbon metabolism and provides a basis for future studies of glucose-associated metabolic capacity during mammalian infection.ImportanceEnvironmental reservoirs play a central role in the transmission of many bacterial pathogens, yet the metabolic mechanisms that enable adaptation to both environmental and host-associated niches remain largely unknown. Using a prediction-driven framework that combines contextualized genome-scale metabolic modeling with multi-omics analyses and experimental validation, we discovered that pathogenic Leptospira activates glucose uptake and metabolism only under host-like conditions. This finding resolves a long-standing misconception arising from studies performed under conventional laboratory conditions and fundamentally revises our understanding of Leptospira physiology. More importantly, our study establishes an integrative systems biology strategy for uncovering condition-dependent metabolic traits that would be difficult to identify experimentally alone, with broad applicability to diverse environmentally transmitted pathogens.
authors: Ozuru R, Yoshimura M, Powers DA, Sonoda T, Papin JA, Obata F, Kolling GL, Hiromatsu K.

title: Host genetics structure Symbiodiniaceae and prokaryotic assemblages and their co-variation in sympatric fire coral species
abstract: ABSTRACT  Host genetic and environmental filtering are key determinants of microbiome assembly, yet their relative influence across multiple symbiotic compartments remains poorly understood. In coral holobionts, studies typically focus on either algal or bacterial symbionts and rarely account for host genetic variation below the species level. Here, we combined host microsatellite genotyping with ITS2 and 16S rRNA metabarcoding to investigate the drivers of Symbiodiniaceae and prokaryotic assemblages in three sympatric fire coral species (  Millepora cf.  exaesa ,  M. tenera , and  M. cf.  platyphylla ) across three adjacent but environmentally contrasting reef habitats on Réunion Island. Both symbiont assemblages were structured by host identity and habitat, although host genetics consistently outweighed environmental effects on the microbiome composition. At the subspecies level, host genotypes explained up to 54% of the variation in Symbiodiniaceae assemblages compared to 20% for the prokaryotes. Symbiodiniaceae communities were dominated by  Symbiodinium A16 and A3 radiations, while showing marked specificity across species and habitats. All  Millepora species consistently associated with the Spirochaetaceae, Kiloniellaceae and Desulfobacteraceae bacterial families across all habitats, suggesting evolutionarily maintained core associations. Integrative analysis further demonstrated genotype-specific co-variation between algal and bacterial symbionts, with some genotypes maintaining stable and co-varying symbionts across clones, while others exhibited more flexible assemblages. Together, our results indicate that sympatric fire coral acquire symbionts from locally available pools through host genotype-dependent filtering. This study highlights host genotype as a major determinant of coral holobiont assembly, shaping the composition and co-variation of both Symbiodiniaceae and prokaryotic assemblages.
authors: Pozas-Schacre C, Derome N, Boissin E, Mercière A, Martineau G, Mercier P, Bourmaud CA, Dubé CE.

title: Gut microbiota dysbiosis in adrenoleukodystrophy: a new piece in the puzzle?
abstract: ABSTRACT  X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD) is the most common monogenic disorder affecting brain white matter, presenting a broad clinical spectrum from slowly progressive adrenomyeloneuropathy (AMN) to rapidly advancing cerebral demyelination. Factors influencing the variable disease expressivity remain poorly understood. We conducted shotgun metagenomic profiling of fecal samples from X-ALD patients and integrated these data with targeted plasma metabolomic analyses of amino acids and key metabolic intermediates. We identified distinct microbiome-associated metabolic signatures across X-ALD phenotypes. Notably,  Bacteroides cellulosilyticus and  Helicobacter apodemus abundance were significantly altered in AMN compared with childhood CALD patients. In parallel, X-ALD patients exhibited evidence of microbial metabolic remodeling characterized by altered amino acid metabolism, reduced folate biosynthetic potential, and enrichment of stress-adaptive pathways, including redox-associated functions, glyoxylate shunt activity, lipid A modification, lipopolysaccharide assembly, biofilm adhesin biosynthesis, and curli fiber production. Consistent with these microbial changes, plasma levels of branched-chain amino acids and methionine, as well as serum folate concentrations, were significantly reduced. Importantly, methionine levels showed an inverse correlation with neurofilament light chain (NfL) concentrations in patients with cerebral disease. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized link between gut microbial metabolic capacity and systemic metabolic alterations in X-ALD. Our results reinforce previous evidence implicating methionine metabolism in disease severity. Collectively, these data support a modulatory role of the microbiota–gut–brain axis in neuroinflammatory and mitochondrial-related processes underlying X-ALD progression and highlight new opportunities for biomarker development and microbiome-informed therapeutic interventions.
authors: Torreni L, Schlüter A, Marti S, Ruiz M, Vélez-Santamaria V, Rodríguez-Palmero A, Artuch A, Guilera C, Arias A, Mochel F, Aguilera-Albesa S, Cantarin V, Casasnovas C, Artuch R, Köhler W, Pujol A, Fourcade S.

title: A multi-scale cell-type resolved map of trans-regulatory architecture in the aging human brain
abstract: Mapping genetic effects on distal genes and regulatory programs is essential for understanding how genetic variation influences complex diseases; yet trans-QTL discovery remains limited by weak effect sizes, extensive multiple testing and poor reproducibility. Here, we introduce TransMap, a generalizable computational framework that combines multi-scale trans-QTL mapping with multi-phenotype genetic colocalization to improve the discovery and interpretation of distal regulatory variants. Beyond individual trans-eGenes, TransMap constructs local co-regulatory program phenotypes that account for background expression variation to improve the detection of weak, coordinated distal genetic effects. Across a broad range of simulation settings, TransMap achieved 9.2-36.7% higher trans-QTL discovery power than existing methods while maintaining well-controlled type I error rates. We applied TransMap to bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomic profiles from the aging human brain in the ADSP Functional Genomics Consortium (FunGen-AD), further integrating proteomic, glycoproteomic and metabolomic biomarker measurements (average N=476 donors). Genome-wide fine-mapping of TransMap single-gene and program-level QTL yielded variant annotations with 2.75-2.88x heritability enrichment across 57 complex diseases and traits (average N=307K), with complementary heritability information captured across regulatory scales. Multi-phenotype colocalization identified 49,532 trans-regulatory events supported by shared genetic signals with cis-eQTL or biomarker-QTL, including 1,825 candidate cis-trans-biomarker regulatory configurations. TransMap further revealed an asymmetric cross-cell-type regulatory architecture in which neuronal cis-regulatory signals preferentially associate with coordinated glial trans-regulatory responses, supported by co-culture experiments and spatial transcriptomics. Alzheimer's disease (AD) GWAS-prioritized colocalization identified trans-regulatory associations in 115 AD-associated loci, including a KNOP1 cis-eQTL associated in trans with a microglial regulatory program containing MS4A4E, with additional support from statistical mediation analysis. TransMap provides a multi-scale, cell-type-resolved atlas of trans-regulatory variation and a generalizable framework for elucidating the regulatory architecture of complex diseases.
authors: Cao X, Wang Y, Sun H, Feng R, Zhang H, Li Y, Lee H, Karaahmet B, Li B, Gersbach C, Crawford GE, Taga M, Beeri MS, Buchman AS, Klein H, De Jager P, Bennett DA, The Alzheimer's Disease Functional Genomics Consortium, Wang G, Dey KK.

title: cpr0186 contributes to promoting sporulation in Clostridium perfringens SM101.
abstract: ObjectivesAlthough the precise mechanism underlying activation of Spo0A needs to be clarified to fully understand C. perfringens sporulation, the molecules directly interacting with Spo0A have not been fully elucidated. This study aimed to identify proteins interacting with Spo0A during C. perfringens sporulation by a yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) assay.MethodsPrey libraries constructed using the genomes of C. perfringens SM101 and str. 13 and a bait plasmid encoding the receiver domain of Spo0A in C. perfringens SM101 were used for Y2H assay. The deletion mutant and its complemented strain were constructed by homologous recombination. Phenotypic analyses included measurements of bacterial growth, sporulation efficiency, cell morphology, mRNA expression of sporulation-related genes, and the amount of phosphorylated Spo0A. Potential protein interactions were evaluated using AlphaFold 3.ResultsY2H screening identified CPR0186, a hypothetical protein in C. perfringens SM101, as a Spo0A-interacting candidate, and AlphaFold 3 modeling supported the possibility of the direct interaction with the receiver domain of Spo0A. The cpr0186-null mutant exhibited growth comparable to that of the wild-type strain, but showed significantly reduced sporulation. The mutant also showed significantly decreased mRNA expression of spo0A, sigF, sigE, sigG, and sigK. No apparent difference in the ratio of Spo0A∼P to unphosphorylated Spo0A was observed among the strains under the conditions tested.Conclusioncpr0186 promotes sporulation in C. perfringens SM101 and is suggested to contribute to the expression of Spo0A-regulated genes. CPR0186 may interact directly with Spo0A although the functional significance of this interaction remains to be determined.
authors: Yasugi M, Sugimoto M, Kusakabe S, Miyake M, Nariya H.

title: Aniline Biodegradation and Nitrogen Removal by Salt-Tolerant Pseudomonas sp. H1: Performance and Potential Mechanisms of Catechol-Mediated Enhancement.
abstract: Industrial wastewater containing salts, nitrogen, and aromatic pollutants presents challenges for biological treatment. Although salt-tolerant microorganisms have shown potential for nitrogen removal and aromatic pollutant degradation, their functional versatility and the effects of co-substrates on pollutant biodegradation remain insufficiently understood. Here, we investigated the aniline degradation and nitrogen removal capabilities of salt-tolerant Pseudomonas sp. H1, with particular emphasis on catechol-mediated enhancement of aniline biodegradation. Strain H1 degraded only 9.11% of aniline (200 mg⋅L-1) within 60 h as sole substrate, but the degradation rate approached 100% within 24 h with catechol as co-substrate. Moreover, the strain tolerated high salinity (20-60 g⋅L-1 NaCl), achieving a maximum average NH4+-N removal rate of 10.98 mg⋅L-1⋅h-1. Whole-genome sequencing, nitrogen balance analysis, and enzyme activity assays supported ammonium assimilation as an important nitrogen removal pathway. Transcriptomic analysis revealed differential expression of genes associated with antioxidant defense, carbon metabolism, and aromatic compound degradation under catechol-supplemented conditions, suggesting potential transcriptional responses associated with enhanced aniline biodegradation. These findings demonstrate that catechol supplementation can substantially improve aniline biodegradation by a salt-tolerant bacterium with nitrogen removal capability, providing a basis for the potential application of strain H1 in saline wastewater treatment.
authors: Zha Z, Ren Y, Chen F, Yu C, Lei L, Li Z, Chen H.

title: Efficacy of Two Antimicrobial Peptides Against Pseudomonas syringae pv. actinidiae in Kiwifruit.
abstract: Kiwifruit bacterial canker caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. actinidiae (Psa), has led to substantial economic losses worldwide and represents a major challenge to kiwifruit cultivation. Due to the inadequate effectiveness and environmental safety of current treatments, there is a pressing demand for novel antimicrobial compounds, such as antimicrobial peptides (AMPs). In this study, two AMPs, P255 and P256, previously designed by our group, were used to determine their efficacy against Psa in kiwifruit. P256 with a minimum inhibitory concentration of 18.75 µg/mL demonstrated stronger antimicrobial activity against Psa than did P255. P256 and P255 showed synergistic effect when combined with EDTA. In addition, they effectively inhibited the biofilm formation, and regulated the expression of genes related to Psa biofilm formation. Both peptides bound with the lipopolysaccharide of Psa, targeted the membrane and increased the permeability of Psa cell membrane, resulting in calcium leakage. P256 and P255 disrupted the cellular morphology and intracellular structure of Psa cells. They also bound to the genomic DNA of Psa and induced the accumulation of intracellular reactive oxygen species. In experiments on infected leaf discs, P256 and P255 displayed superior control of Psa compared to commercial agricultural streptomycin. Collectively, P256 and P255 efficiently controlled Psa in kiwifruit and could be further developed as a new eco-friendly bactericidal agents.
authors: Zhou Y, Yang Y, Wang L, Gao Y, Xu X, Ying F, Dang X.

title: First contact: biophysical insights into non-enveloped viruses from VLPs to packed virions.
abstract: Precise biophysical characterization of non-enveloped viruses and virus-like particles (VLPs) is essential for evaluating assembly, structural integrity, and sample heterogeneity - key parameters that influence infectivity, manufacturability, and therapeutic performance. Analytical ultracentrifugation, light scattering, and mass photometry provide complementary information on particle size distributions, empty/full ratios, and assembly quality. Native and charge-detection mass spectrometry extend this, enabling accurate mass determination and genome-loading assessment. Solution-based structural techniques, such as SAXS and spectroscopy, provide dynamics. High-resolution X-ray crystallography, cryogenic electron microscopy, and tomography reveal global architectures, quaternary arrangements, and conformational switching essential for entry and maturation. Besides these methods, atomic force microscopy also allows nanoscale visualization in conjunction with mechanical profiling, linking physical stability with functional behavior. Thermal, chemical, and mechanical stress assays offer insight into unfolding pathways, pH-dependent disassembly, and genome-driven capsid pressurization, informing both viral biology and formulation science. Finally, mass spectrometry-based methods enable site-specific mapping of post-translational modifications and conformational perturbations. Together, these approaches establish a comprehensive framework for characterizing viral particles and VLPs, supporting rational engineering of stable, homogeneous, and functional assemblies for vaccines, gene delivery, and nanobiotechnology. This review summarizes current label-free methods for assessing size, mass, structural organization, and stability of intact viral particles.
authors: Rothe J, Uetrecht C.

title: MOCHI enables systematic identification of candidate independent intronic transcriptional signals from short-read RNA-seq data
abstract: Standard short-read RNA-seq analysis pipelines quantify expression over annotated exons and disregard signals mapped to introns, thereby missing independently transcribed intronic RNAs. Existing strategies depend on annotation, biologically crude whole-intron quantification, or subjective, low-throughput manual genome-browser inspection. We present MOCHI (Mapping of Cryptic Hidden Intronic Transcripts), a framework that couples reference-independent, k-mer-based signal discovery with reference-guided genomic interpretation and a custom multi-step filtering module to systematically curate potential independent intronic transcription units from strand-specific short-read RNA-seq data. On two simulated datasets, MOCHI recovered annotated sense-intronic long non-coding RNAs removed from the reference and distinguished them from intronic signal confounders. Across paired ribosomal RNA-depleted and poly(A)-selected libraries from ten cancer cell lines, MOCHI curated candidates whose host introns are strongly enriched for a transcription-initiation signal. Candidate expression is largely uncoupled from host-gene exons, and their genomic features resemble those of annotated long non-coding RNAs. In ten matched cohorts from The Cancer Genome Atlas, candidates were detected in tumor samples, and a subset was associated with overall survival after adjustment for age and host-gene expression. Consequently, MOCHI extends the transcriptomic landscape that can be mined from existing short-read RNA-seq data and provides a curated resource of candidate intronic transcripts for downstream analyses.
authors: Gurer-Er DC, Karakulah G, Gautheret D, Akgul B.

title: Foodborne Bacterial Protein Toxins: Structural Genomics, Stability, and Prospects for Enzymatic Detoxification in Food and Gut Environments.
abstract: Foodborne bacterial toxins remain a major global health threat, causing millions of diarrheal cases annually by disrupting ion balance, inhibiting protein synthesis, and dysregulating immune responses. Key agents include AB5 enterotoxins such as cholera toxin, heat-labile toxin, and Shiga toxins; heat-stable peptides (STa/STb); staphylococcal superantigens; and pore-forming toxins from Bacillus cereus and Clostridium perfringens. Encoded on mobile genetic elements or chromosomal loci, these structurally robust toxins often resist host proteolysis, limiting natural detoxification. Despite abundant data on individual toxins, an integrated synthesis that links high-resolution structural and genetic features with practical implications for enzymatic neutralization is lacking. This review addresses this gap by compiling the structural genomics of major toxin families and mapping toxin architecture and gene context onto stability profiles and enzymatic vulnerability. We examine their genetic organization, structural stability, and susceptibility to enzymatic neutralization by microbial proteases, probiotic-mediated modulation, and engineered biocatalysts. Enzymatic detoxification of mycotoxins is discussed only as a limited translational analogy: small-molecule conversion by lactonases, oxidoreductases, or hydrolases is biochemically distinct from proteolysis of large, conformationally complex protein toxins. Thus, mycotoxin studies inform enzyme-discovery and engineering workflows but do not constitute direct evidence that these pathways can neutralize AB5 holotoxins, superantigens, or pore-forming toxins.
authors: Pham THH, Nguyen TL.

title: Borrelia-specific cell-free DNA in plasma from adults with Lyme neuroborreliosis: an explorative study.
abstract: Current blood-based diagnostic modalities for LNB have significant limitations. Using Next Generation Sequencing, we investigated blood samples from patients with LNB and non-LNB controls for Borrelia burgdorferi-specific cfDNA (Bb-cfDNA). Blood-samples from 61 adults suspected for LNB were analysed with amplification-free Nanopore metagenomic sequencing and detected cfDNA was cross-referenced with human and Bb-genome databases to identify Bb-specific-cfDNA. Bb-cfDNA was detected in 3 of 45 patients with LNB (6.7%) and in none of the 16 controls. Positive samples contained low levels of Borrelia-classified reads. Bb-cfDNA is unlikely to become a relevant blood-based diagnostic test for LNB in immunocompetent adults.
journal: European journal of clinical microbiology & infectious diseases : official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology
authors: Fjordside L, Pedersen MS, Ellegaard K, Stegger M, Florescu AM, Dos AH, Brandt CT, Jepsen MPG, Stenør C, Mens H, Lebech AM.

title: Genomic Profiling of the Virulence Potential and Antimicrobial Resistance of Shiga Toxin-Producing Escherichia coli from Surface Water and Animal Sources.
abstract: The aim of this work was to characterize the pathogenic potential of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) circulating in environmental and animal reservoirs. To achieve this, 225 genomes were analyzed: four genomes were obtained from bovine mastitis isolates, and 221 were obtained from the NCBI Pathogen Detection database originating from surface water and animal fecal samples. All genomes were analyzed to identify virulence-associated factors and antimicrobial resistance profiles in strains collected from surface water and animal samples. Virulence analysis revealed that stx1 and stx2 were detected in 32% and 44% of isolates, respectively. Environmental genomes frequently carried adhesion and LEE-associated genes, while mastitis isolates lacked these markers but exhibited enriched iron uptake systems and hemolysins, indicating niche-specific virulence repertoires. Resistance analysis identified 105 genes that contribute to antimicrobial resistance against multiple antibiotic families, including beta-lactams, quinolones, tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, and polymyxins. Phylogenetic analysis classified the strains mainly into phylogroups B1 (63.56%) and E (28%), and serotyping identified 41 serotypes, with O157:H7 being the most common (25.33%). MLST revealed 46 STs, with ST11 being the predominant one in animal fecal isolates. Overall, the data indicate a genetically diverse STEC population, with shared lineages among water, feces, and mastitis, as well as combined virulence and multidrug resistance profiles. This supports the need to incorporate genomic surveillance in environmental and livestock reservoirs to anticipate and mitigate the risks of transmission to the human population.

title: Temporal changes in genetic variation during the invasion of Lygodium japonicum in North America
abstract: Premise of the study. Invasive species are now widespread and have detrimental ecological and economic impacts. They also offer opportunities to investigate rapid evolution in colonizing populations. Here, we leverage nuclear DNA from herbarium specimens of Lygodium japonicum, an invasive fern to 1) identify the putative source(s) of its invasion, 2) test for climate adaptation in its invaded range, and 3) characterize the effects of genetic bottlenecks on adaptive and neutral variation during its establishment. Methods. We use low-coverage genome skimming data from specimens spanning 1905 through 2017 to identify the source region(s) of the L. japonicum invasion of North America. We use a genotype-environment analysis of invaded range samples to identify genomic regions associated with local adaptation to variation in five bioclimatic variables. Finally, we compare heterozygosity between native and invasive individuals and their changes through time in non-coding, coding, and putatively adaptive loci. Key results. We identify mainland Asia as the most likely source region for this invasion. Our genotype-environment analysis found 144 candidate SNPs significantly associated with climatic variation in the invaded range, with precipitation of the driest month associated with the greatest number of SNPs, suggesting rapid genomic adaptation in the invaded range. Finally, we found conflicting trends in individual-level heterozygosity over time when analyzing different types of genetic variation: in non-coding loci, there was a small, yet significant decrease in genetic diversity, but in putatively adaptive loci we did not find evidence of a genetic bottleneck. Conclusions. Natural history collections provide exceptional opportunities to explore evolutionary processes, by capturing genomic sequences across time. Here, herbarium specimens reveal rapid evolution, maintenance of adaptative variation, and accumulation of noncoding diversity in the Lygodium japonicum invasion, highlighting the potential for adaptative variation to fuel the success of invasive species.
authors: Pelosi JA, Pearse AR, Northing PC, Markley M, Altergott E, Beck JB, Dlugosch KM.

title: Somatic structural variation discovery on cancer pangenome graphs
abstract: Somatic structural variants (SVs) drive tumorigenesis across most cancers, yet low variant allele frequencies in subclonal populations often necessitate multi-sample sequencing per patient. Existing somatic SV callers rely on whole-genome read alignments against a single linear reference, incurring high computational costs and reference bias. We present JANUS, which discovers somatic SVs directly within a personal pangenome, a colored de Bruijn-like graph of locally consistent parsing (LCP) cores built from matched normal and tumor PacBio HiFi reads. JANUS identifies candidate SV sites traversed exclusively by tumor reads without prior alignment, mapping only short read snippets surrounding each site. Across five tumor-normal pairs in the CASTLE panel, JANUS leads the 18-caller consensus with a mean F1 score of 0.887 (next-best caller: 0.858), widening its lead under low-signal regimes (0.489 versus 0.362 at 5x; 0.683 versus 0.520 at 20% purity). End to end, JANUS analyzes a tumor-normal pair in ~11 minutes on average with 16 threads, which is ~24x faster than read alignment alone on the same machine. In a 20-tumor patient simulation, joint graph calling outperforms independent pairwise runs in speed and accuracy, particularly at low depth. By processing multi-sample cohorts jointly and maintaining sensitivity at low coverage and purity, JANUS provides an efficient, reference-unbiased framework for cancer genomics. JANUS is available at https://github.com/BilkentCompGen/janus.
authors: Kara M, Ashyralyyev A, Alkan C.

title: Evolutionary dynamics of the pan-centromere architecture in oaks
abstract: Centromeres ensure faithful chromosome segregation and genome stability, yet their DNA evolves rapidly, presenting a long-standing centromere paradox. Here we characterise the genomic and epigenomic architecture of >1,300 candidate centromeres from 111 high-quality Quercus (oak) genomes. We show that lineage-specific expansion of QuCEN146 satellite drives centromere turnover in oaks by displacing ancestral LTR-rich sequences into flanking regions, with genetic drift facilitating fixation of satellite-rich centromeres. Population-scale analyses in Q. serrata reveal extensive variation in satellite rich centromeres, generated by array expansion and contraction, strand-orientation shifts, and interspecific introgression. By contrast, LTR rich centromeres of Q. variabilis exhibit extremely low polymorphism and high collinearity across populations, sustained by suppressed local recombination, linked selection, and constrained LTR dynamics. We further demonstrate chromosome-independent evolutionary patterns for both satellite-rich and LTR-rich centromeres. Collectively, these findings demonstrate how evolutionary processes drive centromere turnover and shape contrasting centromeric sequence landscapes in forest trees.

title: The Geography of Speciation Across Andean-Centred Clades
abstract: Aim:  Mountains harbour a disproportionate share of global biodiversity, yet the geographic pathways through which this diversity arises remain debated. In the Andes, diversification has been linked both to geographic isolation generated by complex topography and climatic dynamics, and to ecological divergence across steep environmental gradients. Here, we assess the predominant geographic modes of speciation across Andean-centred clades using a large-scale comparative framework, while evaluating how alternative representations of species distributions influence macroevolutionary inference. Location: Andes, South America. Taxon: A total of 102 Andean-centred genera of animals, plants, and fungi. Methods: We combined time-calibrated phylogenies with species distribution data derived from two alternative spatial representations: concave polygons and potential distribution models. For each genus, we estimated 13 summary metrics capturing range overlap, range asymmetry, and phylogenetic structure. We then used simulation-trained, likelihood-free classification approaches, including linear discriminant analysis and two approximate Bayesian computation methods, to assign each clade to its most probable geographic mode of speciation: vicariant, peripatric, parapatric, sympatric, or mixed geographic scenarios. Results: Across clades, overlap-associated scenarios, corresponding to parapatric or sympatric classifications, were inferred as predominant in 57–67% of genera, whereas strictly allopatric scenarios, that is, vicariant or peripatric speciation, accounted for 23–30%, depending on the spatial representation and classification method used. Sympatric scenarios alone were inferred in 38–52% of genera, particularly when potential distribution models were used. At least one-third of clades showed congruent classifications across both analytical methods and spatial representations. However, several genera were sensitive to how species distributions were represented, with some shifting between allopatric and sympatric classifications depending on the spatial input used. Main Conclusions: Our results suggest that Andean diversification has not followed a single dominant geographic pathway, but instead reflects a mosaic of spatial contexts involving both isolation-driven and overlap-associated scenarios. However, classifications as parapatric or sympatric should be interpreted as hypotheses of geographic overlap during lineage divergence, rather than as direct evidence of speciation with gene flow. By shifting from single-clade case studies to a broad multi-taxon comparative perspective, this study suggests that the geography of Andean speciation reflects a heterogeneous process shaped by multiple spatial pathways to lineage divergence, while identifying candidate clades for future phylogeographic, ecological, cytogenetic, and population genomic studies of mountain biodiversity.
authors: Ramos Torres A, Molina-Henao YF.

title: Acquire and rewire: mobile genetic elements co-opt the bacterial core genome
abstract: It is assumed that bacterial genomes are streamlined, with genes encoding core functions integrated with one another and with aligned fitness interests. Such genes can gain little from horizontal transfer, as any recipient would already carry its own copy better adapted to resident networks. These restrictions motivated the ‘complexity hypothesis’, which predicts that core genes are rarely transferred. Yet homologues of core genes are repeatedly found outside their native chromosomal context, carried by mobile genetic elements such as plasmids and phage-plasmids, and by domesticated replicons such as chromids. Explaining this pattern requires us to ask whether a copy rides a mobile, self-interested element or a domesticated, host-aligned one. On domesticated, vertically inherited carriers, a second copy plausibly serves the host, through dosage, niche-specific benefit or functional specialization. On mobile, selfish elements, it may instead serve the element, by promoting behaviors that favor onward transmission. Because they enter cells that already have a host-encoded copy, we propose that mobile variants can act through dosage or through effects disproportionate to their abundance, for example by co-assembling with the chromosomal product. Here, we discuss the evolutionary drivers and consequences of extrachromosomal core genes and argue that these overlooked copies deserve systematic study.
authors: Carvalho R, Hall J, Botelho J.

title: Discovery of Apis mellifera filamentous virus in the blue orchard bee: Characterization of impacts and interactions with an organosilicone surfactant
abstract: Abstract    While RNA viruses have received attention in impacts on bee health, research is limited for DNA viruses. DNA viruses, such as  Apis mellifera filamentous virus  (AmFV), have been identified in solitary bees; but infection dynamics and impacts are not well studied. We detected AmFV in diapausing  Osmia lignaria  adults and dead larvae from wild populations using metagenomic sequencing. Finding AmFV in diapausing adults in cocoons indicated an active AmFV infection. Unmodified larval provisions from nests had significant levels of AmFV, suggesting virus transmission may occur via fecal/oral routes via pollen. Using established rearing methods, we fed  O. lignaria  larvae AmFV and monitored survival, development, and adult weight metrics. Increased amounts of AmFV in larval provisions resulted in increased mortality. Co-exposure to an organosilicone surfactant (OSS) in provisions synergistically increased AmFV titers in larvae and adults, indicating that agrochemicals could affect viral infections. With increased development time from 2nd instar to pupation, bees of both sexes weighed more; however, male and female bees were impacted differently by AmFV and OSS. OSS plus AmFV exposure significantly increased the time to pupation in female bees. Male bees exposed to OSS weighed more. These results provide crucial insights into AmFV disease dynamics.
authors: Williams MF, Schaeffer RN, Cox-Foster DL.

title: From Genomics to Diagnostics: Combating the Spread of Vascular Streak Dieback in North America.
abstract: Vascular streak dieback (VSD) has emerged as a major threat to woody ornamental production in the United States (U.S.), currently affecting at least 50 tree and shrub species across 25 botanical genera in at least twelve U.S. states. The putative causal agent, here termed the VSD-associated Ceratobasidiaceae lineage (Csp), presents diagnostic challenges due to its fastidious growth requirements and vascular colonization pattern. Here, we integrate genomics-guided marker discovery with multi-platform genome-anchored tools (SSR, TaqMan qPCR, and LAMP that target unique genomic regions identified through comparative genomics) to deliver a field-deployable, genome-anchored toolkit for detection and genotyping of Csp across nurseries and landscapes. We evaluated the performance of these tools using 103 samples representing DNA isolated from 64 VSD-symptomatic plants or their fungal isolates and 39 non-target Ceratobasidiaceae outgroups. Genome assembly of Illumina reads yielded ten informative microsatellite markers with an overall amplification success rate of 95.8% (91.7%-100.0% across Csp samples). These markers demonstrated strong performance in distinguishing the Csp samples from the outgroups. Among the three TaqMan probes developed, VSD048 exhibited superior performance with 100% detection across Csp samples, characterized by cycle threshold (CT) values of 26.8 ± 4.2, and no cross-reactivity with C. theobromae or other Ceratobasidiaceae species. A multi-laboratory ring trial confirmed the reproducibility of the VSD048 TaqMan assay across various testing platforms. The loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) assay targeting the Csp-unique region achieved a sensitivity of 0.82 [95% CI 0.68-0.968] and specificity of 1.00 [95% CI 1.00-1.00], with a practical detection threshold of approximately 25 copies of the target region. Our molecular survey of the disease revealed a surprisingly broad host range beyond Cercis canadensis (Eastern redbud), encompassing eight additional genera, and confirmed its geographical distribution across the eastern and midwestern U.S. These validated molecular tools provide rapid, sensitive, and specific detection methods for Csp surveillance and management. The field-applicable LAMP assay and laboratory-based TaqMan/SSR protocols offer complementary approaches for different diagnostic scenarios, thereby enabling early detection and supporting efforts to limit the spread of this emerging pathogen in nursery and landscape settings.
authors: Nowicki M, Boggess SL, Avin FA, Baysal-Gurel F, Bonkowski JC, Cubeta MA, Huff ML, Junaid M, Kilbourne K, McVay J, Meinecke CD, Shoemaker D, Staton ME, Trigiano RN, Turner JH, Villari C, Williams-Woodward J, Hadziabdic D.

title: Evaluation of ITS copy number variation among Clarireedia jacksonii isolates using single-copy genetic markers cam and hsp60.
abstract: Molecular tools are widely used for plant pathogen detection and quantification. Recent quantitative PCR applications for the turfgrass disease causal agent Clarireedia jacksonii were developed targeting the ITS region and showed potential utility in improved disease management. However, accurate and consistent pathogen quantification is contingent on stable copy numbers of the target genes across populations. In this study, we evaluated the genomic copy number of molecular markers in C. jacksonii using in silico analyses, quantitative PCR, and digital PCR. Calmodulin (cam), elongation factor 1-alpha (ef1α), and minichromosome maintenance protein 7 (mcm7) were consistently identified as single-copy loci, whereas ITS exhibited multiple copies in two out of nine assemblies. Digital PCR confirmed that cam and heat shock protein 60 (hsp60) closely followed theoretical single-copy expectations across a genomic DNA dilution series of C. jacksonii isolate HRS10. In the analysis of 27 C. jacksonii isolates, ITS was consistently detected as a multicopy locus, with copy number estimates ranging from 33 to 48 copies per genome when normalized using cam and from 34 to 52 copies per genome when normalized using hsp60. These results demonstrate that ITS copy number variation among C. jacksonii isolates was consistently observed, independent of the single-copy reference locus used for normalization. Therefore, single-copy genetic markers, such as cam and hsp60, may represent superior choices for accurate and stable estimation of fungal genome equivalents in C. jacksonii.
authors: Lopes da Silva L, Chou MY.

title: First Comprehensive Characterization and Highly Sensitive Detection of Hop Stunt Viroid in Chinese Sweet Cherry.
abstract: Hop stunt viroid (HSVd) is an emerging threat to sweet cherry production in China, yet its geographic distribution and genomic characteristics remain poorly understood. Here, we report the first occurrence of HSVd in cherry in Hebei Province and the complete genome sequences of three local isolates: YT-HSVd-1 (PQ580329), YT-HSVd-14 (PQ580330), and YT-HSVd-15 (PQ580350). Phylogenetic analysis placed them within a distinct plum-type clade alongside the isolates SC-17, SC-13 (Shandong sweet cherry), FP2 (Japanese plum; AB098502.1), HSVd.apr9, and HSVd.apr10 (Moroccan apricot), sharing 91.45 to 97.01% nucleotide identity with other known HSVd variants. Additionally, we developed a cherry-adapted SYBR Green I-based RT-qPCR assay using optimized primer sets (HSVd-q117F/R and HSVd-q168F/R) at 10 μmol/liter with annealing temperatures of 55.0 and 56.9°C, respectively. The assay demonstrated high sensitivity, with detection limits of 12.9 and 1.29 copies/μl and excellent reproducibility (Ct value [CV] < 5%). When applied to field samples, HSVd was reliably detected (100% detection rate) across all tested tissues, showing the highest viral titer in branch bark, followed by leaves and fruit stalks, and the lowest in fruit peels. This study provides the first complete HSVd genomes from Hebei Province and establishes a rapid, sensitive detection tool to support future surveillance and etiological research.
authors: Pan Y, Yu P, Li Z, Wang S, Cao K, Wang Y.

title: Variety-specific interrelationships between glucosinolate-related metabolite profiles and microbial communities in fermented mustard with divergent physicochemical and volatile properties.
abstract: Mustard exhibits varietal diversity in glucosinolate (GSL) composition, potentially affecting fermentation microbiota and product quality. Two varieties, LM01 (Brassica juncea var. longepetiolata Yang et Chen) and LM05 (Brassica juncea var. latipa), were selected from eight varieties and analyzed using volatile profiling, widely targeted GSL metabolomics, and metagenomics. After 20 d fermentation, LM05 had lower reducing sugars content but higher total acidity than LM01 (0.71 vs. 0.53 g/100 g) and retained higher levels of differential GSLs. The relative abundance of Lactiplantibacillus reached 89% in LM05 compared with 77% in LM01, accompanied by the enrichment of glycoside hydrolase-related functions, indicating distinct microbial functional potential associated with GSL transformation. Correlation analyses revealed distinct association patterns: LM01 exhibited a relatively simplified LAB-dominated network suggestive of a "stress-adaptive" pattern, whereas LM05 showed broader associations among LAB, yeasts, and GSL-derived metabolites. These findings provide a basis for targeted inoculation to improve fermentation performance across mustard varieties.
authors: Mei Y, Ge L, Wang Y, Yang M, Lai H, Zhao J, Du Q, Li H, Liu S, Hu K, Liu D, Zhao N.

title: Genomic Features and Risk Factors of Carbapenem-Resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa Bloodstream Infections.
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa (CRPA) bloodstream infection is associated with high mortality and limited treatment options. This retrospective cohort study was conducted at a single Chinese hospital from January 2020 to January 2026 and included adult patients with P. aeruginosa bloodstream infection. Clinical data were extracted from the hospital information system, and whole-genome sequencing was performed on 48 CRPA isolates to determine multilocus sequence types, carbapenemase genes, and capsular serotypes. Univariate and multivariable logistic regression were used to identify factors associated with CRPA acquisition. Among 110 patients, 48 (43.6%) had CRPA bloodstream infection. Prior ICU stay within 1 month (adjusted OR = 5.67, 95% CI: 2.81-11.45, p < 0.001) and prior carbapenem exposure within 30 days (adjusted OR = 3.89, 95% CI: 1.92-7.88, p < 0.001) were independent risk factors for CRPA acquisition. ST-3757 was the predominant sequence type (39/48, 81.3%), KPC-2 was the predominant carbapenemase gene (32/48, 66.7%), and O11 was the most frequent serotype (12/48, 25.0%). All ST-3757 isolates shared pairwise average nucleotide identity above 98.5%, and phylogenetic analysis placed them in a single well-supported clade. These findings indicate that prior healthcare exposure and carbapenem use drive CRPA bloodstream infection in this setting and that an ST-3757-O11-KPC-2 lineage is locally epidemic, supporting targeted antimicrobial stewardship and genomic surveillance.
authors: Fu H, Yao Y, Wang X, Chen X.

title: Personalization and evaluation of human whole-body metabolic models and community microbiome models using Persephone.
abstract: Human metabolism and human gut microbiome co-metabolism can be difficult to investigate in vivo owing to the complexity of the systems involved. Genome-scale metabolic modeling with human whole-body metabolic models (WBMs) offers a computational approach to address this challenge. However, personalization and analysis of WBMs requires comprehensive knowledge of metabolic modeling, which can be daunting for beginners. To reduce the computational expertise required and to standardize the process of working with and analyzing WBMs, we present Persephone: a personalization and evaluation pipeline for human WBMs. Persephone has functionalities to create community microbiome models from raw sequencing data or taxonomy-assigned read tables, use physiological and metabolomic data to create personalized WBMs, combine community microbiome models with WBMs or personalized WBMs to create community microbiome (personalized) WBMs, optimize WBMs according to user-defined metabolic reactions, perform statistical analyses to describe the data, and visualize significant results in various figures. Persephone saves intermediate results as well as a log file with all changes made to the model, data and any warnings encountered during the various steps. Persephone is designed for use by anyone with basic research-computing experience and access to modest computer hardware. Applications include the investigation of human-microbiome co-metabolism and the evaluation of the effects of various physiological parameters, such as weight, on human metabolism. Using a dataset of 100 metagenomic samples, it can take several days to a week to run Persephone on a single computer, depending on the number of reactions optimized and whether taxonomic assignment is performed.
authors: Nap B, Hensen T, Barton W, Sheehy A, Widder J, Chenna S, Thiele I.

title: Computational Structural Dynamics and Preliminary Heterologous Expression Suggest a "Rigid-Anchor, Flexible-Melting" RNA Chaperone Mechanism for Rice OsCSP1.
abstract: Cold and drought are major abiotic stresses that severely constrain rice (Oryza sativa) growth and productivity. Cold shock proteins (CSPs) act as RNA chaperones that facilitate post-transcriptional adaptation under environmental stress. In this study, we combined phylogenetic analysis, prokaryotic heterologous expression, and all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to elucidate the evolutionary features, stress-protective capacity, and working mechanism of rice OsCSP1. Promoter analysis revealed enrichment of low-temperature responsive (LTR) and MYB-binding drought-responsive (MBS) cis-elements upstream of OsCSP1. Heterologous overexpression of OsCSP1 in Escherichia coli showed no cytotoxicity at 37°C. Under 17°C cold stress, recombinant strains overcame initial metabolic burden and exhibited superior biomass accumulation (OD600) compared with empty vector controls during late log phase. Spot dilution assays indicated enhanced colony-forming ability at 10-3 dilution. Sector-plate assays further demonstrated strong induction-dependent cytoprotection against both prolonged cold (17°C) and 15% (w/v) PEG6000-induced osmotic stress in E. coli, highlighting its potential protective efficacy in heterologous systems. AlphaFold 3 modeling of the OsCSP1-U6 RNA complex yielded a moderate interface confidence (ipTM = 0.66), which is expected for proteins containing intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). Subsequent 100-ns all-atom MD simulations revealed rapid contraction in radius of gyration (Rg) and solvent-accessible surface area (SASA), forming a compact, solvent-resistant conformation. RMSF analysis showed a rigid N-terminal CSD anchor coupled with a highly dynamic C-terminal IDR. MM/PBSA binding free energy decomposition indicated that the interaction is primarily driven by van der Waals and electrostatic forces. We propose a "rigid-anchor, flexible-melting" model in which the CSD is predicted to provide stable RNA binding while the flexible IDR is hypothesized to facilitate the destabilization of misfolded RNA secondary structures. These findings provide a foundational biophysical framework that facilitates future in planta functional validation of OsCSP1 as a potential target for engineering climate-resilient rice.
authors: Liang Y, Zhang J, An X, Kong Y, Xu L, Liu J, Zhao F, Wu J.

title: Bacterial 2',3'-cGAMP signaling induces membrane splitting in antiphage CBASS immunity.
abstract: Bacterial cyclic-oligonucleotide-based antiphage signaling systems (CBASS) are evolutionarily related to the mammalian cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway. The bacterial CdnB-Cap14 CBASS system is notable for producing 2',3'-cyclic GMP-AMP (2',3'-cGAMP), the same second messenger used by the mammalian cGAS-STING pathway; however, its functional mechanism has remained unclear. Here, we show that CdnB-Cap14 protects against phage infection through abortive infection (Abi) by triggering cell death. Structures of apo CdnBΔC and its complexes with ATP and guanosine triphosphate (GTP), together with inactive and activated 2',3'-cGAMP-bound Cap14, reveal that CdnB is autoinhibited by its C-terminal AGS-C domain and becomes activated by DNA together with intracellular ATP/GTP depletion to synthesize 2',3'-cGAMP in vitro. This signal drives Cap14 assembly from dimers into zipper-like two-layered filaments that partition the membrane and disrupt its integrity. We further show that phage-encoded Acb2 sequesters 2',3'-cGAMP to block signaling. These findings reveal mechanistic parallels between bacterial CBASS and eukaryotic cGAS-STING immunity and provide a molecular basis for therapeutic engineering.
authors: Li Z, Chen W, Li Y, Xia Y, Wei XY, Yang L, Zhang JT, Wang C, Jia N.

title: Decolorization and detoxification of aniline blue dye by Cloacibacterium normanense Gsp-T3 newly isolated from amphipods: Novel of bacterial community composition, synthetic dye-degrading bacteria, ligninolytic potential, and biodegradation pathway.
abstract: Synthetic dye contamination negatively affects ecological creatures and health because of the durability and toxicity of dye molecules. This study aimed to isolate dye-degrading bacteria from three amphipod species, comprising Floresorchestia amphawaensis (FA), Quadrivisio meufong (QM), and Grandidierella sp. (Gsp), and assess the potential of natural bacterial isolates for dye decolorization and detoxification. Based on analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequences, six novel strains that decolorize a wide range of dyes were closely related to Stenotrophomonas nitritireducens (isolate FA-T13), Isoptericola nanjingensis (FA-T16), Klebsiella quasipneumoniae (QM-T13), Acidovorax temperans (QM-T15), Bacillus subtilis group (QM-T27), and Cloacibacterium normanense (Gsp-T3). Among them, the promising strain C. normanense Gsp-T3 had the highest decolorization capability of 60.51% for a harmful triphenylmethane dye, aniline blue, and demonstrated the highest activity of ligninolytic enzymes, including laccase, manganese peroxidase, and lignin peroxidase. Decolorization by Gsp-T3 was monitored using UV-Vis spectral and HPLC analyses, and the products derived from dye biodegradation were analyzed using FTIR and GC-MS analyses. Eight degradation products were identified as aromatics, short-chain aliphatic acids, and aliphatic alcohol, and a degradation pathway of aniline blue by Gsp-T3 was proposed. Moreover, alterations in bacterial cell surface morphology were detected by SEM. In detoxification assays, the biodegradation products had a reduced cytotoxicity effect on Vero cells and did not elevate phytotoxicity (mung bean, and rice). As culture-independent method, 16​S rRNA metagenomic analysis revealed diverse amphipod-associated bacterial communities, containing several genera potentially involved in pollutant biodegradation. The findings provided knowledge of amphipod-associated bacteria and their capability for synthetic dye bioremediation.
authors: Meeto C, Chanworawit K, Lueangjaroenkit P, Srinoi P, Deevong P.

title: Immunomodulatory natural products via toll-like receptor 2 signalling: from agonists to inhibitors across diverse natural sources.
abstract: Covering: up to 2025Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) is a versatile pattern recognition receptor whose activity can be tuned in either direction-agonism or antagonism-to produce distinct therapeutic outcomes, ranging from vaccine adjuvants and cancer immunotherapeutics to anti-inflammatory agents for sepsis, neuroinflammation, and autoimmune disease. Natural products from bacteria, fungi, plants, and marine organisms have emerged as a structurally rich source of TLR2 modulators, encompassing acylated lipopeptides, glycolipids, polysaccharides, flavonoids, non-flavonoid polyphenols, an aromatic aldehyde, an aporphine alkaloid, and even large bacterial antagonist proteins. This review surveys these natural TLR2 agonists and inhibitors, highlighting how the effective allocation of hydrophobic chains between the TLR2 pocket and its partner receptor, rather than total acyl-chain number alone, combines with chain branching, stereochemical presentation and polar head-group interactions to govern TLR1/TLR6 heterodimer selectivity among bacterial and gut-commensal lipids, and how mechanistically distinct inhibitory strategies-direct receptor competition, transcriptional downregulation, and TIR-domain interference-converge on a shared druggable interface exploited independently by plant polyphenols and staphylococcal virulence factors alike. Persistent experimental challenges are also discussed, including microbial contamination of natural extracts and structural heterogeneity of isolated lipids, along with how total synthesis and chemically defined oligomers have resolved these ambiguities, underscoring natural products as a promising yet still underexploited chemical space for developing selective TLR2-targeted therapeutics.
authors: Lee J.

title: A symbiont-derived biosurfactant couples bacterial surface properties to host-mediated clearance
abstract: Abstract  Host mechanisms that regulate intestinal colonization are viewed as acting on microbes, yet microbial traits that determine susceptibility to host control remain poorly understood. Using the association between Caenorhabditis elegans and its symbiont Pseudomonas lurida MYb11, we identify the cyclic lipopeptide biosurfactant massetolide as a bacterial factor that couples microbial physiology to host-mediated clearance. An unbiased screen of >11,000 bacterial mutants coupled to a host transcriptional reporter, combined with bacterial and host genetics, chemical complementation, transcriptomics, and physiological analyses, revealed that massetolide triggers host TGF-β and serotonergic signaling to promote intestinal peristalsis, limiting colonization. Massetolide also alters bacterial surface properties and promotes swarming. Experimentally increased serotonin-dependent peristalsis selectively reduces colonization by massetolide-producing bacteria, whereas massetolide-deficient bacteria remain resistant to host-mediated expulsion. Together, our findings reveal a symbiont-derived biosurfactant that links host neuroimmune control of intestinal peristalsis with bacterial susceptibility to expulsion, coupling host and microbial physiology to regulate symbiont abundance.
authors: Pees B, Escudero-Hernández C, von Hoyningen-Huene A, Rosenstiel P, Schmitz R, Dierking K.

title: ProteoKnight: Image-Based Encoding for Phage Virion Protein Classification and Uncertainty Estimation
abstract: Abstract  Accurate prediction of Phage Virion Proteins (PVPs) is essential for genomic studies due to their crucial role as structural elements in bacteriophages. Machine learning has emerged as a promising approach for annotating phage protein sequences obtained via high-throughput sequencing. However, effective annotation requires informative sequence encoding. This paper introduces ProteoKnight, an image-based encoding method that adapts the classical DNA-Walk algorithm using amino-acid-specific pixel colors and adjusted walk distances. It addresses the spatial information loss inherent in the previously reported image-based representation for PVP classification, frequency chaos game representation (FCGR). Moreover, this study bridges a gap in uncertainty analysis for protein sequence classification by evaluating prediction uncertainty in binary PVP classification through the Monte Carlo Dropout technique.In this study, variance and entropy measures were used to assess prediction uncertainty across proteins of various classes and lengths, forming the foundation of this investigation into protein classification and uncertainty quantification.The experiments highlight the efficacy of our approach in binary classification, achieving approximately 89% accuracy, demonstrating competitive performance with previously reported methods. Nevertheless, multi-class classification accuracy remains suboptimal. Furthermore, the uncertainty analysis unveils variability in prediction confidence influenced by protein class and sequence length, contributing novel insights to protein classification research.Combined with parameter-efficient convolutional neural networks, ProteoKnight enables accurate PVP prediction. Moreover, our uncertainty investigation identifies data points associated with low-confidence predictions, enhancing the comprehensiveness of our analysis.
authors: Khan MI, Bhuiyan AA, Neha SA, Rahman MK, Noor J.

title: A systematic review of whole-genome sequencing studies of Mycobacterium bovis that determine the direction of transmission between badgers and cattle
abstract: Abstract  Background: Tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium bovis, is a bacterial disease affecting cattle and other domestic species, wild mammals, and with resilience to survive in the wider environment for many months. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) methods can distinguish closely related isolates and local transmission clusters. However, the relatively slow evolutionary rate of M. bovis, with substitutions accumulating more slowly than individual transmission events occur, results in limited genetic divergence between epidemiologically linked isolates and a weak temporal signal, greatly limiting the ability to determine precisely ‘who infected whom’ and to estimate transmission rates. Differences in surveillance, sampling intensity, geographic coverage, and detection probability between cattle and the European badger Meles meles warrants a review to examine the strength of evidence, to better inform disease control considerations. Methods: Following PRISMA guidance, we searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and Embase for peer-reviewed studies using WGS data from sympatric cattle and European badgers. Studies were assessed according to their sampling design, temporal and geographic coverage, genomic diversity, analytical framework, treatment of unsampled and environmental transmission pathways, and integration of genomic and epidemiological data. Evidence was considered separately for host sharing, local persistence, maintenance, spillover, and transmission direction. Results: The reviewed studies consistently showed close genetic relationships and local sharing of M. bovis strains between cattle and badgers. However, estimates of transmission direction varied substantially between studies with large variation in sampling quality and analytical approaches. Some studies reported patterns compatible with greater badger-to-cattle transmission, while others indicated the opposite, and some emphasized within-species spread and cattle movement. Directional estimates were potentially sensitive to unequal host sampling, differences in surveillance processes, weak temporal signal, incomplete observation of infection chains, the treatment of environmental or unsampled transmission pathways, and especially model assumptions. Close genomic similarity supported shared local transmission histories but generally did not establish direct transmission or its direction. Collectively the evidence base is considered insuﬀiciently rigorous for findings to be definitive and this is recognised by most authors. Conclusions: Current WGS studies demonstrate shared local M. bovis strains and epidemiological connections, but directionality and reservoir status remain highly uncertain and particularly sensitive to sampling and modelling assumptions some of which show signs of confirmation bias. Existing caveated estimates of transmission are presently insuﬀicient to inform generalised conclusions about variation in interspecies transmission rates and their use to validate badger intervention in disease control strategy.
authors: Torgerson P, Ghielmetti G, Langton T.

title: Breakpoint structure and inter-clade exchange in recombinant duck circovirus genomes
abstract: Abstract    Recombination shapes the evolution of circoviruses, yet its extent and its breakpoints in duck circovirus (DuCV) are known only from regional datasets analysed in different alignment coordinates. We screened 444 non-redundant complete DuCV genomes from GenBank with the pairwise homoplasy index, a genetic algorithm for recombination detection (GARD) and a phylogenetic discordance score, and confirmed the 14 most discordant genomes with three independent breakpoint analyses, all reported in the numbering of one reference genome. Recombination signal was significant (p = 0.001), and GARD placed four breakpoints at positions 585, 971, 1141 and 1697. The 14 extreme genomes fell into four breakpoint signatures and, after grouping by shared breakpoints and parents, represent at most nine events, and the ten group 1 genomes are not one lineage. Breakpoints lay in the replicase gene (  rep  ), the capsid gene (  cap  ) and the intergenic regions. In 13 of the 14 genomes the two parental arcs came from different major clades, DuCV-1 and DuCV-2, so exchange crosses the deepest split in the species, and because breakpoints cut through  rep  , a clade call from  rep  was ambiguous in 12 of the 14 genomes and in none of the others. The data carry no clock-like signal (R² = 0.01), so the events cannot be dated. Selection on recombination-free parts of  rep  and  cap  was mostly purifying, with five candidate positively selected sites that survived stricter filtering. All 14 genomes are Sanger sequences without public raw reads, so the events should be confirmed from reads.
authors: Shil S, Debnath A.

title: Population genetics reveals adaptive signatures of Exidia glandulosa across diverse climates from China
abstract: Abstract    Background  Wood-decaying fungus  Exidia glandulosa  , as the type species of the genus  Exidia  , is widely distributed in China. However, the scarcity of genomic limits the development of subsequent resources mining and utilization. Results  Here, we firstly assembled the high-quality reference genome of  E. glandulosa  using third-generation and next-generation sequencing technologies, systematically analyzed the population structure and adaptive evolution characteristics of  E. glandulosa  across diverse climatic regions in China based on 78 samples. This assembled genome revealed an abnormally high level of genome heterozygosity, suggesting elevated ancestral genetic diversity or historical inter-lineage hybridization events. Population genetic analyses indicated that genetic differentiation among  E. glandulosa  populations, likely driven by regional climatic variations. Selection signal analysis suggested that temperate populations mainly responded to climate variations through enhancing signal transduction and stress responses, subtropical populations focused on energy metabolism, and plateau populations through multidirectional regulation of pathways including energy sensing, autophagy regulation, and DNA damage repair. Conclusions  This study elucidates the significant roles of climatic and geographic factors in driving population differentiation and local adaptation in  E. glandulosa  . The rich genetic diversity and flexible molecular regulation mechanisms identified here underpin its wide ecological distribution. Additionally, this work provides a valuable genomic resource for future  Exidia-  related omics research and contributes to birding the gap in studies on climate adaptability of wood-decaying fungi within the framework population genetics.
authors: Liu S, Zhao H, Li W, Ablat T, Wu F.

title: Qiliqiangxin Capsule ameliorates post-myocardial infarction heart failure: associations with gut microbiota remodeling, altered fecal short-chain fatty acid profiles, and myocardial HDAC3-associated histone acetylation and JNK/TGF-β-related signaling.
abstract: BackgroundQiliqiangxin Capsule (QLQX) is a guideline-recommended adjunctive therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, but mechanisms underlying post-myocardial infarction heart failure (post-MI HF) remain incompletely defined, particularly gut-heart microbial metabolism.PurposeThis study aimed to characterize the gut microbial and fecal short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) alterations associated with the cardioprotective effects of QLQX and to determine whether gut-associated factors contribute functionally to its therapeutic effects in post-MI HF.MethodsA rat model of post-MI HF was established by permanent ligation of the left anterior descending coronary artery. Cardiac function, ventricular remodeling, histopathological injury, and inflammatory indices were evaluated after QLQX treatment. An integrated analytical strategy comprising fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing, targeted fecal SCFA quantification, untargeted fecal and myocardial metabolomics, myocardial transcriptomics, and targeted protein analyses was used to characterize gut and cardiac responses. A publicly available human ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction transcriptomic dataset was included for exploratory pathway-level comparison. Spearman correlation analysis with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction was performed to examine associations among microbial taxa, SCFAs, inflammatory markers, and cardiac functional indices. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations were used to assess the structural plausibility of selected candidate interactions, and surface plasmon resonance (SPR) was performed to experimentally evaluate the predicted interaction between isobutyrate and JNK1. Antibiotic treatment and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) were further performed to evaluate the functional contribution and transferability of gut-associated fecal factors.ResultsQLQX improved cardiac dysfunction, adverse ventricular remodeling, myocardial injury, and inflammatory responses in post-MI HF rats. Treatment reshaped the fecal microbial community and altered the fecal SCFA profile, including restoration of butyrate and isobutyrate. Selected SCFAs and bacterial taxa were associated with inflammatory markers and cardiac functional indices. Integrated omics and protein analyses further showed that these gut-associated alterations were accompanied by coordinated changes in myocardial cAMP, nuclear HDAC3 abundance, histone H3 acetylation, AMPK/mTOR signaling, and JNK/TGF-β related molecular indices. SPR analysis further demonstrated concentration-dependent binding of isobutyrate to JNK1, with an equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) of 5.89 × 10⁻⁵ M. Antibiotic treatment attenuated the therapeutic response to QLQX, whereas FMT from QLQX-treated donors partially transferred the protective phenotype, supporting a functional contribution of fecally transferable gut-associated factors.ConclusionQLQX ameliorated post-MI HF in association with remodeling of the gut microbial ecosystem, alterations in fecal SCFA profiles, and coordinated myocardial metabolic, epigenetic, and stress-signaling responses. The antibiotic and FMT experiments suggest that gut-associated factors partly contribute to the cardioprotective effects of QLQX. Butyrate and isobutyrate emerged as prioritized candidate metabolites, with SPR providing direct binding evidence for the isobutyrate-JNK1 interaction, although their broader causal roles and myocardial exposure require further validation.
journal: Phytomedicine : international journal of phytotherapy and phytopharmacology
authors: Liu K, Liu Y, Wan H, He Y.

title: The SbNAC gene family in sorghum: Genomic characterization, functional diversity, and roles in abiotic stress responses.
abstract: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench) is an important cereal for water-limited environments, yet drought, salinity, and temperature extremes constrain its growth and productivity. The plant NAC transcription-factor family is named after NAM (No Apical Meristem), ATAF (Arabidopsis Transcription Activation Factor), and CUC (Cup-shaped Cotyledon). SbNAC (Sorghum bicolor NAC transcription factor genes) refers to the NAC family genes in sorghum. Genome-wide studies have characterized a diverse SbNAC family, although reported gene numbers differ among analyses using distinct genome annotations and identification criteria. Transcriptomic studies have documented SbNAC responses to drought, salinity, cold, and abscisic acid, with expression patterns varying by genotype, tissue, developmental stage, and sampling time. Functional evidence in sorghum is concentrated in a small number of genes: SbNAC2 has been linked to activation of the stress-responsive gene SbAP37, while manipulation of SbNAC9 alters drought-related traits, including photosynthetic performance, root development, and reactive oxygen species scavenging. Conversely, SbNAC56 overexpression has been associated with increased sensitivity to salt-, osmotic-, and hormone-related treatments during germination, highlighting context-dependent effects within the family. Multi-omics and network studies identify candidate pathways but do not alone establish direct SbNAC-mediated regulation. In this review, we synthesize previous genomic, expression, functional, and multi-omics studies of SbNACs, distinguish candidate responses from experimentally supported mechanisms, and identify priorities for validating their roles in sorghum stress adaptation and crop improvement.
authors: Seck EM, Sun R, Wang F, Rehman FU, Diack O, Kanfany G, Di P, Zhang J.

title: Alterations of fecal microbiome and metabolome in patients with diminished ovarian reserve.
abstract: Study questionAre there distinct variations in the gut microbiome and metabolism among infertile women diagnosed with diminished ovarian reserve (DOR), and how might the gut microbiome influence ovarian function?Summary answerIn DOR patients, Hoylesella abundance correlated with anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH)/antral follicle count (AFC), and stearic acid was identified as a key differential metabolite that was associated with activated PI3K-Akt signaling.What is known alreadyAccumulating evidence underscores the presence of a 'gut-ovary axis', highlighting a substantial interplay between the intestinal microbiome and ovarian function. However, the specific microbial and metabolic profiles characterizing infertile individuals with DOR remain largely uncharacterized.Study design, size, durationThis study was a cross-sectional observational study. We enrolled participants receiving frozen embryo transfer at the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University between 1 October 2024, and 31 December 2025. Each participant was limited to a single frozen embryo transfer within the study.Participants/materials, setting, methodsA total of 190 participants were included: 91 with DOR and 99 with normal ovarian reserve (NOR). Clinical information and stool specimens were collected from every subject. Sequencing of 16S rRNA and non-targeted metabolomics were implemented to characterize the gut microbiome and metabolome, respectively. Molecular docking analysis and network pharmacology were then implemented to screen for overlapping genetic targets among DOR-associated targets and key metabolite-targeted proteins.Main results and the role of chanceRelative to NOR controls, the DOR population exhibited significantly lower Gut Microbiota Health Index (P = 2.52 × 10-22) and higher Microbiota Dysbiosis Index (P = 8.31 × 10-10). The genus Hoylesella was significantly depleted in the DOR group (P = 0.018). Spearman analysis demonstrated that Hoylesella proportions were significantly positively correlated with AMH and AFC levels. Metabolomics analysis identified 243 differential metabolites across the study cohorts. Among these, four metabolites were associated with Hoylesella, and stearic acid exhibited high predictive performance (area under the curve = 0.89) for distinguishing DOR. Network pharmacology analysis of stearic acid and DOR identified five core targets: tumor necrosis factor, AKT serine/threonine kinase 1, SRC proto-oncogene, non-receptor tyrosine kinase (SRC), peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARG), and epidermal growth factor receptor. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathway enrichment indicated that the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway was the most significantly enriched.Large scale dataRaw 16S rRNA sequencing data have been deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive under BioProject accession PRJNA1444490. Untargeted metabolomics data have been deposited in MetaboLights under accession MTBLS14194.Limitations, reasons for cautionThe current investigation represents an initial effort to identify the alterations in intestinal microbes and associated metabolites in women with DOR-related infertility through 16S rRNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics; however, experimental validation of the underlying mechanisms is still missing. Furthermore, the metabolomics analysis in this study did not further stratify by age.Wider implications of the findingsThrough immunological dysregulation and inflammatory reactions, aberrant alterations in key intestinal microbes and metabolic products likely participate in the underlying mechanisms of DOR. These results provide direction for further research into the causal connections between important microbial species and metabolites in patients with DOR.FundingThis research was supported by grant 32271169 from the National Natural Science Foundation of China and the Henan Province Young and Middle-aged Health Science and Technology Innovation Leading Talent Project (Grant No. LJRC2024009).DisclosuresThe authors have no conflicts of interest.Trial registration numberN/A.
authors: Sun L, Li J, Zhu Y, Li D, Yin B, Kong H, Wang F, Guo Y, Zhang Y.

title: On the trail of novel bacteria: time to scale up the species description process.
abstract: Bacterial taxonomy provides a framework for classifying, naming, and identifying microbial diversity, yet the number of formally described bacterial species remains remarkably small compared with the vast bacterial diversity estimated to exist on Earth. The reasons for this include the historical difficulty of cultivating microorganisms and the traditional polyphasic taxonomy practice. Culturomics, that is, the combination of diverse cultivation conditions with high-throughput identification methods such as MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, has demonstrated that many bacteria previously considered uncultivable can, in fact, be isolated and characterized. Coupling culturomics with whole-genome sequence analysis paves the way for scaling up the species description process.
authors: Vandamme P, Wieme AD, Peeters C.

title: GeneFamHunter: annotation-independent recovery of divergent and tandemly arrayed gene-family members from genome assemblies
abstract: Motivation  Gene families expand by tandem duplication, diverge and decay, so their members are often missing, fragmented or fused in automated genome annotations, and divergent copies escape pairwise similarity searches. These challenges are particularly pronounced in non-model organisms, for which well-annotated genomes and reference proteomes are often unavailable, limiting the applicability of protein-based gene family recovery methods. Results  We developed GeneFamHunter to recover gene-family members directly from nucleotide assemblies. It searches continuous six-frame translations of overlapping genomic windows using four complementary domain- and profile-based methods, clusters hits while distinguishing tandem paralogs, predicts and validates gene models, and constructs gene trees. Across six Quest for Orthologs genomes, window-based HMMER searches recovered all 130 reference papain-like (C1A) loci, with 21 off-target hits, compared with 45 for stop-to-stop ORF searches; whole-contig HMMER searches recovered 108 (83.1%). With 11 distantly related queries, PSI-BLAST and DELTA-BLAST recovered all reference loci, whereas RPSTBLASTN recovered 98.5–99.2% and TBLASTN, as used by BITACORA, recovered 94.6– 95.4%. Across six mite genomes, GeneFamHunter recovered all 209 previously reported C1 loci and identified 37 additional candidate loci. In a separate comparison, it recovered all 128 reference UniProt C1A proteins and identified five additional loci without annotated gene models; OrthoFinder included 35 non-C1A proteins, whereas OMA recovered 98 reference proteins. Availability and implementation  GeneFamHunter is implemented in Bash for Linux and SLURM clusters and is freely available at  https://github.itap.purdue.edu/HeLab/GeneFamHunter (MIT license). Benchmark code and data:  https://github.itap.purdue.edu/HeLab/GeneFamHunter_benchmarks and Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23744704).  Supplementary information  Supplementary data are available at  Bioinformatics online.
authors: Klimov PB, He Q.
