title: Deterministic DNA-first discovery reveals recurrent genomic architectures
abstract: Genome mining typically begins with known genes or protein families, which can make systems defined primarily by genomic organization difficult to detect. We developed a DNA-first framework combining asymmetric-ovariance natural-vector representations with generic positional recurrence, joining separately calibrated signals through genomic coordinates. In benchmarks of array-associated reverse transcriptase (ART) loci, the target-free mathematical arm localized seven of eight predeclared loci, including all seven with exact-array coordinates. Dual-arm signals occurred in none of three non-array RT controls and in one of five UG27 systems, indicating selectivity within these small control sets. A separate profile-guided search of 6.12 Gb identified five candidate array-associated RT-like systems. In an independent 54.38-Gb evaluation of this profile-guided arm, structural compatibility was 24/32 under a historical-rule mirror, 12/32 after novelty-only selection, and 0/17 for architecture-selected complete ORFs; the two 32-member panels shared six exact sequences. Together, these results suggest that mathematical features of raw DNA can complement protein-directed searches in nominating genomic architectures for experimental RNA-to-DNA studies.
authors: Hu G, Wang H, Yau SS.

title: Detection, Genetic Characterization, and Evolutionary Analysis of Jingmen Tick Virus in Ticks from Border Regions of Yunnan Province, China
abstract: Abstract    Background  Jingmen tick virus (JMTV), an emerging tick-borne arbovirus of global public health concern, is a segmented positive-sense RNA virus assigned to the genus Flavivirus of the family Flaviviridae. Although JMTV has been detected in ticks and mammals across Asia, Africa, Europe, and the Americas, epidemiological data from the border regions of southwestern China remain limited. This study investigated the prevalence and genetic characteristics of JMTV in ticks collected from border areas of Yunnan Province, China. Methods  A total of 1,035 ticks infesting cattle were collected from five border regions of Yunnan (including Ruili and Malipo) between May 2024 and August 2025. Tick species were identified by PCR amplification and sequencing of the mitochondrial  COI  and 16S rDNA genes. JMTV was detected by RT-qPCR, and genetic and phylogenetic analyses were performed on near-full-genome sequences of positive samples; attempts were made to isolate the virus in Vero, BHK-21, and C6/36 cells and in Kunming mice. Results  Three tick species were identified:  Rhipicephalus microplus  ,  Haemaphysalis longicornis  , and  Haemaphysalis bispinosa  . The overall JMTV-positive rate was 70.82% (733/1,035), with JMTV detected exclusively in  R. microplus  ; the regional positive rates were 93.90% in Ruili and 71.33% in Malipo, a statistically significant difference (P R. microplus  along the China–Myanmar and China–Vietnam borders of Yunnan, posing a potential public health risk and providing epidemiological evidence to support local JMTV prevention and control. Because sampling was uneven across regions, more balanced future surveys are needed to refine regional epidemiological estimates.

title: Deciphering Viral Antigenic Relationships Through Antigenic Cartography: A Narrative Review
abstract: Background:  Antigenic cartography is a computational approach that quantitatively visualizes antigenic relationships among viral strains using serological data, including hemagglutination inhibition and virus-neutralization assays. Since its introduction in the early 2000s, it has substantially advanced the study of viral antigenic evolution by transforming complex serological measurements into interpretable antigenic maps, thereby facilitating assessment of antigenic diversity, immune escape, cross-reactivity, and vaccine–virus relationships. Objective: This review examines the historical development, methodological principles, applications, limitations, and emerging directions of antigenic cartography across clinically relevant viruses, with particular emphasis on its relevance to viral surveillance, antigenic drift monitoring and vaccine-strain selection. Methods: The literature was synthesized comparatively across major applications of antigenic cartography, encompassing human seasonal influenza and other viruses, including dengue, lyssaviruses, foot-and-mouth disease virus, Enterovirus A71, norovirus, rotavirus, SARS-CoV-2, and HIV. Particular attention was given to real-world applications, methodological advances, sources of uncertainty, and integration with genomic, structural, evolutionary, and computational approaches. Findings: Influenza remains the most extensively studied viral pathogen, where antigenic cartography has supported recognition of epidemiologically relevant antigenic transitions and informed vaccine decisions. Examples include the emergence of A/Fujian/411/2002-like H3N2 viruses during 2004–2005 and assessment of A/California/07/2009 during 2010–2011. Applications to other viruses demonstrate broader utility for characterizing antigenic landscapes and evaluating cross-protective immunity and vaccine performance. However, map reliability is influenced by serological assay variability, serum-panel composition, measurement noise, incomplete and geographically biased datasets. Limited inter-operability among serological, genomic, and structural datasets further restricts reproducibility and cross-study comparability. Future Directions and Conclusions: The field is transitioning from retrospective visualization toward predictive and mechanistically informed antigenic surveillance. Integration of artificial intelligence, protein language models, evolutionary modelling, structural vaccinology, and real-time genomic–serological surveillance could enable earlier prediction of antigenic drift, identification of emerging vaccine mismatches, and prioritization of candidate vaccine strains. Future platforms should incorporate standardized and automated serological measurements, inter-laboratory calibration, harmonized data standards, geographically representative datasets, experimental validation, and interpretable continuously updated models. Such integration could establish antigenic cartography as a scalable predictive framework for vaccine design and for strengthening preparedness against emerging viral threats.
authors: Biswas D, Subaschandrabose RK, Ningombam JD.

title: A heat-induced HagF-HrcA regulatory loop promotes chlamydial fitness and infectious progeny yield under stress.
abstract: Bacterial survival under environmental stress requires precise regulation of protein homeostasis, yet how this is achieved in organisms with streamlined genomes remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify HagF as a previously unrecognized protein that antagonizes the conserved heat-inducible transcriptional repressor HrcA in Chlamydia. Using genetic and biochemical approaches, including overexpression and CRISPRi-mediated knockdown, we show that under non-stressed conditions, HrcA represses hagF along with its five known targets, including hrcA and four chaperone genes. Upon heat stress, HagF is induced and binds HrcA, attenuating its repressor activity. This negative feedback loop enhances chaperone gene induction, particularly from the hrcA-grpE-dnaK operon, and promotes infectious elementary body yield. Notably, HagF is conserved across members of the order Chlamydiales, highlighting a lineage-specific adaptation. Together, these findings define a regulatory circuit in which a specialized antagonist modulates a widely conserved repressor, enabling Chlamydia to couple heat-responsive gene expression with developmental progression and enhance fitness under restrictive conditions.
authors: Huang Y, Wang Y, Pan M, Wan D, Wang L, Fondell JD, Wu X, Zhong G, Fan H.

title: Effect of continuous application of pig manure on soil antibiotic resistance genes.
abstract: The large-scale application of livestock and poultry manure in protected agriculture is common; however, research on the spread of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) from this practice remains limited. Herein, 16 S and metagenomic sequencing methods were used to investigate the effects of eight consecutive years of pig manure application on tetracycline (TC) antibiotics in protected soil and to evaluate the ecological consequences. In addition, the characteristics of soil ARGs and bacterial diversity were explored, and the potential hosts of ARGs in protected soil and the influence of environmental factors on these potential hosts and ARGs were preliminarily investigated. After 8 years of applying composted pig manure, the total tetracycline residues in the protected soil was as follows: commercial organic fertilizer soil > pig manure soil > rapeseed cake fertilizer soil. Soil enzymes indirectly affect ARG abundance by influencing the microbial community structure. g__unclassified_p__Acidobacteria and g__unclassified_c__Actinomycetia may be the two most important ARG hosts, with a highly significant positive correlation with 32 ARG subtypes. Total nitrogen (TN) and soil organic matter (SOM) significantly promoted the abundance of these two important potential hosts. Nocardioides, g__unclassified_o__Solirubrobacterales, Actinoplanes, and Methyloceanibacter are potential hosts for intI1. TC, Soil urease(S-UE), Soil acid phosphatase(ACP), Soil β-glucosidase(S-β-GC), TN, total phosphorus (TP), and SOM significantly promoted the abundance of potential intI1 hosts. Soil environmental factors collectively accounted for 72.27% of ARG variation, making them the most important factor affecting ARGs. Our research will support manure management in protected agriculture to reduce ARG spread.
journal: International microbiology : the official journal of the Spanish Society for Microbiology
authors: Wang L, ZHao J, Huang H, Yu X, Xu W.

title: Identification of Vibrio cholerae proteins that bind 3',3'-cyclic guanosine adenine dinucleotide.
abstract: Cyclic dinucleotides are used as signaling molecules in both antiphage defense and normal cellular functions. Horizontal gene transfer can introduce antiphage defense systems that encode specific signaling molecules into a new host. Whether these new signaling molecules interact with existing host signaling proteins and whether such interactions have evolutionary implications remain unknown. Vibrio cholerae represents an organism in which a new cyclic dinucleotide signaling molecule, 3',3'-cyclic guanosine adenine dinucleotide (3',3'-cGAMP) produced by DncV, is introduced by horizontal gene transfer of an antiphage system. 3',3'-cGAMP activates CapV phospholipase activity, leading to reduced growth and swim motility. To identify additional 3',3'-cGAMP-binding proteins, we performed a 3',3'-cGAMP-binding screen of the V. cholerae El Tor ORFeome. In addition to the expected 3',3'-cGAMP-binding proteins CapV and three V-cGAP proteins, this screen identified seven additional 3',3'-cGAMP-binding proteins that were previously found to bind c-di-GMP. These seven all bind to c-di-GMP with greater affinity, suggesting that these proteins do not bind 3',3'-cGAMP specifically. We assessed the function of 3',3'-cGAMP-binding proteins by testing the expression of DncV, CapV, or both in V. cholerae. Expression of DncV alone did not affect growth or swimming motility, in contrast to co-expression with CapV. In Escherichia coli, which lacks native 3',3'-cGAMP-signaling pathways, co-expression of CapV and DncV also led to reduced growth and swimming motility. In contrast, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which also lacks endogenous 3',3'-cGAMP, is less susceptible to CapV and DncV co-expression. Signaling nucleotides from antiphage systems primarily function in phage defense but have the potential to regulate other processes when the phage pressure subsides.IMPORTANCEIn this study, we systematically identified 3',3'-cGAMP-binding proteins in V. cholerae, which also uses the similar cyclic dinucleotide c-di-GMP for signaling. In addition to previously observed 3',3'-cGAMP-binding proteins, including 3',3'-cGAMP-activated phospholipase CapV and V-cGAP proteins, this screen identified seven new 3',3'-cGAMP-binding proteins that bound c-di-GMP as well. We found that both 3',3'-cGAMP production and CapV phospholipase activity were necessary and sufficient to inhibit growth and swimming motility as previously observed. In heterologous bacteria that use c-di-GMP but lack 3',3'-cGAMP-signaling pathways, 3',3'-cGAMP activation of CapV phospholipase was similarly required to inhibit growth and swimming motility as observed in V. cholerae. These results suggest that the acquisition of signaling nucleotides from antiphage systems may evolve to regulate cellular processes.
authors: Kim S-K, Carter JA, Park JH, Kung WC, Jiang X, Yildiz FH, Lee VT.

title: Antibiotic class shapes O-antigen-dependent phage outcomes in a clinical Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate.
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a high-priority opportunistic pathogen characterized by significant genetic plasticity and increasing multidrug resistance. Although phage-antibiotic combinations are increasingly explored to combat antimicrobial resistance, whether these interactions are synergistic or antagonistic and how different antibiotic classes influence phage replication and the subsequent development of resistance remain unclear. In this study, we examined combinations of the O-antigen-dependent phage phipa10 with amikacin (AMK), levofloxacin (LEV), or meropenem (MEM) against P. aeruginosa ZS-PA-35. At 24 h, the combinations showed antibiotic-dependent patterns of bacterial growth suppression. High concentrations of amikacin and meropenem reduced the extracellular yield of infectious phipa10. The highest tested levofloxacin concentration also reduced the recovered phage yield. Whole-genome sequencing of phage-resistant mutants showed that meropenem treatment drove large chromosomal deletions encompassing galU and hmgA, resulting in a characteristic brown pigmentation phenotype. LEV-selected isolates carried smaller deletions involving galU, whereas AMK-selected isolates shared a galU substitution. In a Galleria mellonella infection model, phipa10-antibiotic combinations improved host survival relative to either treatment alone, although the magnitude of the benefit varied across antibiotic classes. The meropenem combination yielded the highest observed survival proportion despite reduced phage yield in vitro. These results show that bacterial suppression, infectious phage yield, and resistance outcomes can diverge among the three tested antibiotic partners.IMPORTANCEPhage-antibiotic combinations may affect bacterial suppression, phage yield, and resistance-associated phenotypes differently. We compared three antibiotic partners in a single Pseudomonas aeruginosa-phage system. The observed growth, genetic, and larval survival outcomes varied across the tested treatments. Reduced phage yield did not preclude improved survival in the infection model. These observations support evaluating multiple outcomes when assessing a phage-antibiotic combination. Their broader relevance requires validation with additional isolates, phages, and antibiotics.
authors: Yang Y, Wu Y, Chen Z, Li N, Li D, Zhu B, Jin W, Wang K, Cheng Z, Pan J, Zhou C, Gao X, Lin J, Chen F, Bao R, Wang S, Shan Y, Hu B, Tan D, Hu L.

title: Sulfite disproportionation by Desulfotomaculum from marine sediments.
abstract: Sulfite disproportionation is a critical pathway of global sulfur cycle since primordial Earth, yet the microbial diversity underlying this process remains incompletely explored. Here, we report an autotrophic enrichment culture from marine sediments capable of producing both sulfate and sulfide by disproportionating sulfite. This culture was dominated (>95% relative abundance) by a novel bacterial strain closely related to Desulfotomaculum profundi. Genomic analysis revealed a complete pathway for dissimilatory sulfate reduction, which likely facilitates sulfite disproportionation by operating the enzymes for sulfate reduction to sulfite in reverse. Unlike the characterized species within the Desulfotomaculum genus, this highly enriched organism apparently lacked the physiological capacity to respire sulfate when tested with acetate and formate as electron donors, suggesting a specialized metabolic adaptation for sulfite disproportionation. Our findings represent the first experimental evidence linking sulfite disproportionation to the genus Desulfotomaculum. Given the widespread occurrence of functional genes across diverse ecosystems, we propose that Desulfotomaculum-mediated sulfite disproportionation is a biogeochemically significant yet underappreciated process in sulfur-enriched modern ecosystems.IMPORTANCEBacteria within the ubiquitous genus Desulfotomaculum (known as Desulfotomaculum subcluster Ia) are key actors in the sulfur cycle across diverse terrestrial and marine anoxic environments. Historically, cultivated strains have been characterized exclusively as sulfate reducers. Here, we expand the metabolic profile of this genus by characterizing a highly enriched Desulfotomaculum population capable of autotrophic sulfite disproportionation. In contrast to known Desulfotomaculum species, the enriched population showed no detectable sulfate reduction when tested with acetate or formate. These results indicate that Desulfotomaculum lineages can actively participate in sulfate formation and autotrophic carbon fixation, suggesting an expanded role in coupling the sulfur and carbon cycles across anoxic subsurface and sedimentary ecosystems.
authors: Su J-Y, Wu X-T, Bao P, Ren H-Y, Li S, Chen S-C.

title: Bacterial vaginosis as a polymicrobial biofilm ecosystem: microbial interactions, host responses and therapeutic challenges.
abstract: The vaginal mucosa is a hormonally responsive barrier ecosystem in which epithelial integrity, immune tone and microbial composition are interconnected. In eubiotic states, estrogen-supported, Lactobacillus-dominated communities help maintain low pH, reinforce epithelial barrier function and modulate mucosal immunity through lactic acid and antimicrobial metabolites. Disruption of this equilibrium can lead to bacterial vaginosis (BV), a polymicrobial dysbiosis characterized by depletion of lactobacilli and formation of structured biofilms adherent to the vaginal epithelium. Genomic, transcriptomic and metabolomic studies increasingly support the view that BV reflects a spatially organized, metabolically integrated biofilm network rather than simple bacterial overgrowth. Gardnerella species are considered key early colonizers, forming an epithelial scaffold that recruits secondary anaerobes. Interspecies cross-feeding, glycan degradation, amine production and density-dependent regulation contribute to biofilm maturation, antimicrobial tolerance and persistence. These biofilms degrade mucus and weaken epithelial integrity through cytolytic and enzymatic activities, triggering low-grade mucosal inflammation with limited neutrophilic infiltration, favoring recurrence and increasing susceptibility to sexually transmitted infections and adverse reproductive outcomes. This review examines the establishment and organization of BV-associated polymicrobial biofilms in bacterial vaginosis, key interspecies interactions and virulence mechanisms, experimental approaches used to study these communities and implications of biofilm persistence for recurrence and emerging therapeutic strategies.
authors: Bernard L, Baud D, Stojanov M.

title: Changes in the Gut Microbiota Composition and Metabolic Pathways in Six-Week-Old HIV Exposed Breastfed Infants Receiving Antiretroviral Prophylaxis.
abstract: IntroductionUnderstanding the association of HIV exposure, antiretroviral therapy (ART) prophylaxis and human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) on the gut microbiota of breastfed infants is crucial for developing strategies to promote infant health. Our study explored gut microbiota diversity and development in breastfed infants, analysing the influence of nevirapine (NVP) in HIV Exposed infants and HMOs in HIV Unexposed infants.MethodsInfants delivered vaginally and exclusively breastfed were recruited from City Council Clinics in Harare, Zimbabwe, at six weeks postpartum. A total of 110 infants were enrolled, and stool samples were collected for shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Dried blood spots from HIV-exposed infants were analyzed for nevirapine using HPLC-MS/MS, and breast milk from HIV-uninfected mothers was analyzed for human milk oligosaccharides using UPLC-MS. Of the collected samples, 93 stool specimens passed all bioinformatics quality filters. Alpha diversity and beta diversity were assessed, and associations between microbial diversity and HIV exposure, nevirapine levels, and HMO concentrations were evaluated using MaAsLin2.ResultsOur analysis showed no significant differences in microbial diversity across various NVP concentrations in HE infants or in 3'SL and 6'SL in the HU infants group (p ≥ 0.05). HIV exposure was associated with higher levels of Stenotrophomonas maltophilia and Mediterraneibacter faecis (corrected p-values 2.08×10-5 and 0.00246), respectively. Moreover, HIV exposure was linked to changes in specific metabolic pathways.ConclusionAlthough overall diversity remained stable across NVP concentrations in HE infants and HMO levels in HU infants, specific taxa and functional pathways differed by HIV exposure, highlighting that compositional and functional changes can occur independently of global diversity metrics. Therefore, HIV exposure itself may influence gut microbiota composition and metabolic functions at species level, particularly with an increased abundance of specific bacteria and altered metabolic pathways leading to disturbances in vitamin metabolism.
authors: Mudhluli TE, Nel Van Zyl K, Kujawska M, Mashingaidze-Mano R, Marsh CC, Chitsike I, Zia N, Manasa J, Hall LJ, Gomo E, Zhou DT.

title: Cross-Cohort Transcriptomic and Oral Microbiome Analyses Identify Ferroptosis-Associated Signatures in Periodontitis and Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma.
abstract: BackgroundPeriodontitis (PD) and oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) have been investigated in relation to inflammation, oral microbial alterations, and iron/redox biology. Whether ferroptosis-associated expression patterns overlap across independently sampled periodontal and cancer cohorts remains uncertain. We characterized these patterns without presuming that the available datasets represent matched individuals or a temporal disease sequence.MethodsWe analyzed gingival single-cell RNA-sequencing data (GSE171213), an OSCC discovery expression cohort (GSE30784), and an independent oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma validation cohort (GSE13601). Periodontal microbial functional gene profiles (GSE54290) and a cross-study OSCC 16S abundance resource were examined separately. Analyses included cell annotation, KEGG ferroptosis gene-set scoring, sample- and cell type-level comparisons, differential expression, external transcriptomic signature validation, microbial diversity and abundance analyses, and LPS-stimulated cell-line RT-qPCR and ELISA measurements. The transcriptomic and microbial cohorts were not linked at the individual-patient level.ResultsQuality control retained 34,342 cells from 12 gingival samples (four healthy controls [HCs], five PD, and three treated periodontitis [PDT]), assigned to 11 annotated cell populations. Mean sample-level ferroptosis gene-set scores were 0.081 in HC, 0.114 in PD, and 0.076 in PDT; these descriptive scores do not measure ferroptotic cell death. SAT1 showed a positive PD-versus-HC association in cell type pseudobulk analysis (log2 fold change, 0.546; false discovery rate [FDR], 0.012) and positive effects across all three transcriptomic cohorts. A discovery-derived ferroptosis-associated OSCC signature achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.933 in GSE13601. Periodontal functional profiling identified 25 advanced PD-associated annotations (FDR ConclusionsIndependently sampled periodontal and OSCC cohorts show ferroptosis-associated transcriptomic changes, with SAT1 emerging as a cross-cohort candidate. Parallel microbial datasets identify disease-associated functional gene and taxonomic differences but do not demonstrate within-patient host-microbe interactions or causal mediation. LPS-exposed cell-line measurements show expression changes in selected ferroptosis-associated markers, not ferroptotic cell death or functional resistance. The results are exploratory associations; in the absence of direct ferroptosis assays, paired longitudinal cohorts, and prospective clinical validation, they cannot establish a disease-progression mechanism, clinically deployable biomarker or therapeutic efficacy.
authors: Qiu C, She P, Wu L.

title: A hidden T-DNA-linked inversion-duplication is associated with a light-dependent Arabidopsis mutant phenotype.
abstract: Key messageA hidden T-DNA-linked genomic rearrangement alters gene dosage and exacerbates light-dependent phenotypes in Arabidopsis, highlighting the importance of structural genome validation for reliable interpretation of mutantphenotypes. T-DNA insertion mutants are widely used to study gene function, yet associated genomic alterations can confound phenotypic interpretation. We investigated mutants affecting mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase (MDH1) and heterodimeric NAD-dependent malic enzyme (ME1/ME2) under different photoperiods and irradiance regimes. Under long-day conditions, mutant combinations showed no major phenotypic differences from wild type. Under short-day, low-light conditions, mdh1.1 me2 mutants were markedly smaller than wild type and, unexpectedly, more severely affected than mdh1.1 me1 me2 triple mutants. ME1 was undetectable in mdh1.1 me2, indicating that both genotypes effectively lack heterodimeric NAD-ME. Whole-genome analysis identified a 137-kbp inverted duplication downstream of the MDH1 insertion in mdh1.1 me2, absent from the triple mutant. The original mdh1.1 population segregated for the severe phenotype, whereas an independent mdh1.2 allele did not reproduce it, linking the defect to the mdh1.1-associated rearrangement. The duplication increased gene dosage and transcript abundance, particularly under low light. Proteomics detected only five of 38 proteins encoded within the duplicated region, including phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase 1 (PEPC1). mdh1.1 me2 accumulated oxaloacetate-derived amino acids and exhibited altered carbon/nitrogen balance. These findings suggest that the duplication contributes to the phenotype, potentially through increased PEPC1 activity and consequent perturbation of carbon-nitrogen metabolism. However, interactions with MDH1 deficiency cannot be excluded, making PEPC1 a candidate contributor rather than the sole causal determinant. Our results highlight how T-DNA-linked structural variation can confound condition-dependent phenotypes and emphasize the need for structural validation of insertion loci, particularly given the widespread use of Agrobacterium-mediated DNA transfer in plant genome editing.
authors: Del Pilar Martinez M, de Oliveira JAVS, Nica I, Ditz N, Zheng K, Wewer V, Metzger S, Westhoff P, Eubel H, Finkemeier I, Schwarzländer M, Pucker B, Maurino VG.

title: Humic acid with manure promotes fungal necromass carbon accumulation in saline-alkali soils.
abstract: Microbial necromass carbon is increasingly recognized as a vital precursor for stable soil organic carbon (SOC). However, how diverse organic amendments regulate its accumulation and the underlying mechanisms in saline-alkali soils remains poorly understood. Based on a 4-year field experiment and an additional 13C-labeling incubation, we investigated the variation in fungal necromass carbon (FNC) and bacterial necromass carbon (BNC) under four organic amendments (organic manure (OM), organic manure plus crop straw (OM + CS), organic manure plus humic acid (OM + HA), and an unamended control). OM stimulated nitrogen mineralization through leucine aminopeptidase activity, while structural C sources in crop straw amendments (OM + CS) enhanced cellulolytic enzyme activities and biomass accumulation. In contrast, OM + HA upregulated N-acetyl-glucosaminidase at 0-20 cm and alkaline phosphatase activity at 20-40 cm, concurrently enriching K-strategist fungi (e.g., Basidiomycota) through deterministic assembly. This was accompanied by more complex, highly modular fungal networks. Glucose-derived C was preferentially retained in the FNC pool after 150 days, with 13C-labeling confirming FNC contributes 28.8%-30.4% of 13C-SOC versus merely 4.6%-4.7% for BNC. While OM + CS promoted necromass via biomass-enzyme co-enhancement, OM + HA synergizes enzyme-driven FNC/BNC co-transformation with K-strategist fungal enrichment and increased 13C-BNC efficiency by 19.0% versus OM. These findings highlight OM + HA as a promising strategy for promoting microbial necromass C accumulation in degraded saline-alkali ecosystems.

title: Tourmaline enhances nitrogen removal efficiency in partial Nitrification/Anammox systems via an adsorption Enrichment-Gene Regulation-Electron transfer triple mechanism.
abstract: The partial nitrification (PN) / anaerobic ammonium oxidation (anammox) coupled process offers distinct advantages, including reduced aeration energy consumption and elimination of organic carbon dependence. Nevertheless, its full-scale application faces several critical challenges, particularly the difficulty in sustaining a stable nitrite accumulation rate (NAR) during the PN stage, coupled with the inherently long doubling time of anaerobic ammonium oxidation bacteria (AnAOB) in the anammox stage. Natural tourmaline (Tur), a mineral distinguished by its unique physicochemical characteristics and potential for microbial regulation, provides a promising approach to overcoming these limitations. Experimental results indicated that Tur promoted the enrichment of functional microorganisms (e.g., Nitrosomonas) and the nitrogen removal efficiency (NRE) of the PN/Anammox_Tur system showed a relative increase of 14.77%. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations further demonstrated that the active sites on Tur surfaces exhibited selective adsorption affinity for key substrates-namely NH4+, NO2-, and O2-thereby providing a theoretical foundation for Tur-enhanced NRE in PN/Anammox system. Analysis of microbial community structure revealed that Tur induced a significant restructuring of the microbial consortium. Moreover, metagenomic analysis confirmed the directional reconstruction of metabolic gene networks and pathways, and elucidated the differential regulation of electron transport chains by Tur via its micro-electric field. This study proposed and refined a novel mechanistic framework-termed the "Adsorption Enrichment-Gene Regulation-Electron Transfer" triple mechanism-through which Tur enhances the NRE of the PN/Anammox system. These findings provide a theoretical basis for applying natural mineral materials, particularly tourmaline, advancing mineral-based materials for biological nitrogen removal and enhancing their engineering-scale implementation feasibility.
authors: Ren S, Yuan M, Qiu S, Jing B, Fu M, Jiang Z, Deng F.

title: Facilitating efficient anammox bacteria enrichment with loofah sponge: coupled roles of physical retention, slow-release carbon supply, and metabolic synergy.
abstract: Anaerobic ammonium oxidation (anammox) provides an energy-efficient and sustainable strategy for nitrogen removal. However, the slow growth and challenging enrichment of anaerobic ammonium-oxidizing bacteria (AnAOB) remain key constraints on its engineering application. In this study, the biodegradable biomass material loofah sponge was introduced into the system to enrich AnAOB from nitrification-denitrification sludge and achieve a rapid commencement of the anammox process. During the AnAOB maturation period, the system achieved TIN (Total Inorganic Nitrogen) and NH4+-N removal efficiencies of 66.8% and 99.6%, respectively. Extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) analysis indicated that biofilms formed on the loofah sponge exhibited a high protein-to-polysaccharide (PN/PS) ratio, thereby enhancing microbial aggregation and facilitating AnAOB enrichment. Analysis of the microbial community structure showed that the relative abundance of the key anammox genus Candidatus Brocadia in the loofah sponge significantly increased from 0.03% in the seed sludge to 17.07%. Metagenomic analysis detected genes associated with cellulose and hemicellulose degradation, while the effluent COD profile supported gradual loofah sponge biodegradation and soluble organic matter transformation. The loofah sponge also exhibited higher abundances of genes related to central carbon metabolism, the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway, and heme biosynthesis, indicating greater metabolic potential. Overall, AnAOB enrichment on loofah sponge may have resulted from the combined effects of physical biomass retention, gradual biodegradation, and associated microbial interactions. This study offers a feasible pathway for integrating agricultural waste valorization with low-carbon nitrogen removal and steers the anammox process toward greater economic and environmental sustainability.
authors: Ji J, Du J, Hu F, Wu G, Liu L, Wang L, Shen B, Wei X.

title: Engineering rhizosphere microbial consortia for soil bioremediation: Mechanisms, field constraints, and evidence-based design.
abstract: Soil contamination continues to threaten ecosystem health and agricultural productivity worldwide. However, rhizosphere-mediated bioremediation has emerged as a nature-inspired, sustainable approach for mitigating these impacts. This review advocates field-scale implementation of rhizosphere microbiome engineering by exploiting interactions among plants, microorganisms, and soil. Unlike previous reviews that primarily summarize rhizosphere-mediated remediation processes, it integrates mechanistic, ecological, and engineering perspectives to identify critical barriers limiting field performance. This review synthesizes recent advances in rhizosphere microbiome engineering, with an emphasis on root-exudate manipulation, synthetic microbial communities (SynComs), biochar-assisted remediation, and multi-omics technologies. The evidence reviewed indicates that root exudates are key regulators of microbial recruitment, biofilm formation, and expression of contaminant-degrading genes, while engineered microbial consortia enhance functional complementarity and pollutant transformation. A comparative analysis of laboratory and field studies reveals substantial performance gaps, with highly efficient degradation observed under controlled conditions often declining following field deployment because of microbial competition, environmental variability, and contaminant sorption dynamics. The review further shows that integration of SynComs with biochar carriers and precision root-exudate engineering can improve microbial establishment and remediation efficiency. Advances in metagenomics, metabolomics, and systems biology are enabling more predictive design and monitoring of rhizosphere processes. Collectively, this review provides a mechanistic synthesis, identifies key translational bottlenecks, and outlines practical directions for developing scalable rhizosphere-based remediation technologies.
journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
authors: Asemoloye MD.

title: Soil amendments reshape alpine meadow microbial communities across degradation gradients by modulating nutrient availability.
abstract: Climate change and overgrazing have led to the continued degradation of alpine meadows on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, thereby severely impairing the ecosystem services provided by these grasslands. Soil amendments are an important strategy for restoring degraded grasslands; however, the regulatory effects of different amendment measures across varying degradation gradients and the underlying microbial response mechanisms remain unclear. This study systematically investigated the effects of three soil amendments (humic acid, superabsorbent polymer, and Bacillus subtilis) on soil physicochemical properties and microbial community structure in mildly, moderately, and severely degraded alpine meadows. The results indicated that the regulatory effects of soil amendments are significantly dependent on the degradation gradient: In the severe degradation stage, amendments significantly increased available nutrients, lowered pH, and alleviated alkalization, whereas their regulatory effects were limited in the mild degradation stage. Amendments selectively altered the abundance of microbial groups involved in organic matter degradation, nitrogen cycling, and stress-tolerant symbiosis. Humic acid demonstrated the optimal regulatory effect in the mild degradation stage, whereas superabsorbent polymers and Bacillus subtilis were more suitable for restoration in the moderate and severe degradation stages. Redundancy analysis indicated that bacterial communities were primarily subject to deterministic selection by soil pH, available potassium, and organic matter gradients, with the intensity of environmental selection increasing with increasing degradation severity; fungal communities exhibited significant environmental responses only in the moderate degradation stage, while stochastic processes dominated community assembly in the mild and severe degradation stages. In summary, alpine meadows at various stages of degradation require differentiated remediation strategies. Precise, stage-specific remediation tailored to degradation severity can facilitate synergistic restoration of the soil-microbial system, providing a theoretical basis and practical guidance for restoring degraded alpine meadows on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.
authors: Wang N, Zhang Z, Zhou H, Wen Y, Wang X, Song H, Du Y.

title: Core effectors of the Fusarium pan-effectome contribute to host specificity.
abstract: Fusarium fungi cause economically important diseases of cereal crops, including Fusarium head blight, ear blight, and root rot. Central to these interactions are secreted effector proteins that manipulate host biology to promote infection. In turn, plants have evolved to recognize effector activity to activate immune responses and restrict disease. Despite their importance, the diversity, conservation, and evolution of Fusarium effectors remain poorly understood. Here, we present the Fusarium sambucinum Species complex Effector Compendium (FUSEC), a sequence-defined pan-effectome constructed from 188 high-quality genomes representing 27 species. FUSEC comprises 4,057 sequence-defined effector families, including a conserved soft-core repertoire of 235 families present in at least 95% of isolates. Structure-guided comparisons reorganized these conserved families into 184 structure-defined groups, revealing relationships that extend beyond sequence similarity and identifying similarities to numerous experimentally characterized fungal (a)virulence factors. Despite their broad conservation, soft-core families exhibited substantial within-family sequence diversity, and analyses of diversifying selection identified 44 candidate families undergoing adaptive evolution. Functional screening revealed that the majority of these candidates altered wheat immune responses, and CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene deletions in Fusarium graminearum demonstrated that multiple conserved effectors contribute to cultivar-dependent Fusarium head blight severity.

title: Genetic Characterization of Avian Influenza H14 Viruses in Guangdong, China: Evidence of Intercontinental Transmission and Reassortment in the East Asian-Australasian Flyway.
abstract: AbstractH14 avian influenza viruses (AIVs) are rare, with limited data on their circulation in mainland China. This study investigated the ecological origins and zoonotic potential of H14 viruses in southern China. Active surveillance was conducted in Guangdong (2022-2025). The isolates underwent full-genome sequencing and phylogenetic analysis. Receptor binding specificity for avian- and human-type receptors was evaluated using a solid-phase assay. In vitro replication was assessed in avian, mammalian, and human cell lines. In vivo pathogenicity was evaluated in mice. In this study, four H14 AIVs (one H14N6, two H14N7, and one H14N8) were isolated. We identified a novel H14 transmission network involving Mareca penelope and multiple shorebird species (Tringa, Himantopus), suggesting a multihost dispersal mechanism. Phylogenetically, the Guangdong isolates formed a distinct subclade within the Eurasian lineage, closely related to strains from Russia and Cambodia. Importantly, the three isolates (SZ3742/H14N6, ZJ3523/H14N7, and SZ3536/H14N8) exhibited dual receptor-binding specificity, recognising both avian-type (α-2,3) and human-type (α-2,6) sialic acids. Replication in human A549 cells was strain-dependent: SZ3742/H14N6 reached a peak titre comparable to that in DF-1 cells but lower than that in MDCK cells, whereas ZJ3523/H14N7 and SZ3536/H14N8 reached lower peak titres than in both reference cell lines. All three tested isolates replicated transiently at low titers in mouse lungs with limited viral pathogenicity, despite reduced fitness in human A549 cells. Molecular characterization revealed key mammalian adaptation markers and a typical HA cleavage site motif (PDKQTR↓GLF). This study provides the first evidence of H14 AIV circulation in Guangdong Province, China. The virus demonstrates a broad host range in migratory birds and possesses genetic markers associated with mammalian adaptation, highlighting the need for increased surveillance in the East Asian‒Australasian Flyway.
authors: Liu J, Li Y, Huang R, Yao Q, Yang Q, Shen X, Ge Y, Gao Y.

title: Biosensor-guided genome-wide CRISPR screens enable  cis  ,  cis  -muconic acid overproduction in yeast
abstract: ABSTRACT  Classical pathway metabolic engineering relies on enhancing strain productivity through the introduction of rationally identified genetic perturbations, which while useful, are time-consuming and miss unintuitive targets. Genome-wide CRISPR screens offer an alternative by efficiently sampling genomes, enabling the engineering of novel phenotypes, and are further enhanced when combined with high-throughput strain interrogation methods. Here, using  Saccharomyces cerevisiae , we engineered small molecule biosensors into population enrichment tools using zeocin resistance and fluorescence as signal outputs. We then introduced the multi-functional genome-wide CRISPR (MAGIC) library that targets every gene for activation, interference, or deletion, thus creating biosensor-aided MAGIC, or senMAGIC. As a case study, we utilized senMAGIC to identify single genetic determinants that improve productivity of the nylon precursors protocatechuic and  cis ,  cis -muconic acids (PCA and ccM). These were then randomly assembled as triple gRNA-tRNA arrays for multiplexed gene perturbations to identify combinatorial effects. Top gRNA hits were then confirmed using direct genomic integrations in senMAGIC-free production strains, resulting in identifying known as well as novel targets that increase PCA and ccM titres. Our results demonstrate senMAGIC as a robust automation-friendly whole-genome evolution tool and highlight limitations of the method, providing a roadmap for future multifunctional CRISPR screens to optimize host metabolism for efficient bioprocesses.
authors: Nasr MA, Knoops A, Thornbury M, Davies M, Kwan DH, Martin VJ.

title: Resurrecting host–microbiome interactions: combining resurrection ecology and microbiome transplants to test temporal local adaptation
abstract: Host-associated microbiomes can influence fitness, respond rapidly to environmental change, and potentially contribute to host adaptation. Yet, determining whether host–microbiome associations evolve adaptively over ecological timescales remains challenging because historical host genotypes and their associated microbial communities are rarely available for experimental comparison. Resurrection ecology offers a means of recovering historical host genotypes from dormant propagules, while microbiome transplantation provides an experimental approach for testing the effects of microbial communities on host performance. Combining these approaches could enable direct tests of temporal local adaptation in host–microbiome associations. Freshwater Daphnia provide a promising model because their dormant eggs can persist in lake sediments, allowing historical host genotypes to be resurrected. However, the microbiota associated with dormant eggs may originate from multiple sources, including ancestral hosts, lake water, and surrounding sediment, complicating the recovery of historically associated microbial communities. We outline a framework combining sediment archives, host resurrection, microbiome characterisation, and reciprocal transplantation experiments to test whether historical and contemporary hosts perform better with microbiomes from their respective time periods. We discuss the conceptual predictions, methodological challenges, and experimental controls required to distinguish temporal local adaptation from microbial environmental effects, host-genotype specificity, and changes in community composition. This framework could extend resurrection ecology beyond host evolution to experimentally investigate the historical evolution of host–microbiome interactions.
authors: Paplauskas S, Frisch D.

title: Direct whole-plastome alignment systematically inflates long-branch artifacts in chloroplast phylogenomics: a 468-paper audit and three-method reanalysis
abstract: Abstract  Plastid genomes are the workhorse of plant phylogenomics, but their quadripartite structure, inverted-repeat (IR) and small single-copy (SSC) orientation changes, gene rearrangements and length-variable noncoding regions make direct whole-plastome multiple sequence alignment (MSA) problematic. We audited 468 chloroplast/plastid genome papers published in Mitochondrial DNA Part B between October 2023 and October 2026, extracted their materials and methods, and flagged 53 papers with suspicious long branches or topology. Each candidate was reanalyzed with three independent strategies: (C) whole-genome MAFFT + trimAl + IQ-TREE, mimicking the common published workflow; (A) SibeliaZ locally collinear blocks (LCBs) concatenated and analyzed with a patched RAxML-NG implementing T92+F+FreeRate (2-10 categories, BIC-selected); and (B) single-copy orthologs + IQ-TREE TESTMERGE. We compared Robinson-Foulds distances and branch-length diagnostics across methods and manually reviewed every case against the published tree. Thirty-six papers were strict positives: the published long branch was reproduced by C and disappeared or shortened under A/B, giving a confirmed positivity rate of 7.69% (95% CI 5.61-10.47%; 10.75% among 335 branch-length-auditable papers); 34 of the 36 (94.4%) had used direct whole-plastome MSA in the original materials and methods, including one case with an ambiguous figure legend that we mark with an asterisk and test separately. The remaining candidates comprised eight CDS/PCG-based studies, six whole-genome cases attributable to local-clock or genuine rate heterogeneity, and three negatives, one of which was reclassified after re-review. A BLAST screen of the 24 positives that lacked SSC/IR assays, plus a LASTAL re-check of the nine whose original assays were negative, attributed 16 additional cases to SSC orientation discordance and 16 to complex rearrangement; all 36 positives now have a structural attribution. Positivity was 20.0% in 2023 and approximately 6.7% in 2024-2026. All 36 positives deposited supplementary material, but none deposited a machine-readable alignment, partition scheme or tree topology. Direct whole-plastome MSA is therefore not a neutral shortcut: in this corpus it systematically inflates long branches, and distance-matrix residuals localize the effect to the curated long-branch taxa (26/27 C-A and 25/27 C-B comparisons; A-B shows no directional difference). Shared alignment errors can also produce supported clades when several close relatives carry the same structural variant, so topology alone is not a safeguard. It is not the only cause of long branches; routine locus extraction, LCB- or ortholog-aware alignment, alignment inspection, and explicit rooting/IR-SSC checks are required to separate alignment artifacts from biological rate variation.
authors: Xu Z.

title: SwinePan for pig graph-based pangenome and multiomics data mining.
abstract: Pigs are one of the most important livestock species worldwide. Although multiple high-quality reference genomes exist, reliance on a single linear reference limits the detection of structural variants (SVs) and the characterization of population-specific genetic diversity. To address this limitation, we developed SwinePan, a comprehensive and integrated multiomic database for pigs built on a graph-based pangenome framework. SwinePan incorporates a variome derived from the graph-based pangenome, covering 2598 individuals across 35 breeds, including 185,759 SVs, 117 million SNPs, and 6.8 million indels. The database also integrates transcriptomic data from liver, loin muscle, abdominal fat, and backfat, along with more than 150,000 phenotypic records. The online toolkit deployed in SwinePan enables genome-wide association studies (GWAS), expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) mapping, and colocalization, whereas interactive modules visualize population structure and multiomic associations, streamlining candidate gene and variant exploration. Additionally, two proof-of-concept analyses demonstrate how SwinePan pinpoints trait-associated loci and deciphers their potential regulatory mechanisms.
authors: Lin M, Liu L, Cai G, Huang S, Qiu Y, Yao Z, Deng S, Wang S, Liu Y, Ruan D, Zhou F, Wu J, Zhang Z, Zheng E, Yang J, Wu Z.

title: Iron-associated functional differentiation between granules and flocs enhances resilience and phosphorus recovery in a CEPT-PDA treating low-strength wastewater.
abstract: Carbon fluctuations destabilize microbial ecosystems by disrupting metabolic interactions, yet how community heterogeneity drives resilience remains unclear. Using a CEPT-PDA system, we show that iron associates functional differentiation between granules and flocs under alternating COD disturbances. High‑COD shocks allowed recovery within 5-7 days, whereas low‑COD starvation required 12-15 days. Iron accelerated recovery, achieving NH4+‑N (99.1%), PO43-‑P (70.0%), and TN (99.2%) average removal rate. Mechanistically, iron promoted niche differentiation: granules sustained anammox (Candidatus. Brocadia, 33.3%), while flocs supported denitrification (Thauera, 50.1%). Metagenomics revealed distinct Fe utilization: granules enhanced Fe(II) transport, flocs enriched Fe(III) uptake, iron-sulfur cluster assembly, and denitrification-related pathways. Iron also sequestered P as ferric phosphate and vivianite. Thus, iron acts as an ecological regulator that reorganizes microbial resource use and spatial functional differentiation, enhancing resilience to carbon fluctuations while enabling nutrient removal and recovery.
authors: Sun X, Tang M, Gu P, Cao S, Du R, Peng Y.

title: BAHD acyltransferase ApAT2 catalyzes the acetylation of protostane-type tetracyclic triterpenes in Alisma plantago-aquatica.
abstract: Alisma plantago-aquatica L. is a traditional Chinese medicinal herb used to treat urinary disorders. Acylated protostane-type tetracyclic triterpenes such as alisol B 23-acetate and alisol C 23-acetate are its major bioactive components and have been reported to exhibit improved antiviral activities. However, the content of these compounds is relatively low in plants, and the enzyme that catalyzes this acetylation process has not yet been identified. In this study, we constructed a transcriptome dataset for A. plantago-aquatica. Using co-expression analysis and enzyme activity screening, we successfully identified a benzyl alcohol O-acetyltransferase, anthocyanin O-hydroxycinnamoyltransferase, anthranilate N-hydroxycinnamoyl/benzoyltransferase, deacetylvindoline 4-O-acetyltransferase (BAHD), ApAT2. This enzyme catalyzes the acetylation of alisol B and alisol C but does not exhibit any catalytic activity toward alisol A. Molecular docking and site-directed mutagenesis confirmed that the M412 residue of ApAT2 played a critical role in its substrate specificity. Phylogenetic analysis suggests that the active pocket of ApAT2 possibly diverged via lineage-specific evolution, conferring specificity for protostane-type tetracyclic triterpenes. Furthermore, we established a semi-biosynthetic platform in Escherichia coli expressing ApAT2 to produce alisol B 23-acetate from alisol B. In conclusion, we identified the BAHD enzyme responsible for the acetylation of protostane-type tetracyclic triterpenes, thus providing new systems to produce these valuable compounds. We also identified a new molecular basis for the recognition and modification of diverse substrates by the BAHD family during plant evolution.
authors: Zhu S, Cui M, Li B, Chen J, Chen Q, Pei T, Fang Y, Liu J, Kong Y, Li J, Cao Y, Bai F, Wang H, Fu R, Zhang Y, Zhao Q.

title: Identification and functional characterization of pineapple AcGPX5 in oxidative stress response.
abstract: Pineapple (Ananas comosus), a globally significant crop, stands as the world's third most important tropical fruit. Throughout its extensive domestication history, mitotic recombination has contributed to the formation of terminal homozygosity regions on chromosomes. However, the functional genomic landscape and biological significance of these regions remain largely unexplored. In this study, we systematically investigated these regions. Functional enrichment analyses revealed that genes residing within these regions are predominantly associated with critical biochemical processes, including ADP binding, oxidoreductase activity, response to oxidative stress, and the catabolic metabolism of macromolecules. Utilizing transcriptomic profiling across fruit developmental stages, we classified these genes into five distinct clusters, each exhibiting unique expression patterns. Notably, genes within these clusters showed significant transcriptional dynamics during fruit ripening, suggesting a coordinated regulatory role in this process. Among these genes, AcGPX5, a cluster 1 gene, was identified as a strong candidate because of its markedly high expression levels during fruit development. To elucidate its functional role, we characterized AcGPX5 in terms of sequence architecture, predicted protein structure, and subcellular localization. Additionally, we conducted preliminary functional validation through enzyme activity assays and transgenic experiments. The enzyme activity assays confirmed that recombinant AcGPX5 possesses thioredoxin-dependent glutathione peroxidase activity, while multiple transgenic assays demonstrated that AcGPX5 plays an essential role in plant oxidative stress resistance. Collectively, this study identifies a set of ripening-related candidate genes embedded in chromosome terminal homozygosity regions and functionally characterizes AcGPX5 as a representative member. These findings advance our understanding of pineapple genome evolution and domestication and provide an experimental basis for exploiting these unique genetic resources in crop improvement.
authors: Guo LN, Liu BQ, Liu YY, Nie L, Liu XX, Li X, Fu BL, Chen LY.

title: In silico characterization of copy number variation (CNVS) in Renibacterium salmoninarum genomes from farmed salmonids.
abstract: Renibacterium salmoninarum is a highly clonal intracellular pathogen responsible for bacterial kidney disease (BKD) in salmonids. Although previous studies have demonstrated limited genomic diversity within this species, the contribution of copy number variations (CNVs) to its genomic variability remains poorly understood. Here, we analyzed CNVs in 41 Chilean R. salmoninarum isolates recovered from Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar), Rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) and Coho salmon (Oncorhynchus kisutch) hosts using short-read sequencing data mapped against the genome of the type strain ATCC 33209. CNVs were detected throughout the chromosome and comprised both duplications and deletions. While the overall CNV burden was not significantly associated with lineage, geographic origin, or year of isolation, CNV profiles differed significantly between host genera. Specifically, duplications were more frequent among isolates recovered from Oncorhynchus spp., whereas deletions occurred more frequently in isolates derived from S. salar. Functional annotation identified host-associated genomic differentiation in CNV patterns, including variation affecting the dCTP deaminase gene, which plays a key role in nucleotide metabolism. Collectively, these findings reveal that CNVs constitute an additional source of genomic variation in R. salmoninarum and highlight patterns of host-associated genomic differentiation whose biological significance remains to be determined.
journal: Comparative biochemistry and physiology. Part D, Genomics & proteomics
authors: Sandoval A, Avendaño-Herrera R, Gallardo-Escárate C, Valenzuela-Miranda D.

title: Computational identification of EBNA1-binding candidates using machine learning-based virtual screening and molecular docking.
abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is associated with several malignancies and multiple sclerosis, and Epstein-Barr nuclear antigen 1 (EBNA1) plays an essential role in viral genome replication and episome maintenance. The experimentally characterized KVD-associated pocket within the EBNA1 DNA-binding domain provides a structurally defined site for computational ligand prioritization. This study aimed to identify and prioritize predicted EBNA1-binding candidates using an integrated machine-learning and structure-based virtual screening framework. A PubChem EBNA1 bioactivity dataset comprising 304,124 records was curated to obtain 4,584 unique compounds. Molecular representation combined 1,024-bit Morgan fingerprints with 11 RDKit molecular descriptors. Random Forest, SVM-RBF, Logistic Regression, and XGBoost models were evaluated using scaffold-based independent testing. The optimized XGBoost model was applied to a non-overlapping DrugBank library of 12,287 compounds. Compounds with predicted activity probabilities ≥0.5 were subjected to Lipinski-based filtering, followed by molecular docking against the KVD-associated binding pocket of EBNA1 (PDB ID: 6NPM). Docking validation was performed by independent KVD redocking at exhaustiveness values of 8, 16, and 32. Post-docking candidates were further evaluated using PAINS, aggregation, frequent-hitter/promiscuity, assay-interference, redox-associated structural-alert, and ADMET assessments. XGBoost demonstrated the highest test-set ROC-AUC (0.835), PR-AUC (0.408), and best Brier score (0.067), and was selected for virtual screening. Screening identified 116 compounds above the probability threshold, of which 40 satisfied Lipinski criteria and were docked. Thirty-two compounds achieved docking scores ≤ -7.0 kcal/mol. Sequential liability assessment and integrated prioritization identified 10 computationally prioritized EBNA1-binding candidates with favorable combined machine-learning, docking, and structural-filter profiles. The integrated computational framework enabled systematic prioritization of structurally diverse predicted EBNA1-binding candidates for further experimental investigation. The identified candidates represent computationally prioritized molecules for subsequent biochemical and functional evaluation of EBNA1 binding and activity and should not be interpreted as experimentally validated antiviral or disease-modifying agents.Graphical abstractVirtual screening for drug discovery using trained ML model for EBNA1 protein, Molecular Docking, and ADMET analysis.
authors: Pauskar AP, Natarajan E.

title: Integrative transcriptomic and gut microbiota analysis reveals thermal stress-induced physiological regulation in the narrow-clawed crayfish Pontastacus leptodactylus.
abstract: This study systematically investigated the effects of acute temperature stress on transcriptional levels and gut microbiota in the narrow clawed crayfish (Pontastacus leptodactylus). GO enrichment analysis showed that upregulated genes were significantly enriched in biological process terms (chitin-based cuticle development, vacuolar acidification, and lysosomal lumen acidification), the cellular component term sarcomere, and molecular function terms (structural constituent of cuticle and proton channel activity). In contrast, downregulated genes were primarily associated with normal growth and development, exoskeleton mineralisation, and enzymatic degradation processes, such as molting cycle, chitin breakdown, and skeletal mineralisation, indicating suppression of routine physiological activities under stress conditions. KEGG pathway analysis further showed that upregulated genes were significantly enriched in apoptosis, gap junctions, mTOR signaling, and Toll like receptor pathways, reflecting activation of cellular defense and immune regulatory networks. In contrast, downregulated genes were mainly enriched in oxidative phosphorylation and thermogenesis, suggesting impaired mitochondrial energy metabolism. RT-qPCR validation of 14 representative DEGs strongly agreed with transcriptomic data, confirming the results' reliability. Meanwhile, alpha-diversity analysis of the gut microbiota revealed numerically higher Chao1 and observed species richness estimates but lower Simpson and Shannon diversity indices under acute temperature stress, although none of these differences reached statistical significance (all P > 0.05). At the genus level, acute temperature stress substantially increased the relative abundances of Hafnia-Obesumbacterium, Enterobacter, and Raoultella, while dominant genera such as Prevotella and Agathobacter declined significantly, as confirmed by LEfSe analysis. Functional prediction results indicated a significant increase in proportions of biofilm formation, stress tolerance, and potentially pathogenic bacterial phenotypes in the stressed group, along with notable reductions in the relative abundances of multiple KEGG orthologs and COG functional categories, suggesting a reduction in predicted gut microbial functional potential. Overall, acute temperature increased profoundly reshaped the transcriptional expression profile and intestinal microecological structure of the narrow-clawed crayfish, providing essential molecular and microbiological insights into its adaptive mechanisms to acute high temperature.
authors: Li Y, Tay YJ, Han M, Yao Z, Li B, Lv M, Li Y, Gao P, Cheng Z, Lai Q.

title: Genome-wide selection signatures in Turkish Awassi sheep: uncovering the genetic basis of production traits and adaptation.
abstract: The Awassi sheep is one of the leading fat-tailed breeds of the Fertile Crescent, known for its high milk yield and resilience in arid and semi-arid environments. Despite its socio-economic importance, a high-resolution genomic characterization of selection signatures in Turkish Awassi populations remains limited. This study aimed to investigate the genomic diversity, demographic history, and selection signatures of Turkish Awassi sheep using double-digest restriction-site-associated DNA sequencing (ddRADseq). Genome-wide single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) discovery was performed on 40 unrelated Awassi sheep. Genetic diversity parameters, historical effective population size ( Ne ), and linkage disequilibrium (LD) decay were assessed. Selection signatures were identified using both runs of homozygosity (ROH) islands and Tajima's D analyses, followed by functional annotation of candidate genes. A total of 397 315 high-quality SNPs were identified. The average minor allele frequency (MAF) was 0.333, and the ROH-based inbreeding coefficient ( FROH ) was low (0.025), indicating high genetic integrity. The historical Ne showed a consistent decline, reaching 147 in the most recent generations. Selection signature analysis identified 21 and 48 protein-coding genes by means of ROH and Tajima's D , respectively. The key candidate genes were associated with milk yield and lactation (AKR1C3, AKR1D1, OXT, AVP, ZNF131), meat production and growth (PBX1, KBTBD8, HOXA cluster, ADGB), fat-tail formation (HOXA cluster, HMGCS1, STARD4), and environmental adaptation (ABCB1, TSLP, IL6). Our findings reveal that the Turkish Awassi genome is a rich genetic reservoir shaped by combined natural and artificial selection. The selection signatures identified in this study provide fundamental genomic targets for future breeding strategies to enhance productivity without compromising environmental resilience. These findings support the use of Turkish Awassi as a genetic resource for breeding programs in arid and semi-arid production systems.
authors: Meydan H, Demir E, Bilginer Ü, Doğru H, Kaya S, Argun Karsli B, Aktaş Y, Atmaca V, Perini F, Karsli T.

title: A gut symbiotic bacterium enhances baculovirus resistance in Spodoptera frugiperda by maintaining peritrophic matrix integrity.
abstract: BackgroundSpodoptera frugiperda is a major agricultural pest worldwide, whereas Spodoptera frugiperda multiple nucleopolyhedrovirus (SfMNPV) serves as an important microbial control agent against this pest. Resident gut bacteria are increasingly recognized as important modulators of insect-pathogen interactions; however, whether and how they influence SfMNPV infection in S. frugiperda remains unclear. We therefore investigated how gut bacteria modulate host resistance to SfMNPV.ResultsAntibiotic-mediated depletion of gut bacteria increased larval susceptibility to SfMNPV. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed that gut bacterial depletion downregulated midgut genes associated with immune defense, digestive functions and peritrophic matrix (PM) maintenance. Among seven culturable midgut bacterial isolates, reinoculation with Glutamicibacter soli significantly enhanced larval resistance to SfMNPV. Pre-feeding with either the G. soli culture supernatant or cell lysis precipitate also increased larval resistance and partially reversed transcriptional changes caused by gut bacterial depletion before viral challenge, including the downregulation of peritrophin-1. RNAi-mediated silencing of peritrophin-1 disrupted PM structure, increased PM permeability, and enhanced larval susceptibility to SfMNPV. Consistently, G. soli reinoculation restored PM integrity impaired by gut bacterial depletion.ConclusionThese findings identify maintenance of PM integrity as an important mechanism contributing to gut symbiotic bacterium-mediated resistance to SfMNPV. The study advances our understanding of how gut bacteria influence baculovirus infection in insect hosts and provides potential microbial and molecular targets for improving baculovirus-based pest management. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
authors: Guo L, Jin W, Kang Q, Tong Y, Shi H, Zhang J, Li X, Wang H, Qin Q, Meng Q, Zhang H.

title: A RecBCD-like enzyme regulates expression of bacterial defense operons in response to DNA damage
abstract: ABSTRACT  Bacteria must quickly respond to stress signals including bacteriophage (phage) infection, invasion by mobile genetic elements, and other threats. DNA damage is a stress-signaling nexus in bacteria, initiating global responses such as the SOS response and triggering expression of specific defense and immune pathways through DNA damage-sensing transcriptional regulators. Here we identify a three-protein pathway termed Cerberus that senses dsDNA ends that become available during DNA damage or inhibition of the key DNA repair complex RecBCD, and controls expression of an associated defense/immune operon. The central player in Cerberus is a large peptidase-helicase-nuclease fusion protein, CerC, that is architecturally similar to the RecBC complex itself. Upon DNA damage or RecBCD inhibition, CerC binds and unwinds free DNA ends to allosterically activate its fused HExxH metallopeptidase domain. CerC specifically cleaves the adjacently encoded anti-sigma factor CerB to release its cognate sigma factor CerA, allowing CerA to mediate transcription of a defense/immune operon encoded nearby. Cerberus therefore represents a pathway that has co-opted a key DNA repair machine for DNA damage sensing, and linked that activity to transcriptional control through anti-sigma factor cleavage.
authors: Chambers LR, Patel KM, Gong M, Basu D, Tian E, Ouderkirk SN, Zhou Y, Ye Q, Pham BQ, Mishanina TV, Whiteley AT, Corbett KD.

title: Molecular and Structural Characterisation of the MERS-Coronavirus Polymerase
abstract: MERS-CoV (Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus) belongs to the  Betacoronavirus genus, which also includes SARS-CoV-2, the causative agent of the COVID-19 pandemic. MERS-CoV is the pathogen responsible for Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS), a respiratory disease with a 36.5% case fatality rate. Given the capacity of coronaviruses for genetic recombination and mutation, MERS-CoV remains a pathogen of significant pandemic potential, with viral evolution potentially facilitating enhanced adaptation and transmission in humans. There are no approved treatments for MERS-CoV infection. The MERS-CoV replication-transcription complex (RTC), a multimeric protein complex key to genome amplification, has no cellular analogues and a highly conserved sequence, making it a useful target for antiviral compounds; however, structural and biochemical characterisation of the MERS-CoV RTC is limited. Here, we characterise the minimal MERS-CoV RTC using in vitro and single-molecule assays and show that it is susceptible to the RNA-dependent-RNA-polymerase inhibitor suramin. We present a structure of the minimal MERS-CoV RTC in complex with an RNA duplex, which shows strong structural similarity to the SARS-CoV-2 RTC. We use cross-subunit swapping experiments to show that the MERS-CoV NSP12 core can efficiently utilise SARS-CoV-2 cofactors NSP7 and NSP8, whereas SARS-CoV-2 NSP12 exhibits reduced in vitro activity with the MERS-CoV NSP8. This asymmetric cross-species compatibility highlights both the evolutionary conservation and virus-specific adaptation of coronavirus polymerase-cofactor interactions. Together, these findings provide a structural and mechanistic framework for understanding MERS-CoV RNA synthesis and establish its conserved RTC as a potential target for the development of broadly acting coronavirus antivirals.  Significance Statement  Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) causes severe respiratory disease and represents a significant pandemic threat because of the capacity of coronaviruses to mutate and recombine. Despite this risk, there are no approved vaccines or specific treatments for MERS, and no structure of the essential replication-transcription complex (RTC) has been available. Here, we define the biochemical properties of the MERS-CoV RTC and determine its structure bound to RNA, revealing conserved and virus-specific features of coronavirus replication. We further demonstrate inhibition of the polymerase by suramin. By establishing a structural and functional framework for MERS-CoV genome replication, this work addresses a key gap in our preparedness for MERS-CoV and supports the development of antivirals that could be effective against multiple coronaviruses.
authors: Cunnison RF, Philip SS, Deng A, Groves D, Spence AM, Coleman CM, Keown J, Robb NC.

title: DNA Analyser: An Interactive Web Server for Integrated Prediction of Local Non-B DNA Structures in Genomic Sequences.
abstract: BackgroundLocal non-B DNA structures and R-loops are associated with genome regulation and stability. CpX islands and p53 response elements provide complementary sequence annotations. Exploring these features often requires separate tools and repeated sequence submission.Main findingsDNA Analyser web server integrates G4Hunter, G4Killer, R-loop Tracker, Z-DNA Hunter, pretrained Z-DNABERT models running on CPUs, CpX Hunter and a p53-binding predictor. Palindrome analyser is linked as a separate companion server. Inputs include plain-text or FASTA upload, pasted sequences, multiple-sequence workflows and NCBI retrieval. Outputs include analysis settings, sortable regions, interactive graphics and module-specific exports. Guest and registered users have access to the same analytical functions.Biological relevanceA shared sequence workspace supports examination of structural propensity, nucleotide composition and potential regulatory elements. Predictions identify candidates for further investigation; they do not demonstrate structure formation or biological function in vivo.SignificanceIntegrated access reduces repeated sequence handling and helps researchers explore complementary features of the same genomic region. DNA Analyser is freely accessible through HTTPS without identity registration at https://bioinformatics.ibp.cz/#/.
authors: Brázda V, Petrovič M, Šťastný J, Mergny JL.

title: New insights on the dual role of viruses favoring microbial survival and pollutant degradation in the rhizosphere.
abstract: The rhizosphere is widely recognized as a crucial environment for microbial community assembly and pollutant degradation, with numerous mechanisms already elucidated. However, the role of viruses in these processes remains largely unexplored. Viruses can carry auxiliary metabolic genes (AMGs), which shape microbial functions through horizontal gene transfer and may play an important role in the rhizosphere. This study investigated microbial and viral community structures, as well as degradation gene profiles, in rhizosphere and non-rhizosphere soils at a PCBs-contaminated site. More microbial functional pathways were negatively correlated with PCBs concentrations in rhizosphere soils, a pattern consistent with potentially greater functional sensitivity to pollutant-associated stress. Meanwhile, viral AMGs associated with antioxidant defense and DNA repair appeared to help microbes resist PCBs toxicity. Notably, viruses also carried potential PCBs degradation genes associated with both aerobic and anaerobic degradation pathways. More putative transfer events involving these degradation-related genes were observed among microbes in rhizosphere soils than in non-rhizosphere soils, suggesting that viruses may play an important role in PCB degradation. The normalized abundance of degradation genes was significantly correlated with that of antioxidant and DNA repair genes, but not with PCBs concentrations. This association is consistent with a possible ecological link between toxicity resistance and degradation potential. This study provides new insights into the role of rhizosphere viruses in organic pollutant degradation and informs the development of strategies to enhance microbial bioremediation efforts.
authors: Wang Y, Yan W, Song M, Jiang L, Xie Y, Jin LN, Wang S, Luo C.

title: An integrative GWAS, Transcriptomic, and domestication analysis Uncovers Multi-Layered genetic architecture of kernel rate in maize testcross hybrids.
abstract: IntroductionImproving yield efficiency in maize (Zea mays L.) is increasingly important under high-density production systems, where gains from total biomass accumulation are approaching physiological limits. Kernel Rate (KR), or shelling percentage, captures reproductive biomass partitioning within the ear but remains less well characterized genetically than absolute yield components.ObjectiveHere, we evaluated KR together with ear weight (EW), cob weight (CW), and kernel weight (KW) in two testcross populations generated with Mo17 and Zheng58 and assessed across six year-by-location environments. KR was highly heritable, showed only weak correlations with EW, and was consistently negatively correlated with CW, supporting its use as an index of relative kernel-to-cob biomass allocation.MethodsTo investigate the genetic basis of this variation, we applied an integrative analytical framework combining testcross-based genome-wide association studies (GWAS), comparative parental-line transcriptomic comparisons associated with extreme F1 testcross performance, and population genomic signals from domestication scans. Rather than identifying a single set of causal genes, this approach revealed limited overlap among data layers, indicating that yield efficiency is shaped by multiple, context-dependent genetic contributions.ResultsGWAS identified multiple trait-associated loci with limited overlap across environments and tester backgrounds; two CW associations also met FDR_BH ConclusionThese results support a multi-layered and context-dependent genetic basis of biomass partitioning in maize testcross hybrids. The integrative framework provides biologically informed candidate priorities for functional validation and breeding across additional testers and environments.
authors: Xiong X, Duan H, Ding D, Tang J, Zhang X.

title: Design, Synthesis, in silico Studies, and Biological Evaluation of N<sup>4</sup>-Acetyl/Benzoyl Piperazinyl Ciprofloxacin-Amino Acid Conjugates as Broad-Spectrum Antimicrobial Agents.
abstract: This study reports a second-stage optimization of our previously reported ciprofloxacin derivatives through molecular hybridization, with structural modifications aimed at improving antimicrobial potency and activity against resistant strains. Their structures and identities were confirmed by spectroscopic techniques, elemental analysis, and HPLC. In vitro antimicrobial activity showed enhanced potency across a panel of bacterial strains. The derivatives demonstrated promising activity against both wild-type and resistant strains, while the most active derivatives also exhibited promising antimycobacterial activity. The most active compounds were selected for further in vitro and live-cell mode-of-action studies. Several compounds showed biofilm-inhibiting activity against Staphylococcus aureus at sub-MIC. Phenotypic mode-of-action studies indicated topoisomerase inhibition in both Escherichia coli and Bacillus subtilis. Enzyme inhibition studies revealed potent activity against DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Additionally, the best anti-Helicobacter pylori candidates showed promising urease inhibition. Selected derivatives showed bactericidal activity with minimal resistance development compared with ciprofloxacin. The cytotoxicity study indicated low in vitro cytotoxicity under the tested conditions. Molecular modeling supported favorable binding and inhibitory potential, while QSAR linked physicochemical properties to biological activity, providing mechanistic insights and guiding compound optimization toward improved efficacy and development. Overall, the synthesized ciprofloxacin hybrids showed promising antimicrobial activity and potential to combat bacterial resistance.
journal: European journal of pharmaceutical sciences : official journal of the European Federation for Pharmaceutical Sciences
authors: El-Sagheir AMK, Sidarta M, Bunker A, Wenzel M, Yli-Kauhaluoma J.
