title: rmf, a conserved ribosome hibernation marker of convergent dormancy in experimentally evolved Escherichia coli.
abstract: Bacteria adapt to remarkably diverse chemical stresses, yet how far independent adaptive trajectories converge, and on what, remains poorly defined. We reanalyzed transcriptomes from 188 Escherichia coli lineages evolved under 47 different chemical stresses, 4 M9 controls, and 4 ancestral replicates. We used multiple public data sets to test whether divergent lineages converge on a shared physiological endpoint. Lineages evolved under chemically diverse stresses converged on a shared transcriptional axis, with their expression change positively correlated across chemicals (r = 0.157; P = 0.001). This axis corresponds to a slow-growth, RpoS-governed stationary-phase and ribosome hibernation program, aligning strongly with an RpoS/stationary-phase index (r = 0.97) and inversely with a ribosomal index (r = -0.65). The ribosome modulation factor rmf, which forms translationally silent 100S ribosome dimers, rose along the PC1 axis (r = 0.65) and co-expressed specifically with the 100S hibernation factors hpf, yfiA, and sra. In contrast, its associations with persister toxin-antitoxin, multidrug efflux, and oxidative stress genes were weak or inconsistent. Cross-species analysis supported purifying selection on ribosome modulation factor, and a genome-wide analysis placed rmf within the lowest-diversity 4% of core genes, consistent with convergence through regulation rather than coding change. Neither the axis nor rmf expression tracked the resistance level of the lineages, identifying the program as a conserved state of adaptation rather than a resistance mechanism. These findings recast a canonical stress response program as the convergent endpoint of adaptive evolution and identify rmf as a conserved readout of that state.IMPORTANCEBacteria survive antibiotics not only by becoming resistant but also by entering a dormant, slow-growing state that tolerates drugs, and how predictably different populations reach such a state has been unclear. By reanalyzing Escherichia coli populations experimentally evolved under dozens of chemically distinct stresses, we show that each population acquired largely stress-specific mutations, yet their gene expression profiles converged on a shared dormancy program centered on ribosome hibernation. A single gene, rmf, whose product switches ribosomes off, reliably marked how deeply a population had entered this state, was reproducible across many independent data sets, and was almost invariant across hundreds of E. coli genomes. Because this convergence arose through gene regulation rather than mutation and did not correspond to resistance, rmf offers a simple readout of a dormant state associated with tolerance, a distinction useful for understanding and countering how bacteria survive antibiotics.
authors: Yuan J, Sun R, Zhang C.

title: Accuracy of plasma cell-free DNA PCR versus mNGS for non-invasive diagnosis of invasive mold disease.
abstract: Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) detection in plasma is a novel testing modality for non-invasive diagnosis of invasive mold disease (IMD) in immunocompromised patients. The accuracy of PCR compared to metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) for diagnosis of IMD remains unknown. Plasma samples from patients with proven and probable IMD and no IMD were tested with mold PCR and shotgun mNGS. Mold PCR detected Aspergillus species, Mucorales agents, Fusarium species, Scedosporium species, and Lomentospora prolificans. The sensitivity and specificity of mold PCR and mNGS were measured. Ninety-four patients with proven (48) and probable (48) IMD due to Aspergillus species (64), Mucorales agents (13), Scedosporium species and Lomentospora prolificans (13), and Fusarium species (6), and 62 patients with no IMD were included in this study. 99.4% (155) of the patients were immunosuppressed. The overall sensitivity and specificity were 62.5% (60/96; 95% CI 52.0-72.2) and 99.8% (535/536; 95% CI 99.0-100), respectively, for mold PCR and 43.8% (42/96; 95% CI 33.6-54.3; P P = 1.0), respectively, for mNGS. The proportion of mold PCR-positive mNGS-negative results was 16.0% (4/25) in focal cases compared with 25.0% (11/44; P = 0.384) and 18.5% (5/27; P = 0.810) in multifocal and disseminated cases, respectively. The median PCR cycle threshold was 40.6 (IQR, 37.5-41.5) in PCR-positive mNGS-negative cases compared with 37.3 (IQR, 34.5-39.3; P = 0.004) in PCR-positive mNGS-positive cases. Plasma cfDNA PCR is more sensitive than mNGS for the diagnosis of IMD in immunocompromised patients. Lower sensitivity of mNGS was associated with lower mold cfDNA burden.ImportanceInvasive mold disease (IMD) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in immunocompromised patients. Early diagnosis and initiation of tailored antifungal therapy are critical for optimizing outcomes in patients with IMD. Detection of circulating fungal cell-free DNA (cfDNA) in the acellular fraction of blood is a novel testing modality that is increasingly used for early and non-invasive diagnosis of IMD. This study represents the first head-to-head accuracy study to compare the sensitivity and specificity of PCR with mNGS for the diagnosis of IMD. The study showed that the overall mold PCR was significantly more sensitive compared with mNGS, while both assays demonstrated very high specificity. Similar trends were observed in a smaller subgroup of patients with invasive aspergillosis, mucormycosis, and scedosporiosis. The findings have implications for assay selection when seeking to non-invasively diagnose IMD in immunocompromised patients.
authors: Pusz-Bochenska K, Murugesan K, Senchyna F, Lalljie A, Budvytiene I, Banaei N.

title: Short-tailed Salmonella Phage SWJM-03: Isolation, Characterization, and Application in Controlling Contamination on Lettuce.
abstract: AimsSalmonella enterica, a major cause of foodborne outbreaks associated with ready-to-eat leafy greens, like lettuce, poses urgent challenges to food safety. In this study, a lytic phage, SWJM-03, was isolated and evaluated for its potential as a biocontrol agent against Salmonella contamination in lettuce.Methods and resultsPhage SWJM-03 was isolated from sewage using multidrug-resistant Salmonella Typhimurium 2112 as the host, and its biological characteristics, genomic features, antibiofilm activity, and biocontrol efficacy on lettuce were evaluated. Phage SWJM-03 is classified within the genus Berlinvirus, class Caudoviricetes. The phage exhibited a short-tailed morphology and demonstrated rapid adsorption (92.7% within 20 min), a short latent period of 5 min, and a burst size of 97 PFU/cell. SWJM-03 showed high stability across a wide pH range (3-12) and retained high activity within a temperature range of 30-60°C relevant to food processing conditions. Notably, SWJM-03 also exhibited great storage stability, with minimal titer reduction after 4 weeks at 4°C, supporting its practical applicability. Genomic analysis (39 474 bp dsDNA, 48.97% G + C, GenBank Accession no.: OQ818670) confirmed the absence of virulence-associated genes. SWJM-03 significantly reduced biofilm biomass of S. Typhimurium by 56.8%, and demonstrated promising biocontrol potential. Importantly, in a simulated lettuce contamination system under refrigeration (4°C), SWJM-03 achieved up to 4.00 log₁₀ CFU/cm² reduction within 3 days, reducing bacterial counts below detectable levels (ConclusionsPhage SWJM-03 is a rapid-acting and environmentally stable lytic bacteriophage with strong antibacterial activity under refrigeration conditions, highlighting its potential as a promising biocontrol agent for controlling Salmonella contamination in fresh produce.
authors: Zhang L, Huang N, Pan H, Shu M, Li J, Zhong C, Wu GP.

title: The Genetic Legacy of Thermal Processing in Pasteurized Foods: Persistence of Antimicrobial Resistance Genes, Potential for Horizontal Gene Transfer, and a Proposed Genetic Legacy Index.
abstract: Thermal processing inactivates foodborne bacteria but does not necessarily destroy their DNA, membrane vesicles, or bacteriophage particles. Such residues persist in pasteurized milk and heat-treated meat and are ingested by consumers. Whether this material can transfer antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) to gut bacteria remains untested: the only direct human evidence of foodborne resistance-gene transfer involved live bacteria, not material released from heat-killed cells. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on the post-thermal fate of extracellular DNA, membrane vesicles, and bacteriophages, grading that evidence explicitly from detection of a target sequence, through structural integrity, to demonstrated transfer under realistic conditions. Persistence of ARG sequences after pasteurization is well documented, whereas functional transfer from foodborne dead-cell material has not been demonstrated in vivo. A Genetic Legacy Index (GLI) is proposed as a conceptual measurement framework-not a validated index-combining extracellular DNA abundance, ARG load, and ARG-mobile genetic element linkage, with an illustrative formula, normalization strategy, and validation agenda. Current finished-product microbiological criteria are predominantly culture-based and do not establish limits for extracellular or dead-cell genetic material, although integrated antimicrobial resistance surveillance increasingly includes molecular detection and whole-genome sequencing. The GLI is therefore proposed as a research and surveillance tool rather than a product-release criterion: a first step toward evaluating an unquantified exposure pathway within One Health surveillance of the food chain.
authors: Song S, Yan L.

title: Mining of Small Open Reading Frame-Encoded Peptides from Chlamydomonas nivalis without Its Reference Genome.
abstract: Small open reading frame (sORF)-encoded peptides (SEPs) participate in diverse biological processes, yet their identification in nonmodel organisms is limited by the lack of high-quality reference genomes. Here, we developed an integrative proteogenomic pipeline to discover SEPs in Chlamydomonas nivalis by combining sORFs predicted from its transcriptome with those derived from the genomes of the related species, Chloromonas eustigma and Volvox carteri. Using this strategy, we identified 978 endogenous SEPs supported by transcript evidence and 1 999 candidate SEPs supported by cross-species proteogenomic evidence. SEPs predicted from transcriptomic and related-species genomic data showed broadly similar physicochemical and evolutionary features. Importantly, incorporation of related-species genomic data substantially increased identification coverage, with over 95% of SEPs identified through these databases absent from the transcriptome-derived data set. Functional analysis identified several cold-responsive candidates, including an Lhca6-homologous SEP and several intrinsically disordered region-rich SEPs. Heterologous expression of selected candidates in C. reinhardtii further showed that two SEPs enhanced cold tolerance. These results demonstrate the value of integrating transcriptomic and related-species genomic resources for SEP discovery and provide functional evidence for SEP involvement in cold adaptation.
authors: Yao S, Peng Z, Liu G, Huang K, Wan C.

title: IsoPairFinder: A Computational Workflow for Prioritizing LC-MS Feature Pairs Representing Candidate Microbial Pathway Intermediates from Stable Isotope Tracing Metabolomics.
abstract: Functional annotation of microbial genes lags behind the pace of genome sequencing, leaving major gaps in our understanding of microbial metabolism. Combining genetic perturbation with untargeted stable isotope tracing metabolomics provides a powerful strategy for identifying pathway intermediates and elucidating microbial metabolic pathways. To streamline this workflow, we developed IsoPairFinder, a computational tool that prioritizes pathway-intermediate feature pairs by analyzing paired unlabeled (12C) and 13C-labeled metabolomics datasets from genetically perturbed microbes. By consolidating redundant liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) features and pairing features across unlabeled and labeled samples, IsoPairFinder reduces candidate lists to plausible isotope-paired intermediates for downstream validation. We demonstrate the utility of IsoPairFinder in a case study of uric acid catabolism in Clostridium sporogenes, where it filters redundant features and prioritizes LC-MS feature pairs representing gene-associated pathway intermediates. IsoPairFinder is available as an open-source R package and as a web-based workflow within GNPS2. By integrating differential analysis and isotope-pair detection into a single workflow, IsoPairFinder enables microbiologists to connect metabolomic features with microbial gene function more efficiently, thereby accelerating microbial pathway discovery.
journal: Journal of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry
authors: Zhou Z, Liu Y, Wang M, Dodd D.

title: The Potential Role of Gut Microbiome Dysbiosis and Functional Reprogramming in Colorectal Liver Metastasis via the Gut-Liver Axis.
abstract: BackgroundColorectal liver metastasis (CRLM) is a leading cause of mortality in colorectal cancer (CRC), yet current surveillance often misses occult micrometastases, underscoring an urgent need for early non-invasive biomarkers and mechanistic insights.AimsThis study aimed to investigate gut microbiota dysbiosis and functional alterations associated with CRLM and explore potential non-invasive biomarkers.Methods and resultsFecal metagenomic sequencing was performed in 60 participants, comprising healthy controls, patients with non-metastatic CRC, and patients with synchronous CRLM (n = 20 per group). Microbial composition, functional pathways, co-occurrence networks, and clinical associations were systematically analyzed, and a random forest model was constructed to identify potential diagnostic biomarkers. Results showed that gut microbiota dysbiosis intensified as CRC progressed toward CRLM, characterized by the depletion of commensal flora and significant enrichment of specific genera, such as Eikenella and Porphyromonas. Functionally, the gut microbiome displayed stage-specific remodeling, shifting from infection- and virulence-related pathways in CRC to functions associated with microbial secondary metabolism and stress adaptation in CRLM. Furthermore, SPIEC-EASI-based network analysis revealed a sparser and more compartmentalized microbial ecological structure in CRLM, with [Clostridium] symbiosum, Campylobacter concisus, and Coprococcus eutactus emerging as module hubs. A random forest model integrating nine core taxa and one virulence factor (VF0160 FeoAB) achieved an overall 97.5% classification accuracy in discriminating CRLM from non-metastatic CRC, indicating the potential of fecal metagenomic biomarkers for future risk stratification. However, prospective validation in larger multicenter cohorts is required before clinical translational utility.ConclusionCollectively, our findings suggest that gut microbiota dysbiosis and functional reprogramming are strongly associated with CRLM progression, potentially through remodeling the hepatic pre-metastatic niche via the gut-liver axis.
authors: Sheng Y, Dai X, Lu J, Zhang H, Cai P.

title: When cold-bloods heat up: meta-analytical evidence that climatic variability mediates behavioural fever in amphibians and reptiles.
abstract: Fever is an adaptive defence response that enhances immune performance by elevating body temperature above normal values. In ectotherms, fever is expressed behaviourally through the selection of warmer microhabitats following infection, yet its magnitude and determinants vary widely across species and environments. We performed a phylogenetically informed meta-analysis to test whether behavioural fever expression is shaped by climatic thermal variability, pathogen identity and taxonomy in amphibians and reptiles. We predicted that species from thermally variable environments would exhibit stronger behavioural fever than those from stable environments and reptiles would exhibit stronger fever responses than amphibians owing to lower hydrothermal constraints. Across 47 studies encompassing 101 effect sizes, behavioural fever emerged as a widespread but context-dependent response. Behavioural fever was strongest in species from thermally variable habitats, suggesting that thermal opportunity and behavioural plasticity mediate the expression of fever. Contrary to our prediction, amphibians exhibited stronger fever responses than reptiles, possibly reflecting differences in thermoregulatory biology, environmental opportunity or methodological artefacts. Bacterial infections elicited larger body temperature increases than fungal or viral challenges. Our findings demonstrate that temperature is not a background condition for host-pathogen interactions, but an active and environmentally contingent component of immune defence in ectothermic tetrapods.
authors: Giacometti D, Servino LM, Cabanzo-Olarte LC, Bícego KC, Navas C.

title: Early Life Stage Exposure to Environmentally Relevant Concentrations of TCPP Induces Multigenerational Reproductive Toxicity in Estuarine Fish: A Study Based on Whole-Genome Methylation and Steroidogenesis Pathway.
abstract: Tris (1-chloro-2-propyl) phosphate (TCPP) is ubiquitous in estuarine environments. Parental TCPP exposure impaired reproduction and offspring developmental in zebrafish; yet its multigenerational and transgenerational effects and epigenetic mechanisms in estuarine fish remain unknown. Here, Mugilogobius chulae embryos were exposed to TCPP until 25 days posthatching and reared in clean seawater until F2 hatching. Reproductive and gonadal end points were assessed across generations, while gonadal steroidogenesis and whole-body DNA methylation in larvae were analyzed in F0 and F1 to investigate potential endocrine and epigenetic mechanisms. TCPP induced multigenerational reproductive toxicity that was transmitted to F2 embryos, with F1 and F2 lowest observed effect concentrations 1 order of magnitude lower than that in F0. In F0, 100 μg/L TCPP reduced fecundity and male gonadosomatic index. In F1, 10, and 100 μg/L prolonged spawning latency and affected male gonadal development. In F2, 10 μg/L reduced embryonic hatching. Disruption of steroidogenesis gene expression and hormone levels occurred in F0 and F1 male gonads but only in F1 females. Whole-genome DNA methylation revealed persistent hypermethylation of nerve growth factor receptor (NGFR) and calcium voltage-gated channel auxiliary subunit γ 2 (CACNG2) in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway across F0 and F1. Their hypermethylation and reduced expression were associated with decreased steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (STAR) and cytochrome P450 family 11 subfamily A member (CYP11A) in male gonads, suggesting NGFR and CACNG2 may represent candidate epigenetically regulated genes associated with TCPP-induced multigenerational reproductive toxicity. This study reveals transgenerational risks of environmental concentrations of TCPP to estuarine fish and provides epigenetic evidence for multigenerational endocrine disruptors.
authors: Ren J, Peng Y, Sun C, Zhang Y, Guan Z, Li J, Xia S, Gao Y, Wang Y, Gao C, Nie X.

title: Adaptation and Resistance of Nitrifiers to Harsh Engineered Conditions during Partial Nitritation.
abstract: Selective suppression of nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB) is essential for stable partial nitritation (PN), yet NOB often persist or recover under engineered suppression conditions. This study investigated the kinetic, microbial, and genomic responses of NOB and ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB) in a PN system subjected to low pH and high free nitrous acid (FNA) sidestream treatment. A sequencing batch reactor was operated for 283 days under varying treatment intensities. Long-term operation selectively enriched a Candidatus nitrotogafabula-related MAG (bin.69), characterized by a relatively high apparent growth rate (∼1.3 d-1) and low substrate affinity (Ks = 2.3 ± 0.4 mg NO2--N L-1; Ko = 1.1 ± 0.3 mg O2 L-1). Comparative genomic analyses identified stress-tolerance-associated traits related to proton transport, ion homeostasis, protein stabilization, and cellular stress responses. Proteome isoelectric (pI) point analysis further showed a lower genomic pI profile than other known NOB, potentially consistent with persistence under acidic and FNA stress. These findings provide genome-informed insights into NOB persistence under long-term suppression and implications for improving PN stability.
authors: Hu Z, Shao B, Cen X, Duan H, Su Z, He D, Hu S, Ye L, Zheng M.

title: From transcriptomics to structural modelling with AlphaFold: analysis of the central response to stress in bacteria using machine learning and structural bioinformatics
abstract: In this webinar, we will present our research focused on understanding the core mechanisms (perturbome) employed by prokaryotic organisms to survive and adapt to diverse stress conditions. Our analyses are based on transcriptomic datasets from the bacterial models Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Staphylococcus aureus, in which gene expression analyses and the prioritisation of stress-response-associated genes were performed using machine learning, systems biology, functional enrichment, and orthologous analyses. Subsequently, we implemented structural bioinformatics approaches integrating experimentally resolved protein structures available in PDB and AlphaFold-based predictions for proteins lacking experimental structural data. Using these protein structures, molecular docking and other in silico analyses enabled the identification of a preliminary set of compounds and potential conditions capable of inhibiting these molecular targets as a proof of concept. Future experimental validation studies are expected to confirm the computational findings obtained through this integrative framework.
authors: Molina Mora J.

title: Patterns of genetic variation in a range-expanding fruit fly Zeugodacus tau.
abstract: BackgroundRange expansion is often accompanied by reduced genetic diversity and increased environmental stress in populations at range edges, potentially constraining adaptive evolution despite strong selection. This study aimed to investigate these processes during the northward range expansion of the fruit fly Zeugodacus tau, an important agricultural pest. We sampled 217 individuals from 11 geographical populations spanning the species' current distribution across China and genotyped them using double-digest restriction-site-associated DNA sequencing (ddRAD-seq).ResultsThe surveyed populations were genetically differentiated into southwestern and southeastern groups, with an admixed group located in the longitudinal transition zone between them. Northern populations generally exhibited lower genetic diversity than southern populations, whereas populations with admixed ancestry tended to retain higher genetic diversity than non-admixed populations at comparable latitudes. TreeMix supported two historical migration events, and all populations except Shanghai exhibited broadly similar demographic histories. Environmental variables independently explained more genomic variation than geographic variables, both across all populations (53.01% vs 27.28%) and within the admixed group (50.64% vs 17.25%). Genome scans identified candidate SNPs in the admixed group that were potentially associated with responses to environmental stress.ConclusionsOur findings show that the northward range expansion of Z. tau is accompanied by a general decline in genetic diversity, while admixture among differentiated lineages may partially offset this loss. These results highlight the joint roles of demographic history and admixture in shaping genomic variation during range expansion, although the adaptive consequences of admixture remain unresolved. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
authors: Wang YT, Yue L, Cao LJ, Chen JC, Song W, Ma WH, Yang JF, Gao XY, Chen HS, Zhang Y, Tian ZY, Thia JA, Hoffmann AA, Wei SJ, Zhou ZS.

title: Aridity reshapes leaf and root trait dispersion through distinct microbial pathways.
abstract: Aridity is a primary driver of plant community assembly, yet most trait-based studies focus on mean traits rather than trait dispersion. Soil microbes may mediate plant responses to aridity, but whether leaf and root trait dispersion responds to aridity through shared or distinct microbial pathways remains unclear. Using 535 species-by-plot records (247 species) along an aridity gradient in north-west China, we quantified four leaf and four root traits, soil properties, microbial diversity and composition, and microbial carbon use efficiency. We tested whether aridity differentially regulates leaf vs root functional dispersion (FDis), and whether these responses are associated with different microbial predictors. Leaf traits shifted more consistently with aridity and were more tightly linked to environmental variation than root traits. Leaf FDis negatively correlated with CUE, whereas root FDis negatively correlated with fungal diversity and bacterial community composition. These associations weakened toward less arid sites. Structural equation modeling further showed that leaf FDis linked primarily to microbial functioning, whereas root FDis linked more strongly to microbial diversity and composition. Our results reveal that aridity reshapes trait dispersion through organ-specific plant-microbe pathways, highlighting that predicting dryland community responses to increasing drought must treat above- and belowground traits separately.
authors: Hu M, Zhang X, Shi H, Gao J, He R, Zhang Q, Dang H.

title: Hydroxyl-enriched biochar enhances methanogenesis by shaping microbial functional responses in anaerobic digestion.
abstract: Biochar is effective in improving methanogenesis during anaerobic digestion (AD), but its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the role of hydroxyl groups by synthesizing ball-milled biochars (BMBs) with different hydroxyl contents through alkali modification and evaluating their effects on methane production and microbial gene abundance patterns. Hydroxyl content increased from 0.14 mmol/g in BMB0 to 0.70 and 0.60 mmol/g in BMB5 and BMB10, respectively. BMB5 achieved the highest final methane yield of 385.54 mL CH4/g volatile solids (VS), 20.9% above BMB0. The hydroxyl content was positively correlated with final methane yield (P < 0.01). Planktonic and sessile communities also showed distinct compositions, with Methanobacterium preferentially enriched on biochar surfaces. Metagenomic analysis showed higher abundances of pili- and Fpo-related genes in BMB-associated communities than in the Blank, whereas variation in the hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis (HM) gene module was significantly associated with hydroxyl content (P = 0.025). These results link hydroxyl enrichment to differences in methanogenesis-related genetic potential and methane production. Overall, this study identifies surface hydroxyl content as a material property closely associated with the methanogenic performance of biochar and provides a basis for rational design of biochar to enhance methane recovery from AD systems.
authors: Han Y, Luo Y, Guo L, Lin S, Wu X, Zan F.

title: Integrating pangenome and imputation framework reveals structural variants affecting stature and milk composition traits in French dairy cattle.
abstract: BackgroundStructural variants (SVs) are most effectively identified using long-read (LR) sequencing. However, such data remain scarce, and sequenced samples often lack associated phenotypic information. To overcome this limitation, we integrated pangenome-based (variation graph-based) and imputation approaches to enable large-scale SV association studies in the three main French dairy cattle breeds.ResultsA variation graph was constructed using 69,892 deletions, 89,900 insertions, and 17,402 duplications detected in 176 LR samples. We subsequently genotyped 939 samples for each SV in the panel by realigning their short-read (SR) sequences to the graph. Validation analyses showed high genotype concordance rates for deletions (0.79) and insertions (0.79); however, concordance for duplications was low (0.14), leading to their exclusion from further analyses. The retained SVs were combined with single nucleotide variants (SNVs) to build a sequence-level imputation reference panel. Using SNP genotyping array data, we imputed SVs and SNVs for 11,902 Holstein, 3,753 Montbéliarde, and 3,053 Normande bulls. After quality control, more than 14 million SNVs and 40 thousand SVs were retained for within-breed genome-wide association studies (GWAS) using daughter yield deviations for stature and four milk production and composition traits. The GWAS results revealed genetic architectures consistent with previous findings and identified 40 genome-wide significant associations between structural variant and key phenotypes. Conditional analyses identified that ten of these SVs as potential candidate variants underlying QTLs related to milk fat and protein contents, as well as stature.ConclusionsBy integrating LR, SR, and SNP genotyping data within a unified pangenome and imputation framework, we demonstrate a scalable strategy to systematically interrogate the contribution of SVs to complex traits. The resulting genetic architectures were highly consistent with previous findings, validating both the robustness and transferability of our approach. Our findings highlight the added value of integrating SVs into routine genomic analyses and provide a scalable framework for incorporating SVs into genomic selection in dairy cattle.
journal: Journal of animal science and biotechnology
authors: Naji MM, Sorin V, Grohs C, Fritz S, Klopp C, Faraut T, Boichard D, Boussaha M, Sanchez MP.

title: ARTP Mutagenesis and Omics-Guided Target Validation for Improved Human Serum Albumin Fusion Protein Production in Yeast.
abstract: Efficient production of human serum albumin (HSA) fusion proteins in yeast remains constrained by the combined demands of folding, secretion, and cellular resource allocation. Rational optimization of endoplasmic reticulum folding and unfolded protein response pathways can improve production, but additional cellular constraints may persist in engineered strains. Here, we combined iterative atmospheric and room-temperature plasma (ARTP) mutagenesis, activity-coupled screening, and genome- and transcriptome-guided validation to improve production of an amylase-HSA fusion protein (AGSH) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Using extracellular α-amylase activity as the screening indicator, five rounds of ARTP mutagenesis in the folding-optimized strain AH28 generated mutants with enhanced AGSH production. The final mutant N5S14 reached 2.12-fold the AH28 level in AGSH-associated α-amylase activity. Physiological profiling showed that enhanced production was associated with altered growth-production balance and changes in glucose, ethanol, and glycerol profiles. Whole-genome sequencing identified 33 candidate mutation sites, and reverse engineering validated genes associated with improved AGSH production, including BUD27, NPR3, NPR2, and IML1. RNA-seq revealed distinct transcriptional states involving central carbon metabolism, protein folding, and stress-related processes. Transcriptome-guided validation identified PFY1 deletion and SSA3 overexpression as additional beneficial interventions. Overall, this strategy improved AGSH production and identified engineering targets beyond previously optimized folding-related modules.
authors: Wang S, Li Y, Li Y, Zheng L, Zhao M, Pan Y, Huang M.

title: Genomic and Clinical Analysis of Influenza A in Hospitalized Adults, 2019-2024: Exploratory Evidence on Neuraminidase and Polymerase Acidic Protein Mutation-Outcome Associations From a Single Center.
abstract: BackgroundAntivirals are widely used to treat influenza, but potential resistance mutations remain a major challenge, and clinical data on key resistance mutations are limited.MethodsWe conducted a retrospective cohort study of 765 adults with RT-PCR-confirmed influenza A admitted to Ruijin Hospital, Shanghai, between 2019 and 2024 to determine whether specific NA/PA mutations are associated with severe outcomes or prolonged length of stay (LOS) when analyzed alongside key host factors. PA and NA sequences were obtained and linked to the clinical cohort for mutation-clinical outcome analyses. Multiple testing was addressed by controlling the false discovery rate using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure.ResultsAmong 765 inpatients with influenza A virus infection, the median age was 68 years; 5.0% were severe disease and 9.9% died. Older age, higher CURB-65 score, and bacterial/fungal co-infection were the main correlates of mortality, whereas antiviral regimen and Ct value were not independently associated with mortality or severe outcomes. Adjusted observational analyses showed a lower estimate for severe disease with baloxavir but no association with in-hospital death. Major high-level resistance mutations were absent; detected NA/PA mutations showed no robust association with severe disease or mortality. PA-F105L showed an exploratory association with longer LOS, but this finding was attenuated after adjustment and was confounded by clade and calendar period.ConclusionsClinical outcomes were driven mainly by host factors and admission severity. Detected NA/PA mutations were not robustly associated with severe outcomes, while high-level resistance could not be assessed; PA-F105L-LOS association requires phenotypic and external validation.
authors: Feng A, Tan W, Xu W, Zhang X, Wei D, Yang Z.

title: Next-Generation Immunotherapies for Pseudomonas aeruginosa: Monoclonal Antibodies and Immune Checkpoint Modulation.
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa represents a critical healthcare challenge, accounting for 7%-10% of hospital-acquired infections globally, with particularly high prevalence in intensive care, burn, and respiratory units, alongside escalating rates of multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant strains. The bacterium evades host immunity through multiple mechanisms, including Type III Secretion System effector translocation and biofilm formation via polysaccharide matrices (alginate, Psl, Pel). Antibiotic-based therapies are increasingly ineffective, necessitating host-directed immunotherapeutic strategies. This review synthesizes emerging evidence on monoclonal antibody therapy and immune checkpoint modulation for P. aeruginosa infections. Bispecific antibodies targeting PcrV and Psl enhance opsonophagocytic killing and biofilm disruption through Fc-mediated mechanisms. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1/PD-L1) reverse T-cell exhaustion from chronic antigen exposure and LPS-driven upregulation of inhibitory receptors, restoring antimicrobial function. Combination approaches integrating mAbs with antibiotics and checkpoint blockade show potential for synergistic bacterial clearance in preclinical pneumonia and burn wound models. Clinical translation remains limited by antigen variability (Psl and PcrV epitope polymorphisms), biofilm heterogeneity, and host immunogenetic diversity (Fc receptor polymorphisms, HLA variants, cytokine profiles). Multi-omics profiling may enable personalized treatment selection. Safety concerns regarding immune hyperactivation require carefully dosed, biomarker-guided strategies. Future development demands genomic stratification of responders and optimized therapeutic windows for maximal clinical benefit.
journal: APMIS : acta pathologica, microbiologica, et immunologica Scandinavica
authors: Mehmood MS, Wajid T, Saleem M, Khalid R, Mumtaz MH.

title: Sequence-encoded dynamics diversify allostery within a conserved protein scaffold.
abstract: Proteins evolve allosteric mechanisms through sequence variation while preserving a conserved structural fold. How these substitutions reshape the protein's conformational landscape to drive functional diversification remains poorly understood. Members of the cAMP receptor protein family (CRP), a ubiquitous bacterial transcription factor, share a common architecture yet differentially couple cAMP binding to DNA interactions. Here, our results support a model in which allosteric diversification in CRP arises from the tuning of sequence-encoded protein's conformational dynamics. Comparative analysis of sequence conservation and helical propensity across proteobacterial and actinobacterial CRPs reveals lineage-specific distributions of conformational heterogeneity within the dimerization C-helix. These evolutionary patterns map onto the proteobacterial Escherichia coli (E. coli) CRP and the actinobacterial Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) CRP, two protein homologs that respond to cAMP through distinct allosteric mechanisms. Guided by functional and evolutionary differences, we introduced CRPE. coli-inspired C-helix substitutions into CRPMTB to identify sequence, structural and conformational features that contribute to the divergent allosteric behavior in CRPMTB. The resulting C-helix variants preserved the global fold, but displayed altered thermodynamic stability, cAMP binding affinity and cooperativity, DNA recognition properties, and promoter-associated oligomerization. Among these, the C-helix hinge residue, N135, emerges as an allosteric node that redistributes cAMP-induced conformational responses, modulating DNA binding. Together, our results identify the C-helix as an evolvable hotspot where sequence changes reweight conformational ensembles and generate distinct allosteric outputs within a conserved protein scaffold.
journal: Protein science : a publication of the Protein Society
authors: Mohanaraj S, Samuel M, Siminiceanu E, Missaghi N, Maillard RA.

title: Spatial Diversity of Marine Protists Along the Northern Norway Fjords During the Sub-Arctic Summer.
abstract: Polar coastal waters are highly complex and productive ecosystems that experience increasingly higher average water temperatures, shallower and stronger stratification, and higher glacier-melting rates. Yet, the environmental complexity and high microbial diversity within fjords pose challenges to understanding the impacts of these changes and the ecological processes driving them. Here, we studied protists and prokaryote communities, their distribution, and functional ecology along the northern Norwegian coast in summer 2019 using SSU rRNA gene metabarcoding. Physicochemical data provided insights into the main drivers for differences in plankton communities. We found significant differences in alpha and beta diversity among the different fjords and between the western (Vesterålen, Balsfjorden, and Lyngenfjord) and northern areas (Porsangerfjord, Laksefjord, and Tanafjord). Temperature, salinity, and phosphate are the main drivers for community composition differences, positively correlating with the western fjords and negatively with the northern ones. Metabarcoding analyses revealed dinoflagellates, cryptophytes, and ochrophytes as the most abundant groups on the north Norwegian coast and confirmed the bloom of the ichthyotoxic haptophyte Chrysochromulina leadbeateri in Balsfjorden. Our comprehensive spatial study of communities and key contributors across different fjords set a baseline for future environmental monitoring of these unique and productive ecosystems, which are subject to rapid environmental changes.
authors: Gran-Stadniczeñko S, Anestis K, Bunse C, Edvardsen B, Egbers P, Henkel R, Hörstmann C, Klemm K, Kühne N, Moritz F, Neuhaus S, Šupraha L, Tebben J, Voss D, Wilms SN, Wohlrab S, John U.

title: Inflammatory Pseudotumour in Common Seal (Phoca vitulina): A Case Report.
abstract: Pinnipeds, including seals, sea lions and walruses, are marine mammals susceptible to a variety of pathological conditions. Although neoplastic lesions in these species are receiving increased attention, relatively little information is available compared to neoplastic studies in domestic animals. In this report, a 19-year-old intact male common seal (Phoca vitulina) presented with a chronic ulcer on the fifth phalanx. Radiological examination revealed cortical reaction with significant osseous alterations in this animal and in another companion common seal, although the flipper appeared macroscopically normal. Histopathological analysis identified nests of fusiform to oval cells accompanied by mixed lymphohistiocytic inflammation. Immunohistochemical evaluation demonstrated that neoplastic cells were positive for vimentin, α-smooth muscle actin and calponin. Negative results were for pancytokeratin, desmin, CD31 and IRF4, supporting a myofibroblastic phenotype. The Ki-67 proliferation index was low (5%). All histopathological and immunohistochemical features were consistent with an inflammatory pseudotumour. Microbiological culture isolated Vibrio alginolyticus from the lesion, a marine and fish pathogen previously linked to chronic cutaneous infections in humans. No herpesviral DNA was detected by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Chronic bacterial infection and repeated microtrauma may have contributed to lesion development, consistent with reports of inflammatory pseudotumours arising in the context of persistent inflammatory stimuli.
authors: De Pablo-Moreno JM, Canales R, Mainez M, Aradilla N, Chinchilla B, Porras N, Vargas-Castro I, Rodríguez-Bertos A.

title: Telomere-to-telomere co-mapping of transposable elements and human genes identifies a cluster of young L1 elements in the interferon-alpha domain with potential evolutionary arms-race.
abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) have played a central role in major evolutionary transitions across the human lineage, from eukaryogenesis to the emergence of the eutherian placenta, and are currently reactivated in cancer and autoimmune diseases. The complete telomere-to-telomere (T2T) assembly enables comprehensive investigation of TE contributions to gene regulation. Using a 10 kb window around transcription start sites, we mapped 3,709,429 human TEs to 28,738 genes against a 500-permutation background and assessed the enrichment and functional associations of 6 TE classes and 44 families. We identified a 220 kb interferon-alpha domain enriched with young L1 elements: 77 of its 175 TEs are evolutionary young L1 copies from 36 subfamilies, at mean divergence 135.7 against 188.2 genome-wide. This is consistent with recent L1 activity and could indicate a recent evolutionary arms-race affecting innate immune gene regulation. Distinct TE classes exhibited specific functional associations: SVA elements were enriched near genes involved in transcription termination; Alu elements were linked to RNA processing and splicing; MIR elements were associated with zinc homeostasis and voltage-gated potassium channel genes; LINE elements were enriched near genes related to lipid metabolism and olfactory perception; and LTR elements were associated with ion transport. This correlative map provides a positional baseline against which epigenomic and functional TE studies can be normalized, and a set of candidate loci for further investigation of evolutionary arms race.
authors: Nikitin D.

title: Age-dependent genetic effects contribute to immunosenescence in Drosophila melanogaster.
abstract: Immunosenescence, the age-related decline in immune function, varies widely among individuals. Although both genetic and environmental factors contribute to variation in immunosenescence, the extent to which age-specific genetic effects shape age-related immune decline remains poorly understood. Here, we tested whether age-related variation in bacterial clearance is shaped by age-dependent genetic effects by measuring clearance of Escherichia coli infection in 175 genotypes at 1 wk of age and 183 genotypes at 5 wk of age. Clearance ability declined with age, but the magnitude of decline differed markedly among genotypes. Age-specific genetic effects explained substantially more phenotypic variation than age-independent genetic differences, and the genetic correlation in clearance ability across ages was modest, indicating that genetic effects on immune performance were only partially shared across ages. Consistent with these findings, genome-wide analyses identified largely distinct sets of candidate genes associated with clearance in young and old flies, including genes exhibiting genotype-by-age effects. Network and gene ontology analyses revealed enrichment for plasma membrane-associated genes and pathways involved in cell adhesion and cell migration. Functional follow-up of 14 candidate genes using hemocyte-specific RNA interference produced limited effects overall but confirmed that nebulosa contributes to bacterial clearance. Together, our results demonstrate that immunosenescence is shaped by age-dependent genetic effects and identify conserved pathways and candidate genes for future mechanistic studies of age-related immune decline.
authors: Campbell S, Gudino I, Rhee M, Harbison S, Leips J.

title: Response to divergent selection on meiotic recombination in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
abstract: Meiotic recombination is a key driver of evolution in sexually reproducing species, reshaping genetic diversity by generating novel allelic combinations. The rate of recombination varies substantially across living organisms depending on cis- or trans-acting genetic elements, as seen in many species, including the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Here, we report on an experimental evolution-based study to better understand the factors shaping this natural variation. Starting with a genetically diverse population of S. cerevisiae, we have carried out recurrent divergent selection on recombination rate using a fluorescence-based sorting approach in 4 independent lineages. After 10 generations, we observed an average response of recombination rate of +28% after positive selection and -24% after negative selection, within the interval used for selection. In the adjacent region, however, we observed a weaker response in the opposite direction, and no response in 4 other unlinked genomic regions. Whole-genome sequencing of individuals selected for high recombination revealed mixed outcomes in the 4 independently evolved lineages for high genome-wide recombination rates. However, all 4 lineages showed selection for high recombination locally, with particular haplotypes heavily favored and sequence- or structural variation-based heterozygosity selected against within the selection interval. Overall, this experimental evolution approach provides original and useful insights into the evolvability of the meiotic recombination rate and the associated genetic determinants.
authors: Raffoux X, Saayman X, Abuelgassim WA, Maret T, Venon A, Dumas F, Tattini L, Martin OC, Liti G, Falque M.

title: Genetic determinants that permit growth without the core septin Cdc12 in Cryptococcus neoformans.
abstract: Septins are conserved cytoskeletal GTPases that regulate morphogenesis, cytokinesis, and cell-surface organization in fungi. In most model and pathogenic yeasts that proliferate by budding, including Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Candida albicans, core septin subunits such as Cdc3 and Cdc12 are essential and their loss results in lethal cytokinetic defects. In Cryptococcus neoformans, by contrast, deletion of CDC12 or CDC3 yields viable cells that grow normally under permissive conditions, raising the question of how this pathogen maintains cell integrity without a functional septin complex. To address this, we compared the transcriptomes of wild-type cells and a cdc12Δ mutant. The cdc12Δ strain showed a focused set of transcriptional changes, with induction of genes involved in cell wall remodeling, stress-dependent morphogenetic programs, and pathways that promote fitness under compromised cytoskeletal conditions. Genetic analysis of the most highly induced genes uncovered factors that contribute to proliferation in the absence of Cdc12, including a previously uncharacterized aspartic-type endopeptidase that exhibits a genetic interaction with the loss of septin function. These findings outline the compensatory circuitry that permits septin-independent growth in C. neoformans and help explain why this pathogen can tolerate the absence of the septin complex. This intrinsic plasticity highlights C. neoformans as a powerful comparative model for studying the evolution and function of septins.
authors: Stempinski PR, Akahoho HS, Noorai RE, Shankar V, Kozubowski L.

title: Impact of corneal microbial latency detected by metagenomic next-generation sequencing on postoperative recovery after keratorefractive lenticule extraction.
abstract: PurposeTo investigate the microbial species latent in corneas of healthy individuals and determine whether small-incision lenticule extraction (SMILE) serves as a risk factor for pathogen reactivation.SettingOphthalmology Department of Peking University Third Hospital, Beijing, China.DesignProspective cohort study.MethodsMetagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) was used to analyze the microbial composition of corneal lenticules from SMILE. Based on the results, patients were categorized into viral group (VG) and nonviral pathogen group (NVPG). 2 Matched groups (MG1 and MG2) were established by selecting pathogen-negative individuals at a 1:4 ratio relative to 2 positive groups. Using SPSS to analyze baseline characteristics, preoperative ocular parameters, and postoperative ocular parameters among groups.ResultsAmong the detected pathogens, latent Herpesviruses were identified in 9 cases (4.31%), Papillomavirus were 4 cases (1.91%), and nonviral pathogens were 20 cases (9.57%). Both VG and NVPG groups showed no significant differences in baseline characteristics or preoperative ocular parameters compared with MG groups. In postoperative ocular parameters, no significant differences were found between VG and MG1, although intergroup variations in intraocular pressure and corneal thickness were observed ( P > .05). However, NVPG demonstrated significantly poorer results than MG2 in 1-month spherical equivalent ( P = .033) and corneal epithelial staining ( P = .044).ConclusionsThese findings indicate pathogen latency does not affect ocular status and SMILE surgery is unlikely to reactivate latent viruses or exerts minimal influence. Viral latency has almost no impact on postoperative recovery, while latent nonviral pathogens may interfere with postoperative recovery.
journal: Journal of cataract and refractive surgery
authors: Tang Y, Lin Z, Liu Z, Guo J, Yang C, Feng L, Wang Y, Zhang P, Chen Y.

title: Mechanistic insights into viral-host interactions during transcription.
abstract: Viral transcription strategies vary significantly depending on the nature of the viral genome and the site of transcription within the host cell. A common challenge for all viruses is to circumvent host defense mechanisms while simultaneously exploiting host cellular machinery to facilitate their own transcription. DNA viruses and retroviruses often hijack the host's RNA polymerase II (Pol II), while RNA viruses typically encode their own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). Through these diverse mechanisms, viruses effectively manipulate host transcription, translation, and immune responses, thereby evading immune surveillance and completing their replication cycle. This article systematically reviews the transcription strategies employed by major DNA and RNA virus families, providing insights that contribute to a deeper understanding of viral transcriptional regulation mechanisms.
authors: Huang Z, Peng T, Li Z, Zhu G, Zhu Z.

title: A computational-experimental strategy identifies K-7174 against African swine fever.
abstract: African swine fever (ASF), caused by the African swine fever virus (ASFV), poses a catastrophic threat to global swine production due to the absence of effective vaccines or therapeutics. Targeting the virally encoded RNA polymerase (RNAP), which is essential for viral transcription, offers a promising antiviral strategy. Capitalizing on our previously resolved high-resolution structure of ASFV RNAP, we conducted a rigorous structure-based virtual screening of two compound libraries (T001 and LF1000) to identify selective inhibitors. From 100 candidates validated in vitro, nine compounds identified at the genome level by qPCR demonstrated >98% inhibition of ASFV replication in porcine alveolar macrophages (PAMs). The lead compound, K-7174 - a repurposed agent known to modulate proteasome and GATA activity - exhibited potent, dose-dependent antiviral efficacy (IC 50 = 2.502 µmol/L), minimal cytotoxicity, and high binding affinity for ASFV RNAP. Molecular docking simulations indicated potential interactions with key catalytic residues, including Glu1051 and Ala456, proposing a mechanism that may involve active-site disruption. However, definitive confirmation of this binding pose requires further experimental validation through high-resolution structural methods such as cryo-EM. Our study not only nominates K-7174 as a promising anti-ASFV candidate but also establishes an integrated computational-experimental framework for accelerating the discovery of antiviral agents targeting viral polymerases.
authors: Sun B, Xi F, Liu Z, Liu H, Song H, Zhao Y, Zhu Z, Zheng H, Zhu G.

title: Map-based cloning and functional validation of Xa50, a wall-associated kinase gene conferring broad-spectrum bacterial blight resistance in rice.
abstract: Genetically validated broad-spectrum resistance genes are needed to improve bacterial blight resistance breeding in rice. Here, we identified HP178 as a rice accession showing broad-spectrum resistance to geographically diverse Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Xoo) strains and mapped a dominant locus to a 140-kb interval on chromosome 11. Within the mapped interval of the R498 reference genome, annotation and domain analysis identified OsR498G1120741700, which encodes a predicted wall-associated kinase (WAK), as the most likely candidate gene. Genetic complementation in the susceptible cultivar Zhonghua 11 and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing in HP178 confirmed that OsR498G1120741700 contributes to the resistance phenotype. The largely overlapping mapping intervals and the correspondence of this gene to ORF5, one of the candidates previously proposed for Xa50(t) in CX315, suggest a possible relationship between the two resistance loci. We therefore tentatively adopt the designation Xa50 to refer to the gene identified here, although its relationship to Xa50(t) in CX315 requires further investigation. Natural-variation analysis of 3,970 rice accessions showed that 936 were classified as Xa50-like, including 443 accessions with the resistance-associated Hap1 haplotype. Functional tests showed that the K435N lines exhibited partially attenuated Xa50-mediated resistance, whereas lines carrying a Hap4-type kinase-domain variant showed severely compromised resistance and reduced ROS accumulation. Our results identify Xa50 as a WAK-type resistance gene and provide haplotype information to support the selection of resistance-associatedXa50 alleles in rice breeding.Supplementary informationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11032-026-01739-5.
journal: Molecular breeding : new strategies in plant improvement
authors: Zhang M, Yuan M.

title: In silico codon optimization and phylogenetic analysis of various strains of Sapovirus
abstract: Introduction  Sapovirus (SaV) is an emerging enteric pathogen of rising public health importance, responsible for acute gastroenteritis in people of all ages and most often in children under five. Its genome is approximately 7.1-7.7 kb long, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA, comprising two principal open reading frames; processing of the ORF1 product yields seven non-structural proteins and the major capsid protein VP1, while ORF2 encodes the minor structural protein VP2. Given the absence of therapies or an approved vaccine and the low yields of recombinant capsid protein, improving expression remains a priority. Methods  VP1 and VP2 sequences from twelve selected human SaV strains were aligned, phylogenetic trees were reconstructed by maximum likelihood method under the Tamura-Nei model with 1,000 bootstrap replicates, and both genes were optimized  in silico for  Escherichia coli using the OPTIMIZER.  Results  The trees resolved three genogroups, GI, GII and GV, each strain placed alike by both genes. Every optimized sequence reached the ceiling value of 1.000 for the codon adaptation index (CAI). Mean CAI and GC% increased by 3.07 (207.0%) and 1.11 (11.1%) fold for VP1, and 3.11 (210.9%) and 1.14 (14.1%) fold for VP2, while AT% decreased. All changes were statistically significant (p Conclusion  Our findings indicate that Optmization raised host-matched codon usage in both capsid genes with no truncated proteins produced. The redesigned VP1 and VP2 sequences warrant further investigation as potential candidates for biotherapeutic and vaccine development.
authors: Adhikari S, Mani I.

title: Host specificity, seasonality, and urbanicity shape the gut microbiome of a synanthropic insect
abstract: The soapberry bug Jadera haematoloma is a classic model of rapid adaptive evolution, with a well-documented host shift from native herbaceous sapinds to the introduced goldenrain tree (Koelreuteria spp.). This host shift has facilitated the insect's spread into novel anthropogenic urban habitats. Microbial associations are often critical to insect environmental adaptation. Here, we characterize the gut microbiota of J. haematoloma across native and introduced host plants, seasonal transitions, and a gradient of urbanicity. Our findings indicate that the soapberry bug gut microbiome is highly specialized, with a small number of core bacterial amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) primarily from the families Rhizobiaceae, Streptococcaceae, Enterobacteriaceae, and Lactobacillaceae. While traits such as sex and wing morph do not correlate with microbiome structure, the host plant acts as the primary determinant of community composition. Bugs feeding on the ancestral host plant maintain a more diverse and even microbial community featuring Enterobacteriaceae, whereas the gut environment of bugs on the introduced host is overwhelmingly dominated by a single unclassified Rhizobiaceae ASV. Furthermore, seasonal transitions drive significant turnover among accessory microbial taxa. Finally, we demonstrate that urbanization introduces a distinct ecological effect on the insect's microbiome. While the degree of local green space does not systematically alter within-host taxonomic richness, it is associated with modest change in mean community composition and significantly disrupts microbial community variance. Increased urbanization correlates with significantly higher beta dispersion, indicating that anthropogenic environments lead to more stochastic microbiomes, which may be an indicator of environmental stress. Together, these results illustrate how rapid dietary host shifts and the ecological pressures of urbanization interact to shape the microbiome of a synanthropic insect.
authors: Noyes H, Anika N, Combs J, Khan T, Just J, Fitzpatrick S, Angelini RG, Angelini DR.

title: Dynamic evolution of diaphorin biosynthetic genes against a background of genome conservation in  Profftella
abstract: The Asian citrus psyllid  Diaphorina citri (Insecta: Hemiptera), a major agricultural pest, harbors the unusual obligate bacterial symbiont  “Candidatus Profftella armatura” (  Profftella ), which is intimately integrated with its host yet devotes a remarkably large proportion of its highly reduced genome to the production of diaphorin, a bioactive polyketide. To gain insight into the evolution of this distinctive symbiont, we determined the genomes of  Profftella and the co-resident nutritional symbiont  “Candidatus Carsonella ruddii” (  Carsonella ) from  Diaphorina lycii and compared them with previously characterized counterparts from  D. citri and  D . cf.  continua . The  Profftella and  Carsonella chromosomes from  D. lycii were 471 and 174 kb, respectively, and  Profftella harbored an 8-kb plasmid. Genome organization and gene content were highly conserved across the three lineages. The diaphorin biosynthetic system likewise retained its overall organization, consistent with an important role for diaphorin in the  Diaphorina symbiotic system. Remarkably, however, pronounced lineage-specific structural variation was observed in diaphorin synthases DipP and DipT, encoded by two of the 20 diaphorin biosynthetic genes. These synthases contained three extensively amplified tandem arrays of acyl carrier protein (ACP) domains that carry growing polyketide intermediates, with up to seven copies compared with one or two at corresponding positions in the related pederin synthases. All three regions of tandem ACP repeats showed copy-number variation among the  Profftella lineages. This variation indicates that ACP amplification remains evolutionarily dynamic despite the otherwise highly constrained symbiotic genome. Together, our findings show that even highly integrated obligate symbionts retain evolutionary flexibility in specialized functional systems.
authors: Yasuda Y, Piel J, Malenovský I, Gjonov I, Hirose Y, Nakabachi A.

title: Distinct labeling of host and viral genomes highlights redistribution of nuclear proteins during HSV-1 infection
abstract: Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) coordinates viral and cellular proteins during infection. While proteins associated with HSV-1 genomes have been identified, changes in proteins associated with the host genome during infection remain poorly understood. We adapted accelerated native isolation of proteins on nascent DNA (aniPOND) to label and purify cellular and viral DNA then identify associated proteins by mass spectrometry. Using this approach, we confirm observations that cellular transcription, DNA replication, and repair proteins are enriched on viral genomes after the onset of viral DNA replication. We assessed how protein interactions with cellular DNA change during infection relative to protein abundance. Targets of the viral E3 ubiquitin ligase, ICP0, are depleted from the nucleus and cellular genome during infection. Transcription regulatory factors, Pol II, and the proteasome are depleted from the host genome, while association with DNA damage response and nuclear pore proteins increases. We also provide evidence for HSV-1 disruption of ribosome biogenesis. Results demonstrate reorganization of the nucleus during infection and validate this technique to identify changes to host genome-associated factors during infection. Author Summary  Viruses remodel host cells to create an environment conducive to infection. Herpesviruses are known to alter host protein levels and localization to manipulate cellular processes and pathways. In this study, we explored how HSV-1 infection remodels host nuclei through changes to nuclear protein levels and association of proteins with cellular DNA using a novel approach to study host genome interactions during infection. Results provide a comprehensive view of how HSV-1 dramatically remodels host chromatin and nuclear processes and establishes a method that can be used to explore how nuclei are remodeled during infection with other DNA and RNA viruses.
authors: Lloyd AE, Packard JE, Rutan SL, Dembowski JA.

title: Molecular Characterization of a Saudi Arabian DENV-3 Isolate and Identification of Potential Inhibitors Targeting Dengue Virus Proteins.
abstract: IntroductionThe dengue virus (DENV) is a globally significant pathogenic virus. Understanding the genetic characteristics of the DENV is critical to elucidating viral evolution, diversity, and transmission. Furthermore, investigating DENV evolution using advanced molecular approaches can facilitate the identification of new genotypes and expand our knowledge of the DENV proteome, thereby supporting the development of novel therapeutics. Our study examines a DENV-3 isolate sequence at the molecular level and seeks to identify a potential inhibitor targeting crucial DENV proteins.MethodSerum samples collected from confirmed dengue cases in Saudi Arabia (2024) were analysed to characterize crucial targets for potential antiviral development. We performed multiple sequence alignment, phylogenetic analysis, virtual screening, molecular docking, and ligand-protein interaction analysis.ResultsDENV-3 isolate is similar to the DENV virus from a Saudi Arabian isolate from 2016 (MZ857217.1), as demonstrated by phylogenetic research. The findings reveal a stable secondary structure of targets and identify at least four leading chemical compounds as anti-dengue therapeutic candidates that have higher predicted affinities toward the targets compared to the control.ConclusionThese findings enhance our molecular-level understanding of recent dengue isolates in Saudi Arabia and contribute to the development of antiviral medicines. They may inform future therapeutic strategies and outbreak management efforts.
authors: Damfo S, Zaki EA, Alsuhaimi N, Alharbi BAA, Alrashdi HH.

title: Comparison of enrichment strategies for human cytomegalovirus across short- and long-read platforms.
abstract: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) infection is the most common congenital infection globally and an important cause of disease among immunocompromised patients. HCMV genomic characterization is complicated by its genetic diversity, intra-host variability and complex genome structure. We compared the accuracy of Illumina and Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) sequencing platforms to analyze full-length HCMV genomes of laboratory CMV strains enriched by hybridization capture. Both platforms achieved high per-base accuracy with DNA from high viral load (106 international units, IU) samples: 99.97% (95% CI: 0.999-1.000) with Illumina and 99.71% (95% CI: 0.994-1.000) for ONT. Low viral load (103 IU) samples, however, yielded insufficient data for downstream analysis (0.17% genome coverage, 0.01 × mean depth) using Illumina while ONT achieved 99.91% (95% CI: 0.997-1.000) per-base accuracy. Short-fragment DNA enrichment using biotinylated RNA baits produced ONT reads of only 372 ± 28 bp, inadequate for spanning complex genomic regions. To address this, we modified the enrichment method to increase fragment lengths and evaluated its performance using full-length HCMV genomes of CMV laboratory strains. The modified enrichment method substantially improved ONT performance: read lengths increased to 945 ± 363.3 bp, recovering 89% of the genome versus 83% with Illumina at ≥ 5x depth. The modified method also improved assembly contiguity from mean N50 of 150 bp to 1692 bp. Validation of the modified protocol with synthetic DNA confirmed that 5 × depth was adequate for variant calling, with consistent performance metrics across 5-500 × depth. Long-fragment DNA enrichment with ONT sequencing appears to be optimally suited for comprehensive HCMV genomic characterization.
authors: Dungca NT, Gantt S, Smith M.

title: Fish-derived soluble cues remodel the transcriptome of Aeromonas salmonicida in marine environments.
abstract: Aeromonas salmonicida is an important pathogen of freshwater and marine fish, yet little is known about its transcriptional responses to seawater and soluble cues released by susceptible marine hosts. We investigated the response of a highly virulent A. salmonicida strain to seawater and fish-derived cues using dialysis bags that physically separated bacteria from lumpfish (Cyclopterus lumpus) while allowing exposure to soluble host-derived compounds. Immersion challenge with 106 CFU/mL of A. salmonicida for 40 min resulted in 100% lumpfish mortality within 14 days, confirming susceptibility to waterborne infection. Transcriptomic analysis of A. salmonicida identified 1,389 and 1,184 differentially expressed genes after 40 min exposure to seawater (SW) and seawater in the presence of lumpfish (SWF), respectively, relative to culture conditions. Seawater induced extensive remodeling of stress and redox homeostasis, transport, surface and sensory systems, iron homeostasis, and transcriptional regulation, with reduced expression of cell-division and cell-envelope biosynthetic functions. Direct comparison of SWF with SW identified 442 bacterial DEGs, including 225 with higher and 217 with lower expression in SWF. Fish-derived cues were particularly associated with increased expression of amino-acid and central carbon metabolism and nutrient and osmolyte transport. The pASAL5-encoded type III secretion system showed an induction-dominated response to seawater and component-specific modulation by fish-derived cues. These findings demonstrate that seawater initiates transcriptional remodeling of environmental and virulence-associated functions before direct host contact, while host-derived cues further modify metabolic, transport, and T3SS-associated responses.
authors: Vasquez I, Machimbirike VI, Paramanathan T, Cao T, Santander J.

title: Identification and in silico characterization of a thermophilic GH10 xylanase from hot spring metagenomes.
abstract: This study sought to identify xylanases by mining metagenomic reads from high-temperature environments across multiple geographic regions. It also aimed to conduct an in-silico characterization of a promising thermophilic GH10 xylanase, analyzing its sequence, structural features, and dynamic properties. BLASTp results indicated that potentially thermophilic xylanases from different hot spring environments share high sequence similarity with xylanases from diverse phyla, including Cyanobacteria, Dictyoglomi, Bacteroidota, Bacillota, Pseudomonadota, and Acidobacteriota. Additionally, eighteen complete xylanase sequences with melting temperatures above 65 °C showed instability index values below 40 (ranging from 22.32 to 39.13) and aliphatic index values greater than 72 (ranging from 72.04 to 95.54). Molecular docking analysis revealed that the catalytic residues E164 and E270 of HSWMetXyn15 participated in noncovalent interactions within the HSWMetXyn15-X7 docked complex. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated stable behavior of both HSWMetXyn15 and the HSWMetXyn15-X7 complex. Structural analysis confirmed that HSWMetXyn15 belongs to the GH10 family and differs from the reference xylanase XynAS9 in several secondary structural elements. Moreover, P77 and E78 may contribute to the thermal stability of HSWMetXyn15 through their involvement in local noncovalent interactions. Therefore, the favorable structural and dynamic properties of HSWMetXyn15 compared with the reference xylanase XynAS9 highlight its potential as a promising candidate for high-temperature industrial applications, including biofuel production, animal feed processing, paper and pulp manufacturing, and food processing.
authors: Kurt H, Tütüncü HE, Vardar-Yel N, Sarı C, Akçok İ, Hoş BH, Kurt KC, Akarsubaşı AT, Sürmeli Y.

title: Functional characterization of flowering-associated PbMADS33 and PbMADS8 in Phoebe bournei.
abstract: Main conclusionPbMADS8 and PbMADS33 from Phoebe bournei promote flowering when overexpressed in Arabidopsis and interact in the nucleus; their co-expression enhances PbGA20ox1 and PbFBX promoter activity in transient assays. Phoebe bournei has a prolonged juvenile phase that limits breeding, but the functions of its flowering-associated regulators remain poorly understood. Transcriptome analysis of leaves from trees of different ages and floral samples identified 5,921 differentially expressed genes. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) identified a black module associated with leaves from flowering trees and containing three SUPPRESSOR OF OVEREXPRESSION OF CONSTANS 1 (SOC1)-like genes, PbMADS8, PbMADS33, and PbMADS38. Comparative genomic analysis revealed expanded SOC1-like loci enriched in repetitive sequences. PbMADS8 and PbMADS33 were selected for functional analysis because of their higher transcript abundance relative to PbMADS38. Heterologous overexpression of either gene accelerated flowering in Arabidopsis thaliana under long-day conditions. Yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) and bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) assays supported an interaction between PbMADS33 and PbMADS8 in the nucleus. DNA affinity purification sequencing (DAP-seq) identified candidate PbMADS33-binding regions, and promoter assays supported regulation of PbGA20ox1 and the putative F-box gene PbFBX. Co-expression of PbMADS8 and PbMADS33 produced the highest reporter activity for both promoters in Nicotiana benthamiana. Together, these results nominate PbMADS8 and PbMADS33 as flowering-associated candidates and PbGA20ox1 and PbFBX as candidate promoter-associated genes in P. bournei. Their effects on endogenous gibberellin levels, protein turnover, and the juvenile phase of P. bournei remain to be established.
authors: Sun Q, Zhang Y, Qiu Y, Wang B, Zhou S, Li C, Han X, Yang Q, Tong Z, Zhang J.

title: From genetic investigation to viral diagnosis: HSV-1 detection through genome sequencing analysis in neonatal intensive care.
abstract: PurposeNeonatal sepsis and genetic disorders share overlapping clinical presentations in critically ill neonates, making differential diagnosis challenging. We report an incidental detection of herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) through human genome sequencing (GS) initially performed for suspected genetic disease.MethodsA 7-day-old male infant presented with fever and failure to gain weight. Initial investigations revealed inflammatory response and gram-positive cocci in urine; CSF and respiratory microbiological analyses were negative. Trio-based GS was performed under the French Genomic Medicine Plan 2025. Soft-clipped reads from BAM files were analyzed using IGV visualization and NCBI BLAST homology search. Retrospective virological testing was performed on archived samples.ResultsGS variant calling initially identified an apparent de novo insertion in NRROS. Manual BAM file inspection revealed that flanking soft-clipped sequences aligned with the HSV-1 UL47 gene rather than the human genome. Retrospective PCR confirmed HSV-1 in blood and nasopharyngeal samples, despite initially negative CSF testing. The patient died at 14 days of age from disseminated HSV-1 infection with multiorgan failure.ConclusionHuman GS can incidentally detect pathogen sequences through systematic analysis of unmapped reads, highlighting its potential dual diagnostic utility in neonatal intensive care.
journal: Genetics in medicine : official journal of the American College of Medical Genetics
authors: Sauvestre C, Garrigue I, Arcourt A, Thevenon J, Burrel S, Guichoux J, Trimouille A.

title: DBAASP V4: condition-resolved bioactivity and chemical structures for data-driven peptide and peptidomimetic discovery.
abstract: The current peptide renaissance-driven by metagenomic and proteomic mining, molecular de-extinction, protein language models, and generative or evolutionary design-is producing millions of candidates, but useful machine learning depends on experimentally anchored, context-rich labels. The Database of Antimicrobial Activity and Structure of Peptides (DBAASP) is a manually curated resource linking peptides and peptidomimetics to quantitative antimicrobial, antibiofilm, anticancer, hemolytic, and mammalian-cell cytotoxicity measurements and their experimental conditions. DBAASP v4 contains >25 000 entries and extends the resource from a sequence-centered database to a structure-aware repository. Major additions include systematic SMILES representations, enhanced annotation of intrachain bonds and ring architectures, dedicated antibiofilm, and synergy records, PubChem links, >9200 molecular-dynamics trajectories, and new prediction services. The condition-resolved data support supervised learning, strain-, and target-specific models, model calibration, and surrogate fitness functions for genetic algorithms. SMILES representations further enable modeling of noncanonical peptides and peptidomimetics that cannot be adequately described by sequence alone. DBAASP therefore complements large peptide catalogues by providing the experimentally curated activity and structure layers, needed to convert sequence information into testable predictions, design, and optimization of biologically active compounds. DBAASP v4 is freely available at https://dbaasp.org.
authors: Pirtskhalava M, Alimbarashvili E, Grigolava M, Chubinidze M, Vishnepolsky B, Zaalishvili G, Karaputadze R, Samsonidze N, Rosenthal A, Hurt DE, Tartakovsky M, Gabrielian A.

title: Epidemiology and spillover risk of SFTSV in animals across East Asia.
abstract: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is an emerging tick‑borne zoonosis in East Asia, yet the contribution of animals to virus maintenance and spillover remains incompletely characterized. This review synthesizes current evidence of SFTS virus (SFTSV) infection across domestic livestock, companion animals, wildlife, and captive species, focusing on host range, geographic distribution, diagnostics, and reports of viral RNA and virus isolation. Available data indicate that SFTSV exposure and infection occur across a broad range of animal hosts, supporting a multi-host ecological framework rather than a simple single-reservoir interpretation. Domestic ruminants frequently exhibit high seroprevalence and may function as sentinels of enzootic activity, while occasional virus isolation from cattle demonstrates that viable virus can be recovered from naturally infected livestock, although this does not establish reservoir or amplification competence. Companion animals are considered a potential interface for interspecies transmission, as some studies have documented severe clinical disease, high viral loads, and cat-associated human transmission events supported by varying levels of epidemiological and genomic evidence. Studies in wildlife further document exposure and natural infection across diverse taxa, although their specific roles in viral maintenance remain unresolved. Interpretation of these findings depends heavily on the diagnostic modality: serology primarily indicates prior exposure, RNA detection supports current or recent infection, and virus isolation demonstrates that viable virus was present in the sampled material. Integrating animal infection data within an ecological framework reveals major knowledge gaps related to reservoir competence, infectious shedding, phylogenetic connections among animal, tick, and human cases, and implications for prevention. The review underscores the need for One Health surveillance that incorporates clinical data from companion animals and applies evidence‑based interpretation to improve recognition of animal-human interfaces associated with potential spillover risk.
authors: Shin YS, Lee JY, Kang JG.
