title: Constraint-Aware Coding-Sequence Design for Nicotiana benthamiana: A 49,257-Record Benchmark and Codon-Reference Sensitivity Analysis
abstract: Synonymous coding DNA sequence (CDS) design for plant expression constructs must balance host codon adaptation against guanine–cytosine (GC) composition, restriction-site avoidance, and sequence-integrity constraints, yet benchmark outcomes can depend strongly on the chosen codon- usage reference. Using FactorForge v3.2.0, an open-source CDS design and sequence-review workflow, we evaluated four rule-based design presets (Balanced, High-CAI, GC-target, and Assembly-friendly) on 49,257 reference-derived Nicotiana benthamiana CDS/protein records from the Sol Genomics Network (SGN) QLD183 resource (seed 320), scoring sequence integrity, a historical 55–65% GC window, and absence of BsaI/BpiI/BsmBI sites. With the legacy packaged codon reference, Assembly-friendly passed all three criteria for 63.37% of records; with three genome-derived references its combined pass rate was 0.00% after rounding, whereas GC-target attained 22.68% in each derived condition. A separate v3.3.0 dynamic-programming (DP) execution maximizing the codon adaptation index (CAI) within the same GC window found a GC-compliant sequence for 99.83% of records (mean CAI 0.9989), but 28.21% passed all criteria because Type IIS sites are outside the DP objective. These in-silico results characterize candidate generation under a historical policy. Evaluation with the v3.3.0 default settings, against external tools, and in the laboratory remains to be done.
authors: Kim M.

title: Detection of novel Echovirus 25 lineage from patients and sewage in Fukuoka in 2024.
abstract: Echovirus 25 (E25), belonging to the Enterovirus B species of viruses, is known to cause infectious gastroenteriris, aseptic meningitis, and acute flaccid paralysis. Our study aims to conduct enterovirus surveillance and subsequent molecular epidemiology investigations among patients and sewage samples in Fukuoka. In 2024, a total of ten and seven enteroviral strains were detected in 141 clinical specimens and 24 sewage samples, respectively. Among them, five E25 strains were identified, and phylogenetic analysis of VP1 region revealed that these strains constituted a distinct clade separated from previously reported E25 strains. Full-length genome sequences were determined using sequence-independent, single-primer amplification and next-generation sequencing. The five strains had sequence identities ranging from 99.0% to 99.9% among themselves. Through phylogenetic analysis, the five strains were classified as E25 on the basis of P1, and P1-3 sequences, and as E3 and E11 on the basis of P2-3 sequence. Furthermore, SimPlot and RDP4 analysis revealed a unique recombination event between the detected E25 strains and E3 in the region of the 2B gene, which is the non-structural region. These findings indicated the emergence of a novel E25 lineage in 2024, and underscore the importance of continued surveillance to monitor its evolution and circulation.
authors: Furutani T, Yoshitomi H, Kondo Y, Kobayashi T, Kitamura K, Hamasaki M.

title: Stream–lake network position structures freshwater microbial communities across multiple catchments
abstract: Streams and lakes form hydrologically connected freshwater networks. Different environmental conditions and dispersal dynamics along the stream–lake continuum potentially affect bacterial community composition, although the strength of such effects may vary among individual catchments. Here, we analysed 224 water samples from 58 streams draining into eight lakes across Switzerland, covering the full continuum from headwaters to lake outlets. Bacterial community composition analyzed via 16S metabarcoding differed between streams and lakes, with a sharp turnover at stream-lake confluence, and this pattern was repeatable across all catchments. Lake communities had lower alpha diversity and lower overall beta dispersion than stream communities, despite hydrological connectivity with a diverse stream microbiome. Community composition in both lakes and streams differed between catchments, but this pattern was more pronounced in lakes. Lake communities were dominated by a small set of widespread and abundant core taxa, primarily established pelagic freshwater genera, that captured the catchment-level differences through shifts in relative abundance. In contrast, stream communities contained a comparatively less abundant core microbiome dominated by soil- and groundwater-associated genera, together with a larger and more diverse peripheral microbiome. Together, these findings show that bacterial community composition changes repeatably across the different positions of hydrological networks.
authors: Kirtane A, Deiner K, Hall AR.

title: SYMBIO-SCAN, a full-length 16S rRNA gene-based workflow optimized for bacterial symbiont detection and discovery from long read sequencing
abstract: Bacterial endosymbionts are often unculturable, making sequencing-based approaches essential for their discovery and characterization. Here we developed SYMBIO-SCAN, a dedicated workflow for recovering high-quality nearly full-length 16S rRNA gene sequences of symbionts from long reads, which provided an adequate discriminatory power for identification and for accurate phylogenetic analyses. After validation on a mock community, we applied this workflow to 30 beetle (Coleoptera) specimens from 10 species. Beetles were selected since they host a wide variety of bacterial symbionts, able to influence host physiology, ecology, population dynamics, and evolution. Despite their importance, most of these symbionts remain completely unknown or poorly characterized. By the novel approach, we obtained 80 high-quality sequences belonging to diverse bacterial lineages, mostly  Rickettsiales and  Enterobacterales . Putative reproductive manipulators were among the most frequently detected symbionts, including  Wolbachia ,  Rickettsia , “  Candidatus Lariskella”,  Arsenophonus , and  Spiroplasma . Moreover, three putative novel genera and one additional putative novel species were identified, including a possible  Enterobacterales nutritional symbiont of the weevil  Holotrichapion pisi . Overall, our results support that full-length 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing combined with tailored bioinformatic analyses provide a quick, cost-effective, and robust approach for investigating the diversity of host-associated bacterial symbionts, also allowing the discovery of entirely novel lineages.
authors: Croci C, Iamundo G, Baharibabadi A, Sabatelli S, Sassera D, Castelli M.

title: The influence of drug dosing regimen on extinction and adaptation during experimental evolution in  Candida albicans
abstract: ABSTRACT  The antifungal azole drug fluconazole (FLC) is frequently prescribed for treating  Candida albicans infections. Azole drugs are typically fungistatic—they inhibit cell growth rather than kill susceptible cells within a population. Therefore, fungal populations can adapt to fluconazole through increased drug resistance or increased drug tolerance (the ability of a subpopulation of susceptible cells to grow slowly at inhibitory drug concentrations). To our knowledge, no prior experiments have examined how different factors influence extinction propensity, although previous  in vitro studies show that both drug concentration and strain background can influence adaptation. To determine how the drug dosing regimen, namely fluconazole concentration and transfer duration (i.e., the amount of time between transfer into fresh medium), influenced extinction and adaptation in  Candida albicans , we conducted a fully factorial series of short  in vitro evolution experiments. Dosing regimen significantly influenced extinction: all replicates evolved at all drug concentrations survived the 48 h and 72 h transfer experiments, yet the extinction rate increased sharply from low to high drug concentration with 24 h transfers. Increases in drug tolerance were frequent regardless of the dosing regimen. In contrast, drug resistance and growth rate both tended to decrease following evolution at higher drug concentrations. Fluconazole-evolved replicates exhibited frequent increases in cross-tolerance and decreases in cross-resistance in a panel of other azole drugs. Genome size changes were common in some strain backgrounds evolved to higher fluconazole concentrations, regardless of transfer times. Combined, our results indicate that many experimental factors can influence the trajectory of adaptation, and show that extinction in a fungistatic drug occurs readily at high drug concentration with rapid transfers.
authors: Sethi P, Pouteau E, Sumanarathne A, Gerstein AC.

title: Occurrence of Potato Viruses in Taiwan and Biological and Molecular Characterization of Potato Virus Y Isolate.
abstract: Potato production has long been threatened by viral diseases, particularly potato leafroll virus (PLRV) and potato viruses A, M, S, X, and Y (PVA, PVM, PVS, PVX, and PVY). However, current information on the occurrence of potato viruses in Taiwan is limited, and the biological and molecular characteristics of locally occurring virus isolates are poorly understood. To determine the current occurrence and characteristics of potato viruses in Taiwan, a four-year field survey (2023-2026) was conducted in commercial potato production fields across major potato-growing regions. PVY was the most frequently detected virus (46%), followed by PVS (5.1%). Subsequent strain typing showed that recombinant PVY strains predominated, with PVYSYR-I (25.1%), PVYSYR-II (13.7%), and PVYN-Wi (13.3%) being the most frequently detected strain groups. Among the tested isolates, PVY-33, a PVYN-Wi isolate, caused the most pronounced symptoms in Nicotiana benthamiana and induced severe systemic leaf deformation in potato cv. Kennebec. Based on this pronounced biological phenotype, PVY-33 was selected for construction of a full-length infectious cDNA clone, providing a genetically defined and reproducible inoculum source. The infectious clone-derived virus reproduced the PVY-33 phenotype and reduced tuber yield by approximately 50% in both cv. Kennebec and cv. Atlantic. Whole-genome phylogenetic analysis supported the notion that PVY-33 is closely related to PVYN-Wi isolates from the United States. Together, these findings provide an updated understanding of potato virus occurrence and PVY strain composition in the surveyed fields and provide important information about the biological and molecular characteristics of a locally derived PVY isolate.
authors: Chiu SH, Lin MS, Liang YC, Shih PC, Chang L.

title: Decoding dissolved organic matter reorganization and multitrophic regulation of biogeochemical cycling in effluent-dominated hyporheic sediments.
abstract: Continuous wastewater effluent discharge sustains pronounced redox heterogeneity in the hyporheic zone (HZ), with consequences for dissolved organic matter (DOM) transformation and sediment biogeochemistry. However, the ecological pathways linking redox-dependent DOM transformation to multitrophic organization and coupled nitrogen (N) and sulfur (S) cycling remain poorly understood. We integrated fluorescence and molecular DOM characterization, bacterial and eukaryotic community profiling, metagenomics, ecological network analysis, and structural equation modeling across oxic and anoxic zones. The summed relative contribution of protein-like fluorescence did not differ significantly between zones, while tyrosine-like fluorescence was 31% higher in the oxic zone and the median tryptophan/tyrosine ratio was 52% higher under anoxia. FT-ICR MS analysis showed that formulas positively associated with HIX had higher O/C ratios and a median NOSC of 0.35, whereas negatively associated formulas had a median NOSC of -0.90, linking optical humification to molecular carbon oxidation characteristics. Bacterial genera exhibited broader estimated niche breadths than eukaryotic genera, with median Levins' B values of 7.19 and 5.86, respectively. Under oxic conditions, DOM was associated with basal communities within a connected sequence of bacterial, protozoan, and metazoan associations. Bacterial and algal communities were primarily associated with N and S cycling potentials, respectively. Under anoxia, significant DOM associations with basal groups and the bacteria-to-protozoa association were not detected, while both cycling potentials shifted toward bacteria-centered regulation. N and S cycling potentials remained strongly coordinated, while modeled network robustness was 20.5% lower under anoxia. These findings reveal that redox-associated DOM reorganization shifts multitrophic regulation of coupled N and S cycling, thus providing a framework for integrating DOM composition and multitrophic organization when assessing aquatic interfaces exposed to sustained organic matter loading and redox heterogeneity.
authors: Wang Z, Pan X, Li Y, Wang L.

title: Associations of environmental phenols exposure with gut microbiota in a general population from Shenzhen, China.
abstract: The gut microbiota is considered an important target for the toxicity of environmental phenols, yet the epidemiological evidence elucidating their associations in adults remains limited. This study investigated associations between phenol exposure and gut microbiota in 241 adults from Shenzhen, China. We quantified 38 urinary phenols via ultrahigh performance liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) and profiled the gut microbiome via shotgun metagenomics. Linear regression, permutational multivariate analysis of variance (adonis), and Multivariable Association with Linear Models 2 (MaAsLin2) were used to assess links with α-diversity, β-diversity, microbial taxa, and functional pathways. We found that exposure to environmental phenols was significantly associated with altered gut microbiota diversity, composition and function. Bisphenol C was negatively associated with α-diversity, whereas benzylparaben and ethylparaben were positively associated with it. Exposure to methylparaben, triclosan, isopropylparaben and propylparaben was significantly associated with altered gut microbial community structure. Taxa analysis showed that methylparaben was negatively associated with the relative abundance of two beneficial species, Bacteroides salyersiae and Anaerostipes caccae. Additionally, functional profiling revealed that parabens inhibited amino-acid, carbohydrate and terpenoid metabolism, whereas triclosan up-regulated pathways for aromatic compound degradation and mixed-acid fermentation. Further prospective investigations are warranted to validate our findings.
authors: Zou D, Fu Y, Lv Z, Liu Z, Huang Z, Yan B, Liu J, Kuang Y, Li M, Lin L, He M, Jing T, Huang S.

title: Differing patterns in community composition and diversity of biofilm-forming bacteria and fungi along a large salinity gradient
abstract: Aim  Biofilms are complex ecosystems formed by phototrophic and heterotrophic organisms, such as bacteria and fungi. Biofilms are hotspots for microbial activity and crucial for the functioning of all aquatic ecosystems, but they are overlooked and poorly studied, especially along large environmental gradients. We aimed at resolving the responses of bacterial and fungal communities to environmental variation along a gradient with strong variation in environmental factors, especially salinity. We also investigated whether the diversity of biofilm-forming bacteria and fungi follows the pattern predicted by the ‘Remane curve’, which posits that species diversity is lowest at intermediate salinity. Location  2300-km-long spatial gradient in the Baltic Sea, Northern Europe Time period: August 2018 Major taxa studied  Biofilm-forming bacteria and fungi Methods  We investigated the composition and diversity of bacteria and fungi by collecting biofilm samples from 42 shallow benthic ecosystems. We also characterized key environmental variables, such as salinity, nutrient concentrations, wind exposure, and climatic conditions. Bacterial and fungal communities in biofilm samples were identified using Illumina MiSeq sequencing. Results  We found that bacteria and fungi responded differently to environmental variation. Bacterial communities were mainly controlled by salinity, and their diversity was lowest in the intermediate salinity. Bacterial communities were also dominated by different bacterial orders in high, intermediate, and low salinity. Fungal communities, instead, were jointly controlled by several environmental variables, i.e., salinity, water temperature, wind exposure, and nutrients, and their diversity or composition did not show a clear pattern along the salinity gradient. Main conclusions  To our knowledge, this is one of the first studies to investigate the biofilm-forming communities, especially fungal communities, along large environmental gradients. Our results highlight the role of biofilms as complex ecosystems where organisms’ ecological requirements are unique and variable.
authors: Virta L, Wang J, Salonen I.

title: Integrating 16S and 18S sequencing reveals coupled prokaryotic and eukaryotic relationships in drinking water biofilms
abstract: Drinking water biofilms host diverse communities spanning all realms of life. However, despite the known interactions between opportunistic pathogens and microbial eukaryotes such as amoebae, most studies focus only on the prokaryotic populations in these systems. As a result, the degree to which microbial eukaryotes shape biofilm communities and the persistence of opportunistic waterborne pathogens, such as  Legionella spp. is still largely unknown. Here we leveraged a set of 128 non-disinfected drinking water shower hose biofilms collected across Switzerland to characterize both communities and quantify eukaryotes’ role in shaping prokaryotic communities and  Legionella persistence. We found both communities to present a conserved set of core taxa dominated by oligotrophic bacterial families and amoebae. The prevalence of taxa was mainly driven by the phylogenetic diversity among their sequence variants rather than their number alone. We detected prokaryotic and eukaryotic communities to show similar patterns in their richness and composition, influencing each other more than abiotic building-level factors.  Legionellaceae bacteria were detected in 82% of samples presenting a diversity extending known reference species and no clear dominant taxa.  Legionellaceae richness did not correlate with the richness of known amoebal hosts, but rather other amoebae, indicating that eukaryotic taxa relevant for  Legionella persistence extend beyond the classically described hosts. These findings highlight the importance of integrating the eukaryotic communities to understand the microbial ecology in drinking water biofilms and recognize the conditions which allow opportunistic waterborne pathogens such as  Legionella to persist.
authors: Caligaris L, Hammes F, Cristino S, Gabrielli M.

title: Gut microbiome-disease associations revealed by large-scale Mendelian randomization analyses
abstract: Abstract    Background  The gut microbiome has been associated with diverse human diseases, but systematic genetic evidence for potential causal relevance, disease-system clustering, and circulating metabolic pathways remains limited. Methods  We integrated four gut microbiome genome-wide association study (GWAS) datasets with 4,934 disease GWAS outcomes. Two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR), using the inverse-variance weighted (IVW) method as the primary analysis, was performed to evaluate potential causal associations between gut microbial traits and diseases. Multiple sensitivity analyses and reverse MR were conducted to assess robustness and potential reverse causality. Hypergeometric tests were used to examine disease-system enrichment of microbial lineages with significant MR associations. For significant MR associations, Bayesian colocalization analysis was performed to assess shared local genetic signals. Circulating metabolite GWAS data were further incorporated into two-step MR mediation analysis to explore candidate metabolic pathways. Results  We identified 1,943 significant associations between 630 gut microbial traits and 925 disease outcomes across multiple disease systems. Enrichment analysis revealed system-specific clustering patterns, including enrichment of Burkholderiales-related taxa in circulatory diseases, Bacteroidota-related taxa in mental, behavioural, or neurodevelopmental disorders,  Eisenbergiella  -related taxa in musculoskeletal diseases, and  Faecalicatena  -related taxa in endocrine and metabolic diseases. Colocalization analysis identified 58 colocalization signals with supportive evidence of shared local genetic signals, involving 34 microbial traits, 45 disease outcomes, and 33distinct genomic windows. Mediation analysis highlighted triglycerides in intermediate-density lipoprotein (IDL-TG) as a frequent candidate mediator, particularly linking Burkholderiales-related taxa to ischaemic cardiovascular diseases. Conclusions  This large-scale genetic study provides a systematic map of potential causal associations between the gut microbiome and multi-system diseases. By integrating MR, disease-system enrichment, colocalization, and mediation analyses, our findings suggest that specific gut microbial lineages may contribute to disease susceptibility through shared genetic architecture and circulating metabolic pathways. In particular, the Burkholderiales-IDL-TG-ischaemic cardiovascular disease axis may represent a candidate microbiome-metabolism-disease pathway that warrants further validation in experimental and clinical studies.
authors: Che X, Zhang X, Zhang Z, Pan J.

title: Transient overexpression and silencing of tomato SlGLP11-1 gene reveal its crucial role in mediating ROS homeostasis driven disease resistance
abstract: Abstract    Germin and germin- like proteins (GLPs) are known to play various roles in plant development and in response to biotic and abiotic stress. Many GLPs have been reported to show differential expression in response to pathogen infections, indicating their direct roles in host- pathogen interactions. Despite their significant roles in plant immunity, the tomato (  Solanum lycopersicum  L.) GLP members have not been studied comprehensively at the genome- wide scale. Also, very few reports exist on the functions and activities of tomato GLP gene family members. In this study, GLP family members in tomato were analysed and a standardised nomenclature for tomato GLP genes was defined. The chromosomal distribution of GLP genes in tomato was determined, and a phylogenetic analysis was performed. In addition, the in silico subcellular localization of GLPs in tomato was predicted, and gene expression was examined in response to different phytohormone treatments and pathogen infection. Finally, we identified candidate pathogen- responsive  SlGLPs  and functionally characterized  SlGLP11-1  . Transient overexpression of  SlGLP11-1  in  Nicotiana  leaves enhanced resistance against  Botrytis cinerea  . Similarly transient silencing of  SlGLP11-1  by virus induced gene silencing (VIGS) in tomato leaves increased susceptibility to  Botrytis cinerea  infection. We also, estimated endogenous H  2  O  2  levels and catalase activity in the transient  SlGLP11-  1 overexpressed and silenced leaves of  Nicotiana benthamiana  and tomato respectively, all with and without Botrytis infection. Our results establish that  SlGLP11  -1 functions as a positive regulator of ROS-mediated plant defence by promoting H  2  O  2  accumulation during both basal and pathogen challenged conditions, with catalase activity tracking H  2  O  2  levels as a secondary antioxidant response. This study will serve as a foundation for future functional investigations of tomato GLP family members playing role in the plant immunity.
authors: Prajapati P, Khobragade T, Kamble A.

title: Dose-dependent growth and gene expression in marine prokaryotes in response to glacial and non-glacial iron-rich colloids from Kerguelen Island (Southern Ocean)
abstract: Iron (Fe) plays a central role in regulating prokaryotic carbon (C) metabolism through complex processes. In Fe-limited limited ocean regions, new sources can influence prokaryotic activity thereby modulating the microbially mediated cycling of carbon. However, while accelerated glacial melting delivers substantial quantities of Fe-rich material to the ocean, the bioavailability of glacial Fe remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the response of marine prokaryotes to Fe contained in the colloidal fraction (20–200 nm size fraction) originating from the Cook Ice Cap on Kerguelen Island (Southern Ocean). We assessed growth and gene transcriptional responses to dose-dependent additions of Fe-rich colloids from two sources, glacial meltwater and a non-glacial origin. The two colloid types resulted in dose-dependent, but contrasting growth responses. Increasing additions of glacial colloids resulted in a reduction in prokaryotic growth and the opposite pattern was observed with non-glacial colloids. Transcriptional profiles revealed an increasing trend in Fe-limitation, as evidenced by transcripts of the glyoxylate shunt, as a function of the addition of either colloid type. We further observed a dose-dependent increase in transcripts of aromatic compound degradation only in the non-glacial colloid incubations, suggesting that these Fe-rich colloids could also provide C. These results point to the key role of C regulating prokaryotic growth in response to Fe-rich colloids. The quantitative transcriptional responses observed provide insights to the nutritional status of prokaryotes and to compounds and pathways involved in processing Fe-rich colloids.
authors: Pereira Garcia C, Christaki U, Thoppil R, Guénueguès A, Catala P, Crispi O, Blain S, Obernosterer I.

title: Genomic Potential vs. Pathogenic Reality: Functional Virulence Variation in  Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Despite the rapid expansion of bacterial genome sequencing, predicting pathogen virulence from genomic information remains a major challenge. To study this association, we integrate comparative genomics, functional phenotyping, host-pathogen interaction assays, and infection outcomes across a diverse collection of 28  Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates, representing clinically relevant diversity in serotype, type IV pilus group, and flagellar type.  While virulence-associated systems were broadly retained across the strain collection, isolates displayed substantial variation in phenotypic behavior and pathogenicity. Genotypic classifications based on pilus, flagellar, siderophore, or secretion system characteristics were poor predictors of virulence-associated phenotypes. Pathogenicity in a  Galleria mellonella model varied markedly among strains and was most strongly associated with surface-associated motility, whereas other virulence traits and quorum-sensing genotypes showed limited predictive value. In a three-dimensional lung epithelial cell model, inflammatory responses were negatively correlated with activity of the type III secretion system effector ExoS, suggesting a role in modulation of host immune signaling.  Together, these findings demonstrate that virulence emerges from functional deployment of conserved virulence repertoires, rather than their mere presence. By linking genomic diversity to phenotypic expression, pathogenicity, and host responses within a single strain collection, this study highlights fundamental limitations of gene-content-based virulence prediction and underscores the importance of integrating genomic and functional data to better understand  P. aeruginosa virulence.  Importance  The increasing availability of bacterial genome sequences raises expectations that pathogen virulence can be predicted from gene content. However, despite encoding similar repertoires of virulence-associated genes, many  P. aeruginosa isolates exhibit markedly different infection outcomes. This study demonstrates that substantial variation in pathogenicity and host interaction can arise from strains with broadly conserved virulence systems. These findings highlight the important contribution of regulatory and functional variation to virulence and show that genomic information alone provides an incomplete picture of pathogenic potential. They further underscore the need to better understand how genomic variation translates into phenotypic traits and host interactions. By integrating genomic analyses with phenotypic characterization and host-response measurements, this work provides the type of dataset needed to connect genomic variation to functional outcomes. Such datasets may ultimately provide the foundation for more reliable prediction of virulence from genome sequences.
authors: Dehaene R, Poppeliers J, Boon M, Bens L, Voet M, Lood C, Verwimp S, Van Noort V, De Meester G, Van Daele A, Crabbé A, Lavigne R.

title: US Carbapenemase Genomic Panel: An Open and Annually Refreshed State-by-Year Table of Carbapenemase Genes in Public U.S. Gram-Negative Genomes
abstract: Carbapenemase-producing Gram-negative bacteria are among the most urgent antimicrobial resistance threats in the United States, and public health lab-oratories increasingly characterize them by whole-genome sequencing. The NCBI Pathogen Detection project screens every public genome in its scope with AMRFinderPlus, but its outputs are organized by organism group and release rather than by place and time, and sample metadata are free text. This paper describes the US Carbapenemase Genomic Panel v1.0.0, an open, versioned ta-ble of five carbapenemase families (KPC, NDM, OXA-48-like, VIM and IMP) in public U.S. genomes of Klebsiella, Escherichia coli, Enterobacter, Acinetobacter and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, tabulated by state, collection year, organism and harmonized isolation source (clinical, screening, environmental, unknown). Fam-ily membership follows the AMRFinderPlus Reference Gene Hierarchy, and every harmonization decision is published with the data. The v1.0.0 build, from NCBI data retrieved on 12 October 2026, covers 257,965 genomes, of which 38,511 (14.9%) carry at least one of the five families. NDM-carrying genomes (17,736) now outnumber KPC-carrying genomes (16,911), and NDM has exceeded KPC in every complete collection year since 2021. A state could be assigned to only 34.3% of carbapenemase-positive genomes; 90.2% of the remainder come from a single CDC BioProject (HAI-Seq Gram-negative bacteria) that records country only. The panel therefore supports national trend description and state-level description of the located public record, but not comparison of burden between states. The scripted pipeline is designed for annual refresh, with each version archived under a stable concept DOI.
authors: Akhigbe Igbuan E.

title: A genome‑wide screen in E. coli reveals metabolic adaptations that enhance intratumoral fitness and bacterial cancer therapy efficacy.
abstract: Despite decades of investigation, the fundamental molecular and cellular principles that enable bacteria to thrive within the tumor microenvironment have yet to be defined. Here, through a genome‑wide functional screen, we identify the bacterial genes and pathways that govern intratumoral fitness. Targeted deletion of nonglucose phosphotransferase systems to align bacterial metabolic preference with tumor metabolite availability promotes bacterial intratumoral fitness. Integrating multiple metabolic adaptations into a single tumor‑avid Escherichia coli strain (Ec‑TA) results in increased tumor colonization, not only after intratumoral delivery but also after intravenous delivery, leading to increased anti‑tumor efficacy when using Ec‑TA engineered to deliver an encoded immunostimulatory payload. Furthermore, Ec‑TA displaces wild‑type bacteria from pre‑colonized tumors when administered systemically, underscoring its potential for locally delivering therapeutics in the presence of resident tumor microbes. These data demonstrate that adapting bacteria to the unique characteristics of the tumor metabolic microenvironment can drive the development of safer and more effective chassis for next‑generation bacterial cancer therapies.
authors: Chen N, Rouanne M, Yang Z, Mariuzza DL, Fabozzi M, Shin AE, Nishiwaki N, Rajbhandari P, Ringham OR, Schwabe AD, Zhu M, Stockwell BR, Mori H, Danino T, Arpaia N.

title: Stochastic and quantum perspectives on teleost immunity: Linking immunogenetics, structure, and biophysics.
abstract: Teleost fishes possess highly diverse, lineage-specific pattern-recognition receptor (PRR) repertoires shaped by teleost-specific whole-genome duplication (3R-WGD), subsequent duplication, differential retention, functional divergence, and gene loss. Toll-like, RIG-I-like, and NOD-like receptor families show lineage-specific expansion and, in some cases, adaptive sequence evolution, particularly in regions implicated in ligand recognition. Separately, hydrogen tunneling is supported in specific enzyme reactions, while radical-pair chemistry provides a bounded mechanistic precedent rather than evidence for teleost immune function. This review examines whether teleost PRR diversification creates concrete, testable opportunities for investigating analogous biophysical mechanisms, without assuming that receptor diversity or environmental sensitivity entails non-classical effects. A five-level evidence hierarchy is applied: direct teleost evidence, evidence from other systems, indirect teleost evidence, testable hypothesis, and unsupported or contradicted claim. No direct evidence was identified for a functionally consequential quantum-biological mechanism in teleost immune recognition or signaling. However, increasing genomic, structural, transcriptomic, single-cell, and functional-genomic resolution provides a tractable framework for testing such possibilities. Sequence and structural divergence among PRR paralogs can be evaluated using structure prediction, molecular dynamics, and, where chemically justified, quantum-chemical or QM/MM methods, with uncertainty assessed across stages and experimental validation through ligand binding, signaling, and environmental-response phenotypes. The NADPH-to-flavin hydride-transfer step in an immune effector oxidase is proposed as a chemically defined candidate, not an established teleost tunneling mechanism. Quantum mechanisms therefore remain hypotheses rather than established features of teleost immunity. A falsifiable research roadmap is proposed linking receptor evolution to structure-function relationships, signaling diversity, redox processes, and candidate quantum-sensitive molecular events.
journal: Progress in biophysics and molecular biology
authors: Abo-Al-Ela HG.

title: Susceptibility, methodological discrepancies, heteroresistance, and iron acquisition-mediated cefiderocol resistance in Italian Pseudomonas aeruginosa: results from a multicenter prospective study.
abstract: Cefiderocol is a siderophore cephalosporin that leverages bacterial iron uptake systems to overcome resistance in Gram-negative pathogens. Despite strong in vitro activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa, uncertainty remains regarding susceptibility testing accuracy and interpretation of borderline phenotypes. We conducted a prospective multicenter study of 352 non-duplicate clinical P. aeruginosa isolates from eight tertiary-care hospitals in Italy. The study assessed carbapenem resistance epidemiology, cefiderocol activity using reference and commercial methods, and methodological variability, including EUCAST-defined areas of technical uncertainty (ATU). Selected isolates underwent population analysis profiling, including strains showing growth within inhibition zones, and whole-genome sequencing of susceptible, heteroresistant, and resistant isolates. Carbapenem resistance was detected in 17.5% of isolates, with significant inter-hospital variation in carbapenemase distribution. Cefiderocol resistance was rare (0.3%) by reference testing, confirming sustained in vitro activity. Commercial susceptibility methods showed some variability in MIC values, particularly near clinical breakpoints. Disk diffusion occasionally identified isolates within the ATU, sometimes associated with discordant MIC results, although these discrepancies did not affect susceptibility categorization. Heteroresistance was uncommon (0.3%) and observed in a single isolate. Genomic analysis revealed alterations in iron acquisition pathways, including loss of pyoverdine biosynthesis genes in the resistant isolate, but no single genetic determinant fully explained reduced susceptibility, supporting a multifactorial resistance mechanism. Overall, cefiderocol retains strong in vitro activity against Italian P. aeruginosa isolates. However, variability in testing methods and the presence of intermediate phenotypes complicate interpretation. These findings underscore the need to refine susceptibility testing and better link MIC values, resistance mechanisms, and clinical outcomes.

title: Single-cell imaging of the lytic phage life cycle in bacteria.
abstract: Upon infecting a bacterial cell, a lytic bacteriophage commandeers the host's resources to replicate, before lysing the cell to release new virions. As phages are obligate parasites, each stage of the infection process depends on the physiological parameters of the host cell. Given the inherent physiological variability within a population of genetically identical bacterial cells, we ask how the phage infection dynamic reflects such heterogeneity. Here, we introduce a time-lapse imaging assay for investigating the dynamics of individual infection steps by a single T7 phage on a single bacterium. This high-throughput, time-resolved assay enables us to monitor the infection progression simultaneously in multiple cells, uncovering substantial heterogeneity at each step and revealing correlations between infection dynamics and the physiological state of the infected cell. Simulations of competing phage populations reveal that heterogeneity in infection dynamics can significantly impact phage fitness, highlighting it as a potential evolutionary driver of phage-bacteria interactions. A record of this paper's transparent peer review process is included in the supplemental information.
authors: Wedd C, Li R, Yunusov T, Smith A, Hardo G, Hunter M, Mohan AK, Majed R, Fusco D, Bakshi S.

title: Integrative genomic SEM analysis of shared genetic architecture and candidate genes for insulin resistance-related metabolic traits.
abstract: Insulin resistance is a complex metabolic state involving impaired insulin sensitivity, compensatory insulin secretion, abnormal lipid metabolism, and altered fat distribution. However, the shared genetic architecture underlying these correlated phenotypes remains incompletely defined. In this study, we applied Genomic Structural Equation Modeling to genome-wide association summary statistics of fasting insulin, insulin sensitivity index, triglycerides, and waist-to-hip ratio to construct an insulin resistance-related latent genetic factor. SNP-level association analysis was then performed for the latent factor, followed by risk locus annotation, fine-mapping, transcriptome-wide association analysis, gene-level prioritization, enrichment analysis, and exploratory structural biology assessment of selected missense substitutions. The single-factor model showed acceptable but not optimal approximate fit and captured a biologically consistent genetic pattern, with positive loadings for fasting insulin, triglycerides, and waist-to-hip ratio and a negative loading for insulin sensitivity index. The latent factor showed detectable SNP heritability and revealed 3,067 genome-wide significant candidate SNPs, with Q_SNP retained as a complementary SNP-level heterogeneity diagnostic.. Functional annotation identified 100 genomic risk loci and 1,530 FDR-significant genes in MAGMA. Fine-mapping prioritized multiple candidate regions, including loci near PPARG, RSPO3, SLC38A11, SLC39A8, BCL2, GDF5, and SPATA5. TWAS and FOCUS further highlighted candidate genes involved in adipocyte biology, glucose-lipid metabolism, insulin secretion, and expression regulation, including PPARG, MLXIPL, TCF7L2, FAM13A, CCDC92, and SLC22A3. Enrichment analyses suggested that genetic signals associated with the insulin resistance-related latent factor were mainly linked to fat distribution, cardiometabolic traits, adipose tissue, mesenchymal cell lineages, and active regulatory genomic regions. In a separate exploratory analysis, AlphaFold3 modeling, ThermoMPNN prediction, and molecular dynamics simulations suggested structural perturbations for three ultra-rare missense substitutions in nominated candidate proteins: BCL2-W188G, GDF5-C400Y, and RSPO3-C129Y. These substitutions were selected using functional-impact annotations and modeling feasibility, were not GWAS lead or fine-mapped causal variants, and do not establish the mechanisms underlying the GWAS associations. These findings provide an integrated genetic and structural framework for understanding shared mechanisms underlying insulin resistance-related metabolic abnormalities, while emphasizing the need for further experimental validation.
authors: Li S, Liang Y, Zhu G, Wu L, Li H, Li Y, Chen Q.

title: Persistent pseudolysogeny of bacteriophage phiSASD1 in Streptomyces avermitilis and its extrachromosomal plasmid-like DNA form.
abstract: Pseudolysogeny represents a distinct phage-host interaction mode that differs from the classical lytic and lysogenic cycles, yet it remains poorly characterized in filamentous actinomycetes. In this study, bacteriophage phiSASD1 infecting Streptomyces avermitilis was investigated. Three phiSASD1-carrying strains exhibiting pseudolysogenic characteristics were obtained through a plaque survival assay combined with PCR verification. Physiological characterization revealed that these strains exhibited stable resistance to superinfection by the homologous phage, while SAPL-1 continuously released high titers of infectious phage particles (up to 4.62 × 10⁷ PFU/mL) and maintained substantial mycelial biomass during the tested cultivation period. Adsorption assays showed that the representative strain SAPL-1 displayed markedly reduced adsorption capacity for phiSASD1, and mitomycin C treatment did not induce significant phage production, suggesting an atypical infection pattern distinct from classical integrative lysogeny. Southern blot analysis showed that the phiSASD1 genome was present in both total DNA and plasmid DNA fractions, with restriction patterns consistent with those of the free phage genome. Pulsed-field gel electrophoresis further supported the presence of an extrachromosomal phage-derived DNA molecule, while transmission electron microscopy revealed population heterogeneity, including intact and lysing cells. Functional assessment of the putative recombinase-associated region did not detect chromosomal integration under the tested conditions. Collectively, these results support a persistent pseudolysogenic association in which phiSASD1 is maintained as an extrachromosomal plasmid-like DNA form. This study provides new insights into alternative survival strategies of actinobacteriophages and provides a basis for further mechanistic studies and for phage monitoring and control in industrial fermentation systems.IMPORTANCETo our knowledge, this study provides systematic evidence that bacteriophage phiSASD1 can establish a persistent pseudolysogenic association with the industrially important actinomycete Streptomyces avermitilis, while its genome persists outside the host chromosome as an extrachromosomal plasmid-like DNA element. These findings extend the classical lytic-lysogenic framework by illustrating a persistent phage-host coexistence mode characterized by non-integrated phage DNA maintenance, continuous production of infectious phage particles, and population heterogeneity. The study therefore provides a basis for further investigation of the molecular mechanisms underlying phage persistence and phage-host coexistence and may inform phage monitoring and contamination control strategies in industrial fermentation systems.
authors: Lu N, Wu J, Hu Z, Chen H, Liu L.

title: Stable isotopes indicate consistent trophic structures but marked spatial variation in isotopic values across contrasting high-altitude Andean salars.
abstract: High-altitude Andean salars are poly-extreme wetlands that support communities dominated by microorganisms and important populations of flamingos. Much of the work on these systems has focused on microbial community composition and function, but little is known regarding their trophic ecology. We evaluated the use of stable isotopes to compare food web organisation and consumption pathways in three contrasting Andean salars. We analysed δ13C, δ15N and δ34S of primary producers, aquatic invertebrates and flamingos (feathers and faeces) in Laguna Puilar (Salar de Atacama), Salar de Tara and Salar de Pujsa. We quantified the isotopic niche volume and overlap between trophic components and used Bayesian mixing models to estimate the relative contribution of putative prey resources to flamingo diet. The trophic organisation was quite similar among the salars, however, the relative size of community and consumer isotopic niches differed markedly. At Puilar and Tara, most invertebrate niches were narrow and largely nested within the isotopic space occupied by flamingos, suggesting restricted resource use and limited dispersion in three-isotope space. In contrast, Pujsa showed a broader and more heterogeneous occupation of isotopic space among consumer taxa. Mixing models indicated that one or two dominant groups of aquatic invertebrates, together with diatoms, contributed substantially to the flamingos' diet, consistent with previous studies. The isotopic values of the feathers showed high variability, consistent with integration between multiple wetlands and, potentially, multiple species of flamingos, rather than simple local trophic generalism. Despite limitations related to the inability to assign feathers to specific species and incomplete coverage of meiofauna, the triple isotope approaches provided robust information on dominant energy sources and revealed local 'trophic identities' among salars. Stable isotopes therefore offer a non-invasive and effective framework for monitoring trophic structure in remote and difficult to study Andean salars under increasing anthropogenic pressure.
journal: Isotopes in environmental and health studies
authors: Salazar G, Aguilar P, Saccò M, Harrod C.

title: Natural and engineered bacteriophages against multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens: current landscape and clinical translation.
abstract: The worldwide emergence of antimicrobial resistance and the need for non-conventional alternatives to conventional antibiotics have been increased by multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens, which cause the majority of nosocomial infections and are starting to develop resistance to even the most potent drugs. Engineered bacteriophages are promising precision antimicrobials because of their ability to selectively infect and lyse bacterial hosts, multiply at infection sites, and co-evolve with bacterial populations to overcome resistance. Advances in synthetic biology, such as tail fiber modification, depolymerase and endolysin enhancement, genome editing using the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR), and computationally designed phage cocktails, have opened new possibilities for therapeutics that were hindered by the limitations of natural phages. These engineering strategies expand host range, enhance biofilm penetration, and target resistance genes. In spite of promising evidence in preclinical models, the use of engineered phages in routine clinical practice remains difficult. Specific key challenges include unclear regulations, lack of good manufacturing practice (GMP)grade production, variable pharmacokinetics and limited clinical trial data. This review critically examines engineering approaches to improve phage activity against ESKAPE pathogens, identifies the scientific and regulatory barriers limiting clinical use, and outlines the key steps needed for wider adoption.
authors: Nautiyal D, Sahu M, Jain U.

title: mito-overview: a mitochondrial report software
abstract: Interpreting mitochondrial DNA variation requires relating allele representation and genomic annotation to the sequencing evidence available for each sample. We developed mito-overview to integrate mitochondrial coverage, candidate allele fractions, genomic annotations and long read co-occurrence in mitochondrial genomic reports. Analysis of a subset of public GM12878 long read data from Vandiver and colleagues’ Cas9 enrichment study of full-length mitochondrial genomes (SRR18110025) identified 16 candidate variants. Among these candidates, co-occurrence analysis showed that m.8860A>G and m.14831G>A occurred together in all 366 jointly callable query names, demonstrating how mito-overview extends individual allele measurements to quantify shared read support between mitochondrial sites. Analysis of public GM11906 short read data (GSE142741), pooled from three single-cell ATAC-seq libraries, recovered the previously characterized disease-associated m.8344A>G variant in MT-TK at an alternate allele fraction of 72.1% (740 of 1,027 callable observations). The recovered variant identity and MT-TK assignment agree with Lareau and colleagues’ original study, providing a disease-relevant example of mito-overview’s combined candidate detection and genomic annotation. We also examined ONT data from blood, fibroblast and muscle of one patient using a separate internal workflow. Heteroplasmy was estimated from alternate allele fractions calculated separately for each tissue. The respective analyses yielded 90, 52 and 60 candidates, with 19 candidate identities shared across all three lists. For these shared candidates, the tissue-specific estimates enabled examination of both variant presence and allele representation across the sampled tissues, illustrating the application of mitochondrial genomic reports to heteroplasmy assessment in disease research. By combining candidate identification with allele measurements, genomic annotations and shared read support, mito-overview enables researchers to examine which variants are observed, their representation within a sample and their co-occurrence with other mitochondrial alleles. These complementary measurements support the selection and characterization of candidate variants for further study in mitochondrial disease research.
authors: Lopes E, Ahuja K, Gai X.

title: Variation in hypoxia tolerance is driven by evolutionary changes in gene regulation in the eastern oyster
abstract: Understanding the genomic basis of stress tolerance is crucial for predicting biological responses to environmental change. Here, we investigated the genomic basis of divergence in hypoxia tolerance between two populations of eastern oyster (  Crassostrea virginica ) from Louisiana and Texas, USA. We combined low-coverage whole-genome sequencing data with previously generated transcriptomic evidence to understand the mechanisms underlying population-specific variation in hypoxia tolerance. Genome-wide analyses revealed substantial population differentiation (global F  ST = 0.21), indicative of a clear genetic break between our study populations. We combined estimates of genomic differentiation (F  ST ) with diversity metrics to generate a set of exploratory candidate regions showing signatures consistent with recent selection. Several candidate genes identified through this approach were associated with the maintenance of homeostasis under environmental stress. We additionally tested whether genes previously identified as differentially expressed (DE) under hypoxia exhibit elevated genomic divergence between populations. While these hypoxia DEGs did show higher than expected between-population differentiation, this pattern also holds for other environmentally responsive genes. This suggests that transcriptomically responsive genes in general may generally show elevated divergence among populations, possibly due to a weaker effect of purifying selection. Furthermore, we found that hypoxia DEGs did not show an enrichment of nonsynonymous fixed differences (p = 0.9155, as compared to the genome-wide background), suggesting that the elevated divergence seen in these genes is not driven by rapid protein-coding evolution. Together, our results support a model in which population-scale differences in hypoxia tolerance occur primarily through evolution of gene regulation acting on environmentally responsive pathways.
authors: Eaton KM, Vaidya RV, Peyre JL, Pollack JB, Sirovy KA, Kelly MW.

title: Adaptive responses to antifungal selection depend on dose and drug combination in experimentally evolved yeast
abstract: Natural populations rarely face a single stressor at a single intensity, yet most laboratory evolution experiments impose exactly that. Theory predicts that stronger or compounded selection pressures should change the magnitude of adaptive change as well as the specific loci involved, but this prediction is rarely tested directly. Here, we use an evolve-and-resequence approach to compare genomic responses in  Saccharomyces cerevisiae across antifungal environments differing in the concentration and number of drugs applied. Twelve replicate populations founded from a genetically diverse ancestor were evolved for >50 generations under low and high concentrations of caspofungin or clotrimazole alone, a combination of the two drugs, or no drug, with pooled-population sequencing at three timepoints. We found little overlap among candidate loci between concentrations of the same drug or between single and combined treatments. Alleles favored in one environment did not shift predictably in the others, departing from expectations of additivity. We also observed that most candidate loci fell outside known antifungal resistance genes, except for  FKS1 in all caspofungin treatments and a putative gain of the  ERG11 -containing chromosome VIII in 9 of 12 populations evolved under high clotrimazole. Remaining candidates implicated diverse cellular functions that differed among environments. Furthermore, we found little evidence of fitness costs in drug-free medium across all evolved populations. Our results collectively show that stronger and combined antifungal selection redirects genomic responses rather than simply amplifying those favored under less challenging conditions, highlighting the limits of predicting adaptation from simpler selection regimes.  Significance statement  Predicting evolutionary responses across environmental contexts remains a major challenge. Populations exposed to similar stresses often show repeatable patterns of adaptation, but whether these patterns persist as stress intensifies or multiple stresses occur together is less clear. By evolving yeast under different concentrations of two antifungal drugs, alone and in combination, we found that the genetic changes responding to selection differed substantially across treatments. Stronger and combined antifungal selection favored distinct genomic responses beyond the drugs’ primary targets, while retaining some shared responses at known resistance-associated loci. These findings show that evolutionary responses observed under one set of conditions may be poor predictors of adaptation under stronger or more complex stress, with implications for anticipating antimicrobial resistance across different drug concentrations and combination therapies.
authors: Sandoval-Powers M, Crestani G, Dugo H, Shearman E, Burke MK.

title: Short- and long-read hybrid-capture viral metagenomics reach high sensitivity and specificity with data-driven cut-offs compared with routine diagnostics in CSF and BAL specimens
abstract: Background  Hybrid-capture viral metagenomics improves sensitivity over untargeted metagenomics, but its performance across sequencing platforms and the definition of data-driven analysis cut- offs using real clinical samples have not been systematically evaluated. This study benchmarks the hybrid-capture workflow on mock and clinical specimens across short- and long-read platforms while introducing a new, reproducible approach for setting pathogen-calling cut- offs. Methods  The Twist Comprehensive Viral Research Panel was used with both AVITI short-read and Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read sequencing on 12 mock cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) external quality assessment (EQA) panel samples and on 14 CSF and 21 bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) clinical specimens. Data-driven cut-offs for pathogen calling were derived using Latin hypercube sampling across genome coverage, abundance, and bleed-ratio parameters, then validated on the independent EQA datasets. Results  After cut-off application, both platforms detected 22 of 23 expected viral targets in EQA samples (95.7% detection-level sensitivity) with 100% specificity in negative controls. In clinical specimens, AVITI corroborated 26 of 30 (86.7%) and ONT 25 of 30 (83.3%) routine viral detections while maintaining 100% diagnostic specificity. Sensitivity was 100% for CSF but lower in BAL, particularly for low viral load targets, and all detections below a Cq value of 32 were identified by both platforms. Metagenomics also identified a potentially clinically relevant pathogen not tested by routine testing in two CSF samples. Conclusion  Hybrid-capture viral metagenomics performed comparably on AVITI and ONT for routine viral targets, with AVITI showing slightly higher genome recovery. In addition, the newly developed data-driven cut-off selection strategy offers a practical, reproducible method other laboratories can apply to their own workflows.
authors: Karatas M, Cuypers L, Laenen L, Bloemen M, Rector A, Maes J, Vanrenterghem M, Ranst MV, Wollants E, Desmet S, Matthijnssens J.

title: The molecular biophysics of extreme environments: From its beginnings to future prospects.
abstract: In the 1970s, biophysicists took up the challenge of studying life under high stress after biologists isolated and characterised organisms that thrived in extremes of salinity, temperature, or pressure. The main methods and results of early experiments through to the latest discoveries regarding the molecular mechanisms of adaptation, as well as their significance in the search for extraterrestrial life, are reviewed here. The presence of liquid water is vital for life's processes, and a section on water describes its biologically relevant dynamic diffusion in extreme environments and inside microbial and human tissue cells. Research on halophilic proteins in solution permitted quantification of interactions with solvent involved in protein solubility, stability, and dynamics. Crystallographic studies on halophilic and hyperthermophilic proteins identified the features of adaptation to high salinity and temperature. The discovery of bacteriorhodopsin, a retinal-binding protein, in the membrane of an extreme halophile unlocked the structural study of membrane proteins in general. The study of a lactate dehydrogenase-like malate dehydrogenase in an extreme halophile opened up the exploration of evolutionary relationships and allostery in the malate/lactate dehydrogenase superfamily. The study of hyperthermophilic protease complexes provided important information on this functional group across domains. Adaptation via molecular dynamics measured in vivo by neutron spectroscopy in bacterial and archaeal cells is also discussed. In the conclusion, future research directions are outlined on microbial extremophiles in the deep sea and underground, in particular with respect to their global importance in climate change biology.
authors: Zaccai G.

title: Beyond Blood Cultures and Echocardiography: Emerging Diagnostics for Infective Endocarditis.
abstract: Management of infective endocarditis (IE) is often confounded by the presence of prosthetic valves, transcatheter prostheses, and cardiovascular implantable electronic devices, as well as by changing epidemiologic risks and antimicrobial resistance patterns. For the diagnosis of IE, blood cultures and echocardiography remain foundational, but important gaps persist, particularly in culture-negative and prosthetic/device-associated infections. Contemporary diagnostic criteria and guidelines now support a multimodality approach incorporating molecular microbiology and advanced imaging. This review summarizes emerging technologies including broad-range 16S/18S/28S rRNA polymerase chain reaction and sequencing, fluorescence in situ hybridization coupled with sequencing, targeted and shotgun metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), plasma microbial cell-free DNA, cardiac computed tomography, and 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron-emission tomography/computed tomography. We also examine the potential role of artificial intelligence in echocardiographic interpretation and of large language models in multimodal data integration. Current evidence suggests that tissue-based molecular testing generally provides greater microbiologic yield than valve culture in culture-negative IE, while blood-based mNGS and microbial cell-free DNA may extend pathogen detection after antibiotic exposure and reduce reliance on tissue-based diagnosis. However, heterogeneity in specimen handling, sequencing pipelines, contamination control, reporting thresholds, and clinical interpretation remains a major barrier to implementation. Future progress should move beyond pathogen detection toward rapid, reproducible, clinically actionable diagnosis that integrates organism identification, anatomic localization, disseminated disease, and personalized treatment. Prospective outcome trials, standardized workflows, cost-effectiveness studies, and multidisciplinary Endocarditis Team integration can help determine whether these technologies translate into better antimicrobial stewardship, procedural decision-making, and patient outcomes.
authors: Park H, Dhand A.

title: Mucin-rich environment shapes Pseudomonas aeruginosa cytotoxicity and phage-mediated epithelial protection.
abstract: Chronic respiratory diseases (CRDs) are characterized by excessive mucin accumulation that alters host-pathogen interactions within airway epithelia. Although bacteriophage therapy is increasingly considered as an alternative to antibiotics, it remains unclear how mucin-rich environments influence bacterial virulence and phage efficacy. Here, we show that exogenous mucin reshapes outcomes during Pseudomonas aeruginosa in epithelial cells. Mucin exposure induces transcriptional changes, increases epithelial susceptibility to bacterial cytotoxicity, and reduces bacterial adhesion and internalization. Surprisingly, mucin simultaneously enhances phage-mediated protection, preserving epithelial viability without impairing phage amplification. Moreover, prolonged bacterial exposure to mucin increases the cytotoxicity activity of cell-free secretomes, while altering the phenotypic and genotypic characteristics of phage-resistant bacteria. Together, these findings reveal that mucin-rich environments exert opposing effects on infection dynamics by increasing host vulnerability while enhancing phage-mediated control of bacterial infection. Our results highlight the mucosal environment as a key determinant of phage therapy outcomes and bacterial adaptation.
authors: Patricio DO, Niitti K, Salminen I, Granella LW, Suokko V, Almeida GMF, Sundberg LR.

title: Integrated genomic and transcriptomic profiling identifies PFKM as a candidate biomarker of nodal metastasis in oral squamous cell carcinoma.
abstract: ObjectivesNodal metastasis is a key prognostic determinant in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), yet its underlying molecular basis remains poorly defined. This study aimed to identify prognostic genes and pathways associated with nodal metastasis in OSCC using integrated genomic, transcriptomic, and experimental approaches.DesignGenomic and transcriptomic data from The Cancer Genome Atlas and Gene Expression Omnibus were analyzed to compare pN2 and pN0 OSCC tumors and identify differentially mutated and expressed genes. Pathway enrichment analyses were conducted using gene set enrichment, Gene Ontology, and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes analyses. Candidate genes were validated by WES in 28 institutional OSCC specimens, and their expression was assessed by RT-qPCR in metastatic OSCC cell lines.ResultsNine metastasis-associated prognostic genes-WNT2, PTH1R, PFKM, CCDC59, ACTN2, ARL4C, KCTD9, DLGAP3, and PITPNM3-were identified across pN0 and pN2 stages. Among these, PFKM showed the most consistent multi-level association, characterized by increased DNA mutation frequency, elevated RNA expression in pN2 tumors, unfavorable survival outcomes, and upregulation in highly metastatic OSCC cell lines. WNT2 and PTH1R similarly demonstrated increased mutation burden and transcript expression in pN2 samples, whereas KCTD9 exhibited features consistent with negative regulation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling. Pathway analyses revealed enrichment of epithelial-mesenchymal transition, actin cytoskeletal remodeling, myogenesis, and metabolic programs in pN2 tumors, while immune- and inflammation-related processes predominated in pN0 tumors.ConclusionsThis integrated analysis identifies PFKM as a stable biomarker candidate associated with nodal metastasis in OSCC and highlights the coordinated involvement of metabolic and Wnt/β-catenin-related pathways in metastatic progression.
authors: Kuk SK, Lee JH, Kim HJ, Park DG, Choi SJ, Il Lee J, Cho SD.

title: Evaluation and genomic characterization of endosulfan-degrading Streptomyces spp. isolated from a tropical environment.
abstract: Endosulfan was banned worldwide under the Stockholm Convention in 2011, generating large amounts of waste to be disposed of and sporadic reports on its illegal usage. Microorganism-assisted treatment can be a cost-effective and environmentally friendly strategy to remove this chemical. Screening of bacteria from tropical agricultural sources heavily treated with endosulfan enabled us to isolate two Streptomyces spp. with ability to degrade α- and β-endosulfan isomers via hydrolytic pathway within 20 days of incubation in both sulfur-free medium (SFM) and carbon-free medium (CFM), producing endosulfan diol as metabolite. During the 20-day incubation in SFM, strain S12 degraded 99% (α) and 93% (β) of the isomers, while 68% (α) and 80% (β) were degraded in CFM. A similar tendency was observed for strain S9, with 96% (α) and 92% (β) degradation in SFM, compared to 40% (α) and 70% (β) degradation in CFM. Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis identified endosulfan diol as a single metabolite in both strains. Based on genome and RNA-Seq analyses, homologous genes of known endosulfan degradative genes, esd and ese, were found in both genomes; however, their expression levels were negligible or not induced in SFM supplemented with endosulfan, suggesting that these genes are not involved in endosulfan degradation. In contrast, other genes that were highly expressed and showed different expressions in SFM- and CFM-containing endosulfan were discovered, implying that novel genes may be involved in endosulfan metabolism. This report provides evidence of newly isolated Streptomyces species and their potential to transform endosulfan into endosulfan diol.
authors: Alias A, Suzuki-Minakuchi C, Mok KM, Shamsol Anuar NS, Vejarano F, Ahmad Sabri NS, Yusof N, Okada K, Hara H, Nojiri H.

title: Why does apical periodontitis persist? A shotgun metagenomic survey of the microbial community in primary and persistent periapical granulomas.
abstract: ObjectiveThis cross‑sectional observational study used shotgun metagenomic sequencing to compare the microbiomes of periapical granulomas from primary and persistent apical periodontitis to identify microbial taxa and functional pathways associated with persistent lesions.MethodsSeventeen patients with untreated primary apical periodontitis (UA), 19 with persistent apical periodontitis (PA), and 19 healthy gingival reference samples (HC) were enrolled. Periapical granuloma and healthy gingival samples were collected during tooth extraction for whole-metagenome shotgun sequencing. Alpha diversity was assessed by the Shannon and Chao1 indices. Beta-diversity was evaluated using PERMANOVA based on Bray‑Curtis distances. Differential abundance analysis of species and predicted functional pathways between UA and PA was performed using the Mann‒Whitney U test with Benjamini‒Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Clinical associations were examined using Spearman's correlation. The HC group served as a descriptive reference.ResultsAlpha diversity showed a significant difference in species richness (Chao1, p p > 0.05). Beta diversity revealed a trend toward separation but did not reach statistical significance (PERMANOVA, R2  = 0.05085, p = 0.051). Metagenomic sequencing revealed differences in species composition and functional potential between UA and PA. Taxonomic profiling identified 503 species in UA versus 255 in PA. At the species level, several taxa showed nominal differences between UA and PA (p q > 0.05). Functionally, several KEGG pathways showed nominal differences between UA and PA (p q > 0.05), with the top three pathways all below 3% relative abundance. Swelling duration correlated negatively with several taxa and pathways (p ConclusionsPersistent apical periodontitis granulomas showed lower species richness and abundance, but similar predicted functional capacity, compared with primary infections. Further longitudinal and multi‑omics studies are needed to investigate the associations.

title: Study on the Correlation Between Fermentation Microbial Communities and Flavor Compounds in Sauerkraut.
abstract: This study aimed to investigate the microbial community structure and its association with flavor compounds in mature sauerkraut fermentation. DNA high-throughput sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) were employed to analyze the microbial communities and volatile flavor compounds in sauerkraut samples on the 20th day of fermentation. A total of 104 volatile compounds were identified, including aldehydes (28.98%), alcohols (3-methyl-1-butanol, 18.28%), esters (methyl thiolacetate, 3.14%), and organic acids (acetic acid, 4.28%). These compounds were associated with the characteristic sour, fruity, and grassy aroma profiles of sauerkraut. Microbial community analysis indicated that bacteria exhibited greater diversity than fungi, with Firmicutes (69.37%) and Proteobacteria (29.92%) being the dominant phyla. The genera Enterococcus and Lactococcus accounted for over 50% of the bacterial community, representing dominant taxa associated with fermentation characteristics. These microorganisms may participate in flavor development through metabolic activities related to carbohydrate utilization, amino acid metabolism, and volatile compound formation. Correlation analysis further demonstrated a significant positive relationship between Lactococcus, Enterococcus, and several acetate-derived esters, suggesting a close statistical association between these genera and the accumulation of these compounds. This study provides further evidence for the association between microbial community structure and flavor profiles in sauerkraut, providing a scientific basis for the optimization of traditional fermented food processes and quality improvement.
authors: Lu X, Guo S, Zhao H, Yang Y, Ma X, Shi S, Hu B, Luo A.

title: Cascading effects of nano-biochar mitigate antibiotic resistance via phage-host interactions in the soil-crop ecosystem.
abstract: Controlling the spread of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in agroecosystems is central to One Health, yet whether nano-biochar-amended organic fertilizers can mitigate phage-mediated ARG dissemination along the fertilizer-soil-crop continuum remains poorly understood. Here, we analyzed 120 viral metagenomes to examine how biochar-amended organic fertilizers modulate ARG dynamics, phage-associated functions, and phage-host interactions across the fertilizer-soil-lettuce continuum. The lettuce phyllosphere served as a key endpoint for ARG accumulation, exhibiting 4.1-4.9 times the total ARG abundance and 56.8-66.3% higher phage-encoded ARG abundance compared with rhizosphere and non-rhizosphere soils. Source-tracking analysis indicated that manure and soil inputs accounted for 50.8-57.0% of phyllosphere ARGs, while 111 manure-associated viral populations were shared with the phyllosphere at the viral cluster level. Notably, nano-biochar-amended vermicompost exerted a cascading mitigation effect, reducing manure- and soil-derived ARG inputs to the phyllosphere by 20.4-21.6% and manure-associated viral sharing by 51.6%. Meanwhile, nano-biochar-amended vermicompost reduced lysogenic phage-host interactions, phage-encoded ARGs, and auxiliary metabolic genes associated with antibiotic-resistant bacteria, which may contribute to reduced phage-associated ARG dissemination potential. Consequently, total ARG abundance in the phyllosphere decreased by 68.9-76.3%, while lettuce biomass increased by 54.1-61.5%. This work suggests that nano-biochar-amended vermicompost may mitigate antibiotic resistance risks and enhance crop productivity partly by attenuating phage-associated ARG dissemination across the fertilizer-soil-crop continuum, highlighting its potential for One Health-oriented resistance-risk control in agricultural production.
authors: Xie T, Lin D, Du S, Wu D, Zhu D.

title: Microbiome-Mediated Pharmacokinetics and Informed Dosing of Mycophenolate in Kidney Transplantation.
abstract: Background and objectivesThe gut microbiome contributes to interindividual variability in drug pharmacokinetics; however, its role in guiding dose adjustments remains unclear. Mycophenolic acid (MPA), the active metabolite of the immunosuppressant mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), exhibits high pharmacokinetic variability, potentially linked to microbial activity. This study aimed to characterize the gut microbiome effect on MPA pharmacokinetics and determine if these effects necessitate dose modifications.MethodsIn 84 kidney transplant recipients, plasma and urine concentration-time profiles for MPA and its glucuronide metabolites were characterized using population pharmacokinetic modeling in NONMEM®. Stool samples were collected within 2 days of pharmacokinetic sampling for microbiome shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Machine learning was used to identify microbial species associated with pharmacokinetic variability. The impact of these species and clinical covariates was evaluated using full fixed-effect modeling. Simulations were conducted to assess the effect of microbial relative abundance on MPA therapeutic target attainment across various MMF doses.ResultsFive bacteria were associated with the magnitude or duration of enterohepatic circulation (EHC). High relative abundance of Eubacterium callanderi increased EHC and MPA exposure by 29-63%, requiring a 17% lower MMF dose. Conversely, high Faecalibacterium SGB15315 abundance reduced EHC and MPA exposure by 13-26%, requiring a 50-75% higher dose. While Gemmiger formicilis and Eisenbergiella tayi prolonged EHC by >100% and Anaerostipes caccae decreased it by 30%, these taxa did not clinically impact therapeutic target attainment.ConclusionWe identified several stool microbial species affecting MPA pharmacokinetics. Specifically, Eubacterium callanderi and Faecalibacterium SGB15315 may identify patients who require additional therapeutic drug monitoring or possible dose modifications to reach target concentrations.Clinical trial registrationClinicaltrials.gov, NCT04953715.
authors: Saqr A, Mohamed ME, Staley C, Onyeaghala G, Vo D, Remmel RP, Teigen L, Guan W, Oetting WS, El-Rifai R, Dorr CR, Gupta K, Matas AJ, Israni AK, Jacobson PA.

title: Genetics and genomics of enteroarthroconidial development in  Coccidioides
abstract: Regulated cell death is a cornerstone of plant and animal development. Distant orthologs of some cell death genes are also found in microbes, with roles that remain incompletely understood. The human fungal pathogen  Coccidioides causes the disease Valley fever when infectious spores called enteroarthroconidia are inhaled from soil. These spores develop via an unusual checkerboard-style differentiation in which alternating segments of hyphae (cellular filaments) die and disarticulate, releasing mature spores on either side. The molecular mechanisms are unknown. Adapting single-cell transcriptomics for filamentous fungi, we catalogued expression across the specialized cells of a developing  Coccidioides colony. With the resulting profiles, and cell-biological validation via protein tagging, we characterized high expression of the pyroptosis-like cell death pathway in hyphal segments destined to die. Genetic knockout of pyroptosis-like pathway genes resulted in developmental arrest at a late stage in the colony, preserving hyphal growth but abrogating cell death and spore production. Together, these findings reveal the pyroptosis-like pathway as a requirement for enteroarthroconidial development, and thus infectivity, in  Coccidioides . We propose that regulated cell death may prove to mediate events in development in many fungi with multicellular life cycles.
authors: Fleming KE, Christensen KC, Szewczyk E, Homer CM, Brem RB.
