title: AltORF-encoded microprotein recruits primary-ORF-encoded dehydrogenase to cell poles upon heat shock
abstract: Alternative open reading frames (altORFs) initiating from in-frame or out-of-frame start sites within annotated protein-coding genes represent a largely unexplored source of protein-coding potential and remain poorly understood in terms of regulation, function, and impact on physiology. Here we investigate  Escherichia coli GndA, encoded by an out-of-frame altORF within  gnd , which encodes 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase. We observe that the GndA protein is induced by heat shock, consistent with the initial identification in a quantitative membrane proteomics screen, but is unstable, while the levels of the stable Gnd dehydrogenase are unchanged. Using translational fusion assays and in vivo RNA structure probing, we show that an internal complementary sequence upstream of  gndA acts as a thermo-responsive secondary RNA structure controlling GndA translation. Mutagenesis of either  gnd or  gndA reduce heat shock survival of  E. coli indicating both gene products are important for resistance. GndA fractionates with membranes consistent with in silico predictions that the protein forms an amphipathic α-helix. In contrast, Gnd is predominantly cytoplasmic but shows GndA-dependent relocalization to cell poles upon heat shock. Together, our results demonstrate that an altORF-encoded microprotein is required for stress-dependent relocalization of its primary ORF partner, revealing a functional interplay between proteins encoded by overlapping ORFs in bacterial stress adaptation.  Significance  Alternative translation from internal translation initiation sites enables bacteria to expand their proteomic versatility without increasing genome size. Here we show that a single  Escherichia coli transcript encoding the well-characterized dehydrogenase Gnd also produces an additional microprotein from an internal alternative open reading frame (altORF), whose translation is controlled by an RNA thermometer-like structure. We further demonstrate that this heat shock-induced microprotein promotes spatial relocalization of its primary ORF-encoded partner during aerobic heat stress. Together our findings highlight how alternative translation can expand the cellular response to stress.
authors: Schmidt JJ, Ramos-León F, Zhang A, Zeinert R, Shabalina SA, Storz G.

title: A host-virus arms race over FAM134B in African swine fever virus infection.
abstract: Although reticulophagy, the selective autophagy of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), restricts several RNA viruses, whether this pathway constrains DNA virus infection remains unknown. Recently, we found that FAM134B (family with sequence similarity 134 member B), an ER-resident cargo receptor that mediates reticulophagy, restricts African swine fever virus (ASFV), a large cytoplasmic DNA virus, by targeting the major capsid proteins p72 and pA137R for lysosomal degradation, thereby blocking capsid assembly at perinuclear viral factories. ASFV counters this restriction through the virulence factor pMGF300-2R encoded by the MGF300-2R gene of ASFV, which binds to FAM134B, recruits LC3B (microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 beta), an ATG8 (autophagy-related protein 8) family member, via the C-terminal LC3-interacting region (LIR) motif, and directs FAM134B into autophagic degradation. Deletion of the MGF300-2R gene in the ASFV genome restores FAM134B abundance, reduces viral replication, and attenuates virulence in pigs. These findings establish reticulophagy as a previously unrecognized antiviral barrier against a large DNA virus and reveal a host-virus arms race centered on the reticulophagy receptor.Abbreviations: ASFV: African swine fever virus; ER: endoplasmic reticulum; FAM134B: family with sequence similarity 134 member B; LC3B: microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 beta; LIR: LC3-interacting region; VFs: viral factories.
authors: Wang T, Luo R, Huang R, Sun Y, Qiu HJ.

title: Emergence and characterisation of bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid resistance in recurrent rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis patient: A case report.
abstract: BackgroundBedaquiline (BDQ), pretomanid (Pa) and linezolid (LZD)-based (BPaL) regimens have transformed rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (RR-TB) treatment. However, resistance to these drugs is increasingly reported, while longitudinal data integrating clinical, phenotypic and genomic evolution remain limited.Case presentationWe report a fatal case of recurrent RR-TB in a 40-year-old South African woman with HIV infection who received BPaL therapy. Following treatment completion, recurrent disease was complicated by pregnancy, treatment interruption and loss to follow-up. She subsequently re-presented with advanced cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis and respiratory failure. Despite re-initiation of BPaL, she deteriorated and died from septic shock. Routine drug susceptibility testing, available posthumously, confirmed resistance to BDQ, Pa and LZD. Seven sequential Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates collected during treatment underwent minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) testing and whole-genome sequencing. All demonstrated phenotypic resistance to the three BPaL drugs. Serial genomic analysis identified progressive Rv0678 diversification associated with a two-fold increase in BDQ MIC, while resistance-associated rrl and fbiC mutations remained comparatively stable despite persistently elevated LZD and Pa MICs.ConclusionsThis case demonstrates the interaction of treatment interruption, delayed resistance detection and continued within-host bacterial adaptation during BPaL therapy. Longitudinal phenotypic and genomic findings revealed distinct resistance trajectories among BPaL drugs, highlighting the importance of treatment retention, timely susceptibility testing and genomic surveillance for preserving BPaL effectiveness.
authors: Kaapu KG, Ntsoane RV, Raphiri C, Lekalakala-Mokaba MR, Rukasha I.

title: A genome-wide scan for signatures of selection in two indigenous Sicilian chicken breeds.
abstract: Natural and artificial selection can leave distinctive genomic signatures that provide insights into the evolutionary history of populations. In this study, we used high-density SNP arrays to investigate genomic signatures of selection in two indigenous Sicilian chicken breeds: the Siciliana, also known as Coronata (SIC), and the recently recognized Cornuta di Caltanissetta, also known as Cornuta di Sicilia (COR). We combined two extended haplotype homozygosity (EHH)-based methods, iHS and Rsb, with a complementary site frequency spectrum (SFS)-based analysis using SweeD software, to identify genomic regions potentially affected by selection. Several candidate regions were identified in COR, with regions on chicken chromosomes (GGA) 1, 8, and 21. On GGA1 strong iHS signals coincided with elevated composite likelihood ratio (CLR) values from SweeD, whereas regions on GGA8 and GGA21 showed overlapping iHS and Rsb signals, supported by additional exploratory evidence from SweeD. These regions contain several genes associated with nervous system development and function, including PCDH9 on GGA1; ASTN1, TNR, and BRINP2 on GGA8; and CLSTN1, NMNAT1, UBE4B, and KIF1B on GGA21. Additional candidate genes identified within regions showing differential selection signals on GGA3, including TTBK1, SLC8A1, TTL, and VSX1, also have reported roles in neural processes. Collectively, these genes highlight potential links between the identified genomic signals and neural processes that may contribute to phenotypic differentiation between the two breeds, although their involvement in breed-specific traits remains to be established. Beyond these candidates, we identified selection signatures encompassing genes associated with gene regulation, including transcriptional co-regulation and alternative splicing. Several highly significant variants were also located within long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) regions, pointing to a possible contribution of regulatory variation to the observed genomic patterns. Overall, our results identify candidate genomic regions containing genes involved in neural function and gene regulatory processes, providing a basis for future investigations into the evolutionary history and phenotypic differentiation of these indigenous Sicilian chicken breeds.
authors: Ben-Jemaa S, Chessari G, Lasagna E, Cassandro M, Cesarani A, Sardina MT, Criscione A, Mastrangelo S.

title: Discrepant responses of abundant and rare taxa to polyethylene microplastic and nanoplastic perturbations in cold seep sediment.
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) and nanoplastics (NPs) are emerging contaminants in deep-sea ecosystems, yet their specific impacts on the internal heterogeneity of cold seep microbiomes remain poorly understood. Here, microcosm experiments with cold seep sediments exposed to polyethylene particles were conducted to investigate the response patterns of abundant and rare taxa to MP/NP-induced disturbances. The results indicated that MPs/NPs exposure reshaped bacterial community structure, with significant enrichment of Epsilonbacteraeota, a phylum associated with chemoautotrophic metabolism. In contrast, archaeal alpha diversity showed no significant response to MPs/NPs exposure. Abundant and rare taxa exhibited contrasting responses in community composition, assembly patterns, and network associations. Despite stochastic processes largely governing overall community assembly, the assembly mechanism of rare bacteria shifted toward heterogeneous selection under NPs exposure, which contrasted sharply with the homogeneous selection observed in the rare archaea. Furthermore, network analysis revealed that rare taxa constituted the majority of nodes in both co-occurrence networks. Functional predictions suggested contrasting responses, with lower relative abundances of taxa assigned to sulfate respiration in abundant bacteria under most treatments and higher relative abundances of taxa assigned to sulfur oxidation and nitrogen cycling in rare taxa under some treatments. Overall, this study highlights the contrasting responses of abundant and rare taxa to MPs/NPs exposure and provides insights for assessing the ecological risks of plastic pollution in deep-sea environments.
authors: Yuan Y, Ma B, Xu Z, Wang J, Tang Q, Yin Q, Zhou H, Chen C, Zhang C.

title: A secreted NanoLuc luciferase-expressing PRRSV for high-throughput antiviral screening identifies lithocholic acid as a post-entry inhibitor of viral replication.
abstract: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) is an economically important swine pathogen without effective antiviral agents. Here, we constructed recombinant PRRSV reporter viruses expressing secreted NanoLuc luciferase (Nluc) based on the PRRSV TA-12 strain and established a quantitative antiviral screening platform. The selected rGNluc reporter virus exhibited stable replication characteristics and enabled rapid evaluation of PRRSV replication. Screening of a library of 146 gut microbial metabolites identified several antiviral candidates, among which lithocholic acid (LCA) exhibited potent inhibitory activity against PRRSV replication with a favorable selectivity index. LCA exhibited antiviral activity against multiple PRRSV-1 and PRRSV-2 strains, although susceptibility varied among strains, and primarily inhibited viral replication at post-entry stages. Mechanistic studies demonstrated that LCA reduced viral genomic RNA and subgenomic RNA synthesis and early viral protein expression, while its antiviral activity was independent of the bile acid receptors FXR and TGR5. Furthermore, cholesterol supplementation almost completely rescued PRRSV replication inhibited by LCA, suggesting the involvement of host cholesterol homeostasis in its antiviral activity. These findings establish a robust high-throughput screening (HTS) platform and identify LCA as a promising host-directed antiviral candidate.
authors: Zhang L, Shi J, Li Q, Xu T, Li C, Li Y.

title: HIV-1 Integrase C-terminal Domain Mutations Regulate ALLINI Sensitivity
abstract: ABSTRACT  HIV-1 integrase (IN) performs two essential functions in virus replication: catalyzing the integration of reverse-transcribed viral cDNA into host DNA and promoting proper virion maturation. The latter is mediated by IN binding to the genomic RNA (gRNA) through basic residues in its C- terminal domain (CTD), thereby ensuring correct repackaging of the gRNA inside the remodeled capsid lattice. Allosteric integrase inhibitors (ALLINIs) bind within a V-shaped pocket at the interface of the catalytic core domain (CCD) of IN dimers, promote the engagement of the CTDs from adjacent dimers, and thereby occlude gRNA binding. However, virological evidence supporting a role for the IN-CTD in ALLINI mechanism of action is lacking, as mutations in CTD residues implicated in ALLINI-induced multimerization typically yield non-infectious viruses. Here we demonstrate that IN-CTD mutants bearing compensatory substitutions that restore infectivity exhibit markedly altered sensitivity to ALLINIs. Specifically, we show that R269A/K273A substitutions within the IN-CTD confer ∼100-fold enhanced sensitivity to ALLINIs. This correlates with a loss of IN-gRNA binding at low ALLINI concentrations, while exerting minimal effects on IN multimerization  in vitro and in virions. In contrast, we found that the IN I268T substitution which arose as a suppressor mutation of I268A confers partial resistance to ALLINI-induced inhibition of gRNA binding. Collectively, these findings provide the first direct genetic evidence that CTD residues, despite being distal to the primary drug binding site at the CCD dimer, modulate sensitivity to ALLINIs and highlights IN-gRNA binding as a central target of ALLINIs.  SIGNIFICANCE  In addition to its catalytic role in viral DNA integration, HIV-1 integrase (IN) is essential for virion maturation. IN binding to the viral RNA genome (gRNA) through basic residues in its C-terminal domain (CTD) ensures the proper repackaging of the gRNA inside the mature capsid lattice. Allosteric integrase inhibitors (ALLINIs) bind to a pocket within the catalytic core domain (CCD) of an IN dimer and are thought to disrupt IN-gRNA interactions by triggering aberrant IN multimerization through the engagement of the CTDs of a nearby dimer. However, direct genetic evidence supporting a role for the IN-CTD in ALLINI mechanism of action is lacking. Herein, we show that IN-CTD mutants bearing compensatory substitutions that restore infectivity have significantly altered sensitivities against ALLINIs. Our findings provide the first virological evidence that residues within the CTD, away from the primary drug binding site at the CCD dimer, can alter ALLINI sensitivity.
authors: Kumar A, Dinh T, Mugisha CS, Boateng A, Zhou Q, Kvaratskhelia M, Kutluay SB.

title: FapA extends the flagellar cage-dependent network into the cytoplasm to control surface-associated behaviors in  Helicobacter pylori
abstract: Flagellar systems enable many host-associated bacteria to colonize successfully. One such pathogen is  Helicobacter pylori , which assembles an elaborate, high-torque flagellar motor that has a wide C-ring, 18 stator complexes, and is surrounded by a cage that includes homologs of the type IV pilus proteins PilM, PilN, and PilO. PilMNO act to repress soft-agar migration while promoting cell aggregation, microcolony, and biofilm formation, but the pathway linking the flagellar cage to these behaviors is unknown. Here we identify FapA, a member of the flagellar assembly protein A (FapA) family, as a component of this pathway. Deletion of  fapA increased soft-agar migration and reduced microcolony and biofilm formation, similar to deletion of  pilMNO . Epistasis analysis placed FapA downstream of the PilMNO flagellar cage. Using fluorescent fusions and protein-protein interaction experiments, FapA was found to localize to the cell poles, the sites of flagellar motor placement, and interact with the cytoplasmic PilM component of the cage. Indeed, cryo-electron tomography experiments detected cytoplasmic density near PilM that was lost in the Δ  fapA deletion mutant. Phylogenetic analysis suggests that FapA proteins are more widespread than previously appreciated, being found in multiple bacterial phyla including Campylobacterota, Bacillota, Spirochaetota, Desulfobacterota, Thermotogota, Synergistota, and Pseudomonadota. Together, these findings support that the  H. pylori flagellar cage has additional components that reside in the cytoplasm but similarly function to limit motility and activate a sessile/biofilm lifestyle. Given the widespread nature of FapA, our results suggest that many other bacteria might employ FapA homologs for similar purposes.  Importance  The flagella of  Helicobacter pylori enable it to colonize the stomach, but its flagellar motor appears to do more than propel the bacterium. A protein cage surrounding the motor helps determine whether cells swim or settle into microcolonies and biofilms, yet the molecular components that link this structure to cellular behaviors remain poorly understood. This knowledge gap is particularly intriguing because  H. pylori lacks the cyclic-di-GMP signaling system that many bacteria use to coordinate motility and biofilm development. Our identification of FapA as a cytoplasmic component of the cage-dependent regulatory network provides a foundation for understanding how  H. pylori coordinates motility and surface-associated growth and given the widespread nature of FapA, raises the possibility that many other bacteria use similar mechanisms.
authors: Fong JNC, Witt CD, Huang EHL, Yue J, Liu X, Roujeinikova A, Liu J, Ottemann KM.

title: Weak cross-trophic coupling of multidimensional stability in plankton communities under multiple stressors.
abstract: Nutrient enrichment and biological invasions frequently co-occur in freshwater ecosystems, yet it remains unclear whether stability of entire planktonic groups responds uniformly to these combined stressors. To address this question, we conducted a fully factorial mesocosm experiment that crossed three nutrient regimes with two invasive species that impose distinct disturbance pathways. We quantified temporal stability, resistance, resilience, and recovery across functional and compositional facets in zooplankton, phytoplankton, and bacterioplankton communities. Our results revealed highly taxon- and dimension-specific responses. Snail bioturbation significantly reduced the functional resistance of zooplankton under high nutrient conditions. Meanwhile, the functional resistance of bacterioplankton declined with increasing nutrient levels. This suggests that functionally distinct stressors may affect different trophic guilds through distinct mechanisms. Species richness was consistently positively associated with compositional temporal stability, resistance and recovery across all trophic levels, but was negatively associated with resilience, revealing a fundamental trade-off between maintaining community robustness and enabling rapid adaptability. Functional and compositional stability were positively correlated only in the temporal stability dimension, but exhibited negative associations in the resistance and recovery dimensions. This indicates that biomass-related functions and community structure can follow divergent trajectories throughout perturbation and recovery. Most critically, the multivariate analyses and pairwise correlations among trophic levels indicated generally weak cross-trophic coupling, suggesting that, under the conditions of this mesocosm experiment, no single planktonic group provided a consistently reliable proxy for multidimensional whole-community stability. These findings highlight the value of assessing multiple dimensions of ecological stability across trophic groups. Consideration of stability indicators across multitrophic groups may provide complementary information for adaptive lake management as global pressures from nutrient loading and biological invasions continue to intensify.
authors: Wang Y, Li R, Sun S, Zhong M, Wang C, Chu Y, Qin Y, Zhang X, Rao Q, Chen J, Su H.

title: Sewer-relevant aging of microplastics drives plastic-class-dependent N<sub>2</sub>O emissions from denitrifying sludge.
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) accumulate in sewer systems and wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs), where they undergo aging processes distinct from photo-oxidation in surface waters. How such sewer-relevant aging impacts denitrification-associated nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions remains unknown. Here, we simulated sewer-relevant aging (sulfidation and mechanical abrasion) for non-biodegradable, compostable and biodegradable MPs (NMPs, CMPs, BMPs) and evaluated their effects on N2O emissions relative to pristine MPs, while linking MP-derived dissolved organic carbon (DOC) characteristics to microbial physiological and community responses. Aging increased DOC release from CMPs and BMPs by 30.0% and 115.8%, respectively, and generated plastic-dependent molecular signatures enriched in aromatic and sulfur-containing compounds. Rather than bioavailable carbon sources, aged MP-derived DOC could barely be consumed as the electron donor yet acted as a potent physiological disruptor. Correspondingly, aged CMPs and BMPs increased N2O emissions to 2.5- and 8.0-fold those of their pristine counterparts, with a stimulation order of BMPs > CMPs > NMPs under carbon-sufficient conditions (C/N = 4:1). Stronger N2O stimulation was associated with more severe membrane damage and greater impairment of electron supply. Metagenomic analysis further revealed enrichment of Paracoccus under stronger N2O stimulation, together with shifts in denitrification-related genomic potential. As a genus capable of degrading diverse plastic additives while harboring a complete denitrification pathway, Paracoccus could favor N2O accumulation under electron-limited conditions, where N2O reduction is disadvantaged relative to upstream denitrification steps. These findings showed that sewer-relevant aging reshaped MP effects on denitrification-associated N2O emissions in a plastic-dependent manner and challenged the presumed environmental benignity of compostable and biodegradable plastics, underscoring the need to incorporate MPs aging into risk assessment for WWTPs.
authors: Yue H, Guan X, Shen Y.

title: Multi-layer analysis of gut metagenomic functional potential in major depressive disorder.
abstract: BackgroundMajor depressive disorder (MDD) is associated with gut microbiota dysbiosis, but previous studies have mostly focused on species composition and are subject to confounding factors such as age and diet. Robust differences at the functional pathway level remain unclear.MethodsWe included 98 indigenous residents of Xinjiang, China, whose families had resided there for three or more generations (49 MDD patients and 49 healthy controls) and performed shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Functional profiles were annotated with HUMAnN3 across seven levels: GBM, GMM, KO, EC, Module, Pathway, and PathAbundance. Features were transformed using the centered log-ratio (CLR) method. After controlling for 10 covariates (age, sex, BMI, bowel movement frequency, diet, gastrointestinal symptoms, years of smoking, alcohol consumption, physical activity, and sleep), OLS regression was performed with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction (q ResultsAfter covariate adjustment, overall functional profiles did not differ significantly between groups (PERMANOVA R²=1.9%, p = 0.071; PERMDISP p = 0.98). After FDR correction, 33 significant features were detected across five levels: EC, Pathway, Module, GMM, and PathAbundance (no significant signals at the GBM or KO levels). Key biologically meaningful signals included: propionate CoA-transferase (EC 2.8.3.1, β=-1.42, q = 0.022)↓, teichoic acid biosynthesis (map00552, β=-0.34, q = 0.045)↓, vancomycin resistance module (M00651, β=-1.28, q = 0.014)↓, galacturonate degradation II (MF0023, β=+1.82, q = 0.048)↑, and heme b biosynthesis I (PathAbundance, β=+0.93, q = 0.033)↑. MaAsLin2 effect sizes were correlated with the main OLS results at the Pathway level (R²=0.84) with consistent direction. title: Bacterial community profiles of soils from the Mount Makiling Forest Reserve, Philippines.
abstract: The Mount Makiling Forest Reserve harbors diverse microorganisms with potential biotechnological applications, yet bacterial taxonomic profiling across its watersheds remains limited. Amplicon metagenome sequencing targeting the 16S rRNA gene revealed Proteobacteria and Acidobacteriota as dominant phyla, with Actinobacteriota, Verrucomicrobiota, Chloroflexi, Myxococcota, Methylomirabilota, Bacteroidota, Nitrospirota, and Planctomycetota present at varying abundances.
authors: Creencia AR, Arguelles EDLR, Tan Gana NH, Capanzana RMAD, Martinez JP, Lanceras JC, Salaan CAM, Del Castillo RAM, Cadao DFB.

title: The core interaction network of transcription elongation factors is broadly maintained across diverse bacteria.
abstract: Bacterial transcription elongation has been investigated most thoroughly for the model bacterium Escherichia coli. The E. coli elongation factor NusG associates through its N-terminal domain with the transcription elongation complex (TEC), while its C-terminal domain forms mutually exclusive interactions with either ribosomal protein S10 or Rho termination factor. The E. coli NusG:S10 complex bridges the TEC with a pioneering ribosome for coupling of transcription and translation. NusG also participates in antitermination complexes (ATC) that inhibit Rho-dependent termination and increase transcription of rRNA operons. A characteristic sequence in the nascent rrn RNA, called boxA, loads E. coli NusB:S10 onto the NusG-bound TEC, leading to the formation of the rrn ATC. However, these findings may not extend to all bacteria. Rho-dependent termination is less important in gram-positive bacteria, including some that do not encode Rho, and transcription and translation remain uncoupled in Bacillus subtilis and many other gram-positive bacteria. It is therefore unclear whether the interaction network for E. coli elongation factors is conserved in these organisms. We identified boxA-like sequences upstream of 16S and 23S genes in Bacillus species and found that they associate directly with NusB. We also found that B. subtilis S10 associates with both NusB and NusG, and that Rho can also associate with NusG. Bioinformatic analyses revealed conservation of interaction interface residues across multiple phyla. Together, these data demonstrate that the core interaction network of bacterial elongation factors is broadly conserved across diverse bacteria, despite differences in how these interactions function in individual species.ImportanceEscherichia coli is known to use several key elongation factors that promote direct coupling of transcription with translation. These factors also trigger the formation of an antitermination complex that protects the synthesis of ribosomal RNA and CRISPR transcripts from interference by the Rho termination factor. However, Bacillus subtilis is not thought to couple transcription with translation. It is also not known whether B. subtilis needs to suppress Rho, given that its Rho is dispensable. Therefore, we purified B. subtilis elongation factors and mapped their interaction network. Surprisingly, we find that the B. subtilis elongation factors form complexes that closely resemble E. coli counterparts, despite the significant mechanistic differences in how these bacteria control transcription elongation.
authors: Tran TNP, Peterson RE, Jiang X, Sevugan SA, Ranaweera S, Babitzke P, Fushman D, Winkler WC.

title: Periodontal Infectogenomics in Africa: The Biological Case for a Population-Centred Research Agenda.
abstract: African populations harbour the greatest human genetic diversity on earth and carry the highest global burden of severe periodontitis, yet their absence from periodontal infectogenomics represents a biological limitation of the field with profound implications for host-microbe interaction research. This Perspective builds the biological case for African populations as an urgent research priority and proposes a research roadmap integrating genomics, metagenomics and multiomics approaches.
authors: Kabbashi S, Chetty M.

title: Genomic characterization of a novel bunyavirus FsBV1 from Fusarium solani.
abstract: A novel bunyavirus, tentatively named Fusarium solani bunyavirus 1 (FsBV1), was identified in the phytopathogenic fungus Fusarium solani. The complete sequence of the L segment of FsBV1 is 7,186 nucleotides (nt) in length and contains a single open reading frame (ORF) encoding an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) of 316 amino acids (aa). The RdRp contains six conserved bunyaviral motifs, including the SDD tripeptide. The M segment is 1,422 nt long and contains a single ORF encoding a YwqJ-like deaminase of 81 aa. The S segment is 1,301 nt long and contains a single ORF encoding a protein containing putative multifunctional flavoprotein (SiRFP) domain. BLASTp analysis showed that the RdRp of FsBV1 shared the highest amino acid sequence identity (48.73%) with that of Cheeloo tick associated virus 2. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that FsBV1 clusters with unclassified bunyaviruses. Based on its genome organization, protein sequences, and phylogenetic position, FsBV1 is proposed as a novel virus within the class Bunyaviricetes.
authors: Xiao H, Peng Y, Deng Z, Chao J, Mao H, Zhang Y, Tan W, Xie Y, Cai C, Zheng L, Liu T.

title: Hormesis as a universal cellular strategy for growth.
abstract: Our review synthesizes a vast and dispersed literature to demonstrate that subtoxic doses of structurally diverse chemicals can induce a conserved growth-stimulatory (hormetic) response across bacterial, microalgal, plant, and mammalian cells. Stimulation is concentration- and exposure-time-dependent, with higher concentrations inhibiting growth. In eukaryotic models, moderate ROS signaling and activation of DNA-PKcs/Akt, ERK1/2, PI3K/AKT, mTOR, or AURKA accompany growth stimulation, with Cyclin D-CDK4 promoting G1/S transition in mammalian cells. The proliferative DNA-PKcs/Akt response is observed in human hepatic cells, while bacterial examples involve LuxR-dependent signaling and fatty acid β-oxidation. Metabolism rewires, with some microalgae enhancing glycolysis and Krebs cycling, whereas other photosynthetic microorganisms reroute photosynthetic carbon toward lipid or starch storage while downregulating selected carbohydrate-catabolic proteins. Nrf2-driven antioxidants in mammalian cells, carotenoids, and detoxifying enzymes are upregulated, establishing a preconditioned state that can attenuate apoptosis upon subsequent challenge. Within the Catabolic-Anabolic Cycling Hormesis (CACH) model, some time-dependent responses are consistent with an anabolic overshoot following a transient catabolic decline (ATP depletion). This anabolic reprogramming accompanies biofilm formation, altered motility, and, in neoplastic cells, anchorage-independent growth. Thus, cell proliferation is a metabolic strategy shaped by adversity, with functional consequences that depend on cellular context and the endpoint assessed.
authors: Agathokleous E, Markouizou A, Calabrese EJ, Saitanis CJ.

title: Copper exposure induces the release of methyl iodide from coastal wetlands and seawater.
abstract: Methyl iodide (CH3I) is the main organic carrier for iodine transport from both marine and terrestrial ecosystems into the atmosphere, playing an important role in the global iodine cycle and ozone depletion. The widespread input of heavy metal copper (Cu(II)) deposition in marine environments due to anthropogenic activities may affect the production of CH3I, yet relevant studies are still lacking. Here, we explored the effects of Cu(II) on emission of CH3I in coastal wetlands and seawater. The results showed that Cu(II) addition significantly enhances CH3I emission from coastal wetland soils, with emissions under hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) co-addition reaching approximately five times those observed with Cu(II) alone. Notably, this promotional effect was more pronounced in coastal wetland soils with higher organic matter content. In seawater, addition of 400 nM Cu(II) further stimulated the abiotic processes, with emission of CH3I increased 136% (day 8) in filtered seawater (biologically reduced). In unfiltered seawater, despite 400 nM Cu(II) addition inhibition of biological activity evidenced by an 81.7% decrease in chlorophyll-a and a 49.2% reduction in bacterial abundance, the overall CH3I emission was further amplified, which we tentatively attributed to the release of organic matter from the decay of phytoplankton. These findings elucidate that elevated copper stress promote CH3I emission from both salt marsh soil and ocean into the atmosphere. This study provides an important scientific basis for assessing the impact of heavy metal pollution on CH3I emissions from coastal wetlands and seawater under climate change scenarios and anthropogenic perturbations.
authors: Yu WR, Liu SS, Ni J, Wang WQ, He Z, Yang GP.

title: Phylogeographical structure and genetic introgression in Salmonella enterica serotype Napoli: a genomic epidemiology study.
abstract: BackgroundSalmonella enterica serotype Napoli (S Napoli), a non-typhoidal Salmonella serotype that has been emerging in Italy, Switzerland, and France since the mid-1990s, has an unusual epidemiological profile that suggests a role for the environment in the transmission of these bacteria. The genomics of S Napoli has been inadequately characterised; we, therefore, aimed to provide a robust genomic framework for S Napoli surveillance.MethodsIn this genomic epidemiology study, we performed short-read sequencing of 1145 S Napoli isolates from national surveillance in four European countries (Italy, Switzerland, France, and Spain) and complemented this dataset with 175 additional genomes (174 published and one unpublished). We used the EnteroBase core genome multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST) scheme and its associated Hierarchical Clustering algorithm, along with other genome-based bioinformatics approaches such as single nucleotide variant-based phylogenetic analyses, ResFinder, PlasmidFinder, and RefSeq genomes, to characterise population structure, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) prevalence, and differences in gene content among genetic lineages.FindingsWe analysed 1320 S Napoli genomes, collected between April, 1945, and September 14, 2022, from human (n=1088, 82·4%) and non-human (n=232, 17·6%) sources in Italy (n=317, 24%), Switzerland (n=181, 13·7%), France (n=773, 58·5%), and Spain (n=48, 3·6%), confirming that the rising prevalence of S Napoli is driven by a single monophyletic serotype within cgMLST superlineage HC2000_1289. However, this serotype displays considerable genetic diversity (15 lineages falling into 12 HC900 clusters), strong spatial structuring, and a low frequency (2%) of AMR determinants. We also detected genetic introgression between S Napoli and the sympatric, closely related Salmonella enterica serotype Veneziana.InterpretationUnlike successful non-typhoidal Salmonella serotypes, for which globalisation has had a homogenising effect, S Napoli forms distinct lineages isolated by geographical distance. This study suggests that the persistence of S Napoli as a geographically structured metapopulation, causing localised human infections, could reflect the natural ecology of Salmonella before the rise of agribusiness. Future research should investigate the environmental reservoirs and transmission pathways of S Napoli.FundingFondation Le Roch-Les Mousquetaires, Institut Pasteur, Santé publique France, Investissement d'Avenir programme, Laboratoire d'Excellence 'Integrative Biology of Emerging Infectious Diseases', and Institute of Health Carlos III 'Acción Estratégica de Salud Intramural'.
authors: Frézal L, Villa L, Bloemberg G, Bonifait L, Leclerc V, Accou-Demartin M, Fabre L, Hächler H, Angermeier H, Pino-Rosa S, Cadel-Six S, Chemaly M, Pardos-de-la-Gandara M, Herrera-León S, Stephan R, Carattoli A, Weill FX.

title: Bacteria inside kidney tumors associate with myeloid inflammation and disease progression: A TRACERx Renal study.
abstract: BackgroundIntratumoral bacteria are increasingly recognized as active contributors to neutrophil-driven inflammation and disease progression in solid tumors. Yet, in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), where myeloid inflammation is a key feature of aggressive disease, live bacterial presence, their intratumoral distribution, and interaction with the tumor microenvironment remain unexplored.MethodsWe genetically characterized the microbiome of primary ccRCC tumors across two independent cohorts (TRACERx: 616 samples, 143 patients; The Cancer Genome Atlas [TCGA]: 511 samples and patients), confirming live bacterial presence through culture. Multi-regional sampling enabled within-tumor analysis of bacterial distribution. Associations with the tumor microenvironment were explored at scale using bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) across both cohorts and corroborated in depth through spatial transcriptomics and in vitro infection assays.FindingsAcross both cohorts, the commensal Cutibacterium emerged as the dominant genus, accumulating in discrete niches enriched toward the tumor center and associating with more advanced (TRACERx p = 0.024; TCGA p = 0.0011) tumors and shorter progression-free survival (TRACERx p = 0.0022; TCGA p = 4.4 × 10-4). Both across and within tumors, Cutibacterium accumulation associated with neutrophil recruitment and myeloid inflammation. In vitro, Cutibacterium induced sustained expression of neutrophil-attracting chemokines in macrophages, recapitulating patient tumor findings.ConclusionsThese findings establish intratumoral bacteria as novel prognostic components of the ccRCC tumor microenvironment and suggest an active role in shaping local myeloid inflammation, laying the groundwork for investigating their potential as therapeutic targets.FundingThis work was supported by the Francis Crick Institute (Cancer Research UK, MRC, Wellcome Trust). TRACERx Renal is funded by Cancer Research UK (C50947/A18176).

title: Selective attenuation of wastewater resistomes and residual ARG-MGE co-occurrence in semi-arid lagoon-treated effluents.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs), mobile genetic elements (MGEs), and clinically relevant bacterial taxa are environmental-health concerns in wastewater-impacted ecosystems. However, the capacity of lagoon systems to attenuate these AMR-related signals before effluent discharge or reuse remains insufficiently characterized in semi-arid regions. Shotgun metagenomics was applied to 34 influent and treated-effluent samples collected approximately weekly during January-March 2025 from two Moroccan lagoon systems: Settat (urban, n = 18) and Ouled Said (rural, n = 16). TPM-normalized taxonomic, resistome, and mobilome profiles were analyzed using diversity metrics, PERMANOVA, differential-abundance testing, and correlation networks. Lagoon treatment produced site-dependent microbial restructuring, with a marked shift in Ouled Said (Aitchison PERMANOVA, R2 = 0.376, p = 0.002) but a weaker, non-significant shift in Settat (R2 = 0.125, p = 0.054). ESKAPE-associated bacteria declined from approximately 38% to 32% of CARD-annotated taxa but remained detectable in effluents. The resistome was broadly attenuated, but last-resort antibiotic resistance genes (LR-ARGs) responded unevenly: most mcr variants decreased by 82.4-89.9%, with significant reductions for several variants, whereas blaVIM-1 and tet(X) showed limited or non-significant reductions. The mobilome declined, although transposases and insertion sequences remained prominent. Network analysis indicated denser residual statistical ARG-MGE-taxa co-occurrence after treatment, without implying increased genetic mobility or HGT. Overall, the systems acted as selective, context-dependent barriers, reducing AMR-related burdens while retaining clinically relevant residual signals. The contrasting site responses indicate that treatment performance should not be assumed to be uniform across lagoon systems and support targeted effluent surveillance for safer discharge and reuse.
journal: International journal of hygiene and environmental health
authors: Raqraq H, Barguigua A, Ressmi A, Aniba R, Dihmane A, Jihane F, Bennani M, El Goundali B, Shafiq M.

title: Microbial priming controls terrestrial carbon burial in marine sediments
abstract: Marine sediments are a globally important sink for organic carbon of both marine and terrestrial origin, yet far less terrestrial carbon is ultimately buried than rivers deliver to the ocean margins. This long-standing “terrestrial carbon conundrum” has resisted explanation, largely because conventional bulk proxies cannot distinguish marine, terrestrial and microbial-degrader carbon pools. Here we use sedimentary ancient DNA from five records spanning the Bering Sea to the Sea of Okhotsk over the past 30,000 years to reconstruct organic carbon resolved simultaneously by taxonomy and habitat. Integrating these taxon-resolved carbon estimates with environmental proxies across the last glacial–interglacial cycle, we find that terrestrial carbon burial is governed not only by supply but by biogeochemical interactions previously documented only in soils. Microbial processing splits into two competing pathways: under priming, marine organic matter fuels the degradation of terrestrial organic matter, whereas under preferential substrate utilization microbes consume marine organic matter and spare terrestrial carbon. Both pathways are triggered only once marine organic-matter availability crosses a critical, temperature-governed threshold. This temperature-sensitive cascade reveals a previously unrecognized vulnerability of the ocean’s carbon sink to global warming.
authors: Weiß JF, Stoof-Leichsenring KR, Boeckel C, Lembke-Jene L, Meyer VD, John U, Herzschuh U.

title: Metabolomics profiling of Calocybe indica for identification of potential ligands that bind to bacterial DNA Gyrase B.
abstract: The increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance has intensified the search for novel antibacterial agents from natural sources. In the present study, the antibacterial potential of Calocybe indica KUFC144 was investigated through metabolite profiling and computational analysis. Tissue culture was established from fruiting bodies and molecularly identified based on ITS and 28 S rRNA gene sequences, confirming its identity as C. indica. The methanolic mycelial extract exhibited antibacterial activity against both Bacillus subtilis and Klebsiella pneumoniae, with inhibition zones of 10.33 ± 0.43 mm and 13.78 ± 0.07 mm, respectively. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) further demonstrated greater antibacterial efficacy against K. pneumoniae. Liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry analysis identified 33 metabolites belonging to diverse chemical classes, including phenylethanoid glycosides, flavonoids, limonoids, thiophene derivatives, lipids and organic acids. Based on identification confidence, relative abundance, structural diversity, and reported antimicrobial or pharmacological activities, six metabolites: forsythiaside, leonoside A, myricoside, salannin, (10)-gingerol and 5-(4-hydroxybut-1-ynyl)-2,2'-bithiophene, were prioritized for molecular docking against the ATPase domain of Escherichia coli DNA gyrase B (PDB ID: 1EI1). Among the tested ligands, forsythiaside exhibited the highest Vina score (predicted binding affinity of - 9.7 kcal/mol), followed by leonoside A (- 9.0 kcal/mol) and myricoside (- 8.7 kcal/mol), with extensive hydrogen-bonding and hydrophobic interactions within the active site. STRING analysis further placed GyrB within a functionally interconnected network associated with DNA topology, replication, repair and transcription. ADME profiling revealed distinct pharmacokinetic characteristics among the metabolites, with (10)-gingerol and 5-(4-hydroxybut-1-ynyl)-2,2'-bithiophene showing comparatively favourable predicted gastrointestinal absorption and drug-likeness. In contrast, the highly polar glycosidic metabolites exhibited low predicted gastrointestinal absorption. Normal mode analysis indicated favourable structural stability and flexibility of the protein-ligand complexes. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that C. indica KUFC144 is a rich source of antibacterial metabolites and highlight forsythiaside as a promising GyrB-targeting lead based on the Vina score (predicted binding affinity). At the same time, the ADME analysis provides additional information for prioritizing the identified metabolites. The study provides a foundation for future biochemical validation and the development of mushroom-derived antibacterial agents.
authors: Sarkar R, Datta B.

title: Integrated metabolomic and genomic characterization of antifungal Streptomyces halstedii S14 from Melipona mondury larval food
abstract: Abstract    Although the larval food of stingless bees harbors microorganisms with potential for natural-product discovery, the chemical and genomic potential of actinobacteria associated with  Melipona mondury  remains poorly explored. We investigated the antagonism of  Streptomyces halstedii  S14 against  Trichoderma atroviride  by integrating co-culture, spatial UHPLC-HRMS/MS, Feature-Based Molecular Networking, and genome mining with antiSMASH and BiG-SCAPE. S14 produced an inhibition zone of 1.28 ± 0.38 cm. Of 771 molecular features evaluated, 515 showed significant spatial variation across the co-culture gradient after accounting for plate identity. Pre-specified contrasts retained seven robust features associated with the inhibition zone (IZ) and 11 with the halo–fungus interface (TP). Among annotated candidates,  m/z  295.1294, putatively assigned as glutamylphenylalanine, was associated with IZ, whereas  m/z  522.3565, putatively assigned as 1-oleoyl-lysophosphatidylcholine, was associated with TP. Genome mining identified 59 biosynthetic regions. The strongest genome–metabolome convergence involved  m/z  256.0608, putatively annotated as caboxamycin, and NODE_598, closely related to the caboxamycin reference BGC (BiG-SCAPE distance 0.03). A family-level association linked a bafilomycin C1-like signal (  m/z  743.399) to NODE_118 (distance 0.34). These findings reveal a spatially structured chemical interaction and show how regional metabolomics combined with genome mining can prioritize biosynthetic hypotheses without assigning the antifungal phenotype to a single compound.
authors: Diogo YR, Cappelini LTD, Lira KDL, de Carvalho AC, Santos NGd, Vital VG, Soares JKC, Kuriki FK, de Medeiros LS, Francoy TM, de Vasconcellos SP, Morais MM.

title: MET18 deficiency leads to elevated single-stranded DNA at the replication fork and destabilizes the yeast genome.
abstract: Iron-sulfur (Fe-S) clusters often act as protein cofactors, and many enzymes involved in DNA replication and repair require them for proper function. However, the precise mechanisms by which Fe-S clusters influence enzyme activity remain incompletely understood. It has been shown previously that a mutation in the MET18 gene, encoding a key component of the cytosolic Fe-S cluster assembly machinery, elevates the rate of mutations in haploid Saccharomyces cerevisiae cells. In the current study, we demonstrate that in diploid yeast cells, the met18 mutation results in an elevation in loss-of-heterozygosity (LOH) events and large interstitial chromosomal deletions and duplications. We also found 46-fold and 55-fold increases in terminal deletions and duplications, respectively. By expressing the human APOBEC3B gene in yeast, we show that the rate of CG to TA mutations increased threefold in the met18 strain, and these mutations were enriched four-fold on the lagging-strand template relative to the leading-strand template, indicating the presence of elevated levels of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) at replication forks. Overall, this study shows that loss of MET18 causes extensive genome instability in yeast, providing additional insights into how Fe-S clusters regulate genome stability.
authors: Tang XX, Qi L, Tian LY, Li KJ, Zhang K, Petes TD, Zheng DQ.

title: Integrative genomics and regulomics reveal the molecular architecture of complex traits in domestic chickens.
abstract: Domestic chickens (Gallus gallus domesticus) exhibit exceptional phenotypic diversity and provide a valuable model for studying domestication and artificial selection. We integrated whole-genome resequencing data from ~3000 individuals with 20 slaughter-related traits. Population genomic analyses revealed pronounced genetic differentiation between northern and southern Chinese indigenous chickens, accompanied by distinct signatures of domestication and local adaptation. To dissect the gene regulatory networks of slaughter-related traits, we developed an Integrated Weighted Regulatory Network Analysis (iWRNA) framework that combines genome-wide association signals with multi-tissue transcriptomic and epigenomic data. This approach enabled the identification of tissue-specific regulatory modules and candidate causal genes underlying economically important traits. Notably, liver-weight-associated loci converged on a hepatic metabolic network in which enhancer activity coordinates gene expression and phenotypic variation. These findings establish a comprehensive regulatory atlas for complex trait variation in chickens and provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms of domestication, adaptation, and vertebrate phenotypic evolution.
authors: Han W, Zhou C, You Y, Li G, Zhu Y, Tang Y, Zeng T, Zhang H, Xue Q, Yin J, Chen L, Ju X, Jiang Y, Cai J, Li L, Zhang X, Lin Z, Ren J, Lu L, Chen D.

title: A chromosome-level genome assembly of Amaranthus spinosus provides insights into its evolution and invasion.
abstract: BackgroundSeveral Amaranthus species native to the Americas have become widespread invasive weeds, posing threats to agricultural production and ecosystems worldwide. Amaranthus spinosus is a tropical America weed that has established populations across tropical, subtropical, and warm-temperate regions. However, limited genomic resources have constrained our understanding of its invasion history and adaptive evolution.ResultsWe generated a chromosome-level genome assembly of Amaranthus spinosus comprising 17 chromosomes, with a genome size of 420.11 Mb and 98.0% BUSCO completeness. Comparative genomics analyses identified Amaranthus palmeri as the closest relative and revealed expansion of cytochrome P450 (P450), UDP-glycosyltransferase (UGT), and glutathione S-transferase (GST) gene families, which may contribute to environmental adaptation. A genus-level pan-genome of eight Amaranthus species identified 24 274 orthologous gene families, including 13 410 common, 9366 dispensable, and 1498 species-specific orthogroups. Genome-wide single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) analysis of 61 accessions from five geographic regions identified six genetic subpopulations, including two strongly differentiated subpopulations within the United States (USA-1 and USA-2). Demographic history inferred from genome-wide SNPs supported an invasion history originating in the Americas, followed by spread to China and Zimbabwe and subsequently dispersal to Kenya. Selective sweep analyses identified candidate genes involved in environmental adaptation, with the two Africa populations showing enrichment of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) binding cassette (ABC) transporters and stress-response genes.ConclusionThe chromosome-level genome and genome-wide SNPs generated in this study provides insights into the invasion history and adaptive evolution of Amaranthus spinosus. These resources establish a valuable foundation for functional investigation of invasive traits and may facilitate the development of genomics-informed strategies for monitoring and managing invasive Amaranthus weeds. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
authors: Deng Y, Cao L, Cheng Z, Wei S, Chen Y, Sun J, Xing L.

title: Antifungal resistance landscapes in major fungal pathogens in Zhejiang, China.
abstract: BackgroundInvasive fungal infections caused by Aspergillus fumigatus and other pathogenic fungi represent a major global health threat, with treatment increasingly complicated by the emergence of antifungal drug resistance. Azole antifungals serve as the first-line therapy for aspergillosis, but resistance rates vary substantially across geographical regions. This study aimed to characterize the antifungal resistance landscape among clinical fungal isolates from Hangzhou and Yiwu cities in Zhejiang Province, Eastern China, and to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying azole resistance in Aspergillus fumigatus.ResultsWe analyzed 110 Aspergillus clinical isolates for antifungal susceptibility. Among A. fumigatus strains, 8.6% exhibited azole resistance, with half of these harboring the tandem repeat mutation TR34/L98H in the cyp51A gene. One resistant strain carried the TR46/Y121F/T289A mutation combination. Minimum inhibitory concentration testing revealed that 8.6% of A. fumigatus isolates were resistant to amphotericin B We identified one resistant isolate without known resistance mutations and characterized it through whole-genome sequencing and transcriptomic analysis. Novel mutations S437F in cyp51A and P298T in hmg1 were discovered; however, functional validation using CRISPR-Cas9 demonstrated these mutations do not directly confer resistance. Instead, transcriptomic profiling revealed significant upregulation of ergosterol biosynthesis pathway genes and efflux transporter genes, suggesting alternative resistance mechanisms. Among non-A. fumigatus species, all A. niger isolates displayed resistance to itraconazole and posaconazole.ConclusionsThis comprehensive regional surveillance reveals concerning patterns of antifungal resistance among major human pathogenic fungi in Zhejiang Province, China. The identification of both classical resistance mutations and novel transcription-mediated resistance mechanisms highlights the complex and evolving nature of antifungal resistance. These findings emphasize the critical need for continued surveillance programs and rapid resistance detection methods to inform clinical treatment strategies and improve patient outcomes.
authors: Wang H, Zhang J, Zhang N, Ji Y, Hong X, Sámano-Sánchez H, Xu F, Han Y, Xiong X, Welburn SC, Schulze H, Bachmann TT, Ge Y, Scharf DH.

title: Differentially Expressed Infection-Associated Genes in a Shewanella algae isolate From a Deceased Northern Bottlenose Whale.
abstract: Diseases are an important but poorly understood influence on marine ecosystems. However, many pathogens of wild marine organisms remain poorly characterized, limiting our understanding of their ecology and potential impacts. This study investigates the potential virulence mechanisms of a Shewanella algae strain isolated from the brain tissue of a deceased northern bottlenose whale (Hyperoodon ampullatus). Using long-read Oxford Nanopore RNA Sequencing, differential gene expression analysis (DGEA) was conducted comparing growth in standard media, Tryptic Soy Broth (TSB) and TSB supplemented with 5% brain homogenate (BH) to stimulate expression of genes potentially associated with virulence. Twenty-eight significantly differentially expressed genes (23 identified using the assembled genome and five additional non-overlapping genes detected using a closely related reference genome) were identified out of 7,213 genes with at least two primary mapped reads. These genes were associated with processes that have been linked to bacterial virulence in previous studies, including protein translocation (e.g., small signal recognition particle), flagellar motility, chemotaxis, and iron acquisition. Functional analysis indicated an increased expression of pathways related to amino acid metabolism and motility, whereas carbohydrate and inorganic ion transport were downregulated. These results suggest that environmental cues, potentially including factors related to iron metabolism, may influence bacterial virulence, obtained using Oxford Nanopore RNA sequencing for pathogen transcriptomics.

title: Molecular epidemiological characteristics and pathogenicity of Chinese PRRSV-2 L1B sublineage strains in piglets.
abstract: PRRSV evolves through mutation and recombination during circulation, contributing to the emergence and spread of genetically diverse lineages. Among these, the PRRSV-2 L1B sublineage has been detected in multiple countries, but its molecular epidemiology and pathogenicity remain poorly characterized. We investigated the molecular epidemiology of L1B PRRSV in China and assessed its pathogenicity in piglets. L1B strains were detected in multiple Chinese provinces. Phylogenetic analysis based on the ORF5 sequences revealed that all Chinese L1B PRRSV strains cluster within the L1B sublineage of PRRSV-2. These strains harbor a 131-amino-acid discontinuous deletion (111 +1 +19) in the Nsp2 protein and carry cluster-associated amino acid substitutions at positions 137 and 178 of the GP5 protein. Whole-genome analysis revealed that Chinese L1B strains possess complex genetic backgrounds, likely arising from recombination between indigenous circulating strains (NADC30-like and HP-PRRSV) and the introduced L1B strains. Animal challenge experiments demonstrated that inoculation with the representative isolate TZJ2547 induced clinical symptoms including fever, coughing, and decreased feed intake, accompanied by persistent viremia, high viral RNA loads in multiple tissues, and pathological lesions in the lungs and lymphoid tissues. These findings indicate that TZJ2547 exhibits moderate pathogenicity in the challenged piglets. This study characterizes the epidemiological distribution, genomic characteristics, and recombination profile of L1B PRRSV in China. To the best of our knowledge, this study reports the first systematic pathogenicity evaluation of a Chinese L1B PRRSV isolate in piglets. Collectively, these findings provide fundamental data to inform the surveillance and control of this viral sublineage.
authors: Li J, Shi J, Qi H, Zhang X, Li C, Gong B, Guo Z, Feng Z, Kang H, Song Z, Wang G, Chen T, Yang S, Dong A, Tang YD, Xiang L, Zhao K, Wang Q, Peng J, Zhou G, An T, Cai X, Tian ZJ, Xu H, Zhang H.

title: Bovine keratoconjunctivitis: a review of the bovine ocular surface microbiome and related epidemiological risk factors.
abstract: Bovine keratoconjunctivitis (BK) is a common inflammatory condition of the ocular surface (OS) of cattle, with a complex epidemiology. This review summarises current knowledge about the bovine ocular surface microbiota (OSMt) and discusses how it integrates with agent, host and environmental factors involved in BK epidemiology. A comprehensive literature review, from 1950 to 2026, was conducted to identify known constituents of the OSMt and symbionts with pathogenic potential within this community. Information about key epidemiological factors associated with BK was simultaneously collected. After applying a structured literature search and selection criteria, 321 papers remained. A directed acyclic graph was used to construct a conceptual framework that visualised the role of the bovine OSMt in BK within the epidemiological web. The graph indicated that cattle are exposed to six injurious environmental factors acting from outside the ocular surface microbiome (OSMe)-(i) ultraviolet B, (ii) lachryphagous insects, (iii) desiccation stress, (iv) nutritional deficiencies, (v) large particulate matter, and (vi) small particulate matter-and two factors acting from within the microbiome-(vii) pathogenic stages of Thelazia spp. and (viii) pathogenic viruses. Metagenomic analyses revealed marked diversity within the bovine OSMt and symbionts of both high (e.g., Moraxella bovis) and low pathogenic potential (e.g., Mesomycoplasma bovoculi). The symbiotic relationship is influenced by damaging or disruptive environmental influences impacting on barrier integrity. Integrating the OSMe within a network of agent, host, and environmental factors provides a new perspective on BK that may inform future control strategies.
authors: Maartens LH, Thompson PN, Grewar JD, Picard JA, Gummow B.

title: Lineage-associated genomic features and phenotypic heterogeneity in clinical borderline oxacillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
abstract: Borderline oxacillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (BORSA) represents a mecA/mecC-negative phenotype characterized by oxacillin minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of 1-8 mg/L. The molecular basis of this resistance, particularly regarding lineage-associated differences in induction profiles, remains incompletely understood. In this study, 11 clinical BORSA isolates from pneumonia and bloodstream infections were identified among 374 clinical S. aureus isolates. Resistance-associated features were investigated using phenotypic profiling, whole-genome sequencing (WGS), RT-qPCR of blaZ expression, and time-kill assays. All BORSA isolates were cefoxitin-susceptible, β-lactamase-positive, and distributed across six clonal backgrounds, with ST25 and ST7 each represented by three isolates. WGS identified a shared GdpP N105D substitution in all isolates, together with lineage-associated variations in pbp1 and pbp4. Following oxacillin exposure, blaZ was significantly upregulated in all three ST25 isolates (all P gdpP variation, inducible β-lactamase activity, and alterations in penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs). The cefoxitin susceptibility of these isolates presents a diagnostic challenge that may lead to therapeutic misclassification and subsequent inappropriate therapy. β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations demonstrated promising in vitro activity and warrants further investigation for BORSA isolates exhibiting strong inducible β-lactamase activity.IMPORTANCEBorderline oxacillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (BORSA) is difficult to detect because it lacks mecA/mecC and remains susceptible to cefoxitin, increasing the risk of misclassification and inappropriate β-lactam therapy. This study suggests that BORSA resistance in this cohort is multifactorial, involving candidate gdpP variation, lineage-associated variations in penicillin-binding proteins, and inducible β-lactamase activity. Importantly, the ST25 isolates in this cohort exhibited rapid blaZ induction and stronger responses to oxacillin/sulbactam than to oxacillin alone. These findings improve understanding of BORSA biology, highlight a significant diagnostic blind spot in routine susceptibility testing, and support further evaluation of β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations as a promising treatment strategy for BORSA isolates exhibiting strong inducible β-lactamase activity.
authors: Bian Q, Xi L, Li S, Fang H, Ma C, Yang X, Shi X, Li N, Yang P, Dong W, Wu H, Wang X, Wu J, Guo B, Zhang J, Fan Y.

title: Primer: Orbiviruses.
abstract: Orbiviruses comprise numerous species and are transmitted by insect vectors. They are non-enveloped viruses with a multilayered capsid and a segmented double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) genome. Bluetongue virus (BTV), the prototype species of the genus Orbivirus, is a significant pathogen of livestock and is widely distributed throughout the world, causing serious periodic outbreaks with substantial economic consequences. Consequently, BTV has been extensively studied as a model orbivirus, resulting in a comprehensive understanding of its molecular epidemiology, genetics, biochemistry, structure, and replication cycle. This includes detailed insights into virus entry into host cells, synthesis of progeny viral components, assembly of new virions, and subsequent cell-to-cell transmission. This review summarizes the current literature on each of these aspects and discusses how this knowledge has been applied to develop novel vaccines against BTV and related orbiviruses. In addition, the review highlights important gaps in our understanding of virus replication within insect vectors, particularly Culicoides biting midges (gnats), at the molecular level. Addressing these gaps will provide valuable insights into orbivirus evolution, transmission, and the emergence of new viral strains.
authors: Roy P.

title: Expanding the Orchidaceae virome through analysis of public-domain sequencing data.
abstract: Orchidaceae is one of the largest plant families and includes species of major ornamental, economic, and ecological importance. Despite this diversity, the viruses associated with orchids remain poorly characterized. The growing availability of high-throughput sequencing data offers new opportunities to explore plant virus diversity across broad taxonomic scales. Here, we conducted a large-scale meta-analysis of orchid-associated viruses by reanalyzing 2,789 publicly available RNA-seq data sets representing 41 genera across 18 subtribes and five subfamilies. We identified sequences corresponding to 163 viruses, including 13 new associations with orchids. Notably, 117 sequences likely represent putative novel species, including tentative new genera within the families Benyviridae, Betaflexiviridae, Phenuiviridae, and Tymoviridae. This analysis also reveals patterns of virus co-occurrence within the orchid virome and uncovers links between viral taxa and orchid life forms. Overall, these findings greatly broaden the known diversity of orchid-associated viruses and offer a comprehensive global framework for understanding their composition, ecological interactions, and potential scope.IMPORTANCEOrchids are among the most diverse plant families, yet little is known about the viruses associated with them. Plant viruses pose significant risks to agriculture and may also threaten orchid conservation, particularly when infected plant material is moved through trade or cultivation. A comprehensive understanding of the orchid virome is therefore essential for improving virus detection, managing diseases, and producing virus-free planting material. In this study, we used large-scale analysis of publicly available RNA-seq data to identify viral sequences associated with orchid-derived transcriptomic data sets and to characterize the diversity of orchid-associated viruses. Our results substantially expand the catalog of viruses associated with Orchidaceae, revealing numerous previously undescribed viruses and candidate virus-orchid associations. By providing a global perspective on the Orchidaceae virome, this work highlights the power of data mining approaches for virus discovery and establishes a foundation for future studies on plant virus ecology, evolution, and surveillance.
authors: Pérez A, Sánchez-Yali J, Higuita M, Jiménez-Arias C, Ortiz-Reyes A, Gutiérrez PA.

title: Sustained release of beneficial microorganisms for corals from alginate beads under marine conditions.
abstract: AimCoral reefs support more than one-third of the global marine biodiversity, but global stressors have negatively impacted their health by disrupting fragile microbial partnerships, leading to widespread mass bleaching events. To address this issue, the use of beneficial microorganisms for coral (BMCs) has been shown to enhance coral resilience. In this study, we evaluated the potential of alginate beads as a delivery method for BMCs underwater.Methods and resultsBMCs were encapsulated in alginate beads and incubated in artificial seawater at 26°C and 32°C. Microbial viability within the beads and bacterial release were monitored over a three-week period. Cell viability and sustained release rate were maintained throughout the experiment, with viable cell release averaging 106 cells h-1 per 50 mL flask by the third week at both temperatures. Co-encapsulation of multiple BMC strains resulted in changes in bacterial dynamics.ConclusionsThese findings demonstrate that alginate beads can provide sustained delivery of viable BMCs under marine conditions and represent a promising platform for probiotic-based coral restoration strategies.
authors: Alsaggaf AA, Garcias-Bonet N, García FC, Antony CP, Peixoto RS.

title: The replication checkpoint prevents fork stalling by reducing transcription
abstract: The replication checkpoint is essential for maintaining genome stability during replication stress. The prevailing view is that, without this pathway, stalled DNA replication forks lose structural integrity and collapse, preventing replication resumption and ultimately causing cell death. Here, we show that transcription is a major cause of replication stress in budding yeast checkpoint mutants. Checkpoint signaling limits replication defects by reducing RNA polymerase II and III occupancy at highly transcribed genes, particularly those encoding ribosomal proteins. Reducing transcription at these loci reduces fork stalling and the sensitivity of checkpoint mutants to hydroxyurea-induced replication stress. In human cells, transcription inhibition likewise improves replication recovery when ATR is inhibited, suggesting that this function is conserved. Together, our findings extend the canonical view of critical checkpoint functions: in addition to stabilizing stalled forks, it actively reduces RNA polymerase roadblocks that would otherwise impede their progression. Highlights  - The replication checkpoint acts upstream of fork stabilization to prevent stalling - Replication defects is caused by highly expressed ribosomal proteins genes - Reducing ribosomal genes transcription partially rescues checkpoint mutants - This protective checkpoint function is evolutionarily conserved in human cells.
authors: Heuzé J, Grassin S, Pasero P, Poli J.

title: A smartphone-integrated plasmonic biosensor for amplification-free detection of African swine fever virus.
abstract: African Swine Fever Virus (ASFV) poses a catastrophic threat to global swine production, with recent outbreaks across Europe, Asia, and the Caribbean, significantly elevating the biosecurity risk to the United States' billion-dollar pork industry. Current diagnostic gold standards are laboratory-dependent and introduce critical delays in outbreak response. To address this gap, a plasmonic biosensor based on functionalized gold nanoparticles (GNPs) was developed for the rapid, amplification-free detection of ASFV. GNPs were surface-functionalized with 11-mercaptoundecanoic acid (MUDA) and combined in situ with ASFV-specific oligonucleotide probes targeting a conserved region of the p72 (B646L) gene. The detection mechanism relies on acid-induced aggregation: hybridization of target ASFV DNA to the probe generates a rigid duplex that shields the nanoparticles from acid-induced destabilization, maintaining a ruby-red color, whereas in the absence of target DNA the GNPs aggregate, producing a visible red-to-blue color shift. The optimized plasmonic biosensor demonstrated 100% analytical specificity, with no cross-reactivity against a panel of 19 non-target bacterial genomic DNA samples representative of the swine environment. Detection limits determined by the IUPAC 3σ criterion were 285 copies per reaction for Probe 1 and 402 copies per reaction for Probe 2, within the same order of magnitude as the qPCR reference assay run on the same dilution series (approximately 312 copies per reaction) under the experimental conditions used here. A smartphone-based Bio-Analytics App employing an RGB color-conversion algorithm served as a quantitative reader, yielding signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) that strongly correlated with benchtop spectrophotometric readings (A520/A620 ratio, R2 = 0.96) and achieved diagnostic concordance with qPCR binary calls. This platform offers a robust and low-cost (∼$2 per test), amplification-free approach to ASFV screening with potential for point-of-need deployment, subject to future validation in clinical specimens.
journal: Analytical methods : advancing methods and applications
authors: Singh S, Yancy H, Alocilja E.

title: Isolation and pathogenicity characterization of a tembusu virus from 817 broilers with decreased egg production.
abstract: Tembusu virus (TMUV) is widely distributed in duck and goose populations in Asia, causing significant economic losses to the poultry industry. In this study, a TMUV strain, designated 24SD, was isolated and characterized from 817 broilers with decreased egg production in Shandong province of China, in 2024. The 24SD replicated efficiently in BHK-21 cells and SPF chicken embryos, reaching titers 106.833 TCID₅₀ per 0.1 mL and 103.681 ELD₅₀ per 0.3 mL, respectively. The virus also replicated in duck embryos and caused obvious pathological lesions. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and phylogenetic analysis indicated that 24SD belongs to TMUV Cluster 3. The 24SD strain showed high nucleotide sequence identities (99.00-99.03 %) with other Cluster 3 strains, including YN2020, CTLN, and SD2021. Animal pathogenicity studies demonstrated that 24SD could infect both chickens and ducklings, with stronger replication in chickens. The virus induced transient viremia, replicated efficiently in multiple organs, including the heart and liver, leading to varying degrees of tissue damage and inflammation, and was excreted via feces. Overall, this study expands the genomic dataset of chicken-origin TMUV strains within Cluster 3 and provides valuable information for surveillance and control of TMUV in poultry.
authors: Zhao M, Xie Y, Bei L, Feng C, Zhang R, Meng Y, Zhu Y, Wei L, Jiang S.

title: Astragalus Polysaccharides Alleviate Inflammatory Damage in Murine Rheumatoid Arthritis by Modulating Th17/Treg Balance via the Gut-Joint Axis.
abstract: Astragalus polysaccharides (APSs) have demonstrated protective effects in RA models; however, the underlying microbe-host crosstalk remains unclear. In this study, collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) was established in mice, followed by prophylactic and therapeutic APS administration. The following were then assessed: articular histopathology, splenic Th17/Treg frequencies via flow cytometry, serum and joint cytokine profiles via ELISA and immunohistochemistry, gut microbial metagenomes, and bone erosion via Safranin O-fast green staining. It was found that APS treatment significantly attenuated joint inflammation and bone destruction, rebalanced the Th17/Treg ratio, and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α and IL-17) while elevating anti-inflammatory IL-10 both systemically and locally. Subsequently, fecal microbiota from APS-treated donor mice was transplanted via oral gavage into CIA recipient mice. APS reversed RA-associated gut dysbiosis by enriching Ligilactobacillus, Lactobacillus, Limosilactobacillus, and Bacteroides, and these microbial shifts closely paralleled diminished articular inflammation and preserved bone architecture. Collectively, these findings indicate that APS mitigates RA progression by reconfiguring the gut microbial ecosystem-favoring beneficial taxa while curbing pathobionts-thereby restoring intestinal homeostasis, normalizing the Th17/Treg axis, and suppressing systemic and articular inflammatory responses.
authors: Yao P, Huang J, Liu W, Yuan Q, Lv J.

title: Light Penetration, Dissolved Oxygen, and Riparian Zone Extent Are Associated with the Structure, Gene Expression, and Lipid Production of Riverbed Microbial Communities.
abstract: We analyzed riverbed microbiota structure, gene expression, and fatty acid production across several sites along Little Miami River in Ohio, United States. The sites varied in stream width, shading, surrounding land use, and the size of the riparian zone. Within each site, we observed strong concordance among microbial community composition, functional gene expression, and fatty acid signature. All microbial communities were dominated by the members of phylum Proteobacteria, class Planctomycetacia, and by algal and cyanobacterial cells. The measured concentrations of chlorophyll a, dissolved oxygen, and soluble phosphorus were the main environmental determinants of microbial community structure. These were in turn dependent on the level of penetrating sunlight and, to a lesser degree, on the width of the riparian zone. The level of sunlight affected the expression of light-harvesting complexes, methanogenesis genes, anaerobic respiratory reductases and fermentation pathways, as well as functions of denitrification, ammonification, and sulfate reduction. The expression of phosphorus scavenging and antibiotic resistance genes was highest at the site lacking a riparian zone and surrounded by farmland. Overall, our findings demonstrate that riverbed microbiota exhibit consistent structural and functional responses to interacting geochemical and anthropogenic gradients. Our data also provide support for the hypothesis that phototrophic microorganisms act as central organizers of benthic community metabolism.
authors: Shankar V, Paliy O.

title: Genome-Wide Characterization of the HSF Gene Family in Paulownia fortunei and Preliminary Functional Analysis of PfHSF6 in Drought Response.
abstract: Heat shock transcription factors (HSFs) act as crucial regulatory components in plant stress regulatory network and play essential roles in abiotic stress adaptation, particularly drought tolerance. Here, we identified 36 PfHSF gene family members in Paulownia fortunei through genome-wide analysis. Their chromosomal distribution, physicochemical properties, phylogenetic relationships, gene structures, conserved motifs, cis-acting elements, and post-translational modification sites were systematically characterized. Transcriptome-based expression profiling demonstrated distinct tissue-specific and drought-responsive expression patterns among PfHSF members, with PfHSF6 being strongly up-regulated under drought. Subcellular localization assays confirmed nuclear and plasma membrane localization of PfHSF6. Transient overexpression of PfHSF6 in tobacco significantly enhanced drought tolerance, as evidenced by alleviated wilting, a ~60% reduction in MDA content, ~2-fold increases in SOD and POD activities, and a ~67% reduction in electrolyte leakage relative to the control (p NbRD29A and NbLEA5 were up-regulated by ~6- and ~3-fold, respectively. This study provides a comprehensive characterization of the PfHSF family and preliminary functional evidence for PfHSF6, offering candidate genes for further functional validation and potential drought-tolerance breeding in paulownia.
authors: Liu J, Liu C, Wang L, Zhao Z, Cao Y.
