title: L-Lysine production from glucose and chitin monomers using engineered Vibrio natriegens.
abstract: Despite its industrial importance, microbial L-lysine production has largely been confined to classical producer strains, leaving the fast-growing, non-pathogenic marine bacterium V. natriegens mostly unexplored as an emerging biosynthetic platform. In this work, we established an L-lysine-overproducing V. natriegens DSM759 strain through a stepwise rational engineering strategy targeting the native biosynthetic pathway. Building on our prior systems-level analysis of the strain's genetic and regulatory architecture, we identified key metabolic bottlenecks and targeted interventions to relieve them. The central intervention was relief of feedback inhibition on the two key regulatory enzymes, aspartate kinase (AK, lysC) and dihydrodipicolinate synthase (DHDPS, dapA). Transferring feedback resistance substitutions previously characterized in E. coli to conserved positions in the V. natriegens DSM759 enzymes produced L-lysine-insensitive variants with kinetic parameters comparable to the corresponding wild-type enzymes. Among the tested configurations, the strain co-expressing Vn.lysC2 and Vn.dapA1:E84T reached the highest L-lysine titer (9.0 ± 0.6 mM) and yield (0.11 ± 0.01 molLys molGlc-1), whereas overexpression of additional L-lysine pathway genes provided no further benefit. Exploiting the host's substrate range, we further demonstrated L-lysine synthesis from the chitin-derived amino sugar N-acetylglucosamine (0.09 ± 0.00 molLys molGlcNAc-1), highlighting the potential to valorize chitin-rich waste streams from the seafood industry. This work establishes a minimal rational strategy for L-lysine biosynthesis in V. natriegens DSM759 and positions it as a candidate platform for sustainable amino acid production. KEY POINTS: • E. coli-derived rational engineering strategies were transferable to V. natriegens • Native pathway deregulation was sufficient to enable L-lysine production • Chitin-derived N-acetylglucosamine supports L-lysine synthesis.
authors: Straube E, Tran TVA, Faber A, Ihle N, Crespo Blanco R, Le HT, Fritz G, Frazão CJR, Walther T.

title: More than the sum of its parts: reproductive addiction in the ecology and evolution of fungal-bacterial symbioses.
abstract: SUMMARYReproductive control exerted by endosymbionts over their hosts is an adaptation for maintaining host-symbiont associations across generations. This strategy is particularly well-characterized in endosymbiotic bacteria (EB) associated with arthropods, in which EB of disparate species have independently evolved diverse mechanisms to manipulate host reproduction, thereby ensuring their reliable transmission across host generations. Like arthropods, fungi in the phylum Mucoromycota commonly harbor ancient and highly coevolved EB that significantly affect fungal life histories, including reproduction. In particular, the symbiosis between the mucoromycete Rhizopus microsporus and its Mycetohabitans spp. endosymbionts is significantly contingent on reproductive addiction, as removal of the symbiont results in the loss or severe impairment of host asexual and sexual reproduction. Here, we synthesize the current knowledge on sexual reproduction in mucoromycete fungi and the Rhizopus microsporus-Mycetohabitans symbiosis. We highlight current gaps in the knowledge of mucoromycete reproduction as well as present novel hypotheses for studying these interactions based on the understanding of reproductive manipulation in arthropods.
authors: Branine ME, Hempel N, Pawlowska TE.

title: Integrative structural and functional analysis of full-length hibernation-promoting factor and its association with antibiotic susceptibility in Mycobacterium smegmatis.
abstract: Ribosome hibernation is a critical adaptive mechanism that enables bacteria to survive stress by stabilizing inactive ribosomes and conserving cellular resources. This process is facilitated by hibernation-promoting factors (HPFs). However, structural and functional insights into the full-length architecture of Mycobacterium smegmatis HPF, particularly its C-terminal region, remain limited. Here, we combined in silico and experimental approaches to characterize HPF (MSMEG_1878) from M. smegmatis and investigate its role in ribosome-associated physiology and antibiotic response. Sequence and phylogenetic analyses revealed strong conservation of HPF among mycobacterial species, including the extended C-terminal region. A full-length 230-amino-acid structural model generated using complementary modeling approaches and molecular dynamics refinement showed close agreement with the experimentally resolved region. Structural mapping positioned HPF at the 70S ribosomal intersubunit interface, with the modeled C-terminal region extending toward the vicinity of the 16S rRNA decoding-center. Docking analyses predicted that paromomycin and neomycin localize within the h44-associated decoding-center region, near the HPF-associated surface, whereas chloramphenicol and tetracycline localize to spatially distinct ribosomal regions. Deletion of hpf impaired bacterial growth and reduced susceptibility to paromomycin and neomycin, while complementation restored susceptibility toward the wild-type phenotype. Furthermore, neomycin exposure significantly increased hpf transcript abundance, whereas paromomycin exposure showed a nonsignificant trend toward increased expression. Collectively, these findings suggest that M. smegmatis HPF contributes to ribosome-associated physiology and may influence the cellular response to selected antibiotics, providing insights into the relationship between ribosome hibernation and antibiotic response in mycobacteria.IMPORTANCEThis study provides new structural and functional insights into the full-length architecture and ribosome-associated role of HPF (MSMEG_1878) in Mycobacterium smegmatis, with particular emphasis on its C-terminal region. Using complementary structural modeling approaches, we investigated the predicted architecture of the C-terminal region and its spatial relationship with the ribosomal decoding-center region. Functional analyses further demonstrate that loss of HPF affects bacterial growth and alters susceptibility to selected aminoglycosides. Together, these findings suggest that HPF contributes to ribosome-associated physiology and may influence cellular responses to selected antibiotics. This work provides a potential structural and functional framework for further investigation of how ribosome-associated factors influence antibiotic responses in mycobacteria.
authors: Tiwari PK, Singh VK, Shivani, Verma D, Kushwaha AK.

title: Isolation, Identification, and Whole Genome Sequencing Analysis of Common Foodborne Bacteria from Fresh Fruits, Vegetables, and Their Ready-to-Eat Products in Shijiazhuang, China.
abstract: With evolving lifestyles, consumer demand for fresh fruits and vegetables has increased. However, these products are susceptible to contamination by foodborne bacteria from farm to table. To investigate the contamination status of foodborne bacteria in commercially available fresh fruits, vegetables, and their ready-to-eat (RTE) products in Shijiazhuang City, a total of 406 samples were collected from 2024 to 2025. Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus), Clostridium perfringens (C. perfringens), diarrheagenic Escherichia coli (diarrheagenic E. coli), and Salmonella were identified and analyzed for genomic characteristics using traditional biochemical tests and whole genome sequencing (WGS). The results showed that the detection rate of S. aureus was 4.68% (19/406), of which 5 isolates were identified as methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), accounting for 1.23% (5/406). The detection rate of C. perfringens was 8.37% (34/406), and the detection rate of diarrheagenic E. coli was 0.25% (1/406). No Salmonella was detected. Genomic characterization revealed that S. aureus strains were predominantly ST59 and ST22, with the MRSA strains primarily identified as ST59-SCCmec-IVa (2B)-t437. A total of 20 enterotoxin genes were detected, with 94.74% (18/19) of the strains carrying at least one enterotoxin gene. The sea gene was the most prevalent (52.63%, 10/19), and the tsst-1 gene, which can cause toxic shock syndrome, was detected in 2 strains. C. perfringens isolates were divided into 30 STs, exhibiting high genetic diversity. All toxin types were classified as type A. The mprF gene showed the highest carriage rate of resistance genes (94.12%, 32/34), and the main resistance profile was mprF + cplR (55.88%, 19/34). The diarrheagenic E. coli isolate was identified as enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) and carried multiple antimicrobial resistance genes. This study systematically reveals the contamination levels and molecular characteristics of common foodborne bacteria in fresh fruits, vegetables, and their RTE products sold in Shijiazhuang for the first time.
authors: Wang Y, Chen M, Wang J, Liu S, Jiang Y, Hu X, Sun X, Wang Y, Gao Y, Xu X, Wang J.

title: FRET-based nanoprobes for nucleic acid sensing and disease diagnosis: materials, probe architectures, and analytical trends.
abstract: Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) translates nanometre-scale changes in donor-acceptor separation into ratiometric fluorescence signals, enabling homogeneous and isothermal detection of nucleic acid biomarkers. In this review, we critically survey FRET-based nanoprobes for nucleic acid sensing and disease diagnosis, spanning organic dyes and cationic conjugated polymers to metallic nanoparticles, quantum dots, upconversion nanoparticles, carbon nanostructures, MXenes and polymeric nanoantennae. We organise probe designs by architectures, including sandwich hybridisation, disassembly hairpins, molecular beacons, dynamic junction sensors and enzyme-free DNA circuits, and analyse how these platforms achieve attomolar limits of detection, single-nucleotide discrimination and multiplexing in complex matrices. Representative case studies highlight applications in viral (e.g. SARS-CoV-2), bacterial and fungal pathogens, circulating cancer-related miRNAs and mRNAs, and neurodegenerative disease markers, as well as integration of FRET readouts with PCR and isothermal amplification workflows. We then compare FRET nanoprobes with established nucleic-acid assays in terms of analytical figures of merit, instrumentation, and compatibility with point-of-care (POC) formats. Remaining challenges, including photobleaching, spectral crowding, matrix autofluorescence, nanocarrier toxicity, and inter-laboratory reproducibility, are discussed in the context of emerging solutions such as near-infrared and lifetime-based FRET, CRISPR-coupled assays, DNA-origami nanoantennas, and microfluidic or smartphone-enabled devices. Finally, we outline key trends that could drive translation of FRET-based nucleic acid nanoprobes from proof-of-concept demonstrations to clinically actionable diagnostics.
authors: Ammar IM, Panja SK, Geng J.

title: Identification of candidate host susceptibility genes for viral myocarditis through integrated transcriptomic and mendelian randomization analyses.
abstract: This study investigated the genetic mechanisms underlying myocardial inflammatory responses related to Coxsackievirus B3 (CVB3) infection through an integrative transcriptomic and genetic approach. Gene expression profiles from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between CVB3-infected and control myocardial tissues. These genes were subsequently evaluated using Mendelian randomization (MR) based on publicly available expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data and genome-wide association study (GWAS) data for myocarditis. MR analysis prioritized four candidate genes whose genetically predicted expression levels were significantly associated with myocarditis susceptibility. To ensure the robustness of these findings, multiple sensitivity analyses were performed to assess potential pleiotropy and heterogeneity. Functional analyses suggested that the priority candidate genes (PCGs) were associated with immune regulation, inflammatory signaling, and cellular metabolic processes. In addition, immune cell infiltration analysis suggested alterations in the myocardial immune microenvironment and associations between PCG expression and estimated immune cell proportions. An independent GEO dataset was used for external validation, and in vitro experiments further confirmed the significant upregulation of these genes following CVB3 infection. This integrative strategy combining transcriptomic profiling, human genetic analyses, and experimental validation identified four genetically prioritized candidate genes associated with myocarditis susceptibility and provided preliminary insights into the immune-regulatory mechanisms underlying cardiac inflammatory responses.
authors: Zhang M, Zhang Q, Shen H.

title: Occurrence and Toxigenic Potential of Planktonic Cyanobacterial Blooms and Benthic Mats in the Tropical Rio Grande de Comitán and Montebello Lakes National Park, Southern Mexico.
abstract: The tropical aquatic ecosystems of the Río Grande de Comitán and Lagunas de Montebello National Park (southern Mexico) exhibit signs of advanced eutrophication, with environmental conditions that can promote the proliferation of potentially toxic cyanobacteria. This study assessed the distribution and ecotoxicological risk of planktonic blooms and benthic mats throughout the subbasin. Using a polyphasic approach combining cultured-based analysis, molecular detection and HPLC, we found a low-diversity cyanobacterial community dominated by Planktothrix agardhii, which reached densities up to 2.2 × 105 cells/mL during the warmest months. Benthic Microcoleus sp. and localized blooms of Anabaenopsis elenkinii were documented. Molecular analyses confirmed the presence of microcystin and anatoxin synthesizing genes, with high microcystin concentrations detected (67.5-3169 μg/L). Seasonal analyses revealed significant differences in temperature in both lakes (H = 20.8, p 25 (H = 10.7, p = 0.0169). PCA explained 65% and 64% of the variance in the first two axes for lakes and rivers, respectively, separating sites according to gradients in nutrients, conductivity, and other water-quality variables. In lakes, redundancy analysis (RDA) showed that the first two axes explained 72% of the constrained variation, with total nitrogen, specific conductance, total phosphorous, catchment disturbance index, pH, and dissolved oxygen contributing to the environmental gradients structuring cyanobacterial composition. Wastewater discharges from the upper basin (Comitán) act as a continuous source of nutrients and cyanobacterial inoculant, whereas tourism and fishing activities mechanically disperse these populations across the lakes. These results demonstrate the widespread occurrence of potentially toxic cyanobacteria across the subbasin and highlight the need for early-warning and monitoring programs, particularly in areas affected by wastewater inputs and intensive human activities.
authors: Salas AIS, Borrero APC, Carmona-Jiménez J, Márquez-Santamaria KP.

title: Helicase family proteins promote antiviral ADP-ribosylation of DNA purines
abstract: DarTG defense systems studied to date contain a DarT1 or DarT2 toxin that blocks phage replication by ADP-ribosylating DNA and a NADAR or macrodomain antitoxin, DarG, that reverses this modification at homeostasis. Here, we identify additional DarTG subfamilies, one of which comprises a DarT3 toxin, an ADP-ribosylhydrolase (ARH)-domain antitoxin, and a helicase family protein, DarH. The  Escherichia coli DarHTG3 system confers broad phage defense, requires DarH and, unlike previously characterized DarTG systems, modifies adenine. Characterization of additional DarH-containing DarTG systems reveals that a subset also target guanine. Our data support a model in which ADP-bound DarH functions as a processivity factor by recruiting DarT to its single-stranded DNA substrate and allowing for ADP-ribosylation of multiple target sites. These findings reveal how a helicase family protein regulates an antiviral effector by promoting DNA engagement rather than unwinding and thereby expanding the functional repertoire of helicase family proteins in bacterial immunity.
authors: Griesman T, Arifah AQ, Tomko EJ, Tan Y, Tsao N, Trotter JT, Khochare SS, Carlson NA, Mosammaparast N, Zhang D, Galburt EA, Patinios C, LeRoux M.

title: Prokaryotic Community Structures in the Bering and Chukchi Seas
abstract: Bacteria are essential to marine ecosystems as they remineralize organic matter, cycle carbon, nitrogen, and other key elements, and support higher trophic levels through food webs. The Bering and Chukchi Seas off the coast of Alaska are among the most productive regions in the world, with intense seasonal algal blooms, yet their bacterial communities remain poorly characterized, and the region is warming rapidly as heat transport from the Pacific Ocean increases. Here, we used 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing of 181 samples collected on 0.2 µm filters at three depths (surface, middle, and bottom) across 62 stations during the Arctic Shelf Growth, Advection, Respiration and Deposition Rate Experiments (ASGARD) cruise in June 2017, when sea surface temperatures were anomalously warm. Hierarchical clustering of amplicon sequence variant (ASV) relative abundances resolved 11 sample clusters in three divisions, all dominated by Alphaproteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria, and Bacteroidia. Community structure was related to water mass, salinity, and bloom stage, but not to depth. Clusters ranged from Gammaproteobacteria-dominant, Bacteroidia-poor assemblages in warm and cool Shelf Water (Division A) to Bacteroidia-rich assemblages spanning pre- to post-bloom conditions (Divisions B and C). In distance-based redundancy analysis, temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen, nitrate, and fluorescence together explained 14.8 % of the variation in community composition, with salinity the strongest contributor. These results indicate that water-mass origin, physicochemical conditions, and bloom stage jointly shape bacterial communities, and that changes in temperature, salinity, and the magnitude and timing of blooms could substantially alter bacterial communities of this Pacific gateway to the Arctic.
authors: Shibue R, Collins RE.

title: Making sense of chaos: replication and segregation defects in the yeast    mcm4  Chaos    3  mutant
abstract: Genome instability is a defining feature of cancer and is strongly influenced by alterations in the fidelity and timing of DNA replication. The conserved Mini-Chromosome Maintenance (MCM 2-7) helicase is a central component of the eukaryotic DNA replication machinery, playing critical roles in origin licensing and activation. Genetic screens for genome instability mutations in mice identified  mcm4  Chaos3 , a hypomorphic allele of  MCM4 associated with the formation of micronuclei and tumorigenesis, suggesting that the  mcm4  Chaos3 allele causes genome instability. To define the mechanistic basis of this instability, we examined the effects of the corresponding mutation in  Saccharomyces cerevisiae. We found that  mcm4  Chaos3 selectively compromises origin firing at a subset of early S-phase origins, with pronounced effects at many centromere-proximal origins. Chromosome V, containing the sensitive centromere-adjacent  ARS510, exhibited elevated loss rates that were rescued by replacement with the robust early-firing origin  ARS305 , restoring both origin activity and chromosome stability. Together these findings demonstrate that  mcm4  Chaos3 compromises genome stability by impairing a subset of early, centromere-proximal origins that are intrinsically sensitive to origin activation capacity. Our results establish that robust origin function near centromeres is critical for accurate chromosome segregation and reveal how subtle perturbations in helicase function can lead to chromosome instability.  Author Summary  The defining feature of cell division is the distribution of replicated chromosomes to the two daughter cells. Each chromosome contains a single centromere that is essential for their faithful inheritance. But before a cell divides, it must duplicate its DNA. DNA replication begins at sites called origins that differ in their activity and regulation. We studied a mutant version of Mcm4, a component of the molecular machinery that unwinds DNA during replication, to determine how compromised replication affects chromosome inheritance. This mutation was first discovered in mice, where it causes chromosome instability and cancer. Using Baker’s yeast, we found that the mutation reduces activity at a subset of origins, with origins near centromeres being preferentially affected. We also found an approximately three-fold increases in the rate that a test chromosome (chr V) is lost. These results suggest that the  mcm4  Chaos3 mutation can promote genome instability by compromising timely replication of centromeres. Replacing a sensitive origin near the centromere with a robust origin from elsewhere in the genome restored local replication activity and rescued chromosome loss to normal levels. This rescue depended on origin-associated binding sites and a centromere-associated protein, indicating that both origin features and chromosomal context contribute to replication activity. Our findings show that selective defects in replication initiation can compromise chromosome inheritance and that restoring activity at a single centromere-proximal origin can suppress this instability.
authors: Verhey JI, Moore AK, Armstrong JO, Alvino GM, Dunham MJ, Brewer BJ, Raghuraman MK.

title: Metabolomics-guided discovery of cytotoxic anthraquinones from the Red Sea-derived fungus Aspergillus amstelodami associated with Sargassum aquifolium.
abstract: Marine macroalgae-associated fungi constitute an underexplored reservoir of structurally diverse secondary metabolites with considerable pharmaceutical potential. To assess the chemical diversity and anticancer potential of fungi associated with Sargassum aquifolium, several fungal endophytes were isolated from specimens collected along the Egyptian Red Sea coast. Among the isolated fungi, Aspergillus amstelodami AUMC 16413 (Am-10) was prioritized for in-depth chemical and biological investigation based on its metabolite-rich profile in preliminary screening assays. UPLC-HRMS/MS-based metabolomics and GNPS networking enabled the annotation of 53 metabolites (anthraquinones, dihydro-isocoumarins, and prenylated benzaldehydes), revealing an anthraquinone-rich metabolome. Fractionation and spectroscopic analyses led to elucidation of seven anthraquinones, identified as danthron 1, catenarin 2, questin 3A, rubrocristin 3B, questinol 4, dermolutein 5A, and endocrocin 5B. The fungal extract exhibited cytotoxic activity toward MCF-7 cells (CC50 = 16.5 ± 1.9 µg mL-1; SI = 5.07), with a differential response observed between MCF-7 and normal cells together with alteration in cell-cycle progression and induction of apoptosis. RT-qPCR showed upregulation of Bax and p53, with downregulation of Bcl-2. Among the tested metabolites, compound 1, 3A/3B and 5A/5B mixtures displayed cytotoxic activity, with 5A/5B mixture showing the highest cytotoxic activity and selectivity index among the tested compounds (CC50 = 7.37 ± 0.38 µg mL-1, SI = 8.88). Molecular docking showed predicted interactions with apoptosis-related targets. Moreover, SwissADME and toxicity predictions indicated predicted ADME properties of the investigated compounds. These findings highlight Red Sea-derived A. amstelodami as a source of bioactive anthraquinones warranting further biological investigation.
authors: Badawy ET, Ragab AE, Farag MA, Finkelmeier D, Burger-Kentischer A, Abo El-Seoud KA, Zayed A.

title: Highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1-species-specific histopathology and viral antigen distribution in migratory and resident wild birds, South Westphalia, Germany 2025.
abstract: In late 2025, Germany faced a major outbreak of highly pathogenic influenza virus subtype H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, causing high mortality in migratory and resident wild birds and poultry. We examined 16 deceased birds, including Eurasian cranes, geese, a teal, and raptors found in western Germany between October and December 2025. Here, we provide a comparative analysis of light microscopic findings using histology and viral antigen distribution determined by immunohistochemistry, alongside the underlying viral phylogeny. Lesions and viral antigen distribution varied by species, with cranes showing infection in a broad organ spectrum, including the central nervous system (CNS), pancreas, spleen, liver, and kidneys, whereas other species exhibited a more targeted organ involvement. Phylogenetic analysis identified the EA-2024-DI.2.1 sublineage, with cranes forming a monophyletic cluster, which was consistent with the shared roosting/migratory behavior of cranes, although epidemiologic links were not formally demonstrated. In summary, our findings indicate species-specific lesion patterns and viral tissue tropism, which may influence transmission dynamics and environmental shedding.
authors: Beythien G, Gerhards H, Peters M, Kilwinski J, Pöpperl P, Nägler I, Ahrens AK, Pohlmann A, Beer M, Baumgärtner W, Wohlsein P.

title: Structural characterization of ZIKV M protein as a candidate viroporin: insights from molecular dynamics, evolutionary coupling and DFT.
abstract: Viroporins are small viral membrane proteins that facilitate ion transport and play critical role in viral pathogenicity. In this study, we investigate the Zika virus M protein viroporin to elucidate its proposed pore forming architecture using a combined computational framework of molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Sequence analysis shows 75 amino acid long Zika M protein is highly conserved across the continents and a significant variation is observed within different flaviviruses. The ab-initio model determined by AlphaFold is characterized by two hydrophobic C-terminal alpha helices and a N-terminal compact ectodomain. MD simulations in DPPC bilayers indicate that a pentameric pore-like assembly was the most structurally persistent model tested, featuring a single pore with a mixed distribution of polar and nonpolar residues. Leu12, Ile30, Trp35, Phe42, Ile49, Tyr63, Ile67, and Tyr74 provide structural rigidity and pore geometry, thereby stabilizing oligomeric packing. DFT analyses provide atomistic insights into electronic interactions and energetics that underpin conformational switching. Ca2+ displays well-defined multidentate coordination and strong structural organization, whereas Na+, K+, H+, and Cl- engage more weakly, governed mainly by long-range electrostatics and solvation effects. Virtual screening of >170 marketed ion channel modulators identified Lumacaftor and Gliquidone as the highest-scoring compounds for the Zika M oligomer pore-binding pocket, generating hypotheses for future experimental validation. Our study provides a structural and computational framework for the ZIKV M protein as a candidate viroporin, offering testable hypotheses regarding oligomeric stoichiometry, pore-lining architecture, and ion coordination that motivate future experimental validation.
authors: Zeba A, Mallasandra Krishnappa C, Rajendran S, Javeed N, Periyasamy G, Sekar K, Ganjiwale A.

title: Combinatorial Tuning of Multigene Biosynthetic Pathways based on RNA Interference.
abstract: Fine-tuning the expression level of multigene pathways remains a major challenge in engineering eukaryotic microbial cell factories. Modifications to individual pathway genes and CRISPR-based approaches often require repeated genome reconstruction, large regulatory components, or complex guide-array assembly. Here, we developed a lightweight, post-transcriptional RNAi-based strategy that enables fine-tuning gene expression without iterative genome editing. Size-selected small-RNA sequencing and functional testing were used to identify endogenous Pol III promoters spanning graded transcriptional strengths in Schizochytrium sp. Combining promoter strength with multiple short hairpin RNA (shRNA) target positions expanded the accessible repression range and enabled high-resolution gene-dosage tuning. The RNAi-based combined regulation strategy was applied to the three-gene carotenoid pathway of Schizochytrium sp. and the nine-gene docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) pathway of Yarrowia lipolytica, significantly enhancing the product production in both hosts. Integration of RNAi screening and dosage optimization further identified and tuned bypass pathways, increasing the ratio of DHA to docosapentaenoic acid (DPA) by 4.50-fold versus wild type. These gains were maintained during 5-L fermentation and serial passaging. This work establishes a compact and scalable regulatory framework for engineering complex biosynthetic pathways in eukaryotic microbial hosts.
authors: Zhang Z, Xu Y, Li Z, Du F, Ma W, Yang G, Sun X.

title: Polyethylene microplastics reduce aluminum uptake but obstruct nodulation in broad bean under acidic aluminum stress.
abstract: Soil acidification and microplastic pollution increasingly threaten agricultural systems worldwide, yet their combined effects on crops remain largely unexplored. In this study, we subjected broad bean (Vicia faba L.) to polyethylene (PE) microplastics, aluminum (Al) stress, or their combination, and integrated physiological assays, root metabolomics, and rhizosphere metagenomics to dissect their interactive effects. PE microplastics unexpectedly lowered root Al accumulation by 41.7% compared to Al alone, which was associated with reduced exchangeable Al in the rhizosphere. Despite this reduction, the combined PE and Al treatment still significantly suppressed root (by 50.1%) and shoot (by 42.0%) biomasses and severely compromised nodulation and nitrogen (N) acquisition, with effects similar to or even stronger than those of the mono Al treatment. Metabolomic profiling revealed that combined stress extensively downregulated ten flavonoids and fundamentally rewired flavonoid-rhizobia correlation networks, shifting potential symbiotic signaling away from compatible interactions. Metagenomic analysis further showed that while combined stress increased microbial co-occurrence network connectivity by 54.8%, it simultaneously suppressed the abundance of functional genes related to metal resistance and N cycling, pointing to a systemic metabolic burden rather than a targeted stress response. These results demonstrate that PE microplastics modulate Al bioavailability but do not mitigate phytotoxicity; instead, they exacerbate symbiotic disruption through flavonoid signaling interference and microbiome functional decline. These findings highlight the vulnerability of legume-rhizobia symbiosis to multi-stressor environments and call for a reassessment of soil management practices in regions where acidification and microplastic contamination co-occur.
authors: Yang J, Wang R, Hu N, Li B, Li Y, Xu J, Deng Y, Li Y, Li X.

title: Whole-genome characterization of a food-derived Kurthia gibsonii isolate reveals a tet(L)-str-repUS12 resistance-associated region.
abstract: BackgroundThe emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in environmental and food-associated bacteria has attracted increasing attention within the One Health framework. However, genomic information regarding antimicrobial resistance determinants and mobile genetic elements in Kurthia gibsonii remains limited. This study aimed to characterize a food-derived K. gibsonii isolate (KT09) by whole-genome sequencing, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and comparative genomic analysis, with emphasis on the genetic context of a tet(L)-associated resistance region.Methods and results(KT09), recovered from phyllo dough on gentamicin-supplemented medium was sequenced using Illumina platform. The reported draft genome consisted of 2,944,613 bp in 122 contigs > 500 bp (GC content, 36.65%; N50, 72,389 bp), with 99.34% completeness and 2.87% contamination by CheckM. TYGS analysis confirmed assignment to K. gibsonii. Disk diffusion showed variable inhibition-zone diameters, with particularly small zones for tetracycline and streptomycin. Genome analysis identified tet(L), str, and aadA1, while emrB was detected by genome annotation. The tet(L)-str-repUS12 resistance-associated region was located on contig00014, which showed a mean read depth of 290.97× and 100% breadth of coverage. Comparative BLASTn and synteny analyses showed high nucleotide similarity between this localized region and homologous chromosomal and plasmid-associated sequences from Kurthia, Enterococcus, and Staphylococcus. However, the complete contig was predominantly Kurthia-like and was not resolved as an independent circular component.ConclusionsThe KT09 genome expands the limited genomic information available for food-derived K. gibsonii and documents a tet(L)-str-repUS12 resistance-associated region with close sequence similarity to plasmid-associated loci reported in other Gram-positive bacteria. These findings are consistent with a shared mobile gene pool but do not establish plasmid localization, mobility, or the source or direction of horizontal gene transfer. Long-read sequencing and experimental plasmid characterization are required to resolve the genomic location and transferability of this region.
authors: Özer HK.

title: Aberrant expression of HERV-K envelope in lymphoma represents an opportunity for novel treatments.
abstract: PurposeHuman endogenous retrovirus K (HERV-K/HML-2) is a human-specific endogenous retrovirus family that maintains intact open reading frames and is aberrantly expressed in multiple cancers. We tested whether HERV-K, specifically its envelope (Env) protein, marks clinically relevant diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) states and serves as a tractable immunotherapeutic target.Experimental designLocus-level transposable element (TE) and HERV expression was quantified in two independent DLBCL RNA-seq cohorts using curated TE annotation and a uniform alignment/counting workflow. Env transcript and protein expression (including cell-surface localization) was validated in lymphoma cell lines using RT-qPCR, immunoblotting, and flow cytometry. Functional relevance was assessed by siRNA-mediated Env knockdown. Candidate extracellular linear epitopes were predicted in silico and synthesized for serological and phage display assays. Anti-Env camelid VHHs were isolated, humanized, and tested for binding, antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC), and antigen-dependent internalization.ResultsTE transcripts stratified DLBCL into clinically distinct subgroups, and high HERV-K expression associated with an interferon/viral-mimicry program. Env RNA was detected in patient tumors and cell lines, and the protein was detected on the surface of a subset of lymphoma cell lines, in which Env knockdown reduced proliferation. A humanized heavy-chain antibody (FF-01) bound surface Env, induced selective ADCC in Env-positive models (reporter and primary NK-cell assays), and underwent rapid antigen-dependent internalization.ConclusionsHERV-K activity identifies biologically meaningful DLBCL states and exposes a targetable surface antigen. FF-01 provides proof of principle for antibody-based strategies against HERV-K Env, including ADCC- and ADC-oriented approaches.
authors: Spriano F, Cascione L, Sgrignani J, Bendik N, Zadro A, Napoli S, Sartori G, Guerra C, Cannas E, Gong T, Arribas AJ, Pizzi M, Scott DW, Moretti M, Rossi D, Robbiani DF, Cavalli A, Bertoni F.

title: Global Metabolic Rewiring Induced by HAC1 Overexpression Facilitates Efficient Linalool Synthesis in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
abstract: The present study employs global transcriptional engineering (GTE) to optimize metabolic flux toward linalool synthesis by screening seven key transcription factors in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Overexpression of HAC1 in the strain SA44, the master regulator of the unfolded protein response (UPR), increased 2.9-fold in linalool titers compared to the control strain (SA49). Genome-wide transcriptomic analysis revealed that Hac1p-mediated activation induces a redirection of carbon flux into the mevalonate (MVA) pathway, the glyoxylate cycle, and gluconeogenesis, alongside the substantial repression of master sterol pathway activator (UPC2) and the hexose transporters. Multi-layer network analysis revealed GCN4- centered upregulation of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase genes (aaRS) in the HAC1- overexpressing background, associated with putative HAC1-linked transcriptional repression of ERG9. Functional validation of the Hac1p regulatory networks via co-expression of HAC1 with the succinate-fumarate transporter (SFC1) yielded a synergistic improvement in linalool titer. Furthermore, the co-expression of MAF1, a negative regulator of tRNA biogenesis, and HAC1 has been shown to reduce linalool production. Notably, the high-linalool-titer strain (SA44) exhibited a distinct metabolic profile, with higher glycerol accumulation (~5.0 g/L). SA44 demonstrated superior sterol accumulation compared to SA49, with 1.6-fold higher squalene and 1.2-fold higher ergosterol production. Additionally, qRT-PCR was used to independently confirm the differential expression of seven regulatory genes, yielding a high Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.994. This study reports the first HAC1-mediated enhancement of linalool biosynthesis, establishing a robust strategy for microbial monoterpene production.

title: Enterobacteriaceae and Bacteriophages: Implications Against Antimicrobial Resistance.
abstract: Enterobacteriaceae represent a clinically challenging bacterial family owing to the global emergence of multidrug resistance. Bacteriophages, the natural predators of these bacteria, have emerged as powerful tools for detecting, targeting, and inhibiting these pathogens. This review provides a comprehensive overview of bacteriophages targeting Enterobacteriaceae hosts, focusing on their diversity, virion architecture, and the molecular determinants of host specificity. The dynamic co-evolution between bacterial defence strategies and phage counter-defences is discussed to illustrate the complexity of the phage-Enterobacteriaceae host interactions. Translational applications of Enterobacteriaceae phages, including phage therapy, engineered phages, phage-derived lysins as antimicrobials, and phage-based diagnostics for rapid and specific pathogen detection is also explored alongside their limitations including limited large-scale clinical trials, regulatory and manufacturing hurdles, and the need for robust host-range prediction and standardization. Overall, this review elaborates implications of bacteriophage-Enterobacteriaceae interactions to combat antimicrobial resistance and support the development of next-generation antibacterial therapies and diagnostics.
authors: Ramadoss R, Moovarkumudalvan B, Jothimani P, Lakshmanan D.

title: Enzyme-Antibiotic Liquid Crystalline Nanoparticles for Enhanced Antibiofilm Activity, Bacterial Clearance, and Accelerated Healing of Infected Wounds.
abstract: Biofilm-associated wound infections remain difficult to treat because bacteria are protected within extracellular polymeric matrices that restrict antibiotic penetration, promote antimicrobial tolerance, and delay tissue repair. Here, we developed liquid crystalline nanoparticles (LCNPs) for topical coformulation of gentamicin (GEN) and recombinant human DNase I (rhDNase), combining aminoglycoside therapy with an eDNA-targeting enzyme. GEN + rhDNase-LCNPs were successfully formulated as nanoscale particles with low polydispersity, high encapsulation efficiency, and formulation-dependent in vitro release behavior. LCNP formulation preserved GEN antibacterial activity against planktonic Escherichia coli Xen14 and reduced the MBIC against established biofilms by approximately 4-fold. In a minimum biofilm eradication concentration (MBEC) model, GEN + rhDNase-LCNPs achieved the greatest reduction in biofilm-associated viable bacteria, producing an approximately 6-log reduction compared with untreated biofilm controls and supporting the benefit of combining antibiotic delivery with rhDNase. Notably, GEN + rhDNase-LCNPs markedly suppressed bacterial burden and reduced recoverable bacteria at day 9 to near the limit of detection in a bioluminescent E. coli Xen14 biofilm-associated excisional wound infection mouse model. This antibacterial effect translated into accelerated macroscopic wound closure and improved histological repair, including an approximately 80% reduction in wound gape compared with infected controls. Masson's trichrome staining further confirmed enhanced tissue remodeling, with the collagen-positive wound area increasing to approximately 88% following GEN + rhDNase-LCNP treatment, compared with approximately 21% in infected controls. In conclusion, LCNP-mediated codelivery of GEN and rhDNase improved bacterial clearance, re-epithelialization, and collagen deposition, supporting this platform as a promising topical antibiofilm strategy for infected wounds.
authors: Ahsan A, Nguyen HT, Wignall A, Kopecki Z, Barnes TJ, Thomas N, Ogunniyi AD, Prestidge CA.

title: Breakpoint Mapping and Disrupted Gene Identification in Azoospermic Patients With Chromosomal Balanced Translocation by Nanopore Sequencing.
abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the utility of nanopore long-read sequencing for precise breakpoint mapping in azoospermia patients with chromosomal balanced translocations, and to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying translocation-induced spermatogenic failure.MethodsPeripheral blood specimens were collected from two azoospermic patients with balanced chromosomal translocations. G-banding karyotype analysis and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) results served as the reference standard, and whole-genome long-read sequencing of peripheral blood samples was performed on the PromethION platform. Breakpoint positions were visualized using the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV), and gene annotations were conducted using the UCSC Genome Browser.ResultsSequencing was successfully completed for both samples, yielding mean read lengths of 9713.3 bp and 8129.8 bp, respectively. Nanopore sequencing afforded superior molecular resolution of chromosomal aberrations relative to traditional cytogenetic approaches. A total of eight breakpoints were identified through IGV visualization, with four precisely mapped at single-nucleotide resolution. Annotation revealed that five breakpoints resided within intergenic regions without compromising gene integrity, whereas three breakpoints (ChrX:147,998,514-147,998,515, Chr3:65,894,036-65,899,651, and Chr16:53,815,988-53,815,992) were situated within intronic segments of the AFF2, MAGI1, and FTO genes, respectively, resulting in gene disruption.ConclusionThis study employed nanopore long-read sequencing to precisely map chromosomal breakpoints in two azoospermic patients, including cryptic breakpoints undetectable by conventional karyotyping. Disruption of AFF2, MAGI1, and FTO at three breakpoints provides novel candidate gene evidence for translocation-associated spermatogenic failure, confirming nanopore sequencing as a robust tool for structural variant characterization and the discovery of spermatogenesis-related genes.
authors: Zhang J, Chen XL, Chen JY, Ge YS.

title: Dual role of RBM3 in PEDV infection: stabilization of viral RNA and upregulation of the entry factor HSPA5
abstract: RBM3, a member of the cold shock protein family, functions as an RNA chaperone that stabilizes target transcripts by binding to their untranslated regions (UTRs). Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) is an enteric coronavirus that poses a serious threat to the swine industry, and its replication heavily depends on its genomic and subgenomic RNAs, making these RNAs potential targets for host RNA binding proteins. In this study, we show that RBM3 promotes PEDV replication through a dual mechanism. On one hand, RBM3 exhibits a binding preference for the viral 3’UTR, which prolongs the half-life of viral RNA and thereby promotes PEDV proliferation. RBM3 also interacts with the PEDV nucleocapsid (N) protein and replication-associated double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) signals, suggesting that RBM3 may be associated with viral replication complexes, though its contribution to their functional integrity remains to be determined. On the other hand, RBM3 increases HSPA5 promoter activity and HSPA5 mRNA levels, linking RBM3 to HSPA5, a host factor known to facilitate PEDV attachment and internalization. These two mechanisms together provide a mechanistic basis for efficient PEDV infection. Our findings identify RBM3 as a positive host regulator of PEDV and establish, for the first time, a functional link between RBM3 and HSPA5, offering new insights into coronavirus host interactions and suggesting RBM3 as a potential target for antiviral intervention.
authors: Li S, Zeng Y, Li J, Liu Y, Liu H, Yang X, Qin W, Li T, Chen Z, Liu J, Tong G, Cao X, Kong N, Shan T.

title: DarHTG is a tripartite phage defence system for purine DNA base ADP-ribosylation
abstract: Bacteria evolved a variety of phage defence strategies to combat the constant onslaught of viral threats. DarTG toxin-antitoxin systems provide phage defence by ADP-ribosylation of bases in single-stranded DNA which interferes with viral replication and aborts phage infection. Here, we describe DarHTG, a system widespread among bacteria, that combines DarTG with a non- processive superfamily I helicase functioning as co-toxin for DarT and thereby enabling the ADP- ribosylation of double-stranded DNA. We identified two such DarHTG subclasses which catalyse the ADP-ribosylation of adenosine and guanosine bases, respectively, and reverse these modifications with structurally unique ARH superfamily antitoxins. Thus, DarHTG antitoxins expand the known macromolecular target spectrum of the ARH enzyme class to nucleic acids. These DarHTG systems confer resistance to a broad range of bacteriophages and can be triggered by the highly charged tails of viral single-stranded DNA-binding proteins, which occlude the active site of the ARH antitoxin.
authors: Ledermann R, Gotzler A, Steigenberger B, Wang Y, Zimmermann J, Geiger S, Fu J, Hoffmann J, Suyari O, Zhang Y, Lu Y, Mikoč A, Tang C, Ahel I, Schuller M.

title: Comparative cryo-EM structures of CGMMV and ToMMV reveal divergent coat protein packing and electrostatics indicating  Tobamovirus  host specificity
abstract: Tobamoviruses are a group of economically important plant viruses exhibiting extreme stability and persistence. Despite high morphological similarity, they show extensive host-family specificity, cause a range of symptoms, and cause significant global yield loss in fruit and vegetable plants. Composed of a rod-shaped helical assembly of identical coat proteins encasing a single-stranded RNA, Tobamoviruses have long served as fundamental models for understanding helical assemblies. Here we report the cryo-EM structures of two viruses from this genus, CGMMV and ToMMV, at 2.86 Å and 2.71 Å resolution, respectively. The structures reveal divergent packing strategies within the virion assembly. While ToMMV is genetically similar to the canonical Tobamovirus TMV and displays a structure closely resembling TMV, CGMMV employs a more hydrophobic packing strategy, particularly in the solvent-exposed inner loop region of the coat protein. Comparative biophysical and molecular dynamics analyses from the reconstructed structures reveal more stable and compact protein packing for CGMMV at both the subunit and assembly levels. Furthermore, this study reports a newly identified electrostatic patch existing at the lower alpha-helix region of the coat protein that serves as an additional RNA-stabilizing region, with host family-specific amino acid substitutions among Tobamoviruses. Our study elucidates the structural mechanics and evolutionary strategies driving virion stability and host diversity while maintaining a conserved helical assembly. These findings reveal how subtle electrostatic tuning and divergent packing strategies drive viral stability and host adaptation within a strictly conserved quaternary scaffold.

title: Phylogeny-Guided Global-Local Shrinkage for Microbiome Feature Selection
abstract: Microbiome feature selection is challenging because sequencing counts are sparseand compositional, while evolutionarily related taxa may exhibit similar associations with an exposure. We propose phylogeny-guided global--local shrinkage (PGL), a Bayesian regression method for identifying exposure-associated differences in the relative abundances of individual amplicon sequence variants (ASVs). A multinomial logit-normal working model analyzes relative abundance among ASVs detected in each sample. A zero-sum constraint gives the regression coefficients a log-ratio interpretation relative to the mean across retained ASVs. Global--local shrinkage accommodates weak and large associations, while an estimated weight controls information sharing along a supplied phylogenetic tree. Simulation ablation studies showed that phylogenetic borrowing improved detection power and estimation of nonzero coefficients when associations aligned with the tree, with little change under a tree-independent generator. Estimated borrowing decreased as the supplied tree was corrupted. Comparisons with benchmark methods revealed different trade-offs between detection power and false discovery rates across simulation settings. In an HIV oral microbiome application, ablation analysis showed that phylogenetic borrowing preserved the overall pattern of estimated associations while changing posterior uncertainty and selecting three additional ASVs. PGL provides ASV-level inference with adaptive information sharing across evolutionarily related features.
authors: Zhu Z, Zhang S, Tang X, Zhang L.

title: Severe Intracranial Hemorrhage and Intracranial Infection Caused by Ureaplasma parvum Infection in an Extremely Preterm Infant: A Case Report and Literature Review
abstract: Abstract  Background:Ureaplasma parvum (Up) is an under-recognized pathogen in neonatal central nervous system infections. We retrospectively analyzed the clinical data of one extremely preterm infant presenting with severe intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) and intracranial infection attributed to Up infection, and systematically reviewed the relevant literature. The analysis covered perinatal history, neurological manifestations, serial cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and imaging changes, metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) results, and treatment course. Case presentation:A male infant was born at 26⁺¹ weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 920 g. Intracranial hemorrhage, initially grade I on day 1 of life, progressed to grade IV by day 4. CSF examination showed typical features of intracranial infection: the nucleated cell count was markedly elevated, glucose was profoundly decreased (0.07 mmol/L), and protein reached 7,443 mg/L. Conventional bacterial cultures were repeatedly negative; however, mNGS of CSF identified Up (115 sequence reads; relative abundance 87.19%). Following targeted treatment with azithromycin, CSF inflammatory markers improved. Nevertheless, given the severity of the intracranial lesions, the family ultimately chose to withdraw care. Conclusion: This case suggests that Up infection may act as a synergistic factor in the development or progression of severe ICH in extremely preterm infants. Potential mechanisms include direct injury to the cerebral vascular endothelium and fragile germinal matrix vessels, as well as blood-brain barrier disruption secondary to inflammatory cytokine release. In extremely preterm infants with unusually rapid progression of ICH and poor response to conventional treatment, Up infection should be considered early, and mNGS testing should be arranged without delay. As this is a single case report, the causal relationship warrants confirmation in future studies.
authors: Pu J, Yan Q, Zhang J.

title: Integrative genomic and sequence-to-function analyses prioritize TNRC6B- linked regulatory variants in erysipelas susceptibility
abstract: Abstract  Erysipelas is an acute skin and soft-tissue infection predominantly caused by streptococci, yet the host genetic architecture and non-coding regulatory mechanisms underlying susceptibility remain poorly characterized. We integrated FinnGen R11 erysipelas GWAS data (24,825 cases and 399,149 controls) with GTEx v8 and multiple functional genomic resources. Cross-tissue and tissue-specific TWAS, MAGMA, and Polygenic Priority Score (PoPS) analyses were combined with regional association testing, functional annotation, eQTL/sQTL and colocalization analyses, ENCODE chromatin annotations, rE2G/ABC enhancer-to-gene mapping, and AlphaGenome, Borzoi, and Enformer sequence-to-function models. TNRC6B was the only gene remaining significant after FDR correction in UTMOST (P = 1.21 × 10⁻⁵, FDR = 0.045) and was further supported by FUSION, MAGMA (Z = 3.4697, P = 2.61 × 10⁻⁴), and PoPS (score = 0.7712; genome-wide rank 324/18,383; local rank 2/31). No regional variant reached genome-wide significance. Integrated regulatory analyses prioritized rs4821940 and rs6001827 as Tier A candidates, whereas the 3′UTR variant rs139915 was classified as Tier B. Sequence-to-function models provided context-dependent support, although effect directions varied across models and tissues. Evidence-module integration, leave-one-module-out analyses, and 5,000 random weight perturbations consistently ranked rs4821940, rs6001827, and rs139915 among the top three candidates. These findings prioritize TNRC6B and linked regulatory variants for further investigation but do not establish causal effects.
authors: Peng J, Chen G, Gao X, Zhao P, Yan A, Wang K, Yu Q, Tian W, Cai K.

title: Soil pH, not land-use type, predicts microbial motility and denitrification genes after rainforest conversion in Sumatra and Borneo
abstract: Abstract    Conversion of lowland rainforest to rubber and oil palm alters soil microbial communities, but whether functional gene responses are consistent across regions, and what drives them, is unclear. Public soil shotgun metagenomes from Jambi, Sumatra (32 plots: rainforest, jungle rubber, rubber, oil palm) and Sabah, Borneo (24 plots: unlogged forest, logged forest, oil palm) were reanalysed. The Sumatran workflow reproduced published fold changes (r = 0.998). In Sumatra, land use explained 41% of the variation in functional composition (permutation test, p = 0.0001); flagellar assembly genes declined by 27–35%, chemotaxis genes by 17–20% and secretion-system genes by 10–12% in converted systems, while denitrification genes increased in oil palm (  nirS   + 220%,  nosZ   + 164%). In Sabah, oil palm differed little from unlogged forest, and oil palm effects pooled across sites were not significant and highly heterogeneous (I² = 83–99%). In contrast, relationships with soil pH were consistent in both regions: denitrification (combined ρ = 0.69) and nitrogen-fixation genes (ρ = 0.50) increased with pH, whereas type VI secretion (ρ = −0.64), flagellar motility (ρ = −0.53) and chemotaxis genes (ρ = −0.41) decreased (all p ≤ 0.002). Plantations raised soil pH consistently in Sumatra but not in Sabah. Decimal errors in 32 published soil values and a misassigned  mcrA  gene were also corrected. Soil chemistry, particularly pH altered by liming, predicts microbial functional responses to rainforest conversion better than land-use type alone. Measuring soil pH alongside metagenomes should improve predictions of microbial denitrification potential in plantation landscapes, including in the Philippines.

title: RNA pol II speed controls the level of read-through mediated transcriptional interference
abstract: Abstract    Transcriptional interference, which can be mediated by read-through transcription, is recognized as a mechanism negatively controlling gene expression levels. Recent studies highlighted the importance of transcriptional interference mediated by read-through transcription in response to different kinds of stresses and in response to viral infections. In this study we investigated the extent of transcriptional interference mediated by read-through transcription in different human cell lines. Our results, based on the analysis of transcriptomics and genomics data, reveal that transcriptional interference is widespread in the human genome in unperturbed conditions. Furthermore, through the use of RNA pol II mutants with different velocity, we show that transcriptional interference can be controlled by RNA pol II speed. Finally, we observe that read-through transcription invading downstream genes significantly associates with decreased level of translation of downstream genes in tandem gene pairs, therefore probably affecting protein levels. Together these data indicate that transcriptional interference is a mechanism controlling gene expression in unperturbed conditions. In addition, our results uncover the importance of transcription speed in controlling the expression level of downstream genes in tandem gene pairs.  *Virginie Jouffret and Maurane Eisele contributed equally to this work.  **Didier Trouche and Lisa Muniz contributed equally to this work.

title: A genomic toolkit for surveillance and elimination of the principal malaria vectors in Southeast Asia.
abstract: While substantial progress has been made toward malaria elimination in Southeast Asia, major challenges remain. The principal mosquito vectors,  Anopheles dirus and  Anopheles minimus , inhabit diverse ecological niches and exhibit a wide range of behavioural and physiological insecticide resistance phenotypes, complicating vector control efforts. In Africa, genomic surveillance has transformed our understanding of vector evolution and resistance, supported by open-access tools and data. Comparable resources for Southeast Asian vectors remain limited. Here, we release Adir1.0, a curated, analysis-ready catalog of 540  An. dirus whole-genome sequences, accessible for interactive cloud-based analysis via the malariagen-data-python application programming interface (API). Alongside, we provide an updated Amin1.0 API to enhance functionality and usability, enabling integrated analyses across historical and new datasets. We demonstrate these resources by performing the first exploratory population genomic analysis of  An. dirus from Bangladesh, Thailand, and Cambodia, revealing population structure, candidate regions of physiological resistance, and genomic structural variation. Together, these resources provide a foundation for genomic surveillance studies to inform vector control and malaria elimination strategies in Southeast Asia.

title: Integrative lipidomic and genomic analysis identifies key lipids for wooden breast in chickens.
abstract: BackgroundWooden breast (WB) is a prevalent myopathy in broilers that substantially reduces meat quality and causes considerable economic losses. However, the genetic architecture and lipidomic alterations associated with WB remain poorly understood. This study aimed to integrate untargeted lipidomics and genomic analyses to characterize lipid alterations and their associated genetic factors in WB.ResultsTo characterize WB-related phenotypes, pectoralis major muscles from 312 broilers were evaluated for WB severity, compression force (CF), endomysium thickness, and total lipid abundance. By integrating differential abundance analysis, trend analysis, and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), we identified a core set of 25 lipid species. Further refinement using Mendelian randomization (MR) and mediation analyses prioritized nine lipids as candidate molecular traits associated with genetic variation and WB, seven of which showed consistent associations in an independent cohort (n = 119). Metabolome genome-wide association study (mGWAS) of these lipids identified a consensus genetic locus on chromosome 6 (19.55-20.15 Mb) shared by three candidate lipids. Integration of transcriptomic profiles from genes within this locus prioritized five candidate genes, with MAPK8 and NPY4R showing consistent expression patterns in the independent cohort. Based on its potential biological relevance, MAPK8 was selected for functional characterization in chicken primary myoblasts. MAPK8 overexpression and knockdown produced opposite effects on lipid accumulation, oxidative stress, and fibrosis-related gene expression, suggesting that MAPK8 may participate in cellular processes involved in lipid accumulation, oxidative stress, and fibrotic remodeling associated with WB.ConclusionsThis study provides an integrated overview of lipid metabolic alterations and their genetic architecture in WB-affected chickens. Collectively, these findings identify candidate lipid biomarkers and genetic loci and implicate MAPK8 as a candidate gene associated with lipid deposition and fibrotic remodeling in WB.
journal: Journal of animal science and biotechnology
authors: Chen Y, Bai L, Ma X, Wang M, Tang Y, Li Z, Pei Y, Zhang H, Zhao G, Wen J, Liu R.

title: In silico characterisation of lysis and host-recognition modules in Staphylococcus aureus bacteriophage genomes.
abstract: BackgroundMethicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a leading human pathogen, and declining antibiotic efficacy has renewed interest in lytic bacteriophages, whose efficacy phenotypic assays predict poorly.ObjectivesTo characterise the lysis and host-recognition modules of lytic S. aureus bacteriophages, and to determine how far the detectability of each module depends on the annotation source rather than on the genomes.MethodsTwenty-two S. aureus phage genomes from NCBI GenBank were processed through an identical detection funnel under three annotation sources: the deposited record, Pharokka and Phold. Modules were validated by InterPro, disrupted endolysins resolved by tBLASTn, and each domain aligned separately to measure identity.FindingsThe LysK-type endolysin (CHAP-Amidase-SH3b) was conserved and detected identically under all three sources. Tail fibre/receptor-binding protein (RBP) detection was strongly source-dependent: 14 of 22 genomes from the deposited annotation, 20 of 22 after re-annotation, and 22 of 22 combined. Resolved by domain, conservation was scale-dependent: the amidase domain was invariant within species while SH3b varied by 5.7%.Main conclusionsLysis-module conservation is independent of the annotation source; the apparent variability of host recognition is largely an artefact of incomplete deposited annotation. Module-level surveys require re-annotation before comparative claims.
authors: Hasugian IA, Alifiyah NI.

title: Nutrigenomics in Dairy Cattle: Causes and Implications.
abstract: Nutrigenomics is a rapidly developing interdisciplinary field that investigates the interactions between nutrients and the genome, with particular emphasis on how dietary components regulate gene expression and metabolic pathways. In dairy cattle, nutrigenomics has gained increasing attention due to its potential to improve milk production, metabolic efficiency, health, reproduction, and overall animal performance. Nutrients and bioactive dietary compounds can influence gene activity directly through transcriptional regulation or indirectly through epigenetic mechanisms such as DNA methylation, histone modification, and noncoding RNA-mediated gene regulation. These nutrigenomic interactions affect important biological processes including lipid metabolism, adipogenesis, immune response, mammary gland development, and milk synthesis. Advances in omics technologies including transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and next-generation sequencing have enhanced understanding of the molecular responses of dairy cows to nutritional interventions. Dietary fatty acids, vitamins, methyl donors, and short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate have been shown to regulate key transcription factors including peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), sterol regulatory element binding proteins (SREBPs), and liver X receptors (LXRs), thereby modulating metabolic and physiological functions. Nutritional interventions, feed restriction, and supplementation produce tissue-specific molecular responses in the liver, adipose tissue, mammary gland, and immune system, demonstrating interaction between diet, physiological state, and metabolic regulation. Despite these advances, challenges with genetic and physiological variability, tissue-specific responses, integration of multi-omics data, and translation of molecular findings into practical feeding strategies remain unresolved. Future integration of nutrigenomics with microbiome research, multi-omics, artificial intelligence, and precision livestock technologies may facilitate nutritional strategies to improve dairy cattle health, productivity, feed efficiency, and product quality.
authors: Tamasgen N, Asefa B.

title: CYP123, a sterol C4-methyl oxidase, acts with CYP51 to initiate mycobacterial lanosterol catabolism
abstract: Mycobacteria exploit host cholesterol, both as a carbon source and as a source of catabolites proposed to modulate host immunity, but their capacity to catabolise other host sterols has not been established. Lanosterol, the first sterol intermediate of host cholesterol biosynthesis, accumulates in the activated macrophages these bacteria infect. Here we define the initiating steps of mycobacterial lanosterol catabolism, combining genomic enzymology, transcriptional profiling, mutagenesis, biochemistry, NMR and crystallography. We identify the cytochrome P450 CYP123 as a sterol C4-methyl oxidase. It is encoded with the lanosterol 14α-demethylase CYP51 in a co-oriented region conserved across most  Mycobacteriaceae . The region carries no binding site for the cholesterol-responsive regulators KstR or KstR2, and in  M. abscessus lanosterol induces both genes while cholesterol does not. CYP123 oxidises the C4α-methyl group of C14-demethylated sterols in three steps to the carboxylic acid, yet acts on neither lanosterol nor cholesterol, because Met82 excludes the C14-methylated precursor. An M82A variant binds and oxidises lanosterol. In a single reaction containing both recombinant  M. smegmatis enzymes, CYP51 converts lanosterol to FF-MAS, which CYP123 then oxidises to the C4-carboxylic acid, so the two act in sequence.  M. smegmatis ,  M. phlei and  M. abscessus grow on lanosterol as a sole carbon source. Growth slows in  M. smegmatis cyp123 and  cyp51 mutants. Mycobacterial sterol catabolism therefore extends beyond cholesterol, and blocking the cholesterol route alone may not deprive these organisms of host sterols. Induction where lanosterol confers no growth advantage raises the possibility that the pathway also serves functions beyond carbon acquisition.  Significance  Mycobacteria feed on host cholesterol, a dependence long proposed as a drug target but never exploited therapeutically. This work shows that they also catabolise lanosterol, an early cholesterol precursor that accumulates in activated macrophages. Two cytochrome P450s encoded in a conserved, lanosterol-induced locus act in sequence: CYP51 removes the C14-methyl group, and CYP123 then oxidises the C4α-methyl group to a carboxylic acid. This explains why mycobacteria retain CYP51 despite being unable to make sterols, and identifies CYP123 as the first bacterial P450 sterol C4-methyl oxidase and a third enzymatic solution to C4-demethylation. The locus is conserved across more than 90% of  Mycobacteriaceae , spanning pathogens of humans, livestock and the environment, and contributes to fitness during infection, making both enzymes attractive, azole-binding drug targets. Because cholesterol and lanosterol run through separate routes, depriving mycobacteria of host sterols would require blocking both.
authors: Yuan D, Hatfield LR, Ryan H, Williams H, Dong M, Parker JE, Jin Y, Zallot R.

title: One-step glycan photoaffinity probe synthesis enables identification of human milk oligosaccharide-interacting microbiota
abstract: Glycans are found on the surfaces of all living cells and engage in cell signaling through the binding of various molecular targets. However, chemical probes to detect and identify carbohydrate interactions remain difficult to produce, due in large part to the challenges of late-stage, site-specific functionalization of oligosaccharides. Here, we report the synthesis and application of a minimal bifunctional diazirine/alkyne linker utilizing an  N,O -dialkylhydroxylamine (NODHA) moiety that can readily be installed on the anomeric position of unprotected sugars. Our linker functionalizes glycans with complete β-stereoselectivity, appends less mass than a single hexose unit, and maintains the closed-ring structure of the reducing end sugar. With this molecule, we generate glycan photoaffinity probes in a single step using unprotected human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs). We then validate binding selectivity of our compounds using lectins with known affinity towards our sugars. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of these glycan photoaffinity probes by performing photocrosslinking on a complex microbiota community and use cell sorting paired with metagenomic sequencing to identify potential new HMO-interacting microbes. Together, our work provides a one-step route to synthesize photoaffinity probes from unprotected, reducing glycans for interrogating carbohydrate interactions at the host-microbiota interface.
authors: Chun Y, Leonard JT, Griffin ME.

title: Potential biomarker candidates for improving diagnosis and disease treatment in adenomyosis.
abstract: Adenomyosis remains challenging to diagnose due to its unclear pathogenesis and clinical overlap with conditions such as endometriosis and uterine fibroids. While non-invasive imaging techniques like transvaginal ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging have improved adenomyosis detection, histopathological examination remains the gold standard. As this typically requires hysterectomy, it limits fertility-preserving diagnostic options. Therefore, the search for potential biomarkers is essential to improve the diagnosis of adenomyosis. This review summarises current evidence on genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic and microbiome biomarkers identified using conventional molecular techniques and high-throughput multi-omics approaches in eutopic endometrium, blood, urine, faeces, cervicovaginal lavage and vaginal swab samples with potential clinical applicability, enhancing diagnostic accuracy, and enabling early detection and monitoring. In addition, describing adenomyosis biomarkers may enhance the understanding of adenomyosis pathogenesis and help identify new therapeutic approaches. Although numerous candidate biomarkers have shown promising results (e.g. STEAP1, TOMM20, GLT8D2, and NME5, hsa_circ_008959/hsa-miR-124-3p/SLC15A4 + VAS score, miR-92a-3p or Weissella confusa, and Lactobacillus zeae), the current evidence remains insufficient for their implementation in routine clinical practice owing to the lack of external validation, standardised methodologies, and large multicentre studies.
authors: Merino-Pérez A, Albert AB, Del Mar Mascarell-López M, Pellicer A, Corachán A, Ferrero H.

title: Research progress in the production, purification, and applications of long single-stranded DNA.
abstract: Long single-stranded DNA (long ssDNA) plays important roles in cutting-edge fields such as DNA origami, gene therapy, and synthetic biology. However, the production, preparation, and purification of long ssDNA remain technically challenging. This review systematically summarizes current strategies for long ssDNA production and preparation, including phage-E. coli-based biological production, template-dependent enzymatic amplification, and viral-vector-based generation of ssDNA genomes. CRISPR-Cas-assisted approaches are discussed separately as complementary tools for post-synthetic processing, sequence-selective cleavage, enrichment, and quality control, whereas other enzymatic approaches are considered for post-synthetic strand conversion. We compare the characteristics and limitations of these production and preparation strategies, discuss purification techniques for long ssDNA, and summarize its applications in DNA origami nanotechnology and gene therapy. This review comprehensively synthesizes the bottlenecks in long ssDNA production, preparation, and purification, and outlines further development trends. We highlight template-independent de novo enzymatic DNA synthesis, automated DNA manufacturing, synthetic biology-based production systems, and AI-assisted sequence optimization. These developments are expected to accelerate the transition of long ssDNA technologies from laboratory research toward scalable manufacturing and practical applications.
authors: Wang X, Wu Y, Zhang X, Du Y, Liu N, Wang Z, Zhang H, Gao X, Zheng A.

title: Early-life enteric bacterial infection alters hippocampal cell fate and leads to cognitive deficits.
abstract: Early-life enteric infections are increasingly recognized as a major driver of adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes. However, the cell-type-specific mechanisms linking intestinal inflammation to persistent cognitive deficits in the developing brain remain poorly defined. Here, we demonstrate that transient Citrobacter rodentium infection in mice, which models human pathogenic Escherichia coli infection, disrupts hippocampal development and impairs cognitive function. These phenotypes were observed only during a critical postnatal window, coinciding with transient intestinal permeability. Hippocampal transcriptomics revealed persistent dysregulation of neurogenic pathways, and cellular analyses confirmed alterations in neurons, microglia, and endothelial cells. Critically, we identified accumulation of the microbial metabolite D-lactate in the hippocampus. Oral D-lactate supplementation in a gut barrier disruption model, exacerbated both behavioral deficits and hippocampal neuronal loss. Finally, in the presence of inflammatory stimuli, exposing primary neurons to D-lactate reduced the ratio of NeuN expressing neurons. Together, these findings identify age-dependent intestinal barrier dysfunction as a potential route linking early-life enteric infection with increased D-lactate exposure, hippocampal neuronal alterations, and persistent behavioural impairment.
authors: Tabusi MM, Serapio-Palacios A, Creus-Cuadros A, Octoman A, Lewis V, Metcalfe-Roach A, Snyder JS, Finlay BB.

title: Cyclotides from Clitoria ternatea: Genomic Organization, Biosynthesis, and Roles in Plant Defense.
abstract: Clitoria ternatea, commonly known as butterfly pea, is a perennial legume widely recognized for its ornamental and medicinal value. Beyond its characteristic anthocyanin-rich blue flowers, the plant produces cyclotides, a type of ultra-stable, cyclic cystine-knot peptide, with exceptional biological functions. Unlike other cyclotide-bearing families that carry independent cyclotide genes, C. ternatea integrates cyclotide domains into albumin-1 genes, replacing β-chain domains through divergent or convergent evolution. Genomic and transcriptomic studies reveal a large repertoire of albumin-1 loci and associated biosynthetic enzymes, including asparaginyl endopeptidases (butelase-1), protein disulphide isomerases, and peptidyl-prolyl isomerases, which orchestrate the cyclization, folding, and stabilization of cyclotides. Transcriptome analyses further demonstrate tissue-specific expression patterns, with distinct cyclotides such as cliotides T2 and T3 enriched in flowers and pods, and cliotides T8-T10 specialized in seeds, reflecting adaptive responses to localized biotic stress. Functionally, C. ternatea cyclotides exhibit broad-spectrum defense properties, including insecticidal, bactericidal, nematicidal, and antifungal activities, primarily through membrane permeabilization and disruption of lipid bilayers. Their preferential affinity for phosphatidylethanolamine-rich membranes highlights their selective toxicity toward insect and microbial targets. Recent advances in synthetic biology exploit cyclotides' structural stability as molecular scaffolds for therapeutic peptide design, with applications in immunomodulatory, antimicrobial, and anticancer drug development. This review consolidates genomic, transcriptomic, and functional insights into cyclotide biosynthesis and activity in C. ternatea, highlighting its evolutionary distinctiveness and biotechnological potential. Future research integrating multi-omics and spatial single-cell analyses can further unravel regulatory networks, defense dynamics, and translational applications of these unique plant peptides.
authors: Kumar R, Yeo LM, Singaram N, Mah SH, Bunawan H, Lee KW, Yap WHH.

title: Molecular characterization and phylogenetic analysis of the meq gene of Marek's Disease Virus strains from Vietnamese commercial poultry flocks.
abstract: Marek's disease (MD) is a highly contagious lymphoproliferative disease of chickens caused by Marek's disease virus serotype 1 (MDV-1) and remains a major concern for the global poultry industry despite widespread vaccination. Although current vaccines effectively prevent clinical disease, the emergence of more virulent strains has been recorded. Molecular surveillance of field strains is essential, particularly in regions where data remain limited. This study aimed to molecularly characterize MDV-1 isolates from recent cases in Vietnamese commercial poultry flocks, focusing on the meq gene, a key virulence-associated marker, and to compare variants with vaccine strains CVI988/Rispens. A total of 12 MDV-1 positive samples from multiple regions of Vietnam were analyzed using Sanger sequencing of the full-length meq gene. Phylogenetic analysis grouped the Vietnamese isolates into three genetic clusters (G1-G3). The attenuated-like G1 isolates showed high similarity to CVI988/Rispens clones and contained four to seven proline-rich repeat (PPPP) motifs. In contrast, G2 and G3 isolates were classified as field virulent genotypes and contained two to three PPPP motifs. Comparative sequence analysis revealed multiple amino-acid substitutions in the Meq protein relative to CVI988/Rispens, including conserved mutations characteristic of Asian field strains. Vietnamese isolates clustered primarily with contemporary Asian lineages from China and India. The results demonstrate the presence of both vaccine-derived and virulent MDV-1 strains in this Vietnamese sample set and highlight the importance of continued molecular surveillance to monitor viral evolution and support vaccination strategies.
journal: Avian pathology : journal of the W.V.P.A
authors: Duy HD, Hoang PT, Soster P, Duc DN, Molnár J, Samoy C, Christiaens I, Truong VK, Hao QP, Thien NHL, Kim PDT, Bich THT, Thi TL, Gussem M.
