title: The Journey of Newcastle Disease Virus Across the Indonesian Archipelago.
abstract: Newcastle disease (ND), caused by Newcastle disease virus (NDV), remains a major threat to poultry production, food security, and livelihoods worldwide. ND was first recognized in Java, Indonesia, in 1926, followed by its description in Newcastle-upon-Tyne, England, in 1927. Since then, ND has been repeatedly detected in Indonesian poultry systems, including free-range, backyard, and commercial production, with outbreaks causing substantial mortality and economic losses. Indonesia's archipelagic geography, extensive poultry movement and marketing networks, and heterogeneous production systems create complex conditions for virus persistence and dissemination. This review summarizes the century-long journey (1926-2026) of NDV in Indonesia, highlighting its historical emergence, epidemiological evolution, genetic diversity, and control strategies. Molecular epidemiological studies demonstrate substantial genetic diversity, with virulent genotype VII viruses frequently associated with contemporary outbreaks, while genotypes I, II, VI, and XIII have also been reported in Indonesian domestic and wild birds. The evidence supports repeated endemic circulation and ongoing viral evolution across Indonesia, emphasizing the importance of continuous molecular surveillance to monitor viral diversity and inform control strategies. Understanding the long-term epidemiological and evolutionary dynamics of NDV in Indonesia provides valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying viral emergence and persistence in a unique geographical location. Strengthening representative genomic surveillance, improving vaccination implementation, and enhancing regional cooperation across Southeast Asia will be critical for mitigating the future impact of ND on poultry production and food security.
journal: Avian pathology : journal of the W.V.P.A
authors: Ul-Rahman A, Untari H, Nugroho W, Munir M.

title: Genome characterization of a novel monopartite begomovirus infecting Capsicum annuum in Central India.
abstract: Complete genome sequences of two isolates of a novel begomovirus and its associated betasatellite were determined from two individual Capsicum annuum samples, exhibiting indistinguishable severe leaf curl symptoms, collected from Anuppur, Madhya Pradesh, India. The genome sequences of Anuppur-04 (GenBank accession PZ428100) and Anuppur-05 (PZ428101) isolates were 2760 nt each and contained six open reading frames, typical of the Old World monopartite begomoviruses. They shared 95.8% nucleotide sequence identity, whereas the highest identity was 89.4-89.5% with Tomato leaf curl Joydebpur virus. Phylogenetic analysis placed both isolates in a distinct monophyletic clade. Falling below the ICTV species demarcation threshold of 91% for complete genome sequence, these isolates represent a novel begomovirus species and are tentatively named chilli leaf curl Madhya Pradesh virus (ChiLCMPV). Split-decomposition analysis using a Neighbor-Net network, together with recombination analysis, provided evidence of recombination involving begomoviruses related to different species of tomato leaf curl virus. The associated betasatellite sequences from Anuppur-04 (PZ487063) and Anuppur-05 (PZ487064) were of 1320 nt each and shared 83.1% nucleotide identity, while highest 83.3-85.3% identity and clustered with Betasatellite capsi (chilli leaf curl betasatellite; ChiLCB), indicating that they represented new strains of ChiLCB. Collectively, these findings established the occurrence of the novel begomovirus species ChiLCMPV in association with ChiLCB infecting C. annuum in Central India and expanded the known genetic diversity of begomoviruses and their associated satellites.
authors: Soni A, Maheshwari S, Maurya PK, Maurya DK, Kumar S, Snehi SK.

title: In vitro phenotyping and genomics: a conceptual framework linking plant tissue culture with GWAS, QTL mapping, and multi-omics.
abstract: Main conclusionStandardized in vitro phenotypes provide genetically tractable traits that integrate GWAS, QTL mapping, and multi-omics, enabling mechanistic insight and genetics-informed improvement of plant regeneration. Plant tissue culture (PTC) has traditionally been employed as a technical tool for propagation, transformation, and germplasm conservation. This review reframes in vitro culture systems as quantitative phenotyping platforms that enable rigorous genetic dissection of complex traits, such as regeneration competence, stress tolerance, and developmental plasticity. By operating under highly standardized and reproducible conditions, in vitro systems reduce environmental noise and expose genotype-dependent variation that is often obscured in field or greenhouse experiments. When formalized as quantitative traits, culture responses, including callus induction, organogenesis, somatic embryogenesis, and stress survival, become amenable to genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping. Synthesizing evidence across diverse plant species, this review demonstrates that in vitro traits are genetically structured, polygenic, and biologically meaningful, reflecting coordinated regulation of hormonal signaling, chromatin accessibility, stress response pathways, and developmental gene networks. Numerous GWAS and QTL studies have identified loci and candidate genes underlying regeneration efficiency, embryogenic competence, and stress-responsive culture performance, confirming that tissue culture responsiveness is rooted in genomic architecture rather than protocol effects alone. The interpretive power of genetic mapping is substantially enhanced through integration with bioinformatic and multi-omics layers, including transcriptomics, epigenomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and network-based analyses, thereby refining candidate prioritization and facilitating mechanistic inference. This review further examines the dual role of somaclonal variation as both a constraint on clonal fidelity and a source of genetic and epigenetic diversity that can reveal cryptic genotype-phenotype relationships. Emphasis is placed on study design principles, phenotyping challenges, statistical modeling strategies, and integrative pipelines that connect genotype to in vitro phenotype and ultimately to breeding and biotechnology applications. This synthesis highlights in vitro culture systems as powerful, genetics-informed platforms for precision breeding, gene validation, and supporting efforts to more predictably and rationally manipulate complex traits, particularly in horticultural and clonally propagated crops.
authors: Isak MA, Fatima S, Haider I, Yetişir H, Şimşek Ö.

title: Integrated GWAS and RNA-Seq analyses identify candidate genes for drought tolerance in spring wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) from the cold and arid region of China.
abstract: Key messageUsing germplasm accumulated over 50 years in China's cold, arid region, 20 drought-responsive loci were identified through GWAS, and 7 key candidate genes were further revealed by integrating RNA-Seq data from drought-tolerant and sensitive lines. Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) is a major staple crop central to global food security, yet yield is severely constrained by drought. To dissect the genetic basis of drought tolerance, we evaluated 257 spring wheat germplasm lines, accumulated over five decades of breeding in the cold and arid region of China, under well-watered (WW) and rain-fed water stress (WS) conditions for seven yield-related traits. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) for seven agronomic traits and three drought tolerance indices, utilizing three analytical models identified 20 stable loci significantly associated with drought response. Transcriptome profiling of drought-tolerant and drought-sensitive lines under both conditions revealed 4,411 drought-responsive genes. Integrative analysis of GWAS and RNA-Seq data prioritized seven candidate genes, one of which for plant height overlapped with weighted gene co-expression network analysis hub modules, highlighting potential regulators of drought adaptation. Furthermore, genomic prediction based on the identified loci, using Bayesian ridge regression, achieved high trait-specific accuracies, with plant height reaching 85.4%. Collectively, these findings provide novel insights into the genetic architecture of drought tolerance in wheat and offer valuable molecular resources for marker-assisted selection and the development of drought-resilient cultivars.
journal: TAG. Theoretical and applied genetics. Theoretische und angewandte Genetik
authors: Lyu X, Xie X, Meng X, Cui Y, Zhang W, Ren K, Ni J, Yang F, Dai X, Zeng J, Liu W, Li J, Mu L, Ma W, Xu D.

title: Butyrate reverts  Chlamydia pneumoniae  -induced transcriptional suppression of macrophage polarization markers and promotes chlamydial clearance in macrophages
abstract: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are generated by gut microbiota through fermentation of dietary fibers. SCFAs contribute to human health through immunomodulation, metabolic regulation and other extraintestinal functions. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of SCFAs on the survival and antibiotic susceptibility of the intracellular bacteria  Chlamydia pneumoniae and  Chlamydia trachomatis , both representing prevalent human pathogens associated with chronic sequelae. Despite earlier reports on their direct antimicrobial activity, none of the three major SCFAs acetate, propionate nor butyrate affected the growth of  C. pneumoniae or  C. trachomatis in epithelial cells. However, butyrate decreased  C. pneumoniae genome copy numbers and infectious progeny production in THP-1 macrophages harbouring antibiotic-refractory infection phenotype. In addition, butyrate enhanced the chlamydiocidal efficacy of azithromycin in the macrophages. Similar results were obtained with  C. trachomatis -infected macrophages. To elucidate the underlying molecular changes, impact of chlamydial infection, butyrate treatment and the combination theirof on macrophage polarization and antimicrobial peptide expression was investigated.  C. pneumoniae suppressed the expression of macrophage polarization markers CD80, TLR4, CD64, CD204 and CD206, and the antimicrobial peptide LL-37, while butyrate treatment reverted the expression of both the polarization markers and LL-37 in the infected macrophages. These findings suggest that butyrate may play a role in modulating immune responses in macrophages during  Chlamydia infections, highlighting the role of diet-derived metabolites in shaping  Chlamydia –host interactions and antichlamydial treatment efficacy.
authors: Ylätalo M, Reigada I, Hanski L.

title: The Almond Expression Atlas: A comprehensive multi-tissue transcriptomic resource for almond gene expression
abstract: Background  Improving crop adaptation and enhancing agronomic and quality traits requires a deeper understanding of gene expression regulation, for which expression atlases are valuable tools. Almond (  Prunus dulcis (Mill.) D.A. Webb) is one of the most economically important tree nut crops worldwide. However, an integrated transcriptomic resource for this species is still lacking. Available data remain fragmented across independent studies, limiting their comparability and reuse.  Results  Here, we present the first almond gene expression atlas: a comprehensive multi-tissue transcriptomic resource integrating publicly available RNA sequencing data. A total of 142 high-quality untreated and control samples from 17 independent projects were curated through a metadata standardization process and analyzed using a unified bioinformatics pipeline. Standardized expression profiles were generated for 25,225 annotated genes in the  Prunus dulcis ‘Texas’ v2.0 reference genome. The atlas integrates two complementary expression approaches: a median TPM approach capturing quantitative expression levels and a rank-based strategy implemented using the Bgee expression calling method, designed to improve comparability across heterogeneous datasets. This design enables the identification of tissue-specific candidate genes and the exploration of expression patterns across tissues and developmental stages. Its applicability is demonstrated through two use cases, highlighting its ability to identify biologically meaningful gene sets associated with bud dormancy transitions and to prioritize candidate reference genes for RT-qPCR normalization in almond.  Conclusions  The Almond Expression Atlas v1.0 is publicly available through FruitDBase (  fruitdbase.csic.es ), providing an interactive platform for gene expression exploration and visualization. This resource supports functional genomics studies and facilitates candidate gene discovery in almond, while ensuring data traceability and promoting data reusability.
authors: López-Fernández EM, Zwieniecki M, Tixier A, Botía JA, Martínez-García PJ.

title: Repeated Transitions in Migratory Behavior Across a Songbird Radiation Are Not Driven by Selection on Shared Variation in Candidate Genes
abstract: A  bstract   Understanding the mechanisms facilitating the repeated evolution of traits is a core question in evolutionary biology. While repeated evolution has been observed across many systems, behavioral phenotypes have been less well studied than morphological traits. Migration is a behavioral adaptation to seasonality that has evolved independently in many animals, and repeated gains and losses of migratory behavior have been especially prevalent throughout the diversification of birds. While migratory traits are heritable in many taxa and candidate genes underlying intraspecific variation in migratory behavior have been identified, whether similar genetic changes are responsible for the repeated evolution of migration remains poorly understood. We used a phylogenomic approach to investigate the relationship between variation in candidate genes and migratory propensity across nearly all species in the parulid warbler radiation (  n = 101), a group of songbirds in which migratory behavior has been lost and gained multiple times. Comparisons of candidate gene tree topologies to the parulid warbler species tree revealed cases of discordance, though these were explained by differences in the number of phylogenetically informative sites among genes rather than by elevated genetic similarity among species sharing migratory strategies. Testing models of coding sequence evolution identified sites with elevated dN/dS in five candidate genes, suggestive of positive selection; however, variation at these sites showed no clear association with migratory strategy, nor did we detect recurrent selection across lineages where transitions in migratory behavior most likely occurred. Together, these results contradict the hypothesis that selection on shared variation (ancestral polymorphisms or introgressed alleles) facilitated the repeated evolution of migration in this clade.
authors: Szarmach SJ, Bennett KFP, Toews DPL.

title: Genome-wide and haplotype mapping reveals genetic drivers of biomass productivity per unit water and nitrogen in sorghum
abstract: Abstract    Background  Improving crop productivity per unit of water and nitrogen is central to climate resilient sorghum improvement, yet the genetic architecture of biomass-based resource productivity remains poorly resolved across contrasting production environments. This study integrated multi-environment phenotyping with 1.75 million SNPs derived from whole genome resequencing of 172 cultivated  Sorghum bicolor  and  S. bicolor  ×  S. halepense  derivative lines evaluated across temperate Mediterranean and semi-arid tropical environments. Results  Biomass-based water productivity and partial factor productivity of applied nitrogen displayed extensive genetic variation and high broad-sense heritability of 0.75 to 0.81, whereas grain-based indices were more strongly influenced by genotype × environment interaction. Multi-model genome wide association analyses identified 27 significant SNPs defining 22 genomic regions for biomass-based productivity. A recurrent chromosome 9 signal at S09_55037491 was detected across three analytical models and biomass-derived indices and colocalized with Sobic.009G200500, a nitrate-responsive HAT3.1 homeobox transcription factor. Haplotype analysis independently prioritized two additional loci: a chromosome 9 haplotype associated with a 2.7-fold difference in biomass-based water productivity and containing an AHP-like cytokinin-signaling gene, and a chromosome 5 haplotype associated with a 1.86-fold difference and encompassing DAD1, a phospholipase implicated in jasmonate biosynthesis. Candidate gene prioritization also implicated aquaporin-mediated transport, trehalose-6-phosphate metabolism, oxidative signaling and, provisionally, C4 carbon assimilation. Most favorable common haplotypes occurred within cultivated germplasm rather than the introgressed lines. Conclusions  Together, these findings reveal genetically tractable loci and biological pathways underlying sorghum biomass productivity per unit of supplied water and nitrogen. Following independent validation, the identified SNPs and haplotypes could support diagnostic marker development and haplotype informed selection, while genomic selection remains more appropriate for environmentally sensitive grain-based productivity traits.
authors: Sargar P, Thakur N, Mehtre S, Ruperao P, Hermans C, Kalpande H, Pawar G, Vemula AK, Habyarimana E.

title: Maternal progesterone signaling establishes lifelong oral homeostasis
abstract: Abstract  Pregnancy is accompanied by profound endocrine remodeling, yet the mechanisms by which maternal hormonal signals establish long-term tissue homeostasis remain largely unknown. Here we identify maternal progesterone signaling as a developmental cue that establishes lifelong oral homeostasis through a hormone–lipid–microbiome axis. We show that the membrane progesterone receptor mPRδ is selectively expressed in the developing and maternal submandibular glands, where it mediates non-genomic progesterone signaling to promote epithelial differentiation by driving the selective mobilization of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). Loss of this pathway disrupts salivary gland maturation, reshapes the oral microbial ecosystem through the selective expansion of Pasteurellaceae, and causes local inflammation as well as systemic metabolic dysfunction. Mechanistically, antibiotic treatment abolishes these phenotypes, whereas transfer of the oral microbiota recapitulates disease, demonstrating that developmental defects in the host are translated into long-term pathology through the oral microbiome. Remarkably, maternal—but not adult—DHA supplementation restores salivary gland development and microbial homeostasis and prevents adult disease phenotypes, identifying a critical developmental window during which oral homeostasis is durably established. Collectively, these findings reveal a previously unrecognized maternal endocrine mechanism that establishes lifelong host–microbiome homeostasis and identify developmental programming as a fundamental principle linking maternal physiology to adult health.

title: Nematodes as bioindicators of ecological status in midland Irish peatlands
abstract: Abstract  Peatlands play a critical role in global carbon sequestration, yet widespread drainage and land-use change have disrupted their hydrology and soil biological integrity, accelerating peat decomposition and greenhouse gas emissions. Rewetting is increasingly promoted as a key restoration strategy, but its effectiveness in re-establishing belowground ecological structure remains insufficiently understood. This study assessed the response of nematode-based soil food webs across a broad range of peatland habitats, including intact bogs, degraded systems, rewetted and non-rewetted managed peatlands, fens, wasted peatlands, and semi-natural sites, using a combination of morphological identification and DNA-based molecular sequencing. Nematode community composition and functional structure were evaluated using Enrichment Index (EI) and Structure Index (SI) diagnostics. Intact bog habitats consistently exhibited higher SI and lower EI values, reflecting well-structured food webs dominated by fungal-associated and higher trophic nematode families, including Dorylaimidae and Qudsianematidae. In contrast, degraded and non-rewetted peatlands showed simplified food webs characterized by elevated EI and dominance of opportunistic bacterial-feeding families such as Rhabditidae and Cephalobidae. Rewetted sites generally exhibited reduced EI relative to non-rewetted counterparts, indicating dampened nutrient enrichment and microbial pulses following hydrological restoration; however, SI values remained low in the short term, suggesting limited recovery of higher trophic complexity. Comparisons between morphological and molecular datasets revealed strong concordance at the family level for dominant taxa, while molecular sequencing detected additional rare and cryptic nematode families not consistently recovered through morphology alone, underscoring the complementarity of both approaches. Fen peatlands displayed higher EI values consistent with naturally greater nutrient availability, whereas wasted peatlands supported persistently impoverished food webs regardless of management. Overall, the results demonstrate that rewetting effectively stabilizes nutrient dynamics and initiates early recovery of soil food web functioning, but full restoration of trophic complexity requires long-term ecological recovery. Integrating hydrological restoration with biological monitoring is therefore essential for maximizing peatland carbon storage and climate mitigation potential.
authors: Pulavarty A, Ringholz L, Klappauf T, Cooper E, Molina PM, McMillan D, Kakouli-Duarte T.

title: Gut microbiota ablation depletes secondary bile acids and shifts the cytokine balance in BCG-infected mice
abstract: Abstract    Background.  Antibiotic ablation is the standard test of whether a host phenotype depends on the gut microbiota, but it removes the community and perturbs the host at once, so depletion alone cannot assign a metabolite shift to the community. We built a four-arm mouse model on a single BCG infection background: untreated controls (NC), BCG alone, BCG after mixed-antibiotic ablation (ABX_BCG), and BCG followed by faecal microbiota transplantation with no antibiotic exposure at any point (BCG_FMT). The ablated and transplanted arms were independent branches, not a depletion-then-restoration sequence.  Results.  Dual-polarity untargeted LC-MS (9,706 negative-mode and 11,589 positive-mode features) and shotgun metagenomics showed that ablation left a block of 726 negative-mode and 313 positive-mode features absent from all three ABX_BCG samples but detected in 88–94% of the other nine; total ion signal in the ablated arm exceeded that of the quality-control injections, excluding dilution and matrix loss. Twenty-seven block features were annotated, resolving to 17 unique InChIKeys, 21 of them microbial compound classes including secondary bile acids. Deoxycholic acid eluted at 437.93 s in negative mode and 437.28 s in positive mode; deoxycholic and lithocholic acid were undetected in the ablated samples. Both omics layers resolved the same four groups (PERMANOVA R² = 0.562 for the genus table and 0.635 for the metabolome) yet failed to couple at sample level; exhaustive within-group re-pairing excluded sample mismatch, identifying a shared treatment rather than an individual axis. Ablation accompanied higher TNF-α and IL-6 and lower IFN-γ and IL-10 in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and serum alike.  Conclusions.  The gut community contributes a set of metabolite features whose absence is specific to the ablated state rather than shared with infection or transplantation, and the same arm occupies the extreme of the cytokine readout in both compartments. Running the ablated and transplanted arms as independent branches off the infected baseline is what makes this an antibiotic-specific control, and the two omics layers carry a shared treatment structure rather than a shared individual axis.
authors: Ma Y, Zhu L, Xie Y, Gou Y, Zhang B, Zhang R, Xiao C, Chen J, Zhang L, Wu J, Li Q.

title: Synergistic antibiotic activity and integrated genomic-metabolomic profiling of patch- and plaque-derived Staphylococcus aureus in mycosis fungoides.
abstract: Mycosis fungoides (MF), the most common form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, is frequently associated with skin dysbiosis, and advanced lesions are often dominated by multidrug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. To characterize microbiologically relevant properties of MF-associated S. aureus, we evaluated synergistic antibiotic combinations and performed integrated phenotypic, genomic, and metabolomic profiling. Several antibiotic combinations, most notably carbenicillin combined with either gentamicin or levofloxacin, exhibited pronounced synergistic activity and restored in vitro antimicrobial activity against highly resistant isolates. Comparative genomic analyses revealed substantial variability between isolates in resistomes and virulence repertoires, including enterotoxins, immune-evasion, and stress-response factors. Metabolomic profiling further revealed isolate-specific extracellular signatures, including putrescine and urocanic acid. In summary, this study identifies promising antibiotic combinations against multidrug-resistant S. aureus strains. Furthermore, this exploratory investigation demonstrates phenotypic and genomic heterogeneity among MF-associated S. aureus isolates, warranting further evaluation in larger longitudinal studies.ImportanceDespite its predominance in advanced mycosis fungoides (MF) lesions, the role of multidrug‑resistant Staphylococcus aureus in adverse clinical outcomes remains poorly understood. Bridging the gap between clinical observations and microbiological mechanisms is essential to clarify how S. aureus persists in MF skin and to identify therapeutic alternatives for S. aureus‑positive patients, for whom treatment options remain limited. This study addresses two major clinical needs: the lack of effective antibiotic strategies and the limited understanding of bacterial factors that may contribute to worsened clinical outcomes. By integrating synergistic antibiotic testing with genomic, phenotypic, and metabolomic profiling, our work highlights clinically relevant heterogeneity among MF-associated S. aureus isolates. These findings identify promising therapeutic directions and establish a framework for future large-scale longitudinal studies to better understand the role of diverse S. aureus strains in MF pathogenesis.
authors: Straub FA, Serbin LK, Barkani IE, Grünewald C, Mailänder V, Dominelli N.

title: Development of a TaqMan probe-based PCR for the detection of porcine bocavirus group 3 and identification of a novel genotype strain.
abstract: For specific detection of porcine bocavirus (PBoV) group 3 (G3), we developed a TaqMan probe-based real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) targeting the NS1 gene. The correlation coefficient and amplification efficiency of the PCR were 0.994 and 102.9%, respectively. There were no cross-reactions of the PCR with the genomes of classical swine fever virus, porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus, porcine parvovirus, porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV), transmissible gastroenteritis virus (TGEV), and porcine deltacoronavirus (PDCoV), and the detection limit of the PCR was 100 copies per reaction. The coefficients of variation of the inter-assay and intra-assay of the PCR were 1.38-2.71% and 0.23-0.67%, respectively. A total of 719 field samples collected from Xinjiang, Gansu, Qinghai, Ningxia, and Shaanxi Provinces were detected via the developed PCR, and the positive rates were 80.82%, 44.51%, 97.50%, 98.94%, and 93.60%, respectively. In addition, coinfections of PBoV G3 with PEDV/TGEV/PDCoV/PCV2 were determined, and dual infections, triple infections, quadruple infections, and quintuple infections were observed. Furthermore, the complete genome sequences of 10 positive samples (two per province) randomly selected from five provinces were determined, and phylogenetic analysis placed all 10 within PBoV G3, but one strain formed a distinct branch, indicating it was a novel strain in PBoV G3. The established PCR provides a reliable tool for PBoV G3 detection and facilitates the understanding of its distribution and prevalence.ImportancePorcine bocavirus (PBoV) poses a threat to swine health and has potential public health significance. Owing to the high nucleotide diversity of PBoV, existing detection methods may yield false-negative results. A reliable detection method is needed to monitor its prevalence. Given that porcine bocavirus group 3 (PBoV G3) is the predominant group circulating in Chinese pig populations, we established a rapid and sensitive TaqMan probe-based polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for detection of PBoV G3. We detected 719 field samples collected from northwest China by the PCR and analyzed coinfections of PBoV G3 with porcine epidemic diarrhea virus/transmissible gastroenteritis virus/porcine deltacoronavirus PCV2. The results showed that the positive rate of PBoV G3 was high, and dual infections, triple infections, quadruple infections, and quintuple infections were present. Furthermore, a novel genotype was identified in PBoV G3. Taken together, the developed PCR facilitates the prevalence investigation of PBoV G3. The results enrich the data on the distribution and prevalence of PBoV G3 in China.
authors: Gong C, Zhong Q, Lu Y, Li B, Yang B, Yang J, Liu G, Fu Y.

title: Identification and characterization of a periplasmic phosphate-binding protein in phosphorus-starved Pyropia yezoensis.
abstract: The synthesis of several polypeptides (145, 76, 66, 52, 42, 32, and 16 kDa) in Pyropia yezoensis was markedly induced under phosphorus-starved conditions. The most abundant 32-kDa polypeptide was purified and characterized. Comparison of the genomic and cDNA sequences revealed an intronless gene encoding a 323-amino-acid precursor protein with a 24-amino-acid signal peptide and a 299-amino-acid mature protein. The mature 32-kDa polypeptide showed high sequence similarity to periplasmic phosphate-binding proteins (PBPs) from Escherichia coli and marine cyanobacteria. Both the native and recombinant proteins exhibited phosphate-binding ability in equilibrium dialysis assays. Immunological analyses indicated that the phosphorus-starvation-induced 32-kDa PBP is localized to the periplasmic space. Northern blot and quantitative real-time PCR analyses demonstrated that PBP gene expression was strongly induced by phosphorus starvation. These findings support a model of phosphate acquisition in P. yezoensis under phosphorus-starved conditions involving a periplasmic PBP and alkaline phosphatase.
authors: Miwa Y, Yano Y, Kono T, Yoshimizu M, Yamagishi Y.

title: Nuclear cGAS governs transcription to control lipid metabolism, tumor growth, and therapy response.
abstract: Cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS) is a cytosolic DNA sensor critical for host defense against microbial infections. To prevent aberrant activation, nuclear cGAS is restrained by nucleosome tethering or by barrier-to-autointegration factor-mediated restriction of its access to DNA. However, its physiological roles beyond enzymatic suppression in the nucleus remain poorly understood. Here, we present a genome-wide map of cGAS chromatin localization in human cells and unexpectedly find its binding beyond nucleosome tethering, where cGAS is recruited to chromatin by AP-1 transcription factors via a potentially previously uncharacterized transactivation domain. Integrated CUT&RUN, RNA-seq, and metabolomics analyses reveal that cGAS transcriptionally regulates cholesterol homeostasis. Mechanistically, cGAS promotes LGALS3 transcription, which inhibits ACAA2 activity to suppress fatty acid oxidation and acetyl-CoA production, thereby lowering intracellular cholesterol levels. Reduced cholesterol lowers plasma membrane phosphatidylinositol [3,4,5] triphosphate [PI(3,4,5)P3] levels and decreases mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) activation. In contrast, cGAS depletion results in cholesterol accumulation and elevated PI(3,4,5)P3, driving mTORC2/Akt signaling, promoting xenografted tumor growth, and conferring resistance to DNA-damaging agents. In vivo, the elevated hepatic cholesterol levels observed in cGas-/- mice were largely reversed by inhibition of Akt but not STING, whereas cGAS deficiency had minimal effects on lung physiology. Collectively, our findings uncover an unexpected role for nuclear cGAS in orchestrating a transcriptional program that links lipid metabolism to cell proliferation, stress response, and cholesterol homeostasis in liver.

title: High-efficiency antimony biomineralization by Serratia nematodiphila: process optimization and integrated genomic-transcriptomic-proteomic analysis.
abstract: This study aims to elucidate the transcriptional, protein expression and mineral crystallization response mechanisms of the Serratia nematodiphila strain during the process of converting Sb3+ into Sb2O3 through integrating multi-omics methods and various mineral analysis techniques. The isolate Serratia nematodiphila (MIC > 250 mM) achieved 96.18% Sb3+ removal under Box-Behnken-optimized conditions (27.7 ℃, pH 4.67, 205.6 rpm). Time-resolved SEM-EDS, Raman, XRD, and XPS revealed a non-classical mineralization pathway from an amorphous precursor to crystalline Sb2O3 within 36 h. Integrated genomic-transcriptomic-proteomic analyses resolved a coordinated physiological response: (1) energy metabolic remodeling via upregulated TCA cycle and fatty acid β-oxidation and suppressed anaerobic respiration, may help sustain NAD(P)H and proton motive force that could support ArsB-mediated efflux; (2) Fe-S cluster repair and metal sequestration through Suf assembly, iron/siderophore uptake, and molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis; (3) multi-level antioxidant defense via glutathione, catalase/peroxidase, and SoxR/OxyR systems; and (4) motility suppression, conserving energy and protons while enhanced capsule/EPS functions promote Sb adsorption and mineral nucleation. Together, these processes may promote the hydrolysis and precipitation of aqueous Sb3+ species, leading to the formation of crystalline Sb2O3. Serratia nematodiphila orchestrates a coordinated metabolic reprogramming that enhances energy generation, metal sequestration, and oxidative defense while suppressing motility, effectively transforming toxic aqueous Sb3+ into valuable crystalline Sb2O3. These findings provide a mechanistic blueprint for engineering microbial-based bioremediation and resource recovery from antimony-polluted environments.
authors: Zhou Z, Zhang P, Li Q, Hu H, Hu X, Yang A.

title: Soil Microbes Mediate Contrasting Effects of Plant Diversity on Biotic Resistance and Invasional Meltdown.
abstract: Biological invasions are intensifying worldwide as a major component of global change, with soil microbes increasingly recognized as key regulators of invasion outcomes. Yet how soil microbes interact with biodiversity to determine whether communities resist or facilitate invasion, particularly through their effects on plant growth and species interactions, remains unclear. Here, we conducted a two-phase feedback experiment in which soils were conditioned across a diversity gradient of native or invasive plant communities. We characterized soil fungal communities and quantified microbial effects on plant growth and species interactions between phylogenetically paired native and invasive species. Biodiversity generated contrasting invasion outcomes depending on community origin, driven by distinct microbial pathways. In native-conditioned soils, increasing diversity reduced invader dominance (biotic resistance), primarily mediated by microbial effects on interspecific competition that enhanced native competition strength while reducing that of invaders. In contrast, in invasive-conditioned soils, increasing diversity facilitated invader dominance (invasional meltdown), primarily driven by enhanced invader growth and suppression of natives. These patterns were associated with shifts in key microbial groups. Putative pathogen richness increased with increasing plant diversity and was negatively associated with native growth, whereas AMF richness declined with increasing plant diversity in native communities but increased with increasing plant diversity in invasive communities, promoting invader growth and competition strength. By integrating biodiversity-ecosystem functioning, biotic resistance, invasional meltdown, and competitive interactions within a plant-soil feedback framework, our study advances invasion ecology. It identifies soil microbes as central mediators that link biodiversity to ecosystem invasibility through distinct pathways affecting plant growth and species interactions.
authors: Shen C, Tao Z, Wan J, Xu X, Siemann E, Huang W.

title: From mutations to mechanisms: using AlphaFold 2 to decode gentamicin resistance
abstract: The emergence of antimicrobial resistance poses a major challenge to global health, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying resistance often remain incompletely understood. In this webinar, I will present a case study from my PhD research investigating the genetic and structural basis of gentamicin resistance in experimentally evolved bacterial mutants. The project involved generating gentamicin-resistant mutants in the laboratory, performing whole-genome sequencing to identify resistance-associated mutations, and characterising the resulting protein variants. While mutations were identified across several proteins, the primary focus was on elongation factor G (EF-G), a key component of the bacterial translation machinery. To investigate the structural consequences of these mutations, AlphaFold2 was used to predict mutant protein structures and compare them with their wild-type counterparts. Structural alignments revealed that some mutations produced subtle conformational shifts in domain IV of EF-G, an extended region located near the gentamicin-binding site on the ribosome, while other mutations showed little or no detectable structural change. To place these findings into a functional context, experimental ribosome structures from the Protein Data Bank were integrated with AlphaFold predictions. By superimposing structures of EF-G-bound ribosomes and gentamicin-bound ribosomes, a composite structural model was generated, enabling the spatial relationship between resistance-associated mutations and the antibiotic-binding site to be examined. These analyses provided mechanistic insights into how specific mutations may reduce gentamicin binding through local structural and physicochemical effects. The webinar will discuss the opportunities and limitations of using AlphaFold to investigate the structural consequences of genomic variation, the challenges of interpreting subtle structural differences, and the importance of integrating AI-predicted models with experimental structural data to generate biologically meaningful hypotheses.
authors: Abbara R.

title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Proteomic Analysis Reveals Antibacterial Responses of Staphylococcus aureus to 60Co γ-Irradiation.
abstract: γ-Irradiation is a widely used nonthermal sterilization technology in food processing; however, the mechanisms underlying γ-irradiation-induced inactivation of Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) remain incompletely understood. This study investigated the effects of 60Co γ-irradiation on S. aureus and its molecular responses by integrating physiological assays with transcriptomic and proteomic analyses. γ-Irradiation produced a dose-dependent reduction in bacterial culturability from 0 to 2.0 kGy, with the greatest reduction observed at 2.0 kGy. Although no obvious surface morphological alterations were detected by scanning electron microscopy, γ-irradiation compromised membrane integrity, as evidenced by increased leakage of nucleic acids, proteins, and K+ and decreased ATPase-associated activities. Integrated omics analysis identified 486 differentially expressed genes and 178 differentially expressed proteins following 2.0 kGy irradiation. Functional enrichment analysis revealed alterations in pathways associated with cell envelope biosynthesis, amino acid metabolism, and energy metabolism. Notably, upregulation of MNH antiporters suggested a potential adaptive response to maintain cellular ion homeostasis under irradiation stress. Collectively, these findings indicate that γ-irradiation induces S. aureus inactivation through multiple cellular alterations, including membrane dysfunction, genomic damage, intracellular leakage, and metabolic disturbances.
authors: Cui L, Si Z, Wei Y, Wang X, Yan H, Chen S.

title: Trophic highways and dead ends: Algal traits regulate nutrient flux and energy transfer in stream food webs.
abstract: Primary producers supply energy to ecosystems, but their traits determine whether fixed carbon (C) and nutrients are retained or transferred to consumers. In nitrogen (N)-limited rivers, N fixation can provide a critical nutrient input, yet its role in supporting food webs remains poorly constrained. We investigated how algal traits regulate the flux of newly fixed C and N to consumers in the South Fork Eel River, California, using stable isotope tracers to quantify nutrient flux and transfer to grazers (Gumaga nigricula). While several algal taxa exhibited high rates of nutrient fixation, trophic outcomes differed sharply. Assemblages dominated by Epithemia, a diatom genus with N-fixing cyanobacterial endosymbionts, supported disproportionately high trophic coupling. Conversely, cyanobacterial mats and mucilage-rich green algae were highly productive but little consumed. This decoupling is driven by nutrient packaging: Epithemia diatoms provide accessible nutrients and high-quality lipids, whereas cyanobacteria and filamentous green algae have traits that limit consumption. By quantifying variation in the flow of fixed nutrients into an algal-based food web, we show that transfer to primary consumers is governed by producer functional traits, and that shifts from diatom-dominated assemblages to cyanobacterial or green algal dominance will create trophic dead ends, limiting food supplies and top-down impacts of algivores.
authors: Zampini MC, Wulf MA, Sitati AN, Kariunga SH, Thomas SA, Power ME, Marks JC.

title: Family of β-Propeller Diels-Alderases Directs cis-Decalin Formation in Polyketide Biosynthesis.
abstract: Decalin-forming Diels-Alderases (pericyclases) exemplify how Nature repeatedly recruits unrelated protein folds to control [4 + 2] cycloadditions, yet exo-selective intramolecular Diels-Alder (IMDA) reactions that yield cis-fused decalins remain rare and poorly understood. Here, we uncover a previously unrecognized bacterial pericyclase family that enforces an exo-IMDA trajectory in polyketide assembly. Using alchivemycin A, a macrocyclic antibacterial polyketide whose scaffold is defined by a highly functionalized cis-decalin core, we identify AvmG as the dedicated decalin-forming enzyme. Disruption of avmG diverts pathway flux to trans-decalin shunt isomers consistent with spontaneous, endo-biased cyclization that cannot be processed by the downstream macrocyclase, whereas AvmG enables formation of the authentic cis-decalin intermediate. AvmG is unrelated to known [4 + 2] cyclases and adopts an integrin α N-terminal domain-like β-propeller architecture, revealing an unexpected scaffold for pericyclic stereocontrol. Genome mining shows that AvmG-like proteins are widespread and enriched in actinomycete polyketide gene clusters; characterization of the lydicamycin homolog LymR establishes conserved exo-IMDA activity in a distinct pathway. Structural and mutational analyses implicate a loop-defined catalytic cavity in steering the kinetically demanding cis-decalin outcome. Together, these findings expand the fold and mechanistic diversity of Diels-Alderases, define an exo-selective β-propeller pericyclase superfamily, and provide a new handle for mining and bioengineering cis-decalin biosynthetic pathways.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
authors: Zhao EJ, Ling QY, Ma XX, Liu SH, Zhu A, Yan ZY, Zhu HJ, Mai ZP, Igarashi Y, Jiao RH, Zhang B, Ge HM.

title: Integrative transcriptomic profiling of the phosphatome identifies DUSP15 as a chromophobe renal cell carcinoma-selective epithelial biomarker associated with an immune-metabolic tumour state.
abstract: Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma (chRCC) lacks robust molecular markers and well-defined therapeutic vulnerabilities. Here, 265 protein-coding phosphatases were systematically interrogated using pan-cancer transcriptomic profiles from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), cross-cohort evaluation in seven subtype-annotated Gene Expression Omnibus datasets drawn from a ten-dataset compilation, pathway and immune analyses, and two independent single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets. DUSP15 emerged as the most chRCC-selective phosphatase (Tau = 0.977) and showed high retrospective discriminative performance both between chRCC and clear-cell and papillary RCC (AUC = 0.976) and between chRCC tumours and adjacent normal kidney tissue (AUC = 0.973) in TCGA. Subtype discrimination was independently reproduced across the GEO cohorts (AUC = 0.837). Transcriptome-wide analyses showed that DUSP15-high tumours were characterised by coordinated enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation, MYC target and DNA repair programmes, together with reduced interferon and inflammatory signalling. Immune deconvolution revealed lower regulatory T-cell, dendritic-cell and overall immune enrichment scores, consistent with a relatively immune-poor transcriptional state. Single-cell analyses localised the bulk-tumour DUSP15 signal predominantly to tumour-associated epithelial populations in two independent datasets, with DUSP15 detected in 72.2-83.7% of tumour epithelial cells and pseudobulk abundance ranging from 144.9 to 204.3 counts per million. Expression was substantially lower in immune, stromal, normal renal epithelial and non-chRCC tumour populations. Collectively, these findings identify DUSP15 as a highly selective tumour-epithelial biomarker candidate for chRCC and establish the cellular context of a DUSP15-associated immune-metabolic state with potential diagnostic and biological relevance.
authors: Sarhan AR.

title: Acyldepsipeptide 1 and Furan Derivative from Pseudomonas chlororaphis Are Critical for Biocontrol of Tomato Bacterial Wilt Caused by Ralstonia solanacearum.
abstract: Tomato bacterial wilt, caused by Ralstonia solanacearum, is a destructive soil-borne disease that severely constrains tomato production. Here, we compared two rhizosphere bacterial strains Pseudomonas chlororaphis subsp. aurantiaca YS05 and YS21, with contrasting biocontrol efficiency. YS05 strongly suppressed disease, whereas YS21 showed substantially weaker efficacy. Comparative analyses indicated that both strains shared conserved genomic architecture and colonization-associated traits, but YS05 uniquely harbored secondary metabolite (SM) biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) associated with acyldepsipeptide 1 (ADEP1), furan derivative, and arylpolyene. Deletion of adeB or avrD reduced metabolite accumulation and biocontrol efficacy, whereas neither YS05 derivatives nor the corresponding metabolite standards directly inhibited R. solanacearum in vitro; instead, they activated tomato defense responses associated with salicylic acid, jasmonic acid, and reactive oxygen species homeostasis. These findings link ADEP1 and furan derivative to YS05-mediated bacterial wilt suppression and defense activation, and offer new insights into the development of environmentally friendly biocontrol agents.
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
authors: Liu Y, Zhang S, Huang Y, Jiao Z, Xie X, Shi Y, Chai A, Zhang D, Li B, Li L.

title: Whole-Genome Sequences of Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV, Tobamovirus tabaci) Reveal Its Population Genetic Structure and Transmission Routes in China.
abstract: Viral diseases severely threaten agriculture, particularly in cigar tobacco. Here, we clarified the occurrence and distribution of viral diseases in cigar tobacco in Hainan, China, and identified TMV and CMV as the predominant viruses. Furthermore, we obtained the full-length genomes of two TMV isolates, analyzed their structures and variations, and validated their pathogenicity. Using whole-genome resequencing data from 79 TMV isolates collected over the past two decades─60 from five major tobacco-growing regions of China and 19 from other countries─we constructed a genome-wide SNP data set and analyzed the population genetics and transmission routes. Results indicated that TMV in China originated in northern China and spread via two independent routes: (i) progressive north-to-south spread to the middle and lower reaches of the Changjiang River basin and (ii) direct introduction to Hainan Island. Our study provides insights into viral disease management in the development of the cigar industry.

title: Microbial Characteristics of Weissella cibaria HRL3 and Its Immunostimulatory Effects via TLR3/TLR9-Dependent IFN-α Production.
abstract: Rhinacanthus nasutus (L.) Kurz is a medicinal plant whose roots, stems, and leaves are commonly used in tea and traditional Chinese medicine; however, the beneficial effects of its flowers remain to be investigated. In this study, the lactic acid bacteria (LAB) found in the flowers of R. nasutus (L.) Kurz were isolated using a medium containing fructose, which is abundant in the flowers, and their microbial characteristics were subsequently analyzed. The isolated LAB strain was identified as Weissella cibaria based on whole-genome sequencing and was designated as HRL3. This strain was a facultative anaerobe whose growth was promoted under aerobic conditions, and it was classified as a heterofermentative LAB that produced lactate and ethanol via lactate fermentation. In addition, the HRL3 strain exhibited a unique carbohydrate utilization profile that differed from the type strain of W. cibaria. The immunostimulatory effects of the HRL3 strain were also investigated in this study. When added to mouse spleen cells, the HRL3 strain induced the production of IFN-α, which is a cytokine that plays a key role in enhancing antiviral immune responses. This induction could occur through recognition by endosomal Toll-like receptor (TLR) 3 and TLR9. Dectin-1 may also contribute to IFN-α production induced by the HRL3 strain. In an influenza A virus (IAV)-infected mouse model, oral administration of the HRL3 strain was associated with increased IFN-α mRNA expression, reduced IAV M mRNA expression, and attenuation of pulmonary histopathological changes. These findings provide new insights into the functional potential of R. nasutus (L.) Kurz flowers and the immunomodulatory activity of the HRL3 strain.
authors: Niitsuma F, Sasahara H, Masaki A, Toritani A, Tsukamoto M, Takahashi T, Tanaka S.

title: Toward a Universal Switch for Microbial Granulation: Photogranule Insights to Advance Granular Wastewater Treatment.
abstract: Microbial granulation─the assembly of self-immobilized, spheroidal aggregates─is a transformative approach for high-density, energy-efficient wastewater treatment. By concentrating biomass and enhancing resilience to influent fluctuations, granular systems significantly reduce infrastructure footprints. Current granular technologies primarily leverage upflow continuous reactors or sequencing-batch reactors, where specific external selection pressures are imposed to drive granulation. However, granulation remains neither spontaneous nor reliably predictable, and its fundamental biological drivers are poorly understood. Recent advances in photogranules challenge selection-pressure models. Photogranules form from activated-sludge inocula in hydrostatic and hydrodynamic batches and even in CSTRs where classical selection conditions are weak or absent. Moreover, the recurring emergence of compact spheroidal granules across diverse natural and laboratory systems suggests shared, intrinsic biological drivers rather than purely engineered causes. In this Perspective, we propose that the bacterial second messenger c-di-GMP functions as a conserved, Goldilocks-like molecular switch that integrates diverse environmental cues into a coordinated granulation program. We synthesize transcriptomic, biochemical, and genetic evidence and advance three hypotheses linking c-di-GMP signaling and community physiology to granulation. If validated, targeted modulation of c-di-GMP─by genetic or chemical means─could enable predictable, resilient granulation across a wider range of systems, including the continuous horizontal-flow basins that dominate wastewater infrastructure.
authors: Park C, Risser DD, Morita YS, Nüsslein K, Gikonyo JG.

title: Spike gene evolution in HCoV-OC43: Evidence of post-pandemic selective expansion.
abstract: IntroductionThe aim is to characterise the evolution of the HCoV-OC43 spike from 2014 to 2024, spanning both the pre- and post-SARS-CoV-2 pandemic periods, in cases attended at a tertiary hospital in Catalonia.MethodsRespiratory specimens from patients with suspected acute respiratory infection were collected for laboratory-confirmation using a real-time PCR assay. A random selection of HCoV-OC43-positive specimens was performed per week. The whole spike gene was amplified by a nested RT-PCR using primers and protocol optimised from Gorse et al., 2017 and subsequently sequenced with the Illumina DNA Prep protocol. Further analyses were performed with MEGA and Nextclade softwares.ResultsThe overall prevalence of seasonal coronaviruses was 5.18%, with HCoV-OC43 accounting for 47.93%. Phylogenetic analysis of the S gene revealed the predominance of cluster C. Mutation analysis showed that the RBD accumulated the highest number of substitutions prior to the pandemic, followed by a reduction afterwards, suggesting shifts in selective pressures. Positive Tajima's D values in the pre-pandemic period were consistent with stable endemic circulation, whereas negative values in the post-pandemic period suggested population expansion following a bottleneck. Comparative analyses revealed that HCoV-OC43 also exhibited lower evolutionary rates than SARS-CoV-2, in the S1 and the RBD regions, underscoring differential immune pressures.ConclusionsThe present findings highlight the dynamic interplay between viral evolution and epidemiological changes associated with the pre- and post-pandemic periods in shaping the genetic landscape of endemic HCoVs.
journal: Enfermedades infecciosas y microbiologia clinica (English ed.)
authors: Andrés C, Serra M, González-Sánchez A, Prats-Méndez I, Arnedo-Muñoz M, Saubi N, Rando-Segura A, Nadal-Barón P, Esperalba J, Balada E, Garcia-Comuñas K, Martín MC, Valverde M, Canals A, Larrosa N, Antón A.

title: Multi-locus genetic basis of stomatal density and size in maize revealed by integrated QTL and GWAS.
abstract: Stomatal patterning is a fundamental aspect of plant photosynthetic performance and water-use efficiency, yet its genetic basis in C4 grasses such as maize remains poorly understood. Here, we integrated linkage analysis across three recombinant inbred line populations and a genome-wide association study in a diverse maize panel to dissect the genetic architecture of six stomatal traits. This approach identified 33 quantitative trait loci and 51 association loci for 6 stomatal traits and revealed a significant negative genetic correlation between stomatal density (SD) and size, with multiple genomic intervals showing co-localization of effects on both trait categories. By integrating reported cell-type-specific transcriptomic data, we prioritized high-confidence candidate genes, including conserved stomatal regulators as well as previously uncharacterized candidates involved in processes such as cell wall biosynthesis. Functional analyses of EMS-induced mutants for candidates ZmbHLH140 and ZmCESA6 demonstrated that loss of ZmbHLH140 reduces SD, whereas mutation of ZmCESA6 has the opposite effect. In addition, the signature of selection at the ZmbHLH140 locus is consistent with a role for stomatal regulation during maize domestication. Together, our results establish a comprehensive genetic framework for stomatal development in maize, highlighting both conserved and grass-specific mechanisms that shape stomatal patterning and offering a foundation for future functional studies of stomatal development in cereals.
journal: The Plant journal : for cell and molecular biology
authors: Qin Y, Qiu M, Wang C, Yang Z, Ma X, Pan Z, Sun L, Wu T, Huang Y, Wang H, Zhou Q, Tang J, Fu Z.

title: Integrated Whole-Genome and RNA Sequencing Analysis of FFPE Lung Cancer Samples: Feasibility and Pathological Validation.
abstract: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) can be applied to formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) specimens for genomic and transcriptomic analyses, including gene rearrangement detection. We tested whether PCR-free WGS and RNA-seq could detect driver alterations in FFPE lung adenocarcinoma samples prepared under standardized automated fixation and embedding conditions. Two adenocarcinoma cases were analyzed. Before this study, immunohistochemistry had suggested an EGFR alteration in one case and an ALK alteration in the other, although neither had been confirmed at the genomic or chromosomal level. In this analysis, PCR-free WGS yielded stable sequencing metrics and successfully detected small variants, including the canonical EGFR p.Leu858Arg mutation. By contrast, conventional structural variant calling failed to identify the EML4::ALK rearrangement. However, a custom algorithm based on supplementary alignment tags recovered the fusion candidate from WGS data despite support from only a single junction read, and RNA-seq independently confirmed expression of the EML4::ALK fusion transcript. Break-apart fluorescence in situ hybridization demonstrated tumor-wide clonal ALK rearrangement. These findings show that a single junction read can be biologically meaningful only when supported by orthogonal pathological validation and highlight the importance of integrating sequencing findings with pathological validation for the interpretation of gene rearrangements in FFPE specimens.
authors: Kiyose S, Yamada H, Miyazaki R, Yoshimura K, Takeuchi S, Takahashi S, Tanahashi M, Konno K, Hoshino H, Hoshi G, Ozawa H, Chiba H, Hattori N, Shinmura K.

title: Development of Novel Furan-Chalcone Derivatives as Targeting Bacterial DNA Gyrase and Topoisomerase IV: Design, Synthesis, and In Silico Studies.
abstract: A series of novel furan-chalcone derivatives (Na1-Na8) were synthesized and evaluated for their antimicrobial, antioxidant, DNA gyrase inhibitory, and computational properties using integrated in vitro and in silico approaches. Among the synthesized compounds, Na5 exhibited the most potent antibacterial activity with low MIC values against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial strains. Antioxidant studies revealed significant free radical scavenging activity for Na3, Na4, and Na5. Molecular docking studies against DNA gyrase B demonstrated favorable binding interactions within the ATP-binding pocket. Enzyme inhibition studies against Escherichia coli DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV confirmed that Na5 showed the strongest inhibitory activity among the tested compounds. ADME predictions indicated acceptable drug-likeness and pharmacokinetic properties. Furthermore, DFT analysis of Na5 revealed a suitable HOMO-LUMO energy gap and favorable electronic properties supporting its biological activity. Overall, the results identify Na5 as a promising lead candidate for the development of novel antimicrobial agents targeting bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV.

title: Lactobacillales-Enriched Oral Microbiome Profile as a Potential Link in the Tooth Loss-Cognition Association: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of NHANES 2011-2012.
abstract: AimThis study aimed to examine oral microbial features in the association between tooth loss and cognitive status in older adults from the US population and evaluate the role of oral microbiota in tooth loss and cognition.Methods and resultsEligible 568 participants from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (Nhanes) 2011-2012 were recruited. Oral rinse sampleses were collected, and the 16S ribosomal RNA gene was sequenced. α-diversity and β-diversity was analyzed to depict microbiome profile. Mediation models were used to investigate the role of a-diversity in the association between tooth loss and cognitive function. The co-occurring group exhibited significantly reduced α-diversity and distinct β-diversity compared to CI (cognitive impairment) only group and the control group (p ConclusionThis pioneering study investigated the oral microbiota composition in relation to varying levels of tooth loss and cognitive status. It revealed the complex role of mucosal colonization in both dental and cognitive health, thereby underscoring the need to integrate the oral microbiome into cognitive research.

title: Antimicrobial Resistance in Periodontal Disease: Rethinking Adjunctive Therapy in the Metagenomics Era, the Pressing Need for Precision Treatment and Periodontal Resistome Mapping.
abstract: Systemic antibiotics are effective when used as adjunctive therapy in the treatment of periodontitis; however, their use must be balanced against antimicrobial resistance, which is a major threat to global public health. This review provides an expert synthesis of the literature and a field-level overview of antimicrobial resistance in periodontal therapy, highlighting current knowledge and emerging directions, while examining how adjunctive antibiotic protocols may contribute to resistance within the periodontal microbiome through emerging metagenomic insights. To provide this synthesis, the PubMed database was searched for English-language publications using combinations of the terms periodontitis, systemic antibiotics, antimicrobials, resistance, resistome, therapeutic adjuncts, resistance genes, susceptibility, antibacterial and drug resistance, and the findings are presented as a narrative review. The evidence indicates that a substantial proportion of patients with periodontitis harbour subgingival microbiota that are non-susceptible to at least one antibiotic used in periodontal therapy. Across the included studies, antimicrobial resistance was most frequently reported in Prevotella and Porphyromonas species, while some studies also identified virulence-associated factors in Staphylococcus aureus, a non-classical periodontal organism detected within the subgingival microbiota. Overall, current evidence indicates a high prevalence of antibiotic resistance genes in the subgingival microbiota of patients with periodontitis and highlights the ecological consequences of adjunctive antibiotic use. These findings reinforce the need to optimize antibiotic prescribing protocols within an antibiotic stewardship framework and support further metagenomic investigations to refine understanding of resistance patterns, gene-transfer mechanisms and microbiome disruption, with the aim of advancing precision-based periodontal care.
journal: Journal of cellular and molecular medicine
authors: Alghafri M, Edwards L, Moyes D, Nibali L.

title: An integrated workflow for Mycoplasma detection and removal from cell cultures and viral stocks.
abstract: Contamination of cell cultures and viral stocks with Mycoplasma is one of the most frequent and underdiagnosed problems in laboratories working with these materials, severely affecting experimental reproducibility, data reliability, and biosafety. This article presents an integrated set of robust, sensitive, and broad applicable protocols for the detection, treatment, and mitigation of Mycoplasma contamination in cellular and viral systems. Basic Protocol 1 describes a sensitive qPCR-based method for Mycoplasma detection using DNA extracted from cell cultures and viral suspensions, including clear interpretation criteria based on amplification and melting curve analyses. Basic Protocol 2 outlines a sequential antibiotic treatment strategy for eliminating Mycoplasma from contaminated cell cultures, combining different antimicrobial classes and continuous monitoring of cell viability and morphology. Basic Protocol 3 presents a complementary approach to reduce Mycoplasma burden in viral stocks through serial dilution and controlled replication, aiming to preserve viral infectivity while minimizing bacterial contaminants. Together, these protocols provide a practical and reproducible workflow that enables rapid identification of contamination, implementation of effective corrective measures, and molecular validation of decontamination. The procedures are suitable for virology, cell biology, and experimental virus production laboratories, thereby improving experimental quality and data reliability. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Introduction and Spread of West Nile Virus in Lazio, Italy, 2025: Molecular Epidemiology and Genomic Characterization.
abstract: West Nile virus (WNV) is a flavivirus whose cycle involves mosquitoes and avian hosts that occasionally may infect horses and humans as "dead-end hosts." Human infection is mostly asymptomatic, sometimes leading to febrile or neuroinvasive disease. In 2025, Italy experienced its largest epidemic with an unprecedented geographic spread (79 provinces; 52% of cases in central Italy). Here we report whole‑genome sequencing and phylogeographic analysis of 39 WNV lineage 2 samples collected in Lazio and Campania regions between July and September 2025 from humans and animal samples. All 2025 strains belonged to a Southern Italian clade that diversified around 2020, with evidence of earlier circulation in 2024. All the 2025 genomes shared a substitution that lies in envelope protein domain III (K399R), potentially influencing interactions with the viral membrane. The same mutation was previously detected in Eastern European strains, leading to the hypothesis of introductions in Italy via migratory birds from these regions. Phylogeography identified strong viral dispersal routes within Central Italy supporting a pattern of short‑range spread and local overwintering. Overall, results highlight the roles of ecological conditions and cross‑border transmission dynamics in shaping the 2025 Italian epidemic, underscoring the need for integrated genomic/ecological surveillance.

title: Cellular Senescence Dysregulates Antiviral Interferon Responses in Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis.
abstract: Patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) are highly vulnerable to respiratory virus infections, but the cellular mechanisms linking fibrotic remodeling to impaired local antiviral defense remain unclear. Here, we investigated how cellular senescence shapes the response of patient-derived healthy (HLF) and IPF primary lung fibroblasts to influenza A virus (IAV) infection. Transcriptomic profiling identified infection as the driver of gene expression in both DNA damage-induced senescent HLF and IPF fibroblasts and revealed induction of canonical antiviral pathways in both cell states. However, senescent IPF fibroblasts adopted a distinct antiviral response state characterized by a broader set of uniquely induced genes and differential coordination of antiviral transcriptional networks. Functionally, senescence increased viral titers in HLF and IPF fibroblasts, while senescent IPF fibroblasts displayed an altered inflammatory response. Network analysis linked viral response- and cell cycle-associated modules specifically to the senescent HLF infected state, whereas these programs were weaker in senescent IPF fibroblasts. Transcription factor inference identified IRF3 and STAT1 as candidate regulators of this altered antiviral state in both senescent HLF and IPF fibroblasts. Consistent with the network and transcription factor analyses, siRNA-mediated depletion of IRF3 or STAT1 significantly reduced IFN-β secretion in senescent HLF fibroblasts, whereas IPF fibroblasts showed only milder effects, indicating a disease-specific dependence on these pathways for antiviral control. Together, these findings show that the combination of cellular senescence and fibrotic fibroblast identity creates a dysfunctional antiviral state that may help explain the high susceptibility of IPF patients to virus-associated acute exacerbations and disease worsening.

title: Impact Crater Hydrothermal Systems Support Rapid Microbial Enrichment and Diverse Metabolic Potential.
abstract: Impact crater hydrothermal systems, formed after asteroid and comet impacts, have been proposed as promising habitats for life on early Earth and as key targets in the search for life on planetary bodies such as Mars, since they provide liquid water and active geochemical turnover. Because no newly formed impact structures exist on Earth, studies of microbial establishment in impact-crater hydrothermal systems have largely relied on the direct observation of fossil microbial life or its isotopic signatures. To address this limitation, we established simulated microcosm hydrothermal systems in the laboratory using melt-bearing impact breccia (suevite) from the Ries impact structure, Germany, and temperate soils. Within weeks, these systems hosted taxonomically diverse communities, with broad metabolic potential, partitioned among oxidized impact glass, endolithic suevite habitats, and sedimentary environments. Dominant taxa included thermophiles from primarily heterotrophic lineages (e.g., Meiothermus and Aneurinibacillus spp.), as well as lineages with potentially chemolithotrophic metabolisms (e.g., Brockia spp.). Metagenomic annotations identified genes associated with methane, iron, and sulfur cycling, including sulfate-reduction, indicating metabolic potential for biogeochemically relevant processes under hydrothermal conditions. These results show that impact-generated hydrothermal systems can rapidly support diverse thermophilic microbial communities with habitat-specific community structure and metabolic potential, supporting their relevance as analogue environments for studying early microbial establishment and biosignature formation in planetary impact settings.
authors: Hardy SMC, Aguilar-Pine EJ, Gulick S, Ahmad A, Baker BJ, Scott N, Aitolo G, Felton N, Cockell CS.

title: Structural and mechanistic basis of selective inhibition of the fungal-specific histone deacetylase Hos3 from the pathogenic fungus Aspergillus fumigatus.
abstract: Histone deacetylases (HDACs) are critical epigenetic regulators of fungal growth and pathogenicity and constitute promising targets for antifungal drug development. Hos3 defines a fungal-specific HDAC subclass that lacks a clear mammalian ortholog; however, the structural determinants underlying its selective inhibition remain poorly characterized. Here, we integrated x-ray crystallography with biochemical and biophysical analyses to comprehensively characterize the catalytic properties of Hos3 from the pathogenic fungus Aspergillus fumigatus (AfHos3) and its inhibition by the hydroxamate-based compound T2383. Despite high conservation of catalytic residues, AfHos3 displayed significantly higher intrinsic catalytic activity and markedly enhanced sensitivity to T2383 compared with its yeast homolog ScHos3. The crystal structure of the AfHos3-T2383 complex revealed a canonical zinc-dependent inhibitor-binding mode, coupled with a distinct, fungal-specific architecture of the substrate and inhibitor binding pocket. Structural and functional studies identified an aromatic clamp, comprising residues F371 and F443, that is indispensable for both catalytic activity and ligand stabilization. Furthermore, fungal-specific residues M538 and V205, together with structural elements loopA and α12, shape the catalytic-pocket environment and differentially influence enzymatic activity and T2383 responsiveness. Notably, the dimeric assembly of AfHos3 was associated with optimal enzymatic activity but did not influence inhibitor recognition. Collectively, these findings elucidate how fungal-specific structural elements synergize with the evolutionarily conserved catalytic core to govern selective inhibitor recognition, providing a robust structural and mechanistic framework for the rational design of fungal-selective HDAC inhibitors.
journal: Protein science : a publication of the Protein Society
authors: Yang H, Li T, Liu C, Wang X, Li T, Yang N.

title: The dynamics of gene copy-number mutations: transient changes with long-lasting consequences.
abstract: Gene copy-number mutations are frequent and prevalent yet often overlooked. While initially considered to be the neutrally evolving raw material needed for the emergence of new genes through the process of gene duplication and divergence, recent technical advances and renewed interest start to unravel a fundamentally different picture for duplications in bacteria: rather than being neutral, duplications have strong direct and indirect fitness effects, and rather than giving rise to evolutionary novelty through protein family expansions, duplications allow to transiently simply make more of the same. Tandem duplications arise at frequencies orders of magnitude higher than single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), and they collapse at an even higher rate still. Understanding the biological idiosyncrasies of copy-number mutations is pivotal to understanding their fundamental role in bacterial evolution. Having multiple copies of a gene influences its evolutionary dynamics in surprising ways, slowing down divergence, acting along with purifying selection as a force of conservation, and facilitating "bet-hedging" in fluctuating environments or under diversifying selection. Paying careful attention to structural variation in genomic sequence analyses will yield a more comprehensive understanding of bacterial evolution, especially when it comes to the emergence of novel bacterial lineages, such as human pathogens.
authors: Tomanek I, Guet CC.

title: Computational Insights Into the Conformational Dynamics of the Dengue Virus Capsid Protein.
abstract: The Dengue virus (DENV) capsid protein plays an important role in the viral lifecycle, including encapsidation of the genome, recruitment of lipid droplets, and assembly of particles. Capsid protein includes a hydrophobic pocket, which plays a central role in these functions and switches between closed and open conformations. This work studies the conformational change pathway of the capsid protein, specifically how the molecular mechanisms controlling the opening and closing of the hydrophobic pocket are controlled. By using a combination of different types of molecular dynamics simulations and enhanced sampling methods, we share insights on the structural rearrangements that play a crucial role in governing these transitions. Our results show that lipid binding modulates the accessibility of the hydrophobic pocket through environmental cues. In the open conformation, the pocket is involved in the interaction with lipids, stabilization of capsid dimers, and the promotion of immature virus assembly. Conversely, the closed conformation protects the hydrophobic pocket from the surrounding aqueous media as also preventing premature interactions in the solution phase that might disrupt protein stability. Such insights allow a deep understanding of capsid protein's conformational dynamics and represent a promising set of potent targets for antiviral strategies aiming to interfere with its functional transitions.
authors: Chaudhuri D, Giri K.

title: Evolutionary dynamics of polymorphic endogenous retrovirus insertions across wild house mouse populations.
abstract: Endogenous retroviruses represent a major source of structural variation in mammalian genomes, yet their diversity in wild populations remains poorly understood. Here, we conduct a comprehensive genome-wide survey of nonreference endogenous retrovirus insertions in wild house mice (Mus musculus) to characterize their distribution and evolutionary dynamics. Using a newly developed, computationally efficient bioinformatics pipeline, we detected and annotated over 100,000 nonreference endogenous retrovirus insertions from short-read sequencing data across 163 wild mouse genomes sampled across Eurasia. Our analyses revealed marked differences in endogenous retrovirus insertion patterns among subspecies and populations, including variation in genomic localization and population-specific polymorphisms. These heterogeneous patterns suggest distinct evolutionary histories and host-retrovirus interactions across populations. As a case study, we describe the distribution of the endogenous retrovirus-derived Fv4 gene, which is absent in the mouse referenece genome and confers resistance to murine leukemia viruses. Several lines of evidence showed that the spread of Fv4 insertions in Korean population has been driven by adaptive introgression from neighboring populations. Our study provides the first large-scale population genomic scan of endogenous retrovirus diversity in wild house mice. By cataloging extensive polymorphism in nonreference endogenous retrovirus insertions, our results highlight the role of endogenous retroviruses as dynamic genomic elements that contribute to structural variation and adaptive evolution.
authors: Yano T, Takada T, Fujiwara K, Watabe D, Hirose S, Masuya H, Endo T, Osada N.

title: Genetic principles enabling the creation of bacteria-based therapeutics.
abstract: Genetic engineering can transform bacteria (including Salmonella, Escherichia coli, Listeria, and Yersinia) from naturally occurring microbes into programmable therapeutics. Unlike passive platforms, engineered bacteria can localize to defined biological niches, sense environmental cues, regulate programmed activity in situ, interact with host tissues in novel ways, and persist for controlled periods. These properties make bacteria versatile medicines but require genetic control of precision, safety, stability, and activity under clinical conditions. Major design layers include strain or "chassis" selection, attenuation and biocontainment, control of therapeutic activity, targeting and persistence, and genotype-to-phenotype stability during manufacturing and in vivo use. These features also create liabilities, including off-target behavior, unstable expression, and evolutionary loss of function under selection. Progress depends on safe, clinically translatable chassis with integrated, bounded, and durable behaviors. This review examines the genetic design principles and liabilities of bacteria-based therapeutics, approaches used to produce clinical and near-clinical candidates, and the emergence of programmed bacteria delivering complete gene editing systems to therapeutically relevant cells.
authors: Williams AB, Groseclose TM, Holec SAM, Newman D, Mora DSO, Linke L.
