title: Maize gametophytic factor loci Ga3 through Ga11 modify reproductive barriers.
abstract: Gametophytic factor (Ga) barriers are maize (Zea mays ssp. mays) reproductive barriers controlled by molecular incompatibilities between pollen and silks. Twelve distinct Ga loci have been identified in maize populations since the first genetic evidence of a Ga barrier was reported in 1901. Of the twelve, however, only 3 have been validated by modern molecular, functional, and genomic studies: Ga1, Ga2, and Tcb1. The remaining "higher" Ga loci, spanning Ga3 to Ga11, were reported in the historical literature, but their associated phenotypes segregated in unexpected ways or disappeared over subsequent generations. Here we introduce and explore the hypothesis that the higher Ga loci represent modifiers of Ga1, Ga2, and Tcb1 barrier functions. By revisiting the historical literature, we found that barrier phenotypes fall into 2 phenotypic and functional categories. Phenotypically, the 2 categories represent healthy pollen with a silk-length effect and unhealthy pollen without a silk-length effect. These phenotypic categories were supported by genomic data; we identified candidate genes in each higher Ga locus by comparing historical linkage mapping data to the corresponding genomic sequence of maize reference line B73. We discovered candidate genes related to 2 broad pathways: pollen tube growth and RNA-directed DNA methylation. We conclude that the past century of evidence aligns with our hypothesis that maize loci Ga3 through Ga11 modify rather than directly control Ga barriers. This brief investigation provides a starting point for geneticists and evolutionary biologists to explore how strong reproductive barriers are shaped by epistatic interactions.
authors: Cryan EP, Gaut BS.

title: Spore type-specific gene expression profiles underlying development and leaf infection processes of Colletotrichum graminicola.
abstract: Colletotrichum graminicola causes significant losses of the staple crop maize worldwide. The fungus produces two distinct asexual spore types, oval and falcate conidia, which show unique processes in development and plant interaction. Based on genome resequencing of our laboratory strain (CgM2/M1.001), we investigated the gene expression profiles of oval and falcate conidia during development and early leaf infection using RNA-seq. Our results reveal specific gene expression profiles between the two spore types, indicating fundamental differences in their developmental programs that reflect different modes of infection. We identified expression patterns discriminating both conidia types from mycelium and spore type-specific ones for genes encoding transcription factors, conserved fungal developmental genes, transporters, genes of secondary metabolite clusters, and pathogenicity-related functions, including effectors and carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes). Our study shows that despite the identical genomic basis, oval and falcate conidia show unique transcriptomes across vegetative development and early plant interaction. Taking together, these results provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms determining the biology of C. graminicola and its interaction with the plant host.
authors: Rathi D, Andresen K, Daniel R, Guerreiro MA, Kretschmer M, Kronstad J, Nowrousian M, Pöggeler S, Poehlein A, Voll LM, Nordzieke DE.

title: Temporal transcriptomic and microbiome changes in American bison during experimental SARS-CoV-2 challenge.
abstract: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) continues to pose a threat to humans as well as domestic and wild animals. The variability in severity of clinical signs, the zoonotic potential, and the host-specific response to infection contribute to the persistence of circulation of disease. In wildlife species, white-tailed deer have been shown to be more permissive to infection than bovids. However, among bovids, American bison have shown a greater susceptibility than cattle. In this study, we investigate the transcriptomic response to experimental SARS-CoV-2 infection in bison over time. Substantial numbers of differentially expressed genes were identified between pre- and 2, 5, 7, 14, and 21 days post-inoculation. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes and Gene Ontology term analysis identified associations with immune response, inflammatory response, and viral infection including COVID-19. Ingenuity Pathway Analysis of the coronavirus pathway highlighted differences in signaling at days 2 versus 21 post-inoculation. We additionally examined changes in the nasal microbiome of bison over the course of experimental infection, which suggested an increase in opportunity for secondary infection causing pathogens such as Mannheimia. Collectively, this study presents a profile of bison transcriptomic response to SARS-CoV-2 infection and continues to expand our understanding of variation in host response.
authors: Petry B, Boggiatto PM, Buckley A, Cassmann ED, Sarlo Davila K, Olsen SC, Fernandes LGV, Tibbs-Cortes B, Rahic-Seggerman FM, Palmer MV, Putz EJ.

title: Genomic compartmentalization of pervasive sex-biased gene expression in the vine mealybug Planococcus ficus.
abstract: The vine mealybug, Planococcus ficus, is a globally invasive pest of grapevine and a vector of leaf roll viruses. Like other mealybugs, it reproduces through paternal-genome elimination, a sex-determination system that operates without sex chromosomes and is associated with extreme sexual dimorphism. To characterize genome organization and sex-biased expression in this species, we generated a long-read reference genome spanning 369 Mb with 23,489 annotated genes and macrosynteny conserved with the citrus mealybug, Planococcus citri. Resequencing of 4 California field individuals provided the first genome-wide baseline of nucleotide diversity for P. ficus and 132 cross-validated microsatellite markers for population monitoring. Phloem feeders secrete proteins that mediate host interaction; of 2,129 predicted secreted proteins in P. ficus, a conserved core is shared with P. citri, and each carries a lineage-specific set. Comparing adult male and female transcriptomes, we found sex-biased expression to be pervasive and skewed toward females: 41% of tested genes differed between the sexes, with female-biased genes both more numerous and showing larger fold changes. These female-biased genes were not randomly distributed but concentrated in discrete blocks of coordinately expressed, tandemly duplicated gene families, a pattern not previously described in a mealybug. Male- and female-biased secreted proteins also differed in origin, with male-biased proteins drawn from a conserved repertoire shared with P. citri and female-biased proteins spanning a more lineage-specific pool. Together, these results reveal a female-skewed, spatially clustered architecture of sex-biased expression in a mealybug that lacks sex chromosomes, and provide genomic resources for managing an invasive vineyard pest.
authors: Cantu D, Figueroa-Balderas R, Sisterson M, Minio A, Cochetel N, Naegele R, Burbank L.

title: Elevated mutation in haploid yeast driven by error-prone Rev1 polymerase.
abstract: The impact of selection vs genetic drift on the evolution of mutation patterns is unclear. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, which is predominantly diploid in nature, there is evidence that haploid cells have a higher mutation rate than diploids, suggesting that a haploid-specific mutator phenotype may have evolved due to the limited opportunity for selection to act on this rare cell type. Mutation in haploids was primarily elevated in late-replicating regions of the genome, implicating error-prone translesion synthesis (TLS) repair. Additional research has demonstrated that removing REV1, a gene responsible for initiating TLS, causes a reduction in haploid mutation rate. To assess whether the preferential use of this error-prone repair pathway by haploids explains the difference in genome-wide mutation patterns between cell types, we deleted REV1 in both diploid and haploid S. cerevisiae and estimated their mutation rates using a mutation accumulation experiment. Consistent with a previous study, we found a 50% higher single-nucleotide mutation rate in REV1+ haploids than in REV1+ diploids. Deleting the REV1 gene caused this difference to vanish, with mutation rates in haploid and diploid rev1Δ lines converging on 2.4 × 10-10. Our results suggest that the mutagenic effect of TLS is much stronger in haploids, reflecting a limited opportunity for selection to act on mutation rates in rarer cells or smaller populations. We also find evidence that REV1 plays an important role in mitochondrial genome maintenance in both cell types.
authors: Fredette-Roman J, Smith DR, Omari SB, Sharp NP.

title: Gut Pathobionts Translocate into the Liver and Reshape Intrahepatic Microbiome to Facilitate Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
abstract: The role of intrahepatic microbiome in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains elusive. In this study, we profiled matched gut and intrahepatic microbiomes from patients with HCC and healthy subjects. Compared with healthy subjects, we observed increased gut-liver microbiome similarity and a gut pathobiont-centered network in HCC, implying microbial transfer via the gut-liver axis. Consistently, HCC stool transplantation to germ-free mice impaired gut barrier function and increased bacterial load in the liver. Multisite analysis of intrahepatic microbiome and host transcriptome revealed that gut pathobionts in tumor regions positively correlate with host cytokine expression and oncogenic pathways. Administration of HCC-enriched Bacteroides fragilis disrupted gut barrier in mice and led to live bacteria translocation to the liver. B. fragilis exacerbated liver damage and promoted HCC development in mice. Mechanistically, B. fragilis surface protein enolase interacts with and activates vimentin on hepatocytes, triggering oncogenic cascades. Our findings provide insight into how gut pathobionts translocate to the liver to promote hepatocarcinogenesis.SignificanceParallel characterization of stool and intrahepatic microbiomes from patients with HCC and healthy subjects revealed gut-liver microbial transfer. The gut pathobiont B. fragilis disrupts gut barrier and translocates as live bacteria to the liver. Its surface protein enolase binds hepatocyte vimentin to activate proinflammatory and oncogenic signaling, thereby promoting liver tumorigenesis. See related commentary by Chojnacka and Grivennikov, p. 2214.
authors: Liu W, Wang X, Zhang Y, Liu J, Li M, Zhou Q, Wang L, Liu S, Chen W, Chu ESH, Lau HC, Song Q, Zhou X, Gou H, Zhang JX, Tian GB, Wang L, Li X, Peng S, Wong CC, Kuang M, Xu L, Yu J.

title: Adaptive introgression and incompatibility shape interspecific hybrid genomes in ornamental and feral Xiphophorus strains.
abstract: Adaptive introgression can propel the rapid evolution of species, but it is resisted by hybrid incompatibility. Ornamental swordtails are the result of century-old hybridization among multiple ancestries, which is a precious system for understanding interspecific gene flow under artificial selection. We combine Hidden Markov Model (HMM)-based local ancestry inference and simulations to infer the hybridization parameters. We develop new pseudolikelihood statistics for identifying candidate regions under strong adaptive introgression. Candidate regions involved in high-frequency introgressions are enriched for functions such as immunity, reproduction, survival, and life history traits. Compared with short genomic regions harboring a high frequency of the minor ancestry (>90%), which contained lower protein-coding density and lower relative genetic load in the minor parent, strong adaptive introgression occurs more often in regions of higher functional density, suggesting that highly adaptive alleles can potentially overcome the resistance by incompatibility. We further identified incompatibility loci involved in mitonuclear interactions. These findings highlight the interplay between adaptive introgression and hybrid incompatibility in shaping hybrid genomes.
authors: Geng J, Xu W, Chen G, Cai L, Peng X, Wang Z, Zhao B, Cui R.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Tyrosinase Inhibitory Activity in Taxonomically Verified Wood-Inhabiting Fungi.
abstract: Wood-inhabiting fungi represent a taxonomically and metabolically diverse group with potential as sources of bioactive compounds, yet their tyrosinase inhibitory activity remains poorly explored beyond a limited number of well-known medicinal species. In this study, we comparatively evaluated the tyrosinase inhibitory activity of cultured mycelial extracts from 49 phylogenetically verified strains of wood-inhabiting fungi belonging to the Hymenochaetales and Polyporales orders. Strains were cultivated under standardized conditions, and ethanol extracts prepared from three independent biological replicates were evaluated at concentrations of 0.1, 0.5, 1, and 5 mg/mL. Tyrosinase inhibitory activity varied markedly among the tested strains and generally increased with extract concentration. Hydnophlebia alachuana and Nigroporus vinosus showed particularly high activity, including substantial inhibition at the lowest concentration tested. These findings expand the range of wood-inhabiting fungi evaluated for tyrosinase inhibition and identify previously underexplored taxa as promising candidates for further investigation. The results provide a basis for prioritizing active fungal strains for chemical characterization and further evaluation of their tyrosinase-inhibitory potential.
authors: Lupala AS, Choi J, Kim JS, Lim YW.

title: Integrating GWAS, transcriptomics, and machine learning enables genomic prediction of grain cadmium content in malting barley.
abstract: Cadmium (Cd) contamination in arable land poses a serious threat to the production of malting barley, a cornerstone crop for the brewing industry. Excessive Cd in grains undermines malting quality by disrupting germination evenness and reducing enzymatic activity during mashing. Despite this challenge, effective predictive tools for grain Cd levels are scarce, and the genetic architecture controlling this trait remains largely elusive. Here, we employed an integrated strategy combining genome-wide association study (GWAS), RNA-seq, and machine learning across a panel of 100 barley accessions. We benchmarked five genomic prediction algorithms, performed cis-eQTL mapping, and applied multi-omics integration to nominate high-confidence candidate genes. Our GWAS uncovered 3902 Cd-associated SNPs, and the XGBoost model, trained on merely 1000 markers, achieved the highest overall predictive performance (r = 0.86). Through systematic prioritization, we identified 67 candidate metal transporter genes. Among these, HvACA8a emerged as a likely negative modulator of grain Cd loading, whereas HvAHA9 and HvYSL15 were implicated as positive regulators. Collectively, our findings establish a robust genomic prediction framework for early Cd risk evaluation in malting barley. The identified markers and candidate genes offer tangible targets for breeding low-Cd cultivars, thereby helping to safeguard the quality of raw materials destined for the malting and brewing sectors.
authors: Xu C.

title: Grapevine genotype and medium composition as drivers of culturable bacterial communities: From co-occurrence patterns to ISR against Plasmopara viticola.
abstract: Natural bacterial communities (NatComs) represent a promising frontier in sustainable crop protection, yet strain incompatibility and population instability during subculturing remain major bottlenecks in developing reliable bio-inoculants. To address these challenges, we investigated how grapevine scion genotypes with contrasting susceptibility to downy mildew, Chardonnay as susceptible and Voltis resistant, rhizocompartments (endosphere, rhizoplane, and rhizosphere soil), and growth media govern the temporal stability and assembly of culturable NatComs. Using high-throughput SYBR® Green I flow cytometry across successive subcultures, we demonstrated that NatCom stability is largely resilient to environmental shifts, with 87.5% (42/48) of consortia maintaining consistent population densities regardless of host genotype, rhizocompartment, or medium. However, 16S rRNA gene profiling revealed that host genotype exerts a primary selective force on community assembly. Chardonnay NatComs were characterized by co-occurring amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) of Enterobacter and Serratia, whereas Voltis selectively assembled taxa belonging to Achromobacter, Pseudomonas, and Serratia, frequently accompanied by key satellite genera (Rahnella, Stenotrophomonas, Lysinibacillus, and Paenibacillus). Crucially, most NatComs cultured in tryptic soy broth (TSB) significantly enhanced induced systemic resistance (ISR) in grapevine against the biotrophic oomycete Plasmopara viticola. By coupling flow cytometry with high-throughput 16S amplicon sequencing, this work provides a robust culturomics framework for screening stable microbial consortia and highlights scion-selected bacterial populations as effective drivers of induced grapevine resistance against P. viticola.
authors: Duret M, Poncelet L, Wallner A, Aziz A.

title: MC1R residue 223 is a convergent target for coat-colour lightening in domestic and wild bovids
abstract: Whether similar phenotypes evolve through shared substitutions or alternative molecular routes is a central question in evolutionary genomics. Grey-coated taurine cattle provide a powerful system for investigating this question using geographically distinct Podolian and Alpine lineages. We combined whole-genome resequencing data, complementary selection scans (hapFLK, DCMS and FST) and contrasts between grey-coated and non-grey-coated breeds to investigate the molecular evolution of grey coat colour. Selection analyses identified candidate regions associated with Podolian/steppe divergence and a prominent pigmentation-related signal on BTA18 contaning  FANCA ,  MC1R , and  SPIRE2 . Most grey breeds shared a BTA18 haplotype containing MC1R p.Arg223Trp and additional candidate variants. Tyrolean Grey cattle lacked this predominant haplotype but carried the coding duplication p.Gly220_Arg223dup, together with differentiation near the  ASIP regulatory region. Thus, different candidate coding changes affect the same MC1R residue in different cattle lineages. Haplotype comparisons supported independent Podolian and Alpine origins for p.Arg223Trp and p.Gly220_Arg223dup insertion, respectively. Ancient-genome screening yielded no validated evidence of either variant except p.Arg223Trp in medieval cattle. Comparisons across 1,108 mammalian taxa identified independent recurrence of p.Arg223Trp in the white-coated mountain goat,  Oreamnos americanus , where the derived allele was fixed in surveyed individuals (JTT-based neutral probability = 0.0043). Our findings support a model in which grey coat colour in cattle evolved through at least two partially distinct molecular routes within interacting pigmentation pathways. More broadly, they identify MC1R residue 223 as a candidate recurrent target of coat-colour lightening and illustrate how domesticated and wild lineages can repeatedly target constrained functional positions during phenotypic evolution.
authors: Nedosekov V, Yurchenko AA, Gao J, Khamzina AK, Choi J, Yudin N, Kantanen J, Larkin DM.

title: Host identity drives distinct prokaryotic and microeukaryotic microbiomes across four cold-water coral species in a near-pristine Mediterranean reef
abstract: Cabliers is the widest Mediterranean cold-water coral (CWC) mound province exhibiting active growth. This area, a ridge-like CWC mound located in the Alboran Sea (SW Mediterranean) is characterized by thriving CWC reefs and accompanying mega-benthic communities (i.e.: gorgonians, black corals, sponges) found in near-pristine conditions and undergoing an almost null human pressure. We provide in this study the first characterization of the prokaryotic and microeukaryotic microbiomes of four key deep corals structuring the Cabliers province:  Madrepora oculata ,  Desmophyllum pertusum ,  Leiopathes glaberrima, and  Acanthogorgia hirsuta . We used DNA metabarcoding of the 16S and 18S rRNA gene V4 regions via Illumina MiSeq technology to elucidate symbiotic relationships that enable the holobiont to thrive. We found that host identity was the primary driver of microbial community structure, identifying specific signature microbiomes within coral species. The octocoral  A. hirsuta showed reliance on microbes for organic matter processing such as the BD1-7 clade, while scleractinians  M. oculata and  D. pertusum displayed distinct symbionts, including  Endozoicomonas (involved in the sulfur cycle) and the SUP05 clade, respectively. We suggest that coral microbiomes are vital for the continuous growth of Cabliers, with physiological needs and host identity shaping unique microbial communities within these deep coral ecosystems.
authors: Ardanaz-Ullate A, Agazzi M, Lo Iacono C, del Campo J.

title: The HSV-1 US1 gene product targets the histone chaperone ASF1 to suppress H3K9 acetylation.
abstract: It is commonly known that the Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) manipulates host gene expression to facilitate its reproduction. HSV-1 regulates host and viral transcription through coordinated effects on transcription factors, RNA polymerase II, transcription initiation and elongation, and host chromatin dynamics. However, how HSV-1 proteins regulate host histone chaperones and histone modifications remains incompletely understood. Here, we identified a functional relationship between the HSV-1 immediate-early protein ICP22 and anti-silencing function 1 (ASF1), a histone chaperone with two human isoforms, ASF1a and ASF1b. ICP22 associated with both ASF1 isoforms in transfected and HSV-1-infected cells. Compared with wild-type HSV-1 infection, deletion of ICP22 largely restored ASF1 transcript and protein levels and attenuated the reduction in histone H3 lysine 9 acetylation (H3K9ac). Loss of either ASF1 isoform reduced basal H3K9ac levels, whereas restoration of ASF1 counteracted the ICP22-associated reduction in H3K9ac, supporting a functional link between ASF1 and H3K9ac regulation. Integrated H3K9ac CUT&Tag and RNA sequencing further showed that the presence of ICP22 was associated with reduced H3K9ac occupancy and concordant transcriptional changes at host genomic loci. ICP22 expression also reduced the detectable association between ASF1 and histone H3 under the experimental conditions examined. Notably, complete loss of either ASF1 isoform impaired the replication of both wild-type and ICP22-deleted viruses, indicating that basal ASF1 function remains necessary for efficient HSV-1 replication. Together, these findings identify ASF1-associated H3K9ac regulation as a previously unrecognized component of ICP22-mediated host chromatin remodeling and reveal that HSV-1 modulates, rather than completely inactivates, an ASF1-dependent host function required for productive infection.
authors: Wang X, Zhou Y, Xu P, Zhao Z, Hu W, Gao J.

title: Optimizing UV-B induced prophage activation for restructuring microbial aggregates and suppressing recolonization in membrane filtration systems.
abstract: Membrane biofouling remains a persistent challenge in membrane filtration systems. Although phage-mediated lysis has emerged as a promising biocontrol strategy, its effectiveness can be limited by the structural protection of microbial aggregates and hydraulic conditions. Herein, we investigated targeted UV-induced prophage activation and the resulting ecological dynamics between host and non-host bacteria within lab-scale membrane filtration platforms by using E. coli phage-host system. The optimized parameters of UV-induced prophage activation under 313 nm UV-B irradiation were set at low energy of 4.6 mW/cm2, with E. coli phage progeny reaching 1.9 × 104 PFU/mL after 2 min treatment. Transcriptome analysis showed the 1.2-fold up-regulation of bacterial redox-regulator genes (soxRS) and down-regulation of biofilm formation genes (csgC, pgaB), indicating a cellular stress response associated with prophage activation. Subsequent recolonization experiments showed altered contributions of host and non-host invasive populations (AS, 34 %), reduced microbial diversity (28 %), and restructuring of membrane-associated microbial aggregates. An experimentally informed Susceptible-Carried-Infected-Lysed (SCIL) model further reproduced the observed trends in host suppression and phage production under UV-induced stress. Moreover, in cross-flow filtration system, prophage activation was accompanied by restructuring of the extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix, with a 55 % decrease in the protein-to-polysaccharide (PN/PS) ratio and a 31.4 % reduction in aggregate thickness, together with delayed transmembrane pressure (TMP) development. These results demonstrate that controlled UV-B-induced prophage activation can act as a phage-mediated ecological disturbance that restructures resident biofilms and alters subsequent microbial recolonization, providing ecological insights and theoretical guidance for future biofouling-control strategies in wastewater membrane filtration.
authors: Zhang S, Ji C, Kong L, Yu Z, Wang C, Zhu L, Tan Y.

title: More than just a centromere: evolution of a structural supergene causing female meiotic drive in monkeyflowers.
abstract: Meiotic drivers capitalize on vulnerabilities in eukaryotic meiosis and gametogenesis to gain greater-than-equal transmission to the next generation. In most plants and animals, asymmetric female meiosis presents an arena for meiotic drive, as centromeric variants may bias their segregation to the one egg cell. Although centromeric drive is predicted to be pervasive, its mechanisms and consequences remain obscure. Here, we build on representative chromosome-scale assemblies of yellow monkeyflowers (Mimulus guttatus species complex) to compare three functionally distinct haplotypes at Meiotic Drive Locus on Chromosome 11 (MDL11). The driving D allele at MDL11 was previously shown to be centromere-containing, costly, and maintained as a balanced polymorphism in wild M. guttatus populations. D has diverged from nondrivers via at least two major rearrangements (including a hemicentric inversion creating linked arrays of centromeric satellite Cent728 separated by > 200 trapped genes), massive expansions of a novel MDL11-specific subfamily of satellite repeats (Cent728D) that increase the length of the driver chromosome by >50% over homologues, and the build-up of a 2Mb D-exclusive pericentromeric region containing ∼37 extra D-associated genes duplicated and translocated from diverse genomic sources. Differences in centromeric satellite arrays, particularly the recent expansion of Cent728D are primary candidates for generating female meiotic drive. However, substantial divergence in gene content and sequence among the three haplotypes also points to candidate genic modifiers that may enhance D drive and contribute to differences in drive-susceptibility among non-drivers. Overall, our findings support the sequential buildup of this model centromeric driver, reveal intriguing parallels with other selfish supergenes, and provide a strong platform for understanding the mechanisms of its dramatic violation of Mendelian rules.
authors: Stark-Dykema E, Finseth FR, Conner W, Plott CB, Fishman L.

title: Characterization of acetaminophen biodegradation performance and genomic features of Labrys sp. XQ-1.
abstract: Acetaminophen (N-acetyl-p-aminophenol, APAP) is a widely used pharmaceutical and an emerging micropollutant of ecological concern in aquatic environments. However, the taxonomic diversity of APAP-degrading bacteria remains poorly understood. An APAP-degrading strain, Labrys sp. XQ-1, was obtained from municipal wastewater and was capable of utilizing APAP as the sole added carbon and energy source for growth. Removal of 99% of 100 mg/L APAP was achieved within 36 h under optimal conditions (30 °C, pH 7.0, 1% NaCl). Kinetic analysis indicated that APAP degradation by strain XQ-1 was best described by a first-order model (R² = 0.988). Genome sequencing further identified a hydrolase-encoding gene, apbH, classified within the Amidase Signature (AS) superfamily. Functional assays confirmed that ApbH could catalyze the initial deacetylation of APAP to 4-aminophenol. Enzyme kinetics, molecular docking analysis, and site-directed mutagenesis supported the functional importance of Lys135, Ser210, and Ser234 in ApbH-mediated APAP transformation. Batch reactor experiments further confirmed efficient APAP removal in both mineral salt medium and simulated wastewater, with transient accumulation and subsequent disappearance of 4-AP. These findings expand the known diversity of APAP-degrading bacteria and provide new insights into its biodegradation.
authors: Wu Q, Ru Q, Ye T, Diao A, Song F, Wang C, Jiang Y, Qiu J, Mu Y, He J.

title: Comparative genomics and phenotypic characterization revealing Staphylococcus gallinarum SP6 as a promising candidate starter culture for salted shrimp paste.
abstract: Staphylococcus gallinarum is a coagulase-negative staphylococcal species commonly found in fermented foods; however, mechanisms underlying its adaptation, safety, and functional role remain poorly understood. The SP6 strain isolated from Vietnamese fermented shrimp paste was identified as halotolerant and proteolytic. Comparative genomic analysis showed that SP6 has the smallest genome (2.8 Mb; 33.1% GC content) among the compared S. gallinarum genomes that display an open pan-genome. The ability of SP6 to grow at 20% NaCl and pH 11.0 may be associated with multiple candidate genes related to osmoprotection, mechanosensing, ion transport, and pH homeostasis. Exposure to 120 mM H2O2 resulted in decreased intracellular thiol levels and differential transcript changes, with an apparent increase in katA, no significant change in bshA, and a decrease in brxA relative to the untreated control. Candidate genes were mapped to five putative metabolic routes potentially relevant to shrimp protein degradation and flavor development, including proteolysis, volatile organic compound synthesis, integration of central metabolic pathways via α-ketoglutarate, branched-chain amino acid metabolism, and esterification. No functional virulence determinants, plasmid replicons, and cytotoxicity against the HT-29 cell line were detected, and SP6 was susceptible to most tested antibiotics, supporting a favorable preliminary safety profile. SP6 produced 190.6 ± 14.7 µg/mL of γ-polyglutamic acid (γ-PGA) with antioxidant activity and reduced histamine levels by 49.2 ± 4.0% under the tested in vitro conditions. Candidate genes potentially associated with histamine metabolism were also identified, although their functional contribution to histamine removal remains to be established. These findings support further evaluation of S. gallinarum SP6 for starter-culture applications.
authors: Nguyen CT, Hoang PQ, Van Le M, Le DH, Nguyen MTQ, Nguyen DH, Ta TTT, Vu THN, Chu NH, Phi QT, Quach NT.

title: RNA recognition and cleavage in archaeal ribosome biogenesis: insights from FAU-1.
abstract: Ribosomal RNA maturation requires nucleases that recognize appropriate precursors and cleave them at defined stages of ribosome assembly. How these activities are organized in archaea remains elusive. Kawai and colleagues determined the crystal structure of the archaeal ribonuclease FAU-1, revealing a homotrimer with peripheral RNA-binding domains and a central assembly formed by its C-terminal domains. The structure identifies similarities to the RNA-recognition region of bacterial ribonuclease (RNase) E while exposing substantial differences in overall architecture. Subsequent work assigned FAU-1 to the RNase W family and demonstrated a catalytic role for its C-terminal domain. Together, these studies illustrate how related RNA-recognition elements can operate within distinct nuclease architectures. They also raise questions about the relationship between oligomerization, substrate selection and catalytic activation. Resolving these questions will require analysis of physiological RNA substrates and their associated proteins, connecting the structures of individual processing enzymes to the assembly of functional ribosomes.
authors: Ito T.

title: Characterization of influenza A(H3N2) viruses detected on a pig farm in Russia in 2017-2018.
abstract: Pigs serve as "mixing vessels" for influenza A viruses, facilitating interspecies transmission and genomic reassortment. Here, we report characterization of influenza A(H3N2) viruses isolated from suckling and weaned piglets at one commercial pig farm in the Irkutsk Region, Russia, in August 2017 and May 2018. Full-genome sequencing revealed that their HA and NA segments clustered with human seasonal A(H3N2) strains circulating in 2002-2004, while the internal gene cassette was derived from A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses. PB1 and PB2 segments of viruses isolated in 2017 and 2018 belonged to different clusters of the A(H1N1)pdm09 lineage suggesting possible additional reassortment event. Hemagglutination inhibition assay and antigenic cartography demonstrated significant antigenic drift, with the swine isolates forming a discrete cluster ≥ 4 antigenic units distant from human seasonal A(H3N2) strains registered in 2007-2024. The viruses accumulated key substitutions, including HA1-A138S, associated with swine adaptation, yet retained full susceptibility to oseltamivir and zanamivir. Repeated detection of closely related reassortants at the same farm suggests their sustained circulation either within the farm or outside it, leading to reintroductions. Further studies are needed to understand the underlying mechanisms of this observation. Thus, our study identified a new genetic lineage of human-origin influenza A(H3N2) viruses in swine in Russia and highlighted once again that seasonal influenza viruses that stopped circulating in the human population long ago might remain undetected for years within swine and/or other unknown intermediate hosts, undergoing independent evolution and generating antigenically distinct variants that may evade pre-existing human immunity.
authors: Danilenko AV, Svyatchenko SV, Bragina MK, Goncharova NI, Kolosova NP, Ivanova KI, Gudymo AS, Danilchenko NV, Perfilieva ON, Maksyutova AV, Onkhonova GS, Susloparov IM, Marchenko VY.

title: Enterovirus A71 upregulates and recruits host ATF3 to promote viral replication.
abstract: To hijack cellular resources, certain viruses such as EV-A71, induce the shutoff of cellular transcription and translation systems globally for establishing infection. However, our previous studies have shown that the translation efficiency of series host proteins is upregulated during EV-A71 infection potentially, including activating transcription factor 3 (ATF3). Here, we validated in RD cells that ATF3 is mount up during EV-A71 infection significantly via increasing mRNA and cap-independent translation. Our findings highlight the critical role of ATF3 in EV-A71 replication: during EV-A71 infection, ATF3 trans-locates to the cytoplasm besides upregulated, where it interacts with the viral 5' untranslated region (5'UTR) and promotes the replication of viral genome RNA. Intriguingly, the nuclear localization signal (NLS) of ATF3 also contributes to this process, including binding to the viral genome and facilitating viral replication.
journal: The international journal of biochemistry & cell biology
authors: Deng Z, Li Z, Wu Y, Zhuang J, Li H, Tan J, Qiao W.

title: Carbapenemases in Germany in 2025 and the impact of changing the isolate submission criteria of the German National Reference Centre for multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria.
abstract: BackgroundThe German National Reference Centre for multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria at the Department of Medical Microbiology of the Ruhr University Bochum offers the free service of carbapenemase detection or confirmation to German laboratories in order to obtain molecular surveillance data on the spread of carbapenemases in Germany. To prevent capacity overload, the NRC had to sharpen the submission criteria in march 2025 to achieve a better pre-selection of isolates submitted and eventually reduce the number of isolates analyzed.MethodsSpecies identification was performed using MALDI-TOF MS. Carbapenemase detection was performed using a set of phenotypic assays and PCRs targeting the common carbapenemase genes in Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii, followed by sequencing of PCR products for allele identification and Illumina whole genome sequencing when indicated.ResultsCompared to 2024, the number of isolates submitted for carbapenemase detection decreased by 18.6% to 8307. Carbapenemase detections on the other hand increased by 13% to 6.058. The major carbapenemases in Enterobacterales were OXA-48, OXA-244, NDM-5, NDM-1, KPC-2 and VIM-1, while in P. aeruginosa, VIM-2 predominated and OXA-23 and OXA-72 were the most prevalent carbapenemases identified in A. baumannii. The proportion of carbapenemase-positive isolates increased significantly, especially for isolates of P. aeruginosa and Enterobacter cloacae complex.ConclusionsThe sharpened submission criteria led to a drop in isolates sent for analysis in 2025. Nonetheless, the number of carbapenemase-positive isolates increased significantly compared to 2024, indicating that the changed criteria had no negative impact on sensitivity, but a positive effect on specificity for carbapenemase production. This alarming observation indicates that carbapenemases are increasingly spreading in Germany.
journal: International journal of medical microbiology : IJMM
authors: Pfennigwerth N, Möller S, Höfken LM, Javadi S, Gatermann SG.

title: Site-Directed Mutagenesis in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
abstract: Precise manipulation of the mycobacterial genome is required to study the effect of specific mutations without confounding influences from the diverse genetic backgrounds in clinical isolates. This is particularly important for interrogating gene function and drug resistance mechanisms, where background mutations may enhance or suppress the effects of a mutation of interest. Here, two targeted site-directed mutagenesis approaches, two-step allelic exchange using a suicide vector and oligonucleotide-mediated recombineering, are described and compared for introducing defined mutations into an isogenic Mycobacterium tuberculosis background. Two-step allelic exchange uses a suicide vector lacking a mycobacterial origin of replication and carrying a mutated DNA fragment, selectable markers such as sacB for sucrose sensitivity, lacZ for blue-white screening, and antibiotic resistance genes (kan or hyg). The process involves generating the mutated fragment via a multi-step polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or synthesis, cloning it into the vector, electroporating it into M. tuberculosis, and selecting single-crossover (SCO) integration events using antibiotic resistance and blue-white colony screening. This is followed by counter-selection with sucrose and X-gal to eliminate bacteria carrying the wild-type sequence. This method ensures stable, unmarked mutations but is time-consuming and labor-intensive. Recombineering uses a recombinase-expressing plasmid, such as pJV75amber expressing Che9c gp61 recombinase under an inducible acetamidase promoter, together with a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) oligonucleotide to introduce precise mutations. Transformants are selected on appropriate antibiotics and confirmed by PCR and Sanger sequencing. This approach is simpler, faster, and more cost-effective, but may be limited by low transformation efficiency, the need for fresh competent cells, and variable efficiency depending on the genomic region and oligonucleotide design. Together, two-step allelic exchange and recombineering offer complementary strategies for introducing defined mutations into M. tuberculosis. Both methods enable experimental validation of mutations, such as variants associated with gene function and drug resistance.
authors: Otum CC, Niemand N, Streicher EM, Van Rie A, Warren RM, Klopper M.

title: Engineering a production platform for the potent antipseudomonal antibiotic mureidomycin A by reprogramming the pacidamycin biosynthetic gene cluster.
abstract: BackgroundUridyl peptide antibiotics display potent activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a pathogen causing severe nosocomial infections. The four subclasses-mureidomycins, pacidamycins, napsamycins, and sansanmycins-inhibit the underexplored bacterial target phospho-MurNAc-pentapeptide translocase (MraY). Structurally, these compounds contain a 3'-deoxyuridine linked to a central diaminobutyric acid. The latter is situated within a pseudo tetra- or pentapeptide moiety, assembled by a non-ribosomal peptide synthetase machinery. The subclasses are distinguished by variations in the incorporated amino acids. Native producer strains typically synthesize numerous different uridyl peptide antibiotics in low yields. Since the pacidamycin gene cluster displays higher overall yields compared to the napsamycin cluster in identical expression systems, we aimed to reprogram it into a selective production platform for the highly bioactive mureidomycin A. This approach is intended to streamline isolation processes and support hit-to-lead optimization.ResultsStreptomyces albus J1074 was identified as the most promising host for heterologous expression of the pacidamycin gene cluster. Subsequently, media screening and precursor feeding were conducted, and regulators of closely related gene clusters were introduced into the heterologous host. The overexpression of the NpsM regulator of the napsamycin gene cluster increased production significantly. Next, the pacidamycin gene cluster was engineered to produce the more potent mureidomycins. Variable positions of the peptide moiety were individually targeted by domain or module swaps of the non-ribosomal peptide synthetase machinery. More specifically, these were replaced by homologs of the napsamycin gene cluster, resulting in strains mainly producing sansanmycin A or mureidomycin A. Promoter engineering enhanced mureidomycin A production in the final strain, correlating with increased transcription levels in RNA sequencing experiments on an intermediate strain harboring the same promoters.ConclusionsHybrid uridyl peptide antibiotic gene clusters were constructed by genetically engineering the pacidamycin cluster, demonstrating the versatility of these clusters. While the native pacidamycin cluster only produced pacidamycin D and S, the final strain yields the more bioactive mureidomycin A and Met-pacidamycin 5. Additionally, sansanmycin A (syn. Met-pacidamycin 4) can be isolated from an intermediate construct of this study. This expands the access to different analogs and highlights further engineering potential, which will facilitate the future development of these promising antibiotics.
authors: Koutsandrea PH, Sonnengrün R, Hauck N, Kulik A, Harbig T, Daniel JM, Nieselt KK, Goss RJM, Schneider T, Mordhorst S, Gross H, Gust B.

title: A beneficial root endophyte buffers natural variation in pathogen susceptibility across Arabidopsis accessions.
abstract: Host genetic diversity shapes pathogen susceptibility within plant populations, raising the question of whether beneficial root microbes can buffer these differences. The fungal root endophyte Serendipita indica (Si) promotes plant growth and can mitigate disease caused by the pathogen Bipolaris sorokiniana (Bs). Here, we assessed how natural host genetic variation influences Si-mediated protection against Bs in Arabidopsis thaliana. We screened 47 A. thaliana accessions for susceptibility to Bs with and without Si colonization and performed phenotypic, transcriptomic, and comparative genomic analyses of two genetically and geographically proximate Swedish accessions, T510 and T530, that differed strongly in Bs colonization. Si conferred consistent protection against Bs across all accessions, despite variation in baseline susceptibility and immune-gene content. T510 and T530 differed in Bs colonization, disease symptoms, transcriptional responses, and immune-gene repertoires, including presence-absence variation of the TIR-NLR gene ISI. T530 lacks ISI, and mutation of ISI in Col-0 increased Bs susceptibility, demonstrating that ISI contributes to root immunity. However, Si-mediated protection was retained in the absence of ISI, demonstrating that ISI is not required for this protective effect. Beneficial fungal endophytes can thus buffer phenotypic consequences of natural variation in pathogen susceptibility, stabilizing disease outcomes across genetically diverse plant populations.
authors: Peltz N, Armbruster L, Stephens C, Joisten-Rosenthal V, Thomsen T, Yan AW, Dunken N, Granado R, Kopriva S, de Meaux J, Langen G, Koprivova A, Usadel B, Zuccaro A.

title: From discovery to engineering: revealing and optimizing the indigoids biosynthesis by FMO from Indigofera tinctoria.
abstract: IntroductionIndigo-producing plants have been used for millennia as natural dyes and traditional medicines. Despite evolutionary divergence, these species converge on a conserved indigo biosynthesis pathway, yet the molecular basis for differences in catalytic efficiency remains largely unknown.ObjectivesThis study aimed to identify and characterize the key genes involved in indigoid biosynthesisfrom Indigofera tinctoria, and to elucidate the structural determinants underlying their catalytic properties.MethodsWe performed transcriptome mining and functional screening of candidate genes fromI. tinctoria, followed by enzyme kinetic characterization, substrate specificity profiling, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using the catalytically competent state, alanine scanning mutagenesis, and metabolic engineering through co-expression and co-cultivation strategies in Escherichia coli.ResultsThree genes, Flavin-containing monooxygenase (ItFMO),Tryptophan synthase α-subunit (ItTSA), and Indole synthase(ItINS), were identified and functionally validated. ItFMO exhibited higher catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km = 0.22 ± 0.05 s⁻1*mM⁻1) toward indole than other plant FMOs tested, and converted 16 substituted indoles into variously colored indigoids. When 2-oxindole was supplied, ItFMO co-produced indirubin (∼70% of total pigments) via condensation of enzymatically generated indoxyl with 2-oxindole. Co-expression of ItFMO with E. coli TnaA (Tryptophanase) yielded the highest indigo titer (41.27 ± 0.84 mg/L), followed by ItINS (30.54 ± 0.33 mg/L) and ItFMO alone (27.58 ± 0.19 mg/L), whereas ItTSA severely reduced production (5.68 ± 0.20 mg/L). Co-cultivation of the two strains achieved a 2.7-fold increase over the monoculture, with a titer of 60.03 ± 0.82 mg/L. MD simulations and alanine scanning identified Q51, Y160, K212, S213, F373, and N427 as critical residues governing ItFMO catalysis, and which were authenticated by site-directed mutagenesis.ConclusionOur findings establish a mechanistic basis for understanding FMO-mediated indigo formation in plants and provide a structural insight for engineering plant-derived enzymes in microbial systems.
authors: Liu C, Zhang D, Zhang M, Chang S, Cheng M, Lou Y, Tan H.

title: Effect of environmental factors on attachment of Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus to polypropylene microplastics.
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) serve as substrates for bacterial colonization, facilitating pathogen transport in aquatic environments. Therefore, this study investigated the attachment of Escherichia coli (E. coli) and Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) to five MP polymers and evaluated the effects of pH, temperature, hydrodynamic conditions, natural organic matter (NOM), and salinity using polypropylene (PP)-MPs. PP-MPs supported the highest bacterial attachment efficiencies due to their hydrophobicity (water contact angle = 98.4°) and weak negative surface charge (zeta potential = -16.6 mV). Bacterial attachment decreased as pH increased (4.5-8.6) because of increased electrostatic repulsion. Increasing temperature (20 to 35 °C) decreased E. coli attachment, possibly through reduced curli production and increased motility, whereas it increased S. aureus attachment, which may be attributed to enhanced EPS production and surface hydrophobicity. Under varying hydrodynamic conditions, E. coli attachment peaked at 150 rpm, whereas S. aureus attachment remained high under both static and high-mixing conditions. Increasing NOM concentrations suppressed E. coli attachment through enhanced electrostatic repulsion but increased S. aureus attachment owing to the charge heterogeneity of its cell envelope. Elevated NaCl concentrations promoted bacterial attachment by screening electrostatic repulsion, consistent with the extended Derjaguin-Landau-Verwey-Overbeek theory, although this effect was less pronounced for S. aureus due to its high attachment. E. coli attachment decreased from 79.72% in sterilized water to 17.10% in lake water and 4.87% in WWTP effluent, whereas S. aureus retained high attachment efficiencies of 78.26% and 90.14%, respectively. These findings highlight how environmental conditions and species-specific traits collectively govern MP-associated bacterial attachment.
authors: Yoon S, Kim N, Lee M, Kim HO, Lim KS, Ha SJ, Oh C, Park JA.

title: Genomic structural equation modeling elucidates the shared genetic architecture of vascular ageing.
abstract: BackgroundVascular ageing is a central driver of age-related cardiovascular morbidity and systemic ageing, encompassing arterial stiffening, hemodynamic alterations, subclinical atherosclerosis, and vascular calcification. The shared genetic architecture underlying these multidimensional phenotypes remains incompletely characterized.MethodsWe applied genomic structural equation modeling (Genomic SEM) to GWAS summary statistics for five vascular-ageing traits in European-ancestry populations-arterial stiffness, pulse pressure, carotid artery thickness, coronary artery calcification, and carotid plaque. A common-factor model defined a latent vascular-ageing phenotype, followed by functional annotation, Bayesian fine-mapping, cross-tissue sCCA-TWAS with colocalization, pathway and cell-type enrichment, partitioned heritability, and polygenic risk score analyses.ResultsThe common-factor model showed good fit (CFI = 0.998; SRMR = 0.047). The resulting multivariate GWAS identified 372 independent lead SNPs across 249 genomic risk loci, including three loci newly implicated in vascular ageing. Bayesian fine-mapping prioritized 49 high-confidence causal SNPs, and transcriptomic prioritization (TWAS-FOCUS-colocalization) yielded 69 putative causal genes. Three-CDH13, FES, and CCN3-converged across MAGMA, fine-mapping, and TWAS evidence, implicating endothelial adhesion, vascular inflammation, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Enrichment analyses highlighted the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, circulatory system processes, and extracellular matrix organization, implicating fibroblast-stromal compartments, smooth muscle cells, endothelial cells, and monocytes/macrophages as candidate cellular substrates.ConclusionThis study provides the first multivariate genomic characterization of vascular ageing using Genomic SEM, uncovering loci newly implicated in vascular ageing, convergent putative causal genes, and cellular substrates that link vascular biology to systemic ageing and may inform precision prevention of age-related vascular disorders.
authors: Liu Y, Ma Y, Liu Y, Sun Z.

title: Persistence of viral full-length genomic RNA and replication-associated RNA transcripts and proteins in sheep tissues following acute Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus infection.
abstract: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is a tick-borne RNA virus responsible for a severe hemorrhagic disease in humans. In contrast, the virus appears to cause only a brief viremia without overt clinical signs in animals such as livestock, following which the infection is traditionally assumed to end with complete viral clearance. Here, we challenge this prevailing view by reporting the recovery of full-length viral genomic RNA sequences from tissues of CCHFV-infected sheep long after the resolution of acute viremia. While viral RNA persistence in these tissues was largely characterized by a lack of extensive viral replication, we detected the sporadic presence of replication-associated viral RNA transcripts and viral proteins. These findings suggest that the biology of CCHFV in animals extends well beyond an acute infection. The possibility that the virus can transition into a dormant state, with potential for reactivation to resume gene expression or replication, a phenomenon documented in other RNA viruses, warrants further investigation.
authors: Li H, Moffat E, Handel K, Nebroski M, Sullivan D, Dufresne A, Embury-Hyatt C, Lung O, Pickering BS.

title: Persistent viral carriage of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus in canine: A potential canine-to-human transmission event in a family cluster.
abstract: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is a tick-borne viral disease with a substantial case-fatality rate. Here, we reported a family cluster of SFTS cases in Southeast China. The index case was a 57-year-old man, whose son and wife subsequently developed SFTS-compatible symptoms at two and three days after his onset, respectively. All three cases were laboratory-confirmed for SFTS, and retrospectively reported close care to a sick golden retriever prior to symptom onset. In contrast, the other two family members without such canine exposure remained serologically and clinically uninfected. All three cases denied a tick-biting history before illness onset. Subsequent testing confirmed SFTS virus (SFTSV) infection in the golden retriever, and SFTSV was also detected in a tick collected from the dog. Longitudinal viral screening of serial canine samples revealed persistent SFTSV shedding: viral positivity was sustained for 23 days in nasal swabs and urethral swabs, 27 days in serum samples, and at least 30 days in rectal swabs following its symptom onset. Genomic analysis showed near-identical SFTSV sequences from the index case and the infected dog, with identities of 99.94% for the small segment, 100% for the medium segment, and 99.98% for the large segment. This study reveals prolonged SFTSV shedding in infected canine, suggests a plausible risk of canine-to-human SFTSV transmission, and highlights the potential role of dogs in the spread and evolution of SFTSV.
authors: Ren J, Gu S, Liu Y, Yang Y, Shi X, Luo X, Li J, Zhu L, Li S, Yao H, Tian J, Sun J.

title: A High-Sensitivity RPA/Cas12a Assay for Rapid Detection of the Select Agent Ralstonia solanacearum R3b2.
abstract: Ralstonia solanacearum is a globally distributed, soil-borne species complex that causes bacterial wilt in many economically important crops. Race 3 biovar 2 (R3b2) is a cold-tolerant, highly aggressive subgroup within this complex that is responsible for an estimated $1 billion in annual global losses. Because R3b2 remains exotic to North America, it is classified as a USDA Select Agent due to its high potential to devastate U.S. solanaceous crops and ornamental industries. However, current diagnostic methods for this pathogen involve trade-offs among cost, sensitivity, specificity, and ease of use, particularly for point-of-care (POC) detection in field settings. CRISPR-based detection platforms have recently emerged as promising tools for high-sensitivity POC diagnostics. Here we developed an isothermal recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA)/Cas12a assay for specific, sensitive and rapid detection of R3b2. By targeting a genomic region associated with the cool-virulence phenotype, the assay reliably differentiates R3b2 from plant hosts and other diverse R. solanacearum strains. Incorporation of a dual-guide RNA system and an 8-mer single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) fluorescent reporter further improved sensitivity and reduced detection time. Using dilution series of R3b2-spiked Pelargonium DNA extracts, the assay detected as few as 4 CFU per reaction. To facilitate POC applications, the system was adapted into a one-pot, contamination-resistan¬t format compatible with portable fluorescence readers such as Genie III device and P51 viewer. By improving both sensitivity and portability, this assay enhances current diagnostic capabilities and, pending validation in real-world conditions, supports early surveillance efforts aimed at preventing the introduction of R3b2 into the United States.
authors: Ostlund S, Yang H, Newberry E, Costanzo S, Yang Y.

title: Multifaceted HPV16 E2 as a potential therapeutic target for cervical cancer and beyond.
abstract: Human papillomavirus (HPV) can cause a variety of epithelial lesions, including the malignant proliferation of host cells and even cervical cancer. HPV E2 can play an important role in regulating viral gene expression, viral replication and transcription, and also can participate in the isolation of viral genome during cell division. HPV16 E2 protein is highly expressed in low-differentiated cervical lesion cells, but decreased or disappeared with the increase of cervical lesion grade. As both the initiation protein for DNA replication and the major transcriptional regulator for HPV16 gene expression, E2 protein may play a key role in the viral life cycle. HPV16 E2 protein as a sequence specific DNA binding protein, can bind with the specific DNA recognition sequence on the promoters of E6 and E7 oncogenes, and then inhibit the transcription and expression of E6 and E7 oncogenes, thus inducing cell apoptosis and suppressing tumor formation. Therefore, therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring or enhancing HPV16 E2 function may hold promise for the prevention and treatment of HPV-related cancers, including (i) gene-therapy-mediated E2 restoration; (ii) direct delivery of E2 protein; (iii) E2 stabilization through modulation of interacting pathways (e.g., TopBP1, Brd4); and (iv) E2-based therapeutic vaccines. These approaches may exert antitumor effects by repressing E6/E7 oncogenes, regulating the cell cycle, inhibiting cell proliferation, and inducing apoptosis.
authors: Mo X, Wang H, Wang Z, Xiao Y, Tang S, Li L.

title: Evaluations of significant loci associated with mammographic breast density in Korean women.
abstract: BackgroundMammographic density is a strong risk factor for breast cancer and comprises four quantitative phenotypes: breast area (BA), dense area (DA), non-dense area (NDA), and percent density (PD). Although genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have identified loci associated with mammographic density, most evidence has been derived from populations of European ancestry. Therefore, we aimed to assess genetic variants associated with breast density phenotypes in Korean women.MethodsWe conducted a GWAS of BA, DA, NDA, and PD phenotypes in 3,701 women. Association analyses were performed under additive, dominant, and recessive genetic models, and genome-wide significance was defined as P - 8. Loci significantly associated with each phenotype were identified using linear regression models after adjusting for age, body mass index, ancestry-informative principal components, and reproductive factors. Genome-wide significant variants from the additive-model GWAS were further investigated using Functional Mapping and Annotation to define genomic risk loci, annotate candidate variants, and map candidate genes.ResultsIn 3,701 women, the mean age at mammographic density assessment was 40.3 years. Mean BA, DA, NDA, and PD were 87.6 cm², 30.7 cm², 56.9 cm², and 37.9%, respectively. Three associated loci were identified at 6q25.1 (rs2046210), 8p11.23 (rs13365225), and 22q13.2 (rs78694459). For DA, two associated loci were identified at 6q25.1 (rs12665607) and 22q13.1 (rs17002034). For NDA, one associated locus was observed at 8p11.23 (rs13365225), and for PD, one associated locus was observed at 6q25.1 (rs12665607). The most consistent signal was observed at 6q25.1, which was associated with BA, DA, and PD phenotypes and mapped to CCDC170/ESR1. The 8p11.23 locus, mapped to KCNU1, was associated primarily with BA and NDA phenotypes, whereas the 22q13 locus, mapped to MKL1, was associated with BA and DA phenotypes. Functional annotation showed that most candidate variants were intronic or intergenic, with only a small number of exonic non-synonymous variants in CCDC170 and KCNU1. Stratified analysis by age also showed comparable results.ConclusionOur findings indicate that mammographic density phenotypes are influenced by a limited number of recurrent loci: 6q25.1, 8p11.23, and 22q13 in Korean women. All three loci identified in this study were previously associated with breast density and breast cancer, validating our findings and suggesting partial genetic overlap between mammographic density and breast cancer risk. Further research is warranted to clarify the genetic basis of breast density and its relationship with breast cancer risk in the Korean population, including larger studies and functional investigations of the implicated loci.
authors: Jeon S, Kim HN, Jang Y, Yoon J, Ryu S, Park B, Chang Y.

title: Strain engineering of Aspergillus species for industrial enzymes bioproduction: a comprehensive review.
abstract: Filamentous fungi of the genus Aspergillus, because of their exceptional secretory capacity and metabolic versatility have been extensively applied in traditional food fermentation and industrial biotechnology for production of diverse bioproducts. Their history of domestication and industrial application has enabled major progress in enzyme production; however, challenges associated with the filamentous growth and strain engineering for future biomanufacturing development still remain. This review summarizes the advances across the spectrum of strain-improvement methodologies, from classical mutagenesis, protoplast fusion, genome shuffling, and adaptive laboratory evolution to the modern era of CRISPR enabled genome editing, synthetic biology, and systems-level metabolic engineering. Previous reviews have primarily focused on individual Aspergillus species, specific industrial products or particular strain improvement approaches. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of classical and modern strain engineering technologies and industrial scale up across a wide range of Aspergillus species for industrial enzyme production. In particular, emerging non-GMO evolution tools such as atmospheric and room temperature plasma (ARTP) mutagenesis, and modern molecular biotechnology coupled with microdroplet-based ultrahigh-throughput screening, now allow the researchers to generate and screen a large number of Aspergillus species mutants with single-cell precision. The discovery of high-performance strains with enhanced secretion, stress tolerance, substrate utilization, and favorable enzymatic profiles for food and bioprocessing applications has been accelerated by the strain innovations. Collectively, these advances establish A. oryzae and the related species as increasingly reliable, scalable, and programmable hosts that can meet the biomanufacturing requirements of future circular and sustainable bioeconomies.
authors: Ullah I, Zhang Z, Geng D, Zhou Q, Zou Y, Xu B, Zhang C, Xing XH.

title: Virulence and genetic determinants of Staphylococcus spp. in human mastitis: a prevalence study.
abstract: BackgroundLactational mastitis is a common inflammatory breast disease affecting breastfeeding women and is associated with Staphylococcus spp. Increasing antimicrobial resistance and virulence among these pathogens complicate treatment and emphasize the need for accurate laboratory diagnostic methods. This study investigated the microbiological profile, antimicrobial resistance, and virulence characteristics of Staphylococcus spp. isolated from lactational mastitis and evaluated the correlation between phenotypic and molecular detection of major virulence and methicillin-resistance determinants.Methods and resultsA cross-sectional study was conducted in central Gujarat, India, using 180 human milk samples collected from 150 women with lactational mastitis and 30 healthy lactating controls. Somatic cell count, bacterial isolation, biochemical identification, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, haemolysis, slime production, biofilm assays, polymerase chain reaction detection of the hla, icaA, and mecA genes, and phylogenetic analysis were performed. All mastitis samples exhibited somatic cell counts exceeding 1,000 cells/µL, whereas healthy controls remained below this threshold (p ConclusionsElevated somatic cell count effectively distinguished mastitis from healthy controls. The high prevalence of virulent and antimicrobial-resistant Staphylococcus spp., particularly mecA-positive isolates, underscores the need for continuous surveillance, targeted antimicrobial therapy, and cost-effective phenotypic screening to support routine clinical diagnosis and epidemiological monitoring.
authors: Patel M, Gondkar P, Patel K.

title: Influenza A Virus at the Exhibition Swine-Human Interface in the USA.
abstract: IntroductionIn the USA, zoonotic influenza A virus (IAV) transmission occurs frequently in youth who exhibit swine at agricultural competitions, presenting an ongoing pandemic risk. However, active surveillance in this high-risk human population is lacking.MethodsTo address this gap, we enrolled 711 youth participants at nine swine exhibitions during 2019-2021 and collected 700 nasal swabs and 400 serum samples. We assessed the neutralizing antibody titers of enrollees against eight influenza A H1 and H3 variant candidate vaccine viruses (CVVs) recommended by the World Health Organization.ResultsWe found that the highest neutralizing titers are not necessarily associated with the specific viruses which are most prevalent in exhibition swine during the same time period. The geometric mean titers of the cohort were low against the Cluster IV-A (clade 3.1990.4.a) CVV, which we determined to be the most prevalent HA lineage circulating in exhibition swine during 2020-2021 based on simultaneous IAV surveillance in swine (n = 430 genome sequences).ConclusionsThe relatively low neutralizing antibody levels in this high-risk population with intense exposure to livestock indicates that sustained outreach and monitoring is needed. Continued monitoring of IAVs in both swine and humans can inform viral risk assessments and provide considerations for candidate vaccine virus selection.
authors: McBride DS, Nelson MI, Cochran HJ, Nicholson HN, Ohl EM, Jang Y, Zanders N, Cui D, Di H, Davis CT, Barnes JR, Wilson MM, Kirby MK, Bowman AS, Nolting JM.

title: Genome-wide fluctuating selection under demographic cycling in Icelandic rock ptarmigan
abstract: Understanding how natural populations adapt to continuously shifting environments is central to evolutionary biology. Multi-annual population cycles impose temporally varying selective pressures, yet disentangling the resulting genomic signals from those of sustained directional selection and genetic drift has been challenging due to a lack of high-resolution temporal data. Here we investigate the genomic consequences of demographic cycling in a population of rock ptarmigan (Lagopus muta) from northeastern Iceland. We analyzed whole-genome sequences from 91 individuals sampled over an 11-year period, encompassing two population peaks (2010 and 2018) and two troughs (2007 and 2013). Testing allele frequency change at each SNP against a null model of drift and sampling, we identified candidate loci and grouped them by correlation of their temporal trajectories. Cluster trajectories fluctuated through time, and two were closely correlated with the regional census, one significantly tracking the demographic cycle, while a smaller set changed monotonically in a manner consistent with sustained directional selection. Each cluster contained loci distributed across many chromosomes, indicative of genome-wide responses to selection. The most strongly fluctuating loci overlapped candidate genes of possible functional relevance, most notably CTNNA2 (Catenin Alpha-2), which is associated with startle response and anxiety-like behaviors and may relate to predator avoidance. Our findings indicate that fluctuating selection comprises much of the temporal genomic response in this natural population, and suggest that multi-annual demographic cycles can drive rapid and widespread allele frequency change, highlighting the value of temporal genomics for clarifying the interplay between demography and natural selection in wild populations.
authors: Rêgo A, Squires TE, Wei W, Rödin-Mörch P, Höglund J, Magnússon KP.

title: Biosynthetic additive manufacturing through mycelium-bacteria consortia
abstract: Lignocellulosic biomass is the most abundant renewable raw material on Earth, yet its structural and carbon-storage potential remains unrealized: microbial decomposition returns stored carbon to the atmosphere before it can be harnessed as a durable material. Distinct microbial processes, such as biosynthesis and biomineralization, offer a natural counterpoint, converting organic carbon into mechanically robust, persistent materials such as polymers and minerals. Here, we establish a biosynthetic additive manufacturing strategy through mycelium–bacteria consortia, by coupling fungal self-assembly with bacterial biomineralization inside fabricated three-dimensional scaffolds derived from lignocellulosic biomass.  Trametes versicolor forms a continuous living mycelial network that serves as both a structural template and a transport pathway, guiding the spatial colonization of  Sporosarcina pasteurii and enabling volumetric calcium carbonate deposition throughout the scaffold interior, overcoming the surface-limited mineralization of conventional microbial systems. Integration with helicoidal Bouligand architectures translates microscale mineral reinforcement into macroscale performance, increasing compressive Young’s modulus by 7-14-fold and ultimate strength by 5-fold relative to unmineralized conventional mycelium-based living composites. The living mycelial network also enables autonomous self-healing and modular self-assembly through hyphal bridging without external adhesives or energy input. This work establishes a scalable route for converting and upcycling transient biomass carbon into durable living structural materials for sustainable construction.

title: Fasting plasma fructose is associated with postprandial ethanol levels and mitochondrial dysfunction: linking fasting fructose to MASLD
abstract: High dietary fructose consumption is a recognized risk factor for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), but the clinical relevance of fasting fructose levels remains unexplored. This study investigated gut microbiota and hepatic transcriptional alterations associated with fasting fructose levels and their potential link to MASLD. We analyzed data from a subset of 49 morbidly obese individuals enrolled in the prospective BARIA cohort. Fasting plasma fructose levels were significantly higher in individuals with MASLD and were associated with polyol pathway downregulation and lipogenic gene upregulation. Fasting fructose also positively correlated with postprandial plasma ethanol increase, suggesting enhanced microbial endogenous production and/or altered ethanol catabolism, the latter supported by suppressed hepatic alcohol dehydrogenase gene expression. In addition, fasting fructose was associated with fecal gut microbiota alterations, including significant shifts in beta diversity and correlations with specific bacterial species. At the transcriptomic level, elevated fasting fructose was linked to impaired mitochondrial energy metabolism and antioxidant defense, signatures associated with MASLD-related metabolic disruption. In conclusion, our data indicate that fasting plasma fructose reflects dietary intake rather than endogenous production and increased levels are associated with metabolic and microbiota changes linked to MASLD. Although not intended to replace established glycemic markers, our findings suggest that fasting fructose may provide complementary insights into the metabolic state of the liver and MASLD-related dysregulation, supporting its potential as a MASLD risk biomarker.

title: Whole genome duplication uncouples cell volume scaling from mitochondrial homeostasis
abstract: Whole genome duplication, or polyploidy, increases cell size and nuclear volume, yet how cells maintain cytonuclear balance and metabolic fitness following ploidy expansion remains unclear. Using isogenic series of  Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains ranging from haploid (1N) to tetraploid (4N), and isogenic human diploid and tetraploid cell lines, we investigated the impact of polyploidy on mitochondrial homeostasis and metabolic adaptation. Quantitative proteomics uncovered a sub-linear scaling of mitochondrial proteins with increasing ploidy, with pronounced depletion of respiratory chain components, mitochondrial DNA maintenance factors, and redox homeostasis proteins. These changes were highly conserved, indicating a conserved consequence of genome expansion. Impaired mitochondrial scaling reduced respiratory growth, membrane potential and oxygen consumption, and elevated oxidative stress. In budding yeast, the mitochondrial dysfunction triggered reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation and an unconventional activation of stress-responsive signaling pathways, including the Hog1 and cell integrity MAPK networks, which converged on Rtg2-dependent retrograde signaling to promote mitochondrial metabolism despite chronic dysfunction. Our findings identify defective mitochondrial scaling as a key consequence of polyploidy and establish ROS- and stress signaling-dependent retrograde response as a key adaptive mechanism linking genome duplication to mitochondrial homeostasis and cellular fitness.
authors: Hertel AR, Sagoe AM, Yahya G, Heusser A, Khan A, Räschle M, Herrmann JM, Storchová Z, Amponsah PS.

title: Sacred Grove Soil as a Novel Source of Protease-Producing Alishewanella aestuarii B11: A First Report from North Gujarat, India
abstract: Abstract    Sacred groves are forest patches that local communities have protected for generations on religious grounds. Their soils have seen little tillage, grazing or chemical input, yet few studies have screened them for bacteria of industrial use. We collected soil from 25 sacred groves in five districts of North Gujarat, India (Sabarkantha, Banaskantha, Patan, Mehsana and Aravalli) and screened it for protease-producing bacteria by serial dilution, spread-plating and clearance-zone assays on skim-milk agar. Of the 98 morphologically and biochemically distinct isolates recovered, the isolate with the largest clearance zone in each district was taken forward for quantitative work. The best producer overall, BKNR-1 from a Banaskantha grove, gave a 29 mm clearance zone on casein agar and was identified by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and phylogenetic analysis as  Alishewanella aestuarii  B11, a Gram-negative, oxidase- and catalase-positive bacterium. In submerged fermentation, one-factor-at-a-time (OFAT) optimization gave maximum protease production after 48 h with 2% (w/v) fructose as carbon source, 2% (w/v) urea as nitrogen source, an initial pH of 7.0 and incubation at 37°C. Activity under these conditions reached about 655–700 U mL⁻¹ min⁻¹, roughly 4.3 times that of the unoptimized medium. Ammonium sulfate fractionation of the crude extract raised specific activity, in line with reports for other bacterial proteases purified by stepwise salting-out. To our knowledge, this is the first report of a strongly proteolytic  A. aestuarii  strain from Indian sacred-grove soil. The genus has rarely been studied as an enzyme producer, and the result supports further bioprospecting of traditionally conserved forest soils for hydrolytic enzymes with uses in the detergent, leather, food and waste-management sectors.
authors: Prajapati D, Gaikwada Z, Patil K, Chaudhari RG, Bhatt SA.

title: Molecular-level characterization of the five regions of excitation-emission matrices across diverse dissolved organic matter sources.
abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) plays a critical role in all aquatic systems. A number of critically important properties of DOM can be elucidated using excitation-emission matrix (EEM) spectroscopy that quantifies the presence and characteristics of fluorescent DOM (FDOM). Fluorescence regional integration analysis (FRI) is widely used to interpret FDOM composition, yet the molecular signatures of DOM molecules statistically associated with these five regions are poorly understood. In this study, we characterized PPL-extractable DOM from 30 samples from rivers, lakes, canals, seas, wastewater, and sediment pore waters using EEM/FRI analysis combined with ultrahigh-resolution mass spectrometry (FT-ICR-MS). Spearman rank correlation analysis between relative region fluorescence intensities and sum-normalized FT-ICR-MS peak intensities identified 1206 molecular formulas significantly associated with one or more fluorescence regions. Tyrosine-like (Region I) and tryptophan-like (Region II) fluorescence were found to be correlated with molecular stoichiometries with higher H/C ratios and greater contributions of N- and S-containing compositions, whereas fulvic acid-like (Region III) and humic acid-like fluorescence (Region V) were statistically associated with highly oxygenated, aromatic-rich molecular stoichiometries (e.g., polyphenolic/tannin-like compounds). Soluble microbial byproduct-like (Region IV) exhibited intermediate molecular characteristics, with associations dominated by lignin-like and protein-like molecules. Distinct source-dependent molecular signatures were also observed, with terrestrial waters enriched in aromatic CHO stoichiometries while wastewater and marine samples showed greater contributions from heteroatom-containing, protein-like formulas. These results establish a molecular framework for interpreting fixed FRI fluorescence regions within PPL-extractable DOM and strengthen the interpretability and transferability of EEM fluorescence data for investigating DOM composition, reactivity, and fate in natural and engineered waters.
authors: Zhang C, Korshin GV, Gao X, Yan M.
