title: Discovery of 3-phenyldibenzo[b,d]furan derivatives as potent multi-stage inhibitors against SARS-CoV-2.
abstract: Since its emergence in early 2020, SARS-CoV-2 has continuously threatened human health and public safety, underscoring the persistent need for novel antiviral agents. Based on our previously identified marine natural product peniterphenyl A, we designed and synthesized 23 novel 3-phenyldibenzo[b,d]furan derivatives (T1 - T23). Their anti-SARS-CoV-2 activities were evaluated using two infection models: recombinant VSV-Venus-VSVΔG-SARS2-SΔ21 in Vero cells (rVSV-s/Vero) and transcription- and replication-competent SARS-CoV-2 virus-like particles in Caco-2-N cells (trVLP/Caco-2-N). Among them, T11 (IC50 = 5.6 and 3.1 μM), T15 (IC50 = 8.1 and 5.1 μM), and T16 (IC50 = 8.2 and 4.2 μM) exhibited moderate to potent inhibitory activities in both models. Preliminary structure-activity relationship analysis indicated that the 3-phenyldibenzo[b,d]furan scaffold serves as the core pharmacophore, with 2-OH on the B ring and 2'-Br on the C ring being favorable for activity. T15 could downregulate IL-1β mRNA expression. It had low cytotoxicity against host cells and no direct virucidal activity. Mechanistically, by targeting on the AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), it inhibited viral entry and almost completely blocked viral replication when added within 4 h post-infection, whereas its antiviral efficacy gradually declined as the addition was postponed. In addition, T15 dose-dependently elevated the phosphorylation levels of TBK1 and IRF3. Collectively, T15 exhibits multi-stage antiviral activity (inhibiting viral entry and early-stage of replication), along with anti-inflammatory effects and low cytotoxicity, positioning it as a promising lead candidate for anti-SARS-CoV-2 drug development. However, its detailed signaling pathway requires further elucidation.
authors: Li C, Xu H, Chu Z, Fang Y, Liu J, Wang J, Liu S, Liu Y, Yao X, Liao S.

title: Arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis enhances salt tolerance in Eucalyptus grandis by coordinating antioxidant defense, hormone accumulation and ion homeostasis.
abstract: Eucalyptus is a globally important timber species, yet its productivity is markedly constrained by salt stress. Although arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi play crucial roles under environmental stress, the integrated physiological and molecular mechanisms by which they confer salinity tolerance in E. grandis remain incompletely understood. In this study, we explored the impact of inoculation with the AM fungus Rhizophagus irregularis on the physiological, biochemical, and transcriptional responses of E. grandis seedlings across a NaCl gradient (0-200 mM). The results indicated that AM symbiosis significantly alleviated salt-induced growth inhibition, membrane damage and water deficit. Relative to non-mycorrhizal plants, AM-colonized seedlings exhibited lower accumulations of osmolytes and oxidative stress markers, while maintaining higher activities of key antioxidant enzymes. Hormonal profiling revealed a coordinated downregulation of stress-related phytohormones in mycorrhizal plants under salinity. Additionally, AM plants accumulated less sodium (Na+) and more potassium (K+) than non-mycorrhizal controls, suggesting enhanced Na+ efflux and K+ uptake under salt stress. Genome-wide analysis identified 23 candidate SOS pathway genes in E. grandis, and qPCR expression profiling revealed that all of these responded to AM symbiosis under salt stress, suggesting that AM symbiosis may regulate SOS pathway gene expression as part of its salt tolerance mechanism. Redundancy analysis suggested strong correlations among enhanced antioxidant enzyme activity, hormonal adjustments, ion homeostasis and the expression of specific EgSOS genes. Collectively, these findings provide integrated physiological and molecular evidence that AM symbiosis improves salt tolerance in a woody species through modulation of antioxidant defenses, hormonal balance, ion homeostasis and SOS pathway gene expression.
authors: Wang S, Xu G, Yu Y, Zhong Y, Li S, Wang J, Chen H, Tang M.

title: Selective Bacteroidota Depletion but Not Global Microbiome Differences in Short Bowel Syndrome on Fiber-Free Enteral Nutrition
abstract: Intestinal dysbiosis in pediatric short bowel syndrome (SBS) is associated with poor growth, but the factors that are driving this dysbiosis remain unclear. Prior studies suggest that parenteral nutrition (PN) dependence and remnant intestinal anatomy are correlated with dysbiosis. However, these studies often compared SBS patients to healthy controls, making it difficult to distinguish SBS-specific factors from alterations due to differences in diet, namely the consumption of enteral nutrition with complex composition and exposure to dietary fiber. In this preliminary report from the GREENBEANS study, we examined baseline stool shotgun metagenomic profiles from 10 SBS patients and 13 non-SBS controls receiving fiber-free enteral nutrition. Alpha diversity did not differ significantly between groups by richness or Shannon diversity. Beta diversity showed minimal separation by Bray-Curtis distance and modest separation in Jaccard distance. Differential abundance analysis identified depletion of Bacteroidota in SBS. Compared to control patients also receiving fiber-free enteral nutrition, SBS was associated with only a small global difference in the gut microbiome, suggesting that diet, and not anatomy as previously assumed, is the predominant determinant of gut microbiome structure. This suggests that the inclusion of complex substrates, such as dietary fiber, in enteral nutrition, may be a modality to prevent the development of a dysbiotic microbiome in patients with SBS. What is known/What is new  What is known  Children with short bowel syndrome (SBS) often demonstrate intestinal dysbiosis characterized by reduced microbial diversity and enrichment of Proteobacteria/Enterobacteriaceae compared with healthy controls. Dysbiosis in SBS is associated with increased PN dependence and poor growth outcomes. The relative contribution of various SBS-associated factors to this dysbiosis remains unclear because prior studies generally used healthy control subjects. What is new  SBS-specific differences while on fiber-free enteral nutrition were driven primarily by selective depletion of Bacteroidota anaerobes rather than broad Proteobacteria expansion. SBS was associated with only a modest global microbiome separation from non-SBS controls when both were receiving fiber-free enteral nutrition, suggesting that the lack of dietary fiber, rather than the alteration of intestinal anatomy or other SBS-specific factors, may be a major factor in the development of the SBS-associated dysbiosis found in prior studies. Our findings shift attention from fixed anatomic factors alone towards potentially modifiable dietary contributors in SBS-associated dysbiosis, including enteral substrate complexity and dietary fiber exposure.
authors: Zong W, Daniel SG, Zarek CM, Wilson NG, Cook C, Riebe N, Kirsch J, Marquez ET, Alame R, Channabasappa N, Nguyen V, Bittinger K, Wu GD, Bales C, Koh AY, Albenberg L.

title: A Naturally Occurring Defective RNA Species of the Tymo-Like Mycovirus FbLFV1 Confers Hypovirulence in the Host Fusarium Head Blight Fungus, Fusarium boothii
abstract: RNA viruses often generate a defective RNA (D-RNA) species that has internal deletion(s) and recombined fragment(s), which are believed to occur during viral replication. Such subviral RNA fragments sometimes exert overt effects on their parental viral replication or pathogenicity and are called defective-interfering RNA (DI-RNA). This study reports a rare example in which a D-RNA acquired a novel function that determines the hypovirulent phenotype of the host fungus, Fusarium boothii Ep-BL13, a causal agent of Fusarium head blight. The parental Fusarium boothii large flexivirus 1 (FbLFV1) is a tymo-like virus with a 13 kb (+)ssRNA genome encoding a single large ORF, and the D-RNA has an approximately 10 kb internal deletion in the ORF with an in-frame connection. Partial virus curing revealed a clear association between viral infection (FbLFV1 + D-RNA) and inhibition of colony growth and the pathogenicity of the host F. boothii. These traits were further confirmed in a fungal strain expressing the D-RNA ORF, specifically under FbLFV1 infection. Moreover, FbLFV1 and D-RNA infection decreased the host fungal production of the mycotoxin deoxynivalenol. Overall, FbLFV1 produced a D-RNA in F. boothii in nature, which carries the rearranged gene (D-RNA ORF) with a virulence-determining function, representing a rare example of gain-of-function by a D-RNA.
authors: Sato Y, Mizutani Y, Abbhi V, Kamiya M, Kikuchi H, Kanamori K, Abraham A, Sato I, Suzuki N, Suga H, Chiba S.

title: Surveillance Readiness Audit: Completeness of Surveillance-Critical Metadata in U.S. Clinical Pathogen Genomes, 2015 to 2026
abstract: A pathogen genome supports early outbreak detection only when it is deposited with basic context: when and where the sample was collected, its source and host, whether it came from a patient, and, for resistance surveillance, its antimicrobial susceptibility. NCBI Pathogen Detection integrates the national public record of bacterial and fungal pathogen genomes, but the completeness of this context has not been measured routinely across organisms. This paper describes the Surveillance Readiness Audit v1.0.0, an open, reproducible audit of six surveillance-critical metadata fields (collection date precision, state geography, isolation source, host, epi type and antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) availability) for every U.S. isolate in 107 organism groups, stratified by organism, year added and submitter type. The v1.0.0 build, from NCBI data retrieved on 14 October 2026, covers 1,239,575 U.S. isolates added from 2015 to 2026, of which 911,265 (73.5%) are clinical. Only 13.4% of clinical isolates record a state, compared with 84.8% of environmental isolates, and only 6.1% carry all five core fields; 0.8% carry AST results. Year-only collection dates rose from 17.0% of clinical isolates added in 2022 to 69.2% of those added in 2024. Submissions owned by federal agencies account for 83.8% of clinical isolates, and 2.7% of them record a state. The gaps that most limit early detection from the public record are therefore geography and date precision in a small number of high-volume network programs, and susceptibility data everywhere.
authors: Igbuan EA.

title: Supramolecular assembly and membrane anchoring alter variant-induced SARS-CoV-2 Spike conformational dynamics.
abstract: Viral surface glycoproteins function within crowded, membrane-anchored supramolecular assemblies, yet their dynamics are often inferred from soluble, engineered ectodomains. For SARS-CoV-2 Spike (S), this distinction is especially important because variant mutations evolved in the context of intact virions, not engineered trimers. Here, we combined cyclic ion mobility mass spectrometry (CIM-MS) for hydrogen deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDXMS) with computational weighted ensemble molecular dynamic (WE-MD) simulations to compare the conformational effects of SARS-CoV-2 mutations in two S protein constructs: soluble recombinant 2P S and full-length S displayed in virus-like particles (VLPs). Our results reveal that membrane anchoring and virion-like assembly substantially dampen global dynamic changes produced by variant mutations. In VLP S, D614G induced decreased dynamics across interprotomer contacts, whereas Omicron BA.1 mutations systematically reversed this decrease in dynamics in the S1 domain while preserving decreased dynamics near the fusion machinery. These effects are more spatially constrained than those observed in recombinant 2P S. Comparison of the 2 constructs further reveals that 2P substitutions alter native interprotomer communication. Recombinant S shows a predominantly fast-exchanging population in the receptor binding domain (RBD) hinge region, consistent with disruption of hydrogen-bonding and salt bridge networks that couple RBD motion to the trimer core. Thus, recombinant S captures important structural features of S without recapitulating the native conformational ensemble presented on virions. Together, these results show that the supramolecular context of S reshapes the conformational dynamics of variant evolution with direct implications for epitope presentation, antibody recognition, and interpretation of recombinant S structural studies.
authors: Gramm AJ, Braet SM, Srinivasu BY, Venkatakrishnan V, Bass EJ, Kearns FL, Amaro RE, Stahelin RV, Wales TE, Anand GS.

title: A glycoengineered yeast-derived HA1-ferritin nanoparticle vaccine confers protective immunity against H7 avian influenza in chickens.
abstract: H7 subtype avian influenza virus is an important zoonotic pathogen threatening the poultry industry and public health. Recombinant subunit vaccines provide a safer alternative to conventional inactivated vaccines, while yeast expression systems offer advantages of low cost, scalability, and engineering flexibility. However, their application in avian influenza vaccine development remains underexplored. In this study, we use the methylotrophic yeast Komagataella phaffii as a low-cost, industrial-scale platform to produce hemagglutinin-1 (HA1) subunits with programmable N-/O-linked glycosylation. The methanol-utilization-slow (MutS) phenotype strain secreted 1.21 g/L HA1, and compared with the standard methanol-utilization-plus (Mut+) phenotype strain, the N-linked and O-linked glycans were significantly reduced [liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS)/MS glycopeptide profile]. Despite hypoglycosylation, the antigen retained native conformation, binding H7-specific mAb Q74 with a KD of 1.34 × 10-7 M. SpyTag/SpyCatcher-directed conjugation to ferritin drove quantitative self-assembly into 30 nm virus-like nanoparticles. Formulated with CpG-ODN 1826, the HA1-MutS-ferritin candidate elicited Hemagglutination inhibition (HI) titers of 6.7 log2 in specific pathogen-free (SPF) leghorns at 28 days post-immunization (dpi), significantly enhancing HA1-specific IgY responses (p + T cells. At 28 dpi, chickens were challenged with 106 embryo infectious dose (EID)50 of H7N9 avian influenza virus; the formulation conferred 100% clinical protection and accelerated viral clearance, matching the performance of conventional inactivated vaccines. Yeast-based processes significantly reduce downstream purification costs and eliminate reliance on chicken embryos, providing a scalable and biosafe platform for rapid avian influenza control.
authors: Liu Y, Shao Y, Su B, Liu P, Huang Y, Zheng H, Xu S, Zhao Y, Li Q, Liao M, Feng S.

title: Bacterial microbiota profiling of human-biting ticks in Yozgat Province, Türkiye.
abstract: In the present study, the bacterial microbiota of ticks infesting humans in Yozgat Province, Türkiye, was investigated. Ticks were collected from 54 patients who were presented to the Emergency Service of the Yozgat Bozok University Research and Training Hospital between March and November 2019. The following tick species were identified: Hyalomma marginatum, Rhipicephalus turanicus, Rhipicephalus bursa, Haemaphysalis parva, Dermacentor marginatus, and Hyalomma aegyptium. 16S rRNA libraries were prepared from tick DNA pools using a two-step PCR protocol targeting the V3-V4 region. In the second (indexing) PCR, dual Illumina indexes and adapters were added using the Nextera XT Index Kit. The resulting libraries were then sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq platform. A total of 3782 operational taxonomic units (OTUs) were identified; an average of 127,823 reads were obtained per sample, and an average of 31,561 reads were retained after taxonomic assignment. The OTUs were classified into 20 phyla, 41 classes, 94 orders, 168 families, 344 genera, and 452 putative species-level taxa. At the phylum level, Proteobacteria were predominant (averaging 63%), followed by Actinobacteriota and Bacteroidota (each approximately 10%) and Firmicutes (9%). At the class level, Alphaproteobacteria (average 37%) and Gammaproteobacteria (26%) exhibited the highest relative abundance, while at the order level, Rickettsiales (34%) and Francisellales (17%) were prominent. At the family and genus levels, the dominant taxa were identified as Rickettsiaceae (33%), Francisellaceae (17%), Rickettsia (33%), Francisella (17%), and Coxiella (7%), respectively. The most prevalent species included symbiotic bacteria such as Francisella sp. and Candidatus Midichloria mitochondrii. The Kruskal-Wallis test, conducted from phylum to genus level to evaluate taxonomic composition differences among tick species, revealed no statistically significant differences (p ≥ 0.05 for all comparisons). In alpha diversity analyses, no significant differences were found between tick species in terms of Shannon and Simpson indices (Shannon: H = 7.69; p = 0.26, Simpson: H = 8.07; p = 0.23). Similarly, no significant differences were observed between sex and developmental stages (Shannon: p = 0.86, Simpson: p = 0.73). The Chao1 and observed OTU values indicated higher richness trends, particularly in the Hyalomma marginatum and Hyalomma sp. pools. However, Spearman correlations between sample size and diversity indices were not significant (p > 0.05). These findings provide a baseline overview of the bacterial microbiota associated with human-biting ticks in Yozgat Province and may serve as a foundation for future studies employing higher-resolution methods to assess pathogen presence and public health risk.
journal: Infection, genetics and evolution : journal of molecular epidemiology and evolutionary genetics in infectious diseases
authors: Arslan-Akveran G, Karasartova D, Simsek H, Sensoz S, Keskin A, Albayrak L, Gokcen E, Caltekin I, Mumcuoglu KY, Taylan-Ozkan A.

title: Essential genes are enriched in semantic error-protected coding sequences: A communication-theoretic analysis of the genetic code.
abstract: The genetic code is commonly described as a redundant mapping from nucleotide triplets to amino acids, but this redundancy does not make all nucleotide substitutions equivalent. A physical mutation rate at the DNA level may translate into silent changes, conservative amino-acid substitutions, severe missense events, or nonsense mutations. Here, we develop a communication-theoretic framework to quantify how nucleotide-level errors are transformed into semantic degradation of protein-coding information. Single-nucleotide substitutions were modelled as an error channel with variable transition/transversion structure, and their effects were weighted using a normalized physicochemical distance between amino acids, with nonsense mutations assigned maximal cost. This allowed the definition of codon-level semantic cost, sequence-level degradation, and synonymous-codon protection scores. The framework first confirmed that the standard genetic code reduces expected semantic cost relative to randomized genetic-code baselines. At fixed nucleotide substitution probability, semantic degradation depended strongly on the transition/transversion spectrum, showing that physical error rate and genetic-information degradation are not equivalent quantities. The model was then applied to real coding sequences from the RefSeq Escherichia coli K-12 MG1655 assembly. Gene-level analysis revealed substantial heterogeneity in semantic vulnerability across CDS, driven by codon composition, synonymous-codon choice, nonsense susceptibility, and sequence length. Protein-preserving synonymous null models were used to separate amino-acid-composition effects from codon-choice effects. Relative to uniformly chosen synonymous alternatives, real E. coli CDS showed lower semantic substitution cost, increased silent-error protection, and reduced nonsense vulnerability. Much of this signal was explained by genome-wide codon-usage bias, but a subset of genes remained locally protected or locally vulnerable after controlling for global codon usage. Importantly, high-confidence essential genes were enriched among locally protected CDS and depleted among locally vulnerable CDS. This association remained robust across essentiality definitions, mutation-channel assumptions, multivariate controls, and random-label permutation tests. These results support a layered view of genetic-information robustness: the standard genetic code provides a primary semantic-protection layer, organism-wide codon usage provides a secondary modulation, and gene-specific synonymous choice introduces local heterogeneity associated with functional constraint. The proposed framework links mutation-channel parameters to interpretable measures of semantic degradation and provides a quantitative bridge between molecular error processes, codon usage, and gene essentiality.
authors: Conde I, Silva-Ramírez EL, Cumbrera FL.

title: Mitochondrial acquisition after the Asgard revolution: Reconstructing eukaryogenesis with insights for mitochondrial transplantation.
abstract: Mitochondria arose from an alphaproteobacterial endosymbiont that became integrated within an archaeal host during eukaryogenesis. The discovery of Asgard archaea has clarified host ancestry and supports reconstructions in which aspects of cytoskeletal and membrane complexity preceded mitochondrial acquisition. Organellogenesis involved genome reduction, gene transfer, protein import, metabolic coupling, and vertical inheritance. These evolutionary principles complement current mitochondrial transplantation recommendations by generating testable predictions about recipient dependence and the duration of rescue. Transplanted mitochondria are mature organelles introduced into cells already equipped to maintain mitochondria; the requirement for transient or durable function must nevertheless be tested for each indication. Aging can modify organelle delivery, recipient quality control, and tissue responses, with particular implications for the neurovascular unit and neuronal function. Extracellular vesicle delivery requires verification of mitochondrial cargo, potency, and compatibility. Measurable criteria distinguish delivery, uptake, cytosolic access, network interaction, persistence, and functional benefit, while separating evidence from aging, acute ischemia, and inherited disease models.
authors: Li YY, Frazier KB, Tay FR.

title: Comparative genomic analysis for selected members of the Ophiostomatales: insights into biosynthetic gene clusters and CAZymes.
abstract: The Order Ophiostomatales includes ecologically diverse fungi, and many are associates of bark and/or ambrosia beetles. This order includes species that cause tree diseases, and many members are sapwood staining fungi. Despite their ecological and economic importance, the genomic basis of their adaptations remains poorly understood. Here, we present annotated genome assemblies for six species (seven strains) spanning three genera within the Ophiostomatales. Genomes ranged from 21 to 32 Mb with high completeness scores. CAZyme analyses revealed broadly conserved repertoires dominated by glycoside hydrolases and glycosyltransferases, with substantial representation of lignin-and cellulose-associated enzymes and marked quantitative variation among taxa, including expanded oxidative auxiliary activity families in Ophiostoma quercus and Leptographium truncatum and a reduced profile in Ceratocystiopsis minima. antiSMASH predicted 12-19 biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) among the seven genomes. Rather than only broad metabolite classes, comparative analysis revealed conservation of specific secondary metabolite families, including a putative 1,8-dihydroxynaphthalene (DHN) melanin cluster present in all genomes, a conserved fujikurin-like type I polyketide synthase (T1PKS) cluster present in all genomes except L. truncatum, and an Ophiostoma-specific NRPSbased metallophore/siderophore-like cluster potentially involved in iron acquisition. The genomic data provide new insights into the metabolic capacity and potential ecological differentiation of the Ophiostomatales.

title: From 16S rDNA-seq count data to microbial interactions: A comprehensive benchmark of co-occurrence network inference methods.
abstract: The study of the ecological interactions within microbial communities is crucial for gaining deeper insights into community ensemble and evolution, enabling targeted modification of the community's functionality. Many inference approaches have been developed to derive ecological associations. Here, we focus on co-occurrence computational methods, in which associations are inferred from metagenomic abundance data by measuring the statistical dependence between species counts across different sampled populations. The limitations in culture-based experiments have hindered the ability to assess these methods' validity, leading to scarce application in metagenomics studies. To provide a comprehensive assessment of network inference method performance, we benchmark 18 different computational approaches across a broad spectrum of experimental scenarios. We use synthetic 16S rDNA-seq count data generated from known underlying interaction networks, enabling systematic and controlled evaluation. The benchmark spans scenarios varying in numbers of species and samples, sample richness, sequencing depth, and interaction network structure. We evaluated the performance of the methods both in terms of accuracy of the inferred network, using various metrics from binary classification theory and metrics coming from network science, and in terms of computational burden. We found that methods have valid results only in a restricted, and often unrealistic, field of application, whereas their effectiveness diminishes with more realistic simulation parameters. Our findings highlight the limits of the co-occurrence-based approach and the need for further development in microbial ecological association inference.
authors: Mariotto P, Baldan M, Di Camillo B, Baruzzo G.

title: In-vitro screening of a potential probiotic isolate from fermented soybean (Akhuni) and targeted antibiofilm activity against the major clinical pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
abstract: Probiotic microorganisms derived from traditional fermented foods have attracted increasing attention because of their potential to improve human health and serve as functional food ingredients. However, the probiotic characteristics and bioactive metabolite profiles of many indigenous isolates remain insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to isolate and comprehensively characterize potential probiotic microbial strains from the traditional soybean-based fermented food Akhuni, from India and evaluate their functional properties. For probiotic characterization, the gastrointestinal stress tolerance and cell adhesion ability were assessed. The potential strain was identified, and phylogenetic analysis was carried out. Antimicrobial activity was checked against Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which is very hard to eradicate due to its high resistance to multiple antibiotics and its thick biofilm formation. The test was conducted by agar well diffusion assay, growth kinetics analysis and further estimated by determining the MIC value. Anti-Biofilm activity of the isolate was also assessed and validated using anti-pyocyanin and anti-quorum-sensing tests and SEM imaging. The isolate FSG6 showed promising results across all probiotic characterization tests. It demonstrated a high survivability percentage and adhesion ability in gastrointestinal conditions. 16 S rDNA sequencing revealed it to be a strain of Pediococcus sp. FSG6 recorded significant antimicrobial and antibiofilm activity against P. aeruginosa with high anti-pyocyanin and anti-quorum-sensing activity. This study represents one of the earliest reports to describe the presence of Pediococcus sp. in akhuni, which expands the current understanding of microbial diversity of these traditional foods and highlights the untapped potential of these indigenous isolates for future probiotic and other value-added applications.
authors: Sarkar A, Das RK, Sinha A, Mandal M.

title: A temperate phage acts as a symbiotic fitness enhancer for UPEC but surrenders to combination therapy through lysogeny suppression.
abstract: Temperate phages are increasingly recognized as key drivers of bacterial evolution. Here, we isolated a myoviral prophage, vB_EcoM_P899, from a clinical uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) isolate and characterized how lysogenization shapes host biology. Lysogenization significantly enhanced biofilm formation, swarming motility, oxidative stress resistance, and adhesion to macrophages (up to 100-fold) without altering antibiotic susceptibility or overall 72-h lethality in the Galleria mellonella larval infection model. Mechanistically, this is associated with upregulation of the fimbrial gene FimA and enhanced inducibility of the oxidative stress response genes KatE and OxyR under oxidative stress. Crucially, combining P899 with ciprofloxacin or kanamycin produced synergistic killing and suppressed new lysogen formation in an antibiotic-class-dependent manner. In contrast, ceftazidime, while synergistic, failed to prevent lysogeny. Our findings demonstrate that while prophage vB_EcoM_P899 promotes bacterial niche adaptation, its lysogenization frequency is significantly reduced under specific antibiotic pressure, facilitating clearance of the challenged UPEC population. This work provides a strong rationale for optimizing phage-antibiotic combination therapies to treat drug-resistant infections by simultaneously enhancing bacterial killing and limiting lysogenic survivors.ImportanceThis study reveals that lysogenization by a temperate phage can enhance the niche adaptation of uropathogenic Escherichia coli without increasing its virulence in the Galleria mellonella larval model or altering antibiotic resistance. Crucially, we demonstrate that combining this phage with select antibiotics (e.g., kanamycin and ciprofloxacin) not only kills the bacteria effectively but also actively suppresses the formation of new lysogens in an antibiotic-class-dependent manner. These findings uncover a novel role for temperate phages as symbiotic regulators within the host and provide direct experimental evidence for a phage-antibiotic combination strategy. This approach holds promise for combating chronic, recurrent urinary tract infections and offers a clinically viable pathway to address antibiotic tolerance in chronic, recurrent urinary tract infections.
authors: Yan B, Yan C, Li Q, Cai S, Zhu H, Song M, Deng X, Huang X, Guo W, Qin K, Fu Q, Ding Y.

title: Complete genomes of blue- and pink-colored Pseudomonas strains isolated from spoiled foods.
abstract: Here, we report complete genomes of Pseudomonas paracarnis str. CASEUS-AZUL, Pseudomonas paracarnis str. ORYZA-AZUL, and Pseudomonas fragi str. ORYZA-ROSEA, which are bacterial strains isolated from refrigerated spoiled foods (panela cheese that had turned blue, and brown rice that had turned blue and pink, respectively).
authors: Mendoza MC, Nigenda-Morales SF, Porman Swain AM, Becket E.

title: The RNA virome of intertidal kelp in New Zealand reveals novel viral lineages associated with unhealthy kelp.
abstract: Pathogens can have major impacts on ecosystem function, especially when they infect foundational taxa such as habitat-forming kelp. Understanding which potentially pathogenic microbes are in an ecosystem is increasingly important as environmental change intensifies ecosystem imbalances, yet few studies have examined which viruses are associated with key habitat-forming macroalgae. Here, we screened multiple populations of intertidal / shallow-subtidal macroalgae in New Zealand for viruses. Samples were collected from three southern bull kelp species: Durvillaea antarctica, Durvillaea poha and Durvillaea willana. Total RNA was extracted and sequenced from both obviously 'unhealthy' kelp tissue and apparently 'healthy' tissue. We identified putative novel viral lineages belonging to the families Mitoviridae, Narnaviridae, Partitiviridae, Totiviridae, and the recently proposed Ormycovirus group. Viral abundance and diversity were notably higher at Lawyers Head (the site closest to a city) compared to other sites, especially in unhealthy kelp samples. The elevated viral presence at Lawyers Head may indicate that human impacts, such as pollution, are influencing viral prevalence. This study reveals that coastal macroalgae in New Zealand host diverse viral lineages, some likely pathogenic, and hints at the potential influence of anthropogenic pollution on marine virome composition.
authors: Harvey LEM, Waller SJ, French RK, Geoghegan JL, Fraser CI.

title: Comparisons among Yanomami populations reveal transitional gut microbiome configurations under urban influence
abstract: Urbanization influences gut microbiome composition and function, yet comparisons between contrasting lifestyles offer limited insight into which microbial features are most sensitive to increasing urbanization. We analyzed gut shotgun metagenomes from Yanomami participants, an Indigenous Amazonian people who maintain traditional livelihoods, across three geographically distinct populations with varying degrees of urban influence, as well as an urban Belgian cohort. Belgian and Yanomami microbiomes differed markedly in taxonomic composition and functional potential. The comparison between Bicho-Açu, the most urban-influenced Yanomami population, and Xamakorona, the least urban-exposed, revealed that although Bicho-Açu presented a broadly Yanomami-associated microbiome, it exhibited selected urban-associated features, including greater  Bacteroides abundance and a higher relative abundance of genes involved in glycosaminoglycan degradation and secondary bile acid biosynthesis pathways. Furthermore, genus-level co-occurrence network connectivity showed an orderly shift across populations, declining progressively with increasing urban influence. Carbohydrate-active enzyme profiles further showed stronger non-starch-polysaccharide-associated signals in Belgium and resistant-starch-associated features in Xamakorona, suggesting distinct carbohydrate-processing strategies. Our findings support a model in which urbanization reshapes microbial composition, their ecological interactions, and metabolic capacity, with transitional configurations emerging through selective shifts across these dimensions.
authors: de Carvalho LAL, Thorp M, Ciers M, Callewaert C, Good D, Allen-Vercoe E, Vereecke L, Paulino LC.

title: Mild extraction preserves labile structural features of Gram-positive bacterial cell wall glycopolymers
abstract: Cell wall glycopolymers in Gram-positive bacteria are crucial for structural integrity, cell division, and stress resistance. Elucidating the structure of these glycopolymers is not only important for understanding fundamental bacterial physiology, but may facilitate vaccine development, phage therapy, antibiotic design and improvements in food fermentation safety. However, extraction protocols have so far relied on harsh chemicals that can damage these polymers, compromise their structural integrity, obscure their biological functions, and result in low yields. We present a straightforward method for isolating cell wall glycopolymers from Gram-positive bacteria that preserves essential structural features including attachment to peptidoglycan. The method was broadly applicable across phylogenetically diverse species and was not restricted to glycopolymer types. In total, we isolated 17 distinct glycopolymers from 11 species, including six with previously unreported structures, with a median yield of 49 mg per litre of culture. The simplicity and mild nature of the method, combined with the exceptional purity of the resulting products, has the potential to transform research on Gram-positive cell wall glycopolymers.
authors: Boehlich GJ, Tsjokajev A, Mrozek P, Reglinski M, Straume D, Kjos M, Horn SJ, Dorfmueller HC, Vaaje-Kolstad G, Westereng B.

title: Population genomics of  Candida albicans  reveals genetic footprints that allow the prediction of antifungal resistance
abstract: Rapid detection of drug resistance in fungi is becoming increasingly urgent. While multiple loci and mutations were linked to antifungal resistance in  Candida albicans , the utility of whole genome sequencing in predicting resistance has not been tested thoroughly. We address this by integrating more than 1000  C. albicans genomes, with associated resistance phenotypes to six antifungals, a curated repository of resistance-causing mutations and variant effect predictors. We used Genome Wide Association Studies and Machine Learning approaches to associate genetic variants to resistance phenotypes. We found that well curated databases like FungAMR are able to accurately identify markers predictive antifungal resistance. Curated mutations were detected in 56–74% of isolates with reduced azole susceptibility and 57–90% of those with reduced echinocandin susceptibility, revealing incomplete coverage of resistance across both drug classes. Complementary variant- and gene-level association analyses recovered established resistance determinants and uncovered additional candidate loci, whereas copy-number changes provided limited independent explanatory power. Genomic prediction declined when genetic backgrounds were absent from training, and when leading predictive features differed among backgrounds. We also found that models trained on a curated list of mutations and variant effect predictors performed well when classifying drug-susceptible strains, but the drug-resistance trait was predicted with a lower accuracy. These findings support the potential of genome-based resistance prediction while highlighting the need for broader population sampling, functional validation of candidate variants and expanded resistance catalogues to improve prediction across genetic backgrounds.
authors: Jay A, Bédard C, Pageau A, Gagnon-Arsenault I, Bautista C, Kus JV, McTaggart L, Dingle TC, Shokoples S, De Luca DG, Bharat A, Dufresne PJ, Fijarczyk A, Landry CR.

title: Thylakoid plasticity primes photoprotection in diatoms
abstract: Summary  For many millions of years, diatoms have been major primary producers in marine ecosystems, supporting food webs and contributing to carbon sequestration through the export of photosynthetically fixed carbon to the deep ocean, mitigating atmospheric carbon dioxide levels and global climate. A key factor in their ecological success is their ability to rapidly adapt to fluctuating light, balancing efficient light harvesting under dim conditions with energy dissipation under excess light. However, the mechanisms behind this regulation have not been fully elucidated. This study shows that several processes contribute to dissipating excess excitation energy in diatoms exposed to light stress: (i) the detachment of the oxygen-evolving complex proteins from the PSII core, leading to energy dissipation via charge recombination, (ii) Non-Photochemical Quenching (NPQ) in the antenna, i.e., thermal dissipation of excited states and (iii) excitation energy transfer from PSII to PSI via energy spillover. The latter process is observed in parallel with high light-induced topological changes of the thylakoids that may favour transient interactions between the photosystems. Along with the accumulation of light-stress-protecting carotenoids on longer time-scales, this ensemble of photoprotective mechanisms provides a dynamic and flexible response to the light challenges expected in coastal marine habitats.
authors: Perez Compte D, Tolleter D, Uwizeye C, Giustini C, Pernet L, Fenel D, Moriscot C, Wietrzynski W, Ünnep R, Nagy G, Garab G, Jouneau P, Schoehn G, Krieger-Liszkay A, Engel BD, Albanese P, Finazzi G, Flori S.

title: Engineered probiotics target granulomas to treat mycobacterial infection
abstract: Granulomas are a pathological niche for mycobacteria that remain difficult to access with conventional therapies. Here we show that probiotic  Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) infiltrates and colonizes granulomas and can be engineered as a delivery system that senses the local microenvironment and releases antimycobacterial payloads. Specifically, we leveraged the hypoxic microenvironment of necrotic granulomas to restrict bacterial growth, and developed a dual-mode lysis circuit combining intracellular and extracellular killing for sustained payload release with limited evolutionary escape. We further engineered EcN to express a mycobacteriophage-derived enzyme, generating a strain that suppressed drug-sensitive and drug-resistant mycobacteria in vitro and potentiated conventional antibiotic activity. Engineered probiotics also reduced mycobacterial burden in vivo, and in a murine model of rifampicin-resistant infection, combination treatment with pretomanid achieved greater bacterial reduction than either monotherapy. Together, these results establish a synthetic biology framework for targeting granulomatous infections with programmable living microbes.
authors: Chen Y, Harimoto T, Makafe GG, Coker C, Kim H, Im J, Jing Y, Jin H, Hu X, Zutshi S, Raneri MR, Weinrick B, Danino T.

title: Regulation, function and evolutionary structure of St18, encoding a Zinc-Finger Transcription Factor, in the oligodendrocyte lineage
abstract: Abstract  Myelinating oligodendrocytes are first observed during evolution in vertebrates above jawless fishes. Oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs) undergo extensive transcriptional and morphological remodelling to initiate differentiation and myelination. We report that the zinc-finger transcription factor St18 (aka Myt3) is upregulated during the OPC-to–newly formed oligodendrocyte (NFOL) transition. Single-nucleus RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) performed after lysolecithin-induced demyelination of the mouse spinal cord revealed that St18 was acutely upregulated in remyelinating OPCs. In primary rat OPC cultures, St18 overexpression promoted differentiation, whereas OPC conditional St18 knockout delayed developmental myelination in the mouse brain. Chromatin accessibility profiling identified candidate cis-regulatory elements for oligodendroglial St18 expression activated by core oligodendrocyte transcription factors, including SOX10, KLF9/13, and MYRF, and we confirmed that St18 expression in OPCs is Sox10-dependent in vivo. Phylogenetic analysis suggests that St18 arose via duplication of Myt1 in early jawed vertebrates, coinciding with the emergence of myelinating oligodendrocytes. These findings define St18 as a transcriptional marker of NFOLs and OLs and provide insight into the evolutionary regulation of central nervous system myelination.
authors: Yamamoto D, Vaquié A, Aberle T, Perry M, Shah D, Diaz DG, Lam G, Xu Z, Jordan G, Girdler G, Wüst H, Morcom L, Wilson A, Rawji K, Dimas P, Gu G, Teichmann S, Franklin R, Káradóttir R, Wegner M, Rowitch D.

title: Biopolyester Production Using Fruit Wastes as a Substrate by Soil Bacteria
abstract: Abstract    The global dependence on petroleum-based plastics has led to severe environmental challenges due to their non-biodegradability and persistence in ecosystems. Biopolyesters, particularly polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs), have emerged as promising biodegradable alternatives due to their microbial origin, biocompatibility, and sustainable nature. The present study focused on the isolation and characterization of soil bacteria capable of synthesizing biopolyesters using fruit wastes—apple, orange, and banana peels—as renewable and cost-effective carbon substrates. Soil enrichment was performed through mulching with fruit and organic waste to stimulate the proliferation of biopolymer-producing bacteria, thereby enhancing the presence of naturally efficient PHA-accumulating strains in the soil environment. Primary screening for biopolyester producers was performed using Sudan Black B dye, while confirmatory screening employed Nile Blue A. Among twelve isolates, seven showed positive results for biopolymer accumulation, confirming their PHA-producing capability. Quantitative analysis using E  ₂  medium revealed that isolates MS-5 and MS-7 have the highest polyester production efficiencies, highlighting their superior metabolic potential. Subsequent fermentation experiments using fruit wastes as sole carbon sources demonstrated that apple peels provided the most favorable substrate for polyester yield, followed by orange and banana peels. The strain MS-7 produced quantities of polyester comparable to the positive control  Ralstonia eutropha  MTCC1285, further supporting its suitability as an efficient biopolymer-producing organism. Phylogenetic identification through 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed that MS-7 showed 99.83% sequence similarity with  Bacillus sp  ., validating its genetic affiliation with this genus and supporting the accuracy of its taxonomic placement. Extraction of biopolyester was optimized through a novel sonication-assisted method employing ethylene carbonate, which achieved comparable yields to conventional chloroform extraction but with significantly reduced toxicity and cost, demonstrating a more sustainable and environmentally safe extraction approach. Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) analysis confirmed the presence of functional groups characteristic of polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB), validating the polymer identity, although slight intensity differences indicated minor impurities in the extracted sample. Plasmid curing experiments using ethidium bromide demonstrated that the biopolyester synthesis ability of isolates was chromosomally encoded rather than plasmid-mediated, indicating stable inheritance of the trait.

title: Genome-Wide Identification, Expression Profiling, and Stress Responses of the Sugar Transporter Gene Family in Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum)
abstract: Abstract    The Sugar Transporter Protein (STP) family mediates monosaccharide transport and plays essential roles in plant development and stress responses, yet systematic analysis in tomato remains limited. Here, we analyzed the 18 previously reported SlSTPs. Phylogeny classified them into four clades designated Clade I, Clade II, Clade III and Clade IV, with Clade I absent in tomato. Tandem duplications on chromosome 3 drove family expansion. Conserved motifs and gene structures showed clade-specific conservation. Promoters contained abundant light-responsive, hormone-responsive and stress-responsive cis-elements. Tissue expression revealed that  SlSTP1  ,  SlSTP12  and  SlSTP16  , which belong to Clade II, were predominantly expressed in roots, while  SlSTP9  and  SlSTP11  of Clade III were flower-specific; most genes were only detectable during early fruit development. Under nematode infection,  SlSTP1  ,  SlSTP2  ,  SlSTP3  ,  SlSTP8  and  SlSTP12  peaked at 21 days post inoculation, coinciding with the giant-cell stage. Under drought, salt and heat stresses,  SlSTP7  and  SlSTP12  showed broad responses;  SlSTP6  and  SlSTP12  were strongly induced in roots under drought stress, with log₂ fold changes exceeding 5.  SlSTP2  was nematode-specific, whereas  SlSTP5  ,  SlSTP  9 and  SlSTP17  responded only to abiotic stresses. This study provides candidate genes for improving sugar metabolism and stress tolerance in tomato.
authors: Liu Z, Gu Y, Wang X, Shen L, Tang Y, Li X, Tian Y, Ma S.

title: Why PCR Won the 120-Year Adoption Race for Mycoplasma pneumoniae Diagnostics
abstract: Diagnosing Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP) has followed three technological paths — seeing the organism, reading the host's antibodies, reading the pathogen's genome — and the winners were rarely the best assays. Culture was analytically supreme and never adopted; serology ruled the clinic for fifty years despite documented misclassification; PCR outperformed both by 1990 yet took a decade and a half to reach routine use. We reconstructed 120 years of MP diagnostics as a diffusion dataset, scoring each technology on Rogers' five adoption attributes against its contemporaneous competitor, and tested the scores against regulatory archives (FDA, CE-IVD, China NMPA; search concluded 30 September 2026). Every documented displacement is consistent with four empirical laws: relative advantage in time-to-result outweighed analytic accuracy; workflow compatibility decided more contests than sensitivity; displacement occurred when a successor's turnaround crossed the clinical decision window; and adoption lagged roughly a decade behind technological maturity (mean 8.5 years across the eight measurable transitions) — a severity-gated lag that relaxed measurably after the 2023 resurgence. Applying the validated rubric prospectively, we predict that CRISPR-based point-of-care testing will obtain first regulatory approvals (NMPA before FDA) by end-2027 and achieve decisive adoption in pediatric emergency settings by end-2028, conditional on extraction-free, sample-to-answer workflow, while metagenomic sequencing consolidates in severe and atypical niches without crossing into first-line use before 2030. The predictions are falsifiable and dated — the archive is offered as an evaluation instrument, not an opinion.
authors: Shen C, Li D, Chen H.

title: Model-based inference of gene expression noise from single-cell RNA-sequencing data.
abstract: The heterogeneity of expression levels among genetically identical cells, termed gene expression noise, is a property of the gene expression process whose importance in the biology of organisms and their evolution is increasingly recognized. Measuring gene expression noise requires single-cell expression data, as obtained from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNASeq). Its estimation, however, is challenging owing to (i) the presence of technical noise in addition to biological noise, and (ii) the heterogeneity of cell types in the sampled population. We propose a maximum-likelihood framework to infer biological noise from scRNASeq data, while accounting for technical noise, dropout probabilities, and distinct cell sequencing depths. We demonstrate the parameter identifiability using simulations and that the resulting noise estimates are uncorrelated from the mean gene expression, and therefore do not need extra correction in downstream analyses, easing intra- and inter- genome comparisons. Using two technical replicates of scRNASeq data from the wild yeast Saccharomyces paradoxus, we show that expression noise can be inferred in a reproducible manner.
authors: Giersdorf F, Rogers DW, Christensen S, Dutheil JY.

title: scMRdb: a comprehensive resource for cell-type-resolved Mendelian randomization of complex traits.
abstract: Mendelian randomization (MR) is a powerful analytical approach to infer putative causal links between gene expression and human disease, using genetic variants as instrumental variables to mitigate confounding and reverse causation. However, existing MR resources predominantly rely on bulk-tissue expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs), which mask cell-type-specific transcriptional effects by averaging expression across cellular populations. Furthermore, cell-type-resolved causal evidence from single-cell eQTL (sc-eQTL) MR analyses remains fragmented across individual studies with inconsistent workflows, prohibiting standardized cross-cell-type comparisons. Here we present scMRdb (https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/scmrdb), a comprehensive resource for cell-type-resolved MR of human complex traits and diseases. scMRdb harmonizes 5206 genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics of European and East Asian ancestry with 585 sc-eQTL datasets spanning 11 tissues and cell systems, including 110 cell types. A uniform pipeline evaluates all gene-trait pairs via MR followed by Steiger directionality testing. Significant associations are assessed by colocalization, and results are stratified into six confidence tiers with integrated drug-target annotation. scMRdb enables systematic recovery of candidate causal genes supported by cell-type-resolved regulatory evidence that is often diluted or obscured in bulk-tissue analyses. We expect scMRdb to serve as a user-friendly portal for generating cell-type-informed mechanistic hypotheses and prioritizing actionable therapeutic targets for complex human diseases.
authors: Pan S, Wang Z, Jia P.

title: Integrating multi-marker phylogeny and morphology reveals hidden diversity and intraspecific morphological variation in the genus Pseudohydnum P. Karst. (Basidiomycota, Auriculariales) from China.
abstract: The toothed jelly genus Pseudohydnum P. Karst. (Basidiomycota, Auriculariales) has historically been treated under a broad morphological concept centered on P. gelatinosum, a view that has long masked substantial cryptic diversity worldwide. However, many Chinese collections remain taxonomically unresolved and species boundaries are poorly defined. Here, we reassess the species diversity of Chinese Pseudohydnum through an integrative approach combining detailed morphology with multi-marker phylogenetics (ITS, nrLSU, and rpb1). We formally describe three new species, P. ellipsosporum sp. nov., P. macroumbrosum sp. nov., and P. roseolostipitatum sp. nov. We also refine the circumscriptions of four previously described taxa and provide new insights into their intraspecific variation, geographic distribution, and ecology. Notably, we document a previously unknown host association: P. brunneiceps was consistently found on decayed bamboo (Phyllostachys edulis), a substrate never before recorded for any Pseudohydnum species. Critically, our results demonstrate that morphology alone is currently insufficient for species delimitation as convergent or plastic characters obscure diagnostic differences, reinforcing the necessity of molecular validation. These findings substantially expand the known taxonomic and ecological diversity of Pseudohydnum in Asia, suggesting that China, particularly the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau, may be a global hotspot for the genus. Overall, this study underscores the essential role of phylogenetic inference in revising species boundaries and elucidating evolutionary patterns in morphologically plastic groups of fungi.
authors: Yu TJ, Zhang WH, Li XJ, Xiong YY, Gao YX, Li T, Xue R, Lu YT, Xu C, Li J, Tang LP.

title: DUF6383-domain containing protein from Parabacteroides distasonis predicts survival in patients with alcohol-associated hepatitis.
abstract: Intestinal dysbiosis is a hallmark of alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD) characterized by a higher abundance of unfavorable species and a reduction of beneficial species. In this study, we aimed to analyze the bacterial proteome of stool samples from patients with alcohol-associated hepatitis (AH) (n = 80), alcohol use disorder (AUD; n = 20), and controls (n = 19) from an international multicenter cohort using quantitative tandem mass tag (TMT)-based metaproteomic profiling. We validated our results in an independent multicenter cohort of 72 patients with AH at the genomic level using qPCR. We detected 2,364 bacterial proteins and identified distinct metaproteomic signatures separating controls, patients with AUD, and AH. Patients with AUD and AH were characterized by depletion of Firmicutes-derived proteins and enrichment of proteins from Bacteroidetes, Proteobacteria, and Actinobacteria. Eighteen bacterial proteins increased with disease severity, many with multifunctional "moonlighting" roles, including enolase and hexokinase. DUF6383 domain-containing protein from Parabacteroides distasonis is correlated with histological injury, inflammatory cell infiltration, and is linked to neutrophil degranulation in the host. Patients with a high abundance of DUF6383 domain-containing protein had significantly lower 90-day survival, and this association was validated by qPCR at the genomic level in a second cohort. Our findings show that microbial proteins are associated with disease severity and progression, and that DUF6383 domain-containing protein from P. distasonis is a potential prognostic biomarker for AH.

title: Immune Cell-Mediated Interactions Between the Gut Microbiome and Endometriosis: A Mendelian Randomization Investigation.
abstract: ObjectiveThe etiology of endometriosis (EM) remains unclear. Evidence indicates a correlation between intestinal microbial communities and immune homeostasis in the pathogenesis of EM. This investigation leverages Mendelian randomization (MR) to delineate causal links connecting gut microbiota composition, specific immune cell phenotypes, and endometriosis, aiming to identify novel therapeutic avenues.MethodsUsing publicly available genetic data from genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary datasets that encompass 473 microbial taxa, 731 immunological traits, and endometriosis cases, we executed bidirectional and two-step Mendelian randomization (MR) frameworks to assess causality and quantify mediation effects, aiming to evaluate the associations between intestinal microbial communities and immune homeostasis in the pathogenesis of endometriosis (EM). Utilizing single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) as instrumental variables (IVs), we ensured robustness through sensitivity assessments, specifically Cochran's Q statistic and MR-Egger regression, to mitigate concerns regarding horizontal pleiotropy and heterogeneity.ResultsOur analysis revealed that Actinobacteria exerted an influence on HLA-DR+ CD8+ T cells (total effect: -0.2736; mediated proportion: 6.45%), whereas Actinomycetales regulated DN (CD4-CD8-) NKT cell populations (total effect: -0.1961; mediated proportion: 5.77%). Furthermore, Aneurinibacillaceae demonstrated a 14.30% mediation effect operating through CD28 expression levels on resting regulatory T cells (Tregs) (total effect: 0.4053). Eisenbergiella sp900066775 displayed pleiotropic impacts on markers associated with both Tregs and B cells (total effect: -0.1447). Notably, protective correlations were identified for Actinobacteria (Odds Ratio [OR] = 0.76, 95% Confidence Interval [CI]: 0.65-0.89) and Bifidobacterium angulatum (OR = 0.88, 95% CI: 0.83-0.94). Conversely, Aneurinibacillaceae abundance was linked to elevated endometriosis susceptibility (OR = 1.50, 95% CI: 1.13-1.98).ConclusionDysbiosis within the gut microbiome fosters endometriosis development by modulating immune cell dynamics, predominantly via pathways involving Tregs and NKT cells. These results underscore the microbiota-immune axis as a promising target for intervention, warranting future clinical trials to evaluate probiotic or immunomodulatory strategies.
authors: Huang X, Zhong R, Pan L.

title: Transcriptome and DNA methylome profiling reveal molecular responses of bovine blastocysts to trophectoderm biopsy and post-biopsy vitrification.
abstract: Trophectoderm biopsy and post-biopsy vitrification are used in bovine embryo selection and cryopreservation, but their molecular effects remain incompletely understood. We investigated associated transcriptomic and DNA methylation changes in individual bovine blastocysts. Fifteen morphologically intact in vitro-produced blastocysts were allocated to non-biopsied fresh (NB), biopsied (B), and biopsied and vitrified (BV) groups (5 each). Cytoplasmic RNA and nuclear DNA from each blastocyst were profiled by Smart-seq2 and whole-genome bisulfite sequencing, respectively. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs), differentially methylated regions (DMRs), and coordinated promoter methylation-expression changes were analyzed through pairwise comparisons and Gene Ontology and KEGG enrichment. B vs NB yielded 822 DEGs (390 up/432 down), BV vs B 1295 (777/518), and BV vs NB 1494 (887/607). Biopsy-associated DEGs were enriched in glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, pyruvate metabolism, mitochondrial biogenesis, steroid biosynthesis, and peroxisome pathways. Vitrification was additionally associated with endocytosis, cell adhesion, and MAPK, TGF-β, FoxO, and estrogen signaling pathways; apoptosis and carbon metabolism featured in BV vs NB. B vs NB had the fewest DMRs, BV vs NB the most hypermethylated, and BV vs B the most hypomethylated. Genes with concurrent hypermethylation and downregulation were enriched in the tricarboxylic acid cycle and fatty-acid, amino-acid, sulfur, and glycerophospholipid metabolism, whereas those with hypomethylation and upregulation were associated with cytoskeleton remodeling, focal adhesion, and PI3K-Akt, Ras, MAPK, and calcium signaling. Biopsy was associated with transcriptional and epigenetic remodeling, and vitrification with broader metabolic, intercellular-signaling, and cellular-stress alterations. These candidate responses need functional validation and may help refine embryo biopsy and cryopreservation protocols.
authors: Feng X, Dong J, Ayantoye JO, Kolachi HA, Wang Y, Zhang Y, Wan P, Wang C, Zhao X.

title: Antimicrobial resistance detection technologies and the role of healthcare workforce: A scoping review of recent research.
abstract: BackgroundReliable determination of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is fundamental to healthcare research and practice. High-quality research evidence is essential for guiding accurate AMR detection which, in turn, informs antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) decision-making. This scoping review is directed at a critical evaluation of the recent strategies in AMR detection across the globe.MethodsPertinent primary studies on AMR-associated strategies were identified by a comprehensive literature search on scholarly databases (PubMed, Google Scholar, and EMBASE) in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. The final set of pertinent studies published during the last 5 years (2021-2026) included 58 studies. Subsequent analysis critically evaluated the evidence of integration of advanced technologies into AMR detection and prediction programs.ResultsWhole-genome sequencing (WGS; n = 37 articles) was the primary method for AMR screening across the included studies. Metagenomic sequencing (MGS) data was used for AMR characterization in 6 studies, while PCR/multiplex PCR was used in 10 articles. An interesting trend was the use of machine learning (ML) models for predicting AMR. Almost all studies which developed, validated and/or employed ML models (n = 21 studies) reported excellent time- and cost-efficiency, high accuracy and precision, and good concordance with conventional methods for AMR screening. Building on this synthesis, we propose the Integrated Diagnostic-Stewardship-Workforce (IDSW) model, a hypothesis-generating, five layered conceptual framework linking diagnostic innovations, workforce-mediated decision making, AMS intervention, contextual modifiers, and outcome feedback loop.ConclusionThe reviewed evidence supports the adaptation of AMR detection practices for clinical decision support systems, with potential downstream implications for technology-enhanced stewardship programs. Further, the proposed IDSW model offers a framework for guiding future research, policy making, and implementation efforts that integrate diagnostics and workforce roles, with AMS as a key downstream application.
journal: Journal of infection and public health
authors: Bantun F, Jalal NA, Faidah H, Babalghith AO, Johargy AK, Ahmad F, Mathkor DM, Haque S, Srivastava V.

title: Distribution patterns of PFASs in intertidal sediments and the effects on reductive dehalogenating bacteria: A nationwide study in China.
abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) are of great concern because of their environmental persistence. The intertidal zone sequesters various halogenated organic pollutants (HOPs) in sediments. Microbial reductive dehalogenation is crucial for HOPs detoxification. However, the nationwide distribution characteristics of PFASs in intertidal sediments and their impact on reductive dehalogenators (RDGs) remain poorly understood. We investigated PFAS distribution profiles in 128 intertidal sediments across China and analyzed their impact on potential RDGs. Sedimentary PFAS concentrations ranged 0.049-2.58 ng/g, with legacy PFASs being dominant. Amplicon sequencing and Spearman rank correlation analysis revealed positive correlation between total organic halogens and relative abundance and/or α-diversity of Anaerolineae and Desulfobacterota (p < 0.05), whereas no correlation was observed for Dehalococcoidia. Despite low ecological risks, Cl-PFESAs showed significant negative correlations with their relative abundance and α-diversity. Cl-PFESAs negatively correlated with abundance of the module associated with elemental cycles (p < 0.05), rather than those linked to organohalide utilization in the co-occurrence network. Microbial cultivation and metagenomic analysis reinforced the crucial role of Desulfobacterota and Anaerolineae in intertidal microbial dehalogenation and the negligible effect of 6:2 Cl-PFESA (0.1 mg/L) on reductive dehalogenating activity. This study provides critical insights into bioremediation strategies for HOPs in intertidal zones co-contaminated with PFASs.
authors: Zhu X, Wang H, Li S, Ni L, Li Y, Zhang D.

title: Genome-guided development of a halotolerant endophytic consortium-based biofertilizer enhances rice plant growth and salinity tolerance with reduced chemical fertilizer inputs.
abstract: Soil salinity is a major abiotic stress limiting rice productivity worldwide and necessitates sustainable alternatives to intensive chemical fertilizer use. We developed a genome-guided halotolerant endophytic bacterial consortium to enhance rice growth and resilience in salt-affected agroecosystems. A total of 101 endophytic bacteria were screened using a multi-phase strategy based on salt tolerance, plant growth-promoting (PGP) traits, retention of PGP functions under saline stress, and enhancement of rice seed germination under increasing salinity. Seven compatible strains were selected and identified as Phytobacter diazotrophicus, Mangrovibacter phragmitis (two strains), Brachybacterium paraconglomeratum, Priestia flexa, Micrococcus luteus, and Staphylococcus haemolyticus, for formulation into a talc-based biofertilizer. Whole-genome sequencing revealed genetic determinants linked to plant growth promotion and salinity adaptation, including genes associated with indole-3-acetic acid biosynthesis, phosphate solubilisation, nitrogen fixation, siderophore production, exopolysaccharide synthesis, osmoprotection, ion homeostasis, antioxidant defence, and plant colonisation. In vitro assays showed that the biofertilizer significantly enhanced rice seedling growth and biomass under saline conditions compared with individual strains and liquid consortium inoculation. Pot experiments showed that combining biofertilizer with a 75% reduced chemical fertilizer dose significantly improved plant growth, physiological performance, nutrient uptake, and stress tolerance under both 4 and 6 dS m⁻¹ salinity. Moreover, biofertilizer application improved soil nutrient status while reducing sodium accumulation and oxidative stress, with the magnitude of these benefits greater under salinity stress. These findings demonstrate the potential of genome-enabled microbial biofertilizers for sustainable rice cultivation in saline environments with reduced chemical fertiliser inputs.
authors: Das G, Jana S, Dhal PK.

title: Experimental benchmarking of in silico annotations at prostate cancer risk loci and hypothesis-generating cross-cancer prioritisation of ovarian risk variants.
abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified numerous non-coding risk variants for prostate and ovarian cancers, yet determining which are regulatorily active and which target genes they control remains challenging. We re-analysed a dinucleotide-barcode massively parallel reporter assay (DiR-seq) of 208 bi-allelic prostate cancer risk single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in three prostate cancer cell lines under false-discovery-rate (FDR) control, identifying 50 regulatory SNPs at FDR < 0.10 (30 at FDR < 0.05), including 9 shared by at least two cell lines. Benchmarking standard in-silico functional annotations against this experimental ground truth revealed poor predictive performance (cross-validated ROC-AUC = 0.55-0.59), demonstrating that computational predictions cannot reliably substitute for measured allelic activity. We therefore treated the ovarian analysis as hypothesis-generating. Convergent annotation evidence prioritised 44 of 176 ovarian cancer GWAS leads (31 independent loci); a core of 21 SNPs (17 loci) was stable under alternative weights, leave-one-feature-out scoring and threshold changes, and candidates were enriched in ovarian and fallopian-tube regulatory chromatin (OR = 7.9, FDR = 5 × 10⁻5). Copy-number recurrence at candidate genes agreed between two tumour cohorts (Spearman ρ = 0.75, 95% CI 0.46-0.88) but no more than for chromosome-arm-matched control genes, so this observation is exploratory. Formal colocalisation with full summary statistics supported a shared causal variant for prostate cancer risk and TLCD3A expression at 17p13.3 (PP.H4 = 0.92), whereas the ovarian 17q21.31 signal could not be resolved to a single gene. Transcription-factor motifs disrupted in both cancers were over-represented for the interferon-regulatory factor (IRF) and STAT families (FDR = 3 × 10⁻6), a motif-level hypothesis. In an independent MPRA in primary ovarian epithelial cells, variants disrupting interferon-stimulated response elements (ISREs) were depleted, not enriched, for allele-specific activity (4.6% vs 9.2%; OR = 0.47, nominal p = 0.06, FDR = 0.10), so the IRF/STAT hypothesis was not supported; the same assay confirmed allele-specific activity at one prioritised ovarian candidate, rs2976384 (skew = - 0.67, FDR = 3 × 10⁻5). These results provide an audited prostate regulatory-SNP catalogue, quantify the limits of annotation-based fine-mapping, and offer testable cross-cancer hypotheses.
authors: Al-Amili WA, Ayyed Najm M, Jumaah SS, Suleiman AA.

title: Integrated Multi-Omics Analysis of Polygonatum odoratum Polysaccharide in D-Galactose-Treated Mice Reveals Changes in Oxidative Stress Markers and Gut Microbiota.
abstract: Age-related changes are associated with oxidative stress, metabolic dysregulation, and alterations in the gut microbiota. Although Polygonatum odoratum polysaccharide (POP) has shown antioxidant and neuroprotective effects, its associations with gut bacterial composition, circulating metabolites, and tissue gene expression remain unclear. Using a D-galactose-treated mouse model, we assessed hippocampal histology and oxidative stress markers and performed bacterial 16S rRNA sequencing, untargeted serum metabolomics, and hippocampal and colonic transcriptomic analyses. POP treatment was associated with improved hippocampal histology, reduced malondialdehyde levels, and increased glutathione levels and superoxide dismutase activity. It was also associated with changes in selected gut bacterial taxa and serum lipid metabolites, lower expression of NF-κB-related genes (Btk, Lat, and Tnfrsf13c) in the colon, and lower Ninj2 expression in the hippocampus. Cross-omics analysis identified correlations among these bacterial, metabolite, and gene-expression features. These findings identify candidate gut-serum-tissue associations accompanying the effects of POP in D-galactose-treated mice. Functional studies are needed to determine whether any of these changes mediate its effects.
authors: Li W, Huang Y, Zhang W, Li S, Li L.

title: Human Saliva Induces Acetoin-Dependent Metabolic Adaptation that Promotes Stress Tolerance in  Streptococcus mutans
abstract: ABSTRACT  Oral microbes are continually exposed to host-derived saliva, yet its effects on bacterial metabolism and stress adaptation remain incompletely defined. We investigated how saliva supplementation alters the physiology of the caries-associated bacterium  Streptococcus mutans using transcriptomics (RNA-Seq), targeted metabolite measurements, specific gene deletions, and transposon sequencing (Tn-Seq). Growth in a chemically defined medium supplemented with pooled saliva altered expression of genes involved in carbohydrate transport, purine biosynthesis, and pyruvate-associated metabolism, including induction of the acetoin dehydrogenase operon. Saliva significantly increased extracellular acetoin accumulation across all  S. mutans isolates tested, whereas little accumulation occurred in two commensal streptococcal species examined. Deletion of acetolactate synthase/decarboxylase (  alsSaldB ) abolished the saliva-associated increase, while deletion of individual acetoin dehydrogenase components (  adhC /  lplA ) enhanced accumulation, supporting the predicted roles of genes in acetoin synthesis and catabolism. Increasing the available carbohydrate concentrations within the media further increased acetoin accumulation, alongside declining terminal culture pH that was significantly lower in cultures supplemented with saliva. Following growth with saliva,  S. mutans exhibited approximately 10,000-fold greater survival during a hydrogen peroxide challenge than cells grown without saliva. Mutants within the acetoin pathway retained saliva-associated protection but showed approximately 100-fold lower survival than the wild type. Serial passage of a pooled transposon library identified previously unrecognized saliva-associated fitness determinants, including depletion of mutants carrying insertions in the acetoin dehydrogenase operon. Together, these findings identify acetoin metabolism as a contributor to saliva-associated metabolic remodeling and oxidative stress tolerance in  S. mutans and establish saliva as a critical modulator of  S. mutans physiology.
authors: Harris JS, Deever AN, Lee K, Kaspar JR.

title: Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury.
abstract: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most devastating gastrointestinal emergency in preterm infants, frequently causing mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment1,2. Although the gut microbiota has been implicated in NEC pathogenesis3-5, the microbial factors driving NEC and the following brain pathology remain unclear. Here we identify Clostridium perfringens pathobionts containing Delta toxin in the gut microbiome of individuals with severe and fatal NEC. Clinically, infected infants show worse outcomes, including aberrant systemic inflammation, severe neurological damage and coagulopathy. We establish a mouse model in which Delta-toxin-positive C. perfringens infection, or Delta toxin exposure alone, recapitulates clinical features of NEC, including intestinal necrosis and acute cerebral injury. Mechanistically, Delta toxin preferentially targets macrophages, potently activating inflammasome signalling and pyroptosis, triggering a rapid inflammatory cascade that compromises blood-brain barrier integrity and drives neuroinflammation. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify the tetraspanin CD9 as the host receptor for Delta toxin. Using systemic, myeloid-specific and intestinal-epithelial-specific Cd9-knockout mice, we show that systemic and myeloid Cd9 ablation protects mice against toxin-induced lethality, blood-brain barrier dysfunction and multiorgan injury, whereas epithelial Cd9 deletion shows partial protection, implicating macrophage targeting as a primary driver of C. perfringens CD9-dependent pathogenesis. Furthermore, a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody confers protection against disease progression. These findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a specific-toxin-mediated disorder and validate the Delta toxin-CD9 axis as a therapeutic target for this subset.
authors: Zhang S, Gong X, Tian S, Yang Y, Tong X, Sheng K, Zhang Y, Amatsu S, Zhang X, Yu D, Zhao H, Ruan L, Sun H, Wu K, Dong M, Xiong X.

title: Bacteriophages versus priority pathogens: resistance mechanisms, therapeutic challenges, and opportunities for novel combinations.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance poses a critical global health threat, and renewed interest in bacteriophage (phage) therapy highlights its potential as a targeted alternative to antibiotic monotherapy. However, phage resistance in bacteria remains a key limiting factor in phage therapy, driven by evolutionary adaptations to phage exposure. Antibacterial modalities (antibiotics, adjuvants, antimicrobial peptides, and RNA-based therapeutics) could help overcome these barriers and represent untapped potential for synergistic, precision antimicrobial interventions when combined with phage therapy. Importantly, bacterial physiology and environmental context could strongly influence treatment outcomes, underscoring the need for clinically relevant models for testing combinations. Integration of multi-omics and artificial intelligence-driven approaches could help predict patterns for the development of precision therapies and support the development of novel antimicrobial interventions.
authors: Byrne S, Collins ACZ, Nolan AC, Wigneshweraraj S, Zeden MS.

title: Multi-omics insights into rare earth element recovery by microalgae under salinity gradients.
abstract: Conventional rare earth element (REE) extraction methods are resource-intensive and generate secondary pollutants, whereas biomining using microorganisms such as microalgae offers a more sustainable alternative. Microalgal growth and metal recovery are strongly influenced by environmental factors, especially salinity; however, the molecular mechanisms driving REE recovery in microalgae exposed to saline conditions remain largely unexplored. The overarching aim of this study is to elucidate the effects of salinity on REE recovery by microalgae using a multi-omics framework. Specifically, nine microalgal strains were screened across salinities of 0-5 %, followed by integrated metabolomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic characterization of Limnospira maxima under control, REE-only, 3.5 % salinity, and combined REE-salinity conditions. Among the tested species, L. maxima exhibited the highest REE recovery efficiency, outperforming other microalgae by a factor of 2-10. In L. maxima, heavy REE (Sc, Y, Tb, and Dy) were recovered 10-15 % more efficiently than light REE (La, Pr, Nd), particularly under salinities between 0.5 % and 5 %. The selective recovery of REE by L. maxima was most pronounced at elevated salinities. Global metabolomic profiles of the combined treatment were primarily associated with salinity, suggesting that salinity establishes the dominant physiological state within which REE-associated responses occur. Multi-omics analysis showed distinct responses to REE and salinity stress, including changes in carbon fixation, photosynthesis, and amino acid and lipid metabolism, with both transcript-protein convergence and pathway-level discordance indicating complex cross-layer regulation. Overall, the results identify L. maxima as a promising candidate for REE recovery under saline conditions while defining molecular responses and knowledge gaps relevant to future development of microalgae-based REE separation.
authors: Vo PHN, Songsomboon K, Kim M, Strezov V, Clark S, Kuzhiumparambil U, Pernice M, Ralph PJ.
