title: TEDEdb: A multicohort analysis and resource for transposable element differential expression in cancer.
abstract: The human genome consists of nearly 50% repetitive DNA, referred to for decades as "junk DNA." These repetitive sequences, usually under the strict control of epigenetic silencing, can become aberrantly expressed in cancer. Some of these expressed sequences, e.g., transposable elements (TEs), can induce innate immune responses when derepressed following treatment with epigenetic therapies. As a result, epigenetic therapy has been suggested to augment cancer therapies. TEs are traditionally ignored in most RNA-seq studies and their expression is often excluded from publicly available data sources. Thus, the vast amount of publicly available RNA-seq data is an untapped resource for exploring the role of TE expression in cancer and cancer treatment. Here, we present a uniform reanalysis of over 7,000 RNA-seq samples, encompassing more than 2,000 differential expression experiments across 220 cancer cell lines and 700 drug treatments. We observed that TE expression is more prone to batch effects than gene expression alone, necessitating the use of meta-analysis techniques to probe the dataset for global trends. We confirm that DNMTi and HDACis are powerful inducers of TE expression. We also show that nonepigenetic compounds such as cyclin-dependent kinase and topoisomerase inhibitors can also induce robust up-regulation of TE-derived repetitive DNA elements and confirm that this induction is consistent with transcriptional signatures of viral mimicry response. We made all data available through a publicly available database called the Transposable Element Differential Expression Database, or TEDEdb, and created an interactive web application for its exploration located at https://dataexplorer.coriell.org/TEDEdb/.
authors: Calendo G, Chaunzwa M, Dehzangi I, Madzo J, Issa JJ.

title: Evolutionarily diverged on-switch for actin assembly in fungal endocytosis.
abstract: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis is a conserved eukaryotic trafficking process where an Arp2/3 complex-nucleated branched actin network provides force for vesicle formation. The mechanisms that initiate endocytic actin assembly are incompletely understood. In the fission yeast, Schizosaccharomyces pombe, actin assembly is initiated by Dip1, an Arp2/3 complex activator. In the budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the initiation of actin assembly has remained a mystery. Here, we show that S. cerevisiae Ldb17, the homolog of Dip1, functions as an on-switch for endocytic actin assembly. Unexpectedly, the regulation of Ldb17 is more complicated than that of constitutively active Dip1. Ldb17 is controlled by a coat protein, Sla1, via separate recruitment and activation steps. This regulation was likely lost in the S. pombe lineage, and this simplification may be related to other changes in actin assembly between these species. Our findings add a key missing piece in the understanding of endocytosis in S. cerevisiae and reveal an intriguing evolutionary tinkering of the actin on-switch.
authors: Sebellin J, Kandiyoth FB, Bagyashree VT, Picco A, Carvalho N, Hakala M, Rivier-Cordey AS, Michelot A, Toret CP, Kaksonen M.

title: Sequence-structured fitness landscapes predict influenza evolution
abstract: Seasonal influenza viruses continually evolve to evade host immunity. Vaccines must be regularly updated to protect against new circulating strains, motivating efforts to forecast viral evolution. Recent experimental and computational methods have made progress on this problem, but learning the fitness landscape driving viral evolution remains challenging because genomic surveillance samples only a small fraction of the possible sequence space. Here, we developed a generative framework that shares information across genetically related variants, inferring effective mutation-level contributions to viral fitness from temporal sequence data. Applied to hemagglutinin and neuraminidase from A/H3N2 and A/H1N1 viruses, the inferred fitness landscapes recovers known determinants of antigenicity and reveals convergent spatial organization across subtypes consistent with common antibody-mediated selection. Forward simulations from these landscapes predicted both the fixation or loss of circulating mutations and the future composition of viral populations, outperforming models based on neutral evolution or multinomial-logistic growth. Collectively, our results show that interpretable representations of pathogen fitness landscapes can reveal biologically important features and improve prospective evolutionary forecasting.
authors: Rodríguez-Horta E, Barton JP.

title: Transcriptomic and metabolomic profiling reveals early responses of tomato plants elicited by compost-derived bacteria
abstract: Compost produced from biowaste has a defined microbiota, and some bacterial species may represent promising resources for low-input crop systems. However, their effects on plant physiology are poorly investigated and remain difficult to predict from standard bacterial traits alone. We isolated several bacterial strains (  Bacillus sonorensis, Glutamicibacter arilaitensis, and  Kocuria rhizophila ) from biowaste compost and examined their early effects on tomato seedlings under controlled in vitro conditions. Responses were assessed by root phenotyping, root and shoot transcriptomics, and mass spectrometry-based profiling of primary metabolites in plant tissues, root exudates and bacterial culture filtrates.  B. sonorensis induces the broadest response, reducing primary root length and lateral root number and density and triggering broad transcriptional changes related to metabolism, redox balance, hormone signalling and defence-associated pathways.  G. arilaitensis elicits a more selective, tissue-dependent response, whereas  K. rhizophila has limited phenotypic and transcriptional effects at this stage. All isolates reshape primary metabolism, with recurrent effects on amino acid-, carbohydrate- and lipid-related pathways, together with isolate-specific changes in root exudate composition. This study characterises the early molecular and metabolic responses of tomato to compost-derived bacteria and identifies common and strain-specific physiological signatures that provide a foundation for future studies under biotic and abiotic stress.
authors: Ghirardello G, Araniti F, Cipriani R, Zanardi W, Bonato T, Baldan B, Nigris S.

title: Selection through soft and incomplete sweeps underlies postglacial ecotype differentiation in an Arctic wide-ranging ungulate
abstract: Abstract  Ecotypes offer a window into the earliest stages of adaptive divergence, before reproductive isolation is complete. In eastern Canada, migratory and boreal caribou (Rangifer tarandus caribou) represent a striking example of recent ecological divergence, differing primarily in movement strategy despite ongoing gene flow. We used low- and high-coverage whole-genome sequencing from migratory and boreal populations in Quebec and Labrador to characterize the timing, demographic history, and genomic signatures of this divergence. Demographic modeling supported a secondary contact scenario, with an estimated divergence time roughly 7,000–11,700 years ago, coinciding with the last deglaciation period. Despite weak overall population structure (genome-wide FST = 0.02) and evidence of continued gene flow, we identified distinct genomic peaks of differentiation, nearly half of which coincided with divergent haplotype length (XP-nSL), a pattern consistent with recent, incomplete soft selective sweeps rather than classic hard sweeps. Combining differentiation-, diversity-, and haplotype-based statistics proved essential for detecting this subtle selection signature. Candidate genes under selection point to a polygenic architecture spanning bone and connective tissue development (including antler-related pathways), mitochondrial energy metabolism, and other traits plausibly linked to the ecological differences between ecotypes. Together, our results suggest that caribou ecotypes are not fixed evolutionary endpoints but a dichotomy that can re-emerge from standing genetic variation as opportunity arises.
authors: Dallaire X, Yannic G, Taillon J, St-Laurent M, Robert C, Côté S, Shafer A.

title: Infection-Induced SRSF2 Downregulation Drives VEGF-A Isoform Switching to Impair Angiogenesis in Diabetic Foot Ulcers
abstract: Abstract    Background:  Impaired vascular repair and infection contribute to delayed healing in diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs). Whether infection-associated inflammatory stress affects endothelial function through altered RNA processing remains incompletely understood. We investigated SRSF2 and VEGFA isoform regulation in this setting. Human DFU tissues and microbiota were assessed across Wagner grades, and bacterial inoculation was examined in a diabetic mouse wound model. Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) were exposed to high glucose (HG) with or without lipopolysaccharide (LPS). SRSF2 was manipulated to assess scratch closure, EdU incorporation, and tube formation. Knockdown RNA sequencing was performed separately in HMEC-1 cells. Isoform-directed RT-qPCR, RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP)-qPCR, and a dual-fluorescence VEGFA minigene reporter were used to examine RNA regulation in HUVECs.  Results:  Higher Wagner grades were associated with lower granulation tissue and CD31-positive areas and differences in microbial composition. In diabetic mice, bacterial inoculation delayed wound closure and was accompanied by reduced vascularization and endothelial SRSF2 staining. HG+LPS reduced SRSF2 expression and impaired endothelial functional readouts. SRSF2 knockdown reproduced these defects, whereas overexpression partially improved them under HG+LPS. Transcriptomic analysis identified widespread splicing changes after SRSF2 depletion. Under HG+LPS, RT-qPCR showed lower VEGFA-165a and higher VEGFA-165b signals; SRSF2 overexpression partially reversed these changes. The minigene reporter shifted toward VEGF-A165b-associated output under HG+LPS or SRSF2 knockdown and toward VEGF-A165a-associated output following SRSF2 overexpression. VEGFA pre-mRNA was enriched in SRSF2 immunoprecipitates.  Conclusions:  SRSF2 contributes to endothelial angiogenic function under hyperglycemic and LPS stress, and its manipulation alters VEGFA isoform-associated readouts. These findings support a potential role for SRSF2-associated RNA processing in diabetic wound vascular dysfunction. They do not establish that VEGFA isoform switching mediates the functional effects of SRSF2 or that the same mechanism operates in human DFUs.
authors: Zeng Z, An J, Mo Z, Luo G, Liu C, Cai Y.

title: Rhizobacterial genetic diversity associated with Paspalum atratum and Paspalum notatum by metagenomic analysis
abstract: Abstract    The genus  Paspalum  belongs to the Poaceae family and encompasses several species native to South America. The  Paspalum  Germplasm Bank of Embrapa Pecuária Sudeste has about 450 accessions of 50 species. Among the conserved accessions,  Paspalum notatum  BGP 26 and  Paspalum atratum  BGP 308 were selected for their importance as turfgrass and forage, respectively. The rhizospheric bacterial community of  P. atratum  and  P. notatum  was analyzed via 16S (V3-V4 region) metabarcoding sequencing. The statistical difference found for the Chao ecological index indicates that the bacterial composition and diversity were associated with each species. Thirty-one operational taxonomic units (OTUs) were identified with a predominance higher than 1% from 9 phyla (Proteobacteria n = 11, Acidobacteria n = 8, Actinobacteria n = 3, Planctomycetes n = 2, Nitrospirae n = 2, Verrucomicrobia n = 2, Chloroflexi n = 1, Gemmatimonadetes n = 1, and Bacteroidetes n = 1). Among these, 19 OTUs significantly differed between the species studied. Soil hydrogen-ionic potential (pH) was one of the most important factors influencing the species-specific difference of bacterial populations among accessions. Acidobacteriaceae (Subgroup 1), from the phylum Acidobacteria, was the most abundant family in  P. atratum  . The main group found in  P. notatum  was related to the family Nitrosomonadaceae from the phylum Proteobacteria. Our findings highlight a significant distinction in the rhizospheric bacterial community among the examined  Paspalum  accessions and underscore the existence of a species-specific association. These results can aid soil management practices, particularly in relation to vital economic aspects. Further research could help optimize agricultural strategies and promote sustainable soil health.
authors: de Paula AF, de Andrade PHM, Matheucci E, Carazzolle MF, de Carvalho LM, Vigna BBZ, Bernardi ACdC, Fávero AP, Cunha AFd, Lacava PT.

title: Bacterial supplementation during black soldier fly rearing improves frass plant growth-promoting properties
abstract: Abstract    Background  Black soldier fly (BSF,  Hermetia illucens  ) frass is increasingly valued as an organic fertilizer, yet how the rearing substrate and its microbial supplementation shape the frass bacterial community and its agronomic quality remains poorly understood. Aims  We assessed whether microbial supplementation of an olive pomace substrate affects black soldier fly larval performance and the agronomic and microbial quality of the resulting frass. Methods  The substrate was supplemented with two commercial  Bacillus velezensis  formulations (CAL, LAL) and two gut-derived strains selected for broad enzymatic capabilities (LG, closest match  Paenibacillus cookii  ; PD, closest match  Shouchella clausii  ), each supplied live or heat-inactivated. Larval performance was recorded, the heat-treated frass (70°C, 60 min) was evaluated on cherry tomato, and the frass bacterial community was characterized by 16S rRNA sequencing. Results  Effects on larval performance were modest and preparation-dependent: inactivated PD increased larval weight, inactivated LG increased harvest weight, and frass production increased with live CAL, LAL and LG. All supplemented frass types increased root dry weight relative to non-supplemented frass, with LG-F performing best, and frass generally promoted greater plant biomass than mineral and organic fertilizers while maintaining germination. Despite similar chemical profiles, treatment explained 79.1% of the variation in frass community structure;  Bacillus  was enriched in LAL-F and  Oceanobacillus  , a genus with plant growth-promoting traits, in three of the four supplemented treatments. Conclusions  Although strain viability was not confirmed, microbial supplementation during rearing altered the bacterial composition and agronomic value of BSF frass, supporting its potential as a tailored biofertilizer.
authors: Fagua DC, Savio C, Fantatto RR, Souza CSe, Garcia-Fraile P.

title: Identification and applicability of azg1 as counter-selectable marker in Trichoderma species
abstract: Abstract    Background  The widespread use of pesticides and antibiotics in agriculture and clinical settings has accelerated the emergence of antimicrobial resistance across diverse organisms. Although this phenomenon is widely recognized in pathogenic microorganisms, much less is known about the effect on beneficial fungi that are playing a role in sustainable agriculture, such as  Trichoderma  . Many  Trichoderma  isolates, especially those originating from intensively treated soils, exhibit low sensitivity to commonly used laboratory antifungals, complicating their genetic manipulation. Results  In this study, we developed new genetic tools to facilitate the characterization and engineering of  Trichoderma  species, exploiting endogenous counter-selectable markers. Using  Trichoderma atroviride  as a model species, we first assessed fungal susceptibility to the nucleobase analogs 8-azaguanine, 5-fluorouracil and 5-fluorocytosine. While the fungus was sensitive to the first two compounds, 5-fluorocytosine showed no inhibitory effect. Using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated protoplast transformation, we generated mutants lacking a putative nucleobase analog transporter and identified the gene responsible for 8-azaguanine uptake. Deletion of this gene conferred resistance to 8-azaguanine without affecting the overall phenotype or growth behavior of  T. atroviride  under a range of tested conditions. This locus was subsequently employed as a counter-selectable marker for targeted integration events in  T. atroviride  and additional  Trichoderma  species. Furthermore, heterologous expression of the  Penicillium chrysogenum  cytidine deaminase gene, which catalyzes the intracellular metabolization of 5-fluorocytosine to 5-fluorouracil, rendered  T. atroviride  sensitive to this compound. Conclusion  Together, our findings establish  azg1  as a multifunctional genomic platform and expand the genetic toolkit available for  Trichoderma  research, providing the foundation for advanced strain engineering in agricultural and biotechnological applications.
authors: Baldin C, Oberdanner A, Schark L, Nagler J, Schreiner U, Huymann L, Gsaller F, Zeilinger S.

title: Exploring the causal role of the human gut microbiome in breast cancer risk
abstract: Background The relationship between the human gut microbiome and breast cancer (BC) risk is uncertain. Methods We used Mendelian randomization (MR) and multivariable linear regression to investigate the causal relationship between the human gut microbiome and BC risk (overall and subtype-specific) and interrogate the role of circulating metabolites as potential mediators. Summary-level data from genome-wide association studies of gut microbial traits (N = 3,890), circulating metabolites (N = 7,824), overall (N = 247,175) and subtype-specific (N = 200,898) BC risk, including triple negative BC (TNBC; N = 120,493), alongside individual-level data from the Flemish Gut Flora Project (N = 2,242). Sensitivity analyses were applied to examine the robustness of causal estimates. Results Initial two-sample MR analyses suggested that the presence of bacteria within the  Ruminococcus genus increased overall BC risk, that higher abundances of bacteria within the  Parabacteroides genus decreased and presence of unclassified bacteria within the  Bacteroidales order increased TNBC risk, and that several circulating metabolites altered BC risk (e.g., homostachydrine with overall BC and Luminal A BC, and betaine with TNBC). Whilst, in multivariable linear regression analyses, several of these metabolites were also associated with the microbial traits that influenced BC risk, given directional inconsistency of associations across analyses of microbial traits, metabolites and BC coupled with sensitivity analyses implying violations of MR assumptions, associations were unlikely to reflect causality nor a causal pathway between the gut microbiome, metabolites, and BC risk. Conclusions In conclusion, whilst our initial analyses suggested that the gut microbiome and certain circulating metabolites may be associated with BC risk, importantly, sensitivity analyses demonstrated that these relationships are complex and, certainly for the case of the gut microbiome, unlikely to reflect causality.
authors: Edmunds G, Robinson T, Yarmolinsky J, Lee M, Hayes B, Hughes D, Gibbs L, Braybrooke J, Raes J, Timpson N, Wade K.

title: Satellite DNA content and distribution along the mitotic and meiotic chromosomes of Coleonyx mitratus (Eublepharidae, Gekkota).
abstract: Satellite DNAs (satDNAs) are repetitive sequences that play important structural and functional roles in vertebrate genomes; however, their genomic composition and behavior during meiosis remain poorly understood in geckos. Here, we investigated the satellitome of the Central American banded gecko (Coleonyx mitratus) using bioinformatic and cytogenetic approaches. We identified fifteen candidate satDNA sequences representing at least fourteen satDNA families and mapped their distribution on mitotic and meiotic chromosomes. Most satellites were concentrated in constitutive heterochromatin regions. One of the satDNA families, CmitSat-10-58, showed compact signals associated with the core of the synaptonemal complex on most chromosomes and co-localized with anti-centromere antibodies, suggesting a possible role in centromeric function. A heterochromatin region on chromosome 6 containing two satDNA families showed delayed synapsis and excessive stretching during the pachytene stage. Differences in satDNA composition between the X and Y chromosomes may be associated with their delayed synapsis. Our results provide new insight into the organization, chromosomal distribution, and potential functional significance of satellite DNA in gecko genomes, and support further investigation of the relationship between repetitive DNA, heterochromatin organization, and chromosome dynamics during meiosis.
journal: Chromosome research : an international journal on the molecular, supramolecular and evolutionary aspects of chromosome biology
authors: Tishakova KV, Lisachov AP, Prokopov DY, Lisachova LS, Borodin PM, Trifonov VA.

title: Comparative RT-qPCR and qPCR Reveal 'Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus' Early and Low-Titer Infection and Relative Cell Activity in Citrus and Psyllids.
abstract: Citrus huanglongbing (HLB) is recognized as the most destructive bacterial disease affecting citrus. Among the causal agents, 'Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus' (Las) is the predominant species causing HLB epidemics worldwide. Detecting this phloem-limited bacterium at early or low-titer stages and assessing its cellular activity remain major challenges for HLB research and management. To address these limitations, we developed a one-step reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) assay for highly sensitive Las detection using total nucleic acids and the established Li 16S rRNA/rDNA primer-probe set. This method simultaneously amplifies both Las 16S rRNA and rDNA in a single reaction, increasing sensitivity by up to 500-fold compared with qPCR, which targets only 16S rDNA. The improved sensitivity reduced false negatives, expanded sampling capacity, and enabled detection of low-titer infections previously undetectable. In addition, the higher abundance of 16S rRNA generated a consistent Ct gap between RT-qPCR and qPCR, which we used to estimate relative Las cell activity in vivo in host insects and plants and to identify the most effective inoculum sources. This comparative detection strategy was further applied to evaluate inoculum potential, to monitor changes in relative cell activity during in vitro cultures, and to assess antimicrobial treatments targeting Las. The persistent detection of long-lasting, low-titer Las infections underscores the complex biology of the HLB causal agents and highlights ongoing challenges for effective disease management.
authors: Patterson R, Zheng D, Luo W, Deng Z, Bock C, Li R, Duan Y.

title: Autophagy and intratumoral bacteria abundance influence the prognosis of patients with pancreatic carcinoma.
abstract: The biological and clinical significance of the intratumoral microbiota in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains poorly defined. Using oncogenic Kras-driven mouse models of pancreatic tumorigenesis and human pancreatic tissue from patients with non-metastatic PDAC treated with neoadjuvant (n = 62) or adjuvant therapy (n = 101), along with samples from intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMN, n = 24), chronic pancreatitis (CP, n = 33), and healthy donors (n = 9), we determined tissue lipopolysaccharide (LPS), 16S rRNA sequencing, high-resolution quantitative multiplex immunofluorescence of autophagy markers (LAMP2, LC3B) and LPS, 16S rRNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) staining, and TLR4 signaling. In KrasCre mice, we identified significant bacterial accumulation in the pancreas, indicated by elevated LPS, increased FISH signals, enhanced TLR4 signaling, and activation of autophagy. Administration of exogenous LPS further amplified autophagy and TLR4 signaling, supporting a mechanistic link between microbial sensing and autophagy. In human tissue, both adjuvant and neoadjuvant PDAC samples showed significantly increased bacterial alpha- and beta diversity compared with controls, while CP showed a similar enrichment pattern that IPMN lacks; the underlying microbial diversity differs fundamentally across these conditions. Increased LPS levels, along with elevated autophagy markers and abundant FISH-positive bacteria, support the presence of intratumoral bacteria. Across four independent transcriptomic datasets, PDAC samples showed elevated expression of bacteria-associated pathways (including TLR4) and autophagy-related genes. Clinically, higher autophagy-associated LAMP2-LC3B colocalization and increased densities of FISH-positive cells were independently associated with prolonged survival in both adjuvant and neoadjuvant or combined PDAC patients. Collectively, these findings link intratumoral microbial enrichment to increased autophagy-associated signaling and improved patient outcomes, suggesting that microbial signals within the tumor microenvironment were associated with favorable survival.
authors: Zhang Y, Gobin TL, Huang Z, Miao B, Kurilov R, Sun H, Tjaden C, Heger U, Hackert T, Hinz U, Schaefer M, Bergmann F, Springfeld C, Mughal SS, Brors B, Schaal P, Cheaib B, Licastro D, Iebba V, Fortunato F.

title: Genome-Wide Characterization of BMP/GDF Genes in Sika Deer: Spatiotemporal Expression During Antler Regeneration and Computational Analysis of the BMP2–BMPR1A Complex
abstract: Antler regeneration involves rapid chondrogenesis and ossification, yet the bone morphogenetic protein/growth differentiation factor (BMP/GDF) genes associated with skeletal development remain poorly characterized in sika deer. We identified 16 BMP genes and two GDF genes belonging to seven phylogenetic subfamilies. Synteny analysis identified segmental and putative tandem duplications; two duplicated pairs had Ka/Ks ratios below 1. RNA-seq data showed differences across regenerative stages, with BMP3B and BMP5 expressed during early regeneration, BMP2, BMP4, and BMP6 during rapid growth, and BMP7 and BMP3 during terminal ossification. RT-qPCR supported distinct spatial expression patterns for five genes in rapidly growing antler tips. AlphaFold 3 modeling and molecular dynamics simulations indicated that the predicted BMP2–BMPR1A complex remained stable over the simulated trajectories. Free-energy decomposition and alanine scanning identified candidate interface residues. Sequence comparisons showed that these residues are conserved across the mammalian species examined. The results describe BMP/GDF family organization and expression during antler regeneration and identify candidate contacts for experimental analysis of BMP2–BMPR1A binding.
authors: Jian L, Lin Y, Cheng X, Zhang H, Liu Q, Xu J, Lu T, Wang Y, Wang Y.

title: Persistent Pediatric Cervical Lymphadenopathy: A Case Report of Kikuchi-Fujimoto Disease Mimicking Infection and Malignancy.
abstract: Case presentationA 10-year-old female presented with 2 months of unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy despite several courses of oral antibiotics. She presented to the emergency department due to persistent pain and swelling along with new fever. On presentation, she was febrile to 39.0°C. Physical examination revealed significant left-sided cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy with tenderness, warmth, and overlying erythema. Initial labs were notable for leukopenia (2.6 × 103/μL), thrombocytopenia (135,000/μL), and elevated liver enzymes. Computed tomography (CT) of the neck demonstrated necrotic left cervical lymphadenopathy with prominent right cervical lymph nodes. An infectious workup, including testing for Epstein-Barr virus, Cytomegalovirus, human immunodeficiency virus, coccidioidomycosis, tuberculosis, and microbial cell-free DNA sequencing, was negative. Initial fine-needle aspiration (FNA) and core needle biopsy showed predominantly necrotic tissue. Cultures obtained during the biopsy showed no growth, and flow cytometry was negative for leukemia/lymphoma markers. Intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone administration resulted in improvement in neck swelling and fever resolution. Histopathologic examination from excisional biopsy revealed histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis consistent with Kikuchi-Fujimoto (KFD) lymphadenitis. Comprehensive autoimmune serologies were negative. Naproxen was prescribed to help with residual inflammation.DiscussionKFD should be considered in children presenting with prolonged cervical lymphadenopathy refractory to antibiotics. This case illustrates several diagnostic challenges inherent in making this diagnosis. The patient's prolonged unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, necrotic imaging findings, and transient improvement with antibiotics strongly suggested bacterial lymphadenitis or malignancy. However, the persistence of symptoms despite multiple appropriate antibiotic courses, the development of cytopenias and elevated liver enzymes, and ultimately nondiagnostic cultures represented key findings prompting reconsideration of the initial differential diagnoses. This case also highlights the importance of considering excisional biopsy when core biopsy is nondiagnostic.
authors: Thomas M, Stevens D, Davis C, Money NM.

title: The miR-176-DcFoxO axis links CLas infection to juvenile hormone signaling and enhanced fecundity in Diaphorina citri.
abstract: BackgroundThe phloem-limited bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus (CLas), associated with huanglongbing (HLB) disease, is transmitted by the Asian citrus psyllid, Diaphorina citri. CLas-positive females display enhanced fecundity and increased metabolic demands, a phenotype that may promote both vector population growth and bacterial proliferation. Although recent studies have revealed that CLas-associated reproductive enhancement involves neuroendocrine and neurotransmitter pathways, the transcriptional regulators linking persistent bacterial infection, energy metabolism, juvenile hormone (JH) signaling, and ovarian development remain poorly understood.ResultsHere, we identify the forkhead transcription factor DcFoxO as a previously unrecognized regulatory node associated with CLas-induced fecundity enhancement in D. citri. DcFoxO expression was significantly elevated in the ovaries of CLas-positive females during reproductive maturation. RNA interference-mediated silencing of DcFoxO reduced triacylglycerol and glycogen reserves, decreased lipid droplet accumulation, impaired ovarian development, reduced fecundity, and lowered CLas titers in the ovaries. Using dual-luciferase reporter assays, RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP), and microRNA (miRNA) gain-of-function experiments, we demonstrated that miR-176 directly targets the 3' untranslated region of DcFoxO and negatively regulates its expression. Overexpression of miR-176 phenocopied DcFoxO knockdown, suppressing energy reserves, ovarian development, fecundity, and CLas proliferation. Mechanistically, DcFoxO silencing or miR-176 overexpression reduced JH titers and down-regulated core JH-responsive reproductive genes, including DcMet, DcKr-h1, DcVg, and DcVgR.ConclusionThese findings reveal a miR-176-DcFoxO-JH regulatory axis that links CLas infection to metabolic reprogramming, ovarian maturation, and enhanced vector fecundity. This study adds a transcriptional layer to the emerging model of CLas-mediated manipulation of D. citri reproduction and identifies potential molecular targets for disrupting vector performance and HLB transmission. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
authors: Zhang S, Tan S, Urbaneja A, Pérez-Hedo M, Cen Y, Nian X.

title: Empirical substitution models of evolution for protein phylogenetics of the Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus.
abstract: Probabilistic methods for phylogenetic inference rely on substitution models of molecular evolution. However, at the protein level, the availability of empirical substitution models remains limited, particularly for viruses. Here, we present empirical substitution models of protein evolution for several Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) proteins, including the nucleoprotein, glycoprotein precursor, and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. For each protein, we estimated the exchangeability matrix and amino acid frequencies at equilibrium from hundreds of sequences using maximum likelihood, and we evaluated the models using independent data. The inferred CCHFV models revealed distinct evolutionary patterns among viral proteins, including patterns in polar and glycosylation-associated regions, while generally preserving common physicochemical features such as amino acid charge, polarity, and hydrophobic packing shaped by selective pressures. Remarkably, the CCHFV protein substitution models consistently outperformed all currently available empirical substitution models, including those inferred from other viral proteins, in terms of phylogenetic likelihood with independent CCHFV protein sequences. These findings support the use of these substitution models to improve the accuracy of phylogenetic reconstructions of CCHFV proteins, thereby enabling more reliable inference of evolutionary trajectories that may be useful for therapeutic design.
authors: Iglesias-Rivas P, Arenas M.

title: Multilevel metabolic engineering of Bacillus amyloliquefaciens for enhanced L-tyrosine production.
abstract: L-Tyrosine is a valuable aromatic amino acid with diverse applications. Although plasmid-based overexpression has markedly improved L-tyrosine production, the dependence on antibiotic selection and genetic instability under nonselective conditions limits its industrial applicability. To address these issues, this study employed a multi-level metabolic engineering strategy to enhance the L-tyrosine biosynthetic pathway at the genomic level in Bacillus amyloliquefaciens. First, an expression cassette containing the mutant prephenate dehydrogenase (TyrAI309A/E330V) was inserted into the genome of the wild-type strain Z1. When the copy number reached three (strain Z4), L-tyrosine production reached 437.43 mg/L. Subsequently, the mutant DAHP synthase (AroAR27A/K38A) was integrated, and the resulting two-copy strain Z7 increased L-tyrosine production to 591.29 mg/L. Systematic identification of rate-limiting steps showed that most pathway genes enhanced production to varying extents. A promoter in situ replacement strategy was then applied to construct strain Z21, which further increased the titer to 813.01 mg/L. Finally, by optimizing precursor supply, the engineered strain Z32 reached an L-tyrosine titer of 1079.94 mg/L. Overall, this plasmid-free and antibiotic-independent platform offers a promising strategy for stable biosynthesis of L-tyrosine and other aromatic amino acids in microbial cell factories.
authors: Zhang D, Jiang P, Wang L, Gu J, Ji A, Feng N.

title: Clinical utility of plasma microbial cell-free DNA sequencing in adult immunocompromised patients: A real-world cohort study.
abstract: BackgroundPlasma metagenomic next generation sequencing (mNGS) enables noninvasive pathogen detection independent of organism viability. Although analytic performance has been described, the real-world clinical impact in immunocompromised hosts remains incompletely defined.MethodsWe conducted a retrospective cohort study of immunocompromised adults undergoing plasma mNGS testing from January 2022 through November 2024 at the Medical University of South Carolina. Immunocompromised conditions included solid organ transplantation, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, active hematologic malignancy, HIV, or biologic immunosuppressants. Clinical impact was adjudicated by infectious disease physicians as positive, negative, or neutral. Positive results were classified as definite, probable, possible, or unlikely infectious based on clinical correlation and concordance with conventional microbiologic testing (CMT).ResultsNinety-eight patients were included (median age 60 years [range 18-76]; 63% male), including solid organ transplant (31%), hematopoietic stem cell transplant (8%), HIV (13%), active malignancy (42%), corticosteroids (3%), and biologic therapy (10%). At testing, 85% were receiving antimicrobials and 88% were hospitalized. Plasma mNGS was positive in 62% of cases, with CMT concordance in 30%. Thirty-two percent of tests had positive clinical impact, identifying unrecognized infection or antimicrobial optimization. Sixty-six percent had no treatment impact and 2% had potential negative impact. More than half of discordant positives were deemed possible or unlikely infections. False-negative cases included invasive mold and nontuberculous mycobacterial infections.ConclusionsIn this antimicrobial-exposed immunocompromised cohort, plasma mNGS frequently detected organisms but less often influenced clinical management. Discordant positives were common, and false negatives occurred in selected syndromes, supporting cautious interpretation and stewardship-guided use.
journal: The American journal of the medical sciences
authors: Charles DW, Alkabab Y, Sharma D, Adekunle RO, Catalano J, Colven R, Curry SR, Dorman SE, Meissner EG, Mills A, Patterson L, Teixeria CS, Tyler RS, Salgado CD, Harris CE.

title: KmerSignificance score: A discriminative and biologically informed framework for viral k-mer prioritization.
abstract: Distinguishing closely related viral strains requires identifying genomic regions where subtle sequence differences carry biological significance. While k-mer-based approaches offer computational efficiency for genome analysis, existing methods lack standardized frameworks for evaluating which k-mers are most informative. Current selection strategies focus primarily on statistical discriminative power without integrating biological context. We introduce KmerSignificance Score (KSS), a k-mer prioritization framework combining three components: an information-theoretic method measuring strain-distinguishing capacity, an optimized amino acid substitution matrix (MIYATA_EVO) for mutation impact assessment, and a protein characterization score derived from annotations and database cross-references retrieved through UniProt. All three component scores and the integrated KSS are bounded in [0,1] by construction, providing a common numerical scale for ranking positions within a dataset. The discriminative component achieved a mean F1 of 0.881, not significantly different from chi-squared (0.876), the strongest of eight baselines. Top-ranked selections from the discriminative component nonetheless differed from those produced by chi-squared, especially for SARS-CoV-2 and HIV-1. The MIYATA_EVO matrix, optimized using a genetic algorithm, increased the composite agreement score across eight amino acid characteristics by 28.4% over the original MIYATA matrix. Across 17,471 viral proteins, the protein characterization score tracked UniProt's five-level annotation score closely (Kendall's τ=0.775), as expected for measures drawing on overlapping annotation content. Within each level, the continuous score provided finer numerical resolution among proteins. Literature cross-referencing on SARS-CoV-2 (278,738 sequences, 19 Pango-derived lineage labels), HIV-1 (12,223 sequences, 15 subtype labels), and human cytomegalovirus (HCMV; 399-646 sequences, 4-8 locus-specific genotypes) found that the top-ranked k-mers reported here map to established variant-defining mutations, subtype-specific polymorphisms, and genotype markers. KSS provides a standardized framework for viral k-mer prioritization with potential applications in variant surveillance, molecular epidemiology, and functional annotation. The tool is available at https://github.com/bioinfoUQAM/KmerSignificanceScore.
authors: Lebatteux D, Corso F, Soudeyns H, Boucoiran I, Gantt S, Baniré Diallo A.

title: Hepatitis C viral variants bear signatures of de novo CD8+ T cell and antibody pressure after spontaneous postpartum viral suppression.
abstract: Progression to chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection entails loss of HCV-specific CD4+ T cell help, emergence of viral variants that escape recognition by CD8+ T cells and neutralizing antibodies, and exhaustion of CD8+ T cells targeting remaining intact epitopes. Once chronic infection has been established, it is generally lifelong without treatment. However, in some chronically infected women, a surprising postpartum viral load decline has been linked to resurgent functional HCV-specific CD4+ helper T cells. A minority of women even spontaneously clear long-standing chronic infection postpartum. To test whether restored T cell help boosts HCV-specific CD8+ T cell or antibody responses in women with postpartum viral control, we performed serial near-full-length deep sequencing of HCV genomes to assess evolution of viral MHC class I epitopes and antibody epitopes in nine women with significant postpartum viral declines (≥ 1 log10 at 3 mo postpartum, "controllers") and 12 with more stable levels ("noncontrollers"). Although not associated with mutations arising early postpartum, at 12 to 24 mo postpartum, viral control was strongly associated with amino acid mutations in epitopes predicted to be targeted by CD8+ T cells and neutralizing antibodies. Plasma from controllers also demonstrated a postpartum increase in neutralization of multiple HCV strains. Together, these findings support the hypothesis that postpartum viral control is mediated by CD8+ T cell and antibody pressure.
authors: Phelps CC, Smith S, Gridley J, Kohout JA, Xu Z, Marcotrigiano J, Rood K, Skinner NE, Grakoui A, Honegger JR, Walker CM.

title: OMICs-based Characterization of Probiotic or Psychobiotic Lactic Acid Bacteria (LAB) from Philippine Fermented Foods: A Scoping Review.
abstract: Fermented foods are rich sources of diverse lactic acid bacteria (LAB) with promising functional potential. OMICs approaches enable comprehensive characterization. In the Philippines, many regions produce unique fermented foods that may contain potentially beneficial LAB. However, the extent of OMICs' application in studying these microorganisms remains unclear. This scoping review aims to determine the extent and availability of OMICs-based research investigating the probiotic or psychobiotic potential of LAB isolated from Philippine fermented foods. It also seeks to identify whether such studies are abundant or remain limited. Multiple databases were utilized to identify eligible studies. Studies were defined as peer-reviewed, English-language research articles (2000-2026) that applied OMICs approaches to characterize LAB isolated from Philippine fermented food sources. These studies also had accessible datasets and original analyses. Only five eligible studies were identified, comprising three publications from 2024 and two from 2025, with most consisting of genome announcements and only two full research articles. The reviewed studies showed limited taxonomic, food-source, and geographic coverage, representing only three LAB genera, three Philippine fermented foods, and samples originating exclusively from Central Luzon (Region III). OMICs-based studies on probiotic and psychobiotic LAB from Philippine fermented foods are markedly lacking. The identified studies were few and predominantly employed genomics, with only one study incorporating metabolomics. They are also limited to a single region and a narrow range of fermented foods. Expanding OMICs-driven research is essential to address these gaps, enable deeper characterization, and strengthen the scientific and cultural value of Philippine fermented foods.
authors: Veluz J, Buenavista CA, Gloria PC, Luague MJ, Austria K, Relucio-San Diego MAC, Siringan MA.

title: Hubei virga-like virus 2 in Aedes aegypti: Identification of a conserved 216-bp sequence missing from the RefSeq standard.
abstract: We report two near-complete genome sequences of Hubei virga-like virus 2 (HVLV-2) from Aedes aegypti in Oaxaca, Mexico. Both genomes contain a 216-bp insertion region absent from the reference sequence but present in all other reported isolates. Split-read analysis and de novo assembly of our samples, along with a reanalysis of raw reads from the reference sequencing project, confirm that this region is present in the original genetic material from which the assemblies were built. Altogether, these findings confirm that A. aegypti is a putative host of HVLV-2 and demonstrate that the insertion is conserved but missing from the RefSeq standard.
authors: Guerrero-Martínez LE, Solís-Vidal S, Yocupicio-Monroy M, Castelán-Sánchez HG, Zárate S.

title: Conjugative Transfer Potential of Antibiotic Resistance from Wastewater-derived Coliforms to riverine Escherichia coli.
abstract: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARB) discharged into rivers from wastewater treatment plants disseminate antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) through conjugative transfer, suggesting that aquatic environments serve as reservoirs for spreading antibiotic resistance. However, the actual extent of such dissemination of antibiotic resistance is unclear. This study investigated changes in the microbiota and antibiotic resistance profiles of other coliforms during the wastewater treatment process and evaluated whether other antibiotic-resistant coliforms persisting in treated wastewater could potentially transfer antibiotic resistance to Escherichia coli in receiving waters. The treatment process substantially reduced, but did not eliminate, E. coli and other coliforms (most probable number [MPN]/100 mL = 5 for E. coli and 4.3 × 10² for other coliforms), which were subsequently discharged into rivers. The resistance rates of other coliforms tended to increase throughout the treatment process, and the proportion of multidrug-resistant bacteria increased (influent: 4.9%, biologically treated water: 4.3%, effluent: 15.8%). Conjugation experiments using the filter mating method revealed the transfer of ARGs from Klebsiella species to E. coli (conjugation frequency: 10- 6-10- 3), suggesting the potential for antibiotic resistance transfer within biofilms. Experiments under simplified riverbed biofilm conditions confirmed the transfer of rifampicin resistance genes introduced into E. coli to antibiotic-resistant other coliforms (conjugation frequency: 9.7 × 10- 5-5.3 × 10- 4). The abundance of antibiotic-resistant other coliforms in the biofilm was 5.08 × 10² MPN/mL, which was lower than the observed conjugation frequencies, suggesting that the discharge area of treated wastewater is unlikely to function as a significant hotspot for ARB dissemination.
authors: Tamai S, Tsuda K, Suzuki Y.

title: U6  promoters in  Ulva prolifera  enable dual small-RNA/mRNA transcription and vector-based CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing
abstract: For establishing vector-based gene editing in the green-tide-forming alga  Ulva prolifera , development of endogenous RNA polymerase III (Pol III) promoters is a prerequisite to drive single-guide RNA (sgRNA) transcription. To meet the need, the promoters of  U6 snRNA genes in  U. prolifera (  UpU6 ) were identified, cloned, and functionally characterized. Results showed that three  UpU6 copies shared identical sequences, with divergent 5’ upstream sequences containing a positionally conserved TATA box but lacking the USE element typical of seed plants. All three  UpU6 promoters were shown to be capable of driving not only small RNA transcription but also protein-coding gene expression in  U. prolifera , exhibiting the dual transcriptional activity. Unexpectedly, all three  UpU6 promoters also supported  GUS reporter gene expression in  Agrobacterium , representing the first demonstration of  U6 promoter activity in a prokaryotic system. The results of the gene-editing experiment showed that, all three  UpU6 promoters supported vector-based CRISPR-Cas9 targeting of the  APT gene, yielding mutant strains. The mutation-positive fraction among resistant thalli was 92.3% (48/52), and the editing frequency calculated from the estimated starting cell number averaged 3.26 × 10⁻⁶ across the three  UpU6 promoters and did not differ significantly among them. In the mutants, high-frequency occurrences of base substitutions (45.5%) and insertions of long Mutator-like element (MULE) (18.2%) were detected, highlighting a potential association between endogenous DNA transposon insertion and CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene editing. These findings expanded understanding of eukaryotic  U6 promoter functionality and enrich the toolkit for vector-based CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing in  U. prolifera .
authors: Hou Q, Wang Z, Zhao J, Jiang P.

title: From chromosome-scale assembly to the mappable genome of rubber dandelion: chromosome reorganization, rubber-pathway coordination, and domestication traits
abstract: Natural rubber supply depends almost entirely on one tropical tree, motivating development of temperate alternatives. Rubber dandelion (  Taraxacum kok-saghyz Rodin) is the leading candidate, with comparatively well characterized rubber biosynthesis pathways, but its large, repeat-rich genome has left breeding genomics far behind pathway biology. In response, we assembled OSU TarKok 3.0, a 1.19-Gb nuclear reference in which eight chromosome-scale scaffolds contain 98% of the sequence. Continuity within chromosomes improved markedly, with contig N50 rising from 1.3 to 37.8 Mb, and conserved gene-space recovery improved accordingly. Macrosynteny showed strong chromosome conservation within Taraxacum and, when compared to lettuce, displayed four nearly intact and four composite chromosomes, a signature compatible with descending dysploidy accompanied by rearrangement rather than a single end-to-end fusion. Across nine Cichorieae genomes, none of six surveyed rubber-related gene families was uniquely enlarged in rubber dandelion. Instead, a  cis -prenyltransferase locus, a rubber transferase activator, and three small rubber particle protein genes were enriched in underground tissues and grouped with rubber elongation factor in a latex-associated co-expression module, favoring coordinated pathway deployment over species-specific family expansion. Intersecting uniquely mappable and nonrepetitive sequence defined the mappable genome, approximately 210 Mb or 18% of the assembly, within which markers can be interpreted allelically. Mapping in an independent F₂ family of 83 plants identified a chromosome 1 locus for filled-seed production under restricted cross-pollination, whereas herbicide response yielded no significant locus in this design. OSU TarKok 3.0 links chromosome reorganization, pathway deployment, and domestication traits into one framework for improving an outcrossing crop.  Core Ideas  OSU TarKok 3.0 markedly improves within-chromosome continuity and conserved gene-space recovery. Repeat-aware defines a ∼210 Mb short-read mappable space (18% of the assembly), enabling reliable marker analysis. Four chromosomes retain conserved relationships, supporting dysploidy with rearrangement beyond simple fusion. No rubber-related gene family is uniquely expanded; rubber production reflects pathway coordination, not dosage. A chromosome 1 QTL for selfing-related filled-seed production overlaps the positional candidate  g7174 .  Plain Language Summary  As the global supply of natural rubber is dependent on one tropical tree, rubber dandelion has been proposed as a temperate alternative. Although scientists already understand many of the genes involved in its rubber production, breeding has been slowed by its large, highly repetitive genome. In response, we built OSU TarKok 3.0, a much more continuous genome that places 98% of the sequence on eight chromosomes. Comparison with related dandelions revealed broad chromosome conservation, while comparison with lettuce was consistent with rearrangements during the reduction from nine to eight chromosomes. Across nine members of the sunflower family, none of six rubber-related gene families were uniquely enlarged in rubber dandelion. Instead, genes involved in building rubber chains and particles were active together in underground tissues and latex-associated samples, suggesting that coordinated gene activity matters more than extra gene copies. We also identified ∼210 million base pairs, 18% of the genome, where short-read genetic markers can be interpreted reliably. Within that space, we mapped a chromosome 1 region associated with producing filled seed when cross-pollination was restricted. This region overlaps a candidate gene from a protein family involved in reproductive development in other plants, providing a testable target for improving seed production.
authors: Vargas-Mejía P, Gutierrez-Manriquez C, Anderson ES, Williams DR, Vega-Arreguín J, Fresnedo-Ramírez J.

title: Scaling a context-aware genomic model for condition-specific edit design in plants
abstract: Engineering agronomically relevant traits in crops often requires changing a gene’s activity in a specific tissue, developmental stage or environmental condition while preserving its roles in other contexts. Designing such selective changes requires predicting how cis-regulatory sequences are interpreted in different biological states, as the same edit can have different effects across contexts. Genomic models have made substantial progress in predicting gene expression from DNA sequence, yet sequence-only predictors do not receive an explicit description of biological states. We introduce CROP-1 (  C ontext-aware  R egulatory  O utput  P rediction model), which combines DNA sequence with transcription factor binding motifs and measured expression to predict gene activity as a function of both sequence and regulatory state. On a held-out test set spanning six plant species, CROP-1 achieves a median per-gene Pearson correlation across contexts of 0.831, compared with 0.486 for its parameter-matched sequence-only counterpart, and 57–246% higher median correlations than three genomic foundation models fully fine-tuned on the same task. Prediction accuracy also improves with scale: increasing model capacity reduces validation error by 48%, while expanding training data to include more diverse biological contexts reduces it by 58%. We then use gradient-based sequence optimisation to translate a desired gene expression pattern into candidate edits of its cis-regulatory sequence, targeting up- or down-regulation in one context while preserving expression in others. In soybean and tomato, edit designs with 1–20 nucleotide substitutions produce strong predicted target responses and much smaller average changes across non-target contexts. By connecting scalable learning of sequence–state relationships to selective edit design, CROP-1 provides a computational foundation for controlling where, when and under which conditions endogenous crop genes are active.
authors: Antinucci P, Wang L, Moss JD, Schwartz D, Hall D.

title: FluxSprout: Single-cell metabolic modeling of vascular sprouting in zebrafish
abstract: Genome-scale metabolic modeling offers a powerful framework for identifying cell-state-specific metabolic vulnerabilities, yet its application to heterogeneous biological systems remains limited by uncertainty in network annotations, thermodynamic feasibility, transcriptome-to-flux inference, and target specificity. Here, we introduce FluxSprout, a single-cell transcriptomics-informed genome-scale metabolic modeling framework to resolve metabolic heterogeneity during zebrafish sprouting angiogenesis. By integrating single-cell RNA sequencing of 10,090 quality-controlled cells with Zebrafish-GEM, we reconstructed network ensembles for 14 endothelial and hemogenic states. We established four safeguards: stoichiometric auditing, loop auditing, cell-cycle-controlled testing, and ensemble specificity screening. First, we identified four inorganic pyrophosphatase reactions misannotated as oxidative phosphorylation, showing that apparent pathway essentiality arose only with unbounded exchange fluxes. Second, 19.5% of reactions could carry thermodynamically infeasible loop flux, including every candidate of a conventional screen. Third, tip-like and stalk-like cells differed mainly in cell-cycle phase, and elevated glycolysis separated sprouting from established vessels only in gene expression. In contrast, sprouting vessels had higher predicted growth capacity at both constraint strengths, with serine and nucleotide synthesis following in fixed proportion. Fourth, screening 825 genes across four network-extraction settings and 13 non-endothelial lineages left no candidate called by more than one setting. Notably, SLC25A20, that screen’s lead candidate, had no predicted effect in any FASTCORE network. Although the data derive from a single pooled clutch and require experimental validation, FluxSprout provides a transferable, uncertainty-aware framework for distinguishing genuine metabolic dependencies from artifacts of network reconstruction, model assumptions, and cellular heterogeneity, and identifies biosynthetic capacity as a testable feature of sprouting vessels.
authors: Zargar MR, Chowdhury R.

title: An improved CRISPR-LICHT screen of 120 “Tdark” genes illuminates new biologically relevant SOX2 targets in human brain organoids
abstract: SOX2 is a transcription factor and central regulator of neural progenitor identity, yet the downstream molecular networks through which it supports human brain development remain incompletely characterized. Here, we applied CRISPR-lineage tracing at cellular resolution in heterogeneous tissue (CRISPR-LICHT) to human cerebral organoids to functionally interrogate SOX2-dependent regulatory networks. Using a SOX2-focused library targeting SOX2 together with conserved neurodevelopmental regulators expressed in neural progenitor cells, we showed that CRISPR-LICHT detects reproducible lineage- depletion phenotypes across genes already known to be involved in progenitor maintenance, fate specification, glial differentiation and neuronal maturation. This extends the application of CRISPR-LICHT beyond the severe neural progenitor phenotypes previously characterized for microcephaly-associated genes and demonstrates its ability to detect perturbation effects across a broader set of neurodevelopmental regulators, involving SOX2 targets previously defined in mouse and now open to further understanding in a human model setting. We further screened 120 evolutionarily conserved, poorly characterized SOX2-dependent genes classified as “Tdark” within the “Illuminating the Druggable Genome framework” and identified 28 candidate hits whose disruption impaired neural progenitor lineage expansion and/or survival. These candidates included proteins associated with cytoskeletal organization, membrane dynamics and intracellular architecture, suggesting that SOX2-dependent developmental programmes may engage cellular processes beyond transcriptional regulation. Individual downregulation of CDC42EP4, a poorly characterized CDC42 effector linked to cytoskeletal organization, revealed altered distribution of targeted progenitors between ventricular- and subventricular- like compartments, with changes consistent with altered progenitor-state progression. Together, these findings expand the functional landscape of SOX2-dependent regulation in human neural progenitors and identify cellular architecture as a potential component of SOX2-associated developmental programs.
authors: Pozzolini G, Haendeler S, Amin S, Baldi R, Cascio A, Edenhofer F, Taverna E, Esk C, Krenn V, Nicolis S.

title: Why is Cyclin A degraded before Cyclin B?
abstract: The Anaphase Promoting Complex/Cyclosome (APC/C) ubiquitin ligase controls mitosis by targeting the mitotic Cyclins for degradation. CyclinA has evolved multiple APC/C degrons that enable its degradation as soon as cells enter mitosis while the Spindle Assembly Checkpoint prevents recognition of CyclinB until all chromosomes have attached to the mitotic apparatus. But why the rapid early degradation of CyclinA is conserved in evolution is not known. Here, we mutated two APC/C-recognition motifs in human CyclinA2 to slow down its degradation. We find that slower degradation of CyclinA induces errors in chromosome congression and chromosome clustering at mitotic exit, leading to aneuploidy and malformed daughter cell nuclei. We identify Ki67 as the candidate that interferes with chromosome clustering since its phosphorylation and behaviour are perturbed when CyclinA is degraded more slowly, and increased microtubule dynamics as a contributing factor to chromosome congression errors. We conclude that rapid early CyclinA degradation is important for genomic stability.
authors: Roberti A, Soto SG, Weiss Y, Roumeliotis TI, Choudhary JS, Pines J.

title: Taxon-in-context reveals ecological individuality in the human gut microbiome
abstract: ABSTRACT  Ecological theory holds that a microbe’s role depends on its surrounding community. Yet abundance profiles and fixed ecological groupings leave its individual context implicit. We introduce taxon-in-context, a reproducible representation of each microbe’s context within an individual’s microbiome. Across 7,700 metagenomes, we show that common gut species occupy different contexts in different people. This flexibility peaked in early life and declined through adulthood, a pattern reproduced in a larger genus-level compendium. For selected species, context within each person’s microbiome revealed age associations beyond species abundance and the person’s context mixture. In an independent longitudinal urinary tract infection cohort, microbes switched contexts within individuals. Taxon-in-context enabled recurrence prediction where an abundance based model performed near chance. Taxon-in-context and these findings expose a measurable, dynamic and individualized layer of microbiome organization, providing a basis for investigating why the same microbe or intervention may have different biological consequences across people.
authors: Gaudillo J, Astrologo N, Canonaco F, Stella F, Barbaresi S, Zelante T, Wopereis H, Cohen Y, Guyard C, Knol J, Lay C, Acerbi E.

title: Structural analysis of the 5' terminal of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 genome RNAs transcribed from proviruses with mutations in the transcription start site
abstract: Abstract  Recent studies have shown that the functional roles of RNAs transcribed from the transcription start site containing three G residues in human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) are regulated by their structural stability, which is determined by the number of G residues at the 5′ terminus. In contrast, most proviruses in newly infected cells generated by HIV-1 have been shown to retain mutations introduced at the transcription start site. When C or U mutations are introduced at the third G residue, transcription from that position is unlikely to occur, suggesting that transcription instead occurs from the first or second G residue. In the absence of mutations, these transcripts are thought to be used for translation rather than incorporated into genomic RNA. Therefore, the mechanisms by which the functions of these RNAs are determined remain unclear. In this study, we designed model RNAs containing mutations and analyzed their structures and stabilities. RNAs transcribed from the second G residue with GC or GU at the 5’-end formed stable structures similar to those of RNAs transcribed from the third G residue in the native virus, which functions as ic RNA. These results suggest that, in the presence of these mutations, RNA transcribed from the second G functions as genomic RNA.
authors: Kashiyama Y, Kawai G, Yoshida T, Suzuki Y.

title: SPxLINCS: a GWAS-guided, tissue-resolved framework for drug repurposing in hepatocellular carcinoma
abstract: Abstract  Background  Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the third leading cause of cancer-related mortality, yet effective therapeutic options remain limited. Although Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) have identified multiple HCC susceptibility loci, translating these discoveries into therapeutic leads has proven challenging. Here we present a reverse transcriptomic repurposing pipeline that combines evidence from multiple GWAS, tissue-resolved transcriptomics, and small-molecule perturbational profiles to identify candidate drugs for HCC. Materials and methods  We developed a reproducible drug-repositioning pipeline linking 12 HCC-related GWAS datasets with multi-tissue GTEx regulatory profiles and LINCS L1000 perturbational signatures through S-PrediXcan and LINCS-based transcriptomic connectivity analysis (SPxLINCS). Previously calculated compound-level evidence scores were retained for ranking and visualization. Candidate networks were visualized in Cytoscape as bipartite and tripartite graphs, and clinical plausibility was assessed by Drug Set Enrichment Analysis (DrugEnrichr vs. SIDER) with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Results  Across the 12 datasets, the SPxLINCS pipeline prioritized compounds that could be grouped into five mechanism-related categories after key-tissue and reverse-signature filtering: cell-cycle and mitotic kinase inhibitors, including CDK- and PLK1-related compounds; focal adhesion kinase inhibitors; DNA-dependent protein kinase and DNA-damage-response agents; topoisomerase I inhibitors; and translation-related inhibitors. Network visualization distinguished compounds that recurred across multiple GWAS datasets from compounds primarily associated with individual phenotypes. Drug-set enrichment analysis identified enrichment of terms related to hepatocellular and other hepatic malignancy indications in the SIDER database. Importazole, ER-27319, and LDN-193189 were recurrently prioritized across multiple datasets and tissues despite limited prior characterization in HCC. These compounds should therefore be regarded as computationally nominated and hypothesis-generating candidates requiring experimental validation. Conclusions  This multi-GWAS reverse transcriptomic approach yields a mechanism-guided candidate list for drug repurposing in HCC. Signal consistency across independent datasets, combined with indication-level enrichment, supports advancing prioritized compounds into biomarker-stratified preclinical and early clinical evaluation.
authors: Peng J.

title: Discovering pathogens and evaluating the microbial and chemical contamination in the Machángara and the San Pedro Rivers in Quito, Ecuador: A temporal and longitudinal analysis
abstract: Abstract    Water pollution poses major environmental and public health challenges, particularly in regions with insufficient wastewater treatment. This study evaluated seasonal changes in microbial and chemical contamination at three sampling points along the San Pedro and Machángara Rivers in Quito, Ecuador, during two rainy seasons and one dry season.  Escherichia coli  , total coliforms, yeasts, molds, and  Candida  spp. were quantified by selective culture, while selected pathogens were identified by PCR and Sanger sequencing.  E. coli  and total coliform levels frequently exceeded international standards.  Giardia intestinalis  ,  Cryptosporidium parvum  , and  Mycobacterium tuberculosis  were consistently detected, whereas  Helicobacter pylori  ,  Campylobacter jejuni  ,  C. upsaliensis  ,  M. leprae  , and several  E. coli  pathotypes were detected sporadically. Physico-chemical parameters showed seasonal variation, with elevated pH and chemical oxygen demand in the Machángara River and excessive nitrite concentrations in both rivers. Several metals, including Al, Fe, Cr, and Mn, exceeded Ecuadorian limits, indicating impaired water quality. Kruskal–Wallis analyses showed significant differences in most microbial and physico-chemical parameters among sampling points, particularly between upstream reference and downstream contaminated sites, whereas seasonal differences in pathogen occurrence were generally not significant. These findings provide an integrated seasonal assessment of microbial and chemical pollution in urban Andean rivers and highlight the need for improved wastewater treatment, continuous water-quality monitoring, and targeted remediation strategies.
authors: Cabrera-Ontaneda A, Yépez-del-Pozo-Tobar MP, Borja-Serrano P, Pineda-Cabrera CC, Zambrano-Romero A, Carpintero-Salvador N, Maurice L, Graham JP, Trueba G, Tejera E, Ochoa-Herrera V, Machado A.

title: Advances and Translational Challenges in mRNA–Lipid Nanoparticle Vaccines Against Helicobacter pylori: From Rational Antigen Design to Mucosal Immunity
abstract: Helicobacter pylori chronically infects more than half of the global population and is the sole bacterium classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer. Despite decades of effort, no prophylactic H. pylori vaccine has reached the market, largely because conventional subunit and whole-cell candidates failed to induce durable, mucosa-protective T-helper 1 (Th1)/Th17 immunity in humans. The clinical success of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) mRNA–lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) vaccines has re-energized nucleic-acid vaccine research and provided a validated, scalable delivery platform. This review synthesizes the emerging mechanistic rationale and early preclinical evidence evaluating whether mRNA-LNP technology can address key bottlenecks in H. pylori vaccine development: cytoplasmic antigen expression naturally favors major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I/II presentation and CD8⁺/Th1 responses (notably, recent human and murine evidence demonstrates that cytotoxin-associated gene A [CagA]-specific gastric CD8⁺ tissue-resident memory T [TRM] cells control early H. pylori infection), multi-antigen and conserved-epitope designs can be generated rapidly by reverse vaccinology, and the LNP carrier itself acts as an intrinsic innate immune adjuvant. We summarize the principal candidate antigens (urease subunit B [UreB], CagA, vacuolating cytotoxin A [VacA], neutrophil-activating protein [NAP], H. pylori adhesin A [HpaA], and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase [GGT]), dissect LNP composition and intracellular trafficking, and critically appraise the nascent body of preclinical H. pylori mRNA and nanocarrier studies published between 2021 and 2026—specifically distinguishing two recent in vivo mRNA-LNP preprints (encoding full-length UreB or UreB₁₉₉–₃₃₈ cytokine/immunoglobulin Z [IgZ] fusions) from peer-reviewed in silico multi-epitope mRNA and self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) designs, LNP-adjuvanted recombinant UreB/NapA protein vaccines, all-trans retinoic acid-loaded gut-tropic nanovaccines, and oral/lipid DNA vaccine benchmarks. We also reconcile classic evidence that bacterial clearance can proceed in B-cell-deficient mice via MHC class II-restricted CD4⁺ T cells with the ancillary role of functional adhesion- and urease-blocking antibodies, and we examine critical safety and immunopathological constraints—including post-immunization gastritis, oncogenic CagA EPIYA motif detoxification, and target-population stratification (uninfected children versus infected adults). We conclude that while mRNA-LNP represents a promising exploratory modality for an H. pylori vaccine, the current experimental evidence base remains narrow and preliminary; peer-reviewed validation of in vivo Th17 induction, antigen breadth, mucosal delivery route, and long-term durability in non-human primate and human challenge models will be required to establish clinical feasibility.
authors: Zhao Y, Cheng H, Zhou S, He L, Xiu C, Huang B, Lu X.

title: Current Insights Into the Genus Yamadazyma: An Overview of Taxonomy, Ecology and Biotechnological Applications.
abstract: Yeasts of the genus Yamadazyma have received increasing attention in the last decade due to the description of new species, their diverse ecological distribution and their biotechnological potential. The genus Yamadazyma was proposed in 1989, but was not accepted until 2005 due to its polyphyletic nature. Over the years, many new species have been described, and several Candida species have been reassigned to Yamadazyma. However, some Yamadazyma species remain unvalidated, and it is unclear whether the genus Keqinozyma is truly a distinct or should be included within Yamadazyma. Currently, the genus Yamadazyma formally includes 72 species. This genus is widely distributed across various environments worldwide, including aquatic habitats, phylloplane, insects, soil, food products, and humans. Although some species and phylogenetic groups exhibit recurring ecological and geographical patterns, such associations are not generally exclusive. Overall, the genus Yamadazyma appears to be ubiquitous. The presence of this genus across various habitats has facilitated studies on its biotechnological applications including cellobiose fermentation for second-generation bioethanol production and biosynthesis of value-added metabolites such as riboflavin. The genus Yamadazyma plays an active role in food production, contributing to product quality through enzymatic and antagonistic activities, while in agriculture it shows potential through biocontrol activity against phytopathogens. Recent descriptions of new species and the reclassification of previously classified Candida species have fragmented information on this genus. This review aims to address knowledge gaps regarding Yamadazyma by providing a comprehensive resource that unifies taxonomy, ecology, biotechnology, and pathogenesis to support further studies.
authors: Avesani M, Zapparoli G.

title: Field Pea Variants affect Nutrient Digestibility and Gut Microbiome in Pigs.
abstract: The digestibility of nutrients in different field pea variants in pigs can vary due to characteristics such as anti-nutritional factors. Undigested nutrients can be fermented in the hindgut, and their amount and composition likely affect microbial composition. This study compared a spring field pea variant (SP) with two winter field pea variants (WP1, WP2) with higher trypsin inhibitor activity and a tannic spring forage pea variant (SFP) in terms of nutrient digestibility and effects on the gut microbiome in growing pigs. Four diets containing 40% of one of the four field pea variants were formulated and randomly assigned to 8 ileally cannulated barrows according to a 4 × 4 double Latin square design with the blocking factors animal and period. The experiment consisted of 4 periods, each lasting 11 days. Ileal digesta and feces were collected for 2 days each to determine nutrient digestibility. On the last day of every period, ileal digesta and feces were sampled and analyzed for digestive enzyme activity, metagenomics, metaproteomics, and metabolomics. The data was integrated using DIABLO. The winter field pea variants decreased the prececal digestibility of 16 amino acids (P ≤ 0.032) and increased the activity of carboxypeptidase A (P = 0.002). Pigs fed the SFP showed decreased hindgut disappearance of total dietary fiber (P < 0.001) and concentrations of acetate, propionate, and butyrate in the feces (P ≤ 0.026). More differentially abundant taxa in metagenomic and metaproteomic data were detected in the feces than in ileal digesta among field pea variants. The SFP increased the abundance of host proteins related to innate immune response in ileal digesta and feces (adjusted P ≤ 0.047). Integration of the acquired data layers revealed a negative association of ileal amino acid concentrations with the abundance of Prevotella and proteins related to starch degradation and propionate production in the ileal digesta for winter field pea variants. For SFP, reduced hindgut disappearance of total dietary fiber was associated with a reduction of proteins from Ruminococcus. In conclusion, field pea variants can affect the ileal and fecal microbiome in pigs, potentially due to anti-nutritional factors that either indirectly influence the microbiome by reducing nutrient digestibility or directly affect individual microbial taxa.
authors: Quinger F, Klein N, Steinhoff-Wagner J, Camarinha-Silva A, Rodehutscord M, Seifert J.

title: The chromosome-level annotated reference genome MakAnk1.0 reveals a putative signature of selection for long horns and provides insights into the demographic history of Ankole cattle.
abstract: Long-horned Ankole cattle belong to the Sanga group of cattle, which is widely distributed throughout sub-Saharan Africa. They are valued for disease, vector, and parasite tolerance, adaptation to harsh tropical environments, in addition to their unique cultural significance. In this study, a haplotype-aware, chromosome-resolved genome of Ankole cattle (MakAnk1.0) spanning 2.84 Gb, with a scaffold N50 of 110.9 Mb was assembled from PacBio HiFi and Omni-C data. The primary assembly attained 99.5% BUSCO completeness, while haplotypes 1 and 2 had lengths of 2.69 and 2.62 Gb, scaffold N50 of 106.41 and 106.48 Mb, and BUSCO scores of 98.9% and 96.7%, respectively. Gene prediction for the primary assembly yielded 19,406 genes, with a BUSCO completeness score of 88.7%. Repeat sequences accounted for 56.41% of the primary assembly, whereas haplotypes 1 and 2 contained 54.71% and 54.86%, respectively. Using the assembled genome, 27.5 million SNPs and 3.6 million INDELs were discovered, while genome-wide RAiSD analysis identified 421 candidate genomic regions under selection, from which 256 genes were subsequently annotated. These included the HLCS gene, which plays a role in biotinylation and keratinization, potentially supporting development of the long horns in Ankole cattle. Moreover, the annotated genes under selection overlapped with economically significant QTLs in tropical cattle, including tick resistance. Furthermore, the estimated recent effective population size (Ne) trajectory revealed a population contraction, with contemporary Ne estimates ranging from 228 to 278. Collectively, this study provides a valuable genomic resource for advancing research, breed improvement, and conservation of the transboundary Ankole cattle.
authors: Okwasiimire R, Pokharel K, Weldenegodguad M, Makgahlela ML, Ghanem N, Ginja C, Gao J, Uimari P, Kantanen J, Kugonza DR, Crooijmans RPMA.
