title: Lytic phage potentiates aztreonam–avibactam in Escherichia coli with layered resistance by disrupting adaptive stress tolerance
abstract: Abstract    Phage–antibiotic synergy (PAS) can enhance bacterial killing; however, the physiological states that make resistant bacteria vulnerable during co-exposure remain poorly defined. We paired the lytic phage EC10P1 with aztreonam–avibactam (ATM–AVI) against a clinical NDM-5-producing  Escherichia coli  isolate carrying a PBP3/FtsI insertion and a frameshifted  ompF  . Time-kill assays showed that EC10P1 plus sub-MIC ATM–AVI produced a discrete 4-6h window of maximal killing, reaching approximately 4-log  10  reduction relative to ATM–AVI alone, while isothermal microcalorimetry was consistent with sustained metabolic suppression in the combination condition that was not observed with either monotherapy. Time-resolved mRNA sequencing at 1h, 4h and 24h with an interaction-based model localized non-additive responses to the 4h killing phase. Interaction-defined responses were concentrated at the 4h killing phase and showed attenuated induction of alternative respiratory, proteostatic and redox-buffering programs during co-exposure. In contrast, the major porin and  mar/acr  responses were predominantly phage-driven or additive, providing no evidence that potentiation resulted from transcriptional restoration of canonical drug influx or suppression of the central efflux pathway. Together, the data support transient functional resensitization through reduced stress-buffering capacity rather than reversal of a single resistance determinant.
authors: Razavi M, Patpatia S, Lundvik H, Joshi A, Ormälä-Tiznado A, Giske CG, Tellapragada C.

title: No evidence that male killing (MK) Wolbachia in Drosophila innubila protects against Drosophila innubila Nudivirus (DiNV) infection.
abstract: Wolbachia can influence host-pathogen interactions, particularly through its protective effects against RNA viruses in insects. Although prior studies failed to find any evidence for Wolbachia protecting against DNA viruses, the viruses utilized in those studies were usually not pathogens found in natural Drosophila populations. In this study, we compared survival, viral genome copy number, and infectious-virus production (as measured by flow cytometry after cell culture infection) between W⁺ and W⁻ flies following Drosophila innubila Nudivirus (DiNV) infection. We found no evidence in any of these assays that Wolbachia protects D . innubila against DiNV.
authors: Adewumi TS, Lewis A, Unckless RL.

title: Biotechnological Approaches in Natural Products Isolation and Characterization.
abstract: Natural products derived from plants, animals, microbes, and minerals remain a cornerstone of modern drug discovery by virtue of their structural-functional diversity and broad spectrum of bioactivities. However, the isolation and characterization of bioactive compounds from complex natural matrices remain a significant challenge in conventional methodologies, primarily due to metabolites' anonymity, low metabolite abundance, chemical instability, dereplication of already known metabolites, time-consuming processes, limited resolution, and the complexity and non-ecofriendly nature of many methods. Recent advancements in biotechnological applications, including high-throughput screening platforms and advanced mass spectrometric techniques such as GC-MS, LC-MS, multidimensional 1D, 2D & 3D NMR, metabolomics-driven chemical profiling, rapid DNA-detection-based plant authentication techniques, green extraction technologies, bioanalytical techniques like biochips, probes, biosensors, immunoassays, and tools corresponding to genome mining and network pharmacology areas have significantly accelerated the identification, isolation, and characterization of lead compounds. However, despite these advancements, biotechnological approaches still present critical limitations and challenges involving low metabolite annotation rates, difficulty distinguishing stereoisomers, and limited reproducibility and scalability of extraction processes. The present review critically examines traditional and some selective modern biotechnological strategies employed in natural product isolation and characterization, highlighting their advantages, limitations, and applicability in Pharmacognosy research. Furthermore, it discusses current bottlenecks and emerging integrative approaches aimed at improving efficiency, accuracy, and translational potential in natural products-driven drug discovery.
authors: Adhami S, Farooqi H.

title: Multi‑omics integration identifies key microbial taxa, metabolites, and genes associated with intramuscular fat deposition in Danzhou chickens.
abstract: Intramuscular fat (IMF) content is a major determinant of meat quality, yet the regulatory mechanisms underlying its deposition remain poorly understood, particularly in indigenous chicken breeds. In this study, an extreme phenotype grouping strategy was adopted. IMF content was measured in 200 Danzhou chickens, from which individuals with low (LIMF, n = 20) and high (HIMF, n = 20) IMF content were selected. Differences between the two groups were compared in terms of phenotypic traits, meat quality, serum biochemical parameters, breast muscle fatty acid (FA) content, cecal microbiota, serum metabolome, and breast muscle transcriptome. The results showed that the HIMF group had significantly increased IMF content, IMF area percentage, and significantly lower shear force (SF) than the LIMF group (P < 0.05). Serum levels of glucose (GLU), free fatty acids (FFA), low‑density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL‑C), and triglycerides (TG) were significantly elevated (P < 0.05), while high‑density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL‑C) was reduced in the HIMF group (P < 0.05). Additionally, the contents of monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFA), saturated fatty acids (SFA), and total FA in the breast muscle were significantly increased in the HIMF group (P < 0.05). Cecal microbiota analysis revealed that the HIMF group had a higher Firmicutes/Bacteroidota (F/B) ratio (P < 0.05) and this group was enriched with p__Bacillota, c__Clostridia, and s__unclassified Megamonas. These microorganisms were positively correlated with the IMF content. The metabolome‑transcriptome integrative analysis identified succinic acid, (4E)‑2‑oxohexenoic acid, and palmiticamide as key metabolites elevated in the HIMF group, which consistently showed positive correlations with the lipid metabolism‑related genes VNN1 and HSD17B12. Furthermore, the relative mRNA expression of intestinal genes involved in fatty acid uptake (CD36, FABP1, and FABP4), fatty acid synthesis (FASN and ACC), and lipid metabolism regulation (PPARβ) was upregulated in the HIMF group (P < 0.05). These results reveal cross-level associations among the microbiota, metabolites, and genes, providing candidate targets for improving the meat quality of native chicken breeds through microbiota-oriented interventions.
authors: Guo C, Shi L, Hou G, Jiang H, Hu X, Shang Y, Xun W.

title: Widespread antibiotic resistance and multidrug resistance in Escherichia coli from surface waters near dairies and a calf ranch in Wisconsin: Implications for hotspot screening and multi-method monitoring.
abstract: Although concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs) are known sources of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), gaps remain regarding AMR dissemination to environments and monitoring methods. Impacts of large dairies and a calf ranch in Wisconsin on the environmental resistome were assessed at nine surface water sites near CAFOs and two nearby unimpaired sites. 1297 Escherichia coli (EC) isolates were tested against a suite of antibiotics by Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion. Up to 68% of EC isolates at dairy-impacted sites and 70% downstream of the calf ranch exhibited multidrug resistance (MDR), versus up to 8% at the unimpaired sites. Fecal indicator bacteria kits modified with antibiotics detected elevated extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing (ESBL) EC at the site exhibiting highest MDR, suggesting use as a screening tool. Metagenomic analysis showed elevated antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), abundance, diversity, and human health risk scores at the calf ranch-impacted site. Follow-up sampling just upstream and downstream of the calf ranch showed dramatic increases in multiple measures, indicating calf ranches may warrant additional monitoring and elucidate more complex processes such horizontal gene transfer. Culture-based results revealed pronounced AMR hotspots and differences among sampling events only partially reflected by metagenomic analysis and a limited quantitative PCR (qPCR) panel, underscoring the importance of monitoring through complementary methods.
authors: Osborn KP, Zhang Y, Ray S, Kong Y, Levy S, Jun S, Chang M, Lin J, Vuong J, Ives C, Jones A, Henning L, Dickerson C, Mahendra S, Bodeau W, Casillas A, Chowdhry R, Chung J, Curristan N, Espinoza A, Alejo GF, Jennings I, Lakhanpal T, Jay JA.

title: Transcriptional responses of parental and adaptively evolved Lactobacillus plantarum and fecal metabolic changes during mono-colonization of germ-free mice.
abstract: This study integrated metatranscriptomic and untargeted metabolomic analyses to characterize the molecular features of Lactobacillus plantarum AR-R and its adaptively evolved variant AR-R3 during mono-colonization of germ-free (GF) mice and to assess associated changes in the fecal metabolome. Both strains successfully colonized the GF mouse gut, exhibiting comparable bacterial loads and gastrointestinal distribution patterns. Metatranscriptomic analysis revealed widespread transcriptional changes during colonization in both strains, including upregulation of the carbohydrate metabolism-associated genes galE, lacS2, and pdhD, together with downregulation of the stress-associated genes hsp1 and clpL. Strain-specific transcriptional differences were identified, with AR-R exhibiting higher expression of glf2 and fhuB, whereas AR-R3 showed higher expression of ribA and gshR2. Untargeted metabolomic analysis revealed changes in the fecal metabolic profiles following mono-colonization, with pathway enrichment analyses implicating nucleotide metabolism and ABC transporter-related pathways. Fecal metabolic profiles were broadly similar between AR-R- and AR-R3-colonized mice, and no individual metabolites remained significantly different between the two groups after multiple-testing correction. Integrated multi-omics analyses further identified candidate associations between bacterial transcripts and fecal metabolites, including positive associations between the expression of pyruvate dehydrogenase complex genes (pdhD) and fecal indole-3-acetaldehyde levels in the AR-R3 group. Overall, this study characterizes shared transcriptional and fecal metabolic responses during L. plantarum AR-R and AR-R3 mono-colonization and identifies candidate strain-specific features potentially associated with adaptation to the in vivo environment.
authors: Dang C, Xia Y, Ai L, Xiong Z, Wang G.

title: MicroRNAs' Therapeutic Potential in Multiple Human Diseases.
abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are a class of short single-stranded non-coding RNAs widely present in multicellular eukaryotes, including animals, plants, and fungi. Typically, approximately 22 nucleotides in length (with some ranging from 22 to 25 nucleotides), miRNAs are predominantly localized to non-coding genomic regions and exhibit high evolutionary conservation. As key post-transcriptional modulators of gene expression, miRNAs are non-protein-coding molecules. They bind complementarily to the 3'UTR of target mRNAs. This interaction triggers mRNA breakdown or inhibits protein translation. In this way, miRNAs regulate nearly 30% of cellular protein expression. MiRNA biogenesis is tightly regulated. Abnormal miRNA expression alters disease-related genes and signaling pathways. It further drives the onset, development, and pathological processes of various human diseases. This review outlines recent progress in research on miRNA functions across multiple illnesses. These illnesses cover neurological, metabolic, tumor, and cardiovascular disorders.
authors: Zhang H, Cai Z.

title: Whole-Genome Resequencing Identifies Loci Associated with Body Weight and Body-Size-Related Head Height in Bighead Carp (Hypophthalmichthys nobilis).
abstract: Growth traits are economically important in bighead carp (Hypophthalmichthys nobilis), but their genetic basis remains unclear. We conducted whole-genome association analyses in 298 fish using 2,891,492 single-nucleotide polymorphisms and linear mixed models controlling for population structure and genomic relatedness. Five variants reached the per-trait genome-wide threshold. The strongest body-weight association occurred at 13:40990738:C:T on linkage group 13 (LG13) (p = 5.09 × 10-10; effect = 5.50 ± 0.87 g). Two LG04 variants were associated with body weight, while two adjacent LG14 variants were associated with head height (lead p = 8.34 × 10-9; effect = 2.59 ± 0.44 mm). However, associations with head dimensions were substantially attenuated after body-length adjustment, indicating that head-specific genetic effects were not established. Regional linkage disequilibrium and conditional analyses distinguished compact LG13 and LG14 signals from a complex LG04 pattern, and complementary sensitivity analyses supported their robustness. Sanger sequencing confirmed all 118 tested LG13 genotypes. The LG13 body-weight association was reproduced in an independent population of 268 fish and remained significant after body-length adjustment. Genotype-stratified reverse-transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction assays detected higher expression of mchr2-like gene13.20, syngr1-like gene32.45, and cacng2-like gene32.46 in effect-allele carriers after multiple-test correction. These findings provide independent support for the LG13 body-weight association, while LG14 and LG04 remain discovery-stage candidate regions requiring independent replication and functional investigation before potential breeding applications can be considered.
authors: Chen G, Peng F, Wang D, Tong J, Xu J.

title: Hospital Drain Microbiomes as Distinct Microbial Signatures Within Urban Wastewater Networks in the Han River Watershed.
abstract: Background: Hospital drainage systems represent an important interface between healthcare facilities and urban wastewater networks and may contribute distinct microbial inputs to downstream aquatic environments. This issue is particularly relevant in Seoul, Republic of Korea, where urban wastewater discharges into receiving waters within the Han River watershed. Methods: In this study, we characterized hospital drain microbiomes to evaluate their microbial and environmental signatures, using residential drains as a non-clinical comparison. Results: Hospital drains exhibited a distinct taxonomic profile, with greater relative abundances of Bacteroidota and Firmicutes and several genera of environmental or potential public health relevance, including Mycobacterium, Legionella, and Pseudomonas. Although microbial richness was comparable between the two environments, Simpson diversity was significantly lower in hospital drains, indicating reduced community evenness. Bray-Curtis and Jaccard analyses showed clear separation between hospital and residential microbial communities, and hierarchical clustering further supported environment-associated community structuring. LEfSe analysis identified distinct hospital-associated taxonomic biomarkers, and predicted functional profiling revealed substantial metabolic differentiation, with 19 of the 25 most significantly differentiated pathways enriched in hospital samples. Conclusions: These microbial and functional differences underscore the ecological uniqueness of hospital drains and support their inclusion in future wastewater-based microbial surveillance strategies. Collectively, these findings establish hospital drains as distinct microbial ecosystems within urban wastewater networks and provide a baseline for future studies examining the persistence of hospital-associated microbial signatures within the Han River watershed.
authors: Shuvo MSH, Ju-Young W, Jo S, Ahmed I, Aziz MT, Atashi A, Raihan MA, Yeji P, Hyunhee C, Kim T, Yu H, Bae H, Kim S, Seo H, Song HY.

title: Construction of Recombinant PRV Expressing PRRSV Antigens and Evaluation of Their Protective Efficacy in Pigs Against Homologous Challenge.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) remains a major threat to the global swine industry, while the emergence of variant pseudorabies virus (PRV) strains has further complicated disease control in China. This study aimed to develop a PRV-based viral vector platform for PRRSV antigen delivery and evaluate its safety, immunogenicity, and protective efficacy. Methods: A five-gene-deleted variant PRV strain, PRV-JM-DF, was used as the vector backbone. Candidate genomic insertion sites and endogenous late promoters were systematically screened, followed by construction of recombinant PRVs expressing PRRSV GP2, GP3, GP4, GP5, and M individually or as tandem antigen constructs. Recombinant viruses were characterized for antigen expression, replication, and genetic stability. Safety and immunogenicity were initially evaluated in female BALB/c mice, and the leading candidates were further assessed for safety, immunogenicity, and protective efficacy in 18 Landrace pigs of either sex following challenge with highly pathogenic PRRSV HuN4. Results: The TK locus supported efficient foreign-gene expression, and pUL39 exhibited the highest activity among the tested endogenous late promoters. The recombinant viruses retained replication competence and genetic stability. Among the candidates, rPRV-C-4T induced robust PRRSV- and PRV-specific neutralizing antibody responses and showed no obvious adverse effects during the experimental observation period in pigs. Following HP-PRRSV HuN4 challenge, all rPRV-C-4T-immunized pigs survived and exhibited reduced viremia, viral shedding and tissue viral loads, together with markedly alleviated pathological lesions. Conclusions: rPRV-C-4T provided protection against homologous HP-PRRSV HuN4 challenge while maintaining PRV-directed immune responses, supporting its potential as a PRV-vectored multivalent vaccine candidate.
authors: Wang S, Liu Y, Han L, Gao L, Ye G, Zhao X, Liu Y, Liu H, Zhang Z, Weng C.

title: Expanding the pig metabolomics QTL catalog.
abstract: BackgroundUnderstanding the genetic regulation of metabolism is essential for improving animal health and productivity and for strengthening the use of pigs as translational models for human metabolic diseases. Metabolomics, when integrated with genomic data, provides a powerful framework for identifying genetic factors that influence intermediate molecular phenotypes closely linked to physiology. While large-scale metabolomics genome‑wide association studies (GWAS) have been extensively performed in humans, comparable studies in pigs remain limited. Among omics disciplines, metabolomics, the systematic study of metabolites central to physiology, represents the omics layer most closely linked to end-point phenotypes in mammals, such as health and production traits (e.g. growth rate). Metabolite levels are influenced by genetics, diet, and microbiome composition, with human studies showing high heritability and identifying numerous metabolite quantitative trait loci (mQTLs). While such findings have advanced our understanding of disease biology in humans, comparable studies in pigs remain limited.ResultsWe performed GWAS of the serum metabolome in 213 three‑way crossbred pigs [(Landrace × Yorkshire) × Duroc], analyzing 248 metabolites and 30,628 metabolite ratios. We identified 41 significant metabolite-variant associations, which were consolidated into 18 mQTLs based on linkage disequilibrium (LD). Several regions were associated with multiple, biochemically related metabolites, while others showed highly specific effects. Cross-species comparison with the human GWAS catalog revealed candidate genes within seven mQTLs. Through an integrative prioritization strategy, putative causal genes-predominantly enzymes and transporters-were identified for 14 of 18 mQTLs.ConclusionsOur results expand the catalog of genetic loci influencing serum metabolite variation in pigs and highlight both conserved and pig specific components of metabolic regulation. These findings provide a foundation for incorporating metabolomics into pig breeding programs and reinforce the value of pigs as a translational model for studying metabolite-associated traits and diseases in humans.
authors: Ibragimov E, Morsing MK, Rydal MP, Cai Z, Stenlund H, Nielsen JP, Fredholm M, Karlskov-Mortensen P.

title: Microbial resistance from genotype to metabolic phenotype.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses an escalating global threat, yet surveillance and mechanistic understanding remain anchored in individual resistance genes, an approach that is inadequate for capturing the ecological, genomic, and metabolic complexity through which resistance emerges and spreads. In this opinion article, we argue that genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) offer a principled framework for advancing AMR research beyond this gene-centric paradigm. Strain-resolved GEMs embed resistance determinants within metabolic networks, with the potential to generate quantitative, context-dependent phenotypic predictions, including minimum inhibitory concentrations and environment-conditional resistance, that sequence-based tools do not provide. Expanded GEM frameworks incorporating mobile genetic elements, horizontal gene transfer, and community-level interactions support ecology-aware resistance profiling. At the therapeutic level, whole-network modelling can identify metabolic vulnerabilities, synthetic lethal interactions, and microbiome-targeted strategies. Integrating GEMs with multiomics and data-driven approaches represents a critical step toward a mechanism-aware AMR platform connecting surveillance, diagnosis, and drug discovery.
authors: Clasen F, Jin Y, Brett J, Garcia-Guevara F, Ehrlich SD, Shoaie S.

title: Detection and characterization of PRRSV-2 viruses with mutations in binding sites of common diagnostic real-time RT-PCR primer and probe sequences.
abstract: During a field study about porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) in Danish pig herds, it was discovered that the quantitative real-time RT-PCR (RT-qPCR) assay used in the study was unable to detect PRRSV-2 in two herds (Herds A and B) exhibiting clinical signs consistent with PRRS. Two additional herds (Herd C, identified through clinical suspicion, and Herd D, identified during the field study) showed reduced assay sensitivity. Sequence analysis of viruses from all four herds demonstrated that the reduced sensitivity was caused by mutations within the primer and probe binding sites. Full genome analysis of Danish PRRSV-2 sequences revealed the existence of two phylogenetically separate mutated variants with a high degree of identity to previously identified Danish variants, suggesting that they were not newly introduced but likely arose separately in Denmark.
authors: Goecke NB, Canuti M, Marving EL, Heiselberg PR, Hjulsager CK, Ryt-Hansen P, Breum SØ, Thorup C, Droce A, Larsen LE.

title: Biochemical characterization of the mannojirimycin biosynthetic enzymes reveals metal ion- and pH-dependent catalysis in Bacillus atrophaeus MBLB1156 isolated from red fermented bean curd (Hong fu ru).
abstract: 1-Deoxynojirimycin (DNJ) and its C2 epimer, 1-deoxymannojirimycin (DMJ), are pharmaceutically relevant iminosugars. Although the gabT1-yktc1-gutB1 gene cluster has been implicated in the biosynthesis of mannojirimycin (MJ), a common precursor of DNJ and DMJ, the coordinated biochemical properties of the pathway enzymes remain poorly understood. Here, we isolated a DMJ-producing strain, Bacillus atrophaeus MBLB1156, from Hong fu ru and identified a gabT1-yktc1-gutB1 cluster by whole-genome sequencing. Comparative genomic analysis of 99 Bacillus genomes further revealed that the cluster of MBLB1156 belongs to a distinct evolutionary lineage. Biochemical analyses showed that rBatGabT1 preferentially aminated fructose-6-phosphate using L-glutamate, while rBatYktc1 exhibited metal ion- and pH-dependent phosphatase activity. rBatGutB1 was characterized as a Zn2+-binding NAD(P)-dependent dehydrogenase with an alkaline pH optimum. The assembled three-enzyme cascade synthesized MJ, which was subsequently converted to DMJ by chemical reduction, providing biochemical evidence for the proposed biosynthetic pathway. Cell extract assays further showed that DMJ production was favored under neutral to mildly alkaline conditions despite the more alkaline pH optima of rBatGabT1 and rBatGutB1, indicating that the distinct biochemical properties of the three enzymes collectively influence pathway activity. These findings advance our biochemical understanding of MJ biosynthesis of B. atrophaeus and provide a foundation for metabolic engineering and biocatalytic production of iminosugars.
authors: Lim HJ, Chun J, Baek S, Lee S, Jung JH, Seo MJ.

title: Approaches to Superefficient Yeast Transformations: DNA Phase Separation, Cell Growth State and Systematic Experimental Design.
abstract: Yeasts are model organisms and protein production hosts of choice, in part due to their ease of genetic manipulation. Yeast transformation with DNA on plasmids or integrated into the genome has been developed since the 1970s and is a routine method in many laboratories. However, transformation frequencies are surprisingly low, with common methods yielding around 1% of transformed cells in budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. In alternative species, there is lower transformation frequency and unreasonably large quantities of input DNA may be required. Surprisingly, the mechanisms by which yeast cells take up DNA are not known. Here we argue that three approaches could deliver a step-change in yeast transformation frequency and efficiency. First, investigating the mechanisms of DNA uptake. The requirement for salts and extraneous polymers-carrier DNA and PEG-in standard protocols suggests that phase separation of DNA may enhance DNA uptake into cells or subsequent nuclear delivery. Second, accounting for the physiological or growth state of the yeast including cell cycle phase and nutrient or stress conditions. Third, systematically determining the factors that affect transformation efficiency using statistical Design of Experiments. These approaches could allow superefficient transformation of S. cerevisiae, and accelerate genetic manipulation of non-model yeasts.
authors: Elfick A, Wallace EWJ.

title: Grapevine rust fungus Neophysopella tropicalis deploys protein effectors with plant immunity-suppressing activity during sequential stages of pathogenesis.
abstract: Germination of urediniospores marks the onset of infection by Neophysopella tropicalis, the causal agent of Asian grapevine leaf rust, yet the molecular mechanisms enabling this obligate biotrophic fungus to establish infection remain largely unknown. We combined transcriptomics, histological analyses, and functional assays to identify and characterize candidate effector proteins deployed during the earliest stages of pathogenesis. RNA sequencing of in vitro-germinated urediniospores identified 303 genes encoding predicted secreted proteins bearing hallmarks of fungal effectors, grouped into 142 sequence families and revealing a remarkably diverse repertoire of effector candidates. Fifteen highly expressed N. tropicalis effector candidate (NtEC) genes, representing thirteen distinct sequence families, were selected for expression profiling by reverse transcription quantitative PCR across infection stages. Chitin-targeted fluorescence microscopy provided a developmental framework for interpreting expression across germination, penetration, and early colonization. Although identified during germination, seven NtECs accumulated transcripts predominantly during host penetration and early biotrophic colonization, suggesting specialized roles in infection establishment. Using the Type III Secretion System of Pseudomonas fluorescens EtHAn, we demonstrated that three NtECs (NtEC-05, NtEC-09, and NtEC-10) strongly suppressed AvrB-triggered hypersensitive cell death in Nicotiana benthamiana, while three others (NtEC-11, NtEC-12, and NtEC-13) exhibited moderate immune-suppressing activity. Together, these findings provide the first comprehensive characterization of the N. tropicalis effector repertoire, demonstrating that early infection involves coordinated, sequential deployment of evolutionarily diverse effectors associated with plant immune suppression. This work establishes an integrated framework for discovery and functional prioritization of rust fungus effectors and provides a valuable molecular resource for future studies on grapevine-rust interactions.
authors: Maia T, Ferro JV, Husein G, Bombardelli RGH, Monteiro-Vitorello CB.

title: Expanding threat of carbapenemase-producing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae in Peru: genomic and phenotypic evidence of high-risk clones dissemination.
abstract: Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales represent a growing global threat due to their extensive antimicrobial resistance and rapid dissemination. This study characterized the phenotypic and genomic features of Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates collected between 2020 and 2022 from four healthcare institutions in Lima, Peru. A total of 320 non-redundant isolates (61 E. coli and 259 K. pneumoniae) were analyzed through antimicrobial susceptibility testing, polymerase chain reaction, and whole-genome sequencing. The most frequent carbapenemase gene was blaNDM (69%), followed by blaKPC (16.9%) and blaOXA-48-like (4.6%). Eleven K. pneumoniae isolates co-produced NDM and KPC, and one E. coli isolate co-harbored NDM and OXA-48-like. All isolates were multidrug-resistant, and 5% were resistant to all agents included in the routine panel; however, aztreonam/avibactam and cefiderocol retained complete in vitro activity among tested isolates. Novel β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations such as aztreonam/avibactam and cefiderocol showed complete activity against all classes of carbapenemases. Genomic analysis revealed predominant E. coli sequence types ST167 and ST410 and K. pneumoniae lineages ST147, ST15, ST45, and ST273. The blaNDM-5 allele was detected for the first time in Peru, mostly in E. coli ST167, and was carried on multireplicon IncF-type plasmids. In K. pneumoniae, ST147 was identified as a dominant clone associated with blaNDM-1, indicating sustained local dissemination of high-risk clonal groups. The coexistence of multiple carbapenemases and plasmid backbones highlights the ongoing evolution of resistance mechanisms. This work provides the first integrative genomic overview of carbapenemase-producing E. coli and K. pneumoniae in Peru and underscores the need for continuous genomic surveillance and antimicrobial stewardship to mitigate their clinical and epidemiological impact.
authors: Gonzales-Escalante E, Champi-Merino RG, Alvarado-Rios L, Gómez-de-la-Torre JC, Sierra-Chávez E, Sandoval-Ahumada R, Pérez-Lazo G, Casanova J, Matta-Chuquisapon J, Morales-Castillo LV, Escobar-Valdiviezo MA, Gonzales-Rodriguez A.

title: Borrelia garinii spirochetemia in a previously healthy child presenting with Streptococcus anginosus group brain abscess: a case report.
abstract: BackgroundThe clinical significance of transient Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato complex (hereafter referred to as B. burgdorferi) spirochetemia remains poorly understood and has rarely been documented. We report the isolation of viable B. garinii genospecies from the blood of a previously healthy child presenting with a Streptococcus anginosus group (SAG) brain abscess.Case presentationAn eight-year-old girl presented with four days of headache, fever, nausea, slightly reduced general condition, and mild facial asymmetry. Initial evaluation, including lumbar puncture, raised suspicion of viral meningitis or Lyme neuroborreliosis (LNB). Based on the differential diagnosis of Lyme disease, she was enrolled in the prospective BRILLIANT study (NCT06045416), with additional blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sampling for B. burgdorferi culture and serology. Following initial outpatient management, she re-presented with clinical deterioration and signs of raised intracranial pressure. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging revealed a brain abscess requiring surgical drainage. Abscess cultures yielded SAG. Dental treatment four days before symptom onset provided a plausible source of infectious spread. Treatment with intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole for six weeks resulted in complete clinical recovery and radiological improvement. Borrelia burgdorferi-specific two-tier serology and CSF culture remained negative. In contrast, blood plasma culture for B. burgdorferi obtained at initial presentation yielded viable spirochetes after seven weeks. Borrelia burgdorferi DNA was confirmed by flaB-targeted qPCR, and hybrid whole-genome sequencing generated a near-complete genome identifying B. garinii genospecies.ConclusionThis case demonstrates viable B. garinii spirochetemia without serological evidence of LNB, incidentally detected during investigation of a SAG brain abscess. It highlights the uncertain clinical significance of transient B. burgdorferi spirochetemia, and the importance of interpreting microbiological findings within the clinical context.
authors: Greiter BM, Hugelshofer M, Seiler M, Sidorov S, Hackenberg A, Kottke R, Egli A, Krayenbühl N, Berger C, Meyer Sauteur PM.

title: Purification and mechanistic characterisation of bacillomycin D homologues from Bacillus velezensis PD9 with antibiofilm activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance continues to undermine treatment of multidrug-resistant infections, necessitating new antimicrobial agents with distinct mechanisms of action. Bacillus velezensis PD9 (BvPD9), isolated from Heterotrigona itama propolis, produces antibacterial lipopeptides; however, the active bacillomycin D homologues and their mechanisms remain insufficiently characterised. Here, an optimised extraction and chromatographic purification workflow was developed, enabling selective enrichment of two bioactive fractions putatively assigned by LC-TOF-MS/MS as C14-enriched bacillomycin D and a C14/C15-bacillomycin D homologue mixture. The C14-enriched bacillomycin D fraction exhibited selective activity against Staphylococcus spp. and vancomycin-sensitive Enterococcus faecium (VSEF), with minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of 16-32 µg/mL, whereas the C14/C15 homologue mixture demonstrated broader antibacterial activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and selected ESKAPE pathogens (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter spp.) (MICs 16-512 µg/mL), with the lowest MIC (16 µg/mL) observed against VSEF. Both compounds retained activity following heat exposure (40-80 °C), wide pH variation (4-12), and proteolytic enzymes. The C14/C15 homologue mixture was prioritised for further evaluation because of its broader antibacterial spectrum and displayed concentration-dependent inhibition of biofilm formation, membrane permeabilisation, and ultrastructural alterations, together with changes in bacterial DNA-content distribution without detectable direct DNA binding. Preliminary safety evaluation demonstrated concentration-dependent haemolysis and cytotoxicity at higher concentrations, while zebrafish embryos showed concentration-dependent mortality with an LC50 of 109.54 µg/mL at 120 hpf. Serial passaging resulted in a four-fold MIC increase only during the final passages, whereas chloramphenicol showed no detectable MIC change under the same conditions. Overall, the findings demonstrate antibacterial and membrane-associated activities of PD9-derived bacillomycin D-enriched fractions and provide a basis for further investigation of individually purified homologues.

title: DksA regulates intestinal colonization of Klebsiella pneumoniae through metabolic plasticity.
abstract: Intestinal colonization by Klebsiella pneumoniae is recognized as a pivotal prerequisite for its systemic dissemination and subsequent invasive infection; however, the metabolic basis and regulatory mechanisms underlying this process remain poorly understood. In this study, we employed transposon insertion sequencing (Tn-seq) to systematically identify metabolic genes associated with intestinal colonization in K. pneumoniae. By integrating high-throughput screening with in vivo phenotypic validation, we identified the global transcriptional regulator DksA as a key factor that markedly enhances K. pneumoniae intestinal colonization. Mechanistically, DksA may contribute to intestinal colonization through modulation of central carbon metabolism. Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses, together with homology modeling and molecular dynamics simulations, suggested that DksA may contribute to allosteric remodeling of key RNA polymerase structural domains, thereby influencing the expression of metabolic genes, carbon source utilization, and intestinal colonization by K. pneumoniae. Collectively, our findings highlight the important role of metabolic plasticity associated with transcriptional regulation in K. pneumoniae intestinal colonization and provide a theoretical framework and potential targets for developing anti-colonization strategies that exploit pathogen metabolic vulnerabilities.ImportanceIntestinal colonization is a critical first step in the pathogenesis and transmission of Klebsiella pneumoniae, yet the bacterial factors that support persistence in the gut remain incompletely understood. In this study, we identified the transcriptional regulator DksA as an important contributor to intestinal colonization through genome-wide genetic screening and in vivo validation. Multi-omics analyses suggest that DksA is associated with the regulation of bacterial carbon metabolism and metabolic adaptation, processes that are likely important for survival in the nutrient-variable intestinal environment. Structural modeling further provides insight into how DksA may influence transcriptional regulation. These findings expand our understanding of the factors that facilitate K. pneumoniae gut colonization and highlight bacterial metabolic adaptation as a potential target for strategies aimed at limiting colonization and subsequent infection.
authors: Wan J, Wang Y, Wang L, Li Y, Xiong S, Chu X, Zhou D, Li J, Li M, Xia X, Wang W, Yang M, Liu W, Wen Y, Qiu Z, Feng S, Tian G-B.

title: Dissecting multiple hybridization events in a yeast lineage.
abstract: We comprehensively surveyed the occurrence of hybridization events in three phylogenetically related yeast genera - Torulaspora, Zygotorulaspora and Zygosaccharomyces - using a dataset of 172 genomes, 123 of which were newly sequenced. We detected five new hybrids in Zygosaccharomyces, three in Torulaspora, and none in Zygotorulaspora. For most of the newly characterized hybrids we were able to identify their parental species. Moreover, we confirmed that Z. sapae is a triple hybrid that contains the contributions of Z. progenitor, Z. rouxii and Z. siamensis. One Torulaspora hybrid resulted from a hybridization event involving members of two very divergent populations of T. delbrueckii, which suggests that conventional mating is impaired and that one of the parental genomes might in fact represent a cryptic species. In general hybrid genomes had mitochondria from only one of the parental species and maintained the chromosomal architecture of their parental species. However, in Zygosaccharomyces the MAT regions tended to be dynamic and variable, a situation also seen, but to a lesser degree, in non-hybrid genomes. Our results suggest that hybridization in Zygosaccharomyces is linked to the colonization of anthropic environments, as all cases of hybridization in this genus are linked to man-made environments. However, this pattern is not evident in Torulaspora. This study and the resources it provides pave the way for a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying hybridization in yeasts.
authors: Ribeiro Silva M, Rosa CA, Gonçalves P, Homem Brito P, Sampaio JP.

title: Diaphorin induces extensive transcriptional remodeling of translation, transport, metabolism, and stress responses in  Escherichia coli
abstract: Diaphorin is a pederin-family polyketide produced by the obligate bacterial symbiont “  Candidatus Profftella armatura” (Betaproteobacteria) of the Asian citrus psyllid  Diaphorina citri , in which it accumulates at millimolar concentrations. Diaphorin suppresses the growth of many bacterial species but promotes the growth and metabolic activity of  Escherichia coli , highlighting the importance of elucidating the mechanisms underlying these contrasting effects. Although cell-free studies show that diaphorin directly affects bacterial translation, how  E. coli transcription changes during growth promotion remains unclear. Here, we analyzed the transcriptome of  E. coli after 7 h of exposure to 5 mM diaphorin, when its growth-promoting effect is most pronounced. Diaphorin altered the expression of 1,278 of 4,269 analyzed genes. Functional enrichment analyses revealed strong negative enrichment of translation- and ribosome-related functions, pathway-specific changes in metabolism, and enrichment of transport-, stress-response, and quorum-sensing-related functions. Ribosomal protein genes were broadly downregulated, whereas coordinated upregulation was observed in  mdtEF ,  prpBCDE , the Gad system, and  luxS /  lsr genes. These findings indicate functionally structured transcriptional remodeling during diaphorin-enhanced growth. Together with previous cell-free evidence, the pronounced translation-related changes observed here highlight bacterial translation as a major process associated with the response of  E. coli to diaphorin. One possible interpretation of the apparently contrasting observations is that an earlier stimulation of bacterial translation is followed by compensatory downregulation of translation-related genes as growth proceeds. More broadly, these transcriptional changes provide insight into diaphorin-enhanced growth in  E. coli and offer a basis for understanding the strikingly different effects of this symbiont-derived polyketide among bacterial species.
authors: Yasuda Y, Takasu R, Hirose Y, Nakabachi A.

title: The relevance of GGCC methylation for cyanobacterial gene expression regulation
abstract: Epigenetic DNA modifications are pivotal in eukaryotic gene expression, but their regulatory significance in bacteria is less understood. In the  Synechocystis 6803 genome, the DNA-specific methyltransferase M.Ssp6803II modifies the first cytosine in the 38,512 GGCC motifs, forming N4-methylcytosine (GG  m4 CC). Previous analyses showed that deletion of the gene encoding M.Ssp6803II (Δ  sll0729 ), caused a “bluish” phenotype due to reduced expression of the  hemJ gene. This effect was caused by the lacking GGCC methylation in the discriminator sequence of the  hemJ promoter in Δ  sll0729 . In the present study, we analyzed the impact of GG  m4 CC methylation on the overall gene expression. Bioinformatic analyses of multiple, independently obtained DNA microarray datasets revealed reproducible changes in the expression of more than 300 genes. We selected 26 genes that had the GGCC methylation motif in different locations of their promoter sequences and verified their differential expression through qPCR experiments. Classification of the promoters according to the relative position of GGCC motifs suggested context-specific effects on gene expression. These findings imply that GG  m4 CC methylation via DNA methyltransferase M.Ssp6803II has an important impact on proper gene expression and thus, cytosine N4-methylation is a relevant epigenetic marker in  Synechocystis and likely many other bacteria.
authors: Stappert N, Schmidt N, Reimann V, Hagemann M, Hess WR.

title: Epstein-Barr Virus in HIV-Associated Conjunctival Squamous Cell Carcinoma and Transcriptional Reprogramming of Conjunctival Epithelial Cells
abstract: ABSTRACT  The involvement of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) in conjunctival squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) remains incompletely defined. This study integrated analyses of primary tumors with an experimental model of the conjunctival epithelium. Five Nigerian tumors from patients with HIV and three Japanese tumors from patients without HIV were examined by EBV-encoded RNA in situ hybridization (EBER-ISH), EBV DNA PCR, and virome analysis of RNA sequencing data. EBER localized to epithelial tumor cells in four Nigerian specimens and none of the Japanese specimens. EBV DNA and RNA were each detected in three Nigerian tumors, with every EBER-positive tumor supported by at least one additional assay. Human telomerase reverse transcriptase-immortalized conjunctival epithelial cells infected with Akata-GFP-EBV expressed latency-associated and lytic viral genes. Comparison of three infected and three control cultures identified 96 differentially expressed host genes and 23 enriched Hallmark gene sets at a false discovery rate below 0.05. RT-qPCR confirmed increased HES1, CXCL8, CXCL2, and LOX and decreased FGFBP1, CSTA, SAPCD2, and TMEM40 expression. Prominent responses involved inflammatory signaling, epithelial remodeling, metabolism, and cell-cycle regulation. These findings identify tumor-cell-associated EBV in a subset of HIV-associated cSCC and establish an epithelial model for investigating infection-associated host responses.
authors: Dochi H, Avilala J, Yamada Y, Takahira M, Kondo S, Yoshizaki T, Morales M, Abdelghani R, Becnel D, Sides M, Morris GF, Feng W, Liu H, Lin Z.

title: When RNA Viruses Converge on Host Membranes: Extracellular Vesicle-Mediated Transfer and Emerging Antiviral Vulnerabilities
abstract: Positive-sense RNA viruses are commonly classified by genome organization, entry route, tissue tropism, and clinical syndrome, but these categories do not explain how viruses construct protected replication niches or route infectious material between cells. The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) provides a shared platform for viral translation, replication-organelle formation, membrane curvature, lipid remodeling, innate immune regulation, and vesicular trafficking. Within this framework, reticulon-3 (RTN3) has emerged as a candidate regulator linking ER-based RNA-virus replication to the generation of infectious extracellular-vesicle cargo. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) and dengue virus (DENV) provide the strongest comparative evidence for this model despite their distinct transmission routes, tissue tropisms, disease courses, and immune pathophysiology. HCV most clearly demonstrates that exosome-enriched fractions can transfer replication-competent viral RNA with defined host cofactors, whereas DENV extends this mechanism to an acute viral infection. Both viruses nevertheless replicate within remodeled ER membranes and can transfer infection-competent material in vesicle-associated form. Current evidence supports a context-dependent model in which RTN3-associated membrane curvature, ER–endosome communication, and cargo routing influence whether replication-associated viral RNA is retained, degraded, assembled into virions, or exported in biologically active extracellular vesicles. Related membrane-remodeling and vesicle-associated processes in Zika virus, West Nile virus, enteroviruses, SARS-CoV-2, and hepatitis A virus illustrate broader exploitation of host membrane organization, although direct evidence for RTN3-dependent infectious extracellular-vesicle transfer varies across these systems. In the best characterized models, vesicles protect viral genomes or replication-associated complexes and deliver biologically active cargo to recipient cells. Advances in isolation and characterization, including density-gradient or size-exclusion separation, immunoaffinity selection, particle and marker profiling, membrane-protection assays, and recipient-cell infectivity testing, now permit more rigorous identification of defined vesicle populations, protected cargo, and biological activity. Nevertheless, RTN3 should not be considered a universal RNA-virus dependency, nor should extracellular-vesicle release be assumed to generate uniformly infectious populations. Instead, HCV and DENV show that divergent viral pathophysiologies can converge on host membrane factors such as RTN3 while retaining virus-specific molecular partners and pathways for replication and vesicular transmission. Defining these shared and virus-specific dependencies may reveal host–virus interfaces suitable for broad-spectrum or resistance-resilient intervention, provided that infection-selective reliance, a measurable therapeutic window, and preservation of essential host-cell functions can be demonstrated.
authors: Noumi T, Bitazar R, Asaba CN, Labonté P, Bukong TN.

title: Th17 Cells Impair Epithelial Defense Against Intracellular Bacteria in Part Through TGF-β.
abstract: While Th1 and Th17 cells are well known for their distinct roles in host defense, how these effector CD4+ T-cell subsets influence epithelial responses to intracellular bacteria remains unclear. Here, we investigated whether Th1 or Th17 cells modulate the intracellular survival of Escherichia coli 7.2 (Ec7.2), a clinical isolate from oral lichen planus (OLP) tissue, in oral keratinocytes. To assess antigen-specific and antigen-independent T-cell effects, we established a co-culture system using IFN-γ-pretreated, Ec7.2-infected immortalized murine oral keratinocytes (IMOK) and Th1 or Th17 cells differentiated from OT-II-restricted CD4+ T cells, in the absence or presence of cognate peptide. Th1 cells reduced intracellular Ec7.2 in an antigen-dependent manner, whereas Th17 cells consistently increased bacterial persistence through largely antigen-independent and contact-independent mechanisms. Transcriptomic analysis of infected IMOK cells revealed that Th17-associated soluble signals broadly attenuated epithelial innate immune and antibacterial responses, including pathways related to type II interferon signaling, chemokine production, and defense response to bacterium. Among these, Nos2 expression was significantly reduced upon Th17 co-culture and was accompanied by decreased nitric oxide (NO) production. Th17 cells expressed higher levels of Tgfb1 than Th1 cells, and elevated TGF-β concentrations were consistently observed under Th17 co-culture conditions associated with increased bacterial persistence. Neutralization of TGF-β was associated with a trend toward increased NO production and reduced intracellular Ec7.2 recovery relative to isotype-treated controls. Together, these findings identify a previously underappreciated role for Th17-associated signals in modulating epithelial defense against intracellular bacteria, in part through TGF-β-associated suppression of NO-associated antimicrobial responses, which may contribute to bacterial persistence in Th17-dominated mucosal environments.
authors: Kang M, Kim HJ, Song J, Acharya S, Choi Y.

title: Clinical pathogen adjudication in metagenomic sequencing using a large language model
abstract: Clinical metagenomic sequencing detects hundreds of organisms whose relevance to infection requires clinicians' manual interpretation. We retrospectively reviewed 4,855 specimens from 19 sampling sites, linked 1.33 million detected organisms to clinical culprit-pathogen determinations, and fine-tuned a large language model on these labels. The model recovered 92.44% of reference culprit calls in the held-out test set and 84.49% in a later cohort. In a blinded re-adjudication of 215 cases, the model matched 90.5% of culprit calls on which both expert reviewers agreed. Adjudication accuracy varied with organism identity and specimen types. mNGS-derived metrics such as read counts or genome coverage alone were insufficient to identify culprit pathogens, and organisms classified as common colonizers could still be judged causative. Certain organisms were frequently co-reported as causative in the same specimen. These findings support further evaluation of human and AI-assisted report review, particularly regarding missed pathogens, excess calls, and differences across specimen types.
authors: Wei M, Zhao Y, Fang C, Zhang S, Xu K, Li S, Liu L, Pang Y, Liang L, Deng Z, Li M.

title: Investigation of prolificacy across sheep breeds reveals new potential genetic contributors
abstract: Abstract    Background  Prolificacy is a major determinant of reproductive efficiency in sheep, yet its genetic architecture remains incompletely understood, particularly in Canadian populations. Several genetic variants affecting ovine fertility have been reported, notably in  Bone morphogenetic protein 15 (BMP15)  and  Growth differentiation factor 9 (GDF9)  , two genes involved in folliculogenesis. Since 2023, more than 5,000 sheep have been genotyped as part of the development of a genomic selection program in Canada, enabling the investigation of these variants. This study evaluated previously reported prolificacy-associated variants and investigated the genetic basis of exceptional prolificacy in the Canadian Rideau Arcott breed. Results  Among 30 candidate loci, three were significantly associated with litter size in specific breeds using nearly 100,000 litter size records analyzed with linear mixed-effects models. The  G6  variant in  GDF9  gene on chromosome 5 was associated with lower litter size in homozygous compared with heterozygous Romanov ewes and compared with both heterozygous and non-carrier Dorper ewes, with significant deviations from an additive effect. In Rideau Arcott, the  G7  variant in  GDF9  , also known as  FecGF  , was associated with increases of 0.15 and 0.25 lambs per litter in heterozygous and homozygous animals, respectively (p GDF9  variant, designated  FecGR  herein, which was associated with an increase of 0.21 lambs per litter in heterozygous ewes (p GDF9  variants, the association at the second locus persisted, and haplotype analyses highlighted several candidate genes within a 1.5-Mb region. These included several  SPINK  family members and  PPP2R2B  , which encodes a regulatory subunit of Protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) complex and has been implicated in reproductive processes. Conclusions  These findings provide new tools for marker-assisted selection that could complement traditional EPD-based genetic selection, while contributing to a better understanding of the genetic architecture of ovine prolificacy and identifying new candidate genes for future investigation.
authors: POISSON W, MICHAUD C, CAMERON J, ST-PIERRE A, PERECIN-NOCITI R, GILBERT I, PAQUET É, FABRE S, ROBERT C.

title: Cyto-genotoxic potential and in silico analysis of emerging contaminants of the Ganges River water.
abstract: The Ganges River, vital for drinking water, agriculture, fisheries, and socio-religious practices, is increasingly threatened by contaminants, compromising its ecological and biological integrity. Present study was undertaken to identify contaminants in the river water using chemical profiling integrated with bacterial and plant bioassays, complemented by in silico analysis. GC-MS analysis of hexane and chloroform extracts revealed the presence of pharmaceuticals, phenolic substances, siloxanes, hormone-disrupting agents, and antibiotics, including spironolactone, nalmefene, desmethylverapamil, bisphenol B, aminopterin, and minocycline. Solvent extracts of the Ganges water demonstrated concentration-dependent mutagenicity in Ames Salmonella reversion assay, exceeding more than two-fold spontaneous reversion frequency. Chloroform extracts exhibited significant mutagenic potential with strain TA98 compared to TA100, suggesting prevalence of frameshift mutagens in the test samples. DNA repair-defective Escherichia coli K-12 mutants revealed decline in survival after 6 h of exposure; recA and lexA mutants displayed higher sensitivity compared to wild-type counterparts, confirming DNA-damaging potential of the samples. Allium cepa assay demonstrated suppression of mitotic index from 51.63% to 20.62%, along with increased chromosomal abnormalities from 2.33% to 26.17%. In Vigna radiata seeds, germination and seedling growth were reduced, followed by root tip damage and reduced root cell viability as detected by confocal microscopy. Computational docking analysis and 100-ns molecular dynamics simulations revealed stable binding of selected contaminants to molecular targets involved in nucleotide biosynthesis, DNA replication, topological regulation, and cell division. These findings suggested that the bioactive compounds may induce genetic and cellular damage, contributing to the biological effects associated with contaminant mixtures in river water.
authors: Akhtar S, Malik A.

title: Biochar-associated persistent free radicals inhibit wheat growth: novel insights into ecoenzymatic stoichiometry.
abstract: Biochar-associated persistent free radicals (PFRs) can directly induce oxidative damage in plants. However, this toxic mechanism may not be fully applicable to plants growing in a real soil ecosystem considering the complexity of the soil environment. In this study, biochar was applied to soil at rates ranging from 0 to 20 g kg-1, and wheat growth was inhibited at 20 g kg-1, but did not at 1-10 g kg-1. Notably, inhibitor and sterilization experiments indicated that PFRs and their derived hydroxyl radical (˙OH) were the primary factors inhibiting wheat growth, and wheat damage degree primarily depended on the impact of free radicals on rhizosphere microbes rather than direct damage to wheat itself. Integrated analyses of enzymatic stoichiometry, microbial community structure, and transcriptomic profiles analysis further revealed that at 20 g kg-1 dosage, PFRs and ˙OH aggravated microbial C and P limitations, prompting rhizosphere microbes to preferentially allocate metabolic energy for alleviating nutrient limitations. This reduces the abundance of disease-suppressive bacteria (e.g., Actinobacteria, Gemmatimonadetes, and Nitrospirae) and bacterial α-diversity, ultimately increasing wheat susceptibility to free radical stress. By contrast, free radicals did not induce stoichiometric imbalance at 1-10 g kg-1 dosage. Rhizosphere microbes could allocate more energy to activate the wheat defense system, including salicylic acid metabolism, L-phenylalanine metabolism, and the MAPK signaling pathway, thereby reducing free radical-induced damage to wheat. These findings highlight a previously overlooked mechanism of free radical-induced phytotoxicity, providing a foundation for developing improved biochar application strategies.
authors: Yang H, Zhang Y, Zhu Y, Tang Y, Yuan Y, Zhu L, Jia H.

title: Synthetic biology as a game-changer for endangered medicinal orchids: biosynthesis, engineering and conservation.
abstract: Covering: 2012 to 2026Medicinal orchids constitute a rich yet vulnerable reservoir of high-value bioactive metabolites. However, their sustainable exploitation is severely hampered by resource depletion and the inefficiency of traditional extraction. Synthetic biology emerges as a transformative game-changer to resolve this impasse. This review delineates how synthetic biology drives a paradigm shift in endangered orchid conservation. Through modular design of biosynthetic pathways, heterologous reconstruction in microbial or plant chassis, directed evolution of key enzymes, metabolic engineering, and scalable production, it offers a disruptive solution, fundamentally redefining sustainable utilization by decoupling supply from ecological extraction. We highlight the successful heterologous biosynthesis of representative compounds like gastrodin and dendrobine. Facilitated by pathway optimization, chassis engineering and synthetic consortia design, these efforts have established cell factories that demonstrate the potential for sustainable and non-plant-based production, offering a viable alternative to wild harvest. Furthermore, the research encompasses recent breakthroughs in decoding orchid metabolic networks, including the elucidation of biosynthetic pathways, identification of core enzyme repertoires and discovery of regulatory switches involving transcription factors and miRNAs. Insights from evolutionary genomics and endophyte symbioses are also discussed as critical guides for pathway optimization. We explore the translational impact of these innovations, highlighting how the integration of multi-omics, artificial intelligence and gene editing accelerates the Design-Build-Test-Learn cycle. In summary, synthetic biology represents an essential paradigm shift, transitioning orchid resource management from a narrative of scarcity to one of predictable engineering creation and thereby securing a robust and sustainable supply chain for these prized medicinal plants.
authors: Qiu L, Chen X, Luo Z, Jiang M, Chen H, Hou B, Yu H, Li N, Zhang L.

title: Two New Metabolites from Moquiniastrum sordidum: Phytochemical Characterization and Multifaceted Bioactivity.
abstract: Recent taxonomic revisions based on molecular phylogenetics transferred species from Gochnatia to Moquiniastrum, which now includes 22 species, 20 of which occur in Brazil with an extra-Amazonian distribution. Here, we report a phytochemical study of Moquiniastrum sordidum (Less.) G. Sancho. Chromatographic separation afforded eight compounds, including two new metabolites: a sesquiterpene (5) and a phenolic glycoside (8). The known compounds were identified as simiarenol (1), oleanolic acid (2), hispidulin (3), tyrosol (4), genkwanin (6), and apigenin (7). The relative configuration of compound 5 was established using pip-HSQMBC-IPAP NMR, which afforded accurate long-range 2,3 J CH coupling constants. Dereplication enabled the putative annotation of 45 metabolites: 12 flavonoids, 10 chlorogenic acid derivatives, 5 hydroxycinnamic acid derivatives, 9 terpenes, and 9 others. The biological potential of the extracts and isolated metabolites was evaluated using antioxidant, cytotoxic, antimicrobial, and antileishmanial assays. The new phenolic glycoside (8) showed potent antioxidant activity (ABTS: 1111 μmol TE g-1; FRAP: 4293 μmol Fe-(II) g-1). Oleanolic acid (MIC = 130 μg mL-1) and apigenin (MIC = 30 μg mL-1) showed activity against the Gram-positive bacterium Bacillus cereus. Preliminary cytotoxic screening against HCT-116 cells showed that the dichloromethane fraction inhibited proliferation by 92% at 50 μg mL-1. Antileishmanial evaluation revealed moderate activity of the crude extract, which was significantly enhanced upon fractionation, with the dichloromethane fraction showing the highest activity against intracellular amastigotes (IC50 = 8.23 μg mL-1; SI = 7.87), indicating a selective antiparasitic effect.
authors: Cordeiro T, Valeze FAP, Balbinot RB, Sahm BDB, Dourado FF, Pires EF, Pivetta A, Tiuman TS, Nakamura CV, Costa-Lotufo LV, do Carmo MRB, Viesser RV, Basso EA, Sarragiotto MH, Baldoqui DC.

title: Unveiling the mechanism of microplastic-mediated antibiotic bioavailability, gut microbiota and antibiotic resistome in marine fish: Importance of microplastic aging and antibiotic-loading.
abstract: Microplastics and antibiotics co-occur commonly in coastal aquatic ecosystems. Environmental aging of microplastics and interactions with antibiotics are inevitable, which alter the fate of antibiotics and associated ecotoxicological effects, yet the distinct impacts and underlying mechanisms remain largely unknown. Here, polyethylene (PE) microplastics, derived from a widely used polymer and frequently detected in aquatic environments, were selected to investigate the effects of aging and ciprofloxacin (CIP) loading on CIP bioaccumulation and toxicity in marine medaka (Oryzias melastigma). The intake of microplastics by fish visualized via a novel in situ hyperspectral imaging revealed aged PE (APE) easily accumulated in the fish gut. The presence of microplastics exacerbated CIP-induced gill and intestinal lesions. CIP-loaded pristine PE (PPE-CIP) increased CIP accumulation by 0.87-fold, 1.18-fold and 0.10-fold in the gastrointestinal tract, gill and muscle, respectively, and CIP-loaded aged PE (APE-CIP) further amplified this promoting effect. Conversely, PPE and APE without CIP-loading decreased CIP accumulation in the fish gut, but this clean effect varied with exposure duration, tissue distribution and microplastic aging status. The presence of microplastics altered the gut microbiota composition, and APE-CIP exacerbated the effects of microplastics on the gut microbiota by decreasing the stability of the microbiome network. The presence of PPE-CIP and APE-CIP amplified the abundance of Vibrio and CIP-associated antibiotic resistance genes (i.e., norM gene) in fish feces via enhancing CIP bioaccumulation, increasing the risk of ARGs spread through fish feces. These findings highlight the importance of considering aging and antibiotic-loading when evaluating the carrier effects and toxicity of microplastics.
authors: Yu X, Liu S, Gutang Q, Wang Y, Yin X, Li Y, Wang X.

title: Transcriptome Analysis of Hepatitis C Virus-Infected Hepatoma Cells Following Stringent Removal of Genomic DNA.
abstract: Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) is a positive strand RNA virus that infects hepatocytes and reprograms cellular gene expression, contributing to chronic liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma. HCV replicates slowly and induces limited changes in the cellular transcriptome. Here, we improved analysis of low-abundance transcripts, including long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), in the context of HCV replication. We stringently removed genomic DNA from total RNA from Huh-7 hepatoma cell lines by a combination of TRIzol, acidic phenol, silica matrix columns and recombinant DNase I. RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) and targeted validation were used to characterize Lnc-ITM2C-1 splice variants and expression of its neighboring gene, G protein-coupled receptor 55 (GPR55), to investigate their potential roles in HCV replication. Challenging our previous findings, under our improved experimental conditions, Lnc-ITM2C-1 and GPR55 were neither involved in a positive regulation circuit with HCV nor induced detectable transcriptome changes. Secondary analysis of RNA-Seq data according to HCV infection status revealed statistically robust HCV-induced expression of 21 host cell genes involved in pathways like stress response (in particular ATF3), lipid metabolism, cytoskeleton organization and growth regulation. In contrast, we found that expression changed for only a limited subset of previously reported HCV-associated lncRNAs (e.g., EGOT). This highlights the necessity of stringent gDNA removal for analysis of low-abundance transcripts like lncRNAs.
authors: Khajouei M, Jost E, Collatz M, Malik AQ, Gerresheim GK, Hofmann N, Hu P, Grahn N, Weitz R, Dreute J, Soppa L, Goesmann A, Glebe D, Marz M, Niepmann M.

title: Shotgun Metagenomics Reveals Systemic Metabolic Pathways Promoting Organic Acid Production in Traditional Sunki Fermentation.
abstract: Salt-free lacto-fermentation is gaining attention owing to the global demand for sodium reduction. Sunki, a traditional unsalted Japanese turnip pickle, provides a unique ecological model. In this study, we investigated the microbial balance and systemic metabolic pathways that promote organic acid accumulation using shotgun metagenomics. We revealed that a high-quality sunki cluster exhibiting an abundant accumulation of organic acids (lactic acid 8.58 ± 2.42 g/L, acetic acid 2.70 ± 0.76 g/L, succinic acid 1.50 ± 0.52 g/L) and low pH (3.91 ± 0.15) was characterized by the co-dominance of specific lactic acid bacteria along with the foundational species Limosilactobacillus fermentum. This co-dominance enables the synergistic operation of both the homofermentative and heterofermentative pathways, whose functional potentials positively correlated with lactic acid (r = 0.50) and acetic acid (r = 0.48) concentrations, respectively, thereby achieving both effective preservation and flavor complexity. Furthermore, we propose a dual-pathway model for succinic acid production involving the reductive tricarboxylic acid cycle from malate and the γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) shunt. Succinic acid positively correlated with the functional potential of the GABA shunt enzyme (puuE, r = 0.57) and negatively correlated with that of glutamate dehydrogenase (gdhA, r = -0.51), suggesting a metabolic switch redirecting glutamate flux toward the GABA shunt. This mechanism highlights an advanced ecological adaptation for pH homeostasis, emphasizing that a balanced co-dominance structure determines the quality of salt-free fermented foods.
authors: Oshima A, Sekiguchi S, Uchikawa S, Fujita N, Yoshida H, Yamada S, Fujita N, Shiwa Y, Tsuji A, Tanaka N, Okada S, Nishida A.

title: Genome-Wide Characterization of a Recombinant BoAHV-1 ΔgE/β-gal Vaccine Strain Reveals an Unintended Multi-Gene Deletion.
abstract: Bovine alphaherpesvirus 1 (BoAHV-1) is a major cattle pathogen, and glycoprotein E (gE)-negative marker vaccines are widely used for disease control and to differentiate infected from vaccinated animals. The genomic architecture of this previously developed recombinant strain beyond the intended gE/lacZ locus had not been characterized at the genome-wide level. Here, we performed whole-genome sequencing of the parental Los Angeles (LA) strain and two passages of the recombinant BoAHV-1ΔgEβgal strain. In addition, plaque area was descriptively assessed in primary fetal bovine kidney cells using measurements from a single experimental run. In addition to the expected replacement of the US8/gE locus with a β-galactosidase cassette, we identified a previously undescribed 3704 nt deletion in the US region. This deletion removed the complete US1.67, US2, and US3 coding sequences, as well as the 5' portion of US4/gG. PCR assays and Sanger sequencing of the amplicon spanning the breakpoint precisely mapped the junction. Comparative annotation showed that the parental genome contained 74 viral CDSs, whereas both vaccine passage genomes contained 69. In the plaque assay, the mean plaque area of p11 was 68.8% lower than that of the parental LA strain. These findings document an unintended structural alteration in a previously evaluated recombinant vaccine strain and illustrate how genome-wide sequencing can complement targeted molecular characterization by identifying changes outside the intended engineered locus.
authors: Maidana SS, Ferreccio C, Marandino A, Panzera Y, Pérez R, Romera SA.

title: Cloning, Expression Analysis, and Functional Characterization of the NAC Transcription Factor SlNAC2-like from Tomato.
abstract: To investigate the regulatory function of the tomato NAC transcription factor SlNAC2-like under high-temperature stress, the high-temperature-tolerant line Hm 2-2 and the high-temperature-sensitive line BY 1-2 were used as experimental materials. The SlNAC2-like gene was cloned from tomato leaves via reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR), and its encoded protein was characterized using bioinformatics tools, phylogenetic analysis, and expression profiling. Subcellular localization and yeast self-activation assays were performed to determine protein localization and transcriptional activity. Virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) was employed to generate SlNAC2-like-silenced plants, and the activities of superoxide dismutase (SOD), peroxidase (POD), and catalase (CAT), as well as proline (Pro) and malondialdehyde (MDA) contents, were measured under high-temperature stress using spectrophotometry. The results showed that the SlNAC2-like cDNA fragment was 1044 bp in length, with an 876 bp open reading frame encoding 291 amino acids containing a highly conserved NAM domain. The protein was localized in the nucleus and exhibited transcriptional activation activity. Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis revealed that SlNAC2-like expression was tissue-specific and induced by high temperature (42 °C), abscisic acid (ABA), salicylic acid (SA), and methyl jasmonate (MeJA). Silencing of SlNAC2-like compromised tomato high-temperature tolerance, as evidenced by reduced SOD, POD, and CAT activities, decreased Pro content, and a marked increase in MDA content, along with significant downregulation of genes involved in ABA, SA, and jasmonic acid (JA) signaling pathways. Collectively, these findings suggest that SlNAC2-like acts as a positive regulator of tomato tolerance to high-temperature stress and that its function is associated with antioxidant defense and the ABA, SA, and JA signaling pathways. However, the present study does not establish how SlNAC2-like regulates ROS homeostasis or hormone signaling, and identification of its direct target genes and interacting partners requires further experimental validation. This study provides valuable genetic resources and a theoretical basis for molecular breeding of stress-resistant tomato varieties.
authors: Lv L, Duan L, Liu J, Li H, Shao Q, Chen N.

title: Live and Heat-Treated Lacticaseibacillus paracasei NB23 Improve Selected Functional and Physiological Outcomes in Naturally Aged Mice.
abstract: Live and heat-treated microbial preparations are candidate nutritional ingredients for supporting function during aging. This study evaluated Lacticaseibacillus paracasei NB23 in naturally aged male C57BL/6NCrl mice. Ten young mice served as a reference group, and forty aged mice received vehicle, live NB23 at 2.05 × 109 or 6.15 × 109 colony-forming units (CFU)/kg/day, or heat-treated NB23 at 6.15 × 109 cell equivalents/kg/day for 12 weeks. Relative to aged controls, NB23-treated mice had shorter water-maze acquisition latency, longer treadmill endurance, higher hepatic antioxidant enzyme activities and glycogen, and lower selected whole-brain oxidative-damage markers. High-dose live and heat-treated NB23 also increased grip strength and muscle glycogen. Gastrocnemius myofiber area and selected femoral microarchitectural outcomes improved, whereas rotarod performance and tibialis anterior myofiber area did not. Exploratory analyses of brain and intestinal transcripts, fecal metabolites, and microbiota-host associations did not establish a gut-mediated mechanism. Among 325 taxon-outcome pairs in the exploratory microbiome-host screen, 49 met nominal p p = 0.08967). Assay-specific subsets comprised four mice per group for micro-CT and five per group for qPCR, fecal metabolites, and microbiome sequencing, with two gene-specific qPCR exclusions. These findings support further evaluation of NB23 as a functional food ingredient, while the small, male-only animal study does not establish clinical anti-aging efficacy or equivalence of the live and heat-treated preparations.
authors: Lee MC, Lin PJ, Lin TC, Chou CH, Hsiao CY, Huang CC.

title: SpliceCOV: Supervised Filtering of RNA-Seq-Derived Transcript Features Improves Transcriptome Assembly.
abstract: Background/Objectives: High-throughput RNA sequencing enables transcript discovery and quantification, but the resulting coverage profiles often contain substantial transcriptional noise, making it difficult to distinguish genuine transcript features from spurious signals. These noisy signals can propagate into transcriptome assemblies, increasing the number of false transcript models and reducing annotation precision. Methods: We present SpliceCOV, a supervised framework for filtering RNA-Seq-derived transcript features. Rather than performing general-purpose segmentation of RNA-Seq coverage, SpliceCOV uses coverage- and junction-derived features to distinguish likely genuine splice sites and transcript boundaries from noisy candidates. We benchmarked SpliceCOV against established changepoint methods and evaluated whether SpliceCOV-filtered features improve downstream transcriptome assembly with StringTie. Results: Across human GTEx tissue datasets, SpliceCOV substantially reduced likely false-positive splice sites while retaining most annotated sites. We included segmentation-based methods as baselines to assess whether generic coverage changepoints can support RNA-Seq transcript-feature filtering. Because these methods are unsupervised whereas SpliceCOV is trained using annotation-derived labels, the comparisons are intended to assess suitability for this specific filtering task rather than to provide a general ranking of the underlying algorithms. Under this evaluation framework, SpliceCOV retained more annotation-supported splice sites at comparable levels of filtering. For transcript start and end sites, SpliceCOV reduced the majority of false positives while retaining substantial overlap with reference annotations. When SpliceCOV-filtered splice sites and transcript boundaries were supplied to StringTie, transcript-level precision increased across the evaluated tissues while the number of reference-matching transcripts remained broadly similar. The model also showed transferability across tissues and chromosomes, and could be applied to mouse RNA-Seq without retraining, although downstream assembly performance was lower than in human datasets. Conclusions: SpliceCOV provides a supervised approach for filtering noisy RNA-Seq-derived transcript features before transcriptome assembly. By improving the quality of splice-site and transcript-boundary evidence supplied to downstream assembly, SpliceCOV can increase transcript-level precision while preserving transcript recovery.
authors: Hoh C, Shinder I, Chao KH, Varabyou A, Pertea M.
