title: Genome-Wide Identification of NLR Gene Family and Expression Patterns in Response to Colletotrichum camelliae Infection in Tea Plant (Camellia sinensis).
abstract: Background: Colletotrichum camelliae is an important fungal disease in tea plants (Camellia sinensis), and NLR gene family play a central role in plant disease resistance recognition. Analyzing the expression characteristics and regulatory network of NLR genes in tea plants in response to anthracnose infection can provide a theoretical basis for exploring key genes for tea plant resistance to anthracnose and elucidating the molecular mechanisms of disease resistance. Method: Using the tea tree reference genome Shuchazao 2 as the material, CsNLR genes were identified based on NB-ARC (Pfam ID: PF00931) and LRR (Pfam ID: PF00560) conserved domains; Conduct bioinformatics analysis using TBtools, MEME, and MEGA; Using quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) to detect the expression changes of CsNLR in the common variety Sucha 120 and the purple variety Ziying 2 after anthracnose infection, and constructing a protein prediction association network. Result: A total of 158 CsNLR genes were identified, and their physicochemical properties, phylogenetics, gene structure, and cis element analysis revealed differentiation among family members. The promoters generally contain stress and hormone response elements; CsNLR is highly expressed in roots, stems, and mature leaves. After 4 days of inoculation with anthracnose infection, the expression trends of CsNLR in the two tea tree varieties were opposite, with Sucha 120 upregulated and Ziying 2 downregulated; The predicted protein association network shows CsNLR as the central node of the network, with 77 CsNLR proteins were included in the predictive functional association network, and there were differences in the connectivity of different members. Conclusions: The CsNLR identified in this study is a potential NLR resistant gene for anthracnose in tea plants, laying the foundation for subsequent functional verification of disease resistant genes and analysis of resistance mechanisms.
authors: Wang J, Li A, Wan Q, Zhang Y, Tang J, Zhang Q.

title: The dietary pathways of heavy metal accumulation in wild fish from the urbanized waterways of Pearl River Estuary at Guangzhou, China: Insights from fatty acid biomarkers.
abstract: Diet critically influences heavy metal bioaccumulation in fish but their corresponding processes were rarely detailed. Given the severe heavy metal pollution in wild fish from heavily urbanized section of Pearl River Estuary in Guangzhou, this study integrated contamination surveys with fatty acid tracing to identify dietary pathways driving metal accumulation, with their impacts further evaluated through health risk assessment. Results showed that As and Pb exceeded maximum residue limits in some fish. 23 fatty acids were detected, which consisted of 40.39%, 37.11%, and 22.50% for MUFAs, SFAs, and PUFAs, respectively. Fish were classified into two groups via bi‑cluster analysis: a PUFA‑rich benthic feeding group accumulating As and Cd, and a SFA/MUFA‑rich pelagic feeding group accumulating other metals. Significant correlations between As, Cd and ω‑3 PUFAs suggested a dietary pathway from algae/detritus, while the rest metals positively correlated with most SFAs and MUFAs, indicating a dietary pathway from plankton/bacteria. Positive correlations of C17:0 and C17:1 with most metals suggested the predominance of bacterial pathways in enhancing metals accumulation, whereas the negative correlations of C18:1ω9 and C18:2ω6 with metals identified dietary pathways from phytoplankton and terrestrial detritus that mitigate metal accumulation. The higher hazard index (HI) of As highlighted its higher risk, especially for children, with nearly 80% of the HI derived from the algae/detritus pathway. Therefore, controlling the risk of fish should focus on the management of the benthic environment. This study demonstrated metals have distinct dietary pathways, and identifying high‑risk metal intake pathways is fundamental for strengthening pollution risk control.
authors: Miao X, Wei X, Yang S, Zhou X, Mu M, Hao Y.

title: Antiviral activity of lapachol and synthetic hydroxynaphthoquinone derivatives against Mayaro virus.
abstract: The Mayaro virus (MAYV) is an arbovirus belonging to the Togaviridae family, genus Alphavirus. MAYV causes several sporadic outbreaks, affecting regions of the Americas. There are no specific antivirals for treating the disease. Therefore, studies are increasingly needed to discover effective antivirals against these neglected viruses. Thus, our study investigates the antiviral potential in vitro of a natural hydroxynaphthoquinone (QHM0001 - lapachol) and its synthetic derivatives (QHM0011, 0020 and 0110) against CMV-MAYV-nanoluc. We observed that the compounds QHM0001, 0011, 0020 and 0110 interfered with the post-entry stages (2 h.p.i.) of the CMV-MAYV-nanoluc, suggesting an effect on the viral genome replication stage. QHM0001, 0011 and 0020 showed high percentages of inhibition in late stages (4, 6 and 8 h.p.i.) of CMV-MAYV-nanoluc replication cycle. Thus, our study highlights the potential of the tested hydroxynaphthoquinones as promising candidates for new broad-spectrum antivirals.

title: Whole-genome sequencing reveals clonal connectivity of Listeria monocytogenes across hygienically separated processing lines in a fresh-cut produce facility.
abstract: Listeria monocytogenes control in fresh-cut produce facilities relies heavily on hygienic zoning and physical segregation of processing lines, under the assumption that these measures limit microbiological connectivity between compartments. However, whether segregated lines within a single facility harbour genomically independent populations has rarely been assessed at high resolution. Here, we investigated the population structure and connectivity of L. monocytogenes in two physically and hygienically segregated processing lines (cut-fruit and cut-lettuce) within a fresh-cut produce facility. Whole-genome sequencing was performed on 100 isolates collected during three pre-sanitation sampling campaigns. High-quality assemblies were analysed using multilocus sequence typing (MLST), core-genome MLST (cgMLST) and high-quality SNP (hqSNP) approaches. The population was dominated by two sequence types, ST155 (81%) and ST6 (19%), both displaying limited intra-lineage diversity consistent with closely related clonal populations (median pairwise distances of 7 and 3 hqSNPs, respectively). Hygienic compartmentalization did not result in genomically independent populations. Within each lineage, processing line accounted for only a minor fraction of genomic variation, between-line genetic distances were comparable to within-line distances, and near-identical genotypes were recovered from both lines. Two distinct connectivity patterns were identified: a facility-wide distribution of ST155, with boot-washer and floor isolates clustering across lines, consistent with transfer through personnel-associated routes; and a more localized, drain-associated connectivity pattern involving ST6. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that hygienic segregation alone does not ensure microbiological independence between processing lines and highlight the importance of monitoring hygienic transition zones, including footwear sanitation stations, mobile equipment and drainage systems.
authors: Illán G, Allende A, Gil MI, Truchado P.

title: Salinity-dependent effects of erythromycin on biofilm development and conjugative plasmid transfer on poly(vinyl chloride) microplastics.
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) and antibiotics frequently co-occur in aquatic environments and jointly influence the dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). However, the modulatory role of salinity, a highly dynamic factor in estuarine and coastal regions, remains underexplored. This study investigated the effects of erythromycin (ERY) on biofilm development and RP4 plasmid conjugative transfer on poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) MPs across varying salinity levels (5‰, 10‰, and 15‰). Results demonstrated that MP hydrophobicity increased with salinity, while the ERY adsorption capacity followed the order: 5‰ > 15‰ > 10‰. A higher salinity (15‰) promoted biofilm biomass and extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) secretion on MPs. Notably, conjugative transfer frequencies within MP-associated biofilms were consistently higher than those in planktonic cultures. Under varying salinities, the conjugation frequencies in biofilms displayed a U-shaped trend, with higher rates observed at 5‰ and 15‰ compared to 10‰. Crucially, the impact of ERY on plasmid transfer was highly salinity-dependent, i.e., the addition of ERY promoted conjugation at 5‰ and 10‰ but significantly inhibited it at 15‰. Physiological assessments revealed that exposure to varying salinities and ERY induced non-lethal oxidative stress, evidenced by elevated reactive oxygen species and upregulated antioxidant enzymes (CAT and SOD), while lipid peroxidation (MDA) remained relatively low. Concurrently, intracellular proline accumulation and cell membrane permeability increased significantly with rising salinity. These findings provide direct experimental evidence that salinity fluctuations and antibiotic residues jointly alter bacterial physiological states and antibiotic resistance dissemination on MPs, which highlights the necessity of considering dynamic environmental variables in ecological risk assessments.
authors: Chen C, Li K, Liu S, Wang J, Wang D, You J.

title: Phenotypic heterogeneity in Pseudomonas aeruginosa virulence revealed through passive exposure in zebrafish (Danio rerio) and nematodes (Caenorhabditis elegans).
abstract: The rapid emergence of diseases and parasites in aquatic wildlife requires improved methodologies to identify and characterize new and future pathogens. While microinjection of pathogens directly into a model organism, such as zebrafish, enables the exploration of infection and immune response in the host, such methodology focuses primarily on identifying causative agents in events of aquatic wildlife mortality due to acute infection. Here, we present an updated protocol of infection by static immersion in larval zebrafish to investigate the possible effect of prolonged environmental exposure to an opportunistic pathogen. By controlling microbial growth and monitoring mortality over 72 h, we show that static immersion can detect minute differences in virulence profiles between and within different strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, an important opportunistic pathogen of animals and humans. We then conducted two sets of passive exposure virulence assays in Caenorhabditis elegans, an alternative model. We demonstrated the virulence phenotype, while showing slight differences between experimental models, and showed similar trends. We believe that passive exposure thus offers a practical host-pathogen model that simulates opportunistic infection occurring in the environment and enables the detection of minute changes in virulence between and within bacterial strains.
authors: Azulai D, Espinosa A, Talamantes M, Bennett HL, Perron GG.

title: Ecological and Genomic Evidence of Cryptic Speciation in the Potato Psyllid (Bactericera cockerelli).
abstract: The potato psyllid (Bactericera cockerelli) is a crop pest that serves as a vector for the bacterial pathogen Candidatus Liberibacter solanacearum (CLso), which causes disease in solanaceous and apiaceous crops. This psyllid species carries substantial haplotypic diversity based on mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase 1 (mtCOI) sequences, associated with strong geographic and temporal separation. Using mtCOI sequencing and genomic ddRADseq analysis of 111,587 SNPs across 590 individuals collected from native Solanaceae and cultivated crops at 50 geographically paired sites in California, we show that the previously described haplotype diversity in B. cockerelli may represent at least three genetically distinct cryptic species. These three lineages exhibited extremely high genomic F ST values across all 13 chromosomes and are strongly partitioned by the host plant. The Northwestern lineage is strictly associated with the native perennial Solanum umbelliferum, while the Western lineage is associated with solanaceous crops, and the Southwestern lineage moves between native and cultivated hosts in desert regions. Hybridization is also rare, suggesting reproductive isolation. SNP and divergence analyses for the obligate bacterial symbiont support conclusions of the host nuclear and mtCOI sequence analyses. We also detected five CLso variants in psyllid samples. The Northwestern lineage housed G, Sumb2, F and B variants, while the Western lineage housed only B and A variants. The largest diversity of CLso variants occurred in coastal regions where psyllid lineages overlap. Exploring the ecology and CLso associations of this potential cryptic species complex provides a foundation for improving biosecurity and management of potato psyllids and CLso pathogens.
authors: Kenney JR, Scarparo G, Molfini M, Tran M, Tran S, Murguia S, Gebiola M, Sarkar P, Purcell J, Mauck KE.

title: Integrating Ecological Niche Dynamics and Population Genomics Reveals Drivers of Rapid Range Expansion in the Silver Pheasant (Lophura nycthemera)
abstract: The ecological and genomic mechanisms underlying contrasting spatial responses among closely related sympatric species remain poorly understood. We therefore examined two closely related pheasants in subtropical forests of China—the rapidly expanding Silver Pheasant (Lophura nycthemera) and the spatially constrained Elliot’s Pheasant (Syrmaticus ellioti)—and integrated their long-term occurrence records (2002–2025) from camera-trapping surveys, public bird-observation platforms, and GBIF. L. nycthemera showed substantially greater expansion (50-fold vs. 25-fold increase in records) and broader spatial coverage (89 vs. 51 protected areas), occupying a significantly wider range of environmental conditions (standardized niche breadth: 0.497 vs. 0.352) with greater tolerance to anthropogenic disturbance and vegetation heterogeneity, whereas S. ellioti remained strongly specialized to undisturbed dense forests. To investigate the genomic basis underlying this contrasting ecological pattern, we performed whole-genome resequencing of L. nycthemera and three phasianid species (S. ellioti, Bambusicola thoracicus, Coturnix japonica) as references. Comparative genomic scans identified lineage-specific differentiation in L. nycthemera relative to the three reference species. Genome-wide screening using population differentiation and nucleotide diversity metrics revealed 619 candidate regions containing 131 genes, functionally enriched in neural development, cell adhesion, and conserved signaling pathways (FoxO and ErbB). Notably, genes involved in synaptic organization (CNTNAP2, NCAM2, SLITRK family) showed differentiation patterns potentially linked to behavioral flexibility. Our findings indicate that the rapid expansion of L. nycthemera may arise from broad ecological tolerance combined with lineage-specific genomic adaptations in neural and metabolic pathways. This integrated framework bridges ecological and evolutionary perspectives, offering mechanistic insights into species-specific responses to environmental change and informing conservation strategies tailored to different ecological strategies. Although limited by sample size, these genomic signatures provide preliminary evidence for adaptive variation potentially underlying the observed ecological flexibility.
authors: OUYANG Y, Huang H, Wang H, Pang J, Cheng Y, Yang Q, Zhang W.

title: Wine Yeast Engineering for Improved Polysaccharide Depolymerization and Lower Ethyl Carbamate Formation
abstract: Engineering wine yeasts to combine efficient extracellular polysaccharide degradation with reduced accumulation of ethyl carbamate, a group 2A carcinogen, may support improvements in winemaking. This study aimed to replace the arginase-encoding CAR1 locus in the genome of the triploid industrial wine yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae I-328 with an expression cassette for the endopolygalacturonase gene PGU1, placed under the control of the PGK1 gene promoter and terminator. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing was performed using an acetamidase-selectable plasmid followed by phenotypic screening and molecular genetic verification. Whole genome sequencing confirmed the replacement of all three CAR1 alleles by the PGU1 expression cassettes. The modified strain I328-Y21 showed enhanced degradation of polygalacturonic acid relative to the parental strain. Consistently, RT-qPCR analysis showed that the transcription level of the PGU1 gene in strain I328-Y21 was about 300 times higher than in I-328. Inactivation of arginase, which forms urea through the breakdown of arginine, resulted in about nine-fold decrease in the content of urea in the growth medium. Since ethyl carbamate is formed as a result of the interaction between ethanol and urea excreted by yeast cells, this strain could be used to reduce its content in wine. Winemaking experiments show that genome editing did not affect fermentation performance and other technological characteristics. The new strain with the replacement of the arginase gene with the endopolygalacturonase expression cassette is promising for use in winemaking.
authors: Vasyagin EA, Urakov VN, Shalamitskiy MY, Cherviak SN, Semenova KA, Lutkova NY, Beletsky AV, Rakitin AL, Mardanova ES, Kushnirov VV, Ravin NV, Mardanov AV.

title: Single-step GWAS reveals candidate genes associated with longevity traits in Iranian Holstein cattle.
abstract: Longevity is a complex, polygenic trait of economic and welfare importance in dairy production. This study aimed to identify genomic regions and candidate genes associated with longevity traits-herd life (HL), productive life (PL), milking life (ML), and age at first insemination (AFI) in Iranian Holstein cattle using a single-step genome-wide association study (ssGWAS) based on pedigree, deregressed proofs, and genotypes from 150 cows (27,228 SNPs). At FDR < 0.05, 17 genome-wide significant SNPs were identified, three of which surpassed the Bonferroni threshold (p < 1 × 10⁻⁶); these mapped to 12 chromosomes (BTA5-BTA23), with the top windows explaining up to 2.8% of genetic variance. Functional annotation within ± 250 kb windows identified candidate genes including PDE7B, PRDX1, CDKN1B, and HMGA2, involved in cell cycle regulation, oxidative stress response, and energy metabolism. These findings provide exploratory insights into the genetic architecture of longevity in Iranian Holsteins, although validation in larger independent cohorts is required before marker integration into genomic selection.
authors: Maddahi N, Sadeghi M, Sarghale AJ, Siar MKD, Kholghi M.

title: Hantaviruses as Emerging Zoonotic Pathogens: Molecular Biology, Epidemiology, Therapeutics, vaccine, and Pathogenesis.
abstract: Hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens belonging to the family Hantaviridae and are responsible for two major human diseases, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). Despite substantial progress in hantavirus research, important challenges remain in understanding the interactions among viral evolution, reservoir ecology, environmental change, transmission dynamics, and host immunopathology. This review provides an integrated One Health perspective that connects molecular virology and host-virus interactions with transmission ecology, global epidemiology, and the mechanisms underlying vascular leakage and severe disease. In addition to summarizing established knowledge, we highlight recent advances in hantavirus taxonomy, genomic and molecular surveillance, ecological and transmission modeling, and the identification of hantavirus circulation in previously underrecognized regions. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of reservoir host dynamics, climate and environmental change, habitat disturbance, and human-wildlife interactions in shaping spillover risk, as well as on endothelial dysfunction, immune dysregulation, and coagulation abnormalities as interconnected mechanisms of disease severity. We also identify persistent knowledge gaps concerning host susceptibility, viral persistence, determinants of differential virulence and tissue tropism, interspecies transmission, and the development of effective antiviral therapies and vaccines. By integrating these complementary perspectives, this review provides a framework for understanding hantavirus emergence and pathogenesis while identifying priorities for future surveillance, prevention, and therapeutic research.
authors: Akbarin MM, Farjami Z, Álvarez HR.

title: Oxidative Stress Potentiates a STAT1-APOL1 Feedforward Loop and Governs Disease Severity in APOL1-Mediated Kidney Disease.
abstract: IntroductionApolipoprotein L1 (APOL1) risk variants (G1 and G2) confer immunity against Trypanosoma infection but markedly increase susceptibility to progressive kidney disease. However, only a subset of biallelic risk-variant carriers develops disease progression, distinct from murine models. Here, we evaluated molecular drivers of progressive kidney disease using a model that reflected the low human disease penetrance.MethodsTo investigate the heterogeneity of APOL1-mediated kidney disease, we generated novel APOL1 bacterial artificial chromosome transgenic mice with doxycycline-inducible systemic interferon-γ expression (G0- or G1-IFNγ mice). Podocyte-specific transcriptomics using translating ribosome affinity purification (TRAP-seq) and single-cell spatial transcriptomics via 10x Genomics Xenium In Situ platform was performed. Mechanistic validation and analysis of factors regulating APOL1 upregulation were conducted in primary podocytes and subsequently validated in mouse kidney and in human kidney biopsy specimens via immunofluorescence.ResultsA subset of G1-IFNγ mice developed severe albuminuria and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, which strongly correlated with the magnitude of APOL1 upregulation. By pairing TRAP-seq with single-cell spatial transcriptomic data, we identified mitochondrial dysfunction and JAK-STAT signaling as a central mediator of podocyte injury. In primary podocytes, APOL1 risk variants triggered mitochondrial-derived oxidative stress, establishing a self-amplifying STAT1-APOL1 feedforward loop that further enhances APOL1 expression and APOL1 oligomerization. This pathogenic loop was consistently enriched in podocytes from both G1-IFNγ mice and in kidney biopsy specimens from patients with APOL1-mediated focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, demonstrating translational relevance.ConclusionsOur findings suggest that biallelic risk variants initiate an oxidative stress-induced positive feedforward loop which promotes and sustains APOL1 upregulation and STAT1 phosphorylation, thereby contributing to disease susceptibility, severity and outcome.

title: Termite-microbiome symbiosis as a bioreactor model for lignocellulosic biomass pretreatment and biorefinery.
abstract: Lignocellulosic biomass conversion is still limited by pretreatment strategies that are energy-intensive, chemically harsh, and difficult to scale. In contrast, termites and their symbiotic microbiota represent one of the most efficient natural systems for lignocellulose deconstruction, achieving rapid biomass conversion under mild physicochemical conditions. This review synthesizes current knowledge on termite-bacteria symbiosis and interprets it from a bioprocess engineering perspective, positioning it as a model for the design of engineered lignocellulosic biorefineries. By integrating gut compartmentalization, microbial community organization, enzymatic repertoires, and interaction networks, we develop a systems-level view of how spatial organization, physicochemical gradients, and cooperative metabolism jointly enable efficient biomass processing. Comparative analysis with conventional microbial platforms and industrial pretreatment technologies highlights the process advantages of termite-inspired systems in energy demand, process integration, and scalability. Rather than providing a purely descriptive synthesis, this review translates biological organization into engineering logic, outlining practical design principles for reactor architecture, consortium assembly, and enzyme deployment. We further identify key bottlenecks that constrain industrial translation, including transport limitations, gradient control, and community stability. Together, these insights provide a structured foundation for the rational development of robust, scalable, and sustainable termite-inspired lignocellulosic bioprocesses.
authors: Wiafe MN, Ahmad F, Berhanu A, Dar MA, Bai Y, Zhu D.

title: Meta-analysis of 990 EBV genomes identifies EBER2 SNP7048 and its interaction with HLA-A*11:01 driving nasopharyngeal carcinoma risk.
abstract: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is a major health burden in East and Southeast Asia (SEA). While EBV infection is a primary driver, the specific viral strains responsible for NPC development and their interaction with host genetics across geographically diverse endemic regions remain poorly understood. We performed a whole-genome sequencing of 388 EBV isolates and matched host whole-exome sequencing in a Singaporean cohort. To define the global significance of these findings, we conducted a meta-GWAS and phylogenetic analysis across three independent cohorts (Singapore, Hong Kong, and Guangdong and Guangxi provinces of China), totaling 990 EBV genomes. Our study identifies high-risk EBV strains-carrying a core variant in the EBER2 locus (SNP7048)-as the key viral determinator of NPC risk, accounting for approximately 68% of the attributable risk in SEA. Meta-analysis reveals these strains are consistently associated with NPC across all populations, resolving previous regional genetic discordances. We demonstrate a potent synergistic interaction between these EBV risk strains and the host HLA-A*11:01 protective allele; individuals lacking this protection while carrying a high-risk strain exhibit a 30.9-fold increase in NPC risk. Phylogenetic analysis further reveals that these high-risk lineages populated SEA through clonal expansion from Southern China, following historical migration routes. These findings establish that NPC development is driven by the distribution of specific high-risk EBV lineages and their synergistic interaction with host immune susceptibility. This provides a definitive genetic framework for precision population screening and early diagnosis of NPC in the endemic regions.

title: Mechanism of HIV-1 capsid rupture and uncoating by reverse transcription.
abstract: One of the key events in the HIV-1 life cycle is reverse transcription (RT), during which single-stranded viral RNA (ssRNA) is converted into double-stranded DNA (dsDNA). This process occurs inside the mature HIV-1 capsid and, once it reaches a critical threshold, drives capsid rupture. This uncoating is essential for infection because it releases viral genetic material into the host cell nucleus. Despite its importance, many mechanistic details of this process remain to be fully understood. To address this gap, we develop a multiscale computational method for simulating RT inside the capsid, termed Coarse-Grained Kinetic Monte Carlo (CG-KMC). CG-KMC stochastically adds deoxynucleotide triphosphates (dNTPs) to the coarse-grained RNA model, enabling stepwise growth of DNA inside the HIV-1 capsid. We implement this method within an integrative coarse-grained framework that combines a "bottom-up" capsid model with a "top-down" representation of the viral RNA/DNA genome. Our simulations phenomenologically capture and predict diverse capsid rupture pathways during RT. The resulting ruptured structures closely match previously identified cryo-ET images. We further perform an extensive analysis of the rupture process, examining its mechanistic and kinetic aspects as well as the role of capsid-DNA interactions. Our findings illuminate how different capsid-DNA conditions give rise to distinct rupture pathways, which differ from ruptures due to simple outward pressure expansion models from within the capsid.
authors: Ghosh K, Gupta M, Voth GA.

title: Comparative genomics of dark septate endophytes: shedding light on the enigmatic lifestyle and biology of DSEs.
abstract: Dark septate endophytes (DSE) are widespread root-colonising fungi with poorly understood lifestyle and ecological functions. We investigated their genomic traits, sexual reproduction signatures, carbohydrate-active enzyme (CAZyme) and secondary metabolites profiles, and tested whether genomic features distinguish DSEs and other endophytes from fungi with other lifestyles. We also reconstructed ancestral states to clarify the evolutionary origins of DSEs. We analysed 107 Ascomycota genomes representing diverse lifestyles, including nine newly sequenced DSE genomes. The dataset allowed us to test whether secreted enzyme profiles differ between fungi colonising roots vs shoots and those associated with grass vs nongrass hosts. DSEs evolved through multiple independent trajectories and diverse lifestyles and show remarkable metabolic diversity. They possess extensive degradative capacities and some of the largest biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) richness among fungi. Despite sharing BGC richness with other endophytes, DSEs form a distinct subgroup with fewer cellulose- and more hemicellulose-targeting enzymes. Genomes also revealed genomic signatures associated with fungi colonising grass vs nongrass hosts and root- vs shoot-associated niches. Our comparative genomics approach highlights how genome-level data can deepen our understanding of endophytic lifestyle and the biology of the enigmatic DSE fungi.
authors: Csíkos S, Merényi Z, Knapp DG, Lipzen A, LaButti K, Pangilinan J, Riley R, Haridas S, Salamov A, Barry K, Kuo A, Drula E, Grigoriev IV, Henrissat B, Martin F, Nagy LG, Kovács GM.

title: Molecular evidence of the eukaryotic parasites Perkinsea and Stylocephalidae in lizard muscle tissue
abstract: Alveolates are a group of single-celled eukaryotes that include many important parasites of vertebrates, including the parasites that cause malaria. However, the group’s diversity and host associations in reptiles remain poorly understood. Here, we used 18S rRNA metabarcoding and phylogenetic analyses to identify novel parasites from tissue of iguanian lizards from the Caribbean and southern United States. This analysis revealed sequences closely related to members of the Alveolate families  Stylocephalidae and  Perkinsea , neither of which has previously been reported in reptiles.  Stylocephalidae sequences clustered with gregarine parasites typically associated with arthropod hosts, while  Perkinsea sequences grouped with environmental and freshwater lineages related to known amphibian pathogens. These findings represent the first molecular evidence of  Stylocephalidae - and  Perkinsea -related DNA in lizard tissues and suggest previously unrecognized ecological interactions between reptiles and alveolate microorganisms. Although infection cannot yet be confirmed, our results highlight the need for targeted environmental sampling, histopathology, and experimental studies to clarify host range, transmission potential, and possible conservation implications.
authors: Brown-Vera ES, Yuan ML, Westeen EP, Grundler MR, Wang IJ, Holmes IA.

title: Structural analysis reveals three families of bacterial tRNA mimics
abstract: SUMMARY  Comparative genomics has identified over 1,000 candidate structured RNA motifs, yet most remain functionally uncharacterized. Here, we combine crystallography, comparative analysis, and bacterial genetics to identify three families of bacterial tRNA-like RNAs. The skipping-rope RNA adopts an L-shaped fold resembling tRNA despite distinct secondary-structure connectivity and tertiary interactions. In  Clostridioides difficile , the skipping-rope RNA RCd1 is abundantly expressed and processed into a highly stable RNA species. RCd1 overexpression suppresses sporulation, whereas its deletion enhances early spore formation, supporting a role in sporulation control. Guided by the skipping-rope structure, we identify a conserved architectural core and use it to recognize additional candidate tRNA mimics. Crystal structures of DUF2693-FD and salivarius-1 RNAs confirm a shared tRNA-like scaffold assembled through distinct interaction networks. Together, these findings expand the repertoire of bacterial tRNA mimics and establish a structural framework for recognizing shared architectures among uncharacterized ncRNAs, linking one such family to bacterial developmental regulation.
authors: Wang J, Boudry P, Xie Y, He Y, Ren Y, Chen Q, Westhof E, Lilley DMJ, Soutourina OA, Huang L.

title: Evolution-Guided Engineering of Non-conserved  N  -Glycosylation Sites Improves Heterologous Production of Sulfotransferases
abstract: Escherichia coli features low cost, mature fermentation technology and high recombinant protein output, but the expression of glycosylation-dependent eukaryotic proteins therein is severely limited. Many glycosylated proteins are key tool enzymes for the biosynthesis of various pharmaceutical molecules, such as glycosaminoglycan-related synthases, but there is a lack of universal protein engineering methods to enable the adaptive evolution of these enzymes in  E. coli . We established an evolution-guided optimization strategy that targets non-conserved  N -glycosylation sites (EGO-  N Gly). The core of this strategy lies in the phylogeny-guided selective reversion of evolutionarily acquired  N -glycosylation sequons to naturally occurring non-glycosylated residues from early-divergent orthologs, thereby improving heterologous production and residual activity stability for selected sulfotransferases in  E. coli . Using heparin 3-  O -sulfotransferase 1 (3OST-1) as a model enzyme apparatus in eukaryotic organisms, EGO-  N Gly extended the residual activity half-life by 4.5-fold. Structural analysis and molecular dynamics simulations indicate that greater surface rigidity and remodeling of intramolecular interaction networks contribute to the improved conformational stability of M7 in an aglycosylated host. EGO-  N Gly was further applied to a panel of 3OST and 6OST homologs, demonstrating its applicability to a subset of the tested enzymes. Furthermore, EGO-  N Gly can be orthogonally integrated with other complementary protein engineering strategies, as exemplified by its combination with the machine learning-aided Protein Repair One-Stop Service, generating variants with 8-fold and 17-fold extensions in residual activity half-life. Collectively, these results establish EGO-  N Gly as a practical and potentially cost-effective engineering strategy for improving the prokaryotic expression and functional performance of selected glycosylation-dependent eukaryotic sulfotransferases.  Significance Statement  Escherichia coli lacks rational engineering methods for the heterologous expression of glycosylation-dependent eukaryotic proteins. We developed an evolution-guided optimization of  N -glycosylation (EGO-  N Gly) strategy that reverts non-conserved glycosylation sequons to the non-glycosylated residues conserved in early-divergent orthologs, improving the heterologous expression, catalytic function, and stability of animal-derived sulfotransferases. In heparin 3-  O -sulfotransferase 1, EGO-  N Gly extended the residual activity half-life at 37 °C by 4.5-fold. The strategy was transferable to several additional sulfotransferase homologs in a sequence-context-dependent manner and could be combined with machine-learning aided stability design to further extend the half-life by up to 17-fold. EGO-  N Gly thus provides a practical and potentially cost-effective strategy for improving the prokaryotic production of selected animal-derived sulfotransferases.
authors: Li C, Li Y, Li X, Zhao Y, Sun J, Cao Y, Guo X, Zheng S, Deng J, Sheng J.

title: A General Computational Framework for Sequence-Level Thermodynamic Analysis of Modeled RNA–DNA and DNA–DNA Duplex States: A Proof-of-Concept Study in HIV-1
abstract: Abstract  We present a sequence-level computational framework designed to be applicable across viral genomes and demonstrate it in a proof-of-concept analysis of HIV-1. Sixteen predefined regions of the HXB2 reference genome (K03455.1) were evaluated using two RNAstructure 6.6 procedures: OligoWalk for an RNA-target/DNA-oligo duplex calculation and DuplexFold for a DNA-DNA bimolecular minimum-free-energy reference. We define a model-specific contrast, ΔΔG_model = ΔG_RD − ΔG_DD, rather than a universal same-algorithm ΔΔG. Fifteen of 16 regions had negative contrasts; the panel mean was −8.00 kcal/mol (SD 5.45). A two-sided one-sample test against zero gave t₁₅ = −5.87, p = 1.54×10⁻⁵. The directional result persisted in overlap-sensitivity analyses excluding TAR and/or R_5LTR. These results constitute a sequence-level, testable computational prediction under the specified modeling procedures. They do not establish cellular R-loop formation, genomic integration, or a causal biological mechanism. The study is limited to one reference genome and to 16 non-independent, partly overlapping regions.
authors: DINANI SS.

title: Non-canonical mutations drive the evolution of persistent Staphylococcus aureus small-colony variants under zinc oxide nanoparticle stress
abstract: Abstract    The widespread application of Zinc Oxide Nanoparticles (ZnO NPs) in industrial and medical products necessitates a rigorous understanding of bacterial adaptive trajectories under sustained exposure to nanomaterials. In this study, we employed experimental evolution, quantitative proteomics and whole-genome sequencing to investigate the long-term response of  Staphylococcus aureus  to subinhibitory concentrations of ZnO NPs. Serial passaging in the presence of 500 µg/ml ZnO NPs for 14 passages progressively enriched Small Colony Variants (SCVs), which exceeded 95% of the population by passage 10 and became dominant by passage 12; the phenotype remained stable after removal of ZnO NPs. Compared with the parental strain, the evolved SCV exhibited approximately fourfold increase in generation time, increased cell diameter (535 versus 390 nm) and cell-wall thickness (44 versus 29 nm), reduced susceptibility to ZnO NPs with about 68% killing compared to 99.9% killing, and increased adherence to A549 cells (75.45 versus 54.72%). Whole-genome sequencing identified nonsynonymous mutations in  mprF  ,  rpsE  ,  gyrA  ,  comEB  , and  yqeH  , and revealed loss of an approximately 19 kb plasmid carrying  blaZ  and its regulatory genes. Remarkably, despite loss of this plasmid, β-lactam resistance increased markedly, with penicillin G and ampicillin MICs increasing from 32 to 512 µg/ml and from 64 to 1024 µg/ml, respectively. These findings show that continuous ZnO NP exposure can select for a stable SCV phenotype accompanied by metabolic and structural remodelling and altered antibiotic susceptibility, highlighting an evolutionary consideration for the prolonged use of ZnO NP based antimicrobial materials.
authors: Jaiswal A, Chakraborty S, Malhotra A, Jana S, Karan R, Chauhan A.

title: Intraspecific variation of virulence and host-specificity in the mycoparasitic fungus Clonostachys rosea
abstract: Abstract    Parasite-host interactions can display a continuum from specialization to generalism.  Clonostachys rosea  is an ascomycete fungus known for its ability to parasitize other fungi, a phenomenon known as mycoparasitism, and for its use as a biological control agent.  Clonostachys rosea  is reported to parasitize range of different hosts, yet our understanding of the evolutionary dynamics shaping its virulence and host range remains limited. In this study, up to 63  C. rosea  strains were assessed for virulence towards host fungi and an oomycete, under the hypothesis that strains differ in virulence and host specialization. Results revealed significant (  P   ≤ 0.05) variation in virulence between  C. rosea  strains towards the host fungi  Botrytis cinerea  ,  Fusarium graminearum  and  Rhizoctonia solani  and an overall lack of correlation between hosts, suggesting a certain level of host specificity. There was no significant correlation between  in vitro  antagonism of  F. graminearum  and biocontrol of fusarium root rot disease on wheat, emphasizing the complexity of the biocontrol trait. Differences in virulence was further hypothesized to partially depend on different interaction mechanisms towards the intrinsically different host fungi. Genome-wide association analysis identified seven single nucleotide polymorphisms significantly (  P   ≤ 1.6 × 10⁻⁶) segregating with virulence or biocontrol. Different genomic regions segregated with virulence towards different hosts, suggest different underlying virulence determinants. These results are important for our increased understanding of the evolution and ecology of mycoparasitic fungi, with implications for their exploitation in agricultural applications.
authors: Ruffino A, Manyara D, Kuper E, Piombo E, Tzelepis G, Friberg H, Dubey M, Karlsson M.

title: Phenylacetylglutamine and memory B cells as mediators of the migraine–tinnitus relationship: a multi-omics two-step Mendelian randomization study
abstract: Abstract    Background:  Migraine and tinnitus often co-occur, and Mendelian randomization (MR) studies have suggested a modest causal effect of migraine on tinnitus risk, but the biological pathways behind this association are unclear. We used a hypothesis-free two-step MR mediation design to screen multi-omics intermediary phenotypes, including circulating metabolites, immune cell subsets, inflammatory proteins, and gut microbiota, for pathways linking the two conditions.  Methods:  Genetic instruments for migraine were derived from FinnGen release 10 (G6_MIGRAINE; ~430,000 participants). The total effect of migraine on tinnitus was estimated against the UK Biobank tinnitus GWAS (Clifford 2020; n = 172,995) with zero sample overlap. In Step 1, 668 mediators (575 metabolites, 61 immune cell traits, 28 dietary factors, and 4 psychological traits), 91 circulating inflammatory proteins, and 211 gut microbiota taxa were screened against migraine instruments. In Step 2, candidate mediators passing prespecified filters were tested against tinnitus. Indirect effects were computed by the product-of-coefficients method with delta-method standard errors. Microbiome instruments were clumped locally with PLINK (1000 Genomes EUR, r² Results:  The total effect of migraine on tinnitus was weak (inverse-variance weighted [IVW] OR = 1.066, 95% CI 0.995–1.142, P = 0.068; relaxed 66-IV panel null), framing the analysis as shared-pathway decomposition rather than direct causation. In Step 1, a coherent cluster of gut-microbiota-derived phenylalanine metabolites was associated with genetically predicted migraine, led by phenylacetylglutamine (PAGln; IVW OR = 1.177, P = 4.3 × 10⁻⁴), alongside higher absolute counts of memory-lineage B cells (β = +0.410, P = 0.028). In Step 2, PAGln (Wald OR = 1.345, 95% CI 1.067–1.697, P = 0.012) and memory B cells (Wald OR = 0.878, 95% CI 0.794–0.971, P = 0.011) were both associated with tinnitus (both q = 0.049, Benjamini–Hochberg FDR). The indirect effect was significant for PAGln (+0.048 log-odds, P = 0.041; 76% of the total effect) and directionally protective but non-significant for memory B cells. Colocalization analysis (coloc.abf) against full MiBioGen summary statistics confirmed a shared causal variant at chr12:57.3 Mb near LRP1 (Ruminococcus gauvreauii group, PP.H4 = 0.88) and supported colocalization at 11p15.4 (Desulfovibrionaceae, PP.H4 = 0.61–0.64). Microbiome results were robust to the LD-clumping strategy.  Conclusions:  Gut-microbiota-derived PAGln was the only mediator with a genetically supported indirect effect; a secondary, protective memory-B-cell axis did not reach significance. This points to the gut–metabolite axis as a candidate modifiable target in migraine-related tinnitus.
authors: Chen L.

title: Fungal Infections in People Living with HIV and Other Immunocompromised Patients: A European and Romanian Narrative Review
abstract: Background:  Fungal infections are a major cause of morbidity and mortality across the growing population of immunocompromised patients, although the underlying immune deficit differs between people living with HIV/AIDS, non-HIV hosts (hematologic malignancy, neutropenia, solid organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation), and critically ill patients rendered transiently immunosuppressed by severe illness itself, as during the COVID-19 pandemic. Objectives. To compare epidemiology, pathogens, diagnosis, treatment, resistance, and prophylaxis across HIV, non-HIV immunocompromised hosts, and COVID-19-associated fungal disease, and to examine, as a regional case study, how this picture is represented in the European literature and in Romania specifically. Methods. Narrative review of PubMed/MEDLINE literature on HIV and non-HIV immunocompromising conditions, including COVID-19 associated conditions, complemented by a targeted search for European cohort data and by pathogen-specific PubMed searches for Romanian primary literature. Diagnostic terminology follows the EORTC/MSGERC consensus definitions, complemented by the ECMM/ISHAM criteria for COVID-19-associated pulmonary aspergillosis (CAPA). Results. CD4+ depletion in HIV produces a predictable, threshold-driven pattern of opportunistic mycoses; non-HIV immunosuppression is more heterogeneous; and critical illness — as exemplified by COVID-19 — introduced a distinct risk state, with COVID-19 Associated Pulmonary Aspergillosis (CAPA) incidence ranging from ~1% to >20% in ICU patients across European cohorts, and COVID-19-associated mucormycosis (CAM) reaching epidemic proportions in India. European cohorts otherwise document a one-year invasive fungal disease incidence of ~10% after allogeneic HSCT, up to 17% in acute leukemia, and 3–14% for aspergillosis after lung transplantation. Romanian evidence consists of single-center mycological studies, three Candidozyma (Candida) auris reports (including a genomic study assigning all sequenced isolates to clade I), case reports and small series of aspergillosis, CAPA and mucormycosis (the latter increasing after COVID-19), a nosocomial fusariosis outbreak in an acute leukemia ward, one cryptococcal-meningitis series, environmental detection of azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus, and a modelled national burden estimate; no dedicated series exist in solid organ transplant recipients or patients with solid tumors. Conclusions. Recognizing these divergent, population- and context-specific patterns is essential to risk-stratified screening and treatment; the Romanian case illustrates how national surveillance can lag far behind recognized burden even within a well-characterized global framework.
authors: Stanciu A, Cernat RC, Moroti R, Zekra L, Dumitrascu M, Dumea E, Mocanu E, Georgescu S, Efrim N, Nicolau A, Postolache P, Dumitru IM.

title: Single-cell profiling of human plaques reveals cellular and molecular signatures of symptomatic atherosclerosis
abstract: Atherosclerotic plaque vulnerability drives ischemic cardiovascular events, yet the cellular and molecular signatures distinguishing symptomatic from asymptomatic human plaques remain poorly defined. Here, we compared 53 symptomatic and asymptomatic human carotid plaques using single-nucleus (snRNA-seq; 17 samples, 19,100 nuclei; AtherOMICS biobank) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq; 36 samples, 68,983 cells; four public datasets), analyzed independently and combined by meta-analysis. Across sequencing approaches, symptomatic plaques showed cell-state shifts toward later or terminal states in osteochondrogenic smooth muscle cells (SMCs) and CD4⁺ T cells, as well as transcriptional changes toward inflammatory and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in endothelial cells (ECs), T cells, and fibroblasts. Nuclear profiling uncovered a depletion of fibroblasts in symptomatic plaques, marked by downregulation of RGS5. Integrating these transcriptomic signatures with genome-wide association data for coronary, cerebrovascular, and peripheral atherosclerotic disease, we found that genetic risk was enriched primarily in vascular wall cells (SMCs, fibroblasts, ECs), rather than immune cell types. The analyses further nominated higher TWIST1 expression in ECs (colocalized with risk across four atherosclerotic phenotypes), lower GUCY1A1 expression in fibroblasts and macrophages, and higher MRAS expression in T cells as candidate driver mechanisms linking genetic risk to symptomatic plaque transition. These findings provide novel insights into cellular and molecular phenotypes associated with plaque vulnerability and identify potential driver mechanisms of symptomatic plaque transformation that could inform therapeutic development.

title: Genome-wide SNP analysis of genetic diversity and selection signatures in ​Black ​Bengal goats.
abstract: The Black Bengal goat, a well-known breed of the Indian subcontinent, is valued for its excellent meat quality, high reproductive efficiency, and ability to thrive under diverse agroclimatic conditions. In this study, genetic diversity and selection signatures were investigated using SNP genotyping data from 90 animals using the ddRAD sequencing approach. Genetic diversity parameters, effective population size (Ne), and selection signatures were evaluated using Tajima's D, composite likelihood ratio (CLR), integrated haplotype score (iHS), and runs of homozygosity (ROH) analyses. Historical analysis of Ne revealed a peak value of 4,930, approximately 368 generations ago, followed by a steady decline to 366 around 13 generations ago. The observed heterozygosity (0.229 ± 0.149) was lower than the expected heterozygosity (0.275 ± 0.139), indicating a deficiency of heterozygotes in the population. The current Ne estimate of 158.4 suggests a reduction in population size over time. Using multiple complementary approaches, we identified 138 genomic regions under positive selection, encompassing 743 genes. Gene Ontology analysis highlighted significant enrichment of negative regulation of complement activation (LOC102169502, LOC102169786), positive regulation of interleukin-12 production (IL12B, IRF8, LEP, MDK), and type II interferon production (IRF8, IL12B, TYK2, CD14), indicating immune regulation and host defense. The candidate genes and enriched pathways identified in this study were mainly associated with immune function, fear response, adaptation, learning, cognition, and visual perception. These findings provide insights into the resilience and adaptation of the Black Bengal goats and may support future breeding and conservation efforts of the indigenous breed.
journal: Mammalian genome : official journal of the International Mammalian Genome Society
authors: Nayak SS, Devadharshini K, Ranjith G, Rath PK, Verma SK, Rajawat D, Panigrahi M.

title: Identification of selection signatures and growth-related candidate genes in Jishen Black pigs using a three-population comparative strategy.
abstract: As a characteristic breed in Jilin Province, China, the Jishen Black (JSB) pig exhibits traits such as roughage tolerance, cold resistance, and excellent meat quality. To generate greater profits for farmers, we designed a crossbred population of JSB × commercial pig breeds, which exhibited better growth traits. Furthermore, whole-genome sequencing data of 60 JSB pigs, 60 commercial (EUC) pigs, and 38 crossbred (CRB) pigs were obtained and integrated to conduct selection signature analyses using a three-population comparative strategy. Using the three-population comparative strategy, twelve significant 50-kb windows were retained and merged into six non-overlapping selected regions associated with growth-related traits. A total of seven candidate genes were identified within these regions, including NFIA, SCFD2, PDGFRA, C17orf113, NKIRAS2, DNAJC7, and ZNF385C. These genes may serve as promising molecular markers for marker-assisted selection to improve the growth performance of Jishen Black pigs.
authors: Zhang X, Sun H, Chen C, Li J, Ning J, Jin L, Dong F, Feng C, Bie L, Bai C, Sun B.

title: The role of capybaras (Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris) as hosts for hemoplasmas in an urban park of Brazilian Midwest.
abstract: Hemoplasmas (hemotropic mycoplasmas) are Gram-negative bacteria that bind to the surface of red blood cells of mammals and may cause hematological alterations in the infected host, and in urban environments, wildlife species may act as important reservoirs of these agents. The study aimed to evaluate, through molecular analysis, the infection of hemoplasmas in capybaras from the Parque das Nações Indígenas, Campo Grande, Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil. Additionally, we evaluated the health status of infected and non-infected capybaras by haematological parameters. The results of PCR assays based on the 16 S rRNA gene confirmed the presence of hemoplasmas in 84.6% (55/65) of the samples. Phylogenetic inferences based on 16 S and 23 S rRNA genes positioned the sequences into the ´Candidatus Mycoplasma haematohydrochoerus´ clade. The findings suggest that the high prevalence, low genetic variability, and unchanged hematological parameters may indicate host tolerance or adaptation to 'Ca. M. haematohydrochoerus' infection.
authors: Pistori JGB, de Macedo GC, Herrera HM, de Assis WO, do Nascimento LF, Junior OF, Santos FM, Sano NY, Santos da Silva JVD, de Mello VVC, Franco EO, Calchi AC, André MR, De Oliveira CE.
